en: Śrīḥ!
The Śabdakaustubha, composed by Bhaṭṭojī Dīkṣita.
[First Part] || Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
I bow to Viśveśa, who is existence-consciousness-bliss, and who is the entire universe.
He moves about, carries [the world], and effortlessly destroys it with ease. || 1 ||
I pay homage to the triad of sages beginning with Pāṇini, who are worthy of worship by the world.
And [he honored] the wise scholars, foremost among whom was the illustrious Bhartṛhari, who established the definitive tenets.
Having bowed to his father Lakṣmīdhara, who is worshipped by multitudes of wise men.
May he extract the *Śabdakaustubha* from the ocean of the commentary (*bhāṣya*) spoken by the Serpent (*phaṇin*).
Having thoroughly studied many books, that meaning which is obtained with difficulty—
O virtuous ones, accept this entire work from me without any effort. || 4 ||
Having devotedly offered this *Śrī-śabdakaustubha* to the Beloved of Lakṣmī.
Bhaṭṭoji Bhaṭṭa desires to attain the fulfillment of his birth. || 5 ||

For the sake of the engagement of discerning persons, the venerable author of the Bhāṣya demonstrated the subject matter of grammar with the words: "Now, the instruction of words" (*atha śabdānuśāsanam*). The word *atha* indicates the beginning, but it is not expressive (denotative) of it, because it is a particle (*nipāta*), like a prefix (*upasarga*).

Nor should it be argued that these [particles] are indeed expressive; for in cases such as "the teacher is served" (*upāsyate guruḥ*) or "pleasure is experienced" (*anubhūyate sukham*), since the suffixes denoting the object cannot be attached to the verbal root without its referring to a transitive action, the expressiveness of the roots being established, it is more appropriate that prefixes are merely indicative (*dyotaka*).

If it is argued that, according to the reasoning already stated, let it be that prefixes (*upasarga*) are merely indicative (*dyotaka*), while other particles (*nipāta*) are indeed expressive (*vācaka*), we say: no. In expressions such as *sākṣātkriyate*, *alaṃkriyate*, and *ūrīkriyate*, the object—the teacher or the like—is denoted by the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) in the passive voice; for this to be established, the status of being an object (*karmatva*) with respect to the meaning of the verbal root must be something directly expressed (*vācya*). Furthermore, since the category of "particle" (*nipātatva*) is more extensive than the category of "prefix" (*upasargatva*), it is logical to postulate their indicative function precisely as delimited by the former category, because all means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) tend toward the general rather than the particular.

Furthermore, regarding the nature of being a *nipāta* (particle), whether it is considered an adventitious property (*upādhi*), a universal (*jāti*), or the very form of the word itself—in all three of these positions, this status is common to both the *prādi* and *cādi* groups alike. Even in the position that [the particle-hood] resides individually in each [element such as *pra*, etc.], since no distinction can be defined between the *prādi*s and the *cādi*s, and because they are never used in isolation, their dependence on other factors for their meaning is exactly the same. This is because, just as in the case of "he conquers" (*vijayate*) where the root conveys a specific kind of victory, in the case of "the jar and" (*ghaṭaśca*), it is possible for the word "jar" (*ghaṭa*) itself to possess a secondary indicative function (*lakṣaṇā*) toward the conjunctive jar.

Furthermore, if particles (*cādi*) were denoters (*vācaka*), the grammatical rule that "there is a relation of non-difference (*abheda-anvaya*) between the meanings of two co-referential nominal stems" would have to be restricted without any evidence, as it currently pertains only to cases other than particles. Moreover, just as there is a genitive case ending for a word like *ghaṭa* when joined with words such as *samuccaya*, it would also occur when joined with *ca* and the rest. Furthermore, just as there is a connection with qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) in what is presented by words like *samuccaya*, the same would apply to what is presented by *ca* and the rest.

However, under the view that they are indicators (*dyotaka*), there is no connection with qualifiers therein, because [the particle] is merely a part of the word-meaning (*padārthaikadeśa*). Moreover—

In passages such as "śarairusrairivodīcyānuddhāriṣyan rasāniva" ("as if with rays [of light], he would draw out the northerners, as if drawing out essences"), the meaning is: "with arrows resembling rays, he will draw out the northerners who resemble essences. This meaning is obtained only if the words *usra* and so on refer to things similar to rays and the like, and if the word *iva* functions as an indicator of that intended sense (*tātparyagrāhaka*). Otherwise, even the rule that suffixes generate a cognition of their own meaning as connected with the meaning of the stem (*prakṛtyartha*) would be violated. Furthermore, the instrumental case-ending after the word *iva* would be difficult to justify, because since *iva* denotes a non-substantial entity (*asattvārthaka*), it cannot be construed with a case-ending denoting a grammatical relation (*kāraka*).

Even so, this does not resolve the lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) with the third case-ending in examples such as *usrābhyām*. If it is argued that, in this way, established doctrines such as the predominance of the meaning of the second member (*uttarapadārtha-prādhānya*) in a negative compound (*nañ-tatpuruṣa*) would be undermined, we reply: no; for its meaning is that there is predominance with respect to what is manifested by the first member (*pūrvapada*). Furthermore, its status as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is established because it possesses meaning even through the sense manifested [by the first member].

For this very reason, it should be noted that the Vārttika "nipātasyānarthakasya" was composed for the sake of those particles (*nipāta*) for which there is no expressed meaning at all—according to the *Amarakośa*, "tu, hi, ca, sma, ha, vai" are used for filling the verse (*pādapūraṇe*), and according to the *Nirukta*, "kam, īm, id, u" are used for filling the verse. This is clearly stated in the works of Kaiyaṭa and others. Consequently, the Bhaṭṭas stated in the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*: "Among the four types of words here, the determination of meaning is undertaken for two types because doubt arises; [it is not done] for prefixes (*upasarga*) and particles (*nipāta*)."
"For those two possess no operation whatsoever in the expression of the object; rather, that which illuminates the object is what is considered the denoter. Thus [it is said].

As for what has been stated by some in the *Arthavat-sūtra*—namely, that in forms such as *adhīte*, the verbal root is devoid of meaning and that the expressive capacity belongs to the root as qualified by the prefix—that is merely a secondary argument (*abhyuccaya*). The commentary of Kaiyaṭa and others on the sūtra *sarvasya dve* is likewise. Furthermore, the passages in various parts of the Pūrva- and Uttara-mīmāṃsā stating that "the negative particle (*nañ*) functions as an exclusion (*paryudāsa*)" are also of this same nature, due to the reasoning already stated.

Or, let there be another view that particles (*nipāta*) are denoters; nevertheless, the position accepted by the Naiyāyikas—that prefixes such as *pra* and so forth are indicators (*dyotaka*), while particles such as *ca* and so forth are denoters—is a "half-old-woman" argument (*arddhajaratīya*) and is simply unauthoritative. This is the direction of the argument.

The root *śās* preceded by the prefix *anu* is seen in the sense of instructing after having discriminated [the truth]. For example: "One who does not know the field, having asked one who knows the field, proceeds when instructed by that knower of the field. Or as it is said: "O Pūṣan, lead us with a wise man who may straightway instruct us, saying 'This indeed is it. For here, Pūṣan is entreated to train us through a true guru endowed with the three qualities (*guṇas*). In that context, "straightway" (*añjasā*) refers to swiftness; "instructing" (*anuśāsat*) refers to the state of being a teacher who causes understanding through discrimination.

In the Vedic language, according to the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi*, there is no elision (*luk*) of the suffix *śap*. The statement "one who would say 'this is exactly thus'" expresses the determination of the object of knowledge (*prameya*). In the word *bravat*, the augment *aṭ* is applied by the rule *leṭoḍāṭau*. Thus, [the term] *anuśāsana* is derived with the instrumental *lyuṭ* suffix in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), meaning that by which things are taught (*anuśiṣyante*), distinguished (*vivicya*), and separated (*vibhajya*) from what is incorrect. Consequently, in the phrase *śabdānām*, the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karman*), and this forms a compound with that [term].

Nor should one suspect that the prohibition of compounding by the rule *karmaṇi ca* applies here; for in that context, the word *karmaṇi* (in the locative case) signifies the meaning of the word itself, and thus the sense of the rule *ubhayaprāptau* is that a genitive ending which occurs when both [the agent and the object] are applicable is not compounded. This is because in the example *citraṃ gavāṃ doho 'gopena* ("The milking of cows by one who is not a cowherd is wonderful"), it is the wonder (*āścaryam*) that is to be expressed; and this wonder is realized only if the milker is untrained and the cows are difficult to milk, but not otherwise.

Therefore, because both the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) are specifically mentioned [in other rules], there is the possibility of both being applied. But here, since this is an instruction regarding words (*śabda*) and not meanings (*artha*), the sentence is intended to exclude the [application of the] meaning, and not to exclude a specific agent; thus, there is no possibility of both being applied. Or, let it be granted that somehow both are applied.

Nevertheless, there is no harm; for since the view that "the option (*vibhāṣā*) applies without distinction" will be stated in the rule *ubhayaprāptau*, the usage *ācāryasya śabdānuśāsanam* is possible under the alternative where the restrictive rule (*niyama*) does not apply. Alternatively, let the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) be one characterized by the "remainder" (*śeṣa*). Therefore, it is established that the subject matter here consists of both Vedic and worldly correct words (*sādhu-śabda*). Those which exist in the Veda are "Vedic" (*vaidika*), with the suffix *ṭhañ* applied according to the rule beginning with *adhyātmādi*. Similarly, those which exist in the world are "worldly" (*laukika*).

Alternatively, those known in the world are "laukika" (worldly). While the term *vidita* (known) is understood [from the previous rule], the addition of the suffix *ṭhañ* after *loka* and *sarvaloka* indicates that the scope here is not merely a portion of the Veda—as it is in the case of the *Prātiśākhyas*—nor is there an exclusion of the archaic (*chāndasa*) forms as occurs in other systems of grammar; thus, both terms are employed.
Thus concludes the determination of the objects of cognition.

It might be argued as follows: the object here is the word "cow" (*gauḥ*) and so forth; and in that [word], the constituent elements are the phoneme *ga*, the vowel *au*, and the visarga. However, what is being explained [in the grammatical treatise] consists of the suffixes *ḍa* and *sup*, the substitutes, and so on. And this does not appear in the cognition "cow"; thus, there is a difference in the objects [of the two].

If it is argued that there exists a specific relation between the established word "cow" (*gauh*) and the suffixes such as *ḍo* and so forth, and that these suffixes serve the purpose of conveying that [relation], thereby necessitating their grammatical derivation—this is not so. For it is difficult to specify a relation or a utility for [the suffixes] that is distinct from other words; furthermore, it would follow that categories such as substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*) must also be derived here [as grammatical elements]. Indeed, those categories possess a relationship with the word "cow," such as the signifier-signified (*vācya-vācaka*) relation.

For this very reason, in verbal cognition, the word appears as a qualifier through the relation of expressive power (*śakti*), just as "cowness" appears in the cognition of a cow through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*). It is accepted that even in visual cognition, the word—recalled by the individual object—is a qualifier. And it has been said: "There is no cognition in the world that is devoid of the accompaniment of words;
all knowledge appears as if permeated by the word."
"Just as light possesses two powers— namely, the state of being the object of apprehension and the state of being the apprehender—
in the very same way, these two exist separately in all words."
In that case, whatever perception and recollection there may be, not even a single word has any other cause.
For it is only when the physical form (piṇḍa) is actually perceived that it is capable of evoking the recollection of the name.

And this is logical; for there is no obstacle to the recollection of a word by its meaning, just as there is none to the recollection of a meaning by a word whose capacity has been grasped. Therefore, since the word "cow" (go-śabda) is no different from the universal "cowness" (gotva) in being a qualifier of the individual, their relation may indeed be identity (tādātmya).

In the same way, with respect to the cow, its qualities, and so forth, because that which is non-different from what is non-different from something else is itself non-different from it—this is the underlying intention. Thus, in the section beginning with "Now, what is the word in the case of 'cow'?", the authors of the Bhāṣya raise the objection that the word is non-different from substance, quality, action, and universal, and then refute it. The intention of that refutation is as follows: difference and non-difference existing at the same level of reality (*samasattāka*) are indeed contradictory.

Otherwise, according to the method you have stated, since there would be no difference between existence (*sattā*), the quality-ness (*guṇatva*), and so forth, it would follow that pleasure, pain, heaven, hell, and the like are also non-different; consequently, there would be no distinction between engagement and withdrawal, nor would there be the cessation of error through the apprehension of difference. Furthermore, the relation between a universal (*jāti*) and its individual (*vyakti*), etc., is indeed something distinct. In this very same way, it is established that substances and the other categories possess a relation with words as well. Moreover, the exposition of substances and the rest is also useful for the present context.

In this context, correctness (*sādhutva*) must be predicated solely by taking the non-distinction of meaning as the primary factor—namely, that "this [word] is correct in this sense. For this very reason, it is established as the final doctrine (*siddhānta*) that the word *aśva* is correct when applied respectively to a swift horse (*vājī*) and a poor man (*daridra*), whereas the word *asva* is incorrect when applied in reverse order.

If it is argued: "Just as the Vaiśeṣikas and others proceed to explain categories by relying on the division of base and suffix—which is established in their own treatises—while their investigation of bases, suffixes, and so forth is only occasional and incidental; likewise here too, there is no contradiction in explaining mere words by relying on the collection of categories well-known in the world and established in other systems," let that be so for now. Even so, the explanation of *ḍo*-suffixes and the like remains entirely fruitless.

If this is argued, it is replied here: expressions such as "the cow stands," "Devadatta cooks," and so forth, are infinite; therefore, even in a thousand lifetimes, they could not be taught or understood by pointing to each one individually (*śṛṅgagrāhikayā*). Consequently, a simpler means is resorted to—consisting of the postulation of the division between base (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*)—just as in the case of writing. Furthermore, the relationship [between word and meaning] in that context is merely superimposed (*āropita*). For the well-known analogies of the "thick Arundhatī," the "branch and the moon," and so on, are established in the world, and the analogy of the "descent through the five sheaths" (*pañcakośa*) is established in the *Uttaramīmāṃsā*.

Validity [of a statement] arises from the non-sublation of its intended object (*tātparyaviṣaya*). This is indeed the same principle that applies to *arthavādas* (eulogistic passages). Even though [the literal acts] such as the cutting out of one's own chest-organ (*vapā*) are sublated, the excellence (*prāśastya*) which constitutes the intended object remains unsublated. And it has been said by Bhartṛhari:
"The methods [employed] for those who are being instructed are merely means of coaxing children;
having first stood upon the path [of falsehood], one thereafter strives for the truth."

"The means for attaining the goal are not fixed. And so it is said. For this very reason, some employ the suffix *supratyaya*, while others use *sim*. Likewise, according to the method of the Sūtra, there is the suffix *it* in the word "pāṭhitam"; according to the method of the Bhāṣya, there is the suffix *tap*. According to the method of the Sūtra, there is the suffix *vatup* in "tāvān"; and according to the method stated in the Vārttika—"because of the distinction in meaning between *ḍāvac* and *ḍāvan*"—there is the suffix *ḍāvat*. This is the general direction.

By this, those who claim that in expressions such as "he cooks" (*pacati*), the suffixes *laṭ* and so forth—being recalled by means of substitutes (*ādeśa*)—are the conveyors of meaning, are refuted. For it is indisputable that the apprehension of word-meaning power (*śaktigraha*) occurs through the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*). Consequently, the expressive power is established only for *tip* and other such suffixes that are actually present in the utterance, and not for the non-empirical *lādi* suffixes. Similarly, verbal roots such as *ḍupacaṣ* and *ḍukṛñ*, as well as suffixes such as *vic* and *kvip*, are not expressive; rather, it is forms such as *apāk* and *papāc*, which are present in actual usages like "he cooked" (*apākṣīt*), "he cooked" (*papāca*), "he is cooking repeatedly" (*pāpacyate*), "he does" (*karoti*), and "he performs repeatedly" (*carkarīti*), that are expressive.

If it is argued that there is a recollection of roots such as *ḍupacaṣ* through what is being heard, and by means of that, there is the comprehension of the meaning—this is not so. Because of parsimony (*lāghava*) and because of the fixed nature [of linguistic usage], it is more appropriate to postulate a semantic connection for the very elements that are being heard. Furthermore, to postulate a recollection of something merely imagined (*autprekṣika*) would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), and it would lead to a lack of systematic consistency (*avyavasthā*).

Furthermore, because this would result in the collapse of the established doctrine—that in the case of "Devadatta cooks" (*pacati devadattaḥ*) and "See him cooking" (*pacantaṃ taṃ paśya*), it is the *laṭ* (present tense suffix) itself, as recalled by the *tip* and *śatṛ* suffixes respectively, that conveys the meaning—wherein in the former instance the effort denoted by the verbal suffix is a qualifier of Devadatta through the relation of locus and located (*ādhāra-ādheya-bhāva*), while in the latter instance the agent denoted by the *kṛt* suffix is a qualifier [of Devadatta] through the relation of identity (*abheda*).

By this, even the Mīmāṃsakas—who, having rejected the view that the agent is the meaning of the verbal suffix in the *Kartradhikaraṇa*, accept in the *Jañjabhyamānādhikaraṇa* that it is the meaning of the injunctive suffix (*śāstra*)—are also refuted.

As for what they have stated regarding the *śānac* suffix—that the grammatical rule "kṛt [suffixes] denote the agent" (*kartari kṛt*) serves as the means of apprehending its denotative power (*śaktigrāhaka*)—that too is merely superficial. This is because it will be explained later that this supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) concerning *kṛt* suffixes applies to those such as *ṇvul* whose referents are not explicitly specified, but not to those such as *śatṛ* (which includes *śānac*), since the latter are already satisfied by the meaning of their substituends (*sthānin*). Furthermore, this follows the maxim that "prescribing what is required is superior. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the *śānac* suffix could not occur in the sense of the object (*karman*), as in the form *kriyamāṇa*.

Furthermore, since the mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*) in the rule *kartari kṛt* is also understood as recurring in the rule *laḥ karmaṇi*, how can there be a difference between *kṛt*-affixes and *tiṅ*-affixes? For in both cases, they are equal in that the [agent] is obtainable through other means (*anyalabhyatva*). As for the claim that the agent is the expressed meaning (*vācya*) in forms such as the present middle participle (*śānac*) because the relation between the name and its referent is strictly identity (*abheda*), that is equally applicable to *tiṅ*-affixes as well, in accordance with examples such as *pacatikalpaḥ*, *pacatirūpaḥ*, and *devadattaḥ*. Therefore, according to the view of others (*pararītyā*), there is no cause for any discrepancy between words ending in *śatṛ* and those ending in *tiṅ*.

According to our view, however, the general rule of the predominance of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha-prādhānya*)—as stated by the author of the *Nirukta* in the maxim "verbs have action as their primary meaning, while nouns have substance as their primary meaning"—is set aside in the case of *tiṅ*-suffixes. This is because of the rule: "The statement that the meaning of the suffix is primary [is overridden] because the meaning [of the word] has other means of proof," and this is also clear from the *Bhāṣya* on the rules for the prescription of the *śatṛ* and *śānac* suffixes, as well as on the rules for the prescription of gender (*rūpa*).

For this very reason, even in the usage "pacativrajati" (he cooks and goes), [the formation] is not justified in the same way as "pācako vrajati" (the cooker goes); furthermore, in forms such as "pacatorūpam" (the form of two cooks) or "pacantirūpam" (the form of many cooks), dual and plural endings do not occur after the suffixes -rūpa and others. Therefore, it will be stated that between verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) and primary suffixes (*kṛt*), there exists merely a reversal of the relationship between qualifier and qualified.

As for the argument by the Bhaṭṭas—that because of the rule for *la*-suffixes stating "the singular number [is used] when there is singularity in the agent (*kartṛ*) is *tib*," and because this is explained as being in syntactic agreement with [Pāṇini’s rules] such as "for two or one" (*dvyekayoḥ*), the fact that the agent is the expressed meaning (*vācyatā*) does not follow from the Sūtra—this too is merely superficial. For the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) such as "dual" and so forth reside in the substitutes (*ādeśa*); consequently, the rule "for two or one" is in syntactic agreement with that which prescribes those [substitutes], and the word "in the agent" (*kartari*) does not occur therein, such that it could somehow be construed as a qualifier of duality and so on.

If it is argued that there is also syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) between the rule for *la* and the rules for the substitutes (*ādeśa*), this is true; however, that is syntactic unity at the level of the sentence (*vākyaikavākyatā*), not syntactic unity at the level of the word (*padaikavākyatā*), because the rule for the substitutes operates by restating the verbal suffixes (*lakāra*) obtained through the rule for *la*. Furthermore, the term "agent" (*kartṛ*) is mentioned in the rule for *la*, and that [agent] is indeed devoid of designations such as the dual number and so forth. For this very reason, according to the view that the verbal suffixes (*lakāra*)—as remembered through their substitutes—are the conveyors of meaning, one must rely solely upon the substitutes themselves for the cognition of singularity and the other numbers.

In this way, one would have to postulate that the recollection of *liṅ* and other suffixes occurs by means of *ṇal* and so forth; this would entail a great deal of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Nor can *ṇal* be the signifier [of the meaning] through a mediated relationship (*paramparā-sambandha*), because it lacks a formal grammatical operation (*vṛtti*). For this very reason, even you must admit that corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*) serve as reminders of correct words (*sādhu*). This is the general direction of the argument. Therefore, just as in rules such as "what precedes is not established" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*), where an interpretation based solely on superimposition (*āhāryāropa*) is universally accepted, so it is in every case within the technical grammatical system (*sāstrīya-prakriyā*).

In reality, however, denotative capacity resides solely in the *sphoṭa*. Regarding this, there are eight positions: (1) the phoneme-*sphoṭa*, (2) the word-*sphoṭa*, (3) the sentence-*sphoṭa*, (4) the indivisible word-*sphoṭa*, and (5) the indivisible sentence-*sphoṭa*—thus five are *vyakti-sphoṭas*; and the *jāti-sphoṭa* is threefold, according to the distinction of phonemes, words, and sentences.

To explain: since the disruption of the sequence that delimits the expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) occurs at every word due to the occasional transposition of phonemes and so forth, and since the apprehension of expressive power (*śaktigraha*) for one or another [sequence] occurs first in some instances, there is no definitive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*) as to which [phoneme] causes the recollection of which [meaning]. Consequently, just as in the case of *ṛṣabha*, *vṛṣabha*, and *vṛṣa*, all phonemes occurring in actual usage—such as *kar*, *kār*, *kur*, and *cakar*—are denotative when delimited by their respective sequences; this is the position of the *varṇasphoṭa* (the theory of the phoneme-sphoṭa).

The core of the disagreement here concerns whether the *kṛt* suffixes and so forth are expressive (*vācaka*) or not. (1) In cases such as "rāmam," "rāmeṇa," "rāmāya," "haraye," "harau," and "harīn," since it is impossible to determine exactly which portion of the fully established form denotes the substance (*dravya*) and so on, and which portion denotes the objecthood (*karmatva*) and so on, the position of the *padasphoṭa* is that the word-form itself—such as "rāmam"—is expressive of the [substance] as qualified by objecthood and the rest. (2)

In cases such as *dadhādam*, *hareva*, and *viṣṇova*, since the lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanāviraha*) is equal [to other instances], the sentence itself possesses the expressive power (*śakti*) for the qualified meaning; thus, there is the theory of the Sentence-Sphoṭa (*vākyasphoṭa*). Just as one says "one cloth" (*ekaḥ paṭaḥ*), so too from the uncontradicted cognition that "one word" or "one sentence," the word or sentence must be something distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*), being an indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*) entity manifested by the phonemes. If it is argued that the cognition of oneness is merely conditional (*aupādhikī*), then the same would apply to the cloth as well. If it is asked, "What is this category of object (*padārtha*)? the answer is: "Being" (*bhāvaḥ*).

If it is asked, "In what [category] among the specific types of existents (bhāva) are these included?"—they cannot be included within the categories such as substance (dravya) and so forth as defined by you; for that much does not permit one to reject what is established by valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa). If it is argued that there is complexity (gaurava) in the theory of indeterminate categories of existence, [we reply: even for you, there is no fixed limit to the number of individual instances (vyakti). However, the limit of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) can be easily stated by everyone, through their division by way of being an existent or a non-existent, or by way of being eternal or non-eternal, and so on. But the limiting adjuncts that divide existents are not necessary, just like the limiting adjuncts that divide jars.

In both of these two positions, even phonemes (*varṇa*) are not necessary. If it is argued that they are established by experience, we reply: no, because it is accepted that the *sphoṭa* itself—qualified by specific manifesting sounds—is conventionally designated as having the nature of the letter *ka* and so forth. This is just as, in the Bhāṭṭa school, one speaks of a "sharp" or "dull" *ga*-sound; or as, in the Advaita Siddhānta, there is a variety in the manifested bliss of the essential nature due to the diversity of mental modifications (*vṛtti*) produced by contact with objects.

For this very reason, Vācaspatimiśra, in his *Tattvabindu*, presented the view of the proponents of *sphoṭa* (sphoṭavādins) as follows: "In reality, since there is no *ga*-sound whose form is distinct from the *ka*-sound [that precedes it]. Or rather, just as even in indivisible phonemes such as *ṛ*, there is the appearance of a single part identical in form to another phoneme, so too will there be the appearance of phonemes in this position. And it has been said by Bopadeva:
"Just as in the case of being the object of a word (*śakyatva*), let the parsimony of the universal (*jāti*) be observed regarding its power (*śaktatva*);
or else, let the difference between phonemes be merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), like the distinction between high and low pitch."
Bhartṛhari also says:
"In a word there are no phonemes, and in phonemes there are no parts;
there is no absolute distinction whatsoever between words and the sentence."

Therefore, the word or the sentence is indivisible. (5) These five are also sub-classifications of the *vyakti-sphoṭa*. However, for those who maintain the theory of the *jāti-sphoṭa*, properties such as "the state of being the letter ṭ following the letter g" (*ghottara-ṭatva*) must be understood, as appropriate, as the delimiters of the expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) even in the first three positions; otherwise, there would be no cognition of specific meanings in cases such as *saraḥ* and *rasaḥ*. And that [delimiter] is of the nature of an adventitious attribute (*upādhi*). Furthermore, the adventitious attribute is simply the universal (*jāti*) connected through a causal chain (*paramparā*). And that [universal] has the nature of Brahman, which is the substratum of all things.

And thus, by parity of reasoning, just as in the case of the denotable aspect (*śakyāṃśa*), so too in the case of the denoting capacity (*śaktāṃśa*), according to the method of the *Akṛtyadhikaraṇa*, the reality of Brahman itself—either as such or as conditioned by those [limiting adjuncts]—is both the denoted and the denoter. However, they say that in the view where the universal (*jāti*) is a specific property consisting of either nescience (*avidyā*) or its products (*vidyaka*), that very [property] should be the denoter. || 6 ||

All eight of these positions are recorded in various places within the Siddhānta treatises. For instance, in the *sthānivat* rule, there is the Bhāṣya passage: "All substitutes are substitutes for entire words. Here, a "word" (*padam*) is that by which a meaning is expressed (*padyate 'rtho 'nena*), and not merely that which ends in a nominal or verbal suffix (*suptiṅanta*). Likewise, the commentary (*Ṭīkā*) passage—"The meaning of *erur* is *atestuḥ*"—is consistent with the theory of phoneme-sphoṭa (*varṇasphoṭa*).

Likewise, the *Mahābhāṣya* states that since a substitute (*ādeśa*) must be capable of expressing the meaning of the original element (*sthānin*), the rule "ta-stha-stha-mi-pām" and others can be accounted for by the *paribhāṣā* on the closest correspondence (*antaratama*) alone; therefore, the sūtra on "correspondence according to order" (*yathāsaṃkhya*) need not have been commenced for that purpose. Furthermore, regarding the word-sphoṭa (*padasphoṭa*) and sentence-sphoṭa (*vākyasphoṭa*), Kaiyaṭa, taking up the introductory portion of the *Mahābhāṣya* beginning with "yenoccāritena," has described them as the intended meaning of that *bhāṣya* within this very section.

By stating that the word or the sentence is distinct from its constituent phonemes (*varṇa*), it is implied that both are partless (*akhaṇḍa*). However, in various places in the *Bhāṣya*, their divisible nature (*sakhaṇḍatā*) has been asserted on the grounds that "in the case of eternal words, the phonemes must be fixed and unchanging. The term *kūṭa* is used in the masculine for deceptive mechanical devices, heaps of fraud and falsehood, an iron mace, a mountain peak, and a plowshare; it is not used in the feminine.

Thus says Amara. In another section of the *Paspaśā* itself, Kaiyaṭa—while commenting on the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "What then... which states, "Some speak of the *varṇa-sphoṭa*, others of the *pada-sphoṭa*, and still others of the *vākya-sphoṭa*"—and while considering the relative strength of the individual (*vyakti*) and generic (*jāti*) *sphoṭas* in the rule *aiuṇ*, concludes at the end of the *Pratyāhārānhika*: "In the occasion of explaining the Bhāṣya statement 'One should know that the syllable (*akṣara*) is not perishable (*kṣara*)', [it is said that] the permanence of usage belongs to the *sphoṭas* of phonemes, words, and sentences, whereas their [ontological] eternity..."

By demonstrating that this refers to the *jātisphoṭa*, and by explaining immediately thereafter that "the very reality of Brahman indeed manifests in the form of speech," all [other] positions are indeed indicated. When, however, the position is that ignorance (*avidyā*) itself is the genus (*jāti*), then with that intention, even for the *jātisphoṭa* there is permanence in conventional usage; this is the alternative reading in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the verse, "One should know the imperishable as not perishable. Furthermore, both the *varṇasphoṭa* and the *padasphoṭa* are mentioned in the *Bhāṣya* itself under the rule *ādyantau ṭakitau*.

Kaiyaṭa states that the intention is to explain the true *padasphoṭa* according to the maxim of the "single cow and the gavaya," by relying upon an unreal division of stem and suffix as well as their respective meanings. This is clearly evident in the *Mahābhāṣya* and Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on such rules as "that which possesses meaning is not a root" (*arthavad adhātuḥ*), "the form of a word is itself" (*svaṃ rūpaṃ śabdasya*), and "a phoneme followed by *t* denotes its own duration" (*taparas tatkālasya*). Enough of this elaboration. Furthermore, Hari has stated that the universal (*jāti*) is of the nature of Brahman:
"Being (*sattā*) itself, when differentiated among cows and other things due to the difference in their relata, is called a 'universal' (*jāti*); all words are established in that [universal]."
"They declare that [Bhāva] to be the meaning of the nominal stem and the meaning of the verbal root;
it is eternal, it is the Great Self (mahān ātmā), and they say that suffixes such as -tva and -tal denote it. Thus [it is said].
In another section, he himself states that the universal (jāti) is the sphoṭa: "The universal, manifested by multiple individuals, is known as the sphoṭa;
by some, the individuals themselves have been designated as its 'sounds' (dhvanis)."

Although eight positions have been stated here, the authors' intention nevertheless lies in the position of the sentence-sphoṭa (*vākya-sphoṭa*). Even there, it should be understood that they intend the *jāti-sphoṭa* (the universal sphoṭa), because each subsequent position is presented precisely by way of refuting the preceding one. And thus, since the first acquisition of linguistic competency depends upon usage, there is no dispute that the initial apprehension of the word's power (*śakti*) pertains to the entire sentence as a specific unit.

The path of other philosophical systems (*darśanāntara*) is that the capacity (*śakti*) of the constituent parts [of a word] is abandoned through the addition and removal of elements (*avāpodvāpa*), supported by logical reasoning (*nyāya*). However, when a dispute arises among grammarians—due to the lack of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*) in cases such as vowel substitution (*ekādeśa*) according to the aforementioned method, and because some accept the elision of the preceding element (*pūrvalopa*) in cases of external form (*pararūpa*) and so forth—the capacity of the constituent parts becomes difficult to establish; thus, the orthodox (*siddhāntika*) position is that the initial apprehension of capacity (*prāthamik-śaktigraha*) alone is the valid means of knowledge (*pramā*). And it has been stated by Bhartṛhari: "In that regard, what is primary for some, for those others there is the reverse."
And as it is said: "Just as there is no meaning of the word 'brāhmaṇa' in the compound 'brāhmaṇakambala', so too would [words] such as 'Devadatta' be meaningless within a sentence."

This being the case, even the investigation into whether particles (*nipāta*) are indicative (*dyotaka*) or whether verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇa*) are meaningless (*anarthaka*), and so forth, pertains only to the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*). And it has been said: "The separate conceptualization of roots and prefixes for the sake of establishing rules such as *akaḍādi* occurs within the treatise; however, in reality, the root alone is of that [ultimate] nature."

The meaning is that such [a word] is indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*). Furthermore, grammatical maxims (*vyutpatti*) such as "the relation between the meanings of two nouns is indeed identity" and "the meaning of the suffix is the primary element" are based solely on the analytical process (*prakriyā*). And it has been said:
"In our view, what kind of embryo is produced from what kind of embryo, and how does it appear?
All investigation regarding the nature of roots and suffixes has thus borne fruit."

Even that which is superimposed is not contradictory as a means (*upāya*) toward the ultimate reality, because worldly examples such as writing, the broad star Arundhatī, a branch, and the moon have already been shown; likewise, the methods for entering [the truth] through the explanatory statements (*arthavāda*), the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*), and so forth—established in other systems (*tantra*) and established in this very treatise through principles such as "not being previously established"—have already been demonstrated. Thus, according to the distinction of positions, it is established that *sphoṭa* is so called by the etymological derivation: "that from which the meaning bursts forth clearly," whether that [source] be ignorance (*avidyā*) itself or Brahman itself.
And it has been said: "In the scriptures, it is ignorance alone that is described through various systematic distinctions (*prakriyābheda*)."
"Indeed, the undertaking of the grammarians is the beginningless, eternal Brahman. Thus it is said.

Therefore, following the maxim from the *Vāsiṣṭharāmāyaṇa*—"one who set out to search for a cowrie shell obtained a wish-fulfilling gem"—the venerable Bhartṛhari, while engaged in the investigation of words, also incidentally elucidated doctrines such as the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavāda*) with the intention that one might become proficient in the non-dual Brahman of the Upaniṣads as well. However, since that [doctrine] is explained clearly in other treatises and is not excessively useful for the present context, it is not elaborated upon here.
Thus concludes the exposition on the nature of the sphoṭa.

It might be argued that, just as a book is useful for children who possess a delusion regarding words—due to common expressions such as "write 'ca', the letter 'ca' is missing"—and who consequently entertain the conceit of denotative power (*vācakatva*) toward those very [phonemes], so too is it useful for those who grasp at distinctions [between parts]. Such is the state of affairs. Likewise here, the scripture is indeed useful even for those who maintain the conceit of ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*) regarding the division into base (*prakṛti*), suffix (*pratyaya*), and so forth. Therefore, why this laborious effort to expound a mere conceptual construction?

If it is argued that for this very reason the author of the Bhāṣya, having proposed the alternatives of whether sound is eternal or non-eternal, would have remained indifferent—concluding that "let it be as it may" since the undertaking of grammar is free from obstacles in either case—it is true; however, the actual state of things was stated for the sake of etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*). For once the various positions, both primary and secondary, have been explained, it becomes possible to establish the systematic arrangement of even those doctrinal texts (*siddhāntagrantha*) that appear to be mutually contradictory.

Even the point to be explained later—that the five factors, beginning with the object for oneself (*svārtha*), appear in succession—can only be established through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*); such is the general direction [of the argument].

Granted that the word *sādhu* (correct) is the object [of grammar], and granted that its derivation is possible through the conceptualization of stems, suffixes, and so forth; nevertheless, if one asks what compels the study of grammar, take it to be the injunction for compulsory study (*nityādhyayanavidhi*). For it is heard in scripture: "The Veda, with its six auxiliary limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), must be studied and known by a Brāhmaṇa as a duty without motive (*niṣkāraṇa*). Here, "without motive" means independent of visible motives, that is to say, "compulsory. A "motive" (*kāraṇa*) is that by which something is caused or performed; it is a result (*phala*).

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that the Veda with its six ancillaries (*ṣaḍaṅga*) must be studied and known by a Brāhmaṇa. Thus, the meaning is that this duty—consisting of the study of the Veda along with its ancillaries and the knowledge of its meaning—is obligatory, like the twilight worship (*sandhyopāsana*) and other such rites. Haradatta and others maintain that this is *śruti* (direct revelation), whereas Bhaṭṭācārya maintains it is *smṛti* (tradition). In that case, if it is authoritative as *smṛti* alone, then even the statement in the *Mahābhāṣya*, "Moreover, there is tradition (*āgama*)," should be explained as *smṛti* itself, since it is rooted in tradition. Furthermore, the status of being an ancillary (*aṅgatva*) [of grammar] is due to its being praised as an ancillary. For it is said in the *Śikṣā*: [The text continues with the verse: "Grammar is the first ancillary; it is the eye of the Vedas. ...and so forth. Grammar is said to be its mouth, astronomy its eye;
etymology is designated as its ear, and the analysis of meters its feet.
"The Śikṣā is the nose of the Veda, while they declare the Kalpas to be its hands. Thus [it is said].

It is also an auxiliary (*aṅga*) by virtue of being helpful. For grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), by relying on specific meanings, prescribes specific accents and so forth, and is thus useful for determining the specific meanings of words. Astronomy (*jyotiṣa*) likewise explains specific times that are useful for Vedic study as well as for ritual performance. Etymology (*nirukta*), however, is essentially an appendix to grammar, since it mostly compiles within itself the elisions, augmentations, and modifications that are established by means of rules such as *bāhulaka*.

Prosody (*chandoviciti*) is also useful for determining the meaning of injunctions such as "one sacrifices with the *gāyatrī*," by means of defining the characteristics of the *gāyatrī* and other meters. Phonetics (*śikṣā*) likewise demonstrates the method of pronouncing phonemes (*varṇa*). The ritual manuals (*kalpasūtra*) also demonstrate the performance of rites by collecting together sets of subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) that are mentioned in different contexts, obtained through logical inference, or studied in other recensional branches (*śākhā*). Therefore, there are six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*). Among these, grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) is the most important, because the comprehension of words and their meanings depends upon grammar.

This is because the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence is rooted in that [grammar]. For this very reason, its study has been described as being of primary importance. Furthermore, the injunctions regarding the study of the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) are well known even in the *Smṛtis* of Manu and others. Thus, it is established that the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) is what compels the study of grammar. Consequently, just as it is accepted that there is demerit (*pratyavāya*) in the absence of the performance of *sandhyā*-worship and other rites, and the destruction of sin (*pāpakṣaya*) through their performance, so too should it be understood regarding the non-performance and the performance of the study of grammar.

There are also other fruits beginning with *rakṣā* (protection) and ending with *phala* (fruit). Thus, the *Bhāṣya* states: "What, then, are its purposes? Protection, [avoiding] omission, addition, brevity, and absence of doubt are the purposes. Here, the word *prayojana* is one [instance] in the masculine gender, referring to an impelling injunction (*pravartaka-vidhi*), derived either from the instrumental *lyuṭ* suffix in the sense of "that by which one is set in motion" (*prayujyate pravartyate 'nena*), or, due to the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), from the agentive *lyuṭ* suffix in the sense of "that which sets in motion" (*prayojayati*). The other [instance] is neuter, referring to a fruit (*phala*).

Regarding both [questions], since the singular collective form (*ekavadbhāva*) in the neuter *ekaśeṣa* (based on the rule "the neuter remains") is optional, it should be understood that the plural is used in the question and the singular in the answer. In this regard, the distinction is that the traditional authority (*āgama*) is the motivator (*pravartaka*), while the destruction of demons, brevity, and absence of doubt are the results (*phala*). Among these, the motivator—the traditional authority—has been explained. Now, the results are being explained.

In this context, "protection" (*rakṣā*) means the preservation of the Veda. For instance, elisions and substitutions of phonemes that are not seen in the common language (*bhāṣā*) are observed in the Vedic language (*chandas*). These might be suspected of being accidental by those who rely solely on actual usage. However, the grammarian, observing the underlying rules (*lakṣaṇa*), establishes that very form. An example of elision (*lopa*) is: *tmanā deveṣu vivide mitadruḥ*. Here, *tmanā* means *ātmanā*; the vowel *ā* is elided according to the rule: *mantreṣvāṅyāderātmanaḥ*. An example of an augment (*āgama*) is: *devāsaḥ*, *brāhmaṇāsaḥ*. Here, the augment *asuk* is added according to the rule: *ājjaserasuk*.

Examples of elision (*lopa*) and augmentation (*āgama*) are as follows: *devā aduha*. This means *aduhat* (he milked). When the substitution of *ad* for the *jha* of the *laṅ* [aorist] ending has been made, there is elision of the *t* by the rule "elision of *t* in the *ātmanepada* endings," and the augment *ru* is added by the rule "frequently in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*). By this, forms ending in the *laṭ* [present tense] such as *nāśiraṃ druhe*, *viśvā itte*, and *cchenavo duhre* are also explained. An example of the modification of a phoneme (*varṇavikāra*) is: *gṛbhṇāmi te saubhagatvāya* (I take hold of you for the sake of good fortune). The letter *bha* occurs here because of the rule "for *hṛ* and *grah*, *bha* in the Veda," and because it must be stated that this applies to the root *hṛ* as well.

The suffix *ghañ* is also Vedic (*chāndasa*). For example: *udgrābhaṃ ca nigrābhaṃ ca*. According to the rule *udgraha* (Pāṇini 3.3.48) and the statement *udgrābhanigrābhau ca cchandasi srugudyamananipātanayoḥ*, the suffix *ghañ* is applied to the root *grah* preceded by *ut* and *ni*. In that context, the suffix *ghañ* after the root *grah* preceded by *ut* is established even in common usage (*loka*) by the rule itself; however, after the root preceded by *ni*, it occurs only in the Veda (*chandas*) as stated in the Vārttika. *Srucaḥ* refers to specific sacrificial ladles characterized by particular arrangements.

In this context, however, only the *juhū* and *upabhṛt* ladles are to be understood, because of the scriptural injunction: "With the words 'udgābham ca,' he lifts up the *juhū*; with the words 'nigrābham ca,' he lowers the *upabhṛt*. The substitution of the sound *bh* is as previously explained.

Modification (*ūha*) is also a purpose [of the *tantra* method]. For instance, that in which the entire collection of constituent parts (*aṅgajāta*) is taught is the archetype (*prakṛti*), such as the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). That in which it is not taught is the ectype (*vikṛti*), such as the sacrifice enjoined by the rule: "One desiring spiritual luster should offer a *caru* oblation to Sūrya. Here, when there is an expectancy for auxiliaries in the sacrifice—which serves as the instrument within the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) that constitutes the scope of the ectype's injunction—the archetypal constituent parts are obtained by way of that [expectancy].

In the Vedic ritual, only such auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) are required as are already established in their capacity within the archetype (*prakṛti*). Furthermore, the specific nature of those auxiliaries—such as having a single deity—is easily ascertainable. Therefore, it is established in the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā* that "the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) should be performed according to the archetype. In that regard, if a particular benefit provided by an auxiliary element in the archetype is impossible to achieve in the modified sacrifice, that element is excluded.

Just as in the archetype (prakṛti), the purpose of threshing is established as the removal of husks (vaituṣya), and because that purpose is impossible in the case of *kṛṣṇala* seeds, the threshing is omitted; so too are the mantras auxiliary elements. Their function is the illumination of the object to be performed. In that regard, if the referent of a mantra in the archetype does not exist at all in the modified rite (vikṛti), then the entire mantra is omitted. For example, the mantra for threshing, "I shall slay the Rakṣas, the rival of heaven," is omitted in the case of the *kṛṣṇala* seeds.

However, for that part [of a mantra] which has no denotable object, only that much is excluded. For example, in the mantra "I offer thee, acceptable to Agni" (*agnaye tvā juṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi*), the word denoting the deity—which is a constituent part of this mantra—is excluded in the *saurya* sacrifice (which is a modification of the *āgneya* sacrifice) because that sacrifice has medicinal herbs as its substance and possesses a single deity; and when the word "Agni" is excluded because its mediating function has been lost, [the rest of the mantra remains].

The *ekāra* (the vowel *e*) is also subject to modification (*ūha*). For the dative case ending of *ekāra* must be expressed only when there is the proximity of a stem other than one ending in *akāra*, whereas that of the word *yas* [from *yaśas*] occurs after a stem ending in *akāra*. Consequently, in the place of the word *agnaye*, which is oxytone (acute-accented on the final syllable) and ends in the dative case as in *sūryāya*, the form *sūryāyāḥ*—which is madhyodātta (acute-accented on the middle syllable)—is to be substituted. This is what is meant by *prakṛtyūha* (modification of the stem). In some cases, there is modification of the gender (*liṅga*). For example: the mantra "O divine waters, you are pure" (*devīr āpaḥ śuddhāḥ stha*), which is prescribed for use with water, undergoes modification when applied to clarified butter (*ājya*), becoming: "O divine clarified butter, you are pure" (*devājya śuddham asi*).

In some cases, there is modification (*ūha*) of the suffix alone. For example, the sacrificial mantra for the *puroḍāśa* offering is: "Do not fear, do not tremble" (*mā bher mā saṃvikthāḥ*). Regarding this, Haradatta and others state that when it is applied to roasted grains (*dhānā*), the modification is: "Do not be afraid, do not tremble" (*mābhaiṣṭa mā saṃvijidhvam*), and so forth. However, ritualists (*yājñika*) maintain that the modification should be "do not tremble" (*saṃvigdhvam*). This is indeed correct, because it is determined that in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the root *vijir* in the sense of "separation" (*pṛthagbhāva*) is used—since it does not take the augment *iṭ*—and not the root *ovijī* in the sense of "fear and trembling."

Simplicity (*lāghava*) is also a purpose [of this treatise]. For instance, teaching is the livelihood of a Brāhmaṇa; its maintenance depends upon scholarship; and scholarship consists in the discrimination between correct and incorrect words. This discrimination is not possible through the method of reciting every single word (*pratipadapāṭha*), because words are infinite. Therefore, there is simplicity in making that knowledge known by means of definitions consisting of general rules (*utsarga*) and exceptions (*apavāda*); otherwise, however, there would be complexity (*gaurava*).

Even the absence of doubt serves a purpose. For instance, it is heard in scripture: "One should sacrifice a large-spotted female ox. In this regard, there arises a doubt: is this a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound) or a *bahuvrīhi* (possessive compound)? In that context, according to the *karmadhāraya* view, by means of *matvarthalakṣaṇā* (indication based on possessing a quality), the word *pṛṣatī* denotes a cow that possesses spots—that is, one marked with dots; and she is indeed the same even when qualified as "large," regardless of whether the spots are large or small. However, in the case of the *bahuvrīhi*, the largeness would apply to the spots themselves.

In the case of [the compound] *gauḥ sthūlaḥ kṛśo vā* ("Is the cow fat or thin?"), there is indifference [regarding the specific state]. There, having observed that the vowel *ā* in *lakāra* is acute (*udātta*), the grammarian determines it to be a *bahuvrīhi* by means of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member. Consequently, because doubt is obstructed by this certainty, no doubt arises; that itself is "absence of doubt" (*asaṃdeha*). If it is argued that, since the *avyayībhāva* [compound] occurs when there is an absence of meaning, the form should be *asaṃdeham*, [we reply: No, for it will be demonstrated in the second [chapter] that both designations—*avyayībhāva* and *tatpuruṣa*—apply here alternatively.

For this very reason, the Sage’s usage is twofold: "in the non-rapid [speech] it is unjoined (*asaṃhita*)," and "or, by means of the unjoined. Likewise, in cases such as "I partake of that which was drunk by Indra, being invited," the determination of the *bahuvrīhi* compound occurs solely through accentuation; thus, the *Indrapītādhikaraṇa* is meaningful for those who are not grammarians. Alternatively, this may be understood according to the principle of *kṛtvācintā* (hypothetical deliberation). This is the direction of the argument.

Thus, the four fruits known as *rakṣā* (protection), *halāghava* (lightness of effort), *asandeha* (absence of doubt), and *āgama* (scriptural authority) have been explained. It has been stated that scriptural authority (*āgama*) is the motivator (*pravartaka*). However, in the Bhāṣya, for the sake of the clarity of the composition, although the motivator for the fourfold fruit should have been mentioned either before or after [the discussion of the obligatory rites], its mention in the middle—by way of "sandwiching" the fruits—indicates that even the obligatory (*nitya*) rites culminate in a fruit. That fruit is either the destruction of sin (*pāpakṣaya*) or the non-arising of transgression (*pratyavāyānutpatti*), as it is said: "One dispels evil through dharma... by the non-performance of what is enjoined and the performance of what is censured."
And from the lack of restraint of the senses, a man undergoes a fall.
Statements such as these serve as proofs here; this is the general direction.

Furthermore, by means of the commentary beginning with "And these again," other injunctive statements have been cited and explained. For example: "Those Asuras, saying 'helayo helayaḥ,' were utterly defeated. Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should not speak like a barbarian (mlecch), nor should he speak incorrectly; for an incorrect word is indeed a barbarian—so says the Brāhmaṇa. In this passage, "nor should he speak incorrectly" is the explanation of "he should not speak like a barbarian."

In both cases, the suffix *tavaī* is applied according to the rule *kṛtyārthe tavaikenkenyatvanaḥ*. Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, the root *mlecch* is used here in the sense of "censuring," and the suffix *ghañ* is added in the passive sense (*karmani*). Thus, there is no contradiction in its coreferentiality with the term *apaśabda* ("corrupt word"). Here, the prohibition "one should not speak barbarously" (*na mlechitavyam*) has the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) "those were the Asuras" as its supporting justification.

Nor should it be argued here that the fruit [of the recitation] is merely an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise) according to the logic of the *rātrisatra* sacrifice; for, by the principle that "in the case of substances, purificatory acts, and rituals, because they exist for the sake of another, the mention of a fruit must be an *arthavāda*," this serves only to indicate excellence—just as the hearing of "fameless verses" does. Furthermore, the fact that this prohibition is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the ritual due to its context will be made clear by the Commentator himself in the subsequent text beginning with "The *Yarvāṇas* and *Tarvāṇas* by name."

For this very reason, it is not concluded here that "Grammar should be studied so that we do not become defeated," but rather, "so that we do not become barbarians (*mleccha*). The sense is that barbarians are contemptible because they perform practices contrary to what is taught by the scriptures. Regarding this, some maintain that the failure to apply the *prakṛtibhāva*—which would have been required by the rule "when *hai* or *he* are used, there is *pluta* for *hai* and *he*"—and the resulting *pluta* itself constitute the cause of being a barbarian.

If it is argued that this is not a fault because the author of the Bhāṣya will state, "Every *pluta* vowel should be applied optionally by one who does not desire to commit a transgression (*sāhasa*")? True; for precisely this reason, others have explained [the rule] differently as "doubling the sentence is barbarism" (*vākyadvirvacanaṃ mlecchanam*), on the grounds that the inclusion of the term "word" (*pada*) was enjoined in the rule *sarvasya dve*. This is their intention.

If it is argued that this is not a grammatical reduplication (*dvirvacana*), but rather a voluntary repetition for the sake of clarifying the intended meaning—just as in the case of "non-return, from the word; non-return, from the word"—then the accentuation of the repeated syllable (*āmreḍita-svara*) would be untenable. If, however, the reading there is indeed devoid of the *āmreḍita* accent, then we must conclude that the substitution of *l* for the *r* in the word *ari* is an incorrect form (*apaśabda*). And this has been explained by following the well-known recitation of the Vedic text (*śrutipāṭha*) as established in the *Bhāṣya* and other works.

And this reading should be sought in some recensional branch (*śākhā*). In the *Mādhyandina* version of the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*, however, after reading "saying 'helavo helava'," it is stated: "Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should not speak barbarously (*na mlecchet*). In that case, the substitution of the letter *va* for the letter *ya* is clearly a corruption (*apaśabda*). For a mantra deficient in accent or phoneme, when wrongly employed, does not convey its intended meaning;
like Indra’s enemy, it strikes down the sacrificer due to the transgression of accent. Thus it is said.

The suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of "from" (*svarataḥ*) because of the rule "from that which is diminishing or connected with evil. "Misapplied" means that when a word is employed for the purpose of conveying a certain meaning, it conveys a different meaning due to defects in accent or phoneme; thus, the meaning is that it does not convey that intended meaning at all. Speech itself is a thunderbolt (*vajra*) because of its capacity to cause harm. It "strikes the sacrificer" means that just as merit arises for the sacrificer from an oblation performed by the *adhvaryu*, so too does demerit arise for the sacrificer from the use of an incorrect word (*apaśabda*) by the *adhvaryu*. The word "just as" (*yathā*) serves as an illustration.

The term *indraśatruḥ* means "Indra is the enemy. It is said that in ancient times, when Viśvarūpa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, had been slain by Indra, the enraged Tvaṣṭṛ performed a malevolent sacrifice (*ābhicārika-yāga*) with the desire to produce another son named Vṛtra who would be the slayer of Indra. In that context, the phrase "O you whose enemy is Indra, grow! (*indraśatrur vardhasva*) was employed to convey the sense: "Being such [an enemy], grow! The suffix *krun* is an *auṇādika* suffix added to the causative form of the root *śad*.

The short vowel [in *indraśatru*] occurs due to its inclusion in the *prajñādi* group as an irregular formation (*nipātana*). Because the state of being Indra’s enemy (*indraśatrutva*) is that which is to be predicated (*vidheya*), the vocative case is not used, since the vocative has as its domain only that which is already established as a subject (*anuvādya*). For this very reason, there is a restriction in usage between the two phrases "O King, fight! (*rājan yudhyasva*) and "Be a king, fight! (*rājā bhava yudhyasva*). When kingship is already established, the vocative is used; it is not used when kingship itself is what is being predicated. This being the case, although the word *indraśatru*—being a *tatpuruṣa* compound—should have been stated as having the acute accent on the final syllable, it was apparently stated with the acute accent on the first syllable due to an error.

And thus, by the original accent of the first member of the compound, the meaning of a *bahuvrīhi* is obtained. For the word *indra* is derived as being acutely accented on its initial syllable (*ādyudātta*) by the addition of the suffix *ran*—according to the rule "ṛjrendra, etc."—to the root *idi*, which is an *auṇādika* formation. Consequently, it is well known from the Vedas, *itihāsas*, *purāṇas*, and other sources that Indra himself has become his slayer; this is stated here as an illustration.

It might be argued: "In the ritual of sacrifice (*yajñakarman*), there ought to be *ekaśruti* (monotone recitation); and that [rule] applies without distinction to both *tatpuruṣa* and *bahuvrīhi* compounds. To this they reply: *Ekaśruti* is prescribed for mantras alone by way of excluding [the rules for] *japa* and so forth. Furthermore, a mantra is not something employed according to one's own will. As Jaimini stated in the *Bhedalakṣaṇa*: "That which is not recorded in the sacred tradition is not a mantra. And Āpastamba says: "Those not recorded [in the Vedic texts] are non-mantras, such as the invocation of the *pravara* and the utterance of personal names."

For this very reason, although the reading "mantro hīnaḥ" is well-known in the *Śikṣā*, the word "mantra" in the *Bhāṣya* is read as "duṣṭaḥ śabdaḥ" with the intention that, since that which is being modified (*ūhyamāna*) is not a mantra, the subsequent phrase "yathehendraśatruḥ" would otherwise be inconsistent; therefore, the word "mantra" refers to speech in general.

[Objection: But is it not the case that "O Indra-śatru, prosper with Svāhā! is indeed recited in the Veda? [Response: True; however, although that which is emended (*ūhita*)—being non-mantric and intended as something to be imitated—is recited as an imitation, the fact that the original object of imitation (*anukārya*) pertains to meaning remains unchanged, and thus its worldly nature (*laukikatva*) persists. [Objection: If the word *indraśatru* is worldly, how can there be the possibility of merit or defect based on accent (*svara*), given that accent is restricted solely to the Veda? [Response: No, for there is no restriction to the Vedic meters (*chandas*) in the rules governing accent.

The difference is indeed this much: in the Vedic language (chandas), the threefold accentuation (traisvarya) and the single monotone (ekaśruti) are adopted according to fixed rules, whereas in common usage (loka), there is an optional choice based on one's will. For this very reason, we shall explain that in various places both alternatives—the recitation of the Sūtras in the monotone or with the threefold accent—are presented.

Surely, if this were the case, since the rule would already be established by the continued application of the option from the sūtra *uccairutarāṃ vā*, the inclusion of the word *vibhāṣā* in the sūtra *vibhāṣā chandasi* would be redundant. However, this fault does not apply if it is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute prohibition), because the word *vibhāṣā* is repeated there to exclude the restriction *yajñakarmaṇi*. Nor should it be argued that the same could be maintained under the view of *paryudāsa* (exclusion), for the distinction between the scope of an obligatory rule and an optional rule is necessarily established, and the very purpose of the initial formulation itself accomplishes the exclusion of the former.

But in the case of a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation), there is no force for the commencement [of the rule], because the prior rule—which has already found its application in non-mantras such as the *ūha* and so forth—could be sublated by the subsequent rule, which has as its scope the *chandas* (Vedic) alone. For the *ūha* and so forth do not possess the nature of *chandas*, since they are other than both mantra and *brāhmaṇa*.

Therefore, one might argue that even by resorting to an *asamartha-samāsa* (an irregular compound), it is appropriate to accept a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* out of necessity. [Response: No; for even in the case of the *paryudāsa* (relative negation) view, since a division of scope is possible—namely, "always in a mantra" or "in a *brāhmaṇa*"—the mention of the option (*vibhāṣā*) can serve to exclude [the rule] from sacrificial acts (*yajña-karman*).

However, precisely because of dissatisfaction with what was stated, some—relying on a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation) regarding recitation and so forth—maintain that since the application [of the rule] occurs here as well due to the single-mention (*ekaśruti*), the non-performance of that [recitation] and the employment of the *bahuvrīhi* accent constitute the meaning of the phrase "an offense by way of accent" (*svarato 'parādhāt*).
And it is heard [in scripture]:
"That which is studied without understanding is merely uttered as a mechanical recitation (*nigada*)."
Like a boat without a rudder, it never blazes forth, being like dry fuel.

"By mere recitation," that is, by the mere reading [of the text]. It should be resolved as "dry fuel" (*śuṣkedhaḥ*) with the neuter form ending in *-ā* (from *edhas*), or as a masculine word ending in *-a*. The meaning is that it does not burn, it does not shine, and it becomes fruitless. However, in the *Nirukta*, beginning with "Now there is praise of knowledge and censure of ignorance," it says:
"This man is like a pillar, a mere bearer of a burden, who having studied the Veda does not understand its meaning.
But he who knows the meaning attains all prosperity and goes to heaven, his sins shaken off by knowledge."

Having cited this mantra, the passage beginning with "that which is grasped but not understood" (*yad gṛhītam avijñātam*) is recited. There too, "grasped" refers to [the word] by means of its sound (*śabdāt*), while "not understood" refers to [it] by means of its meaning (*arthataḥ*), or by means of the division into stem, suffix, and so forth; the rest is as before. It is also heard elsewhere: "A single word, thoroughly known and properly employed, becomes a cow of plenty (*kāmadhuk*) in the heavenly world. And this the author of the *Bhāṣya* will state under the rule *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ*. This very same root is recorded in the verses called *Bhrāja*, composed by Kātyāyana:

"But he who, being skilled in the distinctions [of words], employs them exactly as they are at the time of usage, that knower of the application of speech attains infinite victory in the next world; however, he is defiled by incorrect words (apaśabda). Thus [it is said].
In the phrase "one is defiled by corrupt words," it is understood by implication that the non-grammarian is the agent.
Likewise:
"The ignorant who do not know the prolation (*pluti*) of the name in the return greeting..."
However, having lived abroad among them, one might as well speak of them as of women.

Now, regarding the word *athama*, [the rule] "and an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) that does not end in *iti* is designated as a *gati*" applies; thus, even in a *gati*-compound, there is no elision of the case-ending because it is an imitation, just as in examples such as *asyavāmīyam*.

The ritualists recite: "The *prayāja* offerings should be performed with their case-endings. Although in the archetype (*prakṛti*) the *prayāja* mantras are indeed recited with their case-endings, nevertheless, if after the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) the sacrificer should suffer from stomach pain, or if a great calamity should befall him within the year, then having prescribed the occasional *punarādheya* sacrifice (the re-establishment of the fires), this is enjoined therein: "The *prayājas* [should be] with their case-endings."

In that context, because a bare case-ending (vibhakti) cannot be employed independently, the base (prakṛti) is implied; and that [base] is specifically the form of the word *agni*, not just any word whatsoever. This is because, in the *Devatākāṇḍa* of the *Nirukta*, after introducing the question, "Now, what are the deities of the *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s?", and citing various mantra-texts and other authorities, it concludes with the statement, "But the settled conclusion is that they belong to Agni (*āgneyāḥ*). Therefore, one should observe in Vedic texts such as these that, in the first four *prayāja*s, four case-endings are recited having *agni* as their base.

Likewise, in another place it is said: "He who arranges speech word by word, accent by accent, or syllable by syllable is fit for the office of a priest (*ārtvijīna*). Regarding the term *pada-padam*, the suffix *śas* is applied according to the rule *saṃkhyaikavacanācca vīpsāyām*. An *udātta* and other such accents constitute the *svara* (accent). A syllable (*akṣara*) is a vowel accompanied by a consonant.

One who is worthy of the office of a *ṛtvij* is an *ārtvijīna*, namely the sacrificer (*yajamāna*); one who is worthy of the work of an *ṛtvij* is an *ārtvijīna*, namely the officiating priest (*yājaka*). [The suffix] *khañ* is applied by the rule "yajñartvigbhyāṃ ghaśañau" and by the *vārttika* "yajñartvigbhvāṃ tatkarmārhatīti copasaṃkhyānam. The sense is that only one who is learned has the qualification for performing sacrifices or officiating at them.

In the Ṛgveda as well, there are many mantra-passages such as *catvāri śṛṅgā*, *catvāri vāk*, *uta tvaḥ paśyan*, *saktum iva*, and so forth. Regarding the word *titau*, the commentary states: "The *titau* is a winnowing sieve. Some maintain that Amara’s statement, "The *cālanī* is the *titau*, masculine," is an error; however, in reality, in accordance with the aforementioned commentary, what is to be excluded from the Amarakośa is merely the impossibility of its being masculine, and not even its connection to anything else.

And likewise, in the section on masculine and neuter nouns, the *Trikāṇḍaśeṣa* states: "The word *vāstu* may mean asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) or a sieve (*titau*). For this very reason, the statements of learned authorities such as "he causes a sieve to act, he sieves" (*titāpayati*) are also consistent. This is the general direction [of the argument]. Ritualists recite: "One who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), having employed an incorrect word (*apaśabda*), should perform an expiatory offering (*prāyaścittīyā iṣṭi*) dedicated to Sarasvatī."

Likewise: "After the tenth day, one should give a name to the son who has been born; it should contain a harsh sound [a sibilant], begin with a consonant, have a semi-vowel in the middle, not end in a long vowel (be *avṛddha*), and imitate three ancestors (*tripuruṣānūkam*). For such a name becomes most firmly established. It should be two or four syllables; one should form a primary derivative (*kṛta*) name, not a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). Regarding the naming ceremony: it is called *tripuruṣānūkam* because it "resounds with" or "denotes" the three ancestors of the father who is the authorized person for the rite. The lengthening of the vowel occurs according to the rule "it is seen in other cases as well."

In the word *tripuruṣā*, there is an absence of feminine gender because it belongs to the *pātra*-class, and the suffix *ka* is applied because it belongs to the *mūlavibhujādi* group. As for the alternative view that one first applies the suffix *ka* by the rule *ātaścopasarge* (Pāṇini 3.2.3) to account for the presence of the subordinate term (*upapada*), and subsequently forms a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound—that is inconsistent with the Vārttika on the rule *karmaṇyaṇ* (Pāṇini 3.2.1), which states "after a stem ending in *a*, when no subordinate term is present, the suffix *aṇ* applies by superseding [the application of *ka*] when a karma-subordinate term is present," as well as with the Bhāṣya on the rule for feminine nouns (*nadī-sūtra*), which states "because it belongs to the *mūlavibhujādi* group, the suffix *ka* is applied."

For this very reason, the ancients maintain that words such as *gaṅgādhara* are proper names (*saṃjñāśabda*). In reality, however, there is no fault even when the word is subsequently connected with an object, provided that the word *anūka* is first derived without intending to express the object; the Vārttika and other such works, by contrast, intend the expression of the object at the very first stage.

Otherwise, what would be the status of forms such as *kṛtapūrvī*? For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa will also state in his commentary on the Bhāṣya’s explanation of *śakyaṃ ca kṣud upahantum*: "The internal refinement of the word is not obstructed by the perception of the external feminine gender. Furthermore, the intention to express (*vivakṣā*) follows worldly convention and is not under one's own independent control; thus, even in rules such as *viparābhyāṃ jeḥ*, one should support the view that "the verbal root is first joined with its grammatical factor (*sādhana*)" and conclude that forms like *vijayati* need not be treated as problematic. This is the general direction.

And thus it is recited in the Ṛgveda itself: "O Varuṇa, you are a good god, whose seven rivers flow along toward your palate (kākuda), like a hollow metal tube. The meaning of this is: O Varuṇa, you are one whose divine power (*deva*) is truth. Your *kākuda*—the palate (*tālu*)—is so called because the tongue (*kākuḥ*, which is the same as *jihvā*) is raised (*udyate*) within it; for the root *vad* has the sense of "raising," since verbal roots have multiple meanings.

Then, by the rule *ghañarthe kāḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.58), the suffix *ka* is added; there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*), and in this *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound, the form of the subsequent vowel is substituted according to the *śakandhv-ādi* group. Others hold that from the root *nud* (in the sense of "impelling"), the suffix *ka* is added in the locative sense, and the syllable *nu* is elided due to its being part of the *pṛṣodara-ādi* group; the essential meaning of the *Nirukta* also supports this. The seven case-endings are like the seven rivers (*sindhu*). The meaning is that they "flow toward" the palate—that is, they become manifest upon reaching it.

Here is an illustration: just as fire, having entered an iron image containing a cavity, becomes manifest; for the fire, having reduced the impurity therein to ashes, makes the image pure—so too do the case-endings (vibhaktis) remove the bodily sin. This is the intended meaning. Amara states: *sūrmī* means a pillar or an iron image. And it is recorded in the Smṛti: "One who has violated the Guru’s bed shall embrace a blazing iron image [to meet his death]."

Regarding the form *ami pūrvaḥ*, they say that the substitution of *yaṇ* occurs due to the continued application of the rule *vā chandasi*. Regarding *suṣirām*, they say that the suffix *ac* is applied according to the rule *arśa-ādibhyo'c*, or that it is a metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāraḥ*). However, in reality, the suffix *ra* is added in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*) by the rule *ūṣasuṣimuṣkamadhoraḥ*. Amara states: "A cavity (*randhra*), a hole (*śvabhra*), a membrane (*vapā*), and a pore (*suṣi*)," and also: "*Sarandhra* and *suṣira* [are used] in three genders. Kṣīrasvāmī says: "It is *suṣi* because it flows well (*suṣṭhu syati*). Śāśvata says: "*Suṣira* is used in three genders for a pit, for that which possesses pits, and for a specific type of musical instrument."
Thus ends the detailed exposition of the purpose.
Thus, since the subject matter and the purpose have been stated, the relationship and the qualified student are effectively already mentioned and are therefore not stated separately.

In this context, someone other than the one who asked about the purpose—namely, a bystander—objects as follows: "Just as when a teacher says, 'Study,' students study the Veda without being asked about the purpose, so too they will study grammar, which is an auxiliary limb [of the Veda]. Therefore, why this trouble of describing its purpose? To this, the following is the reply: because people nowadays generally have short lifespans and encounter many obstacles, the Veda, which is the primary subject, is first taught.
