If it is argued that these are merely properties of the sound (dhvani), then let the properties of *katva* (the quality of being 'k') and *gatva* (the quality of being 'g') also belong to that very [sound]; consequently, there would follow the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the identity of the phonemes 'a', 'i', and so on.

This is what is being stated: that an indivisible word or sentence is the signifier. Why say more? Let there be no such thing as a manifested phoneme (*varṇa*), since everything can be accounted for by the very sounds (*dhvani*) which are considered to be the manifestors. And it has been said by Bhartṛhari: "The universal (*jāti*) manifested by many individuals is known as *sphoṭa*;
by some, these very individuals have been designated as 'sounds' (*dhvani*)."

Therefore, if the manifestation [of meaning] is accomplished by the sounds (dhvanis) alone, then it is simply the *jāti-sphoṭa*; if not, then there is indeed a difference between the high-pitched (*udātta*) and low-pitched (*anudātta*) accents, just as there is between the letters *ka* and *kha*. This being established by logic, the phonemes (*varṇas*), following along with these differences residing in the sounds—such as the high-pitched, the low-pitched, and so forth—become the causes for comprehension.

Thus, it is established that the Mīmāṃsaka position should be disregarded because it is like the "half-old woman" fallacy (*ardhajaratīyatva*). And so, if this reference is intended to denote a genus (*jāti*) according to the method accepted by the Naiyāyikas and others—that there are infinite individual phonemes (*varṇa*)—then let it be the same in the rule *asya cvau* (Pāṇini 7.4.32) as well; what then would be the use of the *grahaṇaka-śāstra* (the technical rules defining phoneme groups)? As it has been said: "The inclusion of *savarṇa* [in the sūtra] is not a general rule (*paribhāṣā*), because the genus is what is being denoted. However, the rule concerning *tapara* (Pāṇini 1.1.70) is for the purpose of removing the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) resulting precisely from the denotation of the genus.

In rules such as *tyadādīnām aḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.102), even a single individual instance (*vyakti*) is intended to be expressed as a qualifier of the genus (*jāti*), because it serves as a qualifier of that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*), just like the singularity [of the animal] in the injunction *paśunā yajeta*. However, in rules such as *asya cyau* (Pāṇini 7.4.32), the individual instance is not intended to be expressed because it serves as a qualifier of that which is being referred back (*anuvādya*), just like the singularity [of the cup] in the injunction *grahaiḥ juhoti*. Nevertheless, this position is not what the author of the Sūtras intended by including the mention of the suffix *aṇ*; rather, the position that there is only one individual instance of the vowel *a* has already been refuted.

If, however, one holds the position that there are eighteen distinct individual phonemes (*avarṇavyakti*), then if the statement *aiuṇ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.9) refers to a genus (*jāti*), the subsequent mention of *aṇ* would be redundant. On the other hand, if it refers to individuals (*vyakti*), then according to the reasoning already stated, the inclusion of homogeneous phonemes (*savarṇagrahaṇa*) in rules such as *asya cvau* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.4.32) would be untenable; thus, there is a great dilemma. If it is argued that, therefore, the intention of the Sūtra-author in this matter is difficult to state, it is replied: the validity of the Sūtra is indeed maintained in all three positions.

For instance, on the view that the phoneme *a* is one and the same—based on the force of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that "this very *a* is that"—you yourself have established the systematic arrangement of grammatical properties (*dharmavyavasthā*). Just as the operation [of the rule] *ke aṇ* does not apply, and just as rules such as those concerning suffixes (*apratyaya*) do not trigger long vowels (*dīrgha*) and so forth, so too the rule *asya cvau* (Pāṇini 7.4.32) would not apply in cases such as *mālībhāti*; therefore, the *grahaṇaka-śāstra* is formulated.

And since that [application] depends upon homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*), the expanded nature (*vivṛtatva*) of the short vowel is postulated. If, however, this were restricted only to those vowels included in the *akṣarasamāmnāya* (the alphabet), it would not be established universally; therefore, the postulation is universal. If it is argued that even so, in rules such as *asya cvau* (Pāṇini 7.4.32) and *atyādau*, there would be no capacity to include [other sounds] precisely because they are not *aṇ* (i.e., not short vowels), [we reply: no, because even in those cases, they possess the status of *aṇ* due to the lack of distinction regarding the expanded nature of the short vowel and so forth.

However, qualities such as being dark-complexioned, tall, or having four arms, though enjoined by a mere restatement of the essential form (*svarūpa*) without being restricted by spatial distinction—unlike the case of "matted hair" (*muṇḍa*) or "tufted hair" (*jaṭila*)—do remain fixed. But it will be stated in the *Vṛddhi-sūtra* that accents (acute, grave, circumflex) and nasality, not being conveyed by the word itself, are not differentiators.

In the view that individual instances (*vyakti*) are indeed infinite, and in the view that there are eighteen distinct instances of the vowel *a* (*avarṇa*), although there exists a single genus (*jāti*) common to the short, long, and protracted [vowels] which serves as the delimiting factor for being produced by the throat and other articulators, or as the delimiting factor for being manifested by the sound (*dhvani*) produced thereby, nevertheless, there also exists a genus that is pervaded by that [genus] and resides exclusively in the short [vowel]. Thus, in the sūtra *aiuṇ*, the mention refers to this pervaded genus. Consequently, the quality of being "open" (*vivṛtatva*) established in one instance of that genus is established for all [instances] as well.

Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever in any of these cases. For even in forms such as *avāttām*, this is precisely the solution. Otherwise, when the form *avāta-s-tām* is established, the rule *jhalo jhali* (Pāṇini 8.2.26)—which applies to the single one of two *takāra*s situated between the *s-* of *sic* and the following *t-*—would not operate. The scope of that rule, however, would be limited to forms such as *abhitthāḥ*. Furthermore, this also accords with the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that long vowels, being non-*aṇ* sounds, do not include their homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇagrāhakatva*).

If it is argued that one should accept the instruction as referring only to the pervasive genus (*jāti*) and thus discard the mention of the *aṇ* pratyāhāra, even so, the *grahaṇaka-śāstra* (the rule defining the *aṇ* pratyāhāra) is indispensable for the purpose of including the *ḷ*-vowel in rules such as *upasargād ṛti* (Pāṇini 6.1.91). Nor can it be claimed that this inclusion [of the *ḷ*-vowel] occurs by virtue of the prescription of homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) in the maxim *ṛ-lṛ-varṇayoḥ*, because that maxim finds its utility in rules such as *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.101).

Furthermore, in the absence of a restrictive rule, there would be a confusion between cases where a pervading genus (*vyāpakajāti*) is indicated—as in *asya ccáu* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.4.32)—and cases where a pervaded genus (*vyāpyajāti*) is indicated—as in *tyadādīnām aḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.2.102).

Furthermore, the Mīmāṃsaka boundary—that the qualification of the subject (*anuvādya-viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualification of the predicate (*vidheya-viśeṣaṇa*) may respectively be intended or unintended, as in the cases of the "singularity of the cup" (*graha-ekatva*) and the "singularity of the animal" (*paśu-ekatva*)—cannot be accepted by Grammarians. This is because in the rule *upeyivānānāśvānanūcānaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.109), they accept that while the root *upa-* is not intended, the negative particle *nañ* and the following elements are indeed intended.

In rules such as *ārddhadhātukasyeṅ balādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.34), the Paribhāṣā *anuvādyaviśeṣaṇapratipattir iti* (the understanding of the qualifier of the subject of an enunciation) is the very refuge in the final doctrine (*siddhānta*). Although an explanatory gloss (*vyākhyāna*) is sometimes resorted to in various places for the sake of convenience—since it must conform to the observed linguistic data (*lakṣya*)—it is by the force of the *grahaṇakaśāstra* that it is most clearly understood that "a non-suffix (*apratyaya*) which is not being prescribed [as a whole] includes its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇagrahaṇakṛt*)."

Furthermore, this limit of the Mīmāṃsakas has been transgressed even in the *Dharmaśāstra* in numerous instances, such as in the rule "one should not awaken a superior person" (*na prabodhayec chreyāṃsam*). In this context, the mention of the word "one" (*eka*) in the Pāṇinian sūtra "ekah pūrvaparayoḥ" (Pā. Sū. 3.2.84) is also an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Otherwise, since the singularity [of the vowel] in the sūtra "ādguṇaḥ" (Pā. Sū. 6.1.87) could—as in the case of the singularity of the animal in ritual injunctions—be intended as a specific restriction, what would be the purpose of that [mention of "one"]? This is the direction of the argument.

Alternatively, even if the possession of meaning (*arthavattva*) is not intended [to be expressed], the letter *a* and others, when uttered here, bring to mind six individual instances similar to themselves through the relation known as similarity (*sādṛśya*). Nor does this lead to the impossibility of these being the correlates of syntactic connection (*anvaya-pratiyogitā*) in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), because there is no obstacle to the theory of "supplying the meaning" (*arthādhyāhāra-vāda*). The avoidance of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), however, occurs precisely through the force of the indicators of intention (*tātparya-grāhaka*). Otherwise, for you too, the over-extension resulting from secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), supplying [missing words], and so forth, would remain in its original state.

By the force of the grammatical rule *spṛher īpsitaḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.46), and because the rule *kriyārthopapadasya ca karmaṇi sthāninaḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.4.14) and others establish that in specific instances an implied object (*arthādhyāhāra*) is admitted, otherwise—as will be explained—there would be no understanding in cases such as *gavity ayam āha*.

*Ṛlṛk* (Māheśvara Sūtra 2). Now, one might object: "In the prescriptive rules (*vidhivākya*), just as the letter *ṛ* includes the eighteen sounds beginning with *ṛ* by virtue of the rule for inclusion (*grahaṇaka-śāstra*), it will likewise include the twelve sounds beginning with *lṛ*. Therefore, what is the purpose of teaching the letter *lṛ* separately? Nor should it be argued that it is not included because of a lack of homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) due to having different places of articulation; for by the force of the Vārttika, 'There is a rule for the homogeneity of *ṛ* and *lṛ*,' a scriptural homogeneity must necessarily be admitted."

Otherwise, even when the *ḷ*-vowel is taught [as a substitute], there would be the undesirable consequence that rules such as *upasargād ṛti dhātau* (Pāṇini 6.1.91) and *vā supy āpiśaleḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.92) would fail to apply in forms like *prālkarīyati*. If it is argued: "This *ḷ*-vowel here is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the *ḷ* found in the root *klṛp*; and since that [original *ḷ*] is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) for the purposes of vowel operations, this [imitated *ḷ*] is in fact an *ṛ*-vowel. Thus, rules such as *upasargād ṛti* will be established," [The answer is: No, because although the *ḷ* prescribed by *kṛpo ro laḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.18) is non-existent for those purposes, this imitation of it is not non-existent.

It might be argued that, by the extended application (*atideśa*) rule "an imitation is like its original" (*prakṛtivadanukaraṇam*), this [form] is also indeed unestablished (*asiddha*). And that extended application must necessarily be resorted to, so that in the Taittirīya statement, "He said, 'Let them cook twice' (*dviḥ pacantu ity āha*)," although *pacantu* and so on are recited with an acute accent (*udātta*), nevertheless—in the version from another branch cited in the Bhāṣya—the elision of accent (*nighāta*) of the word *pacantu* may occur according to Pāṇini 8.1.28 (*tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*). For this is not a finite verb (*tiṅanta*), since its meaning is the referent of a finite verb (*tiṅntapadārthakatvāt*).

It will be stated in the *arthavat-sūtra* that the production of the *svādi* suffixes here is optional, depending on the difference in the speaker's intention (*vivakṣābheda*). In cases such as *agnī ity āha*, the status of being a *pragṛhya* is also due solely to extension (*atideśa*). The evidence for this extension is the Pāṇinian rule *yattadetebhyaḥ parimāṇe* (Pāṇini 5.2.39). For, without extension, the substitution of *tyadādi* forms [with *t*] would not be obtainable here; this is because, according to the maxim *abhivyaktapadārthā ye*, that rule operates only when there is a reference to meanings well-known in common usage (*lokaprasiddhārtha*).

"Regarding the principle that 'there is an obligatory connection between *yat* and *tat*': if it is argued that because this very extended application (*atideśa*) necessitates the presence of *atva*, the cited example is indeed untenable, we say no. For the fact that the extended application is non-obligatory (*anitya*) is indicated by the non-employment of *ekaśeṣa* in the rule cited as evidence, namely *tyadādīni sarvaiḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.72), as well as by such references as *etattadoḥ sulopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.132)."

Alternatively, by the rule *prāvṛṭśaratkāladivāṃ ja* (Pāṇini 6.3.15) and the Vārttika *apo yoniyanmatuṣu ca*, both this Paribhāṣā and its non-eternality (*anityatā*) are indicated. To illustrate, in the *Kārīrī* sacrifice, the Śruti states: *apsumantāvājyabhāgau*.

In the mantras "apsu me somaḥ" and "apsv agne sadhiṣṭava," because the word *apsu* occurs there as an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) followed by the suffix *matup*, the rule for elision (*luk*)—as seen in examples such as "asyavāmīyam"—does not apply since an imitation lacks case-inflection (*vibhakti*). Therefore, the prescription of non-elision (*aluk*) makes known the aforementioned technical rule (*paribhāṣā*). Furthermore, since the derivation of the suffix *matup* is difficult to achieve without the word ending in the nominative case, its status as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is also necessary.

Furthermore, since that [term] would be difficult to obtain if it were to end in a suffix, its status as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is established even by the fact that the application of the extended designation (*atideśa*) is permitted to be absent; thus, its non-eternality is also proven. By this, usages such as "of the two objects of the suffixes *yuṣmad* and *asmad*" are explained.

Let us return to the subject at hand. One might ask: "Since the imitation of the sound *lṛ* is also [treated as] non-existent (*asiddha*) by extension (*atideśa*), the rule *upasargād ṛti* (Pāṇini 6.1.91) is successfully applied in cases such as *prāl̥kārīyati*; therefore, what is the use of phonetic similarity (*sāvarṇya*)? This is not so. For if that were the case, even though the status of being followed by *r* (*rephaparatva*) would be established, the status of being followed by *l* (*lakāraparatva*) would remain unestablished due to the non-existence [of the *l*]. Consequently, you too must admit that, because the extension does not apply here due to its being considered non-eternal (*anityatva*), the status of being followed by *l* remains unestablished.

If it is argued that since the status of being followed by *r* is already established, the substitution of *l* for *r* will occur by means of extended application (*atideśa*), we say no; for even so, in the case of the imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the *ḷ*-vowel found in roots such as *gamlṛ*, *sṛplṛ*, etc., there would be no possibility of stating the aforementioned extended application. Therefore, since the quality of being a homogeneous letter (*savarṇatva*) is necessary, the teaching (*upadeśa*) of the *ḷ*-vowel is indeed useless. If this is the objection?

To this it is replied: First of all, the author of the *Sūtras* did not proceed [to compose his work] merely after seeing the *Vārttika*. Furthermore, even if the *Vārttika* had already been composed, the instruction of the phoneme *ḷ* must indeed have been given in order to indicate that the homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between *ṛ* and *ḷ* is non-eternal. By means of that, in the example "klṛptaśikhā," the protracted vowel (*pluta*) is established by Pāṇini’s rule 8.2.83, "guroranṛtaḥ. Otherwise, there would be a prohibition by the word "anṛtaḥ" [in that same rule], because *ḷ* would be included by the mention of *ṛ*.

In forms such as *klṛpyamānaḥ* and *calīklṛpyamānaḥ*, the non-application of the nasalization (*ṇatva*) prescribed by the supplementary rule (*aupasaṃkhyānika*) "after a vowel containing *ṛ*, there is [nasalization] of a *n* [in a suffix]" can also be easily explained by classifying these words under the *kṣubhna*-group. Otherwise, in forms such as *praklṛpyamāna*, the application of nasalization would be unavoidable by Pāṇini’s sūtra 8.4.29, "after a *kṛt* suffix ending in a vowel, there is [nasalization] of a *c* [in a suffix]."

However, this must be noted: according to the *Vārttika* school, the mention of *aṇ* in the rule regarding homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*) is not a governing maxim (*paribhāṣā*). Consequently, since there is no common genus (*jāti*) shared by both *ṛ* and *lṛ*, it is impossible to grasp the form (*ākṛti*) [of the former] as including the latter; thus, the failure to accomplish the grammatical operation in the case of "prālkārīyati" remains as it was. The rule for homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*), however, serves its purpose by preventing the application of Pāṇini 6.1.127 (*iko'savarṇe*) in cases such as "hotṛ lṛkāraḥ," where a long vowel substitution (*savarṇadīrgha*) is required.

Furthermore, there is no application of the rule *ṛtyakaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.128), so how could [the mention of] *sāvarṇya* (homogeneity) indicate its non-eternality? Therefore, the intention must be inferred as follows: for one who rejects the mention of *aṇ*, the mention of *ṛk* should be made in its place, and the mention of *apratyaya* (not being a suffix) need not be performed.

Even though, in this case, for roots such as *pallṛ* which are marked with *lṛ*, the operation prescribed for those marked with *ṛ*—namely, Pāṇini 7.4.1 (*nāglopi śāsvṛditām*)—would apply, the separate assignment of the marker *ṛ* is incapable of ensuring non-confusion because its purpose is fulfilled by the application of the substitute *aṅ* to those marked with *ṛ*. Nevertheless, this too must be resolved by means of the non-universality of the rule regarding homogeneous sounds (*sāvarṇya*).

Alternatively, in the section on vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*), it should simply be stated that the *ḷ*-vowel undergoes the same treatment as the *ṛ*-vowel; furthermore, the rule regarding their homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) need not be added as a supplement (*upasaṃkhyeya*), because the protracted vowel (*pluta*) resides in a different section and thus the extension of the rule (*atideśa*) does not apply there. As for the metarule (*paribhāṣā*) "uraṇ raparaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.1.51), since it operates according to the principle of "time of application" (*kāryakālatā*), it belongs to the section on vowel-sandhi; therefore, it is justified that the term "uḥ" includes the *ḷ*-vowel.

Even in this view, the instruction of the vowel *ḷ* must indeed be performed here so that [the following results may occur]: in the case of *praklṛpta*, there may be the protracted (*pluta*) accent according to the rule "and [in the word] *klṛpta*, it is svarita" (Pāṇini 1.2.39); and in *klṛpta*, there may be doubling; and in *praklṛpta*, there may be the svarita accent. For in this instance, the suffix *kta* occurs in the passive sense after a root whose causative meaning is internalized. Consequently, by the rule "an immediately preceding prefix [retains its original accent]" (Pāṇini 6.2.49), the first member retains its natural accent, because that rule is prescribed for a compound whose final member ends in a *kta* suffix used in the passive sense.

Then, once the remaining *nighāta* (elision of accent) has been performed, the rule "an udātta following an udātta becomes svarita" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 8.4.66) applies. Nor should there be any suspicion here that the rule "the *ra* of *kṛp* becomes *la*" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 8.2.18) is *asiddha* (non-existent for the purposes of the preceding rule), because the former is prior. For that which is subsequent is *asiddha* with respect to what precedes it, but not vice versa. And in this way, even the designation of the *ḷ*-vowel as an *it* (indicatory letter) for roots such as *gamlṛ* is established without effort.

Otherwise, however, the substitution of *yaṇ* (the semivowel) for the vowel *ṛ*—as prescribed by the rule *puṣādidyutādyṛditaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.55)—would have to be somehow established through the technical designation (*it-saṃjñā*) of that *ṛ*, which serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Similarly, on account of the symmetry with such subsequent references as *idito num* (Pāṇini 7.1.58) and with indicative citations such as *ṛtyakaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.128), the vowels *i*, *u*, and so forth would likewise not need to be explicitly mentioned. Nevertheless, we shall speak according to the literal form of the sūtras as they are heard.

When a girl, having begun to pronounce the sound *ṛ*, pronounces *lṛ* due to a lack of proficiency in articulation (*karaṇāpāṭava*), the result is that even for the imitation (*anukaraṇa*), the grammatical operations dependent on vowels (*ackārya*) do not take effect; this is because it is accepted that imitations are always correct (*sādhutā*) when they possess meaning through their prototype (*anukārya*). If it is objected that this contradicts the rule "there are no long vowels for the *lṛ*-sound," since an imitation of it would be easily available there as well, [the reply is: no, because even that which is established by logic is set aside by an explicit statement (*vacana*).

And this is obtained from the *vārttika*: "Because [the form] is logical, there is the assumption [of the phoneme *ḷ*] in names (*saṃjñā*) and so forth. To explain: by the preceding *vārttika*, "The instruction of the phoneme *ḷ* is for the sake of arbitrary words (*yadṛcchā*), words arising from inability (*aśaktija*), imitation (*anukaraṇa*), prolated vowels (*pluti*), and so forth," three purposes for the instruction of the phoneme *ḷ* are stated. Its meaning is as follows: "Give curd to *Lṛtakā*" is an arbitrary word; "The girl said, 'She is straight (*lṛju*)'" is an imitation arising from inability; and prolated vowels, reduplication, circumflex accents, and so forth are the "prolated vowels and so forth"—for these purposes, the phoneme *ḷ* is taught.

In that regard, the following *vārttika*—"because of the existence of what is logical" (*nyāyyabhāvāt*)—is intended to refute the first [proposed] purpose. Its meaning is as follows: *ṛti* is a verbal root (*dhātu*) mentioned in the *sūtra* "from *ṛti*, *īyaṅ*" (Pāṇini 3.1.29); from that, the suffix *kvun* is applied according to the *uṇādi* rules. For it is stated in that context: "The suffix *kvun* occurs after a root—even one not previously established—to denote either a craft (*śilpin*) or a name (*saṃjñā*)" (Uṇādisūtra 2.200). The meaning is that when a craftsman is to be expressed, or when it is a name, the suffix *kvun* occurs after a root, whether it is accompanied by a prefix (*sopapada*) or without a prefix (*nirupapada*).

"Rajaka" (washerman), "takṣaka" (carpenter), and so forth are examples [of names] for artisans; "caraka" (wanderer), "bhaṣaka" (barker), "kaṭaka" (bracelet), "kanaka" (gold), and so forth are examples in the sense of a proper name (*saṃjñā*). Thus, the word *ṛtaka* is correct because it conforms to the grammatical treatises (*śāstra*). Due to its existence [as a valid form], that alone is the proper name. Furthermore, by this, even the *Gṛhya-smṛti*—which states, "One should use a primary derivative (*kṛt*), not a secondary derivative (*taddhita*)" and so on—is corroborated. By speaking thus, it is made clear that a name such as "kūcī," which is created in a regional dialect (*deśabhāṣā*) and does not conform to the treatises, is incorrect (*asādhu*)."

By showing that even in the case of imitation (*anukaraṇa*), one must follow the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭa*)—as indicated by the word "and so forth" (*ādiśabda*)—the author demonstrates the ungrammaticality (*asādhutā*) of an imitation of a long *ḷ* vowel that is made by transgressing the established limits of the treatises (*śāstra-maryādā*), namely that "there are no long forms of the *ḷ* vowel. Therefore, just as in the case of *kūci*, *mañci*, and so on from *ṭi*, *ghi*, *u*, and *bh* suffixes, there is no logical distinction between the imitation of words such as *gāvī* and *goṇī* and the imitation of a long *ḷ* vowel; rather, it is established that [the prohibition] is based solely on explicit scriptural statement (*vācanika*).

In the *mantra-śāstra*, however, although the long vowel *ḷ* is accepted in contexts such as the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*, it should nevertheless be understood that, according to the principles of the *Prātiśākhya*, it is of no use elsewhere. Similarly, by parity of reasoning, the unacceptability of forms such as *vancati*—which are not recognized by the learned—is stated. Thus they say: "The root *vac* is never used with the suffix *anti*. And so, by the *vārttika* "because of the exclusion based on logical principle" (*nyāyyabādhāt*), the first among the three purposes mentioned in the preceding *vārttika* is refuted.

The form *lṛtaka* is indeed incorrect. And this was stated under the view that "the occurrence of words is threefold; there are no arbitrary (*yadṛcchā*) words. For the author of the Bhāṣya maintains that refutations are possible even from other perspectives. However, upon a careful examination of this text, it is understood that according to the fourfold theory (*catuṣṭayī*), forms such as *lṛtaka*—like *ṭi*, *ghu*, and so on—are indeed correct, though they fall outside the category of [standard] correct and incorrect forms, rather than being distinct from *ṭi*, *ghu*, and the like. Otherwise, he would not have said "even from other perspectives."

Nor is there a contradiction with the *Gṛhya-smṛti* rules; for even by that much, since there is no obstacle to accepting the grammatical correctness (*śabdasādhutā*) of forms such as *aupagava*—even if they are formed by transgressing the *Gṛhya-sūtra* on the grounds that "one should perform what has already been done, not what is beneficial [if it violates the rule]"—the matter stands. However, this is a separate point: a person who employs even correct words incurs sin through the transgression of the *Dharma-śāstra*, just like one who reviles the gods or Brahmins.

As for the Vārttika intended to refute the second purpose—namely, "imitation [is valid] in the case of those who are learned, unlearned, or not prohibited"—its meaning is as follows: the imitation of a *śiṣṭa* (learned/standard) word is itself standard (*sādhu*). And that which is both unlearned (*aśiṣṭa*) and not prohibited (*apratiṣiddha*)—that is, forms such as *ṭi*, *ghu*, and *bha* which fall outside the category of standard and non-standard—their imitation is likewise of the same nature; thus, by implication, the imitation of a non-standard word is also indeed non-standard.

However, this [second purpose] has indeed been refuted in the Bhāṣya, because there is no basis for declaring as incorrect those forms such as *helayo helayaḥ* which have been accepted by the learned (*śiṣṭa*). It is not the case that something is so [incorrect] merely by being an ungrammatical word (*apaśabda*) that lacks denotative power; otherwise, the word *apaśabda* itself would incur the status of being incorrect. Nor can correctness be extended [to them] by the rule *prakṛtitadanukaraṇam* (Pāṇini 1.4.62), since what is not established by the grammatical system cannot be the subject of an extension (*atideśa*). This is the general direction [of the argument]. Therefore, although the second purpose was refuted by the author of the Vārttika, it remains established according to the view of the Bhāṣya.

As for the Vārttika intended to refute the third purpose—which states, "Because that which is modified in one part is not different [from the original], [operations such as] elision (*pluti*) and so forth [apply]"—its meaning is as follows: since it will be stated later that "there is a specific counter-exception regarding the *nuṭ* augment, vowel substitution (*lādeśa*), and modification (*vināma*)," once the letter *r*, which is a single part of the vowel *ṛ*, is changed to *l*, the operations pertaining to vowels (*ackārya*) are established by the maxim of "that which is modified in one part" (*ekadeśavikṛtanyāya*). Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence (*pratiṣedha*) of the prohibition "not after *anṛt*" (Pāṇini 8.2.64), because of the alternative formulation (*nyāsa*) "after *arvat*" (8.2.72). For by the maxim of "that which is modified in one part," the status of possessing the letter *r* does not necessarily follow.

For even in the world, an action conditioned by having a tail does not occur for one whose tail has been cut off. Nor does it follow that there would be an undesired prohibition of prolation (*pluta*) for a long *ṛ*-vowel such as in *hotṛkārādeḥ* because of the rule *aravataḥ*, since the established formulation (*nyāsa*) is *ra-hrasvasya ravato na*. However, if this were the case, resorting to a fragmentation of the sūtra (*sūtrabhaṅga*) in order to reject the single *lṛ*-vowel would result in the exact opposite of parsimony (i.e., excessive complexity). Regarding this, the author of the Bhāṣya says: "This is like pulling a small vine from a great bamboo stalk."

*Laṭvā* refers to a specific kind of bird or a specific kind of fruit. [It is derived] from the root *laṭ* in the sense of "longing" (*laulye*) belonging to the *bhvādi* class; the suffix *kvan* is applied according to *Pāṇini* 3.2.157 (*aśū-pruṣi-laṭi-kaṇi-khaṭi-viśibhyaḥ kvan*). There is no augment *iṭ* due to *Pāṇini* 7.2.8 (*neḍ vaśi kṛti*).
According to the *Viśva-kośa*: "The word *laṭvā* may denote a species of crane (*karañja*), a defective fruit, or a particular bird."

Now, one might argue: "Let the rule *kṛpo ro laḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.18) precede *a a* (Pāṇini 8.4.68). In this way, since the substitution of *l* for *r* would be considered non-established (*asiddha*), cases such as *pluti* will be correctly accounted for. This is not so. For if that were the case, the rule *gro yaṅi* (Pāṇini 8.2.20) would also have to be moved [to that position], and consequently, because the substitution of *l* would be non-established, the long vowel required by *hali ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.77) would apply in the form *nijegilyate*.

If it is argued: "But surely, since the *Bahvṛca-prātiśākhya* states, 'The sounds ṛ and ḷ, as well as the sixth sibilant [ṣ], are jihvāmūlīyas' (*Ṛk-prātiśākhya* 1.8), and because of this statement regarding the similarity of place of articulation (*sthāna*) for the sounds ṛ and ḷ, the matter can be resolved by the *grahaṇaka-śāstra* itself; therefore, the instruction of the sound ḷ should remain," we say: No. While the addition of the rule for the homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) of ṛ and ḷ may be rejected according to the aforementioned method, the instruction of the sound ḷ must indeed be maintained in order to establish the pluta-vowel in *klṛptaśikha*, as it serves to indicate that homogeneity is not universal. This is the direction of the argument.

EOṄ | EAUC (MāṇSū 3.4). Although among the Chāndogas the Sātyamugri-Rāṇāyanīyas study [the vowels] as half-e and half-o—specifically in "sujāte eaśvasūnṛte" and "adhvaryo o adribhiḥ sutam"—and their own Prātiśākhya prescribes a half-e and a half-o for a non-y vowel situated within a quarter-verse (pāda), nevertheless, due to the very designation of that Prātiśākhya, they are not included in this treatise which is common to all recensions; this is also because of an indicative mark (jñāpaka).

For if the inclusion of the eighteen vowels by means of *eṅ* were intended in the same way as they are included by *a* and the others, then for the sake of brevity (*lāghava*), he would have taught *eṅ* as consisting of only one mora each, just like *a* and the others. Nor should it be argued that in the rule "adeṅ guṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.1.2), because of the addition of the marker *t* (*taparatva*), the designation of *guṇa* would apply only to those [sounds] having exactly one mora; for in that case, since the long vowels are indicated by their own forms as *e* and *o*, they do not include their homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*) due to being non-*aṇ* sounds, and even so, there would still be the advantage of half-a-mora (*ardhamātrā*) brevity.

For in your view, regarding the instruction of phonemes (*varṇopadeśa*), there are four morae (*mātrā*) for the two long vowels *e* and *o*; however, regarding the technical designation as *guṇa*, there are two morae in the instruction of phonemes and four in the designation as *guṇa*. Thus, when combined, there are exactly six morae. Therefore, by the force of the mention of "two morae," it is determined that [the view] of one mora for each is not intended.

If it is argued that, in this case, Pāṇini’s rule *eca igghrasvādeśe* (Pāṇini 1.1.48) would be redundant—since that rule is indeed intended to exclude the half-*ai* and half-*au* sounds which would otherwise be obtained by the *sthānentaratama* paribhāṣā (the maxim of the nearest substitute)—we reply: no, for that rule was formulated to preclude the optional substitution of *a* that would otherwise result.

For the first part of these [diphthongs] resembles the vowel *a*, while the latter part resembles the vowels *i* and *u*. In that case, since there is no short vowel (*hrasva*) that is most similar to both parts, the vowel *a* would occur by turn, as would the vowels *i* and *u*. Therefore, the sūtra is commenced so that the vowel *a* never occurs [in place of the diphthongs]. In reality, however, this sūtra will be rejected (*pratyākhyāsyate*). And thus the author of the Vārttika will say regarding that: "It is established because *eṅ* has the same place of articulation (*saṃsthāna*); and because *ai* and *au* have a greater degree of the subsequent [element]."

The meaning of this is as follows: by the rule of "prohibition of the subsequent" (*paravipratiṣedha*) regarding the term *śabda*, it is established that for the vowels *e* and *o*, the corresponding closest sounds (*antaratama*) are indeed the *i* and *u* vowels. Alternatively, the meaning is that it is established according to the view that the vowel *e* is purely palatal (*śuddhatālavya*) and the vowel *o* is purely labial (*śuddhauṣṭhya*). Thus, the *Prātiśākhya* of the Bahvṛcas states: "The vowels *e* and *ai* and the consonants of the *ca*-group are palatal; the vowels *o* and *au*, the letter *ya*, and the letter *śa* [are labial]" (*Ṛk-prātiśākhya* 1.9), and also: "The remaining [vowels] are to be produced from the lips" (*Ṛk-prātiśākhya* 1.9).

The remaining collection of phonemes (*varṇarāśi*) from those previously mentioned is to be excluded by means of the two [terms] *oṣṭhya*. The meaning of the sūtra is that the *u*-vowels, the labial class (*pavarga*), *o*, *au*, and the *upadhmānīya* are labial (*oṣṭhya*). This has been explained by the author of the commentary on the *Prātiśākhya*. However, in its commentary (*bhāṣya*), the reading is "the remainder is to be excluded by the labials" (*seṣaoṣṭyopavādya*). In that context, regarding the word *apavādya*, this sūtra is intended for the purpose that will be stated in the subsequent sūtra.

Thus, two solutions have been established for the vowels *eṅ*: "because of the prohibition of the term 'śabda'," or "because of the similarity of their places of articulation according to different opinions. Although this [second solution] applies equally to the diphthongs (*ai* and *au*) as well, he states that there is yet another solution for them: "and of *aic*" (*aicoca*). The word "and" (*ca*) should be understood as displaced in order, following the reason.

The meaning is that according to the view that "the vowel *a* has half a mora (*ardhamātrā*), while the vowels *i* and *u* have one and a half moras (*adyardhamātrā*)", the phonemes *ikāra* and *ukāra* will still occur because they are designated by their predominant [duration], just as in the case of "Mallagrāma" and similar names. Furthermore, it will be explained in the eighth [chapter] that there is also a view of equal division; however, in that case, the two aforementioned solutions are the only recourse.

Even though the first explanation, which prioritizes the prohibition of the subsequent (*para-vipratiṣedha*), is maintained in the *Vivaraṇa*, nevertheless, if that were accepted, it would contradict the *Vārttika* and the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *vipratiṣedhe paraṃ kāryam* (Pāṇini 1.4.2), beginning with the statement: "Or there might be non-comprehension for both. For in the case of the rule *go-striyoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.48), the shortening (*hrasva*) prescribed for the word *go* does not find its scope elsewhere such that it would result in non-comprehension.

If it is argued that, since a distinction between characteristics (*lakṣaṇabheda*) would apply to each respective object of observation (*pratilakṣya*), there should be a restriction (*niyama*) stating that [the subsequent operation] alone takes effect, we say: no. For if this were so, regarding the rule *acaḥ parasmin* (Pāṇini 1.1.57), it would follow:
"The substitution of a semivowel (*parayaṇādeśa*) is permanent; subsequently, this [rule of] establishment [of order applies].
Simultaneous occurrence is impossible; [the desired result] is accomplished by means of the external factor (*bahiraṅga*)."

Thus, the context of the Bhāṣya beginning with these words would be contradicted. For, by the force of that [Bhāṣya], it is understood that the scope of the rule on conflict (*vipratiṣedha-sūtra*) is precisely the sequence of priority and posteriority between two rules of definition, whereas the principle "that which is *antaraṅga* is stronger" applies to other cases. We shall clarify this very point in that same place.

The second explanation is also weak, as it generally disregards what is stated in the *Prātiśākhya*, much like the cases of *ardha-ekāra* and so forth. Now, if one argues that—just as the four-moraic vowel favored by the *Chāndogas* is accepted here despite the rule regarding the *tapara* marker serving to exclude it—one might likewise accept the *vārttika* stating "there is the designation of homogeneous (*savarṇa*) for *ṛ* and *ḷ*" according to the method set forth in the *ṛ-lṛ-ka-sūtra*.

If, on the other hand, the commencement of that *vārttika* is based on following another *Śikṣā*, then the commencement of the sūtra *e-cai-c* (Pāṇini 1.1.48) should be treated in exactly the same way; such is the direction of the argument.

Therefore, it is established that by the force of the rule *eca ikaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.48), the half-*ai* and half-*au* sounds would not be obtained. Now, one might ask: "Even if those two were included here despite being mentioned in the *Prātiśākhya*, what undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭa*) would arise such that you must so strenuously demonstrate their exclusion? The answer is: No. Because in the prescription of short vowels for the diphthongs (*ec*), those two [half-sounds] alone would follow by virtue of being the most similar (*antaratama*). Furthermore, the rule *eca ikaḥ* has already been rejected [by the author of the *Mahābhāṣya*]. Even if this rule were accepted for the sake of this very point, the fault would simply be the excessive complexity (*gaurava*) of the formulation.

It might be argued: "We shall designate [the vowels] with the *tapara* markers by means of the sequence beginning with *et ot ṅ*. Thus, when only those with *tapara* markers are presented by the word *ac* in the rule concerning the duration of *ū* (*ūkāla*), the half-measure *e* or *o* would not receive the designation of 'short' (*hrasva*) because its duration is not included; consequently, it would not even be subject to the rules prescribing short vowels. This is not so, for then even those [vowels] consisting of three morae (*trimātra*) would result in not being *ac*.

Furthermore, in the case of *go 3 trātaḥ*, the doubling (*dvitva*) of the letter *t*—which is prescribed by Pāṇini’s sūtra *anaci ca* (8.4.48) for a consonant following a vowel—would not occur. In *pratyaṅṅautikāyanaḥ* and *udaṅṅaupagavaḥ*, the augment *ṅamuṭ* would not apply. Moreover, because the designation *pluta* (protracted vowel) would be absent, the rule governing *pluta* vowels would not take effect. Nor can it be argued that this [the application of the rules] is established by the force of rules such as *omabhyādāne* (8.2.87), since those rules would already have served their purpose through the prescription of the vowel *u*. This is the general direction of the argument.

The author of the Vārttika states this: "If there is the teaching of *tapara* [markers] for the *saṃdhyakṣaras*, then there is the pronunciation with a *tapara* marker, the rule for *pluti* and so forth, and the designation of *pluta*. And when *ecaḥ* [the diphthongs] are not followed by a *tapara* marker, there is the mention of 'long' (*dīrgha*) in the rule for the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) of *ig* for a short vowel. The meaning of this is as follows: because they consist of parts similar to two merging phonemes, a syllable that is being joined together is called a *saṃdhyakṣara*; this is an etymological designation for the *ec* vowels established by the ancient teachers. It is said to be the purpose [of the rule] through the instrumental derivation: "that by which a *tapara* is taught."

And so, if there is a purpose for pronouncing these vowels with the *tapara* marker (the letter ṛ), then that *tapara* pronunciation must indeed be made. Even when the vowel is *pluta* (protracted), rules concerning *aj*—such as doubling (*dvitva*), the suffix *ṅam*, and so forth—would not otherwise be established. In that case, the suffix *ṅam* and the rest would apply only to the *pluta* itself, while doubling would apply to what follows it. The word "and so forth" (*ādi*) is used to indicate this accumulation of effects. The meaning is that the desired grammatical operation is accomplished both in the *pluta* vowel and in the subsequent phonemes. This is stated as a concessive argument (*abhyupetyavāda*).

In reality, however, because [the vowel] lacks duration (*anactvāt*), the designation *pluta* itself is not established. Therefore, it has been stated in three Vārttikas that the mention of the rule as *tapara* (followed by *t*) is defective. According to the reading of the sūtra as it stands, one would have to formulate the rule as *āta ataparaḥ* in order to exclude [the application of the rule to] the half-īkāra and so forth; such is the meaning. But in fact, it has just been demonstrated that the rule need not be formulated by either [of these two methods]. Consequently, this objection is not worthy of being raised, as it applies equally to both positions.

It might be argued as follows: in the absence of the *tapara* designation (*t* following the vowel), in cases such as *gaṅgodakam* and *rameśaḥ*, substitutes of three or four morae (*mātrās*) would indeed replace [bases] of three or four morae, due to the principle of closest proximity (*āntaratamya*).

Nor should it be said that there is no substitution of three-moraic and other vowels because of the analysis (*yogavibhāga*) of the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.101)—interpreting it within the governing context (*adhikāra*) of *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.84) to mean "that which is prescribed therein becomes long"—for this would lead to errors in forms such as *paśum*, *viddham*, and *pacanti*.

Now, one might object: "Let the rule simply be *ami*. From the rule *prathamayoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.102), the term *pūrvasavarṇa* is understood to carry over, as is *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.84). Since the desired result is thus established, the inclusion of the word *pūrva* [in the rule *ami pūrvaḥ*] is for the purpose that it should be exactly as the preceding sound was, and not a long vowel (*dīrgha*). By this, forms such as *paśum* are established. Furthermore, in the rule *samprasāraṇācca* (Pāṇini 6.1.108), that same word *pūrva* is understood to carry over."

Either by the force of the commencement of the rule *halo* (Pāṇini 6.4.2), or by the fact that a long vowel is not prescribed by the rule *saṃprasāraṇācca* (Pāṇini 6.1.108), the form *viddham* is also established. Furthermore, although the word *paraḥ* (subsequent) would suffice for the rule *ato guṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.97), the inclusion of the term *rūpa* (form) implies that the substitute must be of the same nature as what follows; it cannot be of a different character. By this, the form *pacanti* is also established.

If it is argued that, therefore, by means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule), the position that "a long vowel substitution occurs" is indeed faultless—no; for if that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasanga*) of failure to establish forms such as *kṛṣṇarddhiḥ* and *tavalkāraḥ*. For in these cases, because of the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*), the vowel *a* [of the preceding rule] does not apply; and because of the lack of immediate proximity (*anāntarya*), the vowels *e* and *o* do not apply. Therefore, the *yogavibhāga* stating "therefore, long" is indeed defective. Consequently, in cases such as *gaṅgodakam* and *rameśaḥ*, the occurrence of three or four morae (*mātra*) remains unavoidable.

Nor should it be said that the *pluta* vowel is not recorded as being [subject to] the object [of the rule], for it will be stated later that this applies only when there is the possibility of both *pluta* and non-*pluta*. If it is asked, "Even so, how does it become four-mora (*caturmātra*)? For that is not established in either common usage (*loka*) or the Veda," the answer is: no, because it is established in the *Chāndogya*. In fact, however, it is established even in common usage; thus the author of the *Bhāṣya* will say under the sūtra *plutāvaica idutau* (Pāṇini 8.2.106): "A four-mora *pluta* is indeed desired."

To this it is replied: because of the mention of the *tapara* (the vowel with the *p* marker) in the definitions of both *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, the aforementioned fault does not arise. This very point was stated by the author of the Vārttika: "In the case of a single substitute (*ekādeśa*), there must be the mention of 'long' (*dīrgha*). The intention is that only that [single substitute] is the thing to be named (*saṃjñin*). However, this Vārttika is neither intended to prescribe the necessity of making another mention of "long," nor is it intended as a splitting of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), according to the reasoning already stated.

It might be argued: "Even though *tapara* is prescribed in the *saṃjñā-sūtra*, how can *eṅ* and *aic* denote their own duration? If one were to say, "Because in the rule *sahivahorot* (Pāṇini 6.3.112), the mention of the phoneme (*varṇagrahaṇa*) indicates that even a genitive compound (*pañcamīsamāsa*) is possible [meaning 'that which follows *ta*']"—even so, let it be granted that by the words *eṅ* and *aic* followed by *ta*, only the long vowels (*dīrgha*) are presented; nevertheless, once these long vowels are presented, it is impossible to prevent them from including all their homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*). For these [homogeneous vowels] are not themselves followed by *ta*, since they have not been uttered.

The status of being a *grāhaka* (a term that causes another to be included) certainly exists even for those [sounds] not explicitly uttered, provided they are present through *pratyāhāras* (comprehensive terms), as evidenced by the rule *dīrghāj-jasi ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.105). This is also supported by such references as *lvādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.44) and *pvādīnām* (Pāṇini 7.3.80). Consequently, it will be explained later that forms such as *samūṣu* are established through the substitution of *ṣaṭtvādi* (the status of being *ṣaṣ*, etc.).

If it is argued that the phrase "but [the rule] 'tātparaḥ' [applies] to that duration" would apply only when [the sounds] are actually uttered, that is true; however, just as it is accepted that in the rule *ṅamo hrasvāt* (Pāṇini 8.3.32), the *ṭit*-ness attached to the pratyāhāra *ṅamuṭ* is useless for the technical name (*saṃjñā*) itself, yet by its force (*sāmarthya*), it benefits the named items (*saṃjñin*) such as *ṅ* and the rest, so too here, although being "followed by *t*" is of no use for the technical name, it—by its force—effects the determination of the duration for the named items which are brought to mind by that [name]. Thus, there is no fault whatsoever.

Alternatively, the phrase "not a technical term" (*aśabda-saṃjñā*) is understood to carry over into the rule *aṇuditsavarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.69), as is clear from the *Bhāṣya* on *ūkālo’j* (Pāṇini 1.2.27). We shall establish this point in that very place. Consequently, even in the rules prescribing the technical terms *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, there is no inclusion of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇa-grahaṇa*). The addition of the marker *t* (*taparakaraṇa*), however, is for the sake of clarity, just as in the case of *īdūded dvivacanaṃ pragṛhyam* (Pāṇini 1.1.11). Otherwise, there would arise doubts such as whether only *e* and *ai* are specified here, or whether *ā* is also included, and so forth. In that regard, one would have to undergo the labor of following indicators (*jñāpaka*) such as *mālādīnām* (Pāṇini 6.2.58); such is the direction of the argument.

Furthermore, this very position is more logical. For in the first position, since the designation *vṛddhi* applies to the long vowel *ā*, it is not an *aṇ* (short *a*) and thus does not include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*). Consequently, the purpose of the *tapara* marker (the *ṛ* in *ṛt*) must be admitted to serve both functions. Since its utility has already been exhausted in the preceding case, how could it assist the two designata (*saṃjñin*) *e* and *o*? Therefore, in that context, there would certainly be inclusion of the homogeneous vowels. Even in this position, the Vārttika "the mention of 'long' in the rule for *ekādeśa*" is to be explained exactly as before, on the grounds that only the long vowel is the designatum.

It might be argued: "Even in the first position, since that [suffix] is also a grasper of the time of the subsequent element, it would apply only in cases such as *yavaḥ* and *stavaḥ* according to Pāṇini’s sūtra 3.3.57 (*ṛdorap*), but not in cases such as *lavaḥ* and *pavaḥ*. To this, the Bhāṣya states: "This is not the letter *t*; rather, for the sake of avoiding ambiguity or for the ease of pronunciation, this is the letter *d*."

But would this Bhāṣya not contradict the Bhāṣya on *titsvaritam* (Pāṇini 6.1.185), which is intended to reject the Vārttika *tit-pratyayagrahaṇam* (Kātyāyana)? For in that [latter] context, it is stated: "The mention of the suffix (*pratyaya*) must be made in the case of *ti*."

Let it not be that, having raised the objection against *diva ut* (Pāṇini 6.1.131) in the form "dyubhir aktubhiḥ," and having resolved it by resorting to the view that [the *u*] is a *dittava*, one might then suspect that even the *u* being taught (*bhāvyamāna*) would include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇagrāhakatā*), just as in the case of *adaso'serdād* (Pāṇini 8.2.80). Anticipating this, it was explained in the *tapara-sūtra* that because the letter *d* there is also designated as a *cartva* (a substitute for *c*), the *u* followed by *d* (*dapara*) likewise includes those of the same duration. And thus, in rules such as *ur ṛt* (Pāṇini 7.4.7), it is precisely due to being followed by *d* (*daparatva*) that [the substitution applies].

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the *svarita* accent. Furthermore, this very use of the letter *da* as a designation indicates that even the vowel *u* when being taught (*bhāvyamāna*) includes its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇagrāhaka*); thus it is established. However, in this case, because of the use of the letter *da* in the rule *ṛdoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.57), the desired result is obtained even for long vowels in forms such as *lāvaḥ* and *pāvaḥ*.

On this point, the ancients maintain that the author of the Bhāṣya intends here either the *tha* sound in place of *tha*, or the *da* sound in place of *dha*; therefore, there is no contradiction between what precedes and what follows. The straightforward scholars, however, say that according to the view of the Vārttika, this [statement] exists in the Bhāṣya, and thus there is no contradiction. In reality, however, the letter *da* is not specified in the rule *taparas tatkālasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.70), because there would be no purpose for doing so.

In rules such as *div-aut* (Pāṇini 6.1.131) and *ṛta-aut* (Pāṇini 6.1.111), however, the desired result is achieved precisely because of the inclusion of the marker *t* (*taparatva*). If it is objected that this would lead to the unintended application of *titsvaritam* (Pāṇini 6.1.185), we reply: no; for that objection is resolved by the metarule (*paribhāṣā*) stating, "Between a suffix and a non-suffix, the suffix is to be understood" (*pratyayāpratyayayoḥ pratyayasya grahaṇam*).

As for what Haradatta stated regarding the rule *titsvaritam* (Pāṇini 6.1.185)—namely, "Since this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is not seen here in either the Bhāṣya or the Vārttika, this great effort has been undertaken by us"—to that it must be said: the effort consisting of the view that the letter *da* is a substitute for the letter *tha* or a substitute for the letter *dha* was indeed already stated by the ancient masters while discussing the rule *eṅi pararūpam* (Pāṇini 6.1.94); this is clear from Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on that very passage.

If you argue, "Is it not the case that for this very reason we say [the word *aṅga*] is 'respected' (*ādṛta*) by us, but not 'elevated' (*unnīta*)?"—True, it is respected; nevertheless, the reason [you provide], "because no such technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is seen," is unestablished (*asiddha*), since this very rule is introduced by the author of the Bhāṣya in his own words (*kaṇṭharaveṇaiva*) in order to reject the sūtra "aṅgasya" (Pāṇini 6.4.1).

If it is argued that, since it is established that a rule (*sūtra*) must be formulated to achieve forms such as *nirutaṃ* and *durutaṃ*, this *paribhāṣā* is redundant—nevertheless, the interpretive effort to explain it as meaning "the letter *d* is the substitute for the letters *th* and *dh*" is unworthy of acceptance, both because it is fruitless and because it contradicts the natural intent of the original text. This is because, in rules such as *diva ut* (Pāṇini 6.1.131), there is no possibility at all for the application of *titsvaritam* (Pāṇini 6.1.185); thus, the inclusion of the letter *d* (*dakārapraśleṣa*) and so forth lacks any foundation.

For instance, what has come of the letter *u*—the bearer of the designation (*saṃjñin*)—in the case of this [designation] *ud*? In reality, even the designation ends in *t*, not in *t*. For the rule is formulated as "taparaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.1.70), not as "tit". If the designation were like its bearer and also ended in *t*, then [the substitution of *ais* for *bhisa*] would apply only in cases such as *bhavadbhiḥ* by the rule "ato bhisa ais" (Pāṇini 7.1.9), but not in cases such as *vṛkṣaiḥ*.

Furthermore, the sūtra *taparaḥ tatkālasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.70) would be entirely redundant, as its purpose is already served by *sarvaṃ rūpaṃ śabdasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.68). Nor can a characteristic applied to a technical name (*saṃjñā*)—as in the case of the augment *ṅmuṭ*—be understood as applying to the named object (*saṃjñin*), because here there is no such functional necessity (*sāmarthya*). Consequently, the entire passage from the Bhāṣya and Vārttika on the sūtra *titsvaritam* (Pāṇini 6.1.185) is merely a concessionary argument (*abhyupetyavāda*).

In the rule *stāghvoricca* (Pāṇini 1.2.17), the passage beginning with "of what is the letter *t* [in *at*] the status of being *it*? (*icca kasya takārettvam*) is to be understood in exactly the same way. Therefore, this is not the letter *t*, but rather the letter *d*; thus, the passage in the Bhāṣya on this point is correct exactly as it stands. Discerning scholars should take note that this very passage implies that the subsequent passages are of the nature of *abhyupetyavāda* (provisional arguments). By this, the absence of the status of being followed by *t* (*taparatva*) for the prescribed element in rules such as *aut* (Pāṇini 7.3.118) and *iṭo't* (Pāṇini 3.4.146) is also explained. As for the status of being *t* (*tittva*), however, it is far removed; such is the direction.

In this system, phonemes such as *a* and so forth are held to possess constituent parts (*sāṃśa*). As it is said: "Of that [vowel], the first half-mora is acute" (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.2.32), and "The [sounds] *i* and *u* belong to the latter half of the preceding [vowel]. The author of the Vārttika also says: "And because the greater part of *ai* and *au* belongs to the latter [element]."

In that regard, there are certain portions similar to independent phonemes (*varṇa*): for instance, in [the diphthongs] *ā* and so forth, there are two parts similar to the vowel *a*; in *ai* and *au*, the former part is like the vowel *a* and the latter part is like the vowels *i* and *u* respectively; in the vowel *ṛ*, there is a half-mora (*ardhamātrā*) on both sides belonging to the vowel portion (*ajbhakti*), with a middle half-mora portion similar to the letter *r*; and in the vowel *ḷ* as well, there is a vowel portion on both sides, with a middle portion similar to an independent *l*.

In that context, an operation prescribed by the non-mention of specific individual phonemes does not apply to parts that resemble them; for these [parts] are similar to those [phonemes], but are not those very [phonemes] themselves, because they are pervaded by a different genus (*jāti*), like a man-lion (*narasiṃha*). And the mention of *go* and *nau* here is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of this.

For if even the parts were to trigger grammatical operations prescribed for independent words, then in the two rules *godvyaco’saṃkhyāparimāṇāśvāderyat* (Pāṇini 5.2.39) and *naudvyacaṣṭhan* (Pāṇini 4.4.7), the word *go* and the word *nau* would not have been mentioned, since their purpose would already be served by the mention of the term *dvyac* (containing two vowels). Consequently, in examples such as *agne indra* and *vāyo udakam*, the long vowel substitution (*savarṇadīrgha*) would not occur.

Nor should it be argued that this [substitution] is sublated by Pāṇini’s sūtra *eco 'yavāyāvaḥ* (6.1.78); for the substitutions *ay*, etc., being sublaters of *yaṇ* alone—either by the maxim *yena nāprāpte* or by the maxim of intermediate sublation (*madhyepavāda*)—are already fulfilled in cases such as *agra āyāhi*. However, in cases such as *agne indram*, they would be sublated by the subsequent long vowel (*dīrgha*), because even though the long vowel is internal (*antaraṅga*), it depends only on its constituent parts.

Similarly, in *agna eti*, the rule *eṅaḥ padāntāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.109) does not apply; in *ālūya* and *pramāya*, the substitution of *tuṅ* does not occur; in *mālābhiḥ*, the substitution of *ais* does not occur; in *yātā* and similar forms, the elision (*lopa*) of *at* does not occur; and in *vācā tarati* and *vāco nimittam*, the suffixes *ṭhan* and *ṭhañ* characterized by two syllables (*dvyañ-lakṣaṇau*) do not occur—this is the general direction [of the analysis].

However, a counter-argument must be provided regarding the rules for *nuṭ*, substitutes (*lādeśa*), and euphonic changes (*vināma*). To explain: the mention of "having two consonants" (*dvihal*) should be removed, and the rule should instead be formulated as "after that [root], *nuṭ*. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of *nuṭ* occurring in forms like *āṭatuḥ*—as it would in *ānṛdhatuḥ*—because the rule *aśnoteśca* (Pāṇini 7.4.72) serves as a restrictive rule (*niyama*). This restriction is general in scope: if *nuṭ* occurs after a root with the vowel *a* as its penultimate, it occurs only after the root *aś*, and not after roots such as *aṭ*. If, on the other hand, the intention were merely to exclude the root *aś*, the author would have simply said "not after *aś*" (*nāśnaḥ*).

In the word "rolaḥ," the genus (jāti) common to both independent and non-independent [sounds] is intended to be expressed in both the subject and the predicate. Since it is impossible to extract the single substitute as a separate entity, it follows that, by means of that [genus], the substitution of *lṛ* for *ṛ* is the actual result. This designation does not refer to a genus residing in independent phonemes alone, but rather to one that is common to both parts and the whole.

The evidence for this consists of the following grammatical indications: *luṭi ca klṛpaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.93), *tāsi ca klṛpaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.60), and *ṛdupadhāccāklṛpicṛteḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.110). Alternatively, the analysis is as follows: the division is *kṛpa-u-ra-la*. Here, *kṛpa* is a word with its genitive case-ending elided (*lupta-ṣaṣṭhī*). This should be construed either through *tantra* (a single term serving multiple functions) or through repetition (*āvṛtti*). Thus: "the *la* [substitutes] for that *ra* which belongs to *kṛp*" and "the *la* [substitutes] for that *ra* which is a constituent part of the *ṛ* of *kṛp*," meaning a *ra* similar to the *ṛ*. And for that [similar *ra*], there is the substitution of *la*.

Thus, the statement "it is fashioned" (*kalīklṛpyate*) and so forth is established. From the Bhāṣya itself, which is intent on demonstrating such word-divisions, it is determined that the reading of the rule *kṛpo ro laḥ* is erroneous. In this way, the rules for the insertion of the augment *nuṭ* and the substitution of *la* have been resolved.

*Vināma* is *nati*; its definition is stated in the *Prātiśākhya*: "Nati is the state of becoming a dental or a retroflex" (*Ṛk-prātiśākhya* 5.57). In the present context, however, *nati* refers to the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*. Regarding this, the following counter-argument is offered: one should perform a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule) in the sūtra *chandasyṛdavagrahāt* (*Pāṇini* 8.4.26), as follows: first, *ṛtaḥ*; [this means] after an *ṛ*, the *n* that follows shall become *ṇ*, as in *pitṛyāṇam* and *dyumat*, etc. If it is argued: "Even so, because of the inclusion of the *tapara* marker (*ṛt*), the substitution of *ṇ* would not occur in cases such as *pitṝṇām*," [the response is:]...

If that is so, then here too, in the rule for *ṇatva*, the genus (*jāti*) common to both the letter *r* and its similar portion—as in the rule *raṣābhyām*—is indicated, based on the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) found in the reading of the word *tṛpnoti* among the *kṣubhnādi* group. Nor is there an intervention by a subsequent vowel-element (*ajbhakti*), because the rule is divided as *vyavāye 'pi*, whereby *ṇatva* is prescribed generally even when there is an intervention. Furthermore, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *kṛtena*, due to the restrictive rule (*niyama*) *aṭkupvāṅnumbhiḥ*.

The meaning of the restrictive rule (*niyama-sūtra*) is that if [the substitution of *ṇ*] occurs when there is an intervention by letters belonging to the *akṣarasamāmnāya* or by those indicated by them, then it occurs only by these; or else, by the inclusion of the word *tṛpnoti* and by the indicative mention (*nirdeśa*) in rules such as "of *hotṛ*, *potṛ*, and *praśāstṛ*" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 6.4.11), it is signaled (*jñāpyate*) with greater parsimony (*lāghavāt*) that the substitution of *ṇ* occurs for a letter following an *ṛ*-vowel. For in this way, even the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) stating "even when there is an intervention" (*vyavāye’pi*) need not be made.

In the Bhāṣya, however, the position that "the parts of letters are not grasped by the mention of the letters" is also supported; but because it would require many counter-arguments and out of fear of prolixity, it is not elaborated upon here.

Now, if parts of a phoneme (*varṇaikadeśa*) are not grasped by the term "phoneme" (*varṇagrahaṇa*), then in cases such as *kukkuṭaḥ*, *pippalī*, and *pittam*, the technical designation "consonant cluster" (*saṃyoga*) would not apply; for the entire duration of one mora (*mātrākāla*)—namely, the *kk* in *kṛt*—consists of a single consonant (*ekahal*), and its two constituent parts are not grasped by the term "consonant" (*halgrahaṇa*). If it is asked, "But since an indivisible [unit] is not taught [as such], how can it be a consonant?", then let that [designation] also not exist.

But how can the individual phonemes (*avayava*) possess the status of a consonant (*hal*)? [Objection: In cases such as *saṃyyantā*, *saṃvatsaraḥ*, and *yaṃ lokam*, even single phonemes will have the status of a consonant because they are included by those taught in the *aṇ* [pratyāhāra]. However, the status of a consonant would certainly not belong to the two constituent parts of that [consonant cluster]. Consequently, in the absence of the designation "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), there would be no heaviness (*gurutva*) for the preceding [vowel], and thus the protracted vowel (*pluta*) would not occur. To this, they say: A consonant has a duration of exactly half a mora (*mātrā*). However, due to rapid pronunciation, there arises the illusion of unity between two [consonants] whose forms are identical.

And this must necessarily be accepted during the state of linguistic analysis (*prakriyā-daśā*) on account of the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa-samācāra*). However, in the state of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-daśā*):
"In a word (*pada*), phonemes (*varṇa*) do not exist; nor do parts (*avayava*) exist in phonemes.
There is no absolute distinction whatsoever between words and a sentence (*vākya*)."
According to the method stated in the *Vākyapadīya*, for those who establish the *sphoṭa* as the final doctrine, what occasion is there for this prima facie objection?

In the *Māheśvara-sūtras* (*hayavaraṭ*, MāSū 5), this letter *ha* is taught twice. If it were taught only later [in *haśiṭ*], it would not be included in the rules concerning *aṭ*, *kṣa*, *ś*, and *ṇ*. Consequently, in the case of *arheṇa*, the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*]—which applies even when there is an intervening *aṭ*—would not occur. Furthermore, in the form *mahān hi*, [if *ha* were not present here], the form *mahām̐hi* would not result.

For here, by the rule *dīrghād aṭi samānapāde* (Pāṇini 8.3.9), there is *ru*; by *āto 'ṭi nityam* (Pāṇini 8.3.3), there is the nasalization (*anunāsika*); by *bho bhago agho apūrvasya* (Pāṇini 7.3.17), there is *yatva*; and by *hali sarveṣām* (Pāṇini 7.3.22), there is the elision of *ya*. It will be stated that even in that case, the term *aśi* is understood as a governing word (*anuvartate*). In the example *brāhmaṇo hasati*, the substitution of *utva* [for *o*] by *haśi ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.114) would not occur.

Likewise, in forms such as *lilihadhve* and *lilidhve*, the optional substitution of the retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) [ḍha] by the rule *vibhāṣeṭaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.79) would not occur; for in that rule, the word *iṇaḥ* is understood from the preceding sūtra *iṇaḥ ṣīdhvam* (Pāṇini 7.3.78). Thus, it is established that the purpose of the first instruction [of the letter ṣ] is its inclusion within these four categories: after *aṭ*, after *aś*, after *haś*, and after *iṇ*.

If, however, [the *a*] were not taught as being elsewhere [in the *Śivasūtra*], it would not be included in the rules concerning *val*, *jhal*, and *śal*. Consequently, in forms such as *rudihi* and *svapahi*, the augment *iṭ*—which is conditioned by the status of being preceded by a *val* letter according to Pāṇini 7.2.76 (*rudādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke*)—would not occur. Furthermore, in forms such as *snihitvā* and *snehitvā* from the root *ṣṇiha* (meaning "affection")—and likewise *sisnihiṣati* and *sisnohiṣati*—the status of being a *kit* suffix, which applies according to Pāṇini 1.2.26 (*ralovyupadhāt*), would not occur.

In the forms *adāgdhām* and *adāgdham*, because the substitution of *gh* for *dh* would be considered asiddha (unestablished), the *dh* would not be followed by a *jhala* vowel; consequently, the rule *jhalo jhali* (Pāṇini 8.2.26) would not apply. Furthermore, in the forms *adhukṣat* and *alikṣat*, the suffix *kso* would not occur according to the rule *śala igupadādaniṭaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.45).
Therefore, it is established that there is a specific purpose for the first presentation of the four pratyāhāras and the second presentation of the other four.

It might be argued as follows: the *ya*-operations would apply to the letter *r*. For instance, in the cases of *madrahadaḥ* and *bhadrahadaḥ*, the doubling (*dvitva*) prescribed by the rule *aco rahābhyāṃ dve* (Pāṇini 8.4.46)—which applies to a *ya* following an *ac* after an *r* or *h*—would apply to the *y* in *nadyasti* and similar forms, just as it does here. Nor is the elision (*lopa*) by the rule *rori* (Pāṇini 8.3.14) easily applicable, because doubling is not established with respect to that elision.

Regarding the elision [of *y*] by the rule *halo yamām* (Pāṇini 8.4.64), since it will be stated that this elision is optional, the two *repha*s (*r*) would be heard in one alternative case. One should not argue that this is not a fault because the author of the Bhāṣya will state in the *asiddhavat* sūtra that there is no difference between the pronunciation of a single consonant followed by another consonant and that of multiple consonants; for the meaning of that statement is that the difference is difficult to perceive due to its subtlety, not that a difference is entirely absent.

Otherwise, rules such as *śaro 'ci* (Pāṇini 8.4.49) and *halo yamām* (Pāṇini 8.4.64) would become redundant. Furthermore, in cases such as *caturmukhaḥ*, the rule *yaro 'nunāsike 'nunāsiko vā* (Pāṇini 8.4.45) would optionally apply to produce the nasal *ṇ*, because of the identity of place of articulation (*sthāna*). Similarly, in cases such as *kūṇḍaṃ rathena*, the rule *vā padāntasya* (Pāṇini 8.4.59) would optionally apply to produce the retroflex *r*.

The statement "there are no *savarṇa* [homogeneous] sounds for the *repha* and the sibilants" (*bhāṣyaho*) means that there is no *savarṇa* sound belonging to a different class; however, each sound is indeed its own *savarṇa*, because they possess the same place and effort of articulation (*tulyāsyaprayatna*). The elision prescribed by the rule *ro ri* (Pāṇini 8.3.14) does not apply here, because with respect to that [elision], the subsequent homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*).

Now, if, in order to prevent the substitution of a homogeneous nasal (*parasavarṇa*) for the two nasals [in *harin-nāsa*], the letter *r* were to be carried back from the following rule by means of the word *yavābhyām*, then the rule *ralo vyupadhāt* (Pāṇini 1.2.26) would also apply to words ending in *v*. Consequently, in forms such as *devitvā* and *dideviṣati*, the *guṇa* substitution would be prohibited according to that rule.

If it is argued that one should split the rule *avyupadhāt* and explain it as "after a suffix ending in *ava*, provided there is no *vy* as an upadhā," even so, in forms such as *gaudheraḥ* and *paceran*, the rule *lopo vyoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.76) would not apply, because the letter *r* is not included within the *vli* [of *vy*]. If it is argued that one will state "when *r* follows" (*rali*), then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the letter *y* in forms such as *haya* (meaning "to go") and *hayyāt*.

If it is argued that there is no such fault because one may split the word *vali* into two—reading the word *vali* as containing the letter *ra*, and then explaining it as "if there is a *val* [consonant] followed by *repha*"—even so, all the mentions of *yaṇ* in the sequence of rules such as *iko raṇaci* (Pāṇini 6.1.77), *saṃyogāderātoḍhātoraṇvataḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.43), *udāttaraṇo halpūrvāt* (Pāṇini 1.1.45), and *igraṇaḥ saṃprasāraṇam* (Pāṇini 1.1.45), would have to be understood as referring to the letter *ra*.

Even with this much, the desired conclusion is not established, because there would arise the undesirable consequence of many complications: namely, that by following the order of enumeration (*saṃkhyātānudeśa*) in the rule *iko yaṇ aci*, the letter *ra* would replace *i*, the letter *ya* would replace *u*, and the letter *va* would replace *ṛ*. Now, one might object that even according to the literal reading [of the sūtra], establishing the correspondence by order of enumeration is difficult to justify. For instance, since the letters *ya*, *va*, and *la*—being the items being prescribed (*vidhīyamāna*)—do not include their homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*), there are only four *yaṇ*s; moreover, because grammatical qualities (*guṇa*) do not differentiate [the phonemes], even if nasalized (*anunāsika*) vowels were included, there is no reason here for a separate enumeration.

However, because of the inclusion of *savarṇa* (homogeneous sounds), there are sixty-six [substitutes]. Nor should it be argued that there is indeed a fourfoldness among the vowels beginning with *i*, which are denoted by the word *ik* and serve as the designators of those sixty-six; for since thirty [sounds] would be presented by each of the two *ṛ*s belonging to the third and fourth [classes], it would be unavoidable that the substitute *ṛ* would apply in place of *l*, and the substitute *l* would apply in place of *ṛ*. Therefore, in the present case, the requirement is met solely by the rule "In place of [the original], the most similar [element]" (*Pāṇini 1.1.50*).

The *yathāsaṅkhyasūtra* (Pāṇini 1.3.10), however, will be applied in rules such as *nandigrahipacādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.134); this is the essential point. If it is argued that, likewise, even in the formulation *iko raṇ* (Pāṇini 3.2.164), the same [principle] should suffice for its resolution, we say no, because of the disparity. For, according to the literal reading, since there is no contradiction, both paribhāṣās apply to the rule *iko yaṇ aci* (Pāṇini 6.1.77): namely, "there is a one-to-one correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhyam*)" and "the *yaṇ* substitute should be the most similar (*antaratamaḥ*)."

If it were applied [to the *ra*] during the initial placement (*nyāsa*), then due to the conflict between the two technical rules (*paribhāṣā*), the rule of "correspondence in order" (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) alone would prevail by virtue of its posteriority. Therefore, the extraction of the *repha* from its own position is improper. However, according to the literal reading, the three defects such as doubling (*dvitva*) and so forth are unavoidable.

To this it is replied: by the fact that the letter *r* is heard as a cause for doubling without qualification, its status as the object of the operation (*kāryitva*), which is heard only in a general sense, is sublated. Just as in the case of the statement, "The Brāhmaṇas are to be fed; let Māṭhara and Kauṇḍinya serve the food," the feeding of Māṭhara and Kauṇḍinya—which was established in a general sense—is sublated by the serving of food specifically enjoined for them; so it is here.

Although both [possibilities] are possible here due to the distinction between the indicated form (*lakṣya*) and the individual instance (*vyakti*), there is no fault, because we accept the principle that even when both are possible, what is obtained by way of a general rule is sublated by what is obtained through a specific rule. And thus, since it is established in the rule *aco rahābhyām* (Pāṇini 8.4.46) that the term *yara* refers exclusively to [consonants] other than the letter *r*, the same applies in the rule *anaci ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.47) as well, because one relies on the governing scope of the meaning (*arthādhikāra*). Consequently, in forms such as *haryanubhavaḥ*, there is no doubling of the letter *r*.

If it is argued that, in this case, the *yaṇ* substitution would not occur in instances such as *dadhi-udaka*, because the status of the cause (*nimittatva*) is sublated by the specific mention of the substituendum (*sthānitva*), we say: no. For in those cases, the individualist view (*vyaktipakṣa*) is adopted in accordance with the observed forms (*lakṣya*). Indeed, under the individualist view, the rule (*lakṣaṇa*) applies repeatedly for each individual instance. Alternatively, for every individual instance, all the distinct rules are pronounced simultaneously (*tantra*) as "the *ik* vowels are replaced by *yaṇ* before a vowel" (Pāṇini 6.1.77).

Therefore, there is no fault, because even a single [instance] is established as the cause by way of its intended meaning (*tātparya*). Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of *yaṇ* substitution in cases such as *śrīśaḥ*; for, under the view that the rule applies to individual instances (*vyaktipakṣa*), by the force of the restriction "in case of conflict, the subsequent [rule] alone prevails," one assumes the non-existence of the very rule whose domain concerns that specific instance. This should be understood likewise in the domain of exceptions (*apavāda*), as in *suśrayau*, according to the maxim: "An inclusive rule (*utsarga*) applies after having bypassed the domain of an exception."

It has been stated in the *Paspaśā* itself that the positions regarding both the genus (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*) are adopted according to the requirements of the linguistic data (*lakṣya*): "Therefore, [the rule] *tasmādityuttarasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.67), *patyuttarapadāṇṇyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.85), and other such indications serve as evidence (*liṅga*) in this regard. However, in the *Bhāṣya*, it is said: 'These two, *ra* and *ha*, are not the objects of the grammatical operation (*kāryin*) of reduplication; rather, these two are the cause (*nimitta*)."

In this context, the mention of the letter *ha* is for the sake of illustration; just as *ha*, being excluded from the [class of] *yaṇ*s, does not function as the subject of the operation of doubling (*dvitva*), so too the letter *ra*, even though included within the *yaṇ*s, does not.
