According to the aforementioned method, however, it would not be established for the Northerners, whereas it would be established for the Easterners; thus, it is quite clear that both parties have deviated from their own respective tenets.

And likewise, regarding the rule *ṛto bhāradvājasya* (Pāṇini 7.2.63), a difficulty arises: in forms such as *jaghartha*, once the *guṇa* substitution and the subsequent replacement by *ra* have been applied, the rule *acastāsvat* (Pāṇini 7.2.61) does not apply because the stem no longer ends in a vowel (*anajantatvāt*). Consequently, since the restriction [of 7.2.61] would be inapplicable, the rule *ṛto bhāradvājasya* (7.2.63) would become a positive injunction (*vidhāyaka*), and thus [the prohibition of *iṭ*] would not apply even in cases like *pecitha*. To this objection, [the following is stated]: "For Bhāradvāja, after a root ending in a vowel that lacks an *iṭ* augment, the *iṭ* is always [absent] before *thal*."

But in the *Upadeśa*, it is only "of Bhāradvāja. From that point on—"after *ṛ*," [the phrase] "of Bhāradvāja" ceases to apply. And thus, having resolved the matter by breaking the rule (*sūtrabhaṅga*) so that all the target forms (*lakṣya*) are established, the author of the *Bhāṣya* will say: "It is thus established; however, this Bhāradvāja is made to deviate from his own opinion."

For this very reason, in the rule *acaḥ tāsvat* (Pāṇini 7.2.61), the term *upadeśe* from the preceding rule *upadeśe’tvataḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.62) is removed [from consideration] as the author intends to establish his final position (*siddhānta*); such is the direction of the argument. Furthermore, if the suffix *phin* were used, then in the sense of "the despicable descendant of Āmraguptāyani," the suffixes *cha* and *ṭhak* prescribed by the rule *phak-chau* (Pāṇini 4.1.149) would not apply to the *Sauvīra* gotra. In that context, it is established that only *phiñ* is understood and not *phin*, because of the specific restriction [implied by] the word *vṛddhāt* [in Pāṇini 4.1.158]. Consequently, the forms would have to be *āmraguptāyanīyaḥ* and *āmraguptāyanikaḥ*. And yet, [this is not the case].

Since the *Vṛtti* enumerates only these three—namely, "Yamunda, Suṣāman, and Vārṣyāyaṇi are remembered as [belonging to] Phiñ"—it must be stated that the suffixes *cha* and *ṭhak* do not apply after others; however, this is not so, because the author of the *Bhāṣya* does not accept such an enumeration. Otherwise, the counter-example provided under this very rule—"In the case of Sauvīras, why [is the suffix used]? Taikāyaniḥ"—would be inconsistent, for the word *taikāyani* is not included there [in the list].

For this very reason, it is illustrated under the rule *yūni luk* (Pāṇini 4.1.90): the descendant of *Tika* is *Taikāyaniḥ*, formed by *tikādibhyaḥ phiñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.154). His young descendant (*yuvan*) is *Taikāyanīyaḥ*, formed by *pheśchaca* (Pāṇini 4.1.149). The students of that [young descendant] are called *taikāyanīyāḥ*, once the suffix of the young descendant has been elided (*luk*) by the rule *vṛddhācchaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.114). For if there were a restrictive enumeration (*parigaṇana*), the suffix *cha* would not be possible after *taikāyani*, nor would its elision (*lop*) occur.

For this very reason, Haradatta and others have also stated that the enumeration [of cases] in the *yūniluk* sūtra is a later innovation. Furthermore, if the suffix *phiñ* were applied, the form *āmraguptāyaniḥ*—intended for both father and son, meaning "the young descendant of Āmraguptāyani"—would be derived as follows: from *āmragupta* one forms *āmraguptāyani* by adding *phiñ* according to *prāgdīvyato’ṇ* (Pāṇini 4.1.83), and then the *luk* elision of *phiñ* and *añ* by *ṇyakṣatriyārṣañito yūni lugaṇiñoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.58). However, if the suffix *phin* were used instead, that form would not be possible, because the condition "after a suffix marked with *ñ*" (*ñitaḥ*) would not be met.

Nor can its establishment be achieved by the proposed addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) stating, "the suffix *yu* [should be added] after *abrāhmaṇa*, *gotra*, *mātra*, etc.," because that rule does not apply to the *gotra* of a Brāhmaṇa. Furthermore, in the view that accepts the term as denoting what is yet to be (*tadbhāvita*), the acute accent on the first syllable of the preceding member would be established by the rule "mālādīnām ca" (Pāṇini 6.2.88) alone. Moreover, there is the burden of resorting to devices such as *tantra* and *āvṛtti* regarding the word *vṛddhi*. And finally, there is another burden: in the various rules prescribing operations such as "vṛddhi replaces the root vowel of *mṛj*" (Pāṇini 7.2.114), one would have to understand the designation as referring to what is yet to be (*bhāvisaṃjñā*)—like a tailor's measuring cloth—to avoid mutual dependency (*itaretarāśraya*). Thus, there is further complexity.

To this it is replied: the designation *vṛddhi* applies to the entire set of vowels beginning with *ā*. Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, the aforementioned fault would apply to words such as *sarvabāsa*; for in the rule *uttarapadavṛddhau sarvaṃ ca* (Pāṇini 6.2.105), the term *uttarapada* is marked with an accent (*svarita*). It is understood that an accent indicates an extended scope (*adhikāra*). Therefore, by virtue of the governing heading *uttarapadasya*, only that *vṛddhi* which is specifically prescribed [by that rule] is taken here. For example, in *sarvapāñcālaḥ*, the *vṛddhi* is applied by the rule *susarvārddhāj janapadasya* (Pāṇini 7.3.12).

And this must necessarily be stated even when [the term] *tadbhāvita* (that which is produced by that) is understood; otherwise, there would be over-extension (*atiprasakti*) in cases such as *sarvaḥ kārakaḥ* and *sarvakārakaḥ*. Thus, there is no fault even in the case of the feminine form, because by resorting to the principles of *tantra* (simultaneous application) or *āvṛtti* (repetition), the prohibition of the masculine-like behavior (*puṃvadbhāva*) applies only to that which is the cause of the *vṛddhi* prescribed by the word *vṛddhi*. And with the intention that when the prescription is made by the word *vṛddhi*, the entire *vṛddhi* is understood, it was stated in the Bhāṣya: "that which is the cause of the entire *vṛddhi*."

Nor is there an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) to the word *vaiyākaraṇabhāryā* or *sauvaśvabhāryā*, because it is only that which is endowed with a result (*phalopahita*) that is intended to be the cause (*nimitta*). If it is argued that there is indeed an endowment with a result even in relation to *ai* and *au*, we say no; for those two are not prescribed by the term "vṛddhi. Some, however, maintain that a taddhita suffix is called a "cause" when it is capable of producing vṛddhi and is endowed with some result. In the case of *vaiyākaraṇa*, however, the taddhita suffix is not the cause in relation to *ai* and *au*, since the over-extension is avoided merely by the fact that [the suffix] is taught in conjunction with a prohibition (*niṣedhasanniyogaśiṣṭatā*). Therefore, there is no over-extension in the case of *vaiyākaraṇabhāryā*.

Regarding [the rule] *pariṣado ṇyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.4.44), they say that in examples such as *pāriṣadyā bhāryā*, even though the suffix is merely accompanied by the vowel *ā*, the inherent capacity for the operation exists with respect to all *vṛddhi* substitutions.
Therefore:
Because repetition would result in excessive complexity (*gaurava*), and because forms such as *śālīya* would remain unestablished.
And because of the indicative mark [in the word] "of the garland, etc.," and likewise by the logic of pervasion (vyāpti).
Because of the weight of the designation "future" (bhāvin) in grammatical consciousness,
and because there is no distinction here for the mere vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au*, the designation *vṛddhi* is prescribed for them without exception.

The instruction on correct forms (*sādhvanuśāsana*) is not purposeless; this *sūtra* exists for the sake of restricting usage, for the sake of substitutes (*ādeśa*), for the sake of augments (*āgama*), and for the sake of establishing the relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*). As for the sixfold set of positions (*ṣaṭpakṣī*), it is not elaborated here because it has already been refuted in the *Bhāṣya* and because its arguments are inherently untenable. Even though the relationship between name (*saṃjñā*) and named (*saṃjñin*) exists, there are many logical principles (*nyāya*) that determine the intent regarding which is the name and which is the named. For instance: "Connection with the word *yat*, being mentioned first, and so forth, are the characteristics of the subject (*uddeśya*);
the word *tat* and the particle *eva* are the characteristics of the predicate (*upādeya*)."

Thus, according to the statement of the learned and likewise from experience, priority (*prāthamya*) is indeed an indicator (*liṅga*) for being a technical name (*saṃjñitva*). And this is quite evident in rules such as *adaṅ guṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.2).

In the *Vṛddhisaṃjñāsūtra*, however, although the word *vṛddhi* is placed first for the sake of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), once it has been determined—by means of other principles to be explained—that *ā*, *ai*, and *au* are the technical terms (*saṃjñin*), one accepts that the comprehension of the sentence-meaning occurs only after the knowledge of the word-order *ādaij vṛddhiḥ*. Consequently, since *ā*, *ai*, and *au* alone occupy the initial position in the knowledge of the word-order that generates that [sentence-meaning], there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Furthermore, the very knowledge of the word-order is what is called "knowledge of syntactic contiguity" (*asatti-jñāna*).

Furthermore, for those who do not accept that this [proximity] is a cause for verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), the distinction between "proximate" and "non-proximate" would be abolished; for in a mental apprehension of a collection of words, as well as in the recollection of word-meanings, there is no difference in the status of all the words and all the word-meanings as objects of cognition. Moreover, repetition is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the status of being a name (*saṃjñā*), since a name is established solely for the sake of practical usage. Furthermore, the status of being a named object (*saṃjñin*) and a name (*saṃjñā*) are sometimes determined through identity and non-identity: for it is appropriate for many things to have a single name due to parsimony (*lāghava*), but not for a single thing to have many names.

The designation [of *vṛddhi*] is due to its weightiness (*gaurava*). Indeed, many designations with varying numbers of instances are accepted precisely because of the distinctness of the operations (*kārya*) induced by them—just like the designations *kṛt*, *kṛtya*, and *pratyaya*, or the designations *taddhita* and *tadrāja*. Furthermore, the quality of having fewer syllables (*laghvakṣaratva*) should be understood as an indicator of a designation (*saṃjñāliṅga*) in cases such as *ṭi*, *ghu*, and *bh*. However, since it is established here that the word *vṛddhi* is a designation by virtue of its recurrence (*āvṛtti*) and non-difference (*abheda*), one must also apply the priority of the vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au* by means of that [designation], even though it would disrupt the perceived sequence (*śrutānupūrvī*).

Alternatively, setting aside the view that designations (*saṃjñā*) are created by one's own will, this should be applied to the view that there is a restriction for the sake of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*). Even regarding the first [view], it may be resolved by resorting to the *kāryakāla* (time-of-operation) theory; such is the general direction.

By this, the deviation [of the rule] has been demonstrated even in cases such as "ārddhadhātukaṃ śeṣaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.4.114), "kṛdatiṅ" (Pāṇini 3.1.93), "apṛkta ekāl pratyayaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.2.41), "svaṃ rūpaṃ śabdasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.68), "aṇudit" (Pāṇini 1.1.69), "taparaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.1.70), "ādirantyena" (Pāṇini 1.1.71), and "yenavidhistadantasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.72); for in those instances as well, there is the assumption of an inverse sequence.

Furthermore, since the capacity for imagination (*kalpakatva*) has already been stated, and because the solution can be established even through alternative positions (*pakṣāntara*), for this very reason the *bhāṣya* on the *sthānivadbhāva* sūtra—having raised the objection, "What is the purpose of the suffix *-vat*?"—is also justified by stating, "Lest the designation (*saṃjñā*) [of the substitute] be applied to the original element (*sthānin*). As for the claim that the rule *apṛkta ekāl* (Pāṇini 1.2.41) is a *paribhāṣā* and not a *saṃjñā*, that could be said with equal ease regarding [the terms] *vṛddhi* and so forth as well.

"The inclusion of the term *hal* (consonant) in the definition of *apṛkta* [in Pāṇini 1.2.41] is for the purpose of including consonants in the elision of suffixes beginning with *su* [Pāṇini 6.1.68]; this contradicts both the Vārttika and its Bhāṣya. Therefore, the aforementioned interpretation alone is correct; such is the direction [of the argument]."

Now, an objection may be raised: "In rules such as *mṛjervṛddhiḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.114), there is a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), for a designation (*saṃjñā*) establishes a rule, and a designation applies only to those things already established by a rule. Furthermore, since the application of the designation is possible in cases like *mālā*, one cannot assume here that the designation is understood in its future sense (*bhāvisaṃjñā*). Therefore, the word *vṛddhi* itself must be the substitute (*ādeśa*). For even if the designation *vṛddhi* were applied elsewhere, it would be impossible to extract the vowel *a* contained within words such as *mālā* from that context and prescribe it here [as a substitute].

On this point, they say: In cases such as *mārṣṭi*, since the vowel *ā* is already established by the instruction of the root *mṛj*, its grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*)—which would otherwise be suspected—is taught by rules such as *mṛjer vṛddhiḥ*; it is not, however, that a previously non-existent *ā* is produced, which would lead to the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). And it has been stated by the author of the Vārttika: "In the case of *vṛddhi* and other operations, because they serve as causes for what is already existent, there is no establishment [of the rule] due to mutual dependence; but it is established because words are eternal (*nityaśabdatva*)."

Now, suppose someone whose sole eye is the grammatical definition (*lakṣaṇa*) were to seek to acquire proficiency in usages such as *mārṣṭi* by means of grammar alone; even so, there would be no harm, because when the form *ākāra-* is heard in words like *śālāmālā*, through the proximity provided by the general definition of the vowel *ā* (*ātva-sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-pratyāsatti*), one grasps that all instances of *ākāra-* occurring in usages such as *mārṣṭi* are denotable by the term "vṛddhi."

However, in the view that does not accept the existence of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is avoided by the fact that the apprehension of the word’s power (*śakti*), the experience of that power, the recollection of the word-meaning, and the comprehension of the sentence-meaning possess identical modes of presentation (*samānaprakāraka*). Otherwise, even from the sentence "There is a jar in the house," a previously unperceived individual (*apūrvavyakti*) would not be grasped; such is the direction of the argument.

For this very reason, the author of the Bhāṣya will state under the sūtra *na veti vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 1.1.44): "But if this [the *na vā*] were to be enjoined, then by rules such as *vibhāṣā śveḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.30), there would result an option for that very [term]. Therefore, it is the samprasāraṇa and so forth alone that are optionally applied. This is precisely the principle to be followed in the injunction of the *laṭ* and other tenses.

Nor does this result in the destruction of the status of [the rule] as an injunction regarding that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), because the authors of the *Vivaraṇa* and others have stated in the *Kṛnmejanta-sūtra* that in all cases it is precisely that which is qualified by correctness (*sādhutva*) that is enjoined through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); and even when there is an injunction of the mere form, correctness is established from the sentence by postulating an implied meaning (*śrutārthāpatti*) such as: "Whatever is here fully established, that is correct.

Furthermore, in this context, the completion of the sentence occurs with each individual word, as indicated by the evidence in rules such as *mālādīnāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 6.2.78), and because we observe the same in examples such as *brāhmaṇā bhojyantām*.

Although in cases such as "the Gargas should be fined one hundred," the completion of the sentence is observed even with respect to the collective group—since it is impossible for the "one hundred," which is the primary element, to be repeated in accordance with the Gargas, who are subordinate members of the action and have attained the status of the *apādāna* (ablative/starting point)—nevertheless, in this science (*śāstra*), the rule does not apply to the collective group without a specific effort. For this very reason, the author of the Vārttika will state that the word "together" (*saha*) is used in the rule "both [halves] together constitute the reduplicated base" (*ubhe abhyastam saha*).

The author of the Bhāṣya, however, will state that the mention of "both" (*ubhe*) is precisely for this purpose. Otherwise, since [the doubling] would be established by the continued application of the rule *ekāco dve* (Pāṇini 6.1.1), what would be the use of mentioning "both"? Regarding the technical designations of "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) and "compound" (*samāsa*), the effort made in formulating these as "great designations" (*mahāsaṃjñā*) is intended to convey their etymological significance. For this very reason, it will be established that the mention of "together" (*saha*) in the rule *saha supā* (Pāṇini 2.1.4) serves to introduce compounds with finite verbs (*tiṅanta*) and so forth, through a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*).

In this context, it has been explained in detail under the two sūtras "eoṅ" and "aiauc" (Pāṇini 1.1.4–5) that the addition of the *tapara* marker (*Ṭ*) is for the sake of excluding vowels of the same length (*aj-artham*), for the sake of correct pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtham*), and for the sake of removing ambiguity (*asandehārtham*). As for what was stated here by the author of the Vārttika—that "the addition of the *tapara* marker to the vowel *ā* is for the sake of including its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇārtham*)"—that was said with the intention that "vowels are distinguished by their qualities (*guṇāḥ bhedakāḥ*)" and that the *tapara* rule applies even to non-vowels (*an-aṇi*) as an injunction. However, in the Bhāṣya, it is established that "vowels are not distinguished by their qualities (*abhedakā guṇāḥ*)."

The meaning is that the qualities (*guṇa*)—namely, acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), circumflex (*svarita*), and nasalized (*anunāsika*)—even though they are pronounced as inherent to [the phonemes], are not intended to be expressed without a specific effort. The mention of "acute" (*udātta*) in rules such as *anaṅ udāttaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.75) and *aḍ udāttaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.71) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of this; for otherwise, one would simply pronounce the acute accent alone, due to the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*).

Now, if the *guṇas* were non-differentiators, then what the Bhāṣyakāra will say—namely, "Since the substitute *vadhi* for *han* would, by virtue of being a *sthānivadbhāva*, be *anudātta*, an *iṭ*-prohibition would apply; to prevent that, the substitution of *vadhi* will be pronounced as *udātta*. And thus, in the rule *ekāca upadeśe* (Pāṇini 7.2.10), the mention of *ekāj* need not be made"—this would be contradicted, because it would follow that [the accent] is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣā*).

Now, it might be argued: "Even in that case, because of the rule *sthānentaratamaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.50), when the accent that would naturally belong to the substitute is to be uttered, the fact that an acute (*udātta*) is instead pronounced with effort is understood as being for the sake of specific intention (*vivakṣā*). Even so, this contradicts what will be stated in the sixth [book]: "The acute accentuation of *catasṛ* will be prescribed by way of exception (*nipātana*); that exceptional accent (*nipātanasvara*) will be an annulment of the rule *caturaḥ śasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.167)."

Indeed, regarding the word *catuḥ*, if one follows the view that it is not derived (*avyutpatti-pakṣa*), it is acute-accented on the first syllable by the *phiṭ-sūtra* "vraḥ saṃkhyāyāḥ" (PhS 28). Even if it is derived according to "cateruran" (UṇS 747), it is likewise acute-accented on the first syllable due to the *nitsvara* accent. Since it is possible for the substitute form *catasṛ-* to be pronounced with an initial acute accent by virtue of the accent of its original base (*sthāni-svara*), it is illogical for the rule "caturaḥ śasi" (PāS 6.1.167) to act as a sublater of that [initial acute accent].

Furthermore, since even [the substitutes] *asthi* and so forth have an acute accent on their initial syllable, when the substitute *anaṅ*—which conforms to its original (*sthānin*)—is to be pronounced as unaccented, the fact that it is pronounced with an acute accent will serve to indicate a specific intention (*vivakṣā*). Thus, the mention of the acute accent (*udāttagrahaṇa*) would be entirely useless; on the contrary, its inclusion, despite the additional effort required, would suggest that there is no such intention.

As for the claim that because the Sūtra is recited with a single accent (ekaśruti), the occasional utterance of the acute (udātta) is intended to convey a specific meaning (*vivakṣārtha*), that too must be considered. For if that were the case, since the acute would already be established even for *anaṅ* by its very utterance, the mention of "acute" (*udāttagraha*) in the rule would be redundant, and it would be impossible to derive the aforementioned implication (*jñāpana*). To explain: what is the implication to be derived? Is it that "a quality (*guṇa*) not explicitly mentioned by its own term is not intended to be significant," or rather that "it is not intended to be significant unless there is a specific effort"? In the first case, the accent of an irregularly formed word (*nipātanasvara*) would not be intended as significant.

It is said: having accepted that monotonous intonation (*ekaśruti*) is optional according to the rule *vibhāṣā chandasi* (Pāṇini 1.2.36), it was stated that "in various instances, the initial acute accent (*ādyudātta*) will be prescribed by the maxim that 'refutations can also be provided through alternative positions. However, here, by relying on the recitation of the sūtras with the three accents (*traisvarya*), it was stated that the mention of the acute accent is an indicator (*jñāpaka*), because there is the possibility that a quality (*guṇa*) expressed in its own form may be unintended as a necessary concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*). Therefore, there is no contradiction.

Alternatively, since the rule *amuditsavarṇasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.67) would already be established by the mention of *aṇ* alone, the explicit mention of *aṇ*—made for the purpose of including *ya*, *va*, and *la*, which are distinct from the *guṇas*—indicates that the *guṇas* are indeed distinguishers (*bhedaka*). Regarding the two positions of "distinguishers" and "non-distinguishers," one should understand the *Bhāṣya* passage beginning with "the initial udātta accent will be prescribed" as being based on the two views of "universals" (*jāti*) and "individuals" (*vyakti*).

For this very reason, the nasalization does not apply in cases such as *idam* and its substitutes (*astyadādyatve*), nor in rules like *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau* (Pāṇini 7.2.84). If it is argued that the mention of the term *aṇ* in the rule *aṇo'pragṛhyasyānunāsikaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.57) is intended to indicate the continued application of the optionality (*anyatarasyām*) from the rule *halo yamām* (Pāṇini 8.4.64), we say no; for there is no contradiction even if it serves as an indicator for both. Indeed, there is no restrictive rule that only one thing can be indicated by a single [mention]; rather, whatever cannot otherwise be logically established is what must be indicated.

For this very reason, both the optional substitution of *ā* and the designation (*saṃjñā*) as *ṣaṣ* for that which has undergone the *ātva* change will be indicated by the inclusion of the term "long" (*dīrgha*) in Pāṇini’s rule 6.1.172, *aṣṭano dīrghāt*. Furthermore, by means of the governing heading (*adhikāra*) *saṃhitāyām* (6.1.72), two things are indicated: the non-obligatory nature of *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination) and the application of *ānaṅ* and other such substitutions even when there is an interval of time; such is the direction of the argument. And thus, the inclusion of the letter *t* after the vowel *a* in the rule is for the sake of including its homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*); therefore, the relevant Vārttika is indeed correct under the view that [the letters] are distinguishers (*bhedaka*).

In the Bhāṣya, however, the purpose of [the term] *aij* is stated with the intention of another alternative; that too should be understood according to the *yathoddeśa* (definition-at-the-place-of-enunciation) view, because there is the possibility of *ā*, *ai*, and *au* grasping their homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*) due to their being subject to the rule enjoining the technical name (*saṃjñā*). But under the *kāryakāla* (operation-at-the-time-of-application) view, since *ā*, *ai*, and *au* are themselves to be produced as qualified by the technical name "vṛddhi" by the very rule of prescription, they do not at all obtain the grasping of homogeneous counterparts.

Just as words such as *jyotiṣṭoma* and *rājasūya* are understood to be names because they stand in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the injunction for a sacrifice, and not through any other sentence, so too is it in this view regarding *vṛddhi* and the rest. However, the rule *vṛddhir ādaic* (Pāṇini 1.1.1) serves merely to present the term, just as *iko guṇavṛddhī* (Pāṇini 1.1.3) does; the designation of the presented term as a technical name (*saṃjñin*) occurs only subsequently through the operation of the naming rule (*saṃjñāsūtra*).

But the distinction from the first view is that here, just as the meaning of the word *svarga* is understood in the passage "that which is not [accompanied] by pain," etc., the meaning of the words *vṛddhi* and so forth is understood in this very context.

Thus, this is the distilled meaning of the Sūtra: the designation *vṛddhi* shall apply individually to each of the vowels *ā*, *ai*, and *au*, whether they have been [formally] produced by grammatical rules or not. For example: *āśvalāyanaḥ* and *aitikāyanaḥ*. From the words *aśvala-* and *aitika-*, the *vṛddhi* substitution occurs by virtue of the *naḍādi* group [of suffixes], such as *phañ* and others. Also: *aupagavaḥ*, meaning "the offspring of Upagu."

The designation *guṇa* shall apply to *a*, *e*, and *o*. Here, the inclusion of the marker *t* (in *at*) serves all purposes; thus, in the word "tarati," it is only the short *a* that is substituted, and never the long *ā*. Nor can the restriction be established by proximity based on measure (*pramāṇa*), because once the substitution of *r* for *ṛ* has been made, one [the short *a*] consists of one and a half morae (*mātrā*), while the other [the long *ā*] consists of two and a half morae. Examples: *pacanti*, *cetā*, *stotā*.
The *ik* vowels [are designated as] *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.3)

Wherever it is stated that "there is a *guṇa*" or "there is a *vṛddhi*," one should understand that the genitive form *ikaḥ* is supplied [from the previous rule]. For example: *cetā*, *stotā*, *ahārṣīt*, and so forth. Because of the mention of *ik*, [the rules do not apply] here: *yātā*, *glāyati*, and *ubhnitā*. Thus says the Vārttika: "The mention of *ik* is for the purpose of excluding *āt*, diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*), and consonants (*vyañjana*). Now, these are not actually purposes, since the exclusion of non-*ik* vowels is established by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

To explain: in forms such as *pacati*, although there is a *guṇa* substitution for the vowel *a* by means of the suffixes *śap* and *tip* respectively—according to the rules *pugantalaghūpadhasya guṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.86) and *sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.84)—there is no difference in the resulting form. However, in forms such as *acikīrṣīt*, the *vṛddhi* substitution is superseded by the elision of the *at* suffix, because the *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (priority of application) rule *ṇyallopau* (Kātyāyana’s Vārttika) will be stated hereafter.

Even on the view that this [sūtra] is the beginning of the treatise, this very same principle applies in cases such as *cikīrṣakaḥ*; for in the rule *aco ñṇiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.115), since the reference is to the *sthānin*, the *ik-paribhāṣā* does not apply. However, in forms such as *ayāsīt*, there is no harm even if the *vṛddhi* occurs before the *sic*. In reality, however, that [vṛddhi] is superseded by the *sag* and *iṭ* augmentations because they are subsequent; the refined conclusion is that it is superseded because it is an exception (*apavāda*) according to the maxim of "that which was not previously applicable" (*yenanāprāptinyāya*).

Furthermore, there is no risk of the substitution of *guṇa* for the vowel *ā* in forms such as *yātā* and *vātā*, because it has been indicated that the *ā* does not undergo *guṇa* due to the *ṭak* suffix being marked with *k* in the rule *gāpoṣṭak* (Pāṇini 3.2.8). Indeed, that *k*-marker is applied for the purpose of eliding the long *ā* in forms such as *sāmagaḥ*.

If, however, the *guṇa* were a property of the vowel *a*, then when two instances of *a* undergo the *pararūpa* substitution to form words such as *sāmagaḥ*, what would be the purpose of the designation *kit*? Nor should it be argued that here—in examples such as *cikīrṣakaḥ*—the elision (*lopa*) of the root vowel is more appropriate to cite as the result, due to its higher status and its being a stem-internal (*āṅga*) operation rather than the *pararūpa* substitution; for even with that much, there is no obstacle to its serving as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). In reality, however, there ought to be elision here.

For in that context, because the term *upadeśa* (original enunciation) is understood by way of its recurrence from Pāṇini’s rule 6.4.37 (*anudāttopadeśa*), it serves as a qualifier for the *ārddhadhātuka* affix; thus, the elision of the *at* (the final *a*) is prescribed for that which ends in *a* at the time of the *ārddhadhātuka* upadeśa. Otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *gataḥ* and *gatavān*. Nor can this be resolved by the rule regarding what is "as if unestablished" (*asiddhavat*), since that rule will be rejected by the author of the Bhāṣya.

Furthermore, regarding the forms *at* and *pat*, which Mādhava and others cite from the root *aya paya gatau* (DhP 1.957) with the suffix *kvip*—that too would not be established according to the literal reading [of the rule]. Therefore, the only recourse is to follow the traditional instruction (*upadeśa*). If one asks, "How then is the elision of the *a* in forms such as *dhinutaḥ* and *kuṇutaḥ* achieved by the rule *ato lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.48)? some say: because they are taught in conjunction (*sanniyogaśiṣṭatayā*), the vowel *a* is already mentally present at the very time of the instruction for the suffix *u*.

Others, however, say that there is no such fault because, in accordance with the sequence of the sūtra "dhinvikṛṇvyora ca" (Pāṇini 3.1.80), the substitution of *a* occurs first, and subsequently, by the force of the word *ca*, the suffix *u* is attracted [to the root].

If it is argued that, in cases such as *sāmagāya*, because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is treated as the end of the preceding element, the elision of the final *ā* of the root (*āt-dhātoḥ*, Pāṇini 6.4.140) would occur, Kaiyaṭa has provided the following resolution while commenting on the rule *e-oṅ* (Pāṇini 2.4.32): "The *ya*-suffix, having been applied by depending upon the vowel *a*, does not trigger the elision [of that *a*] due to the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*. However, the lengthening of the vowel occurs by virtue of the specific grammatical exception (*nipātana*) in the rule *kaṣṭāya* (Pāṇini 3.1.14). Thus he has settled the matter.

This is his intention: for in the case of that substitute, the property of having *at* (the short vowel *a*) qualified by shortness (*hrasvatva*) is the cause [of the application of the rule], because the word "at" is understood from the previous rule. Although the portion consisting of shortness is set aside by the long vowel in the substitute, nevertheless the mere property of being *at* continues to apply even to the substitute. If that too were set aside by elision (*lopa*), then there would be a contradiction with the Paribhāṣā. As for the portion consisting of length, the Paribhāṣā is indeed set aside due to an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Nor should it be argued that, in this way, the Paribhāṣā should also be set aside in other portions; for its non-contradiction is also logically possible in those other cases.

In this regard, the author of the *Bhāṣya* is the authority, as he states in the present *sūtra* and in the *eoṅ* *sūtra* that the *kittva* (the property of being marked with *k*) of the suffix *ṭak* in the root *gā-pū-* serves no other purpose. By this [principle], the form *śubhaṃyyaḥ* and others cited by Mādhava—derived from the word *śubhaṃyā-* in the neuter gender after shortening, the substitution of *ṅe* for *ṅasi*, lengthening, and the elision of the final *ā* by *āto dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.140)—are to be considered doubtful, as they contradict the *Bhāṣya*.

For this very reason, those who—contrary to Mādhava’s view—have attempted to explain the neuter form *śrīpam* by breaking down the text "śrīpam jñānavat" according to its literal reading as referring to the form *śrīpāyi*, and have instead interpreted it as "prāyeṇa jñānavat," are refuted. Likewise, in cases such as *glāyati*, there will be no *guṇa* substitution for the diphthongs (*sandhyakṣara*) due to the force of their being taught [in the *upadeśa*]; otherwise, one would have taught only the vowel *e*. This is because, even in the absence of brevity in syllables (*mātrālāghava*), there is indeed brevity in the process (*prakriyālāghava*).

Nor should it be argued that, in this way, even the substitution of *āy* would not occur; for according to the maxim: "That rule for which an instruction is rendered purposeless is sublated, but that rule whose very cause [the instruction] exists is not sublated. For with respect to the *guṇa* substitution, the instruction of *ai* is indeed purposeless, since the root *glai* can be easily read as *gle*. However, the substitution of *āy* is its very cause.

Nor should it be argued that one should simply read "glāya" [in the Dhātupāṭha]; for if that were the case, the form "tvayā glāyate" would not be possible, because it would entail the hearing of two *yak* sounds, and forms such as "jaglau" would fail to be established. As for the objection that forms like "glātā" would not be possible due to the contingency of the augment *iṭ* arising from the absence of the condition of ending in a single vowel (*ekājajanta*), that is not correct, because these roots can be easily read among those taught with anudātta accents.

Nor should it be argued that in this way forms such as *aglāsiṣṭām* would be unestablished, because *s* and *iṭ* could not occur since [the root] does not end in a vowel (*anāntatvena*). For once the *y*-elision has been performed by Pāṇini’s rule *lopo vyor vali* (6.1.66), *s* and *iṭ* become easily available. Furthermore, the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā* (the metarule concerning the destruction of a cause-effect relationship) is non-eternal; this will be made known by the inclusion of the term *tuka* in the rule *kṛti-tuk* (6.1.71). Therefore, the *y*-elision caused by the *val*-sannipāta will indeed trigger *iṭ*, even though *iṭ* destroys that very *val*-sannipāta. It is precisely by resorting to this non-eternality that the elision of the long *ā* occurs in forms such as *dākṣiḥ* and *godaḥ*.

Otherwise, because those two [the suffixes] are dependent upon *iṅ* and *kapratyaya*, the elision (*lopa*) would not occur. Or, even if it were granted that "aglāsiṣṭām" and so forth would not be established due to recourse to the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*, this is another defect in teaching [the root] with a *y*. In any case, by virtue of the capacity of the instruction of the diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*), there is no *guṇa*; however, it is established that *āy* and the others do indeed occur.

It might be argued as follows: "In that case, let the substitution of *ā* by *ādecaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.45) also be sublated. For the instruction of *aij* is not the cause for the substitution of *ā*, since even when *gle* is taught [instead of *glai*], that [substitution of *ā*] would still be easily accomplished. When, in the presence of a *śit* suffix, the *guṇa* [substitution] applies and in its absence the substitution of *ā* applies—thereby displacing the *aic* vowels—the force of the instruction of *aij* implies that there is no criterion (*vinigamanā*) to decide between them which one should be sublated and which should not; consequently, the sublation of both is inevitable."

Nor should it be argued that there is no scope for the prescription of *āt* in this manner; for the scope of [roots] such as *dheṭ* "to drink" (*dīopao*) and *śo* "to thin" is clearly evident. If it is objected: "In that case, one should simply say *ādeṅ*, and thus the mention of *aij* would be entirely without scope," we reply: No, because it is for the sake of what follows.

For in the rule *mīnātiminoti* (Pāṇini 6.1.50), the Vārttikakāra will clarify in the *ghu*-saṃjñā-sūtra that by the continued application of the term *ec*, "the bases ending in *ā* are those ending in *ai*, and the bases ending in *ai* are also those ending in *ī*."

On this point, they say: when a possibility exists by subverting only one of two [alternatives], it is improper to assume a subversion of both. In that case, if even a slight distinction were not discerned, then—due to the absence of a deciding factor (*vinigamanā*)—there would indeed be a subversion of both. However, there *is* a deciding factor here: by the mention of the root *dhyai* with its *ā*-vowel already applied in the rule *na dhyākhyā* (Pāṇini 8.2.57), it is made known that the *ā*-vowel substitution is not subverted. Furthermore, the *ā*-vowel substitution occurs also by virtue of the inclusion of the term *ej-* [in Pāṇini 6.1.45]. As for what was said—that it is for the sake of the subsequent rule—that is so.

That is not so; for by the rule *mīnāti* (Pāṇini 6.1.50), the substitution of *ā* is not prescribed in place of *ni*. Rather, when a suffix conditioned by *e* is intended to be expressed, the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel is prescribed at the very stage of the original form (*upadeśāvasthā*).

Otherwise, in the case of *dāyaḥ* and similar forms, the suffix *ghañ* would be superseded by *ac* according to Pāṇini 3.3.56 (*erac*), so that *īṣadavadānaḥ* and *svavadāna* would not take *yuc* as prescribed by Pāṇini 3.3.128 (*āto yuc*), and *avadāyaḥ* would not take *ṇa* as prescribed by Pāṇini 3.1.141 (*śyādvyadhā*). This point will be clarified by the author of the Bhāṣya in the sixth [chapter] itself.

And thus, even if it were stated that "this [substitution] occurs when there is a condition consisting of a *nimitta* (causal factor)," forms such as *dāpayati* and *māpayati* would still be established; for the *ṇic* suffix remains inherently capable (*svarūpayogyatva*) with respect to the *guṇa* substitution as well, since its capacity is not lost even though the *guṇa* is set aside by the *vṛddhi* substitution. Nor is actual productive efficacy (*phalopadhāna*) intended here, because it is accepted that the substitution of *āt* applies even prior to the domain of *aij*. Otherwise, as was just stated, suffixes such as *ghañ*, *u*, and *ṇap* would not occur. Therefore, the substitution of *āt* certainly takes place. However, it is settled that the *guṇa* is set aside by the force of the instruction (*upadeśa*) of the single vowel *ai*.

It remains only that there would be a quality [transfer] of the consonants (*vyañjana*). Consequently, in the word *īhitā*, because the letter *h* is guttural, the vowel *a* would result; and in *umbhitā*, because the letter *bh* is labial, the vowel *o* would result; thus, [the forms] would become *yetā* and *unavitā*.

When the *yaṇ* substitution is applied to the vowel *ī*, the *guṇa* replacement occurs for the vowel *a* together with the augment *iṭ*, but not the elision (*lopa*) of *a*; for it has been explained that the elision applies only to that which ends in *a* at the time of the instruction of an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix. Furthermore, [one might argue] that because the *anusvāra* and *parasavarṇa* substitutions are treated as *asiddha* when the *guṇa* is to be performed after the root *umbh*. This is not a fault; for in the rule "the suffix *ḍa* is added to the root *jan* in the locative case" (Pāṇini 3.2.97), the fact that the suffix *ḍa* is marked with the *ḍit* designation is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that a *guṇa* does not occur for a consonant.

For if [the suffix were not marked with *ḍ*], then when the half-mora *nakāra* undergoes *guṇa* substitution into the one-mora *akāra*, and the form of three *akāras* is established as a single subsequent form (*pararūpa*) by Pāṇini 6.1.97 (*ato guṇe*), the resulting forms would be *upasarajaḥ* and *mandurajaḥ*. In that case, what would be the purpose of marking the suffix with *ḍ* for the sake of eliding the *ṭi*? *Upasaraḥ* refers to the first mating of bulls with female cattle for the purpose of impregnation. The suffix *ap* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.3.71 (*prajane sartteḥ*), which is an exception to the suffix *ghan*.

According to Amara in the section on mixed categories (*saṅkīrṇavarga*), "prajanaḥ syādupasaraḥ" (Amarakośa 3.2.25). Kṣīrasvāmin explains that *prajana* is the time for the conception of embryos by animals, as they are produced (*prajāyate*) therein. *Upasarajaḥ* means "born during the *upasara*" (the breeding season), while *mandurajaḥ* means "born in the *mandurā*" (stable). The shortening of the vowel occurs according to Pāṇini’s rule 6.3.63: "The feminine suffixes *ṅī* and *āp* are diversely elided in technical names and Vedic meters. Amara states: "A stable (*vājiśālā*) is called *mandurā*" (Amarakośa 2.2.7).

Nor should it be argued that the letter *ḍ* is for the purpose of being heard [in pronunciation], because there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule *prāvṛṭ-śarat-kāla-divāṃ je* (Pāṇini 6.3.15), which contains a reference to the elision of the *ṭi*-affix. [Objection: But this is not an indicative mark, since the reference to *ja* is possible as the form ending in the suffix *kap* belonging to the root *jai* (meaning "destruction") from the *Bhvādigaṇa*.

If it is asked: "How then can the suffix *ka* prescribed after a verbal root when a *kāraka* (object) is the upapada apply in cases such as *prāvṛṣijaḥ*? [The answer is: It applies because, for the sake of establishing forms such as *dvipaḥ* and *pādapaḥ*, a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) is accepted in the sūtra *supi sthaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.4). True; however, if the letter *ḍ* were intended merely for its audible pronunciation (*śravaṇārtha*), the status of being an *it* (the marker *ḍ* would be subject to elision), which would contradict the established usage. Nor is there a lack of purpose, since the *ḍ* serves the purpose of effecting the *ṭilopa* (elision of the penultimate vowel). Nor is this otherwise established by the application of *guṇa*, because the absence of *guṇa* is also what is being indicated.

According to the *niṣādasthapati* maxim (*Jaiminīya-sūtra* 6.1.13), the presence of complexity in the result is not a fault; furthermore, if one were to accept that the letter *ḍ* is for the sake of pronunciation, it would contradict the *vārttika* on the *vṛddhi* rule which states: "If it is argued that the teaching is unnecessary because words are eternal, we reply that it is established as necessary because it serves to exclude [other forms]. Now, it might be objected that without the *ḍit* designation, the correct form would not be established, since there would be the undesirable consequence of a nasalized *guṇa* vowel replacing the *n*.

Nor should it be argued that [the vowel] will become "pure" (śuddha) by means of the *pararūpa* rule together with the suffix-vowel *ā*, which lacks the *anunāsika* quality; for even when *pararūpa* is prescribed, since the *guṇas* do not differentiate [the phoneme], the occurrence of the *sānunāsika* form by way of alternation (*paryāya*) would be unavoidable. Do not say so. For the desired result is established merely by the rule *eṅi paraḥ*; the inclusion of the term *rūpa* (form) makes it possible to intend the specific *guṇa* [of the suffix]. Indeed, the sole purpose of that [term *rūpa*] is this: that the form of the subsequent element—endowed with qualities such as the absence of *anunāsika*—should remain exactly as it is.

Therefore, the mention of *ka* in the rule for the root *jan* (Pāṇini 3.2.97) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that a *guṇa* substitute does not apply to a consonant. Thus, having reached the position that the Vārttika—"The mention of *iK* is for the purpose of excluding diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*) and consonants"—is inconsistent, the venerable Commentator (Bhagavān Bhāṣyakāra) states the following final conclusion (*siddhānta*): Even though diphthongs are excluded by the aforementioned indicator, the rule must still be formulated for the purpose of excluding consonants. As for the claim that the mention of *ka* in the rule for *jan* is the indicator, [it is refuted as follows].

That is not so; for this suffix *ḍa* must also be prescribed after the root *gam*. And when *guṇa* is applied to *gam*, by virtue of internal proximity (*āntarya*), an *o*-vowel would result. Consequently, forms such as *nagāḥ*, *agaḥ*, *abhyudgaḥ*, and *samudgaḥ* would not be established. Therefore, how could the status of being marked with *ḍ* (the *ḍittva*), which has already served its purpose there, indicate the absence of *guṇa* for a consonant?

But surely, the suffix *ḍa* is not prescribed for the root *gam* by the rule *janerḍaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.97); rather, it is another suffix *kaḍ*, introduced by the Vārttika *anyatrāpi dṛśyate*, which is read within the section beginning with *gamaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.47) and *antātyantādhvadūrapāra* (Pāṇini 3.2.48).

And so, how is it that the author of the Bhāṣya stated, "this suffix *ḍa* is also [added] after the root *gam*"? It is true: within the section beginning with "the suffix *ḍa* after the root *jan* in the locative case" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 3.2.97), it is beyond dispute that the suffix *ḍa* is prescribed by the rule "it is seen in other cases as well" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 3.2.101). The literal meaning of that rule is that the suffix *ḍa* is seen after the root *jan* even when other words are present as upapadas. By this, forms such as *ajaḥ*, *dvijaḥ*, and *anujaḥ* are established.

Even so, one might object that because there is no suffix *ḍa* after a different verbal root (*dhātu*), forms such as "parikhā" (a moat)—derived from the sense of "dug all around"—would not be established. Anticipating this, the author of the Vārttika stated: "It is also seen after other [roots]" (*anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate*). This very meaning, which was already indicated by the inclusion of the word *dṛśya* in the Sūtra itself, has been clarified by the Vārttika; it is not something newly included. Accordingly, the commentator (*vṛttikāra*) on that point says: "The word *api* is for the purpose of showing the deviation [of the rule] from all conditions (*upādhi*)."

Therefore, [the suffix] occurs even from other roots—as in *parikhā* (a moat), derived from *pari-khā* ("dug all around"). Because of the inclusion of the term "is seen" (*dṛśi-grahaṇāt*), it is clear in that very [work] that [the suffix applies] after other verbal roots and at other times, and so forth. This being the case, since forms such as *nagaḥ* and *agaḥ* are established by this very rule of the Sūtra—just like *parikhā*—the Vārttika need not have been composed at all. Or, if it were composed, it should be understood as being intended merely to explain the meaning already established by this Sūtra; with this intention, the Blessed One said: "Indeed, this suffix *ḍa* should also be stated after the root *gam*."

But even so, the *ḍit*-ness [of the affix] is indeed useless; for since the affix *ḍo* is prescribed by the rule "gamer ḍoḥ," it is understood that the *guṇa* substitution of the letter *m* does not become the vowel *o*. Therefore, the *ḍit*-ness of the affix *ḍu* is merely an indicator (*jñāpaka*) according to the reasoning stated previously. Furthermore, the prescription of the affix *ḍo* itself indicates that there is no *guṇa* substitution for a consonant. If it is objected: "If that were so, why prescribe *ḍo* when it could be accomplished by the affix *vic* alone?"—we reply: No, because if *vic* were used, the *guṇa* being applied would result in the nasalized vowel *o* (*on*), whereas the affix *ḍo* is prescribed to ensure the non-nasalized form. This is the general direction of the argument.

On this point, they say: "By the rule *tenoterḍauḥ sanvacca*, because the suffix is marked with the *ḍit* indicatory letter, there will be no *guṇa* substitution for the consonant. However, is this an extension (*atideśa*) of the *sāstra* (the rule itself) or an extension of the *kārya* (the grammatical operation)? In the first case, as in *ūrṇunaviṣati*, when [the form] is established as *taṃ-taṃ au* by the rule *dvirvacane 'ci* (Pāṇini 1.1.59), the vowel would become nasalized (*sānunāsika*) by the rule *sanyataḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.79). In the second case, however, the operations pertaining to the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) would be difficult to obtain."

That is not so; for in the first case, since the suffixes themselves serve as the indicators (*vaidaka*), the usage of "these two" (*imau*) or "these" (*ime*) is justified. In the second case as well, for the sake of forms such as *babhruḥ* and *juhūḥ*, the designation of "reduplication" (*abhyāsa-saṃjñā*) is accepted even when the dual number belongs to the base (*dātu*) under the governing rule [Pāṇini 1.4.10]. For this very reason, the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra *liṭi dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.8) states: "The mention of *dhātu* [in that sūtra] is merely a formal insertion (*sāṃnyāsika*)."

Although it was initially suggested in the Bhāṣya that the term *dhātu* (root) is understood [by anuvṛtti] from the rule *ādeca upadeśe’śiti* (Pāṇini 6.1.45), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) in the Bhāṣya on the rule for *ṣyaṅ* is that it is not so understood; therefore, the intention of the Bhāṣya must be described exactly in this way. This is the general direction [of the argument].

Furthermore, just as it was established in the *Hayavaraṭ* Sūtra that the rules for nasalization (*anunāsika*) and homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*)—which are refined by the maxim of "the closest [substitute] in respect of place" (*sthānentaratama*)—find their scope and purpose in cases such as *etanmurāriḥ* and *tvaṃ karoṣi* (where they apply due to similarity in both place and effort), and thus do not operate in cases like *caturmukhaḥ* and *kuṇḍaṃ rathena* (where there is no such similarity), so too here, the rule for *guṇa* before a *sarvadhātuka* suffix ending in *jus*, and the rules for *vṛddhi* and so forth before *sic*, find their application in examples such as *netā*, *abibhayuḥ*, and *anaiṣīt*.

In forms such as *umbhitā*, *anenijuḥ*, and *abhaitsīt*, [the rules for *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*] will not apply because their purpose has already been fulfilled. Nor should it be argued that, in cases like *netā* and *anaiṣīt*, where proximity is obtained through all three—position (*sthāna*), quality (*guṇa*), and measure (*pramāṇa*)—then in forms like *cetā* and *acaiṣīt*, where there is an absence of proximity in terms of measure, *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* would not occur. This is because the fact that proximity in terms of measure is not intended to be significant is indicated by the addition of the marker *k* in the rules *sṛghasyadaḥ kmarac* (Pāṇini 3.2.160) and *knōḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.63).

Nor should it be argued that even so, in the case of *īhitā* and *īśitā*, the *ha* and *śa* sounds—which are produced at the throat and the palate respectively, and are [otherwise] fully opened (*vivṛta*)—would likewise have to be [fully open] in those two words; for at the occasion of the refutation (*pratyākhyāna*) of the rule *nājjhalau* (Pāṇini 1.1.10), it will be established as a settled doctrine (*siddhānta*) that the sibilants (*ūṣman*) are slightly opened (*īṣadvivṛta*).

It should not be argued that, because the articulatory organs (*karaṇa*) are equally open (*vivṛta*), and since the *Śikṣā* states that *e* and *o* are more open than those [vowels], there would be no application of *guṇa* even in cases such as *cetā* and *netā*, owing to the absence of any distinction caused by the degree of openness (*vivṛtatva* vs. *vivṛtatara*). For if that were so, the rule [Pāṇini 1.1.5] would become devoid of scope; furthermore, based on the indications in rules such as "the *kṅit* suffixes are *karana*" (Pāṇini 1.1.5), which assign *kit* status to suffixes like *knasu*, *kmarac*, and others, one infers that *guṇa* must indeed apply to vowels such as *e*.

However, in the case of diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*) and consonants (*vyañjana*), it is more appropriate that the substitution of *guṇa* and other such elements does not occur; and thus there are such rules as "for *yā*, *vā*, *drā*, and *psā*" (Pāṇini 6.1.45), "there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) for the root *dhyai*" (Kātyāyana-vārttika), and "also for *vahati*, *cinoti*, and *degdhi*" (Pāṇini 6.1.46), and so forth.

If it is argued that by making *kn* a *kit*, it should rather be understood that the rule regarding "the nearest [substitute]" (*antaratama-paribhāṣā*) does not apply even when prescribing *guṇa* or *vṛddhi*—this is not so; for even if the rule regarding *ik* (*ik-paribhāṣā*) were present, the rule regarding the "nearest" would still be necessary to exclude *ā* and other vowels in favor of the *ī* vowel. Thus, since the consonant has been refuted in the Bhāṣya itself on account of its being marked with *ḍit*, its lack of proximity, and the specific mention [of *ai* and *au*], and since *ai* and *au* as well as *ā* have been refuted, this sūtra is therefore redundant.
Furthermore, if it is intended for the sake of subsequent rules, why is it desired to be a *paribhāṣā* (a governing rule) rather than having the *yoga* divided?

To this it is replied: In the rule *kṅiti ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.5), by relying on the fact that the word *ca* is a synonym for the word *iti*, it will first be explained that there is a prohibition of those *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* [substitutions] which [would otherwise apply]. Otherwise, even the *guṇa* of *o* would be prohibited in the case of *laugavāyaṇaḥ*; whereas forms such as *aupagavaḥ* would be its scope. Likewise, in the case of *paurohityam*, the initial *vṛddhi* would not occur.

This being the case, if this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) were rejected, then even though the status of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute behaves like the original) would ultimately result in the presence of *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, or a semivowel (*vid*), the prohibition [of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*] would not apply because the term "ik" is not explicitly uttered there, and thus the condition of being characterized by "ik" (*iglakṣaṇatva*) would be absent. Consequently, forms such as *kṛtaḥ*, *kṛtavān*, *kurutaḥ*, *chinnaṃ*, and *chinnavān* would not be established.

Furthermore, the prohibitive rule (*niṣedhasūtra*) would become devoid of scope (*nirviṣaya*) under the view that the technical designation (*paribhāṣā*) is abandoned, because the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* [substitutions] characterized by the term *ik* would not be established. This very point has been clarified by the author of the Bhāṣya: "In that case, the mention of *vṛddhi* is indeed for the sake of what follows, namely for the sake of the *sic*-affix. His intention is as follows: although, according to the method to be explained later, the status of being the substitute (*sthānitva*) is obtained for *ik* alone by elimination (*pariśeṣa*) in the injunction "there is *vṛddhi* before *sic*" (*sici vṛddhiḥ*, Pāṇini 7.2.1), nevertheless, the prohibition would not apply without the characteristic of being defined by *ik*.

Therefore, the mention of *vṛddhi* is for the sake of the subsequent rule and for the purpose of initiating the prohibition. By stating this, it is indicated—on the basis of the same underlying principle—that this very same purpose applies to the mention of *guṇa* as well.

But how is it that, in the rules for the application of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, there is everywhere a determination of a single substitute (*sthānin*) even without the application of the *al-antyaparibhāṣā* (the rule regarding the final letter), such that the [present sūtra] is described as having a prohibitory purpose? Listen: the two *guṇas* prescribed by the rules *sārvadhātukārddhadhātukayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.84) and *jusi ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.83) would, according to the *al-antyaparibhāṣā*, apply to the final vowel of the base (*aṅga*). However, due to the previously mentioned *jñāpaka*s (indicatory marks) and other reasons, they are excluded from vowels (*āt*), diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*), semivowels (*vyañjana*), and nasals (*ajan*), and thus they come to rest only in the case of the vowels *i*, *u*, and *ṛ*.

However, in the case of the *guṇa* substitutions for *mida*, *puganta*, *laghūpadha*, and so forth, the substituendum (*sthānin*) is indeed explicitly specified. For instance, in the rule *miderguṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.82), the meaning is "of *mida*"; that is, *mida* refers to the root *mid*. [In the rule] *pugantalaghūpadhasya ca*, there is a compound consisting of a collective aggregate (*samāhāradvandva*)—namely, *pukanta*, *paganta*, *laghūpadha*, and *laghūpadha*—from which the genitive case is derived. Nor does this lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *yāpayati*, because by the *sannipātalakṣaṇaparibhāṣā*, a grammatical operation characterized by a specific phonological configuration (such as the suffix *puG*) does not trigger another operation (such as *guṇa*) that would destroy that very configuration.

In the rule *ṛcchatyṝtām* (Pāṇini 7.4.11), there is also a *praśliṣṭanirdeśa* (a condensed enumeration) of three items: two instances of *ṛt* and one instance of the long vowel *ṛ*. For example: *ā* and *ṛ* and *ṛt*; or *ā* from *ṛcchati* and *ā* [from *āṅ*], and that [ā] and *ṛt*—thus it is a *dvandva* compound containing within it both a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* and a *dvandva*; or alternatively, it is a three-word *dvandva*: *ṛcchatyā*, *ā*, and *ṛtaḥ*. By this means, the status of being a *sthānin* (original substitute) is obtained for the *ṛ* of *ṛcchati*.

In reality, however, four *praśleṣas* (conjunctive insertions) are to be understood here; by means of these, the *guṇa* substitution for the root *ṛ* in forms such as *ārivān sarvabharuṇānyāruṣi* is established through the force of its being prescribed again [in this rule]. Otherwise, due to the force of making *kvasu* a *kit* suffix, the *guṇa* would be prohibited, just as it is in *titīrvān*. And this is because, even in the rule *kvasuśca* (Pāṇini 7.2.67), the *yoga* is divided as "there is *guṇa* when *u* follows," and from that, *dṛśaḥ* [is added], with *uḥ* etc. being carried over [from the previous rule].

In the rule *sthūladūra* (Pāṇini 6.4.156), a split of the *yoga* (separation of the rule into parts) must also be made: one *yoga* is *sthūladūrayuvahasvānāṃ yaṇādiparam*, and another *yoga* is *kṣiprakṣudrayoḥ pūrvasya ca guṇaḥ*. In that case, forms such as *sthavīyān* are established by the *guṇa* substitution for the vowel (*o*). This is because the non-eternality of the status of "not yet established" (*ābhīyāsiddhatva*)—as taught in the rule *śnasorallopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.111)—is indicated by the inclusion of the *tapara* marker (*ṛ*), and because the author of the *Bhāṣya* has rejected [the application of] that status.

The compound *yaṇādi* means "that which has a semi-vowel (*yaṇ*) as its initial. Thus, the meaning is that when the letters *pa* and *da*—which are the initials of the semi-vowels *ya* and *va* respectively—follow [the vowels *i* and *u*], there is elision of the following letter *ra*, and by those very two [semi-vowels], there is the substitution of a *guṇa* for the preceding *i*-vowel or *u*-vowel. Therefore, in this way, all *guṇas* rest upon the vowels *i* and *u*. Furthermore, in the rule *mṛjer vṛddhiḥ*, the word *acaḥ* ("of a vowel") is also drawn down [from the previous rule]. Thus, the full formulation is: "In place of the vowel of *mṛj*, there is *vṛddhi*; then, when a suffix marked with *ñ* or *ṇ* follows, [there is *vṛddhi*] of the vowel [only]."

Nor should it be argued that, in this way, there would be a *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) for the augment *aṭ* as well in the form *āmārṭ*; for when the substitutes for *l* have been applied, according to the view that *āṭ* [is inserted] before them, the *vṛddhi* occurs first because it is of higher priority, after which *aṭ* is added. Once that has occurred, a further *vṛddhi* does not take place, because the rule has already fulfilled its purpose through its single application (*sakṛtpravṛttyā*).

However, when—rather than rejecting the sūtra as unestablished—one relies on the dual-lakāra notation "luṅ," and either by carrying over one of the two terms "upadeśe" or "ārddhadhātuke," the augment *aṭ* is applied precisely at the stage of the suffixal stem (*lā-avasthā*); or when, having split the rule "eranekācaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.82) and carried over "iṇo yaṇ," one adopts the restrictive rule that if the suffix is non-monosyllabic, then *yaṇ* occurs only for the root *iṇ*, thereby preventing *yaṇ* in forms such as "addhyaiyātām"—then, although the *vṛddhi* substitution does not occur at the stage of the suffixal stem because the *lakāras* possess the marker *ṅ*.

This is because [the augment] is prohibited in cases such as *mṛṣṭaḥ*. Consequently, by virtue of its being antaranga, the augment *aṭ* alone would apply; nevertheless, one must set aside the vṛddhi of *aṭ* by relying on the paribhāṣā: "In the absence of the final [element], [the operation applies] to that which stands in the same position as the final. However, in the view where this paribhāṣā is rejected, the suffix—projected by the term "aṅga"—is qualified by the vowel (*ac*), and the form *amārṭ* and others are established by the principle of non-intervention (*yena nāvyavadhāna*). Furthermore, even when the vṛddhi is to be prescribed in the case of the suffix *sic*, the *ik-paribhāṣā* has no utility, as there is nothing left to be excluded.

Furthermore, the vowel *a* in *acikīrṣīt* is not to be excluded [by the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayordīrghaḥ*], because it is already established by the elision of the suffix (*al-lopa*) itself, according to the statement: "The elision of the suffix (*al*), the *iy-aṅ*, the *yaṇ*, the *guṇa*, the *vṛddhi*, and the long vowel take precedence over each other in order of enumeration" (*pūrvavipratiṣiddham*). Otherwise, forms such as *cikīrṣakaḥ* would not be possible, and *cikīrṣāyakaḥ* would result as an undesirable consequence. As for the vowel *ā*, there is no distinction [in its application], and it has been stated that it is superseded by the augment *sa* and the suffix *ṭ*. Nor is a form ending in *ej* possible, because of the specific prescription of *ātva* (the substitution of *ā*). However, in cases such as *udavoḍhām*, the elision of *ḍh* is treated as non-existent (*asiddhatā*).

In the case of words such as *rāya-nigla-uś* ending in the *kvip* suffix used in the sense of habitual action (*ācāra*), there is no difference whether the *vṛddhi* substitution occurs or not. Furthermore, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) even in the case of *agavīt* derived from the word *go* with the *kvip* suffix; this is because Kaiyaṭa and others explain that, by the recurrence of the term *dhātu* (root) from Pāṇini 7.1.100 (*ṛta id dhātoḥ*), which qualifies the root implied by the *sic* suffix, the rule applies only to that which is a root in its own right and not something that is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) in any way whatsoever.

[Objection: "In that case, Mādhava—who states that 'the vṛddhi [substitution] in the *sic* suffix subverts even an internal *guṇa*'—would be contradicted by such forms as *kaveḥ akavāyīt*, *vidhoḥ avidhāvīt*, and *pituḥ apitārīt*. [Reply: True. However, if there is a firm insistence on ensuring consistency, then it should be explained in this way: both *otaḥ* (of a stem ending in *o*) and *dhātoḥ* (of a verbal root) are understood to carry over [from the preceding rule]. And these, being connected through a division of sentences (*vākya-bheda*), result in a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*): "If there is *vṛddhi* for a verbal root ending in *o*, then it must be for a verbal root [and] not for a nominalized root (*nāmadhātu*)."*

Alternatively, in the rule *neṭi* (Pāṇini 7.2.4), one may divide the connection by the word *na*, and either through the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*) method or by the continued application of the context, one should carry forward the term *gotaḥ*; thus, the *vṛddhi* of a verbal root ending in *au* is prohibited. Or else, carrying forward the term *bahulam* from the rule *bahulaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 7.1.103), the matter may somehow be resolved as follows: the *vṛddhi* occurs in the *sic* affix after a nominal root (*nāmadhātu*) ending in *a*, but not after one ending in *o*.

The over-extension [of the rule] regarding the nasalization (*anunāsika*) and the homogeneous sound (*parasavarṇa*), which occurs by means of the nearest [consonant] among the consonants, has indeed already been removed. However, even granting that [the objection], we say: since the *vṛddhi* substitution characterized by a final consonant (*hal-anta-lakṣaṇā*) is being introduced when the *vṛddhi* [prescribed] for *sic* has not yet applied, it will serve as the sublater.

The prohibition [stated] in *naṭi* (Pāṇini 7.1.4), however, applies to all possible *vṛddhi* that might apply to a stem ending in a consonant—whether by *sici vṛddhiḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.1) or *halantasya* (Pāṇini 7.2.3)—and there is no insistence on its being produced by a specific rule. Therefore, in forms such as *akoṣīt* and *amoṣīt*, both types of *vṛddhi* are prohibited; thus, the matter is well-established. Consequently, it is settled that this rule exists to ensure that the [root-final vowel] is characterized as having the *ik* designation (*iglakṣaṇatā*), so that the prohibition may be effective.

It might be argued: "Let the mention of *guṇa* (vocalization) be for the sake of establishing the prohibition in cases such as *kṛtaḥ*, *kṛtavān*, *chinnaḥ*, and *chinnavān*. However, the mention of *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) is redundant. Nor can its purpose be the establishment of the prohibition in cases such as *mṛṣṭaḥ* and *mṛṣṭavān*, because that is already established through a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule). For instance, immediately after the rule *mṛjer vṛddhiḥ*, a statement in the form *ajādau kṅiti vā* must necessarily be formulated for the sake of deriving forms such as *mṛjanti*."

This being the case, the rule *kṅiti* (Pāṇini 1.2.5) is divided when applied to roots beginning with vowels (*aj-ādi*). This is for the purpose of restriction: "If [the substitution] occurs before *kṅit*, it occurs only before those [roots] beginning with a vowel. By this, forms such as *mṛṣṭaḥ* and *mṛṣṭavān* are established. Then, for the sake of the option even before roots beginning with a vowel, the second rule *vā* (Pāṇini 1.2.6) is stated. Therefore, the result of including the mention of *vṛddhi* [in the rule *vṛddhir ādaic*] is difficult to justify. On this point, they say: "The roots *ṇū* 'to praise' and *dhū* 'to shake' are recited among the *kuṭādi* group. From these two, in the *luṅ* [aorist], the forms *anuvīt* and *adhuvīt* are desired."

In this context, the mention of *vṛddhi* [in the rule *sici vṛddhiḥ parasmaipadeṣu*] is intended to establish that the *vṛddhi* is not characterized by *iK*, so as to trigger the prohibition by the rule *kṅiti*. If it is argued: "But here, since the substitution *uvaṅ* depends only on the *siC* which is internally contained [within the complex], it is an *antaranga* operation; once *uvaṅ* has been applied, the word ends in a consonant (*halanta*), and thus the prohibition by the rule *neṭi* (Pāṇini 7.2.4) is already established"—we say no. This is because of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that there is no *antaranga* operation within the domain of *siC*; consequently, the *vṛddhi* would apply even prior to the *uvaṅ* substitution.

It might be argued as follows: "The internal (*antaraṅga*) is stronger" will indeed be established in the rule *acaḥ parasmin* (Pāṇini 1.1.57). Therefore, let that [principle] apply without distinction even to the *sic* suffix. Nor should it be said that, if this were so, the *guṇa* substitution would occur in forms such as *ahaiṣīt*; for since *vṛddhi* is possible in that very case, we accept the desired result. Indeed, there is no mention of the term *vidhi* at present, by which the *vṛddhi* of the single vowel *e* would not be obtained.

Nor should it be argued that even so, in forms such as *astaupīt*, because the *guṇa* substitution would apply first due to its being "internal" (*antaraṅga*), there would be no possibility of *vṛddhi* under the interpretative view that "the [augment] *it* does not follow a stem ending in *o*" (*oto na*); and that under the alternative view—that by virtue of the mention of "diversity" (*bahulagrahaṇa*), the augment does not follow non-*i*-stem roots—there would likewise be a fault in forms such as *acaiṣīt*. This is because all objections are resolved by adopting the third position: that the rule applies only to verbal roots (*dhātu*) ending in *o*, and not to nominalized roots (*nāmadhātu*). Thus, let there be *vṛddhi* characterized by a consonant-final stem in forms such as *akārṣīt*.

In forms such as *atārīt*, however, because the internal (*antaraṅga*) guna substitution takes precedence, the rule for vṛddhi conditioned by a final consonant (*halanta-lakṣaṇā*) applies; yet, when that vṛddhi is prohibited by *neṭi* (Pāṇini 7.2.4), it overrides the optional vṛddhi prescribed by *ato halādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.7), and the obligatory vṛddhi of *ato lrāntasya* (Pāṇini 7.2.2) prevails.

Even in cases such as *alāvīt*, since the internal (*antaraṅga*) operations of guṇa and āvādeśa have already taken effect, the rule *ato lrāntasya* (Pāṇini 7.2.2) will result in the obligatory (*nitya*) vṛddhi, because the rule *lopo vyoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.76)—which provides for the elision of the *v*—is explained as applying there as well. Thus, one obtains *mā bhavānavīt*. If it is argued that in this case too, the vṛddhi would then be obligatory, [the answer is] no; for by removing the mention of *ṇi* and *śvi* and inserting *avi* and *mavi* in their place, the prohibition of vṛddhi is established.

Indeed, the inclusion of the root *ṇi* (in the rule) would not be necessary in this view; for in forms such as *auṇayīt* and *aśvayīt*, since the rules for *guṇa* and *āy-ādeśa* are internal (*antaraṅga*), the prohibition "not for those ending in *y*" (*yāntānām na*) would already be established. [Objection: If this were so, then just as with the root *av*, there would always be a prohibition for *mav* as well, yet an option (*vikalpa*) is desired.

This is not a fault. In the rule *ato lrāntasya* (Pāṇini 7.2.2), by the inclusion (*praśleṣa*) of the letter *v*, the permanent (*nitya*) *vṛddhi* that would otherwise apply is here prohibited for the root *mav* by the rule *na avimavyoḥ*; however, this does not prohibit the application of *ato halādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.7) as well. This is according to the maxim: "Exceptions (*apavāda*) situated in the middle sublate preceding rules, but not subsequent ones.

Nor does this lead to the same undesirable consequence for the root *jāgṛ*, because in that case, one accepts that by resorting to a consideration of the general class of what is to be sublated (*bādhyasāmānyacintā*), everything applicable within its own scope is sublated.

Alternatively, one must accept that when an exception (*apavāda*) is negated, the general rule (*utsarga*) does not apply; however, in the present case, it does apply. This is because, as will be stated immediately below, the determination of whether the object of negation (*bādhyasāmānya*) proceeds or does not proceed once the exception (*bādhaka*) has been negated—whether based on a consideration of the general or the particular—is governed by the requirements of the specific linguistic examples (*lakṣya*). Nor should it be argued that, by the same logic, the obligatory *vṛddhi* would occur in the form *agavīt* due to the inclusion of the letter *v* [in the root *gū*]; for this too is prevented by the mention of "root" (*dhātu*), just as the *vṛddhi* in the context of *sic* is prevented.

Therefore, since forms such as *anuvīt* and *adhuvīt* are established simply by resorting to the internal (*antaraṅga*) substitution of *sici*, there is no need for the prohibition [of guṇa] stated in Pāṇini 1.1.5 (*kṅiti ca*); consequently, the mention of "vṛddhi" [in the rule under discussion] is indeed redundant.

To this it is replied: If there were the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the letter *va*, then even for the verbal root *śabdhi*—which the author of the Bhāṣya accepts in the *Paspaśā* section as being synonymous with *śavati* (meaning "to go") among the Kambojas, while the Āryas use the very same word as a modification (*vikāra*)—there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of obligatory *vṛddhi*. Or, if that too were prohibited, how could [the forms] *kaṇiśca* and *nimāna* be established? For that would result in excessive complexity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, we do not say that another rule (*sūtra*) is internal (*antaraṅga*) out of mere pedantry; rather, it is on the strength of logic, the force of an indicator (*jñāpaka*), and in accordance with the results [of the system].

For instance, that which is not subject to the rule of non-attainment (*aprāpti*) is sublated by the internal (*antaraṅga*) rule through the operation of *vṛddhi*, because it is accepted that "sublation occurs even when [the rules] are both possible. Otherwise, curd would not be sublated by buttermilk (*takra*), nor would the suffixes *śap*, *kap*, and so on, be sublated by *śnam*, *akac*, and the like; for both would be possible due to a difference in location (*deśabheda*). Nor should it be argued that, according to the maxim of the intermediate exception (*madhyepavādanyāya*), only *uvaṅ* is sublated by *vṛddhi* and not *guṇa* as well. For this would only be the case if there were an intention to express the sublated elements as distinct entities.

However, in the consideration of what is to be sublated (*bādhya*) in its general form, everything that has obtained its own scope and serves as a non-exception (*anapavāda*) is sublated; for example, by the rule *aci ra* (Pāṇini 7.2.100), the *guṇa*, *dīrgha*, and *utva* [substitutions] are all sublated. Otherwise, even there, according to the maxim of "the exception in the middle" (*madhye’pavāda*), the *repha* would sublate only the *dīrgha* and *utva*, but not the *guṇa*, because of its posteriority. Furthermore, regarding the sublated element, both types of consideration are employed—sometimes by way of distinction and sometimes by way of a general form—in accordance with the requirements of the specific linguistic examples (*lakṣya*) in each respective case.

Furthermore, the mention of *ṇi* and *śvi* here serves as an indicator (*liṅga*). Otherwise, since the operations of *guṇa* and *ay-ādeśa* would be internal (*antaraṅga*), the forms *aunayīt* and *aśvayīt* and so forth would be established simply by the prohibition "not for those ending in *y*" (*yāntānām na*); what then would be the purpose of mentioning *ṇi* and *śvi*? Another indicator has also been stated in the Bhāṣya: "And that which [the rule] does—namely, the mention of the letter *a* in the rule *laghoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.94)—even though [the *a*] has already been applied."

The intention here is as follows: regarding the mention of *at* in the rule *ato halādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.7), diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*) and the like are not excluded by it, since they are already ruled out by the mention of *laghu*. Only *it*, *ut*, and *ṛt* remain—namely, in the cases of *acetīt*, *akoṣīt*, and *anartīt*. If these too are superseded by the internal operation (*antaraṅga*) of *guṇa*, then the mention of *at* would be rendered useless.

Nor should it be said that the word *tat* (that) is used for the purpose of excluding the vowel *u* in forms such as *akuṭīt* and *apuṭīt*; for even there, once the *vṛddhi* is sublated by the *guṇa* which is *antaraṅga*, the *vṛddhi* does not apply again even if the *guṇa* is subsequently prohibited by the *ṅit*-affix, according to the maxim: "When the killer of Devadatta is slain, Devadatta does not rise again. For this very reason, when the reading is *nāntaḥpādam*, once the *pūrvarūpa* is prohibited, the *ay-ādi* substitutions do not take effect either.

Therefore, it is accepted in the Bhāṣya that [forms] such as *sujāte aśvasūnṛte* are established. Nor should it be argued that, in the absence of an exception (*apavāda*), the general rule (*utsarga*) would remain in force—such that in cases like *vṛkṣau*, once the substitution of the homogeneous vowel (*pūrvasavarṇa*) by the rule *nādici* (Pāṇini 6.1.104) is prohibited, the rule for *vṛddhi* would likewise not apply. For this is shown by indicative marks (*liṅga*) such as *bhidyoddhyau nade* (Pāṇini 3.1.115) and *tau sat* (Pāṇini 3.2.127), which demonstrate that when an exception is prohibited, the general rule also does not take effect.

This is because it is accepted that this [rule] is not universally applicable (*asārvatrika*). This very point is stated here and there: "Being prohibited, it does not dare to sublate [what has already been established].
