And thus, based on the distinction between different *pakṣas* (theories), it is established that even the mention of the term "beginning with a consonant" (*halādi*) in the rule *ato halādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.7) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

There is also a functional result [of this rule]. For if *sic* were an internal element (*antaraṅga*), then in the case of the *luṅ* [aorist] following roots such as *cin*, *tan*, etc., which take *yaṅluk*, and the roots *ciriṇoti* and *jiriṇoti*, forms such as *acecāyīt*, *anenanāyīt*, *acirāyīt*, and *ajirāyīt* would not be possible; because once *guṇa* and *āy-ādeśa* have been applied, the prohibition "not for those ending in *y*" (*yāntānām na*) would apply. Even if one were to resort to the maxim of "an intermediate exception sets aside [only what follows it]" (*madhyepavādanyāya*) during the consideration of specific sublation—maintaining that only *uvaṅ* is sublated and not *guṇa*—even then, this would still not be established.

Therefore, in order to establish the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that even everything internal (*antaraṅga*) does not exist at all when the suffix *sic* is present, one must rely solely on the consideration of the general sublated element (*bādhyasāmānyacintā*). Indeed, it is for this very purpose that the citation of an indicator (*jñāpaka*) was provided in the Bhāṣya.

Otherwise, since the sublation of even an *antaraṅga* rule is established by logic (*nyāya*) alone, what is the purpose of describing an *jñāpaka* (indicatory mark)? This being the case, in forms such as *nyanuvīt* and *nyadhuvīt*, one must simply rely on the prohibition [of guṇa] stated in Pāṇini 1.1.5 (*kṅiti ca*). Consequently, it is established that the mention of *vṛddhi* here is indeed necessary for the sake of establishing the status of [the rule] as being characterized by *i*. And this being so, because of the impossibility [of both applying simultaneously], all *antaraṅga* operations are sublated by *vṛddhi* in the *sic*-affix.

For if it were so, then in no case would a limb (*aṅga*) ending in *sic* be found; this must be kept in mind. Thus, since it is established that the definition of *it* (the vowel *i*) is necessary for the application of the prohibition, the exclusion of diphthongs (*saṃdhyakṣara*), consonants (*vyañjana*), and so forth in various instances is also accomplished by the very *ik-paribhāṣā*; therefore, the laborious recourse to the description of *jñāpaka*s (indirect evidence) and the like need not be adopted.

Nor should it be argued that, by virtue of the presence of the word *ik* [in Pāṇini’s rule], the substitution of *au*, *ā*, and *at* would likewise apply in cases such as *dyauḥ*, *panthāḥ*, and *imam*; for when the terms *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are carried over [from previous rules], the repetition of the terms *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* serves to indicate that the operation of the words themselves is also intended. Alternatively, this is established through the qualification provided by the two terms as they are carried over: "those which are *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* [substitutions] themselves, and not those prescribed by other words."

But surely, since in the rule *acaśca* (Pāṇini 1.2.28), the term *pada* will be understood through the application of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) by virtue of the continued reference to the mention of "short vowels" (*hrasva*) and so forth, then by that very force, the term *pada* will not apply in rules such as *diva aut* (7.1.84), *pathimadhyṛbhukṣāmāt* (7.1.85), and *tyadādīnāmaḥ* (7.2.102).

If it were so, then the deliberate effort made in the rule *acaśca* (Pāṇini 1.2.27)—stating that when a designation (*saṃjñā*) is prescribed, [the term *ac*] refers to the technical name "vowel"—would be useless. This is not the case; for that effort serves its purpose by excluding the metarule regarding *ac* in rules such as *divaut* (Pāṇini 6.1.131), where *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are designated [as substitutes for vowels]. Furthermore, it serves its purpose in rules such as *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau* (Pāṇini 7.2.84), because the short vowel *ik* cannot possibly occur there.

Therefore, the ancients maintain that the term *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are mentioned again here, even though they have already been defined, in order to establish a restrictive rule (*niyama*) for the application of these technical names (*saṃjñāvidhāna*), so as to ensure the correct formation of words such as *dyauḥ*, *panthāḥ*, and *imam*. But is not *panthāḥ* a poor example? For [the substitution of *at*] in rules such as *ito't* (Pāṇini 7.1.86) is already accounted for by the impossibility of applying the name *ik* there. Therefore, the ancients hold that the mention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* is repeated here to establish a restrictive rule for the application of these technical names, so as to ensure the correct formation of words such as *dyauḥ*, *panthāḥ*, and *imam*.

If it is argued that "pathaḥ" (*panthāḥ*) is not a valid example because the form is already established by Pāṇini 7.1.86 (*itaśca*), and therefore the rule for *āt* has no force since the word *ik* does not apply here; we say no. This is because the rule for *āt* could indeed apply in the sense of the vowels *ṛ*, *u*, *ṝ*, and *ū*. Nor should it be said that this is not the case because of the intended meaning of immediate succession (*anantarya*) between *ik* and *s*, and because of the reliance on non-intervention (*avyavadhāna*); for even so, the force of the rule is exhausted by its purpose of applying to the vocative (*sambuddhi*).

Nor should it be argued that one should simply say "itah āt" instead; for if that were so, the form *ṛbhukṣaṇam indram* would fail to be established. For in the rule prescribing *āt*, its establishment occurs by the rule *vā ṣapūrvasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.9). As for the examples *saḥ* and *imam* cited in the Bhāṣya, those are merely imitations of a portion of a Brāhmaṇa passage stating "he saw this mantra. However, they maintain that the actual example is only *imam* and not even *saḥ*; because when the word *tat* is used, an *ik* vowel is impossible, and thus the restriction *ikaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.3) does not apply.

In reality, however, the example *saḥ* is indeed correct. The rule *tyadādīnāmaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.102) is an injunctive statement. In that context, if the word *ekaḥ* were present [in the rule], the substitution of *atva* would apply only to *dvi* and *idam*, and not to others. The mention of the group (*gaṇa*) by name is for the purpose of excluding technical terms (*saṃjñā*) and secondary members (*upasarjana*), as well as for the sake of subsequent rules. For the substitution of *s* in the rule *tadoḥ saḥ sau* (Pāṇini 7.2.106) is prescribed specifically for the *t* and *d* of the *tyadādi* group.

In this regard, the following should be noted: even for the sake of conforming to the employment of the function of words (*śabdavyāpāra*), the mention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* need not be included; the desired result is established by the mere statement "of *ik*" (*ikaḥ*). In fact, even the word "both" (*tau*) is redundant. Let the rule simply be formulated as "of *ik*" (*ikaḥ*). This is because, by interpreting the rule such that the entirety of the two preceding rules is carried over (*anuvartana*), the term "of *ik*" applies wherever *vṛddhi* is prescribed—as in "vṛddhi is [the substitute] for *āT* and *aiC"—and wherever *guṇa* is prescribed—as in "guṇa is [the substitute] for *eC* and *oC". The internal evidence (*liṅga*) for this interpretation is the inclusion of the term "i" in the rule "i is substituted for the final letter of a root ending in *it*" (*ito't*, Pāṇini 7.1.86).

Otherwise, even in that case, when the word *ik* is presented [in the mind], once the exclusion of *ṛ* and *ṝ* has occurred according to the aforementioned method by the maxim of "that which intervenes does not intervene" (*yenāvyavadhāna-nyāya*), one might ask: "What is the use of that? This very point is indicated by the *bhāṣya*—"What is the purpose of the mention of *ik*?"—as well as by the *vārttika*—"The mention of *ik* is for the sake of [excluding] the diphthongs (*ātsandhyakṣara*) and so forth. For otherwise, he would have simply said, "What is the purpose of the rule (*sūtra*)? and so on.

As for the description of the intent of the Bhāṣya—that the mention of *iK* was stated with the underlying thought that the mention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* must indeed be made for the sake of the subsequent rules—that is not correct; for since the rule is established by the mere carry-over (*anuvṛtti*) from the preceding sūtra, it is difficult to justify its being "for the sake of the subsequent" (*uttarārtha*). Furthermore, whether one considers the whole or adopts the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*) method of connection, you yourself must admit the carry-over of the relationship [from the previous rule]. Moreover, since the mention of *iK* would also serve the purpose of the subsequent rules, the doubt regarding that portion [of the rule] remains unresolved.

If it is argued that the seed of the question—"For what purpose is the rule *ikaḥ* divided [into two parts]?"—is intended, then one should simply ask: "In that case, for what purpose is the sūtra [even] regarding the portions of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, since that [division] is no different there either? This is the direction of the argument.

As for the claim that this is an implication of the whole through its principal constituent parts, that too is not particularly consistent with the natural force of the words. Therefore, the previously stated intention alone is correct. Nor does this lead to an inconsistency with the subsequent passage, "By the force of the repeated mention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* in the section on *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*," because that passage intends the literal meaning [of the repetition]. This is because the word *grahaṇa* (mention) is intended to signify recurrence (*anuvṛtti*), or else it signifies the force of the recurrence of the two complete sūtras; such is the direction of the argument.

Thus, the very fact that there is "only one" (eka) *yogavibhāga* is established through the presentation of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*); this is the ultimate meaning here. Consequently, since all desired results are accomplished by this single *yogavibhāga*, it is settled that the description of an alternative derivation (*anyathāsiddhi*)—by resorting to a much greater number of *yogavibhāgas* such as *mṛjervṛddhiracaḥ* and *uraṅi guṇaḥ*—is not to be respected.

Although seven possible positions may be conceived regarding this metarule—namely, that it is a supplement (*śeṣa*) to the "final-element" rule (*alontyaparibhāṣā*), or its subordinate (*śeṣibhūta*), or conjoined with it, or optional (*vaikalpika*), or an exception (*apavāda*) to it, or a sublater of it by means of the "prior-contradiction" principle (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), or a provider of the word-base (*padopasthāpikā*)—nevertheless, because the first six are defective, only the seventh has been established as the final conclusion.

For instance, in the rule *sārvadhātukārddhadhātukayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.84), two paribhāṣās are present by virtue of their respective causes. In that context, if the genitive case in *aṅgasya* were first taken to refer to the final phoneme—such that "the guṇa [substitution] applies to the final phoneme of the aṅga"—and subsequently the *ik* is qualified [as being part of that aṅga], then the other paribhāṣā (*iko yaṇ aci*) would become the remainder.

If, however, by first qualifying the *aṅga* [with *ik*], the rule of "extension to that which ends in" (*tadantavidhi*) applies such that it means "of an *aṅga* ending in *iK*," and then, by the principle of "the operation applies to the final letter" (*alo’ntyasya*), [the substitution occurs], then this is the second position. Both of these two positions—relying respectively on a genitive *tatpuruṣa* and a *bahuvrīhi*—are referred to in the *Bhāṣya* as the "position of its being a supplement" (*taccheṣapakṣa*). In both of these positions, there is a fault in rules such as "there is *guṇa* for *mid*" (*mider guṇaḥ*, Pāṇini 7.3.82). For that which is the final letter of *mid* is not *ik*, and that which is *ik* is not the final letter.

And likewise, when the restrictive rule (*paribhāṣā*) is necessarily abandoned, since there would be no criterion for selection (*vinigamakābhāvāt*), both [the *sthānin* and the *ādeśa*] would be abandoned, and the *guṇa* substitution would apply to the whole [of the base]. This has been stated by the author of the Vārttika: "If it is argued that 'vṛddhi' and 'guṇa' apply to the final [element], then there must be the mention of *mid*, *mṛj*, roots ending in *puk*, those with a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha*), as well as *ṛcchi*, *dṛśi*, *kṣipra*, and *kṣudra*; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [the substitution] applying to the whole, and this would apply even to a base not ending in *ani*. The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of a reason (*hetu*). Consequently, the result is that there would indeed be the undesirable consequence of the substitution applying to the whole.

Now, if by some means—following the previously mentioned method beginning with "mida irmidiḥ" and "tasya mideḥ"—one were to obtain a single substitute as the locus (*sthānin*) in all these cases, even so, in forms such as *bhinnam*, there would be no prohibition of *guṇa* because [the substitution] is not characterized by *i*. If it is argued that the prohibition applies even when not characterized by *i* due to the indicatory *k* (*kit*) in *knū*, then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *laigavāyanaḥ* and *paurohityam*.

If, on the other hand, the indicator (jñāpaka) pertains only to the scope of the guna substitution for a light penultimate vowel in accordance with the specific forms (lakṣya), then let the position that [the suffix] presents the word-base (pada) be adopted for the sake of establishing those forms; for in this way, even the trouble of resorting to an indicator is avoided. Furthermore, let it be indicated by the *kit* status itself that the word-base is presented; for in this way, there is economy (lāghava), as one need not postulate another separate rule based on the indicator.

"Let the third alternative then be accepted: that both [the *mi* of *mid* and the final letter] undergo *guṇa*, and the *ik* [of the root] also undergoes *guṇa*. Not so; for it is difficult to obtain two distinct meanings—namely, the relation of *sthāna-yoga* (substitution) and the relation of being a part (*avayava*)—from a genitive case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) pronounced simultaneously. This is because the rule regarding the substitution of the final letter (*al-antyavidhi*) cannot apply without a relation of *sthāna*. As will be stated later, the genitive of *sthāna* is indeed the indicator (*liṅga*) for the application of that rule. Furthermore, since the word *ikaḥ* cannot be construed with the genitive of part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) without [an explicit statement], and because there is no evidence for [assuming] repetition (*āvṛtti*) or other such devices.

By this, the fourth alternative—that there is either *vi* or *eka* for the final letter of the root *mid*—is also refuted, because such an optionality (*vikalpa*) is beset by eight logical faults (*doṣa*).

Let it then be the fifth alternative: that this [the rule *guṇo yaṅlukoh*] is an exception (*apavāda*) to that [the rule *iko guṇavṛddhī*]. For instance, in the rule *guṇo yaṅlukoh*, the genitive case in *aṅgasya* is not a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*); rather, it is a genitive of constituent part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) with respect to the *ik*. Consequently, due to the absence of a [specific] indicator (*liṅga*), the paribhāṣā "of the final letter" (*alontyaparibhāṣā*) does not apply. And this very point constitutes the meaning of the term "exception" (*bādha*): if the paribhāṣā concerning the *ik* did not exist, then the genitive would be a genitive of location, and consequently, the paribhāṣā "of the final letter" rooted in that would apply.

In the discussion concerning the nature of truth, the designation "exception" (*apavāda*) is applied merely by the fact that both [the general rule and the exception] do not apply simultaneously; for in reality, the sublation (*bādha*) of what has been established by a statement is impossible, as that would entail the invalidity of the scripture. Therefore, they say that "sublation" is the restriction of the intended scope (*tātparya-saṅkoca*) of the scripture. By this, the statement "the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) is an exception to the *dvandva* (copulative compound)" is also explained.

If the case-ending had not yet been produced, there would be the contingency of a *dvandva* compound; however, if *ekaśeṣa* were not to occur, then each word would individually take its own case-ending and form a *dvandva*. But since *ekaśeṣa* does occur, that [contingency] does not arise—this is the truth. And on this view, the *guṇa* substitution prescribed by the rule *sārvadhātukārddhadhātukayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.84) would apply in cases such as *anenijuḥ* and *paryaveviṣuḥ*, just as it does in *ajuhavuḥ*. Furthermore, the *guṇa* would also apply in *ihitā*, just as it does in *bhavati*.

And so says the Vārttika: "If it is argued that [the rule] applies to every *iṅ* vowel, then there must be a prohibition against [guṇa substitution] for non-final vowels in the case of *jus*, as well as in the case of the four types of guṇa substitutions for *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes beginning with a short vowel. Here, by the phrase "beginning with a short vowel" (*hrasvādi*), the fourfold set of guṇa rules is understood: *hrasvasya guṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.108), *jusi ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.109), *ṛto’ṅi sarvanāmasthānayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.110), and *gher ṅiti* (Pāṇini 7.3.111).

Furthermore, the author of the Vārttika maintains that just as the five-fold *guṇa* ending in *oḥ guṇaḥ* occurs in cases such as *he agne*, *agnayaḥ*, *kartari*, *agnaye*, and *bābhravyaḥ*, so too should it occur in *he agnicit*, *agnicitaḥ santi*, *sukṛti*, *agnicite*, and *sauśrutaḥ*. Although this paribhāṣā is difficult to apply here because [the rule] specifies a particular locus (*nirdiṣṭasthānikatvāt*).

Furthermore, because the word *agnicit* lacks the designation *ghi*, the rule *gher ṅiti* (Pāṇini 7.3.111) would not apply; nevertheless, they describe the possibility of such a statement in the Vārttika as follows: "In the two rules *hrasvasya guṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.108) and *jasi ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.109), [the term] *hrasva* (short vowel) is restricted by *igvali*; and the exclusion of long vowels is the result."

Now, one might ask: how can this restrictive *paribhāṣā* apply here when there is no fixed rule [regarding what is replaced]? For one could argue that if the short vowel (*hrasva*) were the substitute, there would be no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), since the *guṇa* of the vowel *a* would simply be *a* itself. To this, it must be said: the meaning of the sūtra would then be "the *guṇa* of the single substitute for a stem ending in a short vowel. Consequently, [the rule] would apply even to non-final vowels, as in "he upago," while forms such as "agnicit" would have to be excluded by the qualification [of the sūtra].

Thus, between the two rules "hrasvasya" and "ikaḥ," there is no mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified; rather, one is a qualifier of the *aṅga* (base), while the other is the qualified (*viśeṣya*). Alternatively, lest "hrasvasya" become a qualifier of the *aṅga*, the *ik-paribhāṣā* would apply to establish that the genitive case in "aṅgasya" is a genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*), thereby effecting the *guṇa* substitution even for a vowel that is not final.

Thus, for the purpose of prescribing *guṇa* substitution for non-final vowels in both cases—namely by the rules *ṛto ṅi-sarvanāmasthānayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.110) and *auto ’m-śasoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.146)—this *paribhāṣā* would certainly apply. However, adopting the position that the technical designation *ghi* applies only to the two specific phonemes (*ṛ* and *u*) and not to what ends in them, one should apply the objection of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the rule *gher ṅiti* (Pāṇini 7.3.111) in examples such as *agnicitaḥ*. For in this view, there is no difference between *ghi* and the [vowels] *ṛ* and *u* with respect to the suffixes *ṅi*, *am*, and *śas*. This is the general direction of the argument.

If it is argued that in this view there is no fault in forms such as *īhitā* because the rule *pugantalaghūpadhasya ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.86) serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*), we say: no. For if the restriction is "only for a root with a light penultimate vowel [does guṇa apply] before sārvadhātuka and ārdhadhātuka affixes," then the fault remains in the case of roots with short vowels (*hrasva*) and so forth when guṇa is applied. On the other hand, if the restriction is "only before sārvadhātuka and ārdhadhātuka affixes [does guṇa apply] for a root with a light penultimate vowel," even then there is still a fault in forms such as *īhitā*.

Now, if both types of restriction [apply] by way of non-recurrence (*āvṛtti*), then there is a fault in the case of *anenijuḥ*. For this cannot be prevented even by those two restrictions, because the penultimate vowel is light (*laghu*) and because a sārvadhātuka suffix follows. Furthermore, over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to cases where the vowel is not penultimate—such as in *he buddhe*, *buddhayaḥ*, *picavyaḥ* (derived from *picu-* by Pāṇini 5.1.2: *ugavādibhyo yat*), *buddhaye*, *vṛddhaye*, and so forth—is indeed unavoidable; such is the heart of the Vārttika.

In reality, however, since all defects are eliminated by qualifying the *ik* vowel with both the suffix implied by the *aṅga* and the suffix actually heard, such as *jus*, it is indeed possible to support the position that this [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) to that [general rule]. One should note, moreover, that the activity of the Bhāṣya and Vārttika texts proceeds on the assumption that the *aṅga* itself is qualified by the suffix.

If it is argued that the sixth position, which is favored by the followers of Kṛṣṇa (Kroṣṭṛ), is therefore correct—that there should be a "prior prohibition" (pūrvavipratiṣedha)—we say no. This is because the paribhāṣā rule regarding *ik* would then be left without scope (*niravakāśatva*). Indeed, a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) does not arise unless both rules can find their respective scopes by excluding one another. Therefore, if one adopts the principle that "even when coexistence is possible, sublation occurs," then this very rule possesses the status of an exception (*apavāda*) according to the maxim of "that which applies when the other does not" (*yenāprāptinyāya*).

However, if it is maintained that "the relationship of sublated and sublator exists only where there is no possibility [of both being true], whereas here a possibility exists such that both might be so," then it is established that the matter must conclude with one of the remaining options—such as *taccheṣa* (its supplement) and so forth—and there is no room for the doctrine of the followers of Kroṣṭṛ.

Therefore, the seventh position—that it is the "establishment of the word" (*padopasthāpanam*)—is the one accepted as the established doctrine (*siddhānta*). To explain: *ika* is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) ending in the genitive case, and not intended to refer to the named entity (*saṃjñin*), according to the rule "the form itself [is the name]" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 1.1.68). Nor does the prohibition "not for a grammatical technical term" (*aśabda-saṃjñā*, Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.68) apply here, because that which ends in the genitive case is not a technical term. Thus, the meaning is this: wherever it is stated that "there is a guṇa" or "there is a vṛddhi," there the genitive form *ikaḥ* presents itself.

Furthermore, its connection through syntactic unity with that [word] is internal (*antaraṅga*), whereas the application of the *alontyaparibhāṣā* (the rule regarding the final vowel) occurs after the intermediate sentence-meaning has been understood within the prescriptive rules (*vidhivākya*) and then connected through syntactic unity with that; thus, its connection is external (*bahiraṅga*). Consequently, in cases such as *jusica* (Pāṇini 7.3.83), since grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible with the phrase *iko'ṅgasya*, the non-coreferential construction (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) is improper; therefore, when the *ik* is specified as qualifying the *aṅga*, the genitive case is not prescribed as a *sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī* (genitive of replacement), and thus the *alontyaparibhāṣā* indeed presents itself.

In rules such as *miderguṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.82), however, because a construction in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is impossible, there is a construction in grammatical non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), namely "the *iK* of *mid*. Consequently, since the genitive of locus (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) is absent, the maxim *alontyaparibhāṣā* does not apply. Nor should it be argued that although the two [genitives] in *mideḥ* and *aṅgasya* are genitives of part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*), the one in *ikaḥ* is indeed a genitive of locus; for this [latter] is not required for the application of the *alontyaparibhāṣā*. This maxim applies only to a genitive that follows a locus consisting of a collection of *al*-sounds, whereas *iK* is not of the nature of an *al*-collection.

Thus, the paribhāṣā regarding the final letter (ālontya-paribhāṣā) arises immediately after the paribhāṣā regarding the vowel *i* (ik-paribhāṣā), but it does not arise simultaneously with it; for if they were to arise together, there would be no distinction between them, and both would have to be suspended. Consequently, all desired results are established. It has already been stated that the refutations against the positions of "that being a supplement" (taccheṣa) and "that being an exception" (tadapavāda) can likewise be removed. Therefore, among these seven positions, three are indeed defective, while the remaining four are established as correct.

If it is asked: "Why should this sūtra not be for the purpose of a governing heading (*adhikāra*), just like [the headings] *aṅgasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.1) and so forth?"—if that were the case, he would have recited it by joining it with the negative particle *na*, as in *na ikoguṇavṛddhī*. It would have been like [the headings] *sarvasya dve* (Pāṇini 8.1.1) or *pūrvatrāsiddham* (Pāṇini 8.2.1). For there is no reason for such inconsistency, since there is no difference in their status as being present in the subsequent sūtras; one should not recite some by joining them [with a particle] while others are recited separately.

In rules such as *pratyayaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.1) and *paraśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.2), although there is no difference in their being subservient to another (*pārārthya*), the fact that they are stated without being conjoined is not contradictory, because the things to be enjoined (*vidheya*) differ. Nor is this a rule of injunction (*vidhisūtra*), owing to the force of the repeated mention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*; even in the view where that [repetition] is rejected, it is due to the force of the specific continuation (*anuvṛtti*). This is the general direction. Thus ends the third Āhnika of the first Pāda of the first Adhyāya in the illustrious Śabdakaustubha.

*Na dhātulopa ārddhadhātuke* (Pāṇini 1.1.4): When an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix that causes the elision of a portion of a verbal root (*dhātu*) follows, the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions for *ik*-vowels do not occur, provided those substitutions are caused by that very suffix. For example: *loluvaḥ*, *popuvaḥ*, *marīmṛkajaḥ*. When the suffix *ac* (the *kṛt* suffix *a*) is added to *yaṅ*-derived roots such as *lolū* (from *lolūy*), the *yaṅ* is elided by *yaṅo'ci ca* (Pāṇini 2.4.74). At this point, although *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* would apply based on the *ac* suffix itself—which serves as the cause for the elision of the *yaṅ*—they are prohibited by this rule. This is true even though there are instances where the elision of the entire verbal root also occurs.

For example: "durīṇo lopaśca" (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.2.187) [states that] when the word *duḥ* is an upapada, the suffix *rak* is applied to the root *iṇ*, and there is elision (*lopa*) of the root; thus, it means "that which is reached or attained with difficulty," namely *dūra*. Nevertheless, in such a case, since there is an absence of any possibility for *guṇa* or *vṛddhi* substitutions to occur, a prohibition would be redundant. Therefore, in this context, by the word *dātuḥ*, a part of that [word] is indicated through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*).

If "dhātulopa" (loss of a verbal root) were a genitive tatpuruṣa compound, then there would be three possible interpretations: whether the mention of "ārddhadhātuka" (an affix belonging to the ārdhadhātuka class) qualifies the elision (*lopa*), or qualifies the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions, or qualifies both through the principles of *tantra*, *āvṛtti*, and so forth. Among these, according to the first position, the meaning of the rule would be that when there is an elision of a verbal root caused by an ārdhadhātuka affix, *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions do not occur, regardless of what causes those substitutions.

Furthermore, when the suffix *kta* is added to the root *indh* preceded by *pra*, and the *n* is elided by that very cause, the rule for *āṭ-guṇa* (the substitution of one long vowel for *ā* and *i*) would apply to the form *preddhaḥ* and would likewise be prohibited. This is because the principle holds that "that which occurs in place of two elements specified by the genitive case may be designated by either one of them"; thus, since the substitute here stands in the place of the *ik* vowels (*i* and *dh*), it possesses that status as well. Nor should it be argued that even so there is no prohibition because the substitute lacks the character of being defined by an *it* (an indicatory letter), just as the *guṇa* substitution in *laigavāyanaḥ* (from *līgava*) does not undergo prohibition.

They say that there is no evidence in this sūtra for interpreting *ika* as referring to its own form (*svarūpaparatā*), whereas in the subsequent sūtra, the word *ca* serves as evidence that [the term] has the sense of the word *iti*. Or, even if one were to accept that here too *ika* refers to its own form by virtue of relying on the governing topic (*adhikāra*) of the meaning, it should be understood that the fault which will be stated regarding the third position—namely, that there would be no *guṇa* substitution in forms such as *bhedyate*—applies equally to the first two positions as well. Now, one might object: "It is impossible for examples such as *upeddhaḥ* and *preddhaḥ* to be mentioned here at all."

To explain: according to the view that "the verbal root is first joined with its suffix" (*pūrvaṃ dhātuḥ sādhanena yujyate*), in the word *iddham*, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), because it depends on the suffix *kta* which presents itself first. However, according to the perspective that "the root is first joined with a prefix" (*pūrvaṃ dhātur upasargeṇa*), the *guṇa* substitution is the internal operation. In either case, the *guṇa* will indeed take place; for, since the external operation is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), it cannot serve as a ground for prohibition, and furthermore, since the external prohibition itself is non-existent, there is no obstacle to the application of the *guṇa*.

True; however, the paribhāṣā "that which is *bāheraṅga* is asiddha with respect to that which is *antaraṅga*" (Pā. Bhāṣya 50) does not apply here, because of the prohibition: "there is no designation of *bahiṣṭva* when there is immediate sequence of vowels" (Pā. Bhāṣya 51). According to the followers of Haradatta, this paribhāṣā does not apply where either an *antaraṅga* or a *bāheraṅga* operation depends upon the immediate sequence of vowels (*ac*).

However, under this view, it would contradict what Haradatta will state regarding the rule *eta ai* (Pāṇini 6.1.93), where he raises the objection: "Why is there no substitution of *ai* for *e* in forms such as *pacāvedam* and *pacāmedam*? and answers that it is because the *guṇa* [substitution] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) due to its being *bahiraṅga*. Furthermore, it would also contradict the relevant Bhāṣya, which aims to establish the derivation of forms like *preddham* precisely by relying on the principle that a *bahiraṅga* operation is non-existent.

Therefore, the meaning of the paribhāṣā *nājānantarye* (Pā. 1.1.51)—that the *bahiraṅga-paribhāṣā* does not apply where there is immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) of vowels (*ac*) followed by an operation occurring at a later time—is precisely that which is accepted by Kaiyaṭa as correct. For in examples such as *pacāvedam*, the *guṇa* substitution occurs first; and even though the immediate sequence of vowels (*ajānantarya*) is relied upon there, the meaning of *nājānantarye* applies to cases where the vowel-substitution occurs subsequently. Indeed, in *pacāvedam* and similar forms, the *guṇa* operates prior [to the subsequent sandhi].

In that regard, even though the condition of immediate sequence with *a* (*ajānantarya*) is relied upon when a subsequent operation involving a *guṇa* substitute is to take place—as in the rule *eta ai* (Pāṇini 6.1.93)—it is correct to exclude [the application of] that [condition] there because of its being *bahiraṅga*. However, in cases such as *upeddhaḥ* and *preddhaḥ*, the prohibition must be applied after first allowing the *guṇa* to occur; thus, the prohibition operates at a later time. Since the condition of immediate sequence with *a* is not relied upon there, this is indeed established by the *bahiraṅgaparibhāṣā*. Consequently, the Bhāṣya on this point is also consistent.

But surely this *paribhāṣā* will be made known by the rule *ṣatvatukorasiddhaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.86). In that context, in examples such as *ko 'sicat* and *ko 'sya*, the condition of "immediate sequence with a vowel" (*ajānantarya*) applies to the initial application of the rule *eṅaḥ padāntād ati* (Pāṇini 6.1.109), but not to the *ṣatva* substitution which occurs at a later stage; how, then, can Kaiyaṭa’s position be justified?

If it is argued that, therefore, one must resort to the very method stated by Haradatta—namely, that "there is no immediate sequence of vowels (*ac*) whether in an internal (*antaraṅga*) or external (*bahiraṅga*) operation"? No; for in Kaiyaṭa’s view, since the dual number in *acoḥ* is not intended to be significant, this applies to all *sāmaja* vowels. Indeed, there is a reliance on the immediate sequence of vowels when the substitution of *ṣatva* (the change to *ṣ*) occurs at a later stage, as it is stated that [the rule applies] to an *s* following an *iṇ* vowel. Thus, while in the first alternative there is no fault in cases such as *preddhaḥ*, the fact that forms like *bhedyate* remain unestablished is precisely the defect; such is the direction of the argument.

In the second alternative, however, the meaning of the rule would be that when there is elision of a root-vowel (*dhātu-lopa*) caused by any cause whatsoever, the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions [prescribed] for the sake of an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix do not take place. Consequently, from the root *knūyī* (meaning "to sound"), after adding the causative suffix *ṇic*, the augment *puk*, and the elision of *ya*, the *guṇa* substitution conditioned by the suffix beginning with *pu* would be prohibited. Thus, the form *knopayati* would not be established. If, on the other hand, the *guṇa* is admitted here on the basis of the specific mention in the rule *cele kropeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.33), then the very same fault remains: the form *bhedyate* would still be unestablished.

In the third alternative, however, the meaning of the sūtra would be that when there is elision of a verbal root (dhātu-lopa) caused by an ārdhadhātuka suffix, the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions caused by that same ārdhadhātuka suffix do not take place. In that case, the complexity resulting from having to resort to methods such as *tantra* (simultaneous application) or *āvṛtti* (repetition) is evident; furthermore, the fact that the elision and the *guṇa* or *vṛddhi* substitutions share a single common cause would not be obtained.

Furthermore, in the case of *bhid-y-ate* (from the root *bhid* with the causative suffix *ṇic* and the passive suffix *yak*), when the form *bhid-iya* is established, the *ṇi*-elision (*ṇilopa*) would be permanent; consequently, even if a *guṇa* substitution were to be applied by relying on the *ṇic* through the principle of "characterized by the suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), it would be prohibited. Nor should it be argued that the *guṇa* should occur prior to the *ṇi*-elision because it is "internal" (*antaranga*); for this is impossible under the view of analytical derivation (*vibhajyānvākhyāna*), and because of the maxim: "An exception (*apavāda*), even when its cause is yet to arise, overrides a general rule (*utsarga*), even when the latter's cause has already arisen" (Pāṇini Bhāṣya 1.1.3).

In cases such as *dadhati*, because it is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), the substitution of *anta* [for the final consonant] would apply by the rule *jhaontaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.3). Nor should it be argued that once this has been done, and given the reduplication (*ślau*) and doubling, the rule *adabhyastāt* (Pāṇini 7.1.4) should apply by virtue of the status of the substitute being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*); for in a rule concerning an *al* (phoneme), the status of the substitute being like the original is impossible.

Furthermore, regarding the rule *samarthānāṃ prathamādvā* (Pāṇini 4.1.82), it will be stated there that the mention of *samartha* ("capable") is intended to indicate the maxim *akṛtavyūhāḥ pāṇinīyāḥ* (the followers of Pāṇini do not undo what has been done) and the principle that "even what has been performed by the grammar is set aside. It will also be clarified in that very place that these two maxims yield the same result. Consequently, here too, the *guṇa* substitution would either not have been applied previously, or even if applied, it would be set aside—as happens with the augment *iṭ* in forms such as *jagmuṣaḥ*.

Therefore, the analysis *yasmin dhātoḥ lopaḥ* as a *bahuvrīhi* compound alone is correct. For this being the case, the fact that the elision (*lopa*) and the *guṇa* or *vṛddhi* substitutions share a single cause is obtained; thus, none of the previously mentioned defects apply. It might be argued: even if this rule were composed, the *guṇa* substitution would still be unavoidable in forms such as *loluvaḥ*. To explain: in this rule and in the rule *ṅkiti ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.5), when there is an expectancy as to what is to be prohibited, the very presence of the word *ik* established by the previous [rule] must be connected—namely, that the word *ik* does not apply to an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix that is the cause for the elision of a portion of the verbal root (*dhātu*).

Furthermore, the result of this section [of the Paribhāṣā] would merely be the prevention of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* in cases such as *bebhidaḥ*, *marīmṛjaḥ*, *bhinnaḥ*, and *mṛṣṭaḥ*; however, in cases like *loluva*, the *guṇa* would indeed occur. Nor should it be argued that, since the Paribhāṣā is subordinate (*śeṣibhūta*) to the rules it qualifies, the prohibition by implication (*arthataḥ*) should apply only to the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* which are the primary elements; for in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), it is appropriate that only the grammatical primacy (*śābdaprādhānya*) determines the relation of connection (*anvaya*).

For instance, in an expression such as "Bring the king’s man" (*rājapuruṣam ānaya*), although the king is primary in terms of meaning, he does not connect with the act of bringing; rather, it is the man alone who does so. And in the present case, syntactic primacy belongs only to the presentation of the word-meanings which constitute the sentence-meaning, according to the established doctrine that "the sentence-meaning is an action qualified by its factors" (*kāraka*). As it has been said:

"A sentence is said to be that which has expectant parts, whose divisions do not require further expectancy from external words, which has the object (or action) as its primary element, and which possesses qualifiers and expresses a single unified meaning."*10* *10. Vākyapadīya 2.324.*

Furthermore, according to our established doctrine (*siddhānta*), in the case of a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), the negative particle (*nañ*) is always construed with a verb, and not with the meaning of a nominal stem. As it has been said:
"This is a non-presuppositional negation where the negative particle is connected with a verb.

For this very reason, there is no confusion between the [grammatical] persons (*puruṣa*) and the [grammatical] numbers (*vacana*). Otherwise, the distinction of persons would not be established in such cases as "the jar does not exist" (*ghaṭo nāsti*), "you do not exist" (*tvaṃ nāsi*), or "I do not exist" (*ahaṃ nāsmi*); for in all these instances, the first person would invariably apply, just as one might say "the absence of the jar exists," "your absence exists," or "my absence exists."

For in the view of the opponent (*paramata*), there is no difference whatsoever between the meanings of "you do not exist" (*tvaṃ nāsi*) and "there is an absence of you" (*tvadabhāvo'sti*). This is because, even if one accepts that the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) has a qualifier-role (*prakāratā*) with respect to its correlate (*anvayin*)—which is presented by a nominative case-ending word through a relation characterized by a counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) delimited by the delimitor of the correlate-ship (*anvayitāvacchedaka*)—the lack of coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the second-person pronoun (*yuṣmad*) remains unchanged in both cases. Furthermore, just as in the statement "there is an absence of colors in the air" (*vāyau rūpāṇāmabhāvo'sti*), the singular verb "is" (*asti*) would also have to appear in the sentence "colors do not exist" (*rūpāṇi na santi*); this is explained in detail elsewhere.

Thus, even for case endings (*kāraka-vibhakti*), grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) exists only when there is a connection with an action (*kriyā-yoga*), and not otherwise; this is because it will be stated in the sūtra *kārake* (Pāṇini 1.4.23) that "in [the expression] 'there is no jar on the ground,' the status of being a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) is connected only to the action, and not to the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*). Consequently, the meaning of the negative particle is connected to the action as qualified by all its case-factors. However, according to the definitive position (*niṣkṛṣṭa-pakṣa*) that the negative particle is merely indicative (*dyotaka*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the verbal root itself refers to the absence of that action.
In either case, a prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* [substitutions] here is indeed difficult to obtain.

To this it is said: It is indeed true that the verbal connection (*śābdānvaya*) of a prohibition is with the action alone, just as it is with an injunction; however, when there is doubt as to what exactly that "action" is, then—even though it is proximate—the application of the word *ik* (the technical term for vowels) does not connect here according to the method you have stated. For if that were the case, the rule *dīdhīvevīṭām* (Pāṇini 1.1.6) would become redundant. Indeed, in that context, there is no difference in the result between the maxim regarding *ik* (*ikparibhāṣā*) and the maxim regarding the final letter (*alontyaparibhāṣā*).

This being the case, according to the method to be explained in the *Prātipadikārtha-sūtra*—namely, that "the verb *asti*, followed by the form *bhavantī*, is understood even when not explicitly employed"—when there is a connection with the prohibition [of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*] for the word *bhavataḥ* which has been brought to mind and is construed with [the rule] *guṇavṛddhī* and so forth, the result is the absence of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. It is on this basis alone that one says there is a "prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*."

Just as in the *adhikaraṇa* on the *āghāra* and *agnihotra* (Jaiminīya-sūtra 2.2.5), it was established that although every [injunction] is indeed a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), from the perspective of its intended meaning (*tātparya*), some are injunctions of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*); similarly, this should be understood regarding prohibitions as well, because the underlying logic is the same. For this very reason, the learned authorities maintain that both injunctions and prohibitions have the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) as their domain. Therefore, the examples *loluvaḥ*, *popuvaḥ*, and *marīmṛjaḥ* are established.

But a counter-example is stated: why does [the sūtra] say "when there is elision of a root" (*dhātulope*)? Lest there be an optionality regarding *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, as there is with the taking up or not taking up of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup due to injunctions and prohibitions in the context of the *ārddhadhātuka*.

What is the purpose of the condition *ārddhadhātuka*? [Consider the following: from the roots *turvī*, *thurvī*, *durvī*, and *dhurvī* (meaning "to injure," Dhātupāṭha 572–574) and *murchā* (meaning "delusion" or "increase," Dhātupāṭha 212), when followed by an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix such as *tiP* etc. after the *yaṅ-luk* formation, there should be no prohibition [of the elision of *ch* and *v*] in forms such as *totorti* and *momorti*. This is because, according to the rule *rāllopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.21), the elision of *ch* and *v* and the *guṇa* substitution would share a single cause (*ekanimittakatva*).

And this was stated by relying on the view that the mention of *kṅit* does not recur in the rule for the elision of *ra* and *l*. However, under the view that it does recur, one should understand that examples such as *totīrmi* (the first person singular) are to be cited; for in those cases, the elision of *ra* and *l* applies because the suffixes are nasalized (*anunāsika*) and so forth. Now, one might object: let the previously mentioned examples such as *toterti* also serve as illustrations.

If it is argued that even though the elision of *r* does not apply here, the elision of *y* and *v* would still occur by Pāṇini 6.1.66 (*lopo vyoḥ*), we say no; for that rule has as its cause merely the phonemes (*varṇa*) themselves, and thus lacks a common cause with the *guṇa* substitution. Indeed, in that context, there is neither the mention of a suffix (*pratyaya*) nor anything that implies it. For this very reason, in forms such as *godhēra*, the elision of *y* occurs even without the suffix following. Why is the term *ika* specified [in the rule]? Consider the examples *abhāji* and *rāgāḥ*. [The purpose is] so that the *vṛddhi* substitution may take place after the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) has been elided by Pāṇini 6.4.33 (*bhañjeśca ciṇi*) and 6.4.27 (*ghañi ca bhāvakaraṇayoḥ*).

If it is asked, "How then is there a prohibition of *vṛddhi* in the case of *pāpacakaḥ*? listen: from the root *pāpacyati* with the suffix *ṇvul*, in the rule *yasya halaḥ* (*Pāṇini* 6.4.49), the mention of *yasya* as a *samudāya* (composite) is for the purpose of excluding forms such as *aharyāt* and *amavyīt*. When *akap* is applied, and the mere consonant (*hal*) is elided by *ādeḥ parasya* (*Pāṇini* 1.1.54), the subsequent elision of the *a* by *ato lopaḥ* (*Pāṇini* 6.4.48) is treated as a separate operation. Due to the status of that [elision] as *sthānivadbhāva*, there is no *vṛddhi* in *pāpacakaḥ* and similar forms.

However, in this case, the rule *na dhātulope* (Pāṇini 1.1.4) has no application whatsoever. When the suffix *ṇvul* is added to a stem ending in *yaṅ*-luṅ, as in *pāpācakaḥ*, the vṛddhi strengthening certainly occurs, just as in the form *nonāva*.

By this, the author of the *Kaumudī* is refuted, who—on the grounds that the word *ikaḥ* is understood from the rule *na dhātulopa ārdhadhātuke* (Pāṇini 1.1.4)—cites *bebhiditā* and *marīmṛjitā* as examples under the rule *na dhātu-lopa-* (Pāṇini 6.4.54), just like *pāpācakaḥ*. For when the elision (*lopa*) is properly applied separately, as is agreed upon in the *Bhāṣya* and other works, the occurrence of *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) is impossible. It is for this very reason that the authors of the *Vṛtti* and others have cited only words ending in *ac*-suffixes, such as *loluva*, as examples under this rule.

However, if there is *yaṅluk* after the roots *bhid* and *mṛj*, then because that [elision] is not caused by any specific condition (*anaimittika*), guna and vṛddhi do indeed occur, as in *bebheditā* and *marīmārjitā*. But if, on the other hand, there is elision of a portion [of the suffix] according to Pāṇini 6.4.49 (*yasya halaḥ*), then due to the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), there is no possibility of guna and so forth; thus, it should be noted that in either case, these are not examples of this sūtra.

The author of the Bhāṣya, however, rejected this sūtra by relying on a separate elision (*alopa*) even when there is *luk* elision, just as in the case of the elision [prescribed] by "yasya" (Pāṇini 6.4.148). Nor should it be argued that, according to the principle of "that which applies where another does not" (*yenāprāptinyāya*), the *luk* elision of the *yaṅ* suffix would subvert the elision of the *at* vowel; for in the rule "yasya halaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.49), the phrase "yasya" is divided into a separate rule, and by carrying forward the phrase "ato lopaḥ," the elision of the *at* vowel of the word "ya" is prescribed, thereby subverting the *luk*. Thus, the scope for *luk* remains only for the remaining consonantal elements.

Consequently, by the very principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original) applied to the elision (*al-lopa*), there would arise the undesirable contingency of a separate elision even in forms such as *bebhiditā*, *marīmṛjitā*, and *pāpacakaḥ*; for the non-conditional elision (*luk*)—which occurs due to the inclusion of the term *bahulam* drawn in by the word *ca*—being *antaraṅga* (internal), would apply to the entire complex form even prior to the production of the *lakāra*.

If it is objected: "In this case, just as in forms such as *cekrīyaḥ*, *loluvaḥ*, and *toṣṭuvaḥ*—where, due to the status of the elision (*allopa*) as *sthānivat*, the *guṇa* substitution does not occur—likewise, the substitutions *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* should also not occur," [the reply is: True, they would indeed not occur if they depended on a vowel (*ac*), for that reason has already been stated; however, they will occur by depending on the letter *a* obtained through the operation of *sthānivadbhāva*. For that [letter *a*] remains designated as an affix (*pratyaya*) even when the *yakāra* has been elided.

It might be argued as follows: in forms such as *loluva*, when the letter *a* is elided, the sequence is [the suffix] *yaluk*. At that time, prior to the presence of the *y*, the status of being a suffix (*pratyayatva*) was not yet acquired by the *a*. Even when that *a* is elided, it no longer exists, since it had already ceased to exist prior to the elision. How, then, could this [elided *a*], being non-existent, acquire the status of a suffix? If it is argued that the status of a suffix is attributed to it through the "substitution of the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) for its elision—[we reply: indeed, an operation observed in the original element (*sthānin*) is obtained through such extension (*atideśa*), but not one that was never observed there in the first place.

On this point, they say: in that case, only what is *sambhāvita* (potentially possible) is extended by analogy (*atidiśyate*). For if the vowel *a*, which is the original locus (*sthānin*) of the elision, were to remain here even when the *yakāra* has been elided, then it would acquire the status of a suffix (*pratyayatva*) and cause the application of *luṅ* and so forth; how then could there not be an extension? And the prohibition of *vār* is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) here. For that [prohibition] is indeed made for the purpose of preventing the elision of the long *ā* by the rule *āto lopa iṭi ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.64) through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*, after the elision of *yaṅ* and the elision of *yal* have occurred following the root *yā* in its *yaṅ*-intensive form (*yāyāyati*).

But if there were an extension (*atideśa*) only of that which is actually seen in the *sthānin*, what would be the point? For in the state "yā-yā-ya," the elision of the final vowel (*ātolopaḥ*) does not apply, because [the preceding element] is not preceded by a vowel other than *a* (*anajāditvāt*); such is the direction of the argument.

But if this were so, then in forms such as *cekṣiyaḥ* and *toṣṭuvaḥ*, by the rule "even internal [operations take precedence]" (*antaraṅgān api*), the *luk*-elision of the *yaṅ* suffix would occur even before the lengthening prescribed by *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.25). Then, even though the *allopa* (the elision of the *a* of the root) would be treated as *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were still present), the base with a light penultimate vowel—namely *cekṣi-a-a* and *toṣṭuṃ-a-a*—would be followed by the *aṅ* suffix, and thus the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel would certainly apply. True; however, the internal operations *viyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* will indeed occur [at that stage].

As the author of the Vārttika says: "Because that which ends in *śacaṅ* is characterized as internal (*antaraṅga*). Consequently, from the roots *ri* (to go) and *pi* (to go), and *dhī* (to hold)—all belonging to the *tudādi* class—when the suffix *śa* is applied, the forms *riyati*, *piyati*, and *dhiyati* arise. Furthermore, in the cases of *aśiśriyat* and *prādudruvat*, the suffixes *caṅ*, *iyaṅ*, and *uvaṅ* occur by virtue of the rule *ṇiśri* (Pāṇini 3.1.48).

Therefore, since everything can be consistently explained through the elision of the *al* suffix alone, the rule *na dhātulope* (Pāṇini 1.1.4) need not be formulated. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of optional *vṛddhi* in the form *marmṛjaḥ*—based on the *vārttika* *majerajādau saṃkramaḥ*—because in the opinion of Haradatta and others, that rule applies only when a primary vowel-initial (*ajādau*) affix follows; however, according to the final conclusion (*niṣkarṣa*), since the authority of the sages increases in successive order, such an outcome is actually desired. Alternatively, let it be considered a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*).

On this point, they say: since there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of both the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) and the elision of *u* and *ṭ* (*yuṭalopa*), the elision of the penultimate vowel cannot be stated as occurring when *luk* [of the suffix] takes place. To explain: in cases such as *sarvakṣatra*, whether the stems end in long vowels or short vowels, once the *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* substitutions have been applied, the *guṇa* substitution conditioned by a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhalakṣaṇa*) would apply. Nor can the status of being a *sthānivat* be invoked here, because [the *guṇa*] would precede the original vowel that is the substitute (*ādiṣṭādacaḥ pūrvatvāt*). Furthermore, in the case of *jaṅgamaḥ*, there would be the elision of the penultimate vowel according to Pāṇini 6.4.98 (*gamahana...*).

Now, if there were a prohibition [of the augment] by the rule *anaṅī*, then in the form *darīdṛśaḥ*, the suffix *yuṭ* would apply according to Pāṇini 6.4.63 (*ṛdṛśo’ṅi*). Furthermore, in *sanīsraṃsaḥ* and *danīdhvaṃsaḥ*, the elision of the penultimate vowel would occur according to Pāṇini 6.4.24 (*aniditām*). Moreover, in forms such as *yāyāḥ* and *vāvāḥ*, the long vowel *ā* would not be produced. Therefore, the elision of the entire [reduplicated] complex must be accepted, and the sūtra must be formulated for the sake of establishing forms such as *loluva*.

To this it is replied: in cases such as *loluva*, the quality [of being a single substitute] does not apply because, by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* rule, there exists the status of being "prior to a non-specified vowel" (*anādiṣṭādacaḥ pūrvatvam*) through the medium of the original locus (*sthānin*). It is precisely for this reason that the term "homogeneous" (*savarṇa*) was included in the rule *na padānta* (Pāṇini 1.1.58). This was done so that in forms like *śiṇḍhi*, when a homogeneous sound is to be applied to the *anusvāra*, the *sthānivadbhāva* of the elision (*allopa*) of the *śn* and *as* suffixes would not take effect by relying on the status of being "prior to a non-specified vowel" through the medium of the original locus.

If it is asked: "Since the status of being prior to an undesignated vowel (*anādiṣṭādacaḥ pūrvatvam*) lacks the character of a grammatical operation (*śāstrīyakāryatva*), how can there be an extension [of that property]?"—[the answer is: because when the extension rule *acaḥ parasmin* (Pāṇini 1.1.57) is to be applied with respect to the state of being prior to an undesignated vowel, the application of *sthānivad ādeśaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.56) is possible; furthermore, this very point has been established by all [commentators] during the occasion of explaining the inclusion of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇagrahaṇa*).

Now, one might object: "Surely, this substitution of *uvaṅ* for *ū* (in *ūḍha*) may somehow acquire the status of being prior to the preceding vowel by way of its *sthānin*, but no operation is prescribed here for that [substitute] such that the elision of *ā* (*allopaḥ*) would have to behave as if it were the *sthānin*. Furthermore, that for which an operation is prescribed—namely, the letter *u*—is not the substitute, so how could it acquire the status of being prior even by way of its *sthānin*? True; however, by relying on the principle that "all substitutes are substitutes for entire words," the relationship between the *sthānin* and the substitute ultimately rests upon meaningful units.

For this very reason, it will be stated that since the rule *eru* (Pāṇini 3.4.86) results in the meaning *testuḥ*, and since [the desired form] is established by the *sthānivadbhāva* rule alone, the supplementary statement (*upasaṅkhyāna*) regarding "that which is modified in one part" need not be commenced. And for this same reason, it will be stated that although the word "substitute" (*ādeśa*) is already obtained through its being a relative term when "like the original" (*sthānivat*) is mentioned, the explicit mention of "substitute" again is for the purpose of including even an inferred substitute.

In this case as well, the substitution of *lolugh* for *lolū* occurs, and because that [substitution] precedes the vowel that has not yet been subject to grammatical operation (*anādiṣṭādacaḥ*), it is by virtue of its status as a *sthānivadbhāva*. Furthermore, when the substitution of *lolova* is to take effect, it is entirely logical that the elision of *al* (*allopaḥ*) should be treated as a *sthānivat*. Moreover, by the long-vowel pronunciation in the rules *jñājanorjā* (Pāṇini 7.3.79) and *rīṅ ṛtaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.27), the *paribhāṣā* "when an operation has already taken place within a stem (*aṅgavṛtte*), there is no further application of a rule to what is already established (*punarvṛttāvavidhirniṣṭhitasya*)" will be made known.

Therefore, once the augment *aṅ* has been applied, there will be no *guṇa* substitution. In the case of *darīdṛśaḥ*, there is no *guṇa* because the term *aṅ* refers specifically to that which is prescribed by its own rule (*pratipadokta*). This is as in the form *adarśat*. However, in the case of the *yaṅ* suffix, the letter *a* is not an affix at the time of its initial instruction (*upadeśa*), but rather a constituent part (*avayava*) of it; and when the *y* is elided, that [augment] is neither qualified by the *ṅ* nor is it even heard. Nevertheless, because it is accessible only through inference, its presence is delayed, much like that of a term defined by a secondary characteristic (*lākṣaṇika*).

If it is argued that, in this way, since the term *anaṅ* is used as a *paryudāsa* (exclusion), the suffix *ak* would not be included, and thus the elision of *al* (*allopa*) would apply in the case of *jaṅgamaḥ*, we say: no. This is because by the *paryudāsa* "not *anaṅ*," the rule for the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) is prescribed for a substitute (*aupadeśika*) beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*) that resembles the original base (*aṅ*), or for one where the initial vowel is actually heard (*śrūyamāṇa*). Furthermore, the claim that only a meaningful element (*arthavat*) is taken in the rule prescribing *guṇa* for the *aṅ* is incorrect, because verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇas*) are themselves devoid of meaning (*anarthaka*). As for the objection that the suffix *yuṭ* would apply in the case of *dedyaḥ*, that is not so, because of the specific mention of the *anubandha* (indicatory letter). As it has been said: "That which is specified by means of *śtip*, *śap*, an *anubandha*, or a class-marker (*gaṇa*)," [is not affected by other operations].

"Where there is the mention of 'only one vowel' (*ekāc*), these five [rules] do not apply when *yaṅ* is elided" (Pā. Bhāṣya 1.3.1). Furthermore, you yourself have stated that in the rule "yuṭ after *dīṅ* before a vowel" (Pā. Sū. 6.4.63), the mention of the marker *ṅ* (*anubandha*) on *dīṅ* is for the purpose of excluding the case where *yaṅ* is elided. And here, the evidence is the mention of "only one vowel" (*ekāc*) in the rule "after a root consisting of a single vowel in its original form" (Pā. Sū. 1.3.2), which is made with the aim of excluding the case where *yaṅ* is elided. For even if that [mention of *ekāc*] were made, without the aforementioned paribhāṣā, forms such as *bebheditā* would not be established.

This is because, in order to establish [the validity of forms such as] *bibhetsati*, it will be concluded that the mention of *upadeśa* (original enunciation) functions as a qualifier for both [the root and the affix], by resorting to methods such as the repetition (*āvṛtti*) of the rule. Nor should it be asked how this can serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) regarding other portions of the rule, such as *api śtipā śapā*; for it is frequently observed in cases such as *gatikārakopapadānām* (Pāṇini 6.2.139) that a Paribhāṣā recited by earlier teachers is indicated through the acceptance of a single part of it.

Nor should it be argued that, in the same way, the doubling prescribed by the rule *ekācaḥ* would also not occur in the *yaṅluk* formation; for its application is guaranteed by the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in Pāṇini 7.4.82, *guṇo yaṅlukoḥ*. In the case of *yaṅluk* forms such as *bebheditā*, where the augment *iṭ* is added, the aforementioned paribhāṣā alone provides the solution.

Since it will be stated later that "doubling is a double utterance" (*dvirvacanam dviḥprayogaḥ*, Bhāṣya), it is impossible to claim that [the reduplicated form] is a different verbal root (*dhātvantara*). However, in the case of the *yaṅ*-intensive form *bebheditā*, since the elision (*lopa*) is admitted as being separate [from the reduplication], there is no prohibition of the suffix *iṇ* because of the status of that [elided part] as *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original element). This is because it will be stated later that the status of *sthānivadbhāva* applies even to a rule concerning what precedes [an operation]. Furthermore, you yourself have accepted that the elision governed by the rule *yasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.148) is an elision of a constituent part (*avayavalopa*).

In this regard, although it might seem that the suffix *yuṭ* should apply in the case of *dedīyakaḥ*, such an objection is not tenable, because since there is no *hal* (consonant) preceding it, the elision of *y* (*yalopa*) does not take effect here, and the form *dedīyakaḥ* is thus accepted. Furthermore, the elision of the penultimate *n* (*nalopa*) in forms such as *sanīsrasakaḥ* need not be raised as an objection, precisely because it is universally agreed upon. Likewise, the elision of the initial *ā* (*āllopa*) in forms such as *yāyāyakaḥ* and *vāvāyakaḥ* need not be raised either, because in the absence of the elision of *y*, there is no subsequent *ārdhadhātuka* suffix beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*) that possesses the *ṅit* marker.

Nevertheless, in a case such as *jaṅgamakaḥ*, formed by adding the suffix *ṇvul* to the root *gam* with the suffix *yaṅ*, there would be an elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) due to the status of the preceding *al*-elision as *sthānivadbhāva*, just as there is an absence of *vṛddhi*. If, however, the prohibition "not when *anaṅ*" applies here, then in the case of *darīdṛśakaḥ*, the rule "guṇa occurs for *ṛ* and *dṛś* before *aṅ*" (Pāṇini 7.4.16) would apply.

Now, if this is resolved here by the rule regarding the function of a constituent part (*aṅgavṛttaparibhāṣā*) or by the principle that "a rule conditioned by a technical name (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*) is not universally obligatory" (Pāṇini Bhāṣya 94), then even in the case of *yaṅ*-elision, the elision of *n* in *sanīsraṃsaḥ* and the elision of *ā* in *yāyāḥ* and *vāvāḥ* need not be suspected [of being irregular], since the resolution is identical; such is the direction of the argument.

Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.5: *kṅiti ca*. When *guṇa* or *vṛddhi* is prescribed after pronouncing the word *ik*, those [substitutions] which would otherwise apply by depending on a *giṭ*, a *kiṭ*, or a *ṅiṭ* as the cause do not take place. Regarding *giṭ*: *jiṣṇuḥ*. This is formed by Pāṇini Sūtra 3.2.139: *glājisthaśca gsnuḥ*. It should be stated that this [suffix] is indeed *kiṭ*; otherwise, in the case of *sthāsnuḥ*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of *itva* (the substitution of *i*) by Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.63: *ghumāsthā...* [etc.].

Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of the augment *iṭ* in the case of *bhūṣṇuḥ*, because even in the rule *śrūyukaḥ kiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.11), that [augment] is prohibited by relying on the inclusion of the letter *ga* through the process of *cartva* (the substitution of *c* for *k*). Nor should it be argued that, because *cartva* is considered "not established" (*asiddha*), the *visarjanīya* would not occur and the substitution of *u* for *ru* (*rorutva*) would instead take effect; for this is prevented either by the separation of the rule into two parts (*yogavibhāga*)—namely, the word *na* in *na mune* (Pāṇini 8.2.3)—or by its being a Vedic (*sautra*) usage. Thus, regarding the rule *glājistha* (Pāṇini 3.2.139), there is a verse in the *Ślokavārttika*: "Because *ksnu* has the marker *g*, there is no *ī* for *sthā*; for the rule for *ī* applies only to *kit* and *ṅit* suffixes."

"The absence of the *guṇa* [vowel] should be remembered in the three [roots]; the substitution of *i* for *śru*, and the substitution of *i* for the roots *kṛ* and *gṛ*. Thus says Jayāditya as well. Vāmana, however, maintains that since the form *sthāsnu* is established by interpreting the rule *glājisthaśca* (Pāṇini 3.2.139) as containing the vowel *ā*—that is, by explaining that there is only the vowel *ā* for the root *sthā* ending in the suffix *kasnu*, and not the substitution of *ī*—there is no need to insert the letter *ga* anywhere.

But surely, according to this view, by the rule *daṃśecchandasyupasaṃkhyānam* (Kāśikāvṛtti), when the suffix *ksnu* is applied, there would be elision of the nasal *n* in the word *daṃkṣṇavaḥ paśavaḥ* (the biting animals) by the rule *aniditām* (Pāṇini 6.4.24). True; this is to be resolved on the grounds that it is Vedic usage (*chāndasatvāt*). Examples of *kit* [suffixes]: *cita*, *stutam*, *mṛṣṭam*. Examples of *ṅit* [suffixes]: *cinutaḥ*, *sunutaḥ*, *mṛṣṭāt*. Why is the locative case used to express the condition (*nimittasaptamī*)? So that [the rule] may apply even when [the cause] is separated [by other elements], as in *chinnaṃ* and *bhinnam*. Why is *ikaḥ* mentioned [in the rule]? [To exclude cases like] *kāmayate*.

What is the purpose of resorting to the operation of the word [itself]? [Consider the example: *laigavāyanaḥ*. The substitution of *guṇa* for *o* applies only to [the *o*] that ends in *ik*, and not to the presence of the entire word *ik*; this is because [the rule] specifies the locus as being "that which is denoted by *oḥ*". As it has been said: "Because of the context of *ik* in the section on *taddhita* suffixes and *kāmya*."

[Objection: But surely, because the rule *kṅiti* is stated in the locative case, the paribhāṣā *tasminniti nirdiṣṭe pūrvasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.66) would apply; since in that context the word *niḥ* signifies immediate proximity and the root *diś-* denotes the act of utterance, the prohibition would apply only to what is uttered immediately [before], and not even to forms such as *chinnaṃ* or *bhinnam*. [Response: This would indeed be the case, if the term *kṅiti* were directly connected to the action that is being prohibited. However, in this instance, it is connected with the terms *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*.

The locative case [in *kṅiti*] is governed by the rule *yasya ca bhāvena* (Pāṇini 2.3.37). Because it refers to another action, it implies the existence [of the suffix] as its general rule (*autsargika*). Consequently, when the connection is made—"the guna and vṛddhi that would otherwise apply when a *kṅit* [suffix] follows"—the principle of the co-occurrence of the accomplished and the to-be-accomplished (*siddhasādhyasamabhivyāhāra*) results in the fact that the locus of existence, serving as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), generally functions as the cause; however, there is no specific prescription of the locative case here to denote a [direct] causal condition (*nimitta*).

Furthermore, a *paribhāṣā* (technical rule of interpretation) is not applicable here, because *paribhāṣās*, which serve as auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) to injunctions (*vidhi*), operate only in connection with the very action that is to be enjoined or prohibited. This [term "of the vowel"] is an adjective qualifying the agent connected to the action, and not an adjective of the action itself; therefore, a *paribhāṣā* does not apply here. Otherwise, in the rule *vṛddhir yasyācām ādiḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.73), if the *ik-paribhāṣā* were to apply, forms such as *śālīya* would not be established. For in this case, the *vṛddhi* substitution does not occur in place of an *ik*.

For this very reason, the term *sthāne* ("in place of") was included in the rule *udīcāmātaḥ sthāne* (Pāṇini 7.3.46). This is because the technical rule *ṣaṣṭhī sthāne yogā* (Pāṇini 1.1.49)—which restricts a genitive case to mean "in place of"—does not apply here; for *ātaḥ* is a qualifier of the thing being restated (*anūdyamāna*), namely "the vowel *a* which is in place of *āt*. The maxim *guṇānāñca parārthatvādasambandhaḥ samatvātsyāt* (Jaimini Sūtra 3.1.22), "And since subordinate elements exist for the sake of another, there would be no mutual connection between them due to their equality," should also be considered here.

[Objection: "In that case, by this very logic, let the rule *kṅiti* be connected with the action (*kriyā*) which is the primary element, and not with the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* which are subordinate to it; for it is improper to abandon a possible connection with the primary. [Reply: No. For where a subordinate element (*guṇa*), having undergone its own refinement (*saṃskāra*), is capable of rendering great service to the primary, it connects with the primary after first experiencing its own refinement—just as water refined by cardamom and other ingredients is used by a person. And it has been said: "A subordinate element, having undergone its own refinement, serves the primary."
"For it functions in such a way as to provide greater assistance to the primary [cause]. Thus [it is said].

In this context, when *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are qualified by the mention of *kṅit*, a great benefit accrues to the primary element (*pradhāna*), because the prohibition is established even for that which is separated [by intervening elements]. Furthermore, the *kit* designation of *knū* is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) of this point. Otherwise, if there were connection with the primary element alone, and the *nirdiṣṭaparibhāṣā* were to apply, the prohibition would not operate in the case of a separation; thus, the *kit* status of *knū* would be entirely purposeless. Therefore, the explanation exactly as it has been given is correct.

If it is objected: "Is this not a locative of reference (*parasaptamī*)? If so, there would be a fault at the end of the *śapa* suffix because the *guṇa* substitution characterized by a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha*) would apply. [Reply: No, because the application of *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* is internal (*antaraṅga*). [Examples of] *dhi*, *ri*, and *pi* from the *tud*-class roots meaning "to hold" (*dhāraṇa*) and "to go" (*gati*) respectively: *dhiyati*, *riyati*, *piyati*.

Regarding the rule *niśra-idru-srubhyaḥ kartari caṅ* (Pāṇini 3.1.48), in forms such as *aśiśriyat*, *adudruvat*, and *asusruvat*, the *guṇa* substitution that would apply by virtue of the *tip* suffix is *bahiraṅga* (external), whereas the *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* substitutions based on the *śap* and *caṅ* are *antaraṅga* (internal). As it has been said: "Because [the forms] ending in *śap* and *caṅ* possess internal characteristics" (*kārikāvākya*). Furthermore, the *Kāśikā* states: "In the case of *mṛj*, when followed by a suffix beginning with a vowel (*ajādau*) that causes *saṃkrama* (transformation), *vṛddhi* is desired."

This point was stated in the *Bhāṣya* as the opinion of another grammarian, in connection with the rule *iko guṇavṛddhī* (Pāṇini 1.1.3). Its meaning is as follows: by the etymological derivation *guṇavṛddhī saṃkrāmataḥ asmāt*, the suffix *kṅit*—which serves as the cause for the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*—is denoted here by the word *saṃkrama*, due to its being both etymologically and conventionally established (*yogarūḍhi*).

Therefore, it should be noted that in the case of *marīmṛjaḥ*, even though the *ac* suffix is the cause for the prohibition of *vṛddhi* due to its being the occasion for the elision of a portion of the root, this alternative (*vikalpa*) does not apply. For this very reason, the statement "optionally when a *kṅit* or *ac* [suffix follows]" was made there in the Bhāṣya; thus we have *mṛjanti* and *mārjanti*. Regarding this, Haradatta says: although it would be established by the rule "when a suffix is prescribed, the designation *ādi* applies to that which begins with it" (Pāṇini 1.1.72) even if only *ac* were stated, the inclusion of the word *ādi* is for the purpose of including the primary vowels (*aj*) at the beginning.

It is argued that by the principle of *vyapadeśivadbhāva* (treating a thing as if it were what it is designated), [the rule] does not apply to forms beginning with vowels such as *yūyaṃ mamṛja* and *tvayā mamṛje*. This, however, is questionable, because there is no evidence for accepting the primary vowel-initial forms [as the basis for the rule]. Indeed, the *Bhāṣya* does not employ the term "beginning" (*ādi*) such that the aforementioned meaning could be obtained; rather, it reads the statement: *kṅity aci vā*.

As for what was previously stated in the Bhāṣya: "In this regard, other grammarians (vaiyākaraṇas) optionally initiate vṛddhi before an affix beginning with a non-jhal consonant after the root *mṛj*," that is merely a restatement of the sentence-meaning obtained through the force of the *tadādi-paribhāṣā* (the rule concerning "that which begins with that"), and not the actual body of an independent injunctive rule (*vidhi-vākya*) by which your proposed meaning could be indicated. For this very reason, Ātreya states that the absence of vṛddhi occurs because of the inclusion of *mṛj* in the *bhidādi* group and because of its very listing in the *gaṇa*.

For this very reason, even in the *Dhātupradīpa*, which has been protected [as an authoritative work], both forms—*tuṇḍapari-mṛjaḥ* and *tuṇḍaparimārjaḥ*—are shown. However, in the *Durghaṭavṛtti*, it is stated that in the case of *tuṇḍaparimṛjaḥ*, the vṛddhi [substitution] does not occur due to the rule of "restricted option" (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). For this same reason, in the *Dhātuvṛttis*, two forms—*yūyaṃ mamṛja* and *mamārja*—are cited as examples. As for the point that even in the view of those who maintain that the primary [meaning of the term] refers to the *ajādi* group [of vowels], the confusion regarding the vṛddhi here is indeed unavoidable.

For instance, regarding the substitution of *a* for the *th* of the second-person plural ending (*madhyamapuruṣabahuvacana*), which is prescribed by the rule *parasmaipadānām* (Pāṇini 7.1.82), it would follow that this replacement applies only to the final letter of the suffix. One might object that such a rule would be redundant, since its purpose is fulfilled by ensuring the correct sequential correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhya*) with *ṇal* and the other substitutes. Anticipating this objection, the Bhāṣya itself will provide a twofold solution: "This substitute consists of two *a*s; because it has more than one letter (*anekāl*), it replaces the whole [suffix]."

Alternatively, since the governing rule *dātoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.91) applies, the vowel substitution for the letter *th* alone is by the rule *ādeḥ parasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.54). In both these views, because of the application of *pararūpa* (single-substitute replacement) by *ato guṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.97), the status of being "originally beginning with a vowel" (*mukhyājāditva*) still exists due to the treatment as if the original were present (*sthānivadbhāva*) by *acaḥ parasmin* (Pāṇini 1.1.57). Thus, some have stated a refutation of this position based on the opinion of Haradatta Miśra. That is not correct; for just as in the case of the extension (*atideśa*) by *ādyantavat* (Pāṇini 1.1.21), it can easily be argued that even in the case of *sthānivadbhāva*, the quality of being "original" (*mukhyatva*) is absent. This is the direction of the argument.

It might be argued as follows: in forms such as *acinot* and *amārṭ*, because the suffix *tip* would possess the property of being *ṅit* by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute behaving like the original), there would be a prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* by Pāṇini’s sūtra 1.1.5 (*kṅiti ca*). Nor can it be claimed that the application of *sthānivadbhāva* is impossible here because the rule is not an *alvidhi* (a rule concerning phonemes); for the prohibition "not in the case of operations concerning *anubandhas*" (*anubandhakāryeṣvanalvidhau*) does not apply. Otherwise, in forms such as *acinavam* and *amārjam*, since the suffix is not *pit*, it would incur the status of being *ṅit* by Pāṇini’s sūtra 1.2.4 (*sārvadhātukamapit*), which would lead to undesired results.
