And here, the indicator (*jñāpaka*) is the rule *na lyapi* (Pāṇini 6.4.69). Otherwise, since the substitution of *it* would not apply due to the absence of *kit*-tva for *lyap*, what would be the purpose of that rule intended to prohibit it? As for the claim that the mention of *apit* in the rule *serhyaṣicca* (Pāṇini 3.4.87) is the indicator, that is not so; for in examples such as *śṛṇīhi viśvataḥ prati*, the rule has its purpose fulfilled by producing an udātta accent in place of the anudātta *siP*, which—being *pit*—would otherwise have been replaced by an anudātta *hi* according to the maxim of the "nearest substitute" (*sthānentaratama-paribhāṣā*).

For in that case, due to the incapacity of the *apit* [suffix], the *antaratama-paribhāṣā* (the rule regarding the closest substitute) is set aside. Alternatively, let it be understood that the mention of *api*—where one could have simply said "udātta" for the sake of brevity in comprehension—is an indicator (*jñāpaka*). This matter is also established by reasoning: since the *anubandhas* (indicatory letters) are not "non-exclusive" (*anekānta*), they do not enter into the category of the substituendum (*sthānin*); consequently, the prohibition stated in Pāṇini 1.1.56, "in a rule concerning an *al* [phoneme]," does not apply here.

"Since the *anubandhas* are 'exclusive' (*ekānta*), they too are removed by the internal operation (*antaraṅga*) of elision even before their status as *sthānin*s is realized. Therefore, it would be difficult to prevent the *ṅit*-character of the substitutes *tiP* and so forth for the *laṭ* and other suffixes by means of *sthānivadbhāva*. To this, they say: the mention of *ṅit* in the rule *yāsuṭ parasmaipadeṣu* (Pāṇini 3.4.103) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the *ṅit*-character of substitutes for *l*-suffixes does not occur through *sthānivadbhāva*. And thus says the Vārttika: "If it is argued that because the *l*-suffix is *ṅit*, there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of *sthānivadbhāva* in its substitutes, [the answer is] that it is established by the mention of *ṅit* for *yāsuṭ*."

But surely, let the *ṅit*-ness of *yāsuṭ* serve to prohibit the *vṛddhi* not characterized by *iK* in forms such as *stuyāt*, and to prohibit [the substitution of] *guṇa* by the rule "before *jus*" (*jusica*, Pāṇini 7.2.83) in forms such as *cinuyuḥ*. In the rule "vṛddhi before *hal* when *luk* occurs after *ut*" (*uto vṛddhir luki hali*, Pāṇini 7.3.89), the *ik-paribhāṣā* does not apply because the rule specifies *dyuta-* as the locus of the operation. Furthermore, the rule "before *jus*" (*jusica*) is indeed an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule "before *kṅit*" (*kṅiti ca*, Pāṇini 1.1.5).

Consequently, the *ṅit*-ness obtained through the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) is not sufficient to prohibit the *vṛddhi* and *guṇa* substitutions in forms such as *stuyāt* and *cinuyuḥ*. However, by the force of the *ṅit*-ness itself, the prohibition of both will nevertheless take effect.

If it is asked: "In that case, since the *ṅittva* of *yāsuṭ* has already served its purpose in prohibiting *vṛddhi* and *guṇa*, how can it indicate the absence of *ṅittva* based on the *l*-suffixes (*lādeśa*) in those [forms]? It is replied: The mention of *vṛddhi* in the rule *ata aut* (Pāṇini 6.1.93)—where one could have simply said *ata au*—is for the sake of ensuring that a rule preceded by a technical name (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*) is not necessarily eternal (*anitya*). Consequently, there is no *vṛddhi* in *stuyāt*, and likewise no *guṇa* in *cinuyuḥ*. This is because, following the word *aci* from the rule *ksasyāci* (Pāṇini 7.3.82), *guṇa* is prescribed before a *jus* suffix beginning with a vowel (*ajādau*).

In the rule *mider guṇo 'kajusi ca*, one should read the vowel *a* as a *praśleṣa* (an elided element), and by adopting a *karmadhāraya* compound—namely, *acaḥ* and *us*—one avoids the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that would otherwise occur in forms such as *cakruḥ* and *jarhuḥ* if one were to rely on the application of *guṇa* before *us* beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*). The analysis is as follows: *guṇa* is a word with its case-ending dropped (*luptavibhaktika*), and the division is *jus-i*. Thus, the meaning is "in *jus* beginning with *u*. Furthermore, the *vārttika*—"The prohibition of *yāsuṭ* applies when there is *guṇa* before *jus*"—is intended merely to state a conclusion already established by the aforementioned method; such is the intention (*hṛdaya*) of the author of the *vārttika*.

According to the view of the Bhāṣyakāra, however, in the rule *sārvadhātukam apit* (Pāṇini 1.2.4), the term *apit* is divided into two separate yogas (*yoga-vibhāga*), and by carrying over (*anuvṛtti*) the word *ṅit* and relying on repetition (*āvṛtti*), two distinct sentence-meanings are described: "that which is *ṅit* is not *pit*, and that which is *pit* is not *ṅit*. This is clearly stated in the Bhāṣya on the rule *halaḥ śnaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.73).

Therefore, in the case of *brūtāt*, the substitution *tātaṅ* for *bruvaḥ* (the root *brū*) does not possess the status of *ṅit* [by rule P. 3.4.79], because the *antaraṅga* (inherently taught) *ṅit*-status overrides the *bahiranga* (derived by extension) *pit*-status, according to the maxim: "That which is inherently taught is stronger than that which is extended. However, in cases such as *acinot*, the *atideśika* (extended) *ṅit*-status dependent on *liṅ* is overridden by the *aupadeśika* (inherently taught) *pit*-status of *tiP* and other suffixes; thus, the occurrence of *guṇa* and other operations is established. And under this view, the explicit mention of the *ṅit*-status of *yāsuṭ* is not an indicator (*jñāpaka*), but rather it serves to prescribe *ṅit*-status where it was otherwise unobtained, as in *mṛjyāt*.

Consequently, there is an annulment of *pitvasya* (the status of being followed by *pi*), which otherwise finds scope in forms such as *cinoti*. Therefore, in forms like *stuyāt*, the *vṛddhi* prescribed by the rule *halīti* does not apply. As for *cinuyuḥ*, however, it should be justified in the same manner as before. But according to the view of the *vārttika* cited earlier, *iṭ* would result in *brūtāt*. This must somehow be resolved by the principle that "the teaching regarding augments is not universally obligatory" (*āgamaśāsanamanityam*).

In reality, however, by the addition of the *ś* marker (*śit*) to the suffix *śānac* in the rule *halaḥ śnaḥ śānajjhau* (Pāṇini 3.1.83), it is indicated that "the prohibition [of treating a suffix as having no marker] even in the case of operations concerning markers applies in some instances. Consequently, there is no fault in forms such as *brūtāt*. For this very reason, according to the view of the Bhāṣya, there is no *ṅīp* in *bhaviṣīṣṭa* due to its being marked with *ṅ*, nor is there *ṅīp* in *kariṣyamāṇā* due to the conditions of the *ugit* or *aṭ* markers; such is the direction of the argument. [The rule] *dīdhīvevīṭām* (Pāṇini 1.1.6).

In the case of the roots *dīdhī* and *vevī*, as well as for the augment *iṭ*, neither *guṇa* nor *vṛddhi* substitutions occur. [Examples: *ādīdhyanam*, *ādīdhyakaḥ*; *āvevyanam*, *āvevyakaḥ*. [With the suffix *luṅ*: *akaṇiṣam*, *araṇiṣam*; [with the suffix *luṭ*: *kaṇitā śvaḥ*, *raṇitā śvaḥ*. In this context, with respect to the suffix *ām*, the stem (*aṅga*) ends in *sij*. However, with respect to the substitute *ḍā* for the suffix *tip*, the stem ends in *t* (as in *kaṇit* and *raṇit*). Taking that *ām* and the substitute *ḍā*—both of which are *sārvadhātuka*—as the cause, the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha-guṇa*) would otherwise apply; it is prohibited by this rule. As for *vṛddhi*, it simply cannot occur in the case of the augment *iṭ*.

The word *śvas* is employed here to demonstrate that [the suffix] ends in *luṭ*. For there is no possibility of *guṇa* substitution for the *iṭ* augment in the case of suffixes ending in *tṛc* or *tṛn*, because that [augment] is a constituent part of the suffix itself. If one asks: "Why are the roots *dīṅ* (to perish, DhP 1.28), *dhīṅ* (to disregard, DhP 1.30), and *veñ* (to weave, DhP 1.38) not included here?"—it is not so; for the conventional meaning of a whole (*samudāya-prasiddhi*) is stronger than the conventional meaning of its parts (*avayava-prasiddhi*).

Furthermore, if the inclusion of the four [roots] were intended, one should have simply said "dīve-dhīvī-ṭām" for the sake of avoiding ambiguity; moreover, here *iṭ* is understood as the augment alone, not the root *iṭ* meaning "to go" (DhP 3.19). Now, one might argue that by virtue of association with the root *dā*, only the root should be taken. This is not so, because association is not a restrictive factor in all cases.

Otherwise, the mention of the term *kṛtvo'rtha* ("in the sense of times") in the rule *dvistriścaturiti kṛtvortha* (Pāṇini 5.4.18) would not have been made; for, by virtue of association with *dvis* and *tris*, which end in the suffix *suC*, it would be impossible to include *catur* as well, since it does not end in *suC*. For this very reason, in the rule, *dīdhīṅ* is placed first because the base (*prakṛti*) is more important than the augment (*āgama*). If, however, *iṭ* were also considered a verbal root (*dhātu*), then despite there being no difference in their status as bases, *iṭ* alone would have to be placed first because it has fewer syllables (*alpa-actaratva*).

In this regard, it should be noted that the forms *dīdhyakaḥ* and *vevyakaḥ*, which were cited as examples, are derived from the roots *dīdhī* and *vevī* in their simple (non-causative) state with the suffix *ṇvul*, and not even from their causative (*ṇic*) forms.

As for what was stated by Haradatta under the rule *yīvarṇayor dīdhīvevyoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.53)—namely, that the word *varṇa* is derived from the root *varṇa* (Dhātupāṭha 406) with the suffix *ac*, and that since the substitution of a *sthānin* occurs only when [the original] is actually heard (*śrūyamāṇa*), there is no elision (*lopa*) because of this state of being heard; thus, once the *yaṇ*-substitution is applied, the form becomes identical to the simple root in cases such as *dīdhyakaḥ* and *vevyakaḥ*—this very point was addressed by the authors of the Bhāṣya under the rule *nāglopiśāsvṛditām* (Pāṇini 7.4.2).

The form *dīdhakaḥ* derived from the causative (*ṇyanta*) should be disregarded because it contradicts the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), whereas the form *dīdhyakaḥ* is derived from the simple root. For in that context, having raised the objection that the mention of the letter (*varṇagrahaṇa*) is intended so that the rule might apply even when the letter has been elided, [the author] rejects such a mention; since the result is already established through the principle of "behaving like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), the elision by the rule *yīvarṇayoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.66) is established prior to the elision of the causative suffix (*ṇilopa*) due to its being an internal operation (*antaraṅga*). Thus, the explicit mention of the letter is superfluous.

If it is argued that we have spoken by following an intention of the Sūtra-author regarding the mention of *varṇa* that is indeed different from what was stated by the Bhāṣya-author, that is true; nevertheless, because of the increasing authority of the Munis in successive stages, the impurity of form remains exactly as it was—this is the direction of the argument.

It might be argued: since the roots *dīdhī* and *vevī* have the marker *ṅ*, the prohibition [of Guṇa] should apply by the rule itself, "In the presence of an affix marked with *ṅ*" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 1.1.5); what then is the purpose of including *dīdhī* and *vevī* here? Do not say so; for it has been stated that that prohibition applies only to those [Guṇa and Vṛddhi] which are conditioned by an *iK* vowel. Furthermore, the Vṛddhi prescribed by "Before an affix beginning with *ñ* or *ṇ*" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 7.2.115) is not conditioned by an *iK* vowel. Moreover, even if the possessor of the operation were to serve as the cause, the result might still be established by the former rule. However, the possessor of the operation is not accepted as the cause, because if it were, there would be the undesirable consequence of prohibiting Guṇa even in forms such as *cyavate* and *plavate*.

And here, the evidence [for this paribhāṣā] is the inclusion of the root *kūṅ* (DhP 1.211, "to sound") among the roots beginning with *kuṭ*, as well as the technical usage in Pāṇini’s rule *sthāṇḍilācchayitari* (P. 4.2.15). As for the claim that the mention of *dīdhī* and *vevī* in the present sūtra itself serves as the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this paribhāṣā—that is not correct; for its purpose is already fulfilled by the prohibition of *vṛddhi* not characterized by *it*. Furthermore, according to the Bhāṣya’s view, since this sūtra is to be rejected, one must instead seek other indicators for the aforementioned paribhāṣā.

It might be argued as follows: if the effect (*kāryin*) is not accepted as the cause (*nimitta*), then how is it that in the form *ūrṇunaviṣati*, the syllable *nu* undergoes reduplication by the rule *dvirvacane'ci* (Pāṇini 1.1.59)? For although *iṣ* begins with a vowel (*ajādita*), it cannot serve as the cause for reduplication because it has entered into the status of the effect (*kāryimadhye*). This is because reduplication is prescribed for the entire base ending in *san* by relying on the genitive case in the rule *sanyaho* (Pāṇini 6.1.9). Otherwise, in the form *pratīṣiṣati*, there would be no reduplication of the suffix *san*.

As for the argument that even if the locative case in *sanyaṅoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.9) were adopted, reduplication would still occur by virtue of the power of the vocalization of the vowel *a* in *san* and *yaṅ*, that is not correct; for the vocalization of the vowel *a* serves its purpose by preventing the derivation of *yaṅ* after roots such as *ditsa* and *dhitsa*, and by enabling the production of the suffix *yat* according to *aco yat* (Pāṇini 3.1.97). Otherwise, forms such as *aririṣati* would be unestablished. For if, in those cases as well, the substitute were treated as the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), then once reduplication had taken place, the form would have been *ariṣati*.

To this it is replied: the meaning of the *paribhāṣā* is that an element which is itself undergoing an operation (*kāryin*) is not accepted as the cause (*nimitta*) for that very same operation. For in the case of *aririṣati*, the rule *ajāderdvitīyasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.2) applies the doubling (*dvitva*) to the syllable *iris*. Since the syllable *is* is included within that [syllable *iris*], it cannot be the cause for its own doubling, because it is itself subject to the operation.

In the case of *ūrṇunaviṣati*, however, although the doubling (*dvitva*) of the syllable *nav* is obtained, the syllable *iṣ* is not included within it; thus, it remains a cause [for the doubling of *nav*], because it has been made clear by the author of the *Bhāṣya* in the rule *sanyaṅoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.9) that being a cause here consists merely in the fact that [the result] occurs when [the cause] is present. Consequently, by the rule *dvirvacane'ci* (Pāṇini 1.1.59), which prescribes the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*), the doubling of the syllable *nu* is indeed appropriate.

As for the counter-example provided by the ancient grammarians (*prācām*) under the rule *dvirvacane 'ci* (Pāṇini 1.1.59)—namely, "What is the purpose of [specifying] *aci*? [Consider] *jeghrīyate*, *dedhmīyate*"—that is merely superficial. This is because, although the elements *ghrīy* and *dhmīy* undergo reduplication (*dvitva*), the *yaṅ* suffix—which serves as the cause for the substitution of *ī* in *ghrādhyamoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.31)—is not itself the cause for the reduplication.

Therefore, in that context, it should be understood that only the form *adhijage* is excluded by the rule for *aci*. This is because, based on the dual-lakāra notation in Pāṇini’s sūtra *gāṅ liṭi* (2.4.49), the substitution of *gāṅ* is prescribed only in the state of the *lādeśa* (the substitute for the root). Furthermore, the mention of *ac* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the *rūpa-sthānivadbhāva* (the status of the substitute being like the original form). Consequently, even the Vārttika on that [sūtra] should be interpreted as follows: if one were to resort to an extension of the operation (*kāryātideśa*) in the example *adhijage*, the mention of *ac* would be redundant. This is the general direction of the argument.

As for what will be stated in the *Asiddhavat-sūtra*—"In this context, the mention [of the word] is for the purpose of understanding that they share the same substratum (*samānāśraya*)"—that is not correct. "Being the substratum" means simply some form of dependence, whether as the locus of substitution (*sthānitayā*) or as a cause (*nimittatayā*), and there is no insistence that it must be solely as a cause. Therefore, in the rule *śā hau* (Pāṇini 6.4.35), the substitution of *śā* for *hi* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) when the substitution of *dhi* for *hi* is to be applied. Otherwise, since *hi* would be the object of the operation (*kāryitayā*), it would lack the status of being a cause, and thus the non-existence (*asiddhatva*) of the former would not apply. For this very reason, they say that an internal (*ābhīya*) rule is non-existent with respect to another internal rule when they share the same substratum (*samānāśraya*), and not when they share the same cause (*samānanimitta*).

This sūtra has been rejected by both the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika. For instance, the roots *dīdhī* and *vevī* are Vedic; they are not fit for use in common worldly speech (*loka*). Furthermore, the substitution of *guṇa* (vocalization) is observed for these two in the Veda—as in "hotrāya vṛtaḥ kṛpayannadīdhet" and "adīdhayurddīśarajñe vṛtāsaḥ. Nor can this be justified by the principle of diversity (*bāhulaka*), because if that were the case, it would be more appropriate—and simpler—to simply not compose the prohibitive sūtras at all.

Likewise, the inclusion of *iṭ* here is also redundant. For in the rule *ārddhadhātukasyeṭ* (Pāṇini 7.2.35), the mention of *iṭ* from the preceding rule *neḍ vaśi kṛti* (Pāṇini 7.2.8) is understood to follow. And that [mention of *iṭ*] is for the purpose of ensuring that the augment is *iṭ* itself and not something modified by it, as explained in the commentary: "the *iṭ* is *iṭ* alone, not something altered. Consequently, due to the absence of the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*), forms such as *kaṇitā śvaḥ* and *raṇitā śvaḥ* are established.

Nor should it be argued that, in this way, the long vowel would not occur in *pipaṭhīḥ*; for that [rule] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the present restriction (*niyama*). However, the homogeneous long vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*) in *apāṭhīt* is not prevented, based on the indicative evidence (*jñāpaka*) of the rule: "The elision of *sic* is to be stated as established (*siddha*) regarding a single-substitute operation" (*sijlopa ekādeśe siddho vaktavyaḥ*). Alternatively, a restriction (*niyama*) formulated within the governing context of the stem (*aṅga-adhikāra*) excludes only a modification of the stem itself. Consequently, the long vowel occurs precisely by the rules *rvoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.76) and *akaḥ savarṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.101).

In the case of *grahītā*, however, the long vowel certainly occurs by virtue of the very introduction of the rule *graho'liṭi* (Pāṇini 7.2.37). But this remains to be addressed: why in the example *pipaṭhīṃṣi brāhmaṇakulāni* the lengthening [of the penultimate vowel] by the rule *sāntamahataḥ saṃyogasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.10) should not apply? This is because that rule is already established, because it is an internal (*āṅga*) operation, because it has its purpose fulfilled in cases such as *tejāṃsi*, and because this present case differs from the previously cited examples such as *pipaṭhiḥ*, *apāṭhīt*, and *grahītā*. On this point, they say: the usage *pipaṭhīṃṣi* is simply incorrect.

For here the augment *num* is not obtained, because due to the status of the elision (*allopasya*) as *sthānivadbhāva*, the stem does not end in a non-jhal vowel (*ajhalantatvāt*). Nor should it be said that *num* would thus arise by virtue of the stem ending in a vowel (*ajantatva*), for even so, the long vowel (*dīrgha*) does not apply because *num* would follow after the *s*, and there is no *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster) beginning with *s*. In reality, however, *num* does not occur here by virtue of the stem ending in a vowel, precisely because *sthānivadbhāva* is impossible; for a rule applies to what precedes an *ac* (vowel) that has not been previously enjoined (*anādiṣṭādacaḥ pūrvasya vidhau hi saḥ*).

Furthermore, that which ends in a vowel (*ajanta*) cannot precede an unindicated vowel (*anādiṣṭāt*), such that when *num* is to be applied to it, the elision of *al* (*allopaḥ*) would be treated as if it were the original element (*sthānivat*). Now, one might argue that *num* caused by the fact of ending in a consonant (*jhal*) is unavoidable. Nor should one suspect the application of *sthānivadbhāva* in that case, because of the prohibition: "That which is elided before *kvip* is not *sthānivat*" (*kvau luptaṃ na sthānivat*). Otherwise, forms such as *sakhīḥ* from the denominative *sakhīyati* after *kvip*, or *sutīḥ* from *sutīyati*, would not be possible, since the elision of *al* would be *sthānivat* and would thus entail the substitution of *yaṇ*.

To this it is replied: first, the body of the *vārttika* is "An addition [to the rule] regarding *kvip*, elision (*luk*), the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*), the *atva* [change], the *aṅ* suffix, the subsequent [element], shortening (*nirhrāsa*), and the substitution of *ku*. Among these, although the portion concerning *kvip* will be explained in two ways—as "that which is elided by *kvip* is not like its original" (*na sthānivat*) and "with respect to an operation prescribed for *kvip*, [the original] is not like its original"—it is as follows.

Although forms such as *dayūḥ* from *devayati* are established by resorting to either of the two explanations [regarding the status of the suffix], the form *sakhīḥ* from *sakhīyati* is not established without the first explanation, and the form *lauḥ* from *lavam ācakṣāṇaḥ* is not established without the second explanation; therefore, the second explanation—"with respect to an operation prescribed for *kvip*"—is universally applicable.

The phrase "in some instances" (*kvācitkam*) regarding the elision [of the *it*] is based on the *Bhāṣya* and other works in the cases of Pāṇini 6.1.112 (*khyatyāt*) and 7.2.91 (*maparyantasya*), but it is not universal. In this matter, the authority is the very *Bhāṣya* under discussion, which is intent on rejecting the inclusion of the term *iṭ*. Otherwise, how could the author reject the inclusion of *iṭ* when, in forms such as *pipaṭhīṃṣi*, a long vowel is desired and obtained according to the rule of the Sūtra?
Therefore, it is established that the form is simply *pipaṭhiṣi brāhmaṇakulāni*. 7. Consonants following immediately after one another constitute a *saṃyoga* (conjunction). (Pāṇini 1.1.7)

Consonants not separated by vowels shall receive the designation *saṃyoga* (conjunction). The applications of this designation are found in rules such as *Pāṇini Sūtra* 8.2.23: *saṃyogāntasya*. Here, since the word *antara*, meaning "gap" or "opening," is used in a *bahuvrīhi* compound to convey the sense of "without gaps," there should be no application of the designation in cases of *avagraha* (the pause between words in a *pada-pāṭha*). However, when the indeclinable *antare*—which emphasizes the contained—is used with a *bahuvrīhi*, it conveys the negation of an interval (*ttvādeya*), and thus the designation must indeed apply even in the case of *avagraha*.

For there is nothing whatsoever in between—that is, in the middle—there; rather, it is merely a *mātrā*. This is because, according to the authority of the *Prātiśākhya* rule, "A *mātrā* is indeed the interval of an *avagraha*" (*Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya* 1.6), one accepts that the duration of a *mātrā* concludes there. As for the other *Prātiśākhya* statement—"An *avagraha* consists of half a *mātrā"—that intends to show that since a half-*mātrā* duration exists everywhere in *saṃhitā*, there is an additional half-*mātrā* duration specifically in the *avagraha*.

Therefore, there is no contradiction between the two Prātiśākhyas. If it is asked, "Which of these two positions should be adopted here? the commentators maintain that there is no fault in either case. But surely, in examples such as *apsu*, if the designation *saṃyoga* (conjunction) were applied, then by the rule *saṃyoge guru* (Pāṇini 1.4.10), the syllable would be heavy; consequently, by the rule *guroranṛtaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.86), a protracted vowel (*pluta*) would have to occur, and not otherwise—thus there would be a great difference in the result.

If it is asked, "How then can both positions be accepted?"—it is not so; for in the case of *apsu* functioning as a locative (*adhikaraṇavṛtti*), there is no connection with the elision of the suffix *ṅasi* [which would apply] from a distance. However, in rules such as *vicāryamāṇānām* (Pāṇini 8.2.97), the rule *vākyasya ṭeḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.82) is what is being carried over (*anuvartate*), and not *guroranṛtaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.86). Now, one might object: "In the word *apsavyaḥ*, meaning 'born in the waters,' the suffix *yat* is applied because the group beginning with *dig-* includes *ap-*; furthermore, by the Vārttika *apo yoniyanmatuṣu ca*, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending."

If it is argued that, consequently, there would indeed be a difference in the result in the case of the reduplicated form *sambuddhau* (vocative singular) in the word *he apsavya*, [we reply as follows].

Regarding this, they say that the authors of the *padapāṭha* do not apply avagraha (separation) in such cases; here, tradition alone must be accepted as the authority. This has been stated: in examples such as *gobhyo gātum*, *gobhir madāya*, and *citraidrājā rājakā id anyake*, although *gobhyaḥ*, *gobhiḥ*, and *rājakāḥ* are indeed words (*pada*), no avagraha is applied. Furthermore, in cases such as *īyivāṃsam atisridhaḥ*, even though *īyivāṃsam* lacks the designation of a word (*pada*), an avagraha is applied before the suffix *kvasu* at the end of the augment *iṭ*.

By this, the presence of *sattva* (the substitution of *s* for *ṣ*), shortening (*hrasvatva*), and so forth in cases such as *sisāsan*, *ukthaśasaḥ*, and *ririṣaḥ* at the time of the *padapāṭha* are also explained. As for what was stated by the commentators on the Veda regarding the mantra *mā no mahāntam*—namely, that "the shortening at the time of the *padapāṭha* is Vedic (*chāndasa*)"—that too must somehow be understood as being based merely on traditional practice (*saṃpradāya*). This is because the *Mahābhāṣya* states, "The makers of the *padapāṭha* do not follow grammatical rules," and Kaiyaṭa and others have declared that "the division of words (*padavibhāga*) is of human origin. Such is the direction of the argument.

If it is asked, "How then is it said that there is a distinction in the *avagraha* (separation) in various instances? understand this as referring to the general rule (*utsarga*) that an *avagraha* is made when there is an intermediate word (*avāntarapada*). Even in cases such as "apsuyonir vā aśvaḥ," there is no *avagraha* before the word "su"; rather, according to the Vedic tradition, the *avagraha* occurs at a time subsequent to the recognition of multiple intermediate words. For this very reason, in the case of "mayūraromabhiḥ," the *avagraha* occurs before the suffix *bhis*.

The same applies here in the case of *namauktibhiḥ*. And in the case of *indraprāṇaḥ puraeteva*, [the rule applies] before the word *eva*; such is the direction. The use of a technical name (*mahāsaṃjñā*) is for the purpose of understanding that the name is significant (*anvartha*). [It means: "In this collection (*samudāya*), the phonemes (*varṇa*) are joined together. Therefore, the completion of the sentence (*vākya-parisamāpti*) occurs with respect to this collection, and not with respect to each individual element as in the case of the technical names *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. For if it were so, in forms such as *niryāyāt*, the *yakāra* would be a *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster), and consequently, by the rule *vānyasya saṃyogādyoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.68), there would be the substitution of *etva* (the shortening of the vowel).

In the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), however, although doubling occurs by the rule *aco rahābhyām* (Pāṇini 8.4.46), because that [doubling] is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), the substitution of *e* does not take place in forms such as *niryāyāt*. Furthermore, on the view that the designation applies to each individual letter, the augment *iṭ* would occur in *saṃdṛṣīṣṭa* by the rule *ṛtaśca saṃyogādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.43). Also, in *saṃhriyate*, the substitution of *guṇa* would occur by the rule *guṇorttisaṃyogādyoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.29), resulting in *saṃhriyate*.

In the case of *dṛṣatkaroti*, due to the status of the cluster (*saṃyoga*) resulting from the proximity of the letter *k* to the letter *d*, there would be elision of the final member of the cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*). In the cases of *śaktā* and *vastā*, when followed by a *takāra* belonging to the *jhāl* group, there would be elision according to Pāṇini 8.2.29 (*skoḥ*). In *niryātaḥ* and similar forms, there would be the substitution of *ṇatva* for the *niṣṭhā* suffix according to Pāṇini 8.2.43 (*saṃyogāderāto dātoryaṇvataḥ*).

This plural form *halaḥ* is used in the sense of a genus (*jāti*), according to the rule *jātyākhyāyām ekasmin* (Pāṇini 1.2.58). Consequently, the designation *saṃyoga* applies even to a pair [of consonants]. Therefore, in forms such as *śikṣā*, the suffix *ap* is established by the rule *gurośca halaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.103). However, where many consonants are joined together, the designation applies specifically to pairs or to all of them. Nor should it be argued that, by the logic of reduplication of a single vowel (*ekāj-dvirvacana*), the designation would apply only to the entire aggregate; for there is a lack of parity (*vaiṣamya*) between the two cases.

For instance, it is impossible to perform reduplication simultaneously for both a whole and its parts when they consist of a single vowel; however, the designation (*saṃjñā*) can be applied. Thus, when the whole is reduplicated, the parts are also reduplicated, according to the maxim: "When a tree moves, it moves together with its parts. But in this case, the designation *sayoga* (conjunction), which applies to the whole, does not effect that operation for the parts. Therefore, it is established that the designation applies without distinction to both two and many [consonants].

If, however, [the substitution] were to apply only when many [consonants] follow, then in the case of *saṃskriyate*, the *guṇa* substitution prescribed by Pāṇini 6.4.146 (*guṇo’rti*) would not occur; in *gomān karoti*, the elision of the final consonant of the *saṃyoga* cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) would not occur; and in *nirglānaḥ* and similar forms, the substitution of *ṇatva* for the *niṣṭhā* suffix would not occur—this is the general direction of the argument.

Now, if both [the *na* and the *da*] are designated as "saṃjñā" (technical terms), then in the case of the desiderative of *indidrīyati*, the form *indidriyiṣati* would not be possible. For here there are two *saṃyogas*: *na-da* and *da-ra*. In that case, just as for the *na*, the prohibition of doubling (*dvitva*) by the rule *nandrāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.2) would apply to the *da* as well. This is not a fault. For in that rule, the word *ajādeḥ* ("beginning with a vowel") is understood as a governing term (*anuvartate*). And that [genitive] is a genitive in a *karmadhāraya* compound. Therefore, the meaning of the sūtra is: "In the case of a root beginning with a vowel, the *saṃyoga*s beginning with *na*, *da*, or *ra* that follow the initial vowel are not doubled. Thus, the *da* is not subject to the prohibition.

And thus, it will be stated that in the preceding sūtra, the word "of the second" (*dvitīyasya*) need not be included at all. What is the purpose of the condition *hal* (consonant)? Consider the example *titaubhyām*. Here, the suffix *i* is added by the rule *tanoter ḍauḥ sanvac ca* (Uṇādi Sūtra), and due to the treatment as if having *san*, there is reduplication (*dvitva*) and the substitution of *i* for *a* by the rule *sanyataḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.79). The absence of *guṇa* [substitution] occurs by virtue of the separate enunciation [of the consonant]. For if the designation *saṃyoga* were to apply even to two non-consonants (*ac*) that are adjacent, then in this case, the elision of the vowel *u* would occur by the rule *saṃyogāntasya* (Pāṇini 8.2.23).

What is the meaning of *anantarā* (immediate)? For example, *panasam*. If there were the designation of a *saṃyoga* (conjunct) for the letters *s* and *m* here, then by the rule *skoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.29), there would be the elision of the letter *s*; such is the direction [of the argument]. *Anunāsikaḥ* (nasalized) is that which is articulated through both the mouth and the nose (Pāṇini 1.1.8). "Mouth-and-nose" (*mukhanāsikā*) means the nose together with the mouth; that which is pronounced through these two shall have the designation *anunāsika*. The locations where this designation applies are such as *āṅo’nunāsikaś chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.126) and others. Examples include: *abhraām̐ apo vṛṇānā*, *gabhīraām̐ ugraputre*.

Regarding the term *vacana*: according to those who follow the *Vṛtti*, it is derived with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of the object (*karman*), based on the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.3.113), as in the expression "rice for the king’s meal" (*rājabhojanāḥ śālayaḥ*).

However, according to the *Bhāṣya* and Kaiyaṭa, *vacanam* means "that by which something is spoken," with *lyuṭ* in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*). It is used in the neuter gender in a general sense, as in "it is possible to dispel hunger" (*śakyaṃ ca kṣudapahantum*), and follows the pattern of rules such as *tena tulyaṃ kriyā cet* (Pāṇini 5.1.115) and *saṃskṛtaṃ bhakṣāḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.16).

And we shall explain in that very place how this does not contradict the statement "guṇavacanānām" and so forth—which will be stated under the rule *viśeṣaṇānāñcājāteḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.52)—insofar as it pertains to the rule-governed formation (*vācanika*) of words according to the theory of word-formation (*padasaṃskārapakṣa*). Therefore, [the term] is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has speech through both the mouth and the nose. Why include the word "mouth" (*mukha*)? The *Bhāṣya* states: so that [the designation "nasal"] might not apply to the *yama*s and the *anusvāra*s in this manner.

In that regard, among the groups [of consonants], when the fifth letter follows the first four, another letter of the same form as the preceding one is prescribed in the *Prātiśākhyas* as an *āgama* (augment); this is designated as a *yama*. It is called *yama* because it is like a twin (*yama*); for in the world, twins generally have identical forms. For example, in *palikrakrīḥ*, *cakhkhanatuḥ*, *agragniḥ*, and *aghraghnan*, there is the *yama* augment similar to each respective letter following *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, and *gha*.

As for what was stated in the *Vivaraṇa*: "The first [consonants] and so forth, when joined with the fifth of their respective classes, are *yamas*"; that is questionable, because it contradicts the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *hayavaraṭ*, which establishes their status as *ayogavāhas*, and because it also contradicts the *Bhāṣya* stating "only the *yamas* and *anusvāras* are purely nasal."

Just as this commentary does not intend merely to state that [the *nāsikya*] alone is nasal (*nāsikya*), but rather intends to show that while only a portion of sounds such as *ām̐* is nasal, the *yamas* and *anusvāras*, although they are both oral and nasal (*mukhanāsikya*), possess nasality according to the maxim of "one who lives in a palace" (*prāsādavāsinyāya*)—meaning they have a nasal component—but for those [sounds] at the beginning, such [nasality] is simply impossible. Even so, for the first four [sounds], that [nasality] is indeed unattainable.

Furthermore, this contradicts the subsequent portion of the Bhāṣya which states, "There is neither a fault nor a purpose," because in examples such as *yad ghnanti*, a fault is prominent in your position due to the unwanted application of Pāṇini 8.4.45 (*yaro 'nunāsike*).

For this very reason, in the *Prātiśākhya*, after beginning with the rule "The stops (*sparśa*), when followed by non-nasalized *yamas* or nasalized [stops], [become nasalized]" (*Ṛk-prātiśākhya* 6.29), and having begun to prohibit the *yama* in the example "pradodhuvat śmaśruṣu," the word "parastāt" ("subsequent") is employed in the sūtra: "There is no occurrence of a *yama* subsequent to a stop whose original form is a sibilant (*ūṣman*)" (*Ṛk-prātiśākhya* 6.30).

"Yama is by its very nature similar [to the preceding vowel]," as stated in the *Śikṣā*: "Or rather, there is a primary *śruti* [sound] belonging to Yama at the same time" (*Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya* 6.33). In other such sūtras as well, the distinctness of Yama from the other phonemes is clearly established. Likewise, in the *Nāradīya Śikṣā* it is said: "If there is a final [consonant] before and an initial [consonant] after, then in between them stands the Yama, which has the same quality (*savarṇa*) as both the preceding and following letters."

*Savarṇa* means "similar. Here, the doubling of the preceding two sounds (*pūrvavarṇayoḥ*) is not intended to be mandatory. The commentators on this rule state that although there are two *ja*s in examples such as *yajjhaḥ*, there are no two *ja*s in examples such as *jmayā atra vasavorantadevāḥ*. Likewise, Audavraji, the author of the *Ṛktantra-vyākaraṇa*—a treatise on Vedic phonology—also formulated a rule: "In a conjunction of non-final and final sounds, a *yama* occurs in the middle, which is a quality of the preceding sound."

The phrase "the *guṇa* of the preceding" means "belonging to the preceding. [In the rule] "in the middle, the *yama* is the *guṇa* of the preceding," the phrase "the *guṇa* of the preceding" likewise means "belonging to the preceding. By this, he makes clear its status as an augment (*āgama*). Similarly, in the *Autamaśikṣā*, which is known as the *Saṃyogaśṛṅkhalā*, it is also stated: "Now, an example of four-syllable [words]: *sayamāyamābhyām*."

For example, in the word *agniḥ*, there are two *ga* sounds and two *ma-na* sounds; in *yajñaḥ*, there are two *ja* sounds and two *ma-ña* sounds, and so forth. Likewise, at the very beginning of this same work, after dividing conjunction (*saṃyoga*) into three types—namely, the iron ball (*ayasa-piṇḍa*), the wooden block (*dāru-piṇḍa*), and the woolen ball (*ūrṇā-piṇḍa*)—and having stated that the "iron ball" is that which is accompanied by a *yama*, it is said:
"No distinction is perceived in the conjunction of a semi-vowel (*antastha*) with a *yama*;
they call the *yama* bodiless, while the semi-vowel is the leader of the cluster."

Thus it has been stated. Here, "standing within" (*antastha*) refers to the fifth letter of each class (*varga*). "Bodiless" (*aśarīra*) means that, like a *svarabhakti* (vowel-fragment), it is devoid of a specific written character (*lipi*) that manifests it. Since its specific position can be determined solely by the rules of phonetics (*lakṣaṇa*), the teachers who established the tradition of writing did not devise a manifesting script for the *yama*, just as they did not for the *svarabhakti*. For it is well known in the *Śikṣā* and other treatises: "When a sibilant (*ūṣman*) follows, there is a *svarabhakti* between the *ra* and *la*."
However, where it was not possible to determine the place [of articulation] by such characteristics, another script was introduced out of necessity, as in the case of the *visarga* and so forth.
This is also stated in the *Pāṇinīyaśikṣā*:
"The number of phonemes is considered to be sixty-three or sixty-four, according to their occurrence."
They were spoken by the Self-Existent One himself, both in the Prakrit and in the Sanskrit languages.
The vowels are twenty-one, the sparśas (stops) are twenty-five,
the letters beginning with ya are remembered as eight, and the yamas are remembered as four.
The anusvāra, the visarga, the *ka* and *pa* [groups] when dependent on another,
the duḥspṛṣṭa, and the protracted (*pluta*) *ḷ*-vowel are to be known as such.

"(pāośio3|4|5)"—for here, because the *yam* sounds are counted separately, their status as distinct phonemes (*varṇāntaratva*) is quite evident. The enumeration is as follows: there are twelve vowels consisting of the four [vowels] *a, i, u, ṛ*, each having three varieties—short, long, and protracted; the single *ḷ* vowel; and eight [vowels] consisting of the *e, o, ai, au* diphthongs, each having two varieties—long and protracted. Thus, there are twenty-one vowels. There are twenty-five *sparśa* (stops). There are eight [semivowels and sibilants]: *ya, ra, la, va, śa, ṣa, sa, ha*. There are four *yam* sounds, by dividing them according to the distinctions of the first *yam*, second *yam*, and so forth.

For this very reason, the four *yamakas*—*kuṃ*, *khuṃ*, *guṃ*, and *ghuṃ*—are cited at the beginning of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). One should understand that these are intended to somehow demonstrate the subsequent unmanifest consonants by relying on the technical conventions (*paribhāṣā*) such as "ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, and *kaḥ*" and "kha, cha, ṭha, tha, pha, and *khuḥ*". There are four more: the anusvāra, the visarga, the *ka-pāśa* (the bindu), and the *duḥspṛṣṭa* (the jihvāmūlīya), which is well known among the Bahvṛcas in the mantra *īle volveha*. Thus, there are sixty-three. Including the *pluta* (protracted) form of the letter *ḷ*, there are sixty-four. This is what is meant by the phrase "as far as possible" (*sambhavataḥ*).

In the *Hayavaraṭ-sūtra*, Kṣīrodākāra also states: "The *yama* [sounds] are those situated between the final consonant of a varga and the penultimate letter; they have the nose as their place of articulation. As for what someone has said—that the *yamas* are substitutes—and that if they were nasalized, then in forms such as *tajjñaḥ* and *tad ghnanti*, the rule *yaro 'nunāsike* (Pāṇini 8.4.45) would result in the substitution of a nasal, thereby contradicting the *Bhāṣya* statement, "There is neither a fault nor a purpose [for this rule]," because one must resort to the principle of *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (restricted optionality). [This objection is not valid.]

That is hollow, because the position of [the rule being] a substitute (*ādeśa*) has already been discarded—like a miscarriage—due to its contradiction with all the aforementioned texts such as the *Prātiśākhyas*, the *Nāradīya-śikṣā*, and others; and because the assumption of an optionality based on fixed distribution (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) is entirely without foundation.

On account of this misconception regarding the authority of his writing, those who follow him have gone so far as to establish the absence of the *cavarga* in rules such as *anupasargāt jñaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.76) and thereby justify the absence of *ścutva*. However, this is refuted by Nārada’s explicit mention of two *ja*-sounds in the word *yajñaḥ*; for it is well known in the treatises that, just as in the usage of the Āraṇyaka—*nasyaitasya trayasyāsthnāmajñāṃ parvaṇām*—the distinction is not clear due to the proximity of similar sounds (*sajātīya-samabhivyāhāra*).

For this very reason, the *Bhāṣya* states: "There is no distinction whether there is one or more consonants following [the vowel]. Kaiyaṭa has explained this in various places with the intent that for a consonant following another consonant—that is, for that which has a consonant as its subsequent element—the distinction between difference and non-difference is difficult to perceive. And for this same reason, the *Bhāṣya* passage "The Teacher makes this known" appears in many manuscripts. Furthermore, even in the rule *anupasargāt* (Pāṇini 1.3.76), the reading *ścutva* is indeed accepted by some.

As for the alternative reading, [the form] may be justified either by treating it as a Vedic (sautra) usage—similar to the rules *alpāctaram* (Pāṇini 2.2.34), *āluc*, and *tadasahane*—or by not applying the rule of *saṃhitā*. This is the general direction. Having explained all this, the venerable teacher [Nāgeśa Bhaṭṭa] stated in the *Prakriyāprakāśa*: "In cases such as *tajjñānam*, the substitution of *ś* certainly occurs. Regarding the *yama* sound, there are two views: that it is articulated by both the mouth and the nose, or that its place of articulation is the nose alone; for the *Taittirīya Prātiśākhya* states: 'The *nāsikya* sounds have the nose as their place of articulation, or they are articulated by both the mouth and the nose.'"

Regarding the domain of nasalized sounds (*anunāsika*), there are three views: first, that the entire phoneme is articulated by both the mouth and the nose; second, that the preceding portion is articulated by the mouth and the subsequent portion by the nose; and third, the reverse of that. Although in the second and third views only a portion [of the sound] is nasal, due to its coloring (*uparāga*), the other portion also appears as such. Consequently, since the connection with the nose pertains only to a portion, the term "articulated by the nose" (*nāsikya*) would not include those phonemes articulated by both the mouth and the nose (*mukhanāsikya*).

However, in certain specific instances, because only the nasalized sounds (*nāsikya*) would be grasped as *yama*s and so forth, then in the application of rules such as "the *aṅ* [suffix] becomes nasal" (*aṅo'nunāsikaḥ*, Pāṇini 6.1.126), only the *yama*s and *anusvāra*s would be prescribed. Furthermore, in cases of restatement (*anuvāda*) such as "the nasal of *viṭ* and *van* becomes *āt*" (*viḍvanoranunāsikasyāt*, Pāṇini 6.4.42), there would simply be no comprehension at all. This is the intended meaning of the cited Bhāṣya. Therefore, it is established that the inclusion of the word "mouth" (*mukha*) is purposeful in both views.

However, regarding the first mention [of the term *mukha*], it is established that both types of statements [those concerning the nose and those concerning the mouth] apply by resorting to the "Prāsādavāsinī" maxim. Furthermore, at the first mention, the designation is established for both types of statements by resorting to the "Prāsādavāsinī" maxim; and due to the principle of closest proximity (*āntaratamya*), there is no application of *yama*s or *anusvāra*s in the places where the rule is extended (*vidhipradeśa*). Thus, it is established in the Bhāṣya that the inclusion of the word "mouth" (*mukha*) need not have been made. For if it were stated simply as "uttered by the mouth" (*mukhavacana*), then [the designation] would apply even to *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, and so forth.

Consequently, in the case of *śaktaḥ*, there would be the elision of *k*; in *pakvaḥ*, there would be the elision of *c*; in *taptaṃ*, there would be the elision of *p*; and in *odanapaṅ* and similar forms, there would be lengthening according to the rule *anunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.15). This is an etymological designation (*anvarthasaṃjñā*): that in which the nose (*nāsikā*) functions subsequently (*anu*), or rather, that in which the mouth functions behind the nose.

By this, it is indicated that the scope of the rule pertains to the portion situated at the nasalization (*nāsikā-vyāpāra*); thus, it is implied that this is not a case for the *prāsādavāsinyāya* (the maxim of the inhabitants of the palace). Furthermore, this sūtra can be dispensed with; for all desired results can be achieved by relying, within the specific rules themselves, on the previously mentioned connection (*yoga*) expressed as "following the nose" (*nāsikāmanugata*). This is the direction [of the argument].

*Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.9*: "A phoneme having the same place of articulation and internal effort is *savarṇa* (homogeneous). It should be understood that a phoneme is *savarṇa* with another phoneme when both its place of articulation—such as the palate (*tālu*) and so forth—and its internal effort are identical to those of that other phoneme. The applications of this technical term (*saṃjñāpradeśa*) are found in rules such as *Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.101*: "When *ak* [vowels] meet a homogeneous vowel, a long vowel is substituted."

Although the etymological meaning (*avayavārtha*) of *tulya* is "that which is measured by a balance" (*tulayā saṃmitaṃ*), because the rule *nauvayodharmaviṣamūlamūlasītātulābhyastāryatulyaprāpyavadhyānāmyasamasamitasammiteṣu* (Pāṇini 5.1.119) prescribes the suffix *yat* after the word *tulā* in the sense of "measured," nevertheless, this word is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of mere similarity. It is called *āsya* because one emits (*asyanti*) or utters (*uccārayanti*) phonemes (*varṇān*) by means of it; from the root *asu* in the sense of "throwing" (*kṣepaṇe*, Dhatupatha 1210), the suffix *ṇyat* is applied in the instrumental sense (*karaṇa*) by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*).

Alternatively, it is called *āsya* because food flows (*āsyandate*) into it upon reaching it and becomes liquefied; the suffix *ḍa* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.101 (*anyeṣv api*). Or else, it is *āsya* because it is made liquid by food (*annena dravīkriyate*); here the suffix *ḍa* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*) with the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) suppressed internally, as in the case of "a moat" (*paritaḥ khātā parikhā*). That which exists there is the oral cavity (*āsya*), consisting of the palate and so forth; this is formed by the suffix *yat* according to Pāṇini 5.1.6 (*śarīrāvayavād yat*).

When the *it* suffix is elided by Pāṇini-sūtra 6.4.148 (*yasya*), the elision of *y* occurs by Pāṇini-sūtra 8.4.64 (*halo yamām*). One should not suspect that the elision of *a* (*al-lopa*) is subject to the status of being "as if present" (*sthānivadbhāva*) [which would prevent the elision of *y*]; for such a status is prohibited when the elision of *y* is to be performed. *Prayatna* means "exertion" (*yatna*) that is "intense" (*prakṛṣṭa*). Intensity here refers to being internal (*ābhyantaratva*). Alternatively, *prayatna* is "exertion at the beginning" (*prārambhe yatnaḥ*). Indeed, the internal efforts (*ābhyantara-prayatnāḥ*) are active precisely at the time of the commencement of a phoneme (*varṇa*). Thus, the compound *tulyau sthānaprayatnau yasya* is a *bahuvrīhi* containing within it a *dvandva*.

Alternatively, it is a three-member *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "those whose effort (*prayatna*) in the mouth (*āsye*) is equal. The inclusion of the term "in the mouth" (*āsye*) serves to exclude external effort. The singular number in "in the mouth" (*āsye*) is intended to be significant, by virtue of the employment of the word *āsya* ending in a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*). Consequently, this implicitly excludes those sounds produced in different locations. Alternatively, *tulyāsya-prayatna* is a valid compound according to the rule for *mayūravyaṃsaka* and similar formations, meaning "that which has its effort in the mouth equal. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "that whose effort in the mouth is equal. Or again, *āsyaprayatna* means "effort in the mouth"; [the compound refers to] that whose [effort] is equal to that.

The intention to express oneness (*ekatva-vivakṣā*) and so forth is as explained previously. Thus, all four types of compounds are established in the Bhāṣya: "a *bahuvrīhi* containing a *dvandva*, or one consisting of three words, or one containing a *tatpuruṣa* in its prior member, or one containing it in its subsequent member. Furthermore, because the word *tulya* (equal) denotes a relationship, it is understood that "that with which [the organ] has the same place and effort is a *savarṇa* (homogeneous) with it. For when it is said, "one's mother is to be honored," it is not the mother of one's own son or wife who is meant to be honored, but rather the mother of the person performing the honor; such is the general principle.
What is meant by "having the same place"? It is so that [the rule] does not apply to *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, and *pa*, even though they have the same effort (*prayatna*).

Therefore, in the word *tarptā*, the elision of the letter *pa* does not occur by virtue of Pāṇini’s sūtra 8.4.65 (*jharo jhari*). Why is the mention of "effort" (*yatna*) necessary? It is so that [the rule] might not apply to the letter *ca* and the letter *śa*. For if there were phonetic similarity (*sāvarṇya*), then in the case of *vāk ścyotati*, the elision of the letter *śa* would occur; thus, the mention of "effort" is intended to prevent this in the case of *ca* and *śa*. This qualification regarding "internal effort" (*ābhyantara-prayatna*) is for this very purpose. Indeed, even between *ca* and *śa*, there exists a similarity in external efforts known as breath (*śvāsa*), lack of voicing (*aghoṣa*), and openness (*vivāra*).

If it is argued that there is a distinction based on having few articulatory efforts (*alpaprayatna*) versus having many articulatory efforts (*mahāprayatna*), what follows from that? For it is impossible to intend an equality of *all* articulatory efforts; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasanga*) that [the rule] "marked" (*aṅkitaḥ*) and so forth would be unestablished, because even for the sounds *ka* and *ṅa*, there is a difference in external articulatory effort (*bāhyaprayatna*). Indeed, the equality of all articulatory efforts applies only of a sound with itself, not with another. And thus, even the formulation of the technical term "homogeneous" (*savarṇa*) would be useless, since everything would be consistent by simply stating: "An *aṇ* is homogeneous with that which has the same place of articulation and articulatory effort."

Regarding the rule *jharo jhari* (Pāṇini 8.4.65), it has been stated that—just as in the case of *halo yamāṃ yami* (Pāṇini 8.4.64)—if the application were strictly according to numerical correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhya*), then just as the *m* in *māhātmyam* would not be elided, the *ḍh* in *śiṇḍhi* would likewise not be elided. Consequently, the inclusion of the term *savarṇa* (homogeneous) was made in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*). However, that fault of over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) would remain exactly as it was as long as there is an intention to restrict the correspondence to equality of effort (*prayatna*).

Now, even if one were to intend to include both external similarity and internal similarity, in the case of *madhuliṭstānam*, there would still be elision of the *s* by the rule *jharo jhari* (Pāṇini 8.4.65), because the *s* and the *th* share four identical external efforts (*bāhyaprayatna*), namely: being voiceless (*śvāsa*), unvoiced (*aghoṣa*), spread-apart (*vivāra*), and having great breath-force (*mahāprāṇatva*).

Now, the distinction of place and effort: *a*, *ku*, *ha*, and *visarjanīya* are gutturals (*kaṇṭhya*). *i*, *cu*, *u*, *ś*, and *va* are palatals (*tālavya*). *ṛ*, *ṭu*, *ra*, and *ṣ* are retroflexes (*mūrdhanya*). *ḷ*, *tu*, *lu*, and *sa* are dentals (*dantya*). *u*, *pu*, *ū*, *ṣ*, and *upadhmānīya* are labials (*oṣṭhya*). *e* and *ai* are gutturo-palatals. *o* and *au* are gutturo-labials. The letter *va* is dento-labial. The *jihvāmūlīya* has its place of articulation at the root of the tongue. The *anusvāra* is nasal (*nāsikya*).

Effort (*yatna*) is twofold: internal (*ābhyantara*) and external (*bāhya*). Among these, the internal is fourfold: contact (*spṛṣṭatā*), slight contact (*īṣatspṛṣṭatā*), openness (*vivṛtatā*), and closure (*saṃvṛtatā*). Among these, contact belongs to the stops (*sparśa*); slight contact belongs to the semivowels (*antasthā*); closure occurs in the pronunciation of the short *a*-vowel; however, for the purposes of grammatical operation (*śāstrīya-kārya*), openness is postulated, as established in the *aiuṇ* sūtra. As for the statement that "the [vowels] *y*, *v*, *ṛ*, and *ṝ* are closed," this is not universally applicable because it is stated in the *Prātiśākhya*.

The openness (*vivṛtatā*) belongs to the sibilants (*ūṣman*) and the vowels (*svara*). These four [vowels] possess internal effort (*ābhyantara-prayatna*) because they precede the production of the phonemes (*varṇa*). For instance, the vital air (*prāṇa-vāyu*), impelled by effort from the region of the navel, moves upward and strikes the articulatory locations (*sthāna*) such as the chest and so forth; from that, there arises either the phoneme itself or the sound (*dhvani*) that manifests it. Among these, when the tip, the middle, and the root of the tongue touch the respective articulatory locations—such as the palate—at the time prior to the production of the specific phoneme, that is "contact" (*spṛṣṭatā*).

When they touch [the palate] slightly, that is *īṣatspṛṣṭatā* (slight contact). Merely being situated near [the point of articulation] is *saṃvṛtatā* (closure), while being at a distance is *vivṛtatā* (openness). Therefore, although there is no difference in their palatal nature (*tālavyatva*), one should distinguish between them by following both experience and the statements of the authors of the *Śikṣās*: when the utterance of the *ca*-group is to be performed, the tip of the tongue and other organs must make full contact with the palate; for the letter *ya*, there is slight contact; but for the letters *śa* and *i*, there is a state of being situated at a distance, and so forth.

The authors of the Bhāṣya, however, while refuting the rule *nāj-jhalau* (Pāṇini 1.1.10), will state that there is a distinction between the sibilants (*ūṣman*) and vowels in that the former are slightly open (*īṣadvivṛta*) and the latter are fully open (*vivṛta*). This too should be understood by the discerning as being entirely consistent with experience.

The external efforts (*bāhyaprayatna*), moreover, are eleven: opening (*vivāra*), closing (*saṃvāra*), breath (*śvāsa*), resonance (*nāda*), voiced (*ghoṣa*), unvoiced (*aghoṣa*), weak aspiration (*alpaprāṇa*), strong aspiration (*mahāprāṇa*), acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), and circumflex (*svarita*). These arise when the vital air (*prāṇa*)—known as *vāyu*—has struck and turned back at the palate after the production of the phoneme. Therefore, they are called "single external" (*ekabāhya*). Closing occurs from the contraction of the throat cavity; opening occurs from its expansion. And these two are indeed distinct from the internal efforts consisting of the states of being closed (*saṃvṛtatva*) and open (*vivṛtatva*).

It should be noted that these two consist of being situated near and difficult to reach. In this regard: "The first and second letters of the vargas, as well as ś, ṣ, s, visarga, jihvāmūlīya, upadhmānīya, and the two yamas, are produced with the throat wide open (vivṛtakaṇṭha)."

The vowels (*āḥ*) are produced with breath (*anupradāna*) and are voiceless (*aghoṣa*). Among the consonants, the first [in each group] are "weakly aspirated" (*alpaprāṇa*), while all others are "strongly aspirated" (*mahāprāṇa*). In the groups of consonants, the third and fourth letters, the semivowels (*antasthā*), the letter *ha*, the *anusvāra*, and the two *yamas* (the counterparts of the third and fourth letters) have a closed glottis (*saṃvṛtakaṇṭha*), are produced with breath, and are voiced (*ghoṣavat*). The third letters of the groups and the semivowels are weakly aspirated; as are the fifth letters, though their further quality is nasality (*ānunāsikya*)—thus it is established in the *Śikṣās*. And the summary verse:
"The *yamas* of the *kha* and *ya* groups, the *śa*, *ya*, *ka*, *pa*, the *visarga*, and the *śara* (sibilants) [are voiceless]."
These [consonants], being produced with an emission of breath and being unvoiced, are open.

Others, however, are gutturals; they are unaspirated and possess resonance. The odd-numbered members of the classes, the semivowels (*yaṇ*), and the nasals (*yamaga*) are known as having weak breath-force (*alpaprāṇa*).

Although these external efforts are not utilized for the technical designation of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇasaṃjñā*), they will nevertheless be employed in the examination of "most similar" (*antaratama*) status; thus, they are explained here as things to be excluded by the qualification "internal."

If it is argued that the mention of "effort" (*prayatna*) in this sūtra is redundant—since both the place of articulation (such as the palate) and the effort are obtained simply by the force of the word *asya* ending in a taddhita suffix—the answer is no; for both are mentioned in order to exclude [the application of the term] to each one individually. Therefore, the designation applies only when there is similarity in both the place and the effort, and not when there is similarity in only one of the two. This being established, the resulting conclusion is set forth here for the sake of clarity: the eighteen forms of the vowel *a* are mutually homogeneous (*savarṇa*), and likewise the vowels *i* and *u*.

There are eighteen *ṛ*-sounds and twelve *ḷ*-sounds, making thirty in total that are mutually homogeneous (*savarṇa*), because it has been stated that there are no long forms of the *ḷ*-sound and because the mutual homogeneity of the *ṛ* and *ḷ* sounds has been added as a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*). The *e*-sounds, however, are twelve that are mutually homogeneous; yet *ekāra* and *aikāra*, or *okāra* and *aukāra*, are not mutually homogeneous. How this is so has already been explained in the very rule *aiuṇ* (Pāṇini 1.1.9).

It is clearly stated in the Bhāṣya on this very sūtra that there is no *sāvarṇya* (homogeneity) between the vowels *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *au* and the vowel *a*, due to the difference in their articulatory effort (*prayatna*). For this very reason, there is no homogeneity between *e* and *ai* and the letter *ś*, nor between *o* and *au* and the letter *ś*. Consequently, these do not serve as examples under the rule *nājjhalau* (Pāṇini 1.1.10). Nor can the matter be resolved here by appealing to a difference in place of articulation (*sthāna*), because *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *au* share the same place of articulation—the throat (*kaṇṭha*)—with *a*, and *e* and *ai* share the same place of articulation—the palate (*tālu*)—with *ś*.

Indeed, it is not intended here that similarity of place (*sthāna*) [alone] is meant, because otherwise there would result a lack of homogeneity (*asāvarṇya*) between *ñ, ṇ, ṅ, m,* and *p* on the one hand and their respective class members (*svavargya*) on the other; and there would also result a lack of homogeneity between the nasalized (*sānunāsika*) and non-nasalized (*niranunāsika*) versions of *y, v, l*. For the nose is not the place of articulation even for the non-nasalized sounds, such that there could be a complete identity of place for all of them. [Objection: But surely, by the force of the word *āsya* (mouth) ending in a *taddhita* suffix, only similarity with respect to the palate (*tālu*) and so forth is obtained. For the "mouth" (*āsya*) is defined as the region from the lips up to the throat (*kākalaka*).

If it is asked: "How is it that the *kākalaka*—the elevated region on the neck which they call the 'throat-jewel' (*kaṇṭhamaṇi*)—is brought to a state of non-homogeneity (*asavarṇatva*) by way of its distinction from the nose? [The answer is: For the nose is not the cause for the production of external sounds (*varṇa*), because there is an absence of the activity of the tongue-tip and other such organs there; rather, within the mouth there is a stretched membrane like the skin of a drum (*paṇava*), and a specific line connected to that is the nose. This is the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that it is this [line] which is the cause for the production of sounds.

And because there is no distinction [in the articulatory organs] starting from the lips for those [consonants], each member of a varga is homogeneous (*savarṇa*) with the others of that same varga, due to having the same place and effort of articulation (*tulyāsyaprayatna*). Of the letter *repha* (r), only *repha* is homogeneous; likewise, for the sibilants (*ūṣman*), only the sibilants are homogeneous and not others, because they lack the same place and effort of articulation. Although, according to the opinion of the author of the Sūtras, the letters *i*, *ṛ*, *ḷ*, and *a* have the same place and effort of articulation as the letters *ś*, *ṣ*, *s*, and *h* respectively, they are nevertheless not homogeneous, due to the prohibition in Pāṇini’s rule "nājjhalau" (Pāṇ. 1.1.10).

According to the opinion of the author of the Bhāṣya, however, it will be stated that there is indeed a difference in effort (*prayatna*). Here, a Vārttika is commenced to prescribe the designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous), which would otherwise not apply due to the difference in place of articulation (*sthāna*): "There is a rule for the homogeneity of *ṛ* and *ḷ*. Thus, *hotṛlṛkāraḥ* becomes *hotṝkāraḥ*. Since a long vowel most similar to both [the short *ṛ* and *ḷ*] is impossible, by process of elimination, it is the short *ṛ* [that results].

It might be argued as follows: regarding the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.101), he will state that "there is an option for *ṛ* when *ṛ* follows" (*ṛti ṛ vā vacanam*) and "an option for *lṛ* when *lṛ* follows" (*lṛti lṛ vā vacanam*). This is its meaning: when a homogeneous *ṛ* follows an *ak*, in place of both the preceding and the following sounds, there is optionally the substitute *ṛ*. This [substitute] has two moras (*mātrā*); it consists of two *repha*s in the middle, with one mora for each, and another [mora] on either side belonging to the vowel portion (*ajbhakta*). Furthermore, this [substitute *ṛ*] is slightly touched (*īṣatspṛṣṭa*).

In that regard, because it is not grasped by the vowel *ṛ* due to a difference in effort (*prayatna*), and because it lacks the status of a vowel (*anactva*)—and thus the designation "long" (*dīrghasaṃjñā*) does not apply—this rule is prescribed even though it was not otherwise obtained: "Before an *ḷ*, an *ḷ* [is optionally substituted]" (*lṛti lṛ vā*). This [substitute] also consists of two morae (*dvimātra*) and is slightly touched (*īṣatspṛṣṭa*). There are two *ḷ*-sounds in the middle; one mora belongs to them, and another belongs to the *abhitaḥ* (surrounding) *ajbhakti*. As before, this is prescribed even though it was not otherwise obtained. In that context, regarding the mention of the word "optionally" (*vāvacana*), the word *vā* will serve to include the long vowel (*dīrghasamuccaya*). For *vā* is used in the sense of option (*vikalpa*), comparison (*upamā*), the particle *eva*, and also in conjunction (*samuccaya*).

Because of this statement, the long vowel will occur even before [the substitution] has been applied; so what is the use of the technical term *savarṇa* (homogeneous)? [Objection: But in the rule *lṛti lṛ vā*, does the word *savarṇe* (before a homogeneous vowel) carry over or not? In the first case, in the form *hotṛlṛkāra*, the desired result would not be achieved without the prescription of the *savarṇa* designation for the sounds *ṛ* and *lṛ*. In the second case, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in forms such as *dadhlṛkāra* and *madhlṛkāra*. [Reply: No, because in the first Vārttika, by removing *ṛti* and reading it instead as *ṛtaḥ* (in the ablative case), [the desired result is secured].

Because everything is consistent [with this view]. Furthermore, the term *savarṇa* ("homogeneous") is carried over from the previous Vārttika; therefore, there is no over-extension in cases such as *dhāttraṃśaḥ*. However, in the second Vārttika, *savarṇa* is no longer operative; rather, *ṛtaḥ* ("from /ṛ/ and /ṝ/") is carried over. Consequently, since the entire system can be maintained by these two necessary statements alone under the rule *akaḥ savarṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.101), the Vārttika here concerning the prescription of homogeneity between /ṛ/ and /ḷ/ is redundant.

Not so; for it is more logical to reject the two rules of the sixth [chapter] by relying on a single *vārttika* here. To explain: even by one who composes those two rules, the vowel-status (*actva*) of those two [sounds] to be taught—which contain two *repha*s and two *lakāra*s—must first be admitted. For the sake of establishing that, they must be recited in the *varṇasamāmnāya*. Otherwise, there would be merely the prescription of these two, but not the vowel-based operation (*ackārya*) of protraction (*pluta*).

For when that [substitution] is prescribed, the technical rule *acaśca* (Pāṇini 1.2.28) applies the term *acaḥ*. Now, one might object: "Since the slightly contacted (*īṣatspṛṣṭa*) vowel is not a *ac*, let there be no *pluta*; however, since the open (*vivṛta*) *ṛ*-vowel is indeed a *ac*, the *pluta* is already established. True, the open *pluta* is established; however, the two *plutas* consisting of two *r*s and two *l*s, which are slightly contacted, are not established.

For this very reason, there is no escape even by means of the mere designation *ac*; since the application of the technical rules for inclusion (*grahaṇaka-śāstra*) cannot be accomplished by that much alone, it has been stated that the [prolated vowels] must indeed be recited among the *aṇ* sounds. When they are recited among the *aṇ* sounds, because there is an inclusion of even those two prolated vowels (*pluta*) consisting of three morae (*trimātra*), the prolated vowels optionally become slightly touched (*īṣatspṛṣṭa*).

This being the case, let the two [separate] statements regarding the sixth [vowel] not exist; for even those two [vowels] subject to that rule would be long, and this is already established by the rule *akaḥ savarṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.101). If it is argued: "But surely, by the *sthānentaratama-paribhāṣā*, since the substituends (*sthānin*) are *vivṛta*, the two substitutes must also be *vivṛta* long vowels, and not *īṣatspṛṣṭa* ones? [We reply: No, for it is also possible that the substitute is endowed with two *repha*s (i.e., *ṛ*), as it is said to be "very similar" (*susadṛśa*).

And thus, since there is no decisive factor (*vinigamaka*) to determine whether one should attend to the presence of two *repha*s or to the state of being "open" (*vivṛtatva*), both would apply alternately; this results in the accomplishment of the two forms one intends to establish. Even in the case of the phoneme *ḷ*, sometimes it is the nearest relative to *ṛ* (being an open long vowel), and sometimes it is the nearest relative to *ḷ* (containing two *la*s and being slightly touched, *īṣatspṛṣṭa*). Thus, all desired results are achieved. Therefore, it is established that the two statements in the sixth [chapter] need not be formulated.

If it is argued: "Let that [the substitution of *ṛ* for *ṝ*] be so, but let there be no formal designation (*saṃjñā*) of it," we say: No, because the introduction of two separate rules would result in obvious prolixity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, in the absence of such a designation, the inclusion of the vowel *ḷ* by means of the letter *ṛ* in rules such as *ṛtyakaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.128), *upasargādṛti* (Pāṇini 6.1.92), and *uraṇ raparaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.51) would not be possible.

Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of *ra*-paratva (substitution by *r*) even in the established system (*siddhānta*) in cases such as *tavalkāraḥ*, because *la*-paratva is established since the *ra*-pratyāhāra will be shown [later] to be intended. Furthermore, there is no confusion among the *ṛdits* and *lṛdits* regarding operations based on *anubandhas* (indicatory letters), due to the force of the separate assignment of *anubandhas* during the instruction of verbal roots (*dhātūpadeśa*), and due to the force of their separate mention in the prescriptive rules (*vidhivākya*).

Otherwise, having recited all [roots] as either *ṛdits* alone or *lṛdits* alone, one would have referred to them in that very same form even in the rules; for when uniformity is possible, it is improper to resort to diversity.

*nājjhalau* (Pāṇini 1.1.10): *a*, *j*, *la*, and *u* are not mutually *savarṇa* (homogeneous). This rule prohibits the mutual homogeneity that would have been obtained by the preceding rule (*tulyāsyaprayatnaṃ savarṇam*) in four instances: between *a* and *ha*; between *i* and *śa*; between *ṛ* and *ṣa*; and between *ḷ* and *sa*. Consequently, in examples such as *ānaḍuhaṃ carma* and *vaipāśo matsyaḥ*, [the long vowels do not include these]. Otherwise, by the rule *yasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.148), there would be a grasping of *i* and *ś* just as there is for the long vowels.

Likewise, in cases such as *daṇḍahastaḥ*, *dadhiśītam*, and *kartṛṣaṭkam*, there would be the substitution of a long vowel for two similar vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*). Similarly, in cases such as *daṇḍahastaḥ* [repeated], *daṇḍahastaḥ*, and *kartṛṣaṭkam*, there would be the substitution of a long vowel for two similar vowels. Furthermore, in cases such as *dadhisāndram*, there would be the substitution of *yaṇ*. One should not accept the meaning of the sentence here to be that no two vowels and consonants (*aj-jhalau*) are similar vowels (*savarṇau*), because that would result in the futility of formulating this technical designation (*saṃjñā*).

If, however, there were an option based on the distinction between what is prescribed and what is prohibited, the author would have formulated the rule more simply as "tulyāsyaprayatnaṃ vā" (or, those produced by the same place of articulation and effort). Nor is homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between vowels and *aj*-consonants, or between *hal*-consonants, negated; for in the very rule "nājjhalau" (Pāṇini 1.1.10), there is the mention of the long vowel substitution (*savarṇadīrgha*) and the substitution of a preceding homogeneous sound (*pūrvasavarṇādeśa*) in the rule "jhayo haḥ" (Pāṇini 8.4.62).

If it is argued that *jhal* is specifically mentioned here and not *hal*, and that the desired result is achieved by that alone, then let the mention of the long vowels (*dīrgha*) itself be the indicator (*jñāpaka*). For by that, it is indicated that the homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between vowels (*ac*) and semivowels (*aj*) is not prohibited; thus, by the principle of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), the mutual prohibition between vowels (*aj*) and *jhal* follows as the conclusion. This is also supported by the indicator in the rule *jharo jhari savarṇe* (Pāṇini 8.4.65). As for the question: "Why was the rule not formulated simply as *nāṇśalau*?"—[the answer is provided in the following].

That is not so; for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-establishment of forms such as *kartṛṣaṭkam* and *dadhisāndram*, because it has been stated that [the term] *aṇ* refers only to the preceding [vowels] except in the case of the *grahaṇaka-sūtra*. Let it be granted [that this is the case]; nevertheless, even so, there would still be the greater complexity of referring to individual phonetic instances (*vyakti*) rather than the class (*jāti*). Thus, the doubt as to whether one should remove the mention of *ac* and instead employ the mention of *aṇ* is already resolved by its own internal collapse. As for the portion concerning *śal*, although there is simplicity regarding the individual instance, the answer is simply that there is no difference in the pronunciation of the phoneme.
In reality, however, it would have been more appropriate to formulate the rule as *na ak-śalau*.

It might be argued that even the *śar* sounds would be excluded from being *savarṇa* (homogeneous) by this very rule. For those [sounds] are designated as vowels (*ac*) because they are included under the term "beginning with *i*" (*ikādi*), and they are also designated as consonants (*hal*) because they are taught among the *hal*s. Nor can it be said that *ikāra* and the others are not *savarṇa* on account of this very prohibition; for since the apprehension of word-meanings is necessary prior to the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence, at that stage it is unavoidable that the *śar* sounds are presented by *ikāra* and the others.

Furthermore, in cases such as *paraśśatāḥ*, *rāmaṣṣaṣṭhaḥ*, and *yaśassāram*, the rule *jharo jhari* (Pāṇini 8.4.65) would not apply. Consequently, three *śa*-sounds (*śar*) would be heard in each instance, whereas only two are desired. Thus, there is a Vārttika regarding the prima facie argument: "In the prohibition concerning vowels (*ac*) and consonants (*hal*), the prohibition of the sound *ṣ* [should also apply], because it is both an *ac* and a *hal*. Here, the mention of *ś* is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all *śar* sounds. Moreover, there would be no homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) among the eighteen varieties of the vowel *a*.

Consequently, in examples such as *daṇkaḍāgram*, the long vowel would not occur. To explain: because it is included by the letter *ha* [in the *hal* pratyāhāra], the letter *a* is a *hal*; yet because it is recited among the vowels (*ac*) in the alphabet, it is also an *ac*. Furthermore, this rule [Pāṇini 1.1.50] does not apply to this very sūtra [Pāṇini 1.1.69], whereby the teaching regarding the inclusion of sounds (*grahaṇaka-śāstra*) would fail to operate due to the lack of homogeneity (*asāvarṇya*). Regarding this, the author of the Vārttika himself states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "It is established either because it is not an *ac*, or because of the non-completion of the sentence. In that context, the response intended in the first Vārttika is achieved by rejecting the sūtra [altogether].

To explain: in the *Śikṣāvākya*, the rule "of the spirants (*ūṣman*) when [the effort] is wide-open" (*vivṛtam ūṣmaṇām*) is analyzed as a separate *yoga*. There, the term "slightly" (*īṣat*) is carried over; and for the vowels (*svarāṇām*), the term "wide-open" (*vivṛtam*) is carried over, while "slightly" (*īṣat*) is discontinued. Thus, since the spirants and vowels would not attain homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) due to this difference in effort, what is the purpose of the rule? The meaning is that it is already established simply because the *śar* sounds (the sibilants) are not vowels (*anac*). This should also be understood as an illustration of the fact that the letter *a* is not a *hal* (consonant). This is said assuming the commencement of the rule;
in reality, however, the meaning is that the rule itself should not be commenced at all, according to the reasoning already stated.

Accepting that the word *īṣat* does not recur [from the previous rule] and that there is an equality of effort (*samānaprayatnatā*), he states—even in the view that the sūtra was formulated [as a separate rule]—that "it is because of the incompleteness of the sentence" (*vākyāparisamāpteḥ*).
