This is the intended meaning: here, first there is the instruction (*upadeśa*) of the phonemes; then the designation *it*; then the establishment of the *pratyāhāra*s by the rule "the first [phoneme] with the last one including itself" (*ādirantyena sahetā*); and then the comprehension of the meaning of the sentence "vowels and *hal*-consonants are not mutually [complementary]" (*nājjhalau*).

Therefore, once the determination of *savarṇa* (homogeneity) has occurred through the exclusion of those objects subject to the exception (*apavāda*), the application of the *grahaṇaka-śāstra* (the rule for the inclusion of homogeneous sounds) takes place; however, this is not the case at the time of the formation of this [present] sūtra. Otherwise, since that very sūtra would prohibit the homogeneity of *i* with *ś* and other such sounds, *ś* would not be included by *i*. Consequently, the reason "because it belongs to the *hal* class" would be unestablished, and your prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) would be rendered utterly untenable.

Now, if you argue that because the knowledge of word-meanings is the cause for the comprehension of sentence-meaning, at the time of understanding the word-meanings within this sentence there is no grasping of the sentence-meaning—and therefore, since the prohibition of *sāvarṇya* (homogeneity) has not yet been established prior to this point, the letter *śa* would indeed be included by the letter *i* in this sūtra—then why do you not consider that prior to this point, the very "comprehension-script" (*grahaṇaka-śāstra*) itself has not yet come into being? For if that were so, [the rules] such as *tulyāsyaprayatnam* (Pāṇini 1.1.9) and *nājjhalau* (Pāṇini 1.1.10), as well as *akaḥ savarṇe*... [would be untenable].

If it is argued that even the rule for lengthening (*dīrgha*)—namely *pādosūtra* 6.1.101—would not apply, we say no; for the rule for lengthening, which operates at a time subsequent to the application of the technical term *savarṇa*, proceeds here without obstruction just as it does in cases such as *daṇḍāḍhaka*, since there is no difference in its being pervaded by the form that constitutes the delimiting condition of the locus of application (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*).

Nor should it be argued that there is an impossibility of understanding the meaning of this sūtra prior to the application of the rule for lengthening by homogeneity (*savarṇadīrgha*); for when the causal complex beginning with the presentation of word-meanings is complete, no delay in verbal comprehension is observed due to a delay in the knowledge of the sentence-meaning that conveys grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*). Otherwise, those who have not cultivated the study of the science of grammar would never achieve verbal comprehension anywhere.

Likewise, for grammarians as well, since the knowledge of correctness (*sādhutva*) regarding the words constituting a grammatical rule (*vyākaraṇasūtra*) arises from grammar itself, and since the comprehension of the sentence-meaning occurs subsequently, it follows that self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*), mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), and circularity (*cakraka*) are unavoidable. This is the direction of the argument. Furthermore, the knowledge of correctness is not a cause for verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). Or, let there be an inference of correctness based on the statement of an authoritative expert; once the verbal cognition has arisen from that, the application of the rule proceeds toward other instances of usage (*lakṣya*) just as it does toward the words contained within the rule itself. This is the direction of the argument.

In reality, however, there is no harm even if the homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) of the *ś* sounds is prohibited from one another; for even in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), two forms are accepted for words such as *paraḥśata*. When the analysis (*vigraha*) is "those which are beyond a hundred" (*śatāt parāṇi*), the suffix *suṭ* is applied because the compound is formed either by the rule "the agent or instrument with a *kṛt*-suffix [is compounded] diversely" (*kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*, Pāṇini 2.1.32) or by the rule "a case-inflected word with another case-inflected word" (*supsupā*, Pāṇini 2.1.4). Then, due to its inclusion in the *pāraskarādi* group, the augment *suṭ* is inserted, and the *ś* of *śata* undergoes the change to *ścu* (becoming *ś*). Subsequently, doubling occurs by the rule "also before a non-consonant" (*anaci ca*, Pāṇini 8.4.47).

If it is argued that there might be a prohibition of doubling by either *śaro'ci* (Pāṇini 8.4.49) or *anaci* (Pāṇini 8.4.47), we say no; for in those rules, due to the prohibition *nājjhalau* (Pāṇini 1.1.10), the letter *śa* is not included within the *ac* category.

Therefore, because of the optional elision according to *Pāṇini-sūtra* 8.4.65 (*jharo jhari*), there arise forms with two or three *śa*s; thus, even though the rule for homogeneous sounds (*sāvarṇya*) is prohibited, these two forms are indeed established, since doubling (*dvitva*) itself is optional by *Pāṇini-sūtra* 8.4.47 (*anaci ca*). In that regard, the optionality of doubling results either from the recurrence of the word "optionally" (*vā*) from *Pāṇini-sūtra* 8.4.45 (*yaro 'nunāsike 'nunāsiko vā*), or from the occasional prohibition by *Pāṇini-sūtra* 8.4.51 (*sarvatra śākalyasya*).

It should be noted, however, that the optionality of the elision (*lopa*) results from the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *anyatarasyām* from Pāṇini’s sūtra 8.4.62, *jhayo ho’nyatarasyām*. Therefore, whether phonetic similarity (*sāvarṇya*) exists or not, there is no difference between the forms with two *ś*s and three *ś*s in the word *paraśśatāḥ*. [The compound] *paraśśatāḥ* is formed by Pāṇini’s sūtra 2.1.64, *pāre madhye ṣaṣṭhyā vā*, which applies when those for whom the number is beyond a hundred (*śata*) or similar are denoted. The form *paraśśatāḥ* consists of two *ś*s; the form *paraśśatāḥ* consists of three *ś*s. In both cases, the meaning is: "those whose number exceeds a hundred. Thus, the presence or absence of phonetic similarity does not affect the result.

Thus says Amara. The same applies to cases such as *rāmaṣṣaṣṭhaḥ* and *yaśassāram*. For this very reason, in the Bhāṣya—beginning with "Another says" (*apara āha*) and explaining two Vārttikas as having a single underlying cause—it is commented that the word *vā* signifies an alternative to the *pratijñā* (the formal proposition), by supplying the remainder of the sentence: "Or let there be the inclusion of the sibilants [ś, ṣ, s] by means of the vowels [i, u, ṛ, etc.]. In that context, the phrase "Another says" indicates the manifestation of dissatisfaction.

Regarding that seed [of the argument]: although there is no difference in the result regarding the prohibition or non-prohibition of *sāvarṇya* (homogeneity) among *śar* sounds according to the method already stated, the form "daṇḍāgram" and so forth would not be established by the previously mentioned method. Since it is necessary to resort either to the rejection (*pratyākhyāna*) of the rule or to the maxim of the non-completion of the sentence (*vākyāparisamāpti-nyāya*) for that purpose, the assumption that *śar* sounds lack *sāvarṇya* with other *śar* sounds is entirely without foundation.

It might be argued as follows: It has been established that the prohibition "not [before] a vowel or *jhal*" (*nāj-jhalau*, Pāṇini 1.1.10) applies only to those vowels whose homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*) have not been grasped. Consequently, since there would be no prohibition of the homogeneity between *i*-sounds and *śa*-sounds and so forth, one might suspect that in cases such as *kumārī śete*, the long vowel substitution for homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*) would occur. This suspicion was resolved by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *ac*. However, this being the case, in forms such as *mālāsu*, the substitution of *ṣ* (*ṣatva*) would occur; for if the letter *a* were grasped by the letter *ha*, then—as in the case of *gorīṣu*—the status of *iṇ* as a subsequent element (*paratva*) would remain unremoved.

Furthermore, in the case of *viśvapābhiḥ*, there would be the substitution of *ḍha* by Pāṇini 8.2.31 (*ho ḍhaḥ*); in *vāgāśīḥ*, there would be the substitution of *gha* for the vowel *ā* by Pāṇini 8.4.62 (*jhayo ho’nyatarasyām*); in *gāsīdhvam*, there would be the substitution of a retroflex (*mūrdhanya*) by Pāṇini 8.3.78 (*iṇaḥ ṣīdhvam*); in *dāsīṣṭa* and similar forms, there would be the substitution of *gha* by Pāṇini 8.2.32 (*dāderdhātorghaḥ*); and in *rāma āyāti* and similar cases, [the rule] Pāṇini 6.1.114 (*hrasvāt*... [would apply].

If this were the case, then in examples such as *devā āyānti*, there would be the obligatory elision of *y* by the rule *hali sarveṣām* (Pāṇini 8.3.22); in *cākhāyitā* and the like, there would be the elision of *y* by the rule *yasya halaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.49); in *śyenāyitā* and the like, there would be the elision by the rule *kyasya vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 6.4.50); and in *nicāyya* and the like, there would be the elision of *y* by the rule *halo yamām* (Pāṇini 8.4.64). Thus, there would be the undesirable consequence of many such grammatical disturbances (*upaplava*).

To this it is replied: the vowel *ā* is not a *savarṇa* (homogeneous) of the consonant *ha*, because their modes of articulation (*prayatna*) are distinct, according to the method of the *Śikṣā* cited in the rule *aiuṇ* [Pāṇini 1.1.2]. However, according to the view of the Vārttika—"The inclusion of *savarṇa* is not a universal grammatical maxim (*aparibhāṣya*), because the class-form (*ākṛti*) is what is grasped"—there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), precisely because *ha* and *ā* are not subsumed under a single genus (*jāti*). Alternatively, in the rule *ājjhalau* [Pāṇini 1.1.10], one should explain the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the vowel *ā* as follows: *ac* is that which is accompanied by *ā* (i.e., *āc*), and that is both *hal* and *āc*. Thus, *ā* is included within the term *ac*.

Therefore, the homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between the vowel *ā* and the consonants is prohibited. The evidence for the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the long *ā* is found in the grammatical indications (*liṅga*) such as the rule "in the sense of time, occasion, and hour, [the suffix] *tumun* [is used]" (Pāṇini 3.3.164). In this view, one should explain that by the compound *āśca āśca* ("ā and ā"), and by the application of the rule for lengthening homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*), the protracted vowel (*pluta*) following a long vowel is also indicated in the rule "vowels and *hal*-consonants are not homogeneous" (Pāṇini 1.1.10).

Therefore, in cases such as *yiyāsoḥ*, one should note that the substitution of *ṣ* for the *s* of the suffix *san* does not apply after the long *ā* resulting from the *pluta* vowel by Pāṇini 8.2.83 (*guroranṛtaḥ*). However, according to the view of the Bhāṣya, since the sibilants are accepted as being slightly opened (*īṣadvivṛta*), there is no possibility of homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) at all; thus, because the rule is rejected, everything remains free of flaw.
Thus ends the fourth Āhnika of the first Pāda of the first Adhyāya in the Śabdakaustubha.

*Īdūded dvivacanaṃ pragṛhyam* (Pāṇini 1.1.11): A dual ending (*dvivacana*) that ends in *ī*, *ū*, or *e* shall have the designation *pragṛhya*. For example: *harī etau* ("these two tawny ones"), *viṣṇū imau* ("these two Viṣṇus"), and *gaṅge amū* ("those two Gaṅgās"). The commentators on the *Vṛtti* state that the inclusion of the marker *t* (*taparakaraṇa*) is for the sake of removing ambiguity; otherwise, once the *yaṇ* substitution has been applied, one might suspect that this is a reference to the short vowel [as in *hari*]. Consequently, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *akurva hy atra*. This is the intended meaning.

In the Bhāṣya, however, it is stated that the individual phoneme (*vyakti*) is the word-meaning and qualities (*guṇa*) are the differentiators; thus, the *tapara* (the *t* following the vowel) is prescribed for the purpose of including long vowels (*dīrgha*) that possess other qualities. It should be noted that this is the specific result for the first *t* in the term *it*. For by that alone, the rule is established even for the vowel *ū*, since the analysis of *tātparaḥ* as a genitive compound (*pañcamī-samāsa*) is also accepted. Furthermore, because the vowel *e* possesses the property of being an *aṇ*, its inclusion of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇagrāhakatā*) is established by the rule *aṇuditsavarṇasya ca*.

Since *ī* and *ū* are not followed by *an*, an effort was made to include them along with those joined by other *guṇa* vowels; therefore, even according to the view of the Bhāṣya, the addition of the *t* in *ūt* and *et* is solely for the sake of removing ambiguity. However, if one accepts that *guṇas* do not cause differentiation (*abhedakatva*), then the Vṛttikāras stated a uniform treatment (*ekarūpya*) by considering that *īt* would have been formulated in the same way. Here, in the rule *taparaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.70), it could also be well argued that the fifth-case compound (*pañcamīsamāsa*) was not intended, and thus the vowel *e* was specified as being without the *t* (*atapara*).

It might be argued that even if the *tapara* designation (*taḥ paraḥ*) were made for the sake of removing doubt, it would nonetheless exclude the *pluta* vowel, according to the maxim: "The eye opened toward a jar does not fail to see a cloth. If it is argued that this letter *da* [in *taparaḥ*] functions like [the *a* in] Pāṇini’s rule *ṛdorap* (Pāṇ. 3.3.57), then even so, the vowel *e* would include the *pluta* because it belongs to the class *aṇ*; however, the vowels *ī* and *ū* would not, on the principle of the "incompleteness of the sentence" (*vākyāparisamāpti*), because they do not belong to the class *aṇ*. If it is argued that the reference is to the genus (*jāti*) rather than the individual, then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasakti*) to the short vowel as well.

If it is argued that even a long vowel (*dīrgha*) is intended when it functions as a qualifier, how then is the inclusion of the protracted (*pluta*) vowel achieved? Nor should it be said that the exclusion of the *pluta* is indeed desired; for in the case of "agrī 3 iti," although the *prakṛtibhāva* conditioned by *pluta*-status is prohibited by the rule *aplutavad upasthite* (Pāṇini 6.1.129), the *prakṛtibhāva* conditioned by *pragṛhya*-status is still required.

Regarding the rule *aplutavat* (Pāṇini 6.1.129), its purpose being fulfilled in cases such as "Devadatta! (*devadatteti*), one should not suspect it to be redundant. Accordingly, the Vārttika on the sixth book states: "The mention of *vat* is for the sake of prohibiting the operations of a *pluta* vowel; for if there were a prohibition of *pluta*, there would follow a prohibition of *pragṛhya* *plutas* as well, since they are prescribed by another rule. On this point, the author of the Bhāṣya says: "Because we adopt the principle that technical names (*saṃjñā*) and paribhāṣās apply according to their enunciation (*yathoddeśam*), the *pluta* vowel is non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the designation of *pragṛhya*."

And thus, because the cognition of [the vowel] having two morae (dvimātratva) is not obstructed, the designation *asaṃjñā* is established. On the view that the application of rules occurs at the time of the operation (*kāryakālapakṣa*), since the designation *pragṛhya* also falls within the scope of the rule *aṇo 'pragṛhyasya* (Pāṇini 8.4.57), the *pluta* vowel would be established with respect to that [designation]; consequently, the nasalization (*anunāsika*) would indeed apply, and this very fault would arise.

By this, the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of sandhi) in cases such as *agnī 3 iti* is also explained. This is because, although the *pluta* vowel is established as valid for vowel-sandhi (*svarasandhi*) by the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in Pāṇini’s rule *plutapragṛhyā aci* (Pāṇ. 6.1.125), its status as invalid with respect to technical designations (*saṃjñā*) does not disappear; furthermore, it has been stated that the *yathoddeśa* (definition-based) view alone is adopted here. In reality, however, the recourse to the *yathoddeśa* view is taken here solely out of fear regarding the application of the nasalization (*anunāsika*). As for *prakṛtibhāva*, it is easily established even under the *kāryakāla* (operation-based) view.

Nor should it be argued that, because the designation [of *pluta*] is established with respect to the rule "a protracted vowel (*pragṛhya*) remains in its original form (*prakṛti*)," it is difficult to justify the designation of a three-mora vowel (*trimātra*). This is because there is no basis for the establishment of the *pluta*. As for the claim that the very statement "the *pluta* remains in its original form" serves as the *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence), that is not correct; for everything is consistent by means of the secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word *pluta* to refer to its substitute (*sthānin*).

Nor should it be said that the very presence of this technical definition (lakṣaṇā) constitutes a fault; for a technical definition is more desirable than the assumption of another sentence based on the presumption of what is heard (śrutārthāpatti). Or, let the indicator (jñāpaka) be one that requires a specific condition: the protracted vowel (pluta) is established as such, and its resulting *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of sandhi rules) is triggered by its status as a protracted vowel, but not by its status as a *pragṛhya*.

Therefore, although it might be possible to justify the *prakṛtibhāva* by adopting the "time-of-operation" view (*kāryakālapakṣa*), it is settled that the "time-of-enunciation" view (*yathoddeśapakṣa*) is adopted here solely to prevent the application of the nasalization rule (*anunāsika*).

Regarding this, Haradatta says: Although the *pluta* vowel is not established (*asiddha*) for the purpose of forming technical names (*saṃjñā*), it is nonetheless established for the purpose of excluding the nasalized (*anunāsika*) vowel. Consequently, that which has its name formed by this [rule] is not the two-mora (*dvimātra*) substitute in the rule concerning the nasalized vowel, but rather the three-mora (*trimātra*) one. Nor does that [three-mora vowel] possess the status of a *pragṛhya* by virtue of the principle of "acting as the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), because [the application of *pragṛhya* status] is a rule concerning phonemes (*alvidhi*). Furthermore, one must necessarily accept the principle that "the *pluta* is established in the context of vowel-sandhis (*svarasandhi*)," so that in the case of "daṇḍa āḍhakam," the *pluta* may be replaced by the long vowel (*dīrgha*).

For this very reason, in the case of *suślokā 3 iti* (where *iti* follows), the occurrence of the *guṇa* substitution precludes only the protracted (*pluta*) vowel and not its original substitute (*sthānin*). Otherwise, the protracted vowel would be heard in its non-substituted form. Therefore, how is the desired result achieved even under the view that technical names (*saṃjñā*) and rules (*paribhāṣā*) function "according to their location" (*yathoddeśa*), and how is there no contradiction between earlier and later parts of the treatises? These matters should be questioned by the learned.

On this point, they say: although the two-mora [vowel] is sublated by the three-mora [vowel], nevertheless, because the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham* (Pāṇini 8.2.1) teaches that [the preceding operation] is as if non-existent, the designation *pragṛhya* is applied on the basis of the cognition that even in the case of the three-mora [vowel], this is indeed a two-mora [vowel].

For this very reason, in the case of *amunā*, once the substitution of *mu* (*mutva`) has been applied and the substitution of *nā* (*nābhāva`) has been applied by depending upon that [substitution of *mu*], the rule *supi ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.102) would cause a long vowel to apply specifically to the word *mu*—on the basis of the notion that "this is the word *daśan*"—in order to avoid this, it is explained in the eighth book (*Aṣṭādhyāyī*) that when the substitution of *nā* is to be performed and has been performed, the substitution of *mu* is not considered non-existent (*asiddha*). Furthermore, in the rule *kṛnmejantaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.39), the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā* (the maxim regarding the destruction of the cause) was established as the solution.

However, we do not bring over the designation (*saṃjñā*) made for a two-mora [vowel] to a three-mora [vowel] by means of the rule of *sthānivadbhāva*, such that the prohibition "not in the case of a rule concerning an *al*" (*Pāṇini 1.1.56*) would be suspected. For it is not reasonable to say that an activity prompted by the error of [perceiving] silver does not have mother-of-pearl as its object. There is only this much difference: the error of silver is non-artificial (*anāhārya*) and prompts action, whereas here, due to the authority of the grammatical treatise, even an artificial superimposition (*āhāryāropa*) is the regulator for the application or non-application of various rules.

This has been made clear by Kaiyaṭa himself. As he says: "Because one resorts to the status of being 'not established' (*asiddha*) with respect to the treatise, when the cognition of a *pluta* vowel is absent and the state of being a *pragṛhya* is being prescribed, the cognition of its having two morae (*dvimātra*) proceeds. And so he will say: "The statement that [the substitute] is 'not established' is for the purpose of preventing the application of the general rule (*utsarga-lakṣaṇa*) and for the purpose of prohibiting the application of the rule concerning substitutes (*ādeśa-lakṣaṇa*). This is the Vārttika located in the sūtra *ṣatvatukorasiddhaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.86).

The term *utsarga* refers to that which is set aside or replaced by an *ādeśa*; it is the original element (*sthānin*). The meaning is that this is for the sake of the application of an operation—such as the insertion of *tuK*—for which that [original element] serves as the defining characteristic or cause. Thus, the intention is that for the sake of uniformity, the status of being "not established" (*asiddha*) according to the treatise should apply everywhere. By this, the first objection—that the element for which this designation is made is not the original element (*sthānin*) in the rule concerning nasalization—is removed. As for the further objection that in cases such as *daṇḍāḍhakam* or *suślokā*, the protracted vowel (*pluta*) would be heard as the substitute (*ādeśa*): [this is also addressed].

That too is not correct; for, according to the method already stated, even there the *pluta* vowel itself is excluded by the substitute (*ādeśa*). It is a different matter that the other person has no awareness that "the *pluta* is being removed by me.

As for what the Commentator (*Bhāṣyakāra*) will state in the sixth [book]—"The *pluta* is established in the context of vowel-sandhis (*svarasandhi*)"—that is intended with the thought that, since it is established here that one must rely solely on the *yathoddeśa* (propositional) view in order to comply with the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the nasalized (*anunāsika*) vowel, there is no fault even if one relies on an indicator (*jñāpaka*) based on vowel-sandhi in general; however, there is no reason for any insistence on the requirement of generality alone. This is the direction of the argument.

If it is argued: "In the examples, it is only the *īdādi* (the suffixes *ī*, *ū*, and *as*) that are duals, not those ending in them," [we reply: because by the principle of *vyapadeśivadbhāva* (treating a form as identical to what it denotes), they are indeed considered to end in them. If it is further argued: "Why not explain it simply as 'that which ends in *ī*, *ū*, or *as* is a dual'? For if this were the case, one would not have to resort to *vyapadeśivadbhāva*," [we reply: No, because there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to forms that are duals by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the rule that a grammatical operation applies to a form ending in a suffix) in cases such as *kumāryor agāraṃ = kumāryagāram* and *vadhvor agāraṃ = vadhvoragāram* or *vadhvagāram*. This is so because, in the formulation of technical names (*saṃjñāvidhau*), [the suffix itself is not included].

The rule "In the case of the mention of a suffix, there is no inclusion of that which ends with it" (Pā. Bhāṣya 27) is established by the inclusion of the word *anta* ("ending in") in the sūtra *suptiṅantaṃ padam* (Pā. Sū. 1.4.14). By this, the following view is refuted: "A dual ending beginning with *ī* or *ū* is *pragṛhya*; however, in cases such as *kumāryyagārāt*, the dual ending ends in *s*, and does not begin with *ī* or *ū*. This is because, in a rule prescribing a technical term (*saṃjñāvidhi*), when a suffix is mentioned, there is no inclusion of that which ends with it.

As for the other objection raised against this position—that in the case of *aśukle śukle samāpadyetām aśuklyāṃ vāsasī*, because of the application of another suffix (*śī*), the *luk* elision would be superseded by the subsequent *śī*-substitution; and once that *śī* is applied, its *luk* would cause *śuklī-* to become a *pragṛhya* by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule—this is not so. For, by the paribhāṣā "the external *luk* elision supersedes even internal rules" (*antaraṅgān api vidhīn bahiraṅgo lug bādhate*), there is the elision of the vowel *au* itself. And since that [elided *au*] lacks both initial and final status, [the condition for *pragṛhya* does not arise].

If it is argued that *īt* and so forth should then be the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), and thus the meaning is that *īt* and so forth which are duals (*dvivacana*) are *pragṛhya*, [we reply: no, because although forms such as *gaṅge* would be established, forms such as *dṛśyete* would not be. For this *e* is a constituent part of a dual, but it is not itself a dual. Furthermore, since the term *pragṛhya* is in close proximity [to the word *dvivacana*], the dual itself is the thing designated (*saṃjñin*), and not *īt* and so forth, because those are remote. Therefore, the explanation exactly as given [by us] is the most elegant.

Regarding this, the authors of the *Vṛtti*—having read the rule as "the prohibition of *mama-iva* and so forth must be stated"—cited *maṇīva*, *rodasīva*, *dampatīva*, and *jampatīva* as examples. Kaiyaṭa and others maintain that this is not authoritative, because it was not stated by the three sages (Pāṇini, Kātyāyana, and Patañjali).

By those who speak thus, on the grounds of equal reasoning, the desirability of other rules not mentioned by the three sages but stated merely by the author of the *Vṛtti*—such as "after the roots *śaṃs*, *duh*, and *guh*, [the suffix *kvip* is optionally applied]," "in the Veda, after the prefix *kram*, [the suffix *ap* is applied]," and "in both the Vedic and common language, after *aṅga*, *gātra*, and *kaṇṭha*, [the suffix *kan* is applied]"—is declared to be unworthy of consideration. As for the expression "two testicles of a camel hang down," they say it is to be explained by means of the word *vā*, which here functions in the sense of *iva* ("as if").

The author of the *Nyāsa*, however, states that this [form] is obtained because the mention of Śākalya in the rule *sambuddhau śākalyasyetau* (Pāṇini 1.1.16) is connected here by the maxim of the "lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokita*), and because recourse is taken to the optionality of a fixed rule (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Some, however, say that the particle *va* is used here in the sense of *iva* (like), as in the case of *bhīma* for *bhīmasena*, or as in the expression *kādambakhaṇḍitadalāniva paṅkajāni* ("lotuses with petals torn by kādamba birds").

In reality, however, everything is well-established because the commentators on Kālidāsa’s usage of the phrase *vadvāyatātathevaivaṃ sāmye* (Pāṇini 5.1.117) have cited it as an example. Furthermore, this very reading is logical, since the secondary suffix *vat*, occurring after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), would otherwise be inconsistent with the context. By this [reading], [the verse] reads:
"As a pair of bees by their two eyes, which possess clearly blooming lotuses, [behold] the buds of her breasts with longing..."
Having fallen upon her heart, the two drops, darkened by collyrium, shone like two blue, trembling gems;
the usage "naio" found in the work of Śrī Harṣa also conveys this same meaning.

*Adaso māt* (Pāṇini 1.1.12): The vowels *ī* and *ū* following this [stem *adas-*] are *pragṛhya*. Examples: *amī īśāḥ*; *rāmakṛṣṇāvamū āsāte*. It should not be said that the example *amū* is already covered by the preceding rule (*adaso'serdādudo maḥ*), because when that [substitution of *m* for *u*] is to be applied, the substitution of *m* (*mutva*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*). However, with respect to the rule *adasomāt*, there is no such non-existence, due to the force of its specific formulation. Thus states the Vārttika: "And there is established existence [of the substitute] by virtue of its locus, as in the case of the substitution of *u* for *ru*."

The example provided is indeed for the masculine singular; however, in the case of the dual number for both feminine and neuter genders, even though the substitution of *m* (*mutva*) is considered *asiddha*, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is established by the preceding rule itself because the stem ends in *e*. Consequently, it should be understood that both the prevention of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) and the exclusion of the nasalization (*anunāsikaparyudāsa*) are already established.

As for what Haradatta stated: "In the rule *aṇo 'pragṛhyasyānunāsikaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.57), when the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is being applied by means of the preceding rule which is present there, the substitution of *m* (*mutva*) is already established; thus, the exclusion of the nasalization (*anunāsika*) in the case of dual endings across all three genders is accomplished by that very preceding rule. The commencement of this [present] rule, however, is for the sake of non-dual endings, and for the sake of preserving the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) in the masculine dual. This is to be considered doubtful, because the view that the preceding rule belongs to the *yathoddeśa* category (where rules are established as names first) has been firmly established in order to include the protracted vowel (*pluta*).

Therefore, it should be understood that the exclusion of the nasalization (*anunāsika*) in the case of the masculine dual is also a result of this rule, and not merely the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). Nevertheless, if there is a persistent insistence that Haradatta’s statement must somehow be justified, then it may be defended as follows: let the "time-of-operation" (*kāryakāla*) view be adopted for the preceding rule. Nor should it be argued that, under such a view, the exclusion of nasalization would not apply to the protracted vowel (*pluta*); for in the cases *ī ī 3 t* and *ū ū 3 t*, the protracted vowel following the long vowel is also indicated through phonetic combination (*praśliṣṭanirdeśa*). Furthermore, the letter *e* will include the protracted vowel simply by virtue of its being a member of the *aṇ* class.

Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of treating that [pluta vowel] as "another" (para) rather than "the same" (apara), because the intention is that this is simply the letter *da*, just as in the rule *ṛdorap* (Pāṇini 3.3.57). And this is logical: under the *yathoddeśa* view, since the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) has already come into operation before the pluta occurs, there is no further reason for the designation to apply again once the pluta has been produced—even though that very same vowel is now perceived as having two morae (*dvimātra*).

It is appropriate to say that the long vowel is prescribed as a counter-measure (*pratividhīyate*) because, although the substitution of *mu* (the *m* sound) had not yet occurred prior to the absence [of the *pluta*], it would have applied to this word "daśa" by means of the cognition "this is the word *daśa*" once the *mu*-substitution was triggered by the cause of the *pluta*. For this [long vowel] does not apply again simply because it had already applied previously—just as the designation of *pragṛhya* does not re-apply after having applied before the *pluta*—and thus the passage from Haradatta in the previous rule is also revitalized; this remains correct until further contradiction.

The intention of the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa, however, is as follows: although the designation *pragṛhya* would apply prior to the *pluta*, it is not applied because it would serve no purpose. Nor should it be argued that the very occurrence of the nasalized (*anunāsika*) vowel in the *pluta* is the result [of applying the *pragṛhya* designation], for even if the designation were not applied, that result would still be obtained; moreover, it is more appropriate that the result belongs to the specific exclusion (*paryudāsa*) occasioned by *pragṛhya*-status—which is what is directly touched by the rule. In cases such as *suśloka iti*, the *pluta* occurs first due to its being *antaraṅga* (internal), according to the maxim "that which is *antaraṅga* is stronger" (Pā. Bhāṣya 38).

Let us return to the subject at hand: even if this sūtra were being composed, for the sake of maintaining uniformity with the preceding sūtra, one would have to adopt the position that [the rule] is merely an enunciation (*uddeśa*). And in that case, just as the substitution of *u* (in *ruta*) is established only with respect to the substitution of *o* (*utva*), so too the substitutions of *m* and *ī* would be established only with respect to the designation of *pragṛhya*, and not even with respect to the *ay-ādi* substitutions.

Consequently, there would be the undesirable application of the *ay* substitution in *amī āsate*; the *āv* substitution in the masculine form *amū āsāte*; and the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) rule "eṅaḥ padāntād api" (Pāṇini 6.1.109) in *amī atra*. Nor should it be argued that the statement [of the rule] would be redundant if its status as established were restricted only with respect to technical names (*saṃjñā*), because the rule serves its purpose by excluding the nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*).

To this it is replied: if the sole purpose were the exclusion of the nasalization (*anunāsika*), then the author would not have composed the technical rule (*saṃjñā-sūtra*). He could simply have said, "The *a* of *adas*, except when it is a *pragṛhya*, becomes nasalized" (*adaso 'naḥ*); for in cases such as *asau*, *amuke*, and *amukābhyām*, even according to the final established view (*siddhānta*), the nasalization does not occur because the vowel is not an *aṇ* and because it is not in the *avasāna* (pause). Therefore, in those instances, there would be no need to include the mention of *māt* or the mention of *īdūt-adaḥ*.

Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of a prohibition even in cases such as "he amuka," because it is a general rule that pronouns beginning with *tyad* lack the vocative case-ending. Therefore, by the force of the introduction of this technical designation (*saṃjñā*), it is understood that its purpose is to provide for the *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form). By virtue of that, the absence of *ādy-udātta* (initial acute accent) is also established; for since *prakṛtibhāva* takes the form of an *apada* (non-word), the following maxim applies: "Even a general rule (*utsarga*) whose cause has already arisen is set aside by an exception (*apavāda*) whose cause is yet to arise" (Paribhāṣā 65). Thus, the desired result is secured.

As for the argument that, by virtue of the initiation of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*), the *mutva* and *ītva* substitutions are understood to be established with respect to *ayādi* and the designation itself; and that, having set aside *ayādi*, *mutva* and *ītva* apply because they are subsequent (*para*)—that is not correct, because there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in making known the absence of *ayādi*. For presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*) naturally concerns that which directly accounts for the fact in question. Furthermore, *mutva* and *ītva* possess greater strength because they reside in a single word (*ekapada*), according to the maxim: "That which is internal (*antaraṅga*) is stronger" (Pāṇini Bhāṣya 38).

How, then, can there be an objection raised [regarding the conflict]? The prohibition "not when *ajānantarya* [is present]" (*Pāṇini 1.1.57*) applies specifically to the maxim "what is external is as if unestablished" (*Pāṇini 6.4.22*), and not to the maxim concerning the accentuation of *udātta* and *anudātta*. Even though the author of the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra "when there is a conflict, the subsequent [rule prevails]" (*Pāṇini 1.4.2*) will state that a separate maxim—"the internal is stronger"—need not be formulated because its purpose is already served by the rule "what is external is as if unestablished with respect to what is internal," [nevertheless, the objection remains].

For in the case of "vṛkṣa iha," the substitution of *su* [for *s*] with the locative singular ending (*saptamyekavacana*) is internal (*antaraṅga*), whereas the lengthening by *savarṇadīrgha* is external (*bahiraṅga*). Nor can the *guṇa* substitution be obtained here by means of the *asiddhaparibhāṣā*, because of the prohibition: "not when there is immediate sequence of vowels" (*nājānantarye*, Paribhāṣā 51). For this very reason, the author of the Bhāṣya will say under the rule *acaḥ parasmin* (Pāṇini 1.1.57): "Since that [substitution] is obligatory and subsequent, and since their application is determined by priority, there is no simultaneous occurrence; thus, it is established by the external [rule]."

And this will be clarified in that very place. For this reason, the author of the Vārttika stated: "Because [the suffix] saṅanta is characterized by being antaranga," and he cited examples such as *dhiyati* and *adudruvat*. Furthermore, the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in this regard is the inclusion of the term *āṅ* in the rule *omāṅośca* (Pāṇini 6.1.95).

For indeed, in the case of *khaṭvā-ā-ūḍhā*, although the rule for homogeneous long vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*) would apply later, the operation between a verbal root and a prefix (*dhātūpasargayoḥ kāryam*) is internal (*antaraṅga*). Thus, once the *guṇa* substitution has been effected due to its internal nature, and the condition for *vṛddhi* arises, the rule [Pāṇini 6.1.94] is applied so that the *pararūpa* (single substitute of the latter form) may take effect. This is clear from the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra "samprasāraṇācca" (Pāṇini 6.1.108). If so, how is it that the author of the Vārttika stated, "or because of conflict" (*vipratiṣedhād vā*)? True; it is precisely because of this lack of complete satisfaction that the author of the *Bhāṣya* resorted to an alternative view, beginning with "or rather" (*athavā*). Such is the direction of the argument.

"What is [the purpose of] *māt*? [It is to indicate] 'in such-and-such a place here. But surely, in this sūtra, only *ī* and *ū* are carried over (*anuvartita*), and not *e*. True; when *māt* is included, *e* is not carried over, because it is impossible for that [ending *e*] to follow after *adas-* with *māt*. Otherwise, however, it would be carried over. But the carrying over of a single part [of a compound term] is difficult to discern. Therefore, it is established that the inclusion of *māt* serves as an indicator of the intended non-carrying over of *e*. Here, this should be considered:"

"Why was it not formulated as: 'ī and ū in the sense of the locative case are *pragṛhya*, as well as *udas* and the dual ending *ec*'? For in this way, the reference to *ī* and *u* from the preceding rule would not need to be included in the present rule, nor would the reference to *māt* be required, resulting in great economy; furthermore, one would not have to resort to the principle of partial recurrence (*ekadeśānuvṛtti*)."

*Śe* (Pāṇini 1.1.13): This [final *e*] shall be a *pragṛhya*. In *asme indrābṛhaspatī*, the substitute *śe* occurs in place of the dative plural by the rule *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39). Because it is marked with the letter *ś* (*śit*), it replaces the whole [base]. By the rule *śeṣe lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.90), the final vowel is elided. In *na yuṣme vājabandhavaḥ*, the meaning is "in you" (*yuṣmasu*). Here, one should understand the example to be *yuṣme* at the time of the *padapāṭha*; for in the *saṃhitā*, since there is no following vowel *ac*, there is no distinction to be gained whether the *pragṛhya* status applies or not.

In this way, one should understand that examples such as "evaṃ tve rāyaḥ sudughāste hyaśvāḥ" are also to be cited at the time of the *padapāṭha*. According to the rule "between that which is taught by a general definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and that which is taught by its specific form (*pratipadokta*), only the latter is to be accepted" (Pāṇini Bhāṣyavārttika 1.1.4), [the following] do not apply here: "kāśe," "kuśe," "vaṃśe," "hariśe," and "babhruśe. [In these cases], the suffix *śa* is applied after "hari" and "babhru" because they belong to the "lomādi" group; from these, the seventh case singular is then formed.

Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.14: *nipāta ekājanāṅ*. A single-vowel (*ekāj*) particle (*nipāta*), excluding *āṅ*, shall be *pragṛhya*. *ā* is used in the sense of negation and reproach: *a avadyam* ("not blameworthy"). *i* is used in the sense of wonder: *i hanta* ("Ah, Indra!"). *u* is used in the senses of disgust, distress, and "indeed" (*anvartha*): *u umeśaḥ* ("Indeed, the Lord of Umā"). The term *ekāj* is a *karmadhāraya* compound. This is because the meaning of the constituent members (*varti-pada*) takes precedence, which makes it an *antaraṅga* (internal) rule, and also because of the specific grammatical indications such as Pāṇini Sūtra 1.3.83: *vyāharati mṛgaḥ*. Therefore, in the following examples, the *pragṛhya* status applies: *predaṃ brahmavṛtratūrye vāvitha* ("O you who have indeed conquered Vṛtra in the battle for Brahman"), and *preddhaḥ*.

It might be argued as follows: if this were a *karmadhāraya* compound, then the inclusion of the word "eka" (one) would be redundant; for the desired result would be established by the mere statement "the particle which ends in *ac*. Nor should it be said that the meaning is "a particle ending in *ac*"—where the qualifier and the qualified are reversed—because of the rule of *tadantavidhi* (extension to what ends with that) when a qualifier is used. For if that were the case, the qualifier would become useless due to the lack of anything to be excluded (*vyāvartya*). Furthermore, a particle ending in a consonant (*hal*) cannot be the thing to be excluded, because even if such a particle were to receive the technical name (*saṃjñā*), there would be no obstacle [to its functioning as a particle].

Nor is there any need to exclude words ending in a consonant (*halanta*), because even if such a word were to receive this designation (*saṃjñā*), there would be no sublation [of its grammatical operations]. Nor should it be argued that in cases such as *puro 'sti*, if the consonant-ending word received this designation, the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of sandhi) would prevent the change of *r* to *u*; for there is no such fault, since the substitution of *r* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the *pragṛhya* designation.

Nor should it be argued that since the designation *pragṛhya* is not applied to [the word] ending in *s*, then by the principle that "that which undergoes a partial modification is not different [from the original]," the same would apply to the form ending in *r*, and thus the contingency of *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form) would remain exactly as it was; for, just as with respect to the *pragṛhya* designation, the substitution of *r* (*rutva*) is also considered *asiddha* (non-existent) with respect to *prakṛtibhāva*. However, in the case of a form ending in *s*, there is nothing established at the stage of the *siddha* (completed) rule that could be prevented by *prakṛtibhāva*.

Therefore, the mention of *ac* as a qualifier for the particle (*nipāta*) would indeed be useless; this has been well stated. If it is asked: "Could the qualifier not be intended so that [the rule] applies only to that which ends in *ac*, and not to every *ac* in general? No, because by the principle of "designation-like behavior" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), even such a word does not lose its status as ending in *ac*. If it is argued: "The principle of designation-like behavior does not apply here due to the force of the qualifier"? No, because the purposefulness of the qualifier can be easily explained even by abandoning the rule of "specification of what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*).

If it is asked, "Even so, what is the necessary factor for deciding which one must necessarily be abandoned?"—know that it is precisely the mention of *aṅga* (the stem). For if it were intended merely to block the application of the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), its mention would be purposeless. Therefore, because the mention of *aṅga* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that *ac* is a qualifier, there is no extension of the rule to include that which ends in it (*tadantavidhi*). However, if *ac* were the qualificand, there would all the more be an extension to include that which ends in it. Thus, it is established that in either case, the mention of "one" (*eka*) is indeed purposeless. [Objection: But let the mention of "one" be for the purpose of excluding a collection of vowels (*acsamudāya*).

[Objection: The designation [of *prakṛtibhāva*] would apply only to the whole (*samudāya*) "aiu," and not to the individual parts, according to the maxim regarding the reduplication of single vowels (*ekāj-dvirvacana-nyāya*); thus, *prakṛtibhāva* would occur only for the final vowel, and not for the preceding two. [Reply: This is not so; for by the very intention (*vivakṣā*) to express singularity in the word *ac*, the possibility of referring to a whole is excluded. On this point, the author of the Bhāṣya says: "By employing the term 'single' (*eka*) to dispel the doubt that a collection of vowels (*ac-samudāya*) might be intended, he indicates that in references to phonemes (*varṇa-grahaṇa*), the number of individuals (*vyakti-saṅkhyā*) is not intended to be expressed, but rather the genus (*jāti*) alone is indicated."

By this, the point that will be stated by the author of the Vārttika—namely, "it is established because the mention of *hal* in the rule for *dambh-* refers to the genus (*jāti*)"—is indicated by the sūtra itself. The grammatical connection is: "it is established from *dambh-*. The reason for this is: "because the mention of *hal* refers to the genus."

When the suffix *san* is added to the root *dambh*, two forms—*dhipsati* and *dhīpsati*—are established as follows: first, by the rule *sanīvantardha...* (Pāṇini 7.2.49), the augment *iṭ* is optionally absent; then, by the rule *dambha icca* (Pāṇini 7.4.56), the root vowel is replaced by *i* and the penultimate *a* is also changed to *i*; next, by the rule *atra lopo'bhyāsasya* (Pāṇini 7.4.58), the reduplication is elided; and finally, because the suffix *san* is treated as having the *kittva* designation by the rule *halantācca* (Pāṇini 1.2.10), the nasal *n* is elided, and the substitution of *bhaṣ* for the dental *d* is applied. Thus, the two forms *dhipsati* and *dhīpsati* are derived.

If the mention of "hal" (consonant) were intended to refer to individual consonants, then since the single consonant *n* which is proximate here is not followed by [the suffix], and that which is followed [by the suffix] is not the single proximate consonant *bh*, the *kit* designation would not apply. Similarly, in the case of *tṛṃhū* (DhP 1.215) in the sense of "injury," belonging to the *tud*-class, because it is marked with *ū*, there would be an optional *iṭ* augment, resulting in forms such as *titṛṃhiṣati* or *titṛkṣati*; such is the direction of the argument.

It might be argued that the application of the principle of reduplication of a single syllable (*ekāj-dvirvacana*) in the case of *aiu apehi* is improper, because the designation of a whole does not include its constituent parts. For this very reason, in cases such as *nirglāyāt* and *nirgleyāt*, where many [sounds] are in conjunction, the designation was accepted for only two [of them]. Nor can there be inclusion by the mention of "particle" (*nipāta*), since the prescription of the designation is possible for each individual particle. True; however, there would certainly be a mere suspicion of the term referring to a collection of single-syllable words (*ekāj-samudāya*).

The inclusion of the term *eka* (single), which is being employed precisely to exclude that [possibility], makes known the meaning previously stated. In reality, however, since the inclusion of *eka* in the definition of *apṛkta* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the aforementioned meaning, it is better to simply abandon the inclusion of *eka* in the present sūtra. What is the purpose of the word *nipāta* (particle)? [Consider] *cakārātra* ("the particle *ca* is here"). Likewise, *atateḥ ḍaḥ aḥ* [forming] *aḥ*; "O *a*, come! (*he a āgaccha*) is also a counter-example. The author of the Bhāṣya states the distinction between *āṅ* and *anāṅ*:

"One should know that *āṅ* is marked with the *ṅ*-sign (*ṅit*) when it denotes slightness (*īṣadartha*), connection with an action (*kriyāyoga*), limit (*maryādā*), or inclusion (*abhividhi*); whereas in the sense of a sentence (*vākya*) or recollection (*smaraṇa*), it is unmarked (*aṅit*)."

Regarding this, some say that because this word was not previously mentioned here, the substitution of *enad* for *etad* has not been applied. That is not correct; for the author of the Bhāṣya will state that an *anvādeśa* (subsequent mention) is merely a restatement of what has already been said, and not specifically a restatement of what was said by means of the pronoun *idam*. Therefore, an *anvādeśa* occurs when, after prescribing something by one sentence, another thing is taught by a subsequent sentence. In this case, however, the commentary (*vṛtti*) stating "that which functions in the sense of 'slightly' (*īṣat*) and so forth" is not something to be prescribed, but is employed merely as an indicator (*paricāyaka*). Consequently, there is no substitution of *enad*. By this [same reasoning]—

"O Rādhā, this man is afraid at night; therefore, you yourself lead him home"—this too has been explained. For there is no intention to predicate the state of fear itself; rather, the fear, being already established, is restated as a reason (hetu). This is the general direction [of the analysis].

In the sense of "slight" (*īṣadartha*): *ā-uṣṇam* (slightly warm). The particle *āṅ* is treated as having the marker *ṅ* by the author of the *Vārttika* in the rule *kugati* (Pāṇini 2.2.18). In connection with an action (*kriyāyoga*): *ā itaḥ* (come here). It is listed among the *prādi* group as having the marker *ṅ*. Regarding the phrase *maryādā'bhividhau ca*: this is either a collective *dvandva* compound where the absence of the nasal augment (*num*) occurs because the rule for augments is not universally obligatory; or it is a *madhyamapadalopa* compound meaning "in an *abhividhi* [inclusive limit] accompanied by a *maryādā* [exclusive limit]. In the sense of *maryādā*: *ā udakāntāt* (as far as the edge of the water), which becomes *audakāntāt*.

Regarding *abhividhi* (inclusive limit): from Ahicchatra [to] Ahicchatra. The term *maryādā* (exclusive limit) is used with "without that" (*vinā tena*), while *abhividhi* is used with "together with that" (*saha tena*). Furthermore, the particle *āṅ* is prescribed by Pāṇini’s sūtra 2.1.13 (*āṅ maryādābhividhyoḥ*) as being marked with the *ṅit* designation. The vowel *ā* is employed to indicate a change in the sense of the preceding sentence, as in: "Is this indeed how you think? The meaning is: "Previously you did not think so; now you think thus. Others maintain that the vowel *ā* is used to signal the commencement of a new sentence.

Likewise, a form that indicates a recollection (*smṛti*) is employed; from that, the recollected object is pointed out—[as in] "Ah! Indeed, it was thus. And here, the intention regarding the *ṅit*-status [of the particle *ā*] lies precisely in the recollection of the sentence. Therefore, it should be understood that the *ṅit*-status applies even in cases other than those involving the recollection of a sentence, even in the absence of a slight meaning (*iṣadartha*) and so forth. By this, Haradatta and others [state] in the sixth [chapter]: in the passage "āmenyasya rajasoyadabhraām̐ apo vṛṣānāḥ," because the particle *ā* functions in the sense of the locative case (*saptamī*), its *ṅit*-status causes the rule "āṅo'nunāsikaśchandasī" (Pāṇini 6.1.126) to apply.

And this is appropriate: since the distinction between both [the *aṅ* and *idam* stems] is obtained from the meaning by means of either one of the two characteristics (*ṅit* or *idam*), even there, for the sake of brevity, one may assume that the intention lies in the characteristic of *aṅ*, while the other part is merely a partial restatement (*avayutyānuvāda*).
(Pāṇini 1.1.15: *otaḥ*)

An *odanta* (ending in *o*) particle shall be designated as *pragṛhya*. Examples: *āho* and *utāho*. Why specify "particle"? [Consider: *devo'si*, *vaṣaṭ te viṣṇavāsa ā*, *vāyavāyāhi*, and *viṣṇova*. As for the claim that the very phrase "*gavityayamāha*" is the counter-example (*vyāvartya*) for the mention of "particle," that is not correct; for even if the *pragṛhya* designation were applied there, there would be no harm. Nor does this lead to the occurrence of *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form), because the rule prescribing *prakṛtibhāva* has "the end of a word" (*padānta*) as its governing context.

Nor should one be deluded into thinking that this [form] can never be a word-final (padānta); for, by intending to express the non-difference between the original (anukārya) and its imitation (anukaraṇa), it lacks the status of a meaningful unit (arthavattva) and thus lacks the status of a nominal stem (aprātipadikatva). Consequently, since no case-ending (vibhakti) arises, this very form is accepted [as the final element]. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of hearing a case-ending.

Nor should it be argued that such an *apada* (non-word) would result in an inconsistency regarding its usage; for the proclamation "one should not employ an *apada*" has the intended meaning of "one should not employ what is not *pariniṣṭhita* (not finalized). This [proclamation] is rooted in those various prescriptive rules (*vidhiśāstra*) concerning *suptiṅ* suffixes and so forth. In this case, by that same principle, even the *sub*-case ending is not obtained, and thus the form "go" itself is indeed *pariniṣṭhita*. For this very reason, the rule "there is elision [of *s*] according to Śākalya" (*Pāṇini* 8.3.19) does not apply here either.

If it is asked: "How then is the *pūrvarūpa* (single-substitute short vowel) applied in the previous sūtra [Pāṇini 6.1.109] *eṅaḥ padāntāt* according to the Vārttika *śe'rthavadgrahaṇāt*?"—[the answer is: there, having intended to express the distinction between the original form (*anukārya*) and its imitation (*anukaraṇa*), the case ending is added; then, by forming the compound *śe'rthavān* (meaningful in the remainder), the elision of the case-ending (*supo luk*) is applied, as explained in the commentary. By this, even the authors of the Vṛtti, who cite *gavityayamāha* ("He said 'go'"") as an example for the subsequent sūtra [Pāṇini 8.2.86] asking "What is the purpose of [specifying] *saṃbuddhau*?", are refuted.

Therefore, in this context, examples such as "devo'si" should be understood as the counter-examples (*pratyudāharaṇa*). Nor can its establishment be claimed solely on the strength of the introduction of the rule *eṅaḥ padāntāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.109), because that rule already finds its application in cases such as "hare'va gaccha. Furthermore, the inclusion of the term *eṅ* does not serve as a basis for this, since it is intended for the sake of the subsequent rule, *ṅasiṅasośca* (Pāṇini 6.1.110).

However, in the subsequent sūtra, if the mention of *sambuddhi* were absent, there would arise the contingency of an optional application even in cases such as *āho iti*, because of its higher status; for while the preceding sūtra finds its scope in instances like *aho īśāḥ*, the subsequent sūtra finds its scope in instances like *viṣṇo iti*. Nor should it be argued that, since the former concerns a word ending in *o* (*odanta*) while the latter concerns a vocative (*āryitayā*), they belong to different domains and thus a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) is impossible.

In examples such as *trapūṇām*, just as there is a conflict of results between the *num* and *nuṭ* augmentations—which belong respectively to the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*)—so too here, despite the difference in scope (*viṣaya*), a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) is possible due to the contradiction in their results. Furthermore, under the view that the governing force pertains to meaning (*arthādhikāra-pakṣa*), the subsequent rule also applies to that which ends in *o*, making it a *saṃjñin*. Even under the view that the governing force pertains to the word-form (*śabdādhikāra-pakṣa*), just as in the rule *iko jhal* (Pāṇini 1.2.9), where the root (*dhātu*) is implied by the suffix *san* and thus serves as the qualifier for the *ik*, so too here [the same principle applies].

Furthermore, since the possibility of applying the rule of "extension to what ends with that" (*tadantavidhi*) exists when *prakṛti*—which is introduced by the word *san*—is qualified by the word *okāra*, it is established that in both sūtras, the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*) "gavityayamāha" does not apply. However, the commentary (*vṛtti*) should be interpreted on the assumption that the mention of "end of a word" (*padānta*) is not connected to the rule for *prakṛtibhāva*. In this view, according to the maxim of the frog-leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*), the mention of "end of a word" must indeed be connected to the sūtra "iko'savarṇe" (Pāṇini 6.1.127);
otherwise, there would be over-extension (*atiprasakti*) in cases such as "gauryau" and "gauryyaḥ. This is the direction of the argument.

It might be argued that these are collections of particles, such as *āha u*, *āho*, *uta āho*, *utāho*, and so forth; therefore, because they function as if they were single units (*ādivadbhāva*), their designation as particles is established by the rule *nipāta ekāj* (Pāṇini 1.1.14) alone. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of applying the rule *ūm* (Pāṇini 1.1.17) to forms like *āho iti*, because the resolution is that this *u*-vowel is without the marker *ṃ* (i.e., it is *u*), and not *ūṃ*. For this very reason, the pronunciation of the marker *ñ* in the sūtra *uñaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.17) is also meaningful.

For this very reason, the author of the Bhāṣya stated regarding the rules *uñaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.17) and *ūm̐* (Pāṇini 1.1.18): "These two *u*-sounds are distinct; one is without an *it*-marker (*ananubandhaka*), and the other is with an *it*-marker (*sānubandhaka*). Furthermore, one might argue that even so, in the case of *ā u o*, since the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) of *āṅ* and *anāṅ* would be subject to the prohibition by the rule *anāṅ* [Pāṇini 1.1.14], this [the mention of *ūm̐*] must be stated as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*). However, this need not be said, because by adopting the interpretation of *anāṅ* as a preclusion (*paryudāsa*), the single-substitute of *āṅ* and *anāṅ* is treated as being like the first member (*ādivadbhāva*), and is thus included by the term *anāṅ*.

For in the case of a non-presumptive negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), there would be either an ungrammatical compound (*asamarthasamāsa*) or a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*). Furthermore, the statement in the Bhāṣya that "this [sūtra] is for the purpose of excluding [the over-extension]" is merely an incidental remark (*abhyuccayamātra*). Otherwise, how could the author, having immediately raised the objection regarding the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of *ado bhavat*, resolve it by stating that only the vowel *o* explicitly mentioned in the rule (*pratipadokta*) is to be understood? If you argue that all the examples (*lakṣya*) are successfully accounted for even without this sūtra, then [we reply]: [The answer follows: No, because the sūtra is necessary for the sake of brevity (*laghu*). For without it, one would have to state the entire expression *adaso māt* [in the sūtra], whereas with it, the mere mention of *māt* suffices. Moreover, the Bhāṣya’s statement that "this is for the purpose of excluding" is not intended as a refutation of the sūtra, but rather as a justification for its necessity. Otherwise, how could he—having raised the objection regarding the over-extension in *ado bhavat*—subsequently say, "In the case of *adbhuta*, the *u* is not included because it is not *pratipadokta*"? To this it is replied: *āho*, *utāho*, and so forth, are not compounds of particles (*nipāta-samudāya*), but rather indivisible units (*avakhaṇḍa*) themselves. This is determined both by the force of this very sūtra—which implies the inclusion of the vowel *au* as explicitly stated (*pratipadokta*)—and by the authority of the Bhāṣya. Consequently, in the example *ām āho devadatta*, the prohibition of the *nighāta* accent (as prescribed by Pāṇini 8.1.55: "An address [is unaccented] when separated from *ām* by one word") is established. For this very reason, even the makers of the *pada-pāṭha* read such passages as *o ṣu varttam arutaḥ* with the initial *o* as a single word (*ekapadyena*).

Thus, since it is established that there is complete agreement among the author of the Sūtras, the author of the Bhāṣya, and the author of the Padas, those who reject this Sūtra by relying on the view that this is merely a collection of particles (nipāta-samudāya) are refuted.

It might be argued that there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of *anadaḥ adaḥ samabhavat*, because the form ending in *cv-* is a particle (*nipāta*); for even though the designation *gati* is prescribed by the rule "the words beginning with *ūryādi*, those ending in *cv-*, and *ḍāc*" (Pāṇini 1.4.61), the governing heading "those [words] up to *rīśvara* are particles" (Pāṇini 1.4.56) still applies. Nor should it be said that the phoneme *o* derived through a grammatical derivative (*lākṣaṇika*) is excluded by the maxim regarding "that which is taught by a rule versus that which is directly stated" (*lakṣaṇapratipadoktaparibhāṣā*), because that maxim does not apply when individual phonemes are being specified.

Otherwise, even the rule *eco 'yavāyāvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.78) would not apply in cases such as *haraye*, because it would already have found its scope of application (*cāritārthya*) in instances where the substitution is specifically prescribed, such as *cakre* and *cakrire*. If it is argued: "Let the paribhāṣā not apply when the phoneme (*varṇa*) is the predominant element, but it must certainly apply when it is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*)," we say: no, for it is easily established that the paribhāṣā does not apply even when there is no such distinction.

And so we shall explain in the sixth [chapter]: "Even granting [your position], we say: in cases such as *agor gauḥ samabhavat* ('A non-cow became a cow') or *go 'bhavat* ('A cow became [something else]'), since the suffix *ḍo* [is prescribed] by the rule *gameḍo* (Pāṇini 3.2.23), the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would certainly occur because of the specific mention (*pratipadokta*) of the vowel *o*. Now, might there not be a resolution here by means of the principle of the primary and secondary (*gauṇa-mukhya-nyāya*)?"

For instance, in cases such as *saṃghībhavanti brāhmaṇāḥ* ("the Brahmins become a group"), *tvadbhavati devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta becomes like you"), *madbhavasi tvam* ("you become like me"), and *tvadbhavāmy aham* ("I become like you"), the established grammatical conclusion is that in every instance involving the suffix * cvi*, agency belongs solely to the base (*prakṛti*), in accordance with the fixed rules governing number and person.

And thus, when the suffix *cv-* arises from a word denoting a modification (*vikṛti*) by means of superimposition upon its original form (*prakṛti*), the fact that the word "cow" (*go*), as it functions in the sense of a Vāhīka and so forth—which serves as the base (*prakṛti*) for the *cv*-suffix—is used in a figurative sense (*gauṇārthatā*) is quite evident. If it is argued that for this very reason, in examples such as "the moon, having become great (mahān), is *mahadbhūtaḥ*," the substitution of *ā* [for the final vowel] prescribed by Pāṇini’s rule *ānmahataḥ* (Pā. Sū. 6.3.46) does not apply, we say: no, because there is a disparity between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*). To explain: the principle of the distinction between the figurative and the primary applies only when a specific form is being adopted.

Because that [rule] is based on the technical definition "when a meaningful element is mentioned, an element lacking meaning is not included" (Pābhā 1.1.68), and because the presentation of a meaning depends upon the apprehension of a specific form; thus, it is logical that the substitution of *āt* prescribed by "ānmahataḥ" (PāSū 6.3.46)—which is enjoined through the mention of a specific form—does not apply in a secondary (*gauṇa*) sense. However, in this case, how could the designation *pragṛhya*, which is enjoined by "ot" (PāSū 1.1.15) by way of the phoneme *o*, fail to apply to that which functions in a secondary sense?

However, the designation *nipāta* applies to that [particle] as well in its primary sense. For this very reason, in the case of *śvāśuriḥ*—meaning "the offspring of Śvaśura"—the rule *rājaśvaśurād yat* (Pāṇini 4.1.137) does not apply; yet the rule *ata iñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95) certainly does apply. Otherwise, there would be an identity of status (*tulyayogakṣematā*) between the suffixes *iñ* and *yat*.

For this very reason, in examples such as "The Vāhīka is a cow" (*gaur vāhīkaḥ*) and "Teach the Vāhīka [to recite] the cow" (*gāṃ vāhīkaṃ pāṭhaya*), the *vṛddhi* and *ātva* substitutions do indeed occur, because those two are not dependent on the phoneme *a*. This is because it will be stated later that the *tapara* notation in the rule *gotaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.90) is intended to indicate any vowel ending in *u*, including *o*. Accordingly, the author of the Bhāṣya will state regarding the rule *auto'm* (Pāṇini 6.1.93): "In the case of *gām*, even though *vṛddhi* is subsequent, it is set aside by *ātva*, which has no other scope."

On that very point, Kaiyaṭa will also state: "The sūtra should be recited as *otaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.69); or, by way of indicating words ending in *o*, this [sūtra] *gotaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.90) should be explained. This is established in the same manner even in the Vṛtti and other treatises.

As for what they say—that the word *go* applies primarily to its own referent, namely that which possesses a dewlap and so forth, and only through the presence of another word such as *vāhīka* does it acquire the status of being used figuratively; whereas in the case of *gobhavat*, the suffix *cv-* itself would be impossible without a figurative meaning, and thus there is a disparity; therefore, it is established that this principle applies to operations on words (*pada*) but not to operations on nominal stems (*prātipadika*)—that is to be considered, because under the view that sentence refinement (*vākya-saṃskāra*) occurs first, the figurative meaning is understood even before the application of the *vṛddhi* and *ātva* substitutions.

As for the fact that the relationship of the case-factors (*kārakas*) with the action alone is directly expressed by the Vedic word (*śrauta*), therefore, once they are brought under the control of a single action, there occurs a mutual delimitation (*pārṣṇika-avaccheda*) between them according to the principle of the "red one-year-old cow" (*aruṇaikahāyanī-nyāya*). Thus, at the time of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) in the sentence "Bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*), there is no secondary meaning (*gauṇārthatā*); rather, such a meaning arises at the time of the subsequent mutual delimitation with the "cart-puller" (*vāhīka*). Nor does the word-formation (*pada-saṃskāra*), which has already proceeded by virtue of its being an internal factor (*antaraṅga*), cease even when a secondary meaning is subsequently perceived as an external factor (*bahiraṅga*).

That too is not correct; for even on that basis, one must resort to a figurative sense (gauṇatā) precisely for the sake of connecting [the words] with the actions "he speaks" (brūte) and "teach" (pāṭhaya). Even if, in the view where the mat (kaṭa) is also the object and Bhīṣma and others are also [objects], a statement could somehow be made possible, this is because in the alternative view stated in the Bhāṣya—namely, that the second case ending applies to Bhīṣma and others due to grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya)—your proposed reasoning does not apply. Furthermore, in the case of *śvāśuriḥ*, there would result the non-occurrence of the suffix *iñ* as well, because the speaker intends to express the status of being an object (*karmatva*) and so forth as residing specifically in the Vāhīka.

Therefore, because they depend upon phonemes (*varṇa*), the truth is that [the rules for] *vṛddhi* and *ātva* apply; it is not, however, because they are operations of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). For this very reason, in cases such as "ekācca prācām" (Pāṇini 5.3.94), even though [the suffixes *smāt*, etc. are operations of the nominal stem, the forms *smāy* and so on do not occur, because the technical designation of "pronoun" (*sarvanāman*) is prescribed only by virtue of a specific form.

The statement, "Those whose word-meanings are manifested," is intended to explain the meaning established by the maxim of the primary (*mukhya*) and the secondary (*gauṇa*); for it is precisely the state of being well-known or not well-known that constitutes being primary or secondary, as is explained at length elsewhere. For this very reason, in the *sarvādi*-sūtra, Haradatta—rejecting the Vārttika which states "there must be a prohibition regarding technical terms (*saṃjñā*) and secondary elements (*upasarjana*)"—says: "To begin with, a prohibition of technical terms need not be stated, because [the desired result] is already established by the rule 'those whose word-meanings are manifested'."

As for what Kaiyaṭa will say there—"The maxim of the primary and the secondary (*gauṇamukhya-nyāya*), though applicable here due to the presence or absence of conventional usage, is not stated, because it was stated under the rule *ot* (Pāṇini 6.1.95) that this applies to operations on words (*pada-kārya*) but not to operations on nominal stems (*prātipadika-kārya*)"—that is merely a superficial argument.

For [if his reasoning were correct], grammatical operations depending solely on the phonetic form of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* would result in applying even when these stems are subordinate (*upasarjana*), and the same undesirable consequence would follow in rules such as *yuṣmadyupapade* (Pāṇini 1.4.105) and *asmadyuttamaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.107). This is the general direction of the critique.

Thus, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) concludes that in forms such as *adobhavat* and *gobhavat*, the designation of *pragṛhya* by the rule *ot* (Pāṇini 1.1.15) is unavoidable, just as [the designation of] indeclinability (*avyayatva*) and so forth would be.

To this it is replied: since the previous sūtra contains the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "not *āṅ*" (*anāṅ*), only those particles (*nipāta*) similar to *āṅ* that are explicitly mentioned in the text are understood there. Here too, either by virtue of the governing topic of meaning (*arthādhikāra*) or by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the mention of "not *āṅ*," the same principle applies; thus, everything is well-established.

And likewise, in the *Sarvādi-sūtra*, within the section stating that "the two forms [sa and ta] occur after the vowel 'a' only when it is not a secondary (*anupasarjana*) element," Kaiyaṭa raises the objection: "In that case, by the rule *tadoḥ saḥ sau* (Pāṇini 7.2.103), the substitution of *s* would apply even in the case of a secondary element because no such qualification is specified. He resolves this by noting that since the phrase *anupasarjanāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.14) is carried over (*anuvartana*) into the rule for the prescription of *s*—namely *tyadādīnāmaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.102)—there is no fault whatsoever.
Furthermore, regarding the rule *sambuddhau śākalyasyetāvanārṣe* (Pāṇini 1.1.16):

The word *ṛṣi* means "Veda," as seen in such passages as "so it was said by the seer" (*taduktamṛṣiṇā*). The vowel *o*, when caused by the vocative case, is optionally *pragṛhya* before the particle *iti*, provided it is not Vedic. Examples: *viṣṇo iti* or *viṣṇaviti*. Why "in the vocative"? [Consider] *gavityayamāha* ("he said 'go'"), according to the author of the *Vṛtti*. The detailed justification for this has already been stated in the preceding rule. Why "not Vedic"? [Consider] *brahmabandhavityabravīt*. Why "before *iti*"? [Consider] *paṭo'tra*. [Now, regarding Pāṇini’s sūtra 1.1.17: *añaḥ* (the *u* of the particle *uñ*). The *u* of *uñ* is optionally designated as *pragṛhya* before the particle *iti*. Examples: *uiti* or *viti*.

*Ūm̐* (Pāṇini 1.1.17). The words *uñaḥ*, *śākalyasya*, and *pragṛhyam* are understood to carry over [from previous rules]. For a *pragṛhya* vowel, when followed by the particle *iti*, there may optionally be the substitute *ūm̐*. This *ūm̐* is both long and nasalized. Here, if there were a single rule—namely *uña ūm̐*—then only two forms would result from the optional substitution: namely, *um̐ iti* and *u iti*. Therefore, having divided the rule, the designation *pragṛhya* is also made optional.

Even so, if in the second rule, "ūm̐" (Pāṇini 1.1.18), both the mention of *pragṛhya* and the mention of Śākalya were not carried over (*anuvarteta*), then since the substitution of *ūm̐* would be prescribed as obligatory for *uñ* in its entirety, the substitute would apply to non-*pragṛhya* vowels just as it does to *pragṛhya* ones. In that case, once the substitute is applied to a *pragṛhya*, the form "ūm̐ iti" is established because of the status of being a *pragṛhya* by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute behaving like the original).

Furthermore, regarding the rule *analvidhau* (Pāṇini 1.1.56), since the term *iṭ* is taken as a collective form in the rule *graho 'liṭi* (Pāṇini 7.2.37), the elision of the *sic* suffix in forms such as *agrahīt* is established by relying on the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) for the long vowel; this will be explained in the section on the *sthānivat* rule. However, if an *anunāsika* were substituted for a non-*pragṛhya* vowel, the *yaṇ* would result. Consequently, among the three desired forms, only *ūm̐ iti* would be established, while the other two would not; thus, there would be the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*).

Furthermore, there would be the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*), because it would undesirably apply even to that which is joined with a nasalized *va* (*sānunāsika-vakāra*). If, on the other hand, only the mention of *pragṛhya* were to follow, then the substitute for *uñ* as a *pragṛhya* would be obligatory; consequently, there would be only two forms—*viti* and *ūm̐*—and not the third form, *u iti*.

Now, if only the mention of Śākalya were to follow, then, due to the optional substitution of *uṅ* for *ū~*, there would be four forms in total when combined: two for the *pragṛhya* vowel—namely *ū~* and *u*—and two for the non-*pragṛhya* vowel—namely *v* and *u*. Among these, although three might be desired, the form containing an anusvāra followed by a nasalized *v* (*ū~v*) would result as undesired. Therefore, it has been stated that both the mention of Śākalya and the mention of *pragṛhya* are to be understood as following [from the previous rule].

It has been stated here that, by changing the case endings, both [the rules] "pragṛhyasya" and "uñaḥ" are carried over. Here, it has been explained as "pragṛhyasya uñaḥ" by changing the case endings. It should be noted that even if one explains it as "the *pragṛhya* [particle] *ūm* becomes this substitute (*ādeśa*)", there is no difference whatsoever.

Is it not the case that only that which is already established (*pariniṣṭhita*) is fit for grammatical application (*prayoga*), and that being established means not being subsumed under the delimitors of the object of a non-applicable obligatory rule (*apravṛtta-nitya-vidhi-uddeśyatāvacchedaka*)? The term "non-applicable" (*apravṛtta*) is used to avoid over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) in cases such as verbal roots ending in *tiṅ* suffixes. The term "obligatory" (*nitya*) is stated to avoid over-narrowness in forms like *seddhā*, where the delimitors of the object of an optional augment (*vaikalpika-iḍāgama*) are applicable. For this very reason, the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that forms such as *pac* and *laṭ* are ungrammatical (*alaukika*). Consequently, the form *u iti* would simply not exist.

For here, according to the view of Śākalya, there must indeed be the substitution of *ū~*; however, if it is argued that in the view of others there is simply no *pragṛhya* status at all, this would be so only if the mention of Śākalya were taken literally; rather, its purpose is merely to indicate an option. Thus says the Bhāṣya: "So that for Śākalya there may be an option," and [the rule] "or *ū~* according to Śākalya."

And thus Kaiyaṭa says thereon: "By means of the word *vā*, he demonstrates that this is the very fruit of Śākalya’s tradition," and "it becomes optional (*vibhāṣā*) by way of reference to another Smṛti. Alternatively, let the mention of Śākalya be taken exactly as heard in the text; nevertheless, since [the status of being a *pragṛhya*] is already established by the rule "A single vowel that is a particle" (Pāṇini 1.1.14), the rule "of *uñ*" (Pāṇini 1.1.17) is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). Thus, the meaning of the first rule is that according to the opinion of those other than Śākalya, [the particle *uñ*] is not a *pragṛhya*.

Furthermore, in the subsequent sūtra, since the status of being a *pragṛhya* for the vowel *uṅ* is already established by the mere mention of Śākalya, the fact that the term "Śākalya" is repeated again implies that even according to the opinion of others, there exists an optional *pragṛhya* status. By this, the form *u iti* is established.
