Alternatively, due to the force of the repetition of "Śākalya" in the subsequent sūtra, and by resorting to the governing principle of the word (*śabdādhikāra*), one understands that a different descendant of the sage Śākalya is intended.

And in this view, even the status of being a *pragṛhya* is obtained by the very force of the restatement (*anuvāda*) "of the *uñ* that is a *pragṛhya*" (*asmiṃśca pakṣe pragṛhyasyoña iti*), just as the status of being *ḍhak* is [obtained] by the force of the restatement "elision of *ḍhaki*" (*ḍhaki lopaḥ*, Pāṇini 4.1.133); such is the direction of the argument.

And this [term] *ādeśa* is clearly indicated by the very mention of *anunāsika*. Likewise, in the *Bahvṛca-prātiśākhya*: "The letter *u*, when joined with the suffix *iti*, is called *rakta* when it is nasalized (*pṛkta*) and lengthened according to the Śākala school" (*Ṛgveda-prātiśākhya* 1.18). And it is stated that the one designated as *rakta* is the *anunāsika*. For this very reason, in the imitation of the reading "yadetannūm" as recited by the *padakāras*, the rule "a semivowel (*yar*) becomes optionally a nasal (*anunāsika*) before a nasal (*anunāsika*)" (*Pāṇini-sūtra* 8.4.45) applies.
Also, the rule "and *ī* and *ū* in the sense of the locative case" (*Pāṇini-sūtra* 1.1.19).

The rule *śākalyasyetāv* is no longer operative here. A word-form ending in *ī* or *ū*, occurring in the sense of the locative case (*saptamī*), shall be *pragṛhya*. For example: *adhyasyāṃ māmakītan*. This is derived from *māmakyāṃ tanvām*; these two forms have their locative endings elided by *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39). It should be understood that *māmakī* and *tanū* are the examples for the application [of this rule] at the time of the Pada-text recitation. Furthermore, *somo gaurī adhiśritaḥ* is an example even in the Saṃhitā text.

What is the purpose of the rule *īdūtāv*? [Consider: *priyaḥ sūrye priyo agnā bhavāti*. Here, the locative case (*saptamī*) following the word *agni* undergoes the substitution *ḍā*. Since the authors of the *padapāṭha* have restricted the use of the particle *iti* in the context of *pragṛhya* vowels, there would be the undesirable consequence of using *iti* here as well at the time of the *padapāṭha*; thus, this is provided as a counter-example. What is the purpose of mentioning the locative (*saptamī*)? [Consider: *dhītī*, *matī*, *suṣṭutī*. These forms result from the substitution of the long *ī* vowel for the third-case singular (*tṛtīyaikavacana*), which would otherwise be a *pūrvasavarṇa* (homogeneous) vowel.

Then, by the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.109), there is a single long substitute [for the two vowels]. However, in this case, the elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*) does not apply, because that would result in the undesirable consequence of hearing a short vowel. Why is the word "meaning" (*artha*) mentioned [in the definition]? [Consider] *vāpy-aśvaḥ* ("a horse in a pond") and *nady-ātiḥ* ("a crossing on a river"). These are locative compounds (*saptamī-samāsa*) formed by the rule *saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 2.1.44).

If it is objected: "Surely there is indeed an occurrence [of the word] in the sense of the locative case; so how is the desired result established even when the term 'artha' (meaning) is included?"—it is as follows: In the view that a compound is *jahatsvārthā-vṛtti* (one in which the constituent words abandon their own meanings), just as letters have no meaning in a word, the constituent members of a compound have no meaning in the compound. Therefore, in this context, the item ending in *-ī* is meaningless, and not merely one occurring in the sense of the locative case; this is quite clear. Even in the view that a compound is *ajahatsvārthā-vṛtti* (one in which the constituent words do not abandon their own meanings), a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) does not terminate in its own meaning alone, but rather in the primary meaning as conjoined with that [subordinate meaning].

And because of the capacity to grasp the meaning, only that much meaning which is denoted by the locative case—namely, that which is not yet conjoined with the superstratum (ādheya) and which has the nature of an abstracted substratum (adhikaraṇa)—will be included here as part of the *vṛtti*.

Although it could be argued that, just as in a sentence, even in a compound (*samāsa*), there is first an understanding of the mere locus by the force of the elided locative case, and subsequently a cognition of the integrated whole as the sentence-meaning; nevertheless, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), in accordance with the maxim "A rule concerning words [is applied] when they are semantically connected" (*Pāṇini 2.1.1*), semantic connection (*sāmarthya*) in the case of a compound consists solely in "the unification of meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*), and not in mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*). For this very reason, it will be stated in the second book [of the *Mahābhāṣya*]: "An adjunct (*upasarjana*) does not admit the connection of a qualifier, because it is a part of that which is already denotable."

Even for the Mīmāṃsakas and others, since they accept a secondary figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) regarding that which is related to the meaning of the preceding word—according to the principle of the "Niṣādasthapati" (the chief of the Niṣādas)—the exclusion of words such as *vāpyaśva* (a horse belonging to a pond) and *nadyāti* (one who goes across a river) by means of the inclusion of the [specific] meaning is indeed correct. *Āti* refers to a crane (*balākā*).

"Śarārī, āti, and āṭi, as well as balākā and bisakaṇṭikā" (Amara-kośa 2.4.27). According to Amara, some maintain that the first three are feminine because they appear alongside *balākā*. However, in reality, *śarārī* and the other two denote specific types of birds and are not synonyms for *balākā*. Therefore, their association with *balākā* is irrelevant; nevertheless, their feminine gender certainly exists. This is stated in the *Ratnakośa* in the section on feminine nouns: "Āṭi, śarārī, and varaṭī. Because of its association with them, *āti* is also feminine. The Vṛtti states that the inclusion of the long vowel marker (*tapara*) is for the sake of avoiding ambiguity. On this point, there is a Vārttika: [text follows].

If it were merely "the seventh case endings ī and ū," then because the meaning [of the case ending] is understood even when it is elided, this [vowel] would be considered a homogeneous sound (savarṇa) of the preceding one; consequently, the substitution of āṬ for the augment ām would undesirably apply.
If the word *sarasī* were to occur even in those cases where lengthening occurs by virtue of a specific rule (*vacana*),
then that would serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the fact that [the elision] applies to the end of the word, or else it would apply to the preceding member (*pūrvapada*).

The meaning of this is as follows: one might simply say "īdūtau saptamī" (the vowels ī and ū in the locative case), and there would be no need for the inclusion of the word "artha" (meaning). To this, he provides the answer: "lupte" (when [the suffix] is elided). Because in a rule prescribing a technical name (*saṃjñā-vidhi*), when a suffix is mentioned, there is no extension of the designation to that which ends with it (*tadanta-vidhi*). Consequently, the designation would apply to the locative suffix itself. However, even when the case-suffix (*sup*) is elided, the mention of "artha" must indeed be made so that the designation may be established for the stem portion (*prakṛti-bhāga*). This is the meaning.

One might object: "In examples such as *somo gauḥ*, the case-ending (*vibhakti*) is not elided; rather, just as in *dhītī* and *matī*, when the homogeneous vowel substitution (*pūrvasavarṇa*) has occurred, the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* applies to produce a single long substitute. Because of the *ādivadbhāva* (the status of being like the first element) of that [long vowel], and because the word *saptamī* is mentioned [in the rule], the seventh case-ending is indeed present. Anticipating this doubt, he says: *pūrvasya* ("of the preceding"). Regarding the phrase *āḍāmbhāvaḥ*: the meaning is that the augment *āṭ* and the replacement by *ām* would apply, overriding the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) rule due to their higher status (*paratva*) and their being operations pertaining to the whole (*āṅgatva*). Therefore, since it is established that there must indeed be elision (*luk*), the mention of the "meaning" (*arthagrahaṇa*) is necessary. This is the intended sense.

One might object: "Let there be no mention of the word *artha*; by the force of the statement itself, the rule of *tadanta-vidhi* (extension to that which ends with the specified term) will apply even in the prescription of technical names (*saṃjñā*. Anticipating this objection, he says: "By virtue of the specific statement (*vacanāt*). This [extension] would apply only where lengthening (*dīrghatva*) occurs, as in the example: "dṛtiṃ na suṣkaṃ sarasī śayānam" (like a dry skin lying in a lake). For here, after the word *saras*, the locative singular ending takes the substitute *ī* according to the rule "iyāḍiyājīkārāṇām upasaṃkhyānam," and thus the locative case is heard [in the form *sarasi*].

And thus, the meaning is that [the suffix] would not occur in cases such as *somo gauḥ*. He refutes this with the words "even there" (*tatrāpi*). Even there, there is only the elision (*luk*) of the locative case-ending, and not the addition of the long vowel *ī*; provided that the word *sarasī* also exists [in the feminine]. This is a statement made regarding what is not doubtful as if it were doubtful, as in the maxim: "If these grammatical treatises were authoritative."

For there exists the word *sarasī*, as evidenced by the statement of the Blessed One: "In the southern region, indeed, large lakes are called *sarasya*," and also from the *Amarakośa*: "A pond (*kāsāraḥ*) is a *sarasī* or a *saraḥ*. Furthermore, usage such as "to frequent the *sarasī*s" (*sarasīḥ pariśīlitum mayā*) is also observed. Thus, since the word *sarasī* also occurs with its case-ending elided, it is established that the rule applies to that which ends in [the stem] *sarasī*.

[Objection: Let it be that the word *sarasī* is as stated; the word *saras*, ending in *s*, is also beyond dispute. Thus, let this substitution of *ī* for *i* occur from a stem ending in *s*. For if this were the case, there would be no need to resort again to the principle of "taking what ends in [the specified element]" (*tadantagrahaṇa*), which was previously set aside by the *jñāpaka* in the rule for technical designations (*saṃjñāvidhi*). [Reply: No. If that were so, because the vowel *ī* would be a case-ending (*sup*) and thus unaccented (*anudātta*), and because the word *saras* is derived from the root *sṛ* with the suffix *asun* (which is accented by the *niṭ-svara*), the resulting form *sarasī* would result in being acutely accented on its first syllable (*ādyudātta*). However, [the desired accentuation is not achieved].

In the case of words such as *gaura*, because of the inclusion [of these terms] in the list beginning with *pippalī* according to the rule *pippalyādayaś ca* (Kāśikā), it is desired that the word *saras-*—which falls within that group—be oxytone (*antodātta*) when the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied; this is likewise due to its recitation in the Veda. If this is so, then let this mention of the meaning (*arthagrahaṇa*) serve to indicate that, in the section concerning the designation of *pragṛhya* vowels, the criterion of being a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) does not apply.

And thus, in the rule *idūded dvivacanam* (Pāṇini 1.1.11), both the interpretation that "the dual ending [is marked by *it*] when it ends in *ī*, *ū*, or *ed*" and the interpretation that "that which ends in a dual ending [marked by *it*] when it itself ends in *ī*, *ū*, or *ed*" are established. For in that context, there is the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *kumāryyoragāram* ("the house of two maidens") and *aśukle śukle sampadyetām śuklayāstāṃ vastram* ("the two clothes, being not white, become white"). That fault is dispelled precisely by the absence of the application of the rule for treating a suffix as present (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*); thus he says: "It is an indicator (*jñāpaka*)."

In the section concerning the technical designation *pragṛhya*, the phrase "of the absence of the application of the rule based on the suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇābhāvasya*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Where is this indication useful? To that he says: "in the case of being that-final" (*tadantatve*). The meaning is: even in both of the two alternative views (pakṣa) which contain that-finality. Now, since there is no rule of "being that-final" (*tadantavidhi*) when a suffix is mentioned in a rule prescribing a technical designation (*saṃjñāvidhi*), the view involving that-finality does not stand there; therefore, out of dissatisfaction with that, he says "or rather" (*mā vā*). The meaning is: let it not occur in cases such as *vāpyaśvaḥ*.

In this regard, the following should be stated: while the term *ī* is being carried over from the rule "The suffix *ī* comes after the roots *avitṛ*, *stṛ*, *tan*, and *bhr*" (Pāṇini 3.2.184), three words are derived by means of two subsequent rules: "The suffix *ī* is *kit* and there is vocalization of the semivowel (*ya*) and substitution of *p* for *ā*" (3.2.178), and "Vātapramīḥ" (4.4.117). That by which they go is *yayīḥ*, the path of liberation. That which drinks essences or protects the world is *papīḥ*, the sun. That which measures the wind by running head-on against it is *vātapramīḥ*, a specific animal resembling a deer but lacking horns, known as the "wind-deer."

In the dative singular (*ṅi*), due to the long vowel resulting from the coalescence of similar vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*), the forms *papī*, *yayī*, and *vātapramī* are beyond dispute. However, since the vowel *u* heard here would have to be the locative case ending, the phrase "if there too were a lake" (*tatrāpi sarasī yadi*) is inconsistent; likewise, since the vowel *ī* heard here would have to be the locative case ending, the phrase "if there too were a lake" is inconsistent, because a locative case ending in the form of the vowel *ī* is impossible.

The meaning of the statement "by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), the rule will apply to that which ends in [the specified element]" is as follows: since the application of the rule to that which ends in *ū* is obtained through implication regarding the portion *ū*, the intention is that it will also apply in cases such as *somo gaurī*. However, in cases such as *yayī āsaktaḥ*, the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) must indeed take effect.

Nor should it be argued that this grammatical rule (*yoga*) pertains to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*), because examples of precisely such forms have already been provided; for to assume a word is Vedic merely by one’s own whim, without the authority of the three sages (*munitraya*), leads to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, there is no evidence to support the claim that the *pragṛhya* status does not apply in common worldly usage (*loka*). By the maxim that "what is not prohibited is assumed," it is more logical that words such as *yayī* and *vātapramī* possess the *pragṛhya* status in the world.

For this very reason, Haradatta and others—who explain that in the rule *dṛgdṛśvatuṣu* (Pāṇini 6.3.79), the *vārttika* *dṛkṣe ca* is employed so that the suffix *kṣa* and the substitution of *s* for *ś* occur only in the Vedic language, since the example *sadṛkṣāsaḥ* is cited in the Bhāṣya—have revealed their own dissatisfaction with the view of those who claim [the usage] is Vedic. This is the general direction [of the argument]. *dādhāghvadāp* (Pāṇini 1.1.20).

Roots having the form *dā* and roots having the form *dhā* shall be designated as *ghu*, with the exception of *dāp* and *daip*. Among these, there are four roots having the form *dā*: *ḍudāñ* (juhoty-ādi, 1091) in *praṇidadāti*; *dāṇ* (bhvādī, 3) in *praṇiyacchati*; *do* (divādi, 1148) in *praṇidyati*; and *deṅ* (bhvādī, 962) in *praṇidayate*. There are two roots having the form *dhā*: *ḍudhāñ* (juhoty-ādi, 1092) in *praṇidadhāti*; and *dheṭ* (bhvādī, 902) in *praṇidhayati vatsaṃ mātaram*.

What is the purpose of excluding *dā* [from the definition of *ghu*]? Consider the example: *dāp lavane* (Dhp. 1059), as in *dātaṃ barhiḥ*. The meaning is "cut. Because this root lacks the *ghu* designation, the rule *dodaddhoḥ* (Pāṇ. 7.4.46) does not apply. Consider also *daip śodhane* (Bhvādi 924), as in *avadātaṃ mukham*. Here too, because it lacks the *ghu* designation, the rule *aca upasargāt taḥ* (Pāṇ. 7.4.47) does not apply. The rules that provide the scope for *ghu* are those such as *nergadanadapatapadām* (Pāṇ. 8.4.17).

In this context, having established *dod*, *eṅ*, and *dheṭ* as imitations (*anukaraṇa*), the substitution of *ā* is applied there by the extended rule (*atideśa*) "an imitation is like its original" (*prakṛtivadanukaraṇam*). This is because of the established doctrine that the substitution of *ā* by "ādeca upadeśe 'śiti" (Pāṇini 6.1.45) is unconditional, whereas its prohibition applies when a suffix marked with *ś* follows. Nor does it follow that case-endings would fail to arise, for according to the established doctrine, the prohibition [of the term "root"] by "na dhātuḥ" (Pāṇini 1.2.45) applies only to actual roots.

Nor should it be argued that, in this case, the production of a case-ending (*vibhakti*) would not occur because the designation of *prātipadika* is prohibited by the rule "that which is not a verbal root" (*adhātu*). This is because the term "not a verbal root" (*adhātu*) here is a *paryudāsa* (an exclusionary negation), and not a *prasajyapratiṣedha* (a simple prohibitive negation). Furthermore, in this instance, the status of being "not a verbal root" exists by virtue of its own substratum. Alternatively, as in the case of the rule "from *yat*, *tat*, and *etad*" (Pāṇini 5.2.39), both the application and non-application of the extended designation (*atideśa*) will occur here specifically by taking a particular grammatical operation (*kāryaviśeṣa*) into account.

Therefore, having applied the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) to the four roots beginning with *dā* (to give) and the two roots beginning with *dhā* (to place), a *dvandva* compound should be formed. In cases such as *praṇidātā*, the status of being a *ghu* root is established for *do*, *deṅ*, and *dheṭ* by virtue of their becoming [the forms] *dā* through the substitution of *ā*. However, the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) regarding "that which is taught by its specific form" (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta*) and the rule "when a term without an indicatory letter (*anubandha*) is mentioned, that with an indicatory letter is not included" do not apply here; for all of them are cited here by their very own forms.

For this very reason, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the roots *dārayati* and *dhārayati*, because these two are not included here; since their imitation (*anukaraṇa*) cannot undergo the substitution of *ā* (the *ātvam*), [the forms] *dṛ* and *dhṛ* are not what is intended here. If it is asked: "But since the root is specified in the rule with the *ā* already applied, how can there be the status of being a *ghu* in cases such as *praṇidyati* and *praṇidhayati*, where the *ā* is absent? You are mistaken. We do not imitate a form in which the *ā* has already been applied, which would lead to the aforementioned fault; rather, it was stated that when the roots ending in *eṅ*—namely *dāp* and *dhāp*—are being imitated, the *ā* is produced by the force of the grammatical rule itself.

Furthermore, even when the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) differs due to its formal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), its status as an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) is not lost; for instance, in the rule *sakhyurasambuddhau* (Pāṇini 7.1.92), the word *sakhī* is understood [as an imitation], and in the example *gavityayamāha*, the word *go* is recognized [as an imitation]. However, there is no inclusion of the root *dīṅ* here, because *ātva* (the substitution of *ā*) is impossible in its imitation. This is because, according to the Vārttika view, *ātva* is prescribed for roots such as *dīṅ* that end in *ej* (vowels other than *a*), whereas according to the Bhāṣya view, that prescription occurs only when an element conditioned by *ej* follows.

Therefore, even though the substitution of *ā* for *dīṅ* has been applied before suffixes beginning with *tṛc* and others, because the designation *ghu* is absent, the rule *nergada-* (Pāṇini 8.4.17) does not apply obligatorily in the case of *praṇitātā*; rather, the optional application of *ṇatva* prescribed by *śeṣe vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 8.4.18) would indeed occur. Likewise, in the example *upādāstāsya svaraḥ śikṣakasya*, the substitution of *i* for *dā* according to *sthāghvoricca* (Pāṇini 1.2.17) does not take place; such is the opinion of the author of the Sūtras.

Now, in this view, are *dāp* and *daip* being imitated or not? If it is the first case, then by the combined force of both imitation and exclusion (*paryudāsa*), there would be an option regarding the designation *ghu* for those two. If it is the second case, then the term *adāp* would be redundant, because since they are not imitated, the application of the *ghu* designation would not arise for *dāp* and *daip* anyway. If this is argued, we say no; for if *adāp* were not present, the imitation of those two [roots] might also be possible.

Indeed, by means of the "eye" of grammatical definitions (*lakṣaṇa*) alone, no distinction whatsoever is perceived between roots such as *dod* and *deṅ*, on the one hand, and *dāp* and *daip*, on the other, by virtue of which their inclusion or exclusion [from the rule] could be established. Only the principle that "the specific understanding [of the intended meaning] arises from the commentary" (*vyākhyānato viśeṣapratipattiḥ*) remains; however, this is a resort of last resort, like the doctrine of non-mention (*anabhidhāna*). And it is not fitting to reject what has been established by the force of that very principle.

According to the view of the author of the *Vārttika*, however, this is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) specifically of the forms beginning with *dā* as they occur in actual usage. Nor does this lead to the objection that in forms such as *praṇidyati* and *praṇidayate*, the substitution would not occur before a *śit* affix due to the absence of *ātva*.

Likewise, one might argue that [the substitution of *ā*] would not occur in cases such as *vyatyadhita* from the root *dheṭ* (Bhvādi 902), which begins with *ā*—namely, in forms like *praṇidātā* and *praṇidhātā*—because the substitution of *ā* is based on a technical definition (*lākṣaṇika*), and by the maxim "between that which is taught by a general rule and that which is taught by a specific rule, the latter is taken" (*lakṣaṇapratipadoktayoḥ pratipadoktasya grahaṇam*). However, this need not be said, for the matter is resolved simply by the force of the explicit statement [of the rule]. Accordingly, there is a Vārttika of Kātyāyana: "The mention of the base form (*prakṛti*) in the definition of the term *ghu* is for the sake of the *śit* suffixes."

The followers of Bhāradvāja, however, read: "The *śit* [affixes] are for the sake of modification. Accordingly, having read "the roots *dā* and *dhā* are *ghu*," one should form a *dvandva* compound—*dāśca dhāśca prakṛtayaśca* (the roots *dā*, *dhā*, and the roots)—and it should be explained that, by virtue of proximity, the roots *dā* and *dhā* alone are the "roots" (*prakṛti*) here.

The authors of the Bhāṣya, however, rejected the Vārttika. For instance, regarding the rule *nergada* (Pāṇini 8.4.17), the term *prakṛti* must necessarily be included so that the substitution of *ṇ* occurs even in forms such as *praṇimayate* and *praṇyamayata*. Therefore, we shall extract that very term from its previous position and read it as *ghuprakṛtimāḥ*. This is a *dvandva* compound consisting of *ghu*, *prakṛti*, and *mā*. And by virtue of proximity (*sannidhāna*), the term *prakṛti* will be understood to apply to both the preceding and the following rules.

Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of including the roots *mī* (to destroy) and *minoti* (to measure) under the designation *ghu*, because the root *māṅ* must necessarily be recited there with the indicatory letter *ṅ*; otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in forms such as *māmānaḥ*. Therefore, since forms such as *praṇidyati* and *praṇidayate* are established by reading *māṅ* as having *ghu* as its base, it is settled that the mention of "base" (*prakṛti*) need not be made in the definition of the *ghu* designation for the sake of excluding the root *chi*.

According to the method stated by the followers of Bhāradvāja, it remains to be addressed that "the rule must apply to the modified form (*vikṛta*) of the word. That too is unnecessary, because the designation *ghu* is established even for a word like *dāru*, which is derived through a grammatical operation (*lākṣaṇika*), by the very technical rule (*paribhāṣā*): "In rules involving the mention of *ga*, *mā*, and *ā*, there is no distinction [between the original and its derivative forms]" (Pari. Bhā. 115). And in this technical rule, the fact that the root *daip* is marked with the indicator *p* (*pittva*) serves as the evidence.

The term *taddhyadābi* is employed for the purpose of including the general class [of roots], because the designation *ghu* is based on its technical definition (*lākṣaṇikatva*). Thus, even though the mention of *dā* is absent in the rule for the *ghu* designation, what is the need for the *pit* status [of *dā*] as a means of including the general class when there is a prohibition regarding *tuk*? Nor should it be argued that even so, the root *dheṭ* would not receive the *ghu* designation; for by the mention of *da* in the rule *do dad ghoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.46)—which is made for the purpose of excluding *dheṭ*—it is indicated that *dheṭ* also possesses the *ghu* designation.

Nor can it be argued that the mention of *da* is for the purpose of excluding *dadhāti*, because by that very mention, it is also made known that *dheṭ* possesses the technical designation *ghu*. Nor should it be said that *da* is stated for the sake of excluding *dadhāti*, since in that case, the application of the substitute *hi* (by Pāṇini 7.4.42, *dadhāter hiḥ*) itself precludes the occurrence of the *dadbhāva* [substitution]. [Objection: Even so, just as the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "In the case of the mention of *gām* and *ā*, there is no distinction" (Paribhāṣā 82) would be set aside, so too would the technical rule regarding the mention of meaningful elements (*arthavat-paribhāṣā*) be set aside.

If it is argued that this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) even in cases such as *praṇidārayati* and *praṇidhārayati*, we say no. For the rule is explained as follows: "The prefix *ni-* is [treated as] a prefix with respect to those very roots *gad*-etc., when they follow a cause (i.e., a preceding sound) situated within a prefix that itself precedes *gad*-etc. However, in the case of the components *dārayati* and *dhārayati*, since the forms *dā* and *dhā* are devoid of meaning (*anarthaka*), the prefix does not function as a prefix with respect to them; for it will be stated later that the technical designations of "motion" (*gati*) and "prefix" (*upasarga*) apply only with respect to that action (*kriyā*) with which the prepositions (*prādayaḥ*) are connected.

Nor should it be argued that, by this same logic, the substitution of *ṇ* would not occur in forms such as *praṇidāpayati* and *praṇidhāpayati*; for in those cases, when the designation *ghu* applies at the stage *dā-dhā* prior to the augment *pu*, the form qualified by *pu* is also included under the term *ghu*. Furthermore, according to the view that "substitutes with augments belong to those without augments," the designation *ghu* applies there by virtue of the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*).

If it is argued that there is indeed no proximity (*āntarya*) between these two, or that their association is like that of a lost horse and a burnt chariot—such that even according to the perspective of the *bhāṣya* on the rule *sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ*, forms like *dārayati* are identical to *dāpayati* because there is no distinction between the *repha* and the *puṅ* (the augment) once the *aṇ* has been established as *rapara*—then this is true. However, the resolution is made according to the method of the *vārttika* on the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ*: "But [the desired result] is established through the application [of the rule], because of the status of being *rapara*."

However, the fault that arises according to the manner of the aforementioned commentary must be remedied by resorting to the opinion of the Sūtrakāra as previously stated; for, in the case of an imitation of the two roots *dṛ* and *dhṛ*, the substitution of *ātva* (long *ā*) is not obtained—this is the general direction.

However, this must be noted: in the case of *praṇidāpayati*, the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* by Pāṇini’s sūtra 8.4.17 (*nergadanadapatapadaghumāsyatihantiyāti-vāti-drātipsātivapativahatiśāmyaticinotidegdhiṣu ca*) occurs invariably only when the two prefixes (*pra* and *ni*) qualify the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*). It occurs invariably only when they qualify the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇyartha*). But when they qualify the meaning of the suffix (*ṇyartha*), since [the prefix *pra*] is not a prefix (*anupasarga*) with respect to that which is designated as *ghu*, there is only an option (*vikalpa*) according to the rule "optionally in other cases" (*śeṣe vibhāṣā*), and not an obligatory substitution of *ṇ*.

It might be argued: "In the form *upadidīṣate*, the substitution of *ī* [for *dī*] by the rule *sani mīmā-* (Pāṇini 7.4.54) would apply, because the author of the Vārttika includes the root *dā* in the designation *ghu*. However, this fault does not apply to the author of the Sūtras or the author of the Bhāṣya, because the author of the Sūtras did not include *dī* [in the list], and according to the Bhāṣya, even though the original form (*prakṛti*) is included in the designation *ghu* for the purpose of nasalization (*ṇatva*), that designation is absent here. This is true; however, even in the view of the Vārttika, this is not the original form of *dā*, since it is accepted that roots ending in *e* undergo the substitution of *ā* [before the suffix *san*].

Nor is there a failure to establish the suffix *yuc* based on the fact that [the root] ends in a short vowel (*adanta*), because its establishment is achieved by that very rule which prescribes a suffix characterized by ending in the vowel *ā*. However, it is another matter that in the Bhāṣya, for the sake of rejecting this statement, the substitution of *āt* was established as the final doctrine (*siddhānta*) regarding the domain of *aij*.

However, this remains to be addressed: according to both the Bhāṣya and Vārttika views, in the example *upādāstāsya svaraḥ śikṣakasya*, the substitution of *i* by Pāṇini 6.1.45 (*sthāghvoḥ*) would apply; and that has been refuted in the Bhāṣya by means of the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*. When the form *upa dī sta* is established, the substitution of *ā* for *dī* (by 6.1.45), which operates within the domain of *ej*-vowels, depends upon the fact that the suffix *sic* is not *kit*.

If the designation *ghu* were to apply here, then by the rule *sthādhvoricca* (Pāṇini 1.2.27), the suffix *sic* would possess the property of being *kit*; therefore, since the substitution of *ā* proceeds depending on the absence of *kit*, that *ā* certainly does not trigger the *ghu* designation which causes the application of *kit*.

The author of the Vārttika, however, has simply provided the statement: "There is a prohibition for *dīṅ* regarding the substitution of *i* in place of [the final vowel] of *sthā* and *ghu*. In both systems of thought (*mata*), once the substitution of *ā* has taken place in *dīṅ* before an affix beginning with *tṛc*, the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs in forms such as *praṇidātā* by the rule *nergada-* (Pāṇini 8.4.17). For this very reason, the author of the Vārttika did not merely state "there is a prohibition for *dīṅ*," but rather specified the particular scope [of the prohibition] as being "in the case of the substitution of *i* for *sthā* and *ghu*."

According to the view of the *Sūtra*, however, it is quite clear that the substitution of *ṇ* should not take place. Furthermore, there is not only a contradiction between the *Bhāṣya* and the *Vārttika* regarding the author of the *Sūtra*, but also between the two themselves. For instance, according to the *Bhāṣya*, in forms such as *praṇidīyate* and *praṇidīnaḥ*, the substitution of *ṇ* is obligatory because the root is included in the rule prescribing the *ṇ*. According to the *Vārttika*, however, it is optional, because it accepts only those ending in *ej* (e, o, ai, au) as roots (*prakṛti*), whereas a root ending in *i* (as in *dī*) is not considered a root in this context.

Otherwise, in the case of *upadidīṣate*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the absence of *iṭ*. Thus, in forms such as *praṇidātā*, there is a conflict between [the view of] the two [grammarians] and the author of the Sūtra; however, in cases such as *praṇidīnaḥ*, the conflict between the other two [grammarians] and the author of the Bhāṣya is difficult to resolve.

On this point, the following must be said: Since it is an established tenet that "the authority of the sages increases in successive order," and since, according to the method stated in the Bhāṣya, *ṇatva* is obligatory everywhere when *dīṅ* is followed by a suffix, even in the view of the Sūtra and Vārttika, one must ensure there is no contradiction with the Bhāṣya by relying on a fixed option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) under the rule *śeṣe vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 8.4.18). This is because, as long as a complete resolution of all cases is possible through a single unified interpretation, it is improper to resort to the assumption of conflicting opinions.

If it is argued that in the prohibition *nanv adābi*, it is only appropriate to understand the root *dāp* (as in *dāplavana*) and not *daip*, because when the letter *p* is heard, the substitution of *ā* (ātvā) is impossible—[we reply: no. According to the view that "indicatory letters (*anubandhas*) are non-exclusive" (*anubandhā anekāntāḥ*), even though the letter *p* is heard, it is like a crow perched on the roof; since it is not an integral part (*anavayava*) of the root, the status of the root as ending in *ā* (*ejanta*) remains intact, and thus the application of *ātvā* occurs.

Even in the view that "suffixes with indicatory letters (*anubandha*) are single [phonemes]," the substitution of *ā* for *a* certainly occurs, because of the established principle that "the non-homogeneity [of a vowel] is not caused by an indicatory letter. And in this regard, the mention of *meṅ*—which has already undergone the substitution of *ā*—in the rule "according to the Northern Grammarians, [the substitute of *māṅ* is used] when there is a desire to see" (*udīcāṃ māṅo vyatīhāre*, Pāṇini 3.4.19), serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

Nor should it be argued that this is merely a reference to the rule *māṅ māne* (Pāṇini 3.2.177), since in forms such as *vyatimimīte*, that root also can occasionally function in the sense of reciprocal action (*vyatīhāra*). This is because the suffix *ktvā*, which expresses an action not prior in time, is not prescribed after the root *māṅ māne*; and on this point, they say that the authority is precisely what is stated in the Bhāṣya.

Thus, although one should simply read *meṅ*, the inclusion of the term *māṅo vyatīhāre* with its heavy marker (*ṅ*) is solely for the purpose of indicating the maxim: "The status of being non-*ejanta* is not caused by an *anubandha*" (Paribhāṣā 7).

The authors of the Bhāṣya, however, maintain that this is not the root *daip*, but rather that among the roots beginning with *div* (the fourth class), it will be read simply as *dāp* in the sense of "purifying. Nor is there any difference in accent; for in forms such as *dāyati*, the acute accent falls on the first syllable regardless of which root is used. If it is argued that there is indeed a difference in accent in the case of the suffix *cānaś* (denoting habitual action) in *dāyamānaḥ*—since the root would have the acute accent on the first syllable when followed by *śyan*, whereas when followed by *śap* (the present indicative marker), the *cānaś* suffix itself would have the acute accent on its final syllable—we reply: no, because in both cases the acute accent remains on the final syllable of the word.

Nor should it be argued that the *śyan* suffix possesses greater force due to its being *satiśiṣṭa* (left over after other rules have applied), because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) in the rule "except for *vikaraṇas*" (*anyatra vikaraṇebhyaḥ*). Furthermore, by the force of the *bhāṣya* and *kaiyaṭa* on the rule "the *khaś* suffix is used in the sense of self-respect" (*ātmamāne khaśca*), it is determined that both *khaś* and *cānaś* are also *antodātta* (accented on the final syllable). As for the passage from Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the *sthānivadādeśaḥ* sūtra, it will be stated that it is erroneous because it contradicts both the *bhāṣya* on the *śaraprabhṛti* sūtra and his own statements.

However, roots such as *dhyai* are not listed in the *divādi* class precisely because they end in long *ā*; thus, forms such as "one should not trust the untrusting" (*na viśvased aviśvastam*) and "the wives of travelers, having gained confidence, are breathing a sigh of relief" (*pathikavanitāḥ pratyayād āśvasantyaḥ*)—as found in the *Meghadūta*—are established. As for what was concluded in the *Bhāṣya*, where it begins by stating that there is no fault even under the view that [the root] ends in *ekāra*, and then establishes the position that once the phoneme *pa* is elided, the form will be produced; and that the status of being *dā* (ending in *dā*) must be explained by resorting to a previously existing *anubandha*: [This is the conclusion.]

In this regard, they object as follows: "Even though there is *ejantatva* (the state of ending in a root with the marker *e*), how can there be *ejantatva* in the original instruction (*upadeśe*)? To this it is replied: By the force of the employment of the *pit* designation, the application of *ātva* (the substitution of *ā*) occurs even in the absence of *ejantatva* in the original instruction. In fact, however, the author of the Bhāṣya does not consider the inclusion of the term "in the original instruction" (*upadeśagrahaṇam*). And so he will say there: "The mention of 'in the original instruction' shall not be made. [Objection: If the mention of "in the original instruction" is not made, then [the rule] would apply even in cases such as *cetā* and *stotā*.

In this case as well, the activity of the Teacher indicates that the substitution of *ā* does not occur for a root whose cause is something subsequent; for he teaches the substitution of *ā* for the roots *krī*, *jī*, and *mī* only when followed by the affix *ṇā*. This is not a valid indicator, for that rule would merely be a restrictive one (*niyamārtha*), meaning that the substitution of *ā* for *krī*, *jī*, and *mī* occurs only before *ṇā*. As for the fact that he causes the mention of *ai* to be carried over from the rule "mīnāti-minoti-dīṅāṃ lyapi ca" (Pāṇini 6.1.50), [that too is not sufficient].

If it is objected that in the case of *praṇidāpayati* as well, there would be the prohibition [of *ṇatva*] by the rule *adābiti*, we say no. Under the *yathoddeśa* view, because the designation *ghu* is established at the very stage of the *dā* root due to its being an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), the prohibition does not apply. However, under the *kāryakāla* view, since the *ghu* designation shares the same locus as the *ṇatva* substitution, both the *ṇatva* and the *ghu* designation are considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the *puk* augment; consequently, the *puk* would be applied first, and subsequently the *ghu* designation would not occur—thus the fault certainly persists. For this very reason, it was resolved in two ways in the Bhāṣya: "I shall state *dādhāgvap*."

Alternatively, these two roots end in *b* (*ba*), and the root *satr* also ends in *b*. In all instances, the letter *p* is indicated [in grammatical rules] by means of *c* (which represents both *c* and *j*). Therefore, in the case of "dāpayati," this prohibition does not apply, because that [root *dā*] also ends in *t* and does not end in *b*.
[This is based on the rule: "In a single [element], [the operations of] the beginning and the end [apply]. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.1.21).

In the case of *asahāya*, the grammatical operations (*kāryāṇi*) should be applied as if at the beginning and at the end [of a word]. For example, *aupagavaḥ*. Just as the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*) applies to suffixes such as *tavya* and others, so too does it apply here to the suffix *aṇ*. In *ābhyām*, just as lengthening (*dīrghatva*) occurs in forms such as *vṛkṣābhyām* by the rule *supi ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.102), so too does it occur here. In *eyam*, derived from the root *iṅ* (meaning "to go," belonging to the *divādi* class)—just as the suffix *yat* prescribed after a verbal root ending in *ac* by the rule *aco yat* (Pāṇini 3.1.97) results in forms such as *ceyam* and *jeyam*, so too does it occur here.

However, from the root *iṇ*, by means of the *kyap* suffix according to Pāṇini 3.1.109 (*eti-stu-* etc.), the form *ityam* and so forth occurs; likewise here as well. But from the root *iṇ*, by means of the *kyap* suffix according to Pāṇini 3.1.109, the form is only *yatya*, and not *eyam*. Why [is the condition] "in one [word]" stated? Consider *sābhāsannayanaḥ*, meaning "that which exists in the *sabhāsannayana*. For here, if the vowel *ā* were considered the first [vowel], then depending on that very [vowel], the word *sabhāsannayana* would become *vṛddha*.

Consequently, by setting aside the *aṇ* suffix, the suffix *cha* would apply [by the rule] "cha after a word containing a *vṛddhi* vowel" (*Pāṇini* 4.2.114). Now, one might object that this very same thing is what is excluded by the inclusion of the word "beginning" (*ādi*) in the sūtra "vṛddhir yasyācām ādiḥ" (*Pāṇini* 1.1.73).

If it is argued that by the very force of that [rule], the designation *vṛddha* will not apply to the word *sabhāsannayana*, we say no. For if, on account of the inclusion of the word "beginning" (*ādi*) in the rule defining the *vṛddha* designation, only the primary beginning—which does not involve extension (*atideśa*)—is understood, then a solitary *vṛddha* such as *jñā* in the example *jñā brāhmaṇī* (a Brāhmaṇī woman who knows) would not be designated as *vṛddha*. Consequently, forms such as *jñāyā ayam* = *jñayaḥ* would not be established.

For if the mention of "one" (*eka*) in the present sūtra were not made, then wherever the designation "beginning" (*ādi*) is not primary—namely, in the case of that which is without a companion (an *asahāya*) at the middle or the end—all of that would, without distinction, become the scope of the extended application (*atideśa*). If it is argued, "If the mention of 'beginning' is for the sake of the technical term *vṛddha*, then it is indeed useless," then alas! by the force of this extended application and the mention of "beginning," there would result an undesirable option (*vikalpa*) in all cases. However, when the mention of "one" is made here, the mention of "beginning" in the rule for the *vṛddha* designation becomes meaningful through the exclusion of the final and middle positions. This is the general direction [of the argument].

As for what was stated by the author of the *Nyāsa*: "In the rule concerning extended application (*atideśa*), if the mention of 'one' (*eka*) were absent, the mention of 'beginning' (*ādi*) in the rule defining the technical term *vṛddha* would serve to ensure that the non-extended application of the term applies only to roots like *jñā* which have no companions, and not to *sabhāsannayana*; for in the case of *sabhāsannayana*, since there exist four vowels within the word ending in *sannayana*, the status of being a 'beginning'—even if it is not obtained through extended application—is present therein."

That is to be considered: because, according to the tenet that "that which has nothing before it when another exists is a beginning," even a middle element lacks the status of being a beginning. For this is the only distinction: in the case of a solitary element, there is an absence of the qualified due to the absence of the final qualifier; whereas in the case of a middle element, there is an absence of the qualified due to the absence of the qualificand.

The author of the Vārttika, however, considering brevity, maintained that the basis for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word *ādi* is merely "being first" (*apūrvatva*) and that of the word *anta* is merely "being last" (*anuttaratva*), rather than including the qualification "only when another exists," because that would involve prolixity (*gaurava*). Thus, thinking that the primary senses of "first" and "last" are possible even in the case of a solitary entity, he rejected this Sūtra. And he said: "Since 'first' and 'last' are defined as being 'without predecessor' and 'without successor,' their application to a single thing is established."

The author of the Bhāṣya, however, did not accept this, because the complexity resulting from the addition of the qualifier "provided there is another" is justified by its being based on authoritative evidence. For in common worldly usage, when it is said "this is the beginning" or "this is the end," people invariably understand that something else remains. Furthermore, the constant and determinate presentation [of a meaning] from a word is accomplished through its expressive power (*śakti*).

If, however, one were to disregard actual experience and postulate a denotative power (*śakti*) for only a single part [of a word], then even in the case of words such as *śvaśura* ("father-in-law") and others, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), the denotative capacity-restrictor (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) would be merely the state of being a wife, merely the state of being a father, or merely the masculinity inherent in that [word]; consequently, by destroying the denotative power directed toward the qualified whole (*viśiṣṭa*), there would be a subversion of all the linguistic usage of the learned (*śiṣṭa*).

[Objection: Even so, the rule *vyapadeśivadbhāvo 'prātipadikena* must indeed be stated, so that in forms such as *iyāya* and *āra*, reduplication may occur by relying on the fact that they are parts of a verbal root (*dhātu*), their initial position, and their having a single vowel (*ekāctva*). For it will be stated that the term *ekāc* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

It should not be argued that after the substitution of *vṛddhi* and *āy* for *eṇ*, and the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* in the case of the root *ṛ*, the monosyllabic status (*ekāctva*) of *āy* and *ār* remains primary—just as it does for roots like *pac*—because of the rule "dvirvacane'ci" (Pāṇini 1.1.59), which prescribes the doubling of these very forms, *i* and *ṛ*. Furthermore, in the case of the fifth lakāra (the optative) of the root *yaj*, as in "sa devān yakṣadiṣito yajīyān," the suffix *sip* is applied by the rule "sibbahulaṃ leṭi" (Pāṇini 3.1.34).

Its status as a *ṣat* (retroflex) must be established through the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), according to the established tenet that "the *ṣat* status belongs to the *s* that is part of the affix. Therefore, one might ask: why should the rule "like that which possesses a designation, in the case of a single [element]" (*vyapadeśivadekasmin*) alone not suffice, instead of this present rule? A "designation" (*vyapadeśa*) means a specific, primary application or usage, such as "having a single vowel" (*ekāc*) and so forth; that which has this is "possessing a designation" (*vyapadeśin*), such as the root *pac* and others. The meaning is that the grammatical operation should apply even when there is no actual [separate] designation.

On this point, the author of the Bhāṣya says: "It is established by worldly cognition because it is not explicitly stated. The meaning is that since the status of being like that which has a designation (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*) is established through worldly usage alone, independent of any formal statement, neither of the two rules—"like the first" (*ādyantavat*) nor "like that which has a designation" (*vyapadeśivat*)—need to be formulated as a *sūtra*. For there exists in the world this well-established usage: "This very one is my eldest son," "this is the middle one," and "this is the youngest. Likewise, even when a woman has not yet given birth or is not currently giving birth, people say of her, "She has been killed by her first pregnancy."

Likewise, one might say, "Previously I had not come, nor do I intend to come hereafter; this is my first arrival. [Objection: Surely all these usages are secondary (*gauṇa*); how then could a grammatical rule (*śāstra*), which finds its fulfillment in the primary (*mukhya*) sense, apply to a secondary one? [Response: No, for due to its extreme conventionalization (*nirūḍhatara*), even this secondary usage stands on an equal footing with the primary, and there is also an indicative proof (*jñāpaka*). Namely, that the rule "when *iṭ* follows *iṭ*" (Pāṇini 7.2.27) teaches the elision of *sic*, thereby indicating the principle: "in a single entity, it is as if it possessed a designation" (*vyapadeśivadekasmin*). For otherwise, the *iṭ* would not be obtainable.

Even though [the root *val*] has the form *val*, it lacks the status of beginning with *val*; likewise, rules such as "a long vowel is substituted for *iṇ* before a *kit* suffix" (Pāṇini 7.4.67) are also indicators (*jñāpaka*). For, without the application of the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), the reduplication of *iṇ* could not be obtained; this is the general direction [of the argument].

As for what was stated by Kaiyaṭa—that because of the principle "that which possesses meaning applies as if it were the designation itself" (*arthavatā vyapadeśivadbhāvāt*), in forms such as *kurutaḥ*, the vowel *ā* of the element *ta* is meaningless; therefore, in order to establish the designation *ṭi* for it, the treatment as if it were the beginning (*ādivadbhāvaḥ*) must be established by an explicit rule (*vacanenaiva*)—the following must be said here: first of all, the statement "that which possesses meaning applies as if it were the designation itself" is not a technical maxim (*paribhāṣā*), because it is a subordinate part of a specific injunction (*vidhyaṅga*). Furthermore, since it has been stated that the treatment as if it were the designation itself (*vyapadeśivadbhāvaḥ*) is a worldly (conventional) matter, it cannot be a subordinate part of that [maxim].

However, the intention of the author of the *Śāstra* is simply this: in order to apply the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), he relies on the collection of both word and meaning to demonstrate that "the word is a part of that [collection]," and for this purpose, meaningfulness (*arthavattā*) is required. For this very reason, in the sixth book, during the occasion of the derivation of the rules *nijau*, *catvāraḥ*, and *ekācaḥ*, both the *Bhāṣya* and Kaiyaṭa accept the application of *vyapadeśivadbhāva* even for that which is meaningless (*anarthaka*), because just as in common usage, so too in the *Śāstra* it is possible for that which is meaningless to possess a designation.

Therefore, the claim that "only that which is meaningful [is subject to grammatical operations]" is merely a general rule; the rejection of the rule (*sūtrapratyākhyāna*) is indeed correct. This is the direction of the argument.

*tarap-tamapau ghaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.22): These two [suffixes] are designated as *gha*. [Examples: *kumāritarā*, *kumāritamā*. [In these cases,] by the rule *gharūpa* (Pāṇini 6.3.47), the short vowel [of the feminine suffix] is substituted. However, this does not occur in *nadyāstaraḥ* or *nadītaraḥ*, because, due to association with *tamap*, only the suffix *tarap* is understood here. Alternatively, the form [of *tara*] relied upon for the application of the designation is that which occurs in the *taraP* suffix; since that [specific form] does not exist anywhere in a fully established usage (*pariniṣṭhita*), the form belonging to the *tarap* suffix itself is taken as the basis for the designation. This [form] exists only for the *tarap* suffix.

Furthermore, the quality of being both a *āpi* vowel and a specifically prescribed (*pratipadokta*) one is easily available here; therefore, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the word *nadī* when it is analyzed etymologically [as *na-dī*]. Moreover, shortening is prescribed when a feminine noun in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) follows. Otherwise, it would also apply in the case of *mahiṣī-rūpam*, as in "a form like a buffalo-cow. This is a compound according to the rule *sup supā*; *rūpa* means shape (*ākṛti*), and the sense is: "this shape is like a buffalo-cow."

Because the comparative suffixes (*ātiśāyanika*) are applied in their own primary sense (*svārthika*) when there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and femininity, they do not apply to the word *nadī* (meaning "river") when it means "other than a woman"; therefore, the aforementioned fault does not arise. If it is argued: "In the very section on comparatives, one should simply state *tādī gha* or *pitau gha* for the sake of brevity," we say no. This is because, by elevating the topic here, it serves to indicate that within this section on technical designations (*saṃjñā-prakaraṇa*), there exists another [suffix] *tarap* as well. And since its specific meaning has not been specified, it occurs in its own primary sense. By this, forms such as *alpāctaram* ("having fewer syllables") and *lopaśca balavattaraḥ* ("elision is more powerful") are established.

Some, relying on an indicator that depends upon generality (*sāmānyāpekṣa*), assert that even the suffix *īyasun* has a svārthika function; by this, usages such as "aho mahīyaḥ tava sāhasikyam" (oh, how great is your audacity! are justified. [The rule] "bahugaṇavatuḍati saṅkhyā" (Pāṇini 1.1.23).

These are technical terms for numbers (*saṅkhyā-saṃjñā*). *bahukṛtvaḥ* [is formed] by *Pāṇini Sūtra 5.4.17*: "The suffix *kṛtvasuc* is added after a numeral in the sense of counting the repetition of an action. *bahudhā* [is formed] by *Pāṇini Sūtra 5.3.42*: "The suffix *dhā* is added after a numeral in the sense of distribution. *bahukaḥ* ("bought for many") [is formed] by *Pāṇini Sūtra 5.1.22*: "The suffix *kan* is added after a numeral that does not end in *ati* or *śat*. *bahuśaḥ* [is formed] as follows: while the rule *Pāṇini Sūtra 5.4.42*, "after words meaning 'much' or 'few', the suffix *śas* is added when they function as a *kāraka*," is in force, *Pāṇini Sūtra 5.4.43*, "and also after numerals and singular terms when there is distributive repetition (*vīpsā*)," prescribes the suffix *śas*.

*gaṇakṛtvaḥ*, *gaṇadhā*, *gaṇakaḥ*, *gaṇaśaḥ*; *tāvatkṛtvaḥ*, *tāvaddhā*, *tāvatkaḥ*, *tāvacchaḥ*. [These are derived] by the rule *yattadetebhyaḥ parimāṇe vatup* (Pāṇini 5.1.32) and *ā sarvanāmnaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.91); the rest is as before. *katikṛtvaḥ*, *katikaḥ*, *katidhā*, *katiśaḥ*. [The suffix] *ḍati* is added after *kim* when denoting a numerical measure, according to *kimaḥ saṃkhyāparimāṇe ḍati ca* (Pāṇini 5.2.41); the rest is as before.

It might be argued: "The word *bahu* also occurs in the sense of 'extensiveness' (*vaipulya*) in the *Vaipulya* [sūtras], as in the expression *bahur himavān* ('the vast Himālayas'). Furthermore, the word *gaṇa* occurs in the sense of a 'monastic community' (*saṅgha*), as in *bhikṣukāṇāṃ gaṇaḥ* ('a group of monks'). According to Amarasimha’s lexicon, *samavāyaḥ cayogaṇaḥ* ('a collection or an aggregate is a *gaṇa*'). Thus, since these two words also denote a 'community' and 'extensiveness,' they too should be designated as 'numerals' (*saṃkhyā*). If this is raised, we say: No. This is because the designation is understood to be based on its etymological meaning (*anvarthasaṃjñā*), namely, that which is "counted by means of it" (*saṃkhyāyate'nayā*). Therefore, only the words *bahu* and *gaṇa* when they denote actual numbers are intended here.

And that [specification] is for the purpose of restriction—namely, that among those words expressing an indefinite plurality, the technical designation *saṃkhyā* applies only to these two (dvi and eka) and not to words such as *bhūri* and so on. Consequently, there is no exclusion of the two cases of "many" and "one," nor of the three and so forth which express a definite plurality. Now, if its status as a restrictive rule were established, then your stated arrangement would indeed follow, since a restriction necessarily depends upon its own class (*sajātīya*). However, its status as a restrictive rule is difficult to establish, as it is more appropriate to regard it as an original injunction (*vidhi*).

For instance, there is the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*): "Between the artificial and the non-artificial, the application of the grammatical operation is understood to pertain to the artificial" (Paribhāṣenduśekhara 9). And this is rooted in logic. For how could a technical term, being restricted by its defining rule to a specific object of designation, cause anything other than that to be understood? This being the case, if *bahu* and *gaṇa* were not included here [in the definition of number], they would not be included at all in the rules concerning numbers, because they are non-artificial.

Therefore, the inclusion of the terms *bahu* and *gaṇa* is solely for the purpose of including themselves, and not for the purpose of excluding words such as *bhūri*. On this point, they say: if the restriction of a technical name (*saṃjñā-niyama*) applied to a specific named entity (*saṃjñin*) were intended with reference to the general category, then the exclusion of non-technical (*akṛtrima*) terms would be appropriate; however, if it refers to a specific instance, then by that restriction only another technical term of the same class would be excluded, and not even a non-technical one.

This is explained as follows: "In this treatise, there is a dual application" (*ubhayagatir iha śāstre bhavati*) means that both the technical (*kṛtrima*) and the non-technical (*akṛtrima*) [terms] are included. Furthermore, there is evidence for this dual inclusion in the rules concerning numbers (*saṃkhyāpradeśa*), namely the exclusion of words ending in *śat* in the rule *saṃkhyāyā atiśadantāyāḥ kan* (Pāṇini 5.1.22). For there is no technical number (*kṛtrimā saṃkhyā*) that ends in *śat*; such is the direction [of the argument]. By this, forms such as *pañcadhā* ("fivefold") and *pañcakṛtvaḥ* ("five times") are established.

Although there is no inclusion of the "end of that" (*tadantagrahaṇa*) when a suffix is mentioned in a rule prescribing a technical name (*saṃjñā*), nevertheless, because there is no purpose for the application of the suffixes *vatu* and *ḍati* alone as names, the inclusion of the end of that [word] follows by implication (*sāmarthyāt*). For in the rules prescribing *taddhita* suffixes, the governing rule "from a nominal stem ending in *ṅī*, *ap*, or a nominal base" (*ṅyāpprātipadikāt*) is in force, and it should be understood that a suffix alone cannot possess the status of a nominal base (*prātipadika*). Furthermore, this rule has been rejected in the *Bhāṣya*.

By the rules "bahupūgagaṇasaṅghasya tithuk" (Pāṇini 5.2.21), "vatorithuk" (Pāṇini 5.2.53), and "ṣaṭkatikatipayacaturāṃ thuk" (Pāṇini 5.2.51), which prescribe augmentations when the suffix *ḍaṭ* follows, it is understood that words such as *bahu* possess the status of being numerals (*saṃkhyātva*) in order to justify the application of *ḍaṭ*. What, then, is the purpose of this present rule? [Objection: But surely, since specific conditions are relied upon in rules such as "bahupūgagaṇasaṅgha" (Pāṇini 5.2.52), the words *bahu* and *gaṇa*—even when they denote a multitude or abundance (*saṃghavaipulya*)—[would already be accounted for].

If it is argued that there should be the grammatical operation (*saṃkhyākārya*) [of a numeral] here, we say no. For these two words, even though they denote indefinite numbers, their purpose is fulfilled by merely indicating that the operation of a numeral applies to them; thus, it is redundant and overly cumbersome to assume the operation of a numeral for words that do not convey a number at all. Furthermore, the inclusion of words such as *bhūri* (many) and so on—which denote indefinite numbers—does not occur, because in common usage only words like *pañca* (five) and others, which denote definite numbers, are more widely recognized as "numeral-words" (*saṃkhyāśabda*).

Because, between what is well-known and what is not, it is logical to adopt that which is well-known. Now, one might object: even so, just as with *bahu* and *gaṇa*, there would arise the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of *pūga*, *saṃgha*, and others also undergoing the grammatical operations of numerals (*saṃkhyā*), such as the suffixes *dhā*, *śas*, *khṛt*, *vasuc*, and so on. Nor can it be argued that the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) applies generally to *bahu* and *gaṇa*, whereas for *pūga* and the rest, it applies only in the domain of the suffix *ḍa*; for such an argument is untenable.

If it is argued that there is no reason for this discrepancy because [the two cases] are equal and included in the same sūtra, do not say so. For, in accordance with the requirements of the linguistic forms to be defined (*lakṣya*), one accepts that an indicator (*jñāpaka*) sometimes depends on a general rule and sometimes depends on a specific rule; thus, a lack of uniformity must be tolerated in accordance with those requirements. This is the direction of the argument. However, the ultimate truth is that the author of the sūtras composed this particular sūtra precisely because he could not tolerate such a forced interpretation (*kusṛṣṭi*).

Regarding this, there are the Vārttikas: "The inclusion of the term *adhyardha* is for the purpose of [applying] compound rules (*samāsa*) and rules concerning primary suffixes (*kan*). *Adhyardha* means 'more by half. This word *ardha* denotes a part; when it is compounded with the word *adhi*, the etymological meaning is understood rather than a numerical value. Thus begins the Vārttika.

"Adhyardhaśūrpa" means "bought for one and a half śūrpa. This is a compound formed by the rule "taddhitārtha" (Pāṇini 2.1.51), while the rule "diksaṃkhye" (Pāṇini 2.1.50) is still in effect. Then, by the rule "sūrpādañanyatarasyām" (Pāṇini 5.2.26), the suffix *añ* or *ṭhañ* is applied; subsequently, by the rule "adyardhapūrva" (Pāṇini 5.1.27), there is elision (*luk*) of these suffixes. "Adhyarddhaka" means "bought for one and a half," formed by the rule "saṃkhyāyā atiśadantāyāḥ kan" (Pāṇini 5.1.26), which prescribes the suffix *kan*.

In this context, the genitive case in the phrase *samāsavidhyartham* expresses a general relationship; that is to say, "when a compound is being prescribed" or "when some other operation is being prescribed on account of a compound. By this, even the elision (*luk*) caused by a *dvigu* compound is obtained. Consequently, the mention of *adhyarddha* in the rule *adhyarddhapūrva* (Pāṇini 5.1.28) need not be made. As it has been stated: "And there is no mention [of *adhyarddha*] when there is elision (*luk*). Furthermore, a compound whose prior member is *adhyarddha* ends in a suffix of ordinal number (*pūraṇapratyaya*). The term *saṃkhyā* (number) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule].

The phrase "ending in a ordinal suffix" (pūraṇapratyayānta) means that the final member [of the compound] ends in a ordinal suffix. This is specifically for the purpose of prescribing a compound and a kṛt-suffix. The term *arddhapañcamaśūrppa* is a bahuvrīhi compound meaning "those of which the fifth is half. It refers to something purchased for four *śūrpa*s plus a half, i.e., four and a half *śūrpa*s. As before, there is either the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *añ* or *ṭhañ*. Thus, *arddhapañcamaśūrppa* is formed. Alternatively, *arddhapañcamaka* means "purchased for four and a half [units]. In this case, the suffix *kan* is added.

The inclusion of the word *adhika* is for the purpose of ensuring the *vṛddhi* substitution in the final member of the compound even when there is no elision (*aluk*). For example, in *adhikaṣāṣṭhikaḥ* (“bought with an additional sixth”) and *adhikasāptatikaḥ*, the compound is formed by *taddhitārtha* (Pāṇini 2.1.51), and the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied by *prāgvateṣṭhañ* (Pāṇini 5.1.18). Because of the statement “when there is no elision” (*alukī*), since the designation of *saṃkhyā* does not exist when elision (*luk*) is to be performed, the status of being a *dvigu* does not arise; consequently, the elision of the suffix prescribed by *adhyarddhapūrva-dvigoḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.28) does not take place.

Then, by the rule *saṃkhyāyāḥ saṃvatsarasaṃkhyasya ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.15), there is vṛddhi of the final vowel of the second member [of the compound]. If it is argued: "The mention of *aluk* (non-elision) is redundant, because the very statement that this is for the purpose of the vṛddhi of the second member makes it possible to infer the absence of elision (*luk*)," we say: No. This is because the vṛddhi of the second member finds its scope precisely in cases where suffixes applied after words meaning "deserving" (*arhat*) do not undergo elision. [Furthermore,] the rule *ṣṇāntā ṣaṭ* (Pāṇini 1.1.24) [applies].

A numeral that ends in *ṣ* or *n* should be designated as *ṣaṭ*. For example: *ṣaṭ tiṣṭhanti*, *ṣaṭ paśya*, *pañca*, *sapta*, and so forth. Why specify "numeral"? [Consider] *vipruṣaḥ* and *pāmānaḥ*. If it is argued: "In the case of *śatāni* and *sahasrāṇi*, once the augment *num* is applied, since it is part of the preceding element (*pūrvabhakta*), the numeral would end in *n* and thus should receive the designation *ṣaṭ*," let it be so. Nor should it be said that this would cause the elision (*luk*) by the rule *ṣaḍbhyo luk* (Pāṇini 7.1.22), because the *num* is introduced by the presence of a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix and therefore does not obstruct that [elision]. However, even if this is the case, the form *aṣṭānām* would not be established.

To explain: when the form *aṣṭanām* is established, one might object that since the substitution of *ā* by "aṣṭana ā vibhaktau" (Pāṇini 7.2.84) applies because it is both subsequent and obligatory (*nitya*), the word no longer ends in *n*. Consequently, the designation (*saṃjñā*) of "six" (*ṣaṭ*) being absent, the augment *nuṭ* would not apply by "ṣaṭcaturbhyaśca" (Pāṇini 7.2.55). This is not so. According to the *yathoddeśa* view, the designation of "six" occurs prior to the substitution of *ā*, because it is more internal (*antaraṅga*). Therefore, even after the substitution of *ā* has taken place, the designation of "six" remains valid—since a modification of a single part does not alter the identity of the whole—and thus the application of *nuṭ* is established.

If, on the other hand, you adopt the view that rules apply at the time of the operation (*kāryakālapakṣa*), then the aforementioned defect remains exactly as it was. Furthermore, even under the view that rules apply at the time of their enunciation (*uddiśyakālapakṣa*), extension (*atideśa*) is difficult to obtain because the rule is not one concerning an *al* substitute (*alvidhi*). If it is argued that Kaiyaṭa stated that the purpose of the rule *vavraśca* (Pāṇini 6.1.15) is to provide an occasion for the application of *acaḥ parasmin* (Pāṇini 1.1.57), we say no. This is because the mention of the term "long" (*dīrgha*) in the rule *aṣṭano dīrghāt* (Pāṇini 7.2.84) indicates that the designation *ṣaṭ* applies even to forms where the substitution of *āt* has already taken place.

For instance, the word *aṣṭan* is established as having its final syllable accented (*antodātta*) by virtue of its inclusion in the *ghṛtādi* group, which overrides the rule *nraḥ saṃkhyāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.174) that would otherwise have caused the initial syllable to be accented. Consequently, in the instrumental plural (*bhisi*), two forms arise: *aṣṭabhiḥ* and *aṣṭābhiḥ*. Regarding these, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that when the substitution of *āt* is absent, the form is accented on the middle syllable (*madhyodātta*), whereas in the case of the *āt* substitution, it is accented on the final syllable (*antodātta*).

In this regard, by the rule *ṣaṭtricaturbhyo halādiḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.179), the acute accent (*udāttatva*) of the case-ending—as seen in forms such as *ṣaṇṇām* and *ṣaḍbhiḥ*—would have been obtained; however, that is superseded by the rule *jhalyupottamam* (Pāṇini 6.1.180). For the meaning of that [latter] rule is: "In a word ending in a case-ending beginning with a *jhal* consonant that follows *ṣaṣ*, *tri*, or *catur*, the penultimate syllable becomes acute."

To preclude that [undesired result], the rule "aṣṭano dīrghāt" (Pāṇini 6.1.172) is commenced. The meaning of the sūtra is: "An affix that is not a *sarvanāmasthāna* case-ending following the word *aṣṭan* when it ends in a long vowel (*dīrgha*) becomes acute. In this context, if the designation *ṣaṭ* were not applied to the form with the substitution of *ātva* (i.e., *aṣṭā-*), then the accentuation of *aṣṭan* would have no scope; consequently, in the alternative where *ātva* is absent, the accent of *aṣṭan* would be barred by the *ṣaṭ-svara* (the accent rule for words designated as *ṣaṭ*) according to Pāṇini 6.1.180, which states "in the presence of *jaś*, the penultimate syllable [is acute]. Therefore, what would be the purpose of including the mention of "long vowel" (*dīrgha*)? However, once the designation *ṣaṭ* is established even for the form with *ātva* substituted, the accent of *aṣṭan* becomes an exception (*apavāda*) to the *ṣaṭ-svara*.

Nor should it be argued that the vowel of *aṣṭan* has no scope when followed by the suffix *śas*, because in that case the matter is already covered by the rule "A single substitute for [a preceding] udātta [vowel and a following vowel] is udātta" (Pāṇini 6.1.102); for it was stated immediately prior that "the word *aṣṭan* is udātta on its final syllable. Therefore, just as in the case of the long vowel (*dīrgha*), even in the absence of that long vowel, the accentuation of the case-ending would occur; thus, the inclusion of the term "long" (*dīrgha*) is indeed purposeful, as it serves to exclude that [accident].

Therefore, it is established that by the inclusion of the term "long" (dīrgha), the designation *ṣaṭ* is indicated even in the alternative view where the substitution of *ā* occurs. Nor should it be argued that, in this way, the inclusion of "long" could not serve as an indicator for the optional substitution of *ā*, because it is possible for it to indicate both. For there is no rule that one [indicator] indicates only one thing; rather, whatever is necessary to avoid an inconsistency is what is indicated, whether that be one thing or many. Whether that [indicated object] is singular or plural is another matter. And in the present case, since the purposelessness of including the term "long" cannot be avoided without [indicating] both, such is the direction of the argument.

If, however, in the present sūtra the vowel *ā* were also included by *praśleṣa* [as part of the compound], such that *ṣṇāntā* meant "that which has *ṣ*, *n*, and *ā* at its end," then in the case of the word *dvābhyām*, the case-ending would become udātta according to Pāṇini 6.1.179 (*ṣaṭtricaturbhyo halādiḥ*). However, in examples such as *ā dvābhyāṃ haribhyāmindra yāhi*, the word *dvābhyām* is recited with an udātta on its first syllable. Therefore, the inclusion of the vowel *ā* by *praśleṣa* in this context should not be maintained; rather, it is established that the previously stated method alone is to be accepted.

Likewise, in the seventh [chapter], having performed a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of a rule), the commentary (*bhāṣya*) has also established two ways by means of that [principle]. To illustrate: in the rule *ṣaḍbhyo luk* (Pāṇini 7.1.22), the word *ṣaḍbhyaḥ* is split off. From the preceding rule *aṣṭābhya auś* (Pāṇini 7.1.21), the word *aṣṭābhyaḥ* is carried over (*anuvartate*). Thus, the meaning of the rule is: "That which was prescribed for the six [numerals] shall also apply to *aṣṭan* when it ends in *ā*. Nor should it be argued that, in this way, the elision (*luk*) of the case-endings *jaś* and *śas* would also be extended [to *aṣṭan*], because that would result in the rule prescribing *auś* becoming redundant.

Alternatively, immediately after the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau* (Pāṇini 7.2.84), one should divide the rule *rāyaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.85) and explain that the condition *halī* is a remainder (*śeṣa*) applicable to both rules. By this means, in the form *aṣṭānām*, the substitution of *ā* occurs only after the insertion of *nuṭ*, and not prior to it.

Nor should it be argued that, in this way, the substitution of *ā* for the case endings *jaś* and *śas* would not occur; for although one could have simply stated "from eight" (*aṣṭabhyaḥ*) for the sake of brevity, the fact that the form with the substitution of *ā* (*aṣṭābhyaḥ*) was specified in the rule *aṣṭābhya auś* (Pāṇini 7.1.21) allows us to infer the presence of *ā* in the scope of *jaś* and *śas*. Indeed, the long vowel was pronounced there specifically so that the substitution of *auś* would apply only where *ā* is present.

This might be argued: if the term *hal* were a remainder (*śeṣa*) applicable to both [the preceding and following rules], then the optional substitution of *ā* for the final vowel in the word *priyāṣṭan*—which is desired before the case-endings *au*, *jas*, *am*, *auṭ*, *śas*, *ṭā*, *ṅe*, *ṅasi*, *ṅas*, *os*, *ām*, *ṅi*, *os*, and *sup*—would not be established. Nor can it be said that the substitution of *ā* is simply not desired there, because that would result in an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the previous positions; for in those cases, the substitution of *ā* is indeed obtained, since its prescription applies to all case-endings (*vibhakti*).

Nor should it be argued that, just as the elision (*luk*) and the augment *nuṭ* prescribed by the two rules "ṣaḍbhyo luk" (Pāṇini 7.1.22) and "ṣaṭcaturbhyaśca" (Pāṇini 7.1.55) do not apply when [the word] is used in a secondary sense (*gauṇatā*), so too this [principle of *atideśa*] would not apply; for there is a disparity between the two cases. For in the rules prescribing *luk* and *nuṭ*, because of the use of the plural forms "ṣaḍbhyaḥ" and "ṣaṭcaturbhyaḥ," those two operations proceed only when the meaning of the number six (*ṣaḍartha*) is primary.

However, in the rule prescribing the substitution of *ā* (Pāṇini 7.2.84), because of the singular-number indication in the word *aṣṭanaḥ*, the substitution of *ā* indeed applies even in the case of the secondary (*gauṇa*) sense—as in *priyāṣṭābhyām*—since it will be stated later [in the Paribhāṣenduśekhara] that "under the governing headings of *pada* and *aṅga*, [the operation applies] to that [word] and to what follows it."

Nor should it be argued that, because the rule *aṣṭābhya auś* (Pāṇini 7.1.21) contains a reference to the form with the substitution of *āt* (*aṣṭā-*), this inferred *āt*-substitution will apply even in cases of secondary (guṇa) usage and when the word stands alone—as it does in *aṣṭau* and *paramāṣṭau*—and thus there is no inconsistency in that respect. For the substitution of *auś* does not occur in cases of secondary usage, just as the elision (*luk*) and the augment *nuṭ* do not; this is because of the use of the plural form *aṣṭābhyaḥ*. Otherwise, even if it were an imitation of the form with the *āt*-substitution, he would have indicated it using the singular alone—either as *aṣṭā auś* or as *aṣṭa auś*.

This is clear right here in this very sūtra according to the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa. And likewise, in the rule for the substitution of *au*, even the substitution of *ā*—which is inferred by the strength of the mention of the form with *ātva* applied (*kṛtātvanirdeśa*)—would apply only when [the word] is primary (*prādhānya*), and not when it is secondary (*gauṇatā*); thus, there is an equal lack of justification regarding that portion as well. Therefore: If "after a consonant" (*halīti*) were a remainder for both [cases], then the substitution of *ā* would not occur in *priyāṣṭan*. The same applies to the forms ending in *ṭā*, *ṅe*, *ṅasi*, *ṅas*, *ām*, *su*, as well as those ending in *au*, *jas*, *am*, *auṭ*, and *śas*.
If the substitution of ātva were to occur even in these aforementioned positions,
then since there would be such a great difference in the result, how could there be a choice between alternative positions?

To this it is replied: the substitution of *ā* for the vowel of the word *aṣṭan* before vowels beginning with *a* (aj-ādi) is indeed unintended, because the *Bhāṣya* itself has established as its final conclusion (*siddhāntita*) that the rule *hal-i* applies as a remainder (*śeṣa*) to both [the *aṣṭan* and the *sarvanāmasthāna* endings]. This being so, one might raise the objection that the forms of the nominative and accusative dual and plural would be *priyāṣṭānau* and *priyāṣṭānaḥ* respectively, and not *priyāṣṭau* and *priyāṣṭā*; however, this is refuted by the statement: "According to the grammatical rules (*yathā-lakṣaṇam*), [forms] not actually used [in the tradition] are not employed."

For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa, taking up the phrase *yathālak�ṣaṇam*, explained that the meaning is: "In this case, the substitution of *ā* does not indeed occur. This being the case, the earlier positions must be understood as either being overcome by dissatisfaction, or as being applicable on the basis of the intention that—by virtue of the *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (regulated option)—the substitution of *ā* does not occur in the case of *ajādi* [words] when they are used in a secondary (*gauṇa*) sense, in accordance with the authority of the cited Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa.

Therefore, O King, in all grammatical forms (*vacana*), the form *priya-aṣṭan* shares the same [stem] form; however, in the dual and plural cases, there is another form shared with the word *hāhā*. As for the application of the suffixes *auś* and *naṭ*, the authoritative path is that they simply do not occur at all.
