For this very reason, Haradatta explicitly stated in his commentary on the sūtra *sarvādīni sarvanāmāni* (Pāṇini 1.1.27) that the suffix *auś* does not occur when [the term] is used in a secondary sense (*gauṇatva*).

For this very reason, regarding the rule *aṣṭābhya auś* (Pāṇini 7.1.21), the *Kāśikā* is consistent in stating that "the inclusion of [words] ending in that [stem] is intended here," and after citing *paramāṣṭau*, it explains: "In *priyāṣṭān*, because the substitution of *āt* does not occur, *auś* does not apply. For this same reason, in the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau* (Pāṇini 7.2.84), the application of the rule to words ending in that [stem] is also intended.

The passage from the *Kāśikā*—“so that forms such as *priyāṣṭau* [‘one who has eight beloveds’] may also occur”—is likewise consistent, because the substitution of *ā* [for *aṣṭan*] before vowel-initial suffixes is unimpeded. However, Haradatta, having cited the *Vṛtti* commentary on the rule *aṣṭābhya auś* (Pāṇini 7.1.21)—which reads *priyāṣṭānaḥ* [‘beloved eights’]—and having promised that he will explain how the substitution of *ā* does not occur when [the word] is used in a secondary sense (*gauṇatā*) within that very same rule, proceeds to the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau* (Pāṇini 7.4.84).

Because the singular number is specified, the word-form itself is taken, not the meaning; therefore, the substitution of *aṣṭan* occurs even when it is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*), since that too is subject to optionality. Thus, forms such as *priyāṣṭā*, *priyāṣṭānau*, and *priyāṣṭānaḥ* also occur.

Even in that regard, he has stated—in the portion of the text ending with "in the alternative where *ā* is substituted (*ātvapakṣe*), they desire the elision of the *ā* in the domain of the technical term *bha*, as in 'priyāṣṭaḥ paśya'; and even in the alternative where *ā* is not substituted (*ātvābhāvapakṣe*), there is the substitution of *ṣṭu* due to the elision of the vowel (*allopa*), resulting in 'priyāṣṭa'"—something contrary to the meaning previously promised and in contradiction to the *Bhāṣya*, the *Vṛtti*, and other authorities. His intention regarding this must be asked of him alone.

The statement that "there is also the substitution of *ṣ* for *ṣṭu*" is indeed to be considered problematic. This is because there is a prohibition based on the rule "not as a substitute for what precedes" (*na sthānivat*, Bhāṣya), since that rule has an exception in the rule "the fault [of the *sthānivadbhāva* rule applies] in the case of the elision of the first member of a *saṃyoga* and in the cases of *latva* and *ṇatva*" (*tasya doṣaḥ saṃyogādilopalatvaṇatveṣu*, Bhāṣya).

Now, one might object: "In that context, the *ṇatva* prescribed by the specific rule 'after *ra* and *ṣ*, *na* becomes *ṇa*' (*raṣābhyāṃ no ṇaḥ*, Pāṇini 8.4.1) is what is intended, and not the rule prescribing *ṣṭutva* (*aṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye'pi*, Pāṇini 8.4.2); for the entire rule [prescribing *ṣṭutva*] and the prohibitory rule [concerning *ṇatva*] have been rejected in the Bhāṣya. This is because the authority of the Munis increases in successive order."

Furthermore, there is no discrepancy in the letter *ṇ* being produced by the term *mūrddhanya* or the term *ṣṭu*, according to the method of the author of the Sūtras; yet, even if some logic were somehow possible here, it must be abandoned in favor of the Bhāṣya. Thus, while refuting the Vārttika which states that the mention of *kharpūrva* ("preceded by *khar*") must be made in the rule *śarpūrvāḥ khayaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.61), the Blessed One says: "The substitution of the *jaś* and *car* sounds for the reduplicated syllable is already established; therefore, the mention of *et* and *tu* need not be made."

And thus, Kaiyaṭa has described the intention [of the rule] as follows: since the substitution of *c* for the *t* in *tuk*—which had been produced by the substitution of *c* for *t* under the rule *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*—is also established as *siddha* by the rule *coḥ kuḥ*, the form *ucicchiṣati* is established. Therefore, that single form *priyāṣṭnaḥ* and others alone would be appropriate. It should not be argued that, in this case, one should read only the letter *n* even in forms such as *pūṣṇaḥ*, because in those cases the substitution of *ṇ* occurs by the rule *aṭkupvāṅnumvyavāye’pi* (Pāṇini 8.4.2). This is the direction [of the argument]. And so [ends the discussion on] Pāṇini 1.1.25.

A numeral ending in *ḍati* shall be designated as *ṣaṭ* (six). Examples: *kati santi* ("how many are there?"), *katy adrākṣīḥ* ("how many did you see?"). Because it is a *ṣaṭ*, there is elision (*luk*) of the case-endings *jas* and *śas*. Why specify "numeral" (*saṃkhyā*)? Consider *patayaḥ* ("lords"), derived from the root *pat-* with the suffix *ḍati*; this should not be called a *ṣaṭ*. It need not be stated that this [suffix] would also receive the designation *saṃkhyā*, because in that context, by association with *vatu*, only a *taddhita* suffix is intended. This rule has been rejected in the *Bhāṣya*. The sequence is as follows: after stating *vahugaṇavatusaṃkhyā*, the phrase *ḍati saṃkhyā* is carried over (*anuvartate*). Then, both *ṣṇāntā ṣaṭ saṃkhyā* and *ḍati* are carried over. Thus, the full formulation becomes: "A numeral ending in *ṣ*, *n*, or *ḍati* is designated as *ṣaṭ*."

Because the designation [of *ḍati*] is understood according to its etymological meaning (*anvartha-saṃjñā*) even in the previous rule, only the *ḍati* suffix prescribed for numbers and questions is included, and not the *ḍati* derived from the *Uṇādi* list. **Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.23:** *ktaktavatū niṣṭhā*. These two—*kta* and *ktavat*—bear the technical designation *niṣṭhā*. Examples: *kṛtaḥ*, *kṛtavān*. Now, one might object: "The designation is applied by this rule to the suffixes that have already been prescribed, and the prescription of those suffixes occurs by means of the designation; thus there is a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*). For it will be stated in the third book: 'The *niṣṭhā* [suffixes are used] in the sense of the past tense. This being so, there is mutual dependence. This is not so, because the designation is understood as a future designation, like the expression "the cloth of the thread" (*sūtra-śāṭaka*). The meaning is: "Those two [suffixes] which occur in the past tense and for which the designation *niṣṭhā* will be prescribed shall be understood as such. Thus, there is no fault.

It might be argued as follows: "The *anubandhas* (indicatory letters) are employed for the sake of grammatical operations (*kārya*), not for the sake of being heard, since their elision (*lopa*) is prescribed. Consequently, when there is similarity (*sārūpya*) between two forms that have been finalized after the *anubandhas* have been elided, it is impossible to determine where the operation dependent on the *anubandha* should apply and where it should not."

Nor should it be argued that even a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), like a crow, will possess the capacity to differentiate; for by means of a crow, the sacrificial altar (*vedikā*) or its lotus (*puṇḍarīka*) is identified as something stable, and by virtue of that, even when the crow has flown away, the linguistic usage does not become confused. However, no such other object to be identified is perceived here, because the letters *ka* and *na* are merely like crows [to the suffixes], and once they have departed—leaving only "ta"—it is impossible to state what the mutually distinct object to be identified is.

On this point, they say: it is precisely the meanings—such as specific times (*kāla*) and agents (*kāraka*)—that occupy the positions of the altar (*vedikā*), the lotus (*puṇḍarīka*), and so forth in this context. Upon seeing them, when the recollection of the grammatical rules (*anubandha-smṛti*) occurs, the operation (*kārya*) prompted by each of those meanings is recognized as correct (*sādhutva*). Thus, when someone utters "the rice is harvested" (*lūnaḥ śāliḥ*), one who knows the technical definitions determines that this is the *kta* suffix [denoting the past] by virtue of the force of the object (*karman*) and the time (*kāla*).

When the expression "one should sacrifice a *loṭa*" (*loṭam ālabheta*) is employed, it is determined that the word *loca*—meaning "ram"—is being used with the suffix *-tan*, based on the *Uṇādi-sūtra*: "The suffix *-tan* occurs after the roots *has*, *mṛg*, *ṛ*, *ṇu*, *vām*, *dam*, *il*, *pū*, *dhū*, and *vi*. Furthermore, it is established in the *Pañcapādī-vṛtti* that "the word *loṭa* may denote both a horse and a ram. Similarly, in the usage "Devadatta broke the pot" (*prābhinna ghaṭaṃ devadattaḥ*), because the agency and singularity [of the agent] are understood, it is determined that this is an instance of the root ending in the *luṅ* (aorist) suffix, and not of the form ending in the *niṣṭhā* (past passive participle) suffix.

It might be argued as follows: "The suffix *kta* is derived from the roots *añci*, *ghṛ*, and *si* by Pāṇini’s rule *añcighṛsibhyaḥ ktaḥ* (Uṇādisūtra 3.376), resulting in the forms *aktam*, *ghṛtam*, and *sitam*. In those cases as well, the designation *niṣṭhā* would apply. Consequently, by the rule *niṣṭhā ca dvyajanāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.205), the accent would be [determined]. The meaning of that sūtra is that a word ending in a *niṣṭhā* suffix consisting of two syllables (*dvyacka*) is udātta on its first vowel when it is a proper name (*saṃjñā*), provided that the initial vowel is not *ā*. This is not an acceptable consequence, because in examples such as *ghṛtaṃ mimikṣe*, the word is actually recited with an udātta on the final syllable."

On this point, they say: Since the form [kaṃsa] is already established by the inclusion of *kam* in the rule *ataḥ kṛkami* (Pāṇini 8.3.46), the specific mention of *kaṃsa* indicates that the *uṇādi* suffixes do not, in certain instances, receive the grammatical operations based on etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*). Therefore, the designation of *niṣṭhā* does not apply here. Alternatively, it is established by the *phiṭ*-sūtra *ghṛtādīnāṃ ca* (phiṭ-sūtra 1.21).
Thus ends the fifth section of the first quarter of the first chapter in the venerable *Śabdakaustubha*.

"Words beginning with *sarva* are called pronouns" (Pāṇini 1.1.27). These [words] shall receive the designation of *sarvanāman* (pronoun). This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound of the type where the qualities (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*). A *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* is that [compound] in which there is a cognition (*saṃvijñāna*) of the qualities (*guṇa*)—that is, the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) consisting of the meanings of the constituent members (*vartipada*)—as being connected with the operation (*kārya*), because they pertain to the external referent (*anyapadārtha*). In this case, the analysis (*vigraha*) is: "those of which *sarva* is the first. By the employment of the word *tat* (in *tadguṇa-*), the predominance of the external referent is obtained. The same applies in cases such as "he whose cows are variegated" (*citrā gāvo yasya saḥ*).

Otherwise, in the expression *yasya gāvaś citrāḥ* ("whose cows are variegated"), the primary referent would be the meaning of the word *go* (cow), yet a *bahuvrīhi* compound is not intended in such a sense. As for the analysis of the compound as *citragavām ayam* ("this [person] of variegated cows") provided in the *Mīmāṃsā-vārttika* to ensure that the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) remains the same in both the derivative form (*vṛtti*) and the analytical sentence (*vākya*), that does not accord with the words of the Sage (Pāṇini), because the author of the *Vārttika* will later state that a *bahuvrīhi* occurs when the meaning is not that of the first case ending.

Furthermore, the author of the *Bhāṣya*, in the rule "the remainder is the *bahuvrīhi*" (*Pāṇini* 2.2.23), established the meaning expressed by the very words of the sūtra by relying on the "remainder" from among the three categories (*trika*). For he stated the compounding of the six categories in sequence—beginning with "the second case [ending] with *śrita*, *atīta*, etc. and "the third case [ending] with that which is made by it" (*tatkṛta*)—and in relation to that, the "remainder" consists of the first category. It is precisely this [first category] that receives the designation *bahuvrīhi*. Consequently, the status of being a *bahuvrīhi* is as remote as possible even for an expression such as "of variegated cows" (*citrāṇāṃ gavām*), just as it is for "he has gone when it rained" (*vṛṣṭe deve gataḥ*).

Furthermore, how could there be the application of the *bahuvrīhi* compound in the sense of possession (*matvartha*) in the phrase "of variegated cows" (*citrāṇāṃ gavām*), given the statement of Kātyāyana: "The *bahuvrīhi* occurs in the sense of possession"? If you argue: "But even in cases such as 'staff-bearer' (*daṇḍī*), since we accept the analytical derivation (*vigraha*) as 'this belongs to the staff,' this very [sense] is the sense of possession according to our system," then there would be an even greater contradiction with the words of the Sage. This is because the rule *tadasyāstyasmin* (Pāṇini 5.2.94) prescribes the suffix *matup* in the sense of a possessor (*sambandhin*) following a word ending in the nominative case that has the qualifier "it exists" (*asti*), and [the rule] *samarthānāṃ prathamādvā*... [is intended to apply].

Furthermore, by the rule *pāosūo 4-1-82*, it is established that only that which is first mentioned [in a grammatical operation] possesses the status of being the base (*prakṛti*). If you should object: "We shall somehow twist even these statements from the Sūtras, Vārttikas, and Bhāṣya and interpret them [to suit our view]," we reply: what would a person like you, who is unrestrained, not do? For you might apply rules such as *samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ* (Pāṇini 2-1-1)—which govern word-combinations—to cases like *vrīhibhir yajate* ("he sacrifices with rice"), even though these are not instances of word-composition (*padavidhi*), and you might describe *sāmarthya* (semantic competency) in a manner entirely contrary to what is accepted in the Bhāṣya and other works. However, [this is not permissible].

Consider the following response to the ultimate objection: "How can you, at your own will, disturb the authority of grammar which was established as a settled doctrine in the section on *vyākaraṇa*? Therefore, the analysis *yasya citrā gāvaḥ* (he whose cows are variegated) is the one established by the tradition of all learned authorities and is consistent with the words of the three sages; such is the direction of the argument.

Since the word *ādi* denotes a constituent part (*avayava*), a "collection" (*samudāya*) is a group whose parts have become manifest; and since that collection cannot be employed simultaneously in the object of grammatical operation (*lakṣya*) and is therefore purposeless (*ānarthakya*), the technical designation (*saṃjñā*)—which, according to the maxim "it applies to its constituents" (*tadaṅgeṣu*), operates upon the members of that collection—applies to the word *sarvaśabda* as well due to the absence of any distinction. Thus, it is logical that this is a case of "inclusion of the qualities" (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*). Furthermore, the rule "before a consonant, all [substitute ṣ for s]" (*hali sarveṣām*, Pāṇini 8.3.22) and others serve as indicative evidence (*liṅga*) for this point.

In the rule *jakṣityādayaḥ ṣaṭ* (Pāṇini 6.1.6), however, the word *jakṣiti* is separated into a distinct *yoga*; because of the force of prescribing the technical name (*saṃjñā*) for *jakṣ*, the term *ityādayaḥ* is understood as a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the qualities [of the members] are not included in the reference (*atadguṇasaṃvijñāna*).

By this, the following is refuted: the claim that—just as it will be stated in the fourth [chapter] that there is a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) for both *tatpuruṣa* and *bahuvrīhi* in order to include the word *śakala* in both rules "from those ending in *kata*" (*katantebhyaḥ*) and "from those beginning with *kaṇva*" (*kaṇvādibhyaḥ*)—so too here, either by the rule "the neuter [remains] when combined with a non-neuter" (*napuṃsakamanapuṃsakena*, Pāṇini 1.2.69), or by the principle "among words differing in accent, that for which the subsequent accentual rule applies is retained," when there is a desire to express both *tatpuruṣa* and *bahuvrīhi* together, the *bahuvrīhi* alone remains. For [the desired meaning] is established by the *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna-bahuvrīhi* itself.

Since the inclusion of the word *sarva* itself is already established, its reliance on the grammatical device of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one from a group of identical words) is refuted by the principle of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

The creation of this great technical designation (*mahāsaṃjñā*) is for the purpose of making it a descriptive name (*anvarthasaṃjñā*), namely "the names of all. By the force of that [designation], it is inferred that only those names possessing the capacity to denote all objects are the designated entities (*saṃjñin*). Consequently, since there would be a necessity to recite such [all-encompassing] items in the list, and because there is no evidence for the recitation of those belonging to other categories, neither specific designations nor subordinate elements (*upasarjana*) possess the status of being among the "all-beginning" (*sarvādi*) items.

Therefore, for them, both the operation pertaining to a *gaṇa* (group) and the operation conditioned by a technical name (*saṃjñā*) do not apply. An example of an operation pertaining to a *gaṇa* is as follows: *tyadādīnāmaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.102). Let there be someone named *tat*; one who has surpassed him is *atitat*. For example: *aḍḍutarādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.25). One who has surpassed another is *atyanyam*, or *atikatarām*. An example of an operation conditioned by a technical name is as follows: *sarvanāmnaḥ smai* (Pāṇini 7.1.14). [One says] *atisarvāya*.

With this in mind, the author of the Vārttika stated: "The prohibition regarding technical terms (*saṃjñā*) and subordinate members (*upasarjana*) is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) based on the recitation [of the list]; for technical terms are assigned only to those items actually recited therein. Therefore, it is established that here the term to be designated (*saṃjñin*) must be one that is not subordinate with respect to another, being employed through a well-known ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*)."

It should be noted that an operation which depends solely on the essential form (*svarūpa*) of a word, and does not depend upon its inclusion in a *gaṇa* list or its technical designation (*saṃjñā*), occurs even when that word is in the state of being a subordinate member (*upasarjana*). For example, in rules such as "after *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, *ṅas* becomes *aś*" (Pāṇini 7.2.27), this remains the case even in the subordinate state. However, this does not imply that forms like *tvam* and *aham* would arise even in cases such as "when *yuṣmad* is the *upapada*" (Pāṇini 1.4.105). This is because those rules operate only when the words refer to their meanings as established in common usage (*lokaprasiddha*), according to the maxim: "Those [words] whose word-meanings are already manifested [do not require further derivation]."

In this context, it should be understood that the inclusion of the final member [of the compound] is intended, based on the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) of the rule *dvandve ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.31). This will be explained in that very place, as well as by the statement of the *vārttika*: "The purpose [is to ensure the application] of the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) for pronouns (*sarvanāman*) and indeclinables (*avyaya*). Consequently, in forms such as *paramasarvataḥ*, *paramasarvatra*, and *paramasarvakaṃ*, the suffixes *tasil*, *tral*, and *kak* are successfully derived from the entire compound.

Nor should it be argued that because the word *prātipadikāt* ("from a nominal stem") is understood in the rules for the suffixes *tasil* and so on, and because this is qualified by the term "all" (*sarvanāman*), the rule of *tadantavidhi* ("application to that which ends with [the specified element]") will apply; for there is a prohibition stating: "In the formulation of rules regarding compounds and suffixes, there is no *tadantavidhi*" (Kātyāyana’s Vārttika). Nor does this lead to the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the suffix in forms such as *atisarvāya*, since the exclusion of items used as subordinate members (*upasarjana*) has already been stated. For this very reason, suffixes such as *smāi* and others do indeed occur in forms like *paramasarvasmai*.

It might be argued that in cases such as *asaḥ*, *atasmin*, and *aneṣaḥ*, the substitutions of *atva*, *satva*, and *sminnādi* would not occur because of the status of being an *upasarjana* (subordinate element), just as in the case of *atisarva*. Consequently, they explain *abrāhmaṇa* and similar compounds by means of paraphrases such as "one different from a Brāhmaṇa," thereby asserting the predominance (*prādhānya*) of the meaning of the first member. This is true; however, according to the grammatical school (*vaiyākaraṇa*), the *nañ*-compound possesses precisely the predominance of the meaning of the final member (*uttarapada*). This is because the author of the *Bhāṣya* established that very conclusion in the *Nañ-sūtra*.

For instance, the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is "superimposition" (*āropitatva*). Thus, just as from words such as *māyāmanuṣya* (an illusory man), *māyāmṛga* (an illusory deer), *vyājaniśākara* (a moon in disguise), or *kapaṭabrāhmaṇa* (a fraudulent Brahmin), the verbal comprehension culminates in the form "this Brahmin is superimposed," that is, "illusory"; the elaboration of the meaning as "distinct from a Brahmin" and so forth is an implied (ārthika) sense, not a literal (śābda) one. For this very reason, the phrase "not a compound with a negative" (*anañsamāsa*) in the rule *etattadoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.132) is meaningful. And for this same reason, the general principle that a *tatpuruṣa* compound is dominated by the meaning of its final member is also maintained. This is the direction of the argument.

Now, if the rule of "extension to that which ends in this" (tadantavidhi) is intended here, then there is a contradiction with the Bhāṣya; for therein, having begun the rejection of the Vārttika "prohibition regarding technical terms and subordinate elements" (saṃjñopasarjanapratiṣedha), the over-extension was removed by relying on a qualification of the case-ending (vibhaktiviśeṣaṇa) through its meaning.

If it is argued that, according to the principle stated in rules such as *ṅeḥ smai* (Pāṇini 7.1.14)—which teaches that the suffixes *smai* and others replace *ṅe* when denoting number, case-role (*kāraka*), and so forth, which are inherent in the meaning of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*)—then by applying the rule of "specification of the final element" (*tadantavidhi*), in forms like *atisarvāya*, the entire compound would be considered a pronoun; and thus, even if one relies on the substitution of the case-ending through its meaning, the undesirable application of *smāy* and other suffixes would remain exactly as it was. True. For this very reason, because of dissatisfaction with that [first] view, the Bhāṣya introduces an alternative position: "Or rather, this is a very large technical designation (*saṃjñā*) being made. Understand it in this way.

If it is objected: "If this is an etymological designation (*anvarthasaṃjñā*), then by the rule *pūrvapadātsaṃjñāyāmagaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.3), the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] should occur," we reply: True; for this very reason, there is an absence of *ṇ*-substitution due to a specific irregularity (*nipātana*). However, the form with *ṇ*-substitution is indeed incorrect, because the rule for *ṇ*-substitution is set aside by the irregularity. For this same reason, forms such as *śāśvatkaḥ* are likewise incorrect.

Because of the rule "yeṣāṃ ca virodhaḥ śāsvatikaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.4.9), which is a nipātana (an irregular formation), the application of the rule "isusuktāntāt kaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.51) is superseded. If it is argued that, in this case, the word *santata* would be superseded by the nipātana "aparasparāḥ kriyāsātatye" (Pāṇini 6.1.144), we say no. This is because, in that rule, the phrase "in the sense of continuity" (*sātatye*) serves as an indirect admission (*ekadeśānumati*) of the very verse recited by the ancient teachers: "one should drop [the suffix] when 'ava', 'kṣama', or a kṛtya suffix follows. Thus, it is that verse itself that is being indicated.

But even so, by the rule *purāṇaprokteṣu brāhmaṇakalpeṣu* (Pāṇini 4.3.105), the word *purāṇa* would result in the sublation (*bādha*) of the word *purātana*. True; however, it should be understood that the word *purātana* is included among the *pṛṣodarādi* group [of irregular forms]. The reality is that the mention of *purāṇa* merely indicates the non-universality (*anityatā*) of the augment-rule and the elision of the *ṭi*-portion. That very point—that nipātanas (irregular forms) are indeed sublaters—is established in the Bhāṣya.

Alternatively, this is not a rule for technical designation (*saṃjñā-sūtra*), but rather has as its sole result the purification of the list (*gaṇa-śuddhi-mātra-phalaka*); for the explanation is that only those which are *sarvanāman* (pronominal nouns) are indeed "headed by *sarva*" (*sarvādi*), and not others as well.

For example, in the rule *tiṅo gotrādīni kutsanābhīkṣṇyayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.27), the phrase *kutsanābhīkṣṇyayoḥ* is separated as a distinct *yoga*, and by carrying over (*anuvṛtti*) the term *gotrādīni*, it is explained—specifically for the purpose of purifying the list—that only those words which function in these two senses [of contempt and frequency] are included among the *gotra*-class and so forth. Consequently, in the two rules *canacidiva-gotrādi-taddhita-amreḍiteṣv-agateḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.57) and *kutsane ca supy-agotrādau* (Pāṇini 8.1.69) as well, only those [words] with specific meanings [are intended].

The inclusion of *gotra* and so forth applies here as well. If it is objected: "Granted that an internal-group operation such as *tyadādīnāmaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.102) may be established by the aforementioned method, but an operation such as *sarvanāmnaḥ smai* (Pāṇini 7.1.14) would be over-extended (*ativyāpta*) to words like *kṛtsna* and *sakala*, which are not included in the list," we reply: No, because by the force of the recitation in the *gaṇa*-list, only those words actually listed therein are understood. This is the only distinction.

In the previously mentioned view, the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is what is to be enjoined, while the purity of the *gaṇa* follows by implication; however, in this [present] view, the purity of the *gaṇa* is expressed directly by the words (*śābdī*), whereas the exclusion of *kṛtsna* and so forth follows by implication. Alternatively, both—the purity of the recitation (*pāṭha-śuddhi*) and the technical name—are effected by this [rule], by resorting to one of the methods of *tantra*, *āvṛtti*, or *ekaśeṣa*. In that regard, the *ekaśeṣa* is based on explicit scriptural statement (*vācanika*), even in the absence of a desire to express them together (*saha-vivakṣā*).

For under the view that [the word] denotes the form (*ākṛti*), the *sarūpa* rule [Pāṇini 1.2.64] is rejected; yet rules such as "guṇa and vṛddhi replace iK" (Pāṇini 1.1.3), which serve the purpose of the technical system of grammar, prescribe *ekaśeṣa* even in the absence of a desire to express them together. Thus, five positions have been established. Furthermore, the exclusion of those [words] that function as technical names (*saṃjñā*) is also accomplished by the principle of the primary and the secondary (*gauṇamukhya-nyāya*). Nor should it be said that this [principle] applies only to operations concerning words (*pada-kārya*), for it has been demonstrated in the introduction to the *autsūtra* that it operates everywhere when a specific form is taken up.

According to the *Vārttika*, however, another solution should be understood: within the governing rule (*adhikāra*) for "one designation" (*ekasaṃjñā*), immediately after the designation of "pronominal" (*sarvanāma*), there is the rule that "a designation applies to what resides in a single substance. Thus, by means of this "designation-designation" (*saṃjñā-saṃjñā*), the pronominal designation is sublated. Alternatively, in the *gaṇasūtra* "pūrva-parāvara," one should divide the rule by adding the phrase "provided it is not a technical term" (*asaṃjñāyām*). Then, the remainder of the two preceding rules—namely, that the "sarvādi" group and the "svādi" group (to be mentioned later) are designated as pronominals when they are not technical terms—should be explained.

Therefore, the primary result of resorting to a term that is etymologically meaningful (*anvarthasaṃjñā*) is precisely the exclusion of *upasarjana* [elements]. Now, it may be objected: in the *Bhāṣya*, the rule *anupasarjanāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.14) was explained by another method, and by the force of that very explanation, the operation pertaining to the internal group (*antargaṇakārya*) was prevented. For instance: the word *anupasarjana* is a term with its sixth case ending elided; the division is *aḥ* and *āditi*; and *āt* is the collective compound (*samāhāra*) of *a* and *ac*.

The meaning of the *paribhāṣā* "wherever the substitutes *a* and *at* are prescribed after the letter *a*, there the term 'not being a subordinate element' (*anupasarjana*) is understood" is as follows: by this rule, the substitution of *at* for the pronouns beginning with *tyad* (as in *tyadādyatvam*), and the substitution of *aḍḍ* (as in *aḍḍatarādibhyaḥ*), do not occur when [the word] is in a secondary sense (*gauṇatā*). What is the purpose of qualifying [the substitute] as "following the letter *a*" (*akārāt paratvena*)? [It is to exclude cases such as: *atiyuṣmat* from *yuṣmānatikrāntebhyaḥ* (by *pañcamyā at*; Pāṇini 7.1.32), and *atiyuṣmat* from *yuṣmānatikrāntāt* (by *ekavacanasya ca*; Pāṇini 7.1.32).

For this [suffix] is not prescribed after the letter *a*. Thus, if it is argued that since the exclusion of the *upasarjana* is established otherwise, what is the purpose of the technical term (*mahāsaṃjñā*)? No; for [the form] *atisarvāya* and the like, which involve phonemes (*vārṇa*), must be accomplished by that [term] alone. Indeed, this cannot be established by the rule *anupasarjanāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.14). It is precisely because of dissatisfaction with this [first view] that the Bhāṣya resorts to an alternative position. This is the direction [of the argument]. And thus, it should be noted that the rule *anupasarjanāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.14) is not even useful as a *paribhāṣā*, and therefore its rejection follows by implication.

It might be argued as follows: the sūtra must be commenced for the sake of establishing the form *kaumbhakāreya*. For in that case, the suffix *ḍhak* must be produced from the word *kumbhakārī* itself; otherwise, there would be no *vṛddhi* substitution for the vowel *u* in *kumbha*. Furthermore, the status of the entire complex as ending in a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) must be accepted. And that [status] is only possible if, in the sūtra *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15), by means of the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*), the term *aṇ* is taken to mean "that which ends in *aṇ*" (*aṇanta*); and by that [term], through the qualification of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the base (*prakṛti*) would be that which ends in a suffix ending in *aṇ*.

And this is clear: by the prohibition "there is a negation in the rules for compound and suffix formation" (*Kāśikāvṛtti*), and by the rule "a *prātipadika* that possesses a [specific] marker does not undergo extension to what ends with it" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 1.1.72), the negation of the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) implies that the extension to what ends with it applies to the principal member; thus, *kaumbhakāreyaḥ* is established.

Nor should it be argued that, by the *paribhāṣā* "when a *kṛt*-affix is mentioned, [it includes] even that which is preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka*" (*Pābhāṣā* 28), the feminine suffix should be applied to the word *kumbhakāra* itself; for in the rule "after [a stem ending in] *aṇ*" (*aṇi*), the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) *aṇ* is also included, as in the example *aupagavī*. However, the *paribhāṣā* "when a *kṛt*-affix is mentioned" applies only when there is a mention of a *kṛt*-affix alone, and not when there is a mention of both *kṛt* and *taddhita* affixes. It is precisely for this purpose that the author of the *Mahābhāṣya* will establish this *sūtra* in the fourth book (*caturtha*).
How is it that it is stated here: "this rule *anupasarjanāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.14) is rejected"?

To this it is replied: In the fourth [chapter], one will merely describe the intention of the author of the Sūtras; however, with the thought that if a definitive conclusion (*niṣkarṣa*) were drawn, the rule would simply result in being purposeless (*vaiyarthya*), the Blessed One has stated here that it is "rejected."

For instance, even when the suffix *ṅīp* is produced after the word *kāra*, the form *kaumbhakāreyaḥ* is indeed established; this is because, by the paribhāṣā "there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the element ending in *ṣyaṅ*, provided that the feminine suffix is not a secondary member (*anupasarjana*)" (Paribhāṣenduśekhara 26), the restriction regarding the initiality of the stem (*tadādiniyama*) is prohibited in the case of a feminine suffix that is not a secondary member, thereby allowing the suffix *ḍhak* to be produced from the word *kumbhakārī*. For this very reason, in the example *paramakārīṣagandhīputraḥ*, the vocalization prescribed for that which ends in *ṣyaṅ* occurs for the word *paramakārīṣagandhyā* as well.

Nor does such an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) occur in cases such as *atikārīṣagandhyaputraḥ*, because the rule "provided it is not a secondary member" (*anupasarjana*) has been stated, and thus the restriction that the compound begins with that [word] applies to secondary members. Nor should it be argued that, in this case, the elision of the final vowel and consonant (*hal-ṅy-ādi-lopa*) would not occur in forms such as *adhīpippalī*; for by the force of the inclusion of the term "long" (*dīrgha*) in the sūtra *hal-ṅy-āp-...*, it is indicated that even in the case of a secondary member, the restriction that the compound begins with that [word] does not apply there.

In reality, however, this is not an indicator (jñāpaka) [of the fact that the rule applies to the whole compound], because in cases such as *niṣkauśāmbi*, although the whole (*samudāya*) ends in a feminine suffix (*ṅī* or *āp*), the individual member (*avayava*) also ends in a feminine suffix; consequently, the elision of the case-ending *su* following it would already be established by the general rule. Furthermore, in cases such as *ardhapippalī*, the same result is achieved simply by the fact that the member ends in a feminine suffix (*ṅī*). Nor can it be argued that the term "prescribed" (*vihita*) must be taken as a qualifier [of the whole], for that would lead to an over-narrow application (*avyāpti*) in forms such as *yā* and *sā*.

Nor can the derivation be accomplished there by virtue of being prescribed after a base ending in a consonant (*hal*), because that would result in the non-elision [of the *su*] in forms such as *kartā* and *hartā*, and would result in the elision [of the *su*] in forms such as *yaḥ* and *saḥ*. Alternatively, the base is implied by the suffixes *su*, *ti*, and *si*; for this is how it is described in the *Vivaraṇa* for the sake of maintaining Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the rule *halantyam*. And thus, the indicator (*jñāpaka*) is well-established, since a single part [of the suffix] does not constitute the base.

For this very reason, at the conclusion of the fifth [chapter], Kaiyaṭa, in his commentary on the sūtra *go-striyor upasarjanasya* (Pāṇini 1.2.48), has stated only the view that [the rule] serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Now, one might object: even so, in cases such as *mālā hṛṣṭā*, the suffix *su* (nom. sg. would apply due to the fact that the entire compound ends in an ā-vowel; consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence of [the word] being treated as a single pada and having a single accent.

If it is argued that even in the view that [the suffix] is a prescription (*vidhi*) by virtue of forming a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*), one must necessarily resort to the rule "the singular number is the default" (*ekavacanam utsargaḥ*) in order to establish forms such as *pacatikalpam*, we say: no. This is because the mention of the suffixes *ṅī* and *ap* serves another purpose; for it will be stated later that when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned in some way, it includes the form qualified by gender, and that the case-ending (*sup*) arises because the form ends in *ṅī* or *āp*. Furthermore, in the present case, the entire complex is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadikatvāt*). For it will be established that the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) regarding meaningful complexes is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*).

Nor should it be argued that even so, the suffix *ḍhak* might occasionally arise from the word *kāra*; for, by the maxim of reduplication of a single vowel (*ekāj-dvirvacana-nyāya*), the suffix arises only from the entire compound, and it is impossible to say that the word *kumbha*, having already entered into a unified relation with another meaning (*ekārthībhūta*), is subsequently extracted and joined with the sense of "offspring. Furthermore, this same reasoning applies even to one who proposes the rule (*sūtra*). Just as in the case of *aupagavī* and similar forms, there is the possibility of the suffix *ṅīp* arising even from the isolated word *kāra*, and thus the occasional fault in the form *kaumbhakāreyī* would be equal in your position as well.

This might be the case: if this sūtra were not composed, the suffix *ṅīp* would not occur in the word *kumbhakārī*. This is because the element ending in *aṇ* (i.e., *kāraka*), which has entered into a single unified meaning (*ekārthībhūta*) with *kumbha*, cannot be connected with femininity; and that which is connected with femininity is the specific compound, not the element ending in *aṇ*. Therefore, since the rule "provided it is not preceded by *mahat*" implies the application of the principle of "extension to what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*), this principle must be accepted for subsequent rules as well.

Just as that [suffix] occurs even when [the word] is a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) in the previous cases—as in *priyapañcā draupadī* by the rule *na ṣaṭsvastrādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.10), and *atidhīvarī* by the rule *vano ra ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.7)—so too would it occur in the case of [feminine suffixes] beginning with *ṭi*. Consequently, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in forms such as *bahukurucarā*. Therefore, this prohibitive rule is meaningful.

[Objection: "Is it not the case that in the previous rule (*strī*), the term ending in that [suffix] (*tadanta*) is qualified by the word *strī* (feminine), whereas in rules such as *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15), it is only the *ṭit* element and so forth that is qualified? Therefore, in forms like *bahukurucarā*, since the *ṭit* element and so forth do not denote a feminine, the suffix *ṅīp* does not apply; however, in forms like *kumbhakārī*, since the suffix *aṇ* occurs in the feminine, *ṅīp* will indeed apply even after a stem ending in that [suffix]. [Reply: No, because the distinction between these cases is difficult to discern, and it is therefore appropriate to compose the sūtra precisely for the sake of knowing that distinction.
[Counter-reply: This is not so, because even if this sūtra were composed, one would still have to rely solely on a formal commentary (*vyākhyāna*) to determine its application.

Otherwise, in the case of *pañcājī*, even though the word *ajā* itself is not feminine, the suffix *ṭāp* would undesirably apply because that which ends in it (*pañcājī*) functions as feminine. Therefore, since there is freedom in choosing the relationship between qualifier and qualified, in rules such as *ajādyataṣṭāp* (Pāṇini 4.1.4) and *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15), the term *strī* (feminine) mentioned therein qualifies the [base] itself; however, in rules such as *vano ra ca* (Pāṇini 4.1.7), it qualifies that which ends in it. Consequently, since all desired results would be unestablished, the present sūtra would be entirely redundant.

It might be argued that this sūtra must indeed be commenced for the purpose of making known the rule of "extension to the end" (*tadanta-vidhi*). Nor should it be said that this is already established by the rule *amahatpūrvā* (Kāśikā 4.1.11), for that [rule] cannot serve as a *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence). For it will be stated later that, in order to establish forms such as *pañcājī*, femininity (*strītva*) is qualified by terms beginning with *aja*.

And thus, in the case of *mahāśūdrī*, even though the whole (*samudāya*) functions as feminine, the constituent part (*avayava*) does not; therefore, even if the rule for "ending in that" (*tadantavidhi*) were applicable, the suffix *ṭāp* would not be obtained. How then could the prohibition result from first establishing the *tadantavidhi*? Do not say so; for although the other [suffixes] beginning with *aj* (i.e., *ṭāp*, etc. are qualified by femininity, the word *śūdra* itself is not so qualified. And in this way, the status of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) is clearly established. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) in the case of *pañcaśūdrī*, because *śūdra* is qualified here by the term *jāti* (genus).

It might be argued that the rule is meaningful according to the method stated by Kātyāyana: "Or rather, the mention in the preceding sūtra is for the sake of [the word] *āpiśalam adhīte*. For instance, *upasarjana* is that which is subordinate; this is because such usage occurs both in the sūtras of the ancient teachers and in common worldly parlance. Consequently, the suffix *iñ* [is applied] to *āpiśali*, and by the rule *iñaś ca* (Pāṇini 4.2.112), the suffix *aṇ* is added. Then, for the female student, the suffix *aṇ* is added by the rule *tad adhīte* (Pāṇini 4.2.59). This [suffix] is elided by the rule *proktāl luk* (Pāṇini 4.2.64), resulting in *āpiśalā brāhmaṇī*.

In this case, because the *aṇ* prescribed by the rule [Pāṇini 4.2.61] is not the predominant element (*apradhāna*), the suffix *ṅīp* does not apply after that which ends in it. This is due to the qualification in the rule that *anupasarjana* means "that which is not predominant. Nor should it be argued that even so, since the *aṇ* produced after the word *adhyetrī* is itself *anupasarjana*, the *ṅīp* would necessarily apply based on it; for that *aṇ* has been elided. Nor should one suspect the application of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the rule that an operation dependent on a suffix applies as if the suffix were present), because that is prohibited when the operation depends on a mere phoneme (*varṇa*). For in the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15), the term *ataḥ* (from that which ends in *a*) is understood from the previous context, and by the *aṇ*, the vowel *a* is specifically qualified.

The [rule] "aṇ-yaḥ akāraḥ" (the *aṇ* suffix followed by an *a*) does not involve a reversed relationship between the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*). For if the phoneme (*varṇa*) were not primary, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of applying the rule for suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), as in the case of *tṛṇahaim* in the form *atṛṇeḍ*. If it is argued that the aforementioned fault does not arise because the word *striyām* (in the feminine) qualifies the *aṇ* suffix, we say no. [Otherwise], from the statement "the *mīmāṃsā* taught by Kāśakṛtsna is *kāśakṛtsnī*; she studies it," one would derive *kāśakṛtsnā brāhmaṇī* (a Brāhmaṇa woman who is a *kāśakṛtsnī*).

In this case, when the second *aṇ* is elided by the rule *proktāluk* (Pāṇini 4.2.64), the first *aṇ* also arises only in the feminine; consequently, the suffix *ṅīp* would apply after that [first *aṇ*] which denotes a Brāhmaṇī. Therefore, this sūtra must be commenced for the purpose that [the suffix] should apply from the primary [element], and not from the non-primary.

To this it is replied: when the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is to be applied to the word *adhyetrī*, it ought to be replaced by *ī*. Now, that *aṇ* which was not produced in the word *adhyetrī* has indeed been elided. As for the *aṇ* that is actually heard [in the base], the *ī* produced from it is also elided; thus, it does not occur again, because a grammatical rule (*lakṣaṇa*) has fulfilled its purpose through a single application. Therefore, the statement of the Venerable One—that the rule "anupasarjanāt" (Pāṇini 4.1.14) may be rejected—is entirely beyond reproach. This is the direction of the argument.

The thirty-five words beginning with *sarva* are as follows: *sarva*, *viśva*, *ubha*, *ubhaya*, *ḍatara*, *ḍatama*, *anya*, *anyatara*, *itara*, *tvat*, *tva*, *nema*, *sama*, *sima*; and *pūrva*, *para*, *avara*, *dakṣiṇa*, *uttara*, *apara*, *adhara* when used in their specific sense (*vyavasthā*) and not as proper names (*asaṃjñā*); *sva* when not referring to kinsmen or wealth; *antara* when meaning "outside" (*bahiryoga*) or "inner garment" (*upasaṃvyāna*); and *tyad*, *tad*, *etad*, *idam*, *adas*, *eka*, *dvi*, *yuṣmad*, *asmad*, *bhavat*, and *kim*.

In this context, the words *sarva* and *viśva* are synonyms for *kṛtsna*. Although the word *sarva* would normally take an udātta accent on its first syllable by the rule *svāṅgaśiṭām* (Pāṇini 6.2.177), its being oxytone (udātta on the final syllable) is prescribed as a *nipātana* within the [Gaṇapāṭha] list. Consequently, in the formation *sarveṣāṃ vikāraḥ*, the suffix *añ* is established by the rule *anudāttāder añ* (Pāṇini 4.3.140). This is because that suffix is prescribed after a base whose initial syllable is *anudātta*; thus it is settled in the Bhāṣya on the *ṅyāpprātipadikāt* sūtra. However, in actual usage, the word *sarva* takes an udātta accent on its first syllable by the rule *sarvasya supi* (Pāṇini 6.1.191).

The word *ubha* denotes that which is qualified by duality; for this very reason, it always ends in the dual number. If this is so, then for what purpose is it listed among the *sarvādi* (the group beginning with *sarva*)? For here [in the case of *ubha*], forms such as *smāy* (the feminine suffix) and so forth are not possible. Furthermore, there is no difference in form or accent between [the forms derived from] *ka* and *kañ*. As for the *avagraha* (separation in the Pada-pāṭha), it is not applied by the makers of the Padas even when the suffix *ka* is present—as in "citra id rājā rājakāḥ" and "id anyake"—because it has been determined to be exactly so in those instances.

Nor should it be argued that this [entry] is included here for the sake of optionally establishing the third case ending in expressions such as *ubhābhyāṃ hetubhyām* and *ubhayor hetvoḥ*, by means of the rule *sarvanāmnaḥ tṛtīyā ca* (Pāṇini 2.3.27); for its purpose is already served by the Vārttika: *nimittakāraṇahetuṣu sarvāsāṃ prāyadarśanam*.

Nor should it be argued that because this *vārttika* is read in the rule *sarvanāmnaḥ tṛtīyā ca* (Pāṇini 2.3.27) by the author of the *Vṛtti*, it too must depend upon the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "pronominal" (*sarvanāman*); for it is read in the *Bhāṣya* under the rule *hetau* (Pāṇini 2.3.23). For this very reason, Haradatta has cited the examples: *annena kāraṇena vasati* ("he dwells for the sake of food") and *annasya kāraṇasya*.

To this it is replied: First of all, the word *ubha* has as its scope only the dual number (*dvivacana*). However, in a compound (*vṛtti*), because the dual ending is elided, that word is not employed; for we observe such usage as *ubhayapakṣa* (Pāṇini 5.2.42) in the analysis (*vigraha*) "awakened from sleep by both wings" (*ubhābhyāṃ pakṣābhyāṃ vinītanidrā*). If one asks, "How then is the word *ubhaya* established in place of *ubha*?"—it is thus: in the rule *ubhādudātto nityam* (Pāṇini 5.2.44), the word *ubhāt* is analyzed [as *ubha-āt*].

The suffix *ayac* should be applied after the word *ubha*, which denotes a number and functions as a part (*avayava*), in the sense of a whole (*avayavin*). Thus, *ubhaya-maṇi*. Consequently, by the rule "nityam ubhaśabdād vṛttiviṣaye," the suffix *ayac* must necessarily occur when *ubha* is used in a compound; since no specific meaning is otherwise indicated, it occurs in its own sense (*svārthe*). This has been stated by the author of the Vārttika: "ubhayo 'nyatra" (ubhaya occurs elsewhere). This being the case, since *ubhaya* alone would be expected even when the suffix *kap* is applied—as in *ubhayataḥ* and *ubhayatra*—the form *ubhakau* and so forth is established only through the addition of *akac*.

Nor should it be argued that the form *ubhaye* would necessarily occur here as well; for the addition of *ayac* in the list of *sarvādi* words is for the sake of the suffix *akac*, which subverts [the application of] *ayac*. Otherwise, the inclusion in the list would be rendered purposeless—this is the general direction of the argument. Furthermore, it is not correct to say that the inclusion [of *ubha*] in the list is for the sake of making it ādyudātta according to the rule *svāṅgaśiṭāmadantānām* (Pāṇini 6.2.177), because within the very list (*gaṇa*), it is prescribed as being antodātta.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the initial syllable being udātta in such cases as *ubhe bhadre joṣayete*, *ubhāu nūnam*, *ubhābhyāṃ deva savitaḥ*, and *sapatyata ubhayornṛmṇamayoḥ*. The word *ubhaya*, however, refers to a whole (*avayavin*) composed of two parts, as in the example *ubhayo maṇiḥ* (a gem consisting of both [colors]). The meaning is that it is composed of two parts, black and red. The singular number is used because the distinction between the individual parts is concealed.

In such cases as "The wise say both," however, the meaning is a collection composed of two groups; the fact that the distinction between the parts is obscured remains exactly the same. But when it refers to a great aggregate formed by two groups, then—because the distinction between the parts is manifested through the desire to express a great difference by means of the two groups which are distinct from the individual members—it takes the plural ending alone, as in "both gods and men" (*ubhaye devamanuṣyāḥ*). [As it is said: "Those who are his friends and those who are his enemies, and those kings who are both."

Thus, for example: when, according to the previously mentioned method, one explains "maṇi" as "both [are] jewels" (*ubhayo maṇiḥ*) and intends to express two such identical jewels together, then by means of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one), a dual number would result. However, it does not occur because of non-expression (*anabhidhāna*).

And thus, while introducing the *bhāṣya* on the rule *taddhitaścāsarvavibhaktiḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.37)—which states, "The inclusion of *kṛt* and *taddhita* [suffixes] is by way of their enumeration"—Kaiyaṭa says: "Because the dual number does not arise for the word *ubhaya*, it is 'not possessing all case-endings' (*asarvavibhakti*). However, Haradatta, accepting the dual number from the word *ubhaya* in that very same rule, states that the recourse to the enumeration is for the purpose of avoiding over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *pacatikalpam* and *pacatirūpam*.

In this case, because the substitute *ayaja* is treated as the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) and thus ends in the suffix *tayap*, the rule *prathamacarama* (Pāṇini 1.1.33) would seemingly allow for the optional application of the *sarvanāman* designation before the nominative plural suffix *jas*. However, some maintain that through the principle of *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (restricted optionality) or by means of a prior prohibition (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), the *sarvanāman* designation applies invariably before *jas*. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is that the obligatory designation—which is internal (*antaraṅga*) because it does not depend on a case-ending—supersedes the optional one, which is external (*bahiraṅga*).

Regarding the sūtra *na veti vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 1.1.44), the author of the Bhāṣya states: "The suffix *ayaC* is indeed a distinct suffix; it is not a substitute for *tayap*, because in the sūtra *ubhādudāttaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.44), there is no recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of *tayap*. Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* would not apply in the word *ubhayī* by virtue of its being formed with *tayap* under the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.15); for in that context, the term *mātrāJ*—beginning from the word *mātra*—includes a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated reference) consisting of the letter *C* following *ayac*.

And thus, even the mention of *tayap* need not be made there; or rather, *dvayasaC* is a pratyāhāra (a collective term). Consequently, there is no need to include *daghnaC* and *mātraC* as well, which results in great economy of effort (*lāghava*). In fact, the intention of the Bhāṣya is that the rule should be read as "the suffixes *mātrac*, *dvayasaC*, and *daghnaC* [denote] measure" (*pramāṇe mātrac-dvayasaC-daghnaCaḥ*). And thus, there is even greater economy than before. Nor does this lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *kati striyaḥ*.

This is because the word "ataḥ" is understood from the previous context, or because of the prohibition "not after [stems ending in] ṣaṣ, svasṛ, etc. (Pāṇini 6.4.137). Nor does this lead to over-extension in cases such as *tailamātrā*, for even though this [suffix -mātra] is similar, it is not included within the pratyāhāra.

Regarding this, someone says: "The designation 'both' (*ubhaya*) is intended to refer to the meaning (*artha*); by this, the usage in Māgha’s *Praharṣiṇī* verse, 'The earth is useless for both types of kings' (*vyarthā dvayeṣāmapi medinībhṛtām*), is justified. That is not correct, because no statement from the author of the *Vṛtti* or other authoritative scholars is found to support such an intentionality regarding the meaning. If it is argued that this is merely inferred on the strength of the usage by great poets, we say no; for great poets themselves have frequently employed the term in its opposite sense. For instance, Māgha writes: "For the two teachers of the two teachers" (*gurudvayāya guruṇoḥ*).
Kālidāsa also says: "In this pair, there is an effort toward the creation of beauty. And Śrīharṣa says:
"Alas, that very pair which my tongue has praised is now useless; there is no purpose in bowing to it.

Therefore, the form *dvayeṣām* should be understood as derived from the root *iṣ* (to desire) with the suffix *kvip*, meaning those who desire or go toward the pair (*dvayam*), that is, duality (*dvaidham*).

As for what someone has said—that because the *Cākravarmaṇa-vyākaraṇa* accepts that even the word *dvaya* is a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), this usage is valid according to its system—that too is not correct. For the distinction between the correct and incorrect forms is currently established according to the opinion of the three sages (*munitraya*), as it is precisely that which is accepted by contemporary learned authorities (*śiṣṭas*) as an auxiliary to the Vedas. Indeed, we see that Smṛtis are restricted to specific times; for example, "the Pārāśara-smṛti [applies] in the Kali age," and so forth. This is because it has been established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) in accordance with the entire body of rules in the sūtra *śatācca ṭhanyatāvaśate* (Pāṇini 5.1.22).

Although the suffixes *ḍatara* and *ḍatama* do not include the final member [of the base] when a suffix is mentioned in a rule defining a technical term (*saṃjñā*), according to the principle that "when a suffix is mentioned in a rule for defining a technical term, there is no inclusion of what ends with it" (Paribhāṣā 27), nevertheless, here there is an explicit extension to the end of the word based on the statement: "The purpose [of this rule] lies in the technical designation of pronouns and indeclinables" (Kātyāyana-vārttika). Alternatively, this is because the mere suffixes themselves have no utility as technical terms. *Kanyaḥ* means "different. Regarding the words *anyatara* and *anyatama*, Kaiyaṭa states in the *Paspaśā* [section of the Mahābhāṣya]: "These two words are underived (*avyutpanna*); by their very nature, they function to denote a selection from among two or many [respectively]."

In this regard, because the word *anyatama* is not included in the list [of the *anyatara*-group], it does not undergo all the grammatical operations prescribed for nouns (*sarvanāma-kārya*), nor does it undergo the specific operations of the internal sub-group (*antargaṇa-kārya*) such as those in Pāṇini’s sūtra 7.1.25, *aḍḍatarādibhyaḥ*. Accordingly, it is used in the expression: "Among the general categories (*sāmānya*) and so forth, darkness is not one of them (*anyatama*). Śākaṭāyana, however, has derived both *anyatara* and *anyatama* from the suffixes *-ḍatara* and *-ḍatama*.

Even in that view, because the reading of the word *anyatara* is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*), the word *anyatama* does not obtain the internal class-based operation (*antargaṇakārya*) nor the operation pertaining to the technical name *sarvanāman*; thus say its commentators. Amara states: "The word *itara* [is used] in the senses of 'other' and 'low'. Both *tva* and *tva* are nominative forms ending in *-a*, both being synonyms for "other"; among them, one is udātta and the other is anudātta. The udātta form is employed in the passage: "I consider this [child], O Tvaṣṭṛ, to be a source of ten sons" (*etaṃ tvaṃ manye daśa putram utsam*).

The distinction is that [the form] beginning with "uta tvaḥ paśyan" is for the case of an unaccented (anudātta) [pronoun]. However, some read it as ending in -t (tvat), as Jayadeva employed it: "pibantaṃ tvadadharamadhuramadhūni" (drinking the honey-sweet nectar of your lower lip). Here, "tvadadhara" is a genitive tatpuruṣa compound meaning "the lower lip of someone other than you," and not "your own lower lip" (tavādharaḥ); for if it were the latter, there would be a lack of syntactic connection with the preceding sentence, "paśyati diśi-diśi rahasi bhavantam" (he sees you in secret in every direction).

This word is unaccented (*anudātta*), according to the *Phiṭ-sūtra*: "The words *tva*, *tvas*, *sama*, *simā*, *iti*, and *anu* are unaccented" (PhiS 4.78). Accordingly, it is employed in the usage: "The barren cow becomes like you (*tvat*)," and "the son-in-law becomes like you (*utvat*). In their commentary on this, the authors of the Vedic commentaries state that this word *tvad*, listed among the pronouns (*sarvanāman*), is an unaccented synonym for "another. Here, according to the method previously stated, the authenticity of the forms ending in *a* with either the acute (*udātta*) or grave (*anudātta*) accent, as well as the form ending in *t*, is beyond dispute; the disagreement lies only regarding its placement in the list of pronouns (*gaṇapāṭha*).

In that regard, there is no doubt that the form ending in *a* which is unaccented (*anudātta*) is included in the list of the *gaṇa*, as evidenced by usages such as "uto tvasmai tanvam. However, regarding which of the two remaining forms is read in the *gaṇa*, there is doubt because the cited examples remain indifferent toward that point. Therefore, the truth must be determined by those of great learning after investigating whether forms such as *akac* are used for the accented (*udātta*) form ending in *-t*, or whether forms such as *smāy-* are used for it in some recensional branch (*śākhā*). This is the direction of the argument.

In reality, however, it is more appropriate to treat the first instance as a case of *tāntaccheda* (separation of the suffix). Otherwise, since—as in the case of the word *aikṣvāka*—it would have been possible to include both forms under a single accent (*ekaśruti*) by means of a pronominal substitute for the vowel, the author would have recited only the form *tva*. This is to be kept in mind. As for instances such as *tve vasūni* and *tve rāyaḥ*, these are uses of the pronoun *yuṣmad* ending in the *śe*-suffix, and not of the word *tva*; this is established in the Vedabhāṣya on the basis of the use of the particle *uti*, which is applied by the Padakāras to indicate the status of being a *pragṛhya*.

The word *sama* is not a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) when it means "equal" (*itardve*). Its usage is seen in such passages as: *pra nemasmin dadṛśe somaḥ* ("Soma was seen in this one [of them]"), *nabhantām anyake same* ("May the others, all [of them], perish"), *mā no vṛkāya vṛkye samasmai* ("Do not [give us] over to the wolf, nor to the she-wolf, nor to any equal [enemy]"), *uruṣyāṇo aghāyataḥ samasmāt* ("Protect us from every one who intends evil"), and *uto samasmin* ("And also in this one"). However, the word *sama* when it is a synonym for *tulya* ("equal") does not possess the status of a pronoun, as indicated by the rule: *yathāsaṃkhyam anudeśaḥ samānām* (Pāṇini 1.3.10).

This is because of the rule *kṛnmejantaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.39), and also because of the usage of the author of the Bhāṣya: "These faults are equal or even greater. By this, the usage *same yajeta* ("one should sacrifice on level ground") is explained. The word *sima* may mean "entirety," "capability," "limit," or "bound."

Thus ends the Nighaṇṭu. Regarding the examples: "ādrātrīvāsastanute simasmai" and "ucchukramatkamajate simasmāt. Although here the rule "tvattvasamasimetyanuccāni" (Pāṇini 8.1.60) would have applied [to make the word *sima* unaccented], nevertheless, its acute accent is established by the rule "simasyātharvaṇe'nta udāttaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.1.61). It should be noted that this is because authoritative commentators have explained that this applies even to mantras found in the Ṛgveda and other Vedas when they have entered into the Atharvaveda.

The five terms *pūrva*, *para*, *avara*, *uttara*, and *apara* denote both direction and time, as well as that which is delimited by them. For example: "in the eastern direction," "in the earlier time," "in the eastern pond," or "in the elder teacher," and so forth. The words *dakṣiṇa* (south) and *adhara* (lower) likewise denote both direction and that which is delimited by it. This restriction of meaning is understood from the statement that they function in the sense of "distinction" (*vyavasthā*). For "distinction" is indeed the restriction of a limit (*avadhi*) relative to that which is denoted by the word itself. Indeed, the aforementioned meanings of the words *pūrva* and the others necessarily depend upon some limit.

Since the suffix *ktin* would otherwise apply by the rule "sthā-gā-pā-paco bhāve" (Pāṇini 3.3.25), the suffix *aṅ* is used here precisely because of this specific irregularity (*nipātana*). What is the purpose of specifying "in the sense of a fixed condition" (*vyavasthā*)? [Consider: "The singers are skilled with the *ikṣu* (sugar-cane)"—the meaning being that they are proficient. Or: "He is capable in the lower [matter]," or "capable in the answer or the counter-argument."

How then are we to explain Kālidāsa’s usage in "tathā pareṣāṃ yudhi ca" (Raghuvaṃśa 3.21), as well as "apare pratyavatiṣṭhante" and so forth? On this point, they say: the words *para* and *apara*, which primarily denote spatial direction and the domain of established order (*vyavasthā*), are used metaphorically for the enemy and the opponent respectively. Nor does this constitute a state of being a subordinate term (*upasarjanatā*). For being figurative (*lākṣaṇikatva*) does not mean being subordinate; rather, it is the transfer of the word's own primary meaning onto another object qualified by that primary meaning.

But that [pronoun] does not refer to a *pradhāna* (principal element) even when it has entered into a grammatical operation (*vṛtti*), nor to a *lakṣaṇika* (metaphorical) element even when it has not entered into a grammatical operation. For this very reason, in expressions such as "therefore he possesses fire," the function of the pronoun (*sarvanāma-kārya*) occurs even under the view that there is a cognition characterized by indication (*jñānalakṣaṇā*). Likewise, in the case of "He who is I, he is that; he who is that, he is I," the function of the pronoun proceeds even when there is indication through the exclusion of parts (*bhāgatyāgalakṣaṇā*). Thus Kaiyaṭa states regarding the rule *bhūvādi*: "'These too' means these things which are to be expressed."

In reality, however, the truth is this: while the cognition of the qualifier "enmity" and so forth arising from words such as "enemy" is merely implied—just like [the cognition] of "distinctness" from words such as "non-horse"—the cognition arising from the word itself has as its qualifier precisely [the property of] residing in another location and so forth.

What is the purpose of [defining] *asaṃjñā* (non-designation)? [It is to exclude] Uttarakuru. Since the word "uttara" (northern) is applied to the Kurus with reference to Sumeru as a limit (*avadhi*), there is indeed a fixed determination (*vyavasthā*) here. However, because this is well-known, the mention of the limit is not employed. Just as in the expression "the cloud rains," where [the rain] refers to water, so too in cases such as "be a co-wife of the southern direction," there is in fact a fixed determination; thus, the operation of a pronoun (*sarvanāma-kārya*) is certainly possible. Nor is there a prohibition based on it being a "designation" (*saṃjñā*), for a "designation" is merely a modern convention (*ādhunika-saṅketa*).

And Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others state in the fifth section on the suffix *astāti* that "it does not exist in the directions. Regarding the distinction here that the convention [of the word *svo*] is ancient in the case of "directions" (*dikṣu*) but recent in the case of "Kurus" (*kuruṣu*), the word of the commentators themselves is the sole authority. Furthermore, the word *sva* has four meanings: self (*ātman*), one's own (*ātmīya*), kinsman (*jñāti*), and wealth (*dhana*). As the Amarakośa states: "The word *sva* means kinsman or self; *svam* in the three genders means one's own; *svaḥ* in the non-feminine gender means wealth. (Amarakośa 3.3.219).

Thus says Amara. Although the word *sva* is accepted as denoting "lordship" (*aiśvarya*) by the rule *svāminnaisvarye* (Pāṇini 5.2.126), even there it is restricted solely to the suffix *manic*, and is not fit for independent usage. In that context, because relatives and wealth are excluded, the designation applies only to "self" (*ātman*) and "one's own" (*ātmīya*). Why is the term "designation" (*ākhyā*) included [in the definition]? It is so that when the word is applied to relatives and wealth by taking their "belongingness" (*ātmīyatva*) as the primary factor, they may still function as pronouns (*sarvanāman*).

However, it is more appropriate here to state [the meaning] as "of self and what belongs to self" (*ātmātmīyayoḥ*). This is also the case in the *Aṣṭādhyāyī* sūtra (4.1.3) which prescribes the optional rule for the *jas* ending, namely *svasminnityādi*. As for the claim made by some that it would be more appropriate there to say simply "self and what belongs to self" (*svamātmīya*), because the word denoting "self" is neuter and thus has no utility in the optional rule for the *jas* ending—that is questionable; for by the very force of the sūtra, the masculine gender is obtained even when referring to the self. For this very reason, in the *Amarakośa*, the word *ātmani* connects with the preceding [definition], while *svam* connects with the following. And so says Hemacandra:
"Dyaus" [is used] for heaven and the sky; "svaḥ" for kinsman and self; "svam" for one's own and wealth. Thus says Medinīkāra.

Furthermore, in reality, the definition of the meanings in the three sūtras beginning with "pūrva-parau" (Pāṇini 1.1.34–36) is merely a specific reading [of the list]. Therefore, other readings are excluded by that very fact. Consequently, in the section beginning with "vibhāṣā jasi" (Pāṇini 1.1.32), one should simply have said "pūrvādīni nava" (the nine beginning with 'pūrva') for the sake of brevity. The conclusion is that the three sūtras should not have been recited at all.

Alternatively, in the *Gaṇapāṭha* itself, immediately after the recitation of the group beginning with *pūrva*, one should insert the rule "optionally before *jas*" (*vibhāṣā jasi*). Furthermore, the words beginning with *pūrva* should be understood as being carried over (*anuvartanīya*) as qualified by their specific meanings. Nor should it be suspected that the *sarvādi* class is also being carried over here, because the optional rule for *nemā* is initiated specifically for the case of *jas*. Or else, a formal insertion (*nyāsa*) should be made in the seventh book [of the *Mahābhāṣya*] regarding the following rules: "for *jas*, *ṅasi*, and *ṅi*, [the suffixes] *śi*, *smāt*, and *smin* [are substituted]; optionally for the nine beginning with *pūrva*; *śī* is substituted for *auṅ* after a feminine stem ending in *āp*; and [the same applies] after a neuter [stem]."

But as for the ultimate truth, let it remain exactly as it is in the seventh [chapter]. As for the rule *pūrvādibhyo navabhyo vā* (Pāṇini 7.1.16), it will be connected by way of a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) with the rule *jasaḥ śī* (Pāṇini 7.1.17), just as the rule *vā chandasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.203) is connected with *ami pūrvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.107). Thus, it is established that these three rules are not to be recited within the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*.

However, the term "in the absence of a name" (*asaṃjñāyām*) need not be applied here, because the name [of the compound] has already been excluded by the etymological name itself, according to the maxim: "Those whose meanings are clearly manifest [do not require a formal name]. The word *antara*, moreover, has multiple meanings; as Amarasimha states: *Antara* [is used] in the sense of space, limit, clothing, disappearance, division, purpose, hole, one's own, exclusion, outside, below, supreme, middle, and within the self. (Amarakośa 3.3.94)

In this context, the technical designations apply specifically to the two meanings of "outer" (*bahiḥ*) and "undergarment" (*upasaṃvyāna*). The term "outer" (*bahiḥ*) denotes both an uncovered space and that which is external. Regarding the first [meaning], the sense is "houses within" or "between," namely the houses of *caṇḍālas* and others located outside the city. Regarding the second, the sense is "houses inside the city. The word *upasaṃvyāna*, derived through the instrumental case (*karaṇa*), refers to an upper garment; however, when derived through the accusative case (*karman*), it refers to an undergarment.

It is established in the Bhāṣya that the mention of *upasaṃvyāna* (the inner garment) need not be made, because the meaning is already conveyed by the connection with "outer" (*bahis*) in either case. However, some maintain that the mention of *upasaṃvyāna* must be made for the sake of pairs of garments and so forth—such as the third garment connected to the body among three pieces of cloth, or the fourth among four, or the third connected to that [body]—because it lacks the connection with the "outer. This very intention of the Vārttikakāra is understood from the word *ādi* (and so forth).

According to the view of the Bhāṣya, however, the inclusion of the term *bahiryoga* (external connection) is intended to be significant; thus, as in the case of *śītoṣṇābhyāṃ kāriṇi* (Pāṇini 5.2.72), they say that because of the mention of the "secondary" (*gauṇa*), the designation will apply even to that which is indirectly connected to the exterior. Nevertheless, even when there is external connection, if the reference is to a city (*purī*), the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāmatā*) does not arise, based on the Vārttika: "And it should be stated that [the designation does not apply] to a city."

For that [vṛddhi] is a supplement (śeṣa) to the Gaṇasūtra, but not to the rule prescribing the optional [vṛddhi] before *jas*; because, under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) "from *at*," the substitution of *śī* for *jas* is prescribed, and since a feminine stem ending in long *ā* cannot be a patronymic (*apatya*), [the vṛddhi] would otherwise apply. The meaning of "in an inner city" (*antarāyāṃ puri*) is "in one situated outside the ramparts or within them. It should be understood that the application [of the rule] occurs either by the *paribhāṣā* regarding words qualified by gender, or by the inclusion of the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) as part of the preceding element through the principle of "taking the preceding end" (*pūrvāntagrahaṇa*).

*tyad* and *tad*—these two refer back to what has been previously mentioned; among them, the first (*tyad*) is Vedic. As for the statement by the author of the *Gaṇaratna*, "This is *syabhānu*," that is incorrect, because if that were the case, the inclusion of the term *chandas* in the rule *śyaśchandasi bahulam* (Pāṇini 6.1.133) would result in redundancy. *Yad* serves to introduce the subject (*uddeśya*). *Etad* and *idam* refer to what is perceptually present. *Adas* refers to what is remote. The word *eka* is used in the sense of "other," as well as for "principal," "first," "exclusive," "common," "equal," and "number."

The word *dvi* is devoid of gender and is qualified by duality; its scope is restricted to the vocative case. The referent of the word *yuṣmad* is the person addressed. The word *asmad*, however, refers to the speaker; it possesses gender and does not deviate from the vocative. This [word *bhavat*] is derived from the rule "from the root *bhā*, the suffix *ḍvatu*" (*Pāṇini* 5.2.126). Although suffixes such as *smāy* cannot occur after this [base *bhavat-*], the matter is already covered by the rule "the third case ending is also used [with pronouns]" (*Pāṇini* 2.3.27) and the Vārttika "in the sense of cause, motive, or reason, all case endings are generally seen" (*Kātyāyana*). Nevertheless...

The prior placement of *phiñ*, *adri*, *mayaṭ*, and *ṭac*; likewise, *ṭhak* and *cha*; the substitution of *ātva*; the formation of a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*); the absence of *ṣyañ*; and *akac*: these are the results [of the rule].

*Phiñ*: *bhāvatāyaniḥ*. Because it belongs to the class beginning with *tyad* (the pronominal class), it is "old" (*vṛddha*); hence, by the rule *udīcāṃ vṛddhāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.157), the suffix *phiñ* is applied. *Bhavadryaṅ*: [This is derived] from the sense "one who goes toward you" (*bhavantam añcati*). By the rule *viṣvag-devayoś ca* (Pāṇini 6.3.91), the word *sarvanāman* ("pronominal") is drawn back by the particle *ca*, resulting in the substitution of *adri*. *Bhavanmayaḥ*: [This is derived] by the suffix *mayaṭ* according to the rule *nityaṃ vṛddha-śarādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.144). *Bhavanmitra*: [In this compound], there is prior placement [of the pronominal] according to the Kāśikāvṛtti rule *sarvanāma-saṃkhyayoḥ*.

*bhāvatkaḥ* and *bhavadīyaḥ*: In the rule *bhavataṣṭhakchasau* (Pāṇini 4.2.115), the term *vṛddhāt* is understood as a carry-over (*anuvartate*) in order to exclude forms ending in the present participle suffix *śatṛ*. Regarding the substitution of *ā*—as in *bhavādṛk*—the rule *ā sarvanāmnaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.72) applies as a single-remainder compound (*ekaśeṣa*). Furthermore, in the expression *bhavato bhāvo bhavattā*, the absence of the suffix *ṣyañ* is also a result [of this analysis], because the designation of "possessing a quality" (*guṇavacana*) is sublated by the designation of "pronoun" (*sarvanāman*). Otherwise, the form would have been *bhāvatyam*.

Regarding the term *akacca-bhavakān*: by the rule "in all derivative formations (*vṛttimātre*)," the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) is also a result; thus, "the son of your ladyship" is *bhavatputraḥ*. The word *kim* is used in the sense of inquiry and censure; such is the general direction [of the analysis].

The word *vṛt* belongs to the *sarvādi* group; "completed" (*vṛtta*) means "finished. In the passage, "O Indra and Agni, [you who] stand upon the lowest earth, the middle one, and the highest," the augment *syāṭ* occurs in the words *avama*, *madhyama*, and *parama* due to the general license of rules in Vedic (*chandas*). However, one should not conclude that the status of being a *kṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class) for the *sarvādi* stems is based on this instance alone. For this very reason, even in the Veda, the application of the designation "pronominal" (*sarvanāman*) to these [words] is not mandatory.

In passages such as "the middle ancestors" (*ye madhyamāḥ pitaraḥ*) and "in the highest step of Viṣṇu" (*viṣṇoḥ pade parame*), that [suffix] is absent. However, in cases such as "both those arrays from one another" (*vyūhāvubhau tāvitaretarasmāt*) and "touching one another with their lotuses" (*anyonyeṣāṃ puṣkarairāmṛśantaḥ*), [the forms are established] under the view that reduplication (*dvirvacana*) consists of a double application (*dviprayoga*), by means of the rule *tadantavidhi*. Under the view that reduplication consists of substitution (*sthāne dvirvacana*), it should be understood that [the forms are established] by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original).

If it is argued that—just as in the case of *vasna-sāda* and the like—due to the confusion regarding the division between base (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*), even by means of the *sthānivadbhāva* rule there would only be the status of being a *pada*, but not the status of being a pronoun (*sarvanāmatā*), because that [status] is absent in the substituendum (*sthānin*) when it is qualified by a case-ending (*sup*)—we say no. This is because, by virtue of being taught as a simultaneous injunction (*sanniyogaśiṣṭa*), the elision (*luk*) caused by the application of the rule "and like a compound, optionally" (*samāsavacca bahulam*, Kātyāyana-vārttika) occurs first, thereby overriding even the internal (*antaraṅga*) doubling (*dvitva*). As it is said: "The external (*bahiraṅga*) elision (*luk*) overrides even internal rules" (*antaraṅgān api vidhīn bahiraṅgo lug bādhate*).

Because this will be stated [later], one relies on the status of being a *pada* by means of the characteristic of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), and thereby the application of reduplication (*dvitva*) occurs. By this, expressions such as "tattattāmasabhūtabhītayaḥ" are explained. Now, while the formation of "itaretarasmāt" may be established according to the method described, how is "anyonyeṣām" formed? If you ask, "Is there not a lack of the status of being a compound (*samāsavadbhāva*) here?", the answer is that the division between base and suffix is established by the force of the rule itself: namely, that the first member of the compound ends in the nominative singular, while the second member begins with the dative and so forth.
