Alternatively, let there be a displacement of the mention of "place" (sthāna) right here, according to the maxim of the lion’s backward glance (*siṃhāvalokananyāya*); however, it has already been stated that a correspondence based on numerical order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) is difficult to establish. If it is asked, "How then is there no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of *aduhitarām*?"—the answer is: by resorting to methods such as *tantra* (simultaneous application) or *āvṛtti* (repetition), because in the rule regarding *saṃprasāraṇa*, the term refers to that which is to undergo such a change (*tadbhāvitagrahaṇāt*).

Alternatively, according to the *kāryakālapakṣa* (the view that a rule operates at the time its effect is to be realized), since the sentence-meaning is "the *saṃprasāraṇa* [vowel] becomes an *iK* in place of the *yaṇ*," there is no status as a mere restatement (*anuvāda*). Consequently, when the *paribhāṣā* [of *yathāsaṃkhya*] applies there, the technical term (*saṃjñin*) itself is what operates according to the sequence of enumeration. That very [term] then presents itself in rules such as *samprasāraṇasya*. Or rather, the connection based on the order of positions is easily established even in a restatement because it is proven by worldly logic; thus, the *yathāsaṃkhya* sūtra simply does not apply—this is the general direction.

In the case of *dyubhyām*, the long vowel [substitution] prescribed by Pāṇini 6.4.2 (*halaḥ*) does not apply because of the *tapara* marker in Pāṇini 6.1.131 (*diva ut*). For this very reason, in the case of *dyulokaḥ*, the long vowel substitution prescribed by Pāṇini 6.3.139 (*saṃprasāraṇasya*) does not apply.

If it is asked: "In that case, how can this [sūtra] be cited as a *jñāpaka* for the purpose [of establishing] the meaning 'even when being taught (*bhāvyamāna*), the vowel *u* includes its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*)'"? No; because it has already been stated under the view that the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is the technical name (*saṃjñin*), or because in the rule *saṃprasāraṇasya* (Pāṇini 6.3.139), there is the inclusion of that which is substituted by it (*tadbāvitagrahaṇa*). However, according to the other alternative view, it should be understood that *ṛta ut* (Pāṇini 6.1.111) is the *jñāpaka*.

If it is objected that, in this case, in forms such as *akṣadyuvau* and *akṣadyuva*, once the *ūṭh* substitution has received the designation of *saṃprasāraṇa*, the rule *saṃprasāraṇācca* (Pāṇini 6.1.107) would cause the single-substitute (*pūrvarūpa*) to occur; we say no, because the author of the Vārttikas established the requirement that for the application of the rule regarding the priority of *saṃprasāraṇa*, the two elements must belong to the same stem (*samānāṅga*). However, even on the view where that requirement is rejected, the substitution *uvaṅ* will occur by the principle *vārṇādāṅgaṃ balīyaḥ* (a rule pertaining to vowels is stronger than one pertaining to phonemes). Furthermore, under alternative views such as that the sentence-meaning itself is the technical term (*saṃjñin*), there is no possibility of the single-substitute occurring at all.

In cases such as *hūtaḥ* and *jīnaḥ*, however, by the force of the rule *halaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.2), the long vowel occurs even when there is a substitute for that which has been produced through *samprasāraṇa*. This is because, even under the view that [the term *al*] denotes a phoneme (*varṇasaṃjñā*), since the status of being a *sthānin* is impossible in an operation concerning a phoneme (*alvidhi*), one must admit that the operation applies to the substitute of the *samprasāraṇa* due to the force of the formulation of the rule *halaḥ*. This is the general direction [of the argument].

*Ādyantau ṭakitau* (Pāṇini 1.1.46): Those [suffixes] designated as *ṭit* and *kit* are respectively the initial and final constituents of that [element] for which they are prescribed. For example: *bhavitā*, *yāpayati*. By the maxim *purastādapavādāḥ* (Pāṇini Bhāṣya 60), this [rule] is an exception to the rule regarding the application of an element in place of another (*sthāneyoga*). However, it is superseded by the rules *pratyayaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.1) and *paraśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.2) because of their higher status [in the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*]. Consequently, suffixes such as *ṭaḥ* in *careṣṭaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.8), *ṭak* in *gāpoṣṭak* (Pāṇini 3.2.16), and *ḍhak* in *vrīhiśālyorḍhak* (Pāṇini 5.2.2) occur only after [the base], not in its place.

This is a *paribhāṣā* (technical rule) because of its association with the subsequent section on *paribhāṣās*. However, in the *Bhāṣya*, the view that it is a *saṃjñā* (technical term) has also been established. To explain: in the rule *ṭakitau*, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound; the letters *ṭ* and *k*, bearing the *it*-designation, are the technical terms for the beginning and the end [of an element]. Likewise, *iṭ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, analyzed as "that which has *i* as its initial *ṭ*" (*iḥ ṭ ādir yasya*). Thus, by the *paribhāṣā* "the most similar [substitute] in place," the desired result is achieved when *tavya* is replaced by *itavya*.

Thus, in the case of *yāpayati*, there is the substitution of *yāp* for the root *yā*, based on the analysis *puḥ k yasya*. Nor should it be argued that one should simply state "the *ṭ* and *k* are the initial and final [elements]," because that would lead to the undesirable consequence that the *ṭ* and *k* in rules such as *ālajāṭacau* (Pāṇini 5.2.125) and *ṭhasyekaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.50) would also be designated as initial and final. Rather, by virtue of being designated as *it*, a specific location is indicated; therefore, the *ṭ* and *k* situated in the location occupied by that which bears the *it*-designation are the technical names (*saṃjñā*).

The *cāṭa* and *caṣṭa* [rules] apply to the single-substitute *ikāra*, and likewise to the *kakāra*; thus, the aforementioned defect does not arise. [Objection: But on this view, by the rule "in *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *lṛṅ*" (*Pāṇini* 6.4.71), there would be the substitution of *abhū* for *bhū*, and since that [substitute] is [prescribed as] acute, it would follow that it is finally acute. [Reply: This is not a defect. For one may resort to a three-membered *bahuvrīhi*: "that which has *aḥ*, *ṭ*, and the acute accent. Even though it is a qualifier, the acute accent is placed at the end according to Vedic usage (*sautra*). Thus, it is established that the substitute begins with an acute *ākāra*.

Nor should it be argued that even so, the defect remains as it was in the rule *āḍajādīnām* (Pāṇini 6.4.72), because a *bahuvrīhi* compound is impossible with the word *udātta* as it occurs in the *anuvṛtti*. This is not to be said, because the rule *āḍajādīnām* (Pāṇini 6.4.72) is about to be rejected; for he will say: "The [augment] *aṭ* is established for words beginning with vowels," and so forth.
Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.47: *midaco 'ntyāt paraḥ*.

Among vowels that are situated [in a word], that which is the final vowel (*antya ac*)—the marker *m* shall follow it, and it [the *m*] is treated as the final part of the preceding element (*pūrvānta*). This is an exception to the rules of substitution (*sthāne-yoga*) and the rule of being "subsequent" (*para*). Examples: *vanāni*, *yaśāṃsi*, *rūṇaddhi*.

If it is argued: "Surely, as in the previous rule (*pūrvayoga*), let this too be an exception (*apavāda*) by the logic of priority, applying only to the connection with a *sthāna* [substitute], but not to the rules 'pratyayaḥ' (Pāṇini 3.1.1) and 'paraśca' (Pāṇini 3.1.2)," we say: No. This is because we accept here that, by relying on a consideration of the general object of sublation (*bādhyasāmānyacintā*), everything that would otherwise apply to its own domain is sublated. Otherwise, the addition of the marker *m* in the rule for *śnam* would be purposeless.

Nor should it be said that the *m* of *śnam* exists solely for the sake of pronunciation (*śravaṇārtha*), because of the rule "tṛṇaha" (Pāṇini 7.3.92). The singular number in the word *acaḥ* is used with reference to the genus (*jāti*). The genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). And one should not argue that since there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *antyāt*, the word *acaḥ* should instead be in the ablative case; for in rules such as "śe mucādīnām" (Pāṇini 7.1.59), since a final vowel (*anta-ac*) is impossible, this specific paribhāṣā would not apply, and consequently, the general paribhāṣā "al-antyasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.52) would take effect.

Furthermore, in that case, there would be the undesirable consequence of the rule for the *mit* designation being redundant. Although in the previous sūtra the compound *ādyantau* was used, here only the mention of *anta* is carried forward, because it is specifically declared to be *svarita* as a single part [of the compound]. Therefore, the *mit* [augment] belongs to the end of the preceding element. If, however, it were not an integral part (*abhakta*) of the word, then in forms such as *tātā piṇḍānām*, when the elision of the *śi* suffix occurs by the rule *śeśchandasibahulām* (Pāṇini 6.1.70), the elision of the *n* would not take place, because it would no longer be at the end of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

Likewise, in the case of *vahaṃlihaḥ*, the suffix *khaś* would be applied by Pāṇini 3.2.32 (*vahābhre lihaḥ*), and then the augment *muṭ* would be applied by Pāṇini 6.3.67 (*arurdviṣadajantasya*). Consequently, the substitution of *anusvāra* for *m* by Pāṇini 8.3.23 (*mo'nusvāraḥ*) would not occur, because [the *m*] would not be at the end of a word (*apadānta*).

If, however, by carrying over the mention of "ādi" (beginning), the augment were made to belong to the subsequent element (*parādi*), then in forms such as *vāriṇe*, the rule *gher ṅiti* (Pāṇini 7.3.111) would cause the substitution of *guṇa*; in *vahaṃlihaḥ*, the *anusvāra* would not occur; and in the case of *atisakhīni brāhmaṇakulāni* ("Brāhmaṇa families whose friends are exceedingly great"), the rule *sakhyur asaṃbuddhau* (Pāṇini 7.1.92) would result in the *vṛddhi* substitution caused by the designation *ṇit*. For that [vṛddhi] is desired even when [the word] is secondary (*gauṇa*), just like the *anaṅ* substitution in *asthān* and so on. This is clear from the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa on this sūtra. Therefore, the position of the *pūrvānta* (belonging to the preceding element) alone is maintained here.

Regarding this, the *Vārttika* states: "The letter preceding the final one [is included] in the root *masj-* for the sake of the elision of the *anuṣaṅga* and the initial of the *saṃyoga*. Examples are *magnaḥ* and *magnavān*. By the rule *oditaśca* (Pāṇini 8.2.45), there is the substitution of *ṇ* for the final consonant in the past participle (*niṣṭhā*). Because that substitution is considered *asiddha*, the *kutva* (substitution of *g*) applies. Furthermore, by the rule *masjinaśorjhali* (Pāṇini 7.1.60), the augment *num* is added. If this *num* were placed after the final vowel, then by the rule *aniditām* (Pāṇini 6.4.24), the elision of the *anuṣaṅga* would not occur. According to the tradition of the ancients, the term *anuṣaṅga* refers specifically to the nasal *n* when it serves as a penultimate (*upadhā*) element.

Now, if it is argued that once the *s* has been elided by the rule "skoḥ" (Pāṇini 8.2.29), the *n* should also be elided because it is an *upadhā* (penultimate letter)? No; for the elision of *s* by "skoḥ" is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) with respect to the elision of *l*. Furthermore, according to the view that in an assembly of many [consonants], the designation *saṃyoga* (cluster) applies only to the entire group, the elision of *s* does not even apply here. Likewise, forms such as *maṅktā* and *maṅktavyam* should also be understood as further purposes [for this analysis].

Regarding *bharji* and *marca*: the phrase "the letter preceding the final one is *mit*" is understood to carry over. From the root *bhṛjī* in the sense of "roasting" (*bhvādi* 178), when the suffix *ac* is added via the *uṇādi* rules, the augment *ūm* is applied, resulting in *bharujā*. The root *marca* in the sense of "sound" (*curādi* 1650) is a *curādi* root; from this, the *uṇādi* suffix *ipratyaya* is added with the augment *īm* according to *aciḥ* (*uṇsū* 4.588). This is established by irregular derivation (*nipātana*). For the word *bharujā* is listed among the *aṅguli*-group [of feminine bases ending in *ā*], and the word *marīci* is listed among the *bāhu*-group [of masculine bases ending in *i*].

In the *Uṇādi-sūtras*, however, the word *marīci* is derived by applying the suffix *īci* according to the rule "from the roots *mṛ* and *kaṇi*, [the suffix] *īci*" (*UṇSū* 4.519). That should be understood as an alternative method.

Regarding the rule *eca igghrasvādeśe* (*PāSū* 1.1.48): among the short vowels being prescribed as substitutes, an *ec* vowel must be replaced by an *ic* vowel. For example: *kulam atihi* becomes *atiki kulam*; *citraguḥ*; *atiriḥ*; *atinu*. Whatever needs to be said on this matter has already been stated under the rule for *eṅ* (*PāSū* 1.1.50).

The sixth [case-ending] denotes "in place" (*ṣaṣṭhī sthāne yoga*). It should be understood that when the genitive case is liable to be interpreted as having multiple types of relations, it is to be understood as signifying a relation based on "place" (*sthāna*). In the rule *asterbhūḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.52), there arises the doubt whether [the substitute *bhū*] belongs to the root *as* or is something adjacent to it; the meaning is that it is to be pronounced in its place. And "place" (*sthāna*) means "occasion" (*prasaṅga*), as in the expression: "In the place of *darbha* grass, one should spread *śara* grass."

And thus, when the utterance of *i* (the short vowel) is applicable, since the meaning results in "that which is to be uttered as *yaṇ*," relations such as proximity (*sāmīpya*) are excluded by implication. *Yoga* means relation; that [relation] is manifold, and this [word] possesses it, hence it is *yogā*. The suffix *ac* is used here in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*), according to the rule for words beginning with *arśas*. And this suffix denotes abundance (*bhūman*), because otherwise the qualifier would be rendered meaningless. Therefore, the sense obtained is "one in whom many relations are possible. Alternatively, there is a word-break as *ayoge 'ti*; the meaning is "one whose specific relation is not determined."

What is the point of [discussing] "connection" (*yoga*) or "non-connection"? [It is so that rules such as] *udupadhāyā gohaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.89) and *śāsa idaṅhaloḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.34)—in the case of *śāsa* here—do not apply. For if there were "connection by position" (*sthāneyoga*) even there, then in the place of *goḥ* and *śāsaḥ*, the substitutes *ū* and *it* would apply to the entire verbal root and to the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*), respectively; such is the direction of the argument.

Alternatively, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has its application (*yoga*) in its proper place (*sthāne*). Precisely for this reason, there is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending due to the rule of irregular formation (*nipātana*). Or else, the analysis is "that which has its application by means of the position (*sthānena*). Here too, the change to *e* [from *ai*] occurs due to irregular formation. Nor does an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) occur in rules such as *gohaḥ śāsaḥ* under these two interpretations, because paribhāṣās are intended to restrict what is unrestricted. And this is logical, because a relationship is preceded by expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*); and here, since it is determined that the genitive denotes a part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*) due to the proximity of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*), the expectancy is satisfied.

For even in the world, when one asks the way and is instructed, "In that space the right [path] is to be taken, in that [other] space the left," this instruction applies only where there is doubt due to a fork in the road, and not in the case of an unambiguous path such as a straight track; such is the general direction.
The authors of the Bhāṣya, however, say: "For *as*, *bhū*" (Pāṇini 2.4.52).

In cases such as these, even though there is the possibility of multiple relations, the relation with the *sthāna* (original locus) alone will be explained on account of the requirement of the target forms (*lakṣya*), because of its being more internal (*antaraṅga*), and because of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule "an *ādeśa* is like the original" (Pāṇini 1.1.56). Therefore, this is not the meaning of the sūtra; rather, the meaning of the sūtra is that only that which is actually uttered in the genitive case is connected with the *sthāna*, and not that which is merely implied. This is stated as: "Substitutes apply to that which is being specifically pointed out" (Paribhāṣā 12).

Therefore, the meaning of the rule *pādaḥ pat* (Pāṇini 6.4.130) is this: when a stem ends in the word *pāda*, the entire word *pāda* that constitutes a part of that stem is replaced by *pad*. However, the two rules *alo'ntyasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.52) and *ādeḥ parasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.54) are superseded by this [present rule] due to the force of its specific formulation. As for the rule *anekālśitsarvasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.55), since there is no conflict with it, this [present rule] operates in conjunction with it.

This being the case, even the meaning of the Sūtra previously stated can be easily explained by resorting to the Tantras and other sources. However, the result is clear comprehension; this is the general direction.
"In its place, the most similar [substitute occurs]. (Pāṇini 1.1.50)

Among those [substitutes] being obtained, the most similar one should be the substitute. And similarity is fourfold: by position (*sthāna*), by meaning (*artha*), by quality (*guṇa*), and by measure (*pramāṇa*). By position, for example: *sudhyupāsyaḥ* (to be worshipped by the pure), *madhvariḥ* (the honey-foe), *dhātraṃśaḥ* (the portion of Dhātṛ), *lākṛtiḥ* (the form of *la*). As for what was stated in the Bhāṣya and other works that this is otherwise established by the rule of "correspondence" (*yathāsaṃkhya*) alone—that is merely an incidental remark; for when there is a desire to express equality in meaning, correspondence is obtained. This is because there is a disparity: there are sixty-six *ik* vowels, whereas there are seven *yaṇ* consonants.

If it is argued that there is indeed equality because, from the sound *i* and the sound *yaṇ*, four [sounds] each are first presented, then how can there be the substitution of *yaṇ* for the long vowel in *sudhyupāsya*? If it is argued that this is because of its being included by the sound *i*, then how can there be the substitution of *yaṇ* for the long vowel in *sudhyupāsya*?

If it is argued that this is because of its being included by the sound *i*, then—since the third sound *ṛ* and the fourth sound *lṛ* would include one another—the consequence would be the occurrence of the letter *ra* in the word *lākṛti*, and the occurrence of the letter *la* in the word *dhātraṃśa*; furthermore, the distinction between the nasalized (*sānunāsika*) and non-nasalized (*niranunāsika*) forms of *ya* and *va* would not be established. This is the direction of the argument.

*Daityāriḥ* (the enemy of the Daityas), *śrīśaḥ* (the lord of Śrī), and so forth, are also examples here by virtue of their meaning. For example: *vātaṇḍayayuvatiḥ*. From the word *vataṇḍa*, the suffix *yañ* is applied in the sense of "descendant" according to *vataṇḍācca* (Pāṇini 4.1.108). That suffix is elided in the feminine according to *luk striyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.109). Because [the base] belongs to the *śārṅgarava* group, the suffix *ṅīn* is applied. In the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound as "she who is both a *vataṇḍī* and a young woman," the compound is formed according to *poṭāyuvati* (Pāṇini 2.1.65) and so forth.

By the rule *puṃvat karmadhāraye* (Pāṇini 6.3.42), when the masculine form is extended [to the feminine], the word *vātaṇḍya*—which denotes the offspring of the word *vataṇḍī*, itself denoting the offspring of Vataṇḍa—is derived. As for [change] by way of quality (*guṇataḥ*): in *pākaḥ* and *tyāgaḥ*, according to the rule *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.52), the unaspirated, voiceless *k* replaces the unaspirated, voiceless *c*; and the voiced, unaspirated *g* replaces the voiced, unaspirated, sonorous *j*.

According to the rule of quantity—as in *amum*, *amūn*, *amūn*—the vowel *u* is substituted [for the final syllable] by the rule *adaso'seḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.80), whereby a short vowel is replaced by a short *u* and a long vowel by a long *u*.

While the term *sthāne* (in place of) is already understood from the context, its mention again here indicates that another meaning of the sentence is also intended: namely, that among those [sounds] which are being substituted, that which is the most similar (*antaratama*) with respect to the point of articulation (*sthāna*)—that is to say, possessing a similarity based on that—is what should occur. This has been stated: "Where there is a multiform similarity, similarity of place is more powerful. Consequently, in forms such as *cetā* and *stotā*, the vowel *a*—though it possesses similarity in terms of measure (*pramāṇa*)—does not take its place.

Furthermore, the inclusion of the superlative suffix *-tamap* is itself the indicative mark for a difference in the statements (*vākya-bheda*). For if only a single sentence-meaning were intended, one would simply say "in place of an *antara*. However, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), in cases such as *vāgghariḥ*, the second [consonants] are applicable by the rule "of a sibilant (*soṣman*), a sibilant," and the third are applicable by "of a sonant (*nādavat*), a sonant"; yet, due to the inclusion of *-tamap*, they become fourth [consonants]. For these are indeed both sibilant and sonant. "Sibilance" (*ūṣmatva*) is a property of the phoneme; those accompanied by that are "sibilant" (*soṣman*).

And likewise, the *Prātiśākhya* of the Bahvṛcas states: "In each group (*varga*), the first two are voiced (*aghoṣa*), the pair [the second and third] are aspirated (*soṣman*), and the last is nasal (*anunāsika*)"; and the *Śikṣā* says: "The letters beginning with *śa* are the *ūṣmans*; the second [letters of each group] are [aspirated] by their place of articulation (*sthāna*), and the fourth [letters] by the letter *ha*. Here there are three sentences. The word *ūṣman* denotes the substratum (*dharmin*). The meaning of the first sentence is: "The letters *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ha* are the *ūṣmans*. In the phrase "by their place of articulation" (*sasthānena*), the instrumental case is used in the sense of a characteristic mark (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇe tṛtīyā*, Pāṇini 2.3.21).

The letters *ha*, *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa* are, in order, the counterparts (*sasthāna*) of the second letters of the *kha*, *cha*, *ṭha*, and *tha* groups. The meaning is that just as *ha* and the others are sibilants (*ūṣman*), so too are *kha* and the others. Although there is no sibilant that is a counterpart of the letter *pra*, its status as a sibilant must nevertheless be understood as being specifically established. By the rule "by *ha*, the fourth [letters]," the meaning is that just as *ha* is a sibilant, so too are those [fourth letters]. But if this were the case, then in words such as *iṣṭaḥ* and *uptaḥ*, by virtue of proximity (*āntarya*), a half-mora *ik* would take the place of the half-mora *yaṇ*.

If it is argued that in cases such as *dadhy atra* and *sudhy upāsyaḥ*, the *yaṇ* substitute for the short (*mātrika*) and long (*dvimātrika*) *ik* vowels would likewise be of that same duration, we say no; for neither a half-mora (*ardhamātra*) *ik* nor a consonant (*vyañjana*) of one or two morae is established in common usage or in the Veda. That which exists [in the Vedic tradition] will indeed be what occurs here.

In this commentary (*bhāṣya*), even the reading ending in the locative case, *antaratama*, is presented and then refuted. To explain: the author of the Sūtras (*sūtrakṛt*) recited it as a *saṃhitā* [compound]: *antaratamauraṇ raparaḥ*. However, the commentators (*vyākhyātāraḥ*) who divide the words may interpret it as having a locative ending. In that case, the meaning of the Sūtra would be: "The genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) [of the original sound] is to be applied to the most similar (*antaratama*) substitute (*sthānin*)," with the word *ṣaṣṭhī* being understood from the previous context.

And thus, in the rule *akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.101), the desired result is established because the genitive case in *akaḥ* is restricted (*upasaṃhāra*) to the long vowel as the most similar substitute (*antaratama*). Similarly, in the rule *vānto yi pratyaye* (Pāṇini 6.1.79), since the genitive case of the term *ecaḥ*, which is carried over (*anuvṛtta*), is restricted to the most similar substitutes *o* and *au*, the desired result is established. Otherwise, the substitution of *vānta* would apply to every *ej* vowel.

In this regard, the following objection is raised: according to the rule *iko yaṇ aci* (Pāṇini 6.1.77), the substitution of *yaṇ* would apply only to short vowels (*hrasva*) and not to long ones (*dīrgha*). For, since a single-mora (*mātrika*) sound is more proximate to a half-mora (*ardhamātra*) sound, the genitive case in the word *ikaḥ* is restricted to that [short vowel] alone. Similarly, by the rules *iko guṇavṛddhī* (Pāṇini 1.1.3) and *aco ñṇiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.115), the genitives [of *ik* and *ac*] would be restricted to those *ik* and *ac* sounds which are the most similar to the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutes; consequently, [the rules would apply] only in cases such as *netā*, *lavitā*, *nāyakaḥ*, and *lāvakaḥ*.

However, [the suffix] would not occur in cases such as *cetā*, *stotā*, *cāyakaḥ*, and *stāvakaḥ*; this is the general direction [of the argument]. Thus, since the position involving the locative case-ending is defective, it is established that only the position involving the nominative case-ending is logical.

It might be argued: "If this were the case, would not *ej* alone be replaced by *vānta*? To this they reply: In the preceding rule (*pūrvasūtra*), the application was either according to the respective order (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) or by means of the maxim regarding the closest substitute (*antaratama-paribhāṣā*). Here, however, the governing topic of meaning (*arthādhikāra*) is relied upon. The meaning of the sūtra is that the same kind of *vānta* replacement seen previously—namely, *au* in place of *o* and *av* in place of *āv*—occurs when the suffix *yi* follows. Alternatively, the term *vānta* need not even be employed.

Nor does such an over-extension apply to cases like *ceyam* or *neyam*, because the rule *kṣayyajayyau* (Pāṇini 6.1.81) is analyzed as follows: by interpreting it as a restrictive rule (*niyama*)—namely, that the suffixes occur only after the roots *kṣi* and *ji* when they have the sense of "being able" (*kaṇṭhatālavya*)—the meaning of the second sūtra is established as "only in the sense of possibility (*śakya*) do [the suffixes] apply to *kṣi* and *ji*. Consequently, it should be understood that even for these two roots, the suffixes do not apply in senses such as "deserving" (*arha*).

But even so, the form *nārī* would not be established for the word *nara* by the rule *nṛnarayor vṛddhiśca* (Pāṇini’s Gaṇasūtra 125), which is recited in the *Śārṅgarava*-group. For in that case, the *vṛddhi* prescribed in conjunction with the suffix *ṅīn* would apply to the final letter of *nara* according to the rule *alo 'ntyasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.52). And thus, since that [final vowel] would be eliminated by the elision rule *yasyeti ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148), the prescription of *vṛddhi* would be rendered useless.

Nor should it be argued that this [suffix] has the meaning of the word *nṛ*; for if that were the case, one would simply have said, "There is *nṛ* and *vṛddhi*" (*nur vṛddhiśca*). Nor should it be argued that even in the word *nara*, since the suffix occurs later, once the elision by *yasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.148) has taken place, the *vṛddhi* that occurs is not purposeless; for because it is prescribed in conjunction with the suffix (*pratyaya-sanniyoga-śiṣṭa*), the *vṛddhi* is *antaraṅga*. Now, one might ask: should the elision be set aside by the *vṛddhi* on the strength of the explicit statement (*vacana-sāmarthya*), or is it more logical to set aside the *antaraṅga-paribhāṣā* itself?

As it has been said: "And in the case of a conflict between the quality of a subordinate member and the whole, [the former prevails] because it is for the sake of that" (Jaimini Sūtra 12.2.25). Furthermore, since the rule *vāha ūṭh* (Pāṇini 6.4.132) is established as being implied by a *paribhāṣā* (technical maxim), it is more appropriate to justify the matter by subverting that very *paribhāṣā* than to subvert the elision (*lopa*) of *y* in *yasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.148), which is directly heard in the text. Thus, if one argues that the form *nārī* is established by applying the *vṛddhi* substitution after the elision has taken place, this is true—it is indeed established—but only under the interpretation that takes the locative ending (*saptamyanta*) as the word division.

For in that case, since the substitution occurs according to the closest [phonetic] similarity by nature (*prakṛti*), the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is restricted to the substitute which is the closest in place; thus, the *vṛddhi* replacement occurs for the letter *a*. However, in the alternative view where the first case (*prathamā*) is elided, the substitution occurs according to the closest similarity by way of the substitute; consequently, by the rule "of the final [al]" (*alo'ntyasya*, Pāṇini 1.1.52), it would apply to the letter *r*. Therefore, the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the form *nāgī* from the word *nara* is difficult to establish under the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

On this point, they say: the author of the Bhāṣya intended precisely the rejection of the reading of the word *nara*, as can be inferred from the fact that he refutes the alternative involving the locative case (*saptamyanta*) in his commentary. Nor should it be argued that if the suffix *ṅīṣ* were applied to the word *nara* by virtue of its denoting a genus (*jāti*), the form would have to be *nari*; for such an outcome is actually desired. Thus, it is employed in usage: "of the *kinnarīs* and the *nāgīs*. Alternatively, let the word *nara* simply remain fixed in the masculine gender.

And so, where is there any over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)? In the case of the aforementioned usage, the suffix *ṅīṣ* will apply by virtue of the rule for feminine forms derived from connection with a male (*puṃyoga*), since that [suffix] would be unavoidable even under the alternative formulation (*anyāsa*). Alternatively, in the rule *nṛnarayoḥ* (Gaṇasūtra 125), the word *ataḥ* (from the rule *ajādyataṣṭāp*, Pāṇini 4.1.4) is understood to carry over. By the force of this grammatical carry-over (*anuvṛtti*), that [word *ataḥ*] is transformed into the genitive case and connects with the word *nara-* in a non-co-referential relationship (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), but not with the word *nṛ-*, because that would be impossible. Therefore, the form *nārī* is established.

In this regard, the following must be said: Granted that the word *nara* may be rejected; however, how could such a statement be possible according to the view of the author of the Sūtras, who reads [the rule] as *nṛnarayoḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.87)? Nor can it be argued that *narī* alone is intended, for that would result in the futility of including the word *nara* within the Sūtra that prescribes the Vṛddhi substitute. Furthermore, an attempt to justify this by means of the word *ataḥ* being understood from a previous rule is also strained, as it necessitates resorting to partial recurrence (*ekadeśānuvṛtti*) and the modification of case endings (*vibhaktivipariṇāma*).

Furthermore, "nṛnarayoḥ" is recited in the *Gaṇapāṭha* (under Gaṇa 125), but not in the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*. Moreover, in that *Gaṇa*, the word "ataḥ" is not the subject under discussion. Likewise, in the rule "śārṅgaravādyañaḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.73) and so forth, one would have to bring to mind the *Gaṇasūtra* by implication and then state the connection of "ataḥ" there; this is clearly more cumbersome. Therefore, it should be resolved as follows: "nara" ending in 'r' is an imitation of [the form] with the vowel 'a' elided, [yielding] "naraḥ". Then, "nuśca narasyeva" is a *dvandva* compound.

Furthermore, the suffix *ṅīn* is applied because [the word] is recited in the *cādgaṇa*. Alternatively, in the rule "In its place, the most similar" (*sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ*), the author of the Sūtras intended a twofold division by means of *tantra* (simultaneous application). Even in the view that the Sūtra is superfluous (*pratyākhyāna*) by resorting to common worldly maxims according to the method stated in the Bhāṣya, the exclusion of the non-most-similar occurs in both ways: from the perspective of the original element (*prakṛti*) and from the perspective of the substitute (*ādeśa*). In the opinion of the Sūtrakāra, this [exclusion] is based on explicit statement (*vācanikī*); however, for the Bhāṣyakāra, it is established by logic (*nyāyasiddha*)—this is another matter.

And thus, [rules] such as "vānto yi" (Pāṇini 6.1.79) and "nṛnarayoḥ" (Gaṇasūtra 125) are all perfectly established. For this very reason, even Haradatta—who, in the fourth [chapter], establishes the form "nārī" by relying on the exclusion of the most similar substitute (*antaratama*) for the original element (*sthānin*)—is not contradicted. Only the objection of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) remains in cases such as "iko yaṇaci" (Pāṇini 6.1.77).

And that [objection] is to be resolved by relying on the non-eternality (*anityatā*) of the substitution of the most similar (*sthānin* → *antaratama*), whether based on an explicit statement (*vācanikī*)—as indicated by rules such as *lvādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.44)—or on reasoning (*nyāyamūlikā*), such as *pvādīnāṃ hrasvaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.80); this is the general direction.

The manner in which the Sūtra is rejected is now stated: For when it is said, "Let everyone sit down," the wise sit together with the wise, the brave with the brave, and the poets with the poets, but not in a confused mixture. What need is there for further elaboration? Even among animals, such an order is observed: a cow runs toward a herd of cows, and a horse toward horses. Therefore, since the meaning of the first sentence is obtained from common worldly usage itself, the Sūtra need not be commenced for that purpose.

Thus, the principle that "proximity by position (*sthāna*) is more powerful" (Pāṇini 1.4.106) is also established from common worldly experience. For instance, when two horses or two oxen that have frequently been seen together are joined with other members of their own species, they are observed to seek one another out based solely on the equality of their position, even while disregarding similarities in qualities such as leanness or paleness. Since this is thus established through worldly experience, what is the purpose of a formal statement?

*uraṇ raparaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.51): An *aṇ* substitute in place of an *ṛ*-vowel shall be followed by the letter *r* (*rapara*) at the very stage of its application. When thirty sounds homogeneous with the letter *ṛ* are presented, one must distinguish that, according to the maxim *sthāne'ntaratamaḥ* (the most similar substitute takes the place), an *aṇ* having the sound *r* is followed by *r*, whereas an *aṇ* having the sound *l* is followed by *l*. Thus, [we derive] *kṛṣṇārddhiḥ* and *tavalkāraḥ*. However, the textual reading "an *aṇ* in place of both *ṛ* and *ḷ*" is both inconsistent and misleading, as it would give rise to the error of assuming a correspondence based on numerical order (*yathāsaṃkhya*), since such a correspondence cannot be established merely through phonetic similarity.

For there are not two [distinct] words in the Sūtra; moreover, in terms of meaning, there is certainly no equality [between them]. Now, if sequential correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhya*) is not intended here, then what is the purpose of specifically mentioning both within the *vṛtti*? Furthermore, a *dvandva* compound is difficult to justify, whether by analyzing it as "from *ā* to *ā*, [the place of] *r* and *l*" (*ā ca ā ca ralau ṛloḥ sthānam*), or by analyzing it as "*u* and *ū*, [the place of] *ṛ* and *ḷ*" (*uśca ūśca ṛlor iti*). For that [compound] is sublated by the rule for *ekaśeṣa*: "Even of dissimilar forms, if they have the same meaning... (*Kātyāyana-vārttika*).

Just as in the case of the word *citragu* when it refers to "one who possesses brindled cows," one might somehow justify its application by resorting to *lakṣaṇā* (indication) for the sake of maintaining grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*), and then arriving at the primary meaning (*śakyārtha*) through *lakṣitalakṣaṇā* (indication based on indication); however, such a justification should be accepted only by those who have faith in the text. This is the direction of the argument.

In this regard, four possible positions (pakṣas) are conceivable: The first position is that "in place of *u*, *aṇ* followed by *r* should occur"; thus, *aṇ* qualified by being followed by *r* (*rapara*) is prescribed. The second position is that there is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) stating that when there is the contingency of *am*, *āman*, or *aṇ* in place of *u*, it must be *aṇ* alone; and by means of a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*), the quality of being followed by *r* (*raparatva*) is prescribed for that *aṇ*. The third position is that having referred back (*anūdya*) to that *aṇ* which occurs in place of *u*, its quality of being followed by *r* (*raparatva*) is prescribed.

The fourth [position] holds that the substitution of *ra* for the final element (*raparatva*) is prescribed only in the state of *prasaṅga* (the occasion for application). Regarding this, in the first alternative, since the *aṇ* is prescribed when the acute (*udātta*) and other accents have not yet been applied, it would sublate them; for there is no scope left for them once they have been excluded. Thus, the formulation of the rule would be: "When a substitute occurs for that which is designated by the genitive case, it shall be the most similar (*antaratama*); however, for the vowel *ṛ*, the *aṇ* shall be followed by *ra*. Consequently, there would be a fault regarding the acute, grave, circumflex, and nasalized vowels.

For instance, in the case of *kṛtiḥ*, the rule *ṇ-nityādir nityam* (Pāṇini 6.1.197) would be set aside, and the *ṛ*-vowel would instead be followed by an *aṇ* suffix with a following *r*. Similarly, in *prakṛtam* and *prahṛtam*, once the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member is applied by the rule *gatiranantaraḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.49), it would subvert both the low-pitched accent (*anudātta*) prescribed by *śeṣanighāta* and the circumflex accent (*svarita*) prescribed by *udāttādanudāttasya* (Pāṇini 7.4.66).

Likewise, in the case of *nṝn pāhi*, although the long vowel of the same class (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*) would be possible by the indicatory power (*jñāpaka*) of the rule *nṝn pe* (Pāṇini 7.3.10), the *aṇ* [substitute] followed by *r* (*rapara*) would occur, overriding the nasalized vowel (*anunāsika*). Furthermore, in the cases of *karttā* and *kārakaḥ*, since there is no restrictive rule stating that when *aṇ* occurs in place of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* it must be the letter *a* alone, the letter *i* or the letter *u* might occasionally occur instead.

Furthermore, in the case of those substitutions such as *it* and *ut* that are explicitly prescribed by rules like "ṛta id dhātoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.101) and "udoṣṭhyapūrvasya" (Pāṇini 7.1.102), the substitution of *r* for the final element would not occur. However, in the second interpretation, there is no fault regarding *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* operations; for when both an *aṇ* and a non-*aṇ* are applicable, the restrictive rule "only an *aṇ*" ensures the correct forms such as *kartā* and *kārakaḥ*.

Now, in the case of a short vowel as the substitute, all *vṛddhi* vowels would be equally proximate (*anantaratama*); however, in the case of a long vowel—as in *tārakaḥ* and so on—all [vowels] are equally proximate in terms of their measure (*pramāṇataḥ*). Thus, since there is no distinction, if all *vṛddhi* vowels were to apply in both cases, let there be a restrictive rule (*niyama*). But in the case of *guṇa*, as in *karttā* and so on, only a one-mora (*mātrika*) vowel is obtained; whereas in *taritā* and so on, only a two-mora *eṅ* vowel is obtained. Consequently, since there is no possibility of application for either an *aṇ* or a non-*aṇ* vowel, the restrictive rule does not operate, and thus in the case of long vowels, only *eṅ* would result.

In the case of short vowels (*hrasva*), even though the letter *a* is present, it shall not be followed by *ra*. For while the first rule restricts [the substitute] to being simply a vowel (*aṇ eva*), this second rule prescribes for that same [substitute] the property of having *ra* as its subsequent element (*raparatva*). If it is argued that there is indeed a fault in this regarding the *guṇa* substitution, [we reply: no, because the rule *uraṇ raparaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.51) overrides the application of *raparatva* in the context of *guṇa* substitution, thereby subverting the *sthānentaratama-paribhāṣā* (the paribhāṣā concerning the closest substitute in place), which otherwise finds scope in rules such as *cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.52) and is already fulfilled by the prescription of *vṛddhi* substitution.

Therefore, it is established that in the second alternative there is no fault regarding *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*; however, there would certainly be a fault regarding the acute (*udātta*) accents and so forth, as well as regarding the *it*-augment and others prescribed by specific rules (*pratipadokta*). In the third alternative, however, there is no fault regarding the acute accents and so forth, because those respective rules—being refined by the *antaratama* (most similar) paribhāṣā—prescribe the substitution of the *ṛ*-vowel itself. Furthermore, there is no fault in cases such as *kirati*; yet, regarding *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, there is indeed a fault.

To explain: although forms such as *karttā* are established through immediate proximity (*āntarya*)—wherein the substitute is a vowel-matrix (*mātrika*), a vowel-matrix, and the substitution of *r* for *a*—nevertheless, in cases such as *taritā*, only *eṅ* would result. Furthermore, since [the rule] would apply without distinction to all three types of *vṛddhi*, when the substitution of *r* for *a* is made because the vowel *a* is an *aṇ*, forms such as *phārakaḥ* and *tārakaḥ* are indeed established; however, undesirable forms such as *kāyakaḥ* and *tāvakaḥ* would also follow.

As for that which was resolved by the authors of the Bhāṣya on the previous sūtra by resorting to this position—namely, "the very absence of immediate succession is their immediate succession"—and as for what was stated there by the authors of the Vārttika—"or it is a conjunction like [the case of] the lost horse and the burnt chariot"—both of these should be understood as being merely optional.

For instance, when it is examined who is the "nearest" (*āntaratama*) for that which is delimited by the class *ṛtvij*, and for whom that which is delimited by the class *atvija* is [the nearest], then the proximity between these two is determined solely by the absence of a corresponding correlate. Indeed, there is no statement by the three sages (Pāṇini, Kātyāyana, and Patañjali) that proximity is fourfold; on the contrary, from the Bhāṣya—"of a sibilant (*soṣman*), a sibilant"—and from the Vṛtti, it is understood that there is indeed no fixed rule. And thus, even the maxim of the "lost horse and burnt chariot" applies only to an examination delimited by class.

If, however, the examination is conducted by prioritizing the individual phonemes (*vyakti*), then this position is faulty according to the method already stated. Accordingly, the *Vārttika* on this *Sūtra* states: "If it is argued that the *aṇ* in the place of [the vowels] is followed by *r*, then there would be no apprehension of the vowel *a* in the case of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. Furthermore, under this view, it would be difficult to establish the distinction as to where the *repha* (the sound *r*) follows and where the *lakāra* (the sound *l*) follows.

Even if one were to argue that there is no mutual exchange because of the rule "the agent is independent" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 1.4.54), and that there is no optionality because of the introduction of the rules "ru for *yaṅ*" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 8.2.20) and "optionally before *ac*" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 8.2.21), there would still necessarily be a burden of comprehension (*pratipatti-gaurava*).

To establish that the *repha* belongs to the prior limit (*pūrvāntatā*), one would have to carry forward the term *anta* from the sūtra *ādyantau* (Pāṇini 1.1.46)—which is a part of a compound—and explain its connection with the *repha*, which serves as an attribute for the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) in the expression *rapara*; thus, there is great difficulty and labor. However, we shall explain that this is not required in the fourth alternative. Therefore, because it is free from defects, the fourth alternative alone is adopted. It should be established in this manner:

Two instances of the word *sthāna* recur here; one is for the purpose of securing the connection with "place" (*sthāna*) even when there is a restatement (*anuvāda*) such as "the *aṇ* in place of [something]," while the second is for the purpose of prescribing the time [of occurrence], meaning that it becomes followed by *r* or *l* precisely at the stage of occasion (*prasaṅga*). Although the word *sthāna* in the rule *sthānentaratamaḥ* refers to the "places of articulation" such as the palate (*tālu*), it should be understood here as referring to "occasion," by virtue of relying on the governing topic of "word" (*śabda-adhikāra*).

And thus, since at the very stage when *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are about to apply, the *aṇ* [substitutes] have already become followed by *r*, they do not replace the nearest (*antaratama*) vowels *eṅ* and *aiC* on the basis of phonetic similarity (*pramāṇataḥ*), but rather only the nearest *aṇ* on the basis of positional similarity (*sthānataḥ*); therefore, there is no fault whatsoever. In the same way, it should be understood that even in the rules for accents (*udātta* etc.), the long *ṛ* occurs because of its positional proximity, and not *ar* or *ir*. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasanga*) of the substitute being a replacement for the whole (*sarvādeśa*) in forms such as *karttā* due to having more than one *al* (the *t* and *ā*), because the rule is established through sequential order (*ānupūrvyeṇa*).

For instance, *raparatva* (the substitution of *r*), which functions by depending upon [a substitute] having a single *ṛ* as its locus (*ṛsthānitva*), does not cause it to become a substitute for the whole (*sarvādeśatā*), because that would contradict its own basis (*upajīvyavirodha*). Accordingly, there is a *vārttika* on the preceding rule: "But there is the undesirable consequence of [the substitute] being a replacement for the whole because it has more than one [indicatory] letter (*anekāltvāt*). Or rather, this is not so; since the possession of more than one letter depends upon that [substitution], there is no obstruction to the substitution of the vowel *ṛ*."

What is the purpose of including the mention of *an*? It is so that the substitution of *r* for the final element (*raparatva*) does not apply to *rīṅ*, *riṅ*, and others. [Otherwise, one would derive] *mātrīyati* and *kriyate*. Furthermore, after *tataḥ*, when the suffix *ḍhak* is applied, the elision (*lopa*) would also be followed by *r* (*rapara*). [If that were the case,] because the rule [Pāṇini 1.1.52] would otherwise become redundant, it would—by virtue of its own capacity (*sāmarthya*)—sublate the rule regarding the substitution of an element for the final letter (*alontyavidhi*) and result in a replacement of the entire stem. Likewise, in the case of *hotāpotārau*, if *anaṅ* were also followed by *r* (*raparatva*), and the final consonant cluster (*saṃyogāntalopa*) were then applied, the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) would not occur because that [cluster-elision] would be considered non-existent (*asiddha*). This is the general direction of the argument.

Now, if it is asked why the *a* in *riṅādiṣu* is not followed by *ra* (i.e., why it is not *rapara*), the answer is: because it is not a substitute (*ādeśa*). For the status of being a substitute rests upon the entire complex (*samudāya*). Nor should it be argued that in forms such as *kṛṣṇarddhiḥ*, there would likewise be no substitution of *ra* because the preceding and following elements together constitute the locus of substitution (*sthānitva*); for by the use of the dual number in the term *pūrvaparau*, it is understood that the status of being the locus of substitution belongs only to those two constituent parts. Precisely for this reason, in rules concerning *bhinnādi* and others, the singular marker *eka-* was employed so that there might not be two distinct substitutes for the two different loci of substitution, just as there is [only one] substitution for *na*.

Therefore, the status of being a substitute (*sthānitva*) belongs to the vowel *ṛ* as well. As it has been said: "That which occurs in the place of both receives its designation from either one" (*Bhāṣya*). Consequently, it is established that even in the case of a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*), the substitution of *r* (*raparatva*) takes place.

It might be argued as follows: "According to the method stated, even for the substitution of *u* by the rule *ṛta ut* (Pāṇini 6.1.11), there would be the status of being followed by *r* (*raparatvam*). Consequently, when *ru* is substituted for the *s* of the case-ending, and the preceding *r* is elided by *rori* (Pāṇini 8.3.14), a long vowel would result by *ḍhralope* (Pāṇini 6.3.111), leading to the forms *mātūḥ* and *pitūḥ*. This is not so. Because the substitution of *ru* is considered *asiddha* (unestablished) [for the purposes of the subsequent rules], the *s* is elided by *rātsasya* (Pāṇini 8.2.24), and the form is established through the *visarga* of the *r*.

But surely, in this case, the substitution of *ṣ* would occur in the word *mātuḥkāryam*, according to the rule *idudupadhasyacīpratyayasya* (Pāṇini 8.3.41). Nor should it be argued that this [visarga] is exclusively the visarga of a suffix (*pratyaya*), because although the vowel *a* is a constituent part of the suffix, it is not itself the suffix; therefore, its substitute (*ḥ*) is all the more not a suffix. To this it is replied: Since the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) resulting from *ṛta ut* (Pāṇini 6.1.111) is included within the scope of the term "subsequent portion" (*parādi*), the designation of "suffix" (*pratyayasañjñā*) applies to that which ends in *s*. Thus, when the *s* is elided, [the condition for the rule is met].

The designation *pratyaya* (suffix) applies only to what remains [of the original element], either because of the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) regarding that which is modified in one part, or because of the inclusion of the term *ādeśa* (substitute) in the rule *sthānivad ādeśaḥ*. For this very reason, it has been stated that when the *yakāra* of the *yaṅ* suffix is elided, the *akāra* retains the designation *pratyaya*. Thus, the prohibition of the *ṣatva* suffixation by the rule *apratyayasya* is established.

Nor should it be argued that even if the substitute occupies the position of a portion of the suffix (*pratyayāvayavasthānika*), the change to *ṣ* would still necessarily occur because it does not occupy the position of the suffix itself (*pratyayasthānikatvābhāva*). For when the term "not a suffix" (*apratyayasya*) is restated as a governing rule (*anuvāda*), the technical maxim (*paribhāṣā*) [which restricts the meaning of the genitive] does not apply; thus, the connection with the "position" (*sthāna*) is difficult to establish. This is because the relationship between part and whole (*avayavāvayavibhāva*) can indeed constitute the meaning of the genitive. [Objection: But surely "not a suffix" is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*). In that case, since the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is included by virtue of being a prior-final element (*pūrvāntatva*), the change to *ṣ* would certainly occur.

Furthermore, even in the view that this is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation), grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible; since non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) is improper, the meaning of the sentence would be: "Let there be the substitution of *ṣ* for that *visarga* which is not a suffix. Consequently, in examples such as *agniḥ karoti*, because the *visarga* possesses the status of being a suffix by virtue of the rule of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute behaves like the original), let there be no substitution of *ṣ*.

If it is argued that [the rule] would indeed apply in cases such as *mātuḥkāryam*, here is the truth: the inclusion of the word *brātuṣputra* in the *kaska*-group (*kaskādi*) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that, by virtue of the rule for single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) formation, there shall be no *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) after what has been produced by that rule. Alternatively, it is precisely the non-co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) of the negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) that is being indicated. As for the Bhāṣya statement: "The suffix is elided; [there is *ṣatva*] of the *s* after *r*."

As for the commentary composed by Kaiyaṭa—"Once *ut* has been applied, only the remaining *s* is designated as an affix (*pratyaya*), and that [affix] is elided"—both of these points are to be considered further. Here, although under the view "it is established because of the substitution of *r* for *ṛ*" (*siddhaṃ tu prasaṅge raparatvāt*) there is no suspicion at all regarding [the *ṛ*] not being a part of the suffix (*abhakta*) since it is prescribed in the form of *ar*, *ār*, and so on, nevertheless, following the method stated in the preceding sūtra (*samprayoge vā*), the Bhāṣya considers three alternative views based on the third position.

In that regard, under the view that [the substitute] does not take the place of the whole (*abhaktatva-pakṣa*) and under the view that it begins with the subsequent letter (*parāditva-pakṣa*), when *urat* substitution and *rapara* substitution have been applied in forms such as *vavre*, the *repha* would not be eliminated by the rule *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*; for by that rule, only a non-initial consonant (*anādi-hal*) which is a constituent of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) is eliminated. Therefore, the summary is this: by carrying forward the mention of "end" (*anta-grahaṇa*), the view that it is a prior-end (*pūrvānta-pakṣa*) alone is established here. [This is governed by] *alo'ntyasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.52).

Whatever is stated regarding that which is indicated by a genitive of locus (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*) should be understood as applying to the final [element] of that [locus], such as in *atalaḥ* (in place of *at*). For example: *tyadādīnām aḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.102), resulting in *saḥ* and *yaḥ*. Why "genitive of locus"? Consider: *ārddhadhātukasyeṭ* (Pāṇini 7.2.35); [if it were not a genitive of locus,] the augment *iṭ* would not necessarily be placed before the *ṛ* of *tṛc*. This is obtained through the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā* (Pāṇini 1.1.49).

What is the purpose of the term *ala*? It is so that the substitution of *d* prescribed by the rule *vasusraṃsu* (Pāṇini 8.2.72)—which is formulated under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of *padasya* (Pāṇini 8.1.16)—should not apply to the final syllable of a word ending in *ad*, as in the example *paramānaḍudbhyām*. By this [use of *ala*], those who explain that substitutes consisting of *al* (vowels) should apply to the final [sound] by relying on the form *alaḥ* (nominative plural) are refuted; for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the rule applying even to the final syllable of a word. Furthermore, if this were the case, one would simply have composed the rule as *alantyasya* for the sake of brevity.

Furthermore, by the rules "arurmanaścakṣuścetorahorajasāṃ lopaḥ" (Pāṇini 5.4.51) and "pādaśatasya saṃkhyādeḥ" (Pāṇini 5.4.1), there would be elision [of the final syllable], and in the case of the suffix *ḍhak*, this elision would apply as a total replacement (*sarvādeśa*). Consequently, forms such as *virajīkaroti* would not be established.

As for the argument that, under the view that *ala* is in the nominative plural (*jas*), the mention of *anekāl* in the rule *anekālśitsarvasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.55) need not be made—thereby describing a simplification—that too is incorrect. For even under the view that it is in the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*), the mention of *anekāl* could be dispensed with by relying on the restrictive interpretation of *ṅicca* (Pāṇini 1.1.53), which would mean that only a substitute ending in *ṅit* that is *anekāl* replaces the final letter, whereas one that is not *ṅit* does not. In reality, however, the mention of *anekāl* must indeed be made in both views.

Otherwise, in the case of fifth-case (ablative) specifications such as *ato bhisa ais* (Pāṇini 7.1.9), even a substitute consisting of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*) would replace only the first letter of the subsequent element. If the term *anekāl* were not included [in Pāṇini 1.1.55], then by virtue of its higher status (*paratva*), it would be a total replacement (*sarvādeśa*). For this very reason, the rule was not formulated as *tasmādityuttarasyādeḥ*. Indeed, there are two exceptions to the rule *alo'ntyasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.52): namely, *ādeḥ parasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.54) and *anekālśitsarvasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.55).

In that regard, the scope for the first [rule] is: "īdāsaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.83) and "bahorlopaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.158), as in "āsīnaḥ" and "bhūyān". The scope for the second [rule] is: "asterbhūḥ" (Pāṇini 2.4.52), and so forth.

Therefore, because [the rule] "ato bhisa ais" (Pāṇini 7.1.9) and others follow later in the sequence, their status as a universal substitute (*sarvādeśa*) is established for forms such as *rāmaiḥ*. Nor should it be argued that forms like *rāmaiḥ* must be derived by carrying over the word *al* (in the nominative plural) from the rule "ādeḥ parasya" (Pāṇini 1.1.54); for if that were the case, forms such as *bhūyān* and *bhūmā* would result in being unestablished. Thus, the principle of the operation being at the end has been explained, as it is consistent with the subsequent context beginning with "ṅicca" (Pāṇini 1.1.53).

Alternatively, this is a restatement of the genitive case itself: "That genitive which is used in the sense of 'in place of' should be understood as referring to the final phoneme. On this view, the meaning of Pāṇini’s sūtra *ṅicca* (Pāṇ. 1.1.53) is: "Wherever a substitute beginning with *ṅ* is prescribed, the genitive [there] refers to the final phoneme. The same applies to subsequent rules as well. Thus ends *ṅicca*.

Furthermore, this [rule] would apply to that which has more than one letter (*anekāl*) as its final element, as in *dadhnā* and *dadhne*. However, since this rule finds its scope of application in cases like *anaṅ* and others where the *ṅit*-markers serve no other purpose, it is superseded by the subsequent rule, *anekālśitsarvasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.55), when *tātaṅ* follows. If it is argued that a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) between a general rule (*utsarga*) and an exception (*apavāda*) is improper, that is true; nevertheless, even in the case of *tātaṅ* being a replacement for the whole word (*sarvādeśa*), a purpose is conceivable in the form of the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* [substitutions].

To that extent, this exception (*apavāda*), having proceeded with some delay, has attained equality with the general rule (*utsarga*) regarding this specific subject; thus, a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) is justified. Alternatively, since the term *ṅit* is prescribed immediately after "eru" (Pāṇini 3.4.86), when it could have simply been stated as "tihyostāt," the inclusion of *ṅit* serves solely for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*; hence, the occurrence of the conflict is established.

Or, let there be no conflict at all, yet the substitution of the whole (*sarvādeśa*) follows from the fact that the stated purpose of prohibiting *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* would be untenable without such a total substitution.

*Ādeḥ parasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.54): That which is prescribed for what follows [an element] should be understood as applying to its initial [sound]. *Īdāsaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.83): Here, the rule *Tasmāditsuttarasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.67) applies. By this, the vowel *ī* is substituted at the beginning; thus, *āsīnaḥ*.

*anekāl śitsarvasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.55): An *ādeśa* consisting of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*) and one beginning with *śit* shall replace the whole [of the original]. Regarding the rules *asterbhūḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.52) [resulting in] *bhavitā*, and *idama is* (Pāṇini 5.3.3) [resulting in] *itaḥ*: although the desired result is established by the restriction *ṅicca* (Pāṇini 1.1.53), it has been stated that the mention of *anekāl* is for the purpose of preventing a conflict with an exception (*apavāda*). As for the example of *śit* given by the authors of the *Vṛtti* under *jaśśasoḥ śiḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.20), that is questionable; for without total replacement (*sarvādeśatā*), the status of being *śit* cannot even be obtained there.

Furthermore, since being a substitute for the whole (sarvādeśatā) is established precisely by the fact of having multiple phonemes (*anekāl*) according to the sequence [of rules], as in the case of *ṇal*, *ḍā*, *śi*, and so forth. To explain: when *ṇal*, *ḍā*, *śi*, and the others are substitutes for the whole, they are designated as "suffixes" (*pratyaya*). From that, the designation "it" (*itsaṃjñā*) applies because they begin with a suffix-initial. Then follows elision (*lopa*). Consequently, even though they possess the property of having a single phoneme (*ekāltva*), there is no loss of their status as substitutes for the whole, because that would result in a contradiction with what they depend upon (*upajīvya-virodha*). For this very reason, it has been stated that in forms such as *kartā*, there is no substitution for the whole.

Since forms such as *iś* and others are already established as being substitutes for the whole (sarvādeśa) simply by virtue of having multiple phonemes (*anekāl*) due to the suffixal marker *ś*, the explicit mention of *śit* (in Pāṇini’s rule Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.1.55) is for the purpose of making known the principle: "The status of having multiple phonemes is not caused by a suffixal marker" (*nānubandhakṛtamanekāltvam*). By this, it should be understood that rules such as *diva ut* (6.1.131) and *arvaṇastrasau* (6.4.127) do not result in substitution for the whole. But how can this serve as a *jñāpaka* (indirect indicator)? For the mention of *śit* has its own legitimate purpose (*caritārthatva*), namely, to account for the rule *ghvasoreddhāvabhyāsalopaśca* (6.4.119).

If it is argued that the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that in the rule *lopaś*, the term is split as *lopaḥ* [ca] *śit*, and although the status of being *śit* is applied there [to the suffix], it remains unused in that context and instead bears fruit upon the named element (*saṃjñin*), just as the *ṭi*-status of *ṅamuṭ* does; this is true under the view that "the markers (*anubandha*) are non-exclusive" (*anekāntā anubandhāḥ*). However, according to the view that "the markers are exclusive" (*ekāntā*), the aforementioned indicator (*jñāpaka*) is necessary, because under the former view, the statement "the fact of having multiple phonemes is not caused by a marker" (*nānubandhakṛtamanekāltvam*) would otherwise lack purpose, and thus the split *lopaś* is intended for that specific purpose. Under the view that they are exclusive, the indicator is indispensable in the manner described.

In the rule *ghvasoḥ*, however, the division is simply *lopaḥ*. Since the rule *lopo yi* (Pāṇini 6.4.118) already prescribes the elision (*lopa*) when followed by *yi*, the fact that the term *lopa* is repeated here with force indicates that this elision is a universal substitute (*sarvādeśa*). According to the view of the Vārttikakāra, however, this is established by the principle *nānarthake 'lontyavidhiḥ* (Paribhāṣā 105). Nor is this the scope of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "not in the case of non-verbal modifications" (*na cānabyāsavikāreṣu*), because elision (*lopa*) is not a modification (*vikāra*). For a modification consists in the attainment of another form.

For example: *bhṛñām it* (Pāṇini 7.4.76), *arttipipartyośca* (Pāṇini 7.4.77), and so forth. For this very reason, in the *Paspaśā*, elision (*lopa*) is mentioned separately from modification (*vikāra*): "One who knows elision, augments, and the modification of phonemes will indeed preserve the Veda. And it has been stated by Kaiyaṭa on the rule *pṛṣodarādīni* (Pāṇini 6.3.109): "There are two others: the modification of phonemes and their destruction. In reality, however, the designation *it* occurs precisely at the stage of instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*), because it is internal (*antarahgata*).

Therefore, the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that even though [phonemes] perish as soon as they are uttered, they bring about their effect only when they exist as being remembered (*smṛyamāṇa*). This is made clear by Kaiyaṭa in the commentary on the subsequent sūtra. Consequently, in rules such as *diva ut* (Pāṇini 6.1.131) and *arvaṇas tṛ* (Pāṇini 6.4.127), because [the substitutes *ut* and *tṛ*] consist of a single phoneme (*ekāl*), there is no possibility of them being a replacement for the whole (*sarvādeśatā*), even under the view that [the substitute] consists of a single phoneme (*ekāntapakṣa*).

And thus, because of the rule *nānubandhakṛtamanekāltvam* (Paribhāṣā 6), let there first be the elision of the *n* in *īś*—which is derived from *kim* and *idam* by *idaṃ kimorīśakī* (Pāṇini 5.2.40)—due to the power of the pronunciation of the letter *ś*. As for what Haradatta stated—that even if the substitution of the whole word (*sarvādeśa*) were to occur, the letter *ś* would not receive the designation *it* because there would be no purpose for it—this is incorrect, because the very elision of the *n* is the purpose. Nor is the pronunciation of the *ś* redundant, as it has served its function by effecting the status of being a substitute for the whole word; such is the direction of the argument.

Therefore, the intention of the author of the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya here must be considered: having read "anekāl śit" in this context and carrying forward [the words] "antyasya" and "ādeḥ," when there is a prohibition of the two types of subsequent application (anusaṃhāra), it would have been possible not to state "sarvasya."
Thus ends the seventh section (āhnika) of the first quarter (pāda) of the first chapter (adhyāya) in the venerable Śabdakaustubha.

*sthānivadādeśo’nalvidhau* (Pāṇini 1.1.56): An *ādeśa* (substitute) obtains the grammatical operation of the *sthānin* (original element) and causes it to function as such, provided the operation does not concern an *al* (vowel or consonant). This is because the sentence-meaning obtained from the suffix *-vat* following a word in the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is "it behaves in the same manner as the *sthānin*. When an extension (*atideśa*) is sought because a grammatical rule (*upadeśa*) would otherwise fail to apply due to a deficiency in form, that form must not be unique to the *sthānin*’s *al*. [Example: *āvadhiṣīṣṭa*. Here, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), which is prescribed for the root *han*, also applies to the root *vadh* by virtue of this extension. *Āvadhiṣīṣṭa*.

In this context, the ātmanepada suffix prescribed for the root *han* also applies to the root *vadhi* by way of extended application (*atideśa*). For in the rule *āṅo yamahanaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.28), the condition of having a *liṭ* affix (*liṭ-lakāra*) is not required. In forms such as *rāmāya*, although the condition of being followed by an affix beginning with *yañ* is relied upon when the lengthening (*dīrgha*) prescribed by *supi ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.102) is to be applied, nevertheless, the non-application of *supi ca* is not triggered by the absence of that [yañ-beginning affix] condition; this is because the substitute *yā* itself begins with *yañ*. Rather, the non-application of the original instruction (*upadeśa*) is due to the deficiency of the *yus* affix.

Although the term *e* occurs here [in P. 1.1.43] as *ec-ih-a-li*, nevertheless that *al* is not unique [to this rule], because [the designation *sup*] rests upon the whole [stem] such as *bhyām* and so on. And this has been stated by resorting to the view that the application of rules is determined by their effect (*kāryakāla-pakṣa*). However, according to the view that the application is determined by the original enunciation (*yathoddeśa-pakṣa*), since the designation *sup* is also scripturally authoritative, it is that very [designation] which is extended. Consequently, the long vowel [of the stem] is established by the original instruction itself; thus there is no difficulty whatsoever. By this, the augment *iṭ* in forms such as *aruditām* and *aruditm* is also explained, because there too the extension of the designation *sārvadhātuka* is possible. This is the general direction.

Regarding this, the authors of the *Vṛtti* state that the purpose [of the term *dhātu*] is for the sake of *dhātu*, *aṅga*, *kṛt*, *taddhita*, indeclinables (*avyaya*), nominal endings (*suptiṅ*), and substitutes (*ādeśa*). One should not be misled into thinking that this is an exhaustive enumeration; rather, it is merely an illustration of the direction. For instance, in the rule *cleḥ sic* (Pāṇini 3.1.44), since an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix is intended to follow, the root (*dhātu*) is mentioned separately from the stem (*aṅga*). Because it is a root, root-suffixes apply—as in *bhavyam*. [In the case of *kena*, *kābhyām*, *kaiḥ*,] because they are stems (*aṅga*), there occur the substitution of *in* for *at*, lengthening, and the absence of *is*. As for *kṛt* suffixes: *prakṛtya*, *kṛtvā*.

The augment *tuk* is applied by the rule *hrasvasya piti kṛti* (Pāṇini 6.1.71). Because it ends in a *taddhita* suffix, the form *adyatana* receives the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) by virtue of ending in such a suffix. Regarding *kad-aśva*, they say that because it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) by the principle of "as if occupying the original position" (*sthānivadbhāva*), it takes the original accent of the first member of the compound according to the rule for indeclinables. However, this is questionable, as the point is already covered by the maxim of "the most similar substitute" (*sthānentaratama-paribhāṣā*). As for the example *adho'dhaḥ*, it is possible because the doubling in the eighth book (*aṣṭādhyāyī*) consists of reduplication in place of the original; yet even there, the result [of the accent] is difficult to state.

Therefore, "adho'dhaḥ kāmaḥ" should be cited as an example. By the rule *ataḥ kṛkami* (Pāṇini 8.3.46), the substitution of *s* would otherwise apply; however, because [the word] is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), that substitution is excluded. As for the example "prastutya" given in the Vṛtti as an instance of an indeclinable substitute, that is questionable, because the suffix *-ktvā* alone is not an indeclinable. This is because the principle of *tadantavidhi* (application of a rule to a word ending in a specified element) has been established as a settled doctrine throughout the entire grammatical system.

Nor should it be argued that this [rule] applies with the intention that "all [substitutes] are substitutes for entire words," because the suffix *ktvā* would otherwise be rendered meaningless in a substitution where its own meaning is abandoned; for in that case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the elision (*tuk*) by the rule *hrasvasya piti kṛti* (Pāṇini 6.1.71). This is the general direction. *sup*: *suprāmāya*. *tiṅ*: *apacatām*. Because it ends in a *tiṅ* suffix, it possesses the status of a word (*padatva*). *vaḥ*, *naḥ*: Because they possess the status of a word, there is the substitution of *ru* and so forth. If it is objected: "In that case, the form *adho'dhaḥ* would also have its purpose already explained simply by being a substitute for a word," the answer is: True. However, this is because the term *avyaya* (indeclinable) is included [in the definition of a word], according to the maxim of the cow and the bull (*gobalīvardanyāya*). This is the general direction.

In this context, the distinction is that in forms such as *kābhyām*, the substitute (*ādeśa*) undergoes its grammatical operation (*kārya*), whereas in forms such as *kena* and *kaiḥ*, it causes the subsequent element to function [as the original].

Now, one might object: let the suffix *-vat* not be used; for even by stating merely "the original (*sthānin*) is the substitute (*ādeśa*)," the sense of *-vat* is obtained—just as in rules such as *asaṃyogalliṭ kit* (Pāṇini 1.2.5). As they say: "The word 'subsequent' (*para*), when employed in reference to another, conveys the meaning of *-vat* even without the suffix *-vat*. Nor should it be asked: why not simply take the sentence-meaning to be "the original assumes the form of the substitute"? For that would already be understood from the very rules that prescribe those respective substitutes.

Nor should it be argued that a substitute does not assume the form of its original locus (*sthānin*), and that because of the authority of two rules, there is an option (*vikalpa*); for this is established by the introduction of the rule *vā liṭi* (Pāṇini 2.4.55). Furthermore, one should not argue that since the substitute *khyāñ* for the root *cakṣiṅ* is the locus of something, and because of the authority of two rules, an option would apply everywhere, that rule [vā liṭi] must therefore serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) to limit it to the *liṭ* tense alone; for even so, in the case of optional rules where the option was not previously established—such as *vibhāṣā luṅlṛṅoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.50)—the inclusion of the word *vā* would result in redundancy.
Furthermore, if two forms were established by [the rules for] *asti* and *bhū*, the rule "asterbhūḥ" (Pāṇini 2.4.52) would result in being rendered superfluous.

On this point, they say: in the absence of the use of the term *vat*, the original element (*sthānin*) would become the name (*saṃjñā*) for the substitute (*ādeśa*). For, in this pāda, rules that establish names (*saṃjñā-sūtra*) are generally commenced. Consequently, in the rule "after *āṅ* [the roots] *yam* and *han* take the middle voice" (*āṅo yamahanaḥ*), the middle voice would apply only to *vadhi*, and not to *han*. Nor could there be a reference to *han* itself under the rule "its own form" (*svaṃ rūpam*), because of the prohibition "not when it is a technical grammatical term" (*aśabda-saṃjñā*). Furthermore, according to the view that the original element is applied to the named entity, the name itself would occupy the position of the thing to be designated (*uddeśya*).

Nor should it be argued that one should simply say "āṅo vadhiyamaḥ," for this would result in the unintended inclusion of the root *vadha* belonging to the *bhūvādika* class, which means "to injure. Nor should it be argued that one should instead read "āṅo vadhayamaḥ," and that there would be no over-extension to the *bhūvādika* root because the vowel *a* is intended to be significant; for the rule "āṅo yamahanaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.3.28) must be stated exactly as it is, in order to include all substitutes ending in *h*.

And thus, as in the case of *avadhiṣṭa*, the Ātmanepada is established here in *ājaghne* as well. To explain: after the root *han*, when the suffix *liṭ* follows, because [the substitution of] *tiP* and so forth is internal (*antaraṅga*)—due to its dependence on the general category of *l* suffixes—it sets aside the *ka* suffix prescribed by "the remaining [roots take *śap*], in the sense of the agent" (*śeṣāt kartari*, Pāṇini 3.1.78), owing to its being subsequent (*para*) and obligatory (*nitya*). Then, by the rule "in *liṭ*, [there is reduplication] of the root" (*liṭi dhātoḥ*, Pāṇini 6.1.8), there is a double application [of the root]. When the *cutva* (change to *c*) occurs in the reduplicated syllable, and the *ghatva* (change to *gh*) occurs for the letter following the reduplication, the entire complex becomes a substitute for the whole root *han*—since a partial modification cannot apply to a single part—the result is that the whole is treated as a substitute for the whole. Thereafter...

The direction is that [the substitute] shares exactly the same acquisition and preservation (*yogakṣema*) as the original element (*sthānin*). Alternatively, even if the designation (*saṃjñā*) were applied to the substitute (*ādeśa*) rather than the original element, the undesirable consequence would remain exactly the same. To illustrate: in the rule *asyativaktikhyātibhyo’ṅ* (Pāṇini 3.1.52), only the root *cakṣiṅ* is understood by the word *khyāti*, because it is the technical term (*kṛtrima*). Consequently, in the form *samacakṣiṣṭa*, the suffix *aṅ* would apply, whereas in *ākhyata*, it would not.

Nor should it be argued that one could simply say "of the root *cakṣiṅ*," since it is possible to exclude the *yaṅ*-luṅ by means of the reference to its *anubandha*; for even so, one might argue that in the rule *gāṅkuṭādibhyaḥ...* it would be possible to exclude the *iṅ-luṅ* by means of *gāṅ*. However, even then, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the word *gāṅ* in the rule *gāṅkuṭādibhyaḥ...* being understood as referring to both *iṅ* and *āṅ*, because the mention of *iṅ* alone would otherwise have no purpose; thus, by the force of that specific mention, both would be understood. But in the rule *gameḥ parasmaipadeṣu* (Pāṇini 7.2.58), there would be the inclusion of only the *ṅit* form of *iṅ*.

Therefore, the suffix *vat* must indeed be employed. If it is argued: "In that case, since the suffix *vat* would be absent, for the sake of brevity of expression, let this section on the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) be placed elsewhere—just as the section on technical names (*saṃjñā*) is located outside the main body of rules? We say no; for if that were so, without the explicit mention of the term *ādeśa* (substitute), the meaning of the sentence could not be established, resulting in excessive complexity.
