In the Siddhānta, however, the inclusion of the term *ādeśa* (substitute) serves the purpose of including [changes] that are inferential (*ānumānika*); by virtue of this, the Vārttika stating "an addition must be made for that which is modified in one part" (*ekadeśavikṛtasyopasaṃkhyānam*) will be rejected. Furthermore, the statement to be made later—"Let it be extended [by analogy] as desired" (*kāmamatidiśyatāṃ vā*)—is dependent upon the use of the particle *iva*; such is the direction.

This might be so: if, in the section on technical names (*saṃjñā-prakaraṇa*), an extended application (*atideśa*) cannot be obtained without the use of the suffix *-vat*, then what is the solution for rules such as *kit* and *ṅit*? It is said in reply: *kit* is not a technical name, because of the *jñāpaka* [in the rule] *na ktvā seṭ* (Pāṇini 1.2.18). For if *kit* were a technical name, its application would have been already established and could not be prohibited.

If it is argued: "Let that [the designation *kit*] which would apply by the rule *mṛḍamṛda* (Pāṇini 1.2.7) be prohibited, and let there be an option (*vikalpa*) so as to make both rules meaningful," we say no. For the mention of the word *vā* ("or") is possible in that very rule *mṛḍamṛda* itself. Furthermore, if this were the case, rules such as *niṣṭhāśīṅ* (Pāṇini 1.2.19) would be rendered useless; for indeed, no designation [of *kit*] could ever apply to the *niṣṭhā* suffix after roots like *śīṅ*. Likewise, the extension of the term *ṅit* [in the rule *niṣṭhāśīṅ*] is due to its association with *kit*.

Furthermore, if *ṅit* were a technical term (*saṃjñā*), then only this [term *ṅit*] would be understood in the rule *grahijyā-vayi-vyadhi-vas-ti-sū-vṛś-hu-tī-nāṃ ṅiti ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.16), because it is an artificial (*kṛtrima*) designation. Consequently, the rule *na vaśaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.20) would be rendered useless, since no vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) would apply in the case of *vāvaśyate*. Moreover, it would not be included in the rule *ṅkiti ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.5), because its own form as a technical term is not explicitly uttered there. Thus, in the rule *gāṅkuṭādibhyaḥ...* (Pāṇini 1.2.1), the transfer (*atideśa*) of the number [of the following elements] applies.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that only single-syllable designations (saṃjñā) should be formed, as in the case of *ṭi*, *ghu*, and so forth. Furthermore, rules such as *kikinau liṭ ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.171) do not belong to the section on technical designations; therefore, the extension (*atideśa*) "as if it were the *liṭ*" remains unimpeded. This is the general direction of the argument.

Now, what is the purpose of including the term *ādeśa* ("substitute")? One might argue that by the mere statement "like the original" (*sthānivat*), the meaning is obtained through the power of the word being a relative term—just as when it is said, "he studies like his father," it is understood that he is the son. True; however, there are two kinds of substitutes: the direct (*pratyakṣa*), such as "for *as*, *bhū*" (*asterbhūḥ*), and the inferential (*ānumānika*), such as "for *ti*, *tu*" (*testuḥ*). Here, by the *i* in *ittuḥ*, an original ending in *i* is inferred, and by the *u* in *tuḥ*, a substitute ending in *u* is [inferred]. Thus, the realized meaning is "for *ti*, *tu*."

In that case, if the term "substitute" (*ādeśa*) were not mentioned, only what is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*) would be included, and not what is inferred (*ānumānika*). However, by the force of mentioning "substitute," both are encompassed; thus, the designation of *pada* is established for forms such as *pacati* because they end in a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). If it is argued: "Let [the rule] *eruḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.91) and so forth remain exactly as heard, and since a form modified in one part is not different from the original, the status of being a *pada* will still obtain"—we say no. For the relationship between the original element (*sthānin*) and its substitute (*ādeśa*) must rest upon that which possesses meaning, and it is only in such a case that the contingency (*prasaṅga*) for the application of the rule can arise.

For instance, it is stated: "The genitive case [is used] when there is a relation of *sthāna* (Pāṇini 1.1.49). And *sthāna* means occasion (*prasaṅga*). That [occasion], moreover, belongs to that which possesses meaning, because a word is employed for the purpose of conveying meaning. Even though [the replacement] of *cli* by *sij* and so forth is impossible [in the sense of being an occasion], nevertheless, when such a possibility exists, it is precisely the occasion based on meaning that must be understood; this is indicated by the very mention of "substitute" (*ādeśa*). And it has been said:
"All substitutions are of entire words for Pāṇini, the son of Dākṣī;
for if there were a modification of only a single part, its permanence (*nityatva*) would not be tenable."

The word *pada* here is meaningful, based on the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) that "it is traversed by this. Although the absolute eternity [of the word] is even more untenable in the case of all modifications (*vikāra*), the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is nevertheless that no modification occurs here at all. Thus, the *Vārttika* states: "Or, because of the transformation of the effect" (*kāryavipariṇāmādvā*). Here, "effect" (*kārya*) refers to cognition (*jñāna*) by virtue of its capacity (*yogyatā*). Therefore, the sense is that production, destruction, and so forth, which reside in cognition, are superimposed upon the object.

But if, in this way, the mere modification of the intellect constitutes the status of the substitute for the original, then even in the case of an exception (*apavāda*), the operation of the general rule (*utsarga*) would still apply. For instance, from a word ending in the suffix *kap*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp*—which is conditioned by the presence of the suffix *aṇ*—would also occur. Regarding this, the author of the Vārttika says: "It is established, however, because that which is designated by the genitive is declared to be like the original" (*siddhantu ṣaṣṭhīnirdiṣṭasya sthānivadvacanāt*). The meaning is that the phrase "the genitive [case] is used in connection with the original" (*ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā*, Pāṇini 1.1.49) is understood [in the sūtra]. An exception is not prescribed in place of that which is designated by the genitive.

In cases such as *nābhi* and *nabhaḥ* (*kāovāo*), however, it should be understood that the nominative case (*prathamā*) takes the place of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*). As for words like *viśravaṇa* and *ravaṇa*, they should be understood as distinct lexical items (*śabdāntara*) that fall within the scope of the suffixes. The point is that the suffix does not apply after the word *viśravas* because of a lack of conventional usage (*anabhidhāna*). Thus, the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *vidūrāñ ñyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.84) states: "Either *bālavāya* and *vidūra* are [the forms], or they are indeed different base stems (*prakṛti*). One should certainly not say 'it is not so' there; rather, one should treat them just like the word *jitvarī*."

In this view, the statement in the Bhāṣya on the *vṛddhi* sūtra—that "substitutes are prescribed in the place of that which is indicated by the genitive case"—is established exactly as it was heard, without any contradiction. As for Kaiyaṭa’s analysis, where he explains [the rule] by breaking it down to mean that only that which is capable of expressing the meaning of the original element (*sthānin*) can be a substitute (*ādeśa*), that should be understood as being intended for another alternative position presented here. Alternatively, the addition of the marker *ś* to *śyan* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that what is effected by a general rule (*utsarga*) does not apply when an exception (*apavāda*) is present.

Nor should it be said that the *nit* designation is for the purpose of preventing the *pit* designation; for that [the *pit* designation] is already established by virtue of being a *nit*. Indeed, the *nit* designation is for the sake of the initial acute accent (*ādyaudātta*). However, if the *śyan* suffix were *pit*, then because it would be *pit*, it would be unaccented (*anudātta*), and since the *l-sārvadhātuka* suffixes are also unaccented, the accentuation would be established by the accent of the root itself—so what would be the use of the *nit* designation? Nor is there any distinction in the case of multi-syllabic roots, because that [the *nit* designation] is absent in the *div* class. If it is argued that [the root] *vāvṛtu* exists in the sense of "turning" (*vartane*) [in the *div* class], [we reply] no, because the word *vā* has the meaning of an option (*vikalpa*).

Nor is that [root *vṛt*] useless because its formation is established by its inclusion in the *bhvādi* class; for the inclusion in the *bhvādi* class is exhausted in providing the internal-group (*antargaṇa*) operations such as those prescribed by Pāṇini 1.3.92: *vṛdbhyaḥ syasanoḥ*. But if this is so—[then how do you explain:
"Then, turning back from there, she gazed toward Rāma’s dwelling" (*Bhaumakāvya*)?

If it is argued that, for this reason, Bhaṭṭi’s usage is untenable, we say no. In that instance, the word *vā* has the sense of *iva* (as if); thus, [the meaning is] "as if she were desiring, but not actually so," rather than "she came for the sake of deception. On this point, Kaiyaṭa says: "In the case of suffixes such as *-āni*, which denote habitual action (*tācchīlya*) and the like, the *nit*-designation of *syaN* would serve to make the initial syllable of the base (*prakṛti*) udātta. For in that case, since there is no *lasārvadhātuka* suffix, the rule for being unaccented (*anudātta*) does not apply; consequently, by the rule *citaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.163), the final syllable would be the one that receives the udātta accent, which is indeed what is desired.

His intention is: "In that case, why should *nittva* itself not be [the cause of the accentuation] for the sake of an undesired result? However, this is not tenable; because the accentuation of *śyan* is weaker due to the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) in the rule "except for the *vikaraṇas*. Nor can its sublation be justified by the force of *nittva*, because *nittva* already serves its purpose in relation to the *l-sārvadhātuka*. If it is argued that its purpose is already served there by *pitva* obtained through the principle of "behaving like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), we say no. For here, since one of the two—either the extended application (*atideśa*) or the exclusion (*paryudāsa*)—must necessarily be sublated, it is more logical to sublate the extended application. This is in accordance with the maxim: "The former [rules] sublate the latter, but not the former" (*pūrvān bādhante nottarān*).

As for the interpretation of Kaiyaṭa’s text by some who explain it as intending that the suffix *cānaś* is desired to have an udātta accent on its first syllable—and who further state: "The exclusion (*paryudāsa*) 'except for verbal suffixes' applies only to those cases where the suffix bears the accent; however, here the suffix does not bear the accent, because of the established principle that 'locatives [referring to] Svarita vowels are locatives referring to word-final elements'"—this should be disregarded, as it is baseless and contradicts both the Bhāṣya located at the end of the *ghu*-naming rule and the Bhāṣya located under the rule on accents.

Furthermore, the fact that the suffix *ṭak* is marked with the *k*-sign in the rule "gāpoṣṭak" (Pāṇini 3.2.8)—which is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule "āto 'nupasarge kaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.3)—is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that what is prescribed by a general rule (*utsarga*) does not apply when an exception is present.

What is the purpose of the phrase *analvidhau*? It is so that [the rule of] substitution (*sthānivadbhāva*) does not apply in an operation concerning *al* (vowels and consonants), nor in an operation concerning *tasmāt* (from that), *tasya* (of that), or *tasmin* (in that). Regarding an operation concerning *al*: as in *vyūḍhoraskena*. Here, because the *s* substituted for the *visarga* by the rule *so ’padādau* (Pāṇini 8.3.38) is treated as the original (*sthānivat*), the *visarga* is considered to have been taught with the augment *aṭ*; consequently, by the rule *aḍvyavāye*, the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] would occur. Regarding an operation concerning what follows [an element]: as in *dyauḥ*, *panthāḥ*, *saḥ*. Here, the elision of the final vowel and following consonant (*halṅyādi-lopa*) does not take place.

In a rule concerning *u*, for example: *diva ut* (Pāṇini 6.1.39), as in *dyukāmaḥ*. The elision prescribed by *lopovyorvali* (Pāṇini 6.1.66) does not occur here. However, the prescription of *utva* finds its application in cases such as *aharvimaladyu*. In a rule concerning *ali* (a consonant), for example: the suffix *kta* applied to the root *yaj* results in *iṣṭaḥ*. In the derivation of *ka iṣṭaḥ*, because the semivowel-vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) is treated as *sthānivat* (as if it were the original element), the *utva* substitution required by *haśi ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.114) does not take place, as would occur in examples like *koyaṣṭā*.

In the example *sa iṣṭaḥ*, the elision of *su* after *etad* and *tad* does not occur. Although it is possible—even when *analaḥ* is stated—that the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) used for expressing a general relationship may include the various case-meanings previously mentioned, nevertheless, the employment of the word *vidhi* (rule) is for the purpose of prohibiting [the application of the rule] even when *al* is resorted to as a subordinate element. By this, forms such as *prapaṭhya* are established; for here, in the expression *valādeḥ*, *al* is resorted to as a subordinate element, and not as a primary one.

It might be argued: "In that case, the operations pertaining to the *sthānin* (the original element) and its *anubandhas* (indicatory letters) would also be prohibited. Consequently, in the form *pradīvya*, the quality of being *kit* would not be obtained through the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*. This is not so. Under the view that "indicatory letters (*anubandhas*) are non-exclusive" (*anekāntā anubandhāḥ*), the *sthānin* lacks the status of being an *al* (a vowel or consonant) due to the presence of the *anubandha*. Even under the view that they are "exclusive" (*ekāntapakṣa*), the *anubandhas* are removed by the internal operation (*antaraṅga*) of elision (*lopa*) prior to any connection with the substitute; furthermore, this is supported by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule *na lyapi* (Pāṇini 6.4.69).

As for the argument that the rule *serhyapicca* (Pāṇini 3.4.87) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), that is merely optional; for it can equally be maintained that, by virtue of the mention of *api*, the low-pitched accent (*anudāttatva*) obtained through the *sthānentaratama* paribhāṣā does not take effect.

Although the established principle (*siddhānta*) is that "when there is an extension of a general rule, there is no extension of specific details," this is because once the requirements of the injunction are fulfilled by the properties associated with the presented general rule and by the properties of the encompassing general category implied by them, there is no evidence for the inclusion of a specific detail that has not been presented. For this very reason, when it is said, "One should behave toward this Kṣatriya as one does toward a Brāhmaṇa," the specific duties pertaining to [sub-classes such as] the Māṭhara and others are not extended.

For this very reason, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) regarding the rule *āśaṃsāyāṃ bhūtavacca* (Pāṇini 3.3.132) is that there is an extension (*atideśa*) only of the *luṅ* and *niṣṭhā* suffixes prescribed for the general past tense (*bhūtasāmānya*), and not of the *laṅ* and *liṭ* suffixes prescribed for specific types of the past as well. Nevertheless, in this present rule, a specific [past tense] is also extended on the basis of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule *na lyapi* (Pāṇini 6.4.69). For the rule *na lyapi* (Pāṇini 6.4.69) is commenced precisely to prohibit the *it*-augment which is prescribed when a *kit* suffix follows.

Furthermore, *kittva* is a specific property (*viśeṣadharma*), because it is absent in cases where a *seṭ* affix follows. By this, forms such as *pradīvya* are established. Therefore, it is settled that the rule *na lyapi* (Pāṇini 6.4.69) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for both the extension of specific properties and the extension of operations conditioned by an indicatory letter (*anubandhakārya*).

As for what the ancients have said—that the prohibition in Pāṇini 1.1.56 (*analvidhau*) indicates a rule of specific extension (*viśeṣātideśa*)—that is to be reconsidered, because that prohibition finds its purpose in cases such as *vyūḍhoraskeṇa* and *ka iṣṭaḥ*, where the properties of being a non-vowel (*aṭ-tva*) and being a vowel other than *ha* (*haś-tva*), which are more extensive than the status of being a visarga or a semi-vowel (*yaṇ-tva*), are already precluded by that very prohibition. Furthermore, regarding the statement made by the Miśras—that after the substitution of *kvā* has occurred, since the extension of the status of being a *kṛt*-affix or a *pratyaya* is accepted, the extension of specific properties such as *haś-tva* does not apply in examples like *ka iṣṭaḥ*.

In this regard, let the learned themselves discern how the properties of *visarga* and *ṇatva* can be considered specific attributes (*viśeṣadharma*) when [the original sounds] have become *aṭ* and *ah*. Although it is established by logic that what occupies the place of something acquires its properties—just as threshing and other operations characteristic of rice are performed upon *nīvāra* grain (which serves as a substitute for rice) even without an explicit scriptural injunction—nevertheless, since those properties are prompted by the grain's being a means to the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the archetype (*prakṛti*), their performance in the case of *nīvāra* and the like is indeed appropriate.

Regarding the rule *āṅo yamahanaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.28), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) for the root *han* is not occasioned by the prescription of meanings such as "injury" (*hiṃsā*), which would apply in the case of *vadhau*. Rather, it is occasioned by the specific form itself, according to the rule *svaṃ rūpam* (Pāṇini 1.1.68). For this very reason, it does not occur in forms such as *atṛṇeḍ*. Therefore, the commencement of this extended application (*atideśa*) is indeed appropriate.

It might be argued: "Let it not be that the matter is already established by logic (*nyāya*); rather, it shall be established by an *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence). For instance, in the rule *yuṣmadasmadoranādeśe* (Pāṇini 7.2.86), the inclusion of the term *anādeśe* ("except when there is a substitute") indicates that a substitute (*ādeśa*) should behave like its original (*sthānin*). Furthermore, in the rule *ado jagdhiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.36), although the result would have been established simply by [the condition] *kiti*, the inclusion of the term *lyapi* indicates two points: first, the portion of the rule stating *na lvidhau* ("not in the case of an operation concerning an *al*"); and second, the portion stating that the prohibition applies even when the *al* is relied upon only as a subordinate factor."

If this is so, what is the purpose of the sūtra? It is said: first of all, for the sake of what follows, the rule "an ādeśa is like that which it replaces" (sthānivadādeśaḥ) must indeed be formulated. Since its establishment is possible merely through a division of the yoga (yogavibhāga), one should not assume a statement based on presumptive implication (arthāpatti). This being the case, the portion "not in the prescription of an element beginning with *a*" (analvidhau) is also stated for the sake of clear understanding and for the purpose of carrying over the term "second prescription" (dvitīyavidhi) into the subsequent sūtra; its specific purpose will be explained in that very place. Having considered all of this, the Blessed One [Patañjali] said: "Even when this sūtra is being commenced..."

This might be so: let there be the commencement of the *sūtra*; nevertheless, why must this be an extension (*atideśa*) of the effect (*kārya*) alone? Because other types [of extension] are also possible. For instance, extension is sixfold, based on the distinctions of: (1) cause (*nimitta*), (2) designation (*vyapadeśa*), (3) identity (*tādātmya*), (4) scripture (*śāstra*), (5) effect (*kārya*), and (6) form (*rūpa*). Among these, a cause cannot be extended, just like Brahminhood (*brāhmaṇya*). Indeed, the Brahminhood that serves as the cause for a Brahmin’s priority in eating and so forth cannot be extended to a Kṣatriya even by a hundred utterances.

Even in the rule *pūrvavatsanaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.62), the cause residing in the base (*prakṛti*), such as its being marked with the *ṅit* indicator, is not extended (*atidiśyate*) to the form ending in *san*. Rather, only this much is extended: that which resides in the base itself causes the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) to operate even when there is an intervention by *san*. It is precisely because of this that the convention "this is an extension of the cause" (*nimittātideśa*) is employed. Nor should it be argued that this should instead be an extension of the grammatical effect (*kāryātideśa*), for if it were so, the augment *iṭ* would undesirably apply in forms such as *cikraṃsate* and *pracikraṃsate*.

In the view that the cause (*nimitta*) is extended [to the compound], however, it is precisely *krami*—preceded by *pra* and not preceded by any prefix—that brings about the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), even though it is separated by the suffix *san*. Consequently, the augment *iṭ* does not occur, because of the restriction in Pāṇini’s rule 7.2.36, *snukramoranātmanepadanimitte*, which states that [the augment applies] when there is no cause for the non-middle voice. For we shall explain that in that context, the "cause" is understood only as something actually endowed with the result (*phalopahita*), and not merely as a state of formal suitability (*svarūpayogyatāmātra*).

"According to the view of the Vārttika—that 'because [the suffix] siddhaṃka is in the ātmanepada, there is a prohibition of iṭ when it resides in the same word'—it can also be easily stated here that this is a transfer of operation (*kāryātideśa*), and this will be explained in that very place. As for the transfer of designation (*vyapadeśātideśa*), however, the idea is that by the rule *ādyantavadekasmin* (Pāṇini 1.1.21), even in the case of a single entity, the designations 'beginning' and 'end' are transferred; thus, the operations are carried out by those very rules themselves. And so the ancients said:
'The transfer of the designations "beginning" and "end" is the cause, as in the case of the desiderative suffix *san*, which is like the preceding. "

And Haradatta states in that very same sūtra that this [interpretation] is "without foundation. His intention is as follows: in that case, it is only the extension of the operation (*kāryātideśa*) that is logical, because all extensions are for the sake of the operation, and thus the operation itself is primary. For this very reason, when one accepts the extension of the operation, one resorts to an alternative method only where an obstacle arises; however, such an obstacle does not exist in the rule regarding "beginning and end-like" (*ādyantavat-sūtra*), on the contrary, there is an obstacle specifically to the position that extends the designation (*vyapadeśātideśa*).

For instance, in forms such as *kurute* and *kurve*, let there be both the designation of the final [element] and the designation of the initial. Nevertheless, because the referent of the *bahuvrīhi* compound—namely, "that which has an *ac* vowel as its initial and a final"—is absent, the designation *ṭi* would not apply, and consequently, the substitution of *e* for the *ṭi* would not occur. However, if one extends (*atideśa*) the grammatical operation observed in *kurvāte* and similar forms—specifically the substitution of *e* for the *ṭi*—then no fault arises. An extension of identity (*tādātmyātideśa*), however, is the extension of non-difference between two distinct things, as in the rule: *subāmantrite parāṅgavatsvare* (Pāṇini 2.1.2).

Therefore, in such instances as *yatto divo duhitarmarttabhājanam*, the *nighāta* (anudātta accentuation) applied by the eighth-century rule *āmantritasya ca* (Pāṇini 8.1.19)—which prescribes the accent for a vocative following another word—occurs over the entire compound *divo duhitar*. However, the extension (*atideśa*) of a grammatical operation (*śāstra*) will be discussed optionally under the rule *karmavatkarmaṇā* (Pāṇini 3.1.87), while the extension of a specific grammatical effect (*kārya*) is seen in rules such as *goto ṇit* (Pāṇini 7.1.90).

As for the extension (*atideśa*) of form, there are rules such as *dvirvacane 'ci* (Pāṇini 1.1.59) and *tṛjvakrauṣṭuḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.95). If it is asked, "What is the determining factor here that this is indeed an extension of the operation (*kāryātideśa*)?"—it is said in reply: because the operation is primary, this is an extension of that [operation] alone; furthermore, because other types of extension would involve contradictions. To explain: it has been stated that the extension of causes and designations (*nimitta-vyapadeśātideśa*) are merely optional. The same applies to the extension of grammatical rules (*śāstrātideśa*). However, an extension of identity (*tādātmyātideśa*) could only occur between two things existing simultaneously.

Just as in the case of two words that have been properly conjugated, here, however, the original element (*sthānin*) has been superseded by the substitute (*ādeśa*), and thus that [transfer of properties] is impossible. If it were a transfer of form (*rūpātideśa*), the prescription of the substitute would be redundant. Nor can there be an option based on the authority of two rules, because an option has already been initiated by the rule "optionally in the *luṅ* and *luṅ* tenses" (*vibhāṣā luṅlṛṅoḥ*, Pāṇini 2.4.50). Therefore, it is established that this is indeed a transfer of grammatical operation (*kāryātideśa*).

As for what was stated by the author of the *Nyāsa*—"In the view that [the suffix -vat] expresses a technical name (*saṃjñā*), the extension of designation (*vyapadeśātideśa*) is ultimately reached; and that [extension] will not occur precisely because of the force of the inclusion of the word *vat* itself"—to this it must be said: there is a difference here from the view that it is a technical name. For instance, in rules such as "of *yama* and *hana* following *āṅ*" (*āṅo yamahanaḥ*, Pāṇini 1.3.28), only the root *vadha* would be included, and not the root *han*; likewise, in forms such as *kena* and *kasmāt*, the operations pertaining to the *aṅga* (stem) and so forth would not take place. Thus, there are two defects in the view that it is a technical name.

And this [transfer] does not apply to the transfer of designations (*vyapadeśātideśa*). For, by the rule "one's own form" (*svaṃ rūpam*, Pāṇini 1.1.68), the designation *han* belongs to *han* alone. If there were a transfer of that designation even to *vadh*, then the ātmanepada would be obtained for both [roots], and not for *han* alone. Thus, because the designations such as "root" (*dhātu*) and "stem" (*aṅga*), which reside in the original element (*sthānin*), are transferred to the substitute (*ādeśa*), the operations dependent on being a root, a stem, and so forth, are indeed easily obtained. Therefore, the truth is simply this: it is a transfer of operations (*kāryātideśa*) based on their predominance.

Regarding this, the authors of the *Vārttikas*—beginning with the rule *tasya doṣaḥ* (*Bhāṣya*)—recorded such points as: "In the case of a substitute (*ādeśa*), there is a prohibition of both [the original and the substitute]," "in the mention of *ṅī* and *āp*, [the rule applies to] what is not long (*adīrgha*)," and "the prohibition of *īṭ* for the roots *āhi* and *bhū*," and so forth. Among these, the manner in which there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding the word "both" (*ubhaya*) has already been established during the explanation of the *sarva*-class of pronouns. Furthermore, even in the case of the mention of *ṅī* and *āp*, because the long vowels are included by splitting the compound as *ṅī-ī-ā-āp*, there is no over-extension in forms such as *atikhaṭvena* and *atikhaṭve*.

Even so, the defect does not remain in the case of *atikhaṭvāya*, because the rule of "beginning with that" (*tadādinīyama*) applies when a feminine suffix is an *upasarjana*. Nor is the description involving *praśleṣa* (elision/insertion) redundant; for in cases such as *atikhaṭve*, in the absence of the governing heading *aṅgasya* (of the stem), there would arise the undesirable consequence of the elision of the *ṭāp* by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt...* on the grounds that it follows a portion ending in *ṭāp*. Indeed, it is not proper to resort to the qualification "that which is prescribed" (*vihitaviśeṣaṇa*) in that context, because it would result in over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in forms like *yaḥ* and *saḥ*, and under-extension (*avyāpti*) in forms like *yā* and *sā*, as has already been stated.

For this very reason, the author of the Sūtras also included the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) in that rule. As for the doubling of the long vowel (*dīrghapraśleṣa*), it is described as a means to reject that [specific] reading; however, this is a separate matter. And this is logical: for according to the Vārttika view, although one might somehow manage cases like *atikhaṭvāya* by the force of the governing heading (*adhikāra*) on the "stem" (*aṅga*), the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in forms such as *jarase*, *nase*, and *pṛte* would be difficult to avoid, and there would also be the undesirable consequence of eliding the *su* in *sutīḥ* (desiring a daughter) and similar forms. This is the general direction of the argument.

Or rather, let there be another interpretation by connecting [the word] *ākāra* as well; by the force of that, the objection regarding the short vowel (*hrasvatvam*) occurring in the middle is avoided—this is the direction [of the argument]. As for the Vārttika "āhibhuvoḥ," the authors of the Bhāṣya rejected it in this manner: even though [the substitution of] *āh* would apply in the case of *āttha* by virtue of being a *sthānivadbhāva*, the *īṭ* augment does not occur for *brū*. This is because of the *jñāpaka* [provided by] Pāṇini’s rule 8.2.35, "āhasthaḥ. For by that rule, the substitution of *th* is prescribed when *jhal*-beginning suffixes and so forth follow.

Nor should it be argued that even after [the substitution] has been applied, by virtue of its former state (*bhūtapūrvagatyā*), the *thakāra* should be considered as beginning with a *jhal* sound; for if that were the case, one would simply prescribe *ātha* out of parsimony (*lāghava*), since all five suffixes beginning with *ti* begin with a *jhal*, and because the suffixes beginning with *ṇal* also possess the status of beginning with a *jhal* by virtue of their former state. Therefore, it is established that, based on the *jñāpaka* rule *āhurutha* (Pāṇini 8.2.35), there is no *sthānivadbhāva* when the augment *iṭ* is prescribed after the root *āh*.

It need not be stated that there is a prohibition against regarding the substitution of *bhu*—prescribed by the rule *asterbhūḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.52)—as being like its original (*sthānivadbhāva*). This is because, by the dual mention of the letter *s* in the rule *astisico'pṛkte* (Pāṇini 7.3.96), the augment *iṭ* is prescribed only after the root *as* ending in *s*.

It might be argued as follows: In the case of the dual mention of the letter *s* in *as-s-iti*, since it would lack the status of a verbal root (*dhātu*), the suffix *śtiP* would be untenable; furthermore, because the *s* situated in the middle of the word cannot qualify the *s* of *sic*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the augment *īṭ* being applied based on that *sic*. Nor should it be said that even if the *īṭ* caused by *sic* does not apply due to the capacity of the qualification "ending in *s*" (*sānta*) for the root *as*, this is so because the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of *īṭ* to the independent root *bhū* remains unavoidable.

Thus, even though there is no difference in meaning, two forms—*abhūvīt* and *abhūt*—would result from the independent (*svatantra*) and non-independent (*asvatantra*) [interpretations] of the two roots. Regarding this, Mādhavācārya has stated, after presenting this objection: "Since *sic* is to be placed first because it is fewer syllables (*alpāctva*) and more important due to its wider scope (*bahuviṣayatva*), the statement *astisicaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.96) allows us to understand, through the method of *tantra* and so forth, that the sense is 'of the existing *sic*' (*vidyamānāt sicaḥ*). For this very reason, the use of the suffix *śtip* is also meaningful."

Otherwise, one would simply have said "si-jas-bhyām. Nor is there an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) to the case of *as* and *asti*, because an unaccented (*apṛkta*) sārvadhātuka suffix cannot follow those two when they are separated by a vikaraṇa. This [explanation] is to be considered, for even so, the Bhāṣya’s statement that "it is an indication of a form with two *s*s" remains unaccounted for due to the failure to resolve the *śtip* suffix. By this [analysis], *sic* and *as* are *sicas*; in a collective dvandva compound, the word has its fifth case ending elided. Because it is a *bha*-stem by virtue of belonging to the *ayasmaya*-class, the *kutva* and *jaśtva* substitutions do not apply.

Furthermore, the analysis as a *karmadhāraya* compound—namely, "that which has *sic* and is *asti*"—is also refuted by the assumption that [the rule applies] after the root *as*, from which *sic* has been elided and which has undergone the change to *bhū*. This is because, even if the desired form were established by that method, it would still fail to account for the *Bhāṣya*. Therefore, one must state that the Blessed One’s intention here is indeed something else.

To this it is replied: there is the elision of the *s* of *asti* and *sic*. However, this applies to *asti* ending in *s*, not to that which has undergone the change to *bhū*. This means that the elision occurs when *sic* is heard with a final *s*. Thus, the letter *s* is understood as being inherent (*praśliṣṭa*) immediately after *sic*, and not before the *śtip* suffix, which would otherwise result in the fault pointed out by Mādhava regarding the impossibility of the *śtip* suffix. For this very reason, it is stated in the Bhāṣya that the form *sico 'pṛkte* contains two *s* sounds; otherwise, he would have simply said *aster akhyati*.

If it is asked, "In that case, how is the *saṃhitā* reading of *asti-sico 'pṛkte* (Pāṇini 7.3.96) to be accounted for?"—the answer is as follows: by the rule *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.23), the second *s* is elided. Now, one might object: the word *s* here has its case-ending (*vibhakti*) dropped; it is not a word ending in a *saṃyoga* (a cluster of consonants). Therefore, since the elision prescribed by the rule applies only to a word that ends in a *saṃyoga*, how can this elision occur here? This objection is invalid, because the rule is explained to mean: "There shall be elision of a *saṃyoga* that occurs at the end of a word. Thus, the elision takes place.

The term *saṃyoga* is indeed a separate word with its genitive case ending elided; both "of the conjunction" (*saṃyogasya*) and "of the word" (*padasya*) are qualifiers of "final" (*antasya*). This alone is the intention of the author of the Sūtra as well. For if this were accepted as the commentary provided by the Vṛttikāra—namely, that it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound where "word" (*pada*) is the external referent (*anyapadārtha*)—then he would not have included the mention of "final" (*anta*), because the status of being final would already be obtained simply by qualifying the word with "conjunction."

Furthermore, regarding the *sarūpa-sūtra*, there is a concern that if one adopts the view of *ekaśeṣa* (retaining only one from all [homogeneous] words) after they have been individually declined (*vibhaktau*), the form *vṛkṣas s-* would result; anticipating this, the *Bhāṣya* states, "It is established by the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct" (*saṃyogāntalopāt siddham*). This passage of the *Bhāṣya* is indeed consistent with the current explanation. As for what Kaiyaṭa will say there—"In reality, it is due to the elision of the final member of a conjunct (*saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ*) and the elision of [consonants] following *hal* and *ṅī*"—that contradicts the intent of the original source, because it begins with the phrase "here they explain" (*atra vyācakṣate*) and implies dissatisfaction [with the previous position].

For this very reason, in the *halantyam* sūtra, while introducing the point that the designation *it* for the final letter *l*—for which the *lit* status of *ṇal* is prescribed for the sake of accent—is an *jñāpaka*, he will raise the objection: "But surely the letter *l* is intended for the purpose of being heard [and thus should remain]," and then resolve it by stating that the mention of *hal* in the rule *apṛktaṃ hal* is made to exclude *ṇal*, thereby making known that *ṇal* is indeed *apṛkta*. For his intention is as follows: in forms such as *bhettā*, the substitute *ḍā* cannot be the object excluded by the mention of *hal*.

By the implication of the term *pratyaya* [in the rule] *sutiṣṛti-pratyayaiḥ*, there is the elision (*lopa*) of the case-endings (*svādi*) following a base (*prakṛti*) that ends in a consonant (*halanta*). Furthermore, with respect to the substitute *ḍā*, the base ending in *tās* is not considered a *prakṛti*. Thus, even in this case, since *vṛkṣas* lacks the status of being a *prakṛti*, how could there be elision by the rule *halṅyābbhyaḥ*? The statement in the current text—that the reference in *astisico 'pṛkteliṭi* (Pāṇini 7.3.96) consists of two *s* sounds—is indeed consistent with the aforementioned explanation.

[Objection: "Granted that the elision of the final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) occurs according to the method stated above; nevertheless, because that elision is considered *asiddha* (non-existent for the purposes of subsequent operations), the substitution of *u* for *r* (*ror utvam*) remains difficult to achieve. [Reply: No, for the non-*asiddha* status [of the elision] is prohibited by the Vārttika: "The elision of the final *saṃyoga* is not *asiddha* with respect to the substitution of *ru*," as seen in examples such as *harivo medinaṃ tvā*. Furthermore, the very mention of the present topic in the rule *sicopṛkte* (Pāṇini 7.2.45) should be understood as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the meaning stated in the Vārttika. Alternatively, let the meaning of the sūtra *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.23) be exactly as stated by the author of the Vṛtti.

However, let the term *antagrahaṇa* (specification of the "end") be intended to convey the sense of duality—namely, that "those two which have a *saṃyoga* at their end"—under the view that the designation *saṃyoga* applies to each [consonant] individually, since this is precisely how it is stated by both the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa in the *Saṃyoga-saṃjñā-sūtra*. But in the present case, let there be no elision of a final *saṃyoga*, since this is precisely how it is stated by both the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa in the *Saṃyoga-saṃjñā-sūtra*.

However, when *ru* is substituted for two instances of *sakāra*, there will be only one substitution of *u* by virtue of the rule *ato roḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.113). This is because the singularity of the attribute of the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*) is intended to be significant, just as the singularity of the animal [in the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal"]. Furthermore, since the mention of *ror* refers to the genus (*jāti*), it is possible for both that which follows *at* and that which precedes it to be included. Let the fact that the mention of the base (*prakṛti*) refers to the genus itself be the proof for this.

Nor should it be argued that because [the *ru* substitute] follows a *ha*, the rule *haśi ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.114) would cause the *ru* to apply to the first *r* alone; for since the substitution of *ru* is considered *asiddha*, there is no subsequent *ha* (*haśparatva*). Nor should it be argued that [the *ru*] is established by virtue of its basis (*āśrayāt siddhatvam*); for while this might apply to the portion concerning the substituendum (*sthāny-aṃśe*), it is impossible in the case of the *ha* which serves as the cause (*nimittībhūta-haś-aṃśe*). This is precisely the intention of the Bhāṣyakāra when he maintains the reading with two *s*-sounds (*dvisakāraka-anirdeśa*). It is not, however, the case that [the *ru* applies] due to the elision of a final conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*).

For this very reason, in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule *nudavid-* (Pāṇini 8.2.54), having raised the objection as to how the letter *n*—which is separated from many rules such as *śuṣaḥ kaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.51)—can be understood as continuing (*anuvṛtti*), it is stated that there is an elision (*praśleṣa*) of another *n* through the *saṃhitā* reading of the rule *anyatarasyāmnadhyākhyā* (Pāṇini 8.2.57). For his intention is that [the *n*] is deleted by the rule *halo yamām* (Pāṇini 8.4.64).

However, since the form is established by the elision of the final consonant (*saṃyogāntalopa*) according to the method previously stated, one need not carry the discussion as far as the *saṃhitā* reading. For even in the *saṃhitā*, because the elision prescribed by *halo yamām* (Pāṇini 8.4.64) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) due to its being *bahiraṅga* and situated within the "tripādī" section, the elision of the final *saṃyoga* must indeed occur. This is because, among the three positions stated in the Vārttika—"there is a prohibition of the *yaṇ*-elision," "or rather, no [prohibition]," or "because of the elision of the *jhal* [consonant]," or "because it is characterized as *bahiraṅga*"—the first and the last alternatives would make that [elision] unavoidable.

Therefore, the meaning of the Bhāṣya is that two solutions are established here in accordance with two alternative views: namely, that the designation *saṃyoga* applies either to the aggregate as a whole or to each individual [consonant] within it. According to the method previously stated, one may also interpret this Bhāṣya by relying on the collective compound *sicaḥ* (as in P. 1.2.11) and taking the division there as *s-it*, thereby justifying the rejection (*pratyākhyāna*) of the mention of the root *as-*. This is the general direction.

By this, the statement in the *Padamañjarī* that "the mention of the word *anta-* in the rule *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.23) could have been omitted" is refuted, because the purpose [of the term] has been stated for both positions. Alternatively, it may be applied to the position where *sicaḥ* is understood as being present. In reality, however, just as in the case of *jhalaḥ*, the word *saḥ* is elided [from *sicaḥ*]; by the force of that [elision], even in the absence of the status of being a *pada* for what ends in a *saṃyoga*, there is elision—enough of this.

As for what some have said—that since *īṭ* would apply due to its higher status [in the order of rules], there is a prohibition by virtue of the Vārttika "prohibition of *īṭ* after *āh* and *bhū*"—that is not correct. This is because, starting with the words "its fault," the aforementioned Vārttika is intended to prohibit the application of *sthānivadbhāva*; thus, even if the *īṭ* that functions depending on the posteriority of *ās* is blocked, the *īṭ* occasioned by *sic* remains unavoidable. Consequently, the aforementioned defect persists in forms such as *asthāt* and *agāt*.
Therefore, one of the previously mentioned paths alone must be taken as the refuge; enough of this prolixity.

There is another *vārttika*: "The prohibition of *vṛddhi* and *tatva*, and the prescription of *iṭ*, [apply] when the substitute *vadha* occurs. Its meaning is as follows: when the suffix *ṇvul* is added to the root *han*, the substitute *vadha* is applied by the *vārttika* "for the sake of technical terms (*saṃjñā*) and the Veda (*chandas*), [the forms] *anta*, *ṇyat*, *nava*, *dhaka*, *gātra*, *vicakṣaṇa*, *ajira*, etc. Considering that this substitute *vadha* ends in a consonant (*halanta*), one might apply *vṛddhi* according to *Pāṇini* 7.2.116 (*aco ñṇiti*) and the substitution of *takāra* according to *Pāṇini* 7.3.32 (*hanasta ca ṇinloḥ*). The purpose of the *vārttika* is to prohibit the treatment of these two operations as if they were *sthānivadbhāva* (as if they were the original element).

Similarly, in forms such as *āvadhiṣīṣṭa*, by virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), the element is treated as an *aṅga* (stem), and thus the prohibition of *iṭ* by Pāṇini 7.2.10 (*ekāca upadeśe 'nudāttāt*) would apply. It must be stated that even when that [prohibition] is to be applied, the status of being an *aṅga* does not exist due to *sthānivadbhāva*. This very point is effectively stated by the rule regarding the prescription of *iṭ* (*iḍvidhiśca*). However, this too has been rejected in the Bhāṣya. For instance, the substitute *vadh* is short-voweled at the end (*adanta*); otherwise, in the form *avadhīt*, there would be the undesirable application of *vṛddhi* by Pāṇini 7.2.7 (*ato halāder laghoḥ*).

This is made clear in the Bhāṣya on the subsequent sūtra. As for the form *vadhaka*, this is not derived from the suffix *ṇvul*; rather, the suffix *kvun* is applied by the Uṇādi sūtra *hano vadhaśca* (Uṇādi Sūtra 204). Consequently, there is no occasion here for either vṛddhi or the substitution of *tatva*. Furthermore, in forms such as *āvadhiṣīṣṭa*, the prohibition of *iṭ* does not apply, because the specific accentuation of the initial vowel (*ādyudātta*) in the substitute *vadha* possesses the force of a restrictive indicator (*jñāpaka*). Nor should it be argued that, if this were the case, the accent of the suffix in forms like *yadāvadhiṣīṣṭa* would be sublated by that [substitute] which is taught later (*satiśiṣṭa*).

This is because the substitutes belonging to the *ārddhadhātuka* category apply merely by the desire to express a suffix (*pratyayavivakṣāmātreṇa*), and thus the accent of the suffix itself is the "later remaining" (*sati śiṣṭa*) one. It might be argued: "If this is a rule for the insertion of *iṭ*, then the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is already weak. For instance, the insertion of *iṭ* is prohibited after a root that is unaccented (*anudātta*) in its original enunciation (*upadeśa*), and *vadhi* is not such [a root]. If it is argued that it becomes so by virtue of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāvena*), we say no; for there is an absence of *sthānivadbhāva* in a rule concerning an *al* (phoneme). True, we do not here speak of *sthānivadbhāva*. Rather, the very enunciation of *vadhi* is itself an enunciation of the root *han*.

Just as in the case of the instruction regarding the root *kṛ* in forms such as *kartā* and *kartum*, where the status of *kar-* and so on is treated as *sthānivadbhāva* (as if being the original element), it has already been stated that the designation of the *aṅga* (stem) must be sought for its purpose. But even so, the explanatory passage (*parihāra-grantha*) remains inconsistent. For if the substitution of *vadh-* is admitted to occur even prior to the production of the suffix, then the Vārttika on the *syasicsūtra*—which states, "The status of *ciṇvat* [is applied] to the *sīyuṭ* [augment] by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) because of the absence of *vadh-*"—would be contradicted; this is because a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) is impossible between what is *antaraṅga* (internal) and what is *bahiraṅga* (external).

Consequently, in the case of the *karmaṇi* (passive) voice with the suffix *sīyuṭ*, there would be only one form, namely *vādhiṣīṣṭa*; however, a second form, *ghāniṣīṣṭa*, is also desired. To this, it is said according to the Vārttika: "Even though the rule *ārddhadhātuke* [P. 6.4.46] is a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*), since rules such as *liṅiluṅoḥ* [P. 6.4.71] are accepted as locatives of sequence (*parasaptamī*), a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) is indeed possible. For this very reason, since the introduction of an initial acute accent (*ādyudāttanipātana*) is impossible here, the prescription of *iṭ* has been added as a supplement (*upasaṃkhyāta*)."

The intention of the commentators (*bhāṣyakāra*), however, is as follows: like the term *ārddhadhātuka*, the term *liṅ* and so forth is also a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*). Thus, since the desired result is established by the very citation of the word with an initial acute accent (*ādyudāttanipātana*), the rule for the insertion of *iṭ* need not be formulated at all. What remains to be addressed is how the form *ghāniṣīṣṭa* is to be derived; the answer to this is that the substitution of *ciṇvat* takes place because a specific rule (*pratipadavidhi*) is more powerful. This has been clearly stated by Kaiyaṭa in his commentary on the rule *syasicsīyuṭ...*.

Therefore, the distinction is that according to the *Vārttika* view, the treatment as *ciṇ* (*ciṇvadbhāva*) occurs due to conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), whereas according to the *Bhāṣya* view, it occurs because [the rule] is stated as a specific injunction (*pratipadoktatva*). By this, the passages of the *Bhāṣya* on the rule "ekāca upadeśe" (Pāṇini 7.2.10), such as "the *ārddhadhātuka* suffixes apply generally," are also explained. As for what Kaiyaṭa stated there—that "in the case of a conflict, the justification must be considered"—that is intended merely to remind one of the justification already mentioned above.

It might be argued: what is intended here by "being prescribed by a specific rule" (*pratipadavidhitvam*)—is it being *without scope* (*anavakāśatvam*), or merely being directly mentioned (*sākṣādupādānamātram*)? It cannot be the first, because the mention of *han* in the rule for *syas* and *sic* finds its scope in forms such as *pradhāniṣyate*; and the mention of *sīyuṭ* there has already served its purpose in forms such as *kāriṣīṣṭa*. Furthermore, since the four roots beginning with those ending in long *ā* are connected with the four suffixes beginning with *sy*, and because they are not marked with the *svarita* accent, the principle of "correspondence in order" (*yathāsaṃkhyam*) does not apply; thus, the portion of the rule stating "of *han* [before] *sīyuṭ*" would indeed be rendered meaningless.

It should not be argued that because the substitution of *vadh* for *han* is internal (*antaraṅga*), once that substitution has taken place, the substitute *vadh* would be included by the mention of *han* through the rule of *sthānivadbhāva*; thus, when the *ciṇvadiṭ* augment is applied to the *sīyuṭ*, and the *al*-elision occurs by the rule "ṇyallopāviyaṅ" (P. 6.4.51) according to the principle of prior contradiction (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), the form would necessarily be *vadhiṣīṣṭa*. This is incorrect, because when an internal operation such as *vadh* is due to take effect, the connection of *han* with the *sīyuṭ* is impossible precisely due to that lack of possibility (*asambhava*).
For a qualifier is meaningful only when there is both possibility (*sambhava*) and deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

This is according to the aforementioned rule. For this very reason, it will be stated in the *bhastrādi* sūtra that the phrase "in place of *āt*" (*ātaḥ sthāne*) is a qualifier of the word *sva* itself, and not of the *bhastrā* group. Likewise, regarding the sūtra *nityaṃ krīḍājīvikayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.17), it will be stated that since a *tṛc* suffix is impossible in the sense of "play" (*krīḍā*), the connection [of the compound] occurs with only one [of the two members].

Not the latter [alternative], because even in the case of the substitute *vadha* in the *liṅ* [optative] mood, the direct mention [of the root] by the rule "for *han*, *vadha* in the *liṅ*" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 2.4.42) remains the same; and furthermore, [the substitute *vadha*] possesses the additional quality of being *antaraṅga* (internally conditioned). If this is argued, it is replied here: By interpreting the particle *ca* in the rule "and like *ciṇ*" (*ciṇvadiṭ ca*, *Pāṇini Sūtra* 6.4.62) as having the sense of an inclusive conjunction (*anuktasamuccaya*), the *ciṇvat*-treatment is prescribed for the *sīyuṭ* suffix that follows *han* as well. And its status as a *pratipadavidhi* (a rule applying to a specific word-form) consists precisely in its lack of meaning [independently].

The commentator himself will state that this [particle *ca*] has the sense of including what has not been mentioned: "But the Blessed One used *ca* for that purpose. For this very reason, even when the view of rejecting the rule (*sūtra-pratyākhyāna*) is adopted, the elision of the *ṇi*-affix after the augment *iṭ* is established. However, it should be understood that if the rule were actually composed, then *iṭ* would be treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), and thus the *ṇi*-affix would be elided according to what will be stated later: "therefore, my *ṇi* is elided. Alternatively, *liṅi* is the general term referring to the *ārdhadhātuka* suffixes, while *sīyuṭi* is the specific term; *hanter* remains common to both cases.

Thus, since [the rule] *ciṇvad iṭ* is indeed an exception (*apavāda*), there is no impossibility whereby the root *han* would not connect with the suffix *sīyuṭ*. Consequently, Kaiyaṭa’s statement regarding its being a "rule by specific mention" (*pratipadavidhi*) is also entirely correct.

And this is logical: for if [the application] is impossible, then because even that which is impossible cannot be prescribed, the previously mentioned position is weak. Alternatively, according to the method of final determination to be stated later, since the rule *antaraṅgaṃ balīyaḥ* ("that which is internal is stronger") is rejected by *asiddhaṃ bahiraṅgam* ("that which is external is as if non-existent"), and since that [rule] is non-permanent due to the inclusion of the term *tuggrahaṇa* in the context of *kṛt* suffixes, its abandonment here in accordance with the observed forms (*lakṣya*) makes the conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) justified. Or else, let *liṅi* be taken as a locative absolute (*parasaptamī*).

Furthermore, the augment *ciṇvadiṭ* [is applied] because of its being "other" (*paratva*). However, let there be no introduction of the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttanipātana*). Nor should it be argued that, in this case, the prohibition by *iṇ* would undesirably apply to forms such as *vadhiṣīṣṭa*, just as it does in *karttā* and similar forms. For the root *vadh* has two upadeśas: the upadeśa as *han* and the upadeśa as *vadh*; this is clear from the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *ekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.10). Thus, since the upadeśa as *vadh* consists of more than one syllable (*anekāctva*), the prohibition of *iṇ* will not apply. Indeed, by the force of the qualifier *eka* ("single"), the upadeśa consisting of more than one syllable is excluded.

If it were stated simply as *acaḥ*, it would apply only to that which ends in a vowel (*ajanta*). This is not so; for otherwise, the designation of the roots beginning with *pac* as *anudātta* (unaccented) would become redundant. Precisely for this reason, by intending to express singularity (*ekatva*), the meaning of *acaḥ* is obtained as "that which possesses a single vowel. Consequently, by the force of the inclusion of the word *eka*, the expressed meaning [of singularity] is not lost. Nor is it correct to say that the inclusion of *eka* is for the sake of applying the *paribhāṣā*: "Where there is a mention of *ekāj*" (Pbh. 92); for the *paribhāṣā* applies by relying on the meaning "having one vowel" (*ekācaḥ*) itself, without regard for any specific word-form.

Because it is easy to state [otherwise]. Nor should it be argued that if the qualifier is thus meaningful only in this specific instance, then the rule *śtipā śapā* (Pā. 1.1.131) and others could not serve as indicators (*jñāpaka*) for the relevant technical rules; for it is possible that the very mention of an indicatory letter (*anubandha*), such as in *śīṅaḥ sārvadhātuke guṇaḥ* (Pā. 7.4.21) and *dīṅo yuḍ aci* (Pā. 6.4.63), serves as the indicator for that purpose. Thus, it is established that in every respect, the augment *iṭ* certainly follows the root *vadh*.

For this very reason, Vyāghrabhūti excluded roots ending in *a* in the *aniṭ-kārikās*, stating: "Roots ending in *a*, those ending in ū, and those ending in ṛ—namely *vṛṅ* and *vṛñ*, etc. As for the fact that in the *Kaumudī*, at the point of explaining the *lakāras* in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*), the form *ghāniṣīṣṭa* is cited and it is stated that the substitute *vadh* occurs optionally, that is entirely unobjectionable according to either the method described above, whether following the view of the *Bhāṣya* or the view of the *Vārttika*.

While this position is thus established, the author of the *Prasāda* commentary, upon taking up the phrase "the substitution of *vadh*" (*vadhādeśa*), remarked: "But this contradicts the final doctrine (*siddhānta*), because the substitution of *vadh* is not accepted in the *Bhāṣya* and other such works. In doing so, he has instead revealed his own blemish. Furthermore, as for the *Vārttika* which he cited as the source of his own confusion—"and there is a prohibition of the substitution of *han*, *ṇi*, and *ṅi*"—this is not intended as a prohibition of what applies to the *liṅ* [optative] mood; rather, it concerns what applies even to the *syādi* [periphrastic] moods by means of the extended application (*atideśa*) of the rule *ciṇvat*.

For this very reason, because of the governing heading (*adhikāra*) concerning "a stem" (*aṅga*), the extension (*atideśa*) applies only to that which is a stem, and not to the substitutes for *han*, *iṇ*, or *ṅi*, since these are not stems; thus, by the force of the heading on "stems" alone, the Vārttika was rejected in the Bhāṣya. Although this is beyond dispute in the works of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), we have nevertheless clarified it so that beginners, having seen the Prasāda commentary, might not fall into error according to the maxim: "like one blind man clinging to another who is blind."

Let us return to the subject at hand. There are five Vārttikas concerning the prohibition of *nuk* and *śuk* after roots ending in long vowels, the prohibition of the substitution of *śā*, *jab*, *dhittva*, the elision of *hi*, and *itva* when there is a substitute for the imperative (*loṭ*), the prohibition of the substitution of *sran* for the root *trai*, the addition of *ām* in the prescription [of the periphrastic future], and the accentuation when there is the substitution of *vas*. These five Vārttikas have also been rejected. For instance, in the forms *vilāpayati* and *bhāpayati*, the suffixes *nuk* and *śuk* will not occur; this is because of the inclusion of the vowel *ī*—that is, reading *lī-ī* and *bhī-ī*—or because of the inclusion of a short vowel.

Likewise, in the cases of *śiṣṭāt*, *hatāt*, *bhintāt*, *kurutāt*, and *stāt*, although the rules "śā hau" (Pāṇ. 6.4.35), "hanter jaḥ" (Pāṇ. 6.4.36), "hujhalbhyo herdhiḥ" (Pāṇ. 6.4.101), "utaśca pratyayād asaṃyogapūrvāt" (Pāṇ. 6.4.106), and "ghvasoreddhau" (Pāṇ. 6.4.119) would apply—since the substitute *tātaṅ* is included by the mention of *hi* through its status as a *sthānivadbhāva*—nevertheless...

"According to the maxim *sakṛdgatau vipratiṣedhe yadbādhitaṃ tadbādhitaṃ eva* (Pao Bhāṣya 40)—'when two rules conflict and apply simultaneously, that which is once superseded remains superseded'—they do not occur. Likewise, in the case of *puṣṇītāt*, the rule *halaḥ śnaḥ śānajjhau* (Pā Sū 3.1.83) does not apply, because *tātaṅ* prevails due to its being subsequent to both of those [rules], both of which are *nit*. Similarly, in the case of *tisṛṇām*, since the substitution of *tisṛ* prevails by virtue of being subsequent, the substitution of *traya-* in *trestrayaḥ* (Pā Sū 6.3.48) is likewise superseded."

Thus, in the case of *catasrastisṭhanti*, the suffix *ām* prescribed by *caturanaḍuhoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.98) is superseded by the state of being *catasṛ*. Similarly, in *aśāsantvāviduṣī sasminnahan*, the rule *videḥ śaturvasuḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.36) prescribes the substitution of *vasu* for the *śatṛ* [present participle suffix]. Because this *vasu* is included under the term *śatṛ* in the rule *śaturanumo nadyajādī* (Pāṇini 6.1.173), one might expect the feminine suffix *nadī* to be udātta, based on its following an antodātta word ending in *śatṛ*. However, [this expectation is not fulfilled] because... [the text continues with the specific grammatical analysis].

In the phrase *viduṣo 'gnihotraṃ juhvati*, the genitive case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in *viduṣaḥ* does not become udātta, because of the prohibition by the rule *anunāsikaḥ*. To explain: *anum* is a bahuvrīhi compound meaning "that in which *um* is absent. The term *um* refers to a pratyāhāra beginning from the vowel *u* in the sūtra *sanāśaṃsabhikṣa-uḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.168) up to the *m* in *anu-m* (the marker for the ārdhadhātuka suffix *kṛt*), or alternatively, it begins from the *u* in *tanādikṛñbhya uḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.79). Within that range, the rule *vasoḥ saṃprasāraṇam* (Pāṇini 6.4.131) is also included.

But surely, if this were the case in the second alternative, there would be the undesirable consequence of the prohibition applying even in examples such as *lunatā acchāravaṃ prathamā jānatīgāt*, because even though the suffix *śnā* does not apply in the initial rule *tanādikṛñbhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.79), the status of being a *śatṛ*-anukaraṇa (an imitation of a *śatṛ* form) is not lost. For even under the view that the mention of *num* is significant, the absence of that [num] is a qualifier of the *śatṛ* itself, and not of the *śatṛ* ending; otherwise, the prohibition would undesirably apply even to forms like *muñcatā* and *muñcate*.

However, this Vārttika remains established even in the final Siddhānta: "There is a prohibition [of the substitution] for *go* when followed by a vowel (*a*), a nasal augment (*ṇit*), or in matters of accent. For in the case of *citragvagram*, the formation of the single preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*) would apply by the rule *sarvatra vibhāṣā goḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.122).

This is because that reading is established in the commentary on the *Ṣaṣṭha* (the sixth book) regarding the rule *nānta-pādam* (Pāṇini 6.1.115), as well as in the commentary on the rule *iko guṇavṛddhī* (Pāṇini 1.1.3); and according to that method, it is appropriate that the rule *sarvatra* (6.1.122) also functions as a prescriber of the single preceding form (*pūrvarūpa*).

Kaiyaṭa, however, based on the observation in the Bhāṣya under the Śākala-sūtra that "by the word *ca* in [Pāṇini 6.1.128] *hrasvaśca*, the term *prakṛtyā* is drawn forward," and following the reading *prakṛtyāntaḥpādam* [from Pāṇini 6.1.115], indicated that the term *pūrvapada* found in the Vārttika is an indicator (*upalak�ṣaṇa*) for the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) preceded by the occurrence of that [shortening].

Nor can it be argued that in the rule *sarvatra vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 6.1.122), by carrying forward the term *eṅaḥ* from the previous sūtra, the prohibition [of vṛddhi] is easily established because it is an operation dependent on an *al* (*alvidhi*). For even in the case of *he citrago agram*, such an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would still occur; for here there is no reliance on an *al* as the substitute (*sthānin*), since the word is already *eṅ*-ending by its very nature. Furthermore, in the case of *citraguḥ*, the condition of being a *ṇit* suffix would apply by the rule *goto ṇit* (Pāṇini 7.1.90). And in the cases of *citragum* and *citragūn*, the substitution of *ā* would apply according to the sixth-century Vārttika *āgotaḥ śasoḥ*.

In this context, the mention of *ṇit*-ness (*ṇittva*) could indeed be omitted; for by the very force of the inclusion of the long vowel marker (*tapara*) in the rule *gotaḥ*, the application of *ṇit*-ness is precluded, and because the reading *aut* will be established [in its place]. Furthermore, any over-extension (over-application) in forms such as *acinavam* can be prevented by means of association with *śas*. [Examples: *svara-bahu-gumān*.

Regarding the prohibition in the rule *nagośvan* (Pāṇini 6.1.182) against the acute accent prescribed by *hasvanuḍbhyāṃ matup* (Pāṇini 6.1.176), the commentary (*vṛtti*) on the rule *nagośvan* states that in forms such as *bahugunā* and *bahugubhyām*, the accent that would otherwise apply by the rule *antodāttād uttarapadād anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 6.1.169) is prohibited. This, however, is questionable, as it contradicts both the *Bhāṣya* and the *Vārttika*.

*acaḥ parasmin pūrvavidhau* (Pāṇini 1.1.57). An *ādeśa* (substitute) for a vowel (*ac*) caused by something subsequent shall be treated as the original (*sthānin*), provided that a rule is to be applied which depends on what was seen as preceding that [original] vowel, or on that [original] vowel itself acting as the cause. In the case of *vavraśca*, here, by virtue of the status of the substitute being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) according to *uraṇ raparaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.50), the substitution of *at* (as per *uraṇ raparaḥ*) is subject to the prohibition in *na saṃprasāraṇe saṃprasāraṇam* (Pāṇini 6.1.37); thus, there is no *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) of the letter *v*. Nor is this redundant because of the previous rule (*pūrvasūtra*), since the present rule concerns a non-vowel (*al*) operation (*alvidhi*).

Nor should it be said that having another as its cause (*paranimittatva*) is unestablished, because [the substitution] has as its cause a suffix implied by the *aṅga*. Nor should it be said that the section on *aṅga* begins prior to the modifications resulting from repetition (*abhyāsa*), for the position that it extends until the end of the seventh chapter is what will be established as the final doctrine (*siddhānta*). As for an example of a rule based on a preceding element: *tanvanti*, *tanvate*. Here, due to the status of the substitute as being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), the augment *iṭ* does not occur. For in that case, the *aṅga* "tan" is the cause, and that [cause] precedes the vowel *u*. Why [is the condition] "vowel" (*acaḥ*) stated? [Consider] *viśnaḥ*, *praśnaḥ*.

Having played at dice (*dyūtvā*), having sewn (*syūtvā*), having approached (*abhigatya*). For instance, in the words *viśnaḥ* and *praśnaḥ*, the substitution of *ś* for *ch* is conditioned by what follows; because of the status of that [substitute] as if it were the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), the augment *tuk* would have been required by the rule *che ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.73), but it does not occur because of the explicit mention of the vowel *ac*.

This might be argued: here, because it is *antaraṅga*, the *tuk* replacement should occur first. Nor should it be said that the letter *ś* [of the suffix] would apply by virtue of the rule "that which pertains to a phoneme (*vārṇa*) is stronger than that which pertains to a morphological element (*āṅga*)" (Paribhāṣā 55); for that rule—"that which pertains to a phoneme is stronger than that which pertains to a morphological element"—applies only where both the *āṅga* and the *vārṇa* operation apply simultaneously with reference to one and the same cause. As in such cases, there the *āṅga* operation is stronger. But here, there is no simultaneous application of both with reference to a single cause. Thus, the *tuk* should indeed occur first.

For example, when the root *kṛ* is followed by the *liṭ* suffix with the *ṇal* augment, resulting in the form *kṛ-a*, the rule *vṛddhi* prescribed by *aco ñṇiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.115)—which finds its scope in forms such as *gaurī*—sets aside the *yaṇ* substitution that would otherwise apply due to its being an *antaraṅga* operation; thus, *vṛddhi* itself prevails. However, in the word *praśnaḥ*, the *naṅ* augment is the cause for the change of *ś* [to *ṣ*], whereas the *tuk* augment is the cause for the change of *ch*. Furthermore, the application of these two rules occurs at different times.

If it is asked: "What is the proof that this *paribhāṣā* applies only where there is simultaneous application (*prāpti*) to a single object?"—understand that the very means of apprehending the subject (*dharmigrāhakamāna*) is the proof. For instance, in the rule *abhyāsasyāsavarṇe* (Pāṇini 6.4.78), the mention of the term *asavarṇa* ("non-homogeneous vowel") is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) of this *paribhāṣā*. And this is established in the *Bhāṣya* at the end of the first daily lesson (*āhnika*) of the sixth book.

For that [rule] is not useful for excluding forms such as *īṣatuḥ* and *ūṣatuḥ*, because in those cases the internal (antaraṅga) rule of homogeneous lengthening (*savarṇadīrgha*) subverts the *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* substitutions; for those two, depending upon both the designation of the stem (*aṅga-saṃjñā*) and the designation of the reduplication (*abhyāsa-saṃjñā*), are external (bahiraṅga). Nor should it be argued that even so, those two [substitutions] would still occur by virtue of being exceptions (*apavāda*), because according to the maxim "that which is not otherwise applicable" (*yena nāprāpti-nyāya*), they are exceptions specifically with regard to the *yaṇ* substitution.

If it is argued that even when *guṇa* has already applied in cases such as *hayeṣa*, and *vṛddhi* has already applied in cases such as *hayāya*, both are set aside by the formal extension (*rūpātideśa*) under the rule *dvirvacane 'ci* (Pāṇini 1.1.59); and once the doubling (*dvitva*) has been performed, since the long vowel of the same class (*savarṇadīrgha*) would also apply, it too—by the maxim *yenāprāpte*—would be superseded by *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*, then [we reply]: in that case, even if the mention of *savarṇa* were made, the rule would end up being without scope (*nirviṣayatā*).

If it is argued that by the force of the mention of "non-homogeneous" (*asavarṇa*), the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions would again take effect, overriding the long-vowel substitution for homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*), we say no; for [the mention of "non-homogeneous"] has its purpose fulfilled in cases such as *iyarti*. If it is further objected: "In that case, since the mention of 'non-homogeneous' is superfluous—given that by the principle of 'what was not previously applicable' (*yenāprāptinyāya*), the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* would already succeed in blocking the *yaṇ* substitution in forms like *hayarti*—one should not have included it," then the resulting meaning is this: by the force of its necessity (*sāmarthya*), the application of *guṇa* and so on occurs in cases such as *hayeṣa*. And thus, the mention of "non-homogeneous" remains entirely redundant once again.

Having treated "artteśca" as a sūtra and carrying forward "yvoh," since the substitution of *iyaṅ* for the *ikāra* of the root *ṛt* could be prescribed for the sake of brevity, forms such as "iyeṣa" are easily established even by the force of the explicit mention of "abhyāsasya" (of the reduplication). If it is objected: "In the case of the citation 'artteḥ' using the *śitap* affix, *iyaṅ* would not occur in the *yaṅluk* form 'ariyarti'," [we reply: let it simply be stated as "ṛtaḥ. Furthermore, due to the association with "iṇo yaṇ" (Pāṇini 6.4.81), the term will refer to the verbal root; or alternatively, because the element *u* serves as a qualifier for the *aṅga*.

Therefore, there is no over-extension [of the rule] in cases such as *artāram* and *atikrāntairatyartṛbhiḥ*. If it is objected that even so, *iyaṅ* would occur in *īṣatuḥ* just as it does in *iyeṣa*, we reply: no, because it has already been stated that the long vowel (*dīrgha*) sublates [the *iyaṅ*] due to its being an internal operation (*antaraṅga*). Nor should it be argued that the same applies to *iyeṣa*, for in that case, the long vowel does not apply because its cause is on the verge of destruction when the possibility of *guṇa* arises.

For it will be stated under the rule *samarthānāṃ prathamād* (Pāṇini 4.1.82) that the inclusion of the term *samartha* ("capable") serves to indicate the metarule (*paribhāṣā*) *akṛtavyūhāḥ pāṇinīyāḥ* ("the followers of Pāṇini do not [allow the application of a rule] once a grammatical configuration has been established"). For this very reason, in the cases of *sautthitiḥ* and *vaikṣamāṇiḥ*, the inclusion of *samartha* is intended to prevent the undesirable forms *sāvutthitiḥ* and *vāyīkṣamāṇiḥ*; otherwise, because the future initial *vṛddhi* would subvert the cause of the internal *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel by homogeneous merger), the latter would fail to apply. Thus, the inclusion of *samartha* ensures that the desired forms are maintained.

In that context, the meaning of the word *samartha* is "already completed" (*pariniṣṭhita*). Alternatively, let it be understood that [the rule] causes even what has already been accomplished to cease. The result, however, remains exactly the same; the only difference is the additional burden of complexity—this is the direction of the argument. Consequently, in forms such as *īyiṣe*, once the *guṇa* substitution has taken place, the long-vowel rule for homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*) does not apply. Since the *yaṇ* substitution would then be applicable, this [rule for *iyaṅ*] serves as an exception (*apavāda*) specifically to that *yaṇ*. In cases such as *īṣatuḥ*, the *savarṇadīrgha* prevails due to its being an internal operation (*antaraṅga*); thus, the inclusion of the term *asavarṇa* (non-homogeneous) is purposeless and serves merely as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the aforementioned maxim.

If it is objected: "How can there be a sublation of the cause (*nimitta*) by a quality (*guṇa*), since the substitution of the long vowel *savarṇadīrgha* remains applicable by virtue of the rule *acaḥ parasmin* (Pāṇini 1.1.57), which prescribes the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*)? We reply: No, because the long vowel is a result of a rule concerning both the preceding and following elements (*pūrvaparavidhi*); therefore, when that [long vowel] is to be produced, the status of the original element does not apply. For it is only for the preceding element that [the status of the original applies].

For that [is the case], but not for the preceding and following [sounds], as will be demonstrated during the analysis of what is excluded by the mention of *vidhi* (rule). Furthermore, since a rule (*vidhi*) concerning a homogeneous sound (*savarṇa*) would also be a rule for that homogeneous sound, the prohibition "na edānta" (Pāṇini 1.1.58) would apply when that [substitution] was to be performed. By this [argument], if the term *asavarṇa* (non-homogeneous) were employed, then in the case of *iyeṣa*, the substitution *iyaṅ* would not occur by virtue of the status of being like the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*). Nor should it be argued that, by the force of employing *asavarṇa*, *iyaṅ* should proceed based on a non-homogeneous sound perceived through direct audition (*śrauta*), just as the substitution of *gh* occurs in *ghnanti*; for if that were the case, it would be impossible to establish the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*).

It has been refuted [by others] on the grounds that, since the single purpose of the rule *iyarti* would otherwise require only the statement *uśca*, the explicit mention of *abhv-asaṃyogapūrvasya* (of what is not preceded by a consonant cluster) implies that *iyaṅ* and *uṅ*—which end in *v*—would, like *ṇal* and *ātus*, indiscriminately subvert even the long vowel; thus, the inclusion of the term *asavarṇa* (non-homogeneous) serves to exclude those cases. This refutation is based on the adoption of a *prasajyapratiṣedha* (absolute negation), meaning "it does not occur when a homogeneous vowel follows."

In that case, since the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) has been prohibited by the aforementioned method, *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*—which are determined to be exceptions to the application of *yaṇ* in forms such as *iyeṣa* because *yaṇ* alone would otherwise apply—are capable of being superseded by the internal (*antaranga*) long vowel (*dīrgha*) in forms such as *īṣatuḥ*. And that [supersession] being indicated is restricted to specific cases characterized by the conditions "having the same locus" (*samānāśraya*) and "simultaneous application" (*yugapatprāpti*), according to the requirements of the grammatical rules; such is the view of the ancients.

For this very reason, in the case of *syonaḥ*—where the suffix *na* is added to the root *siv* by an *auṇādika* rule, and after the elision of *v* and the substitution of *ūṭ* have been applied, resulting in the sequence *si-ū-na*—the *yaṇ* replacement occurs first because it is *antaraṅga*. This is despite the fact that the *guṇa* of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) is also an *aṅga*-operation; for the former depends on two distinct elements (*vyāśrayatva*), whereas the latter does not. Nor should one suspect that the *guṇa* should apply instead of *ūṭ* due to its being subsequent in the order of rules, because the *guṇa* is actually *bahiraṅga*, as it depends upon many factors: the light vowel *i* characterized as the *upadhā* and the entire *aṅga*. This point is made clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the rule *yena vidhiḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.72), and the author of the *Vṛtti* holds the same view.

Let us return to the subject at hand. If the *tuk* augment were applied according to the method stated, the substitution of *śa* would follow; thus, since *tuk* would indeed be heard in the cases of *viśna* and *praśna*, another effort must be undertaken to prevent it, and there must be another counter-example for the rule *acaḥ*. If this is argued, it is true that such an effort does exist, because the inclusion of *tuk* in the formulation of *cchvoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.19) is established in the Bhāṣya on the sixth book and other works.

It might be argued: "Since the forms *viśna* and *praśna* are established by the two paribhāṣās—``akṛtavyūhāḥ pāṇinīyāḥ`` (Pāṇinian grammarians do not undo what has been formed) and ``kṛtaṃ vā nivartayanti`` (or they do undo what has been formed)—what is the purpose of the explicit mention of the augment *tuk*? Nor can it be said that the result of this is to indicate the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of the aforementioned paribhāṣās; for by means of this [mention of *tuk*], the form *cākhāyitā* is established."
