Otherwise, one would have to argue that the substitution of *āt* [for *adas*] should not be applied beforehand—anticipating the future elision by the rule *yasya halaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.45)—or that even if applied, it should be revoked; furthermore, the *ākac* suffix would not be heard in forms such as *tvakatpitṛkaḥ* and *atibhavakān*. However, this need not be asserted, because the mention of *lyap* in the rule *ado jagdhiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.36) and the mention of "the subsequent word" (*uttarapada*) in the rule *pratyayottarapadayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.98) serve respectively to indicate that these rules override the internal (*antaraṅga*) operations of *lyap*-substitution and its elision (*lyap-luk*).

For it is possible that the two aforementioned technical rules (*paribhāṣā*) serve as indicators of the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) well-known in the treatises on final conclusions (*siddhāntagrantha*). If you argue: "The traditional doctrine of the *siddhānta* is not to be trusted because it is devoid of logical justification; for the mention of the suffix *-lyap* and the subsequent word (*uttarapada*) is intended to enjoin what was otherwise unobtained, since it is clear that [the desired result] would not otherwise obtain due to the force of the *akṛtavyūha-paribhāṣā* (the rule regarding the non-modification of a completed formation)," then let even the mention of *-lyap* and the subsequent word be unnecessary. For if the *akṛtavyūha-paribhāṣā* is non-eternal, the very statement of the "return to the original form" (*prakṛtipratyāpatti*) can itself serve as the indicator (*jñāpaka*).

Or let that [objection] be set aside, for the very rules such as *ke'ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.13) and *so'ci lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.134) serve as indicators (*jñāpaka*). To explain: in the case of *ka i sa u*, when the *yaṇ* substitution prompted by another word has been applied to the vowels *i* and *u*, the *guṇa* resulting from *ādguṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.87) would not occur according to the maxim *akṛtavyūhāḥ pāṇinīyāḥ* (Patañjali’s Bhāṣya on Pāṇini 1.1.56), because the cause for that *guṇa* has already disappeared.

Nor can one find a solution by means of the two *paribhāṣās*, "that which is external (*bahiraṅga*) is unestablished" (*asiddham bahiraṅgam*) and "the internal (*antaraṅga*) is stronger" (*antaraṅgaṃ balīyaḥ*); for in cases such as *vṛkṣa i idam*, even after the long vowel (*dīrgha*) has been applied, there is no sublation of those two *paribhāṣās*—which both have scope in cases like *pacāvedam*—by the maxim of "that which is not otherwise applicable" (*yena nāprāptinyāya*), because the cause [for their application] remains unimpaired. Otherwise, forms such as *upeyuṣā* and *jagmuṣaḥ* would also not be established.

Thus, the fact that the *ṅ* in *naṅ* is marked with the *ṅ*-sign (*ṅit*)—which is applied here to prohibit *guṇa* in the case of *viśnaḥ*—would itself indicate the existence of the *akṛtavyūha-paribhāṣā*. Furthermore, let the rule *samarthānām* not exist. For this very reason, the *bhāṣya* on the sūtra *samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.1), which states, "That which ought not to be done is nevertheless done [by saying] 'of those that are semantically connected, starting from the first,'" becomes consistent. Therefore, it is established that all five operations—the attainment of the status of being a suffix (*pratyayatva*), semantic connection (*samarthatva*), the mention of the subsequent member (*uttarapada-graha*), and the presence of *tuk*—need not be performed.

To this it is replied: the mention of *satuk* and *kv* is intended to indicate that the maxim *vārṇādāṅgaṃ balīyaḥ* (Pā. Pa. Bhā. 55) is not universally obligatory. For instance, what was stated previously—following the works of the ancients that [the rule applies] only when the locus (*āśraya*) is identical—is not capable of withstanding scrutiny, since that [application of the maxim] is accepted in many cases even where the loci are different. Thus, Kaiyaṭa, under the rule *asiddhavat* (Pā. 6.4.22), states regarding the form *śunaḥ* that the elision of *a* (*allopa*) occurs by overriding the prior single-substitute (*pūrvaikādeśa*), on the grounds that a rule concerning phonemes (*vārṇa*) is stronger than one concerning constituent parts (*āṅga*).

Nor should it be argued that in those cases there is indeed a common substratum (*samānāśrayatva*) regarding the portion of the vowel *a* in both [the suffix and the preceding element], for that would contradict the presentation of them as having different substrata (*vyāśrayatva*) based on the similarity of the portions of the letter *ch* and the vowel *i* in the words *viśnaḥ* and *syonaḥ*.

Furthermore, there are [rules concerning] a stem (*aṅga*): *ācchīnadyoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.80), *śīṅo ruṭ* (7.1.6), *acaḥ parasmin* (1.1.57), *yena vidhiḥ* (1.1.72), *upeyivānanāśvān* (3.2.109), *āḍajādīnām* (6.4.72), *ajāderdvitīyasya* (1.1.2), *adasa au sulopaśca* (7.2.107), *sārvadhātukamapit* (1.2.4), and *upasargādhrasva ūhateḥ* (7.4.23).

It is clear to those who have mastered the established conclusions (*siddhānta*) that in the rules beginning with *snukramoranātmanepade* (Pāṇini 1.3.36), all the works of Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others proceed by sometimes accepting and sometimes not accepting the principle of having a common substratum (*samānāśrayatā*). Furthermore, even the purposes (*prayojana*) of the maxim (*paribhāṣā*) "that which concerns the phoneme (*vārṇa*) [takes precedence] over that which concerns the suffix (*āṅga*)" (Paribhāṣenduśekhara 55) at the end of the first section (*āhnika*) of the sixth book of the Mahābhāṣya are indeed common to both views.

The same is the case in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the rule *na māṅyoge* (Pāṇini 6.4.74), and likewise in the Mahābhāṣya on the rule *ātonupasarge kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.3). Therefore, just as with the *bahir-aṅga-paribhāṣā* and the *akṛtavyūha-paribhāṣā*, one must resort to the fact that the principle *vārṇād āṅgam* (Paribhāṣā 55) is also non-eternal (*anitya*). And this [non-eternality] is indicated by the inclusion of the augment *tuk* in the word *satuk* [in the rule *sātpadādyoḥ*].

Nor can that [the mention of *sa*] serve to prevent *tuk* by means of the *sthānivadbhāva* even in the preceding rule (*pūrvavidhi*), because its purpose is already served by the requirement of the word *acaḥ*, which must necessarily be formulated for other reasons. Thus, while the inclusion of *satukka* is made for another purpose, let it—if it so desires—inform us of the non-universality (*anityatā*) of the principle *akṛtavyūha* (Pāṇini 1.4.2). As for the counter-example "viśnaḥ" in the present sūtra, it stands according to the literal reading.

This being the case, since the *ṅit*-ness of the negative particle (*nañ*) has already served its purpose in prohibiting *guṇa*, another indicator (*jñāpaka*) must be accepted for the *akṛtavyūha-paribhāṣā*. And that [indicator] would be either the mention of "affix" (*pratyaya*), the mention of "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*), or the mention of "possessing the same meaning" (*samartha*). However, the final conclusion is that the mention of *lyap* itself is the lightest among these. For it will be established that the mention of "affix" is for the sake of the *kvip* affix used in the sense of "behaving like" (*ācāra-kvip*), while the mention of "subsequent member" is for the sake of overriding *tava-mama* and the like, and for the sake of rules that would otherwise not apply.

Haradatta’s conjecture—that the continuous application [of the rule] up to the end of the section is itself the indicator—is incorrect because an *antaraṅga* operation is sublated by an exception (*apavāda*); this will be explained in the seventh [chapter]. And thus, in the *gaṇasūtra* for the class beginning with *pāman*, the inclusion of the term "without sandhi" (*akṛtasandheḥ*) in the rule "after *viṣvak*, there is elision of the final member [of the compound], provided sandhi has not been applied" (*viṣvagityuttarapadalopaścākṛtasandheḥ*) is also unnecessary. Alternatively, let it be for the purpose of making it clear that the secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) are added only after words like *vīkṣamāṇa* where sandhi has already been applied.

Thus, Kaiyaṭa is indeed correct in stating that this *paribhāṣā*—namely, "the rule *striyāḥ puṃvat* (Pāṇini 6.3.34)—is relied upon everywhere. However, Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the *ābhāt* sūtra (*ātaḥ sthaḥ* 7.4.50), which asserts that the *paribhāṣā* "when the cause [of a grammatical operation] has ceased" (*nimittāpāye*) is not supported by the *Mahābhāṣya*, is merely superficial. Likewise, Haradatta’s work in the commentary on *chvoḥ śūḍanunāsike ca* (6.4.19), which claims that this is neither a stated rule nor a logical principle (*nyāya*), is also merely superficial, given the refinement of this *paribhāṣā* in the commentary on the sūtra *samarthānām* (2.1.1).

Because it is self-evident. Alternatively, between the two stated paribhāṣās, the *akṛtavyūha* paribhāṣā alone should be accepted due to its parsimony (*lāghava*), and not the one stating "even what has been performed," because of its prolixity (*gaurava*). The text should be interpreted in this sense in some way. The result, however, is beyond dispute, as other indicators (*jñāpaka*) are also easily available. For example, the rule *cau* (Pāṇini 6.2.138), which prescribes lengthening, serves as an indicator here.

For if the *yaṇ* substitution is applied internally (as an antaranga operation), how could forms such as *pratīcaḥ* provide an occasion for the application of the long vowel (*dīrgha*)? Furthermore, a worldly maxim is easily cited here: in the world, a cause is seen to be of two kinds—that which regulates the persistence of an effect and that which does not regulate it. The first is, for example, the cognition of "two" (*apekṣābuddhi*) in the system of Nyāya, because it is accepted that the destruction of that [cognition] results in the destruction of duality.

Likewise, in the Vedānta system, it is well known that *prārabdha* karma acts as the regulator for the persistence of distractions (*vikṣepa*), just as an adjunct (*upādhi*) acts as the regulator for the persistence of the redness of a crystal and so forth. The second [type of cause], however, is the staff and such; for even when that is destroyed, one does not observe the destruction of the jar.

This being the case, why should there not also be a twofold division here in accordance with the requirements of the subject matter (*lakṣya*)? Thus, Kaiyaṭa and others have cited the worldly twofold usage as a supporting illustration for the established doctrine that "that whose cause is obstructed by another characteristic is not impermanent," which is sometimes accepted and sometimes not. For example, when Vālin was killed by the Blessed One while Vālin and Sugrīva were fighting, people do not describe Sugrīva as having gained superiority over Vālin.

Even though victory was obtained by the Pāṇḍavas with the assistance of the Blessed One, they nevertheless continued to treat the Pāṇḍavas as if they were superior; such is the general direction of the argument.

It might be argued as follows: If the mention of *t* in the rule *chvoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.19) is intended to include the *t*-augment (*satuk*), then that same [augmented form] would carry over into the rule for the elision of *r* (*rāllopa*). Consequently, in forms such as *hūḥ*, *hurau*, and *huraḥ*, the elision would not occur because they lack the *t*-augment. Nor can it be said that by the force of the rule’s continued application (*anuvṛtti*), the rule should apply there even without the *t*-augment—just as in the case of *rādhohiṃsāyām* (Pāṇini 6.4.123), where although *ataḥ* is carried over, it is understood to mean "like the vowel *a*"—for it is equally possible to construe it as referring to the letter *v* alone.

As for the claim that both *satuk* and *vituk* are indicated here, that is not correct; for if they were treated as a collective compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*), a singular form would result, whereas if they were treated as a copulative compound (*itaretara-yoga-dvandva*), a plural form would result. If one suggests that we form a collective compound of the two *cha*s and then form a copulative compound with the *va*, this is also incorrect; for in a collective compound, the suffix *ṭac* would be required, and furthermore, the correspondence between the elements and their respective operations (*yathāsaṃkhya*) would become impossible.

To this it is replied: when a collective *dvandva* compound is formed of the letters *cha* and *va*, let there be another *dvandva* for the subsequent *cha*; likewise, even in the case of the substitute (*ādeśa*), there is a phonetic connection (*praśleṣa*) with the word [of the rule]. Thus, by the principle of closest proximity (*antaratama*) and the maxim of correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhya*), the desired result is established. Alternatively, let the mention be of the letter *ka* itself along with its *tuṭ* augment; however, in the rule for the elision of *ra* and *la* (*rāllope*), only the simple letter [is understood] due to the force of the context, and because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the prohibition of *natva* in the rule "nadhyākhyā" (Pāṇini 8.2.57).

For in the case of the word "mūrtaḥ," without the elision of the *ch* sound, the application of the rule [Pāṇini 8.2.66] would not be possible at all. Likewise, the grammatical indications such as "mūrttau ghanaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.3.77) and "dravamūrttisparśayoḥ śyaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.24) are also consistent with this view. This is the general direction [of the argument]. Under this view, the counter-examples for the rule "acaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.1.57) are "dyūtvā" and "syūtvā. Here, due to the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), the *yaṇ* substitution would not occur. [Objection: But its own inherent nature as an *ac* (vowel) will remain.

If it is argued that "extensions [of grammatical operations] do not cause the cessation of the operation upon their own substratum," we say no; for at the point of explaining the purpose of including the term "vidhi" (rule), it will be established as a settled doctrine (*siddhānta*) in this very sūtra that there is indeed the cessation of the operation upon its own substratum.

If it is argued: "In this case, that which is relied upon in the rule for *yaṇ*-substitution (*yaṇ-vidhi*) is the vowel *a*, and this is not the substitute; whereas the substitute is the entire cluster *ūḍ*, and this cluster is not the cause (*nimitta*) for the *yaṇ*-substitution," [we reply]: No. This is because markers (*anubandha*) are non-terminal (*anekānta*), and even if they were terminal (*ekānta*), the substitute is precisely the form *ūḍ* itself, since it perishes as soon as it is uttered (*uccaritapradhvaṃsin*). Furthermore, it will be stated later that by means of the mention of the suffix *-vat*, even an absence is extended [to the substitute]. Similarly, *abhigatya* is also a counter-example.

For here, since the elision of the nasal (*anunāsika-lopa*) is caused by a subsequent element (*paranimittaka*), due to its status as a *sthānivadbhāva*, the substitution of *tuṅ* [for *u*] by the rule "hasvasya piti kṛti" (Pāṇini 6.1.71) would not apply. Now, for what purpose is the phrase "in the case of a subsequent element" (*parasmin*) used? Consider the example *yuvajāniḥ*. Here, because of the *sthānivadbhāva* of the substitution of *niṅ* for *jāyā*, the elision of the semi-vowel (*yalopa*) would not apply. It has already been stated that the cessation of the original form's own properties (*svāśrayanivṛtti*) and the extension of non-existence (*abhāvātideśa*) will be explained.

Furthermore, [the word] *vyāghrapād* means "one whose feet are like those of a tiger. According to Pāṇini’s rule *pādasya lopo ’hastyādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇ. 5.4.138), there is an elision of the final syllable of *pāda* caused by the presence of the word *vyāghra*. Thereafter, because the base belongs to the *garga*-class, the suffix *yañ* is applied, resulting in *vaiyāghrapadya*. Due to the status of the elided element as *sthānivadbhāva*, the substitution of *pad* for *pāda* prescribed by the rule *pādaḥ pat* (Pāṇ. 6.4.130) would not occur. If one argues that it will occur by virtue of the force of the specific statement [in the rule], then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to forms such as *pādena*.

Furthermore, since the rule *pādaśatasya* (Pāṇini 5.4.1)—which prescribes elision—prevents the application of the *sthānivadbhāva* by its own force, the prescription of the substitution of *pad-* in forms such as *dvipadikā* becomes meaningful; what then is the force of that [prescription]? However, once the word *parasmin* is supplied [to the rule], it is established that because the substitution of *pad-* has its purpose fulfilled in cases like *vaiyāghrapadyaḥ*, there is no substitution of *pad-* in *pādena* and so on, due to the *sthānivadbhāva* of the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*). Now, one might object: the single-substitute is not between two vowels (*acaḥ*), but rather between two consonants (*acoḥ*).

If it is asked, "In that case, how can there be the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*)?"—it is not so, because when individual phonemes (*varṇa*) are specified, the genus (*jāti*) is understood. For this very reason, forms such as *śrāyasau*, *gaumatau*, *cāturau*, and *ānaḍuhau* are established. [The derivation is as follows: from *śreyasaḥ apatyam* ("the offspring of Śreyas"), by the rule *devikāśiṃśapādityavāḍdīrghasatraśreyasām* (Pāṇini 7.3.1), there is the substitution of the vowel *ā*. Consequently, when the suffix *aup* is added to all four bases ending in *aṇ*, the rules for *num* and *ām* do not apply, because the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) is treated as the first element (*ādivat*). Likewise, in the case of *udavāhe*.

The suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *karmaṇyaṇ* [Pāṇini 3.2.1] because it means "it carries water. In the formation of a name (*saṃjñā*), there is the substitution of *ud* for *uda*. Then, because the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) resulting from the *ṅī* ending is treated as the initial element (*ādivadbhāva*), the condition for the substitution of *ūṭh* for *vāh* [by Pāṇini 6.4.132] would apply. Why does the rule specify "in the context of a preceding operation" (*pūrvavidhau*)? Consider the example *naidheyaḥ*. From the root *dhā* preceded by the prefix *ni*, the suffix *ki* is applied by the rule *upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ* [Pāṇini 3.3.92], followed by the elision of the vowel *ā*. Then, the suffix *ḍhak* is applied by the rules *dvyacaḥ* [Pāṇini 4.1.121] and *itaścāniñaḥ* [Pāṇini 4.1.122].

If the elision of the *ākāra* were subject to the rule of *sthānivadbhāva*, then its designation as having three syllables (*tryackatva*) would sublate its designation as having two syllables (*dvyackatva*), because the two are contradictory; for one who has three sons does not receive the designation of having two sons. If it is argued: "Even so, the mention of the word *vidhi* (rule) need not be included, since the meaning 'when an operation (*kārya*) is to be performed on what precedes' can be inferred from the genitive case *pūrvasya*," we reply: No. The mention of *vidhi* is intended to convey two distinct compounds: *pūrvasya vidhiḥ* (a rule concerning what precedes) and *pūrvasmād vidhiḥ* (a rule [arising] after what precedes). As for the example under the compound with the ablative case (*pañcamī-samāsa*), it has already been stated as *tanvanti*.

It might be argued: if even a *pañcamī* compound is desired, then forms such as *vigaṇayya* would not be established, because when the substitution of *ay* is to be applied by the rule *lyapi laghupūrvāt* (Pāṇini 6.4.56), the *allopa* [elision of the penultimate vowel] would be treated as *sthānivat*. Nor can the force of the rule's very formulation be invoked as a justification, since it has its utility in cases like *anugamayya*, where the suffix *mit* applies. To this it is replied: the status of being *sthānivat* regarding an operation conditioned by what precedes is non-permanent (*anitya*), as evidenced by the rule *niṣṭhāyāṃ seṭi* (Pāṇini 6.4.52). For instance:

In this context, the term *seṭ* (having an *iṭ* augment) does not serve to exclude roots that lack *iṭ*, because such an exclusion is impossible from a causative (*ṇijanta*) root. One might object: "But in the example *saṃjñapitaḥ paśuḥ* ('the animal has been caused to be killed'), the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *yasya vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 7.2.15) is indeed possible, since [the root *jñā*] optionally takes *iṭ* by the rule *sanīvanta* (Pāṇini 7.2.49). To this we reply: No, because in the rule *yasya vibhāṣā*, the term *ekācaḥ* ("monosyllabic roots") is understood as a governing word (*anuvṛtti*). Otherwise, the form *daridritaḥ* would not be valid due to the absence of *iṭ*. Therefore, the mention of *seṭ* is for the purpose of determining the time [of application].

The meaning of [the author] who says "with *seṭ*" is that the elision of *ṇi* occurs after [the addition of the suffix], but not prior to it; otherwise, in forms such as *kāritam*, once the elision of *ṇi* has taken place, the prohibition of *iṭ* by Pāṇini 7.2.10 (*ekāca upadeśe*) would apply. However, if there were *sthānivadbhāva* with respect to a rule concerning what precedes, the prohibition would not even arise, because of the intervention of the *ṇic* suffix. Therefore, it is established that the mention of *seṭ* indicates that [the rule regarding the elision of *ṇi*] is not universally obligatory (*anitya*).

And likewise, regarding the sūtra *antaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.20), Haradatta states: "The status of being a *sthānivat* [in place of the original] is not permanent (*anitya*) when there is an operation based on what precedes, because of the mention of *seṭ* in the rule *niṣṭhāyāṃ seṭi* (Pāṇini 6.4.52). And this has been explained precisely in the section on *sthānivadbhāva*. Although this was not explained by the author himself in this particular section, the meaning of that text is that it was explained by the Nyāsakāra and others; otherwise, one must assume either a scribal error or a loss of the text.

By this, the passage from Haradatta’s work stating that "whatever needs to be said here regarding the sūtra *oḥ puyaṇ* (Pāṇini 7.4.80) has already been stated under the sūtra *dvirvacane'ci* (Pāṇini 1.1.59)" is also explained. And thus Kaiyaṭa says in the commentary on the sūtra *vasvekāc* [Pāṇini 6.1.158]: "The rule *pūrvasmād api vidhiḥ* [Pāṇini 1.1.57] is not universally valid."

Mādhavācārya, however, having raised the objection regarding the non-application of the *asiddha* status in the case of *parivraḍhayya gataḥ*, and having set that aside on the grounds of the rule involving different bases (*vyāśrayatva*), he anticipates the possibility of *sthānivadbhāva* by virtue of the rule *pūrvasmād api* (Pāṇini 1.1.57). He resolves this by relying on the force of examples cited in the Bhāṣya, such as *prabebhidayya* and *prastanayya*. Alternatively, he argues that by the rule *lyapi laghupūrvāt* (Pāṇini 6.4.56), since the requirement for the "other word-meaning" (*anyapadārtha*) necessarily implies a reference to a phoneme (*varṇa*), and because in the mention of a phoneme the class (*jāti*) is understood, there is no fault even when there is an intervention [of other elements].

However, some maintain that a genitive compound (*pañcamī-samāsa*) should not be accepted here, as there is no purpose for it. To explain: three purposes have been stated in the Bhāṣya—namely, *bebhiditā*, *māthitikaḥ*, and *apīpacan*. Among these, the form *bebhiditā* is established otherwise, because one must rely on the rule that the term "root" (*ekāc*) in Pāṇini 7.2.10 is a qualifier of what is prescribed (*vihita-viśeṣaṇa*).

In the analysis *māthitika* as "one whose merchandise (*paṇya*) is *mathita*," the suffix *ṭhak* is applied by Pāṇini 6.4.51 (*tadasya paṇyam*). When the *ikādeśa* (substitution of *i*) occurs, the elision of the final vowel (*alopa*) is performed by Pāṇini 6.4.148 (*yasyeti ca*). Consequently, the substitution of *kā* [for *ka*] by Pāṇini 7.3.51 (*isusuktāntāt kaḥ*) will not take place; for, due to the prohibition in Pāṇini 1.1.56 (*analvidhau*), the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original element) is impossible.

In the rule *ṭhasyekaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.50), because the vowel *a* in both the substituendum (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) serves merely for pronunciation, the entire phoneme (*varṇa*) constitutes the substituendum. Alternatively, let us assume that the vowel *a* in both the substituendum and the substitute is intended to be significant. Even so, there is no risk of the substitution of *ka* (for *ṭha*) occurring here due to the rule not being one governed by an *al* (phoneme), because this is resolved by the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*. Furthermore, *apīpacan* is not a valid example [of this rule].

For here, since the *a* of *anta* and the *caṅ* [augment] undergo the substitution of a single subsequent form (*pararūpa*) by Pāṇini 6.1.97 (*ato guṇe*), and because that [substituted form] is treated as the initial element of the following unit, it would be included by the mention of *jhi*; consequently, one might argue that *jus* would apply by Pāṇini 3.4.109 (*sijabhyastavidibhyaśca*). However, this does not occur because of the status of the substitute as *sthānivadbhāva* for either the elision of the *ṇi* or the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) [of the *caṅ*]. This is because, in the case of the root *vid*, a *jhi* immediately following it is possible only in the *laṅ* [tense], and by association (*sāhacarya*) with that, the rule for *jus* is prescribed for *jhi* only after an *abhyasta* [reduplicated stem] in the *laṅ*.

Nor should it be argued that the *luṅ* [suffix] is also included by virtue of its association with the *sic* [suffix], because, according to the rule "In case of conflict, the subsequent [rule prevails]" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 1.4.2), association with the subsequent member is stronger. For this very reason, Mādhava states "abobhūvan" as the *luṅ* form from the *yaṅ*-luṅanta [denominative] of the root *bhū*. However, for the venerable author who cites "apīpacan" as an example to illustrate the purpose of the fifth-case compound (*pañcamī-samāsa*), such association is not accepted here as a restrictive factor.

It has been stated in the commentary on *Pāṇini-sūtra* 1.1.6 (*dīghīvevīṭām*) that because of the specific mention of *kṛt* [suffixes] as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), the principle of association (*sāhacarya*) is not to be relied upon in all cases. Therefore, when there is *yaṅ*-luk, the *jus* suffix alone is appropriate in the *luṅ* tense for the root *bhū*; for Mādhava himself has stated that the restriction (*niyama*) of *Pāṇini-sūtra* 3.4.110 (*ātaḥ*) applies only to that *jus* which is obtained by relying on the condition of being followed by *sic*. This is because the *jus* based on the reduplicated form (*abhyasta*) would otherwise be unavoidable.

If, however, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), the restriction (*niyama*) "ātaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.4.110) were to depend on the general rule [rather than being specific], then in the absence of *jus*, the form would be governed by "ad abhyastāt" (Pāṇini 7.1.4). In this way, two forms—*abobhūvuḥ* and *abobhūvat*—are obtained according to different alternatives, because the augment *vuk* is permanent and thus subverts the *guṇa* substitution. As for the form *abobhūvan* cited by Mādhava, it is indeed questionable, since a final substitute (*antyādeśa*) is difficult to justify in this context.

However, the form *apīpacan* is indeed questionable, because the substitution of *ḍh* at the end is difficult to justify. To establish this form *apīpacan*, one must resort to a genitive compound (*pañcamī-samāsa*). As for the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *vigaṇayya*, the previously mentioned solutions should be recalled; this is the correct path. If it is asked: "Why was it not raised that, in the view of one who says 'let there be no genitive compound,' the augment *iṭ* would occur in *tanvanti*?"—the answer is: No, because the *yaṇ* substitution is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) due to being extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*).

Nor does the prohibition "not when there is immediate succession of vowels" (*nājānantarye*) apply here, because Kaiyaṭa accepts that this prohibition applies only where the rule prescribing the grammatical operation concerns the immediate succession of vowels. If it is asked, "How then is the example *tanvanti* for a compound with a fifth case-ending (*pañcamī-samāsa*) previously cited?"—understand that it was given according to the opinion of Haradatta. For he explained [the rule] as applying wherever there is the immediate succession of vowels, whether in an internal (*antaraṅga*) or external (*bahiraṅga*) context.

But if this were so, would it not contradict the statement of Miśra, who—citing the commentary on the rule *padānta* (*Pāṇini 6.1.86*) regarding the form *dadhyatra*—maintains that the *paribhāṣā* concerning "external" elements (*bahiraṅga-paribhāṣā*) does not apply due to the force of the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva*? For, since the *yaṇ*-substitution is external, its dependence on two vowels (*acau*) triggers the very prohibition "there is no [application of a rule] when there is immediate sequence of vowels" (*nājānantarye*, *Paribhāṣā* 51), which alone prevents the operation of the *paribhāṣā*. Furthermore, in the rule *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ* (*Pāṇini 8.2.23*), the principle "the external is unestablished" (*asiddhaṃ bahiraṅgam*, *Paribhāṣā* 50) is cited...

Furthermore, the rejection of the *vārttika* "the prohibition of *yaṇ*" (*yaṇaḥ pratiṣedhaḥ*), which is performed by relying on the *paribhāṣā*, would also be contradicted. Moreover, regarding the statement in the rule *laṇ* (*Māheśvara-sūtra* 6) that if the subsequent rule *uraṇ raparaḥ* (*Pāṇini-sūtra* 1.1.51) were applied, two *repha*s would be heard in the word *kartrartham*, that too would be contradicted; for the elision by *ro ri* (*Pāṇini-sūtra* 8.3.14) would be possible, and the *asiddha-paribhāṣā* is prohibited by the aforementioned reasoning.

Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with the *bhāṣya* on the rule *na dhātulopa-* (Pāṇini 1.1.4) regarding the word *preddham*, as well as with the *bhāṣya* that rejects the *vārttika* *yaṇaḥ* (Kātyāyana) under the rule *saṃyogāntasya* (Pāṇini 8.2.23). Moreover, the solution accepted [by the author] based on the principle of "being external" (*bahiraṅgatva*)—which was proposed after raising the objection of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *pacāvedam* under the rule *eta ai* (Pāṇini 3.4.93)—would also be undermined. Such is the direction of the argument.

If it is argued that, therefore, the commentary composed by Haradatta contradicts his own preceding and subsequent texts as well as the Bhāṣya, this is true; for this very reason, we have stated that this commentary is unacceptable precisely at the sūtra concerning the elision of verbal roots (*na dhātulopa-*). Alternatively, it may somehow be justified by relying on the non-universality (*anityatā*) of the principle *nājānantarye* (Pariśiṣṭa 51), based on the indicative power (*jñāpaka*) of rules such as *ke’ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.13).

This might be the case: even in Kaiyaṭa’s view, is the doubling [of the consonant] intended in the rule *aco ra ṛti* or not? In the first case, there would be a contradiction with the fundamental indicator (*jñāpaka*). For in examples such as *ko'sicchat* and *ko'sya*, when the rule for *ṣatva* applies to an immediately preceding vowel, there is no recourse to the condition "not being vowels" (*acaḥ*). In the second case, however, the fundamental indicator could only be possible if the mention of *iṇ* were connected with the preceding sūtra; but it has been established that it is indeed connected with the subsequent one.

Now, if the intention is that even though some consonants (*hal*) might indeed be included within the subsequent *grahaṇa*, the condition of "non-intervening vowels" (*ajānantarya*) has not been accounted for, then let us somehow manage the justification through an *jñāpaka*. However, in cases such as *ayaje indram* and *vṛkṣe indram*, the substitution of a homogeneous long vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*) would be unavoidable due to its higher priority, because the prohibition "there is no [application of a rule] when there is non-intervention of vowels" (*nājānantarye*) does not apply here. This is because the principle "that which is external is as if unestablished" (*asiddhaṃ bahiraṅgam*) cannot take effect in this context.

If it is argued that this is established by another *paribhāṣā* stating "the internal (*antaraṅga*) is stronger," and that accordingly, in the *vipratiṣedha-sūtra*, after introducing the rule "and the internal," the purpose [of the subsequent rule] is stated as "the *guṇa* substitution for *iṇ*, *ni*, and *śī* takes precedence over *savarṇa-dīrgha*"—this is true, it was indeed stated; however, having not enumerated the vast majority of purposes, it was concluded that this [rule] need not be formulated, since its purpose is already served by the *asiddha-paribhāṣā*.

By this, Kaiyaṭa—who, in the context of critiquing the examples *paṭvyā* and *mṛdvyā* in the present sūtra, explained that the maxim cited by the authors of the Bhāṣya as *asiddhaparibhāṣā* was intended as an illustration of the principle *antaraṅgaṃ balīyaḥ*—is also refuted, because that contradicts the Bhāṣya on the rule concerning conflict (*vipratiṣedhasūtra*). Therefore, the true nature of the final conclusion (*siddhāntatattva*) in this matter must be stated otherwise.

It is said: because the *antaraṅga* maxim is without exception (*nirapavāda*), whereas the *asiddha* maxim has an exception in the form of "nājānantarye" (Paribhāṣā 51), both are necessary. The authors of the *Bhāgavṛtti* maintain that the commentary on the rule of conflict (*vipratiṣedha-sūtra*) is intended merely as a supplementary argument (*abhyuccaya*). Kaiyaṭa, the author of the *Laghuvivaraṇa*, and others also hold this view. However, the authors of the *Bṛhadvivaraṇa* argue that the maxim "nājānantarye" need not exist at all.

They say that because [the rule] is accepted as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of that [fact], it indicates precisely the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of the *asiddhaparibhāṣā*. And on this view, the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the *vipratiṣedha* sūtra, "not when there is no proximity of vowels" (*nājāntarye*), must be interpreted by breaking it down as being intended to indicate non-eternality; otherwise, it would contradict the very rejection (*pratyākhyāna*) of the principle "the internal (*antaraṅga*) is stronger" found in that same [commentary].

For this very reason, in the *Vṛtti* on the rule *nalopaḥ sup-svara-* (Pāṇini 8.2.2), after beginning with the statement that the *tuk* augment [prescribed by] *hrasvasya piti kṛti* (Pāṇini 6.1.71) does not apply because the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), an objection is raised that the purpose is already served by the two *paribhāṣās*—namely, the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā* and the *bahiraṅga-paribhāṣā*. In response, it is stated that the mention of *tuk* is intended to indicate that both of these *paribhāṣās* are non-eternal (*anitya*).

For this very reason, it has been stated there by the Bhikṣus as well: "Because the *bahiraṅga-paribhāṣā* is not universally obligatory (*anitya*), in the case of *yā* and *sā*, the *tyadādyatva* (the substitution of *a* for the pronouns *tyad* etc.), though *bahiraṅga*, is not treated as *asiddha* (non-existent) with respect to the *antaraṅga* suffix *ṭāp*. Likewise, in order to establish forms such as *pratidīvnaḥ*, the non-universally obligatory nature of the *asiddha-paribhāṣā* is accepted. And for this same reason, in the case of *akṣadyūḥ*, when the elision of *y* (*yalopa*) is to be applied, the *ūṭh* is not *asiddha*; such is the direction [of the argument].

And this exception is expressed by the rule *akṛtavyūhāḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.2), and so forth. Since both the general rule (*utsarga*) and the exception (*apavāda*) are established as being non-eternal (*anitya*), the sole basis for their application is conformity with the observed linguistic forms (*lakṣya*); thus, everything is well-ordered. It might be argued as follows: the genitive case in the word *pūrvasya* denotes a general relationship (*sambandhasāmānye*). And a relationship is of two kinds: either as that of the recipient of an operation (*kāryitva*) or as that of the cause (*nimittatva*). In this way, even without the mention of the term *vidhi*, the result of the two compounds is obtained.

Even though the word *vidhi* (operation) is mentioned, it must indeed be explained as "from what was previously relied upon as the cause"; otherwise, in the case of *he gauḥ*, when an operation follows the *ga* sound, the elision of the vocative suffix (*sambuddhi*) by Pāṇini 6.1.69 (*eṅhrasvāt*) would occur due to the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) of the *vṛddhi* vowel.

True. The inclusion of the term *vidhi* (prescription) is for the purpose of splitting the rule (*yogavibhāga*). By this, through the restriction that "in a prescription concerning a preceding element, [the substitute] is exactly like the original," its own inherent properties (*svāśraya*) are excluded. Alternatively, let there be no split of the rule; by the force of the inclusion of *vidhi*, the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) will apply to every prescription, whether scriptural (*śāstrīya*) or non-scriptural (*aśāstrīya*). Consequently, in forms such as *paṭayati*, the absence of *vṛddhi*—though non-scriptural—is also established.

But even so, will the term *vidhi* (rule) not be carried over from the previous sūtra itself? True; however, by the repetition of the term *vidhi*, a second restriction is established: that [the *sthānivadbhāva*] applies only in a rule concerning the preceding element (*pūrvasya vidhau*), and not in a rule concerning both the preceding and the following elements (*pūrvaparayoḥ vidhau*). By this, the form *īyatuḥ* is established.

Otherwise, by the rule *iṇo 'ṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.81) and the rule *dvirvacane 'ci* (Pāṇini 1.1.59), which prescribes the substitution of *yaṇ* and extends its original form to the reduplicated element, the *yaṇ* would be removed at the time of reduplication. Consequently, when the rule applies again, because the two rules would depend on different bases (*vyāśrayatva*), the principle *vārṇād āṅgaṃ balīyaḥ* (Paribhāṣā 55) would not apply; instead, since the *savarṇadīrgha* depends on the mere phoneme (*varṇamātra*) and is thus more immediate (*antaraṅga*), the long vowel substitution would occur. Nor can one argue that the *yaṇ* substitution is blocked by the principle *akṛtavyūhāḥ* (Paribhāṣā 56), because there is no destruction of the causal conditions for that substitution.

Even if the *yaṇ* substitution were applied, the long vowel resulting from homogeneous vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*) would apply by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* principle. Consequently, once the *savarṇadīrgha* has been effected, the shortening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*)—by virtue of its being included in the term "beginning" (*abhyāsagrahaṇa*) according to Pāṇini 6.1.85—and the lengthening [of the penultimate] by Pāṇini 8.2.69 (*dīrgha iṇaḥ kiti*) would result in the form *īatuḥ*, because the *yaṇ* substitution for *iṇ* is precluded by the very fact that the rule ordaining the lengthening is stated.

In the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), however, since there is no status as a substitute (*sthānitva*) when both the preceding and following [sounds] are subject to a rule, the desired form is established by means of the *yaṇ* replacement [of *i*], even though the cause [for the preceding rule] has been destroyed, according to the maxim of "the non-application of what has not yet taken effect" (*akṛtavyūhaparibhāṣā*). Alternatively, by the force of the suffix *-vat* in the term *sthānivat*, even non-existence (*abhāva*) is extended [to the substitute]; this is indicated by the inclusion of terms such as "reduplication" (*dvirvacana*) in the subsequent sūtra. The inclusion of the word "rule" (*vidhi*) is for the purpose of indicating that it applies only to the preceding [element] and not to both the preceding and following; such is the direction.

In this context, although there is no distinction in the proximity of the three factors—the original element (*sthānin*), the substitute (*ādeśa*), and the cause (*nimitta*)—priority (*pūrvatva*) is understood only in relation to the original element, and not in relation to the substitute or the cause; for otherwise, in the word *vaiyākaraṇaḥ*, the substitution of *āy* would undesirably apply [to the *i* of *vyākaraṇa*]. As it has been said: "By understanding priority with respect to the vowel (*ac*), the rule regarding *ai* and *au* is established" (Bhāṣya).

If it is argued that, in this way, there would be the undesirable consequence of the substitution of *jagdhi* in the form *samādya*—because once the *ṇi*-suffix is elided by the prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) "the elision of *ṇi* and *al*" (*ṇyallopau*), then, due to the presence of the augment *vṛddhi* by the rule of "characterization by the suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), the substitute *ad* is included by the mention of *ad* because it is not different from the original when a part has been modified—and likewise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the substitution of *vadha* in the form *ghātyāt*; [we reply: no, for even in the case of *ad* and *ghātya*, they are prior to the vowel that has not yet undergone its prescribed modification (*anādiṣṭādacaḥ pūrvatvāt*), by virtue of their original substituends.

[Objection: "Even if the original element (*sthānin*) is prior, what does that have to do with the substitute (*ādeśa*)? For being prior to an unspecified vowel is not a grammatical operation (*śāstrīya-kārya*) that could be extended to the substitute by the preceding rule, 'The substitute is like the original' (Pāṇini 1.1.56). [Response: No. This is because when the rule 'When a subsequent [element] intervenes after a vowel' (Pāṇini 1.1.57) is to be applied—relying upon the fact that the substitute is prior to an unspecified vowel—it is possible for the rule 'The substitute is like the original' (Pāṇini 1.1.56) to operate.

And thus, the meaning established is that only a grammatical operation (*śāstrīyaṃ kāryam*) is subject to extension (*atideśa*) by the rule *acaḥ parasmin* (Pāṇini 1.1.56), and that [extension] is extended by the preceding sūtra. For this very reason, the mention of "homogeneous" (*savarṇa*) was made in the rule *na padānta...* (Pāṇini 1.1.58). Otherwise, when the elision (*lopa*) of *śn* and *as* has occurred, the subsequent anusvāra would not be preceded by a vowel that is not [already] extended; consequently, since there would be an absence of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) in its prescription, the mention of "homogeneous" would be entirely useless.

But in that case, the form *kṣatriyakaṇḍūtiḥ* would not be established. To explain: from the root *kaṇḍūyati*, when the suffix *ktic* is added, after the elision of the *ya* and the elision of the *a*, the substitution *uvaṅ* is applied to the *u* by virtue of the *allopasya sthānivattva* (the status of being a substitute for the elided *a*). Now, since this *uvaṅ* is substituted in place of the *u*—which precedes a vowel not originally present in the base (*anādiṣṭādacaḥ pūrvasya*)—it is considered a *sthānivadbhāva* (a substitute behaves like its original) according to *sthānivad ādeśaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.56). Consequently, because of this *sthānivadbhāva*, the *uvaṅ* is treated as if it were the original vowel; thus, due to the intervention of the vowel *a* (by *acaḥ parasmin* 1.1.57), there is no absence of *ūṭh*. [Therefore, the expected *ūṭh* does not occur, and the form remains problematic.]

Precisely because of the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* substitute, by the absence of the elision of *v* according to *lopo vyor vali* (Pāṇini 6.1.66), and once the lengthening has been applied by *hali ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.77), the form *kaṇḍūvati* would result. As for the argument that the *uvaṅ* substitution which occurred previously by way of the *sthānin* does not apply to the *uṭ*, to what then would it apply? It applies to the *v*. And as for that *v* to which the *uṭ* applies, it is not the one that was previously [replaced] by way of the *sthānin*.

That is not so; for just as *testuḥ* [becomes] *teṣṭuḥ*, *kaṇḍū* is replaced by *kaṇḍuv*. And since that [substitute] must necessarily undergo the status of being "as if occupying the original position" (*sthānivadbhāva*) when the replacement of *kaṇḍū* by *kaṇḍūḥ* is to be performed—it has indeed been stated: "All [substitutes] are substitutes for entire words. Otherwise, in cases such as *nirādya* and *ghātvāt*, the status of being "as if occupying the original position" would not apply, resulting in a collapse of the very foundation [of the grammatical system].

To this it is replied: the requirement that the status of being prior to an unspecified vowel (*acaḥ pūrvatā*) be mediated through the substituend (*sthānidvāraka*) is non-permanent (*anitya*). This is known from the evidence (*jñāpaka*) in the *napadāntasūtra* commentary, where the example *kaṇaaḍūtiḥ* is given for the suffix *ati*. Furthermore, this very conclusion is obtained by reflecting upon the *vārttika* "In the rule for the suffix *ka*, after [roots] having a *prasāraṇa* vowel, there is always *ḍa*" under the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.3), as well as the commentary on that section.

And thus, the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on that point states: "For one who does not recognize the *pūrva* [element] as being previously enjoined, there would indeed be the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*. However, if "being prior" were understood as being mediated by the *sthānin*, then the entire section would be inconsistent; this will be clarified in that very place. Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on that point, however, is merely superficial.

By this, Haradatta’s statement that "one says *titaū* [in the sense of] 'he causes to heat' (*titāpayati*)" is also explained. For in that case, when the *ṭilopa* has been applied after the causative suffix (*ṇi*), although there is no *vṛddhi* by the rule *aco ñṇiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.115) due to the status of the *ṭilopa* as *sthānivadbhūta*, the *vṛddhi* by the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.116) applies, resulting in the vowel *o*. Now, because of the status of the *okāra* as *sthānivadbhūta* with respect to the elision of the *ukāra* during the application of the *puṅ* augment—since it stands in the position preceding the *ukāra* via its *sthānin*—the *puṅ* augment would not otherwise apply. [This objection is resolved by the present explanation.]

It cannot be argued that for a [stem] ending in *ākāra* which has *puk*, that *ākāra* is not "prior," or that for a prior *ākāra*, there is no *puk*; for, according to the principle that "a thing modified in one part is not different [from the original]" and the stated rule that "all [substitutes] are substitutes for entire words," the status of being "prior" is not lost even for that which ends in *ākāra*. Therefore, Haradatta’s only recourse is that the "priority" [of the *ākāra*] is contingent upon its substituendum (*sthānin*) and is thus non-eternal (*anitya*).

On this point, some maintain that *titāpayati* is indeed incorrect. To explain: when *tita-* is followed by *ṇic*, both the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel of the root) and the *vṛddhi* substitution prescribed by Pāṇini 7.2.116 (*ata upadhāyāḥ*) apply simultaneously. Since both are obligatory rules, the *vṛddhi* takes precedence due to its higher status in the order of application. Once the *ṭi*-elision has occurred, the penultimate vowel is no longer long (*ā*), because it was not originally long; furthermore, since it is not preceded by a non-specified vowel (*anādiṣṭādacaḥ pūrvaṃ*), the condition for the *puṅ* augment (Pāṇini 7.3.86) is not met. Therefore, after the addition of *śap*, the *guṇa* substitution occurs, followed by the *vṛddhi* and the replacement with *āy*, resulting in *titāyati*.

Nor should it be argued that, given the rule *titāṇic*, since the substitution of *ā* for *at* is internal (*antaraṅga*), the form would be *titayati* after applying *guṇa* and then the *śap* suffix; for when *guṇa* occurs before *śap*, the rule *vṛddhireci* (Pāṇini 6.1.88) would supersede it, and since the cause for the *guṇa* substitution would thereby be destroyed, the *akṛtavyūha-paribhāṣā* prevents the application of the internal *guṇa* first. Indeed, it has been stated that the *akṛtavyūha-paribhāṣā* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *antaraṅga-paribhāṣā*.

Nor should it be argued that, because of the status as a *sthānivadbhāva* by the rule *acaḥ parasmin* (Pāṇini 1.1.57), the substitution for the vowel (*guṇa*) does not destroy the causal condition (*nimitta-vighāta*) for the preceding *guṇa*; for it has been stated that the status as a *sthānivadbhāva* applies only when there is a prescription for what precedes, and not when there is a prescription for both what precedes and what follows. Therefore, the form is only *titāyati*, and not *titayati* or *titāpayati*.

When *caṅ* is substituted for *tiṅ*, and *ṇic* is substituted for *tip*, the form stands as *caṅ-tip*. Under the view that [the root] is derived by the rule *tanoterḍauḥ sa nvacca* (Pāṇini 6.4.39), the prohibition of reduplication applies by the rule *anabhyāsasya* (Pāṇini 7.2.11). Since the *ṭilopa* is not subject to the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* regarding the elision caused by *caṅ* (Pāṇini 1.1.58), there is no short vowel (*hrasva*). Following the elision of *ṇic*, because that elision is either considered non-existent (*asiddha*) or is subject to the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* with respect to the rule for lengthening (*dīrgha*), the substitution of a long vowel by a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*) occurs, resulting in *atitāt* and not *atitāpat*.

On this point, the following must be said: the statement that "the *vṛddhi* [substitution] takes precedence because it is subsequent" is incorrect, because the *ṭilopa* is obligatory (*nitya*). Nor is the *vṛddhi* obligatory; for even though the *vṛddhi* would apply by means of the extension of an operation according to Pāṇini 1.1.57 (*acaḥ parasmin*), it is nevertheless non-obligatory (*anitya*) by the maxim: "That which applies by another rule is non-obligatory. Thus, Haradatta’s statement is indeed correct. However, one must consider the evidence for the specific point that, despite its non-obligatoriness, priority (*pūrvatva*) based on the *sthānin* is not accepted here.

Thus, it is established that in this context, "being prior to a vowel" (acaḥ pūrvatvam) is understood in both ways: either by way of its locus (sthānidvāraka) or inherently (svataḥ). The term *vidhi* is derived from the root *vidh* with the suffix *kip* in the sense of the object (*karman*), meaning "that which is prescribed. In the expression *pūrvasya*, the genitive case is used in the sense of a remainder (*śeṣe ṣaṣṭhī*), because a technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) does not apply in the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*). Furthermore, the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) applies even to augmentations such as *puk* when they are themselves to be prescribed.

In this context, however, regarding the word *aca*, the acquisition of a relationship with the substituendum (*sthānin*) occurs either through its co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with the term *ādeśa* (substitute) by virtue of semantic fitness, or because the term *sthāne* (in place of), which was carried over from the preceding rule into the current one following the maxim *ṣaṣṭhī sthāne yogā* (Pāṇini 1.1.49). This is the well-established path.

The author of the *Nyāsa*, however, accepted both positions—that priority (*pūrvatva*) is relative to the cause (*nimitta*) or relative to the substitute (*ādeśa*)—since they were both presented in the *Bhāṣya*. Regarding words such as *vaiyākaraṇa* and the like, he stated that there is no fault because the diphthongs *ai* and *au* (which are *bahiraṅga*) are considered non-existent (*asiddha*) [for the purpose of the *guṇa* substitution]. This should be supported by what was previously stated: that the optionality belongs either to the maxim *nājānantarye* or specifically to the *bahiraṅgaparibhāṣā*.

In this view, the suffix *ki* in *vidhiḥ* is used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*). Furthermore, since the object (*karman*) has not been previously expressed, the use of the genitive case is also perfectly sound. However, if [the substitution of] *yat* for pronouns like *tad* were to occur prior to [the application of] the cause, then by virtue of its being a *sthānivadbhāva*, there would be no long vowel in forms such as *dvābhyām*. Likewise, because the substitution of *ī* for *ghu* (Pāṇini 6.4.65) would be a *sthānivadbhāva*, the guna substitution characterized by a final *i* would not occur in *deyam*. Consequently, due to the *sthānivadbhāva* of guna and vṛddhi, the substitutions of *ava* and *āva* would not occur in *lavanam* and *lāvakaḥ*.

Relying on indications such as *dvayorekasya* (Pāṇini 5.3.92), *deyamṛṇe* (4.3.47), and *kiratau lavane* (6.1.150), to resort to [the doctrine of] non-uniformity (*anityatā*) is cumbersome; this is the general direction [of the argument]. Prior-ness (*pūrvatva*) does not consist in the absence of intervention (*avyavadhāna*), but rather is common to cases where there is intervention, as evidenced by the inclusion of the term *nirdiṣṭe* in the rule *tasminniti nirdiṣṭe* (Pāṇini 1.1.66), and because of the formulation of the prohibition regarding the elision of what follows *caṅ*. Consequently, the status of being a "substitute for the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) is established in forms such as *paṭayati* and *avadhīt*; for the substitute *vadh* indeed ends in the vowel *a*.

It might be argued as follows: in the case of *paṭayati*, since the status of being a word (*padatva*) is obtained by relying on the internal case-ending, the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaśtva*) would apply. Nor can the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) be invoked, because that is prohibited in the rule prescribing *jaśtva*. True; however, it will be stated later that the suffix *ṇic* arises from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) alone which conveys the object, and not from a form ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*). Even in the view that *ṇic* is added to a *subanta*, the designation of "word" (*pada-saṃjñā*) is superseded by the designation of "nominal base" (*bha-saṃjñā*), which is extended [to this case] by the rule *iṣṭhavad*.

For since the designation *bha* has already applied to this very form *paṭu*, how could the designation *pada* apply there? And if it does not apply there, how could it possibly apply to that which has undergone a partial modification (*ekadeśavikṛta*)? We shall explain later that even in cases such as *srajayati*—meaning "he describes one who possesses a garland"—the derivation of the suffix *ṇic* occurs from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and the same reasoning applies there as well.

The example "avadhīt," however, follows the view of the Bhāṣya; for since it was established in the preceding rule that the *ārddhadhātukīya* suffixes apply generally, there is the possibility of elision according to the principle: "there is elision of that which ends in /a/ when an *ārddhadhātuka* suffix is taught. According to the view of the Vārttika, however, it has been stated that the term "liṅ" [in the rule] is a locative of reference (*parasaptamī*). Consequently, as in the cases of "ataḥ" and "pat," the elision of the /a/ would not occur. For this very reason, in his view, this substitute (*lā*) is restricted to cases where the root ends in a consonant (*halanta*).

However, no *vṛddhi* occurs, because of the *vārttika* on the preceding rule (*pūrvasūtra*) which states: "In the case of the substitute *vadhi*, there is a prohibition of *vṛddhi* and *tattva*. Similarly, in forms such as *akhaṭvakaḥ* and *bahukhaṭvakaḥ*, the vowel *ā* of the syllable *kha* does not become udātta by virtue of *Pāṇini 6.2.174* (*keṇaḥ*), but rather, by *Pāṇini 6.2.173* (*kapi pūrvam*), the final syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) alone becomes udātta.

In cases such as *acitīkaḥ* and *bahucitīkaḥ*, however, due to the status of the long vowel [substituted] by Pāṇini’s rule *citeḥ kapi* (Pāṇini 6.3.127) as being "as if it were the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*), the vowel *i* of the word *cit* retains its acute accent (*udātta*). Nor should one suspect that the prohibition—"in the prescription of accent, there is no *sthānivadbhāva*"—applies here in both instances; for it will be stated later that this prohibition concerns only those substitutes that result from elision (*lopa*).

Thus, because this has been cited by many commentators as "paṭvyā" and "mṛdvyā," the example is indeed correct even though it is treated [as such] in the Bhāṣya as a preeminent case; for, according to the rule of *akṛtavyūha*, the prior substitution of *yaṇ* cannot take place first.

Nor should it be argued that, in cases such as "kartryā" and "irtryā," the acute accent of the case-ending prescribed by Pāṇini 6.1.174 (*udāttayaṇaḥ*) would not occur; for in rules governing accents, a consonant is treated as if non-existent, and the solution is reached by relying precisely on the prior substitution of *yaṇ*.

Nor should it be argued that, even in the case of a rule concerning what precedes [the original element], the substitute would not be a consonant due to its being treated as the original (*sthānivadbhāva*); for the *repha* is not preceded by a vowel in the original form, and because precedence mediated through the original element is non-permanent, and furthermore, because the treatment of a substitute as the original in rules concerning what precedes is itself non-permanent—as evidenced by the inclusion of the term *seṭ* in the rule *niṣṭhāyāṃ seṭi* (Pāṇini 6.4.52). Therefore, the position that this is a preeminent example (*mūrddhābhiṣikta*) is not particularly flawed.

For this very reason, it has been stated in the *Bhāṣya* and the *Vārttika* that according to the view that "the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) applies only when the original form (*prakṛti*) is actually being resorted to," the following would undesirably apply in sequence to the forms *akurvyāśām*, *alunyāśām*, *vyatyajanyāśām*, and *rāyyāśām*: the elision of *u* by *ye ca* (Pā. 6.4.113), the substitution of *ī* for *i* by *ī halyaghoḥ* (Pā. 6.4.109), the optional substitution of *ī* for *i* by *ye vibhāṣā* (Pā. 6.4.43), and the substitution of *ā* for *ai* by *rāyo hali* (Pā. 7.2.85).

As for the Bhāṣya passage which, relying on the principle that "that which is internal is stronger" or on the *asiddha* paribhāṣā, aims to refute the examples *paṭvyā* and *mṛdvyā*, that must somehow be interpreted as being intended to show the non-eternality (*anityatā*) of the rule regarding the non-application of grammatical operations (*akṛtavyūha*). This is the general direction [of the argument].

Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.58: "Not [is there the status of being] like the original (sthānivadbhāva) in rules concerning the end of a word, doubling, the *vara* augment, elision (*lopa*), vowel-quality (*svara*), homogeneous vowels (*savarṇa*), the nasal (*anusvāra*), lengthening (*dīrgha*), and the substitution of *jaś* and *car* sounds. In rules where the end of a word and so forth are the objects of the operation, the status of being like the original, which would otherwise apply by the preceding rule, shall not occur. Regarding the end of a word: in the examples *kāni santi* ("what are they? and *kau staḥ* ("who are they?"), when the *yaṇ* and *āv* substitutions are to be applied, the elision of the *a* of *śna* and *as* (*allopa*) is not treated as if it were the original.

Nor should it be argued that [the substitute] does not behave like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*) simply because it lacks the status of being "prior to an unindicated vowel" (*anādiṣṭādacaḥ pūrvatvam*); for according to the view that words are refined (*saṃskriyante*) by being extracted from sentences (*vākya*), such prior status to an unindicated vowel does exist. Indeed, there is no rule in this grammar (*śāstra*) that a word must be refined here independently of other words; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the inconsistency of rules such as *yuṣmadyupapade* (Pāṇini 1.4.105). This has been clarified by Kaiyaṭa in the commentary on the sūtra defining the technical term *aṅga*.

In the view that only the word (*pada*) undergoes grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*), one should cite as an example such cases as *adadrīcaḥ*, where the elision (*allopa*) prescribed by Pāṇini 6.4.138 (*acaḥ kaḥ*) does not behave as if it were *sthānivat*.

Furthermore, the word *vidhi* here is not used in the sense of "action" (*karman*). For if that were the case, would it form a *karmadhāraya* compound, or a *tatpuru�ṣa* with a genitive of remainder (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*)? It cannot be the first, because since the word *vidhi* denotes an action (*kriyā*), it would follow that it must be placed first [in the compound]. Nor can it be the latter, because the rule "that which is at the end of a word does not behave like its original when something else is to be applied" would result in the elision of the *val* sound in the word *vṛkṣav*, and because there would be a lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) with the items listed as *dvandva* compounds, such as reduplication (*dvirvacana*) and the rest.

Therefore, it is indeed a *bhāvasādhana* [denoting the action] because of its being *antaraṅga* (internal). For this very reason, there is a compound with a word ending in the genitive case of the object (*karmaṣaṣṭhī*). In forms such as *śukī* and *taṭī*, when the designation *pada* is to be applied, the elision by the rule *yasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.148) is indeed *sthānivat*. For the rule *svādiṣu* (Pāṇini 1.4.17) does not prescribe that the end of a *pada* is to be defined, which would result in a prohibition; rather, it merely prescribes the technical name (*saṃjñāmātra*).

In that regard as well, the position of *yathoddeśa* [is preferred], because if the *kāryakāla* [view] were adopted for rules such as *jaśtva*, there would result the prohibition by the rule *pūrvatrāsiddhe na* (P. 8.2.1). Furthermore, since a partially modified element is not different from the original (*ekadeśavikṛtamananyavat*), the substitution *ru* would apply in the word *vetasvān*; however, it will be stated later that this does not occur because the external factor (*bahiraṅga*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*). In the *Bhāṣya*, however, two solutions are offered: first, by accepting that the technical name *pada* applies even when the suffix *kap* is present, so that "at the end of a *pada*" includes this case; and second, by treating the *bha*-designation itself as a *pada*-operation. Regarding the latter, it should be understood that it is established by the force of the specific wording in the *Ṣaṭka*. The *Vārttika* and *Ṣaṭka* on this point will be discussed in the fifth book (*pañcamādhyāya*).

In the case of reduplication—as in *sud-dhy-upāsyaḥ*—the *bahiraṅga-paribhāṣā* does not apply here either, precisely because of the force of the prohibition against treating [a substitute] as the original (*sthānivadbhāva-niṣedha*), or else due to the prohibition "there is no [application of the *bahiraṅga-paribhāṣā*] when there is immediate sequence of vowels" (*nājānantarye*).

The term *vare* is a nipātana (an irregular form), and due to this, there is no elision (*aluk*) and it forms a *dvandva* compound. An *ajādeśa* (a substitute for a vowel) that occurs in the context of *vare* is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta* (as if it were the original). For example: *yāyāvaraḥ*. [This is derived from] *yāti*. By the rule *nityaṃ kauṭilye* (Pāṇini 3.1.23), the suffix *yaṅ* is applied; then by *yaśca yaṅaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.176), the suffix *varac* is added. The elision of the *a* caused by that [suffix] occurs. And that [elision] is not *sthānivadbhūta* when the elision of the *ā* by *āto lopa iṭi ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.64) is to be performed. [Objection: But in this case, there is no "conditioning by what follows" (*paranimittakatva*) at all, because the locative case in *ārddhadhātuke* is accepted as a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*).

For this very reason, the mention of *aj* was made in the rule *aco yat* (Pāṇini 3.1.97). Otherwise, since *ṇyat* would be specifically prescribed for consonant-final bases, by the principle of remainder (*pariśeṣāt*), *yat* would apply only to vowel-final bases; what then would be the purpose of mentioning *aj*? However, if the locative case is taken in the sense of "scope" (*viṣayasaptamī*), then the mention of *aj* serves to establish *yat* even after bases that were previously vowel-final, as in *ditsyam* and *dhitsyam*; thus, the acute accent on the initial syllable is established by the rule *yato 'nāvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.213). True, by the mention of *vare* [in the rule *vare-alo-yaraḥ*], the alternative of the locative being taken in the sense of "immediate proximity" (*parasaptamī*) is indicated.

Furthermore, in the rule *anudāttetaśca halādeḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.149), the inclusion of the word *ādi-* ("beginning with") was made so that it should not be understood as "ending in a consonant" (*halanta-*). And there exists a purpose for this qualification of "ending in a consonant," namely to exclude forms such as *jugupsanaḥ* and *mīmāṃsanaḥ*. If, however, the locative were taken in the sense of "occasion" (*viṣaya-saptamī*), then here too, because of the elision of the *at* suffix, the suffix *yuc* would necessarily apply due to the fact that the stem ends in a consonant; thus, since the qualification "ending in a consonant" would be redundant, the inclusion of the beginning [of the root] would be established by implication alone, and one would simply have said *halaḥ* ("from a consonant").

And thus, from the root *yā* with the suffix *yaṅ*, when *ktic* is added, the *a* is elided; because the status of being a *sthānin* is prohibited with respect to the rule for the elision of *ya*, and once *ya* is elided, the form *yāyā-* remains. Due to the *sthānivadbhāva* of the elision of the *yaṅ*-augment, the *ā* is elided by Pāṇini 6.4.64 (*āto lopa iṭi ca*), and then *ya* is elided again, resulting in *yāti*. Nor should it be argued that once the *ā* and *ya* are elided, only the *ktic* suffix would be heard, because the elision of *ā* is treated as a *sthānivadbhāva* [and thus prevents the elision of *ya*], or because, according to the maxim of *ciṇo luṅ* (Pāṇini 6.4.62), the subsequent operation is considered as if non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the former.

Regarding the elision of *y*, there is another example as well. For instance: from the root *kaṇḍūy* with the suffix *ktic*, we get *kaṇḍūtiḥ*. The mention of *ktin* in the *Kāśikā* is an error, because that would be sublated by the rule *apratyayāt* (Pāṇini 3.3.102). Nor is it appropriate here to resort to the assumption of the *āb* class (as in *rptiḥ*) or the application of the term *bahulam* (variously), since the author of the *Bhāṣya* himself stated that "it must be *kaṇḍūyā*," thereby declaring this [reading *kaṇḍūtiḥ*] to be ungrammatical (*apaśabda*). Therefore, this is simply *ktic*; from that, the elision of *a* and the elision of *y* occur.

Due to the status of the substitute as being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*), *uvaṅ* occurs. From that, *ūṭh* applies by the rule *cchvoḥ śūḍ* (Pāṇini 6.4.19). Even in the case of *ūṭh*, there is the status of being like the original, because it precedes the vowel that is the designated point of reference (*ādiṣṭādacaḥ*). For this very reason, *uvaṅ* does not occur again for *ūṭh*.

Although one might argue here—relying on the principle that "all substitutes are substitutes for entire words" (*sarve sarvapadādeśāḥ*)—that precedence can be established through the medium of the original locus (*sthānin*), as is done in the *Bhāṣya* regarding forms such as *loluvaḥ* and *popuvaḥ*; nevertheless, it has already been stated in the preceding sūtra that precedence through the medium of the original locus is merely occasional.

From the root *sthā* with the suffix *yaṅ*, the suffix *ktic* is added; after the elision of the *a* and the *ya*, the form *teṣṭhīti* remains. Once the elisions of *a* and *ya* have occurred, the substitution of *yaṇ* by rule Pāṇini 6.4.82 (*eranekācaḥ*) applies, and upon the subsequent elision of *ya*, the form *peptiḥ* arises. Likewise, from the root *śo* (meaning "to sharpen") with the suffix *yaṅ*, after the addition of *ktic* and the elisions of *a* and *ya*, the rule "that which was previously established is not [treated as] a substitute" (*pūrvatrāsiddhe na*) prohibits the application of *sthānivadbhāva*. Consequently, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* by rule Pāṇini 8.2.36 (*chasāṃ ṣaḥ*) is applied, resulting in the form *śāṣṭiḥ*.
This same principle applies to forms such as *cektiḥ* from the root *ci* (in *cecīyate*). Such is the general direction of the analysis.
Thus, it is established that in the case of *vareyalopa*, there are not one but two causes [for the application of the rule].

However, some explain the rule by eliding the vowel *ī* in *varaī*, interpreting it as: "In a rule prescribed after an *ī*-vowel, [the substitute] is not like the original (*na sthānivat*). By this, in the derivation of *āmalakam* from *āmalakyāḥ phalam*—where the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied according to *nityaṃ vṛddhaśarādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.144), followed by the elision of the suffix via *phale luk* (Pāṇini 4.3.163), and then the elision of the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* via *luk taddhitaluki* (Pāṇini 1.2.49)—that [elision] is not treated as *sthānivat* for the purpose of the elision of the *y* in *yasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.148).

In the previously mentioned explanation, however, the rule "that which is elided by *luk* is not treated as a *sthānivṛt*" will be formulated. In that context, since "elided" (*luptam*) is used in the neuter gender to denote an abstract state according to Pāṇini 3.3.114 (*napuṃsake bhāve ktaḥ*), the resulting meaning is: "that which has been elided is not treated as a *sthānivṛt*."

In *svare-cikīrṣakaḥ*, the elision of the *a* of the suffix *san*—which is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta* when the acute accent (*udātta*) on the vowel *i* of the suffix *kak* is to be applied by the rule *liti* (Pāṇini 6.1.193)—is not subject to the prohibition against treating a substitute as the original. Nor can the force of the commencement of the rule *liti* be invoked as a justification [for the non-application of *sthānivadbhāva* here], because that rule already finds its scope in forms such as *kārakaḥ*. In the Bhāṣya, however, *ākarṣikaḥ* is cited as an example; but this is merely superficial, for even when there is an intervention caused by *sthānivadbhāva*, the accentuation of the *lit* suffix is easily established by the very force of the *lit*-designation in *ṣṭhal*, just as the *kutva* substitution occurs in forms like *ghnanti*.

Regarding "sarvarṇānusvārayoḥ" (both homogeneous vowels and the *anusvāra*): [in forms such as] *śiṇḍi* and *piṇḍhi*, the elision (*allopa*) of *a* in place of *śn* and *as* is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*. It has been stated that although the *anusvāra* precedes the vowel that is not yet prescribed (*anādiṣṭāt*), its status as preceding is established by way of its *sthānin* (the original substitute). Even though the *anusvāra* could have been included simply by mentioning "homogeneous vowels" (*savarṇa*), it is possible that the indicator (*jñāpaka*) is intended to convey a specific purpose.

And thus, in cases where there is no possibility of *parasavarṇa*, such as in *śiṃṣanti* and the like, the mention of *anusvāra* is intended to prohibit the application of the *sthānivadbhāva* rule. This is because, according to the reasoning stated in the rule *acaḥ parasmin* (Pāṇini 1.1.57), a prohibition against [the application of] *savarṇa* in rules such as *abhyāsasyāsavarṇe* (Pāṇini 6.4.78) would find its scope of application; consequently, forms such as *śiṇḍhi* would also result in being unestablished (*asiddha*). This is the general direction of the argument.

In *pratidīvnā*, the lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule *hali ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.77) is not treated as *sthānivadbhāva* when the *al* (the *n*) is elided. As for what was stated in the *Kāśikā* regarding the rule *upadhāyāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.78), that is an error. Accordingly, it is stated under the rule *upadhāyāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.78): "In *pratidīvnā*, the lengthening is by the rule *hali ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.77). Alternatively, the form may be accounted for by deriving it from a verbal root ending in *kvip* used in the sense of habitual action (*ācāra*), followed by *kvip* according to the rule *kvip ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.76).

But in that case, would not the rule *anunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.15) cause the lengthening [of the vowel]? True; however, by the *akṛtavyūha-paribhāṣā*, having taken into account the future elision (*al-lopa*), the internal (*antaraṅga*) lengthening will not be applied, just as in the case of the introduction of the augment *iṭ* and the substitution of *k* for *r* in the form *jagmuṣaḥ*. This is how it should be understood.

If it is argued that even in the absence of *sthānivadbhāva*, the long vowel (*dīrgha*) would not occur because the elision of *a* (*allopa*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) by the rule "that which is external (*bahiraṅga*) is non-existent" (Pbh. 50), we say no; for by the inclusion of the term *tugvidhi* in the rule *kṛti-tug-vidhi* (P. 6.1.135), the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of the *bahiraṅga-paribhāṣā* is indicated. Furthermore, according to the *yathoddeśa* view, since the long vowel is non-existent with respect to the sixth-case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) *paribhāṣā*, the *paribhāṣā* itself does not apply due to the absence of the internal (*antaraṅga*) condition.

And let there be *jaś* and *sagdhi* for me; at the end of the word, [there is] *harī*. For instance, *gdhi* is from the root *ad* (to eat). In the formation of the *ktin* suffix, there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-lopa*) by the rule "optionally in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*, Pāṇini 6.4.100). There is elision of the *s* by the rule "of *jhal* before *jhal*" (*jhalo jhali*, Pāṇini 8.2.26), because the author of the *Bhāṣya* did not accept the rule "elision of *sic* before *dh* and *s*" (*dhisakāre sico lopaḥ*). According to the view of the *Vārttika*, this is a Vedic elision of a phoneme (*varṇa-lopa*). Then, there is the substitution of *dh* by the rule "after a *jhaṣ*, *th* and *dh* [become *dh*]" (*jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ*, Pāṇini 8.2.40).

And in that case where a substitution is to be performed, there is no treatment as if it were the original (sthānivadbhāva) even from a preceding rule, because the non-obligatory nature of the compound with the fifth case-ending (pañcamīsamāsa) was already established in the previous sūtra. Thus, when the *jaś*-substitution by Pāṇini 8.4.53 (*jhalāñ jaś jhaśi*) is to be applied to the letter *gh*, the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) is not treated as if it were the original.

*Samānā gdhiḥ sagdhiḥ*: By the rule *sahasya saḥ saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 6.3.78), when the word *sa-* is understood as a continuation from that sūtra, the word *samāna-* becomes *sa-* by the rule *samānasya chandasyamūrddhaprabhṛtyudarkeṣu* (Pāṇini 6.3.84). *Babdhām* is the *leṭ* (subjunctive) form of the root *bhas*. *Tas* becomes *tām*. There is *ślu*-elision of the *śap* suffix. Because it is *antaraṅga*, reduplication and the operations pertaining to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsakārya*) occur first. Then, by the rule *ghasibhasoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.100), the penultimate vowel is elided, and so forth, as previously described.

*cara-* [forms] *jakṣatuḥ*, *jakṣuḥ* [from the root] *ghas*. In the *liṭ* [perfect tense], there are the suffixes *atus* and *us*. By the rule *gamahana* (Pāṇini 6.4.68), there is elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*). Regarding the substitution of *ca* by the rule *khari ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.55), [the elided vowel] is not treated as if it were still present (*na sthānivat*).

Regarding this, the *Vārttika* states: "In the cases of vowel (*svara*), long-vowel (*dīrgha*), and the elision of *y* (*yalopa*), a substitute for an elided element (*lopājādeśa*) is not treated as *sthānivat*; however, any other [substitute] is indeed *sthānivat*. Thus, in the example *pañcāratnayaḥ* ("bought for five *aratnis*"), [the substitution of *ya* for *i*] is *sthānivat*. However, in the Veda, we have *pañcāratnyaḥ*. Because of the rule "In the Veda, there is optionally the mention of *jas* etc. before the section beginning with *ṇau caṅy upadhāyāḥ*" (*Kātyāyana-vārttika*), there is an absence of *guṇa*, and thus the *yaṇ*-substitution occurs. They say that because of the *sthānivat* status of that [substitution], the original accent of the preceding member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*) applies by the rule "A word ending in a vowel [or having *kālānta* etc.]... (*Pāṇini* 6.2.29).

Although this is established even by the rule "that which is external is asiddha" (Paribhāṣā 50), it should nevertheless be applied by resorting to the *akṛtavyūhaparibhāṣā*. It has already been stated in the preceding sūtra that the results in forms such as *acitīkaḥ* and *akhaṭvak* are the sequential application and non-application of the suffix *ka-* according to Pāṇini 6.2.174 (*hrasvānte'ntyātpūrvam*). Furthermore, there is no occasion for the application of the *bahiraṅgaparibhāṣā* in that context.

*kiryoḥ*, *giryoḥ*. In the view that [the suffix] is derived (*vyutpattipakṣe*), the long vowel prescribed by *hali ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.71) would have applied, but it does not occur due to the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) of the *yaṇ* [vowel]. Under the governing rule *aca iḥ* (Uṇādi-sūtra 5.88), the suffix *i* is added after the roots *bhuj*, *kṝ*, *gṝ*, *śṝ*, *pṝ*, *kuṭi*, *bhid*, and *chidi* (Uṇādi-sūtra 5.99–100), and it is marked with the *k*-sign (*kit*). As for what was proposed by Haradatta and the author of the Nyāsa—namely, *kṝgṝericca*—that should be sought in some version of the Uṇādi-vṛtti. In *vāyvoḥ*, there is no elision of the *y*.

In this *vārttika*, the mere mention of the vowel (*svaragrahaṇa*) alone is necessary. As for the forms *kiyoḥ* and *giryoḥ*, they are established even by adopting the view that the *uṇādi* suffixes are non-etymological (*avyutpatti*), according to the method stated by the author of the *Vṛtti* on the rule "upadhāyāṃ ca" (Pāṇini 8.2.78). The form *vāyvoḥ*, however, is established because that which is extrinsically conditioned (*bahiraṅga*) is considered non-existent (*asiddhatva*).
