An addition [to the rule] must be made regarding *kvip*, *luk*, *upadhātva*, *acaṅ-paranirhrāsa*, and *kutva*; and also regarding what is not established in what precedes (*pūrvatrāsiddha*). Its defect [applies] in the case of the elision of the first letter of a *saṃyoga* (*saṃyogādilopa*), *latva*, and *ṇatva*. The meaning of this is: with respect to an operation caused by *kvip*, [the substitute] is not like the original (*na sthānivadbhavati*). For example, from *lav* (the causative stem of *lū*), one says *lauḥ* (using *kvip*). Here, there is the elision of *ṇic* and the elision of *ṇi* caused by *kvip*; both of these are not like the original when the substitution of *ūṭ* for the *v*—caused by *kvip* according to *cchvoḥ śūḍ anunāsike ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.19)—is to be performed. Thus, by *etyedhatyūṭhsu* (Pāṇini 6.1.89), there is the application of *vṛddhi*.

Likewise, the example cited in the sūtra *dīdhīvevīṭām* (Pāṇini 1.1.6), namely *pipaṭhiṣi brāhmaṇakulāni*, is also consistent only with the interpretation that "an operation applies prior to [the application of] *kvip*."

However, if one explains [the rule] as "that which is elided by *kvip* is not like the original" (*sthānivat*), then neither *lauḥ* nor *pipaṭhiṣi* would be established. For in the case of *lauḥ*, since the *ṭilopa* (elision of the suffix) would be *sthānivat* due to the presence of the *ṇic* suffix, the substitution of *ūṭh* would be impossible. Furthermore, in the case of *pipaṭhiṣi*, after the suffix *apratyaya* has been added to *pipaṭhīsati* and the *alopa* of the *at* has occurred, when the *num*—conditioned by the fact that the following sound is a *jhal*—is to be applied in the nominative plural neuter (*śi*), the prohibition of *sthānivattva* regarding the *alopa* would result in the undesirable occurrence of *num*.

And this is clear from the *Miśra-grantha* on the sūtra *dīdhīvevīṭām* (Pāṇini 1.1.6) and on the *kaṇḍvādi* sūtra. Kaiyaṭa also states regarding *dīdhīvevīṭām*: "In this context, the meaning is established as 'with reference to a rule concerning *kvip*', but not as 'that which is elided before *kvip* is not like its original form (*na sthānivat*)'. By saying "is established" (*vyavasthita*) here, he indicates that while the position that "that which is elided before *kvip* is not like its original form" is indeed sometimes adopted, there is simply no universal restriction (*niyama*).

The term *luptam* is used in the neuter gender with the suffix *kta* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). Thus, the form *sakhyuḥ* from *sakhyurgomān* is established as *tvam aimaḥ*. For instance, the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *khyatyātparasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.112) states: "From *sakhīyati*, [we get] *sakhyuḥ*; from *lūnīyati*, [we get] *lūnyuḥ*. In that context, if the suffix *kvip* were applied to *sakhīyati*, there would first be the elision of the *ī* vowel (*alopa*), followed by the elision of the *y* (*yalopa*). Due to the status of the former elision as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*), the subsequent elision of the *kvip* suffix (*kilopa*) would be superseded, and by the rule *iko yaṇ aci* (Pāṇini 6.1.77), a *yaṇ* substitution would occur instead.

Consequently, if there were *yalopa* (elision of *ya*), the forms would have to be *sakhaḥ* and *lūnaḥ*. For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa rejected the application of *yaṇ* in that context by stating that what is elided before *kvip* is not like its original (*na sthānivat*). Similarly, in the rule *ugidacām* (Pāṇini 7.1.70), after stating that the mention of "non-root" (*adhātu*) is for the sake of applying *num* even to that which was previously a root, the *Bhāṣya* provides *gomān* as an example from the nominal stem *gomat* with the suffix *ap*. In that case too, due to the *sthānivadbhāva* of the *yalopa*, the condition of being followed by a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix would not exist, and thus *num* would not occur.

Nor should it be argued that by the force of the inclusion of the term *adātu* (non-root), the augment *num* would apply even when there is an intervention caused by the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*; for [the rule] has its purpose fulfilled in the case of the *kvip* suffix added after a denominative (*ācārakvibanta*) by Pāṇini 3.2.76 (*kvip ca*). Therefore, the only recourse is the principle that "what is elided by *kvip* does not count [as an intervention]. Now, an objection may be raised: whether one derives the form from the root *gomati* or from *gomata*, the form *gomān* cannot be established, because in the rule prescribing the lengthening of vowels (*atvasantasya ca dhātoḥ*, Pāṇini 6.4.14), the qualification *aghātoḥ* ("provided it is not a verbal root") is present.

True; there is no fault here because it will be stated later that in that context, the mention of "non-root" (adhātu) qualifies only that which does not end in a suffix, and not that which ends in a suffix.

Likewise, regarding the rule *yenavidhistadantasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.72), the Bhāṣya states: "The word *pād* exists even as a simple [form]; from the root *pad*, we have *pāt* and *padaḥ*. In this case as well, due to the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute behaving like the original), the substitution of *pad* would not occur because of the intervention [of the suffix]. This is established by the principle that "what is elided before *kvip* does not [cause] intervention. For this very reason, it was not formulated as a rule: *pādasya pādahastyādibhyaḥ*. [The purpose is] so that the substitute *pad* might apply not only to this form explicitly mentioned in the rule (*pratipadokta*), but also to that which ends in *kvip*.

And thus, by the author of the Sūtras himself, who provides the heavy designation "pādasya lopaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.130), it is indicated that what is elided before *kvip* is not like the original (na sthānivat). That this [non-sthānivadbhāva] is only occasional is understood from the very wording of the present Sūtra; such is the meaning of the Bhāṣya's statement "what is elided before *kvip* is not [sthānivat]," as suggested by Kaiyaṭa when he employs the term "vyavasthita" (established/limited) based on the greatness of the word "vi" and the Bhāṣya on the Sūtra "khyatyāt" (Pāṇini 6.1.112).

The word *yuṣmān* becomes *yuṣmayati*. From that, when the suffix *kvip* is applied and the *ṇi*-affix is elided, the rule *tvāhau sau* (Pāṇini 7.2.94) ought to apply; however, the elision of the *ṇi*-affix is not treated as *sthānivat*. As it has been said:

"And the status of being *sthānivat* does not apply here to the *ṇi*-affix because it has been elided by *kvip*. Here, the word "of the elision" (*lopasya*) is to be supplied [as the object of the verb], and the construction is "because of the elision of the *ṇi*-affix by *kvip*. If it is argued: "Let it be that even what is elided by *kvip* is always [treated as *sthānivat*]; for by that much, forms such as *lauḥ*—meaning 'one who speaks of lava'—would be established," we say no, because it would lead to the undesirable consequence of the form *pipaṭhiṣi* being unestablished.

Regarding the example *devayateḥ* given here by Kaiyaṭa—stating that "what is elided before *kvip* is not [treated as] non-existent"—this is his intention: although here the rule regarding *kvip* is established as *siddha* with respect to the operation (*vidhi*), nevertheless, because the elision of the *ṇi*-affix (*ṇilopa*) stands prior to the vowel that has not been previously prescribed (*anādiṣṭāt*) via its substituendum (*sthānin*), the elision undergoes the status of being "as if it were present" (*sthānivadbhāva*). Consequently, there arises the contingency of Vṛddhi substitution by the rule *aco ñṇiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.115). Therefore, the only recourse is the principle that "what is elided before *kvip* is not [treated as] non-existent."

Regarding the statement in the *Pāṣasūtra* 6.1.66 (*lopo vyoḥ*), Kaiyaṭa, while deriving the forms *kaṇḍūḥ* and *kaṇḍuvau* from the *kyaj*-derived root *kaṇḍūyati* with the suffix *ap*, says: "Due to the status of the elision (*allopa*) as *sthānivat*, [the substitution of] *yaṇ* occurs; then *uṭh* follows. Nor should it be argued that there would be an obstruction to the application of *uṭh* by virtue of its being *sthānivat*, because the *v* is prior to the preceding vowel (*adac*) of the *ādeśa*. This, however, is based on the assumption that priority determined through the medium of the *sthānin* is not universally valid (*anitya*). According to that principle, the form *dayūḥ* is also easily established.

If it is argued that in either case, the rule for *vṛddhi* would certainly apply in the word *dayaḥ* by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the treatment of a suffix as present), we say no; because the *ūṭh* substitution, being *bāhir-aṅga* (external), is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) with respect to the *vṛddhi*. Thus, even if the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*) were to apply, there is no harm, since the entire resolution is achieved precisely through its *bāhir-aṅga* nature. Therefore, the truth is simply that *dayūḥ* is established under both alternative views.

If it is argued that because a word modified in one part is not different from the original, the substitution of *au* for *div* should apply [here as well], we say no. This is because, according to the paribhāṣā regarding the absence of an *anubandha*, the term *adhātu* (non-root) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], as is clear from the Bhāṣya on the rule *diva auT* (Pāṇini 7.1.84) concerning the form *akṣadyūḥ*. Even though in the rule *ugidacām* (Pāṇini 7.1.70) the meaning is "that which was previously a non-root," the intention here is that this is a governing heading (*śabdādhikāra*) [referring to the current grammatical context].

By this, the long vowel [substitution] prescribed by *hali ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.77) in the form *divyati*—as found in the section on denominative verbs (*nāmadhātu*) in the *Kaumudī*, the *Prāsāda*, and other works—is refuted. Even Mādhava, who states *ḍiviḥ* in the rule *divo ḍiviḥ* added to the *Nyāsa*, likewise accepted only the short vowel in the form *divyati*. Let us return to our subject. However, regarding reduplication and so forth, the *yaṇ* substitution applies by *oḥ supi* (Pāṇini 6.4.83), resulting in forms such as *dayvau*, *dayvau*, and so on, just like *khalapū*. But in cases such as *kaṇḍūḥ*, *kaṇḍuvau*, *kaṇḍuvaḥ*, and so on, there is only the *uvaṅ* substitution; because the root is preceded by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), the *yaṇ* substitution does not apply. This is the general direction.
Here is the summary:
*saṃkhyuḥ*, *gomān*, and *padastvam* are examples of the elision of the suffix *kvip*;
in the case of its non-eternality, there are two instances of *lup* in the rules for *pipaṭhiṣi* and *kvip*.

The *luk* elision is not treated as if it were present (*asthānivat*). For example, *āmalakyāḥ phalam* results in *āmalakam*. However, in the alternative view where the *luk* elision of the suffix is rejected, one should cite *pañcapaṭuḥ*, meaning "bought for five clever [women]"; likewise, *pañcendrāṇyaḥ agnāyyaśca devatā asya* results in *pañcendraḥ* and *pañcāgniḥ*, wherein the *ānuk* augment and the long vowel *ai* are heard in connection with the feminine suffix *ṅīp*.

Nor can there be an exclusion [of the *ṅīṣ*] by the principle of "that which is taught as a restrictive rule" (*sanniyogaśiṣṭanyāya*), because when the exclusion of the *ṅīṣ*—which is caused by the subsequent *taddhita* suffix *luṅ*—is to be performed, the *ānuk* and the vowel *e* of the preceding elements would, by virtue of being treated as the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*) according to Pāṇini 1.1.57, *acaḥ parasmin pūrvavidhau*, prevent such an exclusion. However, for those who, according to the method previously mentioned, effect the inclusion of the vowel *ī* in the form *vara ī*, the mention of *luṅ* is not required here.

When an operation concerning the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) is to be performed, [the substitute] is not treated as the original (*sthānivat*). Consequently, when the *aṇ* suffix is applied to the word *parikhā* according to the rule for the four types of meanings (*cāturarthika*), and then the *cha* suffix is applied to the word *pārikha* by virtue of the rule "after a word with a long vowel, after *akekānta*, and after a word having *kh* as its penultimate vowel" (*Pāṇini 4.2.141*), the form *pārikhīyaḥ* is established. Otherwise, since the designation *upadhā* is a rule dependent on what precedes (*pūrvavidhi*), the elision of *ā* (*āllopa*) would have to be treated as *sthānivat* when that designation was to be applied.

If it is objected that, in this case, there would be *vṛddhi* in forms such as *paṭayati*, we say no; for it is established in the Bhāṣya that this prohibition applies only where a suffix is intended to be prescribed by depending upon the designation (*saṃjñā*) of the *upadhā*. And in this regard, the very mention of *caṅ-paranirhrāsa* (the shortening following *caṅ*) is the indicator (*jñāpaka*). If it is asked: "How then [is it consistent] with what is established in the Bhāṣya? For there, having given the example *saurī balākā* after the elision of *y* (*yalopa*), it is stated that the rule is already established by simply saying 'not in the case of an operation concerning the *upadhā*' (*upadhāvidhau na*)"? Know that this is merely a statement made without strict adherence to the technical details.

For in that case, regarding the form *saurī*—derived from *saura-* by adding the suffix *aṇ* according to Pāṇini 4.3.112 (*lenaikadik*) and then the feminine suffix *ṅīp*, where both the elision of *al* and the elision of *y* must be applied—the status of the former as a *sthānivadbhāva* is prohibited. Since the elision of the *aṇ* (which shares the same locus) is considered *asiddha* because it is *ābhīya*, the elision of *y* is successfully established. Thus, *saurī* is indeed the illustrative example for the rule "there is no *sthānivadbhāva* in the case of the elision of *y*. It is settled that the status of being a penultimate vowel (*upadhātva*) is relevant to that elision, but not to the prescription of the suffix itself.

When a short vowel occurs before a *ṇic* that is followed by *caṅ*, that short vowel is called "reduced by a *ṇic* followed by *caṅ*" (*caṅparanirhrāsa*); in such a case, it is not treated as if it were in its original state (*sthānivat*). For example: *arvāvadadvīṇāṃ parivādakena* ("he caused the lute-player to cause [someone] to play the lute"). Because the elision of the first *ṇic* would be treated as *sthānivat*, the vowel *a* would no longer be penultimate; consequently, the rule *ṇau caṅi* (Pāṇini 7.4.1), which prescribes the shortening of the penultimate vowel, would not apply. This result is established even by taking *ṇic* in its general sense. However, here is another example: *vāri ākhyat* → *avavirat*.

Nor should one fear the prohibition "na aglopi" (Pāṇini 6.4.94), because we accept that since the *vṛddhi* occurs first due to its higher priority, the *ṭilopa* follows, and thus the condition of being "aglopi" (having no elision of *a*) does not apply. For this very reason, the specific mention of *halakala* as ending in a vowel (*adanta*) is meaningful.

Regarding the rule *kutve na sthānivat*: from the root *arc*, the Uṇādi suffix *kap* is added to form *arka*; and from *pāc*, the suffix *ktic* is added to form *pākti*. In the latter case, although the substitution of *k* for *c* occurs by the rule *coḥ kuḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.30), the elision of the *ṇi* augment (*ṇilopa*) is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta*. The essential point (*niṣkarṣa*) is this: although the result could have been achieved in this sūtra simply by stating "in the case of *jaś* and *car*" (*jaścarṣu*), the inclusion of the term *vidhi* ("prescription") is intended to include other prescriptions based on *dvandva* compounds. To explain that further, there is the Vārttika beginning with *kvilugupadhātvacaṅparanirhrāsakutveṣu*. Even in that context, the inclusion of the cases of *kvip*, *caṅ*, the subsequent reduction (*paranirhrāsa*), the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*), and the *kutva* substitution is necessary.

It should be noted that because the meaning [of the rule] is already established by the elision (*luk*) through the inclusion of the vowel *ī*, the substitution of *ku* is considered as if it were not yet established (*asiddha*) with respect to what precedes it. An example for the substitution of *ku* according to Pāṇini 7.3.52 (*cajoḥ ku ghiṇyatoḥ*) should be sought elsewhere. Furthermore, in the context of what is "not yet established" (*pūrvatrāsiddhe*), the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original element) does not apply. From *pāpacyate* with the suffix *ktic*, we have *pāpāṅktaḥ*; from *yāyajyati* we have *yāyaṣṭiḥ*; from *pācayati* we have *pāktiḥ*; and from *yājayati* we have *yāṣṭiḥ*. Here, the elision of *al* (*allopa*) and the elision of *ṇi* (*ṇilopa*) are not treated as *sthānivat* with respect to the substitution of *ku* and the substitution of *ṣ*. Similarly, one should infer examples such as *leḍhiḥ* from *lehayati*, *dogdhiḥ* from *dohayati*, *veṣṭiḥ* from *veśayati*, and *dāṣṭiḥ* from *dāsyati*.

This is established by logic (*nyāyasiddha*): because a rule belonging to the three final chapters (*tripādī*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the extension (*atideśa*) prescribed by Pāṇini 1.1.57 (*acaḥ parasmin*), that extension does not apply when [the rule from the *tripādī*] is to be performed. Nor should it be argued that, if the *sthānivat* rule were likewise not to apply, the visarga in "rāma" would not occur; for it should be noted that its application is indicated by such indications as Pāṇini 3.1.1–2 (*pratyayaḥ paraśca*) and by the inclusion of the term *aś* in the rule 8.3.17 (*bho bhago agho*).

This being the case, it is established in the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika that the terms *dvirvacana*, *savarṇa*, *anusvāra*, *dīrgha*, *jaś*, and *cara* need not be recited in the rule; rather, only *na-padānta-vare-lopa-svareṣu* should be recited. It might be argued: if the mention of *dīrgha* is abandoned, then the status of being "as if that were there" (*sthānivadbhāva*) would apply in the rule for lengthening vowels in the seventh chapter (*sāptamika*). Consequently, the examples cited in the rule *ciṇṇamuloḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.63)—namely *aśaṃśāmi* and *aśāmi*, derived from a reduplicated form (*yaṅanta*) or a causative form (*ṇijanta*) followed by the causal suffix (*ṇic*) and then the *ciṇ* suffix—would not be established.

Nor can the long-vowel rule (*dīrgha*) override the status of being "like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) by its own force, because—following the method stated by Haradatta and others in the *kamerṇiṅ* sūtra, and following the method stated by Kaiyaṭa and others regarding *Pāṇini-sūtra* 6.4.93 (*ciṇṇamulordīrgha*)—the forms *ahiḍi* and *ahīḍi* are established, thereby precluding *aheḍi*; thus, the long-vowel rule has its purpose fulfilled there.

It is said in reply: By taking the unity of the *ṇit*-class (*ṇittvajāti*), the form *aśāmi* is established. As for *aśaṃśāmi*, however, this will occur from the causative (*ṇic*) of the root with the *yaṅ*-lopa suffix. For there is no difference whatsoever between the *yaṅ* and the *yaṅ*-lopa in terms of accent or meaning, such that one would need to struggle to justify the *yaṅ* alone. In this way, forms such as *grāhitam* are also established; because even when there is an intervention by the causative (*ṇic*), the substitution of the original form (*sthānivadbhāva*) prevents the application of the rule "lengthening occurs before the *liṭ*" (*graho liṭi*, Pāṇini 7.2.37).

According to the view of the *sūtra*, however, because the rule relies on a qualification of what is prescribed (*vihitaviśeṣaṇa*), there is no long vowel in forms such as *grāhita*. For this very reason, in *jarīgṛhita*—derived from the *yaṅ*-stem with the suffix *tṛc*—there is no long vowel, both because of the principle of "as if being the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) and because of the qualification of what is prescribed in the *sūtra*; thus it is established. But Mādhava maintains that when the *yaṅ*-elision (*yaṅluk*) occurs, a long vowel does indeed arise for the augment *iṭ* in forms such as those ending in *tṛc*, because according to the established doctrine that "doubling is the doubling [of the root] taught in the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*," the fact that [the root] *grah* is prescribed remains unchanged.

Mādhava’s intention is that because [the augment] *iṭ* is not caused by the elision (*luk*), is not a substitute for *aj*, and is itself elided by *luk*, there is no application of the rule of "acting as the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*). However, in reality, even in the case of *yaṅluk*, the lengthening of *iṭ* is indeed undesirable; this is determined precisely so by a careful examination of the *Bhāṣya*, Kaiyaṭa’s commentary, and other works on the rule *ekāco dve prathamasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.1).

And there, having cited the *Bhāṣya*—"from the root *grah*, when it is the *aṅga* [of an affix]"—Kaiyaṭa says: "For in *jarigṛhīti*, the *aṅga* is the suffix *tṛc*, not the root *grah*; for by the force of the qualification, one must resort to the form exactly as it is heard. Although this was stated there with reference to the *yaṅ*-intensive (*yaṅanta*), nevertheless, because the reasoning is the same, it is understood that the long vowel does not occur even in the *yaṅ*-lucidated (*yaṅ-luṅ*) forms.

For this very reason, Haradatta, in his commentary on the sūtra *ekāco dve* (Pāṇini 6.1.1), having raised the doubt regarding the long vowel in the case of the *yaṅ*-intensive, states: "In the rule prescribing the long vowel [from Pāṇini 7.4.83], the mention of 'having a single vowel' (*ekāj*) from the rule *ekāca upadeśe* (Pāṇini 7.2.10) is understood to carry over. Indeed, on this view, there is not even the possibility of stating that a long vowel occurs in the *yaṅluk* formation.

If it is argued that this contradicts Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the *vārttika* "and [the rule] stated regarding the elision of *yaṅ*" (*yaṅlope ca*) under the sūtra *graho 'liṭi* (Pāṇini 7.2.37), where Kaiyaṭa avoids the lengthening of the vowel in *yaṅ*-ant forms by either resorting to the status of the original form (*sthānivadbhāva*) or by adopting a qualifier for what is prescribed (*vihitaviśeṣaṇa*), since the purpose of the *yaṅluk* case would already be served by the necessity of either resorting to the form as heard (*yathāśrutarūpa*) or by the continued application of the mention of "having one vowel" (*ekājgrahaṇa*)—then the answer is: no, because of the sūtra *graho 'liṭi* (Pāṇini 7.2.37).

In this regard, Kaiyaṭa’s statement follows the maxim that "one means does not invalidate another means," because his intent there was merely to state an alternative method for the *yaṅ*-affix. For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa says there: "Because this fault has been properly extracted elsewhere. By speaking thus, he intends to show that the solution provided there is not universally applicable, and that the one stated in the rule concerning the single vowel (*ekāca*) must necessarily be adopted.

Furthermore, in the view that the form is exactly as heard (*yathāśrutarūpa*), there is no lack of proof (*asiddhi*) regarding the rule "the [root] has been grasped" (*gṛhīta*) and so on; for at the time of the application of the technical designation *aṅga*, the form is indeed present there exactly as it was heard. However, this is not the case with respect to "having caused to grasp" (*grāhita*) and the like. As for the resolution provided by the rule "a root consisting of one vowel" (*ekāc*), that refers exclusively to a domain distinct from the causative suffix (*ṇic*). Therefore, it is established that the long vowel does not occur in the following cases: after the root *grah* when followed by the suffix *yaṅ-luk*, nor after the causative (*ṇijanta*), nor after the aorist (*caṅanta*), whether occurring twice, thrice, or four times.

As for the work of Mādhava, it appears that one must somehow interpret it by assuming that the position which applies the qualification to the enjoined [element] is primary, while the other positions are merely subordinate; this is the general direction [of the argument].

The meaning of the passage beginning with "there is a fault in that" (*tasya doṣaḥ*) is as follows: there is a fault—that is, an over-extension (*atiprasakti*)—of that rule *pūrvatrāsiddham* (Bhāṣya) in three instances; therefore, the meaning is that a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) must be made there for the status of being like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*). By means of that, in the cases of *vākyārtham* and *vāsyartham*, the elision prescribed by *skoḥ saṃyogādyorante ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.26) is not barred; rather, [the *s*] is elided (*nigāryate*). Thus, the substitution of *l* (*latva*) by *aci vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 8.2.21) is established.

Similarly, in the case of *māṣavapanī*, the substitution of *ṇ* does not occur; because of the status of the elision (*allopasya*) as *sthānivat*, the *nakāra* lacks the character of being a final member of a compound (*samāsāntatva*). Nor should it be argued that even in the absence of *sthānivadbhāva*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* itself constitutes the final member of the compound and not the *nakāra*, for it will be stated in the second [chapter] that the feminine suffix *ṅīp* arises after the compound has been formed. This being the case, one should understand that from the root *takṣ* with the *kvip* suffix we have *tak*, and from *rakṣ* we have *rak*, and so forth.

For here, when the elision of a *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster) and so forth is to be applied, that [elision] does not take effect because of the status of the elision of the *ṇi*-affix as *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original element). However, in the case of the elision of a final *saṃyoga*, since the status of *sthānivadbhāva* is prohibited, that [elision] certainly occurs. On the other hand, the form *goraṭ* should be understood as derived from the root *gu* by means of the suffix *kvip*.

As for what Kaiyaṭa stated regarding the commentary on the word *dadhvatra* in the rule *acaḥ parasmin* (Pāṇini 1.1.57)—namely, that "the principle *pūrvatrāsiddham* does not apply here, because the fault [of the previous rule] remains; thus, the elision of the first member of a conjunct (*saṃyogādilopa*) serves as an illustration for the elision of any [consonant] characterized by being a conjunct"—that is not the actual fact. Rather, it is merely a description of the intention of the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) in that context.

For this very reason, it was stated by that same [author] in the supplement to the sūtra *nāpadāntasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.58): "From the root *skand*, [the substitute] *skan* occurs; from *takṣ*, *tak* occurs. As for what Kaiyaṭa stated during his commentary on the Vārttika "In the section on established forms (*siddhakāṇḍa*), there is *ścutva* in place of *dhuṭ*"—namely, "The form *madhug* is desired, whereas *madhuḍ* would result"—that should be understood as being due to the force of the teaching of the letter *s*.

If it is argued that in the case of *san ścotati*, the letter *s* serves its purpose because the rule *śi tuk* (Pāṇini 8.3.32) does not apply, then the principle *kṛt-luptam* [the elided suffix is considered as if it were present] must be invoked as the solution. Furthermore, in the Vārttika *kusmanāmnovā* (Gaṇasūtra), the form *kūḥ* cited by Mādhava is indeed correct; for in that instance, due to the absence of any [other] capacity [to trigger the rule], the elision of the initial consonant of the conjunct (*saṃyogādilopa*) does not take effect. This is the general direction of the argument.

It might be argued as follows: Let there be no mention of "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) and so forth here. Nor does this entail the undesirable consequence of the elision [of *k*] in examples such as *vākyārtham* by the rule *skoḥ saṃyogādyor ante ca* (Pāṇini 8.2.29). For in that rule, the term *jhalaḥ* is understood from the preceding rule *jhalo jhali* (8.2.26). And that [term *jhalaḥ*] qualifies the subordinate member *saṃyoga*, and not the principal members *s* and *k*, because [the latter] do not deviate [from being *jhals*].

Furthermore, according to the meaning of the rule (*sūtra*)—"there is elision of *s* and *k* at the beginning of a conjunct (*saṃyoga*) that ends in a *jhal* [consonant]"—or because the *yaṇ*-substitution is non-existent (*asiddha*) due to its being extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*), the elision of the final consonant of a conjunct does not apply in cases such as "dadhy atra. Accordingly, there is a Vārttika on the eighth book: "Or rather, [the elision] does not [apply], because of the elision of the *jhal*, or because of the extrinsic nature of the characteristic. Nor should it be argued that even so, forms such as "kāṣṭatak" and "rāṣṭrarak" would still remain unestablished; for, due to lack of usage (*anabhidhāna*), the suffix *kvip* itself is difficult to obtain in those instances.
And its non-expression—that "the *kāṣṭhaśak* itself does not exist"—is determined by the force of the Bhāṣya on the eighth [chapter], due to the equality of the underlying reasoning.

To this it is replied: In order to establish forms such as *kusmayate* → *kūḥ*, the rule *saṃyogādi* must indeed be stated. Furthermore, it must also be stated for the sake of forms such as *tak* and *rak*. Nor can it be argued that these do not exist, for there is no evidence for such a claim, and because they have been cited by Kaiyaṭa and others. Nor is the Bhāṣya statement "there is no such thing as *kāṣṭhaśak*" a proof in this matter, because the underlying logic is different. To explain: in the case of *kāṣṭhaśak sthātā*, that statement was made after raising the objection regarding the elision of the initial *k*-sound of the *saṃyoga* that is preceded by a *jhal* consonant.

Therefore, where there is the possibility of the elision of *kal*, that [elision] is intended by the non-mention [of the rule]. For this very reason, it has been explained with the intent that *kvip* does not occur after roots ending in *ṇic*. Nor is there a possibility of the elision of *kal* when *kvip* follows a root ending in *ṇic*, because of the status of the elided *ṇic* as *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were still present). Nor is this prohibited by the rule "in the case of what is not established in the preceding," because the counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) regarding the elision of the first member of a *saṃyoga* is active. Thus, it is settled that the mention of the elision of the first member of a *saṃyoga* must indeed be made.

However, this must be noted: regarding the rule *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.23), since the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is formulated in two ways—either by the option (*na vā*) of the elision of a *jhal* consonant or by its being a "non-local" (*bahiraṅga*) operation—the elision of the final conjunct (*saṃyogāntalopa*) in the form *kū* is difficult to justify. Consequently, according to the first position, the form would be *kusm*. But Mādhava [proceeds] with the intention of the second position.

But even so, the inclusion of *latva* (the substitution of *l* for *r*) is redundant; for in the case of *nigālyate*, even though the *ṇi*-affix has been elided, the substitution of *l* is established by the rule of "characteristic of the affix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). Nor is there a dependence on a specific phoneme (*varṇāśrayatva*), because the operation is understood to apply to the root itself when that affix follows. This will be made known by the explicit statement (*nipātana*) of the form *bhrauṇahatya* in the *dāṇḍināyana* rule. Furthermore, the substitution of *l* can be easily maintained on the grounds of its being an "internal" (*antaraṅga*) operation.

To this it is replied: In the rule *tṛṇaha im* (Pāṇini 7.3.92), the phrase *na aci* ("not before a vowel") is understood to carry over, while *halī* ("before a consonant") has ceased to apply. Consequently, it is established in the Bhāṣya that the rule on *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the treatment of an element as if it were still present when its substitute has occurred) need not be formulated for the sake of deriving forms such as *atṛṇeṭ*; rather, it is formulated for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*). Thus, the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* sūtra has as its sole fruit the exclusion of [the application of rules] to other cases. As for the various grammatical operations themselves, they are to be accomplished by means of the *sthānivadbhāva* sūtra.

And in that context, by the rule *pradīvya*, a prohibition is established to prevent the application of the suffix *iṇ* when the suffix is not primary (*aprādhānya*) and is not based on a vowel (*anāpyalāśrayaṇa*). Consequently, the substitution of *l* (latva) prescribed for a following vowel suffix (*aci pratyaye*) would be impossible without the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*. As for the argument that the substitution of *l* occurs because it is "internal" (*antaraṅga*), that too is incorrect; for the substitution of *l* does not take effect due to the maxim *akṛtavyūhaparibhāṣā* (the rule that an internal operation does not apply if its result would be subsequently sublated).

Furthermore, regarding the rule *upasargasyāyatau* (Pāṇini 6.1.91), two alternatives will be stated: whether the status of being followed by *ayati* is a qualifier of the prefix (*upasarga*) or of the letter *r*. In the first alternative, while forms such as *palyayate* are established, *plāyate* would not be established; for once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been applied, there is no distinct separation (*vyapavarga*), and because the operation depends on both sides, the treatment of the preceding element as the end (*antavad-bhāva*) or the following element as the beginning (*ādivad-bhāva*) is impossible. Therefore, in that case, the distinct separation must be asserted solely through the principle of "behaving like the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*).

And since that [substitution] is prohibited by the rule *pūrvatrāsiddhe ca*, this counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) regarding the substitution of *l* for *r* is indeed meaningful. However, under the second view, the form *palyayate* would not be possible because of the intervention of the *yakāra*. In the case of *plāyate* alone, the substitution of *l* would indeed occur, because by the prohibition of *sthānivadbhāva* in the rule *pūrvatrāsiddhe ca*, the condition of the *repha* being followed by *āya* is not destroyed there. But when the mention of *latva* is made here, the substitution of *l* is established even in *palyayate* by the maxim *yena nāvyavadhānam*.
This is clearly stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the eighth [chapter]. Therefore, it is established that the mention of *latva* (the substitution of *l*) must indeed be made here;

however, the mention of *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ*) is useless. To explain: first, the form *māṣavapanī* is established even by the *bahir-aṅga-paribhāṣā* (the maxim regarding external operations). Nor should it be argued that it is necessary for the sake of forms such as *prahiṇoti* and *pramīṇīte*, because even without the application of the rule *acaḥ parasmin* (Pāṇini 1.1.57), the application of the rule *hinu-mīnā-* (Pāṇini 8.4.15) is possible due to the principle that "that which has undergone a partial modification is not different from the original."

Nor should it be argued that, according to the method described in the rule *ṣṇāntā ṣaṭ* (Pāṇini 1.1.24), the mention of the letter *ṇ* is for the sake of establishing forms such as *priyāṣṭnaḥ*; for under the *kāryakāla* (operation-time) view, even that is established by the *bahiraṅga-paribhāṣā* itself. Furthermore, the *yathoddeśa* (location-time) view will not be adopted here, so as to ensure equality of result with the *ṇatva* that is to be rejected. By this, the passage from the *Padamañjarī* which maintains the acceptance of *ṇatva* in the form *priyāṣṭṇaḥ* is also refuted.

Even though the *bahiraṅga-paribhāṣā* is considered non-eternal (*anitya*), there is no evidence for its non-application here; therefore, it is established that the mention of *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ*) in this rule is redundant. On the contrary, there is even an objection to accepting *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original) in the case of *ṇatva*.

For instance, regarding the rule *aniterantaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.19), one explanation is as follows: by dividing the rule into two parts—*antaḥ* (8.4.20)—and [applying it] for the sake of establishing the form *he prāṇ*, the rule *antaḥ* (8.4.20) prescribes the substitution of *ṇ* for the final *n* of the root *ani* even when it is at the end of a word (*padānta*), thereby overriding the prohibition found in *dāntasya* (8.4.37). Thus, the form *he prāṇ* is established.

Relying on the word *anta* as a synonym for "proximity," two interpretations are established in the Bhāṣya even without a formal split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*): namely, that there is ṇatva for the letter *n* of the root *ani* which stands in proximity to the cause, and that there is ṇatva for the letter *n* of the root *ani* which stands in proximity to the cause. Among these, according to the first position, in forms such as *prāṇiti*, the substitution of ṇ occurs by virtue of the authority of the rule itself, even when there is an intervention by a single vowel, *ā*.

In the second alternative, however, because the single-substitute (ekādeśa) is treated as being like the first [element], a non-initial *ni* can occur immediately after the *r*, and thus the rule applies. But in the case of *paryaniti*, since there is an intervention by two letters and one letter respectively, it is clear from the eighth [chapter] that the substitution of *ṇ* does not apply in either alternative. If the mention of *ṇatva* were made here [in this rule], then just as in *paryaniti*, it would follow that in *prāṇiti* as well, the substitution of *ṇ* would not occur due to the intervention—whether by two or one letter—as the case may be.

Nor should it be argued that, on the strength of the specific wording [of the rule], one must rely on an intervention caused by the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), as in the case of the *kutva* substitution in "vṛtraghnaḥ"; for [the wording] has already served its purpose in cases such as "niraṇiti" and "duraṇiti."

Nor should it be argued that one should simply state "nirduroraniteḥ" [Pāṇini 8.4.17] rather than formulating the general rule "aniterantaḥ" [Pāṇini 8.4.20]. For it is possible to formulate a general rule by resorting to repetition (āvṛtti), since the word "antaḥ" is used—rather than "nirduroḥ"—both for the purpose of restoring the substitution of *ṇ* in the case of "he prāṇ" and out of consideration for brevity of syllables. Therefore, upon a careful examination of the Bhāṣya on Pāṇini 8.4.17, it is determined that the mention of *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ*) need not be made here.

For this very reason, there is no application of the rule for *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) in the case of *vyūḍhoraskeṇa*. Otherwise, since the *visarga* is treated as *aṭ*, the *s* which is its substitute would undergo *ṇatva* by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being like the original in place of what has been substituted). It has already been stated that there is no purpose for the mention of *ṇatva* here. Consequently, one should simply state: "The fault [of this rule] exists in the cases of the elision of the first letter of a *saṃyoga* (consonant cluster) and in the case of *latva*."

In reality, even that [objection] should not be stated; for it has been said that [the substitution] is established by logic precisely because of its being *asiddha* (not yet established) according to the rule "pūrvatrāsiddhe ca" (Pāṇini 8.2.1). Furthermore, that *asiddha*-status is non-permanent (*anitya*), as evidenced by the following: although one could have simply said "amunā," the statement "namune" (Pāṇini 8.2.3)—rather than "adhunā" (Pāṇini 5.3.17)—is due to a separation of rules (*yogavibhāga*). Likewise, although one could have simply said "nuṭi," the mention of "nāmi" (Pāṇini 6.4.3) serves as an indicator (*liṅga*) [of its non-permanence]. Even though the application of the rule "aṅgasya" (Pāṇini 6.4.1) would exclude cases such as "anaśvaḥ," the rule "nāmi" was nonetheless stated in order to prevent the long vowel in examples such as "akṣaṇvantaḥ."

If it is argued that, upon examining the two sūtras *rudhādibhyaḥ śnam* (Pāṇini 3.1.78) and *śnānnalopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.23), the mention of the term *nām* [in the latter] implies that—just as the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā* is set aside by the force of the rule's very formulation—the *asiddhatva* [of the preceding operation] should likewise be set aside without distinction; we reply: no. This is because the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā* is known to be non-eternal (*anitya*) through the inclusion of the *tuka* augment in rules such as *kṛti-tuk*, and because even on the view that the *paribhāṣā* is set aside by the force of the formulation, there would be the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) in cases such as *akṣaṇvantau*, where both [the *paribhāṣā* and the *asiddhatva*] would have to be set aside.

Therefore, that [rule] is intended solely for the purpose of making non-eternality known; by this, even the *Siddha-kāṇḍa* is included. By this, the following difficulty is also resolved: in forms such as *rāmaḥ* and *rāmebhyaḥ*, since the substitution of *ru* is not established (*asiddha*), how could the *it*-designation and subsequent elision of the *u* in *ru* occur? This is also supported by indicators such as *pratyayaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.1) and *paraśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.2). As for the argument that the *it*-designation and elision do not remain unestablished due to the force of the mention of the nasal (*anunāsika*), [that is refuted].

That is not so; for in examples such as *tarumūlam*, [the rule] finds its application by accepting that in the rule *ato roḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.113), only the nasalized (*sānunāsika*) [anusvāra] is intended, in order to exclude the application of *haśi ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.114). Furthermore, since the hearing of the nasalized sound is indeed to be expected even in cases like *rāmaḥ*, its applicability is clear. This is the general direction [of the argument]. Consequently, because there is no lack of established status (*asiddhatā*) regarding the elision of the first member of a conjunct (*saṃyogādilopa*) and the substitution of *la* (*latva*), the status of being a substitute (*sthānivattva*) will prevail, and thus all desired results are accomplished.

*dvirvacane'ci* (Pāṇini 1.1.59). This is a rule for the transfer of form (*rūpātideśa*). When a reduplication (*dvitva*) is to be performed, any substitute for a vowel (*ajādeśa*) that occurs when a vowel is the cause of the reduplication receives the form of its original (*sthānivadbhāva*). Examples: *cakratuḥ*, *cakruḥ*. Because the vowel is specified as the cause of the reduplication, it does not apply here: *dudyūṣati*, *susyūṣati*; for in these cases, the augment *ūṭh* is not the cause of the reduplication. Objection: If this were so, then even in the case of *yaṇ* in *cakratuḥ*, there would be no status as a *sthānivadbhāva*, because although the suffix *atus* is the cause of the reduplication, the letter *a* is not.

But is it not the case that the *sūtra* [Pāṇini 1.4.2] "in the case of *cakre* etc. allows for an exception? True; here, by the word "cause" (*nimitta*), what is intended is the status of being a motivator for reduplication, whether directly or as a constituent of a complex formation, but there is no insistence that it must be direct alone, because this follows from the requirements of the linguistic data (*lakṣya*). Furthermore, the word "cause" does not even exist in the *sūtra*. Rather, one must understand "the cause of reduplication" either through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), or through the etymological derivation "that in which reduplication is expressed" (*dvir-ucyate 'smin iti dvirvacanam*), or by adding the suffix *ac* (in the sense of possession) to form "that in which reduplication exists" (*dvirvacanam asty asmin iti*).

And these three types [of suffixes] can be easily stated as being applicable to the common efficient cause (*prayojaka*), whether directly or through a traditional lineage (*paramparā*). This is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the sūtra *ṭhasyekaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.50).

For this very reason, from the root *ūrṇu* with the suffix *san*, when the augment *iṭ* is optionally present by Pāṇini 7.2.49 (*sanīvantardha...*) and the *ṅit*-status is absent by Pāṇini 1.2.3 (*vibhāṣorṇoḥ*), the form *ūrṇunaviṣati* is established. This is so because, although the doubling (*dvitva*) is prescribed for the stem ending in *san*, since *san* is the cause of that doubling, when the operations of guna and lengthening (*guṇāvadeśau*) are to be applied to the doubled portion, the status of the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*) is maintained. As it has been said: "In this context, the status of being a cause is based merely on the fact that [the operation] occurs when that [element] is present. In reality, however, the suffix implied by the doubling is qualified by the word *aci* (in the rule *aco ñṇiti*).

The word *parasmin* (in the subsequent) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. Just as when it is said, "Bring from among these the one who is after Devadatta," the person brought is the one who is subsequent and not separated by another human being of the same class (*sajātīya*), so too here, that which is subsequent (*para*) is understood as being not separated by another suffix (*pratyayāntara*). Therefore, the meaning of the sūtra is: when a suffix beginning with a vowel (*ajādi*) that causes reduplication (*dvitvanimitta*) follows, and there exists a subsequent [element] not separated by another suffix, whatever substitute (*ādeśa*) occurs for the [reduplicated] vowel shall be treated as if it were the original (*sthānivat*). In this way, there is no inconsistency whatsoever in forms such as *cakratuḥ*.

By the force of the upcoming indicator (*jñāpaka*), although [the rule] applies even when separated by a *ṇic* suffix, there is no application in cases such as *didevanīyiṣati* because of the intervention of multiple affixes. In *apīpyat*, however, despite the intervention of phonemes, the rule does apply because there is no other intervening affix. It should be understood that even when a *paribhāṣā* is not present during a restatement (*anuvāda*), the requirement of the *paribhāṣā* specified [in the rule] is nonetheless fulfilled. For this very reason, the author of the *Nyāsa* states that the word "parasmin" (when followed by another) is carried over (*anuvartate*) here.

Likewise, Kaiyaṭa also intends this very point when he states that by the repetition [of the suffix], there is an implication of the suffix itself, and thus the indicator (jñāpaka) does not apply when the suffix is separated by something other than the *ṇic*. However, it should be noted that for the sake of establishing forms such as *ūrṇunaviṣati*, it is indeed accepted that [the preceding element] serves as a cause merely by its presence (*tadbhāvabhāvitāmātreṇa*).

But in that case, *aririṣati* would not be established; for when the augment *iṭ* is applied to the root *ṛ* by the rule *smipūṅrañjāśāṃ sani* (Pāṇini 7.2.74), then, due to the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) of the *guṇa* caused by the sound *is*, the rule *ajāderdvitīyasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.2) would entail the doubling of the syllable *i*. However, it is desired that the syllable *ris* be doubled. To this, it is replied:

For it has been established in the rule *dīdhīvevīṭām* (Pāṇini 1.1.6) that an effect (*kārya*) is not resorted to as a cause (*nimitta*); therefore, here the sound *is* is not the cause. Consequently, there is no application of the *sthānivadbhāva* principle. Nor should it be argued that, because the suffix *san* is itself the subject of an operation (*kāryitva*), the form *ūrṇunaviṣati* would also be impossible; for by means of the possessive suffix *-in*, the suffix *san* indeed acquires the status of being the subject of an operation simply by undergoing the operation. However, in that case, it is the second monophthong (*ekāc*) that undergoes the operation of doubling, and not the suffix *san*.

However, in the case of *aririṣati*, there is a disparity because only the word-element *ris* is the recipient of the grammatical operation (*kāryabhāk*). If it is objected: "In that case, the exclusion of *jeghrīyate* and *dedhmīyate* from the rule *acī* [Pāṇini 6.1.4] would be inconsistent; for since the elements *ghrīy* and *dhmīy*—which consist of a single vowel (*ekāc*) starting from the second consonant—are the recipients of the operation, the *yaṅ* suffix itself cannot be the cause of reduplication (*dvirvacana-nimitta*)," we reply: True. Let the very example *adhijage* be the object excluded by the mention of *ac* [in Pāṇini 6.1.4]. For in that case, the rule *gāṅ liṭi* (Pāṇini 2.4.49) [applies].

Thus, relying on the instruction regarding two causal factors (*dvilakāraka*), it is stated quite clearly in the *Bhāṣya* that the substitute *gāṅ* applies only in the state of the suffix *l* (the *l*-affix). This has been said following the opinion of the *Vārttika*, because in that system, rules such as "in the *liṭ*" and "in the *liṅ*" are accepted as having locative case endings referring to what follows (*parasaptamī*). However, according to the *Bhāṣya*’s own view, since it is accepted that the rules pertaining to *ārddhadhātuka* suffixes apply generally, rules such as "in the *liṭ*" are also considered locative case endings referring to the context (*viṣayasaptamī*); this was stated in the commentary on the *sthānivadbhāva* rule. According to that [Bhāṣya] view, however, one should understand that forms such as *jagle* are the examples to be excluded by the condition "before a vowel" (*aci*).

For instance, regarding the rule *ādeca upadeśe'śiti* (Pāṇini 6.1.45), in the view that the term *aśiti* is a locative (*parasaptamī*), one adopts the interpretation of *śa-it* as a *karmadhāraya* compound. Consequently, by the application of the principle *yasmānnirdiṣṭastadādāvalgrahaṇe* (Pāṇinīya-Bhāṣya), the substitution of *ātva*—which is prescribed when something other than *ādiśit* follows—is performed while the root is still in the state of *l* (the *laṭ* suffix). Therefore, it is not subject to the *sthānivadbhāva*. Nor can it be argued that because [the formation of] *tiṅ* suffixes and so on is *antaraṅga*, and once *iṭ* has been applied, *ātva* would occur and thus be subject to *sthānivadbhāva*.

Nor should it be argued that because the *tiP* suffixes and others are *antaraṅga*, once *īś* has been applied, the substitution of *ā* would occur, and thus the status of being *sthānivadbhūta* would be unavoidable. This is not the case, because one relies on the dual-marked (*dvilakāraka*) reference in the rule "na samprasāraṇe samprasāraṇam liṭi vayo yaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.37), and having carried that over here—since it was not applicable there—it is explained in the context of the prescription of *ātva* as applying specifically during the *l*-stage (*lāvasthā*) when the *liṭ* affix follows.

If it is asked, "How then are forms such as *jeghrīyate* and *dedhmīyate* cited as counter-examples (*pratyudāharaṇa*) in the Bhāṣya, the Vṛtti, and other works?"—know that this is according to the method of the Prātiśākhya. For it is stated: "The anusvāra and the consonant are members of the syllable" (*Ṛgveda-prātiśākhya* 1.5), and subsequently, "Consonants between vowels belong to the following [vowel]" (*Ṛgveda-prātiśākhya* 1.5). And thus, in cases such as *nenijati* and *anenijuḥ*, because the entire single root is reduplicated, the formation of the *abhyasta* (repeated) base allows for the application of the substitution of *at* and the suffix *jus*, among others.

In a reduplicated form consisting of two syllables (*dvyacka*), however, since the consonants situated in the middle belong to the subsequent part of the word, only the initial vowel-ending portion should be reduplicated—just as *da* in *daridrā-ti* and *jā* in *jāgar-ti*. There is no undesirable result in this regard that would justify disregarding the *Prātiśākhya* rules and instead adopting the principle "consonants [are repeated] like *naṭa* and *bārya*," which would lead to the reduplication of *dar* and *jāg*. For this very reason, the rule "in *catuḥ*, when *cha* or *ya* follows, there is elision of the first syllable" is consistent; such is the direction of the argument.

However, when, according to the system of the *Bhāṣya* and *Vārttika* on Pāṇini 6.1.36, a monophthong (*ekāc*) subsequent to the second vowel is taken, and it is accepted that the rule *gāṅ liṭi* (Pāṇ. 2.4.49) employs a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*), such that the substitution of *ā* is non-contingent (*anaimittika*)—or alternatively, that there is a prohibition in the presence of a *śit* suffix—or if the locative in *aśiti* is taken as a locative of scope, then since the three types of counter-examples (*vyāvartya*)—namely *jeghrīyate*, *adhijage*, and *jagle*—would be impossible, scholars should consider what the purpose of the restriction *aci* might be.

It might be argued: "The mention of *aj* [in the rule] will be for the purpose of preventing reduplication when the penultimate vowel is elided by Pāṇini 6.4.100 (*ghasibhasor hali*) after the suffix *kvasu* added to the root *bhas*. This is not so; for whether there is reduplication or not, there is no difference in the audible form *psān*. If it is argued that even a subtle difference is unavoidable for one with keen vision, we say no; for reduplication can be absent in cases such as *dāti priyāṇi* and *vīravaddhātu*.

For he will state in the sixth [chapter], under the rule *liṭi dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.8), that "the mention of 'non-reduplication' (*anabhyāsa*) is purposeless, because there is an option (*vāvacana*) in the Vedic language. Nor should it be argued that even so, reduplication would still occur optionally; for in the Vedic language, one must follow what is actually observed. It is precisely for this reason that the learned authorities maintain that the rule *nityaṃ chandasi* (Pāṇini 7.4.8)—which is unnecessary since the result is already established by *urṛt* (Pāṇini 7.4.7)—is fruitless.

In common usage (*loka*), however, the suffix *kvasu* is difficult to find according to the view of the Bhāṣya; moreover, the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) occurs only in the Vedic language.

Thus, the inclusion of the term *ac* (the vowel *a*) in the rule, which is performed for the sake of establishing forms such as *jeghrīyate*, *adhijage*, and *jagle*, serves as the very proof here that this is a transfer of form (*rūpātideśa*). For if it were a transfer of operation (*kāryātideśa*), then only the roots *ghrī*, *gā*, and *glā* would have to undergo reduplication; so what need would there be for that [inclusion of *ac*]? Accordingly, the Vārttika states: "But the inclusion of *ac* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that there is a substitution of the form (*sthānivadbhāva*). Furthermore, *dedhmīyate* and *śāśayyate* are examples on the same footing as *jeghrīyate*.

The vowel *ī* [is substituted] by Pāṇini’s sūtra 7.4.31 (*ī ghrādhmoḥ*), and the substitution of *ayaṅ* for *śīṅ* occurs by Pāṇini’s sūtra 7.4.22 (*ayaṅ yi kṅiti*). However, on the alternative view where the mention of *aci* [in 6.1.91] is rejected, one should explain that here there is an extension of the form (*rūpātideśa*) based on the authority of the word (*śabdādhikāra*), in accordance with the observed forms (*lakṣya*). If it is asked: "What is the purpose of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the genitive *acaḥ* from the preceding sūtra here?"—understand that it is for the sake of establishing forms such as *śuśuvatuḥ*.

For instance, although the rule *vibhāṣā śveḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.30) finds its scope in forms such as *śuśāva* when followed by *pit* suffixes, it nevertheless serves only as an exception (*bādhaka*) to the rule *vacisvapiyajādīnāṃ kiti* (Pāṇini 6.1.15), which has already found its application in forms such as *śūnaḥ*, because the former is subsequent in the order of the rules. However, it does not serve as an exception to the rule *liṭyabhyāsasyobhayeṣām* (Pāṇini 6.1.17), because that injunction concerning the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) of the root *śvi* is itself without scope [in the case of *pit* suffixes].

For this very reason, under the rule *vibhāṣā śveḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.30), the Vārttika begins: "In the case of the root *śvi*, there is a prohibition of the characteristics [of reduplication] when the *liṭ* [affixes] follow. Its intention is that the phrase "except for those beginning with *aśvi*" (*aśvayatīnām*) must be supplied to the rule *liṭy abhyāsasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.17). Otherwise, because it would be both prescribed and prohibited, there would be an option (*vikalpa*), and consequently, the undesirable forms *śuśvāya* and *śuśviyatuḥ* might also result in certain cases.

This being the case, in the rule *dvirvacane 'ci* (Pāṇini 1.1.59), if the term *aci* were not understood as being carried over [from the previous sūtra], then in the form *śuśāva*, just as there would be the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* for the substitution of *vṛddhi* and *āv*, so too would there be the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* for the *saṃprasāraṇa*. Consequently, undesirable forms such as *śiśāva* and *śiśuvatuḥ* would result. Nor can it be argued that because of the principle *saṃprasāraṇaṃ tadāśrayaṃ ca kāryaṃ balavat* (Paribhāṣā 128)—which states that a *saṃprasāraṇa* and the operation dependent upon it are stronger—the *saṃprasāraṇa* occurs only at the stage of the *tiṅ* suffixes and thus the condition *aci* does not apply; for even so, the fault remains inevitable in cases such as *vyatiśuśuvāte*.

Nor should it be said that [the rule] *vibhāṣā śveḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.30) applies only at the stage of the suffix *la*; for even so, defects would remain in forms such as *ījāte* and *ījāthe*, because at the stage of *la*, the *kit* designation is absent, and thus the substitution of semivowels (*samprasāraṇa*) does not apply there. Nor should it be argued that the *kit* designation should also apply, since it is superseded by the *antaraṅga* suffixes *tiP* and others. Furthermore, regarding the form *asuṣupat*, it is desired that the semivowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*) occur according to *svāpeścaṅi* (Pāṇini 6.1.18).

However, if the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) were to apply, then by the prohibition "there is no substitution of *samprasāraṇa*" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 6.1.37), the vowel *u* would not be heard in the reduplicated syllable; such is the general direction [of the argument].

In this context, the determination of time is also established by resorting to one of the methods of *tantra*, *āvṛtti*, or *ekaśeṣa*. Thus it has been explained: "when the state of being doubled (*dvitva*) is to be performed. Consequently, in forms such as *cakratuḥ*, the *yaṇ*-substitution and other operations occur again in their respective places within the subsequent member; otherwise, there would be only the *prakṛtibhāva* (non-application of grammatical changes). However, in the case of *ninyatuḥ*, although *iyaṅ* was first applied, it is removed at the time of doubling; thus, even though it might apply again, it is superseded by the *yaṇ*-substitution according to the rule *eranekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.82).

Alternatively, even previously this *iyaṅ* does not apply, according to the maxim: "Having set aside the domain of the exception, the general rule then takes effect. Or rather, because *iyaṅ* is considered asiddha (non-existent) by virtue of being ābhīya (belonging to the subsequent stage), the *yaṇ* substitution will take place.

It might be argued: "Let us set aside the mention of *sthānivat* and carry forward the negative particle (*nañ*), explaining the rule simply as: 'When a vowel (*ac*) is the cause of reduplication, a substitute for a vowel shall not take effect when the operation of reduplication is to be performed. For if this were the case, there would be no need for the laborious introduction of the term *sthānivat* as a governing heading. True; even on this view, one must still assert that the negative particle (*nañ*) possesses a *svarita* accent. However, since that [property] is already established for the word *sthānivat*, there is greater economy [of effort]. Or, let both explanations stand, as there is no difference in their result. This is the direction [of the argument].

"But even so, the rule that [a substitute] is 'as if the original' (sthānivadbhāva) must be stated for the causative suffix (ṇi), for the sake of forms such as *nunāvayiṣati*, *cukṣāvayiṣati*, and *tuṣṭāvayiṣati*. On this point, they say: the statement in the rule *oḥ puyaṇjyapare* is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the status of being 'as if the original' applies to the causative suffix."

The meaning of this is as follows: when the augment *iṭ* is applied to the roots *yu* and *pū* by the two rules *sanīvantardhabhrasjadambhuśrisvṛyūrṇubharajñapisanām* (Pāṇini 7.2.49) and *smipūṅrañjvaśām ca* (Pāṇini 7.2.74), resulting in the forms *yiyaviṣati* and *pipaviṣate*, the rule *dvirvacane'ci* (Pāṇini 1.1.59) causes the substitute to behave like the original (*sthānivadbhāva*). Consequently, although the vowel *u* is obtained in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) before the subsequent vowels *a* (in *yiyaviṣati*) and *a* (in *pipaviṣate*), the prescription of the substitution of *i* for that *u* renders the inclusion of the letters *p* and *y* in the rule *oḥ puyaṇjyapare* meaningful.

Nevertheless, the mention of the *vargāḥ* (classes of consonants), the mention of the *pratyāhāra* (*at* in *ata upadhāyāḥ*), and the mention of *j* serve as indicators that the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* applies even when the vowel that is the cause of reduplication is separated from the *ṇic* affix. Without these, it would be difficult for a reduplicated syllable ending in an *u*-vowel to occur before *pu*, *yaṇ*, or *ji* followed by an *a*-vowel. Furthermore, by the principle of "that which does not allow intervention" (*yena nāvyavadhāna*), only the single *ṇic* affix is accepted as the intervening element between the vowel that causes reduplication and the subsequent sound.

Therefore, in forms such as *ninavanīyiṣati*, [the substitution] is not treated as *sthānivadbhūta* because of the intervention of the suffixes *lyuṭ* and *kvip*. Likewise, even when *lyuṭ*, *kyac*, or *san* follow a causative (*ṇijanta*) base, there is no *sthānivadbhāva*, as in *nināvanīyiṣati* and so forth. For there is no explicit rule stating that "what is performed upon a causative base is *sthānivadbhūta*"; rather, the status of *sthānivadbhāva* is merely indicated [by implication], and it was stated that this applies only when there is an intervention by a single element for the sake of brevity. In the present case, however, the intervention by multiple elements is clearly evident.

Although the *nirdiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the paribhāṣā concerning that which is specifically mentioned) does not apply because [the term *aci*] functions as a qualifier of the location being restated (*anūdyamāna*), nevertheless, its meaning is established solely by virtue of the locative case *aci* being used in the sense of immediate proximity (*aupaśleṣika-saptamī*). Furthermore, it should be understood that when "slight separation" is obtained, there is no inclusion of what is "extremely remote. In fact, however, it was stated at the beginning of the sūtra that the word *parasmin* is understood (*anuvartate*) from the previous rule.

And thus, in forms such as *abībhavat*, *arīravat*, and *alīlavat*, as well as in *bibhāvayiṣati* and others, the substitution of *it* (short *i*) by Pāṇini’s rule *oḥ puyaṇjyapare* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.4.80) takes effect. However, the purpose of this rule-statement is to indicate that where *oḥ puyaṇjyapare* does not apply, [the substitution should be understood to occur]. For example: *cukṣāvayiṣati*; *uḍavati* (meaning "he acts like a star"); from *uḍavati* with the suffix *ṇic* followed by the desiderative suffix (*san*): *uḍuḍāvayiṣati*; in the reduplicated aorist (*caṅ*): *auḍūḍavat*; *tutāvayiṣati*; *atūtavat*.

This is based on the Sūtra [Pāṇini 6.1.54]: *turustuśamyamaḥ sārvadhātuke*. Due to the status of that [vowel] as a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if being the original substitute), forms such as *pusphārayiṣati* and *apuspharat* are to be understood. Furthermore, this *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence) depends upon a similar class [of vowels]. Therefore, the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* applies only when a consonant (*hal*) follows a vowel (*avarṇa*). Consequently, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *acikīrtat*; thus it is established in the Bhāṣya.

As for what is stated in the *Kāśikā* under the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham* (Pāṇini 8.2.1)—where, having cited *aujaḍhat* as an example for the causative (*ṇic*) of the root *vah* ending in the *niṣṭhā* suffix, it says *aujiḍhat* for the form ending in *ktin*—and as explained in the *Nyāsa* on that very point, that the *ṭilopa* performed after the *ṇi* is treated as *sthānivat*; both of these should be disregarded because they contradict the *Bhāṣya*. It is clear from the *Bhāṣya* that the *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence) applies specifically to the case of a vowel followed by a consonant of the verbal root, as required for the derivation of *acikīrtat*.

In the *vārttika* which aims to reject the present sūtra, by means of the *bhāṣya*—"of that which has *o*, *au*, etc., as its substitute, [the rule applies] when preceded by *c*, *ṭ*, *t*, *u*, *ś*, or *r*"—this very point will be made clear immediately hereafter through the pointing out of the defect of under-extension (*avyāpti*). For this very reason, it is said:
"Śuṣkikā, Śuṣkajaṅghā, Kṣāmimān, and Aujiḍhḍhi."

Thus, in the *Vaiyāghrapadyavārttika*, only the word *ji* is recited; the reading *ja*, however, is merely occasional and erroneous, as Bopadeva established in his *Kāmadhenu* after demonstrating the agreement of Durgasiṃha and others. Furthermore, the *Vaiyāghrapadyavārttika* is intended as a summary of the purposes of the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham* (Pāṇini 8.2.1), and we shall explain that very rule in its proper place.

And thus, by the rule "aṅkapade lakṣaṇe ca" (Pāṇini 6.1.145), because the suffix *caṅ* and the suffix *ṇic* undergo reduplication, the form is indeed *āñcikata*, and not *āñcakat*. Nor should it be argued that the inclusion of the word "pada" in this rule would be redundant; for by the force of that word, when the elision (*allop*) does not take effect, and given the presence of the *vṛddhi* and *puṅ* augmentations, the form *aṅkāpayati* is accepted.

And it should not be argued that, this being the case, the form *aṅkayati* would be impossible; for in the Vārttika on *sūci-sūtri* (*kāovāo*), the Bhāṣya provides examples such as *sosūcyate* and *sosūtryate*, by which it is accepted that the elision of *a* (*allopa*) occurs optionally. Indeed, *sūci*, *sūtri*, and others end in long *ā*. For this very reason, because they have more than one vowel (*anekāc*), they do not belong to the class of roots taught with a cerebral *ṣ* (*ṣopadeśa*), and thus there is no substitution of *ṣ* for *s*. This will be explained [later] by stating that [the status of these roots] is determined through the exclusion of *seg* and others, by their association with *ṣvaṣka*, *ṣvid*, and so forth, and by the examples given in the Bhāṣya such as *sosūcyate*.

In this way, we shall justify the remainder of the statement. Here, the usage of "liṅ in the sense of inquiry and prayer" (*sampraśnaprārthaneṣu liṅ*) and so forth serves as the authority for the application of "prayer" (*prārthana*) and "determination" (*adhyavasāya*). Having considered all of this, they say that there is the elision of *v* (in *vā* = *vikalpa*) in order to make the final *t* meaningful. And it has been stated in the *Kāmadhenu*: "The state of having no elision of the penultimate vowel (*aglopitva*) and the status of being as if present (*sthānivattva*) are the purposes of having a final *t*. Where these two do not exist, there is an option regarding the elision of *a*. Thus [ends the section on] *itaḥ*.

The distinction is that the first half [of the verse] explains the initial intention, while the second half explains the subsequent intention. Now, one might object: "In the form *āñcakat*, since the rule *dīrgho laghoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.94) would apply, the prohibition by *anaglopa* (Pāṇini 7.4.93) serves its purpose by preventing the lengthening of the vowel *a*. This is not so; for the established meaning of the sūtra is: "When a *ṇi* followed by *caṅ* is present, [the lengthening applies] to that which is the reduplication of the *aṅga* [stem]. In this case, however, the reduplication belongs to the state of the *aṅga* as a whole, and not to the *aṅga* itself [as a constituent part].

This is clear from the *Mādhavīya-vṛtti* on the *Candra-vyākaraṇa*. For this very reason, there is no lengthening in forms such as *āṭiṭat*. As for the qualification "beginning with a consonant" (*halādi*) provided in the *Kaumudī* regarding the rule for lengthening, that is without foundation. Furthermore, even if forms such as *orṇunavat* were established, [the qualification] would be over-extended to both forms—*acicakāsat* and *acacakāsat*—since, according to the different views regarding whether the phrase "when followed by *caṅ*" (*caṅpare*) qualifies the stem (*aṅga*) or the light syllable (*laghu*) in the rule *sanvallaghuni* (Pāṇini 7.4.93), both results would be desired.

Alternatively, this may be resolved by relying on the fact that in the rule for long vowels (*dīrghavidhi*), the phrase "when followed by *caṅ*" (*caṅpare*) functions as a qualifier of the light vowel (*laghu*). Thus, it is merely a statement of what is already established by the sense [of the rule]. However, according to the final view (*siddhānta*) following the method stated by Mādhava, it is quite clear that there is no lengthening of the vowel even for the root *cakās*, just as there is none for *ūrṇāvayati*. This is the general direction.

The author of the Vārttika rejected this sūtra. For instance, at the end of the section on the sixth case (the genitive), a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) is stated: "Reduplication [takes precedence] over the *yaṇ* substitution, the substitutions *ay*, *āv*, and *āva*, elision (*alopa*), elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*), elision of the suffix *ṇi*, and the substitution of *u* for *ki* and *kī*. Thus, the *yaṇ* substitution finds its scope in examples such as *dadhy atra*; whereas [the other rules find their scope] in examples such as *cayanaṃ*, *cāyakaḥ*, *lavanaṃ*, and *lāvakaḥ*.

The elision of *ā* in *cāyavāyāvaḥ*; the elision of *ā* in *godaḥ*, *kambaladaḥ*, etc.; the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) in *śleṣmaghnaḥ*, etc.; the elision of the suffix *ṇi* in *kāraṇā*, *hāraṇā*, etc.; the elision of the penultimate vowel in *nipūrttā*, etc.; the elision of the suffix *ṇi* in *kāraṇā*, *hāraṇā*, etc.; and the substitution of *u* (*utva*) in *nipūrttā*, etc.—these nine [rules] are superseded by the rule of reduplication (which finds its scope in forms such as *bibhidatuḥ*) through the principle of prior precedence (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*).

By this [rule], forms such as *cakratuḥ*, *cicāya*, *lulāva*, *cicayitha*, *lulavitha*, *papatuḥ*, *tasthatuḥ*, *jagmatuḥ*, *jaghnatuḥ*, *āṭiṭat*, *taturiḥ*, and *jaguriḥ* are established. If it is argued that in this way the form *ninyatuḥ* would not be possible because *iyaṅ* is not included in the aforementioned list, we say no. This is because, by the rule *eranekācaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.82), *yaṇ* ought to occur here; thus, since *iyaṅ* has not yet applied, the maxim *prakalpya ca* (and having first applied [the subsequent rule]) applies.
Therefore, everything is established even without the rule *dvirvacane'ci* (Pāṇini 1.1.59).

The authors of the Bhāṣya, however, support the Sūtra. For instance, the mutual contradiction (vipratiṣedha) is indeed improper, because the substitution of *āl* and so forth is permanent (*nitya*), whereas doubling (*dvitva*) is non-permanent (*anitya*), and thus they are not of equal strength. Furthermore, if one were to resort to a "prior contradiction" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*), a specific rule would have to be formulated in every such case; here, moreover, it would be even more necessary—so where is the economy of effort? Moreover, if a rule being formulated were to override even internal operations (*antaraṅga*), then in forms such as *ninvanīyiṣati* and *didavanīyiṣati*, the letter *u* would also be heard in the reduplicated syllable.

Now, if you were to argue that because it is *antaraṅga* (internal), the substitution of *av* applies first—on the grounds that a rule does not subvert other *antaraṅga* operations but only those that are *nitya* (obligatory)—even so, in forms such as *cukṣāvayiṣati*, since the *vṛddhi* and the substitution of *av* would have already taken effect, the shortening (*itva*) of the reduplicated syllable would occur. Consequently, to prevent that, the substitution of *ut* must be prescribed. And thus, you would have to formulate the rules in this way: "The *ut* [substitution] for the subsequent *at*" (Pāṇini 7.4.88), "In the case of *ti*" (Pāṇini 7.4.89), and "For the substitute *o*, *au*, etc., when preceded by *cu*, *ṭu*, *tu*, or *śa*" (Pāṇini 7.4.60).

The term *abyāsasya* (of the non-reduplicated) is understood [from the previous rule]. The meaning is: in that stem (*aṅga*) which has *o* or *au* as its substitute, for the vowel *a* belonging to the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*)—provided that the reduplicated syllable begins with *c*, *ṭ*, *t*, *u*, *ś*, or *ṣ*—there shall be *ut*. For example: *cukṣāvayiṣati*, *uḍuḍāvayiṣati*, *tutāvayiṣati*, *ūrṇunāvayiṣati*, *śuśāvayiṣati*, and *pusphārayiṣati*. In these cases, the substitution of *ā* [for the semivowel] occurs by the rule *cisphurorṇau* (Pāṇini 6.1.54).

Although in this case the status of being "śarādi" (beginning with a *śar* consonant) no longer exists once the elision (*kha*) has taken place, it must nevertheless be understood that this status did indeed exist at the time the designation "repetition" (*abhyāsa*) was applied. Why specify "of that which has *o* or *au* as its substitute"? Consider: *cāyṛ* (in the sense of worshiping, *bhvādigaṇa*, root 905) in *cicāyiṣati*; and *khada* (in the sense of steadiness, *bhvādigaṇa*, root 50) in *cikhadiṣati*. Why specify "beginning with *cu*, *ṭu*, *tu*, or *śar*" (*cuṭutuśarādeḥ*)? Consider: *bibhāvayiṣati*.

What is the purpose of [specifying] *ataḥ* (from a short *a*)? It is so that in forms such as *ārjijat*, *āṇiṇat*, *ārttitat*, and *āṃśiśat*—derived from the roots *ṛju*, *aṇu*, *ṛtu*, and *aṃśu* respectively—the rule for *ṭilopa* (elision of the penultimate vowel) does not apply after the augment *saṇic* has been doubled, even though *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) would otherwise take precedence. Furthermore, there is a fault in both cases: in the form *śiśītalayiṣati*—derived from *śītalaluḥ* (one who cuts cold), where *śītaṃ lunāti*—"one desires to express that"—there would be the undesirable consequence of the substitution of *ut* for the *at* following the letter *t*.

If it is asked: "Even so, why was another point of complexity not raised against the author of the Vārttika—that in cases such as *aujaḍhat* and *āñcakat*, a further effort must indeed be undertaken to ensure the hearing of the vowel *a* in the reduplicated syllable? The answer is: No, because it has already been stated that in those instances, the vowel *i* alone is intended. For even in the established system (siddhānta), the evidence (*jñāpaka*) is relative to homogeneous elements (*sajātīya*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of hearing the vowel *a* in the reduplicated syllable of *acikīrtat*. Therefore, it remains the case that two separate rules would have had to be formulated by the author of the Vārttika.

Likewise, for the sake of establishing forms such as *jaglau*, the rule for *vṛddhi* must also be recited in the *vipratiṣedha-vārttika*. Similarly, the third rule, *oḥ puyaṇji* (Pāṇini 7.4.80), must also be formulated so that *itva* may occur in cases such as *pipaviṣate*, *yiyaviṣati*, and *jijāvayiṣati*. For instance, in the case of the roots *pu* and *yu* followed by the suffix *san* with the augment *iṭ*, since *guṇa* would apply by virtue of its higher status, one must indeed state that *itva* occurs via *pūrvavipratiṣedha* (priority of application) before the substitution of *āv*.

Similarly, regarding the rule *ju-caṅkramya-* (Pāṇini 3.2.150), when the desiderative suffix *san* is added to the root *ju* as prescribed in that sūtra—resulting in the form *jijāvayiṣati*—the substitution of *u* by the rule *cu-ṭu-tu-śa-r-ādeḥ* would apply; however, to prevent that, the substitution of *i* must be stated.

Nor should it be argued that one will read only the letter *c* there and not the word *cu*, for if that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence of the failure to establish forms such as *ajūgavat*, *ajūghavat*, *jugāvayiṣati*, and *jughāvayiṣati* from the roots *guṅ* and *ghuṅ* (*ghvanau*, bhvādi 979) when followed by the causative suffix *ṇic* and the *caṅ* aorist marker. Furthermore, in cases such as *didavanīyiṣīta* and *ninavanīyiṣati*, the substitution of *u* [for the penultimate vowel] by the rule *cuṭutuśarādeḥ* would apply; therefore, another statement must be adopted to prevent that.

Alternatively, one should resolve this by carrying over (*anuvartana*) the mention of *san*—even though it has been interrupted by the eight rules beginning with "guṇo yaṅlukoḥ" (Pāṇini 7.4.82)—from the rule "saṃyogāt parasya liṭi" (Pāṇini 7.4.79) via the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*) method; then, according to the principle "there is no intervention by that which [itself] intervenes" (*yena nāvyavadhāna*), it should be understood that the substitution of *u* does not occur when there is an intervention by elements other than the causative suffix (*ṇic*).

Even so, when the suffix *san* follows the causative *ṇic*—whether that *ṇic* is present or absent after the root *tan* with the denominative *kvip* suffix *ācārakvib*—in forms such as *titanaviṣati* and *titanāvayiṣati*, the substitution of *ū* would still occur. To prevent this, the Vārttika "of the substitute *o* for *au*" must be explained in another way, as follows: the genitive in *abhyāsasya* is a partitive genitive (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*), whereas the genitive in *odaud* and so forth is a genitive expressing a general relationship (*sambandha-sāmānya-ṣaṣṭhī*). The genitive in *abhyāsasya* is a partitive genitive; the genitive in *odaud* and so forth, however, is a genitive expressing a general relationship.

Therefore, both [the terms *at* and *ut*] are qualifiers.
