This is the meaning: just as there is a substitute for a constituent part (*avayava*) of the reduplication, so too there arises a substitute for a constituent part of that which begins with *a* or *u*. For example, in *cukṣāvayiṣati*, it is a constituent part; in *pusphārayiṣati*, it is a substitute. Thus, the mention of *at* is also meaningful.

Otherwise, for the sake of forms such as *āṭiṭat*, since there would be no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in cases like *ārjijat* due to the extension (*atideśa*) of the *sanvadbhāva* rule to that which is light (*laghu*) within the *aṅga* when followed by *ṇi* with *caṅ* following, the word *ataḥ* [in the rule] would be redundant; this is the general direction [of the argument]. Thus, compared to the view of the Sūtra, the view of the Vārttika involves a great deal of complexity (*gaurava*).

It might be argued: "Let the present Sūtra not exist, and let the Vārttika not exist either; the rule *oḥ puyaṇ* (Pāṇini 7.4.80) itself will indicate that reduplication should take place, overriding both the *antaraṅga* and the *nitya* [rules]. Then, once reduplication has been performed, the *yaṇ*-substitution and other operations will be carried out as they naturally apply. Do not say so, for in that case forms such as *ninavanīyiṣati* and *didavanīyiṣati* would remain unestablished. Furthermore, does this *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence) depend on general rules or specific ones? In the first case, the form *acikīrtat* would not be established.

In the latter case, forms such as *acakratuḥ* would not be established. Therefore, the sūtra must indeed be formulated. However, for the sake of establishing forms such as *cukṣāvayiṣati*, one must rely on the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in Pāṇini’s sūtra 6.1.91, *oḥ puyaṇjyapare*. And it has been settled that this indicator refers to members of the same class [of sounds]. For this very reason, it was previously explained—with the support of Bopadeva—that the example *ojaḍhat* cited by Vāmana contradicts the Bhāṣya. In reality, however, what Vāmana stated is entirely correct; for— Vāmana and the other great elephants have been swallowed by the mighty crocodile that is Bopadeva.
He was liberated by Mādhava solely through the power of Kīrti’s renown.

To explain: does the objection raised by Vāmana conflict with the Bhāṣya that intends to refute the *vārttika*, or does it conflict with the Bhāṣya that intends to refute [the view] of those belonging to the same school (*sajātīya*), or does it conflict with the Bhāṣya that describes the status of being an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for those belonging to the same school? It is not the first case; for since the two objections—"the impossibility of a contradiction between the eternal and the non-eternal" and "the non-establishment of forms such as *didavanīyiṣati*"—are not mentioned in the Bhāṣya, it is established that the Bhāṣya is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of other objections as well. Consequently, even the substitution of the vowel *a* in the reduplicated syllable of *aujaḍhat* [is included].

Since another objection must also be addressed in the Vārttika—namely, that [the rule] should be formulated as *vidheyaḥ syāt*—the Vārttika should be composed as follows: "Because another objection must also be addressed in the Vārttika: *odaudādaśesya kacuṭutuśarāderabhyāsasyautsani*. Then, *allopavato ṇico'tu*: for the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) of a stem (*aṅga*) that undergoes elision of *a* (*allopa*) following a causative suffix (*ṇic*), there shall be *at* [substitution]. Examples are *aujaḍhat* and *āñcakadat*."

The second [alternative] is not tenable; for the established meaning of the Bhāṣya is that when there is a reduplication, the rule *sthānivat* applies to the first vowel (*aj-varṇa*) of the subsequent portion (*uttara-khaṇḍa*). And in the case of the reduplication of the word *hata*, there is indeed an *a*-vowel in the subsequent portion during the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā-daśā*). If it is argued: "But since it is removed by the application of *ṭilopa* (the elision of the feminine suffix) which recurs, that [vowel] does not actually exist in the final form (*prayoga*)," what of it? For being present in the final form is not a qualifying condition provided in the Bhāṣya.

And thus, in cases such as *anunāvayiṣati*, although there is no *a*-vowel at the time the doubling (*dvitva*) occurs, the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) applies by relying on that vowel which exists later; however, in the case of the word *hata* in *adhyajīgapat*, even though that [vowel] is absent later, if there were *sthānivadbhāva*, then because the root begins with a non-j letter (*ajādi*), the doubling would apply to the *ṇic* suffix itself. Consequently, since there is neither an *a*-vowel at the time the doubling occurs nor one subsequent to it, there is no *sthānivadbhāva*, as in the case of *acikīrtat* and similar forms.

Thus, the stubborn insistence that the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* applies only to that which occupies the place of a vowel (*avarṇa*) is entirely baseless. For this very reason, regarding the rule *lopaḥ pibateḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.4), only *apīpyat* is correct, and not *āñcikṣat*. Forms such as *āṅgapayati* and *āñcakipat* are utterly dismissed, because the elision of the vowel (*al-lopa*) would be unavoidable. As for the pronunciation of the letter *a*, its purpose is fulfilled by the hearing of the vowel *a* in the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) and so forth. Furthermore, as for what was stated—that there is both the absence of elision (*aglopitva*) and the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva*—and so on.

That too is not correct; for since the optionality of the *ṇic* suffix is well-established by the rule *cintipūjikathikumbicarcaśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.27) and by the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *ghuṣir aviśabde* (Pāṇini 7.2.23), the optionality of the elision of the *al* vowel follows as a matter of course. Indeed, in the absence of the *ṇic*, the vowel *ā* serves its purpose through the application of the *ām* suffix (*anekācaḥ* [Bhāṣya]) and through the application of the final acute accent (*udātta*) of the root. Furthermore, in forms such as *aṅkyāt*, the prevention of the elision of the nasal (*n*) is also a result; such is the direction of the argument.

Nor should it be argued that even so, in the case of *aujaḍhat*, the vowel *i* would be heard [instead of *u*] due to the absence of reduplication, because of the statement: "That which is not established in what precedes does not apply to reduplication" (*pūrvatrāsiddhīyam advirvacane*). This is because the rule *ubhe sābhyāsasya* (Pāṇini 8.4.21) makes known the non-eternality (*anityatā*) of that [rule]. As for Bopadeva’s claim that this [non-eternality] pertains only to the domain of word-reduplication (*padadvirvacana*), that is incorrect; for it contradicts the Vārttika on the rule *suvinirdurbhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.88), namely "that which has become *sūpi* is reduplicated," along with its Bhāṣya.

For this very reason, Durgagupta and others maintain that the letter *ḍ* occurs in the reduplication. Consequently, the assumption that the reading *aujaḍhat* in the *Vaiyāghrapadyavārttika* is a mere scribal error is itself erroneous. As for the reading with the root *ji*, it is to be explained by means of the suffix *ktin*. As for the hearing of the vowel *i* in the reduplication in forms such as *mā bhavān ūninat* from the roots *paṣ* and *nad*, that too is caused by a scribal error; otherwise, the traditional reading would be found in the *sub-dhātu* section of the root *kṝta* (meaning "to sound," *cu-ādi-gaṇa*, number 120).

It should be noted that in the rule *nonayatidhvanayati* (Pāṇini 3.1.51), the *Kāśikā* and *Padamañjarī* also hold this very same view. Thus, since it is established that there is no contradiction between the *Bhāṣya* and the *Kāśikā*, it should also be understood that works such as the *Sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇa* are likewise free from objection.

As for what the author of the Nyāsa stated regarding the rule *stautiṇyorṅī* (Pāṇini 8.3.61)—namely, that in the form *siṣecayiṣati*, after the root *sic* has taken the causal suffix *ṇic*, undergone *guṇa*, and then the desiderative suffix *san* with *iṭ*, the *guṇa* and *ayādeśa* substitutions are applied; and subsequently, by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* of the *guṇa*, the word *sic* undergoes reduplication—that must be disregarded. For it contradicts the Bhāṣya because the vowel *a* is absent in the subsequent portion [of the reduplicated stem], and it is also useless, since the desired form is established even without the application of *sthānivadbhāva*.

By this, Śīradeva—who, in order to establish forms such as *aujaḍhat* and *āpīpyat*, asserts dependence on a general rule (*sāmānyāpekṣatā*), yet resorts to the doctrine of non-eternality (*anityatā*) to establish forms such as *acikīrttat*—is also refuted.
Thus ends the eighth section of the first quarter of the first chapter in the illustrious Śabdakaustubha.
Non-appearance is elision (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.60).

The word *sthāne* (in place of) is understood [from the previous rule]. And its meaning is "on occasion" (*prasaṅge*). That which is not uttered when it has become applicable (*prasakta*) shall be designated as *lopa* (elision). The applications of this designation are such as "the elision of *y* and *v* before a consonant" (*lopo vyor vali*, Pāṇini 6.1.66), and so forth. This is a designation of the *meaning* (*artha*), and not of the *word* (*śabda*), because of the force of establishing it as a "great designation" (*mahāsaṃjñā*). Now, one might object: in that case, at the very places of application (*pradeśeṣu*), the worldly meaning of "elision" (*lopa*) will be accepted, just as in the cases of "animal," "offspring," and "deity."

If it is asked, "Is that [the cause] by means of a technical name (*saṃjñā*)?"—no; for the Sūtra is commenced in order to obtain such a specific qualification as "of that which has occurred" (*prasaktasya*). Otherwise, in cases such as *dadhi* and *madhu*, there would be the undesirable consequence of the application of the augment *tuk*; for in those instances, there is the non-appearance (*adarśana*) of the suffix *kvip*, and that is termed "elision" (*lopa*), which would result in the application of the rule regarding the characteristics of a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). Now, if this were so according to the view of the Vārttika, in the view of the Bhāṣya, however, the rule concerning the characteristics of a suffix is intended as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*).

How, then, could there be the contingency of *tuk* in cases such as *dadhi*? The rule *sthānivat* does not apply with respect to *tuk*, because the mention of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is understood to carry over into that context. For this very reason, the operation of the suffix *aṇ* does not take place in forms such as *grāmaṇīḥ*.

If it is argued that, according to the manner of the Bhāṣya, this [rule] need not be stated in the Sūtra—on the grounds of the principle to be stated later, namely, "because the beginning and the end are established by common worldly usage" (*loka-siddhatvāt*)—we say: no. For in cases such as *ghaṭaṃ karoti* ("he makes a pot") and *grāme tiṣṭhati* ("he stands in the village"), there would result the undesired application of the ablative case under the rule *lyablope* (Pāṇini 2.3.28). Furthermore, in cases such as *agnim īḷe* (Ṛgveda 1.1.1), there would result the undesired prohibition of the *nighāta* accent under the rule *cādilope* (Pāṇini 8.1.63). However, when the Sūtra is indeed commenced, since the suffixes *lyap*, *pañcamī*, and so forth do not apply there either according to the technical treatise (*śāstra*) or according to common usage (*loka*), the aforementioned defects do not arise.

If it is argued that, even according to the view of the Vārttika, the rule "of that which is applicable" (*prasaktasya*) would still result in the *vṛddhi* substitution in the word *grāmaṇīḥ* because the suffix *aṇ* (prescribed by Pāṇini 3.2.1) is applicable there, we say: no. Although *aṇ* may optionally occur by the principle of *vāsarūpa* (Pāṇini 3.1.94), in the case of the suffix *kvip*, the applicability of *aṇ* is sublated by that very principle. This is because it is established by the grammatical system that when one of two optional alternatives is employed in a particular usage, the rule prescribing the other alternative loses its authority for that specific instance. [This concludes the discussion of] the elision (*luk*, *ślu*, *lup*) of a suffix (Pāṇini 1.1.61).

Because of the capacity to form multiple designations, those [suffixes] whose designations have been established here are understood by relying on *tantra* (the principle of simultaneous application), *āvṛtti* (repetition), and so forth. The non-appearance of suffixes (*pratyayādarśana*) effected by the terms *luk*, *ślu*, and *lup* shall, respectively, bear these designations. The points where these designations are applied are: "when there is *luk* of a *taddhita* suffix" (Pāṇini 1.2.49), "after roots beginning with *hu*, *ślu*" (Pāṇini 2.4.75), and "in the case of a country name, *lup*" (Pāṇini 4.2.89). Since the designation is understood as being prospective (*bhāvinī*) at the points where the rule is prescribed, there is no circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*).

Even though these technical designations (*saṃjñā*) are specifically prescribed, they do not sublate the designation *lopa* (elision). This is because, as will be stated in the *ākaḍāra* sūtra, there is no relationship of sublation between technical designations outside the governing rule (*adhikāra*) of "one designation" (*ekasaṃjñā*). Consequently, the mention of *pratyayasya* ("of the suffix") could have been omitted.

Nor should it be argued that the non-appearance (*adarśana*) prescribed by the rule *luk taddhitaluki* (Pāṇini 1.2.49) would apply to the word *go-* as well, due to the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the rule *gostriyoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.46). This is because the rule can be analyzed by dividing the connection as *gor upasarjanasya*, thereby making it possible for only the mention of *strī-* to be carried over into the rule *luk taddhitaluki*. Otherwise, even if the term *pratyaya-* were included [in the analysis], there would still be the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *ḍo-* after the root *gam-*.

Regarding the rule *kaṃsīyaparaśavyayoryaññau luk ca* (Pāṇini 4.3.168), the elision (*luk*) will not apply even to the base (*prakṛti*), because of the governing rule *ṅyāpprātipadikāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.1), which prescribes that elision occurs after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). For even if the term "affix" (*pratyaya*) were included [in the sūtra], the elision of the *u* and *s* in *kaṃsaḥ* (derived from *kam-i-s*) and *paraśuḥ* (derived from *parān śṛṇāti*) would still have to be avoided in exactly the same way. Nor can it be argued that the elision applies only to *yañ* and *añ*, for by the force of the specific formulation, there would be an optionality regarding the elision of *yañ* and *añ*.

It should be stated that the mention of *vat* is for the purpose of ensuring that the general [suffix] is not heard when one is already specified by *yañ* or *añ*; however, this is not the case because there can be no relationship between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*) for those [suffixes] perceived at the same time, such as *yañ* and its elision (*lup*). In the rule *ṭyuṭyulau tuṭ ca* (Pāṇini 4.3.23), on the other hand, the augment *tuṭ* is prescribed for *ṭyu* and *ṭyul* by relying on syntactic split (*vākya-bheda*), based on the indicators (*jñāpaka*) found in *ghakālakaneṣu* (Pāṇini 6.3.17) and *anadyatane laṅ* (Pāṇini 3.2.111).
Therefore, the mention of "affix" (*pratyaya*) need not be made merely for the sake of excluding non-affixes.

Nor is it for the purpose of specifying a particular locus (*sthānin*). For instance, in the rule *atribhṛgukutsa* (Pāṇini 2.4.65), the term "in the sense of a lineage" (*gotre*) is understood to carry over from the preceding rule *yaskādibhyo gotre* (Pāṇini 2.4.63). Consequently, the elision (*luk*) of that which is prescribed after Atri and the others is already established.

In the rule *janapade lup* (Pāṇini 4.2.81), because the terms *ṅyāpprātipadikāt* (4.1.1) and *pratyayaḥ* (3.1.1) are understood to carry over, there is elision (*lup*) of the *cāturarthika* suffix prescribed for a *janapada*. However, in the rule *lavaṇālluk* (4.4.24), because *ṭhak* is the suffix under discussion, it is that very suffix which undergoes elision (*luk*). In all these cases, the word "suffix" (*pratyaya*) is construed with a genitive case, according to the rule *tasmādityuttarasya* (1.1.67).

It might be argued as follows: the mention of "affix" (*pratyaya*) is for the purpose of ensuring that the operation applies to the whole [of the element]. Consequently, in rules such as *yañañośca* (Pā. 2.4.64) and *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* (Pā. 2.4.71), where the affix consists of more than one phoneme (*anekāl*), the rule *alo'ntyasya* (Pā. 1.1.52)—which would otherwise apply to the final phoneme—does not take effect. Likewise, in cases such as *lavaṇālluk* (Pā. 4.4.24), the rule *ādeḥ parasya* (Pā. 1.1.54)—which would otherwise apply to the initial phoneme of the subsequent element—does not take effect.

Not so; for the status of being a total substitute (*sarvādeśatva*) is established by the very fact of this being an indicator (*jñāpaka*). For when the elision (*lopa*) [of *ghu*] is already under consideration by the rule *ghorlopo leṭi vā* (Pāṇini 7.2.7), the mention of *luk* in *lugvā duha* (Pāṇini 7.3.73) indicates that *luk* and the other elisions are total substitutes. Indeed, the non-appearance (*adarśana*) of the final letter would already be accomplished by the elision (*lopa*) under discussion. Nor does there arise the contingency of the opposite view, because the paribhāṣā regarding the final letter (*alontyaparibhāṣā*) applies first to the elision (*lopa*), since it is not yet contradicted. Thus, it is established that the indicator pertains generally to the domain of *lup*, and not exclusively to the domain of *luṅ*; everything is therefore settled.

This might be the case: in the rule *āgastyakauṇḍinyayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.70), does the term *luk* carry over from the previous rule *lugaṇiñoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.58) or not? If it does, there would be two substituends (*sthānin*) but three substitutes (*ādeśa*), including *luk*; thus, due to this discrepancy, the correspondence between elements (*yathāsaṅkhya*) would not apply, and consequently, all three substitutes would apply to each of the two substituends in turn. As a result, those who are Agastis would also be Kuṇḍinas, and those who are Kuṇḍinas would also be Agastis.

If [the suffix] *luk* were applied, then because of the *jñāpaka*, it would be a replacement for the whole (*sarvādeśa*), and thus in both cases only the case-ending (*vibhakti*) would be heard. Or, if it were applied, then by virtue of the *jñāpaka*, it would be a replacement for the whole, and in both instances only the case-ending would be audible. Alternatively, if it is removed, then there is no fault whatsoever in forms such as *agastayaḥ* and *kuṇḍināḥ*.

However, in the case of *āgastīyāḥ*—the students of the Agastis—the substitution of *agasti-* would not be barred even when a suffix beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi*) belonging to the *prāgdīvyatīya* group is intended; consequently, because the [original stem] would remain un-elided and thus not be "non-vṛddha" (*avṛddha*), the suffix *cha* would not apply. But when the term "suffix" (*pratyaya*) is included [in the rule], by the continued application of the mention of elision (*luk*), the portion consisting of the suffix of both *āgastya-* and *kauṇḍinya-* is elided, while the remaining portions become respectively *agasti-* and *kuṇḍina-*. By this means, the forms *agastayaḥ* and *kuṇḍināḥ* are established.

However, when a *prādīvyatīya* suffix is intended, the elision (*luk*) prescribed by the rule *gotre lug aci* (Pāṇini 4.1.89) is prohibited; consequently, because it is taught in grammatical connection with that elision, the substitution of *agasti-* also ceases. Thus, from the word *āgastya*, when the suffix *cha* (denoting descent from a *vṛddha* ancestor) is applied and the *yalopa* is effected by the rule *sūryatiṣya...* (Pāṇini 6.4.149), the form *āgastīyāḥ* is established. In the case of *kauṇḍinya*, however, there is no difference.

Even when the substitution [of *kuṇḍina*] for *kuṇḍinaja* has ceased, if the suffix *aṇ* is applied to the word *kauṇḍinya* by the rule "from *kaṇva* and others, in the sense of a lineage" (*Pāṇini* 4.2.111), the elision of *ya* by the rule "of the descendant" (*apatya*) (*Pāṇini* 6.4.151) would result in the form *kauṇḍināḥ* alone. Therefore, the mention of *luk* ("elision") must necessarily be carried over to the rule "of *āgastya* and *kauṇḍinya*" (*Pāṇini* 2.4.70). Consequently, in this case, the mention of the suffix (*pratyaya-grahaṇa*) must also certainly be made.

This is not so; for even by interpreting the rule *āgastyakauṇḍinyayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.70) as meaning "there is elision (*luk*) of that [suffix] which is prescribed in reference to a *gotra*," by carrying over the term *gotra* from the preceding rule *yaskādibhyo gotre* (Pāṇini 2.4.63), the desired result is established. Therefore, it remains settled that the mention of the suffix (*pratyaya-grahaṇa*) need not be made here.

It might be argued: "If this were so, then the technical term *lopa* (elision) would have the same scope (*tulyavyaktikatva*) as the terms *luk* and the others. If you say that the name applies to that which is brought about by those rules, then because there is no distinction, the same would apply to *lopa* as well. It is replied: Because it has not yet encountered any contradiction, the name *lopa* applies first to mere non-appearance (*adarśanamātra*). It is further stated: Since the name *lopa* has not yet encountered any contradiction, it applies first to mere non-appearance. Regarding the names *luk* and the others, because of the capacity of formulating multiple technical terms, there is the inclusion of that which is brought about by those specific rules.

It has been stated that there is no confusion of grammatical designations (*saṃjñā*) due to this [restriction]. However, if such confusion were to occur, then in the case of *hanti* where the suffix *śap* is elided, doubling (*dvitva*) would apply by Pāṇini 6.1.10 (*ślau*). Furthermore, in the case of *juhoti*, since the suffix *ślu* is present, the rule Pāṇini 7.3.89 (*uto vṛddhirluki hali*) would require the substitution of a *vṛddhi* vowel for the *u*. Nor should it be argued that the *vṛddhi* will not occur there because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the prohibition "not for a reduplicated stem" (*abhyastasya na*), as in the cases of *yoyoti* or *nonoti*; for under the view that there is a confusion of designations, the continued application of that [prohibition] is impossible.

Otherwise, the Sūtra would be rendered devoid of scope; there would be no room for forms such as *yauti* or *auti*, because even in those cases, the doubling [of the consonant] would be unavoidable due to the confusion of technical designations (*saṃjñā-saṅkara*). It has already been stated that the designation *lopa* (elision) is more extensive than the designations *luk* and so forth. Consequently, the rule regarding the presence of the suffix (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*) is established in cases such as *pañca*; this is the general direction of the argument.

According to the Bhāṣya view, although forms such as *pañca* are established by the rule *sthānivad ādeśaḥ*, nevertheless, in order to prevent the acute accent on the first syllable of the second member (*uttarapada*) and the lengthening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-dīrgha*) in *sudṛṣad brāhmaṇaḥ*—according to the method to be explained later—it must necessarily be maintained that the restriction "only when there is elision (*lopa*) does the *pratyaya-lakṣaṇa* apply" holds true. Consequently, it should be noted that in that case, even the designation (*saṃjñā*) of "suffix" (*pratyaya*) for the *luk*-elision must be taken into account.
*pratyayalope pratyayalakṣaṇam* (Pāṇini 1.1.62).

Even when a suffix (*pratyaya*) has been elided, the grammatical operation dependent upon it should still take place. This is the view of the *Vārttika* author, who states that "this [rule] is for the sake of operations concerning vowels (*alvidhi*). To illustrate: in the form *atṛṇeṭ*, once the *tip* suffix has been elided by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt...* (Pāṇini 6.1.68), the augment *im*—which is prescribed by the rule *tṛṇaha im* (Pāṇini 7.3.92) as conditioned by a following *sārvadhātuka* suffix beginning with a consonant—is applied due to this statement. It cannot, however, be established by the rule *sthānivad ādeśaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.56), because that rule does not apply to operations concerning vowels (*alvidhi*).

If it is argued that, in this case, the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule would also not apply because of the prohibition stating, "there is no *pratyayalakṣaṇa* when [the operation] depends on a phoneme" (*Pāṇini 1.1.56*), we say: no, for there is no such statement; rather, let it simply be "when a suffix is elided, the operation of that suffix [occurs]" (*pratyayalope tallakṣaṇam*) as stated in the present sūtra. Or, let even "the operation of that suffix" (*tallakṣaṇam*) not be mentioned at all, since the desired result is established by the continued application of the term *sthānivadbhāva* alone. This being the case, the purpose of stating "*pratyayalakṣaṇam*" is recited as follows.

Furthermore, by the force of the repetition of the term *pratyaya* (suffix), it is understood that only that which constitutes the unique form (*asādhāraṇa-rūpa*) of a suffix with respect to a grammatical operation—such as being a *sup* or a *tiṅ*—is to be taken as the cause. Consequently, in the example "go-hitam" (beneficial for a cow), the substitution of *ava* does not occur; for the rule prescribing that substitution depends solely on the property of being a vowel (*actva*), and that property is common to both suffixes and non-suffixes. Alternatively, in this case, there is a prohibition based on the rule "not when there is elision" (*na lupatā*, Pāṇini 1.1.63).

In that case, in the word *suyaśāḥ*, the rule *visarjanīyasya saḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.34) would apply; and in *suvṛṭ* and similar forms, the substitution of *c* for *ṣ* (*cartvam*) would apply by the rule *khari ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.54). This is the general direction [of the argument].

In the *Imāgama* rule, however, the suffix itself is primarily relied upon in the phrase "before all suffixes beginning with a consonant" (*sarvadhātuke*); thus there is a disparity. Therefore, the distinction is this: when the phoneme is primary, the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the treatment as if a suffix were present) does not apply, but when the suffix is primary, it does apply. By this very logic, in the rule *na dhātulope* (Pāṇini 1.1.4), although the term *dhātulopa* is established as a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the status of being a cause [for the application of the rule] is obtained through the force of the mention of *ārddhadhātuka*, which implies its nature as such.

Therefore, by the rule *dhinvikṛṇvyorvici* and the subsequent rule *lopo vyoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.66), although there is elision of the *v* and *y*, this elision is caused by the presence of a *val* sound; since the suffix *vic* is not itself a cause for that [elision] because it is an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, the *guṇa* substitution indeed occurs. Consequently, forms such as *sudhe*, *sudhenau*, *sudhenaḥ*; *sukaḥ*, *sukarṇau*, *sukarṇaḥ*—and so on with *ka* and other suffixes—are established. And they recite: "O Rāma, he who here speaks of two adjectives for the Primordial Creator (*Ādikartṛ*)—namely *sudhe* [as in] 'for the sake of the gods' due to the slaughter of enemies, and *sukaḥ* [as in] 'due to ease'—is indeed a follower of Kaiyaṭa."

Nor should it be argued that the mention of *ārddhadhātuka* is meaningful because it excludes forms such as *totorti*, and therefore how can there be any *sāmarthya* (functional significance)? This is because the *yaṅluk* (elision of the *yaṅ* suffix) is Vedic (*chāndasa*). However, in the view that it pertains to the spoken language (*bhāṣā*), the mention of *ārddhadhātuka* must be repeated to establish its *sāmarthya*. If it is objected: "But this contradicts the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *ṅkiti ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.5), for it is stated therein that the mention of *ārddhadhātuka* in the preceding rule is without scope (*anavakāśa*)," we reply: No, for they say that it was stated in that manner merely as a non-literal expression (*anāsthayā*).
One should consider whether it might not simply be the case that, by virtue of that support, only *j* is intended here.

However, when the suffix *kvip* is applied, *ūṭh* occurs; thus one obtains forms such as *dhinūḥ*, *dhinvau*, *dhinvaḥ*, *kṛṇūḥ*, *kṛṇvau*, and *kṛṇvaḥ*. They say, however, that forms such as *sudhī*, *sudhinau*, *sudhinaḥ*, *sukīḥ*, *sukṛṇau*, and *sukṛṇaḥ* certainly do not occur.

It should also be considered whether, since the optionality of the elision (*yaṅ-luk*) pertains to the domain of speech (*bhāṣā-viṣayatva*), the mention of *ārddhadhātuka* [in Pāṇini 7.3.84] finds its utility in forms such as *totorti*; and since there is no evidence for a repetition [of that rule], let the prohibition of *guṇa* apply so that we have *sudhī* and *sudhinau*. Let there be lengthening for the root *kṛṇoti*, resulting in *sukīḥ*, *sukīrṇau*, *sukīrṇaḥ*, and so forth.

[Objection: But in this way, in the case of *parivīḥ*, both the *tuṅ* (the augment *t*) and the long vowel (*dīrgha*) would apply alternatively; for since both are prescribed by this very rule, there is no sequence of priority, and thus the principle *vipratiṣedhe paraṃ kāryam* (Pāṇini 1.4.2) does not apply. [Response: True; however, there is no fault because one may resort to the extension of the rule (*śāstrātideśa*) or the extension of the designation (*vyapadeśātideśa*). Alternatively, even in the case of the extension of the operation (*kāryātideśa*), there is no fault, because only that operation which is capable of occurring when the suffix is present is extended. Thus, as in *parivīya* and so on, in *parivīḥ* as well, only the long vowel occurs and not the *tuṅ*. Therefore, there is no defect.

The authors of the Bhāṣya, however, say: This sūtra is not for the sake of [the forms] *tṛṇahaim* and *tṛṇahāni*, because its purpose is already served by the rule *sthānivat*. Nor is this a rule concerning vowel-substitution (*alvidhi*), because the condition *halī* (before a consonant) is removed [from the context]. And one should not object that, if this were so, the augment *im* would also apply in *tṛṇahāni*; for [the word] "not" (*na*) is understood from the rule *nābhyastasyāci* (Pāṇini 7.3.87), which prohibits [the augment] before a vowel (*aci*). Nor is this [sūtra] intended for the purpose of the *it* augment in *āśīḥ* by means of the rule *sāsa-ha-kāśibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 6.4.34); for this is already established by the specific extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) of the suffix *kvip* after the root *āsas*.

Indeed, this must also be stated by you: in the rule *śāsa idaṅhaloḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.34), if one holds the view that there is a reference to the root *śās* in general, then [the mention of *kvā*] is for the sake of restriction—so that [the substitution of *ī*] occurs only after *śās* followed by *kvā*, as in *āśāste*, and not in cases such as *āśāste*. However, if one holds the view that because the augment *aṅ* is prescribed for *śās*, only that [root] is included in the rule prescribing the substitution of *ī* due to its association with *aṅ*, then just as [the substitution] does not occur in *āśāste* and so on, it would likewise not occur after *kvip*. Therefore, [the mention of *kvā*] is for the sake of a positive injunction (*vidhyartha*).

Therefore, this sūtra is for the purpose of restriction, stating that when a suffix is elided, only that which is characterized by the suffix [occurs]. Its result is the cessation of any operation that would have been prescribed based on a form common to both a suffix and a non-suffix. Consequently, in the example *sudṛśaḥ*—meaning "this palace has beautiful stones"—the rule *sormanasī alomoṣasī* (Pāṇini 6.2.117), which prescribes an initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) for a final member ending in *man* or *as* following the word *su* within a *bahuvrīhi* compound, does not apply.

For here, even though the *jas* suffix has been elided, the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) still exists by virtue of the *sthānivadbhāva* rule. However, the form *as-* is common to both suffixes and non-suffixes, because it will be stated later that "the mention of *an*, *in*, *man*, and *as* applies the rule of *tadantavidhi* [to what ends with them] whether they are meaningful or meaningless. Consequently, the exclusion of the initial acute accent (*ādyudātta*) is established as a rule; thus, by the rule *nañsubhyām* (Pāṇini 6.2.172), the word becomes oxytone (*antodātta*).

This, however, should be noted: this sūtra is not intended solely for the sake of accentuation; rather, even the lengthening of the penultimate vowel by the rule *atvasantasya ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.14), which would otherwise apply in the very examples cited, must be excluded by the aforementioned restriction. According to the view of the Vārttika, however, another means must be sought to achieve both the desired accentuation and the exclusion of the lengthening.

Now, if the sūtra is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), then how is the commentary (*vṛtti*) on the word "five" (*pañca*) to be construed, which states that "there is the status of being a word (*padatva*) by virtue of the definition of a suffix"? Likewise, how are those authoritative works of the masters to be construed here and there—such as [the statements] that "there is the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadikatva*) because it is a compound," "the augment *iṭ* [is applied] by the rule *snukramoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.36)," and "the genitive case is used for the object when both [agent and object] are applicable" (Pāṇini 2.3.66)? To this it is said: that which is our restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*)...

According to the Mīmāṃsā method, this is first of all clearly established in the *Vivaraṇa* and other works as an *aparisaṅkhyā-vidhi* (a restrictive injunction). In that regard, there are three defects: the abandonment of its own primary meaning (*svārthahāni*), the assumption of a foreign meaning (*parārthaparikalpanā*), and the sublation of what is already established (*prāptabādha*). If one accepts these on the grounds that there is no other way (*agatyā*), then the actual meaning of the restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) is simply a prohibition (*niṣedha*). By the word "pratyayalakṣaṇa," that which is different from it is indicated; and by the word "bhavati" (it occurs), "it does not occur" is meant.

And thus, in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.50), it is stated: "By this [rule], the most similar [substitutes] are not excluded; rather, those that are not the most similar are excluded. For this very reason, the author of the *Vārttika* will also say: "When both [agent and object] are applicable, the prohibition [of the agent's designation as *kartṛ*] applies to the object; however, there is no prohibition when *aka* and so forth are employed" (*Kāśikāvṛtti*). According to this view, the genitive case in the rule *ubhayaprāptau* (Pāṇini 2.3.66) should be explained as being "remaining" (*pariśiṣṭā*), and not as being "prescribed" (*vihitā*).

If, however, in order to avoid the burden of the three defects, one explains the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* sūtra according to its literal meaning and—on the basis of this very indicator (*jñāpaka*)—postulates that the *sthānivat* sūtra pertains to cases other than the elision of an affix (*pratyayalopa*), then you too must indeed postulate a specific intention for a rule that functions by means of a general heading; otherwise, there would be the contingency of an option (*vikalpa*), as in the Bhaṭṭa school’s view regarding the statement, "One does not perform those two [rites] at the animal sacrifice" (*na tau paśau karoti*).

Furthermore, because a general rule can be restricted by a specific rule—just as the injunction regarding the *āhavanīya* fire [restricts] the rule "one offers in the foot" (*pade juhoti*)—it does not follow that this would result in the subsumption (*upasaṃhāra*) of the general into the particular. For if that were the case, the composition of the general scripture would become purposeless. However, since there is no author of the Veda who could be thus questioned, the subsumption of the fourfold division (*caturdhākaraṇa*) into the *Āgneya* sacrifice is accepted in the Mīmāṃsā. But the authors of the Kalpasūtras, on the other hand, are quite free in this regard even here.

And thus it has been stated by the venerable Kātyāyana: "Or both, because there is no distinction" (*Kāśikāvṛtti*). In this way, since both [the primary and secondary meanings] are denotable by the general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*) when a specific definition (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇā*) is present, and since the matter is established in that manner, the position that the three defects need not be tolerated is indeed correct according to the cited texts. However, in the Nyāya school, it is beyond dispute that there is no secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) at all in cases where the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is restricted; for they accept that [secondary signification] only when the objective is a cognition whose qualifier is a property subordinate to another property (*viśeṣa-dharma-prakāraka-bodha*).

The wise should understand that even a case where a general property is the qualifier and a particular is the qualificand can be accounted for without resorting to *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication).
This is according to the rule *na lumatāṅgasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.63).

In the word *lumatā*, when an affix is elided by means of the term *lumat* (indicating elision), the operation of the stem (*aṅga*) conditioned by that affix would not take place. According to the view of the Vārttika, this is a prohibition of what was obtained by the preceding rule; however, according to the view of the Bhāṣya, it is a prohibition of what was obtained by the *sthānivat* rule. As for the principle that restrictive rules (*niyamavidhi*) merely serve to restrict the scope of the intended meaning rather than to prohibit, one should state—following the method previously mentioned—that even in the view of the Bhāṣya, this is a prohibition of what was obtained by the *iyaṅ* [substitution] through the preceding rule. The same applies hereafter as well.

In the examples *gargāḥ*, *mṛṣṭa*, and *juhutaḥ*, because the *yaṅ* and *śap* suffixes are elided by *lumat* (Pāṇini 1.1.63), the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutions do not occur for the base (*aṅga*). Why [is it said] "by *lumat*"? Consider *kāryate* and *hāryate*: when the *ṇiC* is elided by the rule *ṇeraniṭi* (Pāṇini 6.4.51), the *vṛddhi* substitution still occurs with respect to the *ṇiC*. In *amārṭ*, even though the *il* (the *ṛ*) and the following *yaṅ* are elided, the *vṛddhi* still takes place because it is obligatory (*nitya*). Why [is it said] "of the base" (*aṅgasya*)? In the cases of *pañca* and *sapta*, the term "base" is intended to be accented (*svaryate*).

The authors of the Vārttikas maintain that by this [sūtra], "governance" (*adhikāra*) is understood, based on the statement: "Governance [is indicated] by the *svarita* accent" (Pāṇini 1.3.11). However, this is refuted in the Bhāṣya. For if that were the case, in the word *utkrāma*, once the substitution of *luK* for *hi* is made according to "the substitution of *luK* for *hi* after a short vowel" (Pāṇini 6.4.105), the lengthening [of the penultimate vowel] prescribed by "lengthening of the root vowel in *kram-* before Parasmaipada endings" (Pāṇini 7.3.76) would not occur. Similarly, in *jigamiṣa*, the augment *iṭ* prescribed by "the augment *iṭ* follows *gam-* before Parasmaipada endings" (Pāṇini 7.2.58) would not occur.

Likewise, in the case of *vivṛtsa*, the prohibition of *iṭ* by Pāṇini 7.2.59 (*na vṛdbhyaś caturbhyaḥ*) would not apply. Therefore, in the rule *na lumatā* (Pāṇini 1.1.63), the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "stem" (*aṅga*) is not being referred back; rather, when an affix is elided by *lumat*, everything—whether it is a stem (*aṅga*) or not a stem (*an-aṅga*)—is prohibited. Nor should it be argued that the aforementioned defect remains as it was, because in the word *utkrama*, the *parasmaipada* affix has been elided.

With respect to that [suffix], the rule for lengthening is not prescribed for that *aṅga* which ends in a *śap* suffix, but rather for the root *kram*. However, since that [root] is not an *aṅga* with respect to the *śap* suffix—because the prohibition does not apply when [the suffix] is elided—the lengthening occurs by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the treatment of what remains as if the suffix were present). Similarly, in forms such as *jigamiṣa* and *vivṛtsa*, the rules for the insertion (*vidhi*) and prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) of *iṭ* indeed take effect. For those two [rules] do not apply to that *aṅga* ending in a desiderative (*sannanta*) when the Parasmaipada suffix is elided by *lumat*; rather, they apply to the suffix beginning with *s*. And it is clear that this [desiderative stem] is not an *aṅga*.

It might be argued as follows: In both positions, the acute accents (*udātta*) prescribed by the three sūtras—"*ñ-nityādir nityam*" (Pāṇini 6.1.197), "*kitaḥ*" (Pāṇini 6.1.165), and "*pathimathoḥ sarvanāmasthāne*" (Pāṇini 6.1.119)—would still apply even when elision (*luk*) has taken place. For example: *gargāḥ*, *bidāḥ* (where there is elision of *yañ* and *añ*), and *uṣṭragrīvāḥ* (where there is elision of *kan* by the rule "*ive pratikṛtau*" [Pāṇini 5.3.96], and subsequent elision of that *kan* by the rule "*devapathādibhyaś ca*" [Pāṇini 5.3.100]).

Consequently, by the rule *ñ-nityādiḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.197), the initial udātta accent would apply. Then, from *atri*, the derivative *atrīṇām apatyāni* ("the descendants of Atri") yields *atrayaḥ*. Here, the suffix *ḍhak* [which normally gives *āyani*] is elided by the rule *atribhṛgukutsavasiṣṭhagotamāṅgirobhyaśca* (Pāṇini 2.4.65). Subsequently, by the rule *kitastaddhitasyānta udātto bhavati* ("the final syllable of a taddhita suffix ending in *k* is udātta"), the final udātta accent would apply; for that [rule] prescribes the accent for the entire form ending in the taddhita suffix, since the mention of the suffix includes the mention of what ends in it.

It should not be argued that even according to our own established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the word must necessarily be oxytone by virtue of the *phiṭ-svara* accent; for, by the *uṇādi*-sūtra "from *rāśi* and others, *trip*" (*uṇādi-sūtra* 516) and "from *ad*, *trin* and *tri*" (*uṇādi-sūtra* 517), the suffix *trip* is applied to the root *ad*—the *c* of which is drawn over from the previous rule—and since this suffix is marked with *p* (indicating it is *anudātta*), the word *atri* is *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable). Thus, it is employed in usage as in: "Listen to the ancient praise of Atri," and "Hear the deeds of Atri as he performs them."

Similarly, even when the *ḍhak* suffix is elided (*luk*), that which begins with an acute accent (*ādyudātta*) is employed, as in "atrīṇāṃ somam adrivaḥ" and "atrīṇāṃ śṛṇutaṃ havam. However, that which ends in the *triṇ* suffix is oxytone (*antodātta*) and ends in *n*; this is another matter. That too is employed, as in "dūre vā ye anti vā ke cid atrinaḥ. Likewise, in "pathipriyaḥ," meaning "one for whom the path is dear," the rule "supo dhātu... (Pāṇini 6.1.119) would result in the initial syllable being acute.

For this triple rule (*trisūtrī*) does not reside within the domain of *aṅga* (the stem), such that the prohibition "not when [an affix] marked with *lu* follows" (*na lumatā*, Pāṇini 1.1.63) would apply. Nor does it apply because, in reality, these are operations pertaining to what is not an *aṅga*. If it is argued: "Let it be so for the rule *kitaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.165); however, as for the other two rules—*ñniti* and *sarvanāmasthāne*—since they are indicated by locative case endings (*saptamī*), they are indeed operations of the *aṅga* in reality," we say no. This is because, according to the sequence beginning with "of that which ends in *ñ* or *ṇ*, at the beginning," those rules are prescribed specifically for the end of an affix; for the established doctrine is that "locatives referring to vowels are locatives referring to that which ends in them."

And this is made known by the mention of the word "prior" (*pūrva*) in the rule *bhīhībhṛhūmadajanadhanadaridrājāgarāṃ pratyayātpūrvaṃ piti* (Pāṇini 6.1.193), as stated in the Bhāṣya on that very sūtra. For this very reason, the rule *upottamaṃ riti* (Pāṇini 6.1.218) applies to a form ending in *caṅ*.

Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, the rule *caturaśśasi* (Pāṇini 6.1.167) would cause the udātta accent to fall on the suffix *śas*, and consequently, in such passages as *ṣaṭtriṃśāṃśca caturaḥ kalpayantaḥ*, the word *caturaḥ*—which is intended to be middle-accented (*madhyodātta*)—would not be established. For in that case, by the force of the inclusion of the term *śas*, the locative interpretation [of the genitive] in *caturaḥ* is set aside; otherwise, he would have simply said *ūḍidampadādyapumraidyucaturbhyaḥ*.

In that case, because the mention of *sarvanāmasthāna* continues [from the previous rule], the suffix will be only *śas*; for even according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), an acute accent is prescribed for a suffix beginning with a consonant by the rule *ṣaṭtricaturbhyo halādiḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.179). Nor should it be argued that, in rules concerning accents, the genitive case alone should be employed; for in view of rules such as *ritaścaṅi*, the use of the locative case in *riti caṅi* is justified by the possibility of achieving a saving of half a *mātrā*.

To this it is replied: First, regarding the position that the mention [of the suffix] refers to its status as a *aṅga* (stem), the *Vārttika* is commenced in order to avoid the aforementioned defects: "When there is elision by *lumat*, a prohibition must be stated; furthermore, an addition must be made for the accent of a single word (*ekapadasvara*). [The additions are: "Excluding the accent of *sarvanāman*, *āmantrita*, and the elision of *sij*," and "The purpose is for the accents of *ñini*, *kil*, and *lak*, and for the rule 'in the case of the elision of the *sarvanāmasthāna* [suffixes] after *pathin* and *mathin*.'"

The meaning of this is as follows: when *lu* is indicated by the technical designation *lumat*, regarding that prohibition [of an operation], there must be an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) concerning the accent (*svara*) which depends on a single word (*ekapada*). The sense is that even though it would have been applicable by virtue of the rule for "characteristics based on suffixes" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), the accent of a single word does not take place. However, an accent depending on two words (*padadvaya*) would certainly occur; for example, in the case of *dadhitiṣṭhati*, the *nighāta* (suppression of accent) prescribed by *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.28)—which is formulated under the governing rules *padasya* (8.1.16) and *padāt* (8.1.17).

For here, in the case of *dadhī*, the definition of an affix (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*) is required for the sake of its designation as a word (*pada-saṃjñā*); likewise, in cases such as *iha tiṣṭha*, it is also required to obtain the status of being a finite verb (*tiṅanta*). But if this were so, then in the case of *sarvastomo 'tirātraḥ*, the acute accent on the first syllable prescribed by Pāṇini 6.1.191 (*sarvasya supi*) would not occur. Similarly, in *sarpir āgaccha* and *sarpis gacchata*, the acute accent on the first syllable of the vocative prescribed by Pāṇini 6.1.198 (*āmantritasya ca*) would not occur.

Likewise, in the case of *mā hi dātām* and *mā hi dhātām*, the rule *ādiḥ sico 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 6.1.187) would not apply to produce an udātta accent on the initial syllable; therefore, he says "sarva" and so forth. The meaning is that this prohibition applies to other accents, excluding these three specific accents.

Nor should it be argued that in the case of *sarvastomaḥ*, this is the accent of two words based on Pāṇini 6.2.1 (*bahuvrīhau prakṛtyā pūrvapadam*), because by Pāṇini 6.1.191 (*sarvasya supi*), the initial udātta-accent of *sarva-* must necessarily be established first, and this [rule 6.2.1] merely effects its preservation as the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). Thus, the occurrence of that [initial accent] must first be accounted for.

Furthermore, the initial udātta accent of the word *sarpiḥ* cannot be obtained even without the vocative accent, because when the Uṇādi suffix *isi* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.173 (*arci-śuci-hu-sṛpi-chādi-chardi-bhyaḥ*), the word becomes antodātta. This remains the case even in the view that the word is not etymologically derived (*avyutpatti-pakṣa*), as its accent would be determined by the Phiṭ-sūtras. Nor can the initial udātta be established by Pāṇini 6.1.197 (*na-viṣayasya kan*), because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) contained in the rule 6.1.198 (*anisantasya*). However, Kaiyaṭa’s assumption that the word *sarpiḥ* belongs to the *ghṛtādi* group [of the Phiṭ-sūtras] for this purpose is open to question.

Objection: Is it not the case that the word *sapta* is derived from the root *sapa-* with the suffix *kanin* by the rule *sapyaśūbhyāṃ tuṭ ca* (Pāṇini 5.2.163)? Thus, because it has the marker *ni*, it is udātta on its first syllable; and even in the view that words are not derivationally formed (*avyutpattipakṣa*), it is the same, according to the statement *nraḥ saṃkhyāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.175). Response: No, for in either case, it is udātta on its final syllable due to belonging to the *ghṛtādi* group. And so it is used in the Vedic passage: *saptá yuñjanti rátham ekacakram*. In this context, let there be no mention of the elision of the *sic* suffix.

In the rule *gāti-sthā* (Pāṇini 2.4.77), the accent is established for the case of elision (*luk*) by virtue of the inclusion of the term *sic*. Otherwise, for the sake of brevity, he would have prescribed the elision of *cli* alone. For in that way, the laborious effort of inserting an additional *s* in the rule *astisico 'pṛkte* (Pāṇini 8.3.96) to ensure the correctness of forms such as *abhūt* and *apāt* would not need to be resorted to.

One should not argue that, if *cl* were elided in this manner, the rule *ātaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.110) would become purely prescriptive (*vidhyartha*) rather than restrictive (*niyamārtha*), and consequently, one would have to state "when *cl* is elided" (*cliluki*) in order to exclude the *laṅ* [tense] there, resulting in the fault of an inverted complexity (*viparītagaurava*). This is because the *laṭ* [tense] is already excluded by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *ṅitaḥ*. Therefore, the phrase "with the exception of all vocative accents" (*sarvāmantritasvaravarjam*) is indeed necessary. He states the purpose for the composition of the Vārttika: "The purpose... (*prayojanam iti*).

The vowel *i* in the words *ni* and *niś* is for the sake of pronunciation, just as in the rule *suṭ tithoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.107). The meaning is that these vowels serve as the purpose (*prayojana*) by virtue of being subject to elision. He states another purpose with the words "of *pathin* and *mathin*. Thus, it is established in this sūtra that the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the three sūtras must be removed by the force of the specific statement.

In reality, this statement should not be made for this purpose, because [the desired forms] such as *bidāḥ* and *gargāḥ* are established by the force of the *jñāpaka* alone. Accordingly, there is a *vārttika* on the rule *saṃjñāyām upamānam* (Pāṇini 6.1.204): "The prescription that the first member of a comparison (*upamāna*) is acute-accented is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the prohibition of the application of affixal accentual rules (*pratyayalakṣaṇa-pratiṣedha*) applies to accents characterized by phonetic markers (*anubandha-lakṣaṇa*)."

And on this view, the rule "there is no *pratyayalakṣaṇa* when a suffix is elided by *lumat*" must indeed be formulated for the forms *pathin* and *maghavan* in the *sarvanāmasthāna* case endings. For this accent is not one caused by an *anubandha*, such that it could be prevented by the force of the aforementioned *jñāpaka*. Nor can it be argued that the *jñāpaka* pertains only to the domain of accents, because that would result in the failure of the *āmantrita* accent and the accent resulting from the elision (*luk*) of *sij*.

Nor should it be argued that even so, this [Pāṇinian rule] teaches that the designation of an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) does not apply to a vowel specified in the locative case; for if that were the case, the initial udātta accent in the word *sarvasya* in the rule *sarvasyomaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.50) would fail to be established. Alternatively, let this be a teaching (*jñāpaka*) specifically regarding vowels specified in the locative case. One should read *supaḥ* as a genitive case, having removed the locative *supi* from the rule *sarvasya supi* (Pāṇini 6.1.191).

Therefore, the statement for the sake of the *pathi-svara* need not be commenced; however, for the sake of the *nit-kitsvara*, it need not be commenced under either alternative. Thus, everything is well-established. Both of these positions were clearly stated by the authors of the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *saṃjñāyām upamānam* (Pāṇini 6.1.204). This is the final conclusion: having first offered a superficial solution by means of a formal rule (*vacana*) to remove the defect of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) suspected regarding the three sūtras, the ultimate resolution was later established through an interpretative indicator (*jñāpaka*) alone.

And this resolution—that the topic of the auxiliaries (*aṅga*) is being indicated—is equal even in the "extracted" (*niṣkṛṣṭa*) view, which holds that [the term *aṅga*] refers to what is the effect of the auxiliary in reality, as it does in the "position" (*pakṣa*) view. For this very reason, in the rule *saṃjñāyām upamānam* (Pāṇini 6.1.204), the authors of the Bhāṣya have applied the explanatory *vārttika* regarding this indication in a manner common to both views. However, in the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa on the present sūtra, it is understood that in the extracted view, the aforementioned objection simply does not arise.

In this regard, the learned describe the underlying intention as follows: an indicator (*jñāpaka*) is of two kinds—dependent on a general rule and dependent on a specific rule. In that context, regarding the rule *bhīhrī* (Pāṇini 6.1.192), if the term *pūrva* were absent and the suffix-ending elements were subject to the grammatical operation, then by the maxim *alo’ntyaparibhāṣā*, the accent would fall specifically on the final letter of the suffixes *bhi* and so forth. However, if one relies on the locative sense [of the rule], the accent would fall on *bhi* and so forth themselves, setting aside the *pit* marker; thus, there is a clear difference in result.

The same applies to the rules "upottamaṃ ritaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.217) and "cahyanyatarasyām" (Pāṇini 6.1.218). However, there is no difference in result in cases such as "ñnityādirnityam" (Pāṇini 6.1.197) and "pathimathoḥ sarvanāmasthāne" (Pāṇini 6.1.199), because when that which ends in [the suffix] is the subject of the operation, the acute accent falls on the very beginning of the base (*prakṛti*), and likewise when even that which is preceded by *ñ*, *ṇ*, etc., is the subject of the operation.

And thus, since the term *sauvarya* does not apply there, the aforementioned defect does not arise at all, because [the substitute] is not subject to the operation of being "that which ends in" (*tadanta*). As for the passages in the *Bhāṣya*, *Kaiyaṭa*, and other works regarding *Pāṇini-sūtra* 6.1.204, *saṃjñāyām upamānam*, they are to be interpreted by relying on a *jñāpaka* that is general in scope. However, in the case of *atraya*, it is neither itself nor something else; for once the *luk* elision has taken place, the element undergoing the operation (*kāryin*) no longer exists.

For that which has the nature of a suffixal operation (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*) occurs even when that suffix is elided, but not that which is an operation belonging to the suffix itself. Nor should it be argued that the inclusion of the stem ending in that suffix (*tadantagrahaṇa*) would occur by means of the paribhāṣā regarding the mention of a suffix; for it will be stated later that such a result is obtained by the rule *yena vidhis tadantasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.72). Furthermore, there is freedom of choice (*kāmacāra*) in the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified.

If it is argued that even so, the accentuation would still occur by the rule *sthānivad ādeśaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.56), we say no; for since elision (*lopa*) is of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*), it subverts both the finality of the element [to which it applies] and its accentuation. For this very reason, in forms such as *abhūt*, there is no *iṭ* augment for the elided *sic*. Indeed, a positive entity cannot be a constituent part of a non-entity. Furthermore, according to the view of the Bhāṣya, there is also the prohibition [of *iṭ*] by the rule *na lumatāṅgasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.63). However, in the case of *kvip*, *vij*, and others, there is also the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *neḍ vaśi kṛti* (Pāṇini 7.2.8).

And this does not lead to the undesirable consequence [of applying the rule] even when a word is split by a nail (i.e., in a non-sandhi form), because that too is removed by elision (*luk*); such is the direction [of the argument]. In reality, by explaining it as "that which is a *aṅga*," forms such as *rājapuruṣaḥ* are also free from objection; for, due to the prohibition of the *bha*-designation, there is no absence of the elision of *a* (*al-lopa*), and due to the designation of "word" (*pada*) conditioned by being a form ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), there is the elision of *n*. Likewise, the *repha* (the *r* sound) is also established in *ahardadāti*, because the prohibition "not when followed by a case-suffix" (*asupi*)—which in fact applies to an operation on the *aṅga*—does not operate here.

However, this [rule] would apply in the case of a specification regarding a constituent element (*aṅga*). For this very reason, the statement "in the prescription of *ra* for *ahan*" is commenced. Nor should it be argued that, by the force of the rule "not when *su* follows" (*na cāsupi*), the prohibition "not when *su* follows" (*asupi*) does not apply due to the characteristic of the suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*); for in cases such as "dīrghāho nidāghaḥ," even though there is elision by the rule "halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal" (*hal-ṅy-ādi-lopa*), the occurrence of the letter *r* would follow [undesirably].

By this, the interpretation based on the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "not before a *sup*"—namely, the assumption that in the case of *ahardadāti*, the letter *r* occurs because the root *dā* is not followed by a *sup*—is also refuted, because of the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to forms such as *dīrghāho nidāghaḥ*. Although, since the substitution of *r* and *l* (*rutva* and *latva*) are considered unestablished (*asiddha*), the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) would have occurred first, and consequently only the vowel *a* would undergo the substitutions of *r* and *l*, nevertheless, the elision of *n* is not desired in the domain of *rutva* and *latva*. This is because of the inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*) of both *rutva* and *latva* to initiate their own operations; for there is no difference between the vowel *a* and [the resulting] *ra* or *re*.

Nor can it be argued that the prohibition of *nalopa* (the elision of the final *n*) in the case of *sambuddhi* (vocative singular) finds its utility in forms such as "he ahargaccha" and "he dīrghāho nidāgha"; for even so, the substitution of *ru* in "rūparātri" (or "kāovāo") would result in being rendered purposeless (*vaiyarthyāpatti*). If it is objected that this [substitution of *ru*] also finds its utility in the vocative, that is true; however, it is established by repeating the rule "ahan" (Pāṇini 8.2.68), whereby the non-elision of the *n* is prescribed (*nipātana*) by one instance of the repetition. This is the general direction of the argument.

It might be argued as follows: in the cases of *paramavācā*, *paramagoduhā*, *paramalihā*, *paramadaṇḍinā*, *paramadivā*, and *paramakumāryā*, the designation "word" (*pada*) would apply to the subsequent member by relying on the case-ending contained within it.

Consequently, the following rules would apply: *coḥ kuḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.30), *dāderdhātordhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.32), *ho ḍhaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.31), *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya* (Pāṇini 8.2.7), *diva ut* (Pāṇini 6.1.131), and *iko’savarṇe śākalyasya hrasvaśca* (Pāṇini 6.1.127). Nor can the designation *bha* override the designation *pada*, because their scopes of application (*avadhi*) are distinct.

For the designation *bha* applies to the whole [word], whereas the designation *pada* applies to the subsequent portion. Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "In the rule for the *bha* designation, the term *subanta* must be carried over from the rule *suptiṅantam* (Pāṇini 1.4.14)."

Therefore, this is the meaning of the Sūtra: when an affix beginning with *yaj* or similar [consonants] follows that is not a *sarvanāmasthāna*, the preceding aggregate for which that affix is prescribed receives the designation *bha*; and if there exists a *sub*-ending element that constitutes a part of that aggregate, then that too shall receive the designation *bha*, provided it immediately precedes the affix beginning with *yaj*. In this case, the designation *bha* for the aggregate is the primary rule (*pradhānaśiṣṭa*), whereas its application to the constituent part is a secondary or incidental rule (*anvācayaśiṣṭa*), just as in the rule "The *kyaṅ* affix occurs after a word denoting the agent, and there is elision of the *s* [of *sas*]" (Pāṇini 3.1.11).

Therefore, the distinction is this: in cases such as *rājñaḥ*, the [suffixal] operation occurs even though there is no constituent that is a *subanta* (an inflected nominal stem); however, when there exists a constituent that is a *subanta*, it occurs for both that constituent and for the entire aggregate. If it is argued: "Even so, in cases such as *paramāvācau* and *paramavācaḥ*, since the status of being a *bha* (a nominal stem before certain case endings) is absent, the operations pertaining to a *pada* (inflected word) would indeed apply," we reply: No; because even though the status of being a *bha* is absent there, the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of *pada* is prohibited by the rule "not before an *asarvanāmasthāna* [suffix]."

In the rule *svādiṣvasarvanāmasthāne* (Pāṇini 1.4.17) as well, the term *subanta* (that which ends in a case-suffix) is understood by way of *anuvṛtti*. Furthermore, this is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation). By virtue of that, the maxim *anantarasya vidhir vā pratiṣedho vā* ("a rule or prohibition applies to what is immediately preceding") is not resorted to. Thus, the meaning is as follows: when a *sarvanāmasthāna* suffix follows, the preceding aggregate (*samudāya*) shall not be a *pada*, nor shall its constituent part—the *subanta*—be a *pada*.

In that case, the designation *pada* would not apply to the aggregate (*samudāya*), nor would it apply to the inflected word (*subanta*) which constitutes its member. Here, the designation *pada*—which would have applied to the aggregate by virtue of the rule *svādiṣu* (Pāṇini 1.4.17), and to the member by virtue of the rule *suptiṅantaṃ padam* (Pāṇini 1.4.14)—is prohibited by this [present rule]. Thus, forms such as *paramavācau* are established.

If it is argued that, in this case, [rules such as] *kutva* would not apply in examples like *suvāk* or *surājā*, because both types of *pada* designation—belonging to the whole and to the constituent part—would be prohibited even in the presence of the suffix *su*, we say: no. In the rule *asarvanāmasthāne*, by carrying over the word *yajaci* from the subsequent rule, both types of *pada* designation are prohibited when the *sarvanāmasthāna* suffixes beginning with *yaC* follow. However, in the case of *su*, both types of *pada* designation indeed occur. If it is further argued that, in this way, there would be a *pada* designation for what precedes *su* when it is actually heard, we reply: this is accepted as the desired result (*iṣṭāpatti*).

But surely, if this were so, it would contradict what the author of the Vārttika will state regarding the rule *eco 'pragṛhyasyādūrāddhūte pūrvasyārddhasyāduttarasyedutau* (Pāṇini 8.2.107), namely that the term *padānta* must be included in that sūtra to prevent over-extension in cases such as *bhadraṃ karoṣi gauḥ*; for even if [the term *pada*] were applied, the fault would remain if *padānta* were not mentioned. [Reply: No; for in that case, having merely included the word *anta*, [the sūtra] should be understood as following from *vākyasya ṭeḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.82).

Since it is possible to explain [the rule] by carrying over the term "vākya" (sentence) from the previous rule as "at the end of a sentence," it is established that, in this way, the designation *pada* never applies to the final member of a compound when followed by an element beginning with *yaj* and so forth. The distinction is that in some cases there is a prohibition, while in others the designation is blocked by its being termed a *bha*.

If it is objected that, in this case, the *luṅ* (imperfect tense) would not occur in examples such as *dūrānmuktam*, and *ānaṅ* would not occur in *hotāpotārau* because those rules are prescribed when there is an "uttarapada" (subsequent member of a compound), we say: no. This is because the word *uttarapada* is conventionally (*rūḍha*) understood as any member following [the first] in a compound; thus, even in the absence of the technical designation *pada*, the rule applies. Furthermore, this conventional usage refers specifically to the very last member. Consequently, in *hotṛ-potṛ-neṣṭṛ-udgātāraḥ*, since the middle members do not possess the status of being an *uttarapada*, *ānaṅ* does not apply to what precedes them. This is the general direction of the argument.

If it is objected that, in this case, the prohibition of *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) by the rule *sātpadādyoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.3.111) would not apply to forms such as *dadhisecau* and *dadhisecaḥ*, we say: no. This is because the rule is explained as meaning "there is no *ṣatva* for that which begins with a word (*padādiḥ*)," i.e., for the beginning of a word. Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, the prohibition would also apply to forms like *rāmeṣu* and *hariṣu*; for the prohibition does not apply to what follows a word when that word-status depends upon the presence of the suffixes beginning with *su* (i.e., the nominal endings). And this is indicated by the very prohibition of *ṣatva* after *su*.

And it has been said: the explanation is "not after *pada* and so forth," and not "of the beginning of *pada*. For if that were the case, then in examples such as *dadhi-seka*, where the compound occurs prior to the derivation of the nominal suffix (*sub*) according to the rule *gatikārakopapadānām* (Pāṇini 2.2.19), the occurrence of the cerebral *ṣ* would be unavoidable. If it is objected: "Even so, in cases like *bahusecau* and *bahusecaḥ*, the cerebral *ṣ* would still occur, because *bahuca* is not a *pada* and thus the prohibition of *ṣ* does not apply," [the reply is: True; a specific statement must indeed be made here: "There is no [cerebralization] for that which is preceded by *bahuca*."

In this regard, there is the following argument against the Sūtra: "The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* after the root *sāti* should not occur. Consequently, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* following these two words ending in *bahuc* should not occur. Therefore, the mention of 'the beginning' (*ādi*) should not be made, since the desired result is established by the rule *tasmād ity uttarasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.67) alone. Thus, this mention of *bahuc* must be considered as being intended to include the mention of 'the beginning'."

In the Vārttika, however, forms such as *paramavācaḥ* are established by the very rule: "In the application of rules concerning what is not the beginning of a word (*apadādividhau*), [the status of] the subsequent member [of a compound] is that of a word (*uttarapadatva*). When the status of being a word (*padatva*) must be applied to the subsequent part of a compound (*uttara*), there should be no *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (the application of grammatical operations conditioned by a suffix) when a suffix has been elided by *lumat*. Consequently, there is no *kutva* (the change of *c* to *k*) and so forth. However, in the application of rules concerning the beginning of a word (*padādividhau*), there would indeed be *pratyayalakṣaṇa*; thus, by the prohibition of *ṣatva* (the change of *s* to *ṣ*), forms such as *dadhisecā* are established.

And in this view, a compound should not be admitted here prior to the production of the case-ending (*sup*), because its optionality will be stated for the sake of establishing forms such as *dhanakrītā*. Kaiyaṭa, however, says: "In the analysis *dadhnaḥ sec-au*, the compound is formed by [Pāṇini 2.2.8] *ṣaṣṭhī* (the genitive compound), and not an *upapada* compound. Since there is no suffix *vij* after a word with an *upapada*, due to its non-mention, forms such as *dadhiṣecau* do not occur at all."

Even on this view, the rule "bahucpūrvasya ca" must certainly be stated. For, once the suffix *bahuc* has been applied, the resulting complex form becomes a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) by virtue of its meaningfulness; then, after the case-ending (*sup*) has been elided, another case-ending arises again from that complex form—this will be explained under the *arthavat* sūtra. In that context, one might obtain the status of being a word (*padatva*) by relying on the internal case-ending; [the rule is needed] so that this status does not apply when operations such as *kutva* (the substitution of *k* for *s*) are to be performed, but rather so that the prohibition of *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) may take effect.

The essential point here is this: one should read the rule as "uttarapadatve ca padādividhau bahuc-pūrvasya ca" while remaining within the previous sūtra itself. This pair of *vārttikas* should be explained as having a restrictive purpose (*niyamārtha*), meaning that the application of the technical term *pratyaya-lakṣaṇa* (the status of being a suffix) occurs only in the case of operations concerning the beginning of a word (*padādi-vidhi*) and not in the case of operations concerning the end of a word (*padānta-vidhi*). In this way, the negative particle *nañ* need not be employed, which results in brevity (*lāghava*). On this view, the status of being a word (*pada-tva*) does not apply to the form *sau*, because the aforementioned forced interpretation (*kusṛṣṭi*) is no longer necessary.

With reference to these two positions, the authors of the Bhāṣya stated regarding the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.68): "Now, even *sā* is a word (*pada*). Even so, it is like a rope that binds both ends."

If it is argued that, under the view that the suffix *aṅ* is the locus of eligibility (*adhikāra*), and even under the view that it belongs to the base (*vastutaḥ*) itself, the *jus* substitute would apply in the case of *abhūvan*, [the reply is: True. However, because the rule *ātaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.110) is subsequent, the *tiṅ* substitutes take effect first. Now, if it is further argued that in the example *devadattaṃ yājayāñcakāra*, since the *luk* elision is superseded by the subsequent application of the *tiṅ* substitutes, and once those have been applied, their *luk* occurs by the rule *āmaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.81), then by the principle of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* (Pāṇini 1.1.62), the word ending in *ām* would be treated as *tiṅ*-ending and thus be anudātta, while the following word would not be; [the reply is: No.

Since the substitution of *luk* occurs precisely at the stage of the *l* (the *lup* suffix), it sublates the *ti* and other affixes according to the principle of "non-attainment" (*yenāprāptinyāya*). As it has been said: "Because of the elision of *ām*, there is no suppression (*nighāta*); and because of that [elision], there is suppression. If it is objected: "In examples such as *devadatto yuṣmatputraḥ*, the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* prescribed for the genitive case-endings would apply," the answer is: True, they do not apply because of the mention of the *sthānin* (the original element).

Nor should it be argued that the mention of *sthā* (standing) is for the purpose of ensuring that the substitution does not apply merely to the preceding portion when a case-ending (*vibhakti*) follows, but rather to the entire form qualified by the case-ending; for this point is already established by the specific mention of "of the genitive, dative, and accusative" (*ṣaṣṭhī-caturthī-dvitīyānām*), and because the phrase "of the whole word" (*sarvasya padasya*) is understood to carry over from the previous rule. Therefore, the mention of *sthā* is solely for the purpose of preventing the substitution from occurring once the case-ending has been elided.

For "abiding" (*avasthāna*) is possible only when [the case endings] are actually heard; or rather, the root *sthā* (in *tiṣṭhati*) signifies "non-removal" (*ahāni*). This is because the intended meaning is already conveyed by the rule stating "of the sixth, fourth, and second cases," and because the phrase "of every word" (*sarvasya padasya*) continues to apply. Therefore, the mention of *sthā* is solely for the purpose that [the substitution] should not occur once the case ending has been elided. For abiding is indeed possible only when [the endings] are heard; or alternatively, *tiṣṭhati* means "not being removed. As in: "O Sugrīva, abide at this time! (*samaye tiṣṭha sugrīva*).

The meaning is: "Do not abandon the agreement. Thus, by the statement "of those two whose case-endings have not been dropped," the fact that their case-endings are actually heard is clearly obtained. However, this remains to be addressed:

If it is argued that, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that [the substitution] applies to the *aṅga* (stem), then once the *talopa* (elision of *ta*) has occurred by the rule *ciṇo luk* (Pāṇini 6.4.104), the substitutions *in*, *ṇiṅ*, and so forth would not take place—resulting in such forms as *avadhi bhavatā dasyuḥ*, *agāyi bhavatā grāmaḥ*, and *adhyagāyi bhavatānuvākaḥ*—because these rules are prescribed when *luṅ* follows; we say: "Not so. For the substitutions *in*, *ṇiṅ*, and so forth are prescribed specifically for that *ardhadhātuka* which occurs in the context of *luṅ*. Therefore, the position that [the substitution] applies to the *aṅga* is established as being free from fault. [Next: *aco'ntyādi ṭi* (Pāṇini 1.1.64).

The word *acaḥ* is a genitive used in the sense of selection (*nirddhāraṇe*). The singular number is used because the reference is to the class (*jāti*). Among vowels (*acām*), that which is the last, beginning with that [vowel], shall bear the technical designation *ṭi*. The applications (*pradeśāḥ*) of the term *ṭi* include such rules as "for the *ṭi* of the *ātmanepada* endings" (Pāṇini 3.4.79), etc., as in *pacate*, *pacete*, and so forth. The word *antya* means "situated at the end. It is derived from the root *anta-* with the suffix *yat* according to the rule for the *digādi* group. The compound *antyādiḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi*: "that of which the beginning is the last. This compound is valid because it involves a constant mutual dependence (*nityasāpekṣatva*).
The rule "the penultimate (*upadhā*) is that which precedes the final vowel (*al*)" (Pāṇini 1.1.65) [is also relevant here].

The letter preceding the final consonant (*al*) shall be designated as *upadhā*. Examples of *upadhā-guṇa* include: *cetati*, *cyotati*, *vardhate*, and so forth. If it is objected that, since the preceding element is not specifically qualified, the designation would apply to the entire cluster "śā" in the root *śās*, one should not say that the substitution of *i* (by Pāṇini 6.4.34: *śāsa idaṅhaloḥ*) would then apply to the entire cluster "śā. This is because the desired result is established by the *paribhāṣā* "the [designation] applies to the final *al*" (*alontyaparibhāṣā*). This may be so.

"The prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 1.1.57], *nānarthake 'lontyavidhir anabhyāsavikāreṣu*, would apply here. And in this case, regarding the form *bibharti*, the phrase *anabhyāsavikāreṣu* was stated for the purpose that the rule *bhṛñām it* (Pāṇini 7.4.76) should apply to the final letter. A "modification" (*vikāra*) refers to a substitution (*ādeśa*) consisting of a phoneme. For this very reason, in the case of *dehi*, the elision (*lopa*) becomes a substitution of the whole word. To this, it is replied:

This technical convention (*paribhāṣā*) is not accepted by the author of the *Sūtras*, because in the rule "its [elision]" (*tasya lopaḥ*, Pāṇini 1.3.9), the mention of "its" (*tasya*) is for the purpose of effecting the elision of all [the markers] *ñ*, *ṭ*, and *ḍ*. Nor is it accepted by the author of the *Bhāṣya*, since it is stated in the *Bhāṣya* that the purposes of this [convention] can be established otherwise. To illustrate: first of all, the substitution of a final [augment] in the case of an imitation of an indistinct sound (*avyaktānukaraṇa*) does not occur, due to the *jñāpaka* [in the rule] "not of a reduplicated word, but optionally of the final [syllable]" (*nāmreḍitasyāntyasya tu vā*, Pāṇini 6.1.99).

Otherwise, he would have simply said "vā" (or) for the reduplicated form. Even in the rule *ghvasoreddhau* (Pāṇini 6.4.119), because the word *lopa* is mentioned again despite *lopo yi* (Pāṇini 6.4.118) being already in force, it has the force of making the substitution a total replacement (*sarvādeśa*). Thus, the formulation of the sūtra would be as follows: "There is elision (*lopa*) of the root *ghu* and of the reduplicated syllable; by the recurrence of another word *lopa*, there would be total elision. And for the root *as*, 'e' [is substituted]; 'e' occurs in place of both *as* and *ghu* when followed by *dhau*."

Alternatively, there is a word-break as *lopaś* (lopa-ś). An *anubandha* applied to a technical name (*saṃjñā*) bears fruit upon the named object (*saṃjñin*), just as in the case of *ṅamuṭ*. However, in the Bhāṣya it is stated that the reference consists of two *ś*s. In that context, *lope* is a separate word.
