Furthermore, the designation *it* for the sound *ś* occurs only at the time of its initial instruction (*upadeśa*). The result of this, however, appears in actual usage; for the sense is that in all cases, *anubandhas* function as differentiators by not becoming constituent parts [of the word], much like a crow perched on a house.

Even in this view, since the suffix *jhac* begins with a *saṃyoga* when followed by *ac-ac-ac-ac-ac-al*, the reading with only a single *śakāra* is easily justified after the elision of *su*. The intention of the Bhāṣya, however, is that—just as in the case of the vowel *a* in rules such as *ana upadhālopinaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.134)—the elision of the *sakāra* here should not take place for the sake of clarity.

If it is argued that in examples such as *ābhyām*, the elision (*lopa*) of the *id* of *idaṃ*—which is prescribed by the rule *hali lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.113)—would likewise apply to the final letter, we say: no. This is because, by carrying over the word *anaḥ* from the preceding rule *anāpyakaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.112), one interprets the locative case *halī* as a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and thus prescribes the elision specifically for the *an*.

And thus, in that case, by the *alontyaparibhāṣā* (the rule that [an operation] applies to the final letter), the *nakāra* is elided; then, by applying *ato guṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.97) for *pararūpa*, forms such as *ebhyām* and *eṣām* are established. Furthermore, regarding the rule *atra lopo'bhyāsasya* (Pāṇini 7.4.58), because of the interpretation that "here the status of being an *abhyāsa* is the basis [of the operation], and not merely a part thereof," and by the force of the inclusion of the word *atra*, there is the elision of the whole.

Although "san" is required to exclude forms such as *dadau* and *dadhau*, "sādau" is required to exclude *jijñapayiṣati*, the "prakṛti" (the verbal root) is required to exclude *pipakṣati* and the like, and the "viṣaya" (the object of the suffix) is also required to exclude *mumukṣati gām* by virtue of the rule "muco 'karmakasya guṇo vā" (Pāṇini 7.4.57); nevertheless, since all of this is easily obtained through mere *anuvṛtti* (contextual carry-over), it should be understood that the explicit mention [of these terms] here is solely for the purpose of excluding everything else.

If it is argued that even so, by the Vārttika "vibhāṣā bhavadbhagavadaghavatām occāvasya," the substitution of *o* for the final [letter] would apply, we say no. Since the form with *ava* is already established, the use of the heavy syllable *avasya* (instead of *vasya*) serves to ensure that the substitute is for the whole word (*sarvādeśa*). Therefore, it is established that the Paribhāṣā "that which is not meaningless" is useless and is not supported by the Sūtras or the Bhāṣya. And thus, although the vowel *a* is the penultimate (*upadhā*) of the stem *śās-* in the form *śāsa-*, forms such as *śiṣṭaḥ* are correctly established.

Furthermore, usages such as "the mention of *upadhā* [is] for the sake of *kṛ*" are consistent with this view; this is the general direction. Alternatively, the rule that the relationship between a limit (*avadhi*) and that which is limited (*avadhimat*) pertains only to things of the same kind is a general principle (*utsarga*). For in common worldly usage, when it is said, "Bring the one immediately preceding the last among these Brahmins," only a single person who is immediately prior to the last is brought, not the entire group. Likewise, here too, the technical name (*saṃjñin*) is only an *al* (phoneme) that is immediately preceding another *al*, and not a collection, nor an *al* that is separated by others.

The usage [of the term] *saṃyoga* as having a penultimate (*upadha*) is figurative (*bhākta*), because the property of a part is metaphorically attributed (*upacāra*) to the whole. This being the case, it is also easy to explain *alaḥ* as being in the nominative plural (*jas*). [In the rule] *jātvākhyāyām* (Pāṇini 1.2.58), the plural number is used. *Pūrvaḥ* is also in the nominative plural. Furthermore, *antyaḥ* is understood as being like *alaḥ* due to their commonality (*sājātya*). Alternatively, in *alaḥ*, the genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), and the singular number is used for the class (*jāti*). The meaning is: "that which precedes the last among the *als*. Thus, here three positions remain possible: that *alaḥ* is in the nominative plural (*jas*), the genitive plural (*ṅasi*), or the genitive singular (*ṅas*).
When that [tasmin] is specified, it refers to what precedes it (Pāṇini 1.1.66).

In the case of specifications involving the seventh case (saptamī), the grammatical operation should apply to the preceding element alone; and "specified" (nirdiṣṭe) means that it has been uttered immediately [without intervention]. The prefix *niḥ* signifies non-interruption (*nairantarya*), and the root *diś-* denotes the act of uttering. Thus, "specified" (*nirdiṣṭa*) means "uttered without interval. This sūtra is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtham*).

For instance, in the rule *iko yaṇ aci* (Pāṇini 6.1.77), the term *aci* [in the locative case] is used according to the rule *yasya ca bhāvena bhāvalakṣaṇam* (Pāṇini 2.3.37). In that context, the locative case [denoting] "characterization by the state of another" applies equally to what precedes as it does to what follows. The same applies to *upaśleṣa* (proximity) as well.

In that regard, since it is impossible for a single element to simultaneously function as both the cause of an effect and the cause of a nimitta, the rule *pūrvasyaiva* (of the preceding alone) is established to restrict the application of *yaṇ*—which would otherwise occur alternately for the vowels *i* and *u* in examples such as *dadhyudakam* and *madhv idam*—to the preceding vowel only. Similarly, in the case of *agnicid atra*, although *yaṇ* would apply even to the separated [vowel], it is restricted by the rule *pūrvasyaiva* to the preceding one alone. Now, one might object: in cases such as *gavity ayam āha*, the word *iti* functions to indicate that the preceding item is its own form (*svarūpa*), just as it does here.

And in this way, this *paribhāṣā* would apply only to the rule *tasminnaṇi* (Pāṇini 4.3.2). For there is indeed something to be excluded there, because in cases such as *he yauṣmākīṇa asmabhyaṃ dehi* ("O you belonging to us, give to us") and *he āsmākīna yuṣmabhyaṃ dadāmi* ("O you belonging to us, I give to you"), there is the possibility of the substitution [of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*] even after the suffixes *khañ* and *ṇa*. True; however, the particle *iti* effects a reversal of the word-meaning. Since in common usage the focus is generally on the meaning, it makes the focus here instead on the word-form (*śabda*). In the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*), however, the opposite is the case.

Furthermore, if this [rule] were to apply only in the context of *tasminnaṇi* (Pāṇini 4.3.2), then it would have included the mention of *pūrva-* right there. Therefore, this is not an imitation of that specific rule. Rather, this is a reference to the independent pronominal *tat* for the purpose of including all specific cases such as *aci*, *halī*, and so forth—just as in the rules *tasyāpatyam* (Pāṇini 4.1.92) and *tatra bhavaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.53). This is established by the rule *tasmādityuttarasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.67).

In the rules concerning the ablative case (*pañcamī-nirdeśa*), the grammatical operation should apply only to what follows (*uttara*) and that which is uttered immediately after; for example, in *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.28), as in *agnim īḷe*. Here it does not occur in *īle 'gnim*, because an ablative case expressing a spatial relation (*dig-yoga-lakṣaṇā pañcamī*) is impossible here. In that context, just as the word "following" (*uttara*) is supplied, the word "preceding" (*pūrva*) would also be supplied without distinction, even if it is separated by an interval. Thus, even a word that is non-contiguous (*vyavahita*) is included.

And likewise, in the case of *utsaṃsthātā*, there would also be the application of *udaḥ sthāstambhoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.61). Thus, it is established that both the preceding rule and this rule serve the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). Accordingly, the Vārttika states: "In the rules [beginning with] *tasmin* and *tasmāt*, because there is no distinction between the preceding and following applications, the statement is for the sake of restriction, as in *dadhyudakam* and *pacatyodanam*. Here too, *tasmāt* is a reference to the independent pronoun *sarvanāman* as before; it is not a mere phonetic imitation (*anukaraṇa*).

For if that were the case, although this paribhāṣā would not apply in the rule *tasmānnuṅ dvihalaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.74) because the preceding element of the stem (*aṅga*)—which would have to undergo the lengthening by *ata ādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.70)—is impossible and thus there is no purpose for its application, it would nevertheless apply in the two rules *tasmācchaso naḥ puṃsi* (Pāṇini 6.1.103) and *tasmānnuḍaci* (Pāṇini 6.3.74). This is because in those instances, forms such as *uccarata ānupalabhate* and *gauranaśvaḥ*, which are to be excluded [by the prohibition], are possible there. Such is the direction [of the argument].

It might be argued as follows: Let this [present] sūtra serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). Let the preceding sūtra also serve as a restrictor under the view that the locative case is *aupaśleṣika* (based on proximity). However, its status as a restrictor is inappropriate under the view that the locative is *satsaptamī* (locative of existence), because that would contradict the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa on Pāṇini 6.4.1. To illustrate, regarding the sūtra *śnānnalopaḥ* (Pāṇ. 6.4.23), the Bhāṣya states: "This is not a locative of posteriority (*parasaptamī*). What then? It is a locative of existence (*satsaptamī*), meaning 'when a *ṅit* suffix is present'."

On that very point, Kaiyaṭa says: "But how is it appropriate to resort to the locative of existence (*satsaptamī*) when the locative of proximity (*parasaptamī*) is possible? There is no fault, for one may supply the necessary words as desired. For if it were understood simply as 'when a *kit* suffix exists,' since there would be no reliance on priority or posteriority, the application of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) 'tasmin' (Pāṇini 1.1.66) would not occur.

When, however, the locative denotes a locus of immediate proximity (*upaśleṣika-adhikaraṇa*), then because there is no fixed rule as to whether the operation applies to what precedes or what follows, the technical rule is brought into play to provide that regulation."

To this it is replied: there is no contradiction, because the sixth book (*ṣaṣṭhādhyāya*) is concerned solely with what is under immediate discussion (*prakṛta*). For instance, regarding the rule *śnānna-lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.23), when the question is raised, "Let there be no mention of that which possesses the letter *ś*; let it simply be *nād*," the objection is raised that this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *nandana*. If, however, one were to carry forward (*anukarṣaṇa*) the rule *aniditām*, then [the elision] would not apply in the case of *hinasti*. Therefore, it is suspected that by carrying forward the term *ṅkiti* and relying on *śnam* itself as being marked with the *ṅ*-sign, the elision may indeed occur in *hinasti*.

If, moreover, in this state the *paribhāṣā* "tasmin" (Pāṇini 1.1.66) were to apply, then in forms such as *nandamāna*, the elision (*lopa*) of the suffix *anaś* would occur because it is marked with the *ṅit* indicator. Furthermore, the addition of the *śit* indicator to *śnam* would be purposeless; for that *śit* indicator serves a purpose only when, by virtue of being *śit*, [the suffix] is treated as a *sārvadhātuka*, and thus—relying on this very *ṅit* indicator—the elision of *n* is effected in the form *hinasti*, but not otherwise. But surely the *śit* indicator is purposeful because it prevents the designation (*saṃjñā*) of [the suffix] as *ārdhadhātuka*.

For if that [the *śnam* suffix] were present, then in the case of *anakti* and *bhanakti*, there would be the elision of the *at* (by Pāṇini 6.4.110); in the case of *ruṇaddhi* and *bhinatti*, there would be the elision of the *at* in *anakti* and *bhanakti*; and in the case of *ruṇaddhi* and *bhinatti*, there would be *guṇa* substitution; and in the case of *tṛṇoḍhi*, there would be the augment *iṭ*. If it is argued that the rule "not before *vaś*" (Pāṇini 7.2.8) does not apply because [the *śnam*] is not a *kṛt* suffix, we say no; for since the portion preceding the *śnam* is not a complete stem (*aṅga*), the aforementioned rules do not apply.

If it is asked, "How is it not a member (*anaṅga*)?"—it is as follows: the meaning of the rule is that when a suffix is prescribed, whatever is indicated by the fifth case (*pañcamī*), such as "from a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*) or "from a nominal stem" (*pratipadikāt*), that [root or stem] is a member (*aṅga*) with respect to that suffix which follows it. However, in this instance, that which is indicated by the fifth case is "from *rudh* and so forth" (*rudhādibhyaḥ*); the suffix does not follow from this. And that [suffix] which follows is not indicated by the fifth case with respect to the preceding portion when it is being prescribed.

For this very reason, in forms such as *bhanakti*, the rule *ato dīrgho yañi* (Pāṇini 7.3.101) does not apply. Nor should it be argued that the addition of the marker *ś* in *śnasorallopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.111) is for the sake of providing a qualification; for even if one were to state simply *nasorallopaḥ*, there would be no fault. [Objection: But in that case, there would be a grasping of the suffixes *nā* and *asti*.

If it is argued that, in the same way, [the rule] would also apply in the case of *kan* with *yaṅ*-elision in the example "caṅkāntaḥ," we say no. For even according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), since there would be the undesirable consequence of including the suffix *śna* and stems ending in *s*, the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would be equally present in cases such as "vastaḥ. As for the claim that the inclusion of both suffixes and verbal roots is based on association (*sāhacarya*), that is the same for both positions.

But surely, if it were stated as "there is elision of *a* and *al* after *na* and *s*" (*nasorallopaḥ*), then this would apply only where there is immediate succession (*ānantarya*) of a *ṅit* affix following the suffix *nap*; for example, in *yatnataḥ* (from *yatna ivācarataḥ*) and *pāmanataḥ*? Not so; because the term *sārvadhātuka*, which is being carried over [from a previous rule], qualifies the suffix. And thus, since there is no contact with a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*), the technical rule regarding "that which is specifically pointed out" (*nirdiṣṭaparibhāṣā*) does not apply, and the locative case is used in the sense of a causal condition (*nimitta-saptamī*). Therefore, the meaning is: "there is elision of the *a* of the suffix *nap* and of the root *ās*, when a *ṅit* [affix] follows immediately."

If it is objected: "But is it not the case that in the rule *sārvadhātuke* (Pāṇini 6.4.110), the mention of *sārvadhātuka* has been rejected?"—No, for that rejection was made on the assumption that [the suffix] possesses the marker *ś*. Thus, it is established that by the force of making *śna* possess the marker *ś*, the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "before an affix marked with *k* or *ṅ*" does not apply even when there is a locative absolute construction (*satsaptamī*). Alternatively, one may explain that it was stated in that manner merely as a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) and without firm adherence.

In these two sūtras, the position that the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is prescribed [for the subsequent term] is also established in the Bhāṣya. For instance, from the sūtra *ṣaṣṭhī sthāneyogā* (Pāṇini 1.1.49), the word *ṣaṣṭhī* is carried over [as an anuvṛtti]. Thus, when there is an indication of the sense of the locative case, the genitive case shall apply to the immediately preceding element.

In that regard, in rules such as *iko yaṇ aci* (Pāṇini 6.1.77), because the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is explicitly heard, that genitive is restated [as a *pratinirdeśa*], and it is merely stated that "this [substitution] applies to what precedes and is immediately adjacent, but not to what follows, nor even to what precedes if it is separated. However, in rules such as *āno muk* (Pāṇini 7.2.82), because the genitive is not heard, it must be supplied; this is the distinction. And since its connection is not fixed [to a specific relation], it is a genitive of locus (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*).

Furthermore, the restriction of the grammatical operation (*kāryaniyama*) applies only to that [word] which possesses the genitive of location (*sthāna-ṣaṣṭhī*); this too is established by implication. However, where there is a mention of both [the word and the element], neither [of them] can be the determiner (*prakalpaka*), because it is impossible for the status of being the locus of the operation (*kāryitva*) and the status of being the cause (*nimittatva*) to coexist simultaneously in one and the same thing, and because of an explanatory indicator (*jñāpaka*). Thus, Kaiyaṭa says regarding the rule *ekaḥ pūrvaparayoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.84): "Since two rules serve as the authority, there would be two genitive case-endings acting as determiners; therefore, in this instance, the status of being an explanatory indicator is resorted to."

Nor can both alternatives be postulated by way of alternation (*paryāya*), because they are not of equal strength. To explain: in the rule *āne muk* (Pāṇini 7.2.82), the locative case (*saptamī*) is without scope [elsewhere]. It supplants the ablative case (*pañcamī*) of the rule *ato yeyaḥ* (7.2.80), which has already found its application in preceding rules. Similarly, the ablative case in *īdāsaḥ* (7.2.83) supplants the locative case of *āne*. Likewise, in the rule *tāsyanudāttet...* (6.1.186), he will state that the locative designation *sārvadhātuke* applies to the sense of *abhyasta-sij-artha*.

And since that locative case (*saptamī*) finds its purpose later on, the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is postulated for that very [locative]. Similarly, in the rule *bahoḷopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.108), the ablative *bahoḥ* postulates a genitive for the locative *iṣṭhemeyaḥsu*, which has not yet fulfilled its purpose. For this very reason, there is a separate mention of the genitive in the rule *bhūca bahoḥ*.

Likewise, in the rule *goto ṇit* (Pāṇini 7.1.90), the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is interpreted as a genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in relation to the locative *sarvanāmasthāne*; this is because there is no purpose for the *go* word itself to possess the *ṇit* designation. Nor should it be argued that the result [of this interpretation] is the *vṛddhi* substitution of the preceding vowel in examples such as *tiṣṭhati gauḥ*, because the verb *tiṣṭhati* is not a constituent part (*aṅga*) with respect to the word *go*. Thus, it is clear in the Bhāṣya that the ablative case generally remains unfulfilled in its function.

In the rule *āmi sarvanāmnaḥ suṭ* (Pāṇini 7.1.52), the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is also without scope; however, the locative case (*saptamī*) in *āmi* has scope for the sake of subsequent rules. If, however, one were to argue that here the ablative case in *sarvanāmnaḥ* also fulfills its purpose by establishing grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the [implied] ablative *āt* through its recurrence (*anuvṛtti*), then—since the *yathoddeśa* theory is adopted—the rule *tasmādityuttarasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.67) will apply.

As it has been said: "In the case of a conflict between two [possible] designations, the designation of the ablative (*pañcamī*) prevails. However, in reality, there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) here; for this is explained as being for the sake of establishing the form "of those belonging to the castes, stages of life, and others" (*varṇāśrametarāṇām*), based on the rule that the suffix is prescribed after a pronoun (*sarvanāman*), and because it is explained as "after the letter *a*" for the sake of meanings such as "those of whom" or "their. But in the rule "the *tuṅ* augment occurs after a long vowel before *cha*," the ablative stands in place of the genitive; therefore, the *tuṅ* augment occurs only after the long vowel, and not after the letter *cha*.

The mention of "surācchāyā" here serves as an indicative mark (*liṅga*). For otherwise, according to the rule *khari ca* (Pāṇini 8.4.55), the *c* would have been substituted [for the *j*], and he would have indicated it with two *ca*s, as in "surāccāyā. However, in the formulation of a suffix-rule (*pratyayavidhi*), the ablative case endings (*pañcamī*) do not serve as the basis for the derivation, because the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) functions as the referential case (*anuvādavibhakti*). Furthermore, since that which is not already established cannot be referred to, there is no possibility of an unrestricted application; thus, the restrictive Paribhāṣā does not apply in such cases. This is the general direction of the argument.
*Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.68*: "The own form (*svarūpa*) of a word [is the technical term], except for a grammatical technical designation (*saṃjñā*).

In the science of grammar, the own form of a word is the thing designated (*saṃjñin*), provided it is not itself a technical designation. For example: *agner ḍhak* (Pāṇini 4.2.33) results in *āgneyam*; *āṅo yamahanaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.28) results in *āyacchate* and *āhate*. Here, in these sūtras, the actual forms of the words *agni*, *āṅ*, *yam*, and *han* as they occur in usage are the things designated. Why does the sūtra say "except for a grammatical technical designation"? So that [the rule] *upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.92) may apply to the roots *dā* and *dhā*, and not to the root *ghu* when it means "sound."

"Śabda" refers to the science of grammar (*śabdaśāstra*); in this context, "saṃjñā" forms a locative compound with it (i.e., *śabde saṃjñā*), and not a genitive compound meaning "the name of a word" (*śabdasya saṃjñā*). For if it were the latter, then in the case of technical designations such as "object" (*karman*) or "instrument" (*karaṇa*), there would be the undesirable consequence of those terms referring to both their own form and other forms.

It might be argued as follows: even without the mention of *rūpa* (form), that very [word] will be grasped by its own name (*sva-śabdena*), because it does not depend on instruction for its cognition, because it is unique (*asādhāraṇa*), because it is internal (*antaraṅga*), and because its presence is fixed (*niyatopasthitika*). For the meaning (*artha*) depends upon the apprehension of a relationship for its cognition; it is common (*sādhāraṇa*) because it can be conveyed by synonyms; it is external (*bahiraṅga*) because it is the object of the understanding produced by the knowledge of the word; and its presence is not fixed because it is not cognized in the state of imitation (*anukaraṇa*). So, what is the purpose of mentioning *rūpa*? [Response: This is true. However, the mention of *rūpa* is made so that the word itself may be understood as the object of the operation (*kārya*), and not the meaning. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the rule would apply to the meaning as well. Furthermore, the mention of *rūpa* serves to exclude the meaning from being the object of the operation, since the meaning is not the primary object of the grammatical operation. Moreover, the mention of *rūpa* is intended to indicate that the word-form is the object of the operation, and not merely the word as a conventionally established entity (*saṅketita-rūpa*). This is because the word-form is the actual object of the operation, whereas the conventional entity is merely a secondary, inferred object. Therefore, the mention of *rūpa* is necessary to ensure that the operation applies specifically to the form of the word. Thus, the objection is refuted. It is established that the mention of *rūpa* is indeed required. This concludes the discussion. Now, let us proceed with the next topic. What is it? It is the definition of the term *pada*. What is a *pada*? A *pada* is that which possesses a meaning (*arthavattva*). But is this not already established by the previous rule (*pūrvasūtra*)? No, it is not. For the previous rule was stated to establish the status of a *prātipadika*, whereas this rule is stated to establish the status of a *pada*. Since the two are distinct, the previous rule does not suffice. Therefore, the definition of a *pada* must be stated separately. And thus, the definition of a *pada* is stated: "A meaningful element ending in a case-ending (*sup*) or a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) is called a *pada*. This is the definition of a *pada*. Now, one might ask: why is the word *artha-vat* used here? Is it not already implied by the previous rule? No, it is not. For the previous rule was intended to define a *prātipadika*, and the present rule is intended to define a *pada*. Since the two are different, the previous rule does not apply here. Therefore, the word *artha-vat* is used to ensure that only elements possessing meaning are designated as *padas*. Without it, there would be the undesirable consequence that even meaningless elements like *goṇī*, *tarku*, and *mañcaka* would be designated as *padas*. To prevent this, the word *artha-vat* is employed. Thus, the definition of a *pada* is complete. Now, let us consider the following: what is the purpose of the word *artha-vat* in the definition of a *prātipadika*? Is it not already established by the present rule? No, it is not. For the present rule is intended to define a *pada*, while the previous rule is intended to define a *prātipadika*. Since they are distinct, the present rule does not apply there. Therefore, the word *artha-vat* must be explicitly stated in the definition of a *prātipadika* to ensure that only meaningful elements are designated as *prātipadikas*. Without it, there would be the undesirable consequence that even meaningless elements like *goṇī*, *tarku*, and *mañcaka* would be designated as *prātipadikas*. To prevent this, the word *artha-vat* is employed. Thus, the definition of a *prātipadika* is complete. Now, let us proceed with the next topic. What is it? It is the definition of the term *prakṛti*. What is a *prakṛti*? A *prakṛti* is that which, when followed by a suffix (*pratyaya*), undergoes modification (*vikāra*) or elision (*lopa*). This is the definition of a *prakṛti*. Now, one might ask: why is the word *pratyaya* used here? Is it not already implied by the context? No, it is not. For without the word *pratyaya*, there would be the undesirable consequence that the definition would apply to cases where a suffix is not actually present, such as in the case of *gavityaṅkaḥ* or *kakudāvartin*. To prevent this, the word *pratyaya* is employed. Thus, the definition of a *prakṛti* is complete. Now, let us proceed with the next topic. What is it? It is the definition of the term *pratyaya*. What is a *pratyaya*? A *pratyaya* is that which is taught after a *prakṛti*. This is the definition of a *pratyaya*. Now, one might ask: why is the word *prakṛti* used here? Is it not already implied by the context? No, it is not. For without the word *prakṛti*, there would be the undesirable consequence that the definition would apply to cases where a *prakṛti* is not present, such as in the case of *tiṅ* suffixes following a *tiṅ* suffix. To prevent this, the word *prakṛti* is employed. Thus, the definition of a *pratyaya* is complete. Now, let us proceed with the next topic. What is it? It is the definition of the term *samāsa*. What is a *samāsa*? A *samāsa* is a compound formed by the conjunction of two or more words. This is the definition of a *samāsa*. Now, one might ask: why is the word *samāsa* used here? Is it not already implied by the context? No, it is not. For without the word *samāsa*, there would be the undesirable consequence that the definition would apply to cases where a compound is not actually formed, such as in the case of *rājapuruṣaḥ* when analyzed as *rāja-puruṣa-au*. To prevent this, the word *samāsa* is employed. Thus, the definition of a *samāsa* is complete. Now, let us proceed with the next topic. What is it? It is the definition of the term *vākya*. What is a *vākya*? A *vākya* is a collection of words that conveys a single, unified meaning. This is the definition of a *vākya*. Now, one might ask: why is the word *vākya* used here? Is it not already implied by the context? No, it is not. For without the word *vākya*, there would be the undesirable consequence that the definition would apply to cases where a single unified meaning is not conveyed, such as in the case of *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* when uttered separately. To prevent this, the word *vākya* is employed. Thus, the definition of a *vākya* is complete. Now, let us proceed with the next topic. What is it? It is the definition of the term *liṅga*. What is a *liṅga*? A *liṅga* is that which indicates gender, number, and case. This is the definition of a *liṅga*. Now, one might ask: why is the word *liṅga* used here? Is it not already implied by the context? No, it is not. For without the word *liṅga*, there would be the undesirable consequence that the definition would apply to cases where gender, number, and case are not indicated, such as in the case of indeclinables (*avyaya*). To prevent this, the word *liṅga* is employed. Thus, the definition of a *liṅga* is complete. Now, let us proceed with the next topic. What is it? It is the definition of the term *vacana*. What is a *vacana*? A *vacana* is a number (*saṅkhyā*). This is the definition of a *vacana*. Now, one might ask: why is the word *vacana* used here? Is it not already implied by the context? No, it is not

On this point, they say: In this treatise, the inclusion of the term *rūpa* (form) is for the purpose of making known that meaning (*artha*) is also intended [to be included], just like form. By this, the principle "when there is the mention of something meaningful (*arthavat*), that which is meaningless (*anarthaka*) is not [included]" becomes established. In that context, by virtue of the aforementioned indicator (*jñāpaka*), the meaning is to be understood; and by the statement "its own form" (*svaṃ rūpam*), the form is also [understood]. Thus, by implication, there is the mention of the form of that which possesses meaning. Consequently, in the case of *kāśe* and *kuśe*, the designation *pragṛhya*—by the rule "after *śe*" (*śe*, Pāṇini 1.1.13)—does not apply.

This sūtra has been rejected in the Bhāṣya. For instance, even if the sūtra were to be formulated, words such as *paśu* (animal), *apatyam* (offspring), *devatā* (deity), *prāñcaḥ* (easterners), *udañcaḥ* (northerners), and *bharatāḥ* (the Bharatas)—as well as [the technical term] *hatyā*—would simply be understood according to their worldly meanings. However, in rules such as *agner ḍhak* (Pāṇini 4.2.33), the word-form itself would be taken [as the meaning], because it is impossible for a suffix to stand in a temporal sequence (*paurvāparya*) with a meaning, and because of the governing rule *ṅyāpprātipadikāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.1).

However, in rules such as *upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.92), the verbal root *ghu* will not be understood [as including *dā* and *dhā*], because of the introduction of the rule *dādhā ghu* (Pāṇini 1.1.20). For it has been said:
"This restriction of a technical term (*saṃjñā*) to its referent (*saṃjñin*) is for the sake of conventional usage in certain instances."

The paribhāṣā "that which possesses meaning" (*arthavat*) is also established by the fact that, in the rule *vraśca* etc., the root *rāj* is listed and then *bhāj* is listed again; it is also established by reasoning (*nyāya*). For in rules such as *agner ḍhak* (Pāṇini 4.2.33), when a meaning qualified by a word is generally presented, because an operation cannot apply to the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), the operation applies to the qualifying word (*viśeṣaṇa*) only as it is presented as being associated with the meaning. This applies even to a word that is itself meaningless, since the requirement is met simply by the reversal of the qualifier-qualified relationship of the meaning; [this holds] entirely...

Because of the impossibility of its being the skin; the maxim of the primary and the secondary (*gauṇamukhyanyāya*) is also rooted in this, since the secondary sense does not present itself first. By this, the statement "those whose word-meanings are manifested" is also explained. Therefore, since everything can be resolved through logic alone, the Sūtra need not be commenced. If it is argued that the Sūtra *svaṃ rūpam* (Pāṇini 1.1.68) must necessarily be stated for the sake of its recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) in the subsequent four Sūtras, we say no; for such recurrence is not necessary.

To explain: first, in the rule *aṇuditsavarṇasya ca pratyayaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.69), the fact that a sound is its own *savarṇa* (homogeneous) is established precisely because it is identical to itself; otherwise, how could there be the elision by *jharo jhari savarṇe* (Pāṇini 8.4.65) in the form *avāttām*? If you argue that in that case *savarṇya* exists due to a difference between individual instances (*vyakti*), then here too it must be understood as such, because of the difference between the individual instance of the signifier (*bodhaka*) and the individual instance of the signified (*bodhya*). The same applies to the rule *taparas tatkālasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.70). Furthermore, in the rule *ādir antyena sahetā* (Pāṇini 1.1.71), the inclusion of the word "beginning" (*ādi*) is established through the function of the commentary (*vṛtti*).

The indicator (*liṅga*) for [the necessity of] repetition is found in rules such as *nādici* (Pāṇini 6.1.104). However, regarding the rule *yena vidhiḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.71), the author of the Vārttikas will indeed state *tasya ca*. In reality, even that need not be stated, since the desired result is established through the principle of *vyapadeśivadbhāva* (treating a thing as if it were what it is designated as). Furthermore, we shall refute the restriction *aprātipadikena* at that very same place. For this very reason, the Vārttika located in the *ādyantavat-sūtra*—which states that "the purpose [of the rule] is to establish the status of being preceded by or ending with that by which the operation is prescribed"—is consistent. This is the general direction (*dik*).

The mention of *siddha* is for the sake of [illustrating] specific examples such as *vṛkṣa*. Here, *siddha* is an illustration; having attached some gender (*liṅga*) [to the general term], one must state that this is the technical name (*saṃjñā*) for specific instances characterized by that gender. And the meaning is that this gender is to be attached to *vṛkṣa* and so on. The same applies hereafter as well. Consequently, because only the specific instances are understood in the rule *vibhāṣā vṛkṣamṛga...* (Pāṇini 2.4.12), forms such as *plakṣanyagrodham* and *plakṣanyagrodhāḥ* are established.

And [the mention of] the word *pitṛ* as a synonym is for the sake of its own form; by the use of the particle *ca*, there is the inclusion of specific instances and the word's own form. As in: "After *puṣ* when followed by *sva*" (*Pāṇini* 2.4.40): *raipoṣaṃ puṣṭaḥ*, *aśvapoṣam*, *svapoṣam*.

The term *paryāyavacana* (synonym) is used here specifically for the sake of words such as *rājan* (king) and others, as in the rule: "A *sabhā* preceded by a word denoting a king or a non-human being [is feminine]" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 2.4.23). Thus we have *inasabham* and *īśvarasabham*. But not here in *rājasabhā* or *hariścandrasabhā*. For that which expresses a synonym is indeed a *paryāyavacana*. Furthermore, there is no option (*vikalpa*) between a word and itself, nor with its own specific form, because a general term and a specific term produce cognitions of different types and thus lack identical meaning; for according to the maxim, only those of identical meaning may be subject to option. Expressions such as "the word *ina* is a synonym for the word *rājan*" are merely conventional usages, similar to saying "Bhīma is Bhīmasena."

The suffix *ṭhak* applies after the word *jhiṭ* and its synonyms when meaning "one who kills fish" and so forth. [Pāṇini Sūtra 4.4.35 states: "After the words *pakṣin*, *matsya*, and *mṛga*, [the suffix *ṭhak* is applied] in the sense of 'one who kills'. Thus we have *mātsikaḥ* and *śāpharikaḥ*. However, this does not apply to synonyms of these words; for instance, one does not say *animiṣān hanti*. Regarding this, the *Bhāṣya* states: "In the case of *mīna*, [the suffix] is desired. Thus we have *mainikaḥ*. As for *mṛga* and *pakṣin*, however, the mention of the *ṇin* suffix should be made. Consequently, commentators explain that there is the inclusion of the actual forms (*svarūpa*), their synonyms, and their specific varieties (*viśeṣa*).

In the present case, regarding *vṛkṣa* and so on, as well as *rājan* and so on, the intended result is established by the very logic [of the rule], and this will be explained in those respective places. From here onwards, however, it should be understood that everything is based solely on explicit scriptural statement (*vācanika*).
*Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.69:* "An *aṇ* and that which is marked with *u* (*udit*) shall be the designation for its homogeneous (*savarṇa*) sound, provided it is not itself an affix (*apratyaya*).

Here, it is stated that the *ṇ* refers to the subsequent *ṇ*. An *aṇ* and an *udit* shall be the technical name for their homogeneous sounds, except when they are being prescribed [as such]. By the force of the word *ca* ("and"), this also applies to their own form (*svarūpa*). Examples: 1. From *asya cvau* (Pāṇini 7.4.32): *śuklī syāt*, *mālī syāt*. 2. From *eranekāco'saṃyogapūrvasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.82): *cicyatuḥ*, *ninyatuḥ*. 3. From *ṛdorap* (Pāṇini 3.3.56): *yavaḥ*, *stavaḥ*, *lavaḥ*, *pavaḥ*. 4. From *uraṇ raparaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.51): *karttā*, *kirati*.

Nor should it be argued that, in this way, the suffix *ap* would also apply after short-final roots such as *kṛñ* and others under the rule *ṛdorap*; for that would result in the redundancy of the explicit mention of the long vowel (*dīrgha*). [Objection: Even so, in the rule *aṣṭana ā vibhaktau* (Pāṇini 7.2.84), the inclusion of the homogeneous vowels (*savarṇagraha*) remains unavoidable.

If it is argued that there is indeed a functional necessity even there—since the mention of "long" (*dīrgha*) serves both purposes so that when a short vowel is uttered, it may be understood as having the duration of one *mātrā* rather than half a *mātrā*—we say no. This is because of the prohibition in Pāṇini’s sūtra *apratyayaḥ* (P. 1.1.69), and because it has already been stated previously that long vowels, not being *aṇ*, do not possess the capacity to include their homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇagrāhakatā*). If it is then objected: "If long vowels are not *aṇ*, then in forms such as *kārakaḥ* and *hārakaḥ*, the substitution of *ra* for *ṛ* (*raparatva*) would not be obtained," you are mistaken.

We do not say that long vowels are never brought forward by the mention of *aṇ*; rather, in the rule for the mention of *aṇ* (*aṇgrahaṇakaśāstra*) and in the instruction of phonemes (*varṇopadeśa*) which depend upon it, they are indeed included. However, in other instances, because the maxim of the "incompleteness of the sentence" (*vākyāparisamāptinyāya*) does not apply, the inclusion of long vowels by the mention of *aṇ* certainly exists—this is the truth.

The rule *kuhoścuḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.62) [teaches that] the letter *c* [is substituted for *k* and *h*]; thus, [from the root *gad*, we derive] *jagāda*. However, the prohibition regarding what is "not a suffix" (*apratyaya*) does not apply to those marked with the *ugit* designation, because of the very purpose of applying the *ugit* marker. For this reason, they say: "An *aṇ* vowel being taught [as a substitute] does not include its homogeneous counterparts" (Pāṇinian Bhāṣya). But *tuk*, *luk*, *nuk*, *tuṭ*, and so forth, are not [considered] *udit* (marked with *u*), because of the accepted doctrine that "the followers of Pāṇini [traditionally] declare the presence of the *anunāsika* [nasal quality]. Why [specify] "not a suffix"? So that suffixes, augments, and substitutes being taught [with an *aṇ*] do not become grāhakas (inclusive) of their homogeneous counterparts.

In the rules *ata iñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95), *idama iś* (Pāṇini 5.3.3), *ārddhadhātukasyeṅ* (Pāṇini 7.2.35), *bhuvo vuk* (Pāṇini 6.4.88), and *am sambuddhau* (Pāṇini 8.1.99), the designation *it* applies specifically to the words *iñ* and so forth that occur within the sūtras themselves, because of the statement "here, in all cases, [the designation applies] to the instruction" (*iha hi sarvatropadeśe*). Although elision (*lopa*) is sublated there by the sequence of operations, it nevertheless proceeds during the analysis of the actual form of the word.

Therefore, by the force of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) "its own form" (*svaṃ rūpam*, Pāṇini 1.1.68), the presentation of the word-meaning that occurs is necessarily that of the form itself as divested of its *anubandhas*. Consequently, since the indicator (*upasthāpaka*) possesses the property of being *aṇ*, the inclusion of all homogeneous letters (*savarṇagrahaṇa*) which would otherwise follow is appropriately barred.

For this very reason, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that even for those sounds such as *ṇ* and others bearing the designation *it*, as well as for the vowel *a* situated between *la* and *ṇ*—just like the vowel *a* [of the fourteen-sūtra group] whose purpose is mere pronunciation—the designation (*saṃjñā*) operates only by being included within the other [sounds], because upon the examination of the word-form (*pada-paryālocanā*), they are set aside according to the maxim: "And elision (*lopa*) is more powerful. This is clearly stated in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the sūtras *alo 'ntyāt pūrva upadhā* (Pāṇini 1.1.65) and *tasminniti nirdiṣṭe* (Pāṇini 1.1.66).

In rules such as *iṭa īṭi* and *iko yaṇ aci*, the case-ending (vibhakti) follows that which bears an *it*-marker (*sānubandha*) because, in the initial cognition, that [element with the marker] alone possesses meaningfulness (*arthavattva*) by virtue of being the object of the qualified [denotation]. For another element indeed presents itself later, but it is not [the one] employed [in the rule]; so how could a case-ending be formed from that? However, the operation of the *it*-designation applies to the thing signified (*pratyāyya*) according to the maxim *ānarthakyāt tadaṅgeṣu* ("because of meaninglessness, [an operation applies] to its parts"). The application of the meaning of the case-ending is also like this.

Indeed, it is observed that in cases such as the augment *ṅmuṭ*, the gender-mark applied to the indicator (*upasthāpaka*) brings about the result in that which is signified by it. This is the general direction [of the argument].

It might be argued: "In the manner stated, the *it*-designation applied to the word *ut* in the rule *udoṣṭhyapūrvasya* (Pāṇini 7.1.102) would cause the *tit-svara* accent to apply to the *lakṣya* [the actual form]. This is true; therefore, recognize that for this very reason the ancient teachers exerted great effort to provide a solution. If it is asked, "How then was the effort directed toward refuting that in the rule *eoṅ*? understand that it was because the letter *t* has already fulfilled its purpose by determining the duration [of the preceding vowel], and thus differs from other *anubandhas*.

For this very reason, in the word *vaiyākaraṇaḥ*, the *cit-svara* accent does not apply to the diphthongs (*ai* and *au*). Similarly, in *pacasva*, the same applies to the suffix *śap*. This is because, in the rule *na yvābhyām* (Pāṇini 7.3.3) and in the phrase *acaḥ parasya dve* (Pāṇini 6.1.2), the letter *c* in the diphthongs *ai* and *au* has already been consumed in the formation of the *pratyāhāra*. Alternatively, let there be no designation as *it* for the letters contained within the rules themselves, such as *iñ*, *iṣ*, and so on; rather, let that designation apply only to those items which constitute the actual meaning of the words [within the rules], due to their proximity to the result. If it is argued that these [letters in the rules] are not taught [as independent elements], we reply that it is the same for those [items in the *pratyāhāra*], as they do not themselves bear the fruit [of grammatical operations].

If it is argued that, by virtue of contextual capacity (*sāmarthya*), the term *la* refers to the final [element] through a mediated relationship (*paraṃparā-sambandha*), then the same applies to the name (*saṃjñā*): let it also be understood as such by virtue of contextual capacity. For "being final" (*antyatva*) in the instruction (*upadeśa*) is based on a commonality of sequence (*ānupūrvī-sājātya*) residing in the indicator (*pratyāyaka*), since it is impossible for it to exist in the actual linguistic usage (*prāyogika*). And this does not apply to those [sounds] followed by *t*, because the letter *t* is absent from what is to be indicated (*pratyāyya*). This is the general direction of the argument.

Let us follow the explicit statement (*prakata*). Even though the substitution of *u* is being enjoined, it includes its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*) because of the evidence provided by the inclusion of the *t* in the rule *ṛta ut* (Pāṇini 6.1.111). By this means, in forms such as *amunā* and *adbhyām*, the short vowel is replaced by a short vowel and the long vowel by a long vowel, which is thus established. Nor should it be argued that, on these grounds, the suffix *u* in *sanāśaṃsabhikṣa uḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.168) would also include its homogeneous counterparts; for it has been stated that this is an indicatory mark (*jñāpaka*) specifically concerning the domain of substitutes.

Alternatively, in the very rule *adaso'seḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.80), let there be a collective *dvandva* compound consisting of *u* and *ū*. It is for this very reason that the elision (*luk*) of the nominative suffix *su* has been applied in the citation. And it is for this same reason that the authors of the Bhāṣya, in order to reject the mention of the modified form *goha* in the rule *ūdupadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.89), stated that another vowel *ū* is to be inserted (*praśleṣa*).

But even so, in the rule *akaḥ savarṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.101), let the letter *a* be the indicator (*grāhaka*) of the eighteen [variants of the vowel *a*], because it possesses the *am* designation. And let that very same [letter *a*] be the indicator of the vowels *i*, *u*, and so on, since it is stated that "the first [vowel] is [the name] by means of the last [vowel]" (Pāṇini 1.1.71). However, how can the vowels *ī*, *ī*, and so on, be the things indicated (*grāhya*)? For indeed, no word denoting them is employed in that sūtra.

If it is argued that by the word *an* (*aṅ*), the vowels beginning with *i* are also presented, then let them indeed lead to the sentence-meaning, since the sentence-meaning consists in the connection between word-meanings. However, they do not present their own [specific] meanings, as it has been stated that they are not uttered [as such]. For this very reason, in expressions such as *ṛcaṃ vetti* ("he knows the Ṛgveda"), the meaning is "he knows a specific word," and not "he knows its meaning. As it was said by the author of the Vārttika: "In that case, when there is a reference to a pratyāhāra, there is no inclusion of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa*) because they have not been taught [as such]."

If it is argued that [the short vowel] is not mentioned because of the cognition of its long counterpart, [we reply: since a word conveys meaning only when it is being uttered, there is no mention [of the short vowel]. This means that for a word that is not being perceived, there is no "non-utterance," which is to say, it lacks the capacity to convey meaning. To this, it is said: in all cases involving the inclusion of a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviated term), there is a well-established secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding what is expressed by its own constituent parts; this is indicated by the rule *dīrghājjasica* (Pāṇini 6.1.105). For in the rule *prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.102), the term *akaḥ* is understood as a governing element (*anuvartate*).

Furthermore, there is no long vowel not denoted by the term *āc* that could serve as the object of this prohibition. If it is argued that the vowel *ā* [of the root *āp*] exists [as such], we say no; for the prohibition is already established there by the rule *nādici* (Pāṇini 6.1.104). Moreover, the grammatical indications (*liṅga*) such as the rule *pvādīnām* (Pāṇini 7.3.90) also serve as evidence here. If this were so, however, the mention of the root *īṅ* [in the form *īdādīnām*] in the sūtra *iko yaṇaci* (Pāṇini 6.1.77) would be impossible, due to the contradiction of two simultaneous functions [of the same word].

If it is argued that, in that case, forms such as *sudhyupāsyaḥ* and *dadhyānaya* would not be established, we say no; for when there is an intended meaning (*tātparya*), there is no obstacle to accepting two simultaneous operations (*vṛtti*). Moreover, in this context, the grammatical indications (*nirdeśa*) such as *āṇnadyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.112) serve as indicators of that intended meaning. However, if—out of faith in the opinion of the ancient grammarians—you do not accept two simultaneous operations, then let there simply be indication (*lakṣaṇā*) here even for the root *īṅ*, just as there is for the words *ig* and *ac*. This is because there is no difference in the fact that both are equally denoted by their own respective designators (*svavācyatva*).
Furthermore, the fact that they possess a denotative capacity (*vācyatā*) in the ultimate sense is another matter entirely.

But even so, in cases such as *śarīram*, the substitution of *ya* for the letter *śa* would result due to the similarity of their place of articulation (*sthāna-sāmya*), because the long vowel denoted by the term *ik* is indeed a *savarṇa* (homogeneous) of *śa*, and thus *śa* is included by the mention of *ik*. Likewise, in cases such as *śītalam*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of *yaṇ*-substitution; for although the long vowel does not follow, there is no evidence (*māna*) to establish a connection with it based on the fact that the status of being denotable by the word *ak* rests solely upon the long vowel.

To this it is replied: This fault—namely, that there would be the substitution of *y* for *ś*—would occur if we were to assert a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for [the term *savarṇa*] in the sense of what is similar to its own denotation. We, however, speak of it only when there exists something denoted by its own denotation. And the long vowel *ī* is not the denoter of *ś*, because it has been repeatedly established that long vowels, being non-atomic (*anaṇ*), do not include their homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*). Furthermore, according to the view of the Bhāṣya, it has been stated that there is no homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between vowels (*ac*) and consonants (*hal*) at all.

Thus, the resulting meaning here is as follows: the letter *a* is the designation for eighteen [sounds]; likewise, *i* and *u* are so. However, *ṛ* and *ḷ* are synonymous terms that serve as the designation for thirty [sounds], because the homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*) between the *ṛ* and *ḷ* phonemes has been explicitly stated, or else because it is indicated by the very observation of the absence of *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form) in the rule *ṛtyakaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.128), despite the presence of *ṛ* and *ḷ* in the rule *ṛlṛk* (Māheśvara Sūtra 2). Nor is the formulation of two designations for the same set of individual instances purposeless, since no other rule has been formulated here for that specific purpose.

However, there are twelve names for the vowels. *Ya* and *va* are the names for two [vowels each], while *ra* and *ha* are the names for themselves alone. Although it might follow that the letter *ha* is the name for the vowel *ā*, nevertheless, one must not forget that an effort was made precisely in the rule "vowels and consonants do not coalesce" (*nājjhalau*, Pāṇini 1.1.10) to avoid that consequence.

The author of the Vārttika has rejected the inclusion of the term *aṇ* here. In his view, [the desired results] are established through the mention of the genus (*jāti*) in rules such as *asya cvau* (Pāṇini 7.4.32). Furthermore, the shortness (*hrasvatva*), which is an attribute of the subject being restated (*anuvādya*), is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣā*), just as singularity is not intended in the case of "one cow" (*gograha*). However, in the context of an injunction (*vidhipradeśa*), it is intended to be significant, just as the singularity of the animal [is intended] in the rule for sacrificing an animal (*paśvekatva*). Thus, all that is desired is established. Although in this position it is difficult to justify the inclusion of *ḷ* by means of *ṛ*, it may nevertheless be resolved according to the method stated in the sūtra *ṛlṛk* (Pāṇini 1.1.5); such is the direction. *taparaḥ tatkālasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.70).

That which follows *ta* is called *tapara*; that which follows *t* is also called *tapara*. Both types of *tapara* serve as indicators (*grāhaka*) for their own time-period. By this rule, *at* is the name for six vowels, and *ṛt* is the name for twelve. For this very reason, in the rule "after a prefix, before a verbal root beginning with *ṛ*" (Pāṇini 6.1.91), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the *ḷ*-vowel is included due to its homogeneity (*sāvarṇya*), but the long vowel is not included because of the *tapara* designation.

An example of a genitive compound (*pañcamī-samāsa*) is "vṛddhir ādaic" (Pāṇini 1.1.1). For it has been stated here that the status of being subsequent (*tātparatva*), when applied to a technical name (*saṃjñā*), bears fruit for the two things named (*saṃjñin*), just as the *ṭit*-status [of the suffix] bears fruit for the augment *ṅmuṭ*. However, there is no fault whatsoever in the view that the word, though derived through secondary indication (*lākṣaṇika*), serves as a reminder [of the rule] through an indirect connection. This is likewise established in the case of "adeṅ guṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.1.2), because in that instance the letter *t* lacks the functional capacity to serve both purposes.

If, however, according to the method to be explained in the *Kālasūtra*, the phrase "in the case of a technical name (*saṃjñā*)" from the rule *aṇudit* is understood to carry over [to this rule], or if, by resorting to the *kāryakāla* view, the inclusion of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇagrahaṇa*) is excluded precisely because [the vowel] is being taught as something yet to be produced (*bhāvyamānatva*), then the addition of the *tapara* marker in the *vṛddhi* rule is for the sake of clarity. In this case, the *Bhāṣya* is consistent. But under the view that "qualities (*guṇa*) are differentiators," the addition of the *tapara* marker in the *vṛddhi* rule serves both purposes, because [the vowel] would otherwise include those endowed with other qualities.

That the inclusion of the term *amaṇ* in the rule *aṇuditsavarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.69) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for its differentiating function has already been established in the commentary on the rule *hal* (Pāṇini 1.2.10). Likewise, the word *tatkālasya* found in this very rule (*aṇuditsavarṇasya...*) is also an indicator here. Otherwise, since the result would be established simply by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the phrase *svasya rūpasya*, what purpose would that [word] serve? Nor is it intended for the sake of including the *ḷ*-vowel through similarity of place and organ (*sāvarṇya*). For if that were the case, he would have included the *ḷ* there itself, or he would have pronounced the two *r*s situated between [the vowels] as prescribed in the Vārttika *ṛti ṛ vā*.

Since the result is already established by the mere word *ā*, the inclusion of the term "long" (*dīrgha*) in the rule *ato dīrgho yañi* (Pāṇini 7.3.101) is also an indicator (*liṅga*) for this point; such is the direction of the argument. For this very reason, this sūtra has been explained in two ways in the Bhāṣya and other works: as a prescriptive rule (*vidhi*) and as a restrictive rule (*niyama*). To explain: the term *aṇ* does not carry over [from the previous rule]. Consequently, in cases like *ākārāt* (from the letter *ā*), where the vowel is not an *aṇ*, all *sarvaṇa* vowels of the same duration are included by this [sūtra], even though there is a difference in their *guṇa* quality. However, in rules such as *ato bhisa ais* (Pāṇini 7.1.9), when both [rules] would otherwise apply, this [present sūtra] alone takes effect due to its posteriority.

If it is objected that it has been stated that there is no relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) between technical designations (*saṃjñā*), [we reply: True; indeed, coexistence (*samāveśa*) occurs when there is no contradiction and when there is a difference in result. But here, there is indeed a contradiction. For it is contradictory to say "eighteen are to be grasped" and "six are to be grasped," since linguistic usage based on number is observed to function only through mutual exclusion. For this very reason, they say that the Vārttika on the rule *chāder ghe* (Pāṇini 6.4.96)—namely, "it should be stated that [the elision of the *ṭi*] does not apply to a prefix consisting of two or more syllables"—is consistent with our position.

In reality, however, no number is mentioned here in these two technical rules (*saṃjñāsūtra*) such that there would be a contradiction; rather, the truth is that the relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) is inferred from the force of the use of the *tapara* marker in rules such as "ato bhisaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.9). In fact, this technical name is qualified by the letter *t*, and is not merely the phoneme *aṇ*. In the expression "of its duration" (*tatkālasya*), the word "its" (*tat*) refers only to the thing to be qualified (*viśeṣya*), and not to the qualified entity itself. Furthermore, even in the view of the ancients, there is indeed a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) toward something similar to the time of its pronunciation.

Even in the case of pronouns, since *lakṣaṇā* (indirect indication) is established in both the earlier and later systems (*tantras*) in instances such as "of this very [sāman], the Vāravantīya" and "That thou art," there is no possibility at all of the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the suffixes *ṭi*, *ghu*, and *bha*—contained within the term *aṇ*—would be understood as denoting the whole word because they are merely parts of a word and thus devoid of meaning. This being the case, the production of case-endings (*vibhakti-utpatti*) is also consistent.

As for Haradatta’s statement in the *Vṛddhi-sūtra*—"here the vowel *a* is meaningful when accompanied by *sa* and *e* in actual usage"—the conclusion is that it must be interpreted according to the method of the ancients (*prācām rīti*). This, then, is the position that [the mention of *aṇ*] serves the purpose of an injunction (*vidhy-arthatā-pakṣa*).

When "aṇ" is understood to carry over [from the previous rule], then this [sūtra] is for the purpose of restriction: "An *aṇ* followed by *tapara* [denotes] only its own duration. Since vowel qualities (*guṇa*) do not cause differentiation, there is no fault regarding those that are not *aṇ*. In this view, the mention of "its own duration" (*tatkālatva*) could be omitted, and the non-recurrence of the term "aṇ" is also unnecessary; for the desired result is established even by the restriction: "A *tapara* denotes only its own form."

In the rule *diva aut* (Pāṇini 7.1.84), the inclusion of the *ta*-marker (*taparakaraṇa*) is for the sake of the accent (*svarārtha*), and not for the purpose of determining the duration of time; for since the vowel is being taught as a *bhāvyamāna* (an element in the process of formation), there is no possibility of its including homogeneous vowels (*savarṇagrahaṇa*). Thus, the circumflex (*svarita*) is employed—as in: *dyauḥ pitaḥ pṛthivi mātara dhruk*. However, one should understand that the use of the acute (*udātta*) in *pṛthivī uta dyauḥ* pertains to the word *dyauḥ* itself.

However, in the rules *auto ’mśasoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.93) and *acca gheḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.119), the addition of the marker *t* (the *tapara* designation) is for the sake of ease of pronunciation (*mukhasukhārtham*), according to the traditional explanation (*vyākhyāna*). Therefore, the authors of the Vṛtti, Haradatta, and others maintain that in examples such as *samidhāne agnau*, the rule *tit svaritam* (Pāṇini 6.1.175) does not apply.

As for what was stated by Jayāditya and others regarding the rule *na vibhaktau tusmāḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.4)—namely, that the prohibition [of the *it*-marker] does not apply to the rule *iṭo 't* (Pāṇini 3.4.106) because the inclusion of the marker *u* in *idamasthamuḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.24) indicates its non-universality—that is merely a concession (*abhyupagamavāda*), since it would result in the accentuation of the *tit* suffix. Nor is such a result desired, as we hear the final syllable as udātta in examples such as *bhakṣīya tavā rādhas*.

Therefore, even in the rule *iṭot* (Pāṇini 3.4.106), the letter *t* is for the sake of ease of pronunciation (*mukhasukha*). It is the same in rules such as *eta īdbahuvacane* (Pāṇini 8.2.81) and *urṛt* (Pāṇini 7.4.6); this is the general direction. In reality, however, it is exactly the same in the rule *diva aut* (Pāṇini 7.1.84) as well; for when a *hal* [consonant] characterized by falling away (*sraṃsanadharmī*) is made *anudātta*, the *svarita* accent is established simply by the rule *udāttasvaritayoryaṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.4). It might be argued: there are three tempos—fast (*druta*), medium (*madhyama*), and slow (*vilambita*). As it has been said:
"The rapid tempo (*drutā vṛtti*) is for the purpose of practice; the medium tempo (*madhyamā*) is for the purpose of performance;
but the slow tempo (*vilambitā*) is desired for the purpose of instruction for students.

These [tempos] increase by one-third respectively. To illustrate: when a particular *ṛc* is recited in the rapid tempo, nine *palas* of water flow out; when that same *ṛc* is recited in the medium tempo, twelve [palas] flow out; but in the slow tempo, sixteen [palas] flow out.

This being the case, if the author of the Sūtra had employed the *tapara* marker for the slow (*vilambita*) tempo, but not for the medium (*madhyama*) or fast (*druta*) tempos, then the rule *ato bhisa ais* (Pāṇini 7.1.9) would not apply at the time of recitation according to another tempo; for by the restriction of duration, it would exclude other tempos just as it excludes the long (*dīrgha*) and protracted (*pluta*) vowels. Thus states the Vārttika: "If the *tapara* marker is used for the fast tempo, an addition must be made for the medium and slow tempos, because of the difference in duration."

For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa states in the *Saṃhitā-saṃjñā-sūtra* that the vowel in the word "madhya" is short due to its being a *nipātana* (irregular formation). On this point, the authors of the *Siddhānta-vārttika* say: "The phonemes are established as existing; however, their modes of occurrence (*vṛtti*) are distinguished by the speaker’s utterance being either slow or rapid."

The meaning of this is as follows: although the manifesting sound (dhvani) persists for a long duration, it manifests [the phoneme] only up to the limit of a single mora (mātrā). That which is produced at a subsequent time, however, continues by itself and does not manifest another [phoneme]. Alternatively, in all three tempos (vṛtti), the manifesting sound of a short vowel lasts for exactly one mora.

In the case of the medium and slow tempos (*madhyama-vilambitayoḥ*), a further manifestation is produced by another sound that arises subsequently with a duration less than that of the initial sound which was grasped first; however, the manifested entity (*abhivyaṅgya*) itself does not differ. Likewise, even in the case of a long manifestor, the initial sound is always of two moras (*dvimātra*); the subsequent one, however, is less than that—this is the beginning of the argument. The manifested entities, however, are inherently distinct from one another. And all this has been indicated by Kaiyaṭa:
"Therefore, their pronunciation is perceived as having the duration of one mora."

"A phoneme (*varṇa*) is not itself measured by its own duration; it may be two measures (*mātra*) or three measures. As for the statement of the author Rāṇaka in the *Śabdāntarādhikaraṇa*—namely, "How could this [phoneme] not be so?"—this must be considered by the wise. However, phonemes are indeed eternal (*nitya*). But according to the theory of the production of phonemes (*varṇotpatti-pakṣa*), one must necessarily admit some sound (*dhvani*) that arises simultaneously with them and is perceptible even from a distance. It is precisely due to the difference in the duration (*kāla*) of this [sound] that there are three types of manifestation (*vṛtti*). The phonemes, however, remain of a single form despite the differences in their manifestation.
Some have even postulated that the individual instances (*vyakti*) themselves are what constitute this "sound" (*dhvani*). (Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇakāra)

In this view, however, the status of being an individual (vyaktitva) belongs only to that which is delimited by a specific limiting adjunct (upādhi) in the form of time; such is the direction of the argument.
And it has been stated in the Bhāṣya:
"Sound and the sphoṭa belong to words; indeed, it is sound that is perceived."

"Small and great, both [of these] belong to some by their very nature. This is the meaning: sound is twofold, namely the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) and the manifested (*vyaṅgya*). That resonance (*dhvani*) which is the connection between sounds as manifested and [other sounds] as manifestors is perceived as both great and small. Both of these—the manifested and the form of the manifestor—belong only to certain [sounds], namely those produced by the operation of the palate and other [articulatory organs], but not even to those produced by drums and the like. Why? "By their very nature," that is, due to the difference in their causes. Here, the term "both" (*ubhaya*) is a designation emphasizing the state; the meaning is "the state of being both."
"An initial [phoneme], together with the final *it*, [denotes] itself and the intervening [phonemes]. (Pāṇini 1.1.71).

An initial phoneme, or a group of phonemes, being pronounced together with the final *it*, shall be the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) for the intervening phonemes, as well as for its own form. For example, *al* is a single phoneme; however, *kṛñ* is a group. Here, in the sense of "becoming that which it was not before," the pratyāhāra is formed by the letter *ñ* from the rule *kṛño dvitīya* (Pāṇini 5.4.58), following the rule *kṛbhvasti* (Pāṇini 5.4.50). First, there are the two parts, the beginning and the end; by means of these two, the whole—the aggregate—is implied.

And because there is no simultaneous application [of a grammatical operation] to the entire object of reference (*lakṣya*), the technical name (*saṃjñā*) entering into its constituent parts comes to rest upon those situated in the middle, and not on the first and last [letters], since their subservience to another purpose is determined by their inclusion within the very form of the name itself. Therefore, the term *svarūpam* (its own form) is understood to follow [from the previous rule]. And "its own form" is taken as referring only to the initial [letter], not to the final one, because of the latter's lack of predominance. For the instrumental case in *antena* ("by the final") is used in the sense of a subordinate element. Consequently, Kaiyaṭa and others maintain that in examples such as *dadhyatra*, only the letter *y* is applied, and not the letter *y* accompanied by *ṇ*.

In this regard, the following must be stated: "Since, upon examining the Bhāṣya and other works situated within the *grahaṇa-śāstra* (the rule of inclusion), it is established that in the case of *pratyāhāras*, the initial [phoneme] is the denoter (*vācaka*)—as the *grahaṇaka-śāstra* has its scope there—the denotative power rests solely in the first letter, while the final one merely indicates the intended meaning (*tātparya-grāhaka*). Furthermore, because of the inclusion of both [the first and last letters], the case-ending is produced from the [composite] qualified form; thus, it differs from other types of indicators (*dyotaka*). This is the settled conclusion.

In that case, how can there be any possibility of the final letter being designated as the *saṃjñin* (the thing named) when it has already been assigned the technical name *it*? Otherwise, what would be the remedy for the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of names such as "vowel" (*ac*) and so on to the letter *ṇ* and others? Furthermore, even if the specific [substitution] were granted the name *yaṇ*, the application of the term *yaṇ* in the example "dadhy atra" would still be inconsistent; for by the same logic, the letter *ik* itself would be expected to be the *sthānin* (the original element), making it impossible for the vowel *i* to be the *sthānin*.

The commentators [the Vṛttikāras] ask: "What is meant by 'by the last'? They say: "It should not be taken as the final element of the third singular case ending *suṭ*. Their intention is that, based on the grammatical indications in rules such as *ṭāṅasiṅasām* (Pāṇini 7.1.22), it is determined that the letter *ṭ* is not a final element belonging to the preceding part [of the suffix]. If it is objected: "Even so, for a group (*saṅgha*) ending in *ṭ*, the letter *ṭ* would still indeed be the final element of the suffix *ṭā*," we reply: No, because it lacks the status of being the final element of a defined unit (*vyavasita*).

For in this regard, Haradatta, in his commentary on the rule *suḍanapuṃsakasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.43), states that a pratyāhāra consists of that which has the designation *it* by virtue of being final. Nor does this result in the failure of the *rapratyāhāra*, because even though it is not final, a pratyāhāra can still be formed due to the promise (*pratijñā*) regarding the nasalization in the *laṇ* rule.

However, this must be addressed: since the *ṭi*-designation of *auṭ* serves no other purpose, the *suṭ-pratyāhāra* is formed by that very [finality], owing to proximity (*pratyāsatti*). Thus, the mention of "final" (*antya*) should not be necessary. To this, the following solution is offered: let the initial [letter] accompanied by the middle *it* not be a grasper (*grāhaka*) for those that follow it as well.
Thus, the mention of "ādi" (beginning) is for the purpose that the middle [term] joined with the last [term] should not serve as a designation (*saṃjñā*) for the preceding ones.

Why is "iti" used? So that there may be a pratyāhāra consisting of *r*. For it has been stated that this [pratyāhāra] occurs even with the final [term], by virtue of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) concerning nasalization (*anunāsika*). And this is not obtainable in the absence of "iti."

The middle phoneme, together with what precedes it (*saha ādinā*) and what follows it (*saha antena*), is designated by the technical term *aṇ* and so forth; this is the meaning. Because of the mention of both "beginning" and "end," the middle phoneme along with its neighbors is understood. The rule *svaṃ rūpam* ("its own form") also carries over [from the previous sūtra]. Just as in the case of the designations *vṛddhi*, *guṇa*, etc., here too, because of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), it is understood to be a technical designation (*saṃjñā*). And they say that under this interpretation, there is no fear of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) even in the case of the rule *halantyam* (Pāṇini 1.3.3).
Since the representation of a whole through its initial and final parts is already established, this [sūtra] is intended to exclude the final phoneme [from being called *aṇ*].
That by which a rule [is conditioned] applies to that which ends with it. (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.72)

Specifically, there should be a designation for that which ends in it (the suffix), as well as for its own form: *er-ac* (Pāṇini 3.3.56) yields *vayaḥ*, *jayaḥ*, and *ayaḥ*; *or-āvaśyake* (Pāṇini 3.1.124) yields *avaśyalāvyam*. Here, the instrumental case in *yena* denotes the instrument (*karaṇa*), and not the agent (*kartṛ*), because it is superseded by the genitive case characterized by its connection with a *kṛt*-suffix. For the term *vidhiḥ* contains the *kvip* suffix in the sense of the object (*karman*). Since the object is thus already expressed, this is not the domain of the restrictive rule *ubhayaprāptau* (Pāṇini 2.3.66). Furthermore, the instrument is dependent, since it possesses the status of an instrument only when presided over by an agent.

Thus, in this context, dependence (*pāratantrya*) is indicated by the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*). As for the objection raised by the Naiyāyikas that "there is no indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the case of a *sub*-suffix denoting separation (*vimukti*"), it is without foundation. Nor is the basis for that [objection] the consequence of rendering the grammatical rules (*anuśāsana*) for suffixes useless, because that [consequence] applies equally to *tiṅ*-suffixes as well; for even you must admit that there is indication of activity (*vyāpāra*) in cases such as "the chariot goes" (*ratho gacchati*).

For this very reason, regarding the statement "he sprinkles the sacrificial oblations with the remnant of the *prayāja*," the Mīmāṃsakas explained it as "one should sprinkle the remnant of the *prayāja* upon the oblation"—this is the direction of the argument. Furthermore, in rules such as *erac* (Pāṇini 3.3.56), the dependence of the vowels *i*, *u*, and *ṛ* and the independence of the verbal roots and so forth do not exist by their own nature (*svarūpataḥ*), like axes [depending on] carpenters; rather, they are determined by intention (*vaivakṣika*). Consequently, it follows that the qualifier is subordinate, and its function is to serve as the designation for the qualificand, which is itself.

And the status of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) occurs in proximity to the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). This proximity, however, sometimes occurs through direct mention, as in "the dual ending *ī*, *ū*, or *e* is *pragṛhya*" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 1.1.11), where it refers to the dual ending; sometimes from the governing context of a term (*śabdādhikāra*), as in "after *e*, [there is] *ac*" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 3.3.56), where it refers to the verbal root (*dhātu*); and sometimes by implication (*ākṣepa*), as in "after an *ik*, [comes] a *jhal* [beginning suffix]" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 1.2.9), where it implies the verbal root by virtue of the suffix *san*.

In rules such as *iko yaṇ aci* (Pāṇini 6.1.77) and *eco 'yavāyāvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.78), there is no proximity of a qualified element (*viśeṣya*) by any means whatsoever; therefore, this [principle] does not apply here.

It might be argued as follows: In the rule *udoṣṭhyapūrvasya* (Pāṇini 7.1.102), the property of having an *oṣṭhya* [labial] vowel as a preceding element would qualify the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself, and not the *ṛ*-vowel. For that [term *oṣṭhyapūrva*], being a qualifier, is a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) for that which ends in *ṛ*. And a designation brings to mind the designated object (*saṃjñin*), but it does not itself undergo connection with qualifiers and so forth. Consequently, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *śaṅkīrṇam*, and under-extension (*avyāpti*) in cases such as *pūrttam*.

Likewise, in the rule *utaśca pratyayāt* (Pāṇini 6.4.106), the qualification "not preceded by a conjunct consonant" (*asaṃyogapūrvatva*) would apply either to the stem (*aṅga*) or to the suffix (*pratyaya*), but not to that which ends in the vowel *u*. Consequently, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in forms such as *aśnuhi*. If the qualification were applied to the stem, there would be over-extension in forms such as *takṣṇuhi*; if it were applied to the suffix, then while forms like *takṣṇuhi* would be correctly established, there would still be a fault in cases such as *aśnihi*.

On this point, they say: this technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is dependent upon the relationship between the subordinate (*guṇa*) and the principal (*pradhāna*). Thus, in rules such as *utaśca pratyayāt* (Pāṇini 6.4.106), at the time of connection with the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), the subordinate status is not yet manifested; having experienced that [subordination], the specific designation occurs subsequently when there is a connection with the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). For here, there is the qualification of the qualified (*viśiṣṭa-vaiśiṣṭya*), and not the application of a qualifier to the qualificand (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa*), according to the [traditional] commentary. Therefore, there is neither the qualification of the qualified, nor the presence of two [qualifications] in one place; such is the direction [of the argument].

And thus the Vārttika states: "If it is argued that 'by whatever [term] there is an injunction, it applies to that which ends in it,' then there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the qualifiers of the item being mentioned (grahaṇopādhi) would themselves become qualifiers of what ends in that item. But this is established because the qualifier and the qualified may be applied as desired. The meaning is: "of the qualifiers of the item being mentioned"—that is, of those such as "having an *uṣṭha* [labial] preceding," which are accepted as qualifiers of the item being mentioned.

By the phrase "because it is as desired," he shows this: among the four types of cognitions—namely, the cognition of a qualifier, the cognition of a qualified, and the cognition of the relation between the qualifier and the qualified—it is here accepted that only the cognition of the relation between the qualifier and the qualified (*viśiṣṭasya vaiśiṣṭyam*) is intended, and not the other three, both because of the [author's] explanation and in accordance with the observed usage (*lakṣya*). Here, many *vārttikas* have been composed to clarify the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) as it is accepted in our own school’s tenets (*siddhānta*).

For example: regarding the prohibition [of the elision of the case-ending] in rules prescribing compounds and suffixes—such as *dvitīyāśrita* (Pāṇini 2.1.24) and others—the words beginning with *śrita* are the qualificands (*viśeṣya*), and the nominal ending (*sup*) is their qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).
