Similarly, in rules such as *naḍādibhyaḥ phak* (Pāṇini 4.1.99), the words beginning with *naḍa* are the qualificands and the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is the qualifier; this is the resulting meaning.

By this, the statement that "there is no *tadantavidhi* [extension of a grammatical rule] to that which ends in a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that possesses a specific designation" is also explained; for Kaiyaṭa and others have stated in the commentary on the rule *diva ut* that this prohibition also applies to the same domain as the examples cited. For this very reason, in the rule *go-striyoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.48), it is explained as "that nominal stem which ends in *go*. By this, Haradatta and others—who attempt to extend the prohibition "that which possesses a specific designation" (*grahaṇavatā*) to rules such as *śeṣo ghyasakhi* (Pāṇini 1.4.7)—are refuted.

Let us return to the subject at hand. It has been stated that words such as *śrita* (relied upon) function as the qualificands (*viśeṣya*). Consequently, the compound governed by the rule *dvitīyā śrita* (Pāṇini 2.1.24) occurs only in cases like *kṛṣṇāśritaḥ* ("one who has relied on Kṛṣṇa"), and not in cases such as *kṛṣṇaṃ paramaśritaḥ* ("one who has supremely relied on Kṛṣṇa"). Similarly, regarding the rule *naḍādibhyaḥ phak* (Pāṇini 4.1.99), we have *nāḍāyanaḥ*. Here, however, the form *sautranāḍiḥ*—meaning "the descendant of Sutra-naḍa"—does not occur; rather, there is vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) in both members of the compound due to its inclusion in the *anuśatikādi* group.

Now, one might object: "In the case of *kṛṣṇaṃ paramaśritaḥ*, there is no possibility of compounding at all. For here, the case-ending (*sup*) is prescribed after the compound; therefore, that which ends in *śrita* must itself be a word ending in a case-ending (*subanta*). On this point, Kaiyaṭa and Haradatta state: "One should cite the vocative form as the example, namely *kṛṣṇa paramaśrita*. For this [form] becomes a word ending in a case-ending by the rule for the elision of case-endings (*pratyayalopa-lakṣaṇa*), and yet the element ending in *śrita* is heard [in the compound]. This may be so; however, even if in the final view (*siddhānta*) words such as *śrita* function as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), their status as being "ending in a case-ending" (*subantatva*) is nevertheless set aside in that context.

Nor should it be argued that, precisely because of this failure of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), words such as *śrita* and others possess a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) for bases ending in those [suffixes], since these very forms ending in the vocative case (*sambuddhi*) obtain their scope by prioritizing their primary meaning (*mukhyārtha*). For if that were so, expressions such as *kṛṣṇāśritam* would not be established. It is replied: In the section on compounds (*samāsa*) and secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), in all instances, words such as *śrita* and *naḍa* have only a secondary signification for bases ending in those [suffixes]. Even though the status of being a vocative ending is possible in rules such as *khaṭvākṣepe* (Pāṇini 2.1.46), the scriptural indications (*sautra-nirdeśa*) such as *ekavibhaktau* (Pāṇini 1.2.64) would otherwise fail to be established.

Therefore, since it is established that there is a uniform definition (*lakṣaṇa*) for every respective substitute by the force of the evidence dependent upon generality (*sāmānya*), it should be noted that the interpretation provided by Kaiyaṭa and Haradatta in their commentaries on the *Bhāṣya* and the *Vṛtti* regarding this point is to be rejected as being inconsistent with the text.

He states an exception to this: "with the exception of [pratyayas] having an *ugit* [marker], a vowel, and a specific mention. The resulting meaning is that the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is qualified by an *ugit* suffix and by a vowel. In the word *atimahatī* ("exceedingly great"), because it is an *upasarjana* (secondary member of a compound), the suffix *ṅīṣ*—which would otherwise apply by the rule for words beginning with *gaura*—is absent; however, the suffix *ṅīp* applies because it ends in an *ugit* suffix. Some maintain that the words *bṛhat* and *mahat* do not belong to the *gaurādi* group; and this is correct.

In the case of *mahate saubhagāya* and similar examples, the acute accent (*udāttatva*) of the case-ending is established by the fact that the Vārttika—"An addition [should be made] for *bṛhat* and *mahat* when there is the acute accent of a feminine suffix beginning with *nadī* or *aj*" (*nadyajādyudāttatve bṛhanmahator upasaṃkhyānam*)—is being formulated under the rule *śaturanumaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.176); thus, the acute accent of the *ṅīp* suffix is also established. [Regarding the formation of] *dākṣiḥ* from *ata iñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95): one might argue that here a "rule of extension to what ends in that" (*tadantavidhiḥ*) applies by virtue of necessity (*sāmarthyāt*), but this is not so, because the rule already finds its application in cases such as *asyāpatyam iḥ kāmaḥ*.

Nor should it be argued that, in this case, the substitution of *ñ* for *i* (the *ñittva*) would be purposeless; for in the rule *bāhvādibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.96), it serves its purpose through the appropriate application of vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) and the acute accent (*udātta*). If it is objected: "Even so, [the suffix] would apply only in cases like *aupagaviḥ*, but not in *dākṣiḥ*, because here the letter *a* is meaningless," we reply: No, for when a specific phoneme (*varṇa*) is mentioned in a rule, the technical maxim *arthavat-paribhāṣā* (which restricts grammatical operations to meaningful units) does not apply. Consequently, there is a Vārttika at the end of this sūtra which states: *al-eva-anarthakena* ("only when a meaningless phoneme is involved").

For this very reason, [the rule] is meaningful only through the mention of the *saṃghāta* (the entire complex). Consequently, the *iyaṅ* substitution prescribed by Pāṇini 6.4.79 (*striyāḥ*) occurs only here: in *striyau* and *paramastriyau*; it does not occur here in *śastrayau* or *śastryaḥ*. Likewise, in the rules 6.4.12 (*inhanpūṣārthamṇāṃ śau*) and 6.4.13 (*sau ca*), regarding the mention of *han* in the former, there is no inclusion of *plīhan*. Therefore, in forms such as *plīhānau*, the long vowel is established because the restriction (*niyama*) of 6.4.13 does not apply.

In the rule *udaḥ sthāstambhoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.61), even under the view that the term *pada* is carried over from the preceding rule *vā padāntasya* (Pāṇini 8.4.59), the word *ud-* alone is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). However, if it is not carried over, there is no deficiency whatsoever. In either case, because that which is meaningless (*anarthaka*) is not included, the following do not apply here: *garmutsthāsyati* and *garmutsuvarṇatṛṇayoḥ*.

One might object: "In the cases of *śastryau* and *plīhānau*, there is no possibility [of the application of the rule] at all, because of the statement: 'Under the heading of *pada* and *aṅga*, [the operation applies] to that [word] and to its subsequent member' (Pariśiṣṭa 29). For here, this [suffix] is neither at the end of that [word], nor is it subsequent to it. True; if the statement "under the heading of *pada* and *aṅga*" were in force, it would indeed be so. However, this has been refuted in the Bhāṣya, because the purpose is already served by the rule of "extension to what ends with that" (*tadantavidhi*) within the Sūtra itself.

For this very reason, by analyzing the compound as *paramaś cāsau atimahān ca* ("this is both supreme and exceedingly great"), the form *paramātimahān* is established; however, this would not be established if one were to rely on the [standard] rule of word-order (*vacana*). This is because, although the word *atimahat* has *mahat* as its final member (*uttarapada*), it is not an *aṅga* [for the purposes of that specific rule]; and although *parama-viśiṣṭa* is an *aṅga*, it lacks *mahat* as its final member. Nevertheless, by means of the "extension to the end of a compound" (*tadantavidhi*) taught in the Sūtra, both the lengthening of the vowel according to *sāntamahataḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.10) and the addition of the augment *num* conditioned by a vowel beginning with *u* (*ugillakṣaṇa*) are here successfully established.

Nor should the prohibition "by that which possesses [the suffix] *grahaṇa*" (*Pāṇini 1.1.72*) be suspected here, because it has been stated that this [prohibition] shares the same scope as "in the case of compounds and secondary derivatives" (*Kāśikāvṛtti*). By this [it is meant]:
"For those who desire to attain the supremely pure state of Brahman, beyond birth and old age... (*Kirātārjunīya* 5.22).

Thus, the prohibition regarding *bhāra* has been explained. An exception to the rule "in this very case" (*alaiva*) is stated in the Bhāṣya: "The mention of *an*, *in*, and *as* applies the rule of 'that which ends with [the element]' (*tadantavidhi*) both to meaningful and meaningless forms. For example: *an*—with the meaningful *rājñā* and the meaningless *sāmnā*; *in*—with the meaningful *daṇḍī* and the meaningless *vāgmī*; *as*—with the meaningful *supayāḥ* and the meaningless *susrotāḥ*.

[The word] *man-suśarmā* [is an example] with a meaningful [suffix], while *suprathimā* is one with a meaningless [suffix]. And that is established because, in the rule *iṇaḥ kaḥ ṣīdhvam* (Pāṇini 8.3.78), the mention of the term *aṅga* indicates that the paribhāṣā "the mention [of a suffix] refers only to that which has a meaning" (*arthavad-grahaṇa-paribhāṣā*) is not universally obligatory (*anitya*). Since in the case of *pariveviṣidhyam*, the non-inclusion of the word *ṣīdhvam* is already established precisely because it is meaningless, the point is: what is the purpose of the mention of *aṅga* for the sake of excluding that? This is the direction of the argument. The author of the Vārttika states other examples of the rule: * *mā hi dīdhyam* * *mā hi pīpyam* * *mā hi luluvidhvam* * *mā hi luluvīdhvam* * *mā hi luluvadhve* In these cases, the suffixes *hi* and *dhve* are meaningless; therefore, by the aforementioned principle, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* does not occur. However, since the suffix *dhvam* following the root *lū* is meaningful, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* does take place. Thus, the mention of *aṅga* is necessary to exclude the former instances and include the latter. Furthermore, there is no fault in the case of *mā hi dīdhyam*, etc., because the *aṅga* ending in *iṇ* is not followed by *ṣīdhvam*. As for the case of *mā hi luluvidhvam*, the mention of *aṅga* serves to indicate that the paribhāṣā is not universally obligatory. This is the view of the Vārttikakāra. However, the Bhāṣyakāra maintains that the paribhāṣā is indeed universally obligatory (*nitya*). He argues that even in the case of *pariveviṣidhyam*, the mention of *aṅga* is required to prevent the application of the rule to the *ṣīdhvam* belonging to the *liṅ* (optative) mood, which is meaningful. Therefore, the mention of *aṅga* is necessary to exclude the *ṣīdhvam* of the *liṅ* and to include the *ṣīdhvam* of the *luṅ* (aorist). Consequently, the paribhāṣā is established as being universally obligatory. This is the view of the Bhāṣyakāra. Furthermore, the mention of *aṅga* is necessary to exclude the *ṣīdhvam* of the *liṅ* and to include the *ṣīdhvam* of the *luṅ*. Thus, the paribhāṣā is established as being universally obligatory. This is the view of the Bhāṣyakāra. Moreover, the mention of *aṅga* is necessary to exclude the *ṣīdhvam* of the *liṅ* and to include the *ṣīdhvam* of the *luṅ*. Thus, the paribhāṣā is established as being universally obligatory. This is the view of the Bhāṣyakāra. Furthermore, the mention of *aṅga* is necessary to exclude the *ṣīdhvam* of the *liṅ* and to include the *ṣīdhvam* of the *luṅ*. Thus, the paribhāṣā is established as being universally obligatory. The purpose [of this rule] is for the designation (*saṃjñā*) of pronouns (*sarvanāman*) and indeclinables (*avyaya*). The implied meaning is that, by means of a designation based on its literal sense (*anvarthasaṃjñā*), the designatum (*saṃjñin*)—which has been suggested—is specified as "those beginning with *sarva*. This is the resulting sense.

Regarding the inclusion of *bhayāḍhyādi* in the rule for the formation of secondary derivatives (*upapadavidhi*): *bhaya* and *āḍhyādayaḥ* form a *dvandva* compound. Consequently, in the section on the suffix *khac*, under the sūtra "after the root *kṛ*, when *megha*, *ārti*, or *bhaya* are the accompanying words" (*Pāṇini 3.2.53*), the sentence is split so that *megha* and *ārti* qualify the accompanying word (*upapada*), while *bhaya* itself is the accompanying word. However, if one were to form a *dvandva* of the two words *bhaya* and *āḍhya*, and then form a *bahuvrīhi* with the word *ādi*, then even *kṣema*, *priya*, and *madra* would qualify the accompanying word.

In the established doctrine (siddhānta), however, *kṣema* and the others are qualified by a secondary member (*upapada*). For example: *bhayaṅkaraḥ*, *abhayaṅkaraḥ*; *āḍhyaṅkaraṇam*, *svāḍhyakaraṇam*. Regarding the prohibition of the feminine suffix *ṅīp*, there is the mention of the *svasṛ*-class [of words]: *svasā*, *paramasvasā*.

And there is the inclusion of *bista* and so forth among the immeasurables (*aparimāṇa*). The phrase "the purpose [of this] is for the sake of prohibition" continues to apply. The sense is that the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), brought into proximity by the numeral *dvi-* (two), is qualified by *bista* and the others. Thus: *dvibistā*, *dviparamabistā*; *dvyācitā*, *dviparamācitā*. Regarding *diti*: *daitya* and *āditya*. In the rule *dityadityāditya-* (Pāṇini 4.1.85), the mention of *aditi* need not be made; the sense is that it does not occur after *parama-* and so forth due to non-usage (*anabhidhāna*).

The suffix *aṇ* [is applied] after *roṇī* by the rule *rauṇī* (Pāṇini 4.2.78), which belongs to the group of four meanings (*cāturarthika*). Examples are: *rauṇaḥ*, *ājaka-rauṇaḥ*, and *saiṃhaka-rauṇaḥ*. Regarding the phrase "and of that" (*tasya ca*): it should be stated that this is a supplement (*śeṣa*) to all [rules] previously mentioned and those yet to be mentioned. Thus, the resulting meaning here is that the expression *svaṃ rūpam* ("its own form") is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*) into this sūtra. If it is argued that the form *raunaḥ* is established through the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), [the answer is]: no, because of the prohibition: "The principle of behaving like that which possesses a designation does not apply when [the base] is not a nominal stem" (*vyapadeśivadbhāvo 'prātipadikena*; Pāṇini-paribhāṣā 32). This is the view of the authors of the Bhāṣya.

Although the word *roṇī* is not a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), nevertheless, in the rule "not after a non-stem" (*na aprātipadikāt*), since the mention of "nominal stem" includes that which is qualified by gender, the meaning is that there is no application of the principle of "behaving like the designated" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*) even for those ending in feminine suffixes. For it will be stated in the rule on *ṅī* and *āp* suffixes that when a nominal stem is mentioned in any way whatsoever, that which is qualified by gender is included.

If it is argued that if [the word] *tasya* is stated and the term *svarūpagrahaṇa* (the taking of the word-form itself) is understood to follow, then the rule *vyapadeśivadbhāvo 'prātipadikena* (Pāṇini 1.1.27) would be rendered purposeless; we say no, because that rule finds its scope in cases such as *sūtrāntāṭ ṭhak* (Pāṇini 4.2.60) and *daśāntāḍ ḍaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.45).

Nor should it be argued that the designation [of the whole as the base] will not occur there simply by virtue of the inclusion of the word "anta" (end); for the inclusion of "anta" serves its purpose by setting aside the prohibition stated in the Vārttika: "There is a prohibition regarding the prescription of compounds and suffixes. This Paribhāṣā is established through a *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence). The *jñāpaka* here is the division of rules (*yogavibhāga*) found in Pāṇini 5.2.86–87: whereas one could have simply said "pūrvāt sapūrvād iniḥ," the rule is instead split into "pūrvād iniḥ" and "sapūrvācca."

In reality, however, as in the case of *bhayāḍhya* and so forth, even in rules such as *sūtrāntāṭ ṭhak* (Pāṇini 4.2.60) and *daśāntāḍ ḍaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.45), the desired forms are established merely by reversing the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva-vyatyāsa*). Thus, the inclusion of the word *anta* (end) in those rules is easily justified on its own strength; therefore, the recourse to this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) is redundant. Nor should it be argued that, if this were the case, the vowel *go* in *gokula* would undergo shortening, for the rule prescribes shortening for a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that ends in the word *go* when it functions as a subordinate member (*upasarjana*).

Furthermore, because proximity (*sannidhāna*) leads one to rely on the noun stem (*prātipadika*) itself as the qualificand, and because that [proximity] is absent in the case of the word *go*, for this very reason there is no shortening in the expression *rājakumārīputraḥ*. This is also because, even in the rule concerning "the noun stem ending in a feminine suffix which is a subordinate element (*upasarjana*)," one must rely on proximity. This is precisely your own way of accounting for the matter as well.

For the technical rules (*paribhāṣā*) stated here cannot apply; this is because Kaiyaṭa and Haradatta have stated in their commentary on the sūtra *div-au-ti-sū* that both technical rules—"that which possesses a designation behaves like the designated entity" (*vyapadeśivadbhāvaḥ*) and "with that which involves a formal mention" (*grahaṇavatā*)—have as their scope the prescription of suffixes (*pratyayavidhi*). And thus, the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) "from *pūrvādiniḥ*" (Pāṇini 5.2.87) would be redundant.

In short, since the inclusion of "that which ends in [the word]" (*tadantagrahaṇa*) is possible under the rule *pūrvādiniḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.87), the sūtra *sapūrvācca* (Pāṇini 5.2.87) would be redundant. Furthermore, since the desired result is established through the application of the *vyapadeśivadbhāva* principle, the present Vārttika *tasya* need not have been composed either. As for the principle *svaṃ rūpam*, it has already been refuted previously; such is the direction of the argument.

The suffix *yat* is applied after the words *ratha*, *sītā*, and *hala* when they are the basis for the application of a rule (*yadvidhau*). Regarding the rule *tadvahati* (Pāṇini 4.4.76), [the forms] are *rathyaḥ* and *paramarathyaḥ*. *Sītyam* and *paramasītyam* refer to a field; the meaning is "measured by a furrow" (*sītayā sammitam*), that is, "equal to a furrow. Regarding the rule *nauvayodharmaviṣamūlamūlasītātulābhyastāryatulyaprāpyavadhyānāmyasamasamitasammiteṣu* (Pāṇini 4.4.91), [the form is] *halyaḥ*, meaning "the plowing of a plow" (*halasya karṣaḥ*). This is because of the rule *matajanahalātkaraṇajalpakarṣeṣu* (Pāṇini 4.4.7), which prescribes *yat*. Why is it said "when they are the basis for the application of a rule"? Because otherwise, the suffix would be *ṭhak* according to the rule *halasīrāṭṭhak* (Pāṇini 4.3.124).

What is the purpose of the phrase *yadvidhau* ("in the rule prescribing *yat*")? Kaiyaṭa says: "It is so that, in the prescription of *ṭhak* by the rule *halasīrāṭṭhak* (Pāṇini 4.3.124), there may not be an inclusion of that which ends in those [words]. Here, this must be said: the rule *halasīrāt* (Pāṇini 4.3.124) is read twice—once under the governing heading *tasyedam* (Pāṇini 4.3.120) and once under the governing heading *tadvahati* (Pāṇini 4.4.91). In both instances, an application of the term *tadanta* (referring to words ending in those stems) is indeed intended. In the first case, because it belongs to the *prāgdīvyatīya* group, there is elision (*luk*); thus, we have *dvihalaḥ*.

The non-hearing of another [suffix]—as in *dvaihalikaḥ*. This is clearly stated in the fourth book of Haradatta’s work. And this is logical, because it is stated in the Bhāṣya that the word *ratha* is mentioned twice [in the rules *rathādyat* (Pāṇini 4.3.122) and *tadvahati* (Pāṇini 4.4.76)] for this very purpose. For, by the force of the mention of *ratha* and *haya* within the governing context (*adhikāra*) of "it carries" (*vahati*), the rule of extension to what ends in those words (*tadantavidhi*) is obtained; since there is no distinction, it would certainly apply in both cases.

Nor should it be argued that this is incorrect because the phrase "in which [the suffix] occurs" (*yadvidhau*) would be inapplicable; for that [phrase] is merely an incidental indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). Alternatively, although in the rule *rathādyat* (Pāṇini 4.3.121), when the word *voḍhari* is stated as an example of "from *ratha*, [the suffix *yat* applies] when referring to a part of a chariot," it is possible to justify a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) characterized by that [meaning], nevertheless, such justification cannot be maintained in the case of the mention of *hal*. Therefore, by virtue of the mention of *hal*, there is no application of the rule regarding "that which ends in" (*tadantavidhi*). Or rather, let it be that [the rule applies] only when a numeral is the preceding member (*saṃkhyāpūrvapada*); such is the intention of Kaiyaṭa.

In the section beginning with *tasmai hitam* (Pāṇini 5.1.5), under the sūtra *śarīrāvayavādyat* (Pāṇini 5.1.6), there is the vārttika *rathācca*. In that context as well, this rule of "extension to what ends in [the specified stem]" (*tadantavidhi*) should be understood. As for what Kaiyaṭa will say there—namely, that because of the association (*sāhacarya*) with the words *hala* and *sītā*, they claim the *tadantavidhi* applies only to the *yat* suffix prescribed in the fourth chapter—that is incorrect.

Regarding this, they say the following to highlight the lack of propriety: "One should note that because the mention of 'in a non-compound' (*asamāse*) in the rule *niṣkādibhyaḥ* indicates that, within that specific context, the extension of a suffix to include what ends in a particular word (*tadantavidhi*) has been specifically taught; therefore, even if one resorts to the principle of association (*sāhacarya*), the extension of the suffix to include what ends in a particular word remains unavoidable."

The suffix *vuñ* is applied after words for regions (*janapada*) preceded by *su*, *sarva*, *ardha*, or words denoting directions (*dik*), according to Pāṇini 4.2.127: *su-sarvārdha-dik-śabdebhyaḥ janapadasya*. Examples: * *supāñcālakaḥ* (belonging to the good Pañcālas), * *sumāgadhakaḥ* (belonging to the good Māgadhas), * *sarvapāñcālakaḥ* (belonging to all the Pañcālas), * *ardhapāñcālakaḥ* (belonging to half the Pañcālas). In these cases, the suffix *vuñ* is applied even after a region name that does not contain a *vṛddhi* vowel, provided it refers to a plural domain, according to Pāṇini 4.2.125: *avṛddhād api bahuvacanaviṣayāt*. Furthermore, the *vṛddhi* substitution occurs in the final syllable of the compound, according to Pāṇini 7.3.12: *su-sarvārdhāj janapadasya*. Regarding words for directions: * *pūrvapāñcālakaḥ* (belonging to the eastern Pañcālas), * *aparapāñcālakaḥ* (belonging to the western Pañcālas). In these cases, *vuñ* is applied as before, and the *vṛddhi* substitution occurs in the final syllable of the compound, according to Pāṇini 7.3.13: *diśo 'madrāṇām*.

Regarding the rule for the suffixes applied to parts of seasons that possess a suffix causing *vṛddhi*: when there is the application of a suffix that causes *vṛddhi*—that is, a suffix which is the cause of *vṛddhi*—to words denoting seasons, [the rule applies] "when the parts [of the season] stand as the first member [of a compound]. The remainder [of the meaning] is that this is a case of *tadantavidhi* (extension of a grammatical operation to a word ending in such a form), which is indeed expressly stated by the rule itself. For example: *pūrvaśarat* ("the former part of autumn"). This is a *ekadeśisamāsa* (partitive compound) according to Pāṇini 2.2.1 (*pūrvāparādharottaram*). From that [compound], the word *pūrvaśāradam* ("born in the former part of autumn") is derived by applying Pāṇini 4.3.16 (*sandhivelādyṛtunakṣatrebhyo 'ṇ*), which prescribes the suffix *aṇ*.

By the rule *avayavādṛtoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.11), there is vowel-vṛddhi of the second member [of the compound]. Why specify "containing a vṛddhi-vowel"? [Consider: by the rule *prāvṛṣa eṇyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.17), there is vowel-vṛddhi of the second member. Why specify "containing a vṛddhi-vowel"? [It is] so that the rule *prāvṛṣa eṇyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.17) might not apply as an *atadantavidhi* (i.e., not applying when the word ends in *prāvṛṣ*). Consequently, in that case, only the suffix *ṛtvaṇ* applies—as in *pūrvaprāvṛṣam*.

What [is the purpose] regarding the *avayava* [compounds]? In the case of *paurvaśāradikam* ("occurring in the previous autumn"), the suffix *aṇ* does not apply; rather, only *ṭhañ* applies after a word denoting time (*kālāt*). For in that rule, words denoting time are accepted in whatever way possible, and there is no insistence that they must be established by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) alone, because of the specific qualification "after *sandhi*, *velā*, etc., and the names of lunar mansions" in the subsequent rule. It is for this very reason that forms such as *sāyamprātikaḥ* ("belonging to evening and morning") and *paunaḥpaunikaḥ* ("occurring repeatedly") are established.

In the rule prescribing the suffix *ṭhañ*, when the analysis is "two sixties are its measure" (*dve ṣaṣṭhī parimāṇam asya*), and a compound has been formed by *Pāṇini 2.1.51* (*taddhitārtha...*), the suffix *ṭhak* does not apply by virtue of *Pāṇini 5.1.19* (*ārhāt*). This is because, when the rule of "extension to what ends in that" (*tadantavidhi*) applies to "number," the prohibition of *ṭhak* applies even to words ending in a number. Consequently, by *Pāṇini 5.1.18* (*prāgvateṣ ṭhañ*), the suffix *ṭhañ* alone occurs.

The elision (*luk*) does not occur by the rule *adhyardhapūrva* (Pāṇini 5.1.28), because after the rule *so'syāṃśavasnabhṛtayaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.53), the phrase *so'sya* is carried forward (*anuvartamāna*), yet in the rule *tadasya parimāṇam* (Pāṇini 5.1.57), the meaning of the suffix and the governing case-ending are specified once again. Indeed, this repeated specification indicates that the present case is distinct from the preceding context connected with elision (*luk*).

Alternatively, by means of the word *so'sya* (which is being carried over), together with the rule *saṃkhyāyāḥ parimāṇam*, this [rule] first prescribes the suffix. Then, once the *luk*-elision has been applied, by the force of the statement *tadasya parimāṇam* (Pāṇini 5.1.57), a suffix of that same class occurs again in its own sense (*svārthe*). Because of the force of that prescription, or because there is an absence of being caused by a *dvigu* compound, the *luk*-elision will not take place. And this—by the force of that prescription, or because of the absence of being caused by a *dvigu*—the *luk* will not occur.

And this has been stated by relying on the opinion of the *Vṛttikāra*. According to the opinion of the *Bhāṣyakāra*, however, one should form the suffix in the sense of "having become" (*bhūtārtha*) by means of the rule *tam adhīṣṭa* (Pāṇini 5.1.58), and thus derive forms such as *dviṣāṣṭikaḥ*. For in this case, the elision (*luk*) prescribed by the rule *adhyardha-* (Pāṇini 5.1.28) does not apply, because [the word] is not derived from the suffix *-an* used in the sense of "worthiness" (*anārhīyatvāt*).

Although in the rule *tam adhīṣṭaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.86), the term *kālāt* ("from a word denoting time") is understood to carry over, nevertheless, the derivation from the word *ṣaṣṭi* when it functions as a measure of time (*kāla*) is not contradicted; however, it does not occur after words such as *samanīya* due to the absence of such an expression. But the elision (*luk*) for the sake of expressing "measure" (*parimāṇa*) is unavoidable. For instance, by the rule *prāgvateṣṭhañ* (Pāṇini 5.1.18), the suffix *ṭhañ* applies to those meanings beginning with *tena krītam* (Pāṇini 5.1.37) that precede *tadarhati* (Pāṇini 5.1.63), as well as in the sense of "deserving" (*arhati*).

Furthermore, regarding other meanings such as "he employs" (*vartayati*) and so forth, which are denoted by the suffix *ka* according to the rule *ākālikadādyantavacane kaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.114), the suffix *ṭhañ* also occurs there. Thus, although *ṭhañ* is common to both the sense of "worthiness" (*ārhīya*) and its non-"worthiness" counterparts, because the scope of measurement (*parimāṇa*) is specified prior to the rule *tadarhati* (Pāṇini 5.1.63), the *ṭhañ* produced therein belongs exclusively to the "worthiness" category. Nor does its status as "worthiness" disappear merely because of the subsequent mention of *tad asya* ("this belongs to that"). For the status of being "worthiness" is not revoked simply because of the expression "the crow caws."

Furthermore, if the *ārhīya* suffix were excluded [from this context], then the *luṅ* (aorist) would not occur even in cases other than those involving a measure of life, as in: "that which has two *niṣkas* as its measure" (*dviniṣkaḥ*). Nor should it be argued that the form would occur by virtue of the rule "after *niṣka* preceded by *dvi*, *tri*, etc. (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 5.1.30), because that rule finds its scope in the *ārhīya* sense when applied to things exceeding a measure.

Therefore, for one whose lifespan is sixty years, that person is "hired for sixty" (*bhṛtaḥ*); thus, by the rule *tam adhīṣṭo bhṛtaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.80), the form *dviṣāṣṭikaḥ* (one hired for sixty-two) is to be established. However, the rule *tad asya* (Pāṇini 5.1.16) should be abandoned, because the desired result is achieved simply through the recurrence of the word *so 'sya* (Pāṇini 5.1.17). This is settled. Regarding the suffix after *dharma* with the negative particle *nañ*: "He practices dharma" → *dhārmikaḥ*; "He practices non-dharma" → *ādharmikaḥ*. The separate rule *adharmāt ca* (Kāśikāvṛtti) need not be stated.

Regarding the section on *pada-aṅga*, there is a purpose for both that [term] and its subsequent member (*uttarapada*). [The rule] *iṣṭakeṣīkāmālānāṃ citatūlabhāriṣu* (Pāṇini 6.3.65) provides examples: *iṣṭakacitam* (built with bricks), *pakveṣṭakacitam* (built with baked bricks); *iṣīkatūlena* (with the tuft of a reed), *muñjeṣīkatūlena* (with the tuft of a Muñja-reed); *mālabhārī* (bearing a garland), *utpalamālabhārī* (bearing a garland of blue lotuses). Here, Kaiyaṭa and others maintain that because the purpose is illustrated under the heading of the subsequent member (*uttarapadādhikāra*), the word *pada* in the term *padāṅga* refers to the subsequent member.

For this very reason, in the expression "paramamahat-parimāṇam" (the dimension of the supremely great), Udayanācārya explained that it is a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "the dimension (*parimāṇa*) of a substance (*dravya*) that is supremely great. He argued that if there were grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), then by the rule "ānmahataḥ" (Pāṇini 6.3.46), the substitution of *ā* for the final vowel would have occurred. As for what Vardhamāna stated therein—"In the context of 'pada' and 'aṅga,' only the context of 'pada' is understood, not the context of 'uttarapada'"— [The text continues: ...[This is] because the word *mahat* is mentioned in the *aṅgādhikāra* (the section governing grammatical elements), and since the *aṅga* is a portion of the *pada*, the rule applies even when the *mahat* is not the final member of a compound. However, this is not correct; for if it were so, then in the case of *mahābāhuḥ* (long-armed), the *ā* substitution would apply to the *bāhu* as well, resulting in the undesirable form *mahābāhaḥ*. Therefore, the view of Udayana is more consistent with the established tradition. Furthermore, the *ā* substitution is taught specifically for the *mahat* that occurs at the end of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, whereas in the present case, the *mahat* is not the final member of a *bahuvrīhi*. Thus, the genitive *tatpuruṣa* analysis remains the most appropriate. Otherwise, the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) regarding the extension of that [suffix] to compound-final members in the rule *iṣṭakeṣīkāmālānām* (Pāṇini 6.3.65) would be redundant. Furthermore, in the case of *paramamahatparimāṇam*, there would be no possibility of the substitution of *ā* even under the analysis as a *karmadhāraya*; thus, your statement is an inattentive assertion, because the example given for the purpose of *iṣṭakeṣīka* (6.3.65) is precisely this, and any other supplementary rule would be like a flower in the sky. Therefore, what was stated by the Teacher alone is correct.

By this, the objection—"In the usage of Bhāravi, *satatanaiśatamovṛtamanyataḥ* (Ki. 5.2), why is there no elision [of the case-ending] according to Pāṇini’s rule *ojaḥ-saho’m-bhas-tamasas tṛtīyāyāḥ* (Pā. 6.3.3)?"—is refuted by the method stated by Vardhamāna; furthermore, the statement of the author of the *Durghaṭavṛtti*, that "within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) for the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), there is no mention of 'that subsequent member' (*taduttarapada-grahaṇam*)," is also rejected.

As for what Haradatta stated regarding the rule *ojaḥsaho* (Pāṇini 6.3.3)—namely, that for words such as *ojas*, the preceding member is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) with respect to the following member implied by the compound—that too must be disregarded because it contradicts the Vārttika; for, as Kaiyaṭa himself has explained, the activity of the Vārttikas in this context is solely for the purpose of determining the relationship between the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). As for the usage of Bhāravi, it should be resolved in this way: *vṛttaṃ vṛttiḥ* [is the analysis], and "the covering of the nocturnal darkness" (*naiśatamaso vṛtam*) is a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound.

When there is a connection with a *kta*-suffix used in the neuter sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*), the genitive case is employed when one intends to express its status as a "remainder" (*śeṣatva*). Thus, the compound *satatanaiśatamovṛtam* is a *bahuvrīhi*: "that in which there is a constant enveloping by nocturnal darkness. Alternatively, since the root *vṛt* (DhP 1.759) means "to exist" or "to occur," the suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) according to the rule *ghañarthe kavidhānam*. Thus, it means "that in which there is a constant occurrence of nocturnal darkness," as explained previously.

He states the purposes regarding the governing rule for *aṅga*: "The purpose is great in the formation of *apsaras* and *apsavaḥ*; [the word] *mahat* [is used] in the sense of 'great,' [and] *paramamahat* [is used] in the sense of 'supremely great. [In the case of] *āpaḥ tiṣṭhanti*, [the form] is *svāpaḥ*. By the rule *na pūjanāt* (Pāṇini 5.4.69), the application of a compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) is prohibited. [Objection: Even so, by the rule *dvyantarupasargebhyo'pa īt* (Pāṇini 6.3.97), the substitution of *ī* would still apply [to the final vowel of *apaḥ*].

If it is argued that this is not a *samāsānta* suffix, such that the *ap*-suffix would not be prohibited by the rule *ṛkpūrabdhūḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.74), [we reply: True; however, in the rule *dvyantarupasargebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.97), the word *apaḥ* is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the form ending in the *ap* suffix after a compound has been formed. This nominative case is used in the sense of the genitive by transposition (*vyatyaya*), as in the rule *anho’dantāt* (Pāṇini 8.4.7). It should be noted that the commentary’s statement *svāpaḥ* here serves as authority for this interpretation. Examples: *svasārau*, *paramasvasārau*; *naptārau*, *paramanaptārau*.

In the case of *pad*, *yuṣmad*, *asmad*, and words ending in *-asthi* etc., as well as *anaḍuh*, the augment *num* is applied. The purpose [of this rule] is the transformation into *pad*. For example: *dvipadaḥ paśya* ("look at the two-footed one"). However, the example for the word in isolation is derived from the root *pād* without an affix: *pāt*, *padaḥ*, *padā*, and so forth. Here, because the suffix *kvip* has been elided, the elision of the *ṇi*-augment is not treated as *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were present). Under the heading governing the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*), the word *pāda* itself is the qualified term (*viśeṣya*). Consequently, the transformation into *pad* according to Pāṇini 6.3.52—*pādasya padājyātigopahateṣu*—occurs only in cases such as *pādenopahataṃ padopahatam* ("struck by the foot").

But here, "digdhapādopahatam" does not mean "struck by one whose feet are smeared [with poison]. The same applies to the subsequent sūtra as well. Consequently, the substitution of *pad* for *pāda* occurs only in this specific context, according to Pāṇini 6.3.53 (*padyatyatadarthe*) and 6.3.54 (*himakāṣihatiṣu ca*). Thus, in the case of "one who scrapes with the feet" (*pādau kaṣati*), we have *patkaṣī*; however, in this case, we do not have *paramapādakāṣī*. As for the usage *paramapatkāṣī*, it is to be justified by analyzing the compound as "one who is both supreme and a foot-scraping person," as established in the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa.

You, we, you-selves, we-selves; bone, supreme bone; ox, supreme ox. [The rule] "the mention of *dyu*, *pathin*, *mathin*, *puṃs*, *go*, *sakhi*, *catuṣ*, *anaḍuh*, and *tri*" [is applied as follows]: *dyauḥ* (heaven), *sudyoḥ* (good heaven); *panthāḥ* (path), *supanthāḥ* (good path)—there is no suffix for the compound ending according to Pāṇini 5.4.69, "not after a word of praise"; *panthāḥ*, *paramapanthāḥ* (supreme path); *pumān* (man), *paramapumān* (supreme man); *gauḥ* (cow), *sugauḥ* (good cow); *sakhā* (friend), *susakhā* (good friend), *sakhāyau*, *susakhāyau* (two good friends); *catvāraḥ* (four), *paramacatvāraḥ* (supreme four); *anaḍvāh* (ox), *paramānaḍvāh* (supreme ox); *trayāṇām* (of three), *paramatrayāṇām* (of supreme three).

In the Bhāṣya, however, *paramapanthāḥ* and *paramagauḥ* are cited as examples. In those cases, there would be the application of a compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*). Yet, the prohibition by the rule *na pūjanāt* (Pāṇini 5.4.69) does not apply here, because it will be stated later that [the prohibition applies] "only after *su*" and *ati* (Kāśikāvṛtti). For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa maintains that this is an occasional corrupt reading (*apapāṭha*). Alternatively, it may be resolved by considering the rule for compound-endings to be non-universal (*anitya*). Or else, the meaning is that *parama-* is another example.

In the cases of *apanthāḥ* and *agauḥ*, correctness is established by the rule *patho vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 5.4.72), which applies after a *nañ*-tatpuruṣa compound. As for the reading *paramasakhāyau* found in the Bhāṣya, it should be understood there as a *bahuvrīhi* compound. For even when [the term] is used in a secondary sense (*gauṇatva*), these two—namely the absence of *anaṅ* and the absence of the *ṇiṭ* designation—are exactly like those in the case of *anaṅ* in words such as *asthi*. This is clear from the rules *m-antya-t* (Pāṇini 1.1.47) and *dvitīyā śrita-* (Pāṇini 2.1.24).

Furthermore, such usages as "arudryukṣovaruṇa indrasakhā" (Varuṇa joined with Arudryukṣa, the friend of Indra) and "āgneyāhimarutsakhā" (the followers of Agni, the friends of the Maruts) are likewise consistent with this view. By this, the examples cited by Haradatta and the author of the Nyāsa—namely, "susakhiḥ" (one who has a good friend)—under the rule defining *ghisamjñā* are refuted. As for the rule "trestrayaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.3.48), because it is explained as applying when the suffix *i* follows a word expressing a number inherent in the meaning of the word "tri," it does not apply in a secondary (*gauṇa*) sense—as in "priyatrīṇām" (those who have three beloveds) or "atitrīṇām" (those who have surpassed three). It would indeed apply in a primary (*pradhāna*) sense, as in "paramatrayāṇām" (the supreme three), so they say. However, the authority for this particular explanation must be sought elsewhere.

It should not be forgotten that it has been stated that one should simply say *iha padāṅgādhikāre* ("here, in the governing rule for *pada* and *aṅga*"), because by the very inclusion of the final element (*tadantagrahaṇa*), all desired results are established.

Regarding the rule *pratyayagrahaṇe yasmātsa vihitastadādestadantasya grahaṇam* (Pā. Bhāṣya 23): here, because the aggregate consisting of the root, nominal stem, and so forth—which is implied by the term "affix" (*pratyaya*)—is qualified by the affix, the inclusion of that which ends in such [an element] (*tadantavidhi*) is obtained. Furthermore, in the rule defining the technical term *aṅga*, by dividing the formulation into two parts—*yasmāt pratyayavidhiḥ* and *tadādi pratyaye*—and explaining it as a *paribhāṣā* (metarule), the other portion [of the definition] is obtained.

And this [rule] does not apply in the context of the prescription of technical names (*saṃjñā*), because of the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) in the rule "That which ends in a *sup* or *tiṅ* affix is a word" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 1.4.14). Nor does it apply even within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) concerning the subsequent member of a compound, as will be stated on the basis of the mention of the word "lekhā" in the rule "For *hṛdaya*, [the substitution of] *hṛd-* occurs before *lekhā*, *aya*, *daṇ*, and *alāsa*" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 6.3.50). He states the exception to this: "The mention of a suffix (*prakṛtyagrahaṇa*) applies except in the case of the fifth [case-ending]" (*Pāṇinīya Bhāṣya* 24).

The meaning is that where a word ending in the fifth case (ablative) serves as a qualifier of an affix (*pratyaya*), there the inclusion of that which ends in it (*tadantagrahaṇa*) does not apply; as, for example, in the rule *radābhyāṃ niṣṭhātaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.2.42). Consequently, in the form *hṛṣattīrṇā*, the substitution of *na* for the letter *t* of the root *tṝ*—which is a constituent of the affix *niṣṭhā*—does not occur.

In this section concerning the rules for suffixation (*saṃjñāvidhi*) under the heading of "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*), in rules such as *radābhyām* (Pāṇini 8.2.42) and *syatāsī lṛluṭoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.33), the suffix (*pratyaya*) is taken as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*); however, in other instances, it is taken as the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). This is the established conclusion. All of this is accomplished by the Sūtra itself.

The author of the Vārttika states an explicit exception to the rule of "extension to what ends with that" (*tadanta-vidhi*) which is based on the Sūtra: "When there is a grammatical operation [prescribed] for something, it applies to that which begins with it, provided that the term *al* is not being used. Just as the rules *aci śnu-dhātu-* (Pāṇini 6.4.77) result in the forms *śriyau* and *bhruvau*, so too here the forms *śriyaḥ* and *bhrūvaḥ* are established. Thus, this rule of "beginning with that" (*tadādi-vidhi*) is an exception to the rule of "ending with that," and therefore it applies only when there is a qualifying attribute.
That [stem] whose initial vowels are *vṛddhi* is called *vṛddha*. (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.73)

That group [of vowels] among whose constituent parts (*avayava*)—the vowels (*ac*)—the first vowel is designated as *vṛddhi*, shall itself be designated as *vṛddha*. For example: *āmraguptīyaḥ* (derived from *āmragupta*), according to Pāṇini 4.2.114: *vṛddhāccha*. The use of the plural in *acām* refers to the class (*jāti*); therefore, it applies even when there are two [vowels]: *śālīyaḥ* (from *śālā*). It also applies when there is only one [vowel], by virtue of the principle of "behaving like that which has a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*): *jñā* is a Brāhmaṇī woman; her son is *jñīyaḥ*. Regarding the rule *vā nāmadheyasya* (Kātyāyana’s Vārttika): this means that for a proper name (*nāmadheya*), the designation *vṛddha* may optionally apply. For instance, *pauruṣeyam* is a name; for it, the *vṛddha* designation is optional.

This is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) in both cases, because it applies where [the suffix] has not yet been reached for words such as *devadatta*, and where it has already been reached for words such as *vāmana*. Examples: *devadattīyāḥ* (those belonging to Devadatta), *daivadattāḥ* (the same). Śrīharṣa says: "Having assumed a deceptive dwarf form... (*vidhāya mūrtiṃ kapaṭena vāmanīm*). And [the word] whose final member is a *gotra* (patronymic) name is always designated as *vṛddha*; this is the remainder [of the rule]. Examples: *kambalacārāyaṇīyāḥ*, *odanapāṇinīyāḥ*, *ghṛtarauḍhīyāḥ*. The meaning is, for instance: "the disciples of Cārāyaṇa, who is fond of blankets" (*kambalapriya*), and so forth. The act of bargaining is *paṇa*.

The suffix *ka* is applied by the rule "the suffix *ka* is prescribed in the sense of the *ghañ* [suffix]. Thus, one who possesses this [work] is a *paṇin*. The descendant in the lineage (*gotrāpatya*) of *paṇin* is *pāṇinaḥ*, formed with the suffix *aṇ*. By the rule "gāthi-vidathi-keśi-gaṇi-paṇin- and so forth" (Pāṇini 6.4.165), there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). From that, the suffix *yūniñ* is applied, resulting in *pāṇiniḥ*.

It might be argued: "By the rule *ṇyakṣatriyārṣañitaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.58), the elision (*luk*) of the suffix *iñ* would apply here, because [the patronymic] has been derived from an *ārṣa* [name] in the sense of a descendant. This is not so; for by the mention of *ārṣa* in that rule, only the suffix *ṛṣyaṇ* prescribed by the rule *ṛṣyandhakavṛṣṇikurubhyaśca* (Pāṇini 4.1.114) is intended. Furthermore, this [suffix *ṛṣyaṇ*] is the default (*autsargika*) one. Alternatively, the word *pāṇin* is etymological (*yaugika*) and not conventionally fixed (*ruḍha*) to mean a seer (*ṛṣi*). In the rule prescribing elision (*lugvidhi*), however, only that which is conventionally fixed is taken.

And this is determined at the conclusion of the treatise by the indication of the *vārttika*: "Or it is established for the Blessed Pāṇini because of the mention of the *ekaśeṣa* [form]," and by the usage of the author of the *Bhāṣya*: "Of Pāṇini, the son of Dākṣī."

But even so, the form *pāṇinīyāḥ* (the pupils of Pāṇini) would not be established; for the suffix *cha*, prescribed by the rule *vṛddhācchaṃ* (Pāṇini 4.2.114), would be superseded by the suffix *aṇ*, which applies by the rule *iñaśca* (Pāṇini 4.2.112). Nor can it be argued that when *cha* is intended, the suffix *iñ* is elided by the rule *yūni luk* (Pāṇini 4.1.90), and thus this [base] no longer ends in *iñ*; for by the principle of "as if the suffix were present" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), its status as ending in *iñ* is not lost.

On this point, they say: In the rule *iñaśca* (Pāṇini 4.2.112), the term *gotra* is understood by anuvṛtti from the preceding rule *kaṇvādibhyo gotre* (Pāṇini 4.2.111). Moreover, that term is marked with an accent (*svaryate*) in the previous sūtra itself. Consequently, setting aside the worldly *gotra* which would otherwise apply because this [present] rule falls outside the governing heading on *apatya*, the technical category of *gotra* is taken here, according to the principle *svaritenādhikāraḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.11). Furthermore, the *kaṇva*-group is a sub-group within the *garga*-group.

Therefore, the *yañ* prescribed by the rule *gargādibhyo yañ* (Pāṇini 4.1.105) occurs only in the technical sense of "lineage" (*gotra*), because the governing heading for "descendant" (*apatya*) is present there. Consequently, in the rule *iñaśca* (Pāṇini 4.2.112) as well, the resulting meaning is that after a word ending in *iñ* which [denotes] a lineage in the technical sense, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the remaining cases (*śeṣe*). Alternatively, by the maxim *lakṣaṇapratipadoktayoḥ pratipadoktasyaiva grahaṇam* ("between that which is indicated by a general rule and that which is expressed by its specific form, the latter alone is taken"), only the *yañ* occurring in the *kaṇvādi* list is understood; and since that [suffix] is prescribed in the technical sense of lineage, it serves as the indicator (*pratyaya*) for that very [meaning].

And likewise, in the rule *evañcārthādhikārādiñaśca* (Pāṇini 4.2.112), the same applies. As for *pāṇini*, however, the suffix *iñ* is applied in the sense of a *yuvan* (descendant of a grandson or further), and not in the sense of a *gotra*. Therefore, since the suffix *aṇ* does not apply here, the addition of the suffix *cha* remains unimpeded; this is the established conclusion. *Rauḍhiḥ* is the offspring of one who is conventionally known as *ruḍha*; [this is formed] by *ata iñ* (Pāṇini 4.1.95). This may refer either to an immediate descendant or to a *gotra*. Nor does this lead to the undesired application of *aṇ* by the rule *iñaśca* (Pāṇini 4.2.112), because of the prohibition: *na dvyacaḥ prācyabharateṣu* (Pāṇini 4.2.113).

It might be argued: if the designation *vṛddha* is prescribed for a word that has *gotra* as its final member, then in the case of *paiṅgalakāṇvāḥ*—meaning "the students of Piṅgalakāṇva"—the suffix *cha* would apply by the rule *vṛddhāc chaḥ*. However, what is desired is the suffix *aṇ* by the rule *kaṇvādibhyo gotre* (Pāṇini 4.2.111). True; precisely because of this lack of satisfaction, the author of the Vārttika stated: "Or, [the suffix *cha*] may optionally apply after a word ending in *gotra*, like a compound" (*gotrāntādvāsamastavat*).

The meaning is that within the section on secondary derivatives (*śaiṣika*), an extension (*atideśa*) of the rule "the suffix *aṇ* [is used] from before *prāgdīvyataḥ*" (Pāṇini 4.1.83) should optionally be applied. The intention is that because this falls outside the section on lineages (*apatya*), and because the term "lineage" (*gotra*) is understood here in its worldly sense, forms such as *odanapāṇinīyāḥ* are established. Why not simply by the general rule? He says: "No, except for *jivhākātya* and *haritakātya*. The word *kata* belongs to the *garga*-class. *Jivhākātya* refers to one who is fickle-tongued, and *haritakātya* refers to one who is green-colored.
In the sense of "his pupils," only the suffix *aṇ* occurs, resulting in *jaivhākātāḥ* and *hāritakātāḥ*.
"Tyadādīni ca" (Pāṇini 1.1.74):

these [pronouns] shall have the designation *vṛddha*. [Examples: *tyadīyam*, *adasīyam*, *idamīyam*, *kimīyam*; *tvādāyaniḥ*, *mādāyaniḥ*—[the latter two] by the rule "udīcāṃ vṛddhāt" (Pāṇini 4.1.157), which prescribes the suffix *phiñ*; and [the substitution of] *tva* and *ma* for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* occurs by the rule "pratyayottarapadayośca" (Pāṇini 5.2.98).

*eṅ prācāṃ deśe* (Pāṇini 1.1.75). The phrase *yasyācāmādiḥ* ("that which has [eṅ] as the first among its vowels") is supplied here by means of *maṇḍūkapluti* (the frog-leap method of ellipsis). That whose first vowel among its vowels is *eṅ* may optionally be designated as *vṛddha* when denoting a place in the eastern region (*prāc*). Examples: *eṇīpacanīyaḥ*, *gonardīyaḥ*, *bhojakaṭīyaḥ*. Why "eṅ"? Consider *āhicchatraḥ* and *kānyakubjaḥ* (which do not begin with *eṅ*). The mention of *prāc* (eastern) is for the purpose of indicating the specific teacher's tradition, due to the force of the connection with the designation to be enjoined and because of the separate utterance of the case-ending. Furthermore, this is an *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (a restricted option).

Therefore, because the words *kroḍa* and *devadatta* do not denote a region of the East (*prāgdeśa*), they do not receive the designation *vṛddha*; consequently, for *kroḍa* and *devadatta*, only the suffix *aṇ* occurs [resulting in *krauḍa* and *daivadatta*]. However, for the word *devadatta* when it does denote a region of the East, the designation *vṛddha* certainly applies; hence, by virtue of belonging to the *kāśyādi* group, the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭh*—which are characterized as applying to *vṛddha* stems—occur [resulting in *daivadattika* and *daivadattiya*]. It should be stated that this applies to secondary derivatives (*śaiṣika*). Examples: *saipurikī*, *saipurikā*; *skaunagarikā*, *skaunagarikā*. *Sepura* and *skunagara* are villages of the Vāhīkas.

In this case, because [the word] is *vṛddha*, the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭh* do not apply by the rule *vāhīkagrāmebhyaśca* (Pāṇini 4.2.117). Due to the statement "in the sense of *śauṣika*," the suffix *phiñ* applies in the sense of offspring (*apatya*) according to the characteristic of *vṛddha*. Furthermore, the suffix *mayaṭ* does not apply in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*) by the rule *nityaṃ vṛddhaśarāvāṇām* (Pāṇini 4.3.144). Thus, following both the opinion of Kuṇi and the opinion of the Bhāṣya, it has been explained that the mention of *prāk* is for the purpose of indicating the teacher's specific instruction.

Jayāditya, however, explained [the term] as follows: "Those who reside in the eastern region are 'easterners' (prācaḥ); the name for their region is [what is meant here]. His intention was that since it is possible for the word *prācām* to function as an explicit qualifier of the region (*deśa*), one should not assume its connection with the supplied word *matena* ("by the opinion of"). In this view, it is clear that in a Vāhīka village, the suffixes *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭh* do not apply to a name such as *Daivadatta* simply because it is not a *vṛddha* [name]. However, forms such as *Sāipurikī* must be established by the very statement cited in the Bhāṣya; such is the general direction.

What is being taught? The river named Gomatī is located in the eastern region; the fish found there are called *gaumatāḥ*. By the mention of "region" (*deśa*), the river is included, as indicated by the separate mention [of rivers] in the rule: "Rivers and regions that are not villages" (Pāṇini 2.4.7). The division of the regions beginning with the East is as follows: there is a river named Śarāvatī which flows toward the northeast. The region situated to the southeast of that river is the Eastern Region (*prāgdeśa*); the region situated to the northwest is the Northern Region (*udagdeśa*). And it has been said: "The swan separates the milk from the water, just as it separates the East and the North."
"May that Śarāvatī protect us, for the sake of establishing the words of the learned. Thus it is said.
Amarasiṃha also says:
"This world is the land of Bhārata, which lies up to the boundary of the Śarāvatī river."

The regions are the eastern (prācya), the southern (dakṣiṇa), the northern (udīcya), and the western-northern (paścimottara). However, the commentators on the *Amarakośa* state that from the northeast (aiśānī) to the southwest (nairṛtī) lies the Śarāvatī river, which flows toward the western ocean. In either case, there is no dispute regarding the nature of the east and north. As for the Vāhīka region, it lies outside the east and north; this is explained by the grammatical derivation [from *bahiṣ*] according to the rule "the suffix *yañ* occurs with the elision of the final syllable" (*bahiṣaṣṭilopo yañ ca*).

That [interpretation] is questionable, because the venerable author, while explaining the *vārttika* "from *kāśyādi*, *ṭhañ* and *ñiṭha*" (*kāśyādibhyaṣṭhaññiṭhau*) under the rule "after an indeclinable, *tyap*" (*avyayāttyap*), Pāṇini 4.2.104, accepts that the village named Śākala possesses both the characteristics of an *udīcya* and a *vāhīka*. Furthermore, Haradatta and others have likewise restated this very point. Therefore, the truth is simply that a *vāhīka* is a specific region. And so it is said in the *Karṇaparvan*:
"Those regions which lie between the five [rivers] with Sindhu as the sixth are called the Vāhīkas; one should not dwell there for even a single day."

By this, it is meant that they are called *vāhīkas* because they are outside the bounds of the Dharma. Their commentators explain that there are five rivers—the Śatadrū, Vipāśā, Irāvatī, Vitastā, and Candrabhāgā—and the Sindhu river as the sixth; the region situated between them is the *vāhīka*. However, another etymological derivation is shown in that very same source:
"Vahika and Vahīka were two Piśācas on the Vipāśā;
their offspring are the Vāhīkas, who are not the creation of Prajāpati."
And this analysis will be useful in such rules as "vāhīkagrāmebhyaśca" (Pāṇini 4.3.117); thus, everything is well-established.

Thus ends the ninth section (āhnika) of the first quarter (pāda) of the first chapter in the *Śabdakaustubha*, composed by Bhaṭṭoji Bhaṭṭa, the son of Lakṣmīdhara Sūri, the crest-jewel of learned scholars.
And this first quarter is completed.
Śrīḥ.
In the *Śabdakaustubha*,
in the second quarter (pāda) of the first chapter (adhyāya), the first daily lesson (āhnika).

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.1) *gāṅkuṭādibhyo’ñṇinṅit* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.1): After the substitutes *gāṅ* and those beginning with *kuṭ*, suffixes other than those marked with *ñ* or *ṇ* shall behave as if they were marked with *ṅ*. [Example: *adhyagīṣṭa*. By the rule "vibhāṣā luṅlṛṅoḥ" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.4.50), *iṅ* is replaced by *gāṅ*. It will be stated in the sūtra "gāṅ liṭi" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.4.49) that the letter *ṅ* in the substitute *gāṅ* is indeed for the purpose of specification (*viśeṣaṇa*). [Examples: *kuṭitā*, *kuṭitum*. Why "other than those marked with *ñ* or *ṇ*" (*añṇit*)? [Counter-example: *koṭaḥ*. Here, the suffix is *ghañ*. [Another example: *cukoṭa*. Here, by the rule "parasmaipadānām" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.4.82), the suffix *ṇal* is applied.

Regarding the rule *vyaceḥ kuṭāditvamanasīti vaktavyam* (Kāśikāvṛtti), although this was already cited in the Bhāṣya on the sixth-century sūtra *liṭyabhyāsasya* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.17), the author of the Vṛtti has included it here for the sake of clarifying the context. By means of this Vārttika, the status of *vyaci* as belonging to the *kuṭādi* group—which is recited in the *tudādigaṇa* prior to the *kuṭādi* sub-group—is enjoined. Thus, we have *vicitum* and *vicitā*. Why [is it said] "not when *anas* follows"? Consider the example *uruvyacāḥ*. On this point, Haradatta states that because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) indicated by the word *anasī*, this [Vārttika] applies only to the case of the verbal derivative (*kṛtya*).

Therefore, here [the forms] are *navivyacitha*, *avyācīt*, and *avyanīt*. However, some, relying on a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation), claim that the *ṅit* status applies even to suffixes such as *thāl*; but Mādhava and others maintain that this is incorrect because it involves a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) and results in an *asamartha-samāsa* (compound of incompatible meanings). Now, how is it that [the forms] *likhitum* and *svayameva likhiṣyate* [are explained]? On this point, Durghaṭa and others state: just as in the rule *kaṇvādibhyaḥ*, this [rule for] *kuṭādibhyaḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* remaining after a simultaneous intention to express both a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* and a *bahuvrīhi*.

"Therefore, because *likh* is also [a root] beginning with *ku*, it is included here. This is not correct, because it would contradict the usage in the sūtra: *śakuniṣvālekhane* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.142), and because it would contradict the commentary (*vṛtti*) on the sūtras *ralo vyupadhāt* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.26) and *īśvare tosun* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.4.13). For in those [commentaries], it is shown: *likhitvā*, *lekhitvā*, *lilikhiṣati*, *lilekhiṣati*, and *vilekhitum*. Therefore, Hara Datta says that this must be resolved by treating it as being preceded by a technical designation (*saṃjñāpūrvakatva*). How then [to explain] *cukuṭa*?

[Objection: Is it not the case that because the suffix *san* is marked with the *ṅit* indicator, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the *taṅ* (middle voice) endings, just as in the case of a root ending in *yaṅ*? [Response: Not so; for, by continuing the mention of "in the original instruction" (*upadeśe*), the rule is explained as: "the middle voice occurs after a root which is *ṅit* in its original instruction. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.62).

Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.2: *vija iṭ*—after the root *vij*, a suffix beginning with *iṭ* shall be treated as having the marker *ṅ*. [Examples: *udvijitum*. Why is *iṭ* mentioned? [Counter-example: *udvejanam*. Here, from the sūtra *vṛddhiryasya...* (1.1.73), the phrase *yasyādiḥ* is supplied by means of a "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*) [from 1.1.72]. By this, it is understood that the suffix must begin with *iṭ*; it does not refer to the first person singular ending *iṭ*. For if it were so, [the rule] would apply only in cases such as *vijiṣīya*.

Regarding the statement "ovijī bhayacalanayoḥ" (Dhātupāṭha 1290), Haradatta maintains that the root *vij* is understood here [in the sense of trembling], and not the root meaning "separation" (*pṛthagbhāva*) which ends in *-ṝ*, because the latter is *aniṭ*. Nor should it be argued that an *iṭ* augment is indeed possible in the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) due to the rule governing roots beginning with *kṛ* (Pāṇini 7.2.13); for his point is that in that case, the matter is already settled by the fact that the suffix is marked with *k* (which prevents *iṭ*). However, in reality, this is not correct, because an *iṭ* is possible in the suffix *thal* as in *vivejitha*, since the suffix is marked with *p* and thus lacks the *k*-marking.

Therefore, it should be understood that due to its association with *kuṭ* and others, only the roots beginning with *tud* are included, and not those beginning with *hu*. If it is objected that this contradicts Mādhava—who, citing examples such as *udvijitā*, [implies] that even roots beginning with *rudh* possess the *ṅit* designation—then let it be that the exclusion of roots beginning with *hu* follows precisely from the [authoritative] commentary (*vyākhyāna*). Haradatta’s statement, however, is indeed flawed; such is the direction of the argument. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.3) *vibhāṣorṇoḥ*: After this root, an affix beginning with *iṭ* may optionally be *ṅit*. [Examples: *ūrṇuvitā*, *ūrṇavitā*. Why "beginning with *iṭ*"? [Counter-example: *ūrṇavanīyam*.

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.4): *sārvadhātukamapit* | A *sārvadhātuka* suffix that is not marked with *p* should be treated like one marked with *ṅ*. [Examples: *vinutaḥ*, *vinvanti*]. Here, because the word "elsewhere" (*paratra*) is used later in the rule, the suffix *-vat* (denoting "like") should not be understood as being in the locative case—as in the phrase "*ṅiti*" (as if it were *ṅitīva*). If that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence of a locative case for the correlative term, resulting in the form *sārvadhātuke'piti*. In the preceding rule as well, the same would apply, and there would have to be locative forms such as *añṇiti* or *iṭi*. However, in all instances, the nominative case is actually heard.

Therefore, by the rule *tasmāttṛtīyāntādeva vatirṅitaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.1.116), the suffix *vat* also occurs when it is marked with the *ṅ*-sign. If it is objected: "In that case, in the verse *yad dampatī samanasā sunutaḥ*, the rule *tāsyanudāttenṅidupadeśāl la-sārvadhātukam anudāttam* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.186) would cause the *la-sārvadhātuka* affix to be unaccented," we reply: No. This is because the *Bhāṣya* on the sixth book explains that the mention of "in the original enunciation" (*upadeśa*) connects with both [the preceding and following rules], meaning [the prohibition applies] to what is taught as having the *ṅ*-sign and to what is taught as having the vowel *a*. Alternatively, it is because the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) in the rule *anhviṅoḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.39) implies that the term refers to those taught with the *ṅ*-sign in their original enunciation.

The conclusion is that the *Ṣaṣṭhīvṛtti* passage, which intends [the suffix] *vat* to follow a word ending in the seventh case (*saptamyanta*), is merely superficial. In this regard, we have explained in the commentary on the sūtra *kṅiti ca* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.1.5) two types of sentence-meanings: "that which is marked with *pi* is not marked with *ṅ*, and that which is marked with *ṅ* is not marked with *pi*. However, this point is established in the *Bhāṣya* under the sūtra *halaḥ śnaḥ śānajjhau* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.1.83).
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.5)

*Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.5*: *asaṃyogālliṭ kit* (The *liṭ* [perfect] suffix following a root that does not end in a conjunct consonant is *kit*). A *liṭ* suffix that is not marked with *p* (*apit*) shall be *kit* when it follows a root ending in a non-conjunct consonant. Examples: *ninyatuḥ*, *bibhidatuḥ*. Why "not marked with *p*" (*apit*)? Consider *vibheda*. Why "not a conjunct" (*asaṃyogāt*)? Consider *sasraṃse*. Since the status of being *ṅit* was already established [by the previous rule], the designation *kit* is made here for the purpose of causing *samprasāraṇa* according to *Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.15*: *yajādīnāṃ kiti* (In roots beginning with *yaj*, *samprasāraṇa* occurs before a *kit* suffix). Examples: *ījatuḥ*, *ījuḥ*. If one asks: "Why was the *kit* designation not applied in the preceding rule as well? [The answer is: Because in forms such as *vaktaḥ* and *vakyaḥ*, there would be the undesirable consequence of *samprasāraṇa*; and in forms such as *jāgṛtaḥ* and *jāgrati*, there would be the undesirable consequence of *guṇa*.

However, because it is stated that "there is no *samprasāraṇa* for *vac* and others when followed by a *kit* suffix," there is no *samprasāraṇa*. Furthermore, because of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) in the rule "for *jāgṛ*, except before *vic*, *ciṇ*, and *liṅ*" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.3.85), there is no *guṇa*. Regarding the rule "the *liṭ* [suffixes] following roots with *ṛ* as their penultimate vowel are *kit* by means of a prior prohibition of *guṇa*" (Kāśikāvṛtti): the scope of the *kit* status is seen in forms such as *ījatuḥ* and *ījuḥ*; the scope of *guṇa* is seen in *cetati*. In cases such as *vavṛte* and *vavṛdhe*, the *kit* status applies by virtue of a prior conflict (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.6).

*Indhibhavatibhyāṃ ca* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.6). After these two roots, the *liṭ* suffix shall be *kit*. Examples: *samīdhe dasyuhantamam* ("He kindled the greatest slayer of demons"); *putra īdhe atharvaṇaḥ* ("The son kindled [the fire] of Atharvan"). *Babhūva*, *babhūvitha*. The inclusion of *indhī* is for the sake of its occurrence in a conjunct (*saṃyoga*), while that of *bhavati* is for the sake of its being a *pit* root. The mention of *indhī* is by means of the vowel *i* used for pronunciation, as in the rule *suṭ tithoḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.4.107), and not by the *ik* vowel as in *ik-śtipau* (Kāśikāvṛtti), because otherwise the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) would result.

Regarding this, the *Vārttika* states: "Because the root *indh* pertains to the Vedic language (*chandas*), and because the *vuk* augment for *bhū* is obligatory, the rule prescribing the *kit* designation for the *liṭ* [perfect] suffix after these two roots is purposeless. The meaning of this is as follows: In the common language (*bhāṣā*), the root *indh* would necessarily take the *ām* suffix according to Pāṇini 3.1.36 (*ijādeśca*). However, in the Vedic language, by the rule 3.4.117 (*amantre*), the *liṭ* suffix is treated as a *sārvadhātuka*; consequently, due to its *ṅit* status, there is the elision of the nasal in *samīdhe*. Furthermore, the absence of the *śnam* augment occurs because the suffix is *ārdhadhātuka*, or alternatively, by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). As for the root *bhū*, the *vuk* augment—being obligatory—will simply override both *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* strengthening.

Nor should it be said that *vuk* is non-eternal because it applies to a different word-form (*śabdāntaraprāpti*), for etemality is accepted even on the basis of mere "application to what has already been formed and what has not yet been formed" (*kṛtākṛtaprasaṅgitva*) when it conforms to the observed linguistic usage (*lakṣya*). This is because, in the final doctrine (*siddhānta*), non-eternality resulting from application to a different word-form or from the application of a form with a different accent (*svarabhinnasya*) has been rejected in many ways. This is indeed the approach of the author of the Sūtras as well; for in the case of *babhūva*, since the *vṛddhi* substitution is not characterized by the presence of *ni* (as required by P. 1.1.5), the prohibition [of *guṇa*] by the rule "before *kṅiti*" (*kṅiti ca*) is impossible, and one must therefore resort precisely to the non-eternality of *vuk*.

Nor does the prohibition apply to the *vṛddhi* substitution even when it is not characterized by *kit*, because [the rule] finds its application in forms such as *ahaṃ babhūva* under the alternative where the *ṇit* designation is absent, and likewise in the case of the suffix *thali*. For this very reason, in the *yaṅluk* formation, the forms *bobhūva* and *bobhūvitha* are established through the *vuk* augment due to its obligatory nature; for *kit*-ness does not apply there, owing to the mention of the form with the *śtip* affix (*bhū*). Therefore, it is established in the *Bhāṣya* that this sūtra need not be composed.

Regarding this, the *Kāśikā* states: "It should be stated that [the rule applies] to the roots *śranthi*, *granthi*, *dambhi*, and *svañj*. Although this is not found here in the *Bhāṣya* on the present sūtra, it is nonetheless not unauthoritative, just like the expression "in the manner of *maṇi* and so forth. Accordingly, since the elision of the nasal (*na*-lopa) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the elision of the reduplicated syllable by virtue of being an *abhīya* operation under the rule *ata ekahalmadhye* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.120), the *vārttika* *dambheśca* was composed.

Regarding the rule *śnasorallopaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.111), the use of the marker *ta* (in *at*) indicates that this rule is not universally obligatory (*anitya*), or alternatively, it will be explained in the sixth book (*ṣaṣṭha-adhyāya*) that this Vārttika is not strictly necessary. Similarly, regarding the rule *sadeḥ parasya liṭi* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.3.118), the author of the Bhāṣya provided the example *pariṣasvaje* as an illustration for the Vārttika *svañjer upasaṃkhyānam*. Furthermore, the form *tam induḥ pariṣasvaje* is actually employed in usage. Regarding this, Sudhākara states that this *kitva* (the status of being a *kit* suffix) serves both the purpose of the *pit* suffix and the purpose of the *apit* suffix.

Nyāsakāra, Ātreya, and others hold that it is for the sake of the *apid* augment alone. Haradatta, however, was in doubt. In reality, what is stated by Nyāsakāra and others is superior, because this very point has been illustrated here in the *Vṛtti* and in the *Bhāṣya* on Pāṇini 6.1.29. [Examples: From the roots *śrath* and *granth* (DhP 1.513, 514), meaning "to loosen" or "to string together": *śrethatuḥ*, *śrethuḥ*; *grethatuḥ*, *grethuḥ*. From *dambh*: *debhatuḥ*, *debhuḥ*. From *svañj*: *sasvaje*, *sasvajāte*.

However, Haradatta and Mādhava state that some read "śranthi-granthi-dambhi-svañjīnāṃ vā," whereby they optionally apply the *kittva* (the prohibition of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*). According to their view, forms such as *dadambhatuḥ* and *śaśranthatuḥ* are also possible. In the opinion of Sudhākara, however, even with the suffix *ṇal*, the forms are *śretha*, *gretha*, and *debha*. This might be the case: in all these systems, forms such as *śrethatuḥ* and *grethatuḥ* would be difficult to obtain, because [the roots] contain a conjunct consonant (*saṃyukta*) consisting of a *hal* (consonant) situated between two vowels, just as in the case of *sasvaje*. This is true.

For this very reason, Haradatta maintains that the substitution of *e* for *ay* and the elision of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsalopa*) must also be stated here; however, the source for this must be sought. Likewise, the authority of Mādhava—who asserts "śaśranthitha" according to the views of Nyāsa and others, while Sudhākara asserts "śrothitha"—must also have its source investigated. Even though there is disagreement regarding the *kit* designation, the rule "thali ca seṭi" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.121) does not apply here because there is no distinction [in the absence of a *seṭ* suffix]. Similarly, Mādhava’s claim that the statement is necessary because the substitution of *e* would otherwise not apply due to the *asiddha* status of the *na*-elision is also weakly founded.

Regarding the root *śranth*, since it possesses a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) and begins with a *grantha*-type letter, the substitution of *ca* does not apply; thus, due to its prominence, the investigation into whether the elision of *n* is established or unestablished is as futile as examining the teeth of a crow. This is the general direction. For the followers of Kumāra (the Kātantra school), however, all of this is formally enshrined in their sūtras. Accordingly, Śarvavarman has formulated the rule: "In the *parokṣā* [tense], there is the elision of the *anuṣaṅga* of roots ending in *ān*, *ni*, or *anubandhas*, provided no *guṇa* occurs, for the roots *indh*, *śranth*, *granth*, and *dambh*."

Regarding this, [the rule] *asyaikavyañjanamadhyenādeśādeḥ parokṣāyām thali ca seṭi* (Pāṇini 6.1.59), which states that [the substitution of *iṭ*] occurs for the roots *tṛ*, *phala*, *bhaja*, *trap*, *śrantha*, *granthi*, and *dambhi* when followed by the suffix *parokṣā* or *thali* with *iṭ*, Durgasiṃha maintains that because of association (*sāhacarya*) with roots lacking a nasal (*niranuṣaṅga*), the forms *śaśrantha* and so forth are intended here. This being the case, one must somehow justify the fact that the inclusion of *dambhi* and others—which is mentioned elsewhere in the Pāṇinian system—is also accepted there, by relying on the fact that the Vārttika and Bhāṣya on *dambheśca* (Vārttika on Pāṇini 7.2.59) provide a general indicator (*jñāpaka*). (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.7)

Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.7: *mṛḍamṛdagudhakuṣakliśavadavasaḥ ktvā*. The suffix *ktvā* is prescribed as having the *kittva* designation after the roots *mṛḍ*, *mṛd*, *gudh*, *kuṣ*, *kliś*, *vad*, and *vas*. Regarding these roots: for *gudh*, *kuṣ*, and *kliś*, the optionality of *kittva* would have applied by Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.26 (*ralovyupadhāt*). For the others, the prohibition of *kittva* would have applied by Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.18 (*na ktvā seṭ*). Therefore, *kittva* is specifically enjoined here. Examples: *mṛḍitvā*, *mṛditvā*, *gudhitvā*, *kuṣitvā*, *kliśitvā*, *uditvā*, *uṣitvā*. [In *uditvā* and *uṣitvā*,] the augment *iṭ* is added by Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.2.52 (*vasatikṣudhoḥ*). Then, because they belong to the *yajādi* group, there is *saṃprasāraṇa* (vocalization) by Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.8.

Regarding *Aṣṭādhyāyī* 1.2.8: *rudavidamuṣagrahiṣvapipracchaḥ saṃśca*: after these roots, both *saN* and *ktvā* are *kit*. In the case of *rud*, *vid*, and *muṣ*, since the optionality [of *kit*] is already established by *Aṣṭādhyāyī* 1.2.26 (*ralo vyupadhāt*), this rule serves as an injunction for *grah*. For *svap* and *pracch*, however, it is for the sake of *saN*. One should not suspect that the prescription of *kit* for the *aṇiṭ* [roots] *svap* and *pracch* would be merely restrictive (*niyāmaka*) because their purpose is fulfilled by that much alone.

Having wept, he wishes to weep (*rurudiṣati*); having known, he wishes to know (*vividiṣati*); having stolen, he wishes to steal (*mumuṣiṣati*); having taken, he wishes to take (*jighṛkṣati*); having slept, he wishes to sleep (*suṣupsati*); having asked, he wishes to ask (*pipṛcchiṣati*). Due to the *kit* designation, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) for roots beginning with *grah*, and by the rule "after the five beginning with *kṝ*, [the augment *iṭ* is added] to the *san*" (*Aṣṭādhyāyī* 1.2.9), the *iṭ* is added to the *san* of *pracch*.

*Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.9: iko jhal.* A *san* suffix beginning with a *jhal* consonant following an *ik* vowel shall be treated as having the *kit* designation. Thus: *cicīṣati*, *tuṣṭūṣati*, *cikīrṣati*. Now, one might object: when *san* follows the roots *viṣ*, *stṛ*, and *kṛñ*, let there be lengthening by *Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.16* (*ajjhanagamāṃ sani*), which would override *guṇa*; what then is the purpose of the *kit* designation? Nor should it be said that this would apply similarly in cases such as *pipaviṣati*, for the rule *Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.15* (*anunāsikasya kvijhaloḥ*)—by virtue of the continued application of the term *jhal* from that rule—prescribes lengthening only before a *san* suffix beginning with a *jhal* consonant.

If this were not a quality (*guṇa*), then in the case of *jñīpsati*, the long vowel (*dīrgha*) would subvert even the elision of the suffix *ṇi* (*ṇilopa*) without distinction. However, it must be stated that when the *kittva* (the status of having a *k*-marker) is present—as in *cicīṣati* and the like—the long vowel has already served its purpose; thus, in *jñīpsati*, it is subverted by the elision of *ṇi* because the latter is subsequent (*para*). This is because, according to the maxim of "that which was not previously applicable" (*yenāprāptinyāya*), the long vowel is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *guṇa*. Nor should one be deluded into thinking that, by the maxim of "an exception [prevails] over what precedes it" (*purastādapavādanyāya*), the elision of *ṇi* alone is what is subverted; for that maxim only applies when there is a possibility of both being exceptions (*ubhayāpavādatā*).

But here, because there is an absence of the principle *yenanāprāpti* (non-application where [the rule] would otherwise apply), [the present rule does not supersede the elision]. Nor should it be argued that, in a general consideration of the scope (*sāmānyacintā*), the supersession of the elision of *ṇi* is unavoidable; for, based on the grammatical indication in *Aṣṭādhyāyī* 1.4.34, *sthāśapāṃ jñīpsyamānaḥ*, and in accordance with the observed forms (*lakṣya*), it is more appropriate here to adopt a specific consideration of what is to be superseded (*bādhyaviśeṣacintā*).

Nor should it be argued that because the roots *gu* (in the sense of "evacuating excrement") and *dhru* (in the sense of "motion" and "stability") are listed [in the Dhātupāṭha], the long vowel in forms such as *jugūṣati* and *dūdhūṣiti*—which has already served its purpose [by preventing Guṇa substitution for the penultimate vowel]—is sublated by the subsequent Guṇa rule. This is because the inclusion of the pratyāhāra *ajjhan* in the rule [A 6.4.16] is without scope [for application elsewhere] if it were not stated that [the rule applies] to *u*, *ṛ*, and *ṅ*.

Nor should one suspect that the *vārttika* "of the substitute for √gam [in the form] iṅ" (Kāśikāvṛtti) is intended as a rejection [of the rule], on the grounds that the mention of the vowel *a* (*aj*) would be purposeful because √gam would be qualified by *ac* through the principles of *tantra* and so forth, based on the possibilities and exceptions [involved]. For if that were the case, after stating "lengthening of *u*" (*uto dīrghaḥ*), one should have composed the rule as "of *iṅ* and *han*" (*iṅhanoḥ*).
