The word *ibhya* has its initial syllable accented acute (udātta) according to Pāṇini’s sūtra 6.1.213, *yato ’nāvaḥ*. The word *kṣatriya*, however, has its middle syllable accented acute according to Pāṇini’s sūtra 6.1.217, *yāntasyāntyātpūrvam*.

[The suffix *kan*] is applied after words beginning with *aśman* (Pāṇini 6.1.156): *nakha*, *ukhā*, *sukha*, *duḥkha*. Regarding *nakha*, since it is a term for a body part, the rule "for body parts ending in a sibilant" (Pāṇini 6.1.159) would have required the acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable. Regarding *ukhā*—a specific vessel constructed by ritualists for cooking barley-gruel and the like—the rule "when denoting an artificial object, the vowel following *kh* is acute" (Pāṇini 6.1.160) would have required the acute accent on the vowel *u*. Regarding *sukha* and *duḥkha*, the rule "of that which does not have *na* as its scope" (Pāṇini 6.2.172) would have applied. Why say "beginning with *aśman*"? [Consider] *śikhā*, *mukha*.

Regarding the word *mukha*, its initial vowel is udātta (high-pitched) either by Pāṇini 6.2.179 (*svāṅgaśiṭām*) or by 6.2.176 (*nabviṣayasya*). As for the word *śikhā*, although 6.2.179 does not apply because it ends in a long vowel, its initial vowel is nevertheless known to be udātta by virtue of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of words beginning with *aśman* in that same rule.

And so, [the author] says "In reality... out of dissatisfaction with the fact that in many Uṇādi manuscripts the reading is simply "śīṅo hrasvaśca" (Uṇādisūtra 712) and not "śīṅaḥ kho niṭ dhrasvaśca. In the Uṇādi list, the *niṭ* status is stated for "śīḍaḥ kho niṭ dhrasvaśca. In reality, that alone is the refuge.

This is because, according to the lexicon "śaṅkhaḥ nidhau lalāṭāsthina" (Amarakośa 3.3.18), the word "śaṅkha" denotes bone; thus, since the rule "svāṅgaśiṭām" (Pāṇini 6.2.129)—which prescribes an udātta accent for words denoting body parts ending in *śiṭ* consonants—is already fulfilled by its application to such words, it cannot serve as a *jñāpaka* (indicative mark) for the exclusion of the rule "aśmādeḥ" (Pāṇini 6.2.128).

Regarding *hiṣṭha*, *vat*, *sarat*, and those ending in *iṣṭha* (Pāṇini 6.1.208): for these, the final syllable shall be udātta. For example, *atiśayena bahulaḥ* becomes *baṃhiṣṭhaḥ*. This is by virtue of the rule "the initial [syllable] is always [udātta] when a suffix marked with Ñ or Ṇ follows" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.197). Since the initial syllable would otherwise have been udātta, this rule applies. In cases such as *baṃhiṣṭhair aśvaiḥ*, *suvṛtā rathena*, or *yad baṃhiṣṭhaṃ nātivide*, the initial syllable is udātta due to metrical transposition (*vyatyaya*). *Saṃvatsaraḥ*: here, the original accent of the first member of the compound, being an indeclinable (*avyaya*), is superseded. *Saptatiḥ*; *aśītiḥ*.

When the rule *laghāvante* (Pāṇini 6.1.167) would otherwise apply, [the following occurs]: *catvāriṃśat*. Here too, as before, [the accent is on the final syllable]. In *abhyūrṇvānāprabhṛthasyāyoḥ*, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) in the prior member is here set aside. In the sense of "skillful" (*sādhau*), [the word] *dakṣiṇasya* has an acute accent (*udātta*) on the final syllable. Why "in the sense of skillful"? So that, when it functions as a pronoun (*sarvanāma*) in the sense of "fixed position" (*vyavasthā*), it may have the acute accent on the first syllable according to *svāṅgaśiṭām* (Pāṇini 6.2.173). But in other meanings, by the rule *laghāvante* (Pāṇini 6.1.167), the heavy syllable (*guru*) receives the acute accent. The lexicon (*kośa*) states: "Dakṣiṇa [is used] for 'straight,' 'generous,' and 'one who conforms to the will of another.'"

"Regarding a word denoting one's own limb (*svāṅga*), the first syllable is optionally [acute] (Pāṇini 6.2.173). Thus, for the word *dakṣiṇa*, both the beginning and the end are acutely accented alternately. Example: *dakṣiṇo bāhuḥ* ("the right arm"). Why is the term "denoting [one's own]" (*ākhyā*) mentioned? [Because] for one sitting facing west, the left hand becomes the "right" [hand]. "And in the Veda" (Pāṇini 6.2.174). This rule is for the purpose of [words] that do not denote one's own limbs. Example: *dakṣiṇaḥ*. Here, both the beginning and the end are acutely accented alternately.

Regarding *kṛṣṇa* when it is the name of a wild animal (*mṛga*) [Pāṇini 6.2.11]: since the rule "the final syllable of the names of colors" (Pāṇini 6.2.33) would have prescribed an udātta accent on the first syllable, this sūtra prescribes an udātta on the final syllable. Examples: *kṛṣṇānāṃ vrīhīṇām* ("of black rice grains"); *kṛṣṇo nonāva vṛṣabhaḥ* ("the black bull has bellowed"). But when it is the name of a wild animal: *kṛṣṇo rātryai* ("the black one for the night").

[Regarding Pāṇini 6.2.13] *vā nāmadheyasya*: *kṛṣṇasya* remains the same. Or: *ayaṃ vā kṛṣṇo aśvinā* ("this black one, O Aśvins"); *kṛṣṇa ṛṣiḥ* ("the seer Kṛṣṇa"). [Regarding Pāṇini 6.2.13] *śuklagaurayorādiḥ*: some say that the initial syllable should always be udātta. However, it is more logical that the word *vā* ("or") is understood here as well, because we see the final syllable accented in the example: *saro gauro yatā piba* ("the white bull, go and drink from the lake").

Regarding *aṅguṣṭha*, *udaka*, and *vaśā*, [the final syllable] is udātta in the Vedic language (Pāṇini 6.2.179). Since the rule "for body parts other than those beginning with *kūrda*" (Pāṇini 6.2.177) would have resulted in the second syllable of *aṅguṣṭha* being udātta, this sūtra is commenced for the purpose of making the final syllable udātta. The mention of *vaśā* is for the sake of restriction: namely, that it occurs only in the Vedic language. Consequently, they say that in common usage (*loka*), it is ādyudātta (acute on the first syllable).

And for *pṛṣṭha* (PhSū 15): In Vedic, the final syllable shall be acute; in the spoken language (*bhāṣā*), it may optionally be so. This sūtra has as its scope the spoken language alone, like [the rules] "before eleven in non-Vedic" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.3.49), "the penultimate [syllable is acute] before a *jhal*-ending suffix" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.180), and "optionally in the spoken language" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.181). Examples: *pṛṣṭham*. And for *tṛṇa* when it is a name of Arjuna (PhSū 16): This is an exception to the initial acute [prescribed by] "of those ending in *-arvan*" (PhSū 32).

If the name of a noble person (*ārya*) is [used] as a designation for ownership (*svāmī*), [it is unaccented]. (Pāṇini 6.2.17) This rule is stated because the preceding rule, "that which precedes the final vowel of a word ending in *yā*" (Pāṇini 6.2.52), or the rule "after *yataḥ*, except for *nauḥ*" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.213), would otherwise result in an acute accent on the first syllable.

If the name of a direction (*āśā*) is not a designation for a cardinal point (*digākhyā*), [it is unaccented]. (Pāṇini 6.2.18) This is for the purpose of excluding those that are designations of directions. By this very indicator (*jñāpaka*), it is established that synonyms for "direction" (*dik-paryāya*) have an acute accent on the first syllable, as in: *indra āśābhyaḥ pari*.

In the case of names of constellations (*nakṣatra*) ending in *āp*, the final syllable shall be acute (*udātta*). This rule applies to names such as *Āśleṣā* and *Anurādhā*, for which the rule "laghāvante" (Pāṇini 6.1.197) would otherwise apply; and to *Jyeṣṭhā*, *Śraviṣṭhā*, and *Dhaniṣṭhā*, for which the suffix *iṣṭhan* would otherwise cause the initial syllable to be acute. However, this is not the case if the word is preceded by *ku* and is the name of the constellation Kṛttikā. In such a case, the final syllable is not acute; thus, *kṛttikā* (the constellation Kṛttikā) has its accent on the first syllable. Some commentators, however, explain the rule as applying to words ending in *āp* that are preceded by *ku*, and they assert that even in cases such as *āryikā* and *bahulikā*, the final syllable is not acute.

And for *ghṛta* and so forth (Pāṇini 6.1.217), the final syllable is acute (*udātta*). Example: *ghṛtaṃ mimikṣe*. This is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*). In the case of *jyeṣṭha* and *kaniṣṭha* when referring to age (Pāṇini 6.1.218), the final syllable shall be acute. Examples: *jyeṣṭha āha camasān*; *kaniṣṭha ahi caturaḥ*. Why "when referring to age"? [Counter-examples: *jyeṣṭhaḥ* [meaning] "best," and *kaniṣṭhaḥ* [meaning] "smallest. In these cases, because of the *nit*-designation, the initial syllable alone is acute. For *bilva* and *tiṣya*, the circumflex (*svarita*) is optionally applied (Pāṇini 6.1.219). For these two, the final syllable may optionally be circumflex; in the alternative case, it is acute.
Thus ends the first quarter in the Phiṭ-sūtras.

Now, the section beginning with *prāk śakaṭeḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.24) is a governing rule (*adhikāra*). It extends as far as *śakaṭi-śakaṭyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.60). [The initial syllable] of a word ending in a short vowel that is restricted to the feminine gender shall have an acute accent (*udātta*). Examples: *valiḥ*, *tanuḥ*. [The initial syllable] of a word ending in *naP* that does not end in *ani* shall have an acute accent. [Also] that which ends in *van* or *ya*. However, for a word ending in *is*, it is so only when accompanied by *sāP*. *Nap* means neuter.

And [the feminine suffix *ī* is applied] to words for grasses and grains that consist of two syllables (phiṣ sūtra 27). "Consisting of two syllables" is the meaning. Examples: *kuśāḥ*, *kāśāḥ*, *māṣāḥ*, *tilāḥ*. According to the *Bahvṛcas*, however, it is *godhūmāḥ*.
[The suffix *ī* is applied] after a numeral (phiṣ sūtra 28). Examples: *pañca*, *catasraḥ*.

[The suffix *ī* is applied] to words denoting one's own limbs (*svāṅga*) that end in a sibilant (*śiṭ*) but not in the letter *m* (phiṣ sūtra 29). *Śiṭ* refers to all nominal stems (*sarvanāman*). Examples: *karṇaḥ*, *oṣṭhaḥ*, *viśvaḥ*.

In words denoting living beings (*prāṇin*), the first syllable preceding *k* (the *ka*-class consonants) is acute (*udātta*). Examples: *kākaḥ*, *vṛkaḥ*. [In the phrase] *śukeṣu me* ("among the parrots, mine"), why "of living beings"? [Counter-example: *udakam* ("water"). When followed by a *khay* consonant (any consonant except *y*), if it denotes an artificial object (*kṛtrimākhyā*), the first syllable containing the vowel *u* is acute. Example: *kandukaḥ* ("a ball"). In words ending in *un*, *varuṇa*, *voriśāda*, and *svasṛ*, the first syllable containing *u* is acute. Examples: *un*—*unarvann antānām* ("of those ending in *un*"); *varuṇa*—*varuṇaṃ voriśādasam* ("Varuṇa, the devourer of Vṛtra"); *svasṛ*—*svasāraṃ tvā kṛṇavai* ("I shall make you my sister"). *van*—*van pīvānaṃ meṣam* ("the fat ram").
In the case of color-words ending in *ta*, *na*, *ti*, or *ni* (Pāṇini 6.2.33), the first syllable is acute (*udātta*). For example: *etaḥ*, *hariṇaḥ*, *śitiḥ*, *pṛśniḥ*, *harit*.

In the case of a word ending in a short vowel, except for those ending in *ṛ* (Pāṇini 6.2.34), the initial short vowel shall be acute. For example: *muniḥ*. In the case of the word *akṣa* when it does not mean "gambling" (Pāṇini 6.2.35), the first syllable is acute. For example: *tasya nākṣaḥ* ("his dice"). However, when it refers to gambling, as in *akṣair mā dīvyaḥ* ("do not play with dice"), [the rule does not apply].

PĀṆINI SŪTRA 6.2.46: *ardhasyāsamadyotane*. The first syllable of *ardha* is acute when it does not signify an equal portion. Example: *ardho grāmasya* ("half of the village"). However, when it signifies an equal portion, it is *ardhaṃ pippalyāḥ* ("half of a long pepper"). PĀṆINI SŪTRA 6.2.47: *pītadravārthānām*. For words meaning "yellow" (*pīta*) and "liquid" (*drava*), the first syllable is acute. Example: *pītadruḥ* ("the Sarala pine tree"). PĀṆINI SŪTRA 6.2.48: *grāmādīnāñca*. For the group beginning with *grāma*, the first syllable is acute. Examples: *grāmaḥ*, *somaḥ*, *yāmaḥ*.

[The first syllable] of a name of the object compared (*upameya*) [ending in] *lup* [is acute]. "Ending in *sphig*" is an alternative reading; *sphig* here refers to the elision (*lup*). This is a technical term (*saṃjñā*) of the Easterners (*prācām*). Example: *cañcā* (meaning "like a beak"). [The first syllable] of these names of objects compared—namely, *vṛkṣa*, *parvata*, *vyāghra*, *siṃha*, and *mahiṣa*—is not acute. Examples: *tāla* (as in *tāla iva tālaḥ*), *meru* (as in *meruriva meruḥ*), *vyāghraḥ*, *siṃhaḥ*, and *mahiṣaḥ*. [The first syllable] of the name of a specific king (*rājaviśeṣa*) ending in *yaman* or *vā* is acute. *Yaman* means "old. Example: *āṅgaḥ*. Counter-example: *aṅgāḥ*.

"In the case of a light syllable at the end, or when two [light syllables] are at the end, the heavy syllable of a word with many vowels is acute. (Pāṇini 6.2.42). When there is a light syllable at the end, or when two light syllables are at the end, the heavy syllable of a polysyllabic word is acute. For example: *kalyāṇaḥ*, *kolāhalaḥ*. Here, the intended meaning is that which is the first among the heavy syllables. By this, the status of being the initial [heavy syllable] is established in the case of *vṛṣākapiḥ* through the principle of designation (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). Consequently, the commentaries and other texts on rules such as *vṛṣākapyagni-* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.1.37) are not contradicted.

Furthermore, the passages from the Bhāṣya and other texts located in sūtras such as *krītavat parimāṇāt* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.3.146) are also consistent [with this view]. If it is objected: "Even so, does this not contradict Haradatta’s statement in his commentary on the sūtra *anyato ṅīṣ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.2.40), where he says that the words *sāraṅga* and *kalmāṣa* have the middle vowel as udātta according to the rule *laghāv ante* (Phitsūtra 43)? The answer is: True. The essential point is simply that the word *ādi* (and so forth) does not apply here.

PĀṆINI SŪTRA 6.2.43: *strīviṣayavarṇākṣupūrvāṇām* | For these three [categories], the first syllable is acute (*udātta*). *Strīviṣaya* (feminine gender): *mallikā*. *Varṇa* (color/designation): *śyenī*, *hariṇī*. Those preceded by the word *akṣu* are *akṣupūrva*: *tarakṣuḥ*. PĀṆINI SŪTRA 6.2.44: *śakunīnāñca laghupūrvam* | For names of birds, the syllable preceded by a light vowel (*laghu*) shall be acute. Examples: *kukkuṭaḥ*, *tittiriḥ*. PĀṆINI SŪTRA 6.2.45: *na ṛtuprāṇyākhyāyām* | In the case of names of seasons or living beings, that which would have been acute according to the preceding rule is not so. Examples: *vasantaḥ*, *kṛkalāsaḥ*.
In the case of grains ending in *vṛddhi* vowels or *kṣ*, the first syllable is acute (phiṭ-sūtra 46). Examples: those ending in *ka*: *śyāmākāḥ*; those ending in *ṣ*: *māṣāḥ*.

In the case of words denoting inhabited regions (*janapada*) that do not end in *ṣ*, [the first syllable is acute] (phiṭ-sūtra 47). Example: *kekayaḥ*. In the case of words beginning with *haya* and ending in *la* that is not part of a consonant cluster, the final syllable or the preceding one is acute (phiṭ-sūtra 48). *Haya* is a technical term for the letter *ha*. Examples: *palalam*, *śalalam*. Why "beginning with *haya*"? Consider *ekalaḥ*. Why "not part of a cluster"? Consider *mallaḥ*.
And for those ending in -iganta and having two syllables (phiṣ 49), the first syllable is udātta. *kṛṣiḥ*.
Thus ends the second quarter.

Now begins the second [section], prior to *prāgīṣāt* (PhiSū 50). The section on the second case (*dvitīyā*) extends from here until *īṣāntasya hayādeḥ* (PhiSū 66). The section concerning words consisting of three syllables (*tryacām*) extends prior to *makarāt* (PhiSū 51). Until *makaravarūḍha* (PhiSū 57), the rule for three-syllable words applies. Regarding body parts (*svāṅgānām*) that do not begin with *kṛ*, etc.: excluding those beginning with the *ka*-group, *r*, or *v*, for body parts consisting of three syllables, the second [syllable] becomes [nasalized]. For example: *lalāṭam*. However, for words beginning with *kṛ*, etc., we have: *kapolaḥ*, *rasanā*, *vadanam*.
And for words beginning with *mā* (phiṭ-sūtra 53), the second syllable of those consisting of three syllables is udātta: *malayaḥ*, *makaraḥ*.

For words beginning with *śā* that denote vegetables (phiṭ-sūtra 54): *śītanyā*, *śatapuṣpā*. For words beginning with *guru* that end in *p* (phiṭ-sūtra 55): *pādapaḥ*, *ātapaḥ*. But for those beginning with *laghu*: *anūpam*. However, for two-syllable words: *nīpam*.

*Yutānyaṇyantānām* (Pāṇini 6.1.156): For words ending in the triad beginning with *yuta*, the second syllable is udātta. Examples: *yuta-ayutam*, *aṇi-dhamaniḥ*, *aṇi-vipaṇiḥ*. *Makaravarūḍhapārevatavitastekṣvārjidrākṣākalomākāṣṭhāpeṣṭhāpeṣṭhākāśīnāmādirvā* (Pāṇini 6.1.157): For these [words], either the first syllable or the second is udātta. Examples: *makaraḥ*, *varūḍhaḥ*, and so forth. *Chandasi ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.158): This rule applies also in the Vedic language (*chandas*). This sūtra is commenced for the sake of words other than *makara* and the rest. According to the usage of the texts (*lakṣya*), it should be understood that either the first or the second syllable is udātta.

And for words beginning with *kardama* (Pāṇini 6.2.59), either the first syllable or the second is acute (*udātta*). For example: *karhamaḥ*. For words beginning with *sugandhitejana* (Pāṇini 6.2.60), either the first syllable or the second is acute, as well as the word *tejana*. For example: *sugandhitejanāḥ*. For words ending in *phala* (Pāṇini 6.2.61), either the first syllable or the second is acute. For example: *rājādana*.

In the case of a word ending in *y*, the syllable preceding the final one is acute (*udātta*) [Pāṇini 6.1.216]. As in *kulāyaḥ*. Also, in the case of a word ending in *th*, the syllables *na* and *la* are acute [Pāṇini 6.1.217]. In the word *nātha*, both the syllable *na* and the following light syllable (*laghu*) are acute. As in *sanāthā sabhā*. Furthermore, in the words *śiśumāra*, *uduṃbara*, *balīvarda*, *uṣṭra*, *arapūra*, and *purūravas*, the syllable preceding the final one is acute, or alternatively, the second syllable from the end is acute [Pāṇini 6.1.218].

[In the case] of *sāṅkāśya*, *kāpilya*, *nāsikya*, and *dārvāghāṭa* (Pāṇini 6.2.85), the second syllable is optionally acute (*udātta*). [Examples: *sāṅkāśyam*, etc. [In the case] of words beginning with *haya* and ending in *īṣā* (Pāṇini 6.2.86), the first syllable is optionally acute. "Beginning with *haya*" means beginning with a consonant (*hal-ādi*). [Examples: *halīṣā*, *lāṅgalīṣā*.
The first syllable of *uśīra*, *dāśeraka*, *pāla*, *palāla*, *śaivāla*, *śyāmāka*, *śārīra*, *śarāva*, *hṛdaya*, *hiraṇya*, *araṇya*, *apatya*, and *deva* (Pāṇini 6.2.87) shall be acute.
If the word *mahiṣī* or *aṣāḍhā* occurs before *jāyā*, it is called an *iṣṭakā* (bricks) compound; its first syllable is udātta. Example: *mahiṣī jāyā*, *aṣāḍhā upadadhāti*.
Thus ends the third quarter.
In the case of *śakaṭi* and *śakaṭī*, each syllable is acutely accented (*udātta*) in alternation (Pāṇini 6.1.159): *śakaṭiḥ*, *śakaṭī*.

In the case of *goṣṭhaja* when it is the name of a Brāhmaṇa (Pāṇini 6.1.160), each syllable is acutely accented in succession: *goṣṭhajo brāhmaṇaḥ*. In other cases, *goṣṭhajaḥ* refers to an animal; here, it is acutely accented on the final syllable by the rule of the original accent of the second member of a *kṛt*-derived compound. In the case of *pārāvata* (Pāṇini 6.1.161), with the exception of the penultimate syllable, the remainder is acutely accented in succession: *pārāvataḥ*.

Regarding *dhūmrájānu*, *muñjakeśa*, *kālavāla*, and *sthālīpāka* when they do not occur in the sense of "water" (Pāṇini 6.2.72): among these four, with the exception of the four beginning with *dhūmra*, the remaining ones are successively acute (*udātta*). [Examples: *dhūmrájānuḥ*, *muñjakeśáḥ*, *kālavāláḥ*, *sthālīpākáḥ*.
Regarding *kapikeśa* and *harikeśa* in the Veda (Pāṇini 6.2.73): [examples] *kapikeśáḥ*, *harikeśáḥ*.
Regarding *nyaṅ* and *svaḥ* as circumflex (*svarita*) (Pāṇini 6.2.74): this is clear. [Examples: *nyaṅṅ-uttānáḥ*; *vyacakṣayatsváḥ*.
The initial syllable of *nyarbuda* and *vyalkaśa* shall be circumflex (*svarita*) (Pāṇini 6.2.75).

The final syllable of *tilya*, *śikyaka*, *kāśmarya*, *dhānyaka*, *kanyā*, *rājanya*, and *manuṣya* shall be circumflex (Pāṇini 6.2.76). For example, *tilyam*—meaning a field where sesamum grows—is so called; this occurs despite the rule "the acute accent applies after a word ending in /a/ except for *nau*" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.213).
In the Vedic language (*chandas*), the final syllables of *bilva*, *bhakṣya*, and *vīrya* are circumflex (Pāṇini 6.2.77). These [final syllables] shall be circumflex.
*simasme* (Phitsūtra 78): In *tvattvasamasimetyanuccāni*, [the word *simasme*] is not acute. *starīrutvat* | *uta tvaḥ paśyan* | *nabhantāmanyake same* | *simasmai*.

*simasyātharvaṇenta udāttaḥ* (Phitsūtra 79): In *simasyātharvaṇaḥ*, the final syllable is acute. The mention of *atharvaṇaḥ* is for the most part; or rather, it is intended to mean "seen therein. By this, it occurs even in the Ṛgveda, as in *vāsastanute simasmai*. *Nipātā ādyudāttāḥ* (Phitsūtra 80): Particle (*nipāta*) words have the acute accent on their first syllable. *svāhā*.
The prefixes (upasarga), with the exception of *abhi*, [have their first syllable acute];

and the words beginning with *eva* [have their final syllable acute]. There is an alternative reading: "of those beginning with *evam*" (*evamādīnām*). These are: *eva*, *evam*, and *nūnam*. "Together with you, O son, along with the wise. Regarding the word *saha*, in the section of the third chapter of the sixth book [of Pāṇini’s Aṣṭādhyāyī]—"the substitution of *sa-* for *saha-*" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.3.78)—the ancient grammarians maintain that the word *saha* has its initial syllable acute (*ādyudātta*). However, that should be considered doubtful. The words beginning with *vāc* have both syllables acute. The inclusion of the term "both" (*ubhau*) is for the purpose of setting aside the rule "a word [consisting of more than one syllable] is unaccented except for one [which is acute]" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.158).
The particles beginning with *ca* are unaccented (Pāṇini 2.4.82). This is clear.

The word *yathā* [is unaccented] at the end of a metrical foot (Pāṇini 2.4.85), as in: *tannemim ṛbhavo yathā*. Why "at the end of a foot"? [Consider: *yathā no aditiḥ karat*. When there is a reduplication beginning with *pra*, the final syllable of the subsequent member is acute (Pāṇini 2.4.86), as in: *paṭupaṭuḥ*.

"Everything else is unaccented" (Phiṭ-sūtra 87). "The rest" means that which follows [the initial portion] of a word that is reduplicated, such as *nitya* and so forth. Examples: *praprāyam*, *dive dive*. Thus ends the fourth quarter in the Phiṭ-sūtras composed by Ācārya Śāntanava.

Having concluded the incidental discussion, let us return to the subject at hand: (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.42). "A single *al* [phoneme] that is a suffix is called *apṛkta*" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.41). A suffix consisting of a single *al* shall bear the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of *apṛkta*. Regarding the application of this designation, although the mention of the word "single" (*eka*) in the rule "of an *apṛkta* following *vi*" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.14) indicates that when a phoneme (*varṇa*) is mentioned, the entire class (*jāti*) is intended, here—due to the force of the explicit mention of *al*—the reference is to the individual instance (*vyakti*). Furthermore, this very sūtra would be redundant; for in all instances where *apṛkta* is mentioned, the desired result is already established by the mention of *al* alone.

Nor should it be argued that when explaining the term *surā-sut* (one who presses *surā*) as "one who presses *surā*," there would be a deletion (*lopa*) of the *s* which is part of the verbal root (*dhātu*) in the word *surā*. This is because the matter is already settled by the *paribhāṣā* regarding suffixes and non-suffixes (*pratyayāpratyaya-paribhāṣā*), and also due to the association with case-endings (*vibhakti*). Just as even when the rule is formulated as it stands, because of the association with *ti*, only the *tiṅ* [suffix] is understood for *si*, and thus [the substitution] does not apply to the *sic* in "abhaitsīt. Furthermore, in the rule *verapṛktasya* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.67), the mention of *apṛkta* will indeed be rejected by relying on either the *v* or the *e* as being nasalized (*anunāsika*).
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.42)

"A Tatpuruṣa compound whose members have a common substratum (samānādhikaraṇa) is called a Karmadhāraya" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.42). A Tatpuruṣa whose constituent parts share a common substratum shall bear the designation Karmadhāraya. The rules that provide for this designation include "puṃvat karmadhāraye" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.3.42) and others. [The term *samānādhikaraṇa*] is derived from the sense "that which has two words with a common substratum as its basis," by adding the suffix *ac* according to the rule beginning with *arśas*.

However, if— by applying the rule *karmadhārayaśca* at the end of the section beginning with *pūrvakālaika* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.49)— the option were already obtained through the continued application of the term *tatpuruṣa*, and if, by means of the particle *ca*, a conjunction (*samuccaya*) were established as in the case of *gatiśca* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.60) and so forth, then this sūtra (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.43) could have been omitted.

"That which is designated by the nominative case in a compound is the *upasarjana* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.43). A "compound" (*samāsa*) refers to the rule that prescribes the formation of a compound, either because it serves that purpose or by the etymological derivation "that by which [words] are compounded. In that context, whatever is designated by the first case (the nominative) shall be the *upasarjana*. For example, when the second case is used with words such as *śrita*, we have *kṛṣṇaśritaḥ* ("resorted to by Kṛṣṇa"). The creation of this technical term (*saṃjñā*) is for the sake of making the name significant (*nvartha*). For in common usage, they call that which is subordinate an *upasarjana*.

In the case of *rājñaḥ kumārī* and *rājakumārī*, although there is no distinction between the two regarding their being designated as the first member (*prathamānirdiṣṭa*) by the rule *ṣaṣṭhī* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.8), only the word *rājan* is the subordinate element (*upasarjana*), and not *kumārī*. Consequently, the word *kumārī* does not undergo prior placement (*pūrvanipāta*), nor does it undergo the shortening prescribed by the rule *go-striyoḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.48). Furthermore, one should not mistakenly assume that the analysis (*vigraha*) is performed solely with the nominative form, as in *rājñaḥ kumārī*.

And likewise, due to the absence of such a basis, the *Mahābhāṣya* resolves the objection of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)—which arises in rules such as *tatpuruṣe tulyārthatṛtīyāsaptamī* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.2.2) regarding examples like *parame kārake* or *parameṇa kārakeṇa*—by relying on the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) concerning "that which is taught by its specific definition" (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta*). This is also clearly stated in the *Mahābhāṣya* and Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the rule *anekamanyapadārthe* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.24).

There is no rule that the analysis (*vigraha*) must necessarily be with the word ending in the nominative case; rather, it is more appropriate for the analysis to be performed with the word ending in its final, established case-ending. For this very reason, the prohibition of a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) with a word in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), as stated in *Pāṇini* 2.2.11 (*pūraṇaguṇa...*), becomes logically consistent. And for this same reason, the scope of the rule *Pāṇini* 1.2.44 (*ekavibhaktiścāpūrvanipāte*) is secured.

It might be argued: "According to the method already stated, and in accordance with the natural sense of the Sūtras, Bhāṣya, and other texts, as well as logical reasoning, it should simply be said that there is no analysis (*vigraha*) of a word established in the accusative case and so forth by means of a word in the nominative case; why then is it said that 'there is no restriction'? True. There is indeed a basis for that [position]. Why then is it said that "there is no restriction"? True.

Even in that case, there is an objective referent (*ālambana*). For instance, in a common explanatory statement (*vigrahavākya*) intended to demonstrate the meaning of a finished compound—such as "the king’s daughter" (*rājakumārī*) and so forth—it is only the base form (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*āgama*) that are to be explained, and not even the case-ending (*vibhakti*) following the compound. Indeed, the genitive case is not to be explained by another genitive; rather, it is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*). In that context, when there is a desire to explain only the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), who would prevent the use of the nominative case in the explanatory analysis? It is for this very reason that one says: "O King, eat the *harītakī* fruit, which brings benefit like a mother."

Thus, constructions such as these are logically consistent; for there is no obstacle to forming a compound with "mātā" (mother) ending in the nominative case. For this very reason, compounds such as *pacati iti pāka-cakras taṃ pācakam* ("He is one who performs cooking; thus, a cook") are also perfectly correct. This is the general direction [of the argument]. Therefore, the conclusion is that the analysis (*vigraha*) of a word ending in the accusative or other cases—once it has reached its final form—is performed either with another word in its final form ending in the nominative, or with a word in its final form [ending in the same case], but never with a word distinct from both of those.

It might be argued: "If this were a designation based on its etymological meaning (*anvarthasaṃjñā*), then in cases such as *yācakavṛndārakaḥ* ('a beggar who is a noble man') and *gogarbhiṇī* ('a cow that is pregnant'), there would be no prior placement of the substantive. [Response: There is no fault, because in prescriptive rules such as *vṛndārakanāgakuñjaraiḥ pūjyamānam* (Pāṇini 2.1.62) and *catuṣpādo garbhiṇyā* (Pāṇini 2.1.71), the mention of the nominative case serves no other purpose [than to establish the order]. Therefore, it is established that when possible, the etymological meaning serves as the regulating factor. (Pāṇini 1.2.44)

*Aṣṭādhyāyī* 1.2.44: *ekavibhakti cāpūrvanipāte*. Due to the governing topic of meaning (*arthādhikāra*), the term "compound" (*samāsa*) here refers to the non-worldly analytical sentence (*alaukika-vigrahavākya*) which constitutes the meaning of the compound. In that context, although the word conveying the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) may be joined with various case-endings due to different modes of usage, that which possesses a fixed case-ending shall bear the technical designation of "subordinate member" (*upasarjana*) in all operations other than its own prior placement. For example: *atikrānto mālām atimālaḥ* ("one who has surpassed the garland").

In this case, although all case-endings (*vibhakti*) are joined according to the sequence beginning with "that which has been transcended by that which has been transcended," because the word *mālā* is restricted to the second case when it functions as a name (*saṃjñā*), there is shortening [of the final vowel] by the rule "gostriyoḥ" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.48). The same applies to forms such as *niṣkauśāmbi*. Regarding the metarule (*kārikā*) "in a single case-ending, except for the genitive," it does not apply here: *ardhaṃ pippalyāḥ* becomes *ardhapippalī*. But if this is so, would not *pañcakhaṭvī* fail to be established? True.

For this very reason, authoritative scholars maintain that by establishing *vārddhapippalī* through its status as being preceded by a technical name (*saṃjñāpūrvakatva*) and by relying on the *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (the fixed option), the Vārttika stating "after a word ending in the genitive" (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) need not have been commenced. In reality, however, this prohibition concerns the scope of the *ekadeśisamāsa* (part-whole compound). Nor is there a lack of evidence for this; for the second part of the Mahābhāṣya, which provides the example *pañcakhaṭvī*, serves as the proof. Thus ends the first Āhnika of the second Pāda of the first Adhyāya in the *Śabdakaustubha*.
The Second Daily Lesson (Āhnika)

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.45): "That which has meaning, is not a verbal root (*dhātu*), and is not an affix (*pratyaya*) is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Words such as *ḍittha*, which are unanalyzed (*avyutpanna*), serve as examples. This very [sūtra] is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the theory of non-derivation (*avyutpattipakṣa*). As for what Haradatta stated—that even under the theory of derivation (*vyutpattipakṣa*), this [sūtra] is intended for the sake of particles (*nipāta*) and for the sake of imitation (*anukaraṇa*)—that is not correct; for even in that case, the postulation of a base (*prakṛti*) and so forth is possible. In reality, however, this [sūtra] is for the sake of forms such as *bahupaṭavaḥ*.

Nor can the requirement be met by resorting to *matvartha-lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication of possessive meaning) when the term *taddhita* is mentioned, because this would lead to over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *pacataki*. However, the view that [words] are not derivationally formed (*avyutpatti-pakṣa*) is established by the mention of *kaṃsa* itself, since the purpose is already served by the mention of *kami*. Once that is made known, the designation is established even there by this very rule. But is this not itself the indicator (*jñāpaka*)? It should be noted that its purpose is fulfilled in cases where *bahuc* precedes. Why include the condition "having a meaning" (*arthavat*)? So that the designation does not apply to every individual phoneme in examples such as *ghanaṃ vanam*.

It might be argued as follows: even if the technical rule (paribhāṣā) "that which has meaning" (arthavat) does not apply here because its scope is limited to items that take on a specific form through derivation, the desired result is nonetheless established simply by the exclusion (paryudāsa) "not a root, not an affix" (adhātur apratyayaḥ). Nor should it be said that in forms such as *adhīte* and *yāvakaḥ*, the roots *iṅ* and the affix *kan* are indeed present even though they are meaningless; for the meaningfulness of *iṅ* alone is accepted in order to establish the application of augments such as *aṭ*, and affixes that function as suffixes of self-sufficiency (*svārthika*) possess meaning insofar as their base (prakṛti) possesses meaning. Nor should it be said that this is merely a conceptual fiction, for the same would apply to names such as *Ḍittha*.

For it has been said: "Possession of meaning is not possible for [a word] alone because it is not uttered; rather, it is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). For that is the meaning: [meaningfulness belongs] to the imagined *padasphoṭa* and *vākyasphoṭa* alone, since in reality only these possess meaning. True. The mention of "meaningful" (*arthavat*) is for the sake of what follows, but here it is for the sake of clarity. Why say "not a root" (*adhātu*)? [Consider] *ahan*. Let there not be the elision of the *n* (by P. 6.4.24). Nor should it be argued that this is not a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) for a root, because of the inclusion of the term "root" in the rule *supodhātu* (P. 2.4.71).

In forms such as *śpenāyate*, the mention of "dhātu" (verbal root) in the rule is purposeful because it applies to that which ends in an affix. Why [specify] "not an affix" (*apratyaya*)? [So that the designation does not apply to] *tipo* in *pacati*. The same applies to *sup* (nominal endings). Nor is there any persistence of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in words ending in those [affixes], because the mention of "taddhita" (secondary suffix) in the subsequent sūtra serves a restrictive purpose (*niyamārtha*). That is to say, the designation applies only to those ending in taddhitas, and not to others ending in [other types of] affixes. Nor should it be argued that even there, since it is a rule prescribing a technical name (*saṃjñāvidhi*), the inclusion of what ends in that [suffix] (*tadantagrahaṇa*) would be difficult to obtain.

This is established by the force of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "meaningful" (*arthavat*). For the suffix *matup* is used here in the sense of praise (*praśaṃsā*). And the sense of praise consists in being well-known in common usage through its reduction to a single syllable (*ekārpībhāvena*). Although the status of not being a root (*adhātu*) or an affix (*apratyaya*) was already established [by previous rules], the employment of two negatives (*nañ*) is for the sake of clarity. The formation of this great technical designation (*mahāsaṃjñā*) is out of deference to the ancients. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.46)

Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.46: *kṛttaddhitasamāsāśca*. These—namely, primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and compounds (*samāsa*)—when they possess meaning, shall receive the designation of *prātipadika* (nominal stem). Because there is no semantic capacity for [the suffixes] themselves to qualify the specific [meaning], the rule of "extension by the final element" (*tadantavidhi*) applies. For in a compound where the constituent parts lose their own meanings (*jahatsvārthā vṛttiḥ*), there is no longer a separate meaning for the primary or secondary derivative suffixes. However, that interpretation based on a past state of affairs (*bhūtapūrvagati*) is not commendable. In the case of *bhit* and *chit*, since the prohibition "not a verbal root" (*adhātuḥ*) would otherwise apply, and in the case of *karttā* and *harttā*, since the restriction "only those ending in a secondary derivative suffix" would otherwise exclude them, [the present rule is necessary].

And because it is proximate, that which was previously stated regarding the mention of *kṛt* [suffixes] is what is set aside, but not even the restriction caused by the mention of *samāsa*. Consequently, since the paribhāṣā concerning the mention of *kṛt* does not apply here, the sentence *mūlakenopadaṃśam* does not incur [the application of the rule]. If it is objected: "But surely, under the principle of sublation of the general (*bādhyasāmānyacintā*), the restriction regarding *samāsa* would also be set aside," the answer is: True. However, only the first alternative (*pakṣa*) applies here. Nor is there an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the case of a sentence; for, relying on the governing topic of words (*śabdādhikāra*), "meaningful word" (*arthavat-śabda*) is intended here to signify *ekārthībhāva* (integration of meaning).

Because the suffix *matup* is prescribed in the sense of excellence (*atiśaya*). According to the method to be explained, there is the prohibition "not a suffix" (*apratyaya*). However, under the view that this prohibition refers to [suffixes] ending in a suffix (*pratyayānta*), all desired results are established by the maxim of the "intermediate exception" (*madhyepavādanyāya*). Even under the view of rejecting the rule "not a suffix," the desired result is established by the maxim of the "prior exception" (*purastādapavādanyāya*); such is the direction. Regarding the secondary derivative (*taddhita*): *aupagavaḥ*. Here, whether the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) applies by way of a positive injunction or a negative prohibition—either by this [present rule] or by the preceding one—is a point of difference between the opinions already stated.

The same applies to compounds (*samāsa*) as well. Nor should it be said that the mention of "compound" (*samāsa-grahaṇa*) is for the purpose of prescribing [the technical name] even for those compounds that lack semantic connection (*asamartha-samāsa*); for it has already been stated that the term *arthavat* ("meaningful") is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. If it is asked, "How then can there be a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) for those that lack semantic connection?", understand that this is due to the very evidence that establishes the nature of the subject (*dharmigrāhakamāna*). For by rules such as *asūryalalāṭayoḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.2.36), the formation of a compound is prescribed when a *kṛt*-suffix follows an *upapada*. And by virtue of the creation of this great technical designation (*mahāsaṃjñā*), an *upapada* must necessarily be something ending in a case-ending (*vibhaktyanta*).

Nor can it be argued that even in such cases, because there is no rule restricting [the application] to what begins with that [suffix], the word *tat* (in Pāṇini’s sūtra) is intended to serve as an injunction for when the suffix occurs at the end of a compound, as in *rājakumārī*; for the elision (*lopa*) of *hal*, *ṅī*, etc., though an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), takes effect in the domain of elision (*luk*), and thus the compound formation occurs only while the case-ending (*sup*) is still audible. For this very reason, it will be stated later that in forms such as *gomatpriyaḥ*, the augment *num* and others do not occur. Therefore, it is established that in the present context, the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) serves as a restrictive rule (*niyama*), thereby precluding the designation [of "compound"] from a sentence (*vākya*).

And the restriction (*niyama*) is relative to its own class (*sajātīya*). If there should be such a collection where the prior member is a word (*pada*) and the subsequent member is distinct from an affix (*pratyaya*), then it applies only to a compound (*samāsa*). This is because, in all six types of compounds, the status of being a word (*padatva*) for the prior member is never absent. Consequently, since the designation [of *pada*] indeed exists for that which has *bahuc* as its prior member, the acute accent (*udāttatā*) of the letter *ṭ* in "bahupaṭavaḥ" is obtained.

When there is the elision (*luk*) of the first case-ending suffix *jas*, the accent of the *cit* [suffix] is applied according to the rule "the *cit* [suffix], together with its base, [is udātta] for the sake of the forms in *bahuc* and *ka*" (Kāśikāvṛtti), because the case-suffix is produced again. Otherwise, however, the udātta would belong to *jas* itself. Why is it stated "and the following," etc.? So that there may be no exclusion by this [rule] of forms such as *hariṣu*. If it is asked, "Let it be so; what is the harm?", listen.

If that were the case, the mention of "taddhita" in rules such as *janmavān* would be for the purpose of enjoining [the designation] when a taddhita suffix follows; however, by what could the status of *prātipadika* for forms like *rājānau* be prevented? It cannot be by this restrictive rule (*niyama*), because the preceding portion is not a word (*apada*). Nor can it be by the mention of "taddhita," since—as explained above—that mention cannot serve as a restrictive rule.

Nor should it be argued that the mention of the term *dhātu* (root) in the rule *supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.4.71) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that words ending in suffixes do not receive the designation of *prātipadika* (nominal stem). For that [mention] has its purpose fulfilled in cases such as *prāsādīyati*, where the word is not a *prātipadika*—just as in the case of *hariṣu*. Nor is the mention of *ṅyāp* [in the same rule] an indicator; since the matter is already established by the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā* (the maxim regarding forms qualified by gender), it will be demonstrated that its purpose lies elsewhere. Therefore, what has been stated above is correct.

Although this elaboration—that the restriction concerns aggregates that do not stand in the relation of base and suffix—is undertaken to justify the statement "this is its origin" (*utpatti*), it involves unnecessary complexity. However, in the final analysis, let it be exactly as stated. Thus, the mention of *taddhita* [suffixes] serves solely as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). This is precisely Kaiyaṭa’s intention when he states that "the meaningfulness [of a word] is mediated by difference or connection."

The meaning of that passage is that when there is a relation (*saṃsarga*) based on the application of difference (*bheda*) through mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihāreṇa*), the sentence-meaning is mediated by that [relation], but not with the intention that either difference, relation, or both constitute the sentence-meaning; for otherwise, one would not obtain the required diversity (*vairūpya*) between *bahuvrīhi* and *samāsa*. Alternatively, since it is established by the inclusion of the term "sāti" in the rule *sātpadādyoḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.3.111) that a suffix (*pratyaya*) is not a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the mention of "suffix" in the preceding rule must, by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), refer to that which ends in such a suffix (*tadanta*).

The mention of *taddhita* (secondary suffixes), however, is solely for the purpose of a restrictive rule (*vidhi*). It might be argued: "Even in all three positions, in examples such as *rājapuruṣau*, the designation [of *prātipadika*] would unavoidably apply to 'puruṣau' and so on; consequently, by virtue of being a part of a *prātipadika*, there would be elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*). This is not so. In the *jahatsvārthā* theory, [the compound] is devoid of meaning [as a whole]. In the *ajahatsvārthā* theory as well, since the preceding member alone lacks a specific meaning, it is only when combined with the following member that it conveys a specific meaning. For it has been stated: "The suffix *matup* is used in the sense of praise."

Likewise, in cases such as *ghaṭapaṭau* ("pot and cloth"), the two words together alone possess a co-occurrent meaning (*sahabhūtārthatā*), because suffixes convey their own meanings as connected with the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). Thus, the portion "*ghaṭau*" is not itself meaningful [in isolation]. By this, the objection that the mention of "compound" (*samāsagrahaṇa*) in the rule might be for the sake of prescribing [the application of suffixes] even to meaningless compounds—such as *daśadāḍima* ("ten pomegranates") which are like those that are semantically incompetent (*asamartha*)—is refuted; for it has already been stated that the mention of "meaningful" (*arthavat*) here serves a specific purpose. This is the general direction of the argument.

However, if it is maintained—following the view of the Naiyāyikas—that "possessing meaning" (*arthavattva*) means "possessing a grammatical operation" (*vṛttimattva*), and that this is absent in the case of a compound (*samāsa*), such that the mention of "compound" (*samāsagrahaṇa*) is for the purpose of an injunction (*vidhyartha*); and if likewise the mention of "taddhita" is also [for the same purpose]; and if the phrase "not a suffix" (*apratyaya*) is taken as being for the purpose of excluding suffixes (*pratyaya*), even then there is no harm. This is because, by taking the mention of "taddhita" to refer to that which is qualified by it, the form *bahupaṭavaḥ* is easily established.

However, in this view, there would be a contradiction with the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), and there would be over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *mūlakenopadaṃśam* and *pacataki*; therefore, let it remain exactly as it was stated. In this section, one should note that the works of the ancients, taken literally, are indeed flawed. This [rule] is intended for those particles (*nipāta*) which have no meaning even as that which is indicated (*dyotya*). [The example is] *avadyati*. This is established by the particle *ca*, which has the sense of an unmentioned inclusion (*anuktasamuccaya*).

In the case of imitations (*anukaraṇa*), however, when there is an intention not to distinguish the imitation from the original, it lacks meaningfulness (*arthavattva*) and therefore does not possess the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), as in the case of *bhū sattāyām* (Pāṇini 1.3.1). But when there is an intention to distinguish them, it certainly would be a nominal stem, as in the case of *bhuvo vuk* (Pāṇini 6.4.88). Nor does this result in the application of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "not being a verbal root" (*na cādhātuḥ*); for although the extension (*atideśa*) "an imitation is like its prototype" might apply regarding the substitution of *uvaṅ*, it is possible that it does not apply regarding the technical designation (*saṃjñā*), since such extensions are not invariably valid. This has been demonstrated under the rule *ṛlṛk* (Māheśvara Sūtra 2). (Pāṇini 1.2.47)

"A short vowel is substituted for the final of a neuter nominal stem" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.47). In the neuter gender, there shall be a short vowel for a nominal stem ending in a vowel. For example: *śrīpaṃ kulam* ("the Śrīpa family"). Because of the force of the explicit mention of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) in the rule, this does not apply here: *kāṇḍe*, *kuḍye*. However, in these cases, there is indeed an application [of the rule] by means of the extension (*atideśa*) stated in "as if it were the end or the beginning" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.85). Nor should it be argued that the mention of "nominal stem" is purposeful only for excluding forms like *vāriṇī* under the view that the suffix is included; for even in that case, the purposefulness of the mention is easily explained since the result is already established through the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "nominal stem."

Furthermore, because an alternative interpretation is more easily established in accordance with the intended meaning (*lakṣya*). Alternatively, one may adopt [the correct reading] by relying on the view that the application of suffixes occurs at the time of the formation of the word (*kāryakālapakṣa*) and by accepting a *prasajyapratiṣedha* (absolute negation) for the rule "not after that which ends in a suffix" (*neti pratyayāntasya*). Nor should it be argued that, if this were the case, the case-endings (*svādayaḥ*) would not apply in the example "brahmabandhuḥ"; for that is established by the *paribhāṣā* regarding forms qualified by gender (*liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā*), just as in the case of "śvaśrūḥ" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.48).

*Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.48: gostriyor upasarjanasya.* When the word *go* (cow) is an *upasarjana*, and likewise when a word ending in a feminine suffix is an *upasarjana*, the final vowel of that nominal stem (*prātipadika*) shall be short. Examples: *citraguḥ* (one who has brindled cows), *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* (one who has departed from Kauśāmbī). Why "of the *upasarjana*"? Consider *sugauḥ* (one who has beautiful cows) and *rājakumārī* (the king’s daughter). The word *strī* (feminine) is specifically mentioned [in the sūtra]. Therefore, by the rule for taking suffixes taught under the heading of "Feminine" (*stryadhikāra*), this does not apply here: *atilakṣmīḥ* (exceeding Lakṣmī) and *atiśrīḥ* (exceeding Śrī). If one asks how [the forms] *gokulam* (a herd of cows) and *rājakumārīputraḥ* (the son of the king’s daughter) are accounted for, listen.

Since an *upasarjana* (secondary member) is by definition related to something else, this shortening applies only when the word whose stem is subject to the rule stands in a state of subordination (*guṇībhāva*) with respect to the meaning of that [other] word which forms the final member (*uttarapada*)—namely, the words *go* and *strī*. This is not the case here. For although *go* is subordinate with respect to *kula*, it is not so with respect to *gām*; and although *kumārī* is subordinate with respect to *putra*, it is not so with respect to *rājān*. Furthermore, in this context, the technical (*śāstrīya*) *upasarjana* is intended, because it is an artificial designation (*kṛtrima*).

For this very reason, since such a status is impossible for a suffix alone, the term must be understood as ending with that [suffix]. However, if one were to take the worldly sense of being a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) and qualify the suffix itself, then there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of *harītakyaḥ* (the fruits of the *harītakī*), derived from *harītakyāḥ phalāni*. This is clear in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *upamānāni sāmānyavacanaiḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.55). Now, how is it that one who has surpassed a princess is expressed by the word *atirājakumārī*, given that this word ends in a feminine suffix? Understand it thus: [it is so because the compound is formed with a feminine noun as the first member].

For the distinction is that this [suffix] is subordinate (*upasarjana*) with respect to the person surpassed (*atikrānta*), but not with respect to the king. It should be noted, however, that Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on this point is merely superficial. Regarding this, there is a Vārttika: "The statement that [the feminine suffix] is like the masculine (*puṃvat*) applies to a Bahuvrīhi compound ending in *īyas*. (Kātyāyana’s Vārttika). The meaning is that in a Bahuvrīhi compound ending in a feminine suffix derived from a stem ending in *īyas*, the shortening [of the vowel] does not occur. For the shortening is prescribed by the rule "In the case of *go* and a feminine [ending]" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.48).

In this regard, the absence of the short vowel [at the end] is established through the following syntactical formulation: "Just as there is no feminine suffix in that masculine [word], so it should be understood here. Thus, *bahuśreyasī* refers to one for whom there are many *śreyasīs* (most excellent women). By the rule "īyasaśca" (Pāṇini 5.4.156), the suffix *kap* is prohibited. Why is the term *bahuvrīhi* mentioned? [To exclude cases such as] *atiśreyasi*. (Pāṇini 1.2.49)

*luktaddhitaluki* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.49): When there is *luk* elision of a *taddhita* suffix, there shall be *luk* elision of the feminine suffix that constitutes an *upasarjana*. Now, *luk* elision occurs only for a suffix itself, and not for that which ends in it. For this very reason, the *upasarjana* here is the worldly (*laukika*) one, and not the technical (*śāstrīya*) one mentioned previously, because [the latter] is impossible. Indeed, a suffix alone is not a technical *upasarjana*. The fruit of the *āmalakī* is *āmalaka*. By the rule *nityaṃ vṛddhaśarādibhyaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.3.144), there is *luk* elision of the *mayaṭ* suffix when it denotes a fruit.

Consequently, by this [rule], there is the elision (*luk*) of the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* after words such as *gaura*. Here, the scope (*avakāśa*) of the preceding rule is exemplified by *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*; the scope of this [present] rule is exemplified by *āmalakam*. However, in the case of *pañcendraḥ*—meaning "that which has five Indrāṇīs as its deities"—the elision (*luk*) alone occurs because of its higher priority (*paratva*).
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.50)

*Idgoṇyāḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.51). After the word *goṇī*, when a *taddhita* suffix is elided (*luk*), the suffix *id* is applied. This is an exception to [the general] elision (*luk*). A cloth purchased for five *goṇīs* is *pañcagoṇiḥ*; [purchased for ten,] *daśagoṇiḥ*. The word *goṇī* denotes both a measure (*parimāṇa*) and a container (*āvapana*). From the first sense, the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied according to *prāgvateṣṭhañ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.1.18); from the second, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule for items belonging to the *ārhīya* group. By the rule *adhyardhapūrvadvigor lug* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.49), there is elision (*luk*) of those two suffixes. Finally, by this rule (*idgoṇyāḥ*), the suffix *id* is added.

*Lu-pi yuktavad-vyakti-vacane* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.51). Pāṇini restates this sūtra of the Easterners for the purpose of refuting it: when *lup* occurs, the gender and number are like those of the base (*prakṛti*). For example, *pañcālāḥ*, which refers to Kṣatriyas in the masculine plural; their inhabited country (*janapada*) is called *pañcālāḥ*. [Likewise,] the many descendants of Pañcāla.

From the word *janapada* (region), when derived from a *kṣatriya* [name], the suffix *añ* is applied [by Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.1.168]. Those [suffixes] are called *tadrāja* [by Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.1.174]. When there is a plurality [of those denoted by a *tadrāja* suffix], [the suffix is elided] [by Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.4.62]. Then, regarding the suffix *aṇ* [introduced by] "his residence" [Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.2.69], there is elision (*lup*) [by] "elision of the suffix after a region-name" [Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.2.81]. What is the purpose of this elision (*lup*)? [Consider] *lavaṇaḥ sūpaḥ* ("salted soup"). [In the rule] "when mixed" [Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.4.22], there is elision of the suffix *aṇ* after *lavaṇa* [by Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.4.24]. Why is there mention of "individual expression" (*vyaktivacana*)? [It is so that] in cases such as *harītakī* ("yellow myrobalan") or *pañcālāḥ* ("the people of Pañcāla"), there may not be an extension of the genitive case ending.

This rule is for the purpose of restriction regarding the elision (*lup*) of the plural suffix of the *uttarapada* in a compound. Examples: *mathurā-pañcālāḥ*. Because of the restriction that it applies only to the *uttarapada*, it does not apply here: *pañcāla-mathure*. Why "of the plural"? Consider: *godau* (the two *godau* rivers). In *grāma-mathurā-godamathurāḥ*, the transfer of duality to the *pūrvapada* would indeed occur [by the preceding rule]. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.52)

"Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.52: *viśeṣaṇānāṃ cājāteḥ* (And [the gender and number] of qualifiers also [are like those of the base], except for [words denoting] a genus). For the meaning of a base that has undergone elision (*lub-artha*), the gender and number of its qualifiers are also like those [of the base], with the exception of words denoting a genus (*jāti*). Example: *pañcālā ramaṇīyāḥ* (The Pañcāla country is beautiful); *godau ramaṇīyau* (The Godau villages are beautiful). Why "except for a genus"? Example: *pañcālā janapadaḥ* (The Pañcāla country is a region); *godau grāmaḥ* (The Godau are a village). How then is it that one says *pañcālā janapadau ramaṇīyau* (The two Pañcāla regions are beautiful)? Understand that this is because [here] the word is a qualifier of a genus. However, when it qualifies the specific entity [the country itself], it is indeed *ramaṇīyāḥ*.

It might be argued that this [principle] applies elsewhere as well, since in the case of *badarīvṛkṣāḥ* (the jujube trees), a distinction is accepted between the two usages—*sūkṣmakaṇṭakāḥ* (having fine thorns) and *sūkṣmakaṇṭakaḥ* (having a fine thorn)—based on the difference in the gender of the qualifiers. So what is the need for the rule? True. The meaning of the rule is that for words expressing qualities (*guṇavacana*), the gender and number are determined by the substratum (*āśrayataḥ*). That is to say, those qualifiers which are distinct from generic terms (*jāti*) follow the same gender and number as their qualificand (*yuktavat*, i.e., like the qualificand). Although the term "words expressing qualities" is used [in the rule], its intended meaning here is a word denoting a quality that is distinct from a genus. As it has been stated by Amara:

"Whatever [referent] is intended to be qualified by words such as 'woman' or 'wife,' and by whatever kind of words it is introduced—be they words for qualities (*guṇa*), substances (*dravya*), or actions (*kriyā*)—those shall function as its qualifiers. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.57)

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the general rule that the neuter gender is obtained by logical necessity. Therefore, the form *śuklaṃ paṭāḥ* (the white cloths) does not occur. Furthermore, this extended application (*atideśa*) is non-eternal (*anitya*), as evidenced by rules such as *saṃskṛtaṃ bhakṣāḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.16). The settlement [of usage] follows the observed forms (*lakṣya*). In the case of *harītakī* and similar words, the individual entity (*vyakti*) is expressed. This [rule] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*). Consequently, the plural number is not applied as if it were possessed of a quality (*yuktavat*). Thus: *haritakyāḥ phalāni* (the fruits of the *harītakī*) becomes *harītakyaḥ*. Here, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is added according to the *gaura-* group (Pāṇini 4.1.41), and then there is elision (*lup*) of that suffix according to the rule *anudāttādeśca* (Pāṇini 4.3.140).

The mention of *khalatika* and so forth [is for the sake of restriction]. This too is indeed a restrictive rule (*niyama*). Forests situated not far from the mountain *khalatika* are called *khalatika-vanāni*. *Khalatika* refers to a thicket of *varaṇa* trees and the like. Regarding the prohibition [of the suffix] when there is *luP* (elision) signifying a human (*manuṣya-lupi*): there is a prohibition of adjectives when the sense of *luP* denotes a human characteristic (*manuṣya-lakṣaṇe*). However, it does indeed apply to that which ends in *luP*. For example: *cañcā* is a man made of straw; one who resembles him is called *cañcābhirūpaḥ*. Here, *luP* occurs by the rule *saṃjñāyām* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.3.98). A *vardhrīkā* is a specific modification of leather.

Like that, *vardhrikā* is "beautiful. Thus, it is established here that there are two *vārttikas*: the first applies to the former [rule], while the third is an exception (*apavāda*) to the second. However, this must be noted: here, since the gender of the qualifiers (*abhirūpa* and *darśanīya*) is prohibited [from following the gender of the qualified noun], the neuter gender would result. It does not occur, however, by virtue of the force of the examples provided by the author of the *Bhāṣya*. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.53)

"That [usage] need not be taught, because conventional names are authoritative" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.53). "That" refers to the statement that they are used as if they were derived from etymological rules (*yuktavat*). "Need not be taught" means it is unnecessary to prescribe them. Why? Because conventional names (*saṃjñā*) are authoritative. This is the underlying point: words such as *pañcālāḥ* and *varaṇāḥ* are not etymological (*yaugika*). Even though they denote the inhabitants of those places, they are not used for other regions. Furthermore, under the governing rule "with reference to a place bearing that name" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.2.67), suffixes are prescribed for things located nearby; however, these are simply conventional designations (*saṃjñāśabda*).

And those [words] which are well-known in the world according to their gender and number are indeed authoritative in that regard; the meaning is that they have the usage as their authority. For example, in cases such as *āpaḥ* (waters), *dārāḥ* (wife/wives), *vanam* (forest), *gṛhāḥ* (house/houses), *sikatāḥ* (sand/sands), and *varṣāḥ* (rainy season/plural rains). Therefore, no grammatical instruction need be undertaken here in this treatise for that purpose either. Furthermore— (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.54)

"A deletion (*lup*) is also unnecessary because the connection [of the parts] is not manifested" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.54). [This refers to the rules] "Deletion (*lup*) after [words denoting] a country" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.2.81) and "and after *varaṇa* and so forth" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.2.82). Why? Because here the connection—the meaning of the constituent parts—is not manifested, that is, it is not perceived. Thus, in this case, the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) itself would not even arise according to the rules "the place where he dwells" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.2.69) and "that which is not far from it" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.2.70); what, then, is the purpose of prescribing its deletion (*lup*)? This is the meaning. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.55)

"And if [the word were based on] connection (*yoga*), there would be no perception [of it] in the absence of that [connection]" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.55). The particle *ca* has the sense of *hi* ("for"). For if this [word] were the authority—that is, the indicator—of the meaning of the constituent parts (*yoga*) [i.e., etymology], then in the absence of those [parts], it would not be perceived. Yet it is perceived now; for instance, the word *pañcāla* is used for a country even without a connection to Kṣatriyas. Nor can one resort to the notion of "having previously existed" (*bhūtapūrvagati*).

The point is that since there is no determining factor (*vinigamakābhāva*) as to whether the word applies to the country because of its connection with Kṣatriyas, or the word applies to the Kṣatriya because of his connection with the country, the opposite could just as easily be asserted. Therefore, the truth is that these words have multiple meanings (*nānārtha*), like the word *akṣa* and others.

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.56) "The statement that the meaning of the suffix is the primary element [is unnecessary], because the meaning [of the sentence] is established by other means. This statement—that the meaning of the suffix is the primary element—is also not to be taught. Why? Because the meaning is already established through common worldly usage (*loka*). Furthermore, the meaning is that this is contradicted by the fact that in a verbal form (*ākhyāta*), the action (*kriyā*) is the primary element.
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.57)

"And [the rule] regarding time and the subordinate term is the same" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.57). A day joined with the latter half of the past night and the former half of the coming night is "of today" (*adyatana*). Time and the subordinate term (*upasarjana*) have been defined by the ancient teachers in the sequence beginning with "that which qualifies is the subordinate term," and the rule is the same there as well. The meaning is that the status of not requiring further instruction (*aśiṣyatva*) is identical; the intention is that this is because it is already well-established in common usage. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.58)

Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.58: *Jātyākhyāyām ekasmin bahuvacanam anyatarasyām* ("In the case of a word denoting a genus, the plural may optionally be used for a single entity"). For example: *brāhmaṇāḥ pūjyāḥ* ("Brahmins are to be honored") or *brāhmaṇaḥ pūjyaḥ* ("A Brahmin is to be honored"). Even when there is only one referent, the plural form is established through this extended application (*atideśa*), and it is also established by way of qualification. Furthermore, because the term *bahuvacana* is explained as "the expression of many" (*bahūnāṃ vacanam*), this extended application is rendered explicit. Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.59.

*Asmado dvayośca* (Pāṇini 1.4.22): When singularity or duality is intended, the plural may optionally be used for the pronoun *asmad*. Thus, one may say *vayaṃ brūmaḥ* ("we speak"), or in the alternative, *ahaṃ bravīmi* ("I speak") or *āvāṃ brūvaḥ* ("the two of us speak"). There is a prohibition [of the plural] when the pronoun is accompanied by a qualifier (*saviśeṣaṇasya pratiṣedhaḥ*). For example: *paṭurahaṃ bravīmi* ("I, who am clever, speak"). How then is one to explain Bhartṛhari’s verse: *tvaṃ rājā vayamapyupāsitaguruprajñābhimānonnatāḥ* ("You are the king, and we too are elevated by pride in our wisdom cultivated by serving our teachers")? In this case, the plural is indeed valid because "elevatedness" (*unnatatvasya*) is the predicate being enjoined.

Haradatta maintains that this negation is intended to qualify the subject (*anuvādya*). However, in the *Bhāṣya*, this rule has been rejected. For instance, the sense organs such as the eyes are superimposed upon the self as delimited by the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*); therefore, due to their identity with that [ego], they fall within the scope of the expression "I," and there arises the cognition of both difference and non-difference. Just as one says "I hear," one also employs the expression "my ear hears. In that context, because the eyes and other organs are many, when there is a desire to express their plurality and independence, the form "we say" (*vayaṃ brūmaḥ*) is established.

However, when there is a desire to express mere non-difference (*abhedamātra*), the singular number is used, and this does not constitute figurative usage (*gauṇatā*). This is because expressions such as "I am fair" (*gauro 'ham*) remain uncontradicted for as long as worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) persists. By this, even that which was recited by the author of the *Vṛtti*—namely, the rule "for some, [the singular is used] in reference to the teacher Puṣya and others"—becomes redundant, since forms such as "you are the teacher" (*tvaṃ guruḥ*) and "you are the teachers" (*yūyaṃ guravaḥ*) are established by the aforementioned method. For this very reason, common usage such as "the teachers say" (*ācāryāḥ kathayanti*) is also consistent.
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.59–60)

[The suffix *aṇ* is applied] after the constellations *Phalgunī* and *Proṣṭhapadā* (Pāṇini Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.2.60). Because of the attraction [of the word] "two" (*dvayoḥ*) from the preceding rule, either duality or a function conditioned by plurality is prescribed. By this, it is established even when there is a qualifier: *pūrve phalgunyau* (the two former Phalgunīs), *pūrvāḥ phalgunyaḥ* (the former Phalgunīs); *pūrve proṣṭhapade* (the two former Proṣṭhapadas), *pūrvāḥ proṣṭhapadāḥ* (the former Proṣṭhapadas). Why "in the case of a constellation"? [Consider: *phalgunyau māṇavike* (two girls born under Phalgunī). The meaning is "born under the two Phalgunīs. The suffix *ṭa* is applied by the Vārttika "after *phalgunī* and *aṣāḍhā*, [the suffixes] *ṭa* and *na*" (*phalgunyaṣāḍhābhyāṃ ṭānau*). Due to the marker *ṭi*, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied.

However, the two words [“nakṣatra” and “tārakā”] are not employed for the single star Tārā, because the term is conventionally fixed (*nirūḍha*) to the collection as a whole when its constituent parts have become manifest. In the Sūtra, however, *nakṣatre* is the nominative dual, meaning "if both [stars] are denoted" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.61). Furthermore, regarding the two Punarvasus, there is the singular in Vedic usage (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.61); that is, there may optionally be a singular for the two. For example: *punarvasur nakṣatram aditir devatā* or *punarvasu*. But in common worldly usage, because it is conventionally fixed to the collection whose parts have become manifest, the dual alone is used: *gāṅgatāv iva divaḥ punarvasū*.

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.62) *viśākhayośca* (and [the dual ending is used] for Viśākhā). As before. The lunar mansion Viśākhā has Indra and Agni (*indrāgnī*) as its presiding deities. Optionally, it may be *viśākhe*. Because the term *chandasi* (in Vedic usage) is understood to carry over, in common worldly usage it is simply *viśākhe*. However, Amarasimha, by employing the form "rādhāviśākhā" (Amarakośa 1.3.22), does not accept the restriction to the dual number. Regarding the sūtra, he remains neutral. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.63)

In a *dvandva* compound consisting of the two lunar mansions Tiṣya and Punarvasu, the dual number is obligatory in place of the plural number (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.63). The phrase "in the Vedic language" (*chandas*) does not apply here, because it was drawn over from the preceding rule by the particle *ca*. Indeed, it is for this very purpose that there was a separation of rules (*yogavibhāga*) in the preceding section. Tiṣya is one; Punarvasū are two; their *dvandva* compound denotes a plurality. This is an extension (*atideśa*) whereby plurality is treated as if it were duality. Example: *tiṣyapunarvasū udite*. Why [is it specified] "Tiṣya and Punarvasu"? [Counter-example: *viśākhānurādhāḥ*.

What is the purpose of the restriction "when referring to constellations" (*nakṣatra*)? [Consider the example: *tiṣyapunarvasavo māṇavakāḥ* ("The boys Tiṣya and Punarvasu"). By means of the two words *tiṣya* and *punarvasu*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.2.3 (*nakṣatreṇa yuktaḥ kālaḥ*), which is then elided by 4.2.4 (*lubaviśeṣe*). Thereafter, for the sense of "born under" (*jāta*), the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule 4.3.16 (*sandhivelādi*). This *aṇ* is then elided by 4.2.34 (*śraviṣṭhāphalgunyanurādhā...*). This *dvandva* compound refers to the boys (*māṇavaka*), not to the constellations. Nor is this usage figurative (*gauṇa*), because it is based on the literal derivation (*yaugika*).

Is this not already established by the continued application of the rule *nakṣatre*? What, then, is the purpose of mentioning *nakṣatra* again? Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "So that it may apply even to synonyms. Its meaning is as follows: because of the interpretation that it refers to a *dvandva* compound of words denoting asterisms (*nakṣatra*) when they are applied to an asterism that is the referent of the two words *tiṣya* and *punarvasu*, forms such as *puṣyapunarvasū* and *siddhyapunarvasū* are also established.

It might be argued as follows: Just as by the rule *bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.69), the mention of "intransitive" (*akarmaka*) excludes the internal substance-object (*dravyakarman*), but not the external object such as time (*kālādikarman*), so too, even though [the term] is established for cases like *bahavastiṣyapunarvasavo 'tikrāntāḥ* ("many Tiṣyas and Punarvasus have passed") through the exclusion of the internal time, let there be a further mention of "asterism" (*nakṣatra*) for the purpose of excluding the external boy (*māṇavaka*).

Alternatively, by dividing the rule *tiṣyapunarvasvoḥ* and explaining that even when Tiṣya is located in another region, its function remains within the asterism itself, the form *tiṣyapuṣyayoḥ* (as in *tiṣyapuṣyayornakṣatrāṇi yalopaḥ*) is established. Therefore, since the mention of *nakṣatra* has already served its purpose through the exclusion of external factors or through the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), how could it possibly be intended for the inclusion of synonyms?

It is said: It is logical that an intransitive term (*akarmaka-śabda*), by its very hearing (*śruti*), excludes the object (*karman*) and thereby excludes only the primary and internal [object]. However, the word *nakṣatra*, excluding another meaning through the mediation of establishing its own meaning, excludes both [the primary and internal objects] without distinction; thus, it is not the first result. Nor is it the second, because the expression of the meaning "Puṣya" is indispensable. For this very reason, due to dissatisfaction with both positions, an alternative position was stated in the Bhāṣya.

What is the purpose of the term *dvandva* (copulative compound)? Consider: *yastiṣyastau punarvasū yeṣānte tiṣyapunarvasavaḥ*. Here, it is specifically *tiṣya* and the others that are expressed by the *bahuvrīhi* in the reverse order; therefore, this is a *nakṣatra-samāsa* (compound of lunar mansions), but not a *dvandva*. What is the purpose of the plural number? [Consider: *idaṃ tiṣyapunarvasu*. Every *dvandva* optionally takes the singular form (*ekavad-bhāva*). This is established by logic (*nyāyasiddha*), for the rule is that compounds such as those of body parts (*prāṇyaṅga*) must necessarily be collective (*samāhāra*), but the reverse is not the case.

This is because of the separate rule "cārthe dvandvaḥ" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.29), and also because of the inclusion of the plural marker (*bahuvacana*) in the present sūtra; such is the direction [of the argument]. Thus ends the second Āhnika of the second Pāda of the first Adhyāya in the Śabda-kaustubha.

Third Āhnika of the Second Pāda (*Aṣṭādhyāyī* 1.2.64): *sarūpāṇām ekaśeṣa ekavibhaktau*. When words that are identical in form are observed to occur with the same case-ending (*vibhakti*), only one of them remains. Since this *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) is not dependent on any external cause, it is an *antaraṅga* (internal) operation; it applies even before the formation of the nominal suffixes (*sup*) to bases ending in feminine suffixes such as *ṅī* or *āp*. For example, *hariṇī* means both a female deer and a green-colored woman; when there is a desire to express both together, the forms are *hariṇyau* (dual) or *hariṇyaḥ* (plural). Similarly, *kṣamā* denotes both the earth and forbearance.

Śrīharṣa [states]: "In that [king], there was both clothing and forbearance," and also, "Beholding the two splendors of that lord of men. According to the view that "the cognition of meaning arises from hearing the word only once," a *dvandva* compound would occur even when there is phonetic similarity [of the members]. Even if it is accepted that multiple meanings are conveyed through *tantra* (simultaneous application), since there is no rule that everything must always be understood through *tantra* alone, the optional *dvandva* remains unavoidable.

However, when the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) has been initiated, the non-application of *dvandva* follows as a natural consequence due to the absence of two words ending in case-suffixes (*subanta*). For this very reason, there is the well-known declaration that *ekaśeṣa* is an exception (*apavāda*) to *dvandva*. This is because the term "exception" (*apavāda*) was explained in exactly this way in the commentary on the rule *iko guṇavṛddhī* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.1.3), which is an exception to *alontya* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.1.52). Therefore, forms such as *ghaṭau* and *ghaṭāḥ* are also examples here.

Even there, since we frequently observe the use of multiple distinct words—such as "this is a jar, this is a jar"—intended to convey the cognition of multiple individuals according to one's will, it follows that in the same way, when there is a desire to express them together, the formation of a *dvandva* compound such as *ghaṭau* (two jars) would be unavoidable. By this, those who, having seen the Vārttika "And in the case of synonymous words, [the rule applies] without doubt," fall into the error of thinking that only words with multiple meanings (*nānārtha*) are the examples here, are refuted.

Nor should it be argued that because there is no difference in the delimiters of the word-meanings (*padārthatāvacchedaka*), a *dvandva* compound would result in cases such as *ghaṭau* ("two pots"), for the rule "A *dvandva* occurs in the sense of *ca*" (Pāṇini 2.2.29) prescribes it merely for the sake of conjunction (*sāhitya*). And in the case of an *itaretarayoga-dvandva* or an *ekaśeṣa*, this [conjunction] functions either as a qualifier or as a contextual adjunct (*prayogopādhi*) of the compound; however, in a *samāhāra-dvandva*, its manifestation is primary—this is another matter entirely. Furthermore, even so, there is no contingency of a *dvandva* occurring in expressions such as *ghaṭakalaśau* ("pot and jar").

This is due to the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one from a group of identical items) based on the Vārttika rule: "Even for those that are dissimilar [in form], if they have the same meaning" (*kāovāo*). In reality, however, this meaning is already present in the Sūtra itself. A *rūpa* is that which is formed or understood; thus, *sarūpāḥ* refers to those whose *rūpa* (form) is the same. The substitution of *sa-* for *samāna-* occurs according to the rule "jyotirjanapada... (*Aṣṭādhyāyī* 6.3.85). This is explained through *ekaśeṣa* as "those who are both *sarūpa* and *sarūpa*. Nor should it be argued that there is no possibility of an operation upon itself according to the maxim of the "incompleteness of the sentence" (*vākyāparisamāptinyāya*), for...

Because it is pervaded by the form that constitutes the delimiting condition (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) [of the rule], it applies to itself as well, just like the rule *tulyāsyaprayatnam* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.1.9). An analysis of this subject has already been conducted under the sūtra *aiuṇ* (Māheśvara Sūtra 1).
