For this very reason, in the Vārttika—"There is a prohibition regarding *mātṛ* and *mātra* because they are of the same form" (*mātṛmātroḥ pratiṣedhaḥ sarūpatvāt*)—which was composed to prohibit the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one member) for the word *mātṛ* signifying a mother and for the word *mātra* ending in the suffix *tṛc* signifying a measure of grain, the operation of that prohibition applies even to the term *mātṛmātroḥ* contained within the rule itself. Now, an objection might be raised: in that context, there is a restatement (*anuvāda*) only of those two words as qualified by their specific meanings; otherwise, the prohibition would undesirably apply even to the two words *mātṛ* and *mātra* when they signify a mother.

If it is asked, "How then can there be the application of the prohibition when [the word] is a mere imitation (*anukaraṇa*) consisting of sound-forms included within itself?"—understand that it is due to the extended rule (*atideśa*): "An imitation is like its original" (*prakṛtivadanukaraṇam*). According to the view of the Sūtra, however, the particle *eva* is drawn over from the subsequent sūtra here. Consequently, by the interpretation "those which have the same form when in a single case-ending," and because of the lack of identical form (*asārūpya*)—since the rule *aptṛn* (Pāṇini 6.4.11) prescribes lengthening in the *sarvanāmasthāna* [case-endings] for words denoting a measurer—the absence of *ekaśeṣa* follows.

Nor should it be argued that even in the absence of an explicit *ekaśeṣa* (the grammatical rule for retaining one of two identical words), an optional *ekaśeṣa* of "mother" (*mātṛ*) and "measure" (*mātra*) would necessarily occur by resorting to the principle of *tantra* (simultaneous application), as is the case in instances of *śliṣṭarūpaka* (pun-based metaphor). This is because of the restrictive rule: "An *ekaśeṣa* applies only to those words which are of the same form when in the same case-ending. Nor should it be argued that, if this were so, the optional form "ghaṭaghaṭau" (pot-pot) would be unavoidable; for another restrictive rule is invoked: that an *ekaśeṣa* of words with the same form occurs only when they are indeed of the same form [and not when they are merely homophonous].

Therefore, this rule prevents the three undesirable options that would otherwise result—namely, *ghaṭakumbhau*, *kumbhakumbhau*, and *mātṛbhyām*—while the establishment of forms such as *ghaṭau* and so forth would indeed occur even without this rule. This is the summary of the conclusion, whether one adopts the view of the universal (*jāti*) or the view of the individual (*vyakti*). It might be argued: "In that case, even in examples such as *devadeva*, the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) would apply; and it cannot be prevented by the condition *ekavibhaktau* (in the same case-ending)."

This is because [the rule for] *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) serves as a mark of similarity (*sārūpya*), and because *ekaśeṣa* is not contingent upon a specific cause. Now, if you argue that, according to the method to be explained, it functions as a qualifier for *ekaśeṣa*, even then there is no escape from the difficulty. For in the case of *devadeva*, since the single case-ending (*ekavibhakti*) exists after the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), the two internal case-endings have been elided by *luk*, and thus, due to the absence of the "characteristic of a suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), the rule does not apply. Regarding this, they say: *Ekaśeṣa* occurs only when there is a desire to express [the items] together (*sahavivakṣā*), that is to say, in the domain of the *itaretarayoga* copulative compound (*dvandva*). For in this case, there is a mutual connection of several combined meanings; such is the domain [of *ekaśeṣa*]. And it has been said:
"When there is a desire to express them together, a single unified appearance arises as if the distinct [elements] were woven together; this they call the 'dvandva' and 'ekaśeṣa' [compounds].
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.65)

And this restriction regarding the scope [of the rule] is obtained through the force of the statement itself, as well as from the use of the instrumental case in constructions involving *saha* (together) in sūtras such as "vṛddho yūnā" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.65). Alternatively, the term "dvandve" (in a dvandva compound) is carried over (*anuvartate*) from the preceding sūtra; and because of the governing topic (*arthādhikāra*), the understanding is that it refers specifically to the *itaretarayoga* type of dvandva. Thus, by interpreting it as "when a dvandva is about to occur," the aforementioned restriction on the scope is established. Nor should it be argued that one should simply interpret it as "when a dvandva has been formed."

This is because the position that "the single-remainder (ekaśeṣa) applies to those [words] that have already formed a dvandva compound" will be refuted later due to the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of irregular accentuation (svaradoṣa), elision of case-endings (samāsāntadoṣa), and so forth. By this, the usage by Śrīharṣa in the phrase "sāravasāravormijaḥ" is also explained. [In that case,] "sāravāḥ" means "those existing in the *sarayū* river"; however, in the subsequent karmadhāraya compound "te ca te āravasahitāḥ," there is an absence of the intention to express them as co-referential (sahavivakṣā).

In a case such as the *śliṣṭarūpaka* (double entendre metaphor) beginning with "vidvanmānasarājahaṃsa," if the use of the word *mānasa* for both [the lake Mānasa and the mind] by means of *tantra* (elliptical repetition) is not based on the *sūtra*, then the same applies in the alternative case as well; for even by that much, the employment of both forms is successfully accounted for. Nor should it be argued that, since there is an injunction for *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) regarding *samāhāra-dvandva* (collective copulative compounds), the occasional form "ghaṭaghaṭam" and so forth would be unavoidable; for in that regard, one must simply resort to the principle of *anabhidhāna* (non-occurrence). Or, let there be the application of *ekaśeṣa* even in that case.

Nor does this result in the gender becoming neuter, for that [neuter gender] is prescribed specifically for a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*). Thus, according to the view that "a word is applied to each individual object," in cases such as "one should not kill a Brāhmaṇa," there will be an inclusion of all individuals; consequently, a definition need not be repeated for every individual. However, the truth is that due to the *jñāpaka* (indicative rule) in Pāṇini’s sūtra 1.2.69—"and it is optionally singular"—the state of being treated as a single unit (*ekavadbhāva*) does not apply once *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) has been performed.

In cases such as *ekaśca ekaśca* ("one and one") or *dvau ca dvau ca* ("two and two"), both types of *dvandva* (copulative compound) and *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) must be prevented solely by the absence of such usage (*anabhidhāna*). It should be understood that this same principle generally applies even to numeral words. However, in cases such as *viṃśati* ("twenty"), the *ekaśeṣa* is indeed desired; such is the general direction.

This being the case, even on the view that the sūtra should be commenced, since the principle of non-mention (*anabhidhāna*) is frequently resorted to, one might ask: "Let it be the same in cases such as *ghaṭaghaṭau* (pot-pot); what is the point of commencing the sūtra to exclude those? With this intention, the Blessed One rejected the section on *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one of two identical words). Nor should it be argued: "If this were so, how could there be the cognition of the mother in the case of *pitarau* (parents), or of the mother-in-law and so forth in *śvaśurau* (parents-in-law)? For such an objection applies equally even if the *ekaśeṣa* rule were indeed commenced.

If it is argued that "that which remains [of a word] conveys the meaning of what is being elided," then the resulting implication is that words such as *pitṛ* ("father") would possess a primary denotation (*śakti*) or a conventional secondary signification (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) for "mother" and so on, by virtue of the specific condition (*upādhi*) of dual number and the like. And thus, since that [meaning] can be grasped through worldly usage alone, nothing is untenable. Nor should it be said that, if this were the case, suffixes such as *kvip* in forms like *agnicit* should also be rejected; for those [suffixes] are introduced for the sake of the augment *tuk*, the technical designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*), and so forth, by means of the rule regarding the characteristics of suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*).

Thus, although the Blessed One rejected the application of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) for both similar and dissimilar forms, he did so with the intention that the rule concerning similar forms (*sarūpa-sūtra*) alone would still serve to establish *ekaśeṣa* in technical grammatical usage—even without the desire to express them together—just as is the case with technical terms (*saṃjñā*) and interpretive rules (*paribhāṣā*). With this in mind, it was stated in the *Bhāṣya* on Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.1.59, "dvirvacanocī," that *ekaśeṣa* applies there; such is the direction of the argument.

However, when the *sūtra* is being formulated, although six possible positions (*pakṣa*) arise, it should nevertheless be understood that among them three are indeed faulty and three are faultless. To illustrate: there are six positions, namely—(1) "the *ekaśeṣa* [occurs] when all [words] are distinct and followed by a case-ending (*vibhakti*)," (2) "of those ending in the singular number," (3) "or of those not forming a *dvandva* compound," (4) "or from the aggregate when followed by a single case-ending," (5) "or when expressing a simultaneous substratum (*yugapad-adhikaraṇavacana*)," and (6) "or as independent of any cause (*anaimittika*)."

In that regard, in the first case, the word *eka* is a synonym for *samāna*. Thus, when *vṛkṣaḥ vṛkṣaḥ* is established, upon the disappearance of the two initial [visarga] sounds, we have *vṛkṣaḥ s vṛkṣaḥ s*. If one explains the rule *saṃyogāntasya lopah* as "there is elision of a final consonant cluster at the end of a word," then there is elision of the middle *s* (the *su* case-ending). However, if one explains it as "there is elision of the final element of that word which ends in a consonant cluster," then there is elision according to the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt sutisyapṛktaṃ hal*. Even in that case, according to the view that the base (*prakṛti*) is implied by the suffixes *su*, *ti*, and *si*, there is no elision of anything at all.

In every respect, the desired form is simply not established. If the initial and final [sounds] were to cease, the result would be *vṛkṣa s s*. If the subsequent [sounds] were to cease, the result would be *vṛkṣa s*. Likewise, in cases such as *vṛkṣā anityāḥ*, there would be the hearing of the final *sup*-suffix; thus, the first position is indeed faulty. In the second position, however, because the form *vṛkṣa s* would remain with its case-ending, there would be no production of the dual or plural numbers, and only the singular number would be heard.

Although the intended meaning of the sentence can indeed be obtained by carrying over the word *dvandve* from the third [sūtra], nevertheless, when *aśva-aśva-au* is established, because the accentuation of the compound-final (*samāsāntodātta*) is internal (*antaraṅga*) with respect to the requirement for case-endings (*vibhakti*), if the first member were to remain, the entire word would become unaccented (*sarvānudātta*). If, however, the last member were to remain, it would be accented on the final syllable (*antodātta*). But what is desired is an acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*), because of the derivation of *aśva-* from the root *aś* with the suffix *kvanip*, and because such usage is seen in examples like "yo aśvebhir vahate vibhavohyaśvāḥ."

Furthermore, in the case of *ṛk ca ṛk ca ṛcau*, because the suffix *ṛkpūḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.74) is applied as a compound-ending (*samāsānta*) due to its being an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), the *ekaśeṣa* would not occur; this is because the case-ending is separated [from the remaining stem] by the vowel *a* of that suffix. For the compound-ending is a part of the compound itself and thus cannot create a separation between the members of that very compound; however, it certainly creates a separation from its own phonetic form. Even according to the view of the Bhāṣya—that the compound-ending is a constituent part of the subsequent member which expresses the meaning of the compound—the *ekaśeṣa* would be difficult to achieve here due to the dissimilarity (*virūpatva*) of the forms.

Although the rule *virūpāṇām api samānārthānām* (Kāśikā Vārttika) would apply here, nevertheless, in one alternative (*pakṣe*), when the suffix *ṭāp* follows the remainder of the word *ṛc*, forms such as *ṛce* and *ṛcā* would also result. Likewise, in one alternative, forms such as *pathā* and *pathau* would also result. Furthermore, forms such as *karau* and *karāḥ* would not be established, because of the restriction that the term *prāṇyaṅga* (limbs of living beings) applies only to a collective compound (*samāhāra*). Moreover, in cases such as *sarveṣām*, the rules *dvandve ca* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.1.31) and *vibhāṣā jasi* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.1.32) would take effect.

For this very reason, there is no *virūpaikaśeṣa* (retention of one dissimilar form) in cases such as *teṣām*, because if *ekaśeṣa* were applied by the rule *tyadādīni sarvaiḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.72), it would result in the loss of their status as *sarvanāman* (pronouns). Thus, it is established that these three positions are flawed. The final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, is threefold. To explain: in the case of *rāma rāma rāma*, there is indeed a single *prātipadika-saṃjñā* for the aggregate, just as there is for its individual components. There is indeed a single *prātipadika-saṃjñā* for the aggregate, just as there is for those [components] which possess meaning when combined.

Because [the compound] possesses meaning when its parts are combined. Nor should one ask, "How can this be so, given that it has been stated that the mention of 'meaningful' (arthavat) compounds in the rule is for the purpose of restriction? For a restriction applies only to those things of the same class; thus, it operates only in cases where the prior member of the aggregate is a *pada*. It is for this very reason that it was stated under the sūtra *arthavat* (Pāṇini 1.2.45) that in the case of "bahupaṭavaḥ," the status of being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) indeed occurs.

And thus, according to the principle of the singular and dual suffixes, the dual and plural case endings arise from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) of the aggregate itself; for even by that much, it is possible to support the application of number to the individual members [of the aggregate]. Consequently, *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one) occurs when a single case ending follows the aggregate. However, in cases such as *rāmakṛṣṇau*, although a single case ending would have applied to the aggregate according to the aforementioned method, it is nevertheless set aside by the rule for *dvandva* (copulative compound), which carries over the requirement that there be "more than one" inflected word (*subanta*).

In this view, the rule for *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) would also apply to the pair *mātṛ-mātroḥ*. However, this does not occur because of the interpretation: by repeating the rule *ekavibhaktau* and drawing forward the particle *eva*, the meaning is restricted to "those which have the same form when they occur in the same case-ending. Alternatively, *ekaśeṣa* applies to words ending in dual or plural suffixes when there is simultaneous expression of multiple substrates (*yugapadadhikaraṇavacanatā*). A *dvandva* compound is also formed in this way. For in a compound where the individual meanings are not abandoned (*ajahatsvārthā*), in an expression such as "Rāma and Kṛṣṇa," the first member denotes both, and the second member likewise denotes those two.

Nor is either [member] redundant, because the determination of both meanings occurs precisely through their mutual co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*). Thus, although each member is understood to have its own individual meaning prior to the formation of the *dvandva* compound, it is established as a tenet that "the function (*vṛtti*) consists in the expression of the other's meaning. Accordingly, even when the common worldly sentence "Rāma and Kṛṣṇa" (*rāmaśca kṛṣṇaśca*) is presented as the analytical expansion (*vigraha*) without significant distance, in the procedural sentence (*prakriyāvākya*) for the non-worldly *dvandva* and *ekaśeṣa*, the forms *rāma au* and *kṛṣṇa au* enter into the process.

And thus, even the retention of a single form (*ekaśeṣa*) from among words ending in different case-suffixes is entirely unobjectionable. Alternatively, according to the manner explained at the very outset, the *ekaśeṣa* is indeed unconditional (*anaimittika*). Thus, three positions are established in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

On this point, the following must be stated: even among the three positions mentioned, the position that "in the case of a single inflection from a collection" (*samudāyādekavibhaktau*) is indeed defective. This is because, once it is established that the term "in the case of a single inflection" (*ekavibhaktau*) must necessarily function as a qualifier for "only those of identical form" (*sarūpāṇyeva*) in order to avoid over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in examples such as *mātṛ-mātarau*, it is impossible for it to be a qualifier for the "single remainder" (*ekaśeṣa*). Furthermore, there is no evidence for its repetition (*āvṛtti*), nor is there any purpose served by it. Nor can the exclusion of cases such as *payaḥ jarayati* ("it causes milk to digest") be considered the result [of the rule].

This is because the phrase "when there is a desire to express together" (*sahavivakṣāyām*) must necessarily be stated by virtue of the inclusion of the term *dvandva* (copulative compound); otherwise, in the case of "he carries water, [and] water" (*payaḥ payo nayati*), there would result the undesirable consequence of a single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) for both the secondary and primary objects. Furthermore, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as "the god of gods" (*devadeva*). On the contrary, if [the word *saha*] were a qualifier of both through repetition (*āvṛtti*), then the form "alms" (*bhaikṣam*) would not be established.

For instance, when *bhikṣā-ām-a* is present, once the elision (*luk*) is applied by the rule "even internal rules are superseded by external ones," the elision being effected, the formation of a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) would not occur due to the absence of the condition of having a suffix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). Likewise, the view that the word expresses the simultaneous denotation of multiple substrata (*yugapad-adhikaraṇavacanatā-pakṣa*) is also weak; for that is incompatible with the theory of composition where the individual meanings are abandoned (*jahatsvārthā vṛttiḥ*). And so it says in the Bhāṣya on the second book: "This simultaneous denotation of multiple substrata is both difficult and hard to justify. We shall clarify this point in that very place.

Therefore, among the six positions previously mentioned, the position that [the suffixes] are non-contingent (*anaimittika*) is indeed the most powerful; the other five are all to be rejected. It is with this very intention that the Sūtra has been explained. However, in cases such as *pacati*, there is no possibility at all for the application of a dual or plural to the verbal root (*dhātu*), such that one would have to seek a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) [to justify it]. Nor does there arise the contingency of applying the *laṭ* suffix and others to the root in its collective form. This is because the singular number of the term "of the root" (*dhātoḥ*) is intended to be significant (*vivakṣita*). Furthermore, it should not be argued that from a single root alone, two *laṭ* suffixes would occur when there are two agents, or a plurality of *lakāra*s when there is a plurality of agents.

This is because such an objection is acceptable. In the rule *lasya* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.4.77), by intending to refer to the genus (*jāti*), it can be easily stated that the suffixes *tas* and so on apply to two instances of *la*, while *jhi* and so on apply to many. In reality, however, since in rules such as *vartamāne laṭ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.2.123) the singular number residing in the individual (*vyakti*) is intended, there is no fault whatsoever. For this very reason, in expressions such as *vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣaṃ siñcati* ("he waters tree after tree"), there is no succession of case-endings to express multiple singularities; such is the general direction.

Even in cases such as *gargāḥ*, since the father (the progenitor) is one, the base (*prakṛti*) is single, yet the suffixes (*pratyaya*) are many. Because all of them denote that which is connected with the meaning of the base, according to the rule "even for those that are dissimilar in form, if they have the same meaning... (*Kātyāyana-vārttika*), the word *garga* alone remains [as the base]. Nor does it follow that, in some instances, even the word *ya* alone would remain; for an option (*vikalpa*) is marred by eight defects (*doṣa*). Nor is there a lack of a determining factor (*vinigamaka*); for, according to the maxim "even a minute [difference is significant]," the capacity for clear comprehension itself serves as the determining factor.

Alternatively, even in the rule *yañaś ca*, the identity of the individual [referent] (*vyaktyaikya*) is intended. Furthermore, there is the repetition of the subordinate element (*guṇāvṛtti*) for each principal element (*pradhāna*). And there is the retention of only one (*ekaśeṣa*) from among the three words *gārgya*. In both cases, since the suffix *yañ* ends in a vowel, the elision (*luk*) applies by the rule *yaño 'bahuvacanāt*. It should not be argued that, in this way, if one says *kāśyapaḥ* meaning "an image of Kāśyapa," and then intends to express those images collectively as *kāśyapāḥ*, the suffix *yañ* would still refer to a plural number (as it refers to multiple images), and thus the elision (*luk*) would occur. This is because the word *gotra* ("lineage") is understood to carry over (*anuvṛtti*) from the rule *yaskādibhyo gotre* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.4.63).

Although, outside the context of offspring (*apatya*), the term *gotra* refers to the worldly lineage—since Kaiyaṭa, on the rule *strīpuṃsābhyāṃ nañ-snañau* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.1.87), states that "only the progeny of sages (*ṛṣi*) is intended here as *gotra*"—it should be noted that because of this, there is no elision (*luk*) in the forms *pautrāḥ* ("grandsons") and *dauhitrāḥ* ("daughters' sons"). By this [explanation], regarding the section [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*] which begins with "Because of the inclusion of distinctness (*pṛthaktva-niveśāt*), there would be a difference of ritual acts (*karma-bheda*) due to number," and which proceeds to establish that "there is a difference of ritual acts due to number," the example "seventeen *prājāpatya* [animals]" is cited.

The passage from the Bhaṭṭas—"Is this a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) applied after the secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) have been added, or is it that the *ekaśeṣa* is performed first and the connection with the secondary suffix occurs afterwards?"—is also explained as follows: their intention is that there is either a *ekaśeṣa* of those ending in the *ṇya*-suffix, or [a *ekaśeṣa*] of only those ending in the *ṇya*-suffix. Regarding the phrase "those for whom Prajāpati is the deity" (*prajāpatir devatā yeṣām*), the "connection with the secondary suffix" (*taddhita-saṅgati*) refers to being expressed by the secondary suffix (*taddhita-vācyatā*) of those words brought forward by the *ekaśeṣa*-formed pronoun *yeṣām*. Thus, in the popular analytical statement (*laukika-vigraha*), the mention of "those for whom" (*yeṣām*) is intended to convey the relationship with the deity for all the members combined.

In the *Vṛtti*, however, because the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) denoting the deity undergoes *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one), there is a single sacrifice when the animals are combined, since the connection with the deity occurs in the aggregate. This meaning is to be understood from the second half of the cited *Vārttika* regarding passages such as *agnīṣomīya*, where there is a non-dual connection with the deity in the combined [animals]. And this is logical; for the plurality of the meaning of the suffix is directly perceived, and since the *ekaśeṣa* is caused by that [plurality], it would not occur in the case of the base [word]—this being in accordance with the subsequent *Vārttika*.

It might be argued as follows: "The meaning of the base (prakṛti) is a qualifier for one part of the meaning of the suffix (pratyaya). And here, the relationship is identity (abheda); this is the established position regarding [offerings] such as the Āgneya. On this view, the conjunction of those possessing deities is obtained. Even on the alternative view—that the deity resides in that which is to be offered (pradeya), and that the functional capacity (śakti) is held to be distributed fragmentarily among the deity, the offering, and so forth—it remains exactly the same, because the connection with the deity conveyed by a single suffix is more immediate (antaraṅga). To this we reply: True.

This text should be understood with the intention that the primary power (*śakti*) resides in the object to be offered (*pradeya*), whereas the conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) applies to the deity due to its co-occurrence with the suffix. However, passages such as "the deity-denoting *taddhita* suffix arising from 'Agni' alone" must be interpreted according to another school of thought (*matāntara*). Nor should it be argued that even so, under the view of the "residual formation of dissimilar forms" (*virūpaikaśeṣa*), one must necessarily accept the primacy of the connection with the meaning of the stem (*prakṛtyartha*) in order to achieve semantic uniformity.

Regarding the example *yayaya*, although there is no status as a base (*prakṛtitva*) with respect to each individual case-ending, since the possibility of similarity (*sārūpya*) exists when a case-ending follows, the intention is that this is indeed a single-remainder formation (*sarūpaikaśeṣa*). Let us return to the subject at hand. It should be stated: "Among those [bases] distinguished by accent, that one after which an accentual rule applies is retained. By this, in the previously cited example *hariṇyau*, there is the retention of the form ending in *ṅīp*, because that suffix is marked with *p* (indicating it is *anudātta*).

But this does not apply to a word ending in the suffix *ṅīṣ* when it denotes a genus (*jāti*) or a connection with a male (*puṃyoga*), because such a word has its final syllable udātta by the accent of the suffix itself. If you object: "But surely, even for a word ending in *ṅīṣ*, the final syllable would indeed be udātta by the 'udātta-nivṛtti-svara' (the accent of the disappearance of the udātta)," you are mistaken. This is because there is no occurrence of the udātta-nivṛtti at all; for the base (*prakṛti*) is anudātta according to the Phiṭ-sūtra: "The vowels of color-names (*varṇa*), and those ending in *ta*, *ṇa*, *ti*, *ni*, and *ta*, are anudātta" (Phiṭ-sūtra 33). Thus it was said: "from a color-name that is anudātta."

Likewise, *mīmāṃsakaḥ* (one who investigates) is middle-accented (*madhyodātta*) by virtue of the *lit* accent. One who studies the *Mīmāṃsā* is a *mīmāṃsakaḥ*; [this is derived] by the rule *kramādibhyo vun* (Pāṇini 4.2.61). It is initial-accented (*ādyudātta*) by virtue of the *nit* accent. When both [accents] are intended to be expressed together, the initial-accented form remains because the *nit* accent is subsequent [in the order of application]. *Akṣau*, *akṣāḥ*: according to the *Phiṭ-sūtra* "akṣasyādevanasya" (Phiṭ-sūtra 35), the axle of a cart is initial-accented.

In the sense of a die (*devana*), however, the word *akṣa* is oxytone according to Pāṇini’s rule *phiṣaḥ* (P. 6.1.205). Alternatively, because it is formed with a suffix after the root *aś* in the sense of gambling (*devane*), it is oxytone. But in the senses of a part of a cart and the *bibhītaka* fruit, it is ādyudātta (acute on the first syllable) because it ends in the suffix *ghañ*. For this very reason, in the hymn *prāceyām*, during the introduction to the censure of gamblers, many instances of the word *akṣa*—such as in the verse beginning *akṣasyāhamekaparasya*—are used exclusively as oxytones. However, in expressions such as *tasya nākṣaḥ*, it is ādyudātta because it refers to a part of a chariot.

When there is a desire to express both [the masculine and neuter] together, the remainder (śeṣa) is the word with the initial udātta accent. However, when there is a desire to express [the neuter] together with a neuter word denoting a sense organ, one should infer forms such as *akṣam akṣāṇi* according to the rule *napuṃsakamanapuṃsakena* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.69). If it is asked, "How can there be a systematic distinction between masculine, neuter, and so forth for deities who are insentient?"—it is said in reply: First of all, the gender (*liṅga*) consisting of specific physical configurations well-known in the world is not accepted in grammar; for if it were, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the absence of the feminine suffix *n* in words such as *dārān*.

Furthermore, in cases such as *taṭaḥ*, *taṭī*, and *taṭam*, there would otherwise follow the impossibility of establishing grammatical operations based on the three genders according to their respective [natural] genders. Rather, the three genders are merely technical (pāribhāṣika). And that [technical gender] is purely pervasive-positive (*kevalānvayi*). This is the meaning: because words such as *iyaṃ vyaktiḥ* ("this individual") and *idaṃ vastu* ("this thing") have an unrestricted range of application everywhere. In that regard, it must be determined from the rules of gender (*liṅgānuśāsana*) and other sources which word is denotative of one gender only, which of two, and which of all three.

Words such as *kumāra* (boy), *brāhmaṇa* (brahmin), and so forth, however, denote the technical (śāstrīya) masculinity as qualified by worldly (laukika) masculinity, and the technical femininity as qualified by worldly femininity. Otherwise, how could usages such as *kumārī* (girl) and *kumāraḥ* (boy) be established? This is precisely the meaning of Amara’s statement: *kareṇur ibhyāṃ strī nebhe* ("*kareṇu* and *ibhī* denote a female elephant; *kareṇu* and *ibha* denote a male elephant"). But if this is so, how should one interpret the Mīmāṃsaka objection that in the injunction *paśunā* ("with an animal"), the masculinity is intended to be significant (*vivakṣita*)?

If it is argued that a technical (pāribhāṣika) [gender] is non-excluding and thus its intended application is irrelevant, whereas a worldly (laukika) [gender] is not perceived from the word *paśu* (animal), [the reply is: True. However, according to the principle of the final section of the sixth book [of the Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra], "Or the goat [is meant] because of the wording of the mantra," a restriction to the masculine gender must be understood. This is because the word *chāga* (goat) possesses a technical denotative power (*śakti*) qualified by worldly masculinity; such is the direction [of the argument]. And some say that this [masculinity] consists of three classes. As stated by Bhartṛhari: "These three classes alone reside in certain things, being non-contradictory to contradictory classes such as 'cow' and 'human'."
In the Bhāṣya, however, an alternative view is stated under the sūtra *striyām* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.1.3):
"Having adopted, according to their own philosophical tenets, the two genders as contraction (*saṃstyāna*) and procreation (*prasava*), [it is said]:
'The feminine (*strī*) is derived from the root *styai* with the suffix *ḍaṭ* in the sense of contraction; the masculine (*pumān*) is derived from the root *sū* in the sense of procreation.'"

"And that which is the interval between the two is the neuter in their absence. This is the meaning: *saṃstyāna* (contraction) is the female (*strī*), which is the diminution of the qualities (*guṇa*) characterized by *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. *Prasava* (procreation) is the augmentation of the qualities; that itself is the male (*pumān*). The meaning is that from the root *sū*, the letter *s* is replaced by *p*. Mādhava states that the suffix *ḍumasun* is applied to the root *sūṅ*. As for what Ujjvaladatta stated—that the suffix *masun* is applied to the root *yā*—[that is incorrect].

Furthermore, regarding the rule *puṃso 'suṅ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.1.89), the authors of the Nyāsa and the Rakṣita have cited the rule *punāter makāsun hrasvaś ca*; however, both of these are inconsistent with the Bhāṣya. The intended meaning is that when there is neither increase (*upacaya*) nor decrease (*apacaya*), that which is intermediate and similar to both is the neuter (*napuṃsaka*). This is due to the irregular formation (*nipātana*) in the rule *nabhrāṇnapāt* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.3.75). Thus, the neuter is simply the state of stability (*sthitimātra*).

For this very reason, since there is the possibility of intending to express the general state (*sthitisāmānya*) even in the case of manifestation (*āvirbhāva*) and disappearance (*tirobhāva*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that [the word *sattā*] is a neuter pronoun. It should be understood that words such as *strī*, *pumān*, and *napuṃsaka* apply to the substratum (*dharmin*) just as words like *śukti* do to the property (*dharma*). Regarding the term *svakṛtānta*: according to Amarasimha, "The two *kṛtāntas* are Yama and established doctrine" (*kṛtāntau yamasiddhāntau*, Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.3.64). Thus, the meaning is "in the established doctrine of the Grammarians" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.65).

*Vṛddha* [remains when] co-uttered with *yuvan*, provided that the distinction between them consists solely of that characteristic. (*Aṣṭādhyāyī* 1.2.65). *Vṛddha* refers to the lineage (*gotra*). This is because the ancient teachers formulated the rule: "The descendant whose generation is removed [from the founder] is *vṛddha*. When co-uttered with a *yuvan*, the *vṛddha* remains, provided that the entire difference between the two consists merely of the *gotra* and *yuvan* suffixes. For example: *gārgyaś ca gārgyāyaṇaś ca* → *gārgyau*. What is meant by "consisting of that characteristic"? Example: *bhāgavittiś ca bhāgavittikaś ca* (here the difference involves more than just the suffixes). What is meant by "entire"? Example: *gārgyavātsyāyanau* (here the difference is not limited to the suffixes). (*Aṣṭādhyāyī* 1.2.66)

*Strī-puṃvac-ca* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.66): When there is a desire to express [the meaning] together with a masculine [term], the feminine [term] remains, and its meaning becomes like that of the masculine. This must be stated because the previous rule does not apply due to the addition of femininity as a cause of dissimilarity, and it is necessary to prescribe the *puṃvat* treatment. For example: *gārgī* and *gārgyāyaṇau* become *gargāḥ*. While the term *astriyām* ("not feminine") is understood from the context, the elision (*luk*) occurs by the rule *yañañoś-ca* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.4.64). Similarly, *dākṣī* and *dākṣāyaṇaḥ* become *dākṣī*. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.67)

Pumān striyā (Pāṇini 1.2.67): When there is a co-utterance (*sahokti*) among words of identical form (*sarūpa*), the masculine remains, and it behaves exactly like the masculine, provided that the distinction between them consists solely in that characteristic. For example: *sampṛktā* (feminine) and *saṃpṛkta* (masculine) become *sampṛktau*. According to the established principle (*siddhānta*) that "that which remains expresses the meaning of what has been elided," the feminine suffix *ṭāp* would have applied because the feminine gender is still present; however, due to the continued application of the rule "it behaves exactly like the masculine," it does not occur.

In cases such as *haṃsaśca varaṭā ca* ("the male swan and the female swan"), although there is identity in terms of the species (*jāti*) of the swan, a difference in form (*rūpa*) arises solely due to gender (masculinity and femininity); thus, the application of the *ekaśeṣa* rule would have been expected here. However, this is prevented by the continued application of the term *rūpa* (form). And regarding that continued application, the rule *bhrātṛputrau svasṛduhitṛbhyām* (Pāṇini 1.2.68) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Otherwise, because of the commonality of having offspring or being an offspring, even in that case [of brother and sister], it would have been established simply by the rule *pumān striyā* (Pāṇini 1.2.67).

[Objection: Even so, when there is a co-utterance (*sahokti*) of these two—this cow (*gauḥ*) and this female buffalo (*gaurī*)—the form *etau gāvau* would not necessarily result. [Response: This is not a fault. Kaiyaṭa maintains that even when the specific gender-characteristic is conveyed by other words such as *iyam* (this [female]) and *ayam* (this [male]), the application of the rule *pumān striyā* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.67) is possible. [Objection: It might be argued that the cause here is the absence of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭābhāva*), which consists in the absence of those specific gender-characteristics. And that [absence] exists in cases such as *kinnarair apsarobhiś ca krīḍadbhiḥ* (playing with Kinnaras and Apsarases), because of the absence of qualifiers [specifying gender].

However, in the case of *gāvau*, the matter is different because of the absence of a qualified object (*viśeṣya*). If it is asked, "In that case, for what purpose was it stated that [the distinction] extends to being cognizable through another word?"—it is replied: Here, it is not the absence of the qualified object (*viśiṣṭābhāva*) that is the operative factor, but rather the specific feature (*viśeṣa*) conditioned by that alone. Otherwise, in the case of *bhāgāvittibhāgavittikau*, the rule "vṛddho yūnā" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.65) would apply.

For here, even though the suffix *ṭhak* is applied by both [the rules] *kutsā* and *sauvīratva*, the application of *yuvan* still exists; thus, the absence of the qualified [condition] is unassailable. Likewise, in the case of *indrā-indrāṇyau*, the present sūtra would apply, while in cases such as *himahimānyau*, the subsequent sūtra would apply—this is the general direction. If it is objected that this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case of *gārgyavātsyāyanau*, [we reply: no, because through the formulation of the statement "that which is the specific [suffix] is characterized by that," the connection between the subject and the predicate is obtained from the recitation [of the rule].

And thus, it follows that every particularity [of gender] is conditioned solely by those [two meanings]. Consequently, the approach of Kaiyaṭa and others—who follow the interpretation up to the end of the word *padāntara*—is indeed correct; this is the general direction. However, if one intends to express a qualified absence (*viśiṣṭābhāva*) characterized by the lack of any particularity conditioned by anything other than those two, then everything is perfectly sound. By this, the analysis of *sā ca sa ca tau* is explained; for even though the non-conditional *ekaśeṣa* (single-remainder formation) operates at the stage *tad tad*, the restriction to the masculine gender is obtained through this very principle.

However, it does not apply in cases such as *brāhmaṇavatsaśca* (a Brāhmaṇa boy) and *brāhmaṇīvatsā ca* (a Brāhmaṇa girl). The single-remainder formation (*ekaśeṣa*) occurs when there is a desire to express a man and a woman together. Furthermore, this co-expression applies only to the two primary entities. Therefore, since the operation of *ekaśeṣa* takes place only where the distinction between the primary man and woman is the motivating factor for the specific form, or where a distinction is made by the primary entity itself—as is the case here—the rule does not apply here because of the continued implication of the word "only" (*eva*): namely, in *indrāṇī* [with *indra*], for here the distinction is also caused by connection with a male (*puṃyoga*). Likewise, it does not apply in *āraṇyaḥ* (a male forest-dweller) and *āraṇyānī* (a female forest-dweller).

In this case, there is also a distinction based on gender. Why [is it said] "masculine" (*pumān*)? [Consider: *prāk* and *pratīcī* are both "east and west" (*prākpratīcyau*). The word *prāk* is indeclinable (*avyaya*) because it lacks gender (*aliṅga*), due to the rule "A taddhita suffix that does not take all case-endings [is indeclinable]" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.1.38). It is derived from the root *añc* preceded by *pra*, with the *kvip* suffix, and according to the rule "After *añc* ending in *kvin*, [the suffix] *am* is added when followed by *liṅ*" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.4.12). [The rule] "Brother and son [are used in the dual] with sister and daughter" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.68) teaches them in their respective order. Thus: *bhrātā ca svasā ca* = *bhrātarau* ("brother and sister"); *putraśca duhitā ca* = *putrau* ("son and daughter").

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.69) *napuṃsakamanapuṃsakenaikavaccāsyānyatarasyām*: When a neuter [noun] is mentioned together with a non-neuter [noun], the neuter remains, and it may optionally be treated as a singular. This applies provided that the distinction [between them] is based solely on that [neuter] characteristic. For example: *śuklaḥ kambalaḥ*, *śuklā bṛhatikā*, *śuklaṃ vastram*, *tad idaṃ śuklam* (the white blanket, the white cloak, the white cloth—this is white); *tānīmāni śuklāni* (these are white). Why does it say "with a non-neuter" (*anapuṃsakena*)? Consider: *śuklaṃ śuklaṃ ca śukle* (white and white = two whites). In this case, the rule for being treated as a singular (*ekavat*) does not apply. Why does it say "*asya*" (of this)? It is so that the application of the state of being treated as a singular (*ekavadbhāva*) from the subsequent sūtra does not carry over here.

*Pitā mātrā* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.70): When mentioned together with *mātṛ*, *pitṛ* is optionally retained [as the single substitute]. Thus, we have *pitarau* or *mātāpitarau*. This rule (*yoga*) can be dispensed with. For, according to the maxim "that which remains expresses the meaning of what has been elided," it is beyond dispute that in this context the word *pitṛ* alone denotes the mother as well. In that case, whether there is a conventional secondary signification (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) or even primary denotative power (*śakti*), is another matter. Nor is the rule intended for the purpose of precluding the formation of a *dvandva* compound; for such a compound is also desired in certain instances.

In this same manner, it should also be understood in the case of *śvaśuraḥ śvaśrvā* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.71). By this [principle], [the following is explained]: "The wife, the daughters, the parents, and likewise the brothers" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.55).

On the occasion of explaining this [sūtra], the statement of Vijñāneśvara—"first the mother inherits the wealth, and in her absence, the father"—is to be reconsidered, because there is no sequence in the cognition produced by a single word. The same applies to the commencement of the sūtra itself. On the contrary, it is appropriate for the primary meaning to be cognized first, not the secondary (lakṣya) mother. As for the claim that sequence is perceived in the analytical exposition (*vigraha*), that is not so; for the compound (*vṛtti*) and its analytical exposition (*vigraha*) are never used together.

Because in this verse to be explained, only the *vṛtti* (the compound) is employed; furthermore, even when the *vṛtti* is used, the analytical explanation (*vigraha*) should somehow be remembered. However, even there, there is no restrictive rule regarding the sequence of the prior and posterior members; therefore, another means of proof must be sought for determining the order.
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.71)

Pāṇini Sūtra 1.2.71: *śvaśuraḥ śvaśrvā*—when mentioned together with the mother-in-law (*śvaśrū*), the word *śvaśura* (father-in-law) is optionally retained [as the single remainder]. Examples: *śvaśurau* (the two parents-in-law), or *śvaśrūśvaśurau*. By the very fact of the sūtra’s mention of *śvaśrū*, it is established that even a form ending in a suffix is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Otherwise, according to the principle "an imitation is like its original" (*prakṛtivadanukaraṇam*), there would not be an instrumental case ending in *-ūṅ* [as in *śvaśrvā*]. Pāṇini Sūtra 1.2.72.

"tyādīni sarvaiḥ nityam" (Pāṇini 1.2.72). When there is co-utterance (*sahokti*) with *tyad* and the other pronouns as well as others, *tyad* and the rest are always retained. The inclusion of the word "all" (*sarva*) is so that the meaning "only in co-utterance with *tyad* and the others" (by virtue of proximity) should not be understood. Thus, *sa ca devadattaśca tau* ("he and Devadatta, those two"). This statement is for the purpose of excluding the application of the *dvandva* compound rule. However, the form "those two" (*tau*) is already established by the rule "sarūpa" (1.2.64), because it is possible to refer to Devadatta using the very same word *tat*.

When pronouns beginning with *tyad* (the "tyadādi" group) are used together, that which is subsequent remains, due to the rule of "subsequent [application] overriding the previous" (*paravipratiṣedha*). Thus, *sa ca yaśca* becomes *yau*. Regarding this, the *Bhāṣya* states: "An earlier [form] is also seen as the remainder. Thus, *sa ca yaśca* becomes *tau*; and *ahaṃ ca bhāvaśca* becomes *āvām*. The rule *tyadāditaḥ śeṣe puṃnapuṃsakato liṅgavacanāni* [Pāṇini 1.2.66] applies. By the inclusion of *tyadādi* in the list [of particles], the suffix *tasi* is added. The meaning is that when pronouns beginning with *tyad* are intended to be expressed together, the gender and number of the remaining [referent] are determined by whether that referent is masculine or neuter. Thus, *sa ca yaśca* becomes *yau*. Regarding the statement "an earlier [form] is also seen as the remainder," examples include *sa ca yaśca yau*, *sa ca yaśca tau*, and *ahaṃ ca bhāvaśca āvām*. In these cases, although the subsequent form would normally remain, the earlier form is observed to remain instead. This is established by the principle of "subsequent [application] overriding the previous" (*paravipratiṣedha*). Therefore, in the case of *tyadāditaḥ śeṣe*, the gender and number of the remaining [referent]—whether it be masculine or neuter—govern the grammatical forms of the compound. For instance, *sa ca yaśca* results in *yau* because the subsequent form remains; however, in other instances, the earlier form may remain, as illustrated by the *Bhāṣya*. Consequently, the gender and number of the final word are determined by the specific nature of the remaining referent among those being conjoined.

*sa* and *devadattaḥ*—those two; *tat* and *devadattaḥ* and *yajñadattā*—those [plural]; however, when a masculine and a neuter are intended together, the form is determined by the neuter because it is the subsequent one. *tat* and *devadattaḥ*—those two. It should be stated that this applies except for compounds ending in *dvandva* or *tatpuruṣa*, and for qualifiers (Kāśikā Vārttika). These two are a cock and a peahen (*kukkuṭamayūryau*); these two are a peahen and a cock (*mayūrīkukkuṭau*). That is half of a *pippalī*; she is the half-*pippalī*—those two are "half-*pippalīs*" (*ardhapippalyau*).

In this context, by the rule *paravalliṅgam* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.4.26), when the gender of the compound meaning is transferred [to the whole], the pronoun that qualifies it takes that very same gender. However, in the *Bhāṣya*, this rule has been rejected. As he said: "The matter is established because there is no *dvandva* compound between a word expressing a general term and a word expressing a specific term. For when a general term is used in proximity to a specific term, it functions with reference to another specific [instance]. This is just as in the example: "The Brāhmaṇas have arrived, and Vasiṣṭha too."

Kaiyaṭa states that in such a case, this prohibition of the dual number is based on explicit scriptural injunction (*vācanika*). Since the exclusion of forms such as *tau devadattau* (those two Devadattas) is already established by that very rule, the purpose of this *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one member) need not be stated. If so, how then are forms such as *śūdrābhīram*, *gobalīvardam*, and *tṛṇopalām* explained? On this point, they say: Ābhīrī is a distinct caste. As the *Smṛti* declares: "From a Brāhmaṇa and the daughter of an Ugra is born one named Ābhīra;
from a Vaiśya and a Śūdra woman, the Māhiṣya and Ugra are born respectively from the King (Kṣatriya). Thus, [the term *śūdrābhīram* refers to] different castes.

The word *go* here refers to a female cow and is feminine in gender; furthermore, *apām ulapaḥ* is a proper name. This prohibition is not absolute, as is indicated by the reference to the rule *prācyabharateṣu* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.4.66). Consequently, the formation of *dvandva* compounds in cases such as *pramāṇaprameya* is established. By this, usages such as—“Ignorance (*avidyā*), that [nescience], and the mind’s connection with it (*taccito yogaḥ*), these six are beginningless for us; [the term ‘six’ applies] to those two specific [categories] within the fish and so forth”—are explained. However, one should consider with a discerning heart that these would indeed be established even by the initial formulation of the sūtra itself.

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.73) *strī* [remains] when there is a desire to express a collection of domestic animals that are not young. In these cases, when there is a desire to express them together, the feminine form is retained. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule "pumān striyā" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.67). Examples: *imā gāvaḥ* (these cows). Why is the word "domestic" (*grāmya*) mentioned? [Consider: *ime ruravaḥ* (these ruru deer). Why is the word "animals" (*paśu*) mentioned? [Consider: *brāhmaṇāḥ* (Brahmins). Why is the word "collections" (*saṅgheṣu*) mentioned? [Consider: *etau gāvau carataḥ* (these two cows are grazing). Since the application of "single remainder" (*ekaśeṣa*) is already established for multiple objects, the mention of "collections" serves to indicate that a group of many is intended here. Why is it specified "not young"? [Consider: *ime vatsāḥ* (these calves).

"These are goats. It should be stated [in the rule] "among animals with many hoofs" (*anekaśapheṣu*). "These are horses," "these are donkeys. Because they have only one hoof (*ekaśaphatvāt*), there is only the masculine remainder (*puṃśeṣa*). Amarasimha states: "The word *śapha* is neuter; *khura* is masculine" (*Amarakośa* 2.8.49). Haradatta, however, uses the expression "the hooves (*śaphāḥ*) are *khurāḥ*. In that case, another source for the masculine gender of the word *śapha* must be sought. As for camels, because they are wild (*āraṇyatvāt*), there is no feminine remainder. Thus ends the third section (*ānhika*) of the second quarter (*pāda*) of the first chapter in the illustrious *Śabdakaustubha*, and the quarter is completed.
First Daily Lesson of the Third Chapter.

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.1) *Bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.1). Those words listed in the [Dhātu-]gaṇas that denote action (*kriyā*) shall have the technical designation of *dhātu*. Because they possess the status of a *dhātu*, the *laṭ* and other suffixes are applied, as in *bhavati* and *edhate*. Why specify "denoting action"? To prevent the status of *dhātu* from applying to forms such as *yā paśya*, for if that were the case, the elision of the final *ā* would occur by the rule *āto dhātoḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.140). Nor can the semantic definitions provided in the Dhātupāṭha—such as *yā prāpaṇe* (Dhātusūtra 1049)—be considered restrictive, because those definitions are not authored by Pāṇini.

It is recorded in tradition that Bhīmasena and others indeed specified the meaning [of roots]; however, it is clear from the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika that Pāṇini recited [the roots] as *bhū*, *edha*, and so forth. Furthermore, even when meanings have been assigned by authoritative scholars (*abhiyukta*), such an assignment is not intended to exclude other meanings; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [words like] *sukham* and *anubhavati* being treated as verbal roots (*dhātu*).

And it has been said: "The individual meaning was demonstrated in order to declare the state of expressing an action (*kriyāvācitva*). Roots are indeed multivalent; they must be followed according to actual usage."

For this very reason, the particle *eva* is recited in the rule *kurda khurda gurda guda krīḍāyām eva* (Dhātupāṭha 21–24), and rules such as *śliṣa āliṅgane* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.1.46) also serve as indicators (*jñāpaka*) here. Therefore, the qualification "denoting an action" (*kriyāvācin*) is established in order to exclude [words] such as "those which you see" (*yāḥ paśya*). Why specify "those read in the lists" (*gaṇapaṭhitāḥ*)? [It is so that] it may not apply to indeclinables (*avyaya*) such as *hiruk*, *pṛthak*, and *ṛte*, nor to verbal forms (*tiṅanta*) expressing a state of being (*bhāva*), such as *śiśye*. Nor, in this way, does there arise an over-narrow application (*avyāpti*) regarding those [roots] mentioned in the sūtras.

Because the status of being a verbal root (*dhātu*) is inferred from the assignment of the augment *it* to *stambhū* and others, as well as by the prescription of grammatical operations governed by the heading of "verbal roots" (*dhātv-adhikāra*). Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of failing to include colloquial forms such as *culumpa*, for even though the *vṛt*-marker was placed at the end of the *bhvādi* class to signal the conclusion of the *yajādi* group, the *bhvādi* class itself was not thereby concluded; this is because it has been explained exactly so in the *Dhātuvṛttis*. This is also established by the statement of Kātyāyana: "The mention of 'having more than one vowel' (*anekāc*) in the rule for *kāsyap* is for the sake of including *culumpa* and others. (Kātyāyana-vārttika).

Thus, because the formation of the *vṛt* (section marker) at the end of the *bhvādi* class serves the purpose of concluding the *puṣādi* group, the *divādi* classes remain incomplete; consequently, forms such as *mṛgyati* are established. In reality, however, all desired forms are established by means of the *gaṇa*-sūtra at the end of the *curādi* class: "This [list] is a general illustration (*bahulam etan nidarśanam*). For that sūtra has been explained in two ways in the *dhātuvṛttis*: namely, that even from roots listed in the *bhvādi* class, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) may be applied according to usage, such as in *japayati*.

The recitation of ten groups [of roots] is for the purpose of providing a mere illustration; by this, other roots used by the learned (*śiṣṭa*) are also to be included. It might be argued: "In the analysis *bhūr ādir yeṣām* (those of which 'bhū' is the first), when the *yaṇ* substitution occurs, it would have to be *bhv-ādayaḥ*; furthermore, the property of denoting action (*kriyāvācitva*) is not actually mentioned in the Sūtra. To this it is replied: "The Bhāṣya states: 'Becoming is *bhūḥ*, which is action in general; they are called *vādayaḥ* because they denote (*vadanti*), the suffix *iñ* being applied to the root *vad* according to the Uṇādi rules.'"

Although the suffix *iñ* is prescribed after the root *vad* followed by the causative marker (*ṇi*) by the Uṇādi sūtra “*vasi vapi yaji rāji vraji sahi hani vāsi vādi vāribhya iñ*” (Uṇādi-sūtra 574), nevertheless, because of the inclusion of the term *bahulam* ("variously"), the Nyāsakāra and others maintain that it will occur even after the simple root. In reality, however, the Bhāṣya statement “*vadantīti vādayaḥ*” is intended merely as an explanation of the meaning. The suffix *iñ* is indeed added only after the causative form; yet there is no lack of connection with the causative sense here, because the meanings of *pacati* and *pācayati* are identical. The analysis of the compound is thus: *bhūvaḥ vādayaḥ*.

Thus, the quality of denoting action (*kriyāvācitva*) is indeed established by the Sūtra itself. It is inferred that the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) applies only to those roots such as *bhū* and others that are listed in the grammatical recension (*pāṭha*) without an indicatory marker (*anubandha*) and with the verbal suffix *ś* (*śap*) as their conjugational sign (*vikaraṇa*). This is also evident from the commencement of the Sūtra "Those ending in *san* and so forth are verbal roots" (*Aṣṭādhyāyī* 3.1.32). Alternatively, the analysis of the compound may be "those of which *bhū* and others are the first. The augment *vuk* [in *bhūvādayaḥ*] occurs by virtue of a specific grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*). Furthermore, the use of a major technical term (*mahāsaṃjñā*) is for the purpose of understanding the etymological definition (*anvarthasaṃjñā*): "They are called *dhātus* (verbal roots) because they 'bear' (*dadhati*) the action."

Alternatively, *bhū* and *vā* form a *dvandva* compound. Regarding the two instances of the word *ādi*, there is a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) of those words which denote modes of arrangement. Then, the *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed as "those for which *bhū* and *vā* are the *ādis*" (*bhūv-ādīni*). This means that *bhū* and so forth are like *vā* in that they denote action. Or else, it is a *bahuvrīhi*: "those for which *vā* is the *ādi*" (*vā-ādayaḥ*). Then, a *tatpuruṣa* is formed: "the *ādis* of *vā*" (*vā-ādayaḥ*). When there is a *ekaśeṣa* of these two [compounds], according to the rule "of those whose vowels differ," the *bahuvrīhi* remains. Thus, *bhuvo vādayaḥ* is a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*. And the meaning of the genitive case here is the relationship between the signified and the signifier (*vācya-vācaka-bhāva*).

The inclusion of both [the root *bhū* and its synonyms] is obtained either through the rule *dvirvacaneci* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.1.59), by means of repetition (*āvṛtti*), or by other such methods. In any case, it is established that only those roots beginning with *bhū*, which denote action, are *dhātus*. What, then, is action (*kriyā*)? It is said: action is precisely *bhāvanā*, which consists of an activity conducive to production; it has "production" as its synonym and is essentially the meaning of the verb "to do" (*karoti*). For instance, since non-existent things like the sky are not produced, whereas existent things like a jar are produced, the agent of the meaning of "becoming" (*bhavati*) is the object of the action of "doing" (*karoti*).

And thus, because the agent of the action of "doing" (√kṛ) is the instigator of the agent of "becoming" (√bhū), the causative suffix (ṇic) arising in the sense of the instigating activity of "becoming"—which has the meaning of origination—rests upon the meaning of "doing. And it has been said:
"No one [is an agent] of the action of 'doing' without an object that is being done;
and the agent of the meaning of 'becoming' becomes the object of 'doing'."
He who is the agent of the action of "doing" is the instigator (prayojaka) of the one who is to become [the agent];
then, in relation to that instigator, the latter attains the status of the one to be employed (prayojya).
Only verbs with the causative suffix (ṇic) are employed to express the exclusive activity of the instigating agent (prayojyakartṛ) with respect to the actions of that instigator.

"Therefore, those who know the process of manifestation (bhāvanā) say that for an entity which has assumed agency over the various states of being, there is the instigating activity (prayojaka-kriyā) regarding future things. Thus [it is said].

And that [activity] is the common denominator (*vṛtti*) of all verbal roots (*dhātu*). For this very reason, when asked "What does he do?", answers such as "He cooks" (*pacati*) or "He reads" (*paṭhati*) are appropriate. Nor should it be argued that, according to the Mīmāṃsaka view, this [activity] must reside solely in what is denoted by the suffix; for in cases such as *bhoktavyam* ("it is to be eaten"), that [activity] is perceived even without a finite verb (*ākhyāta*). Furthermore, even there, a dependence on a case-factor (*kāraka*) is observed. Moreover, there is also grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the root *paci-* (to cook) in such instances: "What is to be done?"—"It is to be eaten" (*bhoktavyam*); "What did he do?"—"He ate" (*bhuktavān*).

Furthermore, according to your view, just as one says "he causes the pot to exist" (*bhāvayati ghaṭam*), one should also be able to say "the pot exists" (*bhavati ghaṭam*), because the meaning is identical. In the example, the *ṇic* suffix expresses the activity of the agent, the potter; in the case under discussion, however, it is the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta-pratyaya*) that does so. If you argue that there is a difference because the meaning of the *ṇic* is the activity of the instigator (*prayojaka*), whereas the meaning of the verbal suffix is the activity of the agent (*kartṛ*), [we reply: this is not a valid distinction, because if the status of being an agent belongs only to one who employs the entire set of causal factors (*kāraka-cakra*), then the pot itself would not possess such a status. However, if it is held that: "The status of being an agent is always intended for a *kāraka* whose action is already expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*)," [then the pot can indeed be the agent].

Thus, according to the method propounded by Bhartṛhari, you also accept that agency (*kartṛtva*) consists primarily in the state of possessing an operation (*vyāpāra*) denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*). What, then, is the meaning of the finite verb (*ākhyāta*) now? Since the operation is already expressed by the verbal root alone. Furthermore, the distinction between transitive and intransitive roots would be destroyed, and sūtras such as *akarmakācca* (Pāṇini 1.3.26) and others would be contradicted.

If it is objected: "But even in our own system (*siddhānta*), since there is a rule that an action must necessarily depend upon an object (*karman*), how can [the root *yaj*] be intransitive (*akarmaka*)?", we reply: No, because the distinction between transitive and intransitive verbs will be explained on the basis of whether the result (*phala*) and the operation (*vyāpāra*) share the same locus (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) or different loci (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). Furthermore, in expressions such as *jyotiṣṭomayājī* ("one who has performed the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice"), the suffix *ṇini* is justified in our view by Pāṇini’s rule *karaṇe yajaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.2.85), because the other constituent part denoted by the root *yaj*, being included within the verbal root itself, serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) also included within the verbal root.

For roots such as *pac* (to cook) express *bhāvanā* (efficient force) by virtue of being verbal roots (*dhātu*). However, with respect to other components such as softening (*viklitti*), they express them through their specific individual forms, such as *pākatva* (the state of being cooked). And that [specific form] is generally connected as the object to be brought about (*bhāvya*) for those other components that constitute the efficient force. But in cases such as "one who has sacrificed with the Jyotiṣṭoma" (*jyotiṣṭomayājī*), it is connected as the instrument (*karaṇa*), because the meaning understood is: "he has brought about heaven by means of the sacrifice named Jyotiṣṭoma. This is clear in Haradatta’s commentary on the rule for the suffix *ṇini*. By this, the Bhāṣya statement "the root *pac* has two meanings" is explained. And Bhaṭṭi says:

Then Purandara, whose actions are directed toward the ultimate truth, divided his army and appointed the generals against the enemy host, just as the root *kṛ* (to do) employs all verbal suffixes (*karoti*) for various meanings.

Objection: If the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātu*) is action (*kriyā*), then in cases such as *pacati* ("he cooks"), there would not arise a cognition having the action as its primary object—namely, that "the act of cooking has a single agent and exists in the present"—because the status of the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*) as a qualifier of the suffix-meaning (*pratyayārtha*) is already established in examples like *aupagavaḥ* ("the son of Upagu"). Response: This is not so. For while "the suffix-meaning is predominant" is a general rule (*utsarga*), that rule is set aside here, because of the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) that "the verb (*ākhyāta*) has action as its predominant [meaning]," and also because in forms such as *pācikā* ("female cook"), it is accepted that femininity (*strītva*) functions as a qualifier.

On the contrary, there would be an inconsistency in your own view regarding expressions such as *pacati*. Since the predominance of the agent (*kartṛ-pradhānya*) in forms like *pacantam taṃ paśya* (see him cooking) involving the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* is universally accepted, it would follow that the same would apply to verbal endings (*tiṅ*) as well; for there is no distinction between suffixes like *śatṛ* and *tiṅ*s in their status as substitutes (*lādeśatva*) for the *l*-suffixes. Furthermore, since substitutes must either remind one of the original element (*sthānin*) or express its meaning, they are necessarily constrained to have the same meaning as the original.

For this very reason, the established rule for the persons (puruṣa)—such as "the middle [person] occurs when the word *yuṣmad* is in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*), and the highest [person] when *asmad* is"—is consistent. Likewise, rules such as "the nominative case occurs when the agent is expressed" (*abhihite kartari prathamā*) are consistent. One should not claim that by the term "coreferentiality" what is intended is the capacity to be construed with a number denoted by itself, and by the word "expressed" (*abhihita*) what is intended is the state of having a number already expressed; for such an interpretation would be inconsistent with the sūtras.

Because number is not expressed by primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), or compounds (*samāsa*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the third case even when that [number] is already expressed. Nor should it be argued that the non-expression of the verbal action (*kṛti*) is itself the non-expression of the agent; for if that were so, the nominative case would result even for the agent in the case of a verb expressing a state of being (*bhāva-artha-lakāra*). This is the general direction [of the argument]. It might be argued as follows: the status of being a denoter of action (*kriyā-vācitva*) is under-extended (*avyāpta*) to the roots *as*, *bhū*, and *vid*. For in those cases, production (*utpāda*) is not perceived.

If it is argued that there is likewise non-pervasion (avyāpti) even in the case of "it remains thus" (*tiṣṭhati*) and "it is born/arises" (*jāyate*), because arising is indeed connection with the first moment and the operation conducive to that is "causing to arise" (*utpādanā*), while the experience of that [arising] does not exist at all in the case of verbs such as *asti*—for which reason, when asked "What is he doing?", people do not reply "He exists" (*asti*) as they would say "He cooks" (*pacati*) and so on—it is said in response: the meaning of *asti* and similar forms is "maintaining its own nature" (*svarūpa-dhāraṇam*), and maintaining is connection with subsequent moments.

Even so, although the meaning of "doing" (karoti) is present, the expectancy for an object (*bhāvya*) is satisfied by the very act of sustaining (*dhāraṇa*), which is included within the root-meaning; thus, like [the verbs] "he lives" (*jīvati*) or "he dances" (*nṛtyati*), they are intransitive (*akarmaka*). For an action is said to be "production" (*utpatti*) only when it has a locus different from that of the operation (*vyāpāra*). For this very reason, jars and the like possess the status of an object (*karmatā*) in those cases, because they possess production as the result of an operation inherent in another. However, by roots such as *jan* ("to be born"), production is expressed as having the same locus as the operation. For this very reason, they are intransitive.

Even though it possesses an activity conducive to its own production, it lacks the status of an object (*karmatā*)—which is constituted by being inherent in another (*parasamavetatva*)—in the case of jars and the like when they have assumed a subtle form. And as Hari said:
"Bearing itself by means of itself, it is designated as 'it exists'.
Others also say:
"Even in [the cognition] 'it exists' and so forth, there is indeed a mental cultivation (bhāvanā) regarding the objective constituent (dharmyaṃśa) that is to be cultivated;
however, because it is not present in other parts, it does not manifest in that way."

Likewise, although "cooking" (*pacati*) and "being softened" (*viklidyati*) share the commonality of the result of softening (*viklitti*), nevertheless, in the case of "cooking," that result resides in a different locus from the operation (*vyāpāra*), whereas in the case of "being softened," it resides in the same locus as that operation; thus is the distinction between transitive (*sakarmaka*) and intransitive (*akarmaka*) verbs established. For being a "patient" (*karman*) does not consist merely in possessing the fruit that constitutes the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*); rather, the residence of that fruit in a locus distinct from the operation must also be required. As for what was stated regarding the question "What does he do? and so forth—that is unproven.

When someone on the verge of destruction is the object of the question "What is he doing?", the answer "He exists" is universally accepted. In other cases, however, when a person is determined to be in good health, the question "What is he doing? is restricted in scope to specific activities such as cooking; therefore, "He exists" is not an appropriate answer. By this [it is meant]: "Whether already accomplished or yet unaccomplished, that which is designated as being in the state of being accomplished (sādhya) is called 'action' (kriyā), because its nature consists in the assumption of a temporal sequence."

This has also been explained. The point is that the arising of a [cognition] qualified by multiple moments occurring in a temporal sequence is equally possible even in cases such as "the self exists. For even in the case of "he cooks" (*pacati*) and the like, the action (*kriyā*) is the entire collection of operations beginning with placing the pot on the fire and ending with taking it off. Precisely for this reason, because these do not exist simultaneously, the action is not perceptible (*pratyakṣa*). Rather, when each individual operation, such as placing the pot on the fire, is experienced in succession, a synthesis (*saṅkalana*) is performed by the mind.

This has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "This thing called action is absolutely imperceptible; it is impossible to point it out as a solidified whole. Even its unity is merely technical (*pāribhāṣika*), because it is delimited by a single result. And it has been said: "A collection of successive parts, which function as subordinate elements, is designated as 'action' when its non-difference is mentally constructed."

Therefore, it is easy to state that [the word] *bhava* (being) primarily denotes action (*kriyā*). For this very reason, there is a connection with time, as in "it was" (*abhūt*), "it is" (*asti*), and "it will be" (*bhaviṣyati*). Indeed, such a connection with time is not possible without the nature of action. As it has been said:
"Time serves to differentiate actions, whereas number is the differentiator of everything.
And: "That form which conforms to time is perceived as 'it exists' (*asti*)."

In the *Āṣya*, however, the statement of the author of the *Nirukta* has been cited in order to establish the meaning already stated: "The venerable Vārṣyāyaṇi said, 'There are six modifications of being' (*ṣaḍbhāvavikārāḥ*). The meaning is that there are six modes of 'being' (*bhāva*), which is to say, of action (*kriyā*). And among these, because of the reading 'is born' (*jāyate*) and 'exists' (*asti*), the connection with all actions is established. Kaiyaṭa, however, explained it in another manner as well.

"These seven modes of being (*bhāva*), which consist of existence (*sattā*) itself, appear as having the nature of birth and so forth because their form as the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is determined through its connection with the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), even though they are essentially manifold actions. And likewise, in the *Jātisamuddeśa*, beginning with the statement "Being (*sattā*) itself [appears as such] due to the difference in its correlates," it is said: "When specific sequences have been attained, that very [being] is designated as 'action' (*kriyā*); when the form of sequence is withdrawn, it is called 'existence' (*sat-tva*)."

The meaning is that because specific operations (*vyāpāra*) are things to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and are sequential, these [properties] belong to the action as conditioned by them. However, in cases such as *pākaḥ*, the verbal root (*prakṛti*) presents the state of being accomplished as having the nature of non-existence (*asatva*), whereas the suffix *ghañ* presents it in its established (*siddha*) form. And it has been said:
"The established state and the state of being accomplished of an action have been proclaimed.
They maintain that substance (*dravya*) is the established state; it is precisely there that they desire the application of the suffix *ghañ*."

Just as in the case of a verb, the status of being the "to-be-accomplished" (sādhya) and the "means of accomplishment" (sādhana) is conceptually attributed to its two parts according to the treatises, that same principle applies to words ending in *ghañ* and other such suffixes.
"In that context, action is based on the form of the verbal root (*dhātu*) as something to be accomplished (*sādhyatvena*);
however, its state as a substance (*satvabhāva*) is based on suffixes such as *ghañ*.

This means that the suffixes *ghañ* and others bring about the presentation [of the action] in a specific state capable of being construed with gender, number, case-role (*kāraka*), and so forth. By this, the Bhāṣya on the third chapter—"An action expressed by a *kṛt*-suffix shines like a substance"—is also explained. By the word "conceived" (*prakalpita*), he emphasizes that the *padasphoṭa* alone is the reality; for this very reason, rice and other objects are construed with it as its *kārakas*. This is the intended meaning.

For this very reason, suffixes such as *tumun* are established in cases like "cooking in order to eat" (*bhoktuṃ pākaḥ*) and "going after having eaten" (*bhuktvā gamanam*). However, regarding the meanings of *kṛt* suffixes, one must simply take refuge in the principle that they do not occur due to non-expression (*anabhidhāna*). For this same reason, even a doubling [of the suffix] is sometimes observed, based on the usage in the Sūtra and Vārttika stating "the rule for doubling [applies] to *aṇ*" (*dviraṇvidhiḥ*). As for the phrase "but the state of being a substance" (*sattvabhāvas tu*), the meaning is that for this very reason, in cases such as "he performs cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*), it (the action) connects as a *kāraka* (participant in the action).

But in that case, in expressions such as "see, the deer runs," there would be no objecthood (*karmatā*) for the act of seeing on the part of the deer’s rapid movement. Nor should it be argued that although objecthood appears here through the relational capacity (*saṃsarga-maryādā*), the aforementioned fault does not arise because it does not appear as a qualifier (*prakāra*); for even so, this would lead to inconsistency in cases like "he cooks" (*pacati*) or "it exists" (*bhavati*). For the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) in those instances is: "the present act of cooking has a single agent," and "the present act of existing has a single agent."

And in that case, since the meaning of the verbal suffix (lakāra) in the word *bhavati*—namely, the agent—is not understood as being the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) in relation to the action of cooking whose agent is Devadatta, by way of a non-differentiating relation; thus, the property of existence belonging to the action of cooking, just like [the property] belonging to Devadatta, would be unavoidable. Regarding this, they say: "The manifestation of agency and objecthood is accepted on the strength of experience; however, the intended meaning [of the verb] lies merely in the absence of other factors of action (*kāraka*). The verse cited as "In the verbal form, by its two parts... has precisely this intention.

In this regard, we shall clarify in the third [chapter] that the phrase “with reference to whom” is intended in accordance with the subsequent verse. By this, the syntactic connection of the agenthood of forms such as *apākṣīt*, *apākṣīḥ*, *pacataḥ*, *pacanti*, *pakṣyati*, and *pakṣyataḥ* with the verb *bhavati* is also explained; for, just as in cases like *bhāvī varttate* (“the future exists”) or *dhvasto 'sti* (“the destroyed exists”), there is the possibility of a present existence in a subtle state.

"A nasal [consonant] in the *upadeśa* is designated as *it*. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.2). That which is nasal in the *upadeśa* shall be termed *it*. It is called *upadeśa* because "it is taught (*upadiśyate*) by means of this"; here, by the rule "the *kṛtya* and *lyuṭ* suffixes are used diversely" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.3.113), the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) due to its diversity of application. Otherwise, the suffix *lyuṭ* would have been used. This *upadeśa* consists of the Dhātupāṭha, the Prātipadikapāṭha, and the Sūtras and Vārttikas, for by these words are taught. Among these, the reading of nasalized sounds as they were originally recited by the author of the Śāstra has now become corrupted.

For this very reason, the authors of the Vārttikas say: "The followers of Pāṇini [preserve] the nasality of the original enunciation. In that regard, in forms such as *edha* and *spardha*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs because they are marked with an anudātta accent; thus, *edhate* and *spardhate*. In the case of *bhavati*, the augment *num* is applied because of the marker *u* (the *ugit* designation); hence, *bhavān*.
