According to the established doctrine that expressive power resides in those elements present at the stage of grammatical derivation (*prayoga-samavāyin*), the meaning of the *vānta* (the *au* in *hvāu*) is the vowel *ā*. If it is argued that in the case of *dadhnā*, the *nānta* (the *n* in *dadhi-n*) has the meaning of *dadhī*, then it is equally applicable that the *vānta* itself has the meaning of the vowel *e*. For, during the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā-daśā*), when there is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of a form ending in *e*, the substitution of *ā* occurs by virtue of the technical rule (*lakṣaṇa-vaśāt*), but here it is not the form ending in *ā* that is being imitated. Therefore, nothing here is untenable.

As for what was stated by the author of the Nyāsa—that because the term *vyai* (referring to a form where the vowel has already undergone change) is mentioned in the rule *navyo liṭi* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.46), which prohibits *ātva*, this serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that a modified form (*vikṛti*) may also include the original base (*prakṛti*)—this is an effort expended in the wrong place. This is because the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is weakened by the reasoning already stated. Furthermore, if there were such an inclusion of the modified form in rules like *eranekācaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.82) and *oḥ supi* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.83), then the substitution of *yaṇ* would undesirably apply even in forms such as *śiśayiṣate*.

If a derivative (*vikṛti*) were to cause the application of a rule to its base (*prakṛti*), then in the case of *viśvarājau* as well, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of lengthening according to Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.3.128, *viśvasya vasurāṭoḥ*. Furthermore, in *turāsāham* and similar forms, there would be the undesirable consequence of the retroflex nasal (*mūrdhanya*). This is the general direction of the argument. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.31)

*Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.31*: *kṣpardhāyāmāṅaḥ*. The *ātmanepada* [middle voice] ending shall be used after the root *hve* (to call) when preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, provided that the context concerns rivalry (*spardhā*). Example: *mallamāhvayate* ("He challenges the wrestler"). The meaning is: "Being in rivalry, he issues a challenge to him. Why specify "in the case of rivalry"? Consider: *putramāhvayati* ("He calls his son"). Although this root is listed as being used in the sense of rivalry, even so, when preceded by *āṅ*, it does not function there in that sense; rather, it functions in the sense of "calling out" (*śabdane*). For this very reason, it is explained that this rule applies specifically to the domain of rivalry. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.32)

*Gandhana*, *avakṣepaṇa*, *sevana*, *sāhasikya*, *pratiyatna*, *prakathana*, and *upayoga*: after the root *kṛ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.32), the Ātmanepada suffix occurs when these seven meanings are present, even if the fruit of the action does not accrue to the agent. Here, *gandhana* means "hinting" (*sūcana*). For instance, because the roots are listed in the *curādi* group as "√*gandh* in the sense of injury" (*cuoāo* 1685) and "√*ard* in the sense of injury" (*cuouo* 1829), *gandhana* is injury. Since hinting also constitutes injury by way of causing execution, imprisonment, and so forth, that [injury] alone is the meaning of the word *gandhana* here.

*Utkurute* means he indicates or suggests. *Avakṣepaṇa* means reviling. "The hawk *udākurute* the quail" means he reviles it. "He *upakurute* Hari" means he serves him. One who acts with violence is a *sāhasika*; [the suffix] *ṭhak* is applied by the rule *ojaḥ sahombhasā vartate* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.4.27). His action is *sāhasikyam*; [the suffix] *ṣyañ* is applied. "He *prakurute* another's wife" means he acts violently toward her. In the sense of refining or improving (*pratiyatna*): "He *upaskurute* the water with fuel."

The word *avodaidhaudhma* is an irregular formation (*nipāta*) [according to Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.29]. It is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*). The genitive case [in *kṛñaḥ*] is used according to Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.53, "after the root *kṛ*, [the sixth case is used] in the sense of improvement. The augment *suṭ* is applied according to Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.139, "after the prefix *upa*, [the augment *suṭ* is added to *kṛ*] in the sense of improvement," and so forth. Its meaning is "to bring about the acquisition of another quality. *Gāthāḥ prakurute*: the meaning is "he narrates them excellently. *Upayogaḥ samīcīno viniyogaḥ*: "proper application" means correct employment. *Śataṃ prakurute*: the meaning is "he employs a hundred [coins] for the sake of dharma. In these cases, what [is the rule]? *Kaṭaṃ karoti* ("He makes a mat"). [This is governed by Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.33.]

*Adheḥ prasahane* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.33). After the root *kṛ* preceded by *adhi*, the same [rules as before] apply in the sense of overcoming (*abhibhava*) and endurance (*kṣamā*). This is because the root *ṣah* is listed with the meanings "to endure" (*marṣaṇe*) and "to overcome" (*abhibhave*). Haradatta maintains that for those who read the rule as "in the sense of overcoming, in the Veda" (*abhibhave chandasi*), the mention of "in the Veda" is merely a general statement. Thus, *tam adhicakre* means "he overcame him" or "he endured him. By this, the reading "if those like you exercise authority (*adhikurvate*) over pleasure" (*bhavadvidhāśced adhikurvate ratim*) is explained.

And Mallinātha has explained it as meaning "one who takes possession of" or "one who accepts" delight (*rati*) or satisfaction (*santoṣa*). And by that very [commentator], he states: "In this case, because 'overpowering' (*prasahana*) is not applicable, the ātmanepada ending does not occur after the root *kṛ* preceded by *adhi*, according to Pāṇini 1.3.33, which prescribes the ātmanepada for *adhi* in the sense of 'overpowering. The *Kāśikā* defines 'overpowering' as 'insult' (*paribhava*). Nevertheless, since there is no intention here to express that the action benefits the agent, [the rule] does not apply."

It has been stated that the *ātmanepada* ending is well-known by the rule "svaritañitaḥ" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.72) when the action is intended for the agent (*kartṛabhiprāya*). Thus, even the usage by Bhāravi in the verse "vādṛśāścedadhikurvate parān" (Kirātārjunīya 1.43) is explained; for its meaning is "they endure" (*kṣamante*). Regarding the rule "veḥ śabdakarmaṇaḥ" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.34): the *ātmanepada* shall occur after the root *kṛ* preceded by the prefix *vi-* if the object (*karman*) is sound (*śabda*). Example: *svarānvikurute*. The meaning is "he utters [them]. Why specify "if the object is sound"? [Counter-example: *cittaṃ vikaroti kāmaḥ* ("Lust agitates the mind").
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.35) *akarmakācca* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.35). After the root *kṛ*, when it is intransitive (*akarmaka*), the suffixes are applied as before [after the prefix *vi*].
"The lowly, who do not help others, act perversely when they have grown powerful."

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.36): *sammānanotsañjanācāryakaraṇajñānabhṛtivigaṇanavyayeṣu niyaḥ*. In these cases to be understood, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) shall apply to the root *nī* ("to lead"). Among these, "lifting up" (*utsañjana*), "knowledge" (*jñāna*), "reckoning" (*vigaṇana*), and "expenditure" (*vyaya*) are the expressed meanings of *nī*; the others are conditions of usage (*prayogopādhi*). For instance: *ācāryaḥ śāstre nayate*. The meaning is that the teacher, having established the tenets of the scripture through refutations of objections, causes them to reach the students.

And those disciples, being led by means of logical arguments, become honored through the fulfillment of their desired objectives. Thus, in this context, the meaning of the root *nī* (to lead) is simply "causing to reach. However, the honoring of the disciple is its result, which serves as a condition for the correct application [of the verb]. In the case of *utsañjana* (lifting up), one says *daṇḍam unnayate*; the meaning is "he raises it up. In the sense of "acting as a teacher" (*ācāryakaraṇa*), one says *māṇavakam upanayate*. Here, the meaning of *nī* is "causing to reach one's own presence according to the prescribed rule. Its result is the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the youth.

Since that [result] does not accrue to the agent, the *ātmanepada* ending—which would otherwise not apply—is prescribed here in the sense of "making someone one's teacher. For by teaching preceded by the initiation (*upanayana*), a certain excellence is produced in the teacher; that very excellence is the basis for the application of the word "teacher" (*ācārya*). As it is said: "Having initiated a student and having taught him the Veda, he is traditionally called an *ācārya*" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.34).

This [statement] is also intended merely to indicate a specific excellence. Thus, the act of making someone a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇa*) is the result, which serves as a condition for the application [of the suffix]. Nor should it be argued that the *ātmanepada* ending is already established because that result accrues to the agent; for that is not the direct fruit of the act of initiation (*upanayana*), but rather of the act of teaching (*adhyāpana*) preceded by initiation. Furthermore, being a condition for the application exists even for that which has become a result through a mediated succession; such is the direction of the argument.

In the phrase "the teachers trained him, who was dear to his teachers," the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) ending does not occur because the act of making someone a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇa*) is not intended to be expressed. For the intention to express [a particular meaning] depends upon one's own will; this is made known by the rule "upajñopakramaṃ tadādyācikhyāsāyām" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.21), which prescribes the suffix based on the speaker's desire. He leads [them] to the truth of knowledge; that is, he ascertains it. *Bhṛti* means wages. He brings laborers near; that is, he causes them to come into his presence by the payment of wages. *Vigaṇana* is the repayment of debts and the like. He collects the tax.

He clears the portion to be given to the king; the meaning is that he pays it. *Vyaya* is expenditure, such as the application [of wealth] for dharma and so forth. He expends a hundred; the meaning is that he applies it for the sake of dharma. What about these cases? He leads the pot.

*Pāṇini Sūtra 1.3.23*: "And when the object resides in the agent, provided it is not a part of the body. When the *ātmanepada* ending is prescribed for the root *ni*, it shall apply only when the object is distinct from a limb of the body. By the word "body," its limbs are indicated by implication (*lakṣaṇā*). This is because, since the agent has attained identity with the body, it is impossible for the body to reside in itself; however, the experience that the limbs reside in it occurs through a specific relationship. For this very reason, there is the well-known declaration: "The hand and so forth are pervaded by the nature of the person. Example: *krodhaṃ vinayate* ("He restrains his anger").

The meaning is that one causes one's own anger to depart. Since the fruit of removing anger—such as the clarity of mind (*cittaprasāda*) and so forth—resides in the agent, this rule is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), even though [the application] is already established by the sūtra *svaritañitaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.72). Therefore, it does not apply here in the case of *gaḍuṃ vinayati* ("he removes the goitre"). How then is one to explain Bhāravi’s verse: *vigaṇayya nayanti pauruṣaṃ vijitakrodharayā jigīṣavaḥ* ("Those desiring victory, having conquered the force of anger, lead their manliness after due deliberation")? It will be explained by the fact that there is no intention (*avivakṣā*) to attribute the result to the agent.

However, some say that the ātmanepada ending is prescribed here because [the root *āp*] functions in the sense of "removal," whereas in this context it functions in the sense of "doing" or "obtaining," since roots have multiple meanings (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.38).

*Vṛtti-sarga-tāyaneṣu kramaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.38). The verb *kram* takes the ātmanepada when it signifies non-obstruction (*apratibandha*), exertion (*utsāha*), or expansion (*sphītatā*). In the sense of *vṛtti* (non-obstruction): *ṛcy asya kramate buddhiḥ*. The meaning is that his intellect is not impeded by the *ṛc* verses. In the sense of *sarga* (exertion): *vyākaraṇādhyayanāya kramate*. The meaning is that he exerts himself for the study of grammar. The fact that the root *sṛj* has the sense of exertion is well-known from such passages as: "by whom [he] was created for the conquest of Indra’s world. In the sense of *tāyana* (expansion): *kramante 'smin śāstrāṇi*. The meaning is that the sciences expand therein. The form *tāyanam* is derived from the root *tāyṛ* (meaning "continuity and protection," Dhatupatha 4.89) with the suffix *lyuṭ*.

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.39) *upaparābhyām*: In the case of the roots *kram* and others listed in the *vṛtti* and other such works, the Ātmanepada ending shall occur only after the prefixes *upa* and *parā*, and not after any other prefix. For example: *upakramate*. Because of the restriction "only after these two," it does not occur here: *saṅkrāmati*. [The rule applies] only in the case of the *vṛtti* and others; thus, it does not occur here: *upakrāmati*, *parākrāmati*. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.40)

*Āṅ* [is used] in the sense of rising (*udgamana*) [Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.40]. The *ātmanepada* ending shall occur after the root *kram*, preceded by *āṅ*, when it signifies rising. Example: *ākramate ādityaḥ* (the sun rises). The meaning is "it rises. It should be stated that this applies when the rising concerns light (*jyotiḥ*) [Vārttika]. Not here: *ākrāmati dhūmo harmyatalāt* (the smoke spreads from the roof of the palace). However, in the Bhāṣya, the reading is *harmyatalam*. In that case, the root *kram* should be understood as signifying pervasion (*vyāpti*) preceded by rising, and not merely rising alone, because otherwise it would result in the root being intransitive (*akarmaka*).

How then is it that [the text says], "The moon traverses the sky step by step"? It is replied: here the root *krami* (to traverse) occurs in the sense of pervasion (*vyāpti*), not in the sense of rising (*udgamana*).
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.41)

*Veḥ pādaviharaṇe* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.41). The ātmanepada suffix shall occur after the root *kram*, preceded by the prefix *vi*, when it signifies "stepping with the feet. For example: *sādhu vikramate vājī* ("the horse strides well"). Although "stepping with the feet" (*pādaviharaṇa*) means "placing the foot down," even though the root *kram* is listed in the Dhātupāṭha with that very meaning, the meaning is explicitly mentioned in the sūtra because roots possess multiple meanings. Therefore, it does not apply here: *vikrāmatyajinasandhiḥ* ("the joint of the leather armor splits open"), which means it bursts asunder into two parts. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.42)

Pāṇini Sūtra 1.3.42: *propābhyāṃ samarthābhyām*. The ātmanepada [suffix] is used after the root *kram* when preceded by *pra* and *upa*, provided these two have the same meaning (*tulyārtha*). In the analysis of the compound *samartha*—meaning "those two whose meaning is equal" (*samastulyo 'rtho yayor iti*)—the single substitute *sa-* is understood as having the same meaning (*tulyārtha*), following the rule for *śakandhvādi* compounds (Pāṇini 6.1.94). These two prefixes share the same meaning in the sense of "commencement" (*ārambha*). Examples: *prakramate*, *upakramate*; the meaning is "he begins. Why "provided they are synonymous"? Consider: *prakrāmati* (meaning "he goes") and *upakrāmati* (meaning "he approaches").

The rule *upaparābhyām* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.39), however, does not apply here. This is because it has been stated that in that [preceding] context, the mention of *vṛtti* and so forth is understood as a governing factor (*anuvṛtti*), whereas here, *vṛtti* and the rest are not intended to be included. Furthermore, regarding *anupasargādvā* (Aṣ�ṭādhyāyī 1.3.43): after the root *kram*, the Ātmanepada may optionally occur when it is not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*). Thus, one says *kramate*. Since the rule *upaparābhyām* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.39) is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), the sūtra concerning *vṛtti* and so forth applies only to cases where there is no prefix. Consequently, this option does not apply in the case of *vṛtti* and the like. Therefore, this is indeed an option (*vibhāṣā*) for a case where [the Ātmanepada] was otherwise not established.
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.44) *apahnave jñaḥ*: The ātmanepada suffix occurs after the root √jñā when it signifies concealment. For example, *śatam apajānīte*, which means "he denies [the debt of] a hundred.
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.45)

Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.45: *akarmakācca* (and from an intransitive [verb]). The ātmanepada suffix shall be used after the root *jñā* when it is intransitive. Example: *sarpiṣo jānīte*. The meaning is: "He proceeds by means of ghee (*sarpiṣā*) as a stratagem. The genitive case in *sarpiṣaḥ* is according to Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.51: *jño’vidarthasya* ("the [genitive] of *jñā* when not having the sense of knowing"). Why was the rule not simply stated as *sakaraṇāt* ("from [a verb] accompanied by an instrument") instead of *akarmakāt* ("from an intransitive [verb]")? Because that would result in over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *svareṇa putraṃ jānāti* ("he recognizes the son by his voice"). Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.46: *na-anubhūti-kṛ-jñā-ghrā-śru-bhiḥ* ("not with *anubhū*, *kṛ*, *jñā*, *ghrā*, or *śru*"). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding rule. The ātmanepada is not used with these verbs even when they are intransitive. Examples: *mātur anubhavati* ("he experiences his mother"), *pituḥ karoti* ("he honors his father"), *putrasya jānāti* ("he recognizes the son"), *puṣpasya jighrati* ("he smells the flower"), *dharmasya śṛṇoti* ("he hears about dharma"). The mention of *jñā* here is for the purpose of excluding the application of the previous rule (*pūrvasūtra*) to this specific instance. *Samprati-bhyām anādhyāne* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.46). With these two prefixes, the *ātmanepada* ending shall be used after the root *jñā* (to know), provided that the sense is not that of "longing remembrance. *Śataṃ sañjānītaḥ*: the meaning is "they look toward" or "they observe" a hundred [pieces]. *Śataṃ pratijānīte*: the meaning is "he accepts" or "he acknowledges" a hundred. Why "provided it is not longing remembrance"? *Mātuḥ sañjānāti*: the meaning is "he remembers with longing" his mother. Here, the genitive case is used for the object according to *adhīgartha* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.52).

[Objection: But surely, since the term *śeṣe* ("in the case of the remainder") is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*) there, then because the object (*karman*) is intended here as a "remainder" (*śeṣatva*), the [suffix] would apply by the preceding rule, Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.45, which states *akarmakācca* ("and after an intransitive verb"). [Response: To this they say: the term *anādhyāne* ("except for thinking/intellection") is separated [from the previous rule]. And that [term] is a supplement (*śeṣa*) to both rules; therefore, in the case of *ādhyāna*, the suffix does not occur even by the preceding rule. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.47)

*Vada* [takes the ātmanepada] in the senses of *bhāsana* (shining), *upasambhāṣā* (addressing), *jñāna* (knowing), *yatna* (effort), *vimati* (disagreement), and *upamantraṇa* (addressing/consulting) [Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.47]. In these senses, the ātmanepada occurs after the root *vad*. Here, *upasambhāṣā* and *upamantraṇa* are meanings expressed by the verbal root itself; the others are contextual conditions of usage. *Bhāsana* means shining. "He speaks in the treatise" (*śāstre vadate*) means he speaks while shining. Since shining is the cause, it serves as a qualifier: for he shines while being praised by his disciples. And thus, because the meaning of the treatise appears more and more clearly, his eloquent speech succeeds well.

The sense is that one would not be able to speak if one's brilliance (*tejas*) were broken. *Upasaṃbhāṣa* means consolation. In the expression "he speaks to the laborers" (*karmakarān upavadate*), the meaning is that he consoles them. In the expression "he speaks regarding knowledge" (*jñāne vadate*), the resultant meaning is that he possesses knowledge concerning what has been stated. *Yatna* means effort or enthusiasm. In the expression "he speaks regarding the field" (*kṣetre vadate*), the meaning is that he manifests enthusiasm directed toward that [field]. Here, they say that effort is the object (*karman*) of the root *vad*, whose meaning consists of manifestation. It is also easy to state that the meaning of *vad* here is "to distinguish."

They dispute in a field of disagreement; the meaning is that by means of disagreement as the cause, they speak in various ways. *Upamantraṇa* means persuasion. He entices the wife of another family; the meaning is that he requests her in order to engage her in what he himself desires. Why "in these [cases]" (*eṣu*)? [To indicate that] whatever one says [elsewhere does not take this form]. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.48)

Regarding the rule *vyaktavācāṃ samuccāraṇe* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.48): when humans and others speak together, the ātmanepada ending shall be used with the root *vad*. For example: *sampravadante brāhmaṇāḥ* or *devāḥ*. Although the root *vad* is taught [in the Dhātupāṭha] as referring only to articulate speech, nevertheless, by the force of the inclusion of the term *vyaktavācām*, only those whose speech is more commonly known to be articulate are understood here. Therefore, it does not apply to the simultaneous speaking of parrots, starlings, and the like. Example: *varatanu sampravadanti kukkuṭāḥ*.

Now, if the word *tanu* ends in a short vowel, there ought to be a *guṇa* substitution by the rule *sambuddhau ca*; if it ends in a long vowel, the suffix *kap*—characterized as applying to *nadī* stems—would apply. True; however, the word *tanu* is employed by poets in the feminine gender. Therefore, Haradatta maintains that once the suffix *ūṅ* has been applied by the rule *ūṅutaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.1.66), this is a *karmadhāraya* compound (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.49).

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.49) *anora-karmakāt*: After the root *vad* preceded by *anu*, when it is intransitive and refers to distinct speech, the Ātmanepada ending shall be used. Example: *anuvadate kaṭhaḥ kalāpasya*. Here, *anu* signifies similarity; therefore, in connection with the sense of equality expressed by "of Kalāpa," the genitive case is used according to the rule for the residual category (*śeṣa-lakṣaṇā*). Why say "when intransitive"? Consider: *pūrvoktam anuvadati* ("he repeats what was said before"). Why say "distinct speech"? Consider: *anuvadati vīṇā* ("the lute echoes"). (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.50)

*Vibhāṣā vipralāpe* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.50). When the root *vad* is used in the sense of "confused speech"—that is, the utterance of distinct sounds—the ātmanepada may optionally occur. For example: *vipravadante* or *vipravadanti* vaidyāḥ ("the physicians dispute/conflict"). The meaning is that they speak simultaneously or with mutual contradiction. Why say "in the case of confused speech"? Consider: *sampravadante* brāhmaṇāḥ ("the Brahmins speak together"). Why say "of distinct sounds"? Consider: *vipravadanti* śakunayaḥ ("the birds chirp"). Why say "utterance"? Consider: *krameṇa vipravadanti* ("they speak one after another"). *Aṣṭādhyāyī* 1.3.51.

*Ava-agraḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.51). The ātmanepada suffix occurs after the root *gṛ* (to swallow) when preceded by the prefix *ava*. Example: *avagirate*. Why "after *ava*"? [Counter-example: *girati*. Regarding this, the *Bhāṣya* states: "There is no usage of the root *gṛ* (in the sense of 'to speak') preceded by *ava*, because such a form is not expressive.

*Samaḥ pratijñāne* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.52). The ātmanepada suffix occurs after the root *gṛ* preceded by *sam* when it signifies a formal promise (*pratijñāna*). Example: *śabdaṃ nityaṃ saṅgirate*. The meaning is: "He promises that sound is eternal. Why "when signifying a promise"? [Counter-example: *saṅgirati grāsam* ("he swallows a morsel").

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.53) *udaśvaraḥ sakarmakāt* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.53). The ātmanepada [suffix] shall occur after the root *car-* when preceded by the prefix *ud-* and when it is transitive (*sakarmaka*). Example: *dharmam uccarate*. The meaning is "he transcends and goes beyond dharma. Why specify "when transitive"? Consider: *bāṣpam uccarati*. The meaning here is "it rises upward" (as vapor). (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.54)

[Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.54] *sam* when joined with an instrument expressed by the third case [takes the ātmanepada]. The ātmanepada occurs after the root *car* preceded by *sam*, when it is joined with a word ending in the third case. Example: *rathena sañcarate* ("he moves about by means of a chariot"). Why "joined with the third case"? [Consider:
"ubhau lokau sañcarasi imaṃ cāmuṃ ca devala" ("O Devala, you move through both worlds, this one and that one"). [Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.55]

And *dāṇ* [takes the ātmanepada] if that third case has the sense of the fourth (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.55). After the root *dāṇ* preceded by *sam*, the ātmanepada occurs when it is joined with a word ending in the third case, provided that third case has the sense of the fourth. Example: *dāsyā saṃyacchate*. The meaning is: "The lustful man gives her [something] for the sake of sexual union. It should be stated that in the usage of the unrefined (*aśiṣṭa*), the third case is used in the sense of the fourth. This is indicated by this very rule. Alternatively, in this sūtra, the word *cet* has the sense of *ca* ("and"), because particles have multiple meanings.

And the meaning is that this [suffix] occurs in the sense of the fourth case (dative). However, it must indeed be stated that this refers to "the usage of the unrefined. In the Bhāṣya, however, even this rule has been rejected. For it says: "This usage is intended with respect to one who, while eating together with a female slave, eats what is given by her and gives to her himself. In that case, the third case ending is applied simply by the rule *sahayukte* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.19). And the Ātmanepada suffix is used when there is a mutual exchange of action (*karmavyatihāra*). The root *dāṇ* should be understood as signifying enjoyment preceded by giving."

Now, when the Sūtra is being commenced, how is the *taṅ* (the Ātmanepada suffix) justified in the case of *samprayacchate*, given that the rule *samaḥ* [prescribes *taṅ*] by virtue of obtaining immediate succession (*ānantarya*) through its ablative ending? On this point, they say: the term *samaḥ* is a genitive of qualification (*viśeṣaṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*); therefore, the preceding rule also applies in cases such as *aśvena samudācarate*. Thus, having cited *dāsyā samprayacchate* as an example, the author of the Bhāṣya provides the counter-example *brāhmaṇībhyaḥ samprayacchati* regarding the usage of the learned; this is the authority for the present explanation. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.56)

The rule *upād-yamaḥ sva-karaṇe* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.56) [prescribes the Ātmanepada for the root *yami* preceded by *upa*] in the sense of "accepting as one's own," as previously stated. One says *bhāryām upayacchate* ("he takes a wife"). Here, what is not intended is the making of something already one's own into a different form; rather, it is only the production of ownership over that which was not previously one's own. The suffix * cvi* was not employed in the rule because it is optional according to the rule *samarthānāṃ prathamādvā* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.1.82). Therefore, in this case, one does not say *svaṃ śāṭakam upayacchati* ("he makes the cloth his own").

In this matter, the author of the *Vṛtti* maintains that [the action] is intended only in the sense of taking the hand in marriage (*pāṇigrahaṇa*). Therefore, he says: "Here, Devadatta does not *upayacchati* Yajñadatta’s wife; the meaning is that he accepts her as a maidservant. However, this contradicts the *Bhāṣya*, because in that work the *ātmanepada* ending is stated to occur merely upon acceptance (*svīkāra*). Accordingly, Bhaṭṭi employed [the verb] in such passages as:
"He took up (*upāyaṃsta*) great missiles and weapons that were victorious";
"The Ten-faced one did not take up (*nopāyaṃsta*) [them]"; "They did not take up (*upāyaṃsata*) the wine," and so forth.

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.57) *jñā-śru-smṛ-dṛśāṃ sanaḥ*: The ātmanepada [ending] shall apply to these roots when they are followed by the suffix *san*. The ātmanepada for the root *jñā* has been prescribed by rules such as (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.44) *apahnave jñaḥ*; for *śru* and *dṛś*, it is also included as an extension (*upasaṅkhyāna*) under (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.29) *samo gamy-ṛcchibhyām*. In those cases, the result is already established by (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.62) *pūrvavat sanaḥ*. This rule [1.3.57] prescribes it for other contexts; however, for the root *smṛ*, it is a prescription where [ātmanepada] was not previously obtained at all.
One desires to know the Dharma, desires to hear it, desires to remember it, and desires to see it.

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.57). *Nānorjñaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.58): The Ātmanepada [suffix] shall not occur after the root *jñā* when preceded by *anu* and followed by the desiderative suffix (*san*). Example: *putram anujijñāsati* (he desires to know his son). Why "after *anu*"? [Consider: *dharmaṃ jijñāsate* (he desires to know the Dharma). This is a prohibition of what was obtained by the preceding rule. According to the maxim, "A rule or a prohibition applies only to that which is immediately contiguous," it follows that the prohibition applies only to the transitive form.

Since the preceding sūtra pertains to transitive verbs (*sakarmaka*), whereas with an intransitive verb (*akarmaka*) the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) indeed occurs by the rule *pūrvavatsanaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.62)—because that rule prescribes [the middle voice] for the simple [denominative base] by the rule *akarmakācca* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.45)—the genitive case is applied by the rule *jño vidarthasya karaṇe* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.51). In the example *auṣadhasyānujijñāsate*, the meaning is: "he desires to be induced by the medicine" (*auṣadhena pravartitum icchati*).
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.59)

*Pratyāṅbhyāṃ śruvaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.59). After the root *śru* followed by these two prefixes (*prati* and *ā*), the Ātmanepada endings shall not occur when it is in the desiderative form (*sannanta*). For example: *pratiśuśrūṣati*, *āśuśrūṣati*. This mention of the prefixes (*upasargagrahaṇa*) is due to their mutual association (*parasparasāhacarya*). Therefore, in the following case, [the Ātmanepada] does not apply: *devadattaṃ śuśrūṣate*. Here, *prati* is a *karmapravacanīya* according to Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.94 (*lakṣaṇetthambhūta...*) and so forth, and is not an *upasarga*. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.60)

Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.60: *śadeḥ śitaḥ*. The ātmanepada suffix shall occur after the root *śad* when it is followed by a suffix marked with the *śiṭ* indicatory letter (*śit*). For example: *śīyate*, *śīyante*. Why "followed by a *śit* suffix"? Consider *śatsyati* and *aśatsyat*; here the parasmaipada suffix occurs according to Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.78: *śeṣātkartari*. Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.61.

Regarding *mriyati* in the *luṅ* and *liṅ* [moods] (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.61): the *ātmanepada* suffix shall occur only after that which is the base form (*prakṛti*) *mriyati* when followed by a *śit* affix or in the *luṅ* and *liṅ* moods, and not after any other. In this context, its status as a base form when preceded by a *śit* affix should be understood through its suitability even before the actual production of the suffix, as in the previous case. However, in the *luṅ* and *liṅ*, it should be understood as such only when the suffix has already been produced. Examples: *mriyate*, *mriyatām*, *amriyata*, *amṛta*, *mṛṣīṣṭa*. What is the purpose of this restriction? [Counter-examples: *mamāra*, *martāsi*, *mariṣyati*, *amariṣyat*. The *ṅit* designation, however, is for the sake of accentuation: *mā hi mṛta*.

In the *luṅ* [aorist] tense, there is the accentuation of the *sārvadhātuka* suffix characterized by the marker *ṅit*, according to Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.186: *tāsyanudāttet*. However, by Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.1.34: *hi ca*, there is a prohibition of this accentuation when the suffix is a *tiṅ* [ending], as per Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.62.

*pūrvavatsanaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.62). That which was the root preceding the *san* [affix] is treated as equal to it; thus, the *ātmanepada* [middle voice] shall apply even after a root ending in *san*. The meaning is that whatever cause was prescribed for the application of *ātmanepada* to the base (*prakṛti*) of *san*, that very same cause brings about the *ātmanepada* even when it is separated by *san*. In this sūtra, the suffix *vati* is added to a word ending in the third case according to *tena tulyam* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.1.115), and not to one ending in the fifth case, because there is no such indicative mark (*lakṣaṇa*).

And just as in the case of "He studies from a Vaiśya equal to a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇena tulyaṃ vaiśyād adhīte*), where it is understood [from the context] "as from a Brāhmaṇa," so too here it is understood "as from the preceding one. In the example, the similarity of action is established by the fact that while the study has a Brāhmaṇa as its source (ablative), the teaching has a Vaiśya as its source; this is achieved through the word *brāhmaṇa* being used figuratively (*lakṣaṇayā*) to denote the study having a Brāhmaṇa as its source. Otherwise, the suffix *-vat* would be inappropriate. As it is said: "When there is equality with that, provided it is an action" (*tena tulyaṃ kriyā cet*, Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.1.115).

And thus, it should be understood that the same applies to the present case as well regarding the necessity of employing the *ātmanepada* (middle voice) ending. Furthermore, the established meaning is that this [application] is mediated by the equality of the cause (*nimitta*). By this, arguments such as "Sound is non-eternal, because it is produced, like a pot" are explained; for there too, the action of coming into being (*bhavana*) is identical. Otherwise, the suffix *-vat* would result in grammatical incorrectness (*asādhutā*). For this very reason, the ancients employ the expression: "It ought to be non-eternal" (*anityo bhavitumarhati*).

Alternatively, let it be that the meaning of the sentence is the similarity between the two cognitions, where the word "sādhya" (to be accomplished) functions through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to denote "cognition. In any case, this is for the sake of establishing a similarity between the verbal root and the physical object, and not a similarity based on the verbal expression itself; such is the direction of the argument. Examples include: *āsisiṣate* (desires to sit), *śiśayiṣate* (desires to lie down), *nivivikṣate* (desires to enter), *bubhukṣate* (desires to eat), and so forth. However, in these cases, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) does not occur: *śiśatsati* (desires to cut) and *mumūrṣati* (desires to die). This is because the specific forms *śad* (to fall/cut) and *mṛ* (to die) are not the original bases (*prakṛti*) of the root *śī* (to lie down); therefore, they do not serve as the cause for the middle voice. For once the suffix *san* is applied, the entire form ending in *san* becomes the base of the root *śī*.

However, in cases such as *śiśayiṣate*, because the *ṅit*-character of the base (*prakṛti*) remains undestroyed, the extension of the cause is indeed possible; thus, there is a disparity [between these two cases]. If it is objected: "In that case, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the form *anucikīrṣati*, since the meaning 'hinting' (*gandhana*) and so forth, as well as the *ñit*-character which is the cause for the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), would result in being extended [to the desiderative]," we say no. This is because, upon considering the rule "after *anu* and *parā*, [the root] *kṛ* [takes the middle voice]" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.79), it is determined that only that which is characterized by the absence of the prefix *anu* constitutes the cause for the middle voice.

Or rather, let there be an extension (*atideśa*) of the effect itself based on its predominance: that from which the *ātmanepada* was observed before the addition of *san*, from those same roots, it occurs even when followed by *san*. Nor does this lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *śiśatsati* and *mumūrṣati*, because in both of the two rules—"after the root *śad* when followed by *śit*" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.60) and "after *mṛ* in the *luṅ* and *liṅ* tenses" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.61)—the word "not" (*na*) is carried over (*anuvartate*), and thus by means of a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*), a prohibition is established for roots ending in *san*. However, in cases such as *jugupsate*, although this extension does not apply...

[Objection: Because the *ātmanepada* ending is not observed prior to the suffix *san*, [the rule] would apply by virtue of the suffix being eternally present (*nityasannantatayā*). [Response: Nevertheless, the *ātmanepada* occurs precisely by the rule "anudāttaṅitaḥ" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.12). For a characteristic (*liṅga*) that has no purpose in its constituent part qualifies the whole by virtue of its capacity (*sāmarthyāt*). Nor does this lead to the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) [of the rule] to forms such as *jugupsati*; for once the qualification is satisfied by the inclusion of the limit of the suffix *san*, there is no evidence for a further qualification beyond that. [Objection: But in that case, there would be an over-extension to forms such as *gopayati* and *tejayati*.

"Between the two types of *saṇic* [causative], which one is to be qualified [by the rule] and which one is not? There is no factor to determine this. To this they reply: "In cases such as 'blame' (*nindā*) where *saṇic* is prescribed, those roots with anudātta indicatory marks (*anudātettaḥ*) and those that are invariably followed by *saṇic* denote precisely that meaning. However, when there is another meaning, they should be read in the *curādi* group without an indicatory mark (*ananubandhaka*). Otherwise, just as the *ṇic* suffix occurs elsewhere than in 'blame,' 'patience,' and so on, the *laṭ* and other verbal suffixes would likewise occur [in those other meanings].
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.63).

Regarding the rule *ām-pratyayavat-kṛño'nuprayogasya* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.63): the term *ām-pratyaya* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the quality (*guṇa*) is not included in the reference (*atad-guṇa-saṃvijñāna*). Thus, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) shall apply after the verb *kṛ* used as a subsequent application (*anuprayoga*), just as it would after the verbal root that is the base of the suffix *ām*. Since this is already established by the fact that the suffix *ām* has the marker *ñ*, the present rule is for the purpose of including cases where the action does not benefit the agent (*akartrabhiprāya*). Example: *īhāñcakre* ("he exerted himself").

[Objection: Since this [sūtra] prescribes an injunction (*vidhi*), would not the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings also apply in cases such as *indāñcakāra*, even when the action is intended for the agent (*kartrabhiprāya*)? [Response: True; however, the word *pūrvavat* ("as before") is understood to carry over [from the previous sūtra]. By its force, a restriction (*niyama*) is also established through a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*): "the ātmanepada occurs only as before, and not even in the case opposite to what was before. Why is *kṛñ* mentioned? [Consider: *īhāmāsa*, *īhāmbabhūva*. Here, by the force of mentioning *kṛñ*, there is no inclusion of the *pratyāhāra* (the technical abbreviation *kṛñ*). And for this very reason, it is known that the *pratyāhāra* is included in the rule prescribing the subsequent use of the verb (*anuprayoga*). (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.64)

Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.64: *propābhyāṃ yujeḥ ayajñapātreṣu*. After the prefixes *pra* and *upa*, the root *yuj* (meaning "to join" or "to employ") takes the ātmanepada endings, provided it does not refer to sacrificial vessels. Examples: *prayuṅkte*, *upayuṅkte*. The root *yujir* is marked with a svarita accent; this rule applies to its meaning when it does not intend benefit for the agent (*akartrabhiprāya*). The root *yuj* belonging to the *divādi* class (meaning "to concentrate," Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.2.151) is not intended here, because its status as having an anudātta udātta (anudāttet) is sufficient to establish the ātmanepada even without this rule, and because the vowel *i* in the word *yujeḥ* in the sūtra is intended to be significant. Furthermore, the application of the *divādi* root to sacrificial vessels is impossible.

It should be stated [in the Kāśikāvṛtti]: "after a prefix beginning or ending with a vowel. This means: after that which is connected with a prefix whose initial or final element is a vowel. By this, all prefixes other than *sam*, *niḥ*, *nir*, *dur*, and *duḥ* are included. Examples: *udyuṅkte*, *niyuṅkte*. Why say "not in sacrificial vessels"? Example: *dvandvaṃ nyañci pātrāṇi prayunakti*. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.65)

*samaḥ kṣṇuvaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.65). After the root *kṣṇu* preceded by *sam*, it is as stated before. This rule is recited separately from *samo gamyṛcchibhyām* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.29) in order to prescribe [the Ātmanepada] even when the root is transitive. Example: *saṃkṣṇute śastram*.
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.66).

*bhujo'navane* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.66). After the root *bhuji*, when it occurs in a sense other than protection (*rakṣaṇa*), [the suffix *ghañ* is applied] as previously stated. Although it could have been stated simply as *bhujo'bhakṣaṇe* ("after *bhuji* when not meaning eating"), the use of the term *anavana* is intended so that it may also apply to other meanings. For the meaning of *bhuji* includes enjoyment such as protecting, consuming, and making one's own (*ātmasāt-karaṇa*). In *odanaṃ bhuṅkte*, the meaning is "he consumes. In the verse: *babhuje pṛthivīpālaḥ pṛthivīmeva kevalām* ("The protector of the earth enjoyed the earth alone"), Mallinātha’s commentary, the *Saṃjīvinī*, reads *dhruvam*. [Another example: *evaṃ marutvāniva bhokṣyate mahīm* (Raghuvaṃśa 3.4).

In this context, the meaning of the root is not "protecting," but rather "enjoying" or "making one's own. By this, the statement "an old man experiences hundreds of sorrows" is explained. Why [is the root] *avan* (to protect) excluded? Because [the rule] says "he enjoys the earth" (*bhūm bhunakti*). Here, only roots beginning with *rudh* are intended to be included, because of the prohibition regarding *avan*. For they recite, beginning with "conjunction and disjunction," and concluding with "they are the causes for the recollection of particulars. Just as the word *dhenu*, which is synonymous with *dogdhrī* (a milch cow), is established in its specific sense by means of its associated attributes (*saṃsargin*).

"Just as when one says, 'Let a cow with its calf be brought,' or 'with its foal,' or 'with its kid,' a cow, a mare, or a goat is brought accordingly—each being brought without fail according to the sequence—and not any other; so it is here as well. Therefore, because the root *bhuja* in the sense of "crookedness" (*kauṭilye*) belonging to the *tudādi* class is not included [in this specific rule], there is no application here in the case of *vibhujati pāṇim*.
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.67)

*ṇeraṇau yatkarma ṇau cetsa kartā'nādhyāne* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.67). From a root ending in *ṇi*, the Ātmanepada suffix shall occur when it is not denoting "reflection" (*adhyāna*). The phrase "if that which was the object in the non-*ṇi* [state] is the agent in the *ṇi* [state]" constitutes the second sentence. Here, "object" (*karma*) means the action (*kriyā*) itself as presented by the base of the *ṇic* affix; the meaning is that if that very same action is expressed by the form ending in *ṇi*. "And that [agent] is the agent" (*sakartā*) is the third sentence. The word "in the non-*ṇi*" (*aṇau*) and so forth is carried over from the previous rule. Here, "object" (*karma*) refers to the grammatical factor (*kāraka*), because we rely on the governing context of technical terminology (*śabdādhikāra*).

The meaning is that if the *kāraka* which is the object (*karman*) with respect to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) before the causative suffix (*ṇic*) becomes the agent (*kartṛ*) when the suffix *ṇic* is applied, then [the verb takes the ātmanepada ending]. Although the ātmanepada is already established by the rule "ṇicaśca" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.74), this sūtra is intended for cases where the result does not benefit the agent (*akartrabhiprāya*). Furthermore, it is intended to override the optionality provided by the rule "vibhāṣopapadena pratīyamāne" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.77) even when the result benefits the agent, and to override the parasmaipada prescribed by the rule "aṇāvakarmakāt" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.88).

Nor should it be argued that this [rule]—which has already fulfilled its purpose regarding cases where the result does not accrue to the agent (*akartrabhiprāya*)—would be superseded by the subsequent *vikalpa* (option) and *parasmaipada* (active voice) rules; for one must resort to the principle of "prior precedence" (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). And the authority for this is the example cited in the Bhāṣya: *darśayate rājā*. This is the general direction. As for the examples, they consist of verbs whose state (*bhāva*) resides in the agent and those whose action (*kriyā*) resides in the agent; for it will be stated later that in those cases there is no application of the *karmavadbhāva* (passive-like treatment). However, the *ātmanepada* ending occurs by the very rule under discussion (*prakṛtasūtra*).

For instance, the root *dṛś* (to see) denotes the attainment of the state of being an object (*viṣayatva*) as a subordinate factor, and the attainment of the state of being an object as the point of departure (*apādāna*), because it is a rule that transitive roots do not denote [the agent] by means of a verbal suffix. In that context, the agent is the substratum of the operation denoted by the verbal root, while the object is that which possesses a result residing in a locus different from the operation that constitutes the meaning of the root. Thus, the usage "devotees see Bhava" (*paśyanti bhavaṃ bhaktāḥ*) means "they make Bhava an object of visual cognition.

However, when the aspect of instigation is abandoned due to a desire to express an excellence of facility, then the usage "Bhava sees" (*paśyati bhavaḥ*) occurs, meaning "he becomes an object. And it has been said:
"When the causal operation has ceased, the object remains established through its own constituent actions;
as its status as an object ceases, it persists in its own status as an agent."

Then, in the sense that "they impel one who is seeing," there is the usage *darśayanti bhavaṃ bhaktāḥ* ("the devotees cause Bhava to be seen") with the causative suffix (*ṇic*). Its meaning is "they see. And it has been said:

"The causative suffix (*ṇic*) is prescribed after a verbal root when its original meaning [is retained] and the prompting [of an agent] has ceased. Then again, when the causative meaning is not intended to be expressed for the sake of highlighting the ease of the action, as in *darśayate bhavaḥ*, the meaning is "Bhava becomes the object of perception. Thus, here, because the roots *paśyati* and *darśayati* have the same meaning and because the state [of being seen] resides in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvakatva*), the rule of "being like the object" (*karmavadbhāva*) does not apply; consequently, by the present sūtra, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is employed.

For here, the very same meaning that was expressed by the root *dṛś* (to see) in its primitive form (*ṇic*-prakṛti) in the second stage is likewise present in the fourth stage; thus, there is identity of action (*sāmānakriyatvam*). That which was the object (*karman*) in the first stage under the non-causative (*aṇau*) is precisely the agent (*kartṛ*) [in the subsequent stages]. Similarly, "the elephant makes itself mount" (*ārohayate hastī*) is also an example. [The analysis is as follows: "The elephant-keepers mount the elephant"—this means they cause it to descend [to a lower state]. "The elephant mounts"—this means it descends. Then, from the causative (*ṇic*) where the instigation has ceased, we have "they cause to mount," which means "they mount."

Then, when the meaning of *ṇi* (causative) is abandoned, the meaning of "ārohayate" is "he becomes subordinate. Here too, as before, because the meanings of the first and third [voices] and the second and fourth are identical, the fourth stage (*kakṣā*) serves as the illustration. This is the position of the "cessation of the instigation" (*nivṛttapreṣaṇapakṣa*). And it has been said: "In the simple root *ruh*, both the causing of subordination (*nyagbhāvana*) and the becoming subordinate (*nyagbhavana*) are understood; likewise, in the causative (*ṇyanta*), both the causing of subordination and the becoming subordinate are understood."

He describes the fifth state as follows: "The causative suffix (ṇic) is said to be applied in its original sense to a root from which the act of impelling has ceased, when that same object of the action becomes the agent."

In this context, since the two specific denoters—the root and the causative suffix (*ṇic*)—each have two parts of their denotation, these are counted as four due to the difference in the denoters. Thus, there are four stages in the previously mentioned first and third levels; however, in the fourth level, there is a fifth stage, as in the example "the elephant-keepers [drive] the elephant. As before, this is the first level. Then, for the sake of highlighting ease of performance, the *ṇic* suffix is applied by superimposing the instigation (*preṣaṇa*) onto the object itself.

In the cases of *darśayati bhavaḥ* ("the lord causes [them] to see") and *ārohayati hastī* ("the elephant causes [them] to mount"), the meaning is that he impels the one who sees and the one who mounts. Consequently, when both impelments (preṣaṇa)—those conveyed by the two roots from which the causative suffix (*ṇic*) was originally derived and those conveyed by the two causative suffixes themselves—are simultaneously abandoned, the examples are *darśayate* and *ārohayate*. The meanings are, as before, "he becomes the object" (*viṣayībhavati*) and "he becomes subordinate" (*nyagbhavati*).

Regarding this view of superimposed instigation (*adhyāropita-preṣaṇapakṣa*), the second sentence—intended to signify "identity of action" (*samānakriyatva*)—is provided to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the second stage of the process, such as in the cases "the world shows [him]" (*darśayati bhavaḥ*) and "the elephant makes [him] mount" (*ārohayati hastī*). Because of the addition of instigation (*preṣaṇādhikya*) there, no over-extension occurs. Regarding the view of ceased instigation (*nivṛttapreṣaṇapakṣa*), the third sentence takes the form "they show the world [to him]" (*darśayanti bhavam*) and "they make the elephant mount [him]" (*ārohayanti hastinam*).

In this case, however, since the bhava (the act of being) and the elephant are merely objects (*karman*) of the root *aṇ* and not its agents (*kartṛ*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*). Regarding this, the ancients maintain that the sentence "that which is the object of the root *aṇ*" is intended to exclude other objects. For instance, because of the constant connection between the relative pronoun *yat* and the demonstrative *tat*, the word *tat* is implied here by the word *yat*. Furthermore, since no other property is specified, it is the status of being an object (*karmatva*)—which is heard as the subject to be designated—that is prescribed.

And since that [rule] is being enjoined, by virtue of its capacity and because of the proximity of the word *ṇeḥ*, it is enjoined only in the state of the root having the causative suffix (*ṇic*). Indeed, its prescription in the non-causative (*aṇ*) state is not possible; for that is already established by the very force of the reference (*anuvāda*) in the words "that which is the object in the non-causative" (*aṇau yatkarma*). Thus, from the mere statement "that which is the object in the non-causative," the resulting meaning is: "if that same object remains the object in the causative. And by this, the exclusion of another object is effected. It does not, however, establish that what was an object in the non-causative must necessarily be an object in the causative.

Because its status as the object is established by the subsequent sentence, "That is the karma," and because it is impossible for a single entity to simultaneously possess both the status of object and agent in a single action; therefore, [the rule] states:
"When [an object] is already obtained through a reference and a subsequent restatement, its re-mention in a summary is for the purpose of excluding other objects, by means of a syntactical split."

Then they explained that *ṇau cet* is a separate sentence; its meaning is: "if that very thing which is to be conveyed by the root in the *aṇ* [causative] state is also to be conveyed by the root in the *ṇic* [causative] state. Here, this must be considered: although an interpretation intended to exclude other objects (*karmāntara*) can indeed be made, its utility is difficult to establish. If it is argued that the purpose is to exclude cases such as *ārohayamāṇo hastī* ("the elephant being mounted") and *sthalamārohayati manuṣyam* ("he causes the man to mount the dry land"), we say no, because in those instances there is an absence of identity of action (*samānakriyatva*).

It is established in both the *Vṛtti* and the *Padamañjarī* that the rule "if [the action] is in the causative (*ṇau*)" is intended for the purpose of ensuring identity between the actions expressed. However, such identity does not exist here. If it is argued: "Let this be a flaw according to the view of the *Vṛtti* and others; yet in the case of the *Bhāṣya* and Kaiyaṭa, since identity of action is not explicitly stated, the rule—which serves the purpose of excluding other objects (*karma*)—is indeed meaningful," we say no. For even in the view of the *Bhāṣya*, identity of action must be explained. Furthermore, even if it is not explicitly stated there, it is accepted as being valid because it has not been rejected.

Otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the second stage where the prompting (*preṣaṇa*) is superimposed; furthermore, it is possible to explain the word *karman* in both the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika as referring specifically to action (*kriyā*). Even granting this, we say: let the identity of action (*samānakriyatva*) not hold according to the Bhāṣya view, yet Kaiyaṭa, while explaining the example "the king causes his servants to see [himself]" (*darśayate bhṛtyān rājā*), has made it clear that the action in the *ṇic*-form is excluded if it is different from the agent or object in the *aṇic*-form.

And likewise, although "manuṣyān" is the agent under the causative (*aṇi*) and the object under the causative of the root *druh* (meaning "to injure"), the ātmanepada ending would still be unavoidable; for here, the humans and the ground—which were respectively the agent and the object under the non-causative (*aṇi*)—are precisely the object, and there is no other object besides them. Furthermore, the requirement that "the agent [of the non-causative] must be present" is also absent here, because the elephant alone is the agent.

It might be argued: "In the case of *ārohayamāṇaḥ*, the very elephant who was the object (*karman*) of the non-causal (*aṇ*) verb becomes the agent (*kartṛ*); and that same elephant is also the agent in the case of *sthalam ārohayati*. This too is not correct, because the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is avoided precisely by the force of proximity (*pratyāsatti*). For when it is stated that "the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs after a causative (*ṇi*) suffix if that which was the object in the non-causal form is the agent," this is understood through proximity to mean: "If that which was the object in the base form (*prakṛti*) of the specific causative suffix by which the middle voice is intended to be prescribed is the agent."

In this context, however, wherever this condition (*upādhi*) has been applied, there the *ātmanepada* ending is indeed used—as in "ārohayamāṇaḥ. But where it has not been applied, as in "sthalam ārohayati," this condition does not exist, so that there would be no over-extension (*ativyāpti*). As for what Haradatta stated—"lest [the rule] apply in the case of 'hastī hastipakān ārohayati'"—[that objection is addressed by the fact that the condition is not met].

In this regard, the following must be stated: Is this example in the second stage [of the analysis] under the view that the instigation (*preṣaṇa*) is superimposed (*adhyāropita*), or under the view that the instigation has ceased (*nivṛttapreṣaṇa*)? It is not the first, because there is an absence of "identity of action" (*samānakriyatva*) due to the difference between the operations expressed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*). Nor is it the second, because the first two stages lack the non-causative form (*aṇyantatva*), and in the third stage, the elephant cannot logically be the agent, nor is it possible for the mahouts to be the object. Therefore, the fourth stage remains as the only possibility.

In that case as well, because the meaning does not terminate [with the agent], the connection with the object (*karman*) is indeed clear. It might be argued: the example "the king causes his servants to see himself" (*darśayate bhṛtyān rājā*) is accepted in the Bhāṣya; to justify this, Kaiyaṭa states that what is intended is the exclusion of an object other than those which are the agent and the object in the *aṇ* (causative) stage. His intention is as follows: in the rule "that which is the object in the *aṇ*" (*aṇau yatkarma*), the term "agent" (*kartari*), which has been carried over from the rule "when the agent is the object" (*kartari karma*, Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.14), is transformed into the nominative case.

The form *yaśca yacca yat* is a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) according to the rule *napuṃsakamanapuṃsakena* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.69). By this, there is no fault even when both the object and the agent [of the base verb] become the object in the causative (*ṇic*). And thus, the usage by Māgha, "The female elephant causes the rider to mount" (*kareṇurārohayate niṣādinam*), is also justified.

This being the case, since both positions—the one where the instigation has ceased (*nivṛttapreṣaṇa*) and the one where it is superimposed (*adhyāropitapreṣaṇa*)—are intransitive at the final stage, all the works of the *Bhāṣya*, Kaiyaṭa, and others would be entirely inconsistent. Why then direct this censure specifically at Haradatta? For the difference is merely this: according to the view of the *Bhāṣya*, because of the interpretation "those which are the agent or object in the *aṇ* [root]," this is an example; however, according to the views of the *Vṛttikāra*, Haradatta, and others, it is a counter-example, because of the interpretation "that which is the object in the *aṇ* [root]" alone.

To this it is replied: First of all, the lack of logical concomitance (*ananvaya*) is unavoidable. For when a sublation (*bādha*) is firm, the principle applies: "Why should anything else not also be sublated on the basis of similarity to another? Just as in the sentence "A hamlet on the deep river," even after the primary cognition of the non-difference between the referents of the words "deep" and "river" has occurred, the word "deep" retains its significance by taking into account that initial cognition during the subsequent indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the bank; so too here, in the view that the causal impulsion (*preṣaṇa*) is superimposed, once the object is construed with the second-level [causal] suffix, the causal suffix (*ṇic*) is dropped even when the object itself is abandoned.

And the word *karman* (object) may be considered meaningful in some way by taking its primary denotation; for it is accepted that "indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is a relation with that which is to be made known by [the word] itself. It should be understood that this is how Kaiyaṭa’s statement—"the recourse to indication of excellence through explanatory passages (*arthavāda*s)"—is possible. However, the conclusion—that the sentence-meaning consists in the exclusion of the object—is certainly not intended by the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika, because there is no purpose [for it] according to the reasoning stated above. The text, moreover, remains perfectly sound if the word *karman* is taken to mean "action" (*kriyā*).

However, in the examples [given], such as *bhṛtyān* (servants) and so forth, one should understand that the intention is that the rule becomes established when there is no intention to express those [servants] and only the mere operation upon the object (*karmavyāpāra*) is intended to be expressed. This is because, on the occasion of explaining the passage from the *Bhāṣya* and the *Vṛtti*, "The forest thicket itself causes him to remember," both Kaiyaṭa and Haradatta have taken recourse to the intention to express the object (*enam*) as the *karman*. As for the fact that Kaiyaṭa, in the remainder of the *sūtra*, previously demonstrated that there is an intention to express *enam*, that is merely superficial; such is the direction [of the argument]. Therefore:
"Because of the abandonment of servants and others, because of the difference in words, and because of their inclusion..."
"And in the ritual formula, because it proceeds for that purpose, everything is radiant."

It might be argued as follows: since all transitive verbs denote two parts [the action and its result], the examples cited here from the root-text are already established by the extension (*atideśa*) of the *karmavat* rule to the case of the object-agent (*karmakartṛ*). Nor should it be said that under the view of "superimposed instigation" (*adhyāropita-preṣaṇapakṣa*), the *karmavat* rule would not apply in cases such as *ārohayate hastī* ("the elephant causes itself to be mounted")—because there is no status as an object (*karmatva*)—since there is no status as an object within the same verbal root (*samānadhātu*), as in the cases of *pacaty odanaṃ devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta cooks the rice") and *rādhyaty odanaḥ svayam eva* ("the rice ripens by itself").

Since all illustrative examples are subsumed by the very process of the withdrawal of the instigation (*nivṛttapreṣaṇaprakriyā*), there is no deficiency even in abandoning the position that the instigation is superimposed (*adhyāropitapreṣaṇapakṣa*). Nor should it be argued that because the root *dṛś* (to see) has its state residing in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvaka*) and the root *ruh* (to grow) has its action residing in the agent (*kartṛsthakriya*), the status of being "like the object" (*karmavadbhāva*) would not apply; for it is difficult to establish any distinction between these and roots such as *pac* (to cook) or *bhid* (to split). If the states of softening and becoming two-fold were also considered to reside in the agent, the extended application of the rule for "being like the object" would result in having no scope at all.

In that regard, although the aspect of the operation (*vyāpārāṃśa*) resides in the agent, the fruit—consisting of the form of softening (*viklitti*) or being split apart (*dvidhābhavana*)—resides in the object. If it is argued that this is equivalent for *dṛśi* (to see) and *ruh* (to grow), since their states of being an object (*viṣayatva*) and subordination (*anyagbhāva*) likewise reside in the object, and therefore the reason for this difference here must be stated, Bhartṛhari says on this point: "Where there is a perception of a specific [change], the action is established as residing there;
however, for others, the determination of where the action resides is fashioned by words alone."

The meaning of this is as follows: where a specific change resulting from an action is observed—as in the case of cooked rice or, for example, split wood—there the action resides. Therefore, the status of being treated like an object (*karmavadbhāva*) is established in such cases by the expressions "the rice is cooked" (*pacyate odanaḥ*) and "the wood is split" (*chidyate kāṣṭham*). According to the opinion of others, however, the determination of the action belongs to other verbal roots (*dhātu*) themselves; since the operation of the agent is understood primarily through the word itself, the meaning is that [the action] resides in the agent (*kartṛstha*).

It should be understood that the general rule for determination is that in some cases the object (*karman*) is intended, while in others the operation (*vyāpāra*) is intended; this is the restrictive principle. In the present case, since no distinction is perceived between the act of seeing and the act of descending with respect to the object, the state (*bhāva*) and the action (*kriyā*) here reside solely in the agent (*kartṛstha*). This is also due to the requirement of the intended purpose (*uddeśa*); for the intention is "May I see," and not "May this object come into being"; likewise, the intention is "May I go upward," and not "May the elephant descend."

Furthermore, the specific activity denoted by the root *ruh* is precisely the act of moving upward, and not merely the state of being bent downward. This is because the term *ārohati* ("he ascends") is not used even when one bends down a tree branch with both hands while standing on the ground. For this very reason, the *Bhāṣya* on Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.1.56—"yaddhituparaṃ chandasi"—states: "The root *ruh* has the sense of motion (*gatyartha*). And for this same reason, that which is the agent (*kartṛ*) in the non-causative form becomes the object (*karman*) in the causative form.

"In the case of *pac* (to cook) and *chid* (to cut), however, a distinction consisting of softening and bifurcation is observed in the object (*karman*), and the operation of the causal factors (*kāraka*) is directed toward that very [result]; thus, there is a great disparity [between these roots and others]. And so, those who demonstrate the *karmavadbhāva* (the treatment as an object) in the expression ‘*āruhyate hastī*’ (the elephant is mounted) should be disregarded, as they contradict the logic of the Bhāṣya. Thus says Kaiyaṭa. By this [it is implied]: "I bow forever to that Guru, by whose grace the meaning of the scriptures is understood, remembered, and faithfully accepted."

Thus the application [of the rule] has been explained. Nor should it be argued that [the rule] would not apply because "it is not done in this way. For even though this objection might arise for those who maintain that the root *kṛ* signifies effort (*yatna*), we—accepting, in accordance with the Bhāṣya on the *bhūvādi* sūtra, that *kṛ* signifies the manifestation of what was previously non-existent (*abhūtaprādurbhāva*)—maintain full consistency. And thus, since the status of being like the object (*karmavadbhāva*) does not apply to actions and states residing in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvakriyeṣu*), this sūtra is established in the Bhāṣya as being for the purpose of an injunction (*vidhyartha*).

However, in cases such as *lāvayate sveyameva* ("this very one causes herself to be cut"), it should be understood that under the view of the extension of the operation (*kāryātideśa*), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is applied by the rule *karmavatkarmaṇā* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.1.87) because it is subsequent [to the rule *ṇeraṇau...*]. Under the view of the extension of the rule (*śāstrātideśa*), however, it is by the rule *ṇeraṇau* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.67), because it is subsequent to the rule *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.13).

If the author of the Bhāṣya intended by the phrase "other than those [verbs] whose agent and object are minute (aṇau)" the exclusion of objects distinct from those [two], then, since such verbs would fall under the examples of that sūtra among transitive verbs (*sakarmaka*), even those whose action resides in the object (*karmasthakriyā*) would become examples. For in that case, an extension (*atideśa*) would not be easily available, because it will be stated later: "Like the object, for those that are intransitive. Furthermore, there would be an inconsistency with the passages in the Bhāṣya and Vārttika, such as "for the purpose of restricting the application of *yak* and *ciṇ*, and for the purpose of prohibiting them," which are intended to serve as restrictive rules (*niyamārtha*). This is the general direction of the argument.

Therefore, the threefold meaning of the sentence as stated by us alone is approved by the three sages (Pāṇini, Kātyāyana, and Patañjali). A great internal contradiction among all the authors of treatises—such as Jayāditya, the author of the Nyāsa, Haradatta, Kaiyaṭa, and others—must be extracted here by the discerning. Our own statement, however, should be reflected upon after casting aside envy; enough with further prolixity. As for the usage employed by Māgha, namely, "kareṇurārohayate niṣādinam," that is established by the rule *ṇicaśca*. By this [same principle], the following is explained:
"sa santataṃ darśayate gatasmayaḥ | kṛtādhipatyāmiva sādhu bandhutām" (Ki. 1.10).

Thus it has been explained. *Bandhutā* (kinship) sees him; [the agent] causes that [bandhutā] to see [him]. Alternatively, the meaning is that [the agent] causes kinship—which has attained sovereignty over the worlds—to see the animals, or causes that [kinship] to see [them]. In the first case, *bandhutā* is the agent (*kartṛ*) in the non-causative (*aṇau*); in the second, however, it is the object (*karman*) in the non-causative. In both cases, its status as the object in the causative (*ṇau*) is established without dispute; this is the general direction [of the analysis]. Why is the word *ṇeḥ* (in the causative) used? [It is so that the rule does not apply] to *ārohati* (he ascends), which results from the removal of the prompting (*nivṛttapreṣaṇāt*). Nor should it be argued that because the phrase *ṇau cet* (if [the action occurs] in the causative) is heard in the supplementary portion of the sūtra, the rule will apply only to the causative.

Because the term *aṇ* is also heard [in the rule], and furthermore, the word *ṇeḥ* must necessarily be stated for the sake of what follows; therefore, it is stated here for the sake of clarity and to include the causative *ṇic* (*hetumaṇṇic*). This is because that [causative] alone is possible with the roots *bhī* and *smi*. By this, the form *gaṇayate gaṇaḥ svayameva* ("the group counts itself") is established. For the root *gaṇ* functions in the sense of "dividing and placing [things] in parts. And thus, since this root has its state of being (*bhāva*) residing in the object (*karmasthabhāvaka*), when the causative *ṇic* is applied after the removal of the element of instigation (*nivṛttapreṣaṇa*), the desired middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs upon the further abandonment of the element of instigation.

Because of the proximity of the term *ṇer* (from Pāṇini 1.3.67) to the causal *ṇic*, it is understood that in the rule *ṇau* (Pāṇini 1.3.68) as well, that very same [causal suffix] is intended; thus, the rule is established even from a causative (*hetumaṇṇic*) where the agent is the object of the root belonging to the *curādi* class. As for the fact that the commentator (*vṛttikṛt*) cites only the form *gaṇayati* throughout all four stages [of the derivation], there—since the act of counting, which is the cause of the number, consists of a specific cognition and thus resides in the agent—it is assumed that the action expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*) does not reside in the object; consequently, the rule for "object-like behavior" (*karmavadbhāva*) does not apply, and the Parasmaipada ending is justified in the second stage.

In the fourth stage, however, the *parasmaipada* (active voice) is indeed incorrect. This is because even in the rule *ṇeraṇau* (Pāṇini 1.3.67), it is logical that only the causative *ṇic* denoting "instigation" (*hetumaṇic*)—as specified by the rule *aṇāvakarmakāt* (Pāṇini 1.3.88)—is intended to be included. Furthermore, this is precisely how the matter stands in the *Bhāṣya*. However, if the intent is to establish [the action] as being divided into parts, then the *ātmanepada* (middle voice) applies even in the second stage; this is the distinction, since the application of the *karmavat-bhāva* (treatment like an object) is unavoidable here. As for the suffixes *yak* and *ciṇ*, they do not occur due to prohibitions such as *ṇiśranthi* (Kāśikā Vārttika); such is the general direction.

What is the purpose of the condition "if there is *ṇic*"? It is so that [the rule] does not apply in the third alternative, namely *nivṛttapreṣaṇāṇṇau* (when the causative suffix *ṇic* has been elided), as in the example "the elephant-keepers cause [the elephants] to mount" (*ārohayanti hastipakāḥ*). For if the mention of "*ṇau*" were absent, then because it is explicitly stated [in the sūtra], the status of object (*karmatva*) and agent (*kartṛtva*) would be obtained only when there is no *ṇic*. Nor should it be argued that the dual nature of a single entity is contradicted; for there is no dispute that what was an object in the first state becomes an agent in the second state. Why is the condition "not in the sense of remembering" (*anādhyāne*) included? [Consider: "The cuckoo remembers the thicket of the forest" (*smarati vanagulmaṃ kokilaḥ*).

Then, in the fourth stage, the forest thicket causes her to remember; the meaning is that it becomes the object of memory preceded by longing (*utkaṇṭhā*). The root *smṛ* is used in the sense of "meditative recollection" (*ādhyāna*), belonging to the *bhvādi* class (Dhātupāṭha 809), and is *ghaṭādi*. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.68).

Regarding *bhī* and *smi* when fear arises from a cause (*hetubhaya*) [Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.68]: after these two roots when followed by the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the Ātmanepada ending shall occur provided that the fear or astonishment originates specifically from the agent who causes it. In this sūtra, the mention of *bhaya* (fear) is also indicative of *vismaya* (astonishment). *muṇḍo bhīṣayate* ("The shaven-headed man terrifies"). Here, the augment *ṣuk* is applied by the rule *bhiyo hetubhaye ṣuk* [Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.3.40]. In the alternative view where the vowel substitution is optional according to *vibheterhetubhaye* [Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.56], one says *bhāpayate*; here *ṣuṅ* is not applied because of the elision of the long vowel *ī* in the formulation of that rule. *jaṭilo vismāpayate* ("The matted-haired ascetic astonishes").

The substitution of *ā* [for the vowel of the root] occurs by the rule *nityaṃ smayateḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.57). The augment *puK* is added by the rule *arttihrī* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.3.36). What is the purpose of the condition "out of fear" (*hetubhaye*)? [Consider: *kuñcikayā bāyayati* ("He causes [him] to shave with a key") and *rūpeṇa vismāyayati* ("He causes [him] to wonder at the beauty"). Here, the fear and the wonder arise from the instrument (*karaṇa*), not from the cause (*hetu*). Even though the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is prescribed when there is an operation of a cause—since the meaning is "if he is an instigator" (*prayojaka*)—this is due to the force of including the qualification [in the rule]. For this very reason, in the example *mauṇḍyena bāpayati* ("He causes [him] to shave by means of baldness"), the property called 'baldness' is not intended to be expressed as distinct [from the person]; however, in the examples [cited above], identity (*tādātmya*) is intended, so the fear arises precisely from the cause. By this [explanation]—

This has been explained [in the commentary] as: "astonishing the banner of Manu’s lineage with human speech" (Rao 2.33). For here, there is no cause for astonishment from the lion itself, but rather from the instrument of "human speech. Therefore, in this context, the substitution of *ā* (as in *smāpayan*) according to Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.57, "nityaṃ smayateḥ," does not apply. This is because, in the rule prescribing that [substitution], the phrase "bibheterhetubhaye" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.56) follows, and the mention of "fear" (*bhaya*) is interpreted as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for "astonishment" (*smaya*). However, the reading *vismāpayan*, which includes the augment *puK*, is an error.

Alternatively, it is the voice that causes wonder; however, the lion employs the voice which is causing wonder, thus [the sentence] means "he causes [others] to wonder. [The suffix] ṇic is added after the root *vi-smi* ending in *vyanta*. As for the word "vācā," it should be understood that the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is used for the agent of the prompted action (*prayojya*), and not for the instrument (*karaṇa*).
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.52).

Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.69: *gṛdhivañcyoḥ pralambhane*. The ātmanepada suffix occurs after these two roots, *gṛdh* and *vañc*, when they are followed by the causative marker (*ṇic*) and mean "deceiving. Examples: *māṇavakaṃ gardhayate* or *vañcayate* ("he deceives the boy"). Why "in the sense of deceiving"? [Consider: *śvānaṃ gardhayati* ("he makes the dog greedy"); the meaning here is that he arouses a desire in him. *ahiṃ vañcayati* ("he avoids the snake"); the meaning here is that he shuns it. Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.70: [Continuation]. The ātmanepada suffix occurs after the root *ci* when preceded by *pari* and used in the sense of "piling up" (*upacaye*). Example: *puṣpāṇi paricinute* ("she gathers flowers"). Why "in the sense of piling up"? [Consider: *devadattaḥ puṣpāṇi paricinoti* ("Devadatta gathers flowers [for his own use]"); the meaning here is that he collects them. Why "after *pari*"? [Consider: *puṣpāṇi cinoti* ("he gathers flowers [from a tree]"). Why "the root *ci*"? [Consider: *puṣpāṇi pariṣiñcati* ("he sprinkles flowers"). Why "when preceded by *pari*"? Here, because the action is performed for her own sake, the ātmanepada is already established by rule 1.3.72; this specific rule is intended to prevent its application in other senses. Here, because the action is performed for her own sake, the ātmanepada is already established by rule 1.3.72; this specific rule is intended to prevent its application in other senses. Why "the root *ci*"? [Consider: *puṣpāṇi parivapati* ("he scatters flowers"). Why "in the sense of piling up"? [Consider: *puṣpāṇi paricinoti* ("he arranges flowers [on an altar]"). Here, because the action is performed for her own sake, the ātmanepada is already established by rule 1.3.72; this specific rule is intended to prevent its application in other senses. Why "preceded by *pari*"? [Consider: *puṣpāṇi cinute* ("she gathers flowers [into a basket]"). Here, because the action is performed for her own sake, the ātmanepada is already established by rule 1.3.72; this specific rule is intended to prevent its application in other senses. Why "the root *ci*"? [Consider: *puṣpāṇi parivapati* ("he scatters flowers"). Why "in the sense of piling up"? [Consider: *puṣpāṇi paricinoti* ("he arranges flowers [on an altar
