Nor does this mean that the example *sakhī* for the sūtra *yasyeti ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.148)—where the vowel *i* is replaced by *ī*—is untenable; for when the suffix *ṅīṣ* is added to the word *sakhi* by the rule *sakhyāścaśvītibhāṣāyām* (Kātyāyana Vārttika), there is no difference whether the elision (*lopa*) or the lengthening of a homogeneous vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*) occurs.

As for what is stated in the Bhāṣya and the Vṛtti regarding that point—that if elision (*lopa*) were not applied, then in the case of *atisakher āgacchati*, because the homogeneous long vowel (*savarṇadīrgha*) would behave like the final element with respect to the preceding part, the designation *ghisamjñā* would be prohibited by the rule *na sakhī*—this is clearly explained in the Kaiyaṭa and other commentaries as being based on an absolute prohibition (*prasajyapratiṣedha*). For this very reason, since a relative exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is established here only superficially; otherwise, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), an ungrammatical compound (*asamarthasamāsa*), and the undesirable consequence of the forms *susakheḥ* and so forth failing to be established.

If it is argued that the result [of the elision] is difficult to obtain because of the word *tasmāt*, it is replied here: in forms such as *sakhī*, *sakhyau*, and *sakhyaḥ*, the elision of the *i* must be desired so that the substitution of *anaṅ* and the designation *ṇit* do not occur. Nor is the fault unavoidable even in the final system (*siddhānta*), because when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, there is no inclusion of that which is qualified by gender, since a gender-qualified form is not included when a case-ending (*vibhakti*) follows. By this, Haradatta—who says that the elision of the *i* has its illustration only in the context of secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) and not when *ī* follows—is refuted.
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.8)

"Patih only in a compound" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.8). The word *pati* shall be designated as *ghisamjñaka* only when it occurs in a compound. Examples: *bhūpataye*. It does not apply here: *patyā*, *patye*. The particle *eva* is used by Dṛḍhamuṣṭi to prevent a contrary restriction.

It might be argued: let it simply be "śeṣo 'ghy-asakhi-pati" (P. 6.3.20). For the compound as a whole, the desired form is established by the method previously stated. Nor does it follow that the word *sakhi* would also be connected in the subsequent rule (*patiḥ samāsa eva*, P. 1.4.8), because there is no subverting evidence; for the desired forms are established even by that much alone. As for the second [form], although it is correct, it is not required because it is not recited in the Veda. Nor should it be said that, in this case, the mention of "joined with the genitive" (*ṣaṣṭhīyukta*) in the subsequent rule would be redundant, for we accept that consequence.

In this very same way, the mention of *śrī* in the rule *śrīgrāmaṇyocchandasi* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.1.56), as well as rules such as *nityaṃ mantra* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.210), have been rejected [as unnecessary]. Similarly, in the rule *saṃbuddhau śākalyasya* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.1.16), the inclusion of the term *anārṣa* (non-Vedic) is likewise [unnecessary]. True. Just as in the case of *sakhigṛhe*, where there is no fixed rule regarding the prior placement of the compound members (*pūrvanipātāniyama*), so it might be thought that there would be no such restriction in the case of *patigṛhe*; for here, due to the presence of the *ghi* designation, the prior placement is indeed obligatory.

However, in the case of a compound where *bahu* precedes, because it is treated as a *ghi* stem according to the principle of the *susākhi* rule, forms such as *bahupatinā* should be understood. Now, how is it that [the following usages] are possible: "by the monkey-lord Sakhin," "Śukra is not blameworthy when he goes before a woman being led by her husband," and "when the husband has disappeared, died, renounced the world, become impotent, or fallen from his caste"?

Regarding such passages, Haradatta states: "The sages act according to the rules of Vedic meter (*chandovat*). His intention is this: these [forms] are indeed ungrammatical; however, just as in the case of officiating at the sacrifice for Triśaṅku and others who were ineligible to sacrifice, the use of ungrammatical forms does not significantly hinder sages who possess the greatness of ascetic power (*tapas*). For people like us, however, because of the force of the injunctions to study the *Smṛtis*, *Purāṇas*, and so forth, their inclusion within those texts and their recitation therein is not a violation.

Thus, it is established in both the *Bhāṣya* and the *Kaiyaṭa* on the rule defining the technical term *nadī* that those such as ourselves, who employ [the word] in this way independently, certainly incur a grammatical fault (*pratyavāya*). Alternatively, a *sakhi* is one who is called a friend (*sakha*), and a *pati* is one who is called a lord (*pati*); hence, [the forms] *sakhinā* and *patinā*. The suffix *i* is added by the *Uṇādi* rule "after roots ending in *ac*, the suffix *i*" (Pāṇini 3.3.56). Because these two are derived through a secondary derivation (*lākṣaṇika*), they are not included in the exclusion of the technical term *yid* (which applies to words ending in *i* or *u* vowels), and so forth. By this, [it is explained that] Kṛṣṇa is the friend of Arjuna, and Arjuna is the friend of Kṛṣṇa.

This has also been explained. How [is one to understand] the phrase from Māgha, "vaco vācaspaterapi"? For this is not a compound, since no rule for the non-elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending is observed here. True; however, by virtue of the term *bahulam* ("variously") in the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.3.14), there is no elision. By this, *divaspati* and *vāstoṣpati* are also explained. The substitution of *s* for *ṣ* occurs according to the rule *ṣaṣṭhyāḥ pati* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.3.53).

However, those who carry forward the term *chandasi* (in the Vedic language) from that rule [Pāṇini 6.1.159] in order to establish forms such as *śriyaḥ pati-* (Śikṣā 1.1), maintain in their view that the augment *suṭ* is applied because the word belongs to the *pāraskara-* group (Pāṇini 6.1.157). Others, however, say that the non-elision (*aluk*) of the genitive case-ending is due to a general indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) found in the rule *dyāvāpṛthivīśunāsīramarutvadagnīṣomavāstoṣpatigṛhamedhāccha ca* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.2.32); furthermore, the change to *s* occurs because the word belongs to the *kaska-* group (Pāṇini 8.3.48), while the change to *ṣ* applies to a letter following *iṇ*. But the makers of the *pada*-text read words such as *vācaspatiṃ viśvakarmāṇam* and *vāstoṣpate prati* as separate words.
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.9)

"A word joined with a genitive [is optionally termed *ghi*] in the Vedic language" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.9). A word ending in the genitive case joined with the word *pati* may optionally be designated as *ghi* in the Vedic language. For example: *kṣetrasya patinā vayam*. Here, the rule is divided: first, "joined with a genitive in the Vedic language"; then, "optionally (*vā*)"; and finally, "only in the Vedic language (*chandasi*). The meaning is that all grammatical rules are optional in the Vedic language. Expressions such as "frequently (*bahulam*) in the Vedic language" are merely elaborations of this very principle. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.10)

"A short [vowel] is light" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.10). A short vowel shall have the designation *laghu* (light). Regarding the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate (*laghūpadhaguṇa*), we have the example *cetati*. Now, it is not feasible to employ the designation *laghu* alone even in those contexts where *hrasva* (short) occurs; for if one were to do so, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the rule "after a short vowel, when a *taddhita* suffix beginning with *t* follows" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.3.101) failing to establish the *ṣatva* (substitution of *ṣ* for *s*) in forms such as *sarpiṣṭvam*. This is because the designation *guru* (heavy) would subvert the designation *laghu* in that instance. Therefore, since the section on "one designation" (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*) is in force, the formulation of the *hrasva* designation outside of that section is indeed correctly executed.

If this were the case, then the Bhāṣya—which states that "this rule (yoga) will be formulated under the heading 'One Designation' (ekasaṃjñādhikāra), fearing the simultaneous application (samāveśa) of the designations 'long' (dīrgha) and 'protracted' (pluta)"—would be contradicted. This is because, just as the designation 'heavy' (guru) supersedes the designation 'light' (laghu), there would arise the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the designations 'heavy' and 'long' superseding the designation 'short' (hrasva). Nor can it be argued that [the designation 'heavy'] lacks scope (niravakāśatā), for it serves a purpose merely as a means for the application of the designation 'light,' just as the designation 'word' (pada) does in the explanation: "A word becomes possessed of being" (padaṃ sadbhūtaṃ bhavati).

True; the intention is that the inclusion [of the term] should be made by means of the word *ca* and so forth. Or rather, it is precisely because of dissatisfaction with this [view] that other alternatives were stated there; such is the direction [of the argument]. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.11) *saṃyoge guru*: A short vowel shall be designated as "heavy" (*guru*) when followed by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*). Examples: *śikṣā*, *bhikṣā*. [In these cases,] the suffix *a* is applied according to [Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.3.103]: *gurośca halaḥ*.
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.12) "And a long [vowel]" (dīrghañ ca): A long vowel shall have the designation *guru*. Example: *īhāñcakre*.
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.13)

"Since there is a rule for an affix, that which begins with it is the *aṅga* when the affix follows" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.13). A word beginning with that from which an affix is prescribed shall be designated as an *aṅga* when an affix follows. As in *rāmeṇa*. Why is "rule" (*vidhi*) mentioned? [Consider] *strī īyatī*. One should not argue that here, although the affix *vatup* is not prescribed after the word *strī*, the rule nonetheless applies; for the interpretation is that, by virtue of proximity, that which is an *aṅga* is that from which a particular affix is prescribed when that affix follows. Why "beginning with that" (*tadādi*)? [Consider] *vadāmi*, *vadiṣyāmi*.

Therefore, by the rule *ato dīrgho yañi* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.3.101), a long vowel is substituted. Nor should it be argued that this [longening] will occur simply by the force of the present rule's introduction; for [the rule] would already have its purpose fulfilled in cases such as *yāyāmi*, *yāyāvaḥ*, *yāyāmaḥ*, *cācāmi*, *cācāvaḥ*, *cācāmaḥ*, derived from the roots *yā* (to go) and *cāy* (to go) [in the *bhvādi* class, nos. 478–479] when the *yaṅ* suffix is elided (*yaṅluk*). Why specify "before an affix"? [The answer is: so that [the substitution] does not occur for what remains after the affix, or for anything exceeding that. For if it were otherwise, the subsequent conditionality (*paranimittakatva*) of the substitution of *u* for *ṛ* in *vavraśca* could not be established.

And thus, by the rule *avaḥ parasmin* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.1.57), there would be the undesirable consequence of the substitution of *samprasāraṇa* for the letter *v*, because the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* [of the preceding *u*] does not apply. Nor can the status of *sthānivadbhāva* be established by the first sūtra (*sthānivad ādeśo’nalvidhau*), because it is a rule concerning an *al* (a phoneme). For this very reason, it has been stated that even though the term *liṅga* is mentioned in the first sūtra, the feminine suffix treatment (*nadīkārya*) does not apply in cases such as *niṣkauśāmbi*.

In this context, for the sake of brevity, it would have been more appropriate to state simply: "When a suffix follows *prakṛti* and so forth, [the preceding] is the base (*aṅga*). However, the status of the base is established for the *prakṛti* alone by means of the principle of "designation as if possessing its own designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). The truth is that it was stated in that way in order to obtain the meaning of a technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) through the division of the grammatical rule (*yogavibhāga*). *Kartā*, *kārakaḥ*. Here the rule is divided: "When a suffix is prescribed, [the item] beginning with that from which the suffix is prescribed is [the base]. This is a technical rule (*paribhāṣā*). Its meaning is: when a suffix is being taken, that which begins with the element from which its prescription originates is what is understood. By this, [the rule applies to] *ñ*...

In rules such as *nityādiḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.197), where a suffix (*pratyaya*) is indicated by the locative case, there is the inclusion of that which begins with it. Consequently, in the expression *devadatto gārgyaḥ*, the accent of the *ñit* suffix does not apply to the entire compound. In the rule *supa ātmanaḥ kyac* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.1.8) as well, this restriction regarding the beginning [of the element] applies. Therein, because the *sup* [ending] qualifies either the object (*karman*) or that which begins with it, the rule of "inclusion of what ends with" (*tadantavidhi*) applies. Thus, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *mahāntaṃ putram*.

For if [the suffix] kyac were applied after a sentence, one would have *mahatputrīyati*; likewise, in *devadattaścikīrṣati*, the designation "root" (*dhātu*) does not apply to the entire complex; in *devadatto gārgyaḥ*, the designation "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) does not apply to the entire complex; and from *devadatto gārgyāyaṇaḥ*, the suffix phaṅ does not arise from the entire complex—this is the general direction [of the argument].

The exception to this is stated in the *Paribhāṣā*: "When a *kṛt*-affix is mentioned [in a rule], that which is preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka* is also included" (Pā. Bhāṣya 28). In this context, the mention of the word "immediate" (*anantara*) in Aṣṭādhyāyī Sūtra 6.2.49, "A *gati* [is unaccented] when it is immediate," serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). For that [mention] is intended to prevent the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the word *abhi* from being removed in the compound *abhyuddhṛta*, where *abhi* is separated from the *kṛt*-affix by the word *ud*.

Nor should it be argued that, because of the subsequent word, the *nighāta* (elision of accent) will apply by Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.1.70 (*gatir gatau*), and thus—due to the continued application of the rule for the *udātta* accent—the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) prescribed [by 6.2.2] will not occur; for, since the governing heading *apādādau* (except at the beginning of a verse-quarter) applies, the *nighāta* does not take effect at the beginning of a quarter. Furthermore, under the rule of initial determination (*tadādiniyama*), even though the word *hṛta* ends in a *kta*-suffix, the word *uddhṛta* does not end in a *kta*-suffix, so there would be no possibility [of the *nighāta* applying] anyway; what then is the purpose of the mention of *anantara* (immediately preceding)? The purpose, however, concerns the accents of compounds (*samāsa*) and secondary derivatives (*taddhita*).

For instance, in the expression *avataptenakulasthitam*, the compound is formed by Pāṇini 2.1.47 (*kṣepe*), while the rule *ktena* (2.1.46) is understood as a governing rule (*anuvartamāna*). The elision of the suffix *kṛt* is not applied here by Pāṇini 6.3.14 (*tatpuruṣe kṛti*). In *sāṃkṛṭinam*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.4.15 (*aṇinuṇaḥ*) because of the presence of a prefix (*sa-*); for this very reason, the *vṛddhi* strengthening of the vowel occurs specifically in the portion of the prefix. In *vyāvakrośī*, the suffix *ṇac* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.3.43 (*karmavyatihāre ṇac striyām*).

Then, by the rule *ṇacaḥ striyām* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.4.14), the suffix *añ* is applied. By the rule *na karmavyatihāre* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.3.6), the substitution of *aij* is prohibited. In the word *durādāgataḥ*, there is final acute accent (*antodāttatvam*) by the rule *thāthādisvareṇa*. If it is argued: "Even without this paribhāṣā, the final acute accent will occur by the rule *samāsasya* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.223)," we say: not so. For in the word *āgataḥ*, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the object (*karmani*), as in "it was come."

And thus, setting aside the accent of the compound (*samāsasvara*), the middle-accent (*madhyodātta*) would apply by the rule *gatiranantaraḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.2.49). However, when this *paribhāṣā* is present, the accent of the suffix *kṛt* (*kṛtsvara*)—which is an exception to the accent of the suffixes *tha*, *tha*, and *ghañ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.2.144)—is set aside by the accent of the *gati* [particle], and because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], the final-accent (*antodāttatva*) occurs. Objection: But is not the accent of the *gati* also an exception to the accent of the *thāthādi* group? Response: True; however, that is an exception specifically to the final-accent of a word ending in a *kta* suffix that follows a *gati*.

However, it will be stated that for a word following a *kāraka*, only the accent of the *thā-thādi* group applies. Now, let us assume that the word *āgata* is acutely accented on its first syllable by the accent rule for *gatis*. Then, there is a compound with the word *dūra* according to *Aṣṭādhyāyī* 2.1.39 (*stokāntika...*). There is no elision (*aluk*) of the fifth case ending according to *Aṣṭādhyāyī* 6.3.2 (*pañcamyāḥ stokādibhyaḥ*). Consequently, because it is the most remaining (*satiśiṣṭa*), the compound will indeed have the acute accent on its final syllable.

True; however, the intended meaning is that although the word *āgata* would—by the rule *kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*—be expected to have its first syllable udātta because it ends in a *kṛt* suffix, the *thāthādi-svara* (the acute accent on the first syllable of the second member) actually occurs. This is because the *gati-svara* (the accent for a preceding *gati* particle), which would otherwise apply since *ā* is a *gati* and the suffix *-ta* is added after a verb, is itself sublated by the subsequent application of the *thāthādi-svara*. Thus, the accent is not an example of the Paribhāṣā [that "an operation which applies when another operation is about to take effect is stronger than that other operation"] being illustrated by an accent that could not be established otherwise.

And thus, the technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) regarding the designation of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) does not apply here; for, by the maxim of "an exception in the middle" (*madhyepavādanyāya*), the mention of *kṛt*-affixes serves only to set aside the prohibition "not a suffix" (*apratyaya*). However, the prohibition that a composite (*saṅghāta*) containing a preceding member which is a word other than a compound—that is, one bearing the designation of a "word" (*pada*)—is not a nominal stem, is indeed a sublater [of the former rule] due to its superior status (*paratva*). Consequently, in the example "with radish as an accompaniment" (*mūlakenopadaṃśam*), there is no elision (*luk*) of the case-ending (*sup*).

Nor does it possess the capacity to function as an option for a compound, because the prohibition by Śākala—namely, "no compound" (*na samāsa*)—does not apply, since that [prohibition] finds its utility in cases such as *dadhyupadaṃśa*. This is clear from the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa on the rule *puṃyogād ākhyāyām* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.1.48); this is the direction of the argument.

In the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *ṣyaṅaḥ saṃprasāraṇam* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.4; 6.1.13), another exception to the rule of initiality (*tadādiniyama*) is stated: "The restriction regarding initiality does not apply to a feminine suffix that is not a subordinate member (*anupasarjana*). This has been explained as being merely based on explicit scriptural statement (*vācanika*) in the commentary on the *sarvādi* sūtra. Alternatively, here [in the present context], the term *na-strī* ("not feminine") is understood to carry over from the sūtra *neyaṅuvaṅsthānau* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.4). Although that term there refers to the actual form of the word (*svarūpa-padārthaka*), it here results in referring to the meaning (*arthapara*).

When a suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned, that which begins with it is to be understood; the meaning is that this applies provided that a feminine [suffix] is not being denoted. Consequently, it follows that there is no restriction regarding the beginning of the element when a feminine suffix is involved. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of *samprasāraṇa* in the case of *atikārīṣagandhyāputraḥ*, because by the term *astrī* ("not feminine"), the prohibition applies only to the primary feminine (*pradhānastri*), according to the maxim "between the secondary and the primary, the primary is preferred. Thus, it is established that as long as a word denotes a female primarily, it is considered to end in a feminine suffix, but not if it exceeds that [denotation].
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.14)

"A word (*pada*) consists of that which ends in a nominal suffix (*suP*) or a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.14). That which ends in a *suP* suffix and that which ends in a *tiṅ* suffix shall be designated as a *pada*. For example: *brāhmaṇā ūcuḥ* ("The Brahmins said"). The inclusion of the term "ending in" (*anta*) is for the purpose of making known the rule: "In the formulation of a technical designation (*saṃjñāvidhi*), when a suffix is mentioned, there is no inclusion of what ends with it. (Paribhāṣenduśekhara 27). For example: *gaurabrāhmaṇitarā* ("a more excellent Brahmin woman").

In the context of the technical term *ghasaṃjñā*, when there is the inclusion of forms ending in the suffix *-tarap*, the rule *puṃvatkarmadhāraya* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.3.42)—which prescribes masculine substitution for the word *sita-gaurī*—is set aside. Consequently, instead of masculine substitution, shortening would occur according to the rule *khid ghādikeṣu*, resulting in a short vowel as in *paṭvitara*. However, the shortening would not apply to the word *brāhmaṇī*. If it is asked: "How then is the inclusion of words ending in those [suffixes] understood in the definition of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) through the terms *kṛt* and *taddhita*?"—the authors of the *Bhāṣya* state here: "The phrase 'that which has meaning' (*arthavat*) is carried over into that [definition]. By virtue of its presence, the inclusion of words ending in those [suffixes] is established."

This might be so: if ultimate meaningfulness is intended, then that belongs to a word (*pada*) or a sentence (*vākya*), but not to a form ending in a primary (*kṛt*) or secondary (*taddhita*) suffix. Accordingly, there is a *vārttika* on the rule *arthavat*: "Meaningfulness is not established for [a suffix] alone, because it is not taught as such; however, it is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)."

If it is argued that, in accordance with the *Uttaravārttika* on that point, that [meaning] which is postulated during the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā-daśā*) is intended here, then since such a meaning exists for *kṛt* and *taddhita* suffixes as well, [the objection remains]. True; for this very reason, the force of the inclusion of the term "meaning-bearing" (*arthavat*) has been stated. However, what is grasped here is the meaning conveyed by a suffix-ending word that has attained a unified sense (*ekārthībhūta*), because that is more closely proximate to the worldly meaning (*laukika-artha*). Furthermore, since the possessive suffix *matup* is used in the sense of excellence (*prāśastya*), it is precisely that [meaning] which is grasped. For this same reason, its inclusion is purposeful, as it could have been obtained even through the power of the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "not a verbal root" (*adhātuḥ*) in the preceding rule.

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.15) *naḥ kye*: When followed by *kyac*, *kyaṅ*, or *kyaṣ*, that which ends in *-n* alone shall be designated as a *pada*. Examples: *rājīyati* (with *kyac*); *rājāyate* (with *kyaṅ*); *carmāyati*, *carmāyate* (with *kyaṣ*). This example is cited according to the opinion of the author of the *Vṛtti*, who maintains that the letter *k* in *kyaṣ* is for the purpose of including [the suffix] in general. However, in the *Bhāṣya*, since the letter *k* of *kyaṣ* is rejected, only *kyac* and *kyaṅ* are understood here.

The form *carmāyati* is also incorrect, because [the suffix] *kyaN* is admitted to be invariably ātmanepada by virtue of being a *kyaN*-ending. And so it will be stated: "The rule for *kyaṣ* after roots ending in *lohit* and *ḍāj* [is prescribed]; the others [are included] among the *bhṛśa*-type words" (Kāśikāvṛtti). We shall clarify this very point in the third [chapter]. Why is it not the case that only those ending in *n* are [governed by this rule]? For example: *vācyati*, *srucyati*, *tapasyati*. If one asks, "Why is the reverse restriction—that only those ending in *n* take *kyaN*—not accepted? It is not so, because of the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) in the rule *na ṅisambuddhyoḥ* and the *jñāpaka* in the rule *nalopaḥ prātipadikāntasya*. Otherwise, the sūtra would have been formulated simply as *nalopaḥ kye*.

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.16) *siti ca*: When a suffix marked with *s* follows, the preceding element shall be designated as a *pada*. This is an exception to the designation of *bha*. For example: from the rule *bhavataṣṭhakchasau* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.2.115), we have *bhavadīyaḥ*; and from *ṛtoraṇ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.1.105) and *chandasi ghas* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.1.106), we have *ṛtviyaḥ*, meaning "one for whom the season has arrived.
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.17)

*svādiṣvasarvanāmasthāne* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.17). Before suffixes beginning with *su* and ending with *kap*, excluding the *sarvanāmasthāna* case endings, the preceding element shall be designated as a *pada*. For example: *rājabhyām*, *rājabhiḥ*; *rājatvam*, *rājatā*. However, in the case of *sarvanāmasthāna* endings, it is *rājānau*, *rājānaḥ*. There is an extension (*upasaṅkhyāna*) of the *pada* designation for forms such as *bhuvadbhyām* and *dhārayadvadbhyaḥ*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *bha* designation prescribed by *tasau matvarthe* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.19). By means of transposition (*vyatyaya*), there is the elision (*luk*) of the *śap* suffix after the root *bhū*. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.18)

*Yaci bham* (Pāṇini 1.4.18): When followed by suffixes beginning with *ya* or *ca*, as well as by case-endings (*svādi*) that are not *sarvanāmasthāna*, the preceding element shall receive the designation *bha*. Examples: *gārgyaḥ*, *rājñaḥ*. Regarding how the designations *bha* and *abha* apply to *vācika* and *ṣaḍika*, it will be explained in the fifth [chapter]. There is an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for *nabhas*, *aṅgiras*, and *manus* when followed by the suffix *vat*. For example, in *nabhasvat*—meaning "existing like the sky"—the designation *bha* applies, and thus there is no substitution of *ru*. Similarly: *manuṣvad agne* ("like Manu, O Agni") and *aṅgirasvadaṅgiraḥ* ("like Aṅgiras, O Aṅgiras").

In the case of *janerusiḥ* (Uṇādisūtra 280), because of the continued application of the term *bahulam* ("variously"), the suffix *up* is added to the root *man*. The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs by the rule *ādeśapratyayayoḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.3.59). Regarding *vṛṣaṇvasu* and *vṛṣaṇaśva* (Kāśikāvṛtti Vārttika): he whose wealth (*vasu*) is rain-giving (*vṛṣan*, i.e., productive) is *vṛṣaṇvasu*; similarly, [he whose horses are rain-giving is] *vṛṣaṇaśva*. Whether it is a *karmadhāraya* or a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound, etc., should be understood according to the possibility. Here, if one were to rely on the internal case-ending (*vibhakti*), there would be the contingency of the elision of the *n* (*nalopa*) once the status of being a *pada* is established. However, because it possesses the status of a *bha* stem, it does not have the status of a *pada*.

For this very reason, the prohibition of *ṇatva* by the rule *padāntasya* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.4.37) does not apply. Furthermore, the rule *alloponaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.134) does not take effect because of the absence of the designation *aṅga*, since the governing term *aṅgasya* is in force there. Kaiyaṭa states that these supplementary rules (*upasaṃkhyāna*) pertain to the Vedic domain. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.19)

*tasau matvarthe* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.19): A stem ending in *t* or *s* is designated as *bha* when followed by an affix having the sense of the possessive suffix *matup*. For example, *vidyutvān* ("possessing lightning"). Because it is a *bha*, the substitution of a voiced stop (*jaś*) does not occur [for the final *t*]. The word *udaśvit* ("buttermilk") is derived from the root *śvi* ("to swell" or "increase") with the prefix *udaka-*; it means that which swells or increases through water. By the rule *kvip* [Pāṇini 3.2.76], and specifically by the irregularity (*nipātana*) stated in *udaśvito 'nyatarasyām* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.2.19), there is no vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*). Furthermore, by the rule *udakasyodaḥ saṃjñāyām* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.3.57), *udaka-* is replaced by *uda-* in this technical name. Thus, we have *udaśvitvān ghoṣaḥ* ("a settlement possessing buttermilk"). Similarly, we have *yaśasvī* ("famous"). Whether it is the function of the possessive suffix *matup* or of suffixes such as *vin* and others, their operation in expressing the sense of possession is indistinguishable.

Therefore, the application of the designation *bh* occurs in both cases. For example, when it is said, "Let those staying in Devadatta’s house be brought," Devadatta himself is also brought, because he is pervaded by the nature that constitutes the delimiting condition (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) of the referent.
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.20)

*Ayasmayādīni chandasi* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.20). These [words] are correct in the Vedic language (*chandas*). Because of the governing rule for the technical designation *bha*, their correctness is prescribed through both [designations, *bha* and *pad*], as appropriate. Thus, the Vārttika states: "It should be stated that there are words possessing both designations. For example: *ayasmayam pātram* (an iron vessel). Because it has the designation *bha*, the substitution of *u* does not occur. In the sense of "a modification of iron," the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied by the rule *dvayacaśchandasi* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.3.150).

By this, the author of the *Nyāsa*—who, having raised the objection as to how the suffix *mayaṭ* can be used here given the rule "the suffix *mayaṭ* [is optionally used] for these two in the vernacular" (*Aṣṭādhyāyī* 4.3.143), replied that it is due to a specific irregularity (*nipātana*)—is refuted. [The word is] *sasustubhā sarvatā gaṇena*. Here, because of the status of being a *pada*, there is *kutva* (the substitution of *k* for *s*); however, because of its status as a *bha*, there is no *jaśtva* (the substitution of *j* for *s*). This is because the designation of *pada*, which is intended for the application of *jaśtva*, is blocked by its status as a *bha*.
(*Aṣṭādhyāyī* 1.4.21).

"The plural suffix occurs when there is plurality" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.21). This [suffix] should apply when there is multiplicity, as in *vṛkṣāḥ* ("trees"). How then is it that [the word] *dārāḥ* ("wife") is used? It will be so because of the superimposition (*āropa*) of the plurality of parts onto the whole. Nor does this result in the undesirable consequence of using the plural for even a single tree, because there is no evidence (*pramāṇa*) for such a superimposition in that case. However, in the case of *dāra* and similar words, there is a difference because the usage of elders, as well as lexicons which record them as being invariably plural, serves as authoritative proof. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.22)

*Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.22*: "The dual and singular [case endings] are used for two and one. This means that these [terminations] are employed when there is duality or singularity—e.g., *vṛkṣau* (two trees), *vṛkṣaḥ* (one tree). Here, the words *dvi* ("two") and *eka* ("one") refer to the numbers themselves (*saṅkhyā*), and not to the things numbered (*saṅkhyeya*). For this very reason, the dual form *dvyekayoḥ* is used; otherwise, a plural form would have been required. In the preceding sūtra as well, the word *bahuṣu* ("in many") refers specifically to the number. However, the plural form was used by superimposing the plurality residing in the substratum onto the grammatical property itself.

The mention of *bahu* as a synonym for *parvata* (mountain) in the sense of "vastness" is merely intended to indicate that it is not included here; in reality, however, such a mention is redundant, because since it is a remote term (*para*), the singular number is possible. As for the statement, "Numbers [beginning] from one hundred are [themselves] the objects to be numbered," that is merely a general observation. Regarding this, the *Ślokavārttika* states:
"The meanings of case-endings (*sup*) include the objective case and so forth, as well as number (*saṅkhyā*); likewise for verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*).
There is a well-known restriction (*niyama*) in those cases, or there is a restriction regarding the specific bases (*prakṛta*) [of the words]."

The meaning of the first half [of the verse] is that the section beginning with *karmaṇi dvitīyā* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.2) and the rule beginning with *bahuṣu bahuvacanam* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.20) function as prescriptive injunctions by forming a single syntactic unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the *svādi-sūtra* [1.4.1]. Likewise, the rules beginning with *bahuṣu bahuvacanam* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.20) also form a single syntactic unit with the section on *ti*-affixes and so forth. By the third quarter [of the verse], the restriction of meaning (*arthaniyama*) is stated; by the fourth, however, the restriction of suffixes (*pratyayaniyama*) is stated in relation to the subject matter at hand.

The consideration of the relative strength and weakness (*balābala*) among these alternative views was already undertaken by us in the very rule *taddhitaścāsarvavibhaktiḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.1.38). Here, it would have been more appropriate to state: "The singular, dual, and plural [case endings] are used in the sense of one, two, and many. Furthermore, the word *bahu* should be understood as denoting a number (*saṅkhyā*) alone, due to its association with the word *dvi*. For this very reason, the word *eka* is also taken as denoting a number. In reality, however, these two rules need not exist at all; for by adopting the view that the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) such as "singular" and so forth serve the purpose of subsequent application (*anvaya*), all desired results are established.
Thus ends the second Āhnika of the fourth Pāda of the first Adhyāya in the venerable Śabdakaustubha.

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.23) *Kārake* (in the context of a case-role). This is an introductory heading (*adhikāra*). The locative case is used here by way of transference (*vyatyaya*) to convey the sense of the nominative. Thus, in each subsequent rule beginning with *dhruvam*, the sentence is split so that the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "kāraka" is prescribed. For example: "In separation (*apāye*), that which is fixed (*dhruvam*) shall be designated as a kāraka. Thereafter, [it says] *apādānam*: "The aforementioned kāraka shall be designated as the ablative (*apādāna*). Furthermore, because of the force of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *kāraka*, there is a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) with the specific designations, rather than them being mere alternatives (*paryāya*).

Since that [result] is established from the first sentence alone even without the subsequent application (*anuvṛtti*), by this [rule], in cases such as *stamberamaḥ*, the seventh case ending (*saptamī*) is established because of its status as a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), and the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) is established by the rule *gatikārakopapadātkṛt* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.2.139). However, the accent beginning with *thā-tha-* (i.e., the *thāthādisvara*) does not apply, because in that [rule] only vowels (*ac*) are understood due to their association (*sāhacarya*) with the preceding [term].

Nor should it be argued that the *kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara* (the accentuation of the original pitch of the final member of a compound ending in a *kṛt*-suffix) should apply simply because [the words] are *upapada*s; for according to the rule *stambakarmayoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.13), although this applies to the two nominal bases (*pratipadika*) as they are stated, it does not apply to those qualified by the locative case. Indeed, that which is qualified by the locative is not itself stated with the locative, such that it would obtain the designation of *upapada*. This is the general direction of the argument.

This designation is etymologically meaningful: that which "does" (karoti) is a "doer" (kāraka). Therefore, it does not apply to that which is merely connected to an action [without being its cause]. For example: *brāhmaṇasya putraṃ panthānaṃ pṛcchati* ("He asks the son of the Brahmin the way"). Here, the Brahmin is a qualifier of the son, but he is not connected to the action [of asking]. [Objection: But how is the son also a kāraka? For "asking" (*praśna*) is a desire to know (*jijñāsā*). In that case, although the questioner is a kāraka, the one to whom the question is directed cannot be a producer (*janaka*) of that action. [Reply: True, let there be no status as a producer. What is intended here is merely connection to the action.

And that [cause] certainly exists. By this, the status of the recipient (*sampradāna*) as a *kāraka* is explained. Alternatively, since the recipient and others also first ascend to the mind (*buddhyāroha*), they possess the status of a *kāraka*. In the same way, it should be understood that in cases such as "he knows" (*jānāti*) or "he does" (*karoti*), the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) are also [to be understood as *kārakas*]. If it is asked, "How can those things existing at the moment immediately preceding the effect be causes?"—understand it to be like the case of a sacrifice (*yāga*). If it is argued, "In that case, there is an intermediate operation (*vyāpāra*)," we say no; for even by that much, the sacrifice’s existence as a prior factor (*pūrvavartitā*) is not established.

If it is argued that causality (*kāraṇatva*) consists in being either immediately preceding or one’s own operation (*vyāpāra*), we say no; for since the nature of an operation (*vyāpāratva*) already contains the notion of causality within it, this would result in the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). Furthermore, just as one’s own operation might be included, so too could one’s own cognition (*svajñāna*) be included [in the definition]. For this very reason, the older Naiyāyikas maintain that a probans (*liṅga*) and a word (*pada*) are causes of inferential knowledge and verbal knowledge respectively, only when they are being cognized (*jñāyamāna*). Likewise, the Mīmāṃsakas hold that objects (*padārtha*) are causes only when they are being cognized.

For this very reason, the Mīmāṃsakas proclaim that the *rathantara-sāman* and so forth serve as the occasion (*nimitta*) for [the application of] the *aindravāyava* cup and others. Alternatively, just as the designation "subordinate" (*upasarjana*)—which is etymologically meaningful (*anvartha*) where possible, as in *rājñaḥ kumāryāḥ* (the king's daughter) becoming *rājakumārī* (the king’s daughter)—nevertheless occurs in cases like *ardhapippalī* (half-a-pepper) by virtue of an explicit rule (*vacana*), so too the designation of "kāraka" (participant), though enjoined in each individual sūtra, applies to the *sampradāna* (recipient) and others by virtue of an explicit rule. However, in the specific rules (*pradeśa*), the cognition is indeed characterized by the name itself;
whether it is characterized by that specific form or another is a separate matter.

It might be argued: "In expressions such as *vṛkṣasya parṇaṃ patati* ('the leaf of the tree falls'), the tree—which is a qualifier of the leaf—would also incur the status of a *kāraka*, because of the usage *vṛkṣāt patati* ('it falls from the tree'). If you then say that the capacity to be a generator (*janakatva*) and the lack thereof are determined solely by the difference in our linguistic usage, here is the secret of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*): the status of being a *kāraka* and its six sub-divisions, such as agency (*kartṛtva*), are not fixed to a specific entity."

In that case, just as a cow is a cow for everyone and not a non-cow for anyone, it can be rightly said that a qualifier is simply a qualifier, like a qualified object. And thus, to the questions "What is the instrument?", "Who is the agent?", or "What is the object?", the answer would be "Everything."

Since agency (*kartṛtva*), objecthood (*karmatva*), and so forth, as will be explained, are unimpeded even in the case of insentient entities and beginningless [entities], the answer to the question "What constitutes agency and so on in the meaning presented by a particular verbal root (*dhātu*)? is given in the following order: the agent (*kartṛ*) is the substratum (*āśraya*) of the operation (*vyāpāra*) denoted by the specific verbal root under discussion; the object (*karman*) is the substratum of the result (*phala*) that is non-co-referential with that operation; the instrument (*karaṇa*) is that whose operation is intended to be the immediate antecedent to the action (*kriyā*); and the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is the substratum of the agent and the object, and so forth.

The meaning of the root *pac* (to cook) is indeed an operation conducive to softening (*viklitti*). And such an operation is manifold. In this regard, when the primary intention (*tātparya*) of *pac* lies in placing [the pot] on the fire, pouring in the rice, adding fuel, removing it from the fire, blowing upon it, and so forth, then Devadatta, as the locus of those operations, is the agent (*kartṛ*). When the intention lies in the burning [of the fuel], then the fuel-sticks (*edhas*) are the agents. When the focus is on containing the rice, the cooking-pot (*sthālī*) is the agent. When the focus is on the separation of parts and so forth, the rice grains (*taṇḍula*) are the agents. For this very reason, there exists the conventional usage of "agent-as-object" (*karmakartṛ*), "agent-as-instrument" (*karaṇakartṛ*), and so on.

Thus, in the expression "he cooks in a pot" (*sthālyā pacati*), although the pot is the locus of the operation expressed by the instrumental case, it is indeed the instrument (*karaṇa*) and not the agent (*kartṛ*) at that time; for in that context, the operation of Devadatta and others alone is what is expressed by the verbal root. Similarly, when the meaning is expressed by roots such as *ād-* and *khād-*, the boy is the agent (*kartṛ*); when that same meaning is expressed by the root *bhakṣayati*, the boy is the object (*karman*). When the meaning is expressed by roots such as *śīṅ* and *sthā* preceded by the prefix *adhi*, the locus (*ādhāra*) is the object; when expressed by those same roots used alone, it is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), and so forth.

If it is objected that there is thus a lack of uniformity (*ananugama*), we reply: True; for, just as in the case of "Who is whose father? Who is whose brother?", the object of definition is precisely that which lacks such uniformity. For this very reason, the correctness or incorrectness of linguistic usages (*prayoga*) is established. Otherwise, if the status of being an agent were to apply everywhere simply because it applies in some instances, all linguistic usages would become confused. As stated by Bhartṛhari: "In reality, that [agency] cannot be specifically pointed out, for a thing does not remain fixed [in its role].
Since we observe the fixed usage: 'The food is cooked in the pot' (*sthālyā pacyate*)."

For this very reason, although there is no difference in being pervaded by the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka*), in verbal roots such as *pac* (to cook), the one being prompted (*prayojya*) is not the object (*karman*), whereas in roots such as *gam* (to go), it is indeed the object; likewise, in expressions such as *paurāṇikāc chṛṇoti* ("he hears from the Purāṇa-reciter") and *naṭasya śṛṇoti* ("he hears from the actor"), the Purāṇa-reciter is both the source (*upādāna*) and the factor of action (*kāraka*), while the actor is neither—this and other points to be stated later are thus consistent. If it is asked: "In this case, what kind of 'object' (*karman*) is to be understood in rules such as *laḥ karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 3.4.69)?"—know that all [types of objects] are to be included, since there is no determining factor [to the contrary].

If it is argued that, just as in the case of *bhasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.129), everything here is *bha*, then the status of being a *kāraka* (participant in action) or *karman* (object) and so forth would be merely technical (*pāribhāṣika*), like the designations *ṭi*, *ghu*, and *bh*. Who says it is not so? There is only this much difference: while *ṭi*, *ghu*, *bh*, and so on, are names for words (*śabda-saṃjñā*), the others are names for meanings (*artha-saṃjñā*). And thus, it follows that by the rule "the second case ending is used for the object" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.2), the second case ending is prescribed for the locus (*ādhāra*) and other factors as well, according to their respective roles.

It should be noted that even in cases such as "one goes by means of a chariot" (*rathena gamyate*) and "the chariot goes" (*ratho gacchati*), the agentive case-ending is established by the general rule itself; therefore, one need not resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) there. Furthermore, the extraction of the denotative portions (*vācyāṃśa*) of the case-endings will be undertaken later. By this, those who raise the objection regarding the contradiction between the agent and the object in the case of the self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) of cognition are refuted, because agency and so forth—conditioned by specific linguistic factors—are possible to express in perception and other means of knowledge.

By this, those who—having raised the objection that if "being an object" (*karmatva*) consists in possessing the fruit of an action inherent in another, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the agent of the causal verb (*apādāna*)—attempt to refine the definition by stating that it consists in possessing a fruit delimited by the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), are also refuted. This is because in examples such as *grāmaṃ gamayati devadattam* ("he causes Devadatta to go to the village"), there is non-extension (*avyāpti*) to the goer [Devadatta]; for in your view, although going is the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), it is not what delimits the meaning of the root. Or, if it were so delimited, there would be over-extension to the instigating agent (*prayojyakartṛ*) in cases such as *pācayati* ("he causes to cook").

If it is argued that in this context, the status of being an object (*karman*) useful for the technical instruction is established by the force of the statement itself, then you should understand that even in the case of the *apādāna*, that [status] does not exist, because it is sublated by the non-occasional [rule] within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) regarding "one designation" (*ekasaṃjñā*). For this very reason, in cases such as "the self kills the self," the possibility of the designation of object (*karmasaṃjñā*) being sublated by the subsequent designation of agent (*kartṛsaṃjñā*) was raised, and it was resolved in various places in the Bhāṣya by resorting to a distinction between the Self and the self as qualified by the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), etc.; such is the direction of the argument.

If it is objected: "In that case, how can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between 'instrument' (*karaṇa*) and 'agent' (*kāraka*), since the suffix *ṇvul* cannot apply when there is a lack of independence (*asvātantrya*)? Otherwise, if the designation 'agent' were to occur, the designation 'instrument' would result in a mere synonymy," we reply: By the force of the governing rule (*adhikāra*), the independence conveyed by the word 'agent' (*kāraka*) is understood as belonging to a different state. That which is independent in another state is the "most effective means" (*sādhakatama*), i.e., the instrument. This is as in examples such as: "Those residing in Kurukṣetra live in Kāśī."

The independence [of the agent] belongs to the present moment; and that is utilized for the purpose of the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "agent" (*kartṛ*). Alternatively, the word *kāraka* refers to action (*kriyā*), based on the etymological derivation: "it performs (*karoti*) the designations of agent, object, and so forth. Consequently, since the phrase "with respect to an action" (*kriyāyām*) is supplied in the rules prescribing the designations of "ablative" (*apādāna*) and so on, those very designations would apply only to things connected with an action. However, in rules such as "after a *kāraka*, [the suffix *ṅasi* becomes *smāt* before the words] *datta* and *śruta*" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.2.148), the word *kāraka* is uttered with a specific accent (*svarita*).
By this, only the sixfold set beginning with the agent (*kartṛ*), as stated in this governing context (*adhikāra*), is understood. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.24)

*Apādāna* (the ablative case) is that which is fixed (*dhruva*) in separation (*apāya*). (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.24). Here, *apāya* is intended to mean disjunction (*viśleṣa*), separation (*vibhāga*), and specifically a particular kind of motion characterized by being the cause of that [separation]. When such [separation] is to be accomplished, that which serves as the limit (*avadhi*) shall bear the technical name *apādāna*. Example: *vṛkṣāt patati* ("he falls from the tree"). Regarding the word *dhruvam*: it is derived from the root *dhru*, meaning "to go" or "to be steady" (Dhātupāṭha 14.000), belonging to the *kuṭādi* group, with the suffix *ac* (pacādyac). However, for those who read the root as *dhruva* in the sense of "steadiness," the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule for roots ending in *i* or *u* followed by a short vowel (*igupadhāt kaḥ*). Thus, *dhruvatīti dhruvam*, meaning "that which is steady."

"Of one form" means up to this point. "Its quality is constant" is as follows: likewise, when "of one form" is stated in the context of establishing an *apādāna* (ablative/point of departure), it is understood to mean "that which is useful [as a limit] while not being entered by the motion conveyed by the root under discussion. And that, by implication, results in being nothing other than a limit (*avadhi*). Therefore, in cases such as "he falls from a running horse," even though the horse is qualified by the action [of running], its status as a limit with respect to the action conveyed by the root under discussion is not contradicted.

Similarly, in the expression "the two rams move away from each other" (*parasparasmān meṣāv apasarataḥ*), since the root *sṛ* (to go) denotes both movements, the status of the ablative (*apādāna*) is established for one ram with respect to the movement residing in the other. And it has been stated by Bhartṛhari in the *Prakīrṇakāṇḍa*: "That which is indifferent (*udāsīna*) during a departure—whether moving or stationary—is called the 'ablative' (*apādāna*) because it remains fixed (*dhruva*) and does not participate in that [action]."
The horse is certainly the cause of the falling, since the person falls from the horse;
and for that horse’s falling as well, a wall or similar object is held to be the certain cause.
"The status of being a limit (avadhitva) for each of the two rams is distinct, depending on the action of the other ram;
and their status as agents (kartṛtva) is also distinct, depending on their own respective actions. Thus [it is said].
"Because there is no entry into that" means because there is no entry into the state of separation (*apāya*).
For it is said that there is no separation without a limit (*avadhi*).

The sense is that, as stated in that very same work, there is no status of being an *apāya* (separation) for a movement that is independent of a limit (*avadhi*). However, in the case of "He falls from the horse falling from the mountain," the meaning is the fall having Devadatta as its locus, which has as its limit the horse that is the locus of the fall having the mountain as its limit. The ablative (*pañcamī*) is capable of denoting the limit; therein, the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is a qualifier by way of the relation of identity (*abheda*), while the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is a qualifier of the action, because factors of action (*kāraka*) are connected only with the action, otherwise [the usage] would be ungrammatical.

For it is only when there is a connection with an action (*kriyā*) that the designation of a *kāraka* (participant in an action) exists, and the specific designations [of those *kārakas*] are established based upon that. Therefore, they say:
"In all sentences, the relationship of a noun is established in only two ways:
either through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) or, in some cases, by means of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*)."

"By way of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)" refers to the intention [of expressions] such as "the blue pot" (*nīlo ghaṭaḥ*). Even in cases such as "bring the blue pot" (*nīlaṃ ghaṭam ānaya*), there is the intention of conveying a subsequent, secondary understanding once the elements have been brought under the control of a single action following the connection with the primary action. "By the genitive" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for non-agentive case endings (*akāraka-vibhakti*), as in "salutation to Hari" (*haraye namaḥ*). Regarding the phrase "in some cases," the sense is that even non-agentive case endings can be seen to connect with an action, as in "he hears from the actor" (*naṭasya śṛṇoti*).

By this, the Naiyāyikas—who explain in two ways that in the expression "there is no jar on the ground," either the absence of being located on the ground is the qualifier of the jar, or being located on the ground is the qualifier of the absence of the jar—are refuted; for in both cases, since there is no connection with a verb, the case-ending [denoting location] would be ungrammatical, and furthermore, because there is an absence of meaning, it would result in an indeclinable compound (avyayībhāva), as such a compound is obligatory.

If it is argued that the cognition we have described is also attested by the experience of those born within our own tradition, we reply: True; for we do not say that cognition does not arise at all. We accept that all [minds] are capable of cognizing all objects; however, we maintain that [such cognition] is invalid with respect to that particular object.

And thus, the authors of the Bhāṣya, while explaining the Vārttika “When the relationship between word and meaning is established,” say: “While the relationship with the meaning is common [to both], a restriction is made—just as in the case of ‘the permissible’ and ‘the impermissible’ regarding what may or may not be approached—by means of correct and incorrect words. And it has been said: “Grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) is governed by the distinction of limiting conditions (*upādhi*) based on the relationship that differentiates [correct from incorrect] forms; yet, even in the absence of that [correctness], comprehension is not here prohibited.”

Thus, regarding the question "From which sentence does what kind of cognition arise?", the established position is that for one who has acquired proficiency (*vyutpanna*) in a particular way, the resulting cognition is exactly of that same kind. The true point is that the further investigation as to what kind of cognition constitutes grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) and where it does not apply is the proper domain of inquiry. By this, the claim that expressions such as "the pot is the object" (*ghaṭaḥ karmatvam*), "bringing is effort" (*ānayanaṃ kṛtiḥ*), and so forth, are inherently unfit to produce cognition is refuted; for one who is proficient in such usage, the experience of cognition occurs. Otherwise, even if an effect does not arise due to the absence of the auxiliary factor consisting of proficiency, the inherent fitness (*svarūpayogyatā*) of the expression would not be lost.

By this, those who postulate a causal relationship—namely, that "wherever there is a cognition having the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) as its qualifier, there [the cognition] is produced by the suffix (*pratyaya*) as its object," and so forth—are also refuted, because a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) arises in the case of a reversed linguistic usage. In our established doctrine (*siddhānta*), however, expressions such as *ghaṭaḥ karmatvam* ("pot-ness is the object") are indeed ungrammatical. To explain: there is the Vārttika rule, "when [the case-role] is already expressed, the nominative (*prathamā*) [is used]. How then could the nominative occur in *ghaṭaḥ karmatvam*? Furthermore, since both the pot and the bringing are objects with respect to the act of bringing, the genitive would result according to Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.65, *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ*. This is the general direction.
The ablative (apādāna) is said to be threefold: that whose object is explicitly stated, that whose object is implied, and that where the action is not required.

Where the movement is designated by the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself, that is a case of "designated object" (*nirdiṣṭaviṣaya*), as in "he falls from the horse" (*aśvāt patati*). However, where the root expresses its own meaning as a subordinate part of the meaning of another root, that is a case of "included object" (*upāttaviṣaya*), as in "it flashes from the cloud" (*balāhakād vidyotate*). Here, the root *dyuti* (to flash) occurs with the sense of flashing as a subordinate part of the act of emerging. Or, for example, as in "he cooks from the granary" (*kusūlāt pacati*). Here, the root *pac* (to cook) occurs with the sense of cooking as a subordinate part of the act of taking [grain].

However, that [action] is one whose performance is expected (*apekṣitakriya*), where, having kept in mind an arrival established by perception, one asks, "From where do you come? and replies, "From Pāṭaliputra"; for it has been stated that the supply of a word's meaning (*arthādhyāhāra*) is logically justified. Here, "he falls from the caravan" (*sārthāddhīyate*) is also an example of a case where the locus is explicitly indicated.

This might be the case: because it is subsequent, the designation of the caravan (*sārtha*) as the agent (*kartṛ*) would apply; for it has been stated that "the subsequent [rules] supersede the ablative (*apādāna*). Furthermore, if the caravan lacked the status of being the agent, the thing being abandoned would not receive the designation of the object (*karman*), because it would lack the quality of being pervaded by the operation of the agent. Consequently, the verbal suffixes (*lakāra*) and the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) in the forms *hīyate* and *hīnaḥ*—which denote the object—would be impossible. Nor can it be argued that this suffix refers to a "reflexive object" (*karmakartṛ*), because Indu has stated that since the action of the root *jahāti* resides in the agent, this suffix must refer to the object itself.

As for what was stated by the author of the *Nyāsa* in the rule *apādāne cāhīyaruhoḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.28) and by Kaiyaṭa in the section on the *sampradāna* rule—that the mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*) in the definition of the "object" (*karman*) is an indicator of independence (*svātantrya*), and therefore, in this case, that which is desired by the independent ablative (*apādāna*) in the act of abandoning is designated as the "object"—that is questionable. For in the sentence "He ties the horse to the beans" (*māṣeṣvaśvaṃ badhnāti*), the horse, though the object of the action, would in fact incur the designation of "object" based on its independence with respect to the act of eating.

For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa stated in the supplement to the sūtra prescribing the technical designation *karman*: "Since the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka*) is not the meaning of the word [the verbal root], it is incorrect to regard [the object] as an object (*karman*) with respect to that [operation].

Regarding this, they say: in the example "he is abandoned by his wealth" (*sārthāddhīyate*), the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) denotes the reflexive agent (*karmakartṛ*). For instance, the meaning of the root *hā* is "departing. And that [departing] occurs when Devadatta departs due to the affliction of hunger and so forth; the instigation consists in performing what is conducive to that [departure]. However, when he departs by himself due to the affliction of hunger and so forth, then there is the status of being a reflexive agent (*karmakartṛ*). This is clear in the works of Haradatta and Mādhava.

This might be asked: what is the purpose of including the word *dhruva* (fixed)? Nor should it be said that it is for the sake of preventing over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the cart in the example "he comes from the village by means of a cart" (*grāmād āgacchati śakaṭena*), because in that case the designation of instrument (*karaṇasaṃjñā*) applies by virtue of its higher status, as in "he pierces with a bow" (*dhanuṣā vidhyati*). For here, in the act of piercing, the status of instrument arises precisely through the cart’s assuming the state of being a point of departure (*avadhi*) relative to the emergence of the arrow; thus, there would be the contingency of both designations applying.

In examples such as "the leaf of the tree falls" (*vṛkṣasya parṇaṃ patati*), however, the tree is merely a qualifier of the leaf and is not connected with the act of departure (*apāya*). Nor is the mention of *dhruva* intended for the purpose of indicating the technical name (*saṃjñin*), because the definition—namely, "that which persists through the action of departure"—is already implicitly established as sufficient to designate the named element. Alternatively, by resorting to the locative case in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) in the rule *kārake*, the term "kāraka" (participant) is obtained; this is because it has been stated that even in the previous rule, the locative case is used in the sense of the nominative (*prathamārthe*). Therefore, the inclusion of the term *dhruva* is of questionable utility.

[The Vārttika] states: "There should be an addition [to the rule] for the meanings of *jugupsā* (disgust), *virāma* (cessation), and *pramāda* (negligence). One feels disgust toward, ceases from, or becomes negligent regarding *adharma*. Separation (*vibhāga*) is preceded by conjunction; however, that [conjunction] does not exist here. Furthermore, that which is merely imagined by the intellect is not accepted because it is secondary (*gauṇa*). Thus begins the Vārttika. The authors of the Bhāṣya, however, maintain that *jugupsā* and the others here refer to the cessation (*nivṛtti*) preceded by disgust and so forth; thus, this refers to the actual object of the action. And in the context of grammatical relations (*kāraka*), even that which is secondary is included.

This is established by the inclusion of the term *tamap* in the rule *sādhakatamaṃ kārakam* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.42), which serves as an indicator (*liṅga*). Alternatively, because the words *apāya* and so forth are marked with the *svarita* accent, the principle *svaritenādhikāraḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.11) applies, determining that even a secondary (*gauṇa*) meaning may be accepted. Consequently, since separation (*apāya*) exists even when mentally constructed, the point is proven. For indeed, one first perceives unrighteousness (*adharma*) through the intellect and subsequently desists from it upon seeing its defects; thus, there is separation. This same method of detailed explanation should be understood to apply to the subsequent sūtras as well; this is the general direction. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.25)

Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.25: *bhītrārthānāṃ bhayahetuḥ*. Fear (*bhaya*) is *bhī*, and protection (*trāṇa*) is *trā*; when used in conjunction with verbs meaning fear or protection, the cause of fear (*bhayahetu*) shall be the *apādāna* kāraka. For example: *corabhya udvijate bibheti* (he trembles with fear or fears because of thieves), or *rakṣati trāyate* (he protects or saves). The inclusion of the term "cause of fear" (*bhayahetu*) is considered to have a questionable purpose; however, in cases such as *araṇye bibheti* (he fears in the forest), the designation of locus (*adhikaraṇa*) applies because it is a subsequent rule. Thus, the verse from the Rāmāyaṇa should be explained by connecting it with the phrase *kasya saṃyuge* (of whom in battle). Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.26.

*Parājerasoḍhaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.26). When the verb *ji* preceded by *parā-* is used, that which is "not endured" (*asoḍha*) shall be the *apādāna* [ablative case]. For example: *adhyayanāt parājayate*, meaning "he falters in his studies. This verb is intransitive (*akarmaka*). Since the genitive case would otherwise apply there, this rule is stated. Why "not endured"? Consider: *śatrūn parājayate*; here the meaning is "he overcomes them. The past time implied by the suffix *-ta* in the term *asoḍha* is not intended to be significant here. Consequently, forms such as *adhyayanāt parājeṣyate* ("he will falter in his studies") are also established.

In reality, however, the inclusion of the term *asoḍha* ("unable to endure") is redundant, because in the example *śatrūn parājayate* ("he defeats his enemies"), the designation of the object (*karmasaṃjñā*) is established by the subsequent rule [Pāṇini 1.4.29]. In this sūtra, the form *parājeḥ* should be justified in the same manner as in [the rule] *viparābhyāṃ jeḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.19). As for what Haradatta stated—that due to the subsequent rule *gher ṅiti* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.3.111), there is a *guṇa* substitution—that has already been refuted previously as being contrary to the sūtra, the Bhāṣya, and other authorities.
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.27)

Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.27: *vāraṇārthānām īpsitaḥ*. When verbs meaning "to ward off" (*vāraṇa*) are employed, the *kāraka* that is desired to be reached by the action shall be designated as the *apādāna*. Example: *yavebhyo gāṃ vārayati* ("He keeps the cow away from the barley"). The root *vṛñ* belongs to the *curādi* class (Dhātupāṭha 1814). Warding off is the obstruction of an inclination to act. Why is it said "desired" (*īpsita*)? [Consider: *yavebhyo gāṃ vārayati kṣetre* ("He keeps the cow away from the barley in the field"). One might object: "In this case, because it is a subsequent rule, the designation of *adhikaraṇa* (locus) will apply, just as even when 'desired' is included, the designation of *karman* (object) applies to the cows because they are the most desired. True; the inclusion of the word "desired" has a purpose that requires further consideration. Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.28: *antarāntareṇa yukte*. When used with *antarā* or *antareṇa*, [the word denoting what lies between or on both sides] is the *apādāna*. Example: *antarā tvāṃ ca māṃ ca kamaṇḍaluḥ* ("The water-pot is between you and me") or *antareṇa tvāṃ ca māṃ ca kamaṇḍaluḥ* ("The water-pot is without you and me"). The word *yukte* means "when joined with. Why is it said "when joined"? [Consider: *antarā tava ca mama ca kamaṇḍalumatrāste* ("The water-pot is here between you and me"). Here, because the word *atra* ("here") is used, the designation of *apādāna* does not apply. Why is it said "*antarā* or *antareṇa*"? [Consider: *antare gṛhe kamaṇḍaluḥ* ("The water-pot is inside the house"). Here, because the word *gṛhe* ("in the house") is used, the designation of *apādāna* does not apply. Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.29: *kālādhvanor atyantasaṃyoge*. When there is continuous connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*) with time (*kāla*) or distance (*adhvan*), [the word denoting them] is the *apādāna*. Example: *māsam adhīte* ("He studies for a month") or *krośam kuṭilā nadī* ("The river is winding for the distance of a *krośa*"). Why is it said "continuous connection"? [Consider: *māsaṃ guḍadhānāḥ* ("Barley grains with molasses for a month"). Here, because the word *guḍadhānāḥ* is used, the designation of *apādāna* does not apply. Why is it said "time or distance"? [Consider: *abhikramaṇam asmin vidyate* ("The advancing exists in this [place]"). Here, because the word *asmin* is used, the designation of *apādāna* does not apply. Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.30: *apavarge tṛtīyā*. When there is completion (*apavarga*) [of the time or distance], the third case suffix (*tṛtīyā*) is used. Example: *māsena anuvāko'dhītaḥ* ("The lesson was learned in a month") or *krośena anuvāko'dhītaḥ* ("The lesson was learned in a *krośa*"). Why is it said "completion"? [Consider: *māsam adhīto'nuyogaḥ* ("The study of the lesson lasted for a month"). Here, because the word *anuyogaḥ* is used, the third case suffix does not apply. Why is it said "third case suffix"? [Consider: *māsam adhīyānaḥ* ("Studying for a month"). Here, because the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) is used, the third case suffix does not apply. Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.31: *sādhakatamaṃ karaṇam*. That which is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) [for accomplishing an action] is the *karaṇa* (instrument). Example: *dātreṇa lunāti* ("He cuts with a sickle"). Why is it said "most effective"? [Consider: *kāṣṭhaiḥ pacati* ("He cooks with wood"). Here, although the wood is indeed a means, it is not the most effective one; therefore, the designation of *karaṇa* does not apply. Why is it said "*karaṇam*"? [Consider: *kartā kāṣṭhaiḥ pacati* ("The agent cooks with wood"). Here, because the word *kartā* is used, the designation of *karaṇa* does not apply. Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.32: *divaḥ karma ca*. For the root *div* ("to play"), [the most effective means] is both the *karma* (object) and the *karaṇa* (instrument). Example: *akṣair akṣān vā dīvyati* ("He plays with dice"). Why is it said "*ca* (and)"? [Consider: *akṣān dīvyati* ("He plays with dice"). Here, because the word *akṣān* is used, the designation of *karaṇa* does not apply. Why is it said "*divaḥ*"? [Consider: *śalākāyā dīvyati* ("He plays with a counter"). Here, because the word *śalākāyāḥ* is used, the designation of *karma* does not apply. Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.33: *parikrayaṇe saṃpradānam anyatarasyām*. In the sense of hiring (*parikrayaṇa*), [the most effective means] is optionally the *saṃpradāna* (recipient). Example: *śatena śatāya vā parikrītaḥ* ("Hired for a hundred"). Why is it said "optionally"? [Consider: *śatena parikrītaḥ* ("Hired for a hundred"). Here, because the word *śatena* is used, the designation of *saṃpradāna* does not apply. Why is it said "*parikrayaṇe*"? [Consider: *śatena gāḥ krīṇāti* ("He buys cows for a hundred"). Here, because the word *krīṇāti* is used, the designation of *saṃpradāna* does not apply. Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.34: *ādhāro'dhikaraṇam*. The substratum (*ādhāra*) is the *adhikaraṇa* (locus). Example: *kaṭe āste* ("He sits on a mat") or *sthālyāṃ pacati* ("He cooks in a pot"). Why is it said "*ādhāraḥ*"? [Consider: *adhi kaṭe śete devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta sleeps on the mat"). Here, because the word *adhi* is used, the designation of *adhikaraṇa* does not apply. Why is it said "*adhikaraṇam*"? [Consider: *kaṭaṃ karoti* ("He makes a mat"). Here, because the word *kaṭam* is used, the designation of *adhikaraṇa* does not apply.

"In the case of disappearance (*antardhi*), that by means of which one desires to become invisible" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.28). *Antardhau* is a locative case; *yena* is an instrumental case used for the agent (*kartṛ*). Nor does there arise the contingency of the genitive case due to its connection with a *kṛt* suffix, because of the restrictive rule: "When both [agent and object] are possible, [the sixth case ending is used] only for the object. When there is an obstruction, that *kāraka* by means of which one desires the absence of one's own perception shall be the *apādāna*. Example: *māturnilīyate kṛṣṇaḥ* ("Kṛṣṇa hides from his mother"). The root *līṅ* in the sense of "adhering" (*śliṣaṇe*) belongs to the *divādi* class. Here, the inclusion of the word *antardhau* ("in the case of disappearance") is to be considered purposeless.

In the example "he does not wish to see the thieves" (*na didṛkṣate corān*), the status of being an object (*karmatā*) is established because [the rule for the object] is subsequent [in the order of the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*]. Why [is the word] "wishes" (*icchati*) used? It is so that [the designation of object] may apply even when there is seeing, provided that the desire is absent. (Pāṇini 1.4.29) "In the case of formal instruction (*upayoga*). Formal instruction (*upayoga*) is the acquisition of knowledge preceded by a restrictive rule. When that [acquisition] is to be accomplished, the agent (*ākhyātṛ*) is the *apādāna* kāraka. Example: "He studies from the teacher" (*upādhyāyād adhīte*). Why "in the case of formal instruction"? Example: "He listens to the actor" (*naṭasya śṛṇoti*).

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.30) *janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ*. The source (*prakṛti*) of that which is being born shall be the *apādāna* [ablative] case. For example: *putrāt pramodo jāyate* ("Joy is born from the son"). Here, *jani* means "origination" (*utpatti*). Amara states: "Origination, birth, and arising" (*janirutpattirudbhavaḥ*). The suffix *iñ* is applied to *jani* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) by the *vārttika* "iñ ajādibhyaḥ," or else by the *uṇādi* sūtra "janighasibhyām" with the suffix *iṇ*. The prohibition of *vṛddhi* [strengthening of the vowel] applies here by Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.3.35, "janivadhyośca. The compound *janikartuḥ* is a genitive *tatpuruṣa* meaning "the agent of that [origination]."

The prohibition [stated] in *Aṣṭādhyāyī* 2.2.16, *kartari ca*, is non-permanent; this is precisely because of this very indicator (*jñāpaka*). Alternatively, this is a compound with a genitive of remainder (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*). Kaiyaṭa, on the sūtra *kārake* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.23), states that the prohibition, however, concerns the object-genitive (*karman-ṣaṣṭhī*). Thus, because there is the inclusion of the mere meaning, it occurs even in connection with another verbal root, as in: *aṅgādaṅgāt saṃbhavati*.

By this, the Mīmāṃsā-Vārttikakāras—who, relying on the rule *ikśtipau dhātunirdeśe* (Pāṇini 3.3.108), maintain that this is a designation by means of the suffix *ik*, and who raise the objection regarding the lack of semantic consistency in the elision of the penultimate vowel (*upadhālopa*) according to *gamahana-* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.98)—are answered. In this regard, some hold that the mention of the *prakṛti* (root) refers merely to its inclusion [in the grammatical system].

For this very reason, in the section *Prakṛtiśca pratijñādṛṣṭāntānuparodhāt* (Brahma Sūtra 1.4.23), they state that the ablative case in the scriptural passage "from which indeed these beings are born" (*yato vā imāni bhūtāni jāyante*) supports Brahman’s status as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world. Others, however, maintain that based on the natural usage [of language]—as in "joy arises from a son"—the word *prakṛti* here refers merely to a cause in general.

And on this view, although the word *yataḥ* in the phrase *yato vā* is a general term, it refers specifically to the form of the material cause (*upādāna*), according to the principle of the sixth book of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*: "The goat [is meant] because of the wording of the mantra" (Jaimini 6.8.31). For the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is heard in the text: "May I myself become many. This coreferentiality occurs in four ways: in error, in sublation, in non-difference, and in identity (*tādātmya*). In the present context, it is identity; for identity is defined as having a non-different existence despite being distinct, or as a specific relation based on ignorance (*āvidyaka*), as is clear in the *Uttaramīmāṃsā* (Brahmasūtra 1.4.31).

*bhuvaḥ prabhavaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.31). The source (*prabhava*) of that which originates from the earth (*bhū*) is treated as before [i.e., the fifth case ending is used]. *Gaṅgā prabhavati himavataḥ* ("The Gaṅgā originates from the Himalayas"). *Vitastā prabhavati kaśmīrebhyaḥ*. [In this context,] the root *tasu* (meaning "to perish," Dhp. 1213) takes the suffix *kta* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). *Vigatā tā* [becomes] *vitastā*; the meaning is "not subject to drying up. Here, the verb *prabhavati* functions in the sense of the operation of the object (*karmavyāpāra*), meaning "it manifests" (*prakāśate*). Starting from *bhītrārthānām* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.25), this series of seven sūtras has been rejected in the Bhāṣya.

For instance: "He fears the thieves" means he turns away from them out of fear. "He protects" means he causes [others] to turn away from thieves by means of guarding them. "He is defeated" means he turns away due to exhaustion. "He wards off" means he causes [someone] to turn back by obstructing their activity. "He hides" means he turns away by means of concealment. "He studies" means he perceives the sound emerging from the teacher. Even in the case of "the manifestation of the world arises from Brahman," it likewise departs from that [source].

The disappearance [of the fruit] is to be understood by relying on worldly convention, as in the expression "the fruit from the tree. In the case of "it originates" (*prabhavati*) as well, the meaning is emergence preceded by coming into being.

In this regard, the following must be said: even if one were to somehow justify the stated usages by relying on the function [of the verb] in its own sense as qualified by meanings such as cessation, liberation, or another state (*dhātu*), the employment of the genitive case remains unavoidable when the primary meaning is foregrounded—just as in the expression "he hears the actor" (*naṭasya śṛṇoti*). For indeed, no distinction can be asserted between the teacher and the actor regarding the aspect of activity conducive to the action [of hearing]. Furthermore, a rejection [of the rule] based on the "Brahma-weapon" of non-expression (*anabhidhāna*) is not particularly convincing.

And thus, the *vārttika* beginning with "jugupsā-virāma" (*kātantra-vyākaraṇa*) must also necessarily be commenced. Consequently, the view of the Sūtras and the Vārttikas alone is authoritative here; this remains correct until such time as it is sublated. Likewise, the mention of the technical names (*saṃjñin*) in rules such as "the cause of fear that is not endured is *dhruvam*" is meaningful. For even though those respective technical names would apply by virtue of their higher status, when there is a desire to express the remaining relation (*śeṣatva*), the genitive case is desired—as in "one should not eat beans" (*na māṣāṇām aśnīyāt*). Therefore, since the designation of *apādāna* (ablative) would need to be blocked in such instances, it should be stated [that the Vārttika is necessary]. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.24–32)

That which one intends through the object (*karman*) is the recipient (*sampradāna*; Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.32).
