And [in the case of] *abhiniviś-* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.47). This shall be the locus (*ādhāra*) for the preceding root *viś-*; it shall be the object (*karman*). For example: *grāmam abhiniviśate*. "Adherence" (*abhiniveśa*) means insistence; the meaning is that one becomes possessed of that [insistence]. This root is intransitive (*akarmaka*); therefore, the designation of "object" is prescribed here for the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). However, when it has the sense of "entering," [the status of object] is already established. From the rule "In the case of hiring (*parikrayaṇa*), [the agent] is the recipient (*sampradāna*)" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.44), the phrase "optionally" (*anyatarasyām*) is carried over here by the maxim of the frog-leap (*maṇḍūkapluti*).

This is a *vyavasthita-vibhāṣā* (an option restricted by specific conditions). The authority for this is the usage found in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *samartha-sūtra*: "of those who are intent (*abhiniviṣṭānām*) upon these meanings. By this, forms such as *pāpe 'bhiniveśaḥ* ("attachment to sin") are established. In this sūtra, the reason for not placing the word *ni* last—which would have resulted in *alpa-uttara*—is for the purpose of intending the collection [of words] in this specific sequence. Therefore, the form *niviśate yadi śūkaśikhāpade* does not occur here. However, when the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is intended, the accusative case must indeed occur there as well. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.48)

*Upānvadhyāṅvasaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.48): The locus (*ādhāra*) of the root *vas* preceded by these [prefixes] shall be the object (*karma*). Examples: *upavasati*, *anuvasati*, *adhivasati*, or *āvasati* *grāmaṃ senā* ("the army dwells near, along, over, or in the village"). It should be stated that there is a prohibition for the root *vas* when it does not mean "eating" (*aśyarthasya*). The word *artha* here signifies "cessation" (*nivṛtti*). The two genitives (*ṣaṣṭhyau*) are in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*). The meaning of the genitive case is the relationship between the signifier and the signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*). The sense is: "there is no [application of the rule] to that *vas* which signifies the cessation of eating. Example: *grāme upavasati* ("he fasts in the village").

How is it that [the accusative case is used] in the expression “upoṣya rajanīmekām” (“having fasted for one night”)? The accusative will apply by the rule “kālādhvanoḥ” (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.5). How is it that [the locative case is used] in the expression “ekādaśyāṃ na bhuñjīta” (“one should not eat on the eleventh day”)? The case of the grammatical relation (kāraka-vibhakti) will prevail over the case of the secondary word (upapada-vibhakti) by the rule “upapadavibhakteḥ kārakavibhaktirbalīyasī” (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.49).

*The object (*karman*) is that which is most desired by the agent.* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.49). That which is most intensely sought to be attained by the agent shall be designated as the *karman*. It is understood from the context that "what is desired to be attained by means of that very operation through whose substratum [the agent] becomes the agent. Thus, it results in the state of possessing the fruit of the action. For an action is the object of a desire preceded by a desire for the fruit; indeed, the fruit itself is what is most desired. And since that [fruit] is denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*), the object of the desire here—characterized by that [fruit]—is the one to receive the designation. And that [object] is of three kinds. As it has been said:
It is considered to be threefold—as that which is produced (*nirvartya*), that which is modified (*vikārya*), and that which is reached (*prāpya*);
therein, the most desired object (*īpsitatama*) is the *karman*, while another is conceived as fourfold.
That which is obtained through indifference, that which is not desired by the agent,
that which is not designated by other names, and that which has another as its antecedent.
Likewise:
"That which was non-existent comes into being, or that which exists is manifested by birth; that is the *nirvartya* (produced) object.
But the *vikārya* (transformed) object is established as being of two kinds."
Some [destruction] arises from the cutting off of the original nature, like the ashes of wood and so forth;
some arises from the production of another quality, like the transformation of gold and so forth.
That wherein the accomplishment of specific modifications produced by an action is not perceived through either perception or inference is called "attainable" (*prāpya*).

In this regard, an example of the "to-be-produced" (*nirvartya*) is: "He makes a jar. For according to the Vaiśeṣika school, the jar is indeed non-existent when it comes into being; however, according to the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) as held by the Sāṃkhya and others, it is already existent and merely becomes manifest. Thus, there is a distinction between these two definitions. The general definition [of an object], however, consists in its possessing the fruit known as "origination," which is denoted by the verbal root *kṛ* (to do/make). By this, the view that the root *kṛ* signifies "exertion" (*yatna*) is refuted, because [if that were the case], the verb would result in being intransitive, just like the verb *yatate* ("he exerts himself").

Nor can the matter be resolved even by accepting the meaning that extends to making [the object] the domain of speech (*vad-viṣaya*), because it would be simpler to assume the mere production [of the object], and because, since the action resides in the agent (*kartṛ-stha-kriyā*), the status of being treated like the object (*karmavadbhāva*) would fail to be established. In the present case, the destruction of the self, which is the very source (*prakṛti*) of the source, has occurred or come about. For example: "He turns wood into ash. Or, through the production of a different quality (*guṇāntara-utpatti*): "He makes gold into an earring. It should be understood that in these cases, ash and the earring are merely things to be produced (*nirvartyatva*).

[An example of] the [object] reached is: "He sees the sun. That which is thus connected is of two kinds: the odious and the other. There is another [kind] by the rule "and that which is not otherwise mentioned" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.51). And when there is the possibility of other technical designations, there is yet another, such as "and the object of the root *div*" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.43), and so forth. Thus, it is established that the object (*karman*) is of seven types. Here, in the case of the object reached (*prāpya*), although there certainly exists a distinction produced by the action called "being the object of cognition" (*viṣayatā*), for otherwise its status as an object would be untenable.

Nevertheless, it has been stated that no distinction is perceived with respect to a person other than the agent. However, in the case of a product (*vikārya*), such as wood and the like, the question remains: how can it be the substratum for the result denoted by the verbal root? In this regard, the truth is as follows: the status of being the substratum of production is established through the conventional intention to express the non-difference between the material cause (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikṛti*). Alternatively, the meaning is "transforming the wood, he produces ash," just as in the expression "moistening the rice grains, he brings about boiled rice."

This has been explained in the Bhāṣya, beginning with the statement, "The root *pac* has two meanings. In that context, regarding the usage "He cooks rice-grains into porridge," the meaning is: the activity residing in Devadatta which is conducive to both the softening (*viklitti*) residing in the rice-grains and the production (*nirvṛtti*) of the porridge. However, in the case of "He cooks rice-grains," the meaning is "he causes them to soften" (*vikledayati*). In the case of "He cooks porridge," the meaning is "he brings it about by means of softening" (*viklittyā nirvartayati*). And it has been said: "The mere relationship between the two meanings of the verbal root is expressed by the direct denotation (*śruti*); but when [the word] is applied to only one of those two parts, its operation [in expressing the other] does not exist."

Therefore, it is established that *viklitti* (the state of being softened) is connected—either as the object (*karman*) or as the instrument (*karaṇa*), as the case may be—to the action (*bhāvanā*) which is included within the verbal root (*dhātu*) by virtue of being a root-meaning (*dhātutva*). However, it should be noted here: since the action is obtained through the verbal root and the agent (*kartṛ*) is also obtained through words such as "Devadatta," neither the accusative meaning nor the status of being the most desired (*iṣṭatamatva*) and so forth can be the primary referent [of the accusative case], because they are merely contextual adjuncts (*prayogopādhi*) to the usage, just as in the case of roots like *adhi-śīṅ*.

And thus, just as in the case of the [sūtra] *tathāyuktaṃ ca*, here too the meaning is merely the substratum of the result denoted by the verbal root, or simply the thing to be contained (*ādheya*). And that [substratum] connects with the result through non-difference, according to the maxim: "The meaning of a word is that which cannot be obtained otherwise. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of both *tathāyuktatva* (being so connected) and *anīpsitatva* (not being intended) also being denotable meanings, which would contradict all the grammatical authorities (*tāntrika*). If this is the case, let it be simply that "the object (*karman*) is the locus of the result"; what remains for the two sūtras?

To this, the following is the reply: In the case of the expression "he wards off the boy from the fire" (*agner māṇavakaṃ vārayati*), the term *īpsitatama* ("that which is most desired") must first be stated in order to override the designation of the boy as the *apādāna* (ablative). Once that has been stated, the rule *tathāyuktam* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.50) must also be formulated for the purpose of including both the object of aversion (*dveṣya*) and the indifferent (*udāsīna*). However, the mention of the term *anīpsita* ("not desired") can be dispensed with. Furthermore, in such cases, the locus (*ādhāra*) should be expressed by either the agent-case (*kartṛvibhakti*) or the object-case (*karmavibhakti*).

It is established that there is a difference in verbal cognition based on the systematic distinction between connection with the operation (*vyāpāra*) and the result (*phala*). In the case of *kṛt*-derived forms such as "godohanī" (a milking vessel), "paktā" (a cooker), and "pakvaḥ" (cooked), the meaning is the locus (*ādhāra*) itself, because they must conform to the connection with the referent of a noun (*nāmārtha*). However, it should be noted that the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) between the result and the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) is reversed [in these cases].

Pāṇini 1.4.50: *tathāyuktaṃ cānīpsitam* (And that which is not intended [by the agent], though connected with the action in the same way as the most desired object, shall be designated as the object). Even that which is not intended may receive the technical name "object" (*karman*) if it is connected with the action in the same manner as the most desired object. For example: "While going to the village, he approaches the roots of the trees"; "He sees thieves."

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.51) *Akathitaṃ ca* (And that which is unmentioned). A *kāraka* that is not intended to be specified by particular designations such as *apādāna* (ablative) and so forth shall receive the technical name *karman* (object). To prevent over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *naṭasya śṛṇoti* ("he listens to the actor"), an enumeration [of exceptions] must be made: "In the case of the roots *duh*, *yāc*, *rudh*, *prach*, *bhikṣ*, and *ci*, the cause of the employment [is the object], provided it is not already established by another rule."
And that which is connected with the qualities of the verbs *bruvi* (to speak) and *śāsi* (to command) is called *ākīrtita* (indirect narration) by the poet.
It is the settled conclusion that among the roots with two objects, the inclusion of *nī* (to lead), *vah* (to carry), *hṛ* (to take away), and likewise those expressing motion, must be made.

In this case, regarding *prachī*, the substitution of *tu* [for *ch*] by Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.43 (*che ca*) is not applied, because the teaching concerning augments (*āgamaśāsana*) is not invariably mandatory (*anitya*), as in the cases of Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.1.32 (*sanādyantā dhātavaḥ*) and 6.1.77 (*iko yaṇaci*). The term *upayoga* refers to that which is employed—the primary object (*mukhyaṃ karma*) such as milk—and its cause (*nimitta*) is the cow and so forth; that is to say, it is that which is connected with the primary object of verbs such as *duh*. Similarly, for the roots designated as *brū* and *śā*, there is a connection with the factor of action (*kāraka*) known as the quality (*guṇa*) or the object (*karman*); for factors of action exist in relation to the action (*kriyā*).

Because it is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatvāt*). In that context as well, because the object (*karman*) alone is the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*). That which "attaches" (*sacate*), i.e., is connected (*saṃbadhyate*). The root *ṣac* (in the sense of "to join together," *samavāye*; Dhatupatha Bhvadi 997) is marked with the *svarita* accent. However, some read this root along with those that take the *parasmaipada* endings: "ṣaca samavāye, rapa lapa vyaktāyāṃ vāci" (Dhatupatha Bhvadi 998–999). According to that view, one should understand that the root *ṣac* (in the sense of "to serve," *sevane*; Vādi 163), being anudātta, functions in the sense of "joining together" due to the polysemous nature of roots. In either case, the root *ṣac* occurs in the sense of the operation of the object (*karmavyāpāra*) within the verb *saṃbadhnāti*.

For this very reason, the explanation of the meaning of the term *kartṛ* (agent) by means of the term *karman* (object) is not contradictory, just as "the rice is being cooked" (*rādhyaty odanaḥ*) is explained by "the rice is cooked" (*pacyate*). In both cases, there is no difference in the manifestation of the softening (*viklitti*) residing in the rice. The meaning is that the author—the wise author of the Sūtras—did not mention it, and thus it was practiced and employed [by others]. Regarding the phrase "in the case of an original injunction" (*apūrvavidhau*): it means that the domain of the previously mentioned technical designations (*saṃjñā*), such as *apādāna* and so forth, does not exist [there].

Nor should it be argued that there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of this rule regarding the domains of the designations "cause" (*hetu*) and "agent" (*kartṛ*) which are to be mentioned later; for, under the governing principle of "one designation" (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*), the designation "object" (*karmasaṃjñā*) is superseded by the subsequent designations of "cause" and "agent. However, the earlier scholars (*prāñcaḥ*) maintain that the mention of "the preceding" (*pūrva*) is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for anything other than itself; therefore, there is no over-extension regarding the domains of the designations "cause" and "agent" to be mentioned later.

They say that even in the case of the rule *sūtrepyakathitam*, the past tense of the prohibitions (*nodanā*)—which are intended to exclude the mention [of a case]—is not intended to be expressed; just as in the rule *parājerasoḍhaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.26), the status of the ablative (*apādāna*) applies even to that which is not being endured, as in "he will be defeated from his studies" (*adhyayanātparājeṣyate*), so it is here as well. This, however, is questionable, because everything is consistent even according to the literal reading (*yathāśruta*) by the method already stated. Kaiyaṭa maintains that in the verse beginning with *nivahyoḥ*, the term "verbs meaning 'to go'" (*gatyarthānām*) is an elliptical reference (*upalakṣaṇa*) to those verbs mentioned in the subsequent rule, and that by the word *ca*, verbs such as *jayati* ("to conquer") are included. Mādhava also says the same.
The collection [of roots] consists of *jani*, *kṛṣ*, *math*, *muṣ*, *daṇḍ*,
*pac*, *tṛ*, *grah*, as well as *muc*, *arj*, and *dṛp*.

And in the *Kārikā*, it is said: "By the word 'ca' [in the rule], [the agent is included] with the [verbs] *sudhākara* and *sukha*. The detailed explanation of this will be provided later. Here follow the examples in order: *gāṃ dogdhi payaḥ* (He milks the cow for milk). *avinītaṃ vinayaṃ yācate* (He begs discipline from the ill-behaved one). *gāmavaruṇaddhi vrajam* (He shuts the cow in the pen). *māṇavakaṃ panthānaṃ pṛcchati* (He asks the boy the way). *pauravaṃ gāṃ bhikṣate* (He begs a cow from the descendant of Puru). *vṛkṣamavacinoti phalāni* (He gathers fruits from the tree). *māṇavakaṃ dharmaṃ brūte śāsti vā* (He tells or instructs the boy in the Dharma). *ajāṃ nayati grāmam*, *vahati bhāraṃ grāmam*, or *harati bhāraṃ grāmam* (He leads the goat to the village, or carries the load to the village), or *gamayati grāmam* (He causes [the goat] to go to the village), and so forth. *jayateḥ śataṃ jayati devadattam* (He wins a hundred [coins] from Devadatta).

He pulls the branch toward the village. He churns nectar from the ocean of milk. He causes Devadatta to steal a hundred [coins]. He fines Garga a hundred [coins]. He cooks rice grains into boiled rice. He causes the monkeys to cross the ocean. He causes the boy to grasp this. He causes Devadatta to release or abandon his anger. He causes the students to illuminate the meaning of the scriptures.

It might be argued that this designation [of *duh* and other roots as transitive] is based on their meaning and not dependent on their phonetic form (*svarūpa*), because in the *Rājasūya-bhāṣya* of that [Patañjali’s] *Mahābhāṣya*, it is observed that even *cud*, which is a synonym for *pṛcch*, is used with two objects, as in the statement: "I too shall raise this objection, which ought not to be objected to. Likewise, Bhaṭṭi says:
"He spoke these significant words loudly to Mārīca, who was standing firm in battle and smiling," and Kālidāsa also says:
"Even the mountain, as if out of affection, spoke those very same words loudly to the protector of the earth.
And Bhāravi says: "The noble-minded king was addressed with these noble words by Dvaipāyana."

And thus, since *bhikṣ* has the sense of "seeking," it is established that *yāc* also [falls under this rule], because they have the same meaning, as in the example: "He begs a cow from the descendant of Puru" (*pauravaṃ gāmarthayate*). If it is asked, "Why then is there a separate mention of *yāc*?"—to this they reply: here, *yācati* has the sense of "entreaty" (*anunaya*). One entreats for humility; the meaning is that one seeks to persuade for the sake of humility. Let it be, then, that only *yāc* is mentioned.

If it is argued that [the rule] is established even for *bhikṣ* because it has multiple meanings, we say no; for, relying on the view that "there is a difference in words due to a difference in meaning," only the sense of "begging" (*anunaya*) is intended here by the root *pāci*. For this very reason, the inclusion of the root *nī* does not render the sense of "begging" redundant. Others hold that the separate mention of *bhikṣ* is for the sake of clarity. As for what Mādhava and others have stated—that the root *pac* is included by means of the particle *ca*—that is due to a difference in their respective opinions.

Accordingly, in the commentary on the vārttika “*duhipacyorbahulaṃ sakarmakayoḥ*” (Pāṇini 3.1.87) under the sūtra “*karmavat karmaṇā*” (Pāṇini 3.1.87), Kaiyaṭa has clearly demonstrated that the root *pac* (to cook) is transitive with two objects (*dvikarmaka*). As for the Bhāṣya passage under the sūtra “*karturīpsitatamam*” (Pāṇini 1.4.49) stating that “*paci* has two meanings” (*dvyarthaḥ paciḥ*), that is according to another view (*matāntara*). Otherwise, since the usage “*taṇḍulānodanaṃ pacati*” (he cooks rice into porridge) would be established exactly as it is heard, what is the point of this needless trouble?

For this very reason, if the word *akathita* (unmentioned) were taken to mean "that which is not primary," then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the hand and the bronze vessel in the sentence "He milks milk with his hand into a bronze vessel. However, the rules for the instrumental (*karaṇa*) and locative (*adhikaraṇa*) cases provide their own scope; for those cases do not apply there, because [the application of the rule] is restricted to the specific list of roots beginning with *duh*. Thus, there is no contradiction between the earlier and later statements of Haradatta—one who explains the *akathita* sūtra and another who asserts that roots like *pac* have two objects—since they are based on different philosophical positions.

For this very reason, in his analysis of the verbal root *pac* (to cook), Mādhava cited the usage "he cooks rice into porridge" (*taṇḍulānodanaṃ pacati*) as an example of a verb with two objects (*dvikarmaka*). This is the general direction of the argument. Similarly, many did not accept that the root *grah* (to seize/to marry) has two objects. For this very reason [it is said]: "First, the father, the best among those who know the meaning of things, caused him to grasp the meaning of the family sciences; afterwards, he caused him to grasp the hands of the king's daughters."

Thus, regarding the first half of the verse by Kālidāsa, they explained it by taking the root *grah* (to seize) as having the sense of *duh* (to milk), and by applying the rule *agati-buddhi-* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.52)—which prescribes that the agent of a primary verb becomes the object of its causative form—they construed the word *tam* [as the object]. Then, in the second half, they explained it by changing the case ending of the word *tena*. For this very reason, [the following verse is cited]:
"Janaka caused him to take up that bow with which the wielder of the Pināka had afflicted the city of the Daityas;
desiring to test the strength of his arms, the joy of the Raghus, smiling, broke it."

Thus the usage of Bhaṭṭi has been explained in the *Jayamaṅgalā*: "He caused [the Lord] to grasp" means that by means of this bow, the Blessed One performed the burning of Tripura; that is, he compelled [him]. And this is appropriate, because since it would be improper to state a command to the illustrious Lord of the Raghus, it is necessary to present his very nature [as one who acts spontaneously]. By this [it is meant]: "The Mountain was indeed unable to make the God of Gods accept his daughter when she was not asked for."

Thus it has been explained, because the root *grah* (to seize) has the sense of cognition (*buddhi*). Alternatively, the intention is that this is established because the status of being a two-object verb (*dvikarmaka*) for the roots *iṣ* and *śak* when used in conjunction with the suffix *tuman* is settled in the *Bhāṣya*. However, on the view that accepts *grah* as having two objects, the form "jāyāpratigrahitagandhamālyām" (Rgveda 2.1) would not be established; for in that case, according to the rule "ṇyante kartuśca karmaṇaḥ," the suffix *kta* would apply to the object in its causal state—the cow—which is the object of the prompted action (*prayojya*).

Furthermore, in the analysis (vigraha) "she by whom the husband has caused his wife to accept perfumes and garlands," there could not even be a *bahuvrīhi* compound, because it is established in the Bhāṣya that the remainder [of the compound] must consist of three factors (*trikat*). Even if such a compound were admitted, the transformation into the masculine form (*puvadbhāva*) would be difficult to obtain. According to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, the analysis is: "she by whom perfumes and garlands have been caused to be accepted. The meaning is: she who is the agent of that act of accepting which has perfumes and garlands as its object and which is the domain of an instigation residing in the wife.

This is because the formation of a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) is postulated precisely by including the meaning of another word within the compound and through the reversal of the roles of qualifier and qualified, as in the case of *māsajāta* ("born after a month") and similar examples. However, in the view that maintains syntactic dependence (*vyapekṣā*), there must always be the postulation of a distinct grammatical derivation for a *bahuvrīhi* that does not involve the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) meaning. For instance, the meaning of *prāptodaka* is "that which has become the object of the reaching performed by water"; *ūḍharatha* means "the agent of the carrying whose object is a chariot"; and *upahṛtapaśu* means "the recipient of the offering whose object is an animal."

‘Uddhṛtaudanaḥ’ (rice that has been removed) is the source (apādāna) of the removal whose object is the rice; ‘vīrapuruṣakaḥ’ (a place where brave men stay) is the locus (adhikaraṇa) of the staying whose agents are brave men—such is the direction [of the analysis].

It might be argued: "Let there be the status of having two objects (*dvikarmakatā*) when the [apādāna] and other [kārakas] are not intended to be expressed; however, when they are intended to be expressed, forms such as *jāyāpratigrāhita* will be established. This is not so. For, by the word *ca* ("and") in the rule *harateśca*, although verbs such as *jayati* (which are conjoined with *harati*) fall under the scope of the *akathita* sūtra, the status of being the object (*karmatā*) for the agent of the *aṇ* (causative) is nevertheless accepted for those [verbs] conjoined by the phrase *tathaiva ca*. This is because of their association with verbs meaning "to go" (*gatyartha*). For this very reason, [verbs such as] *tārayati* and others are included separately.

And this is appropriate, because if the agency of the one who causes the grasping (*grahaṇakartṛtva*) were not intended, the causative suffix *ṇic* would be impossible in the absence of a prompter (*prayojaka*). Nor should it be argued that the mention of *dīp-* [in the rule] is redundant, since the status of the agent as the object (*karmatva*) would be established in the *ṇic*-form even without it simply by virtue of its being intransitive (*akarmaka*) in the non-causative (*aṇ*) state; for that mention is purposeful when applied to the root ending in *ṇic*. The meaning is: "The disciples illuminate the truth; he prompts them."

Now, one might object: since *tyāja* (the root *tyaj*) is included [in the list of roots ending in long vowels], forms such as *tyājitaiḥ phalam utkhātaiḥ* ("by those who were made to abandon the fruit, being uprooted") and *muktāhāraṃ ciraparicitaṃ tyājito daivagatyā* ("made to abandon his long-accustomed pearl necklace by the turn of fate") are indeed established. Nevertheless, this contradicts the works of Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, and others, which state that the meaning is "he causes the cow to abandon its milk. To this we reply: even though the cow is the object (*karman*) when the specific distinction [of the agent] is intended, there is no obstacle to its being the agent (*kartṛ*) when the intention is to express agency.

It might be argued that all this is established by the two sūtras: "The object most desired by the agent is the *karman*" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.49) and "Likewise, that which is not desired but is connected with the action in the same way [is also called *karman*]" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.50). For instance, just as the meaning of *pac* (to cook) is the act of moistening subordinate to the softening [of the rice], that of *ruh* (to grow) is the act of causing to bend downward, and that of *bhid* (to split) is the act of causing to divide into two, so too the meaning of *duh* (to milk) is the act of causing to abandon subordinate to the act of abandoning; and the meanings of *yāc* (to beg) and *bhikṣ* (to beg) are the acts of causing to give.

One should also request the acceptance [of a gift] from the root *yāc*; the causing to enter or the placing [of someone] is from *rudh*; the making known is from *pracch*; the releasing is from *ci*; the replying is from *brū*; but its specific variety (reproving) is from *śās*, and so forth. And thus, it is clear that the cow and other such entities possess the status of being the locus (*āśrayatva*) for the operation denoted by the verbal root. For this very reason, the statement in the Bhāṣya on the *Akaḍāra* sūtra—"In the case of 'gāṃ dogdhi' (he milks the cow), the designation of object (*karman*) applies because it is subsequent [to the designation of ablative]"—is consistent.

Under the view that the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) consists of five factors, this [example] applies when there is a simultaneous intention to express both the state of being a limit (*avadhitva*) and the state of being the locus of the result (*phalāśrayatva*). The meaning is thus: an instigation residing in the cow (*gopanisthā preraṇā*) which has as its object the activity conducive to flowing that resides in the cow which serves as the limit (*avadhibhūtā yā gaus tanniṣṭhaḥ kṣaraṇānukūlavyāpāraḥ*).

To this it is replied: this sūtra is intended to set aside the genitive case when there is an intention to express the object (*karman*) as a subordinate factor (*śeṣatva*), as in the example "one should not eat beans" (*na māṣāṇām aśnīyāt*). However, when one intends to express only the status of the ablative (*apādānatva*), the fifth case (*pañcamī*) alone occurs. But if the cow is a qualifier of the milk, the genitive certainly does occur; thus, there is no fault whatsoever. Consequently, it is established here that the meaning of the second case (*dvitīyā*) is merely the relation denoted by the genitive. Now, this is considered: regarding verbs with two objects (*dvikarmaka*), do the affixes *kṛtya*, *kta*, and those having the sense of *khala* prescribed for the object apply to the primary object or the secondary one? On this point, the Bhāṣya states:

Regarding verbs that take two objects, they say that the *l*-affixes (*la-kāraka*) and others denote the principal object; for roots such as *duh* (to milk), etc., they denote the non-principal object; and in the case of causative (*ṇyanta*) forms, they denote both the agent and the object. Thus [it is said].

The word "in denotation" (*abhidhāne*) is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. Here, by the phrase "of those with two objects" (*dvikarmaṇām*), three verbs—*kṛṣ*, *nī*, and *vah*—are intended, as these are conjoined by the word "and" (*ca*) [in the rule]; for the specific treatment of others will be stated later. Similarly, by the phrase "of *duh* and so forth" (*duhyādīnām*), those included in the verse are meant, as well as those conjoined by the word "and," such as *daṇḍ* and others which take the causative suffix *ṇic* without an external cause (*ahetumaṇṇyantāḥ*). By the term "causative" (*ṇyanta*), however, those included in the rule beginning with "motion and so forth" (*gatyādi-sūtra*) are meant, as well as those conjoined by the word "and," such as *tṛ* and others.

In that context, the meaning is that when the object of the root (*aṇau karma*) is expressed, the *l*-affixes and so forth [occur]. Even there, according to another opinion, [the rule applies] to roots whose objects are cognition (*buddhi*), consumption (*pratyavasāna*), or sound (*śabda*), with respect to the secondary object (*guṇakarma*). Thus says the Bhāṣya: "When [the primary object] is mentioned (*kathita*)—that is, when it is not expressed (*anabhihita*)—there is the rule for the suffix *am* (the accusative case); however, the rule for the *l*-affixes and so forth applies to the secondary object (*guṇakarma*) when the suffix *saP* follows. Furthermore, in the case of roots involving fixed states (*dhruva*) or effort (*ceṣṭita*), [the rule applies] to the secondary object (*guṇe*). Remember this statement of the one of no small intelligence."* *Note: This verse is traditionally attributed to Patañjali’s Mahābhāṣya, though its precise location remains a subject of scholarly debate.*

The first section [of this commentary] is intended to refute the opinion of certain grammarians (*ekīyamata*) that when the primary object (*pradhānakarman*) is expressed by the *l*-suffixes (verbal terminations) and so forth, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used for the secondary object (*guṇakarman*). This is because the phrase "this genitive is prescribed" implies that this is the view of another, not his own. In the group of roots beginning with *duh* (to milk), which includes those mentioned in the rule on motion (*gatyādisūtra*), the *l*-suffixes etc. are used for the secondary object. Regarding the term "secondary object": since human effort in the case of *duh* and other such verbs is directed toward the milk and so forth, the cow and other such [entities] are called "secondary."

In the causative (*ṇyanta*), however, the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka*) is primary by virtue of its verbal expression, while the operation of the one being instigated (*prayojya*) is secondary; therefore, it is called an "object" (*karman*) based on that [secondary] property. [The rule applies to] roots denoting motion (*gatyartha*) when conjoined with *dhruva* (a fixed point), and those denoting intransitive action (*akarmaka*) when conjoined with *ceṣṭita* (volitional effort). In these cases, the object is the non-primary factor (*aguṇa*). One should not argue that in the case of roots meaning cognition (*buddhi*), consumption (*pratyavasāna*), or having sound as their object (*śabdakarman*), the designation would apply only to the secondary object (*guṇakarman*) because the rule *kartuśca* is sublated by the rule *saparaḥ*. This is because the Bhāṣya statement *apara āha* indicates that this is a different opinion. Here is the summary: [Roots meaning] cognition, consumption, and those having sound as their object—these take the agent (*kartṛ*) as the object in the causative. Others say that for roots meaning cognition and consumption, the agent becomes the object [only] when there is no other [object]. For roots having sound as their object, both [the agent and the primary object] become objects. For others, the agent becomes the object in the causative. For roots meaning motion and intransitives, the non-primary [factor] becomes the object. For others, the agent becomes the object in the causative. This is the summary.
The verbs *duh* (to milk) and others take the secondary object (*gauṇa-karman*), while *nī*, *hṛ*, *kṛṣ*, and *vah* take the primary object (*pradhāna-karman*);
however, in the case of verbs meaning "cognition" (*buddhi*), "consumption" (*pratyavasāna*), or those having sound as their object (*śabda-karman*), it is by choice (*icchayā*).
For other roots ending in the causative suffix *ṇic*, when the object is the prompted agent (*prayojyakarman*), the use of the present participle (*la*),
the gerundives (*kṛtya*), the past passive participles (*kta*), and words having the sense of the suffix *khal* is established here by those who have mastered the Mahābhāṣya.

In that regard, for roots such as *nī* ("to lead"), the connection with the primary object (*pradhānakarman*) is internal (*antaraṅga*); for roots such as *duh* ("to milk"), however, it is the opposite. Therefore, in those cases, the restriction is established by logic (*nyāyasiddha*). Everything else, however, is based on explicit scriptural statement (*vācanika*). The examples in order are: *gaur duhyate payaḥ* (The cow is milked for milk). *dohyā*, *dugdhā*, *sudohā* (the cow is to be milked, has been milked, is easy to milk). *ajā grāmaṃ nīyate* (The goat is led to the village). *neyā*, *nītā*, *sunayā* (the goat is to be led, has been led, is easy to lead). *bodhyate māṇavakaṃ dharmaḥ*, or *māṇavako dharmam* (Dharma is being taught to the boy; alternatively, the boy is taught Dharma). *devadatto grāmaṃ gamyate*, *gamayitavyaḥ*, *gamitaḥ*, *sugamaḥ* (Devadatta is being made to go to the village; he is to be made to go, has been made to go, is easy to go to).

As for the statement in the *Kaumudī* that, having listed the roots beginning with *duh* and those beginning with *nī* in two groups by means of the rule *duhy-acy-artheti* etc., it is said that the *nī*-group is primary (*mukhya*) while the *duh*-group is secondary (*gauṇa*): therein, the inclusion of *grah* is indeed without foundation. Furthermore, the example "He seized Indra [by the] tree" (*jagrāha dyutaruṃ śakram*) is incorrect. As for the other roots, however, their inclusion in the list has the sole purpose of indicating their status as having two objects (*dvikarmaka*). Both instances of the word "etc. (*ādi*)—in *nyādayaḥ* and *duhyādayaḥ*—should be explained according to the sense of "type" (*prakāra*), so as not to contradict the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

For if it were taken according to the literal sense, [the application of the suffix] would occur with respect to the primary [referent] in the case of *daṇḍin* and *muṣin*. And in that case, the Bhāṣya statement, "Let the Gargas be fined one hundred," would be contradicted. For here, "one hundred" (*śatam*) is the primary element; this is because of the supplementary statement (vākyaśeṣa): "The Gargas, being petitioners, become [possessors of] gold through the king. Furthermore, here the word *daṇḍin* has the sense of "one who is to be seized" (*grahaṇārtha*), not "one who inflicts punishment" (*nigrahārtha*). Precisely for this reason, the completion of the sentence occurs with respect to the collective group (*samudāya*), since it is possible for the primary element not to recur according to the subordinate element (*guṇa*). Similarly, in the case of *manthin*, [the suffix] would apply to the primary [referent]. However, it is desired [that it apply] to the secondary [referent]. And thus says Bhāravi:
By whom the ocean was churned for the nectar by gods and asuras, its waters cast aside and the abode of the nagas shattered. Thus it is said.

For here, nectar (*amṛta*) is primary as the intended object, whereas the ocean (*ambunidhi*) is secondary. As for the argument that others, having said "according to one's preference," cited the example: "The cowherd girl was made to laugh by the Infinite One," that too is incorrect, because of the established rule: "In the case of a causative (*ṇyanta*), the agent [of the causative] is also the object [of the base verb]. Alternatively, Bopadeva reads the root *kṛ* in the sense of "cognition" (*vijñāna*) in the curādi class as being ātmanepada; this is an example of that, since both options have been established regarding roots meaning "to understand. As for what Śrīharṣa employs: "She whose moon was awakened by the intense entreaties of the child who was obsessed with catching the swan of her own play... [this is consistent].

That is to be considered: since the moon was requested by the child (*śiśunā*), the *kta* suffix is applied to a non-primary element, and thus a *bahuvrīhi* compound is inappropriate. For he will state later: "And this [suffix] occurs in the sense of a case other than the first. Nor is the *kta* suffix applied to the moon, because it is stated that "the *druh*-class [verbs take the *kta* suffix] when the object is non-primary. Precisely for this reason, Kālidāsa writes: "Having approached him while he was wearing his side-locks (*kākapakṣadhara*), he was entreated. The genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is obtained separately from both the subordinate and the primary objects, just like the accusative (*dvitīyā*), because there is no distinction; as in the examples: "the leader of the village" (*grāmasya netā*) and "the owner of the cow" (*goḥ svāmī*).
Where two distinct levels are expressed by a single word,
it is not logical for one alone to be dependent upon the other.
"The genitive case is restricted to the primary [substance], whereas with respect to a quality, it may occur in both ways";
thus says Goṇikāputra, according to the Bhāṣya, regarding the two types of qualities.

The sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is obligatory for the principal object (*pradhānakarman*) of the verb *netṛ* (as in *netāśvasya strughnasya* or *strughnam*), but according to the statement of the author of the Bhāṣya, it is optional for the secondary object (*guṇakarman*). This is the established position. Now, one might ask: since intransitive verbs lack an inherent object (*prākṛtakarman*), how can they possess two objects (*dvikarmakatā*)? Consequently, the suffix should apply to the object of the causative meaning (*ṇyartha*), as in "the boy is made to sit" (*āsyate māṇavakaḥ*). Thus, the usage *māsam* [as an object] would be inconsistent.

If it is argued that the inclusion of the word *dhruva* (fixed) in the verse “*dhruvaceṣṭitayuktiṣu vāpyaguṇaḥ*” is redundant, we say: no. This is because the *Mahābhāṣya* states: “Time (*kāla*), state (*bhāva*), and distance to be traversed (*adhvagantavya*) are designated as objects (*karma*) for intransitive verbs (*akarmaṇām*), as is place (*deśa*) for intransitives. Thus, “distance to be traversed” refers to what is to be gone over, as in “to be gone today. The word *gantavya* is placed at the end [of the compound] due to its being an irregular formation (*nipātana*). Only those well-known in the world as distances to be traversed with fixed measurements—such as a *krośa* or a *yojana*—are intended to be included.

Therefore, the expression *adhaavanam svapiti* ("he sleeps for the duration of running") does not occur. One says *māsam āste* ("he sits for a month"), *godoham āste* ("he sits for the duration of milking a cow"). The meaning is that he sits for as long a time as it takes to milk a cow. One says *krośam āste* ("he sits for the distance of a *krośa*") or *kurūn svapiti* ("he sleeps throughout the Kuru country"). In the view that any measure whatsoever (*janyamātram*) can serve as a temporal adjunct (*kālopādhi*), although [the duration of] milking a cow and so forth are established as being time, they are nevertheless mentioned separately because in common worldly usage, only things such as a "month" and the like are well-known as being of that nature.

Kaiyaṭa maintains that by the word *deśa* (place), specific collections of villages such as Kuru, Pañcāla, and so forth are understood; therefore, it should be noted that rules such as *adhiśīṅsthāsām* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.46) are not rendered redundant. However, the rule *kālādhvanoratyantasaṃyoge* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.5) must indeed be initiated for the sake of qualities (*guṇa*) and substances (*dravya*), as in: *krośaṃ kuṭilā* ("crooked for the distance of a *krośa*") and *māsaṃ guḍadhānāḥ* ("molasses and parched grain [consumed] throughout a month"). It is also for the sake of transitive verbs (*sakarmaka*), as in: *māsaṃ vedam adhīte* ("he studies the Veda for a month"). Alternatively, [the roots] *ās*, etc., function with respect to the pervasion (*vyāpti*) preceded by that [time or space].

Thus, it is established by the general rule itself, since the meaning is that "one pervades a month by means of sitting. Accordingly, the Bhāṣya on the second [book] states: "This action is indeed primitive (prākṛta). Nor does this lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) even to transitive verbs, because the aforementioned method is accepted only for intransitive verbs in accordance with the observed usage (lakṣya). And it has been said: "In connection with all intransitive verbs, the status of being an object (karmatva) arises for time, state, distance, and location through their association with other actions that are internally contained within them."

Helārāja, however, says: even in the case of transitive verbs, forms such as *māsam odanam pacati* ("he cooks rice for a month") certainly occur; it is for this very reason that [the rule] was stated by all [grammarians] as "by all [verbs]. As for the phrase "by intransitives," it is not intended to be restrictive. Kaiyaṭa also holds this view. On this position, although the accusative would apply to the mat and so forth in the example *māsam āste kaṭe* ("he sits on a mat for a month"), Helārāja maintains that the status of being the object of pervasion (*vyāpana-karman*) belongs only to time and the like, and not to the mat and so forth. In this matter, non-usage (*anabhidhāna*) is the refuge; or rather, it should be understood as being indicated by rules such as *adhiśīṅ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.46).
And here, in this grammatical operation, regarding both the object and the state (bhāva), when the L-affix is applied, both forms—*davadattanāsyate māsau* and *māsam*—are desired.

It might be argued: "Since there is the rule *bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.69), how can [the suffix] *bhaviṣya* occur after a root that has *māsa* and the like as its object? It is said in reply: By the term *akarmakebhyaḥ*, the internal (*antaraṅga*) substance-object (*dravyakarman*) is excluded, but not the external (*bahiraṅga*) time-object (*kālādikarman*). However, regarding the word *karmaṇi* [in Pāṇini 3.4.69], because the view of individuals (*vyaktipakṣa*) is adopted, even when the internal [substance-object] is absent, the prohibition is not contradicted even with respect to the external time-object and so forth; for the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that the application of the two views—of the universal (*jāti*) or the individual—is determined according to the requirements of the linguistic examples (*lakṣyānurodha*). And it was stated by Hari:

"Because of its distinction from the properties of substance—such as power (*śakti*), means of knowledge (*pramā*), and number—the connection with time applies to actions; therefore, the prior connection belongs to the substance and the object.
And: "Therefore, when a verbal root is connected with those objects which are substances, it becomes intransitive (*akarmaka*);
thus it serves as the cause for the [application of] *la*-suffixes in the sense of the object (*karman*) and the abstract state (*bhāva*)."
By this,
the usage of Śrī Harṣa— “*ṣaṣṭimāghamaghābhidhāni yamunā gaṅgaughasaṅge yayā*”— is explained.
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.52):

*gatibuddhipratyavasānārthaśabdakarmākarmakāṇām aṇau kartā sa ṇau*. For verbs whose meanings involve motion (*gati*), cognition (*buddhi*), or consumption (*pratyavasāna*), as well as those having sound as their object (*śabdakarman*) or being intransitive (*akarmaka*), that which is the agent (*kartṛ*) in the non-causative (*aṇau*) becomes the object (*karman*) in the causative (*ṇau*). This is a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*): if [the status of] being made the object by the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇij-artha*) occurs, it occurs only for [verbs] whose meanings involve motion and so forth. Consequently, in the example "Devadatta causes Yajñadatta to cook" (*pācayati devadatto yajñadattena*), since the previously established designation of agent (*kartṛ-sañjñā*) remains uncontradicted with respect to the one to be impelled (*prayojya*), the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is established.
And it is said:
"Because of its independence in the performance of the action, [the agent], having entered into the state of being an object (*karman*) due to the instigation (*preṣaṇa*),
is designated by its own grammatical property (*svadharma*) because of the restrictive rule regarding the technical term 'object'."

The meaning is that [the agent] is expressed by the third case (instrumental) through its own function (*svadharma*). In the example "he causes the boy to go to the village" (*gamayati māṇavakaṃ grāmam*), the meaning is: one who is the locus of the activity conducive to that going which has the village as its object.

A prohibition must be stated for the roots *nī* (to lead) and *vah* (to carry). Although the meaning of these two roots is "causing to reach" (*prāpaṇa*) and not "going" (*gati*), nevertheless, since "going" is also included within the scope of their expressed meaning by virtue of being a specific instance of it, the prohibition is stated on the grounds that [the rule] would otherwise apply. One causes Devadatta to lead or carry a load: *nāyayati* or *vāhayati bhāraṃ devadattena*. The prohibition applies only to *vah* when the agent is not the driver (*aniyantṛkartṛka*). The resultant meaning is that it must be stated that when the agent is a driver (*niyantṛkartṛka*), the person being prompted is the object (*karman*).

The draft animals carry [the load], the charioteer causes the draft animals to carry [it] for the rider. However, in the rule *yā prāpaṇe* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.49), the meaning of the word *prāpaṇa* is simply motion (*gati*), because the cognitions of the meanings of *yāti* and *gacchati* are identical. Therefore, in expressions such as *kālaṃ pācayati* ("he causes the time to cook"), the status of the object (*karmatā*) for the prompted agent (*prayojya*) should be understood. By the inclusion of the term *budh-artha* ("having the sense of 'to know'"), only those roots denoting knowledge in general are included, and not those denoting its specific varieties, such as *smarati* ("he remembers") and so on. For this very reason, a supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) will be made for the roots *śru* ("to hear") and *dṛś* ("to see").

He teaches the Dharma to the young student (*māṇavaka*). "Consuming" (*pratyavasāna*) means eating. He feeds, he causes to eat, the young student rice-gruel (*odana*). It should be stated that there is a prohibition regarding *ādī* (to eat) and *khādī* (to chew): he causes the boy to eat, he causes him to chew, the food.

A prohibition must be stated regarding the root *bhakṣ* when it does not mean "to injure. The rule [prohibiting the *ṇic* suffix] applies to the causative (*hetu-ṇic*) form; since this prohibition concerns that which is not a primary *ṇic*, it follows by proximity that it specifically targets that context. Consequently, because the possibility of the suffix arises even for the *cur*-class causative *bhakṣayati*, a supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) is provided to prohibit it there as well. Example: *bhakṣayaty annaṃ baṭunā* ("He causes the boy to eat the food"). Why specify "when it does not mean 'to injure'"? Consider: *bhakṣayanti balīvardāḥ sasyam* ("The oxen eat the grain") or *bhakṣayati balīvardān sasyam* ("He causes the oxen to eat the grain"). Here, the act of eating involves injury to the grain, so the prohibition does not apply.

The injury (*hiṃsā*) of barley standing in the field while being consumed should be understood [as such], because it is admitted that they possess sentience (*caitanyatva*) in that state. Those for whom sound is the object of the action are "those whose object is sound" (*śabdakarmāṇaḥ*). However, here the word *karman* does not refer to the action (*kriyā*), as it does in the rule "In the case of the agent when there is a reciprocal action" (*Aṣṭādhyāyī* 1.3.14); for, although one could have said "motion, cognition, consumption, and those whose meaning is sound" (*gatibuddhipratyavasānaśabdārtha*), the word *karman* is mentioned separately from the word *artha*. [Example: "He causes the boy to study the Veda" (*adhyāpayati māṇavakaṃ vedam*).
An addition [to the rule] should be made for the roots *jalpati* and others: Devadatta causes his son to chatter, causes him to lament, or causes him to speak.

There should also be an extension [of the rule] to the root *dṛś* (to see). [Example: *darśayati hariṃ bhaktān* ("He causes the devotees to see Hari"). Although this is already established because *dṛś*, when it refers to cognition in general, has the sense of "understanding" (*budh*), nevertheless, it is not established when it refers to a specific kind of cognition; therefore, this extension is undertaken. However, in the case of *śrāvayati ślokaṃ devadattam* ("He causes Devadatta to hear the verse"), it is established because the object is sound (*śabda*). But if the rule were explained as "verbs whose action is sound," then an extension would be required for the root *śru* (to hear), and a prohibition would have to be made for the roots *hvayati* (to call) and *krandati* (to cry out).

[The rule applies] when one causes Devadatta to bathe or causes him to weep. However, for the root *dṛś* ("to see"), it should be added that the rule applies in both ways (whether transitive or intransitive). For the root *śabdāy* ("to sound"), it should be prohibited in both ways; for even though it is intransitive here, there is still the possibility [of the rule applying], because the object characterized by "sound" is included within it and because it lacks connection with any other object. Thus: *śabdāyayati devadattena*. By the mention of "intransitive," however, those roots are included for which no distinct object such as time (*kāla*) etc. is possible, but not those whose objects are merely not intended to be expressed.

By this rule, the status of the object (*karmatva*) is established in cases such as *māsam āsayati devadattam* ("he causes Devadatta to sit for a month"), whereas it does not occur in cases such as *devadattena pācayati* ("he causes Devadatta to cook"). The same applies to the rule *gatyarthākarmaka-* (Pāṇini 1.4.52). For this very reason, the suffix *kta* is not applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) after roots like *pac* ("to cook") and *dā* ("to give") when their objects are not intended to be expressed; otherwise, in the sense of "one who has cooked" or "one who has given," the forms would have been *pakvaḥ* and *dattaḥ*.

In the sūtra *laḥ karmaṇi* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.4.69), however, there is the inclusion of both those roots whose objects are not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣitakarman*) and those for whom an object is impossible (*asambhavadkarman*). For this very reason, there is no contradiction between the earlier and later statements; for while [Pāṇini] states in this sūtra that the *l*-affixes do not occur in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) for roots whose objects are not intended to be expressed, Haradatta—stating under the rule *ṇeraṇau* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.67) that in the example "it is cooked here" (*neha pacyate*), the *l*-affix occurs in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*)—is merely presenting a difference of opinion (*matabheda*). This is the direction of the argument. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.53)

*hṛkroranyatarasyām* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.53). The analysis of the compound is *hā ca krā ca* ("the roots *hṛ* and *kṛ*"), or alternatively *huśca kruśca* ("the roots *hu* [for *hṛ*] and *kṛ*"). In these two cases, that which is the agent (*kartṛ*) when the root is not preceded by the causative suffix (*ṇic*) may optionally become the object (*karman*) when the root is in the causative form. This rule was formulated by the author of the Vārttika as an "option in both ways" (*ubhayatra-vibhāṣā*) within the context of the *na veti-vibhāṣā* sūtras. To illustrate: in the example *abhyavahārayati māṇavakam odanam māṇavakena vā* ("He causes the boy to eat the rice, or he eats the rice with the boy"), this option applies because the root has the sense of "eating" (*pratyavasāna*), which would otherwise trigger the rule [making the agent the object]. In the example *vikurvate chātrāḥ, vikārayati chātrān chātrair vā* ("The students transform themselves, or he causes the students to transform themselves"), this option applies because the root is intransitive (*akarmaka*), which would otherwise trigger the rule [making the agent the object]. In other instances, however, this option does not apply.

It should be stated that for the roots *abhivādi* and *dṛś*, the Ātmanepada is optional. For *abhivādayati*, the option is not otherwise established; however, for *dṛś*, it is established either because its meaning includes "cognition" (*buddhi*) and so forth, or by means of an addition to the rule. *Abhivādayati guruṃ devadattaḥ* (Devadatta salutes the teacher), or *abhivādayate guruṃ devadatto devadattena vā* (Devadatta salutes the teacher, or [the teacher salutes himself] through Devadatta). The Ātmanepada here is due to the rule *ṇicaśca* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.74). But in the Parasmaipada: *abhivādayati guruṃ devadattena*. *Darśayate rājānaṃ bhṛtyān bhṛtyair vā* (The king shows himself to the servants, or [shows them] by means of the servants).

In the view that there is no notion of an object (*karmasaṃjñābhāvapakṣe*), because of the absence of another object, the ancient grammarians maintain that the *ātmanepada* suffix occurs by the rule "ṇeraṇau" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.67), whereas in other cases it occurs by "ṇicaśca" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.74). However, in reality, only "ṇicaśca" is appropriate. It has been demonstrated in that very [work] that "ṇeraṇau" does not apply here, because of the difference in the usage expressed by the *ṇic* suffix. "A person who is independent is the agent" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.54). That meaning which is intended to be expressed as being independent with respect to the action shall be the agent (*kartṛ*). Independence consists in being the substratum of the activity conveyed by the verbal root (*dhātu*). And it is said:

"It is held that when the action denoted by the verbal root is not explicitly stated, the agent is always intended as the *kāraka*. This [rule] applies even to the case of the object acting as the agent (*karmakartṛ*). In the case of the root *pac*, there is the abandonment of the general rule regarding the difference of locus (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) between the result and the operation. This is the same whether one holds the view of separate powers (*viśakalita-śakti*) or the view of a unified power (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*). However, according to the view that "the object whose instigation has ceased remains within a portion of its own operation," the operation here is simply the meaning of the verbal root as the primary element; the status of being a verbal root (*dhātutva*), on the other hand, exists because it refers to the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) that previously occurred. By this, the restriction that *kārakas* must be connected with an operation is also explained in two ways.

"Devadatta cooks. "The pot cooks. Since the meaning of a word is that which cannot be obtained from anything else, the locus (*āśraya*) is the meaning of the verbal suffix (*lakāra*). In the sentence "It is cooked by Devadatta," the meaning is: the operation conducive to softening (*viklitti*), as qualified by the locus whose nature is Devadatta. And this qualification appears through the relation of being the substrate (*ādheyatā*) by virtue of the semantic requirement of connection (*saṃsarga-maryādayā*). (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.55)

"And the instigator of that [agent] is called the *hetu* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.55). The instigator (*prayojaka*) of that agent shall be designated as a *hetu*, and [by the word "and" (*ca*)], also as an agent (*kartṛ*). The particle *ca* is for the purpose of allowing the coexistence of both designations. [Example: *kurvantaṃ prerayati kārayati hariḥ* ("He prompts the one who is acting; Hari causes [him] to act"). Because of its status as a *hetu*, the suffix *ṇic* is applied to its operation by the rule *hetumati ca* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.1.26). Because of its status as an agent, the *l*-suffix occurs in the sense of the agent. Thus ends the third Āhnika of the fourth Pāda of the first Adhyāya in the venerable *Śabdakaustubha*.
The Fourth Daily Lesson in the Fourth Chapter.

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.56) *prāgrīśvarānnipātāḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.56). From the rule *adhirīśvare* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.97) onwards, the term *nipātāḥ* (particles) is governed as being prior [to that point], by virtue of relying on the principle of *tantra*. Consequently, the meaning is that they first possess the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of "particle" and subsequently the designations of "gati," etc.; thus, the coexistence of these designations is established. Otherwise, there would be an option (*paryāya*) between the designations of "gati," "upasarga," and "karmapravacanīya" on one hand, and the designation of "particle" on the other. The proof for this *tantra* principle is precisely the force of the mention of the word *prāk* (prior).

Otherwise, since the word *dik* (direction) would already imply [the rule] by means of the ablative case ending in *īśvarāt*, what would be the purpose of that [sūtra]? Nor does there arise the undesirable consequence of implying the word *para*. This is because, through the acquisition of the two items to be prescribed in the rules "cādayo 'sattve" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.57) and "prādayaḥ" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.58), there would result a lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*). Why is the mention of the specific letter *r* included? It is so that, by the principle of pervasion (*vyāptinyāya*), the rule "īśvare tosunkasunau" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.4.13) should not serve as its limit.

In reality, however, let there be no mention of *repha* (the letter *r*), because the desired result is established through proximity (*pratyāsatti*) and because the designation of an *avyayībhāva* compound as an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is specifically initiated [by the rule]. Nor should it be argued that this [mention of *repha*] must serve as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*)—to the effect that even within a compound, it is only the *avyayībhāva* [that is indeclinable]—because, rather than adopting the path of a restrictive rule based on the principle of pervasion (*vyāpti*) which is burdened by complexity (*gaurava*), it is more logical to accept its status as an injunction (*vidhyarthatā*) based on proximity. For this very reason, the separate mention of *loka* and others in the rule *na loka-* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.69), apart from *avyaya*, is also justified. This is the direction of the argument. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.57)

*Ca-ādayo 'sattve* (Pāṇini 1.4.57): The particles beginning with *ca* shall have the technical designation *nipāta* (particle), but not when they denote a substance (*dravya*). Because they are *nipātas*, they possess the status of indeclinables (*avyaya*). Examples include *ca*, *vā*, and so forth. Where a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) is employed to indicate a thing, that object which is intended to be expressed as something distinguishable is called a "substance" (*dravya*).

Alternatively, substance (*dravya*) is that which possesses gender and number. What is the purpose of the term *asattve* (in the absence of being)? Consider the example: *paśunā yajeta* ("one should sacrifice with an animal"). Here, the word *paśu* is a [substance]. Furthermore, *ca* in the rule *caḥ samuccaye* ("*ca* [is used] in the sense of conjunction") is also a counter-example. Nor should it be argued that here the status of being a particle (*nipātatva*) is unavoidable due to the extended application (*atideśa*) of the rule *prakṛtivadanukaraṇam* ("an imitation follows the form of the original") (Pāṇini 1.4.62); for the non-eternality of such extended applications has already been established in the very sūtra on *ṛlṛk*.

What is *prasajyapratiṣedha* (absolute negation)? [For example: one who blows is a *vā* (wind); one who is wise is a *vipra*. In this case, because it denotes a substance qualified by an action, and because an action is of the nature of non-substance (*asattva*), it would follow that it is a particle (*nipāta*). Consequently, the word *vepra* would also receive the designation of an indeclinable (*avyaya*), since it has been stated [in the Mahābhāṣya]: "The purpose [of the rule] is for the designation of pronouns and indeclinables."

Now, the particles beginning with *atha*—namely: *va*, *vā*, *ha*, *aha*, *eva*, *evam*, *nūnam*, *śaśvat*, *yugapat*, *bhūyas*, *kūpat*—are used in the senses of inquiry, deliberation, praise, and self-reference (*svayam*). Similarly, *sūpat* is also used. *Kuvid* is used in the sense of abundance, as well as in connection with yoga, praise, and existence (*astibhāva*). *Ned* is used in the sense of apprehension (*śaṅkā*), as in: "Lest, being crooked, we fall into hell," and "Lest the gods should be born again, O gods. However, in such instances as these, the two words *na* and *id* are read separately.

Therefore, this should be understood as a collection of particles (*nipāta-samudāya*), for there is a prohibition of the *nighāta* (anudātta accent) by the rule *nipātairyadyadi* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.1.30). Śākaṭāyana, however, maintains that this [particle] is used in the senses of negation, deliberation, and conjunction. *Cet*: This is the particle *caṇ*, which has the marker *ṇ* when it means "if" (*ced-artha*), but is without a marker (*an-anubandha*) in the sense of conjunction and so forth. This will become clear under the rule *nipātairyadyadi* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.1.30). *Kaccit*: [Used in the sense of inquiry. *Yatra*: [Used in the sense of "where" or "in which. *Naha*: Used in the sense of certain negation. *Hanta*: Used in the senses of joy (*harṣa*) and compassion (*anukampā*).

*mākiḥ* and *mākīm* are used in prohibition (*niṣedha*). Examples: *mākir neśan*, *mākīm riṣat*, *mākīm saṃśārike vaṭet*. *Kiḥ* is used for a negation that implies a possibility (*sambhāvita-niṣedha*), as in *kir indra tvad uttaraḥ*. *Na kiḥ* expresses impossibility, as in *evāyathātvaṃ hi kam*. *Kanukam* and *sukan* are particles of inquiry. *Ākī*, *nakī*, *nakiḥ*, *mākīm*, and *mākiḥ* are listed in the *Vedanighaṇṭu* under the category of "mixed" (*āmiśrāṇi*) words, nine in number; thus says Yāska in his commentary (*Nirukta*). The particle *māṅ* contains the marker *ṅ* for the purpose of specification, according to the rule *māṅi luṅ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.3.175).

In the expression *mā bhavatu* (let it not be) and *mā bhaviṣyati* (it will not be), the word *mā* is without the *anubandha* (the marker *ñ*). It is the negative particle *nañ*. The letter *ñ* is for the purpose of specification, as in the rule *nalopo nañaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.73). If it were simply stated as *naḥ*, then [the elision] would also occur in a case such as *vā pāmanaputraḥ*.

Nor should it be argued that even in the established system (*siddhānta*), the suffix *ñ* is unnecessary because the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the word *straiṇaputra* could be avoided by the fact that the negative particle *nañ* must necessarily be qualified by the "prior member" (*pūrvapada*) implied by the rule *aluguttarapade* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.3.1); for by that very [qualification], the form *pāmanaputra* would also be established. This is because the status of being marked with *ñ* (*ñitva*) is also indispensable to prevent over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *naikadhāgamikarmīkṛta-naikanīvṛtta*, where the negative particle *na* in its prohibitive sense forms a compound with a following noun according to the rule *sahasupā* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.4).

It should be understood that the statement in the works of the ancients—that even when the preceding member is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), only a particle (*nipāta*) whose *ñit* status serves no other purpose is included [in the rule], and not even a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) whose *ñakāra* has already served its function through *vṛddhi*—is possible based on the following list: *yāvat*, *tāvat*, *tvai*, and *nvai* (these two are used in the sense of deliberation); *śrauṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *svadhā*, *oṃ*, *tathā*, *hiruk*, *khalu*, *kila*, *atha*, *suṣṭhu*; and *āda* (with *ha*) is used in the sense of "for" (*hi*), as well as in the senses of "commencement" (*sopakrama*) and "censure" (*kutsana*).

In the case of the phrase "ādahasva dhāman," however, the makers of the *padapāṭha* read "ā" as a separate word. There are also particles that resemble prefixes, case-endings, and accents; for instance, in the sense of an initial action, the forms *avadattam*, *vidattam*, *pradattam*, *sudattam*, *anudattam*, and *nidattam* are desired.

In this case, the substitution of *t* for the *ghu*-affixes does not occur by the rule *aca upasargāt taḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.4.47), because although it resembles a preposition (*upasarga*), it is not actually a preposition. Examples of forms resembling case-endings (*vibhakti-pratirūpaka*) are: *aham*, *śubham*, *ahaṃyuḥ*, and *śubhaṃyuḥ*—[the latter two] being derived by the rule *ahaṃśubhamoryus* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.2.40). Also: *cireṇa*, *antareṇa*, *cirāya*, *acirāt*, *akasmāt*, *cirasya*, *mama*, *gatarājyasya mamatvam*, *velāyām*, *mātrāyām*, and so forth. By this, the verse "geye kena vinītau vām" is explained.

The indeclinable *vām* has the meaning of "you two" (*yuvām*). As for *āha*, *āsa*, and so forth, they are merely imitations of verbal forms (*tiṅanta-pratirūpaka*). Vowels (*svara*), however, should be understood according to their occurrence in addressing, scolding, compassion, filling a verse-line (*pāda-pūraṇa*), or prohibition: *a* in "go away! (*apehi*); *ā* in "is this what you think? (*evaṃ manyase*); *i* in "look at Indra! (*indraṃ paśya*); *ī* in "the Lord" (*īśaḥ*); *ū* in "he sows seed in barren soil" (*ūpare bījaṃ vapati*); *e* in "be gone from here! (*ito bhava*); *o* in "cause [them] to hear! (*ośrāvaya*); *ṛ*, *ṛ*, *lṛ*, *ai*, and *au*—these are collections of mantras (*mantra-stoma*). The word *paśu* is used in the sense of "correctly": "they lead the Lodhra tree, thinking it to be a beast."

*Śukam* is used in the sense of speed. *Yathākathāca* is used in the sense of disregard. *Pāṭ*, *pyāṭ*, *aṅga*, *hai*, *he*, *bho*, *aye*, and so forth, are used in the sense of address. *Gha* is used in the senses of assent, lack of opposition, and filling a metrical foot (*pādapūraṇa*). *Viṣu* is used in the sense of "various" (*nānārtha*). *Ekapade* is used in the sense of "suddenly" (*akasmāt*), as in: "He slays his enemies in an instant" (*nihantyarīnekapade*). *Putam* is used in the sense of censure (*kutsā*); one who covers its censured parts is called *puñchaḥ*. [The suffix] *ṅaḥ* [is applied]. According to Śākaṭāyana, *pul* ends in *l*. One who moves (*kasati*) in a censurable manner is a *pulkasaḥ*. *Asmi* is used in the sense of "I."
"I say to you: 'The assembly of the learned is standing here. Here, *ātaḥ* means "from here" (*itaḥ*). This and similar examples belong to this class of words (*ākṛtigaṇaḥ*).
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.58)

*Prādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.58): Words beginning with *pra* and so forth are designated as *gati* when they are connected with a verb. This word *gati* is masculine, as indicated by the rule *gatiranantaraḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.49). It is either an unanalyzed (*avyutpanna*) term or derived from the suffix *ktic*. The rule *na ktici dīrghaśca* (Pāṇini 6.4.39), which prohibits lengthening, does not apply here precisely because of this very usage [of the masculine form]. The particle *ca* is intended to ensure that these terms coexist with the designation *upasarga*; otherwise, they would be considered synonyms.

By this [rule], the substitution of *ṇ* in *praṇeyam* and so forth, as well as the accentuation of the original form of the final member of a compound (*kṛduttarapada-prakṛtisvara*), are established. Furthermore, the coexistence [of the designation *nipāta*] with other designations has already been proven by the inclusion of the word *prāk* (in Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.58). Here, the designations *gati* and *upasaṃkhyāna* (or *upasarga*) apply to those *pra*-words etc. only in relation to that specific action (*kriyā*) with which they are connected, due to the force of the mention of *yoga* (connection) [in the rule]. Consequently, in examples such as *pravṛddham*, *kṛtam*, and *prakṛtam*, the accent prescribed by the rule *gatiranantaraḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.2.49) does not apply, because [the words *pra-* etc. are not *gatis* in relation to the past passive participle (*ktānta*) ending in *karmaṇi*.

However, if they qualify the meaning of the verbal root (*kṛt*), this would indeed apply. Thus, in the case of *prabhāvaḥ* (great manifestation), where "the state has increased," the suffix *ghañ* is established by Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.3.24, *śriṇībhuvor anupasarge*. Similarly, in forms such as *praṇāyayati* (he leads forth) and *abhipācayati* (he cooks thoroughly), the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* and the change to *ṣ* occur when [the prefixes] indicate intensity or directionality pertaining to the meaning of the base. It should be understood, however, that these do not occur when they qualify the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*). Furthermore, the designation of "particle" (*nipāta*) exists even without connection to a verb.

For this very purpose, the rule *prādayaḥ* has been split into a separate *yoga*. By means of that, in the case of *pragata ācāryaḥ = prācāryaḥ*, the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) as the prior member is established.

An addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) must be made to the word *marut* under the definition of *upasarga*. [Thus we have] *maruttaḥ*. They say that by virtue of the power of the rule prescribing the designation *upasarga*, even though the word lacks an *ac* vowel [ending], the substitution of *t* [for *n*] applies according to Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.4.47: *aca upasargāt taḥ*. However, if this were the case, then in the expression *marunnayati*, the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] would also undesirably apply. Therefore, the designation *upasarga* should be stated only for the purpose of that specific substitution of *t*. For this very reason, neither the suffix *ki* nor the designation *aṅ* applies. Furthermore, the designation *nipāta* is not desired for this word.

Therefore, when the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛti-svara*) is applied by the rule *tṛtīyā-karmaṇi* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.2.48), the word *marutta* has its acute accent on the middle syllable (*madhyodātta*). If it were a particle (*nipāta*), however, it would have the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*). Nor should one suspect that the flaw remains as it was based on the *Phiṭ-sūtra* *upasargāścābhivarjam* (Phiṭ-sūtra 81); for Haradatta and others maintain that since the matter is already established by the rule *nipātā ādyudāttāḥ* (Phiṭ-sūtra 80), the latter rule was formulated merely for the purpose of excluding the prefix *abhi*. For this very reason, the rule could simply have been stated as *nābhiḥ*.

Or even if that [derivation] were not accepted, we have already stated that *abhi-* is easily read [as a root] in such cases as *evādi*. And thus, in the derivation of the word *marut* according to the rule "tapparvamarudbhyām," another means [of derivation] should be understood. In that context, the fact that *tap-* is a *pit* [root] is alone correct. As for the occasional reading of it as having a *nit* marker (*nittva*), that is merely an error; otherwise, there would arise the undesirable consequence of the word *marutta* being udātta on its first syllable, which would contradict Kaiyaṭa and others regarding the present sūtra.

The passage by Haradatta, which proceeds by relying on the *nittva* (the initial accentuation of the suffix) of the *tana* suffix in the section on possessive suffixes (*matvarthīya*) and the fact that the word *marutta* is *ādyudātta* (accented on the first syllable), is to be considered doubtful. However, the initial accentuation of the word *parvata*, as recited in rules such as "parvataścinmahi vṛddho vibhāṣā" (Pāṇini 6.1.157), is established in both ways: either by virtue of the rule "nabviṣayasyānisantasya" (Pāṇini 6.1.173), which prescribes an initial accent for words ending in *na* that do not end in the suffix *ani*, or by the following supplementary rule: **Supplementary Rule:** An addition [to the list] should be made for the word *śraddhā* when the suffix *aṅ* is prescribed. [Resulting form: *śraddhā*. This is established either through its inclusion in the *bhidādi* group or by the specific grammatical nipātana (irregular formation) stating "prajñā-śraddhe."
