True; this is not caused by its being a *upasarga*, but rather by the separate mention [of *pra*] in the rule *upasargaprādurbhyām* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.3.87). By this, those who argue that one should read *prāduṣyanti*—claiming that the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* in the root *syati* preceded by the triad of *upasargas* *pra*, *āṅ*, and *dus*, according to the rule *upasargātsunoti* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.3.65)—are refuted. This is because the status of *dus* as an *upasarga* is prohibited in the rule prescribing *ṣ*-substitution, and furthermore, because the meaning of the root *syati* is irrelevant to the present context. [Now follows the discussion of] the substitution of *ṇ*.

*durnītam* (ill-conducted), *durnayaḥ* (bad policy). By this [rule], those who read "there is no substitution of *ṇ* for the following *n* after *dur*" and thus mistakenly believe that the substitution of *ṇ* occurs in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) are refuted. There is an addition (*upasaṅkhyāna*) of the word *kārikā* to the list of items designated as *gati*. Examples: *kārikākṛtya*, *kārikākṛtam*, *yat kārikā karoti*. Because it is a *gati*, there is the suppression (*nighāta*) of the accent according to Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.1.71 (*tiṅi codāttavati*). Since it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) due to its being a particle (*nipāta*), there is elision of the case-ending (*vibhaktiluk*). *Kārikā* means action; the meaning is "the maintenance of a limit. Others say it means "effort. The suffix *ṇvul* is applied according to the rule "in the indication of the meaning of a root" (*dhātvarthanirdeśe*).

However, that which ends in the suffix *ṇvul* when used in the sense of an agent—as in "kārikā" meaning a female servant—and that which denotes a verse (*śloka*), are not included here; for the word "kārikā" is qualified by the phrase "in connection with an action" (*kriyāyoge*), and thus only those [words] whose function is indeed action are taken.

Furthermore, it should be stated that these [two words] are designated as *gati* in the Vedic language (*chandas*). [In the case of] *punarādheyam*: because it is a *gati*, there is a compound. By the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the final member of a *kṛt*-derived compound, according to Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.213, "the vowel following *yat* is acute except for *nau*," the syllable *dhe* is acute. In *punarutsūtaṃ vāsaḥ*, here too there is a compound due to its being a *gati*. As for the accent, because the group beginning with *pravṛddha-* is an open-ended class (*ākṛtigaṇa*), there is an oxytone (acute on the final syllable). Indeed, in the *Kāṭhaka*, it is recited as oxytone. By the rule of the suppression of the remaining syllables (*śeṣanighāta*), the word *punaḥ* is unaccented (*anudātta*).

By stating the rule *gatir gatau* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.1.70), which prescribes the elision of the accent (*nighāta*) [of the first verb], the author of the Vṛtti considers its application to be more logical due to its subsequent position. Regarding *canohitaḥ*: since the word *canaḥ*, which is acutely accented on the first syllable either because it ends in the suffix *asun* or because it is a particle (*nipāta*), according to the rule *cāyaranne hrasvaśca* (Uṇādisūtra 639), it retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) by the rule *gatir anantaraḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.2.49).

*Ūry-ādi-cvi-ḍācaś-ca* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.61): These [words] are designated as *gati* when used in connection with a verb. Since the suffixes *cvi* and *ḍāc* are prescribed in connection with the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*, by virtue of association (*sāhacarya*) with them, words such as *rūpa* and others are also employed only in connection with those [roots] and not otherwise, because they are not so expressed. Furthermore, among those, Mādhava and others maintain that, with the exception of the words *āviḥ* and *prāduḥ*, the others are used only in connection with the root *kṛ*. Although there is no rule for the inclusion of a word ending in a suffix (*tadantavidhi*) when a suffix is mentioned in a rule prescribing a technical term (*saṃjñāvidhi*), nevertheless, here, by virtue of the contextual requirement (*sāmarthya*), the inclusion of words ending in *cvi* and *ḍāc* is understood.

Indeed, the connection with action (kriyāyoga) is not possible for a mere prefix (*pratyaya*), because it is meaningless as a *svārthika* suffix and because the *ci* [of *cvi*] is not heard [in the final form]. Examples: *ūrīkṛtya*, *śuklīkṛtya*, *paṭapaṭākṛtya*. Here, this much should be stated: even though words beginning with *śrauṣaṭ* and ending with *svāhā* are listed among the *ādi* group [of particles], they possess the status of particles (*nipātatva*) even when not connected with an action. Because the word *āvis* is listed among the *sākṣāt-prabhṛti* group, there is an option regarding its connection with the root *kṛ*; however, in connection with the roots *bhū* and *as*, it is obligatory by this rule. How then [is it explained] in the following verse? *vāruṇīmadaviśaṅkam atāviṣvaviśvakṣuṣo bhavad asāv iva* || [He became like one whose eyes were all-seeing, free from fear due to the intoxication of wine. (Note: The commentary implies that *atāviṣu* is used here despite the prohibition against using *āvis* with *bhū* or *as*, justifying it as an archaic usage or a specific poetic license.)
Is this Māgha’s [verse]? "The two parts of his flanks were revealed, licked by a pair of tongues flickering in both directions.

And so it is said: "Poets are unrestrained," says Haradatta. But in reality, we do not see even a trace of a fault here. For instance, your entire previous argument consists in the claim that, because it is a root (*dhātu*), the word *gati* ought to have been placed before [the verb]. That point has already been largely refuted by the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika themselves. Indeed, the rule *te prāgdhātoḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.80) has been explained in two ways: for the purpose of regulating usage (*prayoga-niyama*) and for the purpose of regulating technical designations (*saṃjñā-niyama*).

In that regard, regarding the final position, it is established that [the particles] should be employed both before and after [the word], yet when employed before, they receive their technical designation (*saṃjñā*). It is precisely by relying on this position that, in the rule *anukaraṇaṃ ca* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.62), the phrase *anitiparam* was rejected as unnecessary. In the same way, this explains the consistency of the Bhāṣya and Vṛtti texts under the rule *chandasi pare’pi* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.3.127) with the example *svāyambhavam*, as well as the Vṛtti text under the rule *cvyarthayoḥ kim?* which asks: "What about *svāḍhyena bhūyate*? (How is it that one becomes very wealthy?).

By this, Haradatta—who, asserting that the *vṛtti* is erroneous, instructs that the reading should be "āḍhyena subhūyate"—is also refuted, because under the maxim "there are solutions even through alternative views," everything is consistent within the view that restricts the technical designation (*saṃjñāniyamapakṣa*). By this [same logic], [the following is explained]:
"Before Rāma, he offered his body into the blazing fire."

Thus says Bhaṭṭi; and Kālidāsa’s usage in "tasya sthitvā kathamapi puraḥ" is likewise supported. One should not fall into the error of thinking that the rule "puro 'vyayam" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.67) applies exclusively to the verb *kṛ*, for there is no governing context (*adhikāra*) for *kṛ* here, and because of actual usages such as "turāsāhaṃ purodhāya. This is the general direction.

*jarī*, *ūrī*, and *urarī*—these three are used in the sense of acceptance (*aṅgīkāra*) and expansion (*vistāra*). *vitālī* and *bhūsī*—these two are used in the sense of expansion. *śakalā*, *sraṃsakalā*, *dhvaṃsakalā*, and *bhraṃsakalā*—these four are used in the sense of injury (*hiṃsā*), as in "having made into fragments" (*śakalā kṛta*) and so forth; the meaning is "having injured. *gulugudhā* is used in the sense of affliction (*pīḍā*); as in *gulugudhākṛtya*, the meaning is "having afflicted. *sajūḥ* is used in the sense of accompaniment (*saha*). *phalaphala*, *ciklī*, and *āklī*—these are used in the sense of transformation (*vikāra*). *aloṣṭī*, *kevalī*, *sevālī*, *śevālī*, *varṣālī*, *masamasā*, and *bhasmasā*—these are used in the sense of injury (*hiṃsā*).

*Vaṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, *svāhā*, and *svadhā* [are indeclinables used] in the sense of an oblation (*pāṃpī*). *Karūṇāvilāpe*: having committed a sin (*pāpīkṛtya*), meaning "having lamented piteously" (*karuṇaṃ vilapya*). *Prāduḥ* is used in the sense of manifestation (*prākaṭye*). *Śrat* is used in the sense of speed (*śīghrārthe*). *Śratkṛtya*. *Āviḥ* is used in the sense of manifestation (*prākaṭye*). *Āviṣkṛtya*. Other [terms] are also included in the *Gaṇaratna*; for instance: *pāpālī*, *saṅkalā*, and *kevāsī*—these are used in the sense of injury (*hiṃsāyām*). *Vārdālī*, *yārdālī*, and *ālambī*—these are used in the sense of manifestation and injury (*prākāśye hiṃsāyāṃ ca*). Thus end the *ūryādi* group (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.61–62).

"A sound imitating [another] (anukaraṇa) is a *gati* when not followed by the word *iti*" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.62). It is a *gati* when connected with a verb. Example: *khāṭkṛtya*. Why "not followed by *iti*"? Consider: *khāḍ iti kṛtvā niraṣṭhīvat* ("having made the sound 'khāḍ', he spat"). For if it were a *gati*, then according to the view that restricts usage, it would have to be placed before the verbal root. This prohibition applies when a word belonging to the class of sounds imitating another is followed by the word *iti*. Therefore, in the example *śrauṣaṭ voṣaṭ iti kṛtvā niraṣṭhīvat*, the word *śrauṣaṭ* is also subject to this prohibition.

However, under the view that restricts the technical designation (*saṃjñāniyamapakṣa*), the mention of "not followed by *iti*" need not be made, because there is simply no possibility of the mutual application of these designations.

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.63) *sadasatī ādarānādarayoḥ*: The words *sat* and *asat* are designated as *gati* respectively when they signify respect (*ādara*) and disrespect (*anādara*). Examples: *satkṛtya* (having honored), *asatkṛtya* (having disregarded). Respect is a haste directed toward rising to meet someone and so forth, preceded by affection. Disrespect is indifference toward rising to meet someone and so forth out of contempt. What is the purpose of this rule? [Consider the examples: *satkṛtvā*, *asatkṛtvā*. The meaning here is "having done well" and "having done poorly. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.64)

*Alam* [is a *gati*] when meaning "adornment" (*bhūṣaṇa*). It shall be designated as a *gati*. Example: *alaṃkṛtya* ("having adorned"). Why "when meaning adornment"? Consider: *alaṃ kṛtvā odanaṃ gataḥ* ("having finished with the rice, he went away"). The meaning here is "enough. Mādhava states that the three rules beginning with *anukaraṇam* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.62) concern the verb *kṛ* by their very nature. *Antar* [is a *gati*] when not meaning "appropriation" (*aparigraha*). This is clear. Example: *antarhatya*. The meaning is "having struck in the middle. Why "when not meaning appropriation"? Consider: *antarhatvā mūṣikāṃ śyeno gataḥ* ("the hawk went away after killing the mouse"). The meaning is "having seized [and carried it off]."

In this regard, the following should be noted: coming after having killed is of two kinds—namely, having abandoned [the victim] after killing it, and having taken possession of it. The first is the primary example (*udāharaṇa*); the second is the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*). Furthermore, the condition "not taking possession" (*aparigrahe*) is a syntactic restriction (*prayogopādhi*) and is not included within the scope of the denotable meaning (*vācyakoṭiniviṣṭa*).
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.66)

The words *kaṇe* and *manas* [are used with the verb *han*] when there is an obstruction of faith (*śraddhāpratīghāta*). They become *gatis*. Examples: *kaṇehatya payaḥ pibati* (he drinks the milk until his thirst is satisfied); *manohatya*. The word *kaṇe* is an indeclinable (*nipāta*) resembling a locative case ending, used in the sense of an excess of longing. The word *manas* is likewise. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.68) *astaṃ ca*: The indeclinable (*avyaya*) ending in -m, namely *astaṃ*, shall be designated as a *gati*. Example: *astaṅgatya* (having set). The word "indeclinable" (*avyayam*) [from the previous rule] applies here as well. Example: *astaṃ kāṇḍam* (the arrow has been cast); the meaning is "thrown. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.69)

In the case of *accha* used with verbs meaning "to go" (*gati*) or "to speak" (*artha-vada*), [the word *accha* is a *gati*]. This applies only when it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Examples: *acchagatya*, *acchodya*. The meaning is "having gone toward" (*abhigatya*) or "having spoken facing toward" (*abhimukham uktvā*). Why "indeclinable"? [Counter-example: *jalam acchaṃ gacchati* ("he goes clearly through the water"). In the case of the word *adas* when not used as an instruction (*anupadeśe*), [it is a *gati*]. The word *adas* belongs to the *tyadādi* group; when it is not used as an instruction, it becomes a *gati*. Examples: *adaḥkṛtya*, *adaḥkṛtam*. This is an illustration for when one reflects in this manner by oneself. Why "not as an instruction"? [So that it does not apply] when speaking to another person. Example: *adaḥ kṛtvā gataḥ* ("having done that, he went").

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.71) *tiro'ntardhau* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.71). [The suffix -ktvā is optionally replaced by -lyap after the word *tiras* when it means "disappearance"]. Example: *tirobhūya*. Why "in the sense of disappearance"? [Counter-example: *tirobhūtvā sthitaḥ*. This means "having become situated at the side. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.72)

The rule *vibhāṣā kṛñi* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.72) is an optional rule (*prāptavibhāṣā*), because the preceding rule *tiro'ntardhau* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.71) continues to apply. Thus, we have *tiraḥkṛteḥ*, *tiraḥkṛtya*, and *tiraskṛtya*. In the latter two cases, the substitution of *s* for *r* occurs optionally by the rule *tiraso'nyatarasyām* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.3.42). However, in the counter-example (*pratyudāharaṇa*), the substitution of *s* does not occur, because the term *gati* (particle) continues to apply in that specific rule. For example: *tiraḥ kṛtvā kāṣṭham*. Mādhava maintains that some scholars desire the substitution of *s* even here, and that, following the usage of the word *tiraskāra* in the sense of defeat (*parābhava*), they exclude the term *gati* from the rule prescribing the substitution of *s*.

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.73) *upāje’nvāje*: These two [words] are optionally designated as *gati*s when used with the root *kṛ*. These two are particles (*nipāta*) that resemble case endings; they function in the sense of providing strength to one who is weak. Examples: *upājekṛtya*, *upājekṛtvā*; *anvājekṛtya*, *anvājekṛtvā*. The meaning is "having supported" (*upaṣṭabhya*). (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.74)

*Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.74*: "And *sākṣāt* and so forth [are optionally termed *gati* when used with the root *kṛ*]. These words may optionally be designated as *gati* when used with the verb *kṛ*. It should be stated that this applies to the sense of the suffix *cv-* (the process of becoming something else). Examples: *sākṣātkṛtya* or *sākṣātkṛtvā*. This usage occurs when that which was not previously manifest (*asākṣād-bhūtam*) is made manifest; it does not apply to the mere assumption of a different form by that which is already manifest. However, in the case of words ending in *cv-*, the designation is obligatory by virtue of the prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*) under *Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.61* (*ūryādicvi*). Therefore, in the example *lavaṇīkṛtya*, the status of having a final *m* (which would trigger the substitution of *am* for the preceding vowel) does not occur.

In this context, it is treated as an irregular form (*nipātana*) within the group [of words] by its association with that option; or alternatively, there is a substitution of the suffix *m* for the word *lavaṇa*, resulting in *lavaṇam*. Thus, let there be no prior counter-exception (*pūrvavipratiṣedha*). For our goal is to establish three forms: *lavaṇaṃ kṛtya*, *lavaṇaṃ kṛtvā*, and *lavaṇīkṛtya*. Among these, when the substitution of *lavaṇam* occurs optionally after both the form ending in the *cv*-suffix and the one not ending in it, the resulting form is identical. However, since the other option is also set aside, the designation is constant for the form ending in *cv*; thus, there is no fault whatsoever.

In this context, *agnau*, *vaśe*, and so forth are particles (*nipāta*) that resemble case-endings. Regarding the words *prāduḥ* and *āviḥ*, the option (*vibhāṣā*) applies because they belong to the group beginning with *ūry-*. *Sākṣāt*, *mithyā*, and *cintā* [are used] in the sense of mental activity; *cintākṛtya* [is used similarly]. *Bhadrā* is used in the senses of observation, praise, and auspiciousness. *Rocanā* is used in the sense of producing faith and in praise. *Amā* is used in the senses of secrecy and proximity. *Āsthā* means faith. *Prājaryā* and *vī-jaryā* refer to the action of aging. *Prājaruhā* and *bījaruhā* refer to the action of growing. [Examples include: *lavaṇam*, *uṣṇam*, *śītam*.

*udaka-*; *ārdra-*; it is stated that for the five beginning with *lavaṇa*, the status of ending in *m* is either prescribed by rule (*sanniyoga*) as a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) for their movement, or it is an irregular substitution (*nipātana*) of the suffix *m*. [The following are examples: *agni*, *vaśa*, *vikampana*, *vikasana*, *prahasana*, *santapana*; *prāduḥ*, *namaḥ*, *āviḥ*. This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (a class defined by its form). (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.75)

*Aṣṭādhyāyī* 1.4.75: *anatyādhāna urasimanasī*. These two indeclinables (*uras* and *manas*) optionally receive the designation of *gati* when used with the root *kṛ*. *urasikṛtya* / *urasikṛtvā*: meaning "having accepted" or "having conceded. *manasikṛtya* / *manasikṛtvā*: meaning "having determined" or "having resolved. *Atyādhāna* means "close contact" or "placing upon. This [designation] does not apply there: *pāṇim upari kṛtvā śete* ("he lies down having placed his hand above"). *Aṣṭādhyāyī* 1.4.76: *pari prādayaḥ*. The words *pari*, *pra*, and so forth, are always designated as *gati* when used with a verb.

*madhye*, *pade*, and *nivacane* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.76): these three may optionally be designated as *gati*s when used with the root *kṛ*, provided there is no sense of "placing upon" (*anatyādhāne*). Examples: *madhyekṛtya* / *madhyekṛtvā*; *padekṛtya* / *padekṛtvā*. These two [words, *madhye* and *pade*] are indeclinables (*nipāta*) ending in the vowel *e*. *Nivacanam* means the absence of speech. Its ending in *e* is prescribed unconditionally; it is not prescribed specifically in connection with this technical designation (*sañjñā*), according to the commentary (*vyākhyāna*). Example: *nivacanekṛtya* / *nivacanekṛtvā*, meaning "having restrained one's speech. Why "provided there is no sense of placing upon"? Example: *hastinaḥ pade kṛtvā śiraḥ śete* ("Having placed his head on the foot of an elephant, he lies down"). (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.77)

The two particles *haste* and *pāṇau* are always designated as *gati*s when used with the verb *kṛñ* (*to do*) in the sense of "marriage" (*upayamana*). Some say this refers specifically to the act of taking a wife; others say it refers to mere acceptance in general. Examples: *hastekṛtya* or *pāṇaukṛtya* [he took] a girl [as his wife], or [he took] three great women. Why "in the sense of marriage"? [Counter-example: *hastekṛtvā suvarṇaṃ gato bhṛtyaḥ* ("Having taken the gold in his hand, the servant departed"). (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.77–78)

*Prādhvam-bandhane* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.78). Since *prādhvam* is listed among the *cādi* group, it is an indeclinable ending in *-m* that denotes favorability. That [term] shall always have the designation *gati* when used with the root *kṛ*, provided that the favorability is caused by binding. Example: *prādhvaṃkṛtya*. Why "in the sense of binding"? [Counter-example: *prādhvaṃkṛtvā*. This means having made [someone] favorable through entreaty and so forth. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.79)

The words *jīvikā* and *upaniṣad* are always designated as *gati* when used in comparison with the root *kṛ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.79). They are always termed *gati* when combined with the root *kṛ*. *Jīvikā* means "the means of livelihood" (*jīvanopāya*). Having treated it like a means of livelihood: *jīvikākṛtya*. Having treated it like a secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*): *upaniṣatkṛtya*. Although the *gati*-compound is obligatory, the analysis (*vigraha*) is made with a non-*gati* word because [the compound] rests solely on its own primary meaning; for this very reason, the word *iva* is employed there in the analysis. Why "in comparison"? [Example: *jīvikāṃ kṛtvā* ("having made a livelihood"). (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.80) (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.80) Those [terms designated as *gati*] must be placed before the verbal root.

In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), [the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*] occurs even when [the following word] is subsequent (*parepi*). (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.81) [The substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs] also before a guttural or a labial (*kupi ca*).
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.82)

"And [preverbs] even when separated [from the root]" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.82). This is clear. Examples: *haribhyāṃ yāhi* ("Go with the two bay horses"), *oka ā* ("To the home"), *ā mandrair indra haribhir yāhi* ("Come, O Indra, with the pleasant bay horses"). In this regard, the position that this is a rule for technical designation (*saṃjñā-niyama*) is also established in the Bhāṣya; for by the word *te* ("these"), the preverbs from *pra* up to *upa* are referred to in their own form, and their designation is prescribed by being syntactically unified with the preceding sūtra for those used before the verbal root. And according to this view, it is established that the two sūtras beginning with "In the Veda, even when following" (*chandasi pare’pi*) and the mention of the term *anitipara* need not be formulated.

And this is consistent with the commentary stating, "They are easy to perform. However, under the view that there is a restriction regarding usage, it would have to be justified by the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (in various ways) in the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.3.113). As for the argument that, since it has been determined that a non-indclinable (*anavyaya*) must precede [the suffix] due to the force of the *khit* marker in the formation of *khala*, the intervention of *su-* is established by process of elimination—[this is not correct].

That is to be considered; for, by implication, the suffix *mum* can occur even when there is an intervention, and because the mention of a *kṛt* suffix includes that which is preceded by a *gati* particle, the word *īṣat* does not receive the designation of a *gati*. Furthermore, in the case of "īṣadāḍhyambhavaḥ," the fact that the *kh* in the suffix *khal* has already served its purpose [in the formation of *āḍhyambhava*] is the direction [of the argument]. Why [is the word] "dhātoḥ" (from a verbal root) specified? [So that] in the case of "prācikīrṣat"—meaning he desired to act—there may not be the application of the suffix *san* before the verbal root. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.83)

*Karmapravacanīyāḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.83). This heading, beginning with *īśvarāt*, is now introduced. Those who have expressed (*proktavantaḥ*) an action (*karman*) are called *karmapravacanīyāḥ*; the suffix *anīyar* is used here in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) by virtue of its irregularity (*bāhulakāt*), and it refers to the past tense (*bhūte*). Consequently, it is understood that they do not indicate an action at present. And it has been said:
"This [term] is neither an indicator (*dyotaka*) of an action, nor is it an expresser (*vācaka*) of a relation;
nor does it imply a verbal root for action, but rather it is a differentiator (*bhedaka*) of the relation."

For instance, in the expression *śākalyasya saṃhitām anupravarṣat*, the prefix *anu* does not illuminate a specific action, as is the case in examples such as *anubhūyate sukham*. Nor is it the case that the genitive case alone expresses the relationship, since that [relationship] is already expressed by the accusative itself. Furthermore, in the expression *prādeśaṃ viparilikhati* (he draws around a span), the prefix *vi-* does not imply another action—such as the act of measuring—as one might think from *vimāya parilikhati* (having measured, he draws around), because that would result in the occurrence of two distinct case endings.

However, since it is understood from the second [sūtra] that the relationship connected with *saṃhitā* consists precisely of the nature of the relationship between the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) and the indicated (*lakṣya*), it is the relationship itself that is established as a specific state by this [term]. In some cases, however, this technical designation (*sañjñā*) applies even to that which indicates a specific quality pertaining to an action, because of an explicit statement (*vacana*), such as: "The prefix *su-* [is used] in the sense of honor" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.94), and "*ati-* [is used] in the sense of exceeding" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.95).
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.84)

*anurlakṣaṇe* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.84). When a characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*) is to be indicated, *anu* shall be designated as a *karmapravacanīya*. Although this was already established by the rule *lakṣaṇetthambhūtākhyāna...* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.90), this sūtra is intended to override the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) used for the cause (*hetu*). To illustrate: the scope for the designation *karmapravacanīya* when indicating a characteristic mark is where it is not a cause, as in: "The lightning flashes near the tree" (*vṛkṣamanuvidyotate vidyut*). The scope for the third case ending expressing a cause is, for example: "The family [is distinguished] by wealth" (*dhanena kulam*).

In the case of the expression *saṃhitāmanuprāvarṣat* ("it rained following the *saṃhitā*"), the meaning is that the raining is characterized by the *saṃhitā* which serves as the cause. Consequently, because the indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) functions as the cause, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) would apply by virtue of its higher status [in the hierarchy of rules]. However, due to the force of the specific formulation of this technical designation (*sañjñā*), the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) alone occurs. As it has been said: "When the connection between the cause and the effect has been delimited by the particle *anu*, the third case ending—which would have applied based on the cause being the indicator—is set aside by the subsequent rule."

Nor should it be suspected that the purpose [of this rule] is already served by the sūtra *tṛtīyārthe* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.85); for, according to the maxim of the prior exception (*purastādapavādanyāya*), that [rule] only sublates the specific rule *sahayukte 'pradhāne* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.19). *tṛtīyārthe* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.85): When this meaning [of the instrumental case] is to be indicated, the word *anu* shall receive the technical designation of *karmapravacanīya*. Example: *nadīmanvavasitā senā*. The meaning is: "the army is connected with the river" (*nadyā saha sambaddhā*). The suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) derived from the root *ṣiñ* (Dhātupāṭha 1248), meaning "to bind."

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.86) *hīne* (in the sense of inferiority). When inferiority is to be expressed, the preposition *anu* functions as previously stated [i.e., like *upa*]. Example: *anu hariṃ surāḥ*. The meaning is that the gods possess a relationship characterized by inferiority relative to Hari. The accusative case ending occurs after the superior [referent] alone, and not after the inferior one, due to the inherent nature of the linguistic capacity (*śakti*).
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.87)

*Upa* is designated as *karmapravacanīya* when expressing that which is superior (*adhika*) or inferior (*hīna*). *Upakharī droṇaḥ*: A *droṇa* [is] more than a *khārī*. The resultant meaning is that both exist; [the word *khārī* takes] the seventh case by the rule *yasmād adhikam* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.9). In the sense of inferiority: *upahariṃ surāḥ* (the gods are inferior to Hari). (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.88)

*apa* and *pari* [are used] in the sense of exclusion (*varjana*). When exclusion is to be expressed, these two function as previously described. *apaviṣṇoḥ* (exclusion from Viṣṇu); *pariviṣṇoḥ* (exclusion from Viṣṇu). The ablative case is applied by the rule *pañcamyapāṅparibhiḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.10). The doubling [of the *p*] occurs by the rule *parervarjane* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.1.5). For that doubling indeed takes place even when the exclusion is indicated by a *karmapravacanīya* [particle] accompanied by the ablative, due to the force of the prescription for both. Why "in the sense of exclusion"? [Consider: *pariṣiñcati*. The meaning is "on all sides.
Here, because it is a prefix (*upasarga*), the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.89)

*Āṅ* [is used] in the sense of a limit (*maryādā*) [Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.89]. This means that when *āṅ* occurs as it did previously in a sūtra where the word *maryādā* is mentioned, it possesses two meanings, as stated in the rule *āṅ maryādābhividhyoḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.13). Examples: *ā mukteḥ saṃsāraḥ* ("the cycle of existence extends up to liberation"); *ā bālebhyaḥ haribhaktiḥ* ("devotion to Hari extends down to children"). (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.90)

*Prati*, *pari*, and *anu* receive the technical designation [of karmapravacanīya] when they signify (1) a mark (*lakṣaṇa*), (2) a state of being so (*itthambhūta*), (3) a share (*bhāga*), or (4) distributive repetition (*vīpsā*). (1) As a mark: Lightning flashes toward, around, or after the mountain (*vṛkṣaṃ prati pari anu vā vidyotate vidyut*). (2) Regarding the description of one who has attained a certain state (*itthambhūta*): Devadatta is kind toward his mother (*sādhur devadatto mātaraṃ prati paryanu vā*). (3) Regarding a share (*bhāga*): Whatever may belong to me here, whether it be a portion toward, around, or after [this].

The meaning is: "let that which is my portion here be given. The relationship between possessor and possessed (*svasvāmibhāva*) is the meaning of the accusative case. *Vīpsā* is the desire to attain, that is to say, the wish to express totality. [The examples are: *prati*, *anu*, or *paryu* with *prabhuḥ* in the sense of "lord over every single being" (*sakalabhūtānām*). Nor is this already established by the rule "itthaṃbhūtākhyāne" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.94). This, then, is the example: *vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣaṃ prati siñcati*, *parisiñcati*, *anisiñcati*. Here, the *vīpsā* is indicated solely by the reduplication.

The word *pari*, however, is connected only with the action (*kriyā*). Nor should it be argued that in this case its status as a *karmapravacanīya* would not be established; for there is no loss of its being the domain of repetition (*vīpsā*). For this very reason, Haradatta, while introducing the passage from the *Vṛtti* which states "when repetition is the domain," says: "And these [categories] such as *lakṣaṇa* (mark) and so on are not the meanings of *prati* and the others in the same way that 'case-ending' (*vibhakti*), 'proximity' (*samīpa*), and so on are the meanings of indeclinables (*avyaya*); rather, they are specified as the domains within which *prati* and the others function as technical designations (*saṃjñā*)."

The second [case], however, is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). The designation *karmapravacanīya* is for the purpose of precluding the status of a prefix (*upasarga*). Consequently, there is no change to *ṣ* according to Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.3.65 (*upasargāt sunoti*). Furthermore, the ablative case does not occur in connection with the word *pari*, because in Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.10 (*pañcamy apāṅ*), the word *apa*—which signifies exclusion—is used in conjunction [with the ablative] due to its association with that specific meaning.
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.91).

*Abhi* [is termed *karmapravacanīya*] when not meaning a share (*abhāge*). With the exception of "share," *abhi* shall have the aforementioned designation (*karmapravacanīya*) when used in the sense of a characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*), and so forth. *Vṛkṣam abhividyotate* (It lightens toward the tree). *Sādhur mātaram abhi* (He is kind toward his mother). *Vṛkṣam abhisiñcati* (He waters the tree). Why say "not meaning a share"? [Consider: *Yad atra mamābhiṣyāt tad dīyatām* (Let that which belongs to me here be given).

*Prati* [is termed *karmapravacanīya*] in the sense of a representative (*pratinidhi*) and an exchange (*pratidāna*). It shall have the aforementioned designation. *Abhimanyur arjunāt prati* (Abhimanyu is the representative of Arjuna); the meaning is "he is a substitute for him. *Tilebhyaḥ pratiyacchati māṣān* (He exchanges sesame seeds for beans). The ablative case is used here by the rule: *pratinidhipratidāne ca yasmāt* (Ablative is used after the word from which a representative or an exchange is made).

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.93) *adhi* and *pari* [are termed *karmapravacanīya*] when they are meaningless (*anarthaka*). They receive the technical designation [of *karmapravacanīya*]. For example: *kuto’dhyāgacchati* ("from where does he come?"); *kutaḥ paryāgacchati*. Here, because they lack an additional meaning (*adhikārtha*), *adhi* and *pari* are meaningless; however, since they merely follow the sense of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), they would otherwise have obtained the designation of *gati*. The purpose of this designation is to set aside that [previous designation]. Consequently, by the rule *gatir gatau* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.1.70), the suppression of accent (*nighāta*) does not occur. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.94)

The particle *su-* is used in the sense of praise (*pūjā*) [Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.94]. Examples: *susiktam* ("well-sprinkled"), *sustutam* ("well-praised"). Because it is not a preposition (*anupasarga*), the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur. Why "in the sense of praise"? Consider: *suṣiktaṃ kiṃ tavātra?* ("What have you sprinkled here so well?"). This is a reproach, not praise. How then is *suṣṭutiḥ* ("excellent praise") explained? They say that only excellence (*atiśaya*) is intended, not praise. And they recite: "The particle *su-* is used in the sense of praise, consent, earth, difficulty, and happiness" [Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.95].

And [the word] *ati* [is used] in the sense of transgression (*atiratikramaṇe*) | In the sense of transgression and in the sense of honor (*pūjā*), *ati* shall have the designation of a *karmapravacanīya*. Transgression is the performance of more than what is appropriate. *Atisiktam*, *atistutam*: the meaning is that it was sprinkled or praised excessively, or in a highly excellent manner. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.95–96)

*Api* [is termed *karmapravacanīya*] in the senses of: particle-meaning (*padārtha*), possibility (*sambhāvanā*), permission (*anvavasarga*), censure (*garhā*), and conjunction (*samuccaya*) (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.96). When these are indicated, *api* receives the designation *karmapravacanīya*. In the example *sarpiṣo 'pi syāt* ("There might even be a drop of ghee"), the suffix *liṅ* expresses a wish (*prārthanā*). The word *api*, indicating the rarity of the agent (*kartṛdaurlabhya*) with respect to the occurrence (*bhavana*) that constitutes the very object of that wish, is connected with the verb *syāt*. Because it is not a prefix (*anupasarga*), the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* does not occur. The genitive case in *sarpiṣaḥ*, however, denotes the relationship of part-to-whole (*avayavāvayavibhāva*) between the drop—understood through the force of the word *api*—and the ghee.

This indeed is what is meant by the particle *api* illuminating the meaning of the word (*padārtha-dyotakatā*). However, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) does not apply here when used with a *karmapravacanīya*, because it has been stated that there is a connection with the drop of clarified butter (*sarpiṣo bindunā*), and not with the particle *api*. *Sambhāvanā* (possibility) is an exaggeration intended to manifest the excellence of a power: "He might even water [the tree] with a thousand roots," or "He might even praise Viṣṇu. *Anvavasarga* (permission) is the granting of leave to act according to one's desire: "Water if you wish," or "Praise if you wish. In the sense of reproach (*garhā*): "Fie on Devadatta! He might even praise a low-born man (*vṛṣala*). In the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*): "Water, and praise as well."

The meaning is: "Sprinkle and praise. According to the respective rules *upasargaprādurbhyām* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.3.87) and *upasargātsunoti* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.3.65), the substitution of *ṣ* would have been required; however, it does not occur because the designation of *upasarga* is superseded by the designation of *karmapravacanīya*.
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.97).

*adhir īśvare* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.97). When the relationship between owner (*svasvāmibhāva*) is to be indicated, *adhi* shall be a *karmapravacanīya*. Here, the *karmapravacanīya* case-ending applies optionally to either the owned (*sva*) or the owner (*svāmin*), and not necessarily to only one of them as in the rules *hīne* (1.4.86) and *upo’dhike ca* (1.4.87). Examples: *adhibhūvi rāmaḥ* (Rāma is over the earth); *adhirāme bhūḥ* (the earth is under Rāma). This technical rule (*saṃjñāsūtra*) need not have been commenced; however, we shall explain in the commentary on *yasmād adhikam* (2.3.9) that this rule should not be split, as it is required for subsequent purposes. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.98)

*Vibhāṣā kṛñi* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.98): *Adhi*, when used with the root *kṛ*, may optionally have the designation of *gati*. The term *īśvara* is understood to follow from the previous rule. This is an optional rule (*prāptavibhāṣā*). "That which will appoint me here" (*yad atra mām adhikariṣyati*)—the meaning is "it will employ me. Here, the status of the employer as a master (*īśvara*) is understood. Because [the object] possesses the status of an object (*karman*), the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is applied. Here, the suppression of accent (*nighāta*) does not occur by the rule *tiṅi codāttavati* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.1.71), because the designation *gati* has been superseded.

Furthermore, in the expression *māmadhikṛtya*, there is no *prādi-samāsa* because it has been stated that there is a prohibition regarding *karmapravacanīyas*. It should be understood that in this alternative view, the form is *adhikṛtya* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.94). *laḥ parasmaipadam* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.99): The substitutes for the *lakāra* shall bear the technical designation *parasmaipada*. [Example: *pacantaṃ paśya* ("See him cooking").

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.100) *Taṅānāv ātmanepadam*: The technical term *ātmanepada* applies to the *taṅ* pratyāhāra and to the affixes *āna* and *ān*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding technical designation (*parasmaipada*). Examples: *āste*, *āsīnaḥ*, *cakrāṇaḥ*. Here, only the affixes *śānac* and *kānac* are included because they are substitutes for *l* (the *l* of *laṭ*, etc.); however, *śānan* and *cānaś* are not included. Consequently, the affix *śānan* occurs after the roots *pūṅ* and *yaj* even when the fruit of the action does not accrue to the agent—as in *rasamānasārasena*—and the affix *cānaś* occurs even after roots that are otherwise *parasmaipada*. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.101)

*Tiṅastrīṇitrīṇi prathamamadhyamottamāḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.101). Because of the *ekaśeṣa* [formation] from the *dvandva* compound, there are six technical terms (*saṃjñā*) beginning with "first" (*prathama*). The three triplets of *tiṅ* suffixes shall be designated as "first" and so forth in their respective order. Although the designation *parasmaipada* finds its scope in the *śatṛ* and *kvasu* suffixes, it is not superseded by the designations "first" and so forth; this is indicated by the rule *sicivṛddhiḥ parasmaipadeṣu* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.2.1).

Likewise, although the technical designations (saṃjñā) such as *prathama* and so forth find scope [to apply] to the *taṅ* suffixes, they are not sublated by the designation *ātmanepada*, because the rule for the *pratipadavidhi* (directly prescribed rule) regarding the *taṅ* suffixes is stated through the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) of those that have formed a *dvandva* compound. Nor should it be argued that, even so, there would be an optionality (*paryāya*) between the designations *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada* with respect to the designation *puruṣa* (person), because the rule "ṇaluttamovā" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.1.21) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) based on a general consideration. Furthermore, the use of these "great designations" (*mahāsaṃjñā*) in these three rules is out of deference to the ancient teachers (*pūrvācārya*).

In this context, *iha trīṇi trīṇi* is one word (*ekam padam*), according to Haradatta, or two words (*dve vā*). Even though there is an intermediate word-designation (*avāntara-pada-saṃjñā*) therein, the designation of a "great word" (*mahāpada-saṃjñā*) prevails, because of the application of the rule: "Sandhi is obligatory within a single word" (*saṃhitā ekapade nityā*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of separate word-divisions (*avagraha*) even in compounds and the like, as well as the consequence of the occurrence of other intervening words between reduplicated forms. For this very reason, in the Veda, an *avagraha* (word-division) is made in cases such as *tātā piṇḍānām*.
We shall explain how both the great word-designation and the intermediate designation apply to reduplicated forms under the rule *nityavīpsayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.4).

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.102) *Tāny ekavacana-dvivacana-bahuvacanāny ekaśaḥ*. Those [terms] which have acquired the designation *puruṣa* (person), three by three, shall individually and in order receive the designations *ekavacana* (singular) and so forth. The mention of the word *tāni* (those) is for the purpose of ensuring their coexistence; otherwise, there would be mutual exclusion between the designations *puruṣa* and *vacana*. Consequently, operations such as "āḍ uttamasya" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.4.92) would not apply in certain instances. The form *ekaśaḥ* is derived from the nominative singular *eka* with the suffix *śas* used in the sense of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*). (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.103)

*Supaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.103): The three triplets of *sup* [case endings] shall, respectively, have the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) "dual," "singular," and "plural. Here, by relying on their etymological significance (*anvarthatā*), it is possible to dispense with the rules "the dual and singular are used for two and one" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.22) and "the plural is used for many" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.23). This is because, even though the singular is the default (*autsargika*), its etymological significance can be easily maintained according to the circumstances, just as in the case of technical designations such as "subordinate element" (*upasarjana*) or "governing particle" (*karmapravacanīya*).
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.104)

And [the word] *vibhakti* [is defined]. The [suffixes] *sup* and *tiṅ* are designated as *vibhakti*. The particle *ca* is for the purpose of combining [this designation] with the designations of person (*puruṣa*) and voice (*vacana*). The purpose of the designation *vibhakti* for *tiṅ*s is [to prevent the application of the rule] *na vibhaktau tusmāḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.4); for *sup*s, however, it is also for [the application of rules such as] the substitution of *yat* for *tyad* and so forth. (Pāṇini 1.4.105)

"When *yuṣmad* is present as a coreferential term (*samānādhikaraṇa*), even when [the verb] is not [actually] used, the second person (*madhyama*) [is employed] (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.105). When *yuṣmad* is used—or even when it is not used—as coreferential with the *lakāra* (the verbal suffix), the second person shall occur. For example: *tvaṃ pacasi dṛśyase ca* ("You cook and are seen"). Why "coreferential"? [Consider: *tvāṃ paśyati* ("He sees you") and *tvayā dṛśyate* ("It is seen by you"). In this case, one might argue that it would be sufficient simply to state: "When *yuṣmad* [is present], the second person; when *asmad*, the first person," because this would account for everything. However, it was not formulated in that way.

However, in the case of *atvaṃ tvaṃ bhavati* and *tvadbhavatī*, [the suffix] does not apply, because the intermediate modification (*madhyamavikṛti*) is not the agent (*kartṛ*). For it is the original material (*prakṛti*) alone that is the agent when undergoing transformation into the form of a modification. And thus says the mantra: "O Agni, may I be you, or may you be me. Here, the person (*puruṣa*) is based solely upon the original material (*prakṛti*), [expressing]: "May I be you," or "May you be me."

It might be argued that in the case of "bhavān karoti" (you do), the second person ending would also apply because [the rule] states "also when [yuṣmad] is in its original form. To this they reply: the referent of *yuṣmad* is devoid of gender and has as its sole domain the vocative; whereas the referent of *bhavat* possesses gender and is common to both the vocative and non-vocative. Furthermore, if the referent of *yuṣmad* had the vocative as its sole domain, then the nominative case-ending would necessarily follow after it only in the vocative.

Furthermore, it should be stated that there would be both the acute accent on the first syllable due to being addressed (*āmantrita*) and the *nighāta* (anudātta) accent due to its following a word; however, this is not so, because the vocative is included within the very meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). For it will be explained that the rule "and in the case of address" (*sambodhane ca*, Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.47) is for the purpose of adding [the designation of] address. As for what some, accepting the undesirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), read:
"The meaning of address is accepted by some everywhere in the second person."
Likewise, they know that the entire first case ending is used for the word *yuṣmad* in the vocative.
"Because the referent of *yuṣmad* is already established [as a pronoun], its initial udātta accent is fixed;
provided that this [first case ending] of *yuṣmad* follows immediately after a word [and not at the beginning of a sentence]. Thus [it is stated].

That is not so, because it contradicts the stated rule and contradicts the definition [of a word]. For we observe that even at the beginning of a *pāda* there is an udātta accent on the final syllable, and even when following a word (*padāt paratve*), there is no *nighāta* (elision of accent). For example: *yuvaṃ ha garbhaṃ jagatīṣu dhatthaḥ*, *yūyaṃ yāta svastibhiḥ*, and *ha ye devā yūyam idāpayaḥ stha* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.106).

Pāṇini Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.106 states: "And when *prahāsa* (jesting) is involved, when *manya* is the upapada, the middle [person] occurs for the root [to which *manya* is subordinate], and [the verb] is singular. The realized meaning is as follows: when the root *manya* is the upapada of another root that serves as the base (*prakṛti*), the middle person should be used if jesting is understood; however, for the root *manya* itself, the highest person (the first person) should be used, and it should express a single object. Thus, even when there are two or many persons being thought of, the singular number alone should be employed. The particle *ca* in the rule *ekavacca* functions as a conjunction (*anvācaya*) [meaning "and [it is] singular"].

Therefore, even though there is no formation of a singular compound (ekavadbhāva), the forms *madhyama* and *uttama*, which are taught as the primary [referents], certainly exist. Even when *odana* (rice) is present, a person habituated to joking, such as a brother-in-law (*śālaka*), might use them deceptively, saying: "Come, I think you will eat rice" (*ehi manye odanaṃ bhokṣyadhve*), or "I shall eat rice" (*odanaṃ bhokṣye*) and "We two shall eat" (*bhokṣyāvahe*), and so on; the meanings are respectively "you think" (*manyase*) and "you two think" (*manyethe*), etc. The rule *yuṣmadyupapade* ("when *yusmad* is the attendant word") and so forth continues to apply here. Consequently, it does not occur here: "May you come, sir; I think I shall eat rice" (*etu bhavān manyate odanaṃ bhokṣye*). Because of the specific mention of the suffix *śyan*, it does not occur here either: "Come, I believe I shall go by chariot" (*ehi manuṣe rathena yāsyāmi*).

In what case does this [substitution] not apply? It should not occur when stating the actual fact: *manyase odanaṃ bhokṣya iti bhuktaḥ so'tithibhiḥ* ("You think you will eat rice, but it has been eaten by the guests"). *Asmady uttamaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.107): When *asmat* (the word "I/we") is present in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the *lakāra* (verbal suffix), the first person (*uttama-puruṣa*) shall occur even if [another pronoun] is the original base (*sthānin*). For example: *ahaṃ paśyāmi* or *dṛśye* ("I see"). However, when there is coreferentiality with both *yuṣmad* and *asmat*, the first person alone occurs because it is the subsequent rule. For example: *ahaṃ ca tvaṃ ca vṛtrahan svayujyāvasanibhyāḥ* ("O slayer of Vṛtra, both I and you, through our own union, [attain] dwellings").
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.108) *śeṣe prathamaḥ*: In cases other than those pertaining to the middle and the highest persons, the first person shall be used. For example: *pacati*, *pacataḥ*, *pacanti*.
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.109)

*Paraḥ saṃnikarṣaḥ saṃhitā* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.109). That which is the closest proximity (*atiśayitaḥ saṃnidhiḥ*) of phonemes shall be designated as *saṃhitā*. The applications of this designation are found in rules such as *saṃhitāyām* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.72), and so forth. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.110).

*Virāma* is the term for *avasāna* (Pāṇini 1.4.110). The absence of phonemes shall be designated as *avasāna*. The applications of this designation are found in rules such as *vāvasāne* (Pāṇini 8.4.56) and others. Even in the case of an absence, there exists a sequence of priority and posteriority produced by the intellect, whether in the case of phonemes that perish as soon as they are uttered or those that are eternal and all-pervading. Alternatively, the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*), meaning "that by which one ceases [speaking]"; thus, the final phoneme itself is the designated entity (*saṃjñī*). In this view, although the locative case in *kharavasānayoḥ* is a single form, it is differentiated according to its distinct objects of application.

"When *khari* (voiceless consonants) follows, there is *visarga* for *repha* (*r*), and *repha* is the substitute in the *avasāna* (pause). Regarding this, there is a *vārttika*: "Since *saṃhitā* and *avasāna* are well-known in common usage, [the rule] is established by the mention of *at*. Thus, the meaning is that these two rules need not exist. Thus ends the fourth *āhnika* of the fourth *pāda* of the first *adhyāya* in the *Śabdakaustubha*, composed by Bhaṭṭoji Bhaṭṭa, son of Śrī Lakṣmīdhara Sūri, who has crossed the ocean of the *pada*, *vākya*, and *pramāṇa*.
Now the second chapter begins.

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.1) *Samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ* (A rule concerning words is dependent on their semantic capacity). Any rule relating to words (*pada*) should be understood as being based on semantic capacity (*samartha*). This is a *paribhāṣā* (metarule). The word *samartha* here is used metaphorically (*lakṣaṇā*) to mean "dependent upon that" [capacity]. And in this context, semantic capacity consists in "becoming a single meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*). That is to say, it is the attainment of a specific unified meaning by that which was initially apprehended as having separate meanings during the stage of grammatical analysis (*prakriyā*). Examples: *rājapuruṣaḥ* (king's man), *putrīyati* (he treats like a son), *kumbhakāraḥ* (pot-maker), *aupagavaḥ* (son of Upagu).

In this context, according to the maxim "a quality [is subordinate] when its own refinement has been accomplished," the *mahāvibhāṣā* functions as a qualifier by virtue of its specific capacity; for its meaning is that a word ending in the genitive case, which has optionally attained a unified meaning (*ekārthībhūta*), is compounded. Furthermore, precisely because of the force of this qualification, the view of syntactic dependence (*vyapekṣā*) is also accepted. However, the formal operation (*vṛtti*) is restricted to compounds and the like. For this very reason, the qualifier "of the prosperous one" (*ṛddhasya*) does not apply there [to the compound], because it is a part of the denotable object (*śakyaikadeśatvāt*).

For indeed, in the cognition produced by the word *śvaśura* (father-in-law), the wife—who is presented as a qualifier of the father—is not connected with qualifiers such as *suśīlāya* (well-behaved). Nor does this lead to the consequence of non-connection in cases such as *devadattasya gurukulam* (Devadatta’s teacher’s family), because even there, the meaning of the genitive case following the word *devadatta* is connected with the *kula* (family) itself. The relation expressed by the genitive, however, is mediated solely through the presented teacher (*guru*) and not anything else. As it has been said: "Those [words] whose connection is with a whole, such as 'the teacher's family' (*gurukula*), are joined with that which possesses [the whole] after having touched its parts."

Alternatively, even though a word denoting a relational entity may constitute only a part [of that whole], the connection with a qualifier certainly occurs, as seen in examples such as "Caitra’s grandson" (*caitrasya naptā*). This is also because the wife, who is presented by the word *śvaśura* (father-in-law), serves as a qualifier for her husband, since there is an expectancy (*utthitākāṅkṣā*) regarding that portion. And it has been said: "A relational term is always dependent; all such terms are compounded. Even when in a compound (*vṛtti*), its dependence on its own referent is not lost."

Therefore, in the case of compounds, words ending in *su*-suffixes, verbal roots (*dhātu*), primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), there is no connection with a qualifier; however, such a connection would occur when [the word] is dependent (*sāpekṣa*).

It might be argued: "Since the formation [of the compound] is possible through the power of the parts already established in the sentence, let there be no additional power. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence of a connection with qualifiers, because the prohibition—'there is no application of a compound when it has qualifiers, nor is there a connection with qualifiers for that which has already been compounded'—is applicable. This is true;

however, if one were to establish the properties of compounding for many elements by means of verbal injunctions alone, there would be great prolixity. Therefore, the state of "unification of meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*) is accepted.

The prohibition of the particle *ca* and so forth, as well as the subversion of many established linguistic usages, must be performed by you; however, our position is that such matters are already established by logic.

For instance, in the expression "the Dhava and Khadira trees," the particle *ca* (and) is not employed because its meaning is already encompassed by the compound itself. Similarly, this applies to words such as *citragu* ("possessor of brindled cows"). You, however, must provide an explanation for this. Furthermore, conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) does not differ significantly from primary denotation (*śakti*), especially since the Naiyāyikas do not accept it in the sense of the particle *ca*.

According to the method explained in the *Akathitasūtra*, there is non-difference between the name (the nominal stem) and its meaning, as well as the abandonment of the grammatical derivation that "the meaning of the suffix is primary" (*pratyayārthaḥ pradhānam*), because in examples such as *prāptodakaḥ* ("one who has obtained water"), the meaning is accepted as "the object of the attainment whose agent is water," and so forth. However, in the case of *ekārthībhāva* (unification of meaning), there is brevity (*lāghava*). Although in the final system (*siddhānta*) it is the word or the sentence that possesses the expressive power (*śakti*), the intention is that at the stage of the analytical process (*prakriyā-daśā*), *ekārthībhāva* is adopted for the sake of brevity. For whatever is our own analytical process is grasped by others as being ultimately real; thus, it is appropriate to present the argument regarding complexity (*gaurava*) against them. This is the general direction of the argument.

In some cases, however, a compound occurs despite the presence of mutual expectancy (*sāpekṣatva*), on the authority of the Bhāṣya. For example: *kimodanaḥ śālīnām* ("What kind of rice-gruel?"). The meaning is: "Of which rice-grains is this gruel? *saktvāḍhakam āpaṇīyānām* ("A measure of groats of marketable [grains]"). The meaning is: "A measure of groats that are for sale. *kuto bhavān pāṭaliputrakaḥ* ("From where do you come, O inhabitant of Pāṭaliputra?"). There are two Pāṭaliputras; the meaning is: "From which of those two Pāṭaliputras have you come? The suffix *vuñ* is applied here by the rule *ropadhetoḥ prācām* (Pāṇini 4.2.123).

Likewise, some negative compounds (nañ-samāsa) are also correct, such as "an aśrāddhabhojī brāhmaṇaḥ" (a Brahmin who does not eat at a śrāddha feast). However, some are not correct, such as "akiñcitkurvāṇam" (doing nothing); the intended meaning here is "not doing even the slightest thing."

In this regard, the following should be noted: the semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) in a sentence is threefold—differentiation (*bheda*), relation (*saṃsarga*), and both differentiation and relation. In the first case, the verbal nature belongs solely to the exclusion of what is other (*atadvyāvṛtti*); the relation, however, is extrinsic (*ārtha*). In the second case, it is the reverse. In the third case, both are verbal. But in the non-worldly (*alaukika*) analytical sentence (*prakriyāvākya*), even when any one of the aforementioned three is apprehended, a *vṛtti* (compound formation) is postulated, because in the final (*pariniṣṭhita*) form, the absence of the connection with qualifiers and so forth is observed.

Just as, having observed coreferentiality with a word ending in the accusative case and so forth in examples such as *śatru*, one postulates [that same relation] for the *lakāra* (verbal suffix), for this very reason, since qualities such as being variegated (*citratva*) are seen to refer to the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*), one likewise postulates that [referentiality] even in the non-worldly *prakriyā*-sentence; for its establishment is achieved through the very restatement found in the Sūtra beginning with "in the meaning of another word" (*anyapadārthe*), which establishes the possession of a physical form by the deity. This is the direction [of the argument]. Thus ends the first Āhnika of the first Pāda of the second Adhyāya in the *Śabdakaustubha*.

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.2) *subāmantrite parāṅgavatsvare* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.2). A word ending in a *sup*-suffix (*subanta*) preceding an address (*āmantrita*) shall be treated as if it were the subsequent member (*parāṅgavat*) when an accent is to be applied. It must be understood that this refers to that which causes [the application of the accent]. The meaning is: that which expresses the cause of the sense of that address—that alone shall be treated as the subsequent member, and nothing else. For example: *yatte divo duhitarmartabhojanam*. Because the word *divaḥ* is treated as the subsequent member, it receives the grave accent (*nighāta*) according to the eighth chapter [of the Aṣṭādhyāyī].

Because of the grasping of those signs, [one recites] here: "O Agni, grow strong by this very prayer; O Agni, this singer [praises you]; through this [prayer], O Mitra and Varuṇa, you who increase the cosmic order (*ṛta*) and touch the cosmic order, you have attained great mental power."

It might be argued as follows: The word *ṛta* is indeed oxytone (accented on the final syllable) because it belongs to the *ghṛtādi* group. Let there be no application of the rule regarding "behaving like the subsequent member" (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) to that [word *ṛta*] due to its being the cause for that accent. However, this would not apply to the compound *mitrāvaruṇau* either. For the form *ṛtāvṛdhau* is derived in the sense "the two who increase the *ṛta*" (*ṛtasya vardhayitārau*), where, after the suffix *kvip* is added to the root *vṛdh* with an implied causal sense (*antarbhāvitavyartha*), the lengthening of the first member occurs according to Pāṇini 6.3.137 (*anyeṣām api dṛśyate*). And in that case, *mitrāvaruṇau* is not the cause.

Nor should it be argued that this is to avoid the status of being a subordinate member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) [of the preceding vocative]; for then the rule *ṛtāvṛdhau* would fail to receive the low-pitched accent (*nighāta*), because it begins the second quarter of the verse and is thus barred by the prohibition *apādādau*. For this very reason, in the mantra *imaṃ me gaṅge*, although the low-pitched accent is applied based on the fact that all [vocatives] follow the word *me*—since each preceding vocative is treated as non-existent (*avidyamānavat*)—the accent is applied only to the triad beginning with *gaṅge*, and not even to *śutudrī*.

Regarding this, the authors of the *Vedabhāṣya* say: "Let there be no mention of the condition 'on account of that' (*tannimitta*); for all desired results are established by the rule itself. This is indeed correct. To explain: according to the perspective of the *Bhāṣya* on the *Samartha-sūtra*, which states, "Some hold that semantic expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) constitutes capacity (*sāmarthya*"), capacity is understood here [in the sense of expectancy]. However, under the view of "integration into a single meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*), it is the term "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) itself that is carried over (*anuvṛtti*) here. Furthermore, it should be understood that this is an extension of the governing heading concerning words (*śabdādhikāra*). It is precisely for this purpose that this rule is introduced at this point in the text.

And thus, because the two words *ṛtena* and *mitrāvaruṇau* are construed with the verb *ānaśāthe* (which has the meaning of *ānaśāthe*), they lack mutual syntactic independence (*asāmarthya*). Consequently, there is no absence of the treatment as a subordinate member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*), and therefore the sixth [rule] does not apply to yield an initial acute accent (*ādyudātta*); rather, the eighth rule applies to produce the *nighāta* (anudātta) accent. However, for the word *mitrāvaruṇau*, because of its status as a subordinate member in the phrase *vṛtāvṛdhau*, it is not at the beginning of a *pāda*; thus, it is indeed subject to the *nighāta*.

Furthermore, the rule *Aṣṭādhyāyī* 8.3.44, *isusoḥ sāmarthye*, which prescribes the substitution of *sa* for the suffixes *iṣ* and *us*, does not apply here to achieve forms such as *sarpiṣkāla* or *sarpiṣkāra*. This is because the principle "that which is in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) becomes meaningful" does not operate in this context; for while that principle applies to ensure the formation of *sarpiṣpīyate* and so forth—given the specific qualification "not denoting a verbal root" (*adhātvabhihita*)—in the present case, [the word *sarpiḥ*] denotes a verbal root. If it is argued that, in this way, even the word *śutudri* would lose its accentual status (be *nihata*), since the preceding word *sarasvatī* would, by virtue of being a subordinate member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*), cause the beginning of the compound to be treated as the start of a subsequent word (*apādādi*)—we say no. For although all the words are connected with the verb *sacatā* ("may she attend"), they lack mutual semantic connection (*asāmarthya*). As it has been said:
"And that which is the vocative case is an attribute of the verb.

Now, one might ask: since words such as *gaṅge* ending in the singular cannot have grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with *sacata* ending in the plural, how can there be a single sentence (*ekavākyatā*), and likewise, how can there be the *nighāta* (accentual suppression)? To this, it must be said that the author of the *Vārttika* established the governing rule for "a single sentence" (*samānavākya-adhikāra*). This is because, within the three *sūtras* beginning with "when *yuṣmad* is the attendant word" (*yuṣmadyupapade*, Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.105), both the *Bhāṣya* and the *Vārttika* have justified coreferentiality even when there is a difference in number.

Furthermore, there is no stated obstacle to the application of a different number (*saṃkhyāntara*) even when those things which were not the qualificands of a cognition characterized by individual unitary aspects have been combined; for there are abundant usages in both the Veda and common parlance, such as "O slayer of Vṛtra, you and I shall unite for the sake of the Anasūyas," and "For the two [of us] are taught by the learned as equal, and so too will our future ailments."

By this, those who supply the word *ete* (these) in order to establish the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) for the phrase "the fame of the Creator is said to be broken" in the verse "A spot on the moon, poverty in the virtuous," are refuted. For if that were the case, there would arise the fault of the lack of connection (*ananvaya*) between the supplied word *ete* and the "spot" (*kalaṅka*) and other terms; furthermore, there would be the consequence that the *nighāta* (tonal suppression) rule would not apply in cases such as "O Gaṅgā. This is the general direction of the argument.

If it is argued: "Even so, how can there be the status of being like a subordinate element (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) for *mitrāvaruṇau*, given that by the rule 'an antecedent vocative is as if non-existent' (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.1.72), it becomes as if non-existent?"—do not say so. For this extension (*atideśa*) applies when an operation is to be performed on a subsequent element, but not even for an operation on itself; otherwise, the mention of the word "antecedent" (*pūrva*) would become redundant. Furthermore, the status of being like a subordinate element is not an operation belonging to the subsequent element, but rather to itself.

For this very reason, in cases such as *vāyo yāhi*, *agne naya*, and *indra dehy adhiratham*, the acute accent on the first syllable of the vocative (*āmantrita-ādyudātta*) indeed occurs; the suppression of accent (*nighāta*) prescribed by the rule *tiṅṅ atiṅaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.28) does not apply to what follows. Furthermore, even granting [the opponent's position], we say: in the present instance, the vocative *mitrāvaruṇau* is a general term, while *ṛtāvṛdhau* is a specific term serving as its qualifier.

Therefore, by the rule *nāmantrite samānādhikaraṇe sāmānyavacanam* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.1.73), the status of being treated as non-existent (*avidyamānavadbhāva*) is prohibited. Now, one might object: even so, because the word *mitrāvaruṇa* is treated like a subordinate member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*), it would begin a new metrical foot (*pādādi*), and thus the exclusion *apādādau* [of the vocative accent] would apply. This is not so; for this is not an extension (*atideśa*) of an operation, but rather an extension of identity (*tādātmya*). When that [identity] is extended, whatever can be performed on the basis of the cognition that "this is a qualified vocative" (*viśiṣṭam āmantritam*) is indeed carried out.

Furthermore, even the extension of an operation (*kāryātideśa*) is difficult to establish for that which is not sanctioned by grammatical rules; how much more so, then, the extension of identity (*tādātmyātideśa*)? [Question: Why [is the word] *sub* mentioned? [Consider the example: *pīḍye-pīḍyamānā*. [Objection: Since there is an absence of "single-meaningness" (*ekārthībhāva*) here, the technical rule regarding "capacity" (*samartha-paribhāṣā*) does not apply; nevertheless, because the mention of "capacity" (*samartha-grahaṇa*) is understood as a recurring element (*anuvṛtti*), the treatment as "like a subsequent member" (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) will not occur. And thus, since the vowel *i* is introduced after a base taught with *a* (an *adupadeśa*), when this low-pitched (*anudātta*) *i* undergoes a single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) with the high-pitched (*udātta*) [vowel], the form *pīḍya-* is correctly established as having its final syllable acute (*antodātta*). [Reply: Not so, because capacity (*sāmarthya*) exists here as well. For the meaning of the sentence is: "O you who are being tormented, [this is] a torment. And it has been said:
"And that which is a vocative case is an adjective (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the verb; [thus] in 'vrajāni devadatta' (let me go, Devadatta), there is the *nighāta* (elision of accent) when that is the case.

This is because of the intention [expressed] in the Vārttika author's statement: "In a single sentence, there is the *nighāta* and the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*; a sentence is a verb together with its adjectives. Why is the term "member" (*aṅga*) mentioned? So that both [the verb and the vocative] do not have the acute accent (*ādyudātta*) separately. Why is the term "that" (*tat*) mentioned? So that it may apply even to what is based on itself (*svāśraya*). [Example: *āmū kuṇḍena aṭan*. There is the status of being separated by one intervening word (*ekāntara*) according to Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.1.55: "A vocative, when not near, is separated by one intervening word from *ām*."

What is meant by "in regard to accent" (*svara*)? In the examples *kūpe siñcan* ("pouring into a well") and *varma naman* ("bending armor"), the treatment as if being the prior member (*parāṅgavadbhāvaḥ*) does not apply with respect to the substitution of *ṣatva* and *ṇatva*. An addition (*upasaṃkhyānam*) must be made for the case of a word in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), because [the condition of] immediate succession (*anantarātva*) is absent—as in *tīkṣṇayā sūcyā sīvyan* ("sewing with a sharp needle"). Nor should it be argued that once the treatment as the prior member has been applied to the subsequent element, the same result for the preceding element is already established by the rule itself; for this is restricted by the mention of "in regard to accent. This is because when the treatment as the prior member is to be effected, that [condition of immediate succession] is difficult to obtain. In reality, however, the mention of "in regard to accent" need not be made at all.

In the example *kūpe siñcan*, because the word *pada* and others which serve as its own substratum (*svāśraya*) exist, the prohibition by the rule *sātpadādyoḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.3.22) is possible. However, the substitution of *ṇ* will not occur due to the restriction that this substitution takes place only when [the *s*] follows a preceding member (*pūrvapada*) in a technical name (*saṃjñā*). The *Bhāṣya* states that even in the absence of a compound, the term *pūrvapada* can be understood in its etymological sense alone (*yaugikārtha*) in accordance with the observed linguistic usage (*lakṣya*). Alternatively, since the word *āmantrite* is present [in the context], the status of being like a subsequent member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*) applies specifically to an operation conditioned by the state of being an address (*āmantritatva*), because of its immediate proximity.

Thus, it is established that both the supplementary rule regarding grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) when there is the status of being like a subordinate member (*parāṅgavadbhāva*), and the mention of accent (*svaragrahaṇa*), need not be formulated. Furthermore, it should be stated that in the Veda (*chandas*), even what follows [a word] behaves like its preceding member: *ā te pitarmarutāṃ sumnametu*, *pratitvā duhitardivaḥ*, *vṛṇīṣva duhitardivaḥ*. There is also a prohibition concerning indeclinables (*avyaya*): *uccairadhīyāna*. However, it has been stated that this prohibition does not apply to an avyayībhāva compound.

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.3) *prāk kaḍārāt samāsaḥ*. From the rule *kaḍārāḥ karmadhāraye* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.38) onwards, the term *samāsa* (compound) is the governing heading (*adhikāra*). Furthermore, the word *prāk* (before) is repeated [in each subsequent rule]. By this, it is understood that first the designation *samāsa* is applied, and thereafter other designations as well. Consequently, coexistence (*samāveśa*) with the designations such as *avyayībhāva* and others is established; otherwise, there would be mutual exclusion (*paryāya*). (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.4)

*sa-ha sup* (Pāṇini 2.1.4). Here, the rule is divided (*yogavibhāga*). A word ending in a *sup* suffix is compounded with a word that is "capable" (*samartha*) of being connected with it. This rule has as its scope only a limited number of finite verbs (*tiṅanta*), because of the subsequent introduction of the rule *sup-supā* (2.1.4). Therefore, one should not raise the objection of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). [Examples: *yo jāta eva paryabhūṣat*; *yaḥ śambaraṃ anvavindat*. Since what is established by the division of the rule is not universal, we do not have here: *samprayaccha vṛṣṇyā indrāya bhāgam*.

For this very reason, regarding the statement made by the author of the *Vārttika* under the governing rule *nityaṃ krīḍā* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.17)—namely, that "there is a compound of a finite verb (*tiṅ*) possessing an acute accent (*udāttavat*) and denoting motion with [another] word denoting motion" (*udāttavatā gatimatā ca tiṅā gateḥ samāsaḥ*)—the *Bhāṣya* establishes it here by dividing the rule. Similarly, it is stated that even "compounding with *iva*" (*ivena samāsaḥ*) is established by the rule *sup supā*. And this is indeed correct.

Otherwise, if a compulsory compound (*nityasamāsa*) were to apply according to the method of the *Vārttika*, it would result in the inconsistency of forms such as *ya ānayat* and *āyonayat samprayaccha*; furthermore, it would lead to the contradiction of the Taittirīyas reading *jīmūtasyeva* and so forth as two separate words. For this very reason, even the usage of separated and non-compounded forms in *udvāhuriva* and similar instances is justified, since the authority of the sages increases in successive order. However, a compound with a finite verb (*tiṅsamāsa*) occurs only in the Vedic language (*chandasi*).

For this very reason, Haradatta maintains that there is no single compound (*ekapada*) in the rule *karmaṇā yamabhipraiti* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.32). This is established precisely because [the application of the rule] is not universal. And this is logical, since it must be stated that in that case the elision of the case-ending (*sub-luk*) occurs by virtue of its being Vedic (*chāndasa*). Otherwise, according to the Bhāṣya statement, "The singular number shall be treated as the general rule," even though the elision of the suffix *su* produced after a compound might occur in examples such as *paryabhūṣat* by the rule *halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt* (6.1.68), it would result in the audible presence of the suffix in examples such as *yat prakaroti*.

Nor can the matter be resolved by accepting [the word] as neuter, because in examples such as *yat prakurute*, a short vowel (*hrasva*) would result, and in *prakurvīran*, the elision of the nasal (*nalopa*) would result. Therefore, in usages such as *prabhavati* found in poetry and other literature, the prefix (*upasarga*) is indeed a separate word. As for the word *iva* in examples such as *vāgarthāviva*, it may be either compounded or separate. However, the truth is that in cases such as *udvāhuriva vāmanaḥ* and *kacācitau viṣvagivāgajau gajau*, it is certainly separate.

As for the claim made by someone that this is a *chāndasa* (Vedic) compound with *iva*, that is baseless and contradicts the separate recitation (*pṛthakpāṭha*) of the Taittirīyas; furthermore, it is contrary to the view of the rhetoricians who cite the *śrautī upamā* as occurring within a compound. Moreover: "I experience non-duality, yet I see my body like a wood-apple in the palm of my hand, as if it were a mere skin-casing."

All such constructions are in agreement with the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *anyapadārtha*, which states: "Indeed, [the compound] does not exist with that which ends in the nominative case alone. For this very reason, the examples from the *Pariśiṣṭa*—such as *agnir iva rājā* ("a king like fire") and *vāyur iva pāśaḥ* ("a noose like the wind")—are also consistent. Let this matter rest for now.

However, this remains to be addressed: once a *tiṅ*-compound has been formed, the final accentuation of the compound (*samāsāntodāttatā*)—being the later rule (*satiśiṣṭa*)—would prevail over the subsequent suppression of the accent (*nighāta*) prescribed by Pāṇini 8.1.28 (*tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*). This is not an acceptable conclusion, for in examples such as *paryabhūṣat* and *tadevānupraviśat*, we observe that the final syllable is never accented.

In this matter, the truth is as follows: the rule prescribing the suppression (nighāta) of the accent of a motion (*gati*) when it precedes a finite verb ending in an acute accent—namely, *tiṅi codāttavati* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.1.71)—is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that there is no final acute accent in a *tiṅ-samāsa*. However, according to the view of the Bhāṣya, since the mention of *kṛt*-derivatives in the rule *gatikārakopapadātkṛt* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.2.139) has been rejected, there is no fault whatsoever.

Here, this should be noted: although the rule *suṣupā* (Pāṇini 2.1.4) prescribes compounds formed with indeclinables such as *saha*, specific technical designations like *avyayībhāva* and so forth do not apply in cases such as *vāgarthāviva* or *pūrvaṃ bhūto bhūtapūrvaḥ*, because these are not recited under those respective governing rules (*adhikāra*). The same applies to examples such as *vispaṣṭapaṭuḥ* and *kākatālīyaḥ*, for there too the rule *suṣupā* is operative. In *vispaṣṭapaṭuḥ*, *kākatālīyaḥ*, and the like, the rule *suṣupā* indeed functions.

Rules such as *vispaṣṭādīni guṇavacaneṣu* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.2.24) and *samāsācca tadviṣayāt* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.3.106), although initiated for the purpose of [specific] accentual suffixes (*svarachapratyaya*), serve to establish compounds according to the maxim of the "old maiden seeking a husband" (*vṛddhakumārīvaranyāya*). Thus, even in this view, the absence of a specific technical designation (*viśeṣasaṃjñā*) is exactly the same. The statement that "compound is fourfold" is merely a general rule of thumb. For this very reason, they recite: "When the question 'What is a compound? arises regarding the scope of *vispaṣṭa* and *paṭu*, those who would speak of it as merely a compound are indeed *vispaṣṭapaṭu* (clearly clever)."

Here, the word *vispaṣṭam* (clearly) is an adjective qualifying *pāṭavasya* (of proficiency). Furthermore, there is acceptance here even of partial application (*ekadeśānvaya*). Likewise, [definitions] such as "the *avyayībhāva* is that in which the meaning of the first member is predominant" were formulated by the ancient teachers (*pūrvācārya*).
