Although these are accepted here on the strength of the technical usage of their great designations (*mahāsaṃjñā*), nevertheless all of that is merely the general rule (*autsargika*); for while a *tatpuruṣa* compound like *ardhapippalī* has the predominance of the meaning of the first member, an *avyayībhāva* like *unmattagaṅgam* has the predominance of the meaning of the other member. This is the direction of the argument.

Although in the *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning its own meaning) type of compound the two constituent words (*varti-pada*) are devoid of meaning, whereas in the *ajahatsvārthā* (not abandoning its own meaning) type both possess a qualified meaning, nevertheless—due to the unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*)—one should understand that the maintenance of the aforementioned general linguistic conventions is achieved by relying on the entry of those two distinct word-meanings from the prior state into the compound, by way of predominance and non-predominance. Furthermore, this compound is sixfold. To explain: [the maintenance of the aforementioned general linguistic conventions is to be understood]. Moreover, this compound is sixfold. To explain:

The wise have declared that compound (samāsa) is of six kinds: [the compound] of case-inflected words with case-inflected words, with a verbal suffix (tiṅ), with a noun (nāman), with a verbal root (dhātu), of verbal suffixes with verbal suffixes, and [the compound] with a word ending in a case-suffix (subanta).

*Sup* [nominal suffixes] with *sup*: *rājapuruṣaḥ*. *Ting* [verbal suffixes] with *ting*: *paryabhūṣat*. *Nāman* [nominal stems] with *nāman*: *kumbhakāraḥ*. *Dhātu* [roots] with *dhātu*: *kaṭaprūḥ*. With *ajasram*. *Ting* with *ting*: *pibatakhādatā*. *Ting* with *sup*: *jahijohaḥ*. In this compound (*samāsa*), this division is made by prioritizing the prior member (*pūrvapada*) and the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). Therefore, there is no fault even when the middle members are not fixed, because in the case of *ehi re yāhi re*, the prior and subsequent members are *sub*-ending words. In all these instances, the status of being a "word" (*padatva*) for the prior member is invariable.

For this very reason, the statement that "the mention of *samāsa* [in Pāṇini 6.2.142] is for the purpose of restriction" refers to those cases where the preceding member is a word (*pada*). Consequently, as explained in the *Arthavat-sūtra*, the acute accent (*udātta*) of the vowel following the *ṭakāra* in the form *bahupaṭavaḥ* is established.

*ivena samāso vibhaktyalopaḥ pūrvapadaprakṛtisvaratvaṃ ca*. Here, having referred back to the compound established by the two previously mentioned rules (*sup supā* and *tiṅ supā*), the absence of case-elision and the preservation of the original accent of the first member are prescribed. As for the subsequent placement of the word *iva* before the verbal form, it is due to its inclusion in the class of *rājadanta* and others (*ākṛtigaṇa*). Examples: *vāsayasīva vedhasaḥ*; *jīmūtasyeva bhavati*. Those compounds for which no specific rule exists are governed by this heading: *saha* (Pāṇini 2.1.5). This is an introductory heading (*adhikāra*).

"An indeclinable [compound] is formed with words expressing: division, proximity, abundance, increase, absence, passing away, 'not at present,' the appearance of a word, sequence, simultaneity, similarity, completion, totality, and limit" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.6). Regarding this, the author of the Nyāsa on the sūtras "gambhīrāñ ñyaḥ" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.3.58) and "avyayībhāvācca" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.3.59) analyzes the rule as *avyayam* [separated from the rest]. By this, the form *apadiśam* ("between the two directions") is established. Because it belongs to the *śarad*-class, the suffix *ṭac* is applied. Amarasimha states: "The neuter indeclinable *apadiśam* means the intermediate space between two directions; the feminine term *vidiś* [also denotes this]. (Amarakośa 3.1.5).

In reality, however, we shall explain in the remainder of the Sūtra that the desired result is established even without the formal splitting of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). Here, "case-ending" (*vibhakti*) refers to the kāraka-potency, based on the etymological derivation: "that by which the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is differentiated. The word "number" (*vacana*) is derived as a passive noun (*karmasādhana*). And this [word] is connected with each of the case-endings and so forth through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). The absence of the rule for placing [the shorter term] first is a Vedic (or Sūtra) anomaly.

The meaning is this: an indeclinable (*avyaya*) ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), which functions as an indicator (*dyotaka*) with respect to these meanings and has become a single unified meaning (*ekārthabhūta*) with another word ending in a case-suffix, shall first receive the designation of *samāsa*, and thereafter the designation of *avyayībhāva*. Although the formation of a compound is already established by the rule *sup supā* alone, its non-universality (*asārvatrikatā*) is nevertheless made known by the subsequent rules prescribing specific compounds. For this very reason, even though it is recited prior to the *mahāvibhāṣā*, it does not possess the status of an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*) like the *avyayībhāva*. Consequently, in that case, there occurs an analysis using its own constituent words (*svapadavigraha*).

And likewise, in the commentary (*vṛtti*) on the rule *bhūtapūrve caraṭ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.3.53), it says: "One who existed previously is *bhūtapūrva*; this is a compound according to the rule *sup supā*. Similarly, regarding the *Śākala-sūtra*, Kaiyaṭa explained the following *Bhāṣya*: "The prohibition of the *Śākala* [substitution] applies to *sin* (the nominative singular ending) in obligatory compounds; thus, the mention of 'obligatory' (*nitya*) is unnecessary. By this, the following is also established: *vāpy-aśvaḥ* (a horse at the pond) and *nadī-ātiḥ* (a boat in the river). This is a compound according to the rule *sup supā*.

For in the case of *saṃjñāyām*, the prohibition is established because the compound is obligatory (*nitya*); likewise, Kaiyaṭa has shown the analysis of the words themselves (*svapadavigraha*) in the rule *anudāttaṃ padamekavarjam* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.158) and in the rule *asiddhavadatra* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.22).

If it is argued that, according to the method already stated, compounds such as *paṅkaja* (mud-born) would also lack a formal analysis (*avigrahatva*), just like *saṃjñāyām* [P. 2.1.48], we reply: True; however, although an analysis is provided by relying on a mere similarity based on the derivative meaning (*yaugikārtha*) alone, in reality this is accepted because the status of being a lotus (*padmatva*) is cognizable solely through the compound. By this, compounds such as *kṛṣṇasarpa*, *lohitaśāli*, and others are explained. Let us return to the subject at hand: regarding the rule for the locative case (*vibhaktau*), in the example *adhiharau* ("on Hari"), only that inflection which forms part of the compound with the word ending in a case-suffix is understood, due to proximity (*sannidhāna*). And here, the word *adhi* serves to indicate the meaning of that [locative] inflection.

Nor should it be argued that in this non-worldly (alaukika) context, the locative case (*saptamī*) itself is difficult to obtain because the locus is already expressed by a particle (*nipāta*), given that the restrictive enumeration—“by means of verbal suffixes, *kṛt*-suffixes, *taddhita*-suffixes, and compounds”—is about to be rejected; for we accept that here, by the force of the rule, the locative occurs even when [the locus] is already expressed, just as in the case of a compound with the fourth case (*caturthī-samāsa*), where by the force of the specific statement the word is employed even though its meaning has already been stated, and this is established both by the logic of the "water-drinker" (*abbhakṣa*) maxim and by the force of including the term "vacana" (statement).

Because the term *avyaya* (indeclinable) is understood here as referring only to those that denote the meaning of a case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*), there is no application [of the rule] in the following cases: *gṛhasyopari* ("above the house") and *grāmasya puraḥ* ("in front of the village"). For words such as *upari* and others function with respect to direction, location, and time, and not solely with respect to the meaning of a case-ending. Precisely for this reason, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in examples such as *kramādamuṃ nārada ityabodhi saḥ* ("He recognized him in turn as Nārada"), because the word *iti*—like a pronoun—refers back to the subject at hand and thus does not denote the mere objective case (*karmatva*). Consequently, the word *vibhakti* (case-ending) is restricted to the locative case (*saptamī*).

For this very reason, in the *Pariśiṣṭa*, the sūtra is formulated simply as "adhikaraṇe. Pāṇini, however, employed the word "vibhakti" with a view toward brevity of syllables (*mātrālāghava*). Regarding whether this compound is formed with a nominative-ending term or a genitive-ending term because the meaning is already expressed by the particle (*nipāta*), two views are maintained in the *Pariśiṣṭa*. That distinction, moreover, makes no difference whether one adopts the term "vibhakti" or "adhikaraṇa."

*Upakṛṣṇam* means "in the vicinity of Kṛṣṇa. Because this technical name (*sañjñā*) is based on its etymological meaning (*anvartha*), this compound occurs only when there is predominance of the sense of an indeclinable (*avyaya*) that is not a substance (*asattvarūpa*). However, he will state later that when the proximity itself is predominant, it is a *bahuvrīhi*, according to the rule: "A numeral combined with an indeclinable, 'āsanna' (near), etc. (Pāṇini 2.2.25), as in the example *upadaśāḥ*.

If it is objected that there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *samayā grāmam*, *nikaṣā laṅkām*, and *ārād vanāt*, Rakṣita replies: "Because of the force of the rules prescribing the second and fifth case endings for [the words] *abhitaḥ*, *paritaḥ*, *samayā*, *nikaṣā*, and *anyārāt*, these do not form an *avyayībhāva* compound. As for what was stated in the *Durghaṭavṛtti*—that in examples such as *citrasya grāmaṃ samayā*, since the word is dependent on another (*sāpekṣatvāt*), the rule for case endings has already served its purpose elsewhere, and thus there is no force (*sāmarthya*) [to trigger the *avyayībhāva*]—[Rakṣita’s view counters this].

That is not so; since a compound (*samāsa*) is obligatory, the rule "there is no connection with an adjective for that which has already entered into a compound" (*vṛttasya viśeṣaṇayogo na*) would necessarily apply. Otherwise, even such expressions as *sthūlasya kumbhasya kāraḥ* (the maker of a large pot) would be possible.

However, in the sense of prosperity (*samṛddhi*), *sumadram* means "the prosperity of the Madras. But when the meaning of the final member (*uttarapada*) is predominant, it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound according to Pāṇini 2.2.18 (*kugati*); thus, *sumadrāḥ* means "prosperous Madras."

In the case of "vyṛddhi" (loss of prosperity), the term is "duryavana" (one whose Yavanas have lost their prosperity). Success here does not occur through the absence of the object itself; for a compound is formed when there is an absence of that which is being compounded. In this instance, however, there is no absence of the Yavanas themselves, but rather an absence of their prosperity.

The term *nirmakṣikam* (free from flies) is used when there is an absence of an object; likewise, *avighnam* (without obstacle). This compound occurs in the sense of a relational absence (*saṃsargābhāva*), and not even in the case of mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*). This is because, by the force of the inclusion of the word *artha* (object), only that absence which is opposed to the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) of the cognition produced by the compounded words is grasped. This is because mutual absence is opposed only to its own counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) as delimited by its own counter-positiveness-determiner (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*), and because such an absence, even if it serves as a qualifier (*prakāra*), does not function as a qualificandum (*viśeṣya*).

As for those who claim that even in the case of "The pot is not a cloth," the meaning is simply the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) of cloth-ness, because—according to the principle of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*—the universal (*jāti*) is the word-meaning; even in their view, by the very force of the inclusion of the term "meaning" (*artha*), this compound implies the absence of the substratum (*dharmin*), and thus the result is exactly the same: it is the absence of the substratum and not merely the absence of the attribute (*dharma*). This is precisely the intention of Haradatta’s commentary on this point. By this, those who explain "There is no pot on the ground" as referring to the absence of the pot are refuted.

Because [otherwise] there would be the consequence of an improper formation due to the application of a *nitya-samāsa* (obligatory compound), and because the case-ending denoting a *kāraka* (grammatical participant) would be inapplicable; for this very reason, in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), when an action is supplied by ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) and there is the cognition of an action qualified by a *kāraka*, the negation of that [action] alone is verbal (*śābda*), while the actual meaning is simply the absence of a jar or similar object resting upon the ground. Furthermore, this logical complexity (*gaurava*) is authoritative (*prāmāṇika*), and this is an absence whose counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is delimited by a property residing in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇa-dharma*). For this same reason, even in the case of "The horn of a rabbit does not exist," both the grammatical correctness of the word and the correctness of the meaning are indeed accepted. And the existence of the rabbit's horn—though cognized through the force of the words—is what is negated.

For it is accepted that "a word indeed produces knowledge of an object even when that object is absolutely non-existent. Furthermore, the certainty of inapplicability (*ayogyatā-niścaya*) is not an obstacle [to verbal comprehension]. Otherwise, a word would be as mute to one who has already understood [the meaning], because the opponent would not comprehend the sentence-meaning from the word; consequently, even the discourse of refutation (*khaṇḍana-kathā*) would be cut off. Or rather, let it be that verbal cognition is something superimposed (*āhārya*). By this [it is explained]: "Weapons do not pierce him, fire does not burn him... [and so forth].

"Water does not moisten them in this way, nor does the wind dry them," and so forth has been explained. Otherwise, since the cutting, burning, moistening, and drying of the self and its actions would be unestablished, there would be the consequence of purposelessness; such is the direction of the argument. "Atyaya" means the passing away of snow, i.e., "excessive cold. "Atyaya" means destruction (*dhvaṃsa*). And since the nature of destruction is an indivisible property pervaded by the nature of non-existence (*abhāvatva*), it is mentioned separately from "absence" (*arthābhāva*) for that very reason.
The indeclinable *samprati* primarily denotes the locus (*adhikaraṇa-śakti*). Thus it has been stated by Amara: "etarhi, samprati, idānīm, adhunā, and sāmpratam likewise" (Amarakośa 3.4.23).

It is never appropriate for [a word] to be prompted by a case-role (*adhikaraṇakāraka*); thus, this action is prohibited. Now, "sleep is not appropriate" is *atinidram*. However, in the *vṛtti*, "a garment produced in Tisṛkā" (*atisaisṛkam ācchādanam*) is cited as an example. Tisṛkā is the name of a village. Regarding the suffix *kan* in the sense of "produced there" (*tatra bhavam*), there is a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for the word *tisṛ*. That which is produced there is a "Taisṛka garment. And that is to be used at a specific time—either in the heat or in the cold. Thus, the meaning is: "a Taisṛka garment for the purpose of enjoyment during the cold season."

In this case, the action of enjoyment (*upabhoga-kriyā*) is included within the verbal expression, just as the act of sprinkling is included in the expression "rice-gruel with curd" (*dadhy-upasikta odanaḥ*), or "curd-rice" (*dadhy-odanaḥ*). Haradatta maintains that the compound is formed because the word *taisṛka* is expressive even when independent of the word *ācchādana*. Regarding the manifestation of a word (*śabda-prādurbhāva*), [the example is] *itihari*. Here, the word *iti* refers to its own form (*svarūpa-parah*). Haradatta analyzes this with a genitive case-ending, stating: "the manifestation of that [word]. Thus, regarding the manifestation of a word, [the example is] *itihari*; the word *iti* refers to its own form, and the analysis is by means of the genitive case: "the manifestation of that."

In the sense of "behind," we have *anurathyam*, meaning "behind the chariots. They say that the grammatical correctness of this sentence is established by the fact that the rule regarding the prior placement of the word with fewer syllables (*alpāctara*)—which applies to words denoting a deficiency (*vyṛddhi*)—is understood to be non-universal (*anitya*). Furthermore, because of its association (*sāhacarya*) with words such as *samīpa* (near) which do not end in a secondary derivative suffix (*ataddhitānta*), it is only such a word [ending in a taddhita] that is understood here; this is also supported by the Bhāṣya: "Then, afterwards, it will fall away and perish.
Moreover, the true principle is that it is also supported by the usage in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *anekam anyapadārthe* (Pāṇini 2.2.24): namely, the expression *sarvapaścāt*.

The meanings of *yathā* are fitness (*yogyatā*), distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), non-deviation from the word-meaning (*padārthānativṛtti*), and similarity (*sādṛśya*). In *anurūpam*, the meaning is "suitable for" (*rūpasya yogyam*). In the sense of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), it is *pratyartham*; the meaning is "with respect to each object" (*artham artham prati*). Here, even the sentence form is correct. For in this case, the indeclinable does not function as distributive repetition; rather, because it is a *karmapravacanīya*, it delimits the relationship. Distributive repetition, however, is expressed by reduplication.

Alternatively, because the technical designation *karmapravacanīya* is prescribed for the word *prati* in the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*), there will also be a sentence containing an accusative case when it is used in conjunction with it, as in *yathāśakti*. The meaning is "without exceeding one's capacity. *Sahari* means "similarity to Hari. *Ānupūrvyam* is the absence of the prefix *anu-*; it is derived from the root *pṛ* with the suffix *ṣyañ* according to the *brāhmaṇa*-class of words. Because the suffix *ṣyañ* is marked with *ṣ*, it is also employed in the feminine gender. *Anujyeṣṭham* means "in accordance with the order of the eldest," that is, by seniority.

In the case of simultaneity (*yaugapadya*), it is *sacakram*. This is a compound with the word *saha*. The substitution of *sa-* [for *saha*] occurs by the rule "In an *avyayībhāva*, when not denoting time" (*Aṣṭādhyāyī* 6.3.81). The same applies in the following cases as well.

In the sense of similarity (*sādṛśya*), [the word] *sadṛśaḥ* [forms] *sasakhi* with *sakhi*. However, in the case of a compound (*vṛtti*), *sakakhī* is cited as the example. A female jackal (*śṛgālī*) that is similar to one whose size has been diminished is called *kikhī*. Since the formation is already established by the very fact of "being according to the object" (*yathārthatva*), the explicit mention of "similarity" (*sādṛśya*) is for the purpose of ensuring that the rule applies even when similarity is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*). For in the phrase *sadṛśaḥ sakhyā sasakhī*, the possessor of similarity (*sādṛśyavat*) is the primary element (*prādhānya*). Consequently, because the meaning of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) is not predominant, an avyayībhāva compound would not occur here, just as it does not in the case of *samṛddhā madrāḥ sumadrāḥ*.

"Corresponding to attainment" means a physical body (ātmabhāva) that is commensurate with those [beings] including Brahmā; the meaning is that their state of being Brahman (brahmabhāva) is appropriate to them.
"In its entirety" means he consumes everything down to a blade of grass; the meaning is that he does not reject anything. However, the intention here is not the consumption of grass itself.

In the rule concerning "mentioning the end" (*antavacane*), [it is explained as follows]: words such as *agni* and others refer to the treatises (*grantha*) that have those [names] as their subject matter; at that time, the portion adopted [of the treatise] has *agni* and so forth as its end, but there is no study beyond that. Therefore, because it refers to the entirety [of the work], the mention of "end" (*anta*) is distinct [from the mention of the whole]. The analysis of the compound is not within its own constituent members (*asvapadavigraha*), namely: "the state of having *agni* as its end" (*agnerantatvam*), using the genitive case. Here, the word *vacana* is redundant. By relying on the separate mention of "end" apart from the entirety of the *dvandva* compound, the result of the split of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), such as "apadiśam" and so forth, is easily established; this is the final conclusion. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.7)

Regarding the rule *yathā’sādṛśye* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.7): since the previous rule [2.1.6] already established the compound, this rule is for the purpose of excluding similarity (*sādṛśya*). The meaning is that the word *yathā* is compounded only when there is non-similarity (*asādṛśya*), and not when there is similarity. Therefore, it is not applied here: *yathā haristathā haraḥ*. In this case, the word *yathā* indicates that Hari is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). Thus, what was previously applicable by either [the rule] *sādṛśye* or *yathārthe* is hereby prohibited. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.8)

*Yāvat* [is compounded] with a *sup*-ending word when it denotes limitation (*avadhāraṇa*). This indeclinable *yāvat*, occurring in the sense of "to this extent" (*iyatā paricchede*), is compounded with a *sup*-ending word; that is an *avyayībhāva*. Example: *yāvadamatraṃ brāhmaṇān āmantrayasva* ("Invite as many Brahmins as there are vessels"). Even though *yāvat* is an indeclinable, its analysis (*vigraha*) is performed using its own constituent words (*svapada-vigraha*) with a non-indeclinable ending in a *taddhita* suffix: *yāvanti amatrāṇi* ("as many vessels as there are"). Why "when denoting limitation"? Consider: *yāvaddattaṃ tāvadbhuktam* ("As much was given, so much was eaten"). The meaning here is: "I do not ascertain how much was eaten. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.9)

[The word] *prati* [is compounded with a word ending in a case-suffix] when it has the sense of "a small amount" (*mātrārtha*). "Small amount" (*mātrā*) is a synonym for "a drop" (*bindu*), "a little" (*stoka*), and other such terms. A word ending in a case-suffix is compounded with *prati* when the latter signifies a small amount; that compound is an *avyayībhāva*. Examples: *śākaprati* ("a bit of vegetable"), *sūpaprati* ("a bit of soup"). Why "when signifying a small amount"? [Consider: *vṛkṣaṃ prati vidyotate vidyut* ("the lightning flashes toward the tree"). The mention of *sup* (a word ending in a case-suffix) is for the purpose of terminating the governing rule concerning indeclinables (*avyaya*).

Otherwise, since in the context of compound formation (*vṛtti*) we observe that indeclinables such as *doṣām anyaḥ ahaḥ* ("another day than night") and *divā manyā rātriḥ* ("a night other than by day") prioritize their substantive aspect (*sattvapradhānatā*), the intention is that only such indeclinables would be compounded with *prati* in the sense of "measure" (*mātrārtha*).
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.10)

The words *akṣa* ("die"), *śalākā* ("counter"), and *pari* ("around") form an *avyayībhāva* compound when used in the sense of defeat. This compound is desired in the context of gambling. There is a game of dice called *pañcikā*, which is played with five dice or five counters. In that game, if all fall face up or all fall face down, then the thrower wins; otherwise, he loses. It is in the case of such defeat that this compound occurs: *akṣapari* (defeated by one die), *śalākāpari* (defeated by one counter), *ekapari* (defeated by one), *dvipari* (defeated by two), *tripari* (defeated by three), and at most *catuṣpari* (defeated by four).
But when there are five of a single form, victory alone will occur;
the dice and so forth, ending with the third, are not like that which was previously described.
What would it matter to you in a game of dice if the die and the stick were one and the same?

The meaning of the commentary passage beginning with *parameṇa* is as follows: *parameṇa* means "by way of excellence," that is, beyond anything else; it amounts to saying that there is no fifth category (*pañcamī*). To demonstrate this, there is the verse beginning with *pañcasu*. [Regarding the term] *ekarūpeṣu*: the singular remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) is formed according to Pāṇini 1.2.67, *pumān striyā*. [Regarding the phrase] *tṛtīyāntāḥ*: the sense is "because of being the agent" (*kartṛtvāt*). The meaning is: whereas previously it was defined as having a uniform mode of operation (*ekarūpaṃ vartanam*), if that were not the case now.

The meaning is that a compound occurs when the sense of "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) in the form of a contrary state (*viparītavartana*) is to be expressed. Regarding the phrase "in the case of oneness": otherwise, as in examples such as *rājapuruṣaḥ* ("the king's man"), one would understand non-dual oneness (*abhedaikatva*), rather than pure oneness (*śuddhaikatva*). Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence [of the rule] applying even when duality and so forth are understood through context and other means.
The intention is: "our words are for the purpose of providing an opportunity for your speech," and so forth.
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.11) *vibhāṣā* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.11). This is an introductory heading (*adhikāra*). (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.12)

*apa*, *pari*, and *bahiḥ* optionally form a compound with a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*); that is an *avyayībhāva*. Examples: *apahariṃ saṃsāraḥ* (the cycle of existence is apart from Hari), or *apahareḥ*; *parihari*, or *parihareḥ*; *bahirgrāmam*, or *bahirgrāmāt*; *prāggrāmam*, or *prāggrāmāt*. Here, *apa* and *pari* have the sense of exclusion (*varjana*) due to their mutual association; they are *karmapravacanīya*s according to the rule *apa-parī varjane* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.88).

In connection with that [word *bahiḥ*], the ablative case (*pañcamī*) alone ought to occur, according to the rule "The ablative is used with *apa*, *āṅ*, and *pari*" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.10). Since the root *añc-* is also understood here as an indeclinable due to its association with *apa* and *pari*, the ablative case—by virtue of the rule defining a word ending in *añc-* as the final member of a compound—should likewise occur in connection with it. This being the case, the mention of "the ablative" (*pañcamī*) is intended to indicate that in connection with *bahiḥ*, the ablative is employed in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhy-arthe*).
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.13)

*Āṅ* [is compounded] with a word ending in the fifth case when it signifies either *maryādā* (limit) or *abhividhi* (inclusion). This compound is an *avyayībhāva*. Examples: *āmukti* or *āmukteḥ saṃsāraḥ* ("the cycle of existence up to liberation"); *ābālam* or *ābālebhyaḥ haribhaktiḥ* ("devotion to Hari from [including] children"). Here, the phrase "when it signifies *maryādā* or *abhividhi*" could have been omitted. For the fifth case is prescribed precisely when *āṅ* is used as a *karmapravacanīya*, and its status as a *karmapravacanīya* occurs only in these two senses, according to the rule: *āṅ maryādāvacane* (Pāṇini 1.4.89).

For in that [context], the mention of *vacana* is for the purpose of ensuring that it refers merely to the expression of a limit (*maryādā*). Alternatively, let there be the inclusion of the sense of "inclusiveness" (*abhividhi*) in that very case [as per Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.14].

According to *Aṣṭādhyāyī* 2.1.14, *abhi* and *prati* signify "facing" (*ābhimukhya*) when used with a word denoting a mark (*lakṣaṇa*). These two [particles] indicate the sense of being directed toward. When used together with a word expressing a sign, they are treated as previously described [i.e., like prepositions]. Examples: *abhyagni śalabhāḥ patanti* (moths fly toward the fire), *pratyagni*, *agnimabhi*, or *agniṃ prati*. This is the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound. Because *abhi* and *prati* are designated as *karmapravacanīya* by *Aṣṭādhyāyī* 1.4.91 (*abhirabhāge*) and 1.4.92 (*lakṣaṇetthaṃbhūtākhyāna...*), the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is applied.

In this context, the two words *abhi* and *prati* signify both the relationship between the indicator (*lakṣya*) and the indicated (*lakṣaṇa*), as well as the sense of directionality (*ābhimukhya*). What is the purpose of the indicator? For example: *srughnaṃ prati gataḥ* ("He has gone toward Srughna"). This means he has returned from Srughna; here, Srughna is the object (*karman*) and not the indicator. Why [use] *abhi* and *prati*? For example: *yenāgnistena gataḥ* ("He has gone where the fire is"). Because of the understanding that "he has gone by way of the place where the fire is," the fire serves as the indicator for the act of going.

Since there is also the sense of "facing toward" (*ābhimukhya*), the word *ābhimukhya* could form a compound with the word *agni* through the [use of] *yena-tena-śabda*. Why is the term "facing toward" (*ābhimukhya*) specified? [Consider the examples: *abhyaṅkā gāvaḥ* ("cows marked on the near side") and *pratyakā gāvaḥ* ("cows marked on the opposite side"). These are *bahuvrīhi* compounds meaning "those cows whose mark (*aṅka*) is new (*nava*) either toward (*abhi-*) or opposite (*prati-*) [the observer]. Here, the "mark" (*aṅka*) refers to a branding mark on the cows; however, the sense of "facing toward" is not present. But was it not stated that the general rule (*utsarga*) is that an *avyayībhāva* occurs when the meaning of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) is predominant?

How, then, is there an application [of this rule] here? True; this is for the purpose of indicating that even in the domain of *bahuvrīhi*, an *avyayībhāva* compound may occur in this context. By means of this, forms such as "dvimunivyākaraṇam" ("the grammar of the two sages") are established under the rule *sakhyā vaṃśyena* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.19).
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.15)

Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.15: *anu* [is compounded] with that object (*yat-samayā*) which it denotes as being near to. When the word *anu* is compounded with a thing (*padārtha*) by way of proximity (*lakṣaṇabhūta*), that forms an *avyayībhāva* compound. In the rule, however, the word *yat* is used in the neuter gender as a general term. Example: *anuvanamaśanirgataḥ* ("The thunderbolt has gone along the forest"). This means *vanasyānu* ("along the forest"), i.e., it has gone in the vicinity of the forest. Why is *anu* mentioned? [To exclude: *vanaṃ samayā* ("near the forest"). Why is *yat-samayā* mentioned? [To exclude: *vṛkṣamanu vidyotate vidyut* ("Lightning flashes near the tree"). Since this would already be established by Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.6 (*avyayaṃ vibhakti...*), this rule is for the purpose of making the formation optional (*vibhāṣā*). Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.16.

And [the rule] *yasya cāyāmaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.16): when the length (*āyāma*) is indicated by the word *anu* acting as a mark (*lakṣaṇa*), that [word] is compounded with it, and the compound is an *avyayībhāva*. Length means extension. *Anugaṅgaṃ vārāṇasī* ("Vārāṇasī along the Gaṅgā"): [this means] "along the Gaṅgā. Here, the fact that the length is the mark is indicated by *anu*; however, the object marked (*lakṣya*) is the meaning of the compound. For this very reason, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with Vārāṇasī, because the sense is: "that which is characterized by the length belonging to the Gaṅgā. And the Gaṅgā is the mark by way of its length. Thus, the resulting meaning is: "Kāśī is declared to be characterized by a length similar to the length of the Gaṅgā."

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.17) *tiṣṭhadgu-prabhṛtīni ca*: These are also treated as *nipātana*s (irregularly formed words). "The particular time at which cows stand [to be milked] is *tiṣṭhadgu*, the milking-time. The particle *ca* has the sense of *eva* (only); therefore, there is no other formation for these. The meaning is that forms such as *paramatiṣṭhadgu* do not occur. How then [is it explained] in the following: *ātiṣṭhadgu japan sandhyāṃ paścimāmāyatīgavam*?

If it is argued that this is according to Bhaṭṭi, [we reply: another compound distinct from the *avyayībhāva* is thereby excluded. However, the *jayamaṅgalā* states that here an *avyayībhāva* indeed occurs by virtue of the rule "āṅ in the sense of limit (*maryādā*) and inclusion (*abhividhi*)" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.13). And this must necessarily be stated in order to account for the form *āyatīgavam*. As for *atiṣṭhadgu*, however, it is equally easy to say that it consists of separate words and that there is elision of the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī-luk*). It is equally easy to say that in *atiṣṭhadgu* there is separate wordhood and elision of the fifth case-ending.

Some read *āyatīgavāt* because of the prohibition [stated in] *Pāṇini 2.4.83*, *nāvyayībhāvādataḥ*, and because of the statement that [the ablative case ending] does not occur after a word ending in *-at*. The words beginning with *khalevu* have the nominative case endings; the meaning is that these are used only in the sense of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*) and not elsewhere. *Tiṣṭhadgu* and *vahadgu*: the substitute *śatṛ* is due to irregular derivation (*nipātana*). There is shortening by *Pāṇini 1.2.48*, *go-striyoḥ*. *Āyatīgavam*: here, the substitute *śatṛ*, the absence of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*), and the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) are all irregularly derived. *Khaleyavam*.

*khalebusam*. There is no elision (*aluk*) of the locative case-ending. *lūnayavam* (the barley is harvested), *lūnamāyavam* (the wild barley is harvested), *lūyamānabusam* (the chaff is being gathered), *saṃhriyamāṇabusam* (the chaff is being collected)—these are words denoting time. *samabhūmi* (level ground), *samapadāti* (level with the foot). Because the meaning of the prior member is predominant—namely, "the levelness of the ground"—this is an *avyayībhāva* compound. There is another reading: *samambhūmi*, *samampadāti*; in that case, there is the augment *mum* added to the prior member. Another reading is *sambhūmi*, *sampadāti*; in that case, there is the elision of the final vowel of the second member, or the compound is formed with the word *sam*. *suṣamam* (perfectly beautiful).

*viṣamam*, *duḥṣamam*, *niḥṣamam*, *apasamam*, *āyatīsamā*, *āyatīsamam*. The substitution of *śatṛ* (the present participle suffix) is as before, and there is an absence of the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like treatment). *Samā* means a year (*saṃvatsaraḥ*). Similarly: *pāpasamam*, *puṇyasamam*. *Prāhṇam*, *pramṛgam*, *prastham*, *pradakṣiṇam*. In these four, the analysis (*vigraha*) is "gone beyond" (*pragata*) the day, etc. *Saṃprati* means "present," [derived from] "gone toward" (*saṅgatatvaṃ prati gataḥ*) the current time; *asamprati* is the opposite. The suffix *ic* is applied "in the sense of mutual exchange of action" (*karmavyatihāre*) [Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.4.127]: *daṇḍādaṇḍi* ("stick-for-stick").

This very [rule] is also prescribed for *dvidaṇḍi* and similar compounds; thus, their status as *avyayībhāva*s should be understood there as well (*Aṣṭādhyāyī* 2.1.18). Regarding *pāre* and *madhye* with a word in the genitive case (*Aṣṭādhyāyī* 2.1.18): the words *pāra* and *madhya* may optionally be compounded with a word ending in the genitive case, and that compound is an *avyayībhāva*. Furthermore, the final form in *-e* for these two is established by nipātana (irregular derivation). In the alternative case, it is a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*. For, by the *mahāvibhāṣā*, only the optionality of *ekārthībhāva* (the unification of meaning) is obtained. However, if *ekārthībhāva* does occur, the *avyayībhāva* would subvert the *tatpuruṣa*.

Therefore, the repetition of the word *vāk* here is for the purpose of obtaining that *tatpuruṣa* compound optionally; however, according to the view that "some hold that expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) constitutes semantic competency (*sāmarthya*)," this [repetition] serves to indicate that where a general rule (*utsarga*) and an exception (*apavāda*) are made optional by the *mahāvibhāṣā*, the general rule does not apply once the subject has been released by the exception. The same applies to the rule "udaśvito 'nyatarasyām" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.2.19). Consequently, when the word *pūrva-kāryasya* is already joined with a *ekadeśisamāsa*, a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) does not occur.

The term *dākṣi* is derived from *dakṣa* with the suffix *iñ*; thus, when *iñ* is applied, the suffix *aṇ* does not occur. Rather, in both cases, there is simply a syntactical construction (*vākya*). The specific grammatical rule for the substitution of the final vowel *e* is intended for those instances where the sense of the locative case (*saptamī*) is not possible, as in examples such as *pāregaṅgāt* ("from across the Gaṅgā") or *madhyegaṅgāt* ("from within the Gaṅgā"). However, when the sense of the locative is possible, the form is established even without the elision of the case-ending (*aluk*), by virtue of the word *bahulam* ("variously") in the rule *tatpuruṣe kṛti bahulam* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.3.14).
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.19)

*Saṃkhyā vaṃśyena* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.19). A lineage (*vaṃśa*) is twofold: by learning and by birth; that which pertains to it is *vaṃśya*. A numeral is optionally compounded with a word denoting such a person, and this [compound] is an *avyayībhāva*. For example: "two lineage-holders, Pāṇini and Kātyāyana" is *dvimuni*; "of grammar, three lineage-holders" is *trimuni*. By way of birth, for example: "twenty-one Bhāradvājas."

If it is asked, "How then is there grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expression *trimunivyākaraṇam*? the commentators on the Vṛtti state: "Because of the metaphorical treatment (*upacāra*) of those who possess the science [the grammars] as being non-different from the science itself. However, it was already stated previously that this is established by the very inclusion of the word "toward" (*ābhimukhya*) in the rule *lakṣaṇenābhipratī* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.14). And [there is coreferentiality] with river names (*nadībhiśca*; Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.20). With river names, a numeral forms a compound as before; and this is intended to denote a collective (*samāhāra*). Examples are *saptagaṅgam* ("the region of the seven Gaṅgās") and *dviyamunam* ("the region of the two Yamunās"). Here, the term refers to its own form as a name (*sañjñā*), and the actual river is not what is meant here, because of the use of the plural number in the rule's enunciation.

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.21): *anyapadārthe ca sañjñāyām*. A *sub*-ending word denoting something other than the meanings of its own constituent members (*anyapadārtha*) is always compounded with words denoting rivers (*nadī*) when it forms a proper name (*sañjñā*); this is an *avyayībhāva* compound. Although the governing rule of optionality (*vibhāṣā*) applies here, the commentary (*vṛtti*) states that because the intended name cannot be understood through a loose syntactical phrase (*vākya*), this is a compulsory compound (*nityasamāsa*). This is also the apparent intention of Kaiyaṭa regarding the *Śākala-sūtra*.

Nor does this same logic lead to the undesirable consequence that the *bahuvrīhi* compound must also be obligatory, because even in the sentence "citrayaṣṭīḥ praveśa" ("enter with variegated sticks"), there is the cognition of those who possess the sticks. This is the general direction [of the argument]. Examples: *unmattagaṅgam* (the region named "Mad-Ganges"), *lohitagaṅgam* (the region named "Red-Ganges"), *tūṣṇīgaṅgam* (the region named "Silent-Ganges"), *śanairgaṅgam* (the region named "Slow-Ganges"). What is the purpose of the phrase "in the sense of another word" (*anyapadārthe*)? [Answer: *kṛṣṇaveṇī* (the river Kṛṣṇaveṇī). What is the purpose of the phrase "when it is a name" (*sañjñāyām*)? [Answer: *śīghragaṅge deśaḥ* (the region called Śīghragaṅga). (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.22) *Tatpuruṣaḥ*: This is a governing heading (*adhikāra*) extending up to the *bahuvrīhi* rule.

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.23) *dviguśca* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.23). A *dvigu* compound shall also bear the designation *tatpuruṣa*. Since the coexistence of designations is established merely by the inclusion of the word *ca* ("and") in the rule *saṃkhyāpūrvo dviguśca*, this sūtra is redundant. However, the status of the *dvigu* as a *tatpuruṣa* serves a purpose regarding the suffixes *ṭac* and *ac*. For example: *pañcarājam*. By the rule *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣ ṭac* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.4.91), the suffix *ṭac* is applied. Because the final member of the compound does not end in the letter *n*, there is no feminine gender.

In the view that *samāsāntas* (compound-final suffixes) are those whose meaning is that of the compound as a whole and which end in the final member of the compound, however, one should understand that [the word *pañcarājī*] belongs to the *pātra*-class. In the commentary (*vṛtti*), on the other hand, *pañcarājī* is an occasional incorrect reading. *dvyahaḥ*: By the rule *ahnaṣṭakhoreva* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.145), there is elision of the *ṭi* portion. By the rule *rātrāhnāhāḥ puṃsi* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.4.29), it is masculine. *pañcagavam*: By the rule *gorataddhitaluki* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.4.92), there is the suffix *ṭac*. As before, there is no absence of femininity. By the rule *tatpuruṣasyāṅguleḥ saṃkhyāvyayādeḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.4.86), there is the suffix *ac*. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.24).

A word ending in the second case is compounded with words such as *śrita*, *atīta*, *patita*, *gata*, *atyasta*, *prāpta*, and *āpanna* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.24). A word ending in the second case is compounded with words beginning with *śrita* that end in case-terminations (*subanta*); this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound. For example: *kṛṣṇaṃ śritaḥ* becomes *kṛṣṇaśritaḥ*; *duḥkham atītaḥ* becomes *duḥkhātītaḥ*; *kūpa-patitaḥ*. Precisely for this reason, the augment *iṭ* is applied after the root *pat* [in *kūpa-patitaḥ*]. Otherwise, by the rule *tanipati-* (Kāśikāvṛtti), the *iṭ* would be optional; and because it is an optional *iṭ*, the prohibition [of its application] by the rule *yasya vibhāṣā* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.2.15) would apply.

Alternatively, since the optionality of the augment *iṭ* for roots such as *kṛtī*—by rules such as *seṭ sic* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.2.57)—establishes that the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) is *aniṭ*, the inclusion of the marker *id* in this root indicates the non-universality (*anityatā*) of the rule *yasya vibhāṣā* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.2.15). For this very reason, forms such as *dhāvitam ibharājadhiyā* are established. Examples: *grāmagataḥ* (gone to the village), *tuhinātyastaḥ* (fallen away from the frost), *sukhaprāptaḥ* (attained happiness), *sukhāpannaḥ* (entered into happiness). Here, in the case of words beginning with *śrita*, the suffix *kta* denotes the agent because they signify motion (*gatyartha*). *Atyāsa* is transgression, which is indeed a specific kind of motion.

In this context, even *prāpti* (attainment) is indeed a *gati* (motion), and not a result (*phala*). The same applies to *āpatti* (occurrence). Alternatively, in examples such as *śrita*, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the commencement of an action (*ādikarman*).

It might be argued: "Since forms such as *kṛṣṇaśrita* can be established even by means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound in the sense of the third case (*tṛtīyārtha*) together with a word ending in *kta* denoting the object (*karman*), what is the purpose of this rule? For the cognition—'the agent of the act of resorting to Kṛṣṇa as its object'—is identical in both cases."

If it is argued that, under the view that "the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the object" (*karmaṇi ktaḥ*), the meaning of the suffix—the object—would be the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) with respect to the act of resorting (*śrayaṇa*), we say no. For it has already been stated in the rule concerning the "unspoken" (*akathita-sūtra*) that in the case of a *bahuvrīhi*, a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) must necessarily be accepted precisely through a reversal of the relationship between qualifier and qualificand; this is likewise stated in the *Bhāṣya* on that very sūtra. Furthermore, there is no difference in accentuation (*svara*). For even in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the preceding member retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) after the words *śrita*, *patita*, and *gata*.

This is because of the rule: *ahīne dvitīyā* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.2.47). However, for the sake of establishing the correct accent (*svara*), let a *tatpuruṣa* compound be prescribed with words such as *atīta*. For in that case, when these [words] form a *tatpuruṣa*, the accent would have to be that of the *thā-tha*-class (by Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.2.144), and not the accent of *ahīna*; since there is a prohibition against the *ahīna* accent for *atīta* and *atyasta*. But for *prāpta* and *āpanna*, because of the rule *ahīne dvitīyānupasarga* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.2.47), the *ahīna* accent applies. In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, however, the accent of the original form of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛti-svara*) would apply. Therefore, a compound with *śrita*, *patita*, and *gata* need not be specifically prescribed.

And thus, there would be great economy [of effort] such that even the rule *ahīne dvitīyā* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.47) need not exist. But, one might object: if this were so, there would certainly be a fault regarding the accent when words such as *śrita* follow words denoting genus (*jāti*) and the like, because of the application of the rule *jātikālasukhādibhyonācchādanāt ktokṛtamitapratipannāḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.2.17), which results in the final syllable being udātta. For under the view that begins with the formation of a *tatpuruṣa*, the dual accentuation is established: the *bahuvrīhi* has its final syllable udātta, while for the *tatpuruṣa*, the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) applies.

If it is argued that there is a discrepancy because, under the view of rejection (*pratyākhyāna*), [the word] would necessarily have an udātta accent on the final syllable, we say no; for the dual accentuation (*dvisvarya*) is easily established precisely within the *bahuvrīhi* compound. To explain: regarding the rule *vā jāte* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.2.171), it should be stated that [the suffix *cha* is applied] after words meaning "born," "resorted to," "fallen into," or "gone to. Nor should it be said that there is no advantage in terms of brevity (*lāghava*) in this formulation; for the brevity is evident by the fact that the rule *ahine dvitīyā* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 7.2.47) need not even be commenced.

However, this is the distinction: in your view, there is a dual accent (*dvaisvarya*) in both compound types, whereas in my view, there is a dual accent only in the *bahuvrīhi*. On this point, they say: by means of the *bahuvrīhi*, forms such as *kṛṣṇaśritaḥ* would not be established, because of the contingency of the prior placement [of the past participle] according to the rule "niṣṭhā" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.36). For the subsequent placement of the past participle is prescribed [only] after words denoting genus (*jāti*), time, pleasure (*sukha*), and so forth; it is not prescribed for cases other than those beginning with genus.

Furthermore, even in the case of *jāti* and so forth, the form would differ; for even under the view that the accent of the preceding member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) applies, there would be the contingency of the optional *ka* suffix being added as a secondary derivative (*śaiṣika*). This is because you have formulated the rule for dual accentuation (*dvisvarya*) only for *bahuvrīhi* compounds. In the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, in a *tatpuruṣa*, there is the accent prescribed by "In a *ahīna* compound, the second [member takes the accent]" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.2.47), but there is no *ka*. In a *bahuvrīhi*, however, there is the *ka* suffix, but not the accent of the preceding member. Thus, the aforementioned accent and the *ka* suffix never coexist. Therefore, let it remain exactly as it was stated in the original rule; and it is settled that this complexity (*gaurava*) is authoritative.

The addition of *gamī*, *gāmī*, and others should be stated [as exceptions]. *Grāmaṃ gamī* (one who will go to the village), *grāmagamī* (one who goes to the village). The suffix *ini* is derived from the root *gam* by the Uṇādi rule "gameriniḥ" (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.54). And that [suffix] refers to the future tense, because it is stated: "gamyādayaḥ in the sense of the future" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.3.3). As for the *ini* [suffix] derived from the rule "āṅi ca ṇit" (Uṇādi Sūtra 4.55), that too occurs in the future due to its inclusion in the *gamyādi* group. Because of the marker *ṇ*, there is vṛddhi [strengthening of the vowel]. Thus, *āgāmī* (one who will come). By virtue of the principle of diversity (*bāhulaka*), it also occurs after the simple root; hence Mādhava says *gāmī*. *Grāmaṃ gāmī* (one who will go to the village), *grāmagāmī* (one who goes to the village).

Because of the prohibition of the genitive case characterized by its connection with a *kṛt*-suffix, as stated in Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.70—"In the sense of the future or of debt, [the genitive is not used] after a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix"—the accusative is used for the object (*karman*). Some, however, maintain that the suffix *ṇini* is used here in the sense of necessity (*āvaśyaka*). They argue that even though the meaning is future, the mention of the accusative in Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.12 ("After a verb meaning 'to go,' the second case is used for the object") is intended to apply even to cases where an exception (*apavāda*) would otherwise have applied; thus, they claim that even when a *kṛt* suffix is employed, the accusative alone must be used. But this contradicts the Bhāṣya, because the Bhāṣya rejects (pratyākhyāta) the rule concerning verbs meaning "to go," thereby accepting the genitive alone in connection with a *kṛt* suffix. By this [rejection],—

"The mountain Adūrādri is such that it will become the Koli mountain for you because of its proximity"—thus is the usage of Śrī Harṣa explained. [Examples include] "one desiring to eat food" (*annam bubhuṣuḥ*) as *annabubhukṣuḥ*, and so forth.
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.25)

[By the rule] *svayaṃktena* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.25): the word *svayam*, when ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), is compounded with another word ending in a case-suffix that has *kta* as its base; this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound. The purpose of the compound is to achieve a single word-form (*aikapadya*). By means of this, the prohibition of the *nighāta* accent prescribed by *āma ekāntaram* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.1.55) is established, and the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) in *svāyaṃkṛtiḥ* is also accomplished. However, although the mention of the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) is carried over from the subsequent rule for the sake of what follows, it is not connected here; for since *svayam* has the sense of "by oneself" (*ātmanā*), it functions as an agent (*kartṛ*) and thus cannot logically end in the accusative case. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.26)

*khaṭvā-kṣepe* (Pāṇini 2.1.26). A word ending in the accusative case and having *khaṭvā* as its base is compounded with a word ending in a *su*-affix and having a past passive participle (*ktānta*) as its base, provided there is censure (*nindā*). Example: *khaṭvārūḍho jālmaḥ*. According to Amarasimha, "a *jālma* is one who acts without due reflection" (Amarakośa 3.1.17). After completing the Veda and the vows, one who has returned home (*samāvṛta*) ought to sleep on the ground; he who, though deserving of sleeping on the ground while still in the state of a religious student (*brahmacarya*), ascends a bed (*khaṭvā*), is a *jālma*. This [term] is used in its conventional sense (*ruḍha*).

Whether he actually climbs onto a bed or not, anyone who is intent on performing what is forbidden is called "bed-climber" (*khaṭvārūḍha*). For this very reason, even though it falls under the heading of *vibhāṣā* ("optionally"), this is a compulsory compound (*nityasamāsa*). The author of the *Vṛtti* states that the censure is not understood through the analytical sentence (*vākya*).

*Sāmi* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.27). *Sāmi* is an indeclinable synonymous with the word *ardha*. Because it denotes a non-substance (*asattvavācin*), it has no connection with the second case ending. That [word] ending in a case-suffix is compounded with a word ending in the suffix *kta*; that is a *tatpuruṣa* compound. Example: *sāmikṛtam* ("half-done").

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.28) *kālāḥ*. Words denoting time ending in the second case are compounded with a word ending in *kta*, as previously stated. This rule is for the purpose of excluding cases of non-permanent connection (*anatyantasaṃyoga*). Example: *māsapramitaḥ pratipaccandraḥ* ("the new moon on the first day of the lunar fortnight measured by a month"). [The root] *māṅ* [is used] in the sense of measuring (Dhātupāṭha 1142). The suffix *kta* denotes the agent. The meaning is: "he has begun to measure a month. In this case, there is no permanent connection between the new moon and the month. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.29)

And [the rule] *atyantasaṃyoge ca* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.29). This statement is for the sake of including words ending in *akṣa*. Words denoting time, ending in the second case (*dvitīyā*), are compounded with a word ending in a *sup* suffix when there is uninterrupted connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*), as previously [stated]. For example: *muhūrtaṃ sukham* becomes *muhūrtasukham*. The meaning is "lasting for a moment. The second case is used here by the rule *kālādhvanoratyantasaṃyoge* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.5). (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.30)

The third [rule] is: *tatkṛtārthena guṇavacanena* (Pāṇini 2.1.30). The term *tatkṛta* is a separate word with its instrumental case-ending elided. A word ending in the instrumental case is compounded with a word expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*) or with the word *artha*, provided that [the quality or object] is produced by the meaning of that instrumental word; this compound is a *tatpuruṣa*. By the word *tat* (that), which refers back to the instrumental ending, the "meaning thereof" (*tadartha*) is indicated. And the state of being produced by that meaning is a qualifier of the "word expressing a quality" (*guṇavacana*) by way of its referent. Thus, the resulting meaning is: "a word expressing a quality that denotes a quality produced by the meaning of the word ending in the instrumental case."

*śaṅkulayā khaṇḍaḥ* (broken by a wedge) becomes *śaṅkulākhaṇḍaḥ*. *kiriṇā kāṇaḥ* (one-eyed from a boar) becomes *kirikāṇaḥ*. These two words—derived from the roots *khaḍi* (to split) [DhP 1.581] and *kaṇa* (to close the eyes) [DhP 1.715] with the suffix *ghañ*—first function to denote a quality (*guṇa*) that has taken the form of an action. Subsequently, through the elision of the possessive suffix *matup* or through metaphorical transfer (*upacāra*), they come to denote the substance (*dravya*) possessing that quality; thus, they are "quality-expressing" (*guṇavacana*). *Dhānyenārthaḥ* (need for grain) becomes *dhānyārthaḥ*. *Artha* means that which is sought after (*arthyate*), i.e., a purpose (*prayojana*). Alternatively, *artha* is the act of seeking (*arthana*), i.e., a request (*prārthanā*) or a desire (*abhilāṣa*).

In all cases, there is a compound with an instrumental case ending when [the quality] is produced by that [instrument]. Why does the rule specify "produced by that" (*tat-kṛta*)? [Consider: *akṣṇā kāṇaḥ* ("blind in one eye"). Furthermore, this statement finds its application where, as in the case of *śaṅkulākhaṇḍa* ("a piece cut by a wedge"), there exists a relationship between the meanings of the prior and subsequent members consisting of the relation of action and its factor (*kriyā-kāraka-bhāva*). Thus, it does not apply in cases such as *dadhnā bhuṅkte paṭuḥ* ("he eats skillfully with curd"), because of a lack of semantic connection (*asāmarthya*). Likewise, it would not apply here either in cases such as *dadhnā-paṭuḥ* ("skillful through curd") or *kuṅkumena-lohitaṃ mukham* ("a face red with saffron").

For here, the connection of the instrument (*karaṇa*) is with the action of "doing" (*karoti*) which is understood. Therefore, the inclusion of the term *tatkṛta* ("produced by that") is so that [the rule] may apply even where the action is not understood in the final member, provided it is produced by that; it is so that [the suffix] might not occur when there is a capacity mediated by eating and the like. Why [is the word] *guṇavacanena* ("by a word expressing a quality") used? [Consider: *gobhir vapāvān* ("fleshy from cows"). Devadatta’s possession of fleshiness (or fatness) results from eating curds and other things related to cows; thus, while there is "being produced by that," this [word *vapāvat*] is not a word expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*).

What is the purpose of including the word *vacana* [in the definition]? Since a compound cannot occur with a mere meaning (*artha*), it will be understood as referring to that which expresses such a meaning. On this point, they say: *guṇavacana* means "one who has spoken of a quality. According to *Aṣṭādhyāyī* 3.3.113, *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*, the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the past agent (*bhūte kartari*). Thus, the meaning is: "that which, having previously expressed a quality, now denotes a substance in which the quality is subordinate. By this, a compound like *ghṛtena pāṭavam* ("sharpness by means of ghee"), which refers exclusively to a quality, does not occur. Furthermore, "quality" (*guṇa*) here is taken as that which will be defined later in *Aṣṭādhyāyī* 2.1.31: "that which enters into a substance... (*sattve niviśate...*).

With words meaning *pūrva* (prior), *sadṛśa* (similar), *sama* (equal), *nārtha* (having the same purpose), *kalaha* (quarrel), *nipuṇa* (skillful), *miśra* (mixed), and *ślakṣṇa* (smooth), a word ending in the third case is compounded as previously stated [by Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.30]. Precisely because of this rule, when joined with words such as *pūrva*, the third case should be understood as being used either in the sense of the third case itself or in the sense of a cause (*hetu*). Examples: *māsena pūrvaḥ* = *māsapūrvaḥ* (prior by a month); *mātrā sadṛśaḥ* = *mātṛsadṛśaḥ* (similar to the mother); *mātṛsamaḥ* (equal to the mother). Here, in connection with *sama* and *sadṛśa*, the third case is employed by the rule *tulyārthaiḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.72).

It might be argued as follows: Since the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) also occurs in a compound when it expresses a sense equivalent to the word *tulya* (equal), the formation would be established by a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) alone; therefore, what is the purpose of including the term *sadṛśa* (resembling) here? Nor can it be said that the term is intended for the sake of the original accent (*prakṛti-svara*) of the first member in a *tatpuruṣa* compound—by the rule "in a *tatpuruṣa*, [the first member retains its accent] when joined with words having the meaning of *tulya* or a word ending in the third case" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.2.2)—because that [accent] is already established by the rule "for *sadṛśa* and *pratirūpa*, [the first member retains its accent] when expressing similarity" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.2.11).

Nor should it be argued that there need not even be the apprehension of similarity (*sādṛśya*) in this case; for if one adopts the position of a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), the acceptance of such a compound is necessary to prevent the final syllable from being accented (*antodātta*). Nor should it be argued that the genitive compound itself need not exist due to lack of usage (*anabhidhāna*); for that would result in the failure to establish the form *dāsyāḥ sadṛśaḥ*. Indeed, in this context, the Bhāṣya accepts a compound with elision of the case-ending (*aluk-samāsa*) based on the rule "in the sense of reproach, [the sixth case may be compounded] after the word *ṣaṣṭhī*" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.3.21).

[Objection: Even so, let the inclusion of the word *sadṛśa* (similar) in the present context serve as the meaning of the compound with the third-case-ending word expressing the cause—namely, "one who is similar by means of knowledge" (*vidyayā hetunā sadṛśaḥ*) is "knowledge-similar" (*vidyāsadṛśaḥ*). For in this case, the genitive case is not obtained by the rule *tulyārthaiḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.72), since that rule prescribes it only when there is a correlative (*pratiyogin*). [Response: No, because it is already established by the preceding rule, since the similarity belongs to that which is similar by means of knowledge; for that which is similar by means of knowledge possesses a similarity produced by knowledge. True; this very point was rejected by the author of the Vārttika in the sixth book.

In the sense of "deficient": *māṣonaṃ kārṣāpaṇam* (a kārṣāpaṇa deficient by one māṣa), *māṣavikalam*. Since the formation of the compound was established in the previous rule by means of the word *artha*, the inclusion of the word *artha* here is for the purpose of indicating the denoted meaning (*abhidheya*). And that [word *artha*] connects only with the word *ūna*, not with *pūrva* and the others. For this very reason, *sama* and *sadṛśa* are mentioned separately. Examples: *vākkalahaḥ* (a quarrel of words), *ācāranipuṇaḥ* (skilled in conduct), *guḍamiśraḥ* (mixed with molasses), *ācāraślakṣṇaḥ* (smooth in conduct).

When the term *miśra* is mentioned [in a rule], it includes the form with a prefix as well. For example: *guḍasaṃmiśrā dhānāḥ* ("barley grains mixed with molasses"). This is established by the fact that in the rule *miśraṃ cānupasargamasandhau* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.2.154), the mention of *anupasarga* ("without a prefix") serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this principle. An addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for the word *avara*: *māsena avaraḥ* = *māsāvaraḥ* ("inferior by a month").
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.32).

*kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.32). When the agent (*kartṛ*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*) is expressed by a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix, the third case ending is frequently used with it, as previously stated. For example: *hariṇā trātaḥ* (saved by Hari) becomes *haritrātaḥ*; *nakhair bhinnaḥ* (pierced by claws) becomes *nakhabhinnaḥ*. Since the mention of a *kṛt* suffix includes even those preceded by a *gati* particle, we also have *nakhanirbhinnaḥ*. Why "agent or instrument"? Consider *bhikṣābhir uṣitaḥ* (dwelt on alms); here the third case is used in the sense of cause (*hetu*). Because of the mention of "frequently" (*bahulam*), this does not apply to forms such as the present participles (*śatṛ*, *śānac*) or the past active participle (*ktavatu*). For example: *hastena kurvan*, *bhuñjānaḥ*, or *kṛtavān*.

In some cases, even other case-endings are compounded precisely because of the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (in various ways). For example: *pādahārakaḥ*. [The word] *hārakaḥ* means "that which is carried away" (*hriyate*). By virtue of *bāhulaka* (the principle of diversity), the suffix *ṇvul* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*). Thus, there is a compound with the ablative fifth case ending, *apādāt*, [meaning] "from the feet. *Galecopakaḥ*: from the root *cupa* in the sense of "slow movement" (*mandāyāṃ gatau*), with the causative suffix *ṇic*, and then the suffix *ṇvul* in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). Thus, *galecopakaḥ* ("one who strikes at the throat"). [Here,] by the rule *amūrdhamastakakāt* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.3.18), there is no elision (*aluk*) of the case-ending. Why say "after a *kṛt*-suffix"? [Consider: *kāṣṭhaiḥ pacatitarām* ("he cooks very well with wood"). (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.33)

*Adhikārthavacane kṛtyaiḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.33). An *arthavāda* statement that results in praise or censure is called *adhikārthavacana*. In that context, the third case ending is used with *kṛtya* suffixes, as previously [stated for the instrumental]. This is an elaboration of the preceding sūtra. The river is *kākapeyā* ("drinkable by crows"). The *kṛtya* suffix is used here in the sense of possibility (*śakya*). Because it is full of water, it is possible even for those standing on the bank to drink it; this is praise. Or, because it has very little water, it is possible even for crows to drink it; this is censure. *Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.34.*

*Anna* (food) [is compounded] with *vyañjana* (condiment). A substance used for seasoning is compounded with that which is to be seasoned, as previously stated. *Dadhna upasikta odano dadhyodanaḥ* ("rice sprinkled with curd" = "curd-rice"). Here, the action of sprinkling (*upasikta*) is included within the compound by its very nature; therefore, there is no lack of semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*). Nor should it be argued that even when there is no mutual relationship between the *kārakas*, one might allow an *asamartha-samāsa* here on the strength of the explicit rule (*vacana*), because this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *kiṃ dadhnā? odano bhujyatām* ("What with curd? Let rice be eaten"). (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.34–35)

**Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.35: *Bhakṣyeṇa miśrīkaraṇam* (Mixing with food).** "Food" (*bhakṣya*) refers to that which is eaten and is hard and distinct in its parts; "hard" (*khara*) means solid, and "distinct" (*viśada*) means having clearly separated components. This is because the suffix *yat* is applied only when the word ending in it denotes something that is eaten. However, in expressions such as *abbhakṣaḥ* ("one who lives on water"), the suffix is not the aforementioned *yat*, but rather the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of the object (*karman*). Others maintain that in such cases, the term is used only in a figurative sense. The mixing with food is treated as before [by the previous rule]. For example, *guḍadhānāḥ* ("barley grains mixed with molasses"). It should be understood that in this commentary (*vṛtti*), the act of mixing is included within the compound itself. **Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.36:** [Continues the discussion of compounds.]

Pāṇini 2.1.36: *caturthī tadarthārthabalihitasukharakṣitaiḥ*. A word ending in the fourth case is compounded with words such as *artha* and others that denote that which is for the sake of what is expressed by the fourth-case word; this compound is a *tatpuruṣa*. A compound with a word meaning "for the sake of that" (*tadartha*) is desired only when there is a relationship of material cause and effect (*prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva*), as indicated by the inclusion of the terms *bali* and *rakṣita*. However, the inclusion of *hita* and *sukha* is not an indicator [of this restriction]. For it must be stated that the fourth case occurs in connection with *hita*.

Because of the rule *caturthī cāśiṣi* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.73), the dative case is possible even when [the word] does not express a purpose (*tadartha*). Thus, we have *yūpāya dāru* ("wood for a sacrificial post") and *kuṇḍalahiraṇyam* ("gold for an earring"). However, it is not the case here in *randhanāya sthālī* ("a pot for cooking"). How then are [compounds] such as *aśvaghāsaḥ* ("horse fodder") and *hastividhejibidhā* ("elephant fodder") to be explained? Regarding this, there is a distinction; the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on this point states that *aśvaghāsa* and similar forms are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*).

It might be argued as follows: Let it then be simply a *caturthī-samāsa* (dative compound). Nor does this entail the application of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member by the rule *caturthī tadartha* (Pāṇini 2.1.36), because that rule applies only when there is a relationship of material cause and its modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*). Otherwise, in the case of *gorakṣitam*, since the form would already be established by *caturthī-tadartha* alone, the rule *kte ca* (Pāṇini 6.2.45) would be rendered useless.

Nor should it be argued that the compound *gohita* does not take the *tatpuruṣa* accent because the sense of "for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*) is absent; for although one might expect the rule to state simply *hite*, the general statement *kte ca* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of its inclusion. For this very reason, in cases such as *kuberabali*, since there is no relationship of material cause and effect (*prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva*), the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*) does not apply; rather, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the final syllable of the compound is accented acute (*samāsāntodātta*).

However, in cases such as *randhanāya sthālī* ("a pot for cooking"), if a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is desired, then let a dative compound (*caturthīsamāsa*) be accepted instead—just as in the examples *gogrāsa*, *līlāmbuja*, *krīḍāsaraḥ*, *vāsabhavana*, and *nāṭyaśālā*.

If, however, there is no application of the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) in cases such as *randhanasthālī* ("cooking pot"), then let it likewise be absent in the case of the dative compound (*caturthīsamāsa*) as well. And in that case, the mention of *balirakṣita* would also be useless, as there would be no basis for its being taught. Furthermore, since a genitive compound is possible even in instances such as *yūpadāru* ("wood for a sacrificial post"), this very sūtra need not exist at all. Instead, let the rule *caturthī tadartha* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.36) be changed to *ṣaṣṭhī tadartha*; and by means of this indicative mark (*jñāpaka*), the determination of the accent will be established.

On this point, they say: first of all, a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) with the word *hita* is not possible, because when that word is used, the dative case is obligatory; therefore, only a dative compound (*caturthīsamāsa*) should be prescribed. Consequently, in the rule *kte ca*, the mention of the dative case must also be made for the sake of forms such as *gohitam*. And if this were so, [the form] *gorakṣitam* would not be possible, because the dative case could not occur there. Furthermore, the rule *ṣaṣṭhī tadartha* (Pāṇini 2.1.36) would not apply, because there is no relationship of material cause and effect (*prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva*) between cow and protection. Therefore, even with the word *rakṣita*, only a dative compound should be prescribed.

Since the relationship of being for the sake of that (*tādarthya*) is invariably understood even when joined with the word *artha*, the dative case must necessarily be employed; therefore, by that [word] as well, only a dative compound (*caturthī-samāsa*) should be stated. Likewise, the inclusion of the term *bali* and *sukha* should also be made, so that the relationship of being for the sake of that may be invariably understood from the compound. Therefore, this rule (*sūtra*) must indeed be commenced. However, the purpose of the restriction "only in the case of the relationship between material cause and modification" (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*) remains to be considered.

In this regard, the following must be stated: the manifestation of *tādarthya* (purposefulness) occurs in two ways—namely, as a general relation (*sambandha*) and as a specific form called *tādarthya* which is pervaded by that [relation]. And this is established in the sentence "grass for horses" (*aśvānāṃ ghāsaḥ*) or "grass for the sake of horses" (*aśvebhyo ghāsaḥ*). It is determined by the authority of the *Bhāṣya*, the *Vārttika*, and other works that in the first case a compound (*samāsa*) is formed, whereas in the second case it is not desired. For example, in such expressions as "one should not eat beans" (*na māṣāṇāmaśnīyāt*), the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) denotes a general relation.

However, when a specific form of the object (karma) is intended, the second case (accusative) is used, just as in the example "Let Maithilī be given to the descendant of Daśaratha," where the suffix *aṇ* denotes the general category of relationship. But when the specific form of that [relationship], namely offspring (*apatya*), is intended, only the suffix *iñ* is used. Or, for instance, in "There was a king, a friend of the gods," the suffix *luṅ* is used when there is an intention to express the general past tense; but when there is an intention to express the immediate past (*anadyatana*), only the suffix *laṅ* is used.

For this very reason, in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.2.3), the expression "the venerable Kātya spoke" (*provāca bhagavān kātyaḥ*) is employed when there is no intention to specify the particularity of being a descendant of [Kātya] who is still living. For this same reason, regarding the rule *kṛtalabdhakrītakuśalāḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.3.38), the author of the Vṛtti in the fourth book states that the meanings of "made" (*kṛta*) and "bought" (*krīta*) are not already included by "born" (*jāta*) and "obtained" (*labdha*), because there is a difference in the mode [of acquisition]. You too will establish this very point in that context.

In that case, since the meaning "existing there" is already established, this same reasoning applies to the two rules: *prāyabhavaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.3.39) and *so'sya nivāsaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.3.89). Thus, when the purpose is clear, how can you ask us to deliberate?

If it is argued that even in cases such as *aśvaghāsaḥ* ("horse fodder"), there is indeed a determination of a specific [meaning] through context, this is true; however, in those instances, the cognition does not have "specificity" (*viśeṣa*) as its qualifier. According to the view that "the elided [case-ending] is remembered as the signifier," the cognition has "relation-ness" (*sambandhatva*) as its qualifier due to the remembered genitive case; for according to the view that "the elided [case-ending] is remembered as the signifier," it is precisely a cognition having "relation-ness" as its qualifier that is produced by the remembered genitive.

According to the established tenet (*siddhānta*) that "that which remains [in a grammatical operation] expresses the meaning of what has been elided," there is an absence of the elision of the fourth case-ending (*caturthī-lopa*); consequently, there is no capacity for a cognition characterized by a specific qualifier (*viśeṣa-prakāraka-bodha*). For this very reason, it is clear to those who know the logic of verbal testimony (*śābdānyāya-vid*) that even for one who is well-acquainted with the context and the like, the word *dāśarathi* does not produce a cognition characterized by the quality of being a descendant (*apatyatva*), but rather a cognition characterized only by the quality of being related (*sambandhitva*). Therefore, they say: "Grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) is regulated by the distinctions of the qualifiers (*bhedyopādhi*), the qualified (*bhedakopādhi*), and their relationship (*sambandhopādhi*)."

Therefore, it should be understood that, just as in the case of the words *aśva* and *an-aśva*, ungrammaticality (*asādhutā*) with respect to anything other than its own specific object is not contradicted by grammaticality (*sādhutā*) in certain instances. This being the case, the previously stated point—that the mention of *balirakṣita* and others serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)—is indeed correct. As for the claim that the mention of *balisukha* is intended to ensure that the sense of "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*) is invariably understood from the compound: [this is incorrect].

Even so, it is not [the case that the dative is unnecessary], because even there the optional *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa* (genitive compound) is unavoidable; therefore, the dative case-ending is implied by the necessity of conveying a fixed sense of "being for the sake of" (*tādarthya*), since its establishment is achieved either through the application of the rule *tasmai hitam* (Pāṇini 5.1.5) or through its recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) from that rule. Furthermore, you yourself have stated this during the occasion of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). This is the direction of the argument.

Regarding the word *artha*, it should be stated that it forms a compulsory compound (*nityasamāsa*) and takes the gender of the word it qualifies (*viśeṣyaliṅgatā*). For example: *dvijāyāyaṃ dvijārthaḥ sūpaḥ* ("This soup is for the sake of the twice-born"), *dvijārthā yavāgūḥ* ("The gruel is for the sake of the twice-born"), *dvijārthaṃ payaḥ* ("The milk is for the sake of the twice-born"). In this regard, its compulsory nature is established by the *Nyāsa*. Since the sense of "being for the sake of" (*tādarthya*) is already expressed by the dative case, there will be no analytical dissolution (*vigraha*) using the word *artha*; however, one must simply state that it takes the gender of the qualified word (*viśeṣyaliṅgatā*) in order to override the rule of taking the gender of the final member of the compound (*paravalliṅgatā*).

It might be argued as follows: regarding the rule *tadarthaṃ vikṛteḥ prakṛtau* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.1.12), let the rule be formulated as *tadarthaṃ samartham*. By virtue of being for that purpose (*tādarthyena*), the fourth case ending (*caturthī-vibhakti*) is implied. Alternatively, it is understood as an extension from the rule *tasmai hitam* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.1.5). From a word ending in the fourth case, when the sense of "being for that purpose" is to be expressed, the suffix *sārtha* should be applied. According to the rules *ādir ñiṭuḍavaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.5) and *ṣaḥ pratyayasya* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.6), because the suffix is indicated with two *ṣ*s, the *s* [of *sārtha*] receives the designation *it*.

By the rule *siti ca* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.16), it attains the status of a word (*padatva*). Because it is marked with the *pi*-diacritic, it is unaccented (*anudātta*). It means "for the sake of a king" (*rājārtha*) or "for the sake of a cow" (*gavārtha*). Thus, the rule for the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapadaprakṛtisvara*) in the sense of *ca* (and) need not be prescribed. Furthermore, because it is a suffix (*pratyaya*), there is no dissolution (*vigraha*) by means of that [word]. And because it is a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), its agreement with the gender of the referent (*abhidheyaliṅgatā*) is established. Do not say so; for there is no evidence for the inclusion of the letter *sa* (*sakārapraśleṣa*) in the rule *ṣaḥ pratyayasya* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.6).

Furthermore, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *tṛṇasaḥ* and the like, due to the application of the suffix *sa* by the rule *vuñ-chaṇ-kha-ka-ṭha-ñ-iñ-ca-ya-phak-phiñ-jāṅ-sāny-aḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.80) after words beginning with *tṛṇa*.
