One might object: "In this case, the ablative case ought to be used, because by the explanation that 'a word denoting a direction is a *diś-śabda*,' the ablative is accepted even when joined with a word that currently does not denote a direction. True; however, when joined with words functioning as parts (*avayava-vṛtti*), only the genitive is desired, based on the indicative mark [of the rule] "the subsequent [word] is called *āmreḍita*" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 8.1.2). This word *ekadeśin* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of a part; for this very reason, a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) is added after it, just as in the expression "an anthill possessing a black snake" (*kṛṣṇasarpa-vān valmīkaḥ*).

Although the suffix *ṭañ* would have applied here by the rule *ekagopūrvāt* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.2.118), nevertheless, it must be understood as *in* precisely because of this specific mention [of *ekadeśin*]. However, when denoting a single part, the word *ekadeśīya* itself is used; for it has been stated that suffixes such as *matup* do not apply to a meaning already obtainable through a *bahuvrīhi* compound. What is the purpose of the term *ekadeśin*? [Consider: *pūrvaṃ nābheḥ kāyasya*. This means: the part prior to the navel (*nābheḥ pūrvo bhāgaḥ*) belongs to the body (*kāyasya*). In the expression *nābheḥ*, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used according to the rule governing connection with a direction (*digyogalakṣaṇa*).

In this case, the navel (*nābhi*) is the limit (*avadhi*) of the preceding part, but it is not a single constituent member (*ekadeśin*); therefore, there is no compound with *nābhi*. However, a compound with *kāya* would indeed occur, as in *pūrvakāyo nābheḥ* ("the upper body from the navel"), because the word *pūrva* is invariably dependent [on another term]. What is the purpose of the condition "within a single substratum" (*ekādhikaraṇe*)? Consider: *pūrvaṃ chātrāṇām āmantrayasva* ("First, address the students"). This genitive is not used for selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), but rather expresses the relationship between a whole and its parts (*samudāya-samudāyi-sambandha*). The plural number is used because one intends to express a collection whose internal distinctions among its members have become manifest, as in the expression "the fifth of the students."

Consequently, while students (*chātra*) indeed possess the property of being parts of a whole (*ekadeśitva*), they lack the qualification of the number one (*ekatvasaṃkhyāvaiśiṣṭya*); thus, there is no compound [in *chātraika*]. How then is the form *madhyāhnaḥ* explained? On this point, some say: every word denoting a part of the day (*ahar*) forms a compound with the word *ahan*, because of the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) in the rule "saṃkhyā-visāya-" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.3.110). Otherwise, the state of being "evening" (*sāya*) or "forenoon" (*pūrva*) would not be possible for the day. However, others maintain that this *jñāpaka* regarding the word *ahan* does not depend on a specific instance, but rather depends on the general principle.

The rule that "all [words] denoting a single part [of a whole] are compounded with a word for time" constitutes the body of what is to be understood (*jñāpyaśarīra*). By this, forms such as *madhyarātraḥ* ("midnight") and *upāratāḥ paścimarātragocarāḥ* ("those who have ceased from the sphere of the final watch of the night") are established. Nor should one suspect that these can be accounted for through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—as in the case of *ūrdhvakāyaḥ* ("the upper body")—because the suffix *ac* prescribed by Pāṇini 5.4.87 (*ahaḥsarvaikadeśa...*) and the substitution of *ahan* for *ahar* prescribed by 5.4.88 (*ahaḥsarvaikadeśa...*) would otherwise be untenable without the assumption of a *ekadeśisamāsa* (part-whole compound).

How then [is it that we have] such forms as *dinamadhyaḥ* ("midday") and *rātrimadhyaḥ* ("midnight")? There is no fault here, for this is established by an indicatory mark (*jñāpaka*) and does not apply everywhere. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.2): *ardhaṃ napuṃsakam*. The word *ardha*, which is invariably neuter, behaves as previously described when combined with a word denoting a whole (*avayavin*) that exists within a single substance.

The word *bhitta* is used in the sense of "fragment" (*śakala*) or "piece" (*khaṇḍa*) and is masculine; *ardha* is used in the sense of "half" (*ardha*) when it denotes an equal portion (*sameṃ'śake*). In this context, regarding the rule "in the case of *śakala* and *khaṇḍa*," since the neuter gender is determined by the difference in form, and because there is an option for the masculine gender, it follows that [the word] is not feminine (*astriyām*). Nor should it be argued that why could it not have a feminine form; for it has been established as a technical rule (*paribhāṣita*) that there is no copulative compound (*dvandva*) of words with different genders. Furthermore, this is determined by the very mention [of the word] as "śakalaśca astrī" (śakala is not feminine).

In the case of the word *ardhaḥ*, however, since its masculine gender is understood from its specific form, the feminine and neuter genders are obtained through its optionality (*vikalpa*) because there is no distinction [in the base]. Thus, the resulting meaning is that the word *ardha* occurs in all three genders. But when it refers to an equal portion (*sameṃ'śake*), the meaning is that *ardha* is invariably neuter. For example: *ardhaṃ pippalyāḥ* (half of a long pepper), which becomes *ardhapippalī*. According to the rule "when there is a single case-ending, provided it is not a word ending in the genitive" (*ekavibhaktāvaṣaṣṭhyantavacanam*), the short vowel does not occur here because the word *pippalī* is not a secondary member (*anupasarjana*). Why "in a single substratum" (*ekādhikaraṇe*)? Consider: *ardhaṃ pippalīnām* (half of many long peppers).

How then is the compound *ardhapippala* (half-pippalī) formed? It should not be analyzed as *ardhāni pippalīnām* (halves of pippalīs). Rather, it will occur in the sense of a collection of parts (*khaṇḍasamuccaya*), based on the analysis *ardhapippalī ca ardhapippalī ca*, and so forth. Why is it said "with one who possesses a part" (*ekadeśinā*)? [Consider: *ardhaṃ paśor devadattasya* (half of Devadatta’s animal). Here, Devadatta is the owner and not the possessor of the whole; therefore, there is no compound with him. However, there would indeed be a compound with the animal: *ardhapaśur devadattasya* (Devadatta’s half-animal), meaning "half of the animal belonging to Devadatta."

What is the neuter example? *grāmārdhaḥ* (half of a village), *nagarārdhaḥ* (half of a city). Since the rule is already established by the very mention of *ardham*, the inclusion of the term "neuter" (*napuṃsaka*) in the sūtra is intended to indicate that the gender specification in the rule is not intended to be restrictive. Consequently, by the rule *tasyedam* (Pāṇini 4.3.120), [the suffix] occurs in all three genders. This sūtra...

This [rule] has been rejected in the *Bhāṣya* on *Aṣṭādhyāyī* 2.4.26 (*paravalliṅgaṃ dvandvatatpuruṣayoḥ*). To explain: the form *ardhapippalī* is established by means of a *karmadhāraya* compound, according to the maxim that "words observed to apply to a whole also apply to its parts. For even in cases other than equal division, you too must resort to this very same reasoning, as seen in examples such as *ardhāhāraḥ*, *ardhahāraḥ*, *ardhajaratīyam*, *ardhavaiśasam*, *ardhoktam*, and *ardhavilokitam*.

Nor should it be said that this rule is intended to supersede the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) in the case of equal division, for the genitive compound is also desired there. Thus, Kālidāsa employed [the form]: "She who, out of love, took half of Hara’s body" (*premṇā śarīrārdhaharāṃ harasya*).
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.3)

Pāṇini 2.2.3: *dvitīyatṛtīyacaturthaturyāṇy anyatarasyām* (the words *dvitīya*, *tṛtīya*, *caturtha*, and *turya* may optionally [be compounded] with a word denoting a part of the whole, provided that they refer to a single substance). These [words] may optionally form a compound with a word denoting a part of the whole (*ekadeśin*), as previously described, if they refer to one and the same substance. Examples: *dvitīyaṃ bhikṣāyāḥ* = *dvitīyabhikṣā* ("the second portion of alms") or *bhikṣādvitīyam*; *tṛtīyabhikṣā* ("the third portion of alms") or *bhikṣātṛtīyam*, and so forth. Why "with a word denoting a part of the whole"? Consider: *dvitīyaṃ bhikṣāyā bhikṣukasya* ("the second [portion] of the alms of the beggar"). Why "if they refer to a single substance" (*ekādhikaraṇe*)? Consider: *dvitīyaṃ bhikṣāṇām* ("the second of the alms [in general]").

It might be argued that this too has been rejected, as was done previously in the earlier sūtra. For instance, when a collective term functions with respect to its constituent parts, forms such as *dvitīyabhikṣā* (a second alms-gathering) are established by means of a *karmadhāraya* compound; whereas forms such as *bhikṣādvitīyam* (alms with a second) are established by means of a *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa* (genitive compound). This is not so, because the *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa* is prohibited by the rule *pūraṇa-pratyaya-antena saha na samāsaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.11).

In this established doctrine (*siddhānta*), however, by the force of the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* in this sūtra, a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is obtained as an alternative option, since the formation of the sentence would otherwise be established by the "Great Option" (*mahāvibhāṣā*) alone. If it is argued: "Even without this sūtra, we could form a genitive compound with that which ends in the suffix *an*, having applied the suffix *an* in its own sense (*svārthe*) by the rule 'pūraṇādbhāge' (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.3.48)," [we reply: No, because even in that case, the prohibition remains equally applicable.

In the rule *pūraṇa* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.11), the term *artha* is indeed employed [to mean "meaning"], and not a reference to the suffixes prescribed under the heading of *pūraṇa*, because the word *artha* is connected with each [term] individually. Thus, [the form] *svārthitam* is valid. For this very reason, they say that the compound in the verse *tānyuñchaṣaṣṭhāṅkitasaikatāni* (Raghuvamśa 5.8) is an error.

In reality, however, the mention of *tatpuruṣa* in the rule *paravalliṅgam* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.4.26), the *vārttika* beginning with *dviguprāpta*, and the three rules beginning with *pūrvāpara* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.58) have been rejected in the *Bhāṣya*. Consequently, for the sake of establishing forms such as *bhikṣādvitīyā*, one must resort to the view that the indications regarding [the gender of] technical names (*saṃjñā*) and measures (*pramāṇa*) serve as general indicators (*jñāpaka*). Thus, the prohibition in the rule *pūraṇa-* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.11) is non-permanent (*anitya*). In this way, even *ucchaṣaṣṭhā* is correct; such is the direction. The authors of the *Vṛtti* maintain that the fourth case (*turīya*) is also desired [to take the feminine gender], but this is not found in the *Bhāṣya* and other such works.

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.4) *prāptāpanne ca dvitīyā*. These two [words] are compounded with a word ending in the second case, as previously stated. Optionally, there is the compound [governed by] Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.24, *dvitīyāśrita*. *prāpto jīvikām* results in *prāptajīvikaḥ*, or alternatively *jīvikāprāptaḥ*. Likewise, *āpanno jīvikām* results in *āpannajīvikaḥ*, or *jīvikāpannaḥ*.

Although the form *prāptajīvikaḥ* and others are established by treating the word as a *bahuvrīhi* compound with a past passive participle (*ktānta*) in the objective case—understanding it as "one by whom livelihood has been obtained"—nevertheless, this specific rule is stated for the sake of ensuring the final accentuation of the compound and for forms such as *prāptasukhaḥ*. For in this *bahuvrīhi*, according to the rule *jātikālasukhādibhyaḥ* (Kātyāyana-vārttika), the past passive participle would otherwise be placed at the end of the compound. Furthermore, by the *paribhāṣā* regarding words qualified by gender, this same compound applies to the feminine form *prāpta* as well; thus, *prāptā jīvikā* results in *prāptajīvikā*.

Now, one might object: "Granted that the word *jīvikā* may undergo shortening by virtue of being a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) according to the rule *ekavibhakti* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.44), but how can the same apply to the word *prāpta*? To this, the Bhāṣya states: "In this sūtra, the vowel *a* of the preceding member is also prescribed; because the particle *ca* has a conjunctive sense, the elision of the vowel [of the second member] is inferred. The traditional scholars (*prāñcaḥ*) maintain that the meaning is as follows: the words *prāpta* and *āpanna* form a compound, and for both *prāpta* and *āpanna*, the vowel *a* is substituted [for the final phoneme]. Furthermore, because this is a Vedic-style sūtra (*sautratvāt*), there is no preservation of the original stem-form (*prakṛtibhāva*). Thus they say.

In reality, however, it should be understood that after the word *dvitīyā*, there is an elision (*praśleṣa*) of the vowel *a*. For in this way, it should be understood that the contingency of the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) simply does not arise.

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.5) *Kālāḥ parimāṇinā* (Time-denoting words [are compounded] with the object measured). That by which something is measured or delimited is "measure" (*parimāṇa*); that which possesses such a measure is "the measurer" (*parimāṇī*). Time-denoting words are compounded with a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) that denotes the object to be delimited; that is a *tatpuruṣa* compound. For example: *māsajātaḥ* ("one for whom a month has passed since birth").

If it is argued: "Devadatta has been born, and for him it is factors such as fortune (*diṣṭi*) that serve as delimiters, not time, because time only delimits action," [the reply is: True; although time directly delimits action, it delimits Devadatta through that [action] as its medium. For one whose month has passed since birth is conventionally designated as "born after a month. In that case, the month occurring in the interval between the moment of birth and the conventional time delimits the person who is already born by means of the birth itself.

In this context, it should be understood that even that which is designated by the genitive case in its analytical state (*vigraha*) attains predominance within the compound (*vṛtti*). This is because, as in examples such as *daṇḍī* ("staff-bearer") and *citraguḥ* ("possessor of variegated cows"), the assumption of "unification of meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*) occurs precisely through the reversal of the relationship between qualifier and qualified. Thus, Hari [Bhartṛhari], having begun with:
"In some cases, the status of being subordinate or predominant among meanings is not intended to be expressed," continues:
Whatever has been stated as an illustration of the meaning of a secondary derivative (taddhita) shows a reversal of the relationship between the subordinate and the principal elements therein.

By stating this, the examples of the dice-player (*ākṣika*) and the grammarian (*vaiyākaraṇa*), among others, have been clarified. Thus, the meaning of *māsajātaḥ* is "one whose locus of birth occurred prior to a month. For this very reason, its connection with an action—such as in "Let the one born for a month be seen"—belongs to the one who has been born (*jātasya*) alone, and not to the meaning of the first member of the compound, as is the case in expressions like *ardhapippalī*. [Similarly: *dvyahajātaḥ*. [This is] a collective compound (*samāhāra*) of two days. [The suffix] *ṭac* is applied by the rule *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.4.91).

By the rule *na saṃkhyādeḥ samāhāre* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.4.89), the substitution of *ahna-* is prohibited [in a compound denoting a collective]. How then is the form *dvyahnajātaḥ* ("born after two days") explained? It is said: this is not a *dvigu* compound denoting a collective; rather, it is accepted as a three-word *tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "one for whom two days (*dve ahanī*) have passed since birth," with the subsequent member being the word *jāta*. If it is objected: "Since the rule *sup supā* (2.1.4) intends the singular number, how can there be [the dual] *eti*?"—know that it is due to an explicit statement (*vacana*). For it has been stated by the author of the *Vārttika*: "The formation of a *dvigu* compound is prescribed when the subsequent member is a word expressing a measure (*parimāṇin*)."

The meaning of this is as follows: for the sake of establishing the *dvigu* compound, a rule for composition must be stated using a subsequent word that denotes the object possessing the measure (*parimāṇin*). By implication, it is understood that this refers to two [objects] simultaneously. Furthermore, by virtue of this specific statement, this *tatpuruṣa* compound may also apply to many [objects]. Thus, when there is a prior *tatpuruṣa* compound in the sense of "two months of one born" (*dvau māsau jātasya*), the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛti-svara*) applies according to Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.1.86: *kālānte dvigau*. The form *dvimāsam* (as in *dvimāsaṃ jātasya*) is derived from the collective sense (*samāhāra*) of two months, belonging to the *pātrādi* group. However, if one were to analyze the compound as *dvimāsaṃ jātasya* and then form the compound, the acute accent would fall on the final syllable of the compound (*samāsāntodātta*) because it is a later-enunciated rule (*satiśiṣṭa*). Therefore, the former analysis is preferred.

This might be the case: it is established that a *tatpuruṣa* compound consisting of three words occurs only where the rule explicitly prescribes it, whereas elsewhere it consists of only two words. And so, how is it that Kālidāsa uses the expression “*trilokanāthena satāṃ makhadviṣaḥ*” (by the Lord of the Three Worlds, who is the enemy of the sacrifices of the virtuous), and the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* uses “*tava rasaruciram*”? For in these instances, the compound of the words *triloka-nātha* and *rasa-rucira* cannot be formed by the rule “*viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa bahulam*” (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.57).

This is because of the restrictive rule (niyama): *dik-saṃkhye saṃjñāyām* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.50). Nor can it be a *dvigu* compound in the sense of a collective (*samāhāra*), because that would entail the application of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* according to the rule *dvigoḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 4.1.21). Furthermore, one cannot assume that it belongs to the *pātrādi* group [to avoid the *ṅīp*], for that would result in the ungrammaticality of the usage *trilokī*. Thus, by process of elimination, only the three-word (*tripada*) option remains. In a three-word *tatpuruṣa* where the word *jāta* is the final member (*uttarapada*), the aforementioned [two-word] construction is indeed defective for the reasons stated above.

To this it is replied: here the word *loka* refers to a collection (*samudāya*). Thus, the compound *tryavayavo lokaḥ* (the world consisting of three parts) is a *tatpuruṣa* with the middle term elided (*madhyamapadalopī*). This is made clear in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *dvigor lug anapatye* (Pāṇini 4.1.88). Alternatively, it may mean "the Lord of the three worlds" (*trayāṇāṃ lokanāthaḥ*). Furthermore, the analysis as a *karmadhāraya* containing a *bahuvrīhi*—namely, "she who is both possessed of the nine sentiments (*navarasa*) and beautiful (*rucira*)"—is also easily explained.

Let us return to the subject at hand. Although in expressions such as *rājapuruṣaḥ* ("the king's man") the number one in the sense of identity (*abhedaikatvasaṃkhyā*) appears, this is not the case with *māsajāta* ("born after a month"). Rather, in the case of *śaurpikaḥ* ("bought for a *śūrpa* measure"), just as there is the primary oneness of the *śūrpa*, so too there is the primary oneness of the month; for it should be understood that such is the established usage (*vyutpatti*) regarding words denoting a specific measure (*parimāṇa*).
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.6)

*Nañ* (Pāṇini 2.2.6): *Nañ* [is compounded] with a *sup*-ending word as previously [stated]. Examples: *abrāhmaṇaḥ*, *avṛṣalaḥ*. This compound has the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) as its predominant sense. For it is the status of being superimposed (*āropitatva*) that is indicated by *nañ*, and this resides in the application of the subsequent member. Thus, the compound is denotative (*śakta*) of that which is qualified by the superimposed Brahminhood. The relation between the qualifier and the qualified, however, is precisely the superimposition itself. Therefore, the cognition of non-difference from a Brahmin is derived through implication (*ārtha*). For this very reason, because it is not a subordinate element (*anupasarjana*), the functions of a pronoun (*sarvanāma*)—such as those prescribed for "that which is not this" (*atasmin*) and so forth—are successfully accomplished.

It might be argued as follows: even in the case of *vighnānām abhāvaḥ* (the absence of obstacles), the *tatpuruṣa* compound would apply because of its higher status [in the order of rules]. The *avyayībhāva*, however, would have its scope in cases such as *nirmakṣikam* (free from flies). This is not so; for this [term *vighnābhāvaḥ*] applies only when the meaning of the final member (*uttarapada*) is predominant. Indeed, it was stated previously: "In the conventional usage of the great technical designations such as *avyayībhāva* and so forth, the restriction on the meanings as taught by the ancient masters is also accepted as the general rule (*utsarga*). But if this is so, what is the solution for cases such as *anupalabdhiḥ* (non-perception)? Listen.

Based on the usage in the *Bhāṣya*, "rakṣohāgamalaghvasandehāḥ," it is accepted that in some instances a *tatpuruṣa* compound is also intended. For this very reason, in the *Bhūvādi* sūtra, both "athāsaṃhitayā" and, in the sūtra "virāmo'vasānam" (Pāṇini 1.4.110), "adrutāyāmasaṃhitam"—both forms are employed in the *Bhāṣya* and the *Vārttika*. Alternatively, even in cases such as non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) or non-doubt (*asaṃdeha*), there is a figurative or semantic understanding of the absence of those [perception and doubt].

It might be argued that this compound would have the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) as its predominant sense, for here the indication is primarily of the state (*bhāva*); thus, by the meaning "that in which Brāhmaṇahood does not exist," the *tatpuruṣa* would override the *bahuvrīhi*, just as in *unmattagaṅga* and other examples the *avyayībhāva* overrides it. However, the result [of such an argument] would be the absence of the suffix *kap* in cases such as *akartā* and *abhoktā*, according to the rule *nadyṛtaśca* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.4.153). This is not so, because in cases such as *atasmin*, there would follow the non-establishment of both the operations pertaining to pronouns (*sarvanāma*) and those pertaining to the numerical category (*gaṇa*).

Furthermore, in the case of "the winter is rainless" (*avarṣā hemantaḥ*), there would be the undesirable consequence that the singular number would apply not only to "winter" but also to its qualifier. Likewise, in examples such as "a poor Brāhmaṇa" (*adhano brāhmaṇaḥ*), by the same logic, there would be the consequence of the compound taking the gender of the final member (*paravalliṅgatā*). This is the general direction of the argument. As for another view:
"Austerity, sacred learning, and birth—these are the causes of being a Brāhmaṇa."
He who is devoid of austerity and sacred learning is merely a Brahmin by birth.

On the authority of such statements as these, all collective terms (*samudāyaśabda*) denote *sattā* (Being), which is qualified not only by those individual instances (*vyakti*) but also by the collection of their respective qualities (*guṇasamudāya*), since this [Being] constitutes a genus (*jāti*). Consequently, in expressions such as *apūrṇo brāhmaṇo 'brāhmaṇaḥ* ("an incomplete Brahmin is a non-Brahmin"), the predominance of the meaning of the second member (*uttarapadārtha-prādhānya*) is in every respect unassailable. And here the proof is the inclusion of the term *anañ-samāsa* ("non-negative compound") in the rule *etattadoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.102). In this way, the use of the singular number in rules such as *anekam anyapadārthe* (Pāṇini 2.2.4) is established.

And Māgha says: "She is served by many women with downcast glances. But how then [is one to explain] the verse: "Many fall like waves from the ocean"? On this point, they say: there is no contradiction in using the plural number there to express actual multiplicity, since it functions as the meaning of the base (prakṛti) for those [waves] whose unity has been superimposed. Alternatively, it may be a *ekaśeṣa* compound of "aneka" and "aneka" [meaning "many and many"]. As for the statement:
"Similarity, absence, difference from that, smallness, lack of excellence, and opposition—these six are proclaimed as the meanings of the negative particle (*nañ*)."

For example: *abrāhmaṇaḥ* (a non-Brahmin), *apañca* (not five), *anaśvaḥ* (a non-horse), *anudarā kanyā* (a girl with no belly), *apacasi* (you do not cook), *adharmaḥ* (non-dharma). It should be understood that these [expressions] intend a meaning exceeding [the literal one], according to their respective contexts. However, since in the final system (*siddhānta*) it has been established that conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) is equal in status to primary denotation (*śakti*), and that a distinct power (*śakti*) is asserted [therein], this [use of the negative particle] must somehow be explained as being included within the meaning of that specific function (*vṛtti*).

In this case, when the intention is to express the relationship [of the word *abrāhmaṇa*] with both "existence" (*bhāva*) and "being superimposed" (*āropitatva*) simultaneously—as in the sense that "the state of being a non-Brahmin exists"—the compound itself is formed first; however, the suffixes *-tva* and *-tal* do not follow subsequently. This is because the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), being dependent [on another], lacks the required semantic independence (*asāmarthya*). On the other hand, the negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) is unimpeded because its primary element is independent. Consequently, the accent of the suffix (*pratyaya-svara*)—specifically the accent of the *liṭ*-suffix—is applied as the final remaining accent (*satiśiṣṭa*), and not the accent prescribed by the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha-* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.2.2).
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.7)

*Īṣadakṛta* (Pāṇini 2.2.7). The meaning is clear: *īṣatpiṅgalaḥ* ("slightly tawny"). But is there not an over-narrow application (*avyāpti*) in cases such as *īṣadbhaktam* ("half-eaten") and *īṣadunnatam* ("slightly raised"), and an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *īṣadgārgyaḥ* ("a Gārgya by name of Īṣat")? True. For this very reason, the author of the Vārttika stated: "With a word expressing a quality (*guṇavacanena*). The meaning is that one should remove the word *akṛta* and supplement its place with the word *guṇavacanena*. Consequently, there is neither over-narrowness nor over-extension.

Although excellence and deficiency do not exist in the state of being a descendant of Garga, nevertheless, they are understood to apply to the actions and qualities inherent in that same referent. Thus, forms such as *gārgyataraḥ* ("more of a Gārgya") and *gārgyakalpaḥ* ("almost a Gārgya") are employed.
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.8)

*Ṣaṣṭhī* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.8): A word ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is compounded with a compatible word ending in a *sub*-affix, as previously stated. Example: *rājapuruṣaḥ* ("the king's man"). It should be stated that a sixth-case ending used in connection with a *kṛt*-derived word is also compounded (Vārttika). Example: *idhmavraścanaḥ* ("wood-cutter"). This is an exception to the prohibition [stated in Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.10] regarding compounds formed by specific rules (*pratipadavidhāna*). In reality, however, it will be explained that both that prohibition and this exception need not be stated at all. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.9)

"And by *yājaka* and others" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.9). The genitive case is compounded with these. This is an exception (*pratiprasava*) to the rule "with *tṛc* and *aka*, when denoting the agent" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.15). Examples: *brāhmaṇayājakaḥ* ("one who sacrifices for Brahmins"). The list includes: *yājaka*, *pūjaka*, *paricāraka*, *pariveṣaka*, *snātaka*, *adhyāpaka*, *utsādaka*, *udvartaka*, *hotṛ*, *potṛ*, *bhartṛ*, *rathagaṇaka*, *patti*, *gaṇaka*. [End of] the section on *vṛt*.

Regarding the statement, "it should be stated that [the compound occurs] after a word ending in *tarap* and there is elision of the suffix" (*kārikāvārttika*), this *vārttika* is recited in the *Bhāṣya* under the rule *sarva-guṇa-kārtsnye* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.2.93). The meaning is that a compound is formed with a word denoting a quality (*guṇa*) that ends in *tarap*. The authors of the *Vṛtti* maintain that this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the prohibition found in *na nirdhāraṇe* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.10). The authors of the *Bhāṣya*, however, hold that it is an exception to the prohibition of compounds with words for qualities found in *pūraṇa-guṇa-* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.11). Examples are: *sarveṣāṃ śvetataraḥ* = *sarvaśvetaḥ*;
*sarveṣāṃ mahattaraḥ* = *sarvamahān*. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.10)

Regarding the rule *na nirdhāraṇe* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.10): a genitive case used in the sense of specification (*nirdhāraṇa*) is not compounded. For example: *nṛṇāṃ dvijaḥ śreṣṭhaḥ* ("Among men, the twice-born is the best"). Here, there would be the possibility of compounding with the word *dvija*, for the genitive case is indeed dependent upon it.

How is it that [the term] "puruṣottamaḥ" [is formed]? Regarding this, Kaiyaṭa, relying on the rule *dvivacanavibhajya* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.3.57), states: "Since there must be the presence of these three—the thing from which selection is made (*nirdhāryate*), the part being selected (*ekadeśo nirdhāryate*), and the cause of selection (*nirdhāraṇahetu*)—selection occurs only when these three are present; therefore, this prohibition applies only in that case, and not even in the absence of the presence of these three."

Alternatively, the compound *puruṣottamaḥ* is formed by the rule *saṃjñāyām* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.44), where the locative case is used for selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). As for the objection that, if this were so, the rule *na nirdhāraṇe* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.10) would be rendered useless—that is not correct, because there is a difference in accent. For in a locative compound (*saptamī-samāsa*), the original accent of the first member (*pūrvapada-prakṛti-svara*) applies according to the rule *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha-* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.2.2); whereas in a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*), the word would be oxytone (*antodātta*).

It must be stated that a genitive case ending prescribed by a specific rule (*pratipadavidhānā*) is not subject to compounding (Kāśikāvṛtti). For example: *sarpiṣo jñānam* ("the knowledge of ghee"). Here, the genitive is prescribed by the rule *jño 'vidarthasya* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.51). And this is a genitive prescribed by a specific rule because it applies to all [genitives] other than those prescribed by the general rule *ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.50). Nor should one suspect that the rule *na nirdhāraṇe* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.10) is redundant on the grounds that its purpose is already served by this very statement.

For the rule *yataśca nirdhāraṇam* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.41) does not prescribe the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), but rather the locative (*saptamī*) alone. As for the genitive, it is reintroduced by that very rule so that it may not be sublated; this is another matter entirely. The same applies to rules such as *svāmīśvara-* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.39). By this, forms such as *gṛhasvāmī* ("master of the house") and *sarveśvaraḥ* ("lord of all") are established.

In reality, within the fourteen sūtras beginning with *jño 'vidarthasya* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.51), excluding the group of six sūtras beginning with *divas tadarthasya* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.58), the term *śeṣe* (in the remaining cases) continues to apply in the rest of the sūtras. Thus, as in examples such as *māṣāṇām aśnīyāt* ("one should eat beans"), the case of the genitive is already established by the rule *ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.50); this section [of rules] is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), meaning that the genitive occurs only in these instances, and it is heard [expressed], not elided.

And thus, the resulting meaning is that the designation of a compound (*samāsa-saṃjñā*) itself does not become the cause for the elision (*luk*). Therefore, the statement "those prescribed by specific rules [are not compounds]" need not be made. This being the case, let the *vārttika* "and [the sixth case ending] when connected with a *kṛt*-suffix" (*kṛdyogā ca*) also be omitted. For in the rule "of the agent and the object when a *kṛt*-suffix follows" (*kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*), the word "in the remaining cases" (*śeṣe*) has ceased to apply. Consequently, the rule "of the agent and the object" (*kartṛkarmaṇoḥ*) serves solely to prescribe the sixth case ending. How, then, could there be the undesirable consequence of the exclusion of compounds? And it has been said:
"And when [the agent or object] is designated by its instruments [i.e., the *kārakas*], and the action is explicitly heard again..."
"It is stated that the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhī) is prescribed at every step for the purpose of precluding compounding.

If one asks, "How then is there compounding in cases such as *harismaraṇam* (the remembrance of Hari), *viśeṣasmṛtihetavaḥ* (causes of the recollection of specific [details]), or *padāt padārthasmaraṇam* (the recollection of the word-meaning from the word)?"—you should understand that this is because compounding is not prohibited when the genitive is used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi-ṣaṣṭhī*). Thus, in these instances, because the genitive denotes a *kāraka* (participant in an action), the compound takes the accent of the original form of the final member (*kṛduttarapada-prakṛtisvara*). However, in a compound formed with the residual genitive (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*), the final syllable would be accented (*antodāttatā*). Therefore, this section is intended to prevent the final accent and to ensure the absence of compounding in examples such as *mātuḥ smṛtam* (remembered by the mother).

The explicit meaning is that the agentive genitive (*kartari ṣaṣṭhī*) is not applicable there, because of the prohibition [stated] in *Pāṇini* 2.3.69: *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛnām*. And it has been said: "The genitive referring to the object (*karman*) is prohibited in the case of a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*); a compound with a genitive characterized as 'remainder' (*śeṣa*) is not desired there."

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.11) *pūraṇaguṇasuhitārthasadavyayatavyasamānādhikaraṇena*. A genitive case ending is not compounded with words expressing ordinal numbers (*pūraṇa*), qualities (*guṇa*), the sense of being satisfied (*suhitārtha*), the word *sat*, indeclinables (*avyaya*), the suffix *-tavya*, or words in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). Regarding ordinal numbers: *ṣaṣṭhaḥ satām* ("the sixth among the virtuous"). Here, only the suffixes denoting ordinal numbers are understood [to be excluded], and not even words such as *pūraṇa* or *umbhana*. Consequently, forms such as *kumbhapūraṇabhavaḥ paṭuruccaiḥ* ("the jar-filling potter is skillful") are established. And the proof for this is the employment of the rule: *lope cetpādapūraṇam* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.1.134).

However, the scope of the rule regarding completion (*pūraṇa*) is not accepted here. This is because the prohibition even by means of a word ending in the suffix *an* (when it denotes a part) is made explicit in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra "dvitīyatṛtīya" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.33). For this very reason, it has been stated that in examples such as *bhikṣādvitīyam*, a compound occurs by virtue of the force of the option (*anyatarasyām*) mentioned in the rule. And for this same reason, they say that the usage in Kālidāsa’s verse, "tānyuñchaṣaṣṭhāṅkitasaikatāni" (Raghuvamśa 5.8), is an error.

Alternatively, one may resolve the difficulty by taking *ṣaṣṭha* as derived from the root *khyā* (to call/name) with the suffix *aṇ*, or by deriving it from the causative form of *khyā* using the suffix *ac* according to Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.3.56.

In this context, the term *guṇa* (quality) is understood as that which is defined by the rule "it inheres in substance and departs from it," and it denotes both a quality alone and a substance where the quality is subordinate. This is according to the principle of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Examples are: "the blackness of the crow" and "the white [teeth] of the Brahmin. These are examples when the qualified object—such as teeth—is known through the force of the sense or the context. But how is it then in the case of "a thousand cows"? On this point, they say:

This prohibition is not absolute, because of the usage by the three sages [Pāṇini, Kātyāyana, and Patañjali] such as: "from *niṣka* ending in *śatasahasra*" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.2.119), the *vārttika* "the addition of *krośaśata* and *janaśata*," and the *Mahābhāṣya* "he does not give even a *khārīśata*. Furthermore, this prohibition by means of a quality (*guṇa*) is non-obligatory, due to such indications as "because a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is the measure" and "the predominance of the meaning of the final member. By this, forms such as *karaṇapāṭavam*, *arthagauravam*, and *buddhimāndyam* are established.

However, in cases such as *candanagandhaḥ* ("the scent of sandalwood"), this prohibition does not apply, because there is a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) for the compound based on the rule "by means of qualities residing in that [substance]. For a scent perceived as suchness (as the universal *gandhatva*) is never co-referential with the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*); rather, it is its own primary referent. As for the usage "it carries water and crushes scents," that is based on the genus (*jāti*) such as *candanatva* (sandalwood-ness) and is not a word denoting a quality (*guṇaśabda*), because such usage is not observed in the case of jasmine flowers and the like. The same applies to expressions such as *ghaṭarūpam* ("the form of the jar").

However, words such as *surabhi* (fragrant) and *śukla* (white) do not denote the qualities residing in that [substance], because they are observed to be in grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the substratum of the quality when perceived in that form. This should be understood similarly in cases such as “*śauklyam*” (whiteness). For by words like *śauklya* and *saugandhya*, there is a cognition of the quality as having the mode (*prakāra*) of whiteness, fragrance, and so on. And for that which has assumed that form, there is indeed grammatical coordination with the substance, as in “*śuklaḥ*” (white) and “*surabhiḥ*” (fragrant); this is the general direction.

The term *suhita* has the sense of satisfaction (*tṛpti*). [In the example] *phalānāṃ suhitaḥ* ("one satisfied with fruits"), the sixth case ending is used because one intends to express the instrument (*karaṇa*) as a residual relation (*śeṣatva*). Nor should one fear the prohibition by the rule *na loka-* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.69), because that rule concerns the sixth case ending characterized by its connection with a *kṛt*-suffix. Regarding this, Haradatta says: "In the case of a connection with words having the sense of *suhita*, the intention to express the instrument as a residual relation is indeed fixed. The phrase "they say" (*āhuḥ*) here indicates a lack of full conviction. The reason for this is the absence of authoritative evidence for such a restriction; for it is said: "Fire is not satiated by wood, nor the great ocean by rivers, nor Death by all beings, nor a beautiful-eyed woman by men."

This is because such constructions are established even when there is a partial intention (*vivakṣā*) to express the state of being a "remainder" (*śeṣa*), as indicated by the word *viśeṣa* in the manuscript. For this very reason, Bhaṭṭi employed the instrumental case to express the sense of instrumentality (*karaṇatva*):
"Having been satisfied with various and wonderful fruits and with sweet, cool waters, they asked that radiant woman: 'Whose city is this? (Bhaṭṭikāvya 4.30) Thus [the usage is justified].

If it is argued that even if the *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa* (genitive compound) is thus prohibited, the form *phalatṛptaḥ* would still occur by way of a *tṛtīyā-tatpuruṣa* (instrumental compound), we reply: this is indeed accepted as the desired outcome (*iṣṭāpatti*). Nor is the prohibition redundant, because there is a difference in accent (*svara*). To explain: in a *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*, the word would be oxytone (*antodātta*); however, in a *tṛtīyā-samāsa*, the rule *tṛtīyā karmaṇi* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.2.48)—which is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *thāthādi*-accent—prescribes the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the first member. Thus, the former would result in an oxytone, while the latter results in a barytone on the first syllable.

The root *tṛp* is also transitive, as evidenced by the usage of Bhaṭṭi: "He satisfied the ancestors, honoring the ancestors with funeral cakes. Therefore, one should not suspect that the suffix *kta* cannot occur in the passive sense from this root. However, in cases such as *phalatarpaṇam*, the difference in accent is quite clear, because the suffix follows a kāraka (object), resulting in the accent of the original form of the final member of the compound (*kṛduttarapada-prakṛtisvara*).

In the example *sat—dvijasya kurvan kurvāṇo vā*, the meaning is "being present, doing [something] for the sake of the twice-born"; here, the genitive case is used in the sense of a residual relation (*śeṣe ṣaṣṭhī*). In *corasya dviṣan*, the genitive in the sense of the object is optional, according to the rule: "The genitive in the sense of the object is optionally prescribed after the root *dviṣ* when followed by the suffix *śatṛ*."

Having formed [the compound] with the indeclinable *brāhmaṇa*, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used when one intends to express the relationship of "being for that purpose" (*tādarthya*) in its general form; the meaning is "an action related to a Brāhmaṇa. The phrase "before the rising of the sun" (*purā sūryasyodetoḥ*) is also an example of an indeclinable. Here, the genitive case is applied to the agent (the *kartṛ*) by the rule "not with [words ending in] *la*-affixes, indeclinables... (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.69), and so forth, because of the statement: "In the prohibition regarding indeclinables, there is no prohibition for [suffixes] *-tosun* and *-kasun*" (Kāśikāvṛtti).

In this context, because of the association with the two [terms] *sattva* and *avyaya*, the prohibition of compounding applies only to an indeclinable (*avyaya*) ending in a *kṛt*-suffix. Therefore, according to Rakṣita, forms such as *tadupari* are established. Accordingly, Bhaṭṭi and others employ such usage: "For whose sake do we subdue our enemies?
O Kumbhakarṇa, for what purpose are enjoyments to be accepted by you?"

"Because of you, she is called 'Khañjanamañjulākṣī' (the one with eyes as charming as a wagtail); could it be that both physicians of heaven have descended into her heart so that her hand might fall upon me? And so forth. Likewise, the usage "sarvapaścāt" (after all) in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the rule "anekam anyapadārthe" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.24) is also favorable here. Kaiyaṭa and Haradatta, however, citing "vṛkṣasyopari" (above the tree) as an example under the prohibition regarding indeclinables—[as noted in the *Ādarśa*: "even with a non-kṛt indeclinable"]—consider that the prohibition applies even when the indeclinable is not a *kṛt*-derivative.

However, that [interpretation] is contrary to the usage of Bhaṭṭi, Śrīharṣa, and others. Alternatively, in this view, in the three examples cited above, the word *kṛte* means "in" (*iti yāvat*). The suffix *-cha* (forming *kṛta*) is derived from the root *kṛ* with the *kvip* suffix belonging to the *sampadādi* group, and it refers to the action (*kārya*). Consequently, the fourth case (*caturthī*) is employed. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "a shoe (*pātuka*) for oneself (*ātmanaḥ*). In the sense of "in that which is in the middle of it," the seventh case (*saptamī*) is used according to the rule *saptamī śauṇḍaiḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.40), resulting in either a *saptamī-tatpuruṣa* or an *avyayībhāva* compound; such is the direction [of the argument].

The suffix *tavya* belonging to a *brāhmaṇa* [ending] must be understood as follows: when the suffix *tavya* is taken in the sūtra without its indicatory letter (*anubandha*), a compound indeed occurs, as in *svakartavyam*. There is a difference in accent (*svara*). According to Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.2.139, "after a prefix (*gati*), a kāraka, or an upapada," there is the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the final member of a *kṛt*-derived compound. In that case, because *tavyat* has the indicatory letter *t*, it has a circumflex accent (*svarita*) on the final syllable.

However, since *tavya* has an acute accent (*udātta*) on its first syllable, when a compound is formed with a word ending in the suffix *tavya*, by the rule of the original accent of the final member of a *kṛt*-compound, the word *svakartavyam* would have an acute accent on the middle syllable; this is the meaning. Thus, it is said that the word has an acute accent on the middle.

[The example] "of the serpent Takṣaka" (*takṣakasya sarpasya*) is by way of apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). It has been stated that a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) does not apply here because of the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (in various cases).

This might be argued: "In this case, a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) would indeed be required; for this genitive depends upon an external relation. Thus, according to the maxim 'the mat is the object, as are Bhīṣma and the others,' when both genitive endings are construed with the word 'poison' (*viṣa*) and so forth, a subsequent, secondary relation between the mere nominal stems must be expressed."

And likewise, how could *takṣakasya* and *sarpasya*, which are mutually incapable [of syntactic connection], be compounded? For this very reason, even in cases such as *nīlotpalasya* and *merumahībhṛtaḥ*, it is logical that there is first a compound of the two nominative-terminating words as adjectives (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*), followed by the genitive case; however, a compound of the two genitive-terminating words is not appropriate, because of the lack of mutual capacity (*asāmarthya*) according to the reasoning already stated.

Furthermore, just as in examples such as *citraguḥ*, the nominative case (*prathamā*) occurs because the relationship is already expressed, so too here, in a compound of two words ending in the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*), the nominative alone would result and not the genitive. To this it is replied: "In the view that the mat (*kaṭa*) alone is the object (*karman*), while *bhīṣma* and the others receive their case-ending merely through coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with it—this is what must be understood. And the very prohibition [of the genitive] by means of a coreferential term is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) of this particular position."

For this very reason, even the proclamation that "the case-ending of the qualifier is for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*)" becomes consistent. Nor should it be argued that, even so, the genitive would not arise from a compound; for under the view that the five—namely, the word-meaning (*svārtha*), substance (*dravya*), gender (*liṅga*), number (*saṅkhyā*), and syntactic role (*kāraka*)—are the meanings of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) alone, while the case-endings and so forth are merely its restatement (*anuvāda*), the occurrence of the genitive is as justified as that of the accusative and other endings. This is because, in the case of a *karmadhāraya* compound, which is common to all case-endings, neither [of the two members] is clearly unexpressed.

And this indeed is the way for all cases involving different grammatical categories (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). For instance, regarding the compound *rājñaḥ kumāryāḥ* (the king’s daughter) as *rājakumārī*, the *Mahābhāṣya* (the *Ākara*) addresses the concern that there would be no fixed rule for the prior placement [of one member] by relying on the etymological nature (*anvarthatā*) of the technical term "subordinate element" (*upasarjana*). Furthermore, in that case, it is not even possible to assert the "lack of semantic connection" (*asāmarthya*) that you have mentioned, which would otherwise necessitate that only the nominative-terminating member be compounded.

And thus, for the king [the forms] *rājñaḥ*, *kumārī*, *kumāryai*, and so forth, are indeed the analyses (*vigraha*); this is the meaning of the two sūtras prescribing the technical designation *upasarjana*: Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.43, "In a compound, that which is designated first is the *upasarjana*," and 1.2.44, "That which has a single case-ending is also [the *upasarjana*], provided it does not occur as a prior member [in a subsequent compound]. This is clear in the *Kāśikā* and other works.

This is also clearly stated in the *Bhāṣya* and *Kaiyaṭa* on the two sūtras: *anekam anyapadārthe* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.24) and *tatpuruṣe tulyārtha-* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.2.2). Thus, since there is no restrictive rule that the analytical exposition (*vigraha*) must consist of words ending in the nominative case, it follows that in all instances—even in a *tatpuruṣa* compound—the second and subsequent case endings are to be accounted for in the same manner as in the fivefold classification (*pañcakapakṣa*); this is the essential point.

Furthermore, just as number does not enter into the formation of a compound, so too the relation that has entered into the meaning of the second member (the *uttarapada*) does not enter into the compound itself. This is because, in the analysis (*vigraha*) suitable for usage, only a case-ending of the same class as that which follows the compound is employed—just as in the case of *pacanti* [becoming] *pācakāḥ*. Moreover, according to the view that grammatical refinement applies to the sentence (*vākya-saṃskārapakṣa*), even in the non-ordinary (*alaukika*) stage, it is more reasonable to assume the presence of the genitive and other case-endings, just as one assumes the plural ending. This is the general direction of the argument.

As for what was cited in the *Vṛtti* regarding Śuka the Mārāvika and the king of Pāṭaliputra: there, he is called a *mārāvika* because he says "mārāvī. According to the rule "there is an addition [to the sūtra] for words such as *māśabda*" (*kā.vā.*), the suffix *ṭhak* is applied. A *mārāvika* is one who prohibits the act of making noise; in the reading *mārāvida*, the meaning is the same: one who gives out the sound "mārāvi. Similarly, one who exists in Pāṭaliputra is a *pāṭaliputraka*.

This being the case, if the compound were undesirable here, then this would be consistent as an example for the rule "samānādhikaraṇe"; however, since he himself asserts that the compound is desired, it is not proper for him to cite this as an example.

As for what was established in that very [work]—that if a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) were used, there would be no fixed rule regarding the prior placement [of the members], whereas in a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*), the prior placement of the qualifier alone is established—this must be said in response: since the relationship between qualifier and qualified is not fixed, an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would result; therefore, a systematic restriction is established among words denoting substances, qualities, and so forth, by means of such principles as "the subordinate is the *upasarjana*, and subordination is based on the meaning."

And since that [undesirable consequence] can be easily stated even in the case of a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*), what is the purpose of this prohibition? In reality, however, examples such as *godhenoḥ* ("the cow that is a milch-cow"), *bhojyoṣṇasya* ("the food that is hot"), *kumāraśramaṇāyāḥ* ("the young female ascetic"), and *go garbhiṇyāḥ* ("the cow that is pregnant") should be cited here. For compounds like *poṭāyuvati-* ("a young woman who is also a hermaphrodite") and others, which have already achieved their purpose by overriding the descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) through other case-endings, would otherwise face the undesirable consequence of being overridden by the subsequent genitive compound. Thus, it should be noted that even if the qualifier itself were placed first as a subordinate element (*upasarjana*), the result would clearly be undesirable.
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.12)

Regarding the rule *ktena ca pūjāyām* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.12): the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) ending in a word formed by the suffix *kta* prescribed by the rule *matibuddhipūjārthebhyaśca* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.2.188) is not compounded. Since that [suffix] is prescribed specifically when [the action] pertains to honor (*pūjā*), the mention of "honor" (*pūjā*) serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for that very context—just as the crow [serves as an indicator for the house]. Therefore, this prohibition applies even to the *kta* suffix used in the sense of "thought" (*mati*) and "perception" (*buddhi*). Examples: *rājñāṃ mataḥ*, *buddhaḥ*, or *pūjitaḥ*.

Regarding the rule *ktasya ca vartamāne* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.67), [the example] is *rājñāṃ mato buddho vā pūjito vā*. By the rule *ktasya ca vartamāne*, the genitive case is applied. How then is the usage *kalahaṃsarāmamahitaḥ kṛtāvān* in the *Bhaṭṭikāvya* to be explained? [The root] *maha* [in the sense of] "worship" (*pūjāyām*) [belongs to the Bhvādi class, No. 30]; thus, the meaning is "honored by Rāma" (*rāmasya mahitaḥ*). Similarly, there are forms such as *rājapūjitaḥ*. On this point, they say: in rules such as *ktena ca pūjāyām* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.12), the prohibition of compounding applies specifically to the genitive case used in the sense of a *kāraka* (participant in an action).

However, when the genitive is used with the intention of expressing the *śeṣa* (remaining relation) of the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth, then a compound is indeed formed. There is a difference in accent: for in a compound formed with the genitive of the *kāraka* (participant), the original accent of the final member ending in a *kṛt*-suffix prevails; whereas in a compound formed with the *śeṣa* genitive, the final syllable of the compound is udātta. The author of the *Anunyāsa*, however, says: when the suffix *kta* denotes the present tense, there is a prohibition of the genitive compound; but when *kta* denotes the past, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is used for the agent, as in: "He who was honored by gods and demons."

The compound for that [term] is formed by *Aṣṭādhyāyī* 2.1.32: *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam*. Nor should it be argued that, according to the logic of the curd and Kauṇḍinya (*takrakauṇḍinyanyāya*), the suffix *kta* here in its sense of the present tense (*vartamāne*) supersedes the suffix *kta* in its sense of the past (*bhūte*). This is because of the rule *tena proktam* (*Aṣṭādhyāyī* 4.3.101) under the heading of the third case, and specifically the rule *upajñāte* (*Aṣṭādhyāyī* 4.3.115), which prescribes the *śaiṣika* suffixes after a word ending in the third case when the meaning is "invented by" (*upajñāte*). This is the intended meaning of the reference.

The sense is that, otherwise, if the *kta* suffix were applied in the sense of the past (*bhūte*), the genitive case alone would be obtained [by rule 2.3.65]. This is because, under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "by that" (*tena*), the mention of *upajñāta-* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that there is no sublation [of the past *kta* by the present *kta*]. Nor is it the case that the sublation of the past *kta* by the present *kta* applies only to those verbal roots whose meaning is "to know" (*jñāna*); rather, the indicator has as its scope the general category [of all roots], since it is more logical that it applies generally in accordance with the cited usage.
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.4.21)

[By the rule] *adhikaraṇavācinā ca* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.13): a word ending in a *kta* suffix denoting the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is not compounded with a genitive case-ending [word]. For example: *idameṣām āsitam*, *gatam*, or *bhuktam*. The *kta* suffix here is applied by the rule *kto’dhikaraṇe ca* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.4.76). The genitive case is used for the agent by the rule *adhikaraṇavācinaś ca* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.68). Although the formation would be established by the rule *adhikaraṇe ca* alone, the inclusion of the term *vācin* (denoting) is for the sake of clarity. How then are forms such as *kivṛttam* and *yadvṛttam* explained? On this point, they say: this *kta* suffix is not used in the sense of the locus, but rather in the sense of the action (*bhāva*).

In the phrase *kimo vṛtte yasmin*, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with non-co-referential members (*vyadhikaraṇapada*). Alternatively, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "that in which the occurrence (*vṛtta*) or completion (*niṣpanna*) of 'what' (*kim*) [takes place].
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.14)

Regarding the rule *karmaṇi ca* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.14): the word *ca* has the sense of "and" (*itiśabdārtha*). That genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) which is prescribed or purified (*pariśoṣitā*) by uttering the word *karmaṇi* is not compounded. For example: *citragavāṃ doho 'gopena* ("the milking of the brindled cows by the cowherd"). If the intention here were that "only the genitive of the object (*karma-ṣaṣṭhī*) is not compounded," then the author would not have initiated the prohibition starting from *tṛjakābhyām* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.15), up to *tṛjakābhyāṃ kartari*. For where *tṛc* and *akac* suffixes occur in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), there the genitive of the object (*karmaṇi-ṣaṣṭhī*) must necessarily occur.
It has been stated in the *Paspaśā* [section] that there is no prohibition of compounding in cases such as "śabdānuśāsanam" (Pāṇini 2.2.15).

*tṛjakābhyāṃ kartari* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.15). A sixth-case [genitive] word does not form a compound with a *tṛc* or *aka* suffix when they have the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). The term "agent" (*kartari*) qualifies only *aka*, and not *tṛc* as well, because there is no deviation [in the case of *tṛc*]. Examples: *apāṃ sraṣṭā* ("the creator of waters"), *purāṃ bhettā* ("the destroyer of cities"), *vajrasya bhartā* ("the wielder of the thunderbolt"). Although the word *bhartṛ* is listed among the *yājakādi* group [which permits compounding], nevertheless, due to the greater force of conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*), it refers there to the synonym for "husband"; however, in its etymological sense (*yaugika*), it is indeed prohibited from compounding. Example: *odanasya pācakaḥ* ("the cooker of rice").

What is the purpose of [specifying] the agent (*kartari*)? [Consider: *ikṣubhakṣikā* ("the eating of sugarcane"). This is by means of the rule *paryāyārhārhaṇotpattiṣu ṇvac* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.3.111), which means that the suffix *ṇvul* is prescribed when there is a reference to the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvarthanirdeśe*). How then is it that there is a quarrel between the creator of pots and the creator of the three worlds? On this point, the author of the *Nyāsa* states: this [word *nirmātṛ*] ends in the suffix *tṛn*.

The prohibition of the genitive case by the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛṇām* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.69) is non-obligatory (*anitya*). This is known from the fact that, although one could have simply said *tryakābhyām*, the sūtra employs the form *tṛcaḥ* with its technical marker (*anubandha*), which serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Kaiyaṭa, however, states that the compound is formed with a residual genitive (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*). Many scholars, on the other hand, maintain that this prohibition is non-obligatory because of the indicators found in the rules *janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.30) and *tatprayojako hetuśca* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.54).
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.16)

**Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.16:** *kartari ca* ("And [there is no compound] with a word ending in *aka*, when it denotes the agent"). There is no compound with a genitive of the agent (*kartṛṣaṣṭhī*) and a word ending in *aka*. Example: *bhavataḥ śāyikā* ("your lying down"). The suffix *ṇvuc* is applied here by *Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.3.111*: *paryāyārhaṇa* ("after a verb meaning 'turn' or 'deserving,' the suffix *ṇvuc* is added"). Although the term *tṛc* was mentioned in the preceding rule (*Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.15*) via a *dvandva* compound, it does not carry over here; for when joined with *ṇvuc*, the agent is already expressed [by the verbal activity], and thus a genitive of the agent is impossible. (*Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.17*)

*nityaṃ krīḍājīvikayoḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.17). In these two senses, the genitive case is always compounded with an *aka*-suffix. *Uddālakapuṣpabhañjikā*: this is the name of a particular game. By the rule *saṃjñāyām* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.3.109), the suffix *ṇvul* is used in the sense of the action (*bhāva*). Here, the genitive case in *puṣpāṇām* expresses the object (*karman*). Regarding the sense of livelihood (*jīvikā*): *dantalekhakaḥ*. In that context, since there is an option regarding play (*krīḍā*) and a prohibition by the rule *kartari ca* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.16) regarding livelihood, this specific statement is made.

Jayāditya, however, maintains that in the rule *tṛjakābhyāṃ kartari* (Pāṇini 2.2.15), the word *kartari* ("in the sense of the agent") is a qualifier of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) which is carried over from the previous rule. He argues that since the agent is already expressed by the suffix *tṛc*, a genitive of agency cannot occur in its construction; and so forth. Having stated that [the mention of *kartari*] is for the sake of what follows, he explains the mention of the word *kartṛ* in the rule *kartari ca* (Pāṇini 2.2.16) as being a qualifier of *tṛc* and *aka*. Then, in the rule *nityaṃ krīḍājīvikayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.17), he cites only the suffix *aka* as an example.

In this regard, the following must be said: in the first sūtra, it is appropriate that the mention of the "agent" (kartṛ) serves as a qualifier for *tṛc* and *aka* alone, because those two are explicitly mentioned [in the rule], but not for the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). Furthermore, one should not assume that *tṛc* is intended for the sake of subsequent rules; for only *aka* is carried forward in what follows, not *tṛc*, due to impossibility. Thus, it is proper that the meaning of the two sūtras is understood through their transposition.

Vāmana, however, in the rule *ake jīvikārthe* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.2.73), asked: "What is the purpose of [specifying] *ake*? He provided *ramaṇīyakartā* as a counter-example when the sense is livelihood (*jīvikā*), employing the suffix *tṛc*. His intention was this: let there not be the suffix *tṛc* in the sense of play (*krīḍā*), because there is no grammatical indicator (*lakṣaṇa*) for it; but in the sense of livelihood, since the suffixes *ṇvul* and *tṛc* are both taught by the rule *ṇvultṛcau* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.1.133), the suffix *tṛc* is indeed easily obtained even when *ṇvul* is used. According to this view, they say that the employment of the forced interpretation such as "*tṛjuttārtha*" (for the sake of including *tṛc*) in the rule *nityaṃ krīḍā* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.17) is intended to ward off the suspicion that the mention of *tṛc* might not be connected [to that rule]. (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.18)

*Pāṇini 2.2.18*: "The word *ku* and the group beginning with *pra* are designated as *gati*. The word *ku* and the words beginning with *pra* are always compounded with a compatible term (*samartha*). *Ku* has the sense of "evil" (or "bad"). Examples: *kupuruṣaḥ* ("a bad man"). Although this [word *ku*] falls within the scope of obligatory compounds (*nityasamāsa*), its status as an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is desired for the sake of preserving the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the preceding member. Accordingly, there is a Vārttika: "In the case of an indeclinable, [the rule applies] to *nañ*, *ku*, and particles" (*kātyāyanavārttika*). Therefore, this [word *ku*] should be understood as belonging among the *svarādi* (indeclinables listed in the *gaṇa* of that name).

And it is precisely this [prefix] that is understood here, and not that which functions with respect to "earth" (*pṛthivī*), such as in *adravyārthaka* and so forth, because of its association with [other prefixes] like *ati*. The term *gati* means "having accepted" (*ūrīkṛtya*). The inclusion of the word "beginning with" (*prādi*) is for the purpose of including those that do not have the sense of motion (*agati*). There are, however, many Vārttikas intended to distinguish the specific scope of their application. For instance: in the sense of censure (*nindā*), *duḥ* is used, as in *duḥpuruṣaḥ*; in the sense of praise (*pūjā*), *su* and *ati*, as in *supuruṣaḥ* and *atipuruṣaḥ*; and *āṅ* in the sense of slightness (*īṣadartha*), as in *āpiṅgalaḥ*. Furthermore, this statement regarding the conditions (*upādhi*) is merely illustrative (*prāyika*).

Otherwise, the prescription of the substitution of *kā* for *ku* by the rule *īṣadarthe ca* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.3.105) would be untenable; as in *koṣṇam* ("slightly warm") and *duṣkṛtam* ("badly done"). Here, *dur* is used in the sense of difficulty (*kṛcchra*). However, because such usage is not sanctioned by linguistic convention (*anabhidhāna*), the suffix *khal* does not occur when referring to the past, as in *suṣṭutam* ("well-praised"). In this case, the word *su-* denotes excellence (*atiśaya*) and not honor (*pūjā*). For this very reason, the substitution of *ṣ* [for *s*] occurs based on its status as a prefix (*upasarga*). As in *atistutam*. According to the rule *atiratikramaṇe ca* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.95), there is an absence of the designation *karmapravacanīya* [for *ati*]. This is the reading.

In the *Tattvabodhinī*, regarding the sūtra *atiratikramaṇe ca* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.95), others cite the examples: "atisiktam" and "atistutam. Since [in these cases] there is an absence of the substitution of *ṣ* (due to the preceding *ati* being a karmapravacanīya), one should reflect that the designation *karmapravacanīya* is unimpeded here. [The rule for] *karmapravacanīya* status: "The particles beginning with *pra* (*prādayaḥ*) are compounded with a word in the nominative case when they have the sense of 'gone' (*gatādi*) and so forth. The meaning is that in the context of a compound (*vṛtti*), particles such as *pra* and others, even if they do not possess the technical status of *gati*, are compounded by virtue of the inclusion of the term *prādi* when they convey senses such as 'gone' and the like. For example: *pragata ācāryaḥ* = *prācāryaḥ*; *prāntevāsī*.

The group beginning with *ati* (atyādayaḥ) is compounded with a word in the second case (*dvitīyayā*) when it has the sense of "surpassing" (*krāntādi*). For example: *atimālaḥ*, meaning "one who has surpassed the garland" (*atikrāntā mālām*).

The group beginning with *ava* (*avādayaḥ*) is compounded with a word in the third case (*tṛtīyayā*) when it has the sense of "called out to" (*kruṣṭādi*). For example: *avakokilaḥ*, meaning "one called out to by a cuckoo" (*avakruṣṭaḥ kokilayā*).

The words *pari* and others [are compounded] with a word in the fourth case when they have the sense of exhaustion (*glāna*) and so forth. For example: *pariglāno 'dhyayanāya* becomes *paryadhyayanaḥ*. Regarding *alaṃ kumāryai*, it becomes *alaṃkumāri*. Although this is a compulsory compound (*nityasamāsa*), Rakṣita maintains that by the force of the rule prescribing the fourth case, a sentence may optionally occur. By this, the Bhāṣya statement on the sūtra *ekavibhakti cāpūrvanipāte* (Pāṇini 1.2.44)—namely, *alaṃkumāriḥ*—and Kaiyaṭa’s remark, “there is a compound according to the rule *paryādayo glānādyarthe*,” are explained.

Let it be that this very commentary serves as the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the non-eternality [of the rule]; however, in reality, there is no compound here with this [word *alam*], because *alam* is not included among the *prādi* group. The traditional source (*ākara*) states that this is an elaboration (*prapañca*) of the *prādi* compound. Nevertheless, a *tatpuruṣa* compound preceded by *alam*, which is indicated by the rule *dviguprāptāpannālampūrva-* (Kātyāyana-vārttika), occurs even with the sense of "sufficiency" (*paryāpti*) due to the separate mention of [the word] *dig*; furthermore, by virtue of its being expressed [by usage], it occurs only with a word ending in the dative case. It should be noted that its status as an optional compound (*anityasamāsa*) is entirely unimpeded.

Words beginning with *nis* (and others) [form compounds] with a word in the fifth case when they have the sense of "departing" (*krānta*) and so forth. For example: *niṣkrāntaḥ kauśāmbyāḥ* → *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*. Since the inclusion of the term *prādi* (words beginning with *pra*, etc. is intended to include words other than those meaning "motion" (*agati*), an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would result; therefore, it must be stated that there is a prohibition for those [words] classified as *karmapravacanīya*. For example: *vṛkṣam prati vidyotate vidyut* ("The lightning flashes toward the tree"). How then is [the form] *adhītya* explained? In this case, the status of *karmapravacanīya* is established by the rule: *adhiparī anarthakau* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.93).

It is said: "Because of the rule *adhyāpakadhūrtaiḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.1.65), the prohibition is not universal (*anitya*). For this very reason, compounds such as *sustutam* and *atistutam* are cited as examples where the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur. This is established either by that [rule] or by the statement *svatī pūjāyām* (Kāśikāvṛtti on Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.18)."

*Upapadam atiṅ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.19): An *upapada*, being a word ending in a *sup*-suffix, is always compounded with a word that is semantically related to it; and this compound is one that does not end in a verbal suffix (*atiṅ*). For example, from *kumbhaṃ karoti* ("he makes a jar"), we derive *kumbhakāraḥ* ("jar-maker"). Here, the non-standard, analytical sentence (*alaukika-prakriyā-vākya*) is *kumbha as kāra*. Although there is an addition of the sense of the present tense (*laḍ*) and so forth, the standard sentence (*laukika-vākya*) should be understood as stated [without them], provided there is no great distance [in meaning]. Why "not ending in a verbal suffix" (*atiṅ*)? Consider *mā bhavān bhūt* ("may you not be"). Because of the mention of the locative case in the rule *māṅi luṅ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.3.175), the word *māṅ* is an *upapada*.

[Objection: But surely, because of the governing rule (*adhikāra*) of "sup," [the compound] will not occur with a verbal form (*tiṅanta*)? [Reply: True; its exclusion is indicated by this [rule]. We shall clarify its result immediately below. However, the mention of "sup" ending in the nominative case (*prathamānta*) certainly continues here. For this very reason, in examples such as *rājadarśī*, the word-level operations such as the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) in the prior member are established. As for the statements in the *Bhāṣya*, the *Vṛtti*, and other texts that "sup-supā" does not continue here, they mean simply that the two together do not continue.

Although it is not explicitly stated here in this Bhāṣya that *atiṅ* is not a qualifier of the *upapada* but rather of the compound (*samāsa*), it is nevertheless made clear in the Bhāṣya on the rule *anaṃvaklṛptyamarṣayoḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.3.145). For there, having raised the objection that the mention of *akiṃvṛtta* is redundant because the section concerning *kiṃvṛtta* is not under discussion, the author anticipates the counter-argument that it is intended for the purpose of the technical designation *upapada*. He then establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) that such a designation is unnecessary, because the prohibition of compounds beginning with *atiṅ* already precludes the need for it.

In the same way, in the preceding sūtra as well, the mention of *gati* (preverbs) should be treated separately, and by that [separation], the mention of *atiṅ* (not ending in a verbal suffix) should also be connected. Thus, a *gati* is compounded, and the compound shall not end in a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*). Consequently, in examples such as *prayavati*, there is no compounding of the *gati* with that which ends in a verbal suffix. Furthermore, because of the mention of *atiṅ*, the rule regarding the third case-ending (*sup*) is set aside.

And thus, the ancient maxim (paribhāṣā) of the predecessors—"There is a rule for the compounding of *gatis*, *kārakas*, and *upapadas* with *kṛt*-affixes prior to the arising of case-endings (*sup*)"—is obtained through the mention of *atiṅ* (not being a verbal form), which serves as a general indicator by way of partial acceptance. The meaning is that the compounding of *gatis*, *kārakas*, and *upapadas* with *kṛt*-affixes must take place precisely before the arising of case-endings from the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). It has been stated, however, that the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) is indeed already endowed with a case-ending.

Regarding the [types of] *gatis*, first: she who smells is a *vyāghrī*. The suffix *ka* is applied by the rule *ātaścopasarge* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.1.136). The suffix *śa* is not applied by the rule *pāghrādhmā* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.1.137), because it has been stated: "An exception must be stated regarding the root *jighrati* when a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is intended. The compound *vyāṅoḥ* with the word *ghra* is a *gati-samāsa*. If that [compound] were to depend upon the word *ghra* being in the form of a declined noun (*subanta*), then for the production of the case-ending (*sub*), the connection with number, object, and so forth would have to be intended.

Furthermore, due to its connection with that [gender], the application of the gender-marker (*liṅgayoga*) occurs even earlier, according to the maxim: "Having expressed its own meaning," and so forth. Consequently, if a suffix were to arise based on gender, it would be *ṭāp* alone and not *ṅīṣ*, because the word *vyāghra* by itself does not denote a genus (*jāti*). Therefore, there is a compound with the word *vyāghrī*. Then, although the word *vyāghrā* denotes a genus, the suffix *ṅīṣ*—which is conditioned by being a genus—would not apply because it does not end in the letter *a*. However, the compound, which arises prior to the production of the case-ending (*sub*), occurs because it is "internal" (*antaraṅga*) insofar as it does not depend upon the connection with gender.

Consequently, the *ṅīp* suffix [would apply], and because the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) would be a form ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), word-level operations (*padakāryāṇi*) would indeed occur—such as the substitution of *ru* in *nigataḥ* and the optional substitution of the following vowel (*parasavarṇa*) in *sayyaṃtā*, and so forth.

In the examples *aśvaiḥ krītā* ("bought for horses") and *alpair abhraiḥ liptā* ("smeared with a little cloud"), there is a compound according to the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam* (Pāṇini 2.1.32). If that [compound] were one where the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) ended in a case-suffix, then, as before, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* would occur. Consequently, the suffix *ṅīṣ* would not apply by virtue of the rules *krītātkaraṇapūrvāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.50) and *ktādalpākhyāyām* (Pāṇini 4.1.51), because of the governing context of the word *ataḥ* ("from [a stem] ending in short *a*").

If it is argued that [the suffix] would occur by the force of the statement (*vacana-sāmarthya*), then it would occur in the state of the sentence (*vākya-avasthā*), because the word *pūrva* can possibly have the sense of "establishment" (*vyavasthā*). Alternatively, the governing rule (*adhikāra*) "from this" (*ataḥ*) would be excluded. And thus, the usage in Bhāravi’s *Bhaṭṭi-kāvya*: "For she, bought with wealth, was dearer to him even than his own life-breaths," would not be established. In the final system (*siddhānta*), however, because of the inclusion of the term "variously" (*bahulagrahaṇa*) in the rule *Aṣṭādhyāyī* 2.1.32 (*kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā*), there is occasionally a compound with a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*); therefore, the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply.

The word *kacchapī* means "one who drinks by means of the neck (*kaccha*)"; it is formed like *vyāghrī*. According to the rule *supi sthaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.2.4), and because of the separation of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) [in the rule] *pīti*, the suffix *ka* is applied, and so forth. As for the claim that the mention of *atiṅ* is a qualifier of the *upapada* (the subordinate word), that is not correct; for if that were the case, the mention of the nominative case-ending (*prathamānta*) would be rendered redundant, leading to widespread confusion (*bahuviplava*). By this, even the counter-example *edhānāhārako vrajati* ("he goes carrying fuel")—which was offered to show what purpose the mention of *atiṅ* serves—is refuted.

As for what was stated in the *Prakriyākaumudī* under the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.18)—namely, that because the term *sup-supā* does not recur there, a compound with a finite verb (*tiṅ*) is also possible, as in *ūrīkaroti* and so forth—that too is incorrect. This is because it contradicts the very mention of the word *atiṅ* (not a finite verb), which is treated as a restrictive remainder (*śeṣīkṛta*) in that context. Furthermore, it has already been explained at length that a compound with a finite verb is obtainable only through the force of the *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) in the form *saha*, and that it pertains to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*) within the specific scope of the particular *vārttika* mentioned.
(Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.20)

*Amaiva* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.2.20). An upapada that is prescribed by the same rule as *ama* alone is compounded with an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Examples: *svāduṅkāraṃ bhuṅkte* (he eats making it sweet), *sampannaṅkāram*, *lavaṇaṅkāram*. [The suffix] *ṇamul* is applied after a word meaning "sweet" according to Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.4.26 (*svādumi ṇamul*). The fact that the first member ends in *m* is due to this very irregularity (*nipātana*) of the word *svādumi*. The term *svādumi* is taken here as a reference to the meaning "sweet. The words *sampanna* and *lavaṇa* are also synonyms for "sweet."

In that sentence where only this [suffix] alone is prescribed and not accompanied by any other suffix, it is stated that "that which has the designation *upapada* by virtue of the mention of the locative case in that sentence is subject to the same rule" (*tulyavidhāna*). Furthermore, the phrase "subject to the same rule" (*tulyavidhāna*) is supplied as an ellipsis in the Sūtra. As for the particle *eva*, which constitutes a part of the restrictive rule (*niyama*), it is obtained through the very nature of the restriction itself and is not explicitly contained within the wording of the Sūtra.
