Let the nominative case (prathamā) apply due to its conflict [with other rules]; nor does it follow that the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhī) would consequently apply because it is further [in the order of rules], since there is no remainder [to which it could apply].

It is said in reply: first of all, the enumeration [of the case endings] has already been rejected in the Bhāṣya. However, the rule (*sūtra*) is for the sake of establishing forms such as *kaṭaḥ kartavyaḥ* ("the mat is to be made"). For in this case, the nominative would be superseded by the genitive according to the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* (Pāṇini 2.3.65). Nor should it be argued that the genitive does not apply here because its meaning has already been expressed by the kṛtya suffix; for the rule is formulated on the assumption that number is the meaning of the case ending (*vibhakti*). Indeed, the meaning of the sentence is: when there is singularity in the object, the singular genitive occurs in connection with a kṛt suffix.

And thus, since the singularity of the object—which is denoted by the genitive case—is not expressed by the verbal suffix (*kṛtya*), the use of the genitive would be unavoidable. However, it is established that under the view that the *kāraka* itself is the meaning of the case-ending, the rule need not exist.

However, when the sūtra is applied, this is an *paryudāsa* (exclusion), not a *prasajyapratiṣedha* (absolute negation), because that would result in the fault of an *asamartha-samāsa* (an ungrammatical compound) and the fault of a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). Furthermore, in the example "He sits on the palace" (*prāsāde āste*), the single substratum called "palace" belongs to both the action of sitting (*sadikriyā*) and the action of remaining (*āsikriyā*). Since that [substratum] is expressed by the suffix *ghañ* following the root *sad*, there would be the undesirable consequence of the prohibition of the locative case (*saptamī*). But in the case of *paryudāsa*, the rule for the locative case applies by relying on the unexpressed (*anabhihita*) power of the substratum as determined by the action of sitting.

In cases such as "he sits on the seat" (*āsane āste*) or "he lies on the bed" (*śayane śete*), when the action is presented by the verbal roots of the present tense (*laṭ*), the locative case is employed to indicate the emergence of the potency directed toward that [action], which is otherwise unmanifest and suitable for it; this is the general direction.

This might be so: if this were an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), then the expression "having cooked, rice is eaten" (*paktvaudano bhujyate*) would not be established. For even though the rice is denoted by the suffix of the verb *bhuj*, one would incur the use of the accusative case on the grounds that it is not denoted by the *ktvā* suffix; for it will be stated that the *ktvā* suffix occurs in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāve*). However, in the case of a simple negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), it is easy to maintain the negation by relying on the fact that the rice is denoted by the suffix of the verb *bhuj*; yet, the previously mentioned fault remains unresolved.

To this it is replied: when the power (*śakti*) denoted by the primary element is expressed, the nominative case (*prathamā*) alone occurs, because of the absolute prohibition [of other cases] once [the power] has been expressed. However, in expressions such as *āsane āste* ("he sits on a seat") and *śayane śete* ("he lies on a bed"), there is no expression of the power belonging to the primary element, which would otherwise necessitate the nominative. This is clear from the commentary of Kaiyaṭa and others on the rule *svādumi ṇamul* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.4.26). Hari also says:

"Where two actions belonging to a substance—one primary and the other subordinate—possess separate powers, and the power [of the subordinate] rests upon its quality (*guṇa*), there the primary action is followed [by the grammatical operation]."
"When the power whose primary object is the principal element is expressed by the suffix, then its subordinate element is understood even though it is not explicitly stated. Thus [it is said].

Even in the case of a relative negation (paryudāsa), the injunction proceeds by relying precisely on the primary power that has not been expressed [by another word]. By this, examples such as "he eats what is cooked" (*pakvaṃ bhuṅkte*) and "he accepts what is given" (*dattaṃ gṛhṇāti*) are established under both views. In reality, however, in cases such as "having cooked, it is eaten" (*paktvā bhujyate*), there is no simultaneous verbal comprehension of the connection of the rice (*odana*) with both the roots *pac* (to cook) and *bhuj* (to eat). Rather, the verbal comprehension occurs through one [of the two], while through the other it is inferential (*ārtha*). And in that regard, there is indeed a fixed rule between the nominative and the accusative: "Having cooked, the rice is eaten. (*paktvā bhujyate odanaḥ*)

By implication, it means "having cooked rice" (*odanam eva paktvā*); for it is not possible [to say] "having cooked bricks" (*iṣṭakāḥ paktvā*) and so forth. Furthermore, it is not logical to abandon what is present and imagine what is not present. However, in the usage "having cooked rice" (*odanaṃ paktvā*), the rice is the object (*karman*) with respect to the act of eating (*bhujyate*). For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa states in the *Paspaśā* that the expression "it is possible to make a jar" (*ghaṭaṃ kartuṃ śakyate*) is indeed valid. Therefore, in the case of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), there is both syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) and the excellence of the compound (*samāsasauṣṭhava*).
As for the nature of the quality (*guṇarūpa*), it remains the same in both views. By this—

"Even a poison tree, having been nurtured by oneself, is not fit to be cut down"—thus it has been explained. This is because the meaning is already expressed by the indeclinable *sāmpratam*; for its sense is "proper" (*yuktam*). As for the enumeration [of synonyms], it is indeed rejected.

Here, Haradatta has stated that in the Bhāṭṭa school, number—remaining as a residual factor after the *kāraka*—is the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*). However, this must somehow be interpreted in accordance with the natural drift of the *bhāṣya* as heard in the *Kartradhikaraṇa*. In reality, however, in the Bhāṭṭa school, the powers such as instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) and so forth are qualified by the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) and by number. For this very reason, the inclusion of multiple [qualifications] within a single power is accepted in various places; such is the direction of the argument.

"A second case ending is used for the object" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.2). Words such as "second" (*dvitīyā*) occur within the triplets of *sup* endings according to the maxim "It should be equal, because it is not specifically heard" (Jaimini Sūtra 10.3.13–53) and due to the usage of former teachers. Here, under the rule for *svādi* [case endings], there is either an injunction (*vidhi*) by virtue of being a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*), or a restriction (*niyama*) by virtue of being a separate syntactical unit (*bhinnavākyatā*). Furthermore, with respect to the meanings under discussion, all positions—whether it be a restriction on the suffixes (*pratyayaniyama*) or a restriction on the meanings (*arthaniyama*)—are valid.
And it has been said: "The meanings of the *sup* [endings] are the object and so forth, as well as number; likewise for the *tiṅ* [endings]."
"The rule is well-known there, and the restriction applies to the primary meanings.

This has been explained in the first [section]. And here, by the natural force of the word *tiṅām* (of verbal suffixes), even in the case of nominal suffixes (*sup*), the object and so forth alone are the denotable meanings, and not "objecthood" (*karmatva*). Nor should it be argued that even for verbal suffixes, "objecthood" alone is the meaning; for if that were the case, it would follow that the same applies to the subsequent sūtra, "tayoreva" (Pāṇini 3.4.70), which would lead to the undesirable consequence that in expressions such as "the jar was made" (*ghaṭaḥ kṛtaḥ*), the syntactic relation of identity (*abheda-anvaya*) would be untenable.

And thus, the natural implication of the sūtras "laḥ karmaṇi" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 3.4.69) and "karmaṇi dvitīyā" (Aṣḷādhyāyī 2.3.2) is also consistent [with this view]. In the case of "ghaṭam," when there is a relation of identity (*abheda-anvaya*) such that "the pot is the object" (*ghaṭaḥ karma*), the pot functions as a qualifier through the relation of being an object (*karmatva*) with respect to the act of bringing and so forth. Consequently, one position holds that the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is manifested in two ways: either as a mode (*prakāratayā*) or as a relation (*saṃsarga-vidhayā*). Another position, based on the natural implication of the Bhāṣya statement "the capacity (*śakti*) is the factor (*kāraka*)," maintains that it is that very capacity which is the denotation.

Since it is not obtainable through any other means, the meaning of the accusative case is either the locus (*ādhāra*) or the located (*ādheya*), as these constitute the referent of the word. In the sentence "He cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*), what appears is a softening (*viklitti*) qualified by that which is the locus, namely the rice; this qualification, however, is the state of being the located (*ādheyatā*). Alternatively, the meaning is the softening as located in the rice, because the meaning of the suffix in its form as the located is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) with respect to the meaning of the stem. Furthermore, there is another position: that the relation itself is precisely the state of being the located (*ādheyatva*).

Furthermore, according to the principle of the *ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*, the meanings are simply the state of being a locus (*ādhāratva*) and the state of being located therein (*ādheyatva*). Another view holds that these are merely relations (*saṃsarga*), and that case-endings (*vibhakti*) serve solely to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparya*). All these positions are established here and there in works such as the *Helārājīya* and are in agreement with the *Bhāṣya* and other authorities; this is the general direction. [This applies] in examples such as "he cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*). Regarding the rule: "The second case is employed after *ubha* and *sarvatas*, after *dhik*, *upari*, and the three beginning with *adhi*, when followed by a reduplicated word; it is also seen elsewhere."

The meaning of this is as follows: when the words *ubhaya* and *sarva*, ending in the suffix *tasil*, are employed, the second case (*dvitīyā*) should be applied. For by the word *ubha*, the word *ubhaya* is indicated, since otherwise the suffix *tasil* would be impossible. It has been stated that the word *ubha* is the domain of the dual number and the feminine suffix *ṭāp*. In the expression *dhik*, there is the elision (*luk*) of the seventh case (*saptamī*), due to the extended application (*atideśa*) of the rule "an imitation [of a form] is like its original" (*prakṛtivadanukaraṇam*). However, it is not without a case-ending (*avibhaktika*).

Just as in the case of *gavityayamāha*, where the rule *lopaḥ śākalyasya* (Pāṇini 8.3.19) does not apply because there is no status of being at the end of a word (*padāntatva*), so too here there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-application of the rule for changing a sound to a voiced one (*jaśtva*). Nor should it be said that this [word] ends in *g* alone; for if the rule *kasya ca daḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.72) were not to apply, the form *dhakit* would result in being unestablished. The phrase "at the ends of *āmreḍita*s" means "in those which have undergone reduplication. Examples: *ubhayataḥ kṛṣṇaṃ gopāḥ* (the cowherds are on both sides of Kṛṣṇa), *sarvataḥ kṛṣṇam* (on all sides of Kṛṣṇa), and *dhik kṛṣṇābhaktam* (shame on the one who is not a devotee of Kṛṣṇa).

Hari is above the world, above the world, and below the world. How is it that the genitive case is used in "buddhīnām" (of the intellects)? The meaning is that the genitive case is an exception (*apavāda*) to the accusative case of the subordinate word (*upapada*). How, then, [is it explained]?

It is said: the meaning is that it moves above those who possess higher intellects and superior understandings. And thus, because there is an absence of non-repetition (*āmoḍitāntatva*), the second case ending does not apply. Alternatively, there is the inclusion here of the specifically prescribed form *upary-adhy-adhas* (Pāṇini 2.3.3), which has undergone reduplication; therefore, when there is reduplication for the sake of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), this rule does not operate. Consequently, it was stated "also elsewhere," and the author of the commentary (*vṛttikāra*) enumerates those instances: "abhitaḥ, paritaḥ, samayā, nikaṣā, hā, and prati, even in the sense of connection. Example: *abhitaḥ kṛṣṇam*.

The meaning is "on both sides. *Paritaḥ* means "on all sides. The suffix *tasil* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.3.9 (*paryabhibhyāṃ ca*). There is also an indeclinable particle *abhitaḥ* which functions as a substitute for a case ending; that too is included here. The words *samayā* and *nikaṣā* are synonyms for "nearness. Examples: *grāmaṃ samayā* or *nikaṣā* (near the village). The word *hā* expresses grief. *Hā kṛṣṇābhaktam* means "one who is not a devotee of Kṛṣṇa is pitied"; the accusative case is used here as an exception to the genitive.

In the case of an address, however, the nominative alone is used because it is *antaraṅga* (more internal); for example, "Alas, father! (*hā tāta*). By this, the usage "Fie on you, fool! (*dhiṅ mūrkha*) is explained. "Nothing appears to one who is hungry" (*bubhukṣitaṃ na pratibhāti kiṃcit*): here the word *prati* is a prefix (*upasarga*) because it qualifies the action, and not a *karmapravacanīya*. Other such cases are also to be established by reference to the mention of the root *dṛś* (to see). For example: "As far as Caitra is cold" (*caitraṃ yāvacchītam*), and "Except for the propitiation of the Supreme Person" (*paramapuruṣārādhanam ṛte*).

And likewise, the Cāndra-sūtra states: "Except for the second case-ending (dvitīyā)," where the word "and" (ca) implies the fifth case-ending (pañcamī). And that [usage] will be prescribed in our own treatise by the rule "anyārāt" (Pāṇini 2.3.29).

(Pāṇini 2.3.3): *tṛtīyā ca hośchandasī* (And the third case [is used] after the root *hu* in the Veda). In the Vedic language, the third case may be used for the object of the root *juhoti*, as well as the second case. For example: *yavāgvāgnihotraṃ juhoti* ("He offers the Agnihotra with gruel"). Here, the word *agnihotra* refers to the sacrificial oblation (*havis*), as seen in such usages as *yasyāgnihotramadhiśritam amedhyamāpadyate* ("If the Agnihotra that has been placed on the fire becomes impure..."), and because of its etymological derivation as "that which is offered (*hūyate*) to Agni. The root *hu* means "to cast in" or "to offer. In this very usage, the third case is employed after the word *yavāgū* (gruel), while the second case is employed after the word *agnihotra*.

Because the meanings of two nouns are not constrained by incompatible case-endings, there is a relation of identity between them. The meaning is that one offers—that is, casts into the fire—the oblation known as *yavāgū* (gruel), having dedicated it to the deity. This sūtra has been rejected in the Bhāṣya. For the word *agnihotra* also applies to the fire itself, as seen in the expression "the *agnihotra* is kindled," and because of its etymological derivation as "that in which [the offering] is poured. Furthermore, the root *hu* (to sacrifice) can mean "to please. Thus, when the third case ending follows the word *yavāgū*, the meaning is "one pleases the fire with the gruel."
But when the second [case] occurs, the meaning is that one pours in the sacrificial substance known as *yavāgū* for the *agnihotra*.

The Mīmāṃsakas, however, say: "The word *agnihotra* is the name of a ritual (*karmanāmadheya*), according to the principle that 'there is another scriptural passage which makes that [name] known' (*tatprakhyaṃ cānyaśāstram*). For it is observed [in scripture]: "This sacrifice is fivefold: the *agnihotra*, the *darśapūrṇamāsa*s," and so forth. This being the case, by the principle of the *bhāvārthādhikaraṇa*, since the *homa* (oblation) is placed within the category of the instrument (*karaṇa*), the *agnihotra*—which stands in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with it—is also an instrument; thus, while the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) would be expected, this statement serves to provide the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) in certain instances. But that contradicts the context of the Sūtra, for the term "in the object" (*karmaṇi*) is understood to carry over.

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.4) *antarā* and *antareṇa*, when used in connection with [another word], [govern the accusative case]. When used in conjunction with these two, the second case (*dvitīyā*) shall occur. The word *antarā* occurs in the sense of "in the middle" (*madhya*), which is the meaning of a word ending in the seventh case (*saptamī*). The word *antareṇa*, however, occurs in both that sense and in the sense of "without" (*vinā*). Example: *antarā tvāṃ māṃ ca hariḥ* ("Hari is between you and me"). [Another example]:
*mṛṇālasūtrāmalamantareṇa sthitaścalaccāmarayordvayaṃ saḥ* ("He stood pure as a lotus fiber between the two waving chowries").

"Without Hari there is no happiness. Now, since the word *antareṇa* requires two limits, it is indeed connected with the two meanings of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* (you and I) as the limits, as well as with the two chowries; likewise, it is also connected with the thing contained (*ādheya*). Therefore, the accusative case should also occur after the thing contained. This is not so; because in that case, by virtue of being more internal (*antaraṅga*), the nominative case alone arises. Therefore, it is established that this accusative case, which is an exception to the genitive, applies to the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and not to the qualified (*viśeṣya*) as well.

Now, one might ask: why is there no connection with the word *antarā* ending in the suffix *ṭāp* (i.e., nominative/accusative dual), nor with the word *antareṇa* ending in the third case? It is because only those two [specific forms] are taken here due to their being explicitly mentioned (*pratipadokta*) and because of their mutual association (*sāhacarya*). For example, when it is said "the Guru and Bhārgava," only the two planets are understood, not the teacher [Vasiṣṭha] and Paraśurāma. Thus, the expression "What is the use of going between these two? is established; the meaning is: "What is the use of knowing the distinction between these two? Because of the requirement for a connected form (*yuktagrahaṇa*), this does not apply here: "The form of Kṛṣṇa is between you and me. Here, *kṛṣṇāt* takes the fifth case (ablative) because it does not connect with the word *antareṇa*.

(Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.3.5) *kālādhvanoratyantasaṃyoge* (Pāṇini 2.3.5). Here, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) should occur. For example: *māsam āste* ("He sits for a month"). Although this is established here simply because [the time] functions as an object (*karman*), it is stated that "time, state, and distance to be traversed are designated as objects when [the verb] is intransitive" (*kālabhāvādhvagantavyāḥ karmasaṃjñā hy akarmaṇām*). Nevertheless, this rule is intended for the sake of [verbs] that do have an object (*sakarmaka*), and for the sake of connection with qualities (*guṇa*) and substances (*dravya*). Examples: *māsam adhīte* ("He studies for a month"); *māsaṃ kalyāṇī* ("She is auspicious for a month"); *māsaṃ guḍadhānāḥ* ("Jaggery and parched grain for a month"). *krośam adhīte* ("He studies for the distance of a *krośa*"); *krośaṃ kuṭilā nadī* ("The river is winding for a *krośa*"); *krośaṃ parvataḥ* ("The mountain extends for a *krośa*"). Why "in the sense of continuous connection" (*atyantasaṃyoge*)? Consider: *māsasya dvir adhīte* ("He studies twice a month").
The genitive case is used [by Pāṇini 2.3.6, *kṛtvorthaprayoge kāle 'dhikaraṇe*] when words having the sense of *kṛtvas* (times) are employed.

The third case is used when there is completion (*apavarga*). Completion is the attainment of the result; when this is to be indicated, the third case shall be used for time and distance in cases of continuous connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*). For example: *ahna anuvāko 'dhītaḥ* (the lesson was studied throughout the day) or *krośenānuvāko 'dhītaḥ* (the lesson was studied for the distance of a *krośa*). Why "when there is completion"? [Consider: *māsam adhīto nāyātaḥ* (he has studied for a month but has not mastered it).

(Pāṇini 2.3.7) *Saptamī-pañcamyau kāraka-madhye*: When time (*kāla*) or distance (*adhvan*) fall between two factors of action (*kāraka*), the seventh (*saptamī*) and fifth (*pañcamī*) case endings are used for them. For example: *adya bhuktvāyaṃ dvyahe dvyahād vā bhoktā* ("Having eaten today, he will eat in two days or after two days"). This time lies between the two powers of the agent (*kartṛ-śakti*). Or: *ihastho 'yaṃ krośe krośād vā lakṣyaṃ vidhyet* ("Standing here, he might pierce the target at a distance of one *krośa*"). This place lies between the agent and the object (*kartṛ-karmaṇoḥ*). There is no application of the case endings to time and distance according to their respective order [as in the previous rule], because that rule is not marked with the *svarita* accent. (Pāṇini 2.3.8)
When used in conjunction with a *karmapravacanīya*, the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is employed (Pāṇini 2.3.8). The meaning is clear: *hariṃ prati*, *pary* or *anu*. (Pāṇini 2.3.9)

The rule *yasmād adhikaṃ yasya ceśvaravacanaṃ tatra saptamī* (Pāṇini 2.3.9) applies. The phrase *karmapravacanīyayukte* is understood to carry over [from the previous sūtra]. Because of the usage in the expressions *yasmād adhikaṃ* and *tad asminn adhikam*, when used in conjunction with the word *adhika*, both the fifth (*pañcamī*) and seventh (*saptamī*) case endings occur optionally. However, the meaning of the present sūtra is: when there is that from which something is superior (*yasmād adhikaṃ*) or that which expresses mastery (*yasya ceśvaravacanaṃ*) in connection with a *karmapravacanīya*, the seventh case ending should be employed there. For example: *upaparārddhe harerguṇāḥ*, meaning "the qualities of Hari are superior to the highest number (*parārddha*)."

Regarding the term *aiśvarya* (lordship), the seventh case ending (*saptamī*) is used alternately for both the object (*sva*) and the owner (*svāmin*). To explain: that by which one is called "lord" (*īśvara*) is "lordship" (*aiśvarya*), which is a word denoting the state of being a lord. Alternatively, the word *īśvara* emphasizes the abstract state (*bhāvapradhāna*); the meaning is that the lordship of whichever owner is expressed. Or else, by the word "whose" (*yasya*), the object (*sva*) is indicated; the meaning is then that [the suffix occurs] after the word "object" (*svāt*), because the lord of that object is expressed.

Furthermore, this case-ending is used alternatively because the case-endings for *karmapravacanīyas* governing the remaining relations have been introduced; and because the seventh case (*saptamī*) arising from a word that functions as a qualifier expresses the relation even when it resides in both [terms]. Moreover, since the meaning of the suffix is appropriately a qualifier with respect to the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), which serves as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), the suffix arises precisely from the qualifier. However, from the qualificand, only the first case (*prathamā*) occurs. For example: *adhirāme bhūḥ*. But in the alternative where there is a compound according to Pāṇini 2.1.40, *saptamī śauṇḍaiḥ*, the form becomes *rāmadhīnā*.

The suffix *kha* is applied by the rule *aṣaḍakṣa-* (Pāṇini 5.4.7). An *avyayībhāva* compound, however, functions as the sense of a case ending (*vibhaktyartha*). For example: *adhirāmam*. When it occurs with its own case ending, as in *adhibhuvi rāmaḥ* ("Rāma is on the earth"), the portion of this sūtra stating "when there is a designation of lordship" (*yasya ceśvaravacanam*) is rejected in the Bhāṣya. To explain: when the earth is situated upon its locus, the master, and when either of these is intended to be expressed as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), then the seventh case (*saptamī*) will apply there.

In this way, even the technical rule (*saṃjñāsūtra*) *adhir īśvare* need not be formulated. Nor is it intended to prevent the sublation of [the designation] *upasarga* by [the designation] *karmapravacanīya*; for since the prefix *adhi*—when its domain is sovereignty—lacks connection with an action, that [designation of *upasarga*] does not apply in the first place. If it is argued that the rule is for the sake of the subsequent [sūtra], then the division of the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) need not be made.

By the rule *pañcamyapāṅparibhiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.10), the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) shall be used when these *karmapravacanīya*s are employed: *apa*, *āṅ*, and *pari*. For example: *apaviṣṇoḥ pariviṣṇoḥ saṃsāraḥ* ("The cycle of existence is outside of Viṣṇu"). Because of its association with *apa*, the *pari* here is understood in the sense of exclusion (*varjana*). Therefore, it does not apply in cases such as indication (*lakṣaṇa*), etc., as in: *vṛkṣaṃ pari vidyotate vidyut* ("The lightning flashes around the tree"). *Āṅ* is used in the sense of a limit (*maryādā*): *āpāṭaliputrādvṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("It has rained as far as Pāṭaliputra"). (Pāṇini 2.3.11).

"And [the fifth case ending is used] after the word *yasmāt* when it signifies either a substitute (*pratinidhi*) or an exchange (*pratidāna*). In that context, the fifth case ending shall be used when joined with a *karmapravacanīya*. For example: *pradyumnaḥ kṛṣṇāt prati* ("Pradyumna is a substitute for Kṛṣṇa"); *tilebhyaḥ pratiyacchati māṣān* ("He exchanges sesame seeds for beans"). In this rule, the fifth case ending is applied by this very [sūtra] because of the word *yasmāt*. (Pāṇini 2.3.11). (Pāṇini 2.3.12) [The fifth case ending is also used] after the word *yasmāt* when it signifies the cause (*hetu*). For example: *yasmāt kṛṣṇāt bhaktiḥ tasmāt jayaḥ* ("Because there is devotion to Kṛṣṇa, there is victory"). In this rule, the word *yasmāt* is used as a *hetu* (cause), and thus the fifth case ending is applied. (Pāṇini 2.3.12).

Pāṇini 2.3.12: *gatyarthakarmaṇi dvitīyā-caturthyau ceṣṭāyām anadhvani*. When there is physical effort (*ceṣṭā*), these two [case endings], the second and the fourth, are used for the object (*karman*) of verbs meaning "to go," provided it is not a path (*adhvan*). Examples: *grāmaṃ gacchati* (he goes to the village) or *grāmāya gacchati* (he goes to the village). Why "verbs meaning 'to go'" (*gatyartha*)? [Consider: *odanaṃ pacati* (he cooks rice). Why "for the object" (*karmaṇi*)? [Consider: *aśvena vrajati* (he goes by horse). Why "when there is physical effort" (*ceṣṭāyām*)? [Consider: *manasā hariṃ vrajati* (he goes to Hari mentally). Why "not a path" (*anadhvani*)? [Consider: *panthānaṃ gacchanti* (they go along the road). A prohibition must be stated regarding that which has already been traversed (*āsthitapratiṣedhaḥ*). Example: *āsthitaḥ* (already reached/traversed), *samprāptaḥ* (attained).

The meaning is "presided over by a goer" (*gantrā adhiṣṭhita*). Therefore, when one intends to proceed from a wrong path onto the correct path itself, then the fourth case (*caturthī*) certainly occurs: *utpathena pathe gacchati* ("he goes from the wrong path onto the path"). However, in the expression *ajān nayati grāmam* ("he leads the goats to the village"), the fourth case does not occur because the root does not have the sense of "going. For although "going" is perceived here, it is not the primary meaning of the root *nī*, since its meaning is "causing to reach" (*prāpaṇa*). Similarly, in *striyaṃ gacchati* ("he goes to a woman"), the fourth case also does not occur, because there is no desire to reach a destination not yet reached (*asamprāpta-prepsā*).

For, having set aside the term *anaghvanī* (non-attaining), [the word] *asamprāpta* (not yet reached) is supplied [to complete the definition]. The inclusion of the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is so that [the rule] may apply even in cases where an exception would otherwise apply; thus, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) characterized by its connection with a *kṛt*-suffix does not occur. By stating "one should simply say 'the fourth case (*caturthī*) is for the purpose of connection (*anvaya*)'," the author of the *Vṛtti* cited the example *grāmaṃ gantā* ("one who is about to go to the village") in connection with a form ending in the suffix *tṛc*. However, this is contrary to the *Bhāṣya*. For it is established that since the action itself is a "grammatical object" (*karma*) in the sense of being something to be attained through actions such as seeing, that which is intended for the sake of the action possesses the status of the "recipient" (*sampradāna*).

However, when the distinction between [the acts of] *sandarśana* (showing) and so forth and the act of going (*gamana*) is not intended to be expressed, the accusative case is also established; thus, this rule was rejected in the Bhāṣya. For by speaking in this way, it is maintained that only the genitive case is desired in connection with a *kṛt* suffix. Precisely for this reason, the example "grāmaṃ gāmī" ("one who goes to the village") is cited in the Bhāṣya under the rule *akenoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.70).
(Pāṇini 2.3.13)

The fourth [case ending] is used for the recipient (*sambhprādāna*) [Pāṇini 2.3.13]. This is clear [as in]: *viprāya gāṃ dadāti* ("He gives a cow to the Brahmin"). Regarding the sense of "being for the sake of that" (*tādarthye*), there is a supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*). [Example: *yūpāya dāru* ("Wood for a sacrificial post"). Here, the third case ending governed by the rule "when the cause" (*hetau*, Pāṇini 2.3.23) does not apply to the word *dāru*. For that [third case] applies only in the domain of the sixth case; in the mere sense of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), only the first case ending occurs. If it is argued: "If this supplementary rule is necessary, then the sūtra is indeed redundant," [the answer is: No, for it is also necessary for such purposes as *haraye rocate* ("It pleases Hari").

Regarding the rule *klṛpi sampadyamāne ca* (Pāṇini 1.4.30): the meaning is that the fourth case (*caturthī*) is used after a word expressing a transformation (*vikāra*). For that [transformation] indeed comes into being or manifests. "Devotion conduces to knowledge" (*bhaktir jñānāya kalpate*). When one intends to express the distinction between the material cause (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikāra*), the fourth case is used. But when non-distinction is intended, only the first case (*prathamā*) is used. Some say: "Devotion becomes knowledge" (*bhaktir jñānaṃ kalpate*). Others, however, state that the fourth case is used even when non-distinction is intended. But when the status of the source (*apādānatva*) is intended for the agent of birth (*janikartṛ*), the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is used: "Knowledge arises from devotion" (*bhakteḥ jñānaṃ kalpate*).

Some, however, maintain that even in this case, the fourth [case-ending] is desired. Regarding the rule *utpātena jñāpite ca* (Pāṇini 2.3.45): an "omen" (*utpāta*) is a modification of natural elements that indicates the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness of living beings; for example, "tawny lightning portends wind. Regarding the rule *hitayoge ca* (Pāṇini 2.3.46): it is understood from the prescription of the fourth-case compound that [the word] "beneficial" (*hita*) [governs the dative]; for example, "beneficial for the Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇāya hitam*). (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.14).

"And [the fourth case ending is used] for the object of a word that has another word denoting an action as its subordinate member (*upapada*), provided that [the word denoting the object] is not actually employed" (Pāṇini 2.3.14). The term *upapada* is technical; and since it can only occur in the forms of *tumun* and *ṇvul* when they denote an action for the sake of another action, by the power of this qualification, the qualified element is understood to be precisely those suffixes *tumun* and *ṇvul*. The fourth case ending shall be used for the object when [the word denoting the object] is not being employed. For example: *phalebhyo yāti* ("He goes for fruits"), meaning "in order to fetch fruits. The word *sthānin* is well-known in the house of grammarians as referring to something that is not being employed. (Pāṇini 2.3.15)

*Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.15: tumarthācca bhāvavacanāt*. According to this rule, the fourth case (*caturthī*) shall occur after a word ending in an affix prescribed by the sūtra *bhāvavacanāśca* [3.3.11]. For example: *yāgāya yāti* (he goes for the sake of sacrifice); *pākāya*, *pacanāya*, *bhaktaye* (for the sake of cooking, for the sake of food). Since the sense of being for that purpose (*tādarthya*) is already expressed by the term "bhāvavacana" itself, one might think the fourth case would not apply to express *tādarthya*; thus, the formulation of this sūtra is necessary. *Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.16*.

Pāṇini’s Sūtra 2.3.16 states: *namaḥ-svasti-svāhā-svadhā-alam-vaṣaṭ-yogācca*. When these are used in conjunction [with another word], the fourth case ending (*caturthī*) shall be employed. For example: *haraye namaḥ* ("salutation to Hari"). The case ending determined by the *kāraka* (grammatical participant) is stronger than that determined by a *upapada* (an accompanying word), because the connection with the action—which constitutes the primary element—is more immediate (*antaraṅga*). Therefore, one says *namaskaroti devān* ("he pays homage to the gods"). How then are we to explain the forms cited by Bhaṭṭi: *namaścakāra devebhyaḥ* ("he paid homage to the gods") and *rāvaṇāya namaskṛtyāḥ* ("worthy of being saluted by Rāvaṇa")? On this point, Mādhava explains: since the word *namaḥ* is included among the words beginning with *sākṣāt* in the list of *gatis*, its status as a *gati* is optional. Thus, both the second and the fourth case endings are permissible.

In this regard, according to the view that [pra-] is a *gati* (a verbal prefix), it functions as an indicator (*dyotaka*) like other prefixes; thus, the meaning of *kṛñ* itself is "to honor" (*pramati*). Consequently, the second case is used for its object, as in the example *namasyati devān*. However, if it is not a *gati*, then [the prefix] expresses the act of bowing—which has become the object of the action of "doing" (*karoti*)—as the primary qualificand; therefore, since the gods are not the object [of the action of "doing"], the fourth case alone is used by the rule *namaḥ-svasti-svāhā-svadhā-alaṃ-vaṣaḍ-yogācca*.

In this regard, the following must be stated: even if the dative case is justified by the method already mentioned, the substitution of *s* (in *namas*) would not occur because *namas* lacks the designation of a *gati*. Consequently, the grammatical derivation of such usage remains unestablished. Therefore, the dative should be understood as being prescribed by the rule *kriyārthopapadasya ca* (Pāṇini 2.3.14), since the meaning is "to propitiate the gods. Vardhamāna, however, states that the dative occurs because the term "action" (*kriyā*) should be supplied [from the previous rule], just as in the example "he is bold for the sake of the *śrāddha*" (*śrāddhāya nigalbhate*). Examples: *prajābhyaḥ svasti* ("well-being to the subjects"); *agnaye svāhā* ("hail to Agni").

*svadhā* to the ancestors. *Alaṃ* for Malla against Malla. The inclusion of the sense of "sufficiency" (*paryāpti*) by the word *alam* is intended; therefore, [examples such as] "Hari is *alam*, the lord, the capable, the powerful, against the Daityas," and so forth, are included. If so, how is one to explain Māgha’s verse: "The Lord desiring to become the master of the three worlds"? It is said in reply: the rule regarding *alam* applies only to its sense of sufficiency, and not to its sense of prohibition—as in "Enough with weeping" (*alaṃ rodanena*)—according to another interpretation established in the Bhāṣya.

And thus, due to this difference in interpretation, the genitive case is also correct when used with words such as *prabhu* (lord/master). For this very reason, the author of the Sūtras has taught it in two ways: "He is a master over those [such as] *santāpa*, etc. (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 4.1.101) and "He is their leader" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 5.2.78). Accordingly, Bhaṭṭi says: "No one was able to strike him down, nor could anyone strike him. This is a form of the root *prothṛ* in the sense of "to be sufficient" (*bhvādigaṇa*, *ubhayapada*, No. 867).

In the expression *alaṃ rodanena* ("enough with weeping"), however, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used because it is understood that nothing is to be accomplished by means of weeping. *Vaṣaḍ indrāya*. The particle *ca* serves the purpose of re-enacting [the rule]; therefore, even when a blessing (*āśis*) is intended to be expressed, the fourth case (*caturthī*) occurs, overriding the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). For example: *svasti gobhyo bhūyāt* ("May there be well-being for the cows"). Otherwise, the scope for the fourth case in connection with *svasti* would be limited to cases such as *svasti jālmāyāsti* ("there is well-being for the wretch"). In the statement of a fact (*tattva-kathana*), the scope of the rule *āśiṣi ca* (Pāṇini 2.3.73) is restricted to words meaning "well-being" other than *svasti*. When both [the fourth and sixth cases] would apply simultaneously, the sixth case would optionally occur due to its subsequent position in the rules. (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.17).

Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.17: *manya-karmaṇyanādare vibhāṣā’prāṇiṣu*. When the verb *man* (to think) is used in the sense of disregard, provided the object is not a living being, the fourth case (*caturthī*) may optionally be employed for that object. Examples: *na tvāṃ tṛṇaṃ manye* (I do not consider you a blade of grass), or *tṛṇāya te* (I consider you a blade of grass). Why is the mention of *man* (the root *man*) necessary? [Consider: *na tvāṃ tṛṇaṃ cintayāmi* (I do not think of you as a blade of grass)—here the fourth case is not applied because the root is *cit*, not *man*. Furthermore, the rule specifies the form with the *śyan* affix (*manyate*). Why then would it not apply here: *na tvāṃ tṛṇaṃ manve* (I do not consider you a blade of grass)? This is because the root *man* belongs to the class beginning with *tan* (Dhātupāṭha 8.1), which takes the *u* affix (*manute*), and not the *śyan* affix. One should not ask why the mention of *man* is not simply *manoti*, for the governing rule *anabhihite* ("when not already expressed") is still in force. Thus, the sūtra applies only when the action is not otherwise expressed by another grammatical element.

For indeed, an unexpressed object (*anabhihitaṃ karma*) cannot exist when there is the connection with the suffix *yak*. Furthermore, the suffix *śyan* is merely an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of roots belonging to the *divādi* class, and is not itself intended to be expressed. Therefore:
"Even the joy of the Raghus, considering [him] as a mere blade of grass (*tṛṇāya matvā*), dispatched the Rākṣasa from the battle with an arrow."

Thus, Bhaṭṭi’s usage is consistent. Furthermore, "disrespect" (*anādara*) here does not mean merely the absence of respect, but rather contempt—what is meant by "censure" (*kutsā*). This is because the negative particle *nañ* expresses the opposite [of the following word], as in the case of *adharma* (non-dharma) or *anṛta* (untruth). And that [contempt] is twofold: first, by comparing a superior thing with an inferior one, as in *tṛṇāya matvā* ("regarding [him] as a blade of grass"); the meaning is "having regarded him as if he were a blade of grass. Second, in some cases, through connection with a negation, there is the cognition of the unsuitability of the comparison, as in *na tvāṃ tṛṇaṃ manye* ("I do not consider you a blade of grass"); the meaning is "I do not consider you even to be equal to a blade of grass."
However, this is the distinction: here there is absolute disregard, whereas in the former case there was merely a lack of regard; in both instances, it is established by the Sūtra.

The author of the Vārttika, however, says: "The mention of 'the contemptible' (*kutsita*) should be made as 'exceedingly' (*prakṛṣya*). The meaning is that if there is contempt even from that which is expressed by the word taking the fourth case, and not merely similarity, then the fourth case is employed. And thus, since the rule for the fourth case is prescribed only when there is contempt associated with a prohibition, the aforementioned usage of Bhartṛhari is contradicted according to the system of the Sūtra; however, it is consistent with the system of the Sūtra itself. Likewise, Āpiśali also formulated the rule: "In the sense of disregard toward the object of a verb meaning 'to think,' [the fourth case is used] optionally for the standard of comparison, provided it refers to living beings."

The *Bhāṣya* states that the word "aprāṇiṣu" (among non-living beings) should be removed and "anāvādiṣu" (among those other than dogs, etc. should be read instead. "Nau, kāka, śva, and śṛgāla" constitute the group beginning with "nau. However, in the example "na tvāṃ śune manye" ("I do not consider you a dog"), the dative case indeed occurs despite the referent being a living being; this is the general direction [of the analysis]. The term "anādare" (in disregard) is an adjective qualifying the "object" (*karman*). It means: "that object which indicates disregard. Consequently, the dative occurs only after words such as "tṛṇa" (grass), and not after the pronoun "yuṣmad" (you); or else, this is understood through the application of a restricted option (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). Thus ends the first Āhnika of the third Pāda of the second Adhyāya in the *Śrī-Śabdakaustubha*.
The second daily lesson in the third quarter.

(Pāṇini 2.3.18): *kartṛkaraṇayos tṛtīyā* (The third case ending is used for the agent and the instrument). Example: *rāmeṇa bāṇena hato vālī* (Vālin was killed by Rāma with an arrow). [Commentary: There is an extension of the rule to words such as *prakṛti* (inherently), etc. (Kātyāyana’s Vārttika): *prakṛtyādibhya upasaṅkhyānam*. Example: *prakṛtyābhirūpaḥ* (He is handsome by nature). Since no action (*kriyā*) is explicitly heard here, and since there is no [explicit] agent or instrument, the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would here be expected. [Objection: But surely it is established because the action of "making" (*karoti*) is understood, and thus [nature] functions as an instrument. For, in order to exclude other instruments, it is intended that nature alone (*prakṛti*) be the instrument. The meaning is: "This person is made handsome by his very nature (*svabhāvena*), and not by ornaments and the like."

Is it not the case that multiplicity is the instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the study denoted by the word "sacrificer" (*yājñika*)? For the meaning is that they study the sacrifice together in a group. Even in cases where, upon seeing someone in a particular dress, one generally concludes, "This person is a sacrificer," there too the status of being an instrument is established with respect to the act of cognition (*jñāna-kriyā*) which is understood [therein]. For the meaning is that this person is made known by people as "a sacrificer" through the multiplicity of his conduct and so forth.

However, some say that the word *prāyeṇa* is a particle (*nipāta*) resembling a case ending, used in the sense of "surely" (*nūnam*). And it is seen [used] thus: *prāyeṇa sāmagryavidhau guṇānām* ("Surely, the qualities are for the sake of producing a whole"), and *prāyeṇa niṣkrāmati cakrapāṇau* ("Surely, he goes out when Cakrapāṇi [Viṣṇu] departs"). [Objection: In that case, regarding *gotreṇa gārgyaḥ* ("Gārgya by lineage"), would not either the nominative or the genitive case be required? [Reply: But here too, it is established by the sense: "I am known by this. [Objection: Then consider *samena viṣameṇaiti* ("He goes by level and uneven ground"); here, the accusative case would be required after *sama-* and *viṣama-*.

[Objection: Since a path (*pathin*) is also an instrument (*karaṇa*) for going, let the meaning be "by an even path" (*samena pathā*). [Response: Then consider this: "He buys grain with two *droṇas* (*dvidroṇena dhānyam krīṇāti*); he takes animals for five [coins] (*pañcakena paśūn gṛhṇāti*). In the case of *dvidroṇa*, it is a compound denoting the collection of two *droṇas* (*dvayordroṇayoḥ samāhāraḥ*), such as a measure of liquid and so forth; the meaning is "having made two *droṇas*. Here, either the accusative or the genitive would be expected. In the case of *pañcaka*, it is a group (*saṅgha*) whose measure is five (*pañca-parimāṇam asya*). Therein, because one intends to express the non-difference between the group and its members (*saṅgha-saṅghinoḥ abheda-vivakṣāyām*), the accusative is expected due to its coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇyāt*) with the word "animals" (*paśūn*).

This too has been rejected in the Bhāṣya: since the price of two *droṇas* and so forth is used to purchase exactly those two *droṇas* and so forth, there is no difference in meaning either. (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.19)

*Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.19*: *sahayukte 'pradhāne*. When joined with a word having the sense of *saha* ("with"), the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) shall be used for the subordinate element (*apradhāna*). For example: *putreṇa sahāgataḥ pitā* ("The father has come with the son"). Here, the connection with the action is expressed directly (*śābda*) in the case of the father, whereas in the case of the son it is understood through implication (*ārtha*); thus, the son is subordinate. Although it would have been sufficient to say simply *sahe 'pradhāne*, the inclusion of the term *yukta* (joined) serves to include the sense of the word itself. Thus, even without the word *saha*, when its meaning is understood, the suffix still applies; as seen in the usage in the sūtra: *vṛddho yūnā* (Pāṇini 1.2.65).

The mention of "the principal" (*pradhāna*) could have been omitted. Nor does this result in the father also receiving the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*); for in that case, because it depends on the nominal stem alone (*prātipadika*), the first case (*prathamā*) is appropriate due to its being more internal (*antaraṅga*).
(Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.20)

"By that through which a bodily modification is indicated" (Pāṇini 2.3.20). The third case ending shall be used after that by which a modification of the body (*śarīra*) is characterized. In the sūtra, the word *aṅga* ends in the suffix *ac* derived from the *arśas*-group. And because of proximity, only the limb (*avayava*), which constitutes the base meaning and indicates its modification, is understood. Furthermore, that [limb] must necessarily be modified, for a modification of the body is not possible through an unmodified limb. With this in mind, it is stated in the commentary: "by which limb, being modified," and so forth. Example: *akṣṇā kāṇaḥ* ("blind in one eye"), *pādena khañjaḥ* ("lame in a foot").

A hand that is crooked is called *kuṇi*. When a sentence begins with a general term and the word *akṣṇā* is used, there arises an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), such as "Is he one-eyed? or "Does he describe him as such? In that context, the usage of *kāmaḥ* and so forth is not contradictory. Although it is the eye itself that is one-eyed, nevertheless, through association with it, the designation is firmly established for the body as well. This is an exception to the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī-apavāda*). The meaning is: "one who possesses one-eyedness related to the eye" (Pāṇini 2.3.20). Regarding the rule *itthambhūtalakṣaṇe* (Pāṇini 2.3.21): when something has attained a certain state (*itthambhūta*), the third case ending shall be used to denote the characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*) of that state. Example: *jaṭābhis tāpasaḥ* ("an ascetic by his matted hair"). This means: "one who possesses the state of being an ascetic as indicated by his matted hair."

(Pāṇini 2.3.22): *saṃjño 'nyatarasyāṃ karmaṇi*. An optional third case ending may be used for the object of the verb *jñā* preceded by *sam*. One recognizes [his father] as his father (*pitṛā* or *pitaram sañjānīte*). The *taṅ* (ātmanepada) affix is applied here by Pāṇini 1.3.46: *sampratibhyām ānādhyāne*. However, when used with a *kṛt* suffix, the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) applies because it is of subsequent rule. Thus: *pituḥ sañjñātā*. As for what Haradatta stated—that in the sense of "recollection" (*ādhyāna*), the sixth case ending is applied by Pāṇini 2.3.52 (*adhīgartha...*) because it is of subsequent rule, as in *mātuḥ sañjānāti*—that is not correct, because in that context [of 2.3.52], the governing heading is *śeṣa* (the remainder).

This is because, when there is an intention to express the object (*karmatva*), the use of either the third or the second case must necessarily be accepted; furthermore, it is improper to apply the rule of "prohibition by conflict" (*vipratiṣedha*) between two rules that have different scopes. This is the general direction [of the argument]. (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.23)

[In the rule] *hetau* (Pāṇini 2.3.23): the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) shall occur when there is the sense of a cause (*hetu*). Examples: *dhanena kulam* ("a family [is distinguished] by wealth"); *vidyayā yaśaḥ* ("fame [is gained] by learning"). Here, "cause" refers to a worldly cause that serves as a means to an effect (*phalasādhanībhūta*), and not the technical "cause" (*hetu*) defined as that which prompts an action (*tatprayojaka*). For, since the designation "agent" (*kartṛ*) is prescribed for that [worldly cause] by the word *ca* [in Pāṇini 1.4.55], the third case would already be established by the rule *kartṛkaraṇayos tṛtīyā* (Pāṇini 2.3.18). Furthermore, even for a worldly cause, it is common to be devoid of activity (*nirvyāpāra*). However, an instrument (*karaṇa*) pertains exclusively to an action and is necessarily characterized by activity. As it has been said: "A cause has substances and so forth as its object; a factor of action (*kāraka*) has a restricted action."
And it is said: "When an operation [of the agent] is not dependent [on another], the cause is called the *nimitta*.

Likewise, here the word "cause" (*hetu*) also includes the result (*phala*). This is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the rule *pratyayaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.1), as well as on [the rule] *adhyayanena vasati* (Pāṇini 2.3.24).

*Akartary ṛṇe pañcamī* (Pāṇini 2.3.24). When a debt (*ṛṇa*) other than the agent is the cause, the fifth case ending (*pañcamī*) shall be used after it. This is an exception to the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*). Example: *śatād baddhaḥ* ("bound because of a hundred [debt]"). Why say "other than the agent"? Observe: *śatena bandhitaḥ* ("caused to be bound by a hundred"). Here, the hundred is a debt because it is being held as a loan to be repaid; furthermore, by the word "and" (*ca*) in the rule, it is also designated as the "agent" (*kartṛ*) when it functions as the prompter (*prayojaka*). Objection: It was stated in the previous rule that the term "cause" (*hetu*) refers to a worldly cause. But this [debt] is a technical (*śāstrīya*) cause. Response: True, yet even a technical cause possesses a worldly character.

For that which is pervasive in common usage is not contradictory; or rather, let there be the inclusion of "general" (*sāmānya*) even in the previous rule by virtue of its meaning here. (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.25)

*Vibhāṣā guṇe 'striyām* (Pāṇini 2.3.25). When the cause is a quality (*guṇa*) that is not feminine, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) may optionally be used. For example: *jāḍyāj jāḍyena vā baddhaḥ* ("bound because of dullness"), *pāṇḍityāt pāṇḍityena vā muktaḥ* ("released because of wisdom"). Why "when it is a quality"? [Observe: *dhanena kulam* ("the family [is distinguished] by wealth"). Why "not feminine"? [Observe: *buddhyā muktaḥ* ("released by means of intelligence"). Here, the term "quality" (*guṇa*) is understood as defined by the rule: "that which enters into a substance (*sattva*) and departs from it. This is because the examples and counter-examples conform to that definition. In this context, the rule *vibhāṣā* is divided [into separate applications].

Therefore, [the ablative] occurs even when there is no quality (*guṇa*), and likewise in the case of a woman (*strī*). This is clear in the commentary of Haradatta on the rule *manuṣyebhyo hitamanuṣyebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.3.81). Some, however, say that here the word *guṇa* refers merely to that which is dependent (*paratantra*), as in the expression "due to the state of being twofold" (*dviguṇasya bhāvāt*). They claim that by this, the ablative is established even in cases such as "there is fire because of smoke" (*vahnimān dhūmāt*). But how then is it that one says, "There is no jar here because of non-perception" (*nāstīha ghaṭo'nupalabdheḥ*)?

Regarding this, they say: [the suffix *ṅīp*] occurs even for feminine stems in certain cases due to the rule-split (*yogavibhāga*) "optionally when a quality is expressed" (*vibhāṣā guṇe*). Furthermore, the usage in the Vārttika—"on account of the diversity of verbal roots, because the nature of the base is rarely observed"—serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) here. (Pāṇini 4.1.44). (Pāṇini 2.3.26) *ṣaṣṭhī hetuprayoge*: When a cause is indicated, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) shall be used. Example: *annasya hetor vasati* ("He dwells for the sake of food"). (Pāṇini 2.3.27).

*Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.27*: "And the third case ending [is used] after a pronoun. When a pronoun and the word *hetu* (cause/reason) are employed to indicate the cause, the third case ending shall be used, as well as the sixth. For example: *kena hetunā vasati* (for what reason does he dwell?), *kasya hetoḥ*. According to the *Kāśikāvṛtti*: "In the case of *nimitta*, *kāraṇa*, and *hetu*, all case endings are generally observed. For example: *kiṃnimittaṃ vasati* (for what purpose does he dwell?), *kena nimittena*, *kasmai nimittāya*, and so forth. Likewise: *kiṃ kāraṇam*, *ko hetuḥ*, *kiṃ prayojanam*, and so forth.

This [rule] applies even to words that are not pronouns (*asarvanāman*), because the author of the *Vṛtti* included it in this very reading, whereas the author of the *Bhāṣya* read it under the rule *hetau* (Pāṇini 2.3.23). Due to the inclusion of the term *prāyas* ("mostly"), the first and second case endings do not occur after non-pronouns. For example: *annena kāraṇena vasati* ("He dwells for the sake of food") and *annāya kāraṇāya* ("for the sake of food"), and so forth. The mention of synonyms in the *Vārttika* is for the sake of elaboration, since the status of denoting the meaning is accepted in accordance with words such as *prayojana* ("purpose") and others.
(Pāṇini 2.3.28)

"The fifth case ending is used for the ablative (apādāna)" (Pāṇini 2.3.28). This is clear. Example: *grāmād āgacchati* ("He comes from the village"). There is a supplementary rule (*kārikā-vākya*): "When a verbal root ending in *lyap* is elided, the [fifth case] is also used for the object and the locus. Example: *prāsādāt prekṣate* ("He looks out from the palace") and *āsanāt prekṣate* ("He looks out from the seat"). The meaning is: having ascended the palace and having sat down on the seat, he looks out. Even a verb that is merely implied can serve as the cause for a case-ending of a kāraka, as in the expression *praviśa piṇḍīm* ("Enter; [eat] the cake"). By this principle, forms such as *kutobhavān, pāṭaliputrāt* ("From where do you come? From Pāṭaliputra") are established.

For here, the question and answer proceed precisely regarding the path (*adhvan*), depending upon the traditional authority (*āgama*) established by perception and other means of valid cognition. By this, the Vārttika stating "and in the case of questioning and explaining" is refuted, because the required action is already established as being of the nature of giving (*dāna*). Otherwise, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as "What is the moon? and so forth. And since the measurement of distance and time occurs therein, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is used. (Kāśikā-vṛtti) From a path connected with that [measurement], the first and seventh cases (*prathamā-saptamī*) are used. (Kāśikā-vṛtti) And it should be stated that from time, the seventh case is used. (Kāśikā-vṛtti)

The village is a *yojana* or two *yojanas* from the forest. From the full moon of *Kārttika* to the full moon of *Āgrahāyaṇī* is one month. The full moon joined with the *kṛttikā* [nakṣatra] is the *kārttikī*. The elision (*luṅ*) prescribed by the rule *lubaviśeṣe* (Pāṇini 4.2.4) does not apply to the word *paurṇamāsī*, because of the specific mention in the rule *vibhāṣā phālgunī-śravaṇā-kārttikī-caitrībhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.23), which occurs under the governing heading *sāsmin paurṇamāsī* (Pāṇini 4.2.21). That in which the year (*hāyana*) begins is the *āgrahāyaṇī*.

Since *prajñā* and others belong to the *ākṛtigaṇa* class, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in its own sense (*svārthika*). The change to *ṇ* [in *mārgaśīrṣa*] occurs by virtue of the specific rule (*nipātana*) for *āgrahāyaṇī*, *aśvattha*, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "from that which is connected" (*tadyuktāt*): it means from words such as *māsa* (month) and the like, which denote time and are connected—by way of their meaning—with a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamyanta*). Regarding this, Kaiyaṭa states in his commentary on the *Mahābhāṣya* that because the usage *kārttikyāḥ prabhṛti* ("starting from the full moon of Kārttika") is seen, the fifth case is used in connection with *prabhṛti*. Kaiyaṭa further explains that *prabhṛti* is taken here in its general sense; thus, the meaning is "beginning from that. Kumāra says: "Starting precisely from the shoulder, they are covered in foliage. (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.29).

*Anyārāditarartedikśabdāñcūttarapadājāhiyukte* (Pāṇini 2.3.29). When used in conjunction with these, the fifth case (*pañcamī*) shall be employed. In this rule, *anya* is taken as representing the general sense [of "other"]; however, the inclusion of *itara* is for the sake of elaboration. It should not be argued that this refers to the word *itara* in its sense of "inferior," based on Amarasimha’s statement, *itarastvanyanīcayoḥ* (Amarakośa 3.3.200), because such usage is already established by the rule *pañcamīvibhakte* (Pāṇini 2.3.42), as seen in examples such as *asmāttāro mando vā*.

[The phrase] "different from Devadatta," "distinct," "of a different character," or "a separate entity," and so forth—nor should it be argued that this leads to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in the case of "the jar is not a cloth," because the negative particle (*nañ*) also has the meaning of mutual exclusion (*anyonyābhāva*), and thus, in accordance with expressions such as "difference from the jar," there would be no intention to include the substratum (*dharmin*) within the scope [of the negation]. This is because it has already been stated that the negative particle functions as a mere indicator (*dyotaka*). [In the example] *ārād devadattāt* ("far from Devadatta"), the rule *dūrāntikārthaiḥ ṣaṣṭhyanyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 2.3.34) applies.

Regarding the rule *ārād dūrasamīpayoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.25), it was stated previously that when used with *ṛte*, the second case (*dvitīyā*) is also optionally employed—as in *ṛte kṛśānoḥ na hi mantrapūtam*. A "directional word" (*dikśabda*) is a word observed to denote a direction; by this, [the application of the ablative] occurs even in connection with words currently denoting space or time. For example: *grāmāt pūrvo deśaḥ* ("the region east of the village") and *caitrāt pūrvaḥ phālgunaḥ* ("the month of Phālguna preceding Caitra"). How then is one to explain *pūrvaṃ kāyasya* ("the front part of the body")? It is said in reply: [the ablative] does not occur in connection with words expressing parts of a whole, because of the grammatical indication in the rule *tasya paramāmreḍitam* (Pāṇini 8.1.2).

Although the word *añc* (ending in *-añc*) has the nature of a directional term (*dikśabda*), it is mentioned separately in order to override the rule "with a word ending in a suffix having the sense of *atas* [and others], the sixth case is used" (Pāṇini 2.3.30). Examples: *prāk* or *pratyaṅ* *grāmāt* ("to the east" or "to the west of the village"). One might ask: why is this not intended for the sense of the ablative case in examples such as *tena sahardaṅ*? It should not be so stated, because by association with other directional terms (*dikśabda*), only words like *prāk* and the rest are understood here. Examples with *āc*: *dakṣiṇā* or *uttarā* *grāmāt* ("south" or "north of the village"). Examples with *āhi*: *dakṣiṇāhi* or *uttarāhi* *grāmāt*. The suffixes *āc* and *āhi* are applied by the rules "after *dakṣiṇa*, the suffix *āc*" (Pāṇini 5.3.36), "also *āhi* when far away" (Pāṇini 5.3.37), and "also after *uttara*" (Pāṇini 5.3.38).

(Pāṇini 2.3.30): *enapā dvitīyā*. In connection with a word ending in the suffix *enap*, the second case (*dvitīyā*) shall be used. The sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is also desired; however, that [usage] is to be established by dividing the rule *enapā* into two separate rules. For example: *dakṣiṇena grāmaṃ* or *grāmasya*. Likewise for *uttareṇa*. The suffix *enap* is applied by the rule *enabanyatarasyāmadūre pañcamyāḥ* (Pāṇini 5.3.35). How then [is it explained] in the following verse: "There, our house is to the north of the house of the Lord of Wealth (*dhanapati*)"? [This is explained as follows: The word *uttareṇa* here is derived from the root *ṛ* ("to go") with the suffix *kha*, which is added after the word *uttara* when it signifies direction (*diś*), provided that the sense is not "near" (*adūra*). Thus, it means "that which goes in the northern direction. Alternatively, it may be understood as a Bahuvrīhi compound meaning "that whose northern part is near," or as a Tatpuruṣa compound meaning "that which has a northern part. In this way, the sixth case is established by the rule *enapā*. However, if one does not accept the division of the rule, then the sixth case is established by the rule *ṣaṣṭhyatasarthapratyayena* (Pāṇini 2.3.30), because the suffix *enap* is included among the suffixes having the sense of *atas* (such as *uttareṇa*). The second case is also established by the rule *enapā*. Therefore, both cases are valid. As for the usage *uttareṇa gṛham*, it is explained as being formed by adding the suffix *kha* to the word *uttara* when it denotes direction, provided the sense is not "near. This is because the word *uttara* is included in the group of words beginning with *prāk* (the *prāgdiś* group). Thus, the suffix *kha* is applied, and the feminine form *enap* is derived from it. Consequently, the sixth case is established by the rule *enapā*, while the second case is established by the rule *enapā dvitīyā*. Therefore, both forms are correct. Furthermore, in the phrase *uttareṇa gṛham*, the word *gṛha* is understood to mean "the vicinity of the house" (*gṛhasamīpa*). Since the sense of proximity is present, the suffix *kha* is not applied, and thus the sixth case is established by the rule *ṣaṣṭhyatasarthapratyayena*. Alternatively, it may be explained that the word *uttareṇa* is formed by adding the suffix *kha* to the word *uttara* when it denotes direction, provided the sense is not "near"; and since the word *gṛha* is understood to mean "the vicinity of the house," the sixth case is established by the rule *enapā*. In this way, the usage is justified in both ways. As for the verse: "The house of the Lord of Wealth is to the north of the house of the King of Mountains (*śailarāja*)," the same logic applies: the sixth case is established by the rule *enapā*, while the second case is established by the rule *enapā dvitīyā*. Therefore, both forms are valid. As for the verse: "The house of the Lord of Wealth is to the north of the house of the King of Mountains," the same logic applies: the sixth case is established by the rule *enapā*, while the second case is established by the rule *enapā dvitīyā*. Therefore, both forms are valid. Therefore, both forms are valid. "Because of the governing rule for feminine nouns (*stryadhikāra*), the rule regarding optional forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*) does not necessarily apply here," and so forth. Even the suffix *enap* is optional after the word *para*, when the rule *taddhita* [Pāṇini 5.3.34] "uttarādharadakṣiṇāt" is not being followed. This is true; for this very reason, Haradatta states that this point is indeed subject to deliberation. Others hold that *uttareṇa* is in the singular instrumental case and is in apposition with *toraṇena*. Still others, however, read *dhanapatigṛhān* as ending in the accusative plural (*śas*). (Pāṇini 2.3.32)

*Pṛthag-vinā-nānābhis-tṛtīyā-anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 2.3.32). The inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* is for the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaya*), since particles have multiple meanings. By the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*) principle, the word *pañcamī* (the fifth case) is carried over. When used in conjunction with these [words], both the third and fifth cases occur. However, the author of the *Vṛtti* says: "By means of a word-split (*yogavibhāga*) in the rule *pṛthag-vinā-nānābhiḥ*, the second case is also desired. Examples: *pṛthak grāmeṇa* or *pṛthak rāmāt*; likewise *vinā* and *nānā*. Amarasimha states: "*Hiruk* and *nānā* are used in the sense of exclusion (*varjana*). An example of usage is: "*Nānā nārīr niṣphalā lokayātrā*" ("The course of worldly life without women is fruitless"). (Pāṇini 2.3.33)

And in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*), the third and fifth case endings are used after the words *stoka*, *alpa*, *kṛcchra*, and *katipaya* when they do not denote a substance (*asattvavacanasya*). The third and fifth cases occur after these words when they do not refer to a substance in the sense of the instrument. Examples: *stokena* or *stokāt muktaḥ* ("released with little effort"). Why "when not denoting a substance"? [Answer: *stokena viṣeṇa hataḥ* ("killed by a small amount of poison"). (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.33–34)

Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.34: *dūrāntikāryaiḥ ṣaṣṭhyanyatarasyām*. In connection with these [words], the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) shall optionally be used, as well as the fifth case (*pañcamī*). It has been stated that the fifth case is also included by the rule *pṛthagvinā* (Pāṇini 2.3.32); since this [present sūtra] belongs to the same section, it should be understood in the same way. Examples: *dūraṃ antikaṃ vā grāmasya* or *grāmāt*. Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.35.

Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.35: *dūrāntikārthebhyo dvitīyā ca*. From words meaning "far" (*dūra*) or "near" (*antika*), the second case (*dvitīyā*) shall be used; by the word *ca* ("and"), the fifth (*pañcamī*) and third (*tṛtīyā*) cases are also included. This rule applies to the primary meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). Examples: *grāmasya dūram*, *dūrāt*, or *dūreṇa*; *antikam*, *antikāt*, or *antikeṇa*. Since this [sūtra] is carried forward into subsequent rules, the second case and others may also occur in those respective contexts. Thus, it is also employed in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*): *dūrād āvasathān mūtram* ("urination far from the dwelling"). The meaning is "far from the dwelling. The term *asattvavacana* ("denoting a non-substance") is understood to carry over [from the previous sūtra].

Therefore, in this case [the following forms are used]: *na-dūraḥ panthāḥ* ("not far from the path"), *dūrāya pathe dehi* ("give for the distant path"), and *dūrasya pathaḥ svam* ("the property of the distant path"). (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.36)

Pāṇini 2.3.36 states: *saptamy adhikaraṇe ca* ("The seventh [case-ending] is used for the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), and..."). Because of the word "and" (*ca*) in the rule, it is also used after words meaning "far" (*dūra*) or "near" (*antika*). For example: *kaṭe āste* ("He sits on a mat"). Regarding the words meaning "far" and "near," the first three case-endings have already been mentioned; by this [rule], the seventh case is added, so that four case-endings result from them. The Vārttika states: *ktasyenviṣayasya karmaṇy upasaṃkhyānam* ("An addition should be made [to the rule] regarding the object of a word ending in *kta* when it has *in* as its scope"). Here, *in* refers to a word ending in the suffix *in*. "Scope" (*viṣaya*) means the ground of occurrence for that which ends in *kta*. The meaning is: [the seventh case is used] for the object of such a word. Example: *adhītī vyākaraṇe* ("One who has studied grammar"). The analytical explanation (*vigraha*) is: "by whom grammar has been studied" (*adhītam anena*).

Following the rule *śrāddhamanena bhuktam* (Pāṇini 5.2.85), which includes the word *anena*, the suffix *ini* is applied by the rule *iṣṭādibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 5.2.88) to denote the agent (*kartṛ*). Consequently, since the word *vyākaraṇa* (grammar), having attained a unified meaning with the taddhita-suffix meaning, cannot be extracted and related [to the action] through the accusative case, the suffix *kta* has not already expressed the agent. Therefore, as in the example *kṛtapūrvī kaṭam* ("one who has previously made a mat"), the second case ending would be expected [for *vyākaraṇam*].

For even when the act of studying is subordinate (guṇabhūtā), its connection with the object (karman) is not contradictory, as in the case of expressions such as "he studied grammar together [with someone]. And it has been said:

"Just as an action that is itself without a physical form, yet residing in states such as 'gone,' is connected with objects such as a village, so too is it connected in cases such as 'one who has previously done' (kṛtapūrvī)."

That which has no separate apprehension (*avigrahā*) is one whose [object] is not grasped separately; the meaning is that it is subordinate (*guṇībhūta*). Now, an objection might be raised: would the locative case (*saptamī*) not also apply to the object denoting time, as in examples such as *māsam adhītī vyākaraṇe* ("he has studied grammar for a month")? It is not so, because that [time-denoting object] is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*). Nor should it be said that, in this way, the accusative case (*dvitīyā*) would also not occur there; for in the formulation of that rule, the view of individual instances (*vyaktipakṣa*) is adopted in accordance with the observed usage (*lakṣya*). And in the employment of the words *sādhu* and *asādhu*: *sādhuḥ kṛṣṇo mātari* ("Kṛṣṇa is well-behaved toward his mother"); *asādhur mātule* ("he is ill-behaved toward his maternal uncle").

In this context, although correctness (*sādhutva*) and incorrectness (*asādhutva*) concern objects such as one's mother and so forth, the statement [of the rule] is made because, due to the absence of an action (*kriyā*), there is no status as a locus (*adhikaraṇatva*). Since the result would be established by the rule *sādhunipuṇābhyām* (Pāṇini 2.3.43) alone, the inclusion of the word *sādhu* here is for the sake of excluding cases of mere respect (*arcā*). Therefore, it applies even when stating the truth. However, the inclusion of the word *arcā* in that [previous] rule is for the sake of *nipuṇa*. It should be noted that the inclusion of *sādhu* there was omitted from the sūtra after observing the Vārttika.

[The rule] *kārikā* [states]: "When those who are worthy act, and those who are unworthy do not act, and when this is reversed... [as in the examples] "While the fathers-in-law were crossing, the mothers-in-law remained sitting," and so forth. Although this is already established by the rule *yasya ca bhāvena* (Pāṇini 2.3.37), they say that this statement is made so that [the locative case] may occur even when there is no intention to express the relationship between the indicator (*lakṣya*) and the indicated (*lakṣaṇa*). [The rule] *nimittāt karmayoge* [states]: "After a word denoting a cause (*nimitta*), the seventh case ending occurs if there is a connection with an object (*karman*), provided that connection is a specific type of relation consisting of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*). Here, "cause" (*nimitta*) means "result" (*phala*). The seventh case ending shall be used for a word expressing that [result], if it has a connection with an object—that is, a specific connection characterized by conjunction or inherence.
One kills the leopard for its skin; one kills the elephant for its tusks;
one kills the yak for its hair; and the musk deer is killed for its scent-gland at the base of its tail.

The "hide-slab" (*carmaphalaka*) is made of leopard skin; the meaning is that it is used for striking. In this context, the instrumental case is obtained in the sense of a cause (*hetu*), for there the result is also understood by the word "cause. This was established in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the rule *Pāṇini Sūtra* 3.2.1, *pratyayaḥ*, in order to justify examples such as "he dwells for the sake of study" (*adhyayanena vasati*). Here, the relationship between the leopard skin and the slab is one of inherence (*samavāya*). The feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied to the word *camara* according to the rule for denoting a genus (*jāti*). A *puṣkalaka* is a stake. It was "struck down" (*nihata*)—meaning driven in or buried—along with its boundary-mark, for the purpose of identifying the boundary.

Haradatta and others maintain that the connection (*saṃyoga*) is the contact with the boundary (*sīmā*) by means of the peg (*śaṅku*) being driven in. However, in the *Durgavākyaprabodha*, Kulacandra says: "The boundary (*sīmā*) is the egg-casing (*aṇḍakośa*); the *puṣkalaka* is the musk-deer (*gandhamṛga*). And it is stated in the *Medinīkośa*: "The word *sīmā* is feminine when it refers to a boundary, a place, a field, or an egg-casing.
Furthermore: "And *puṣkalaka* [is used] for the musk-deer, a mendicant, and a wooden pin."
What is the application of *karmayoga*? He reaps grain for wages (*vetana*). (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.37).

And [the rule] "when there is a characterization of one action by another action" (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.37): the locative case shall be used for that whose action characterizes another action. An action whose time is already known is called a "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) because it delimits the time of an action whose time is not yet known. For example: "He departed while the cows were being milked. Likewise, even when it is a quality (*guṇa*), it may serve as a delimiter of space, as in: "There is substantiality (*dravyatva*) in the quality."

(Pāṇini 2.3.38) *ṣaṣṭhī cānādare* (Pāṇini 2.3.38). When there is an excess of disregard (*anādara*) as a characteristic of an action (*bhāva-lakṣaṇa*), both the genitive and locative cases are used. In this sūtra, the word "in disregard" (*anādare*) is a locative absolute with the preceding [sūtra]. It means: when there is disregard, that which characterizes the action. Thus, the predominance of disregard is established as the result. Example: *rudati rudato vā prāvrajīt*. The meaning is: having disregarded his weeping son or others, he renounced the world (*sannyasta*). (Pāṇini 2.3.39)

[The rule] *svāmīśvarādhipatidāyādasākṣipratibhūprasūtaiśca* (Pāṇini 2.3.39): when these seven [words] are joined [with a word], the sixth (genitive) and seventh (locative) case endings occur. Since the sixth case ending alone was already applicable, this statement is for the purpose of optionally allowing the seventh case. For example: *gavāṃ svāmī* or *goṣu svāmī*, *gavām īśvaraḥ* or *goṣu īśvaraḥ*, and so forth. One who takes an inheritance (*dāya*) is called a *dāyāda*; by virtue of this very exception (*nipātana*), the suffix *ka* is applied even after a root with a prefix (*upasarga*).

Although the word *gavām* is an adjective qualifying the whole [compound], nevertheless, by the etymological derivation *dīyate iti dāyaḥ* ("that which is given is a gift"), it touches upon the "portion" (*aṃśa*) which constitutes the meaning of the individual member. Consequently, the resulting sense is: "one who has not taken a portion consisting of cows. The phrase *gavāṃ prasūtaḥ* means "born to experience cows alone.
(Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.40)

Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.40: *āyuktakuśalābhyāṃ cāsevāyām*. When used in conjunction with these two words, the sixth and seventh case endings are employed provided that "practice" (*āsevā*) is understood. "Practice" means devoted application (*tātparya*). *Āyukta* means engaged; *kuśala* means skillful. [Examples: *āyuktaḥ kuśalo vā haribhajanasya* or *haribhajane* ("devoted or skilled in the worship of Hari"). Why "provided that practice is understood"? [Counter-example: *āyukto gauḥ śakaṭe*, meaning "the ox is slightly yoked to the cart. (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.41)

"And from that which there is selection" (Pāṇini 2.3.41). Selection (*nirddhāraṇa*) is the separation of one part from a whole by means of genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), or name (*sañjñā*). Where there is selection, the sixth and seventh case endings occur. Examples: *nṛṇāṃ* or *nṛṣu brāhmaṇaḥ śreṣṭhaḥ* ("among men, the Brāhmaṇa is the best"); *gavāṃ* or *goṣu kṛṣṇā bahukṣīrā* ("among cows, the black one yields much milk"); *gacchatāṃ* or *gacchatsu dhāvan śīghraḥ* ("among those who are walking, the running one is fast"); *amīṣāṃ chātrāṇāṃ devadattaḥ paṭuḥ* ("among these students, Devadatta is clever"). (Pāṇini 2.3.42)

"The fifth case ending [is used] in the sense of separation" (Pāṇini 2.3.42). "Separation" means being distinguished. Where there is a distinction of that which is being singled out (*nirdhāryamāṇa*), and not merely its being subsumed under a common form expressed by the word, there the fifth case ending shall occur based on that which is the locus of the distinction. For example: *māthurāḥ pāṭaliputrakebhya āḍhyatarāḥ* ("The people of Mathurā are wealthier than those of Pāṭaliputra"). For here, as in examples such as *gavāṃ kṛṣṇāḥ* ("the black among cows"), there is no relation of genus and species; rather, there is simply a contradiction between the two properties expressed by the words. And this rule has been rejected in the section on the ablative (*apādāna*) by relying on a separation conceived through the intellect (*buddhi*). As it is said:
"When a speaker, having first conceived the identity [of the Pañcālas] with the Kurus through the intellect,
subsequently divides them again, then a separation (*apāya*) is perceived. (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.43)

*Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.43*: "With *sādhu* and *nipuṇa*, when used in the sense of 'reverence' (*arcā*), the seventh case ending is employed, provided that *prati* is not used. When these two [words] are joined with a word signifying reverence, the seventh case is used, but not when *prati* is employed. For example: *mātari sādhuḥ* or *nipuṇaḥ*. The word *nipuṇa* is derived from the root *puṇ* (meaning "to be auspicious") with the prefix *ni*; the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule for roots having a light penultimate vowel (*igupadhāt*).
