The word *arcā* is derived from the root *arca* (meaning "to worship") belonging to the *bhvādi* class; the suffix *ap* is applied according to the rule *gurośca halaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.103).

However, after roots such as *caur* [in the sense of stealing], the suffix *yuc* would apply by Pāṇini 3.3.107 (*ṇyāsaśranthayuc*). Why [is it said] "in the sense of worship" (*arcāyām*)? [Consider: "The king’s servant is skillful" (*nipuṇo rājño bhṛtyaḥ*). Here, the intention is to state a fact (*tattvakathane*). But when the word *sādhu* is employed, the locative case indeed occurs even when there is no worship; this is because it has already been stated that [the locative applies] "in the employment of *sādhu* and *asādhu*" according to the Vārttika. It should be stated [as a restriction]: "not with *prati* and so on" (Vārttika). Therefore, it does not occur here: "He is skillful or clever toward his mother" (*sādhurnipuṇo vā mātaram prati pary anu vā*). (Pāṇini 2.3.44)

Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.44: *prasitotsukābhyāṃ tṛtīyā ca*. In connection with these two words, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) shall be used, and optionally the seventh case (*saptamī*). For example: *prasitaḥ* or *utsukaḥ* *hariṇā* or *harau*. According to Amarasimha’s lexicon, "one who is intent (*tatpara*) is *prasita* and *āsakta*. Because of its association with *utsuka*, *prasita* here is understood only in the sense of being "intent" (*tatpara*), and not in the sense of "whitened" (*śukla*) by being thoroughly bound (*prakarṣeṇa sitaḥ*). Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.45.

And [the third and seventh case endings occur] when a *nakṣatra* (lunar mansion) is the base meaning (*prakṛtyartha*), provided that the suffix which has been elided by the technical term *lup* expresses that same meaning. When expressing the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), the third and seventh case endings occur after a word denoting a *nakṣatra*. For example:

*mūlenāvāhayed devīm* (one should invoke the Goddess under the asterism Mūla), or *śravaṇena visarjayet* (one should dismiss her under Śravaṇa); or alternatively, *mūle* and *śravaṇe*. [In these cases, the suffix] *aṇ* [is applied] by the rule *nakṣatreṇa yuktaḥ kālaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.3), and it is then elided by the rule *lub aviśeṣe* (Pāṇini 4.2.4). Why specify "in the sense of a locus"? Consider: *puṣyaḥ* (the asterism Puṣya); *puṣyam pratīkṣate* (he awaits Puṣya); *puṣyāya spṛhayati* (he longs for Puṣya). In these instances, the first case ending is used because the asterism itself is the object of expectation or desire, not a locus.

Regarding this, some have explained that the two locative endings [in the sūtra] are used in the sense of the ablative (*pañcamyarthe saptamyau*), meaning "from a nakṣatra-denoting word that has undergone *lup*. According to them, [the rule] would not apply because of the qualification "having undergone *lup*" (*lubantaviśeṣaṇāt*). As Haradatta says: "One should not go by means of the two *Uttara-phālgunīs*," as in the example.
Thus ends the second Āhnika of the third Pāda of the second Adhyāya in the illustrious *Śabdakaustubha*.
The third lesson in the third chapter.

(Pāṇini 2.3.46): *The first case ending occurs when there is merely the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), gender, measure, or number.* The first case ending (*prathamā*) shall occur when there is merely the meaning of the nominal stem, as well as in the cases of mere gender and so forth. Because the word *mātra* is heard at the end of the *dvandva* compound, it is connected with each member individually. Furthermore, it has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). Amara states: "*Mātra* [is used] in the sense of entirety or restriction" (Amarakośa 3.3.186). The analysis of the compound is not within its own constituent words (*asvapadavigraha*): "merely those [things], namely the meaning of the nominal stem and the rest. This is a compound according to Pāṇini 2.1.72: "*Mayūravyaṃsaka* and others."
The meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadika) is existence (sattā). For it has been said: "All words are established in that [existence].
And: "They declare that to be both the meaning of the nominal stem and the meaning of the verbal root."

*Uccaiḥ* (high), *nīcaiḥ* (low). For here, they say, only pure existence (*sattāmātra*) qualified by a particular measure is perceived. Others, however, say that the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) is that which has a fixed presentation. On this view, for words with fixed genders such as *vṛkṣaḥ*, *kuḍyam*, and *bhittiḥ*, the use of the nominative case is established simply by the rule "the nominative is used in the mere sense of the nominal stem. But the phrase "in the mere sense of gender" (*liṅgamātre*) is intended for cases like *taṭaḥ*, *taṭī*, and *taṭam*, because here masculinity and so forth do not have a fixed presentation.

Therefore, it is prescribed even when there is an excess of gender alone. In the case of measure alone: *droṇo vrīhiḥ* ("a *droṇa* measure of rice"). For here the meaning is that the rice is delimited by that measure characterized as a *droṇa*. It should be understood that the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*), the *droṇa*, functions as a qualifier through the relation of identity with the suffix-meaning (*pratyayārtha*), which is the measure; and the suffix-meaning [functions as a qualifier] with respect to the rice through the relation of the delimited and the delimiting. In the case of number alone: *ekaḥ*, *dvau*, *bahavaḥ*.

The word *vacana* (number) likewise [refers to gender] due to the usage of the Easterners (*prācām*). In this context, although number is already expressed by the base (*prakṛti*), this statement is made so that [the rule] may apply even when it is [already] expressed. In this sūtra, only "the first case [is used] for meaning and gender" would have been necessary; the rest, however, is redundant. To explain: the mention of *prātipadika* (nominal stem) is first of all superfluous. For suffixes beginning with *su* (*svādayaḥ*) are prescribed after a *ṅy-āp-prātipadika*. In that regard, when there is an expectation for the word "in the meaning" (*arthe*), it is already understood that the meaning belongs to that from which the suffix is prescribed.

Furthermore, specifying a measure is also purposeless; for, just as in cases such as "the Vāhīka is an ox," since the nominative case endings are applicable to the primary meaning alone, the perception of a secondary meaning can be established through the co-occurrence with another word, because an imposition (āropa) of "one droṇa" and so forth upon rice and the like is possible, just as the imposition of "ox-ness" upon a Vāhīka is possible.

Likewise, the inclusion of the word *vacana* (number) is also redundant; for since it is established by the rules "the suffix alone should not be used" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 1.2.64) and "the suffix comes after [the base]" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 3.1.1), as well as "and it is subsequent" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 3.1.2), the suffix is necessarily required. Furthermore, because the use of a non-referential expression is inadmissible, it is only logical that the usage of a reiterative expression (*anuvādaka*) should be employed. Moreover, the inclusion of the word *mātra* (only) is also redundant; for by the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule "and in the vocative" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 2.3.47), the nominative case does not apply when there is an addition of the object (*karman*) and other kārakas.

If it is argued that in cases such as "the brave man" (*vīraḥ puruṣaḥ*), the nominative case ending would not occur because an additional relation of identity (*abheda-saṃsarga*) appears [in the meaning], we say no; for since the relation constitutes the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), it is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*), and thus it is impossible for it to subvert the grammatical operation (*saṃskāra*) that has already taken effect first.

The author of the Vārttika, however, says: "When [the meaning] is expressed, the first case-suffix occurs. The meaning is that in examples such as *vṛkṣastiṣṭhati* ("the tree stands"), *kṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ* ("the mat is made"), *śatyaḥ* ("worth a hundred"), and *prāptodako grāmaḥ* ("the village reached by water"), the first case-suffix occurs when the agent and so forth are expressed by verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) and the like. Thus, even in cases like *vīraḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the hero is a man"), where there is an excess [of meaning], the first case-suffix is established because [the meaning] is expressed. Nor is there non-pervasion (over-extension) in cases such as *vṛkṣaḥ* ("tree") and *plakṣaḥ* ("fig tree"), because the verb *asti* ("is") is to be supplied.

Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "There would be the over-extension [of the rule] to cases where [the locus] is already expressed. To explain: in the sentence *prāsāda āste* ("He sits on the palace"), the single locus for both the action of sitting (*sad*) and the action of sitting down (*ās*) is called the "palace" (*prāsāda*). This is expressed by the suffix *ghañ* produced after the root *sad*; however, it is not expressed by the *laṭ* suffix after the root *ās*. In that case, the nominative (*prathamā*) would prevail over the locative (*saptamī*) because it is subsequent [in the order of rules]. If it were argued that "the nominative is prescribed when there is coreferentiality with something other than a finite verb (*atiṅ*)," that too is not correct, because in examples such as *devadattaḥ pacati*, finite verbs (*tiṅ*) would become impossible to find.

For instance, when *devadattaḥ paca* is established by the rule *laṭ*, as long as the *tiṅ*-suffixes have not yet been applied, there is no coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a *tiṅ*; consequently, the restriction that "only the first case ending [is used]" would not apply. Thus, since all case endings beginning with *su* (the nominative) could arise from the word *devadatta* without distinction, the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* would also occur, because the condition for them—the coreferentiality with a stem not ending in the first case—is present. However, the injunction for *tiṅ*-suffixes finds its scope in gender and other such factors.

Even regarding the restriction that "only that [person] is the first person," rules such as *vido laṭo vā* (Pāṇini 3.4.83) are satisfied by the mere use of the root *vid*, as in examples like *vettha* or *veda*. This is because the second and third persons are prescribed even when the original form (*sthānin*) is present; thus, there is no necessity for their actual employment once they are determined through context or implication. Furthermore, this fault is merely occasional.

For in the rule prescribing *śatṛ* and so forth, there is a twofold alternative: whether it is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) such as "not the first case" (*aprathamā*), or a prohibitive negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*). In that regard, the aforementioned fault does not apply to the second [alternative], because since the first case [ending] also exists, the prohibition of *śatṛ* and so forth is possible.

As for what was stated in the Bhāṣya regarding the *paryudāsa* (exclusion) view—that "there is no fault in the restriction of case endings"—that is to be reconsidered, because there it relies on the formulation of the rule as "the second case [is used] only when there is an object," and so forth. In that case, let there be no second case for Devadatta; however, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would certainly still occur, for that [sixth case] is restricted to the *śeṣa* (remainder) alone. That which is not governed by the restriction of any other case-ending is the *śeṣa*. Consequently, since the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) is in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the sixth case characterized as *śeṣa* would apply prior to that, and thus the present participles *śatṛ* and *śānac* would be unavoidable. (Pāṇini 2.3.47)
And in the case of addressing (*sambodhana*), [the first case suffix] shall apply (Pāṇini 2.3.47). Here, the nominative case (*prathamā*) occurs: *he rāma* (Pāṇini 2.3.48).

*Āmantrita* (Pāṇini 2.3.48): A word-form ending in the nominative case used in the sense of addressing (*sambodhana*) shall bear the technical designation *āmantrita*. Although it is generally difficult to include the "ending in" (*tadanta*) in a rule that prescribes a technical term (*saṃjñā-vidhi*) when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned, this is nevertheless obtained here because of the use of a "great technical term" (*mahāsaṃjñā*). [Thus,] addressing itself is called *āmantrita*; by metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*), the term applies to the word that effects that addressing. Furthermore, one addresses by means of a form ending in a case-suffix, not by the case-suffix alone. The locations where this technical term is applied are such rules as "and of the *āmantrita*" (*āmantritasya ca*), etc.

What is that [term]? By means of the rule *prātipadikārtha-* (Pāṇini 2.3.46), this designation should apply even to that which ends in the nominative case used in address (*sambodhana*). For example: *he pacan*, *he pacamāna*. For here, since the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* are prescribed in address, that expressed meaning is included [within the nominal stem]; thus, the nominative is applied by the preceding rule alone. However, if those two [suffixes] were devoid of case endings, their capacity would lie solely in expressing the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth.

Just as in the case of the *loṭ* [imperative] suffix when it is devoid of reduplication, so too here the alternative view is that of Pāṇini’s sūtra 2.3.47: *sambodhane ca*. In that case, let the word *set* not be included; for even though the principle *anantarasya vidhir vā* applies, the formation of the desired form is still achieved. (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.49)

The singular number [of the first case] is called *saṃbuddhi* (Pāṇini 2.3.49). That which is the singular number of the first case in address shall bear the technical name *saṃbuddhi*. [Example: *he paṭo*. While the rule *saṃbuddhau ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.106) is in force, the rule *hrasvasya guṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.108) applies. Although it would have been sufficient to say that the *saṃbuddhi* is [the first case], the mention of "singular" (*ekavacana*) is for the purpose of applying the name to the affix alone—since only one thing is expressed by it—rather than to the whole ending. Otherwise, to avoid breaking the continuity of the grammatical context, the name would apply to the entire form ending in that [affix]. (Pāṇini 2.3.50)

*Ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe* (Pāṇini 2.3.50). When there is a "remainder" (*śeṣa*)—that is, a relation such as that between owner and owned which is distinct from the meaning of the *kāraka* or the nominal stem—the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) shall occur. For example: *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the king's man"). Now, one might object: under the view that the rule restricts the application of the suffix, the mention of "remainder" (*śeṣa*) should indeed serve the purpose of restriction, namely, that it occurs only when there is a remainder.

If it is asked: "But since, under the view that the meaning [of the genitive] is restricted, a restriction is possible—namely, that when both the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and another case are applicable, the sixth case alone shall apply—what is the purpose [of the word *śeṣa*]? The answer is: No. The inclusion of the term *śeṣa* here is for the sake of clarity, even though its inclusion is necessary for subsequent purposes. Furthermore, the inclusion of *śeṣa* is not for the sake of denoting what is non-primary (*apradhāna*). Therefore, one should not say that [the genitive] would not occur either alternatively or simultaneously with two [factors], because the meaning of the suffix is primary, and thus it is logical that the sixth case occurs only from that which is non-primary. As for the person who is not the meaning of the base, however, it is indeed appropriate for him to be a qualifier of the meaning of the sixth case, as in "of the king" (*rājñaḥ*). This is the general direction [of the argument]. (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.51)

*Jño vidarthasya karaṇe* (Pāṇini 2.3.51). When the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the verb *jñā*—provided it does not mean "to know" [but rather "to intend"]—is intended to be expressed as a residual relation (*śeṣa*), the sixth case ending shall be used. This section was established for the purpose of preventing compound formation; this was demonstrated precisely during the refutation of the Vārttika *pratipadavidhānā ca* in the context of the rule *na nirdhāraṇe* (Pāṇini 2.2.14). Example: *sarpiṣo jñānam*. The meaning is: an activity related to the ghee (*sarpis*) which has become the actual instrument. There is a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the verb *jñā* when the activity is preceded by knowledge. (Pāṇini 2.3.52)

*Adhīgarthadayeśāṃ karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 2.3.52): For these [roots], when the object (*karman*) is intended as a residual relation (*śeṣe*), the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) shall occur. In the root *iṅ* (meaning "to remember"), the letter *k* is for the sake of specification (*viśeṣaṇārtha*) in this very context. The utterance of the word *adhi*, however, is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) with reference to the general rule that "the roots *iṅ* and *ik* do not deviate from having prepositions (*upasarga*)"; therefore, it was not stated as *smṛtyarthadayeṣām*. Even in the alternative view where the sūtra is split, the *kit* status must indeed be maintained for the sake of specification in the rule *iṇvadikaḥ* (Kāśikā Vārttika).

If the term *eḥ* were used [in the rule], there would be the undesirable consequence of including the root *ā-yat* (meaning "to go") as it is *praśliṣṭa* (coalesced) in the word *kaṭīgatau* (*kāovāo*). The examples for this section in the *Vṛtti* and other treatises are: *mātuḥ smaraṇam* ("remembering one's mother"), and *sarpiṣa udayanam īśanam vā* ("the rising or the ruling over clarified butter"). Although a form ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) is seen here, it has nonetheless been explained by the learned as being indicative (*upalakṣaṇatayā*) of that [rule].
(Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.53)

*kṛñaḥ pratiyatne* (Pāṇini 2.3.53): When *guṇādhāna* (the imparting of a quality) is intended, the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) shall be used for the object (*karman*) of the root *kṛ* when it remains as a residual element (*śeṣe*). Example: *edhodakasyopaskaraṇam* ("the preparation of fuel and water"). In the analysis (*vigraha*) *edhāśca udakaṃ ca*, there is singular collective treatment (*ekavadbhāva*) according to *jātiraprāṇinām* (Pāṇini 2.4.6). The augment *suṭ* is applied by *upātpratiyatne* (Pāṇini 6.1.139), etc. (Pāṇini 2.3.54).

Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.54: *rujārthānāṃ bhāvavacanānām ajvareḥ*. For verbs meaning "to afflict" (*rujārtha*) that denote an abstract state (*bhāva*) and exclude the root *jvari*, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) shall be used for the object (*karman*) when it is treated as residual (*śeṣe*). Example: *caurasya rogasya rujā* ("the affliction of the thief's disease"). The root *ruj* (Dhātupāṭha 1416) means "to break. The form *rujā* is established either by its inclusion in the *bhidādi* group or by specific irregularity (*nipātana*) within this very sūtra. The word *rujā* is conventionally used (*rūḍha*) to mean "disease. Regarding the sūtra, the term *bhāvavacanānām* refers to the agent (*kartṛ*) in the sense of the suffix *lyuṭ*; however, the primary meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) is not intended here. If so, how can there be a speaker (*vaktā*) of the abstract state? [The answer is: the abstract state itself is the speaker.

Therefore, for the sake of establishing the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of the suffix, the root *vac* should be understood [as implied]. It should be stated that [the rule] applies to *jvar* and *saṃtāp*, except for the causative (*ṇic*) (Kāśikāvṛtti). For example: *caurajvaraḥ* or *caurasaṃtāpaḥ*. The meaning is: a fever or the like related to a thief, having the disease as its agent. The suffix *ac* is added after the root *tap* when it is followed by the causative marker *ṇic* and the causal suffix *ṇiC*. In this case, the compound indeed occurs. (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.55)

*Āśiṣi nāthaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.55). When *nāth* has the sense of a benediction (*āśis*), the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) shall be used for the remaining object (*śeṣe karmaṇi*). Example: *sarpiṣo nāthanam* ("the praying for ghee"). Why is it said "in the sense of a benediction"? Consider *māṇavaka-nāthanam*; this means a request related to a boy. Although when the status as an object is intended, the sixth case is applied by the rule *kartṛ-karmaṇoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.3.65), and in that case a compound does indeed occur, nevertheless, in that instance the accent is that of the original form of the final member (*kṛd-uttara-pada-prakṛti-svara*). The conclusion is that while the final acute accent of the compound (*samāsāntodātta*) occurs in cases such as a request, it does not occur in the sense of a benediction. (Pāṇini 2.3.56)

*Jāsi-nipra-haṇana-nāṭa-krātha-piṣām hiṃsāyām* (Pāṇini 2.3.56). For these roots meaning "to injure," the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) shall be used for the remaining object (*śeṣe karmaṇi*). The root *jasu* occurs both as *jasu tāḍane* (curādi-gaṇa 1718) and *jasu hiṃsāyām* (curādi-gaṇa 1668); it is this [curādi] root that is intended here, and not the *divādi* root *jasu mokṣaṇe* (divādi-gaṇa 1211), because of the specific mention of *jāsī* [with the long vowel] and the statement "in the sense of injury" (*hiṃsāyām*). Example: *caurasyojjāsanam* ("the act of striking/destroying the thief"). *Niprahaṇaḥ* refers to the root *han* preceded by the prefixes *ni* and *pra*.

The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule *hanteratpūrvasya* (Pāṇini 8.4.22). The prefixes *ni* and *pra* may be joined together (*saṃhatau*), reversed (*viparyastau*), or used separately (*vyastau*). Thus, one says *caurasya niprahaṇanam*, *praṇihananaṃ*, *nihananaṃ*, or *prahaṇanaṃ*. In the word *praṇīti*, the substitution of *ṇ* occurs by the rule *nergada* (Pāṇini 8.4.17). The root *naṭ* meaning "to cause to flow" (*avasyandane*) belongs to the *curādi* group (DhP 10.1545). However, the root *naṭ* meaning "to dance" (*nṛttau*) from the *bhvādi* group (DhP 1.781) is not included here, because of the mention of the long vowel [in the rule]. An example is *caurasyonāṭanam*.

The root *krath* is listed in the *Ghaṭādi* group (beginning with *ghaṭ*) in the sense of "injury" (*hiṃsā*); the author of the *Vṛtti* states that the vowel lengthening here occurs by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). For this very reason, while [Pāṇini] mentions "kratha in the sense of injury" as being *svarita*-accented in the *Yujādi* group, Deva reads it there as *anudātta*; and Śākaṭāyana is interpreted by Mādhava and others as following a different opinion. The form *caurasya krāthanam* ("the killing of a thief") is thus explained. The inclusion of the suffix *mit* is for the purpose of allowing optional lengthening according to Pāṇini 6.4.93 (*ciṇṇamuloḥ*). Thus we have *akrathi* or *akrāthi*, and *kratham* or *kratham*.
*Krātham krātham*. Here, indeed, the optional long vowel (*dīrgha-vikalpa*) prevails by virtue of its higher status, overriding the *nipātana* (irregular form).

As for what the author of the *Nyāsa* stated—that because of the irregular mention (*vikṛta-nirdeśa*) as *krāthī*, the genitive case applies only where there is *vṛddhi* even when the suffix *mit* is present, whereas in the case of the *caṅ* aorist, due to the absence of *vṛddhi*, one says *coram acikrathat*—that is weak. For Mādhava maintains that since this section is established as being for the purpose of precluding compound formation (*samāsa-nivṛtti*), verbal forms ending in *tiṅ* are not examples here; furthermore, even in the case of the *caṅ* aorist, a "residual" genitive (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*) cannot be denied.

Nor should it be said that the intention of the *Nyāsa* is that the genitive suffix applies only to the remainder (*śeṣa*) after *krāth*, and not to *hrasva*, so that by breaking the context, even a verbal form (*tiṅanta*) may serve as an example in the present case; for even so, the accusative case remains difficult to obtain, and there is no evidence for such a deviation from the established method. Although Haradatta has stated that the inclusion of *ghaṭa* and others in the list is for the purpose of ensuring that the designation *aṅ* occurs when the status of *ṣit* is extended [to these roots] by the rule "ghaṭādayaḥ ṣitaḥ" (Gaṇasūtra).

That too is weak, for it is sūtra-ed in the middle [of the *Gautama-sūtra*] as: "ghaṭādayaḥ ṣitaḥ. By this, the status of being *ṣit* applies only to the preceding [words] and not to the subsequent ones as well; furthermore, this [word in question] is subsequent—this is the direction [of the argument]. "The grinding of a low-caste man (*vṛṣala-peṣaṇam*). Why [is it specified] "in the sense of injury"? [Consider: "the grinding of grain (*dhānya-peṣaṇam*)," which has the udātta accent on the final syllable. Because of the continued application of the term "the remainder" (*śeṣa*), when there is an intention to express the object (*karman*) [as a subordinate factor], only the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) is used. And so says Bhaṭṭi: "We eat the twice-born who sacrifice to the gods; we slay them. As for Māgha’s usage: "To utterly destroy those who harm the world by their own power... (Māgha, Kāvyamīmāṃsā 1.37), it should be understood that here the status of being a "remainder" (*śeṣatva*) is intended. (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.57)

Regarding the roots *vyava-hṛ* and *paṇ* when they have the same meaning: the sixth case ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) shall be used for the object (*karman*) in the remaining cases. It should be understood that these two roots have the same meaning in the context of gambling and in the business of buying and selling. Examples: *śatasya vyavaharaṇam* or *paṇanam*. The meaning is: the application of a hundred [coins] in the form of buying and selling, or gambling. Why "when they have the same meaning"? Example: *śalākā-vyavahāraḥ*; the meaning is "counting. Example: *brāhmaṇa-paṇanam*; the meaning is "praising.
The suffix *āya* is optional because of the rule *āyādaya ārdhadhātuke vā* (Pāṇini 3.1.31). (Pāṇini 2.3.58)

*divastadarthasya* (Pāṇini 2.3.58). Here, the term *śeṣe* ("in the remaining cases") does not apply, because of the commencement of the two subsequent sūtras. If *divaḥ* had been read in the previous sūtra itself, the phrase *tadarthasya* would not have been necessary; yet, although this would have resulted in greater brevity (*lāghava*), the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the sake of the following rules and to prevent its connection with *śeṣa*. The genitive case shall be used for the object of the root *div*, provided it has the same meaning as *vyavahṛ* ("to deal") or *paṇ* ("to bet"). In these three sūtras, forms ending in verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*) also serve as examples: *śatasya dīvyati* ("he plays for a hundred"). Why "having that meaning" (*tadarthasya*)? [Consider: *brāhmaṇaṃ dīvyati* ("he challenges a Brahmin"). (Pāṇini 2.3.59)

*vibhāṣopasarge* (Pāṇini 2.3.59): This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding rule. One plays for a hundred, or wins back a hundred. *dvitīyā brāhmaṇe* (Pāṇini 2.3.60): In usage where *brāhmaṇa* is the subject, the second case (*dvitīyā*) may optionally be used for the object of *div* (to play/dice) when it has that same meaning [as in the previous rule]. This is an exception to the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*). On that day, they should play with his cow as the stake. Although this is already established by the optionality (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*) in the Vedic language (*chandas*) even for the verb with a prefix (*sopasarga*), this rule is commenced for the sake of the form without a prefix (*nirupasarga*).

(Pāṇini 2.3.61): *preṣyabruvorhaviṣo devatāsampradāne*. [The sixth case ending is used] after words denoting a specific sacrificial oblation (*havis*) which serve as the object of the verbs *preṣya* and *brūhi*, when these verbs are employed in the sense of a deity being the recipient (*devatāsampradāna*). The word *preṣya* is the second person singular imperative of the root *iṣ* belonging to the *divādi* class, meaning "to go. By association with this, *brūhi* is also understood as being in that same form (the second person singular imperative). When these two—*preṣya* and *brūhi*—are used in the sense of a matter where a deity is the recipient, the sixth case ending shall be applied to a word expressing a specific sacrificial oblation that serves as their object. Example: *agnaye chāgasya haviṣo vapāyā medasaḥ preṣyānubrūhi vā* ("Command [the Hotṛ] or recite for Agni the fat of the omentum of the goat-oblation").

Why [is it said] "of *preṣya* and *bruvaḥ*"? [Consider: *agnaye chāgaṃ havir vapāmedo juhudhi* ("Offer the goat-offering, the omentum and fat, to Agni"). Why [is it said] "of the *havis* (oblation)"? [Consider: *agnaye gomayāni preṣya* ("Send word for cow-dung for Agni"). Why [is it said] "when there is a deity as the recipient" (*devatā-sampradāne*)? [Consider: *māṇavakāya puroḍāśān preṣya* ("Send word for sacrificial cakes for the boy"). A prohibition must be stated regarding the qualification of the *havis* by its being "prepared" (*prasthita*), or else it should be excluded [from the rule]. [Example: *indrāgnibhyāṃ chāgaṃ havir vapāmedaḥ prasthitaṃ preṣya* ("Send word for the goat-offering, the omentum and fat, prepared for Indra and Agni"). In this sūtra, the mention of "the rest" (*śeṣa*) is not connected [to the rule], because the formation of a compound with a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) is impossible.
And this [rule] applies even in the common language (*bhāṣā*), because of the explicit mention of "Vedic" (*chandas*) in the subsequent [sūtra]. (Pāṇini 2.3.62)

In the Vedic language (*chandas*), the genitive case is frequently used in the sense of the dative (*caturthī-arthe*). Thus, the genitive may occur [in place of the dative]. For example: *puruṣamṛgaś candramase godhākālakādārvāghāṭas te vanaspatīnām* (Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 1.27), meaning "The human-deer, the lizard, the black snake, and the woodpecker—these belong to the trees," that is, they are for the trees (*vanaspatibhyaḥ*). This is established by the rule concerning the transposition of cases (*vyatyaya-vacana*). Furthermore, in the Vedic language, the genitive is frequently used in the sense of the instrumental (*karaṇe*) after the root *yaj* (to sacrifice). Thus: *ghṛtasya yajate* or *ghṛtena yajate* ("He sacrifices with clarified butter").

(Pāṇini 2.3.64): *kṛtvo'rtha-prayoge kāle'dhikaraṇe* (when used in connection with words having the sense of *kṛtvas*, the seventh case is used for time as the locus). Here, although the term *śeṣa* (remainder) has been interrupted by six preceding sūtras, it continues to apply because of the mention of *karman* (object) in the subsequent sūtra. Indeed, [the rule] *kartari ca* (Pāṇini 2.2.16) was not stated [here]. The ancient commentators maintain that the mention of *karman* connected with *śeṣa* does not continue [into this sūtra]. In reality, however, the commentary itself is the refuge, since the mention of *karman* could possibly serve to exclude the immediately preceding *adhikaraṇa*. Example: *pañca-kṛtvo'hno bhojanam* (eating five times a day).

"Twice a day is the meal. What if it were otherwise? This would then be merely a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*), and consequently, the locative case in *dvirahany adhīte* ("he studies twice a day") would not occur, because it would be superseded by the genitive.

[Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.65: "The genitive is used for the agent and the object when a *kṛt* suffix follows. The term "in the remaining cases" (*śeṣe*) is discontinued. When joined with a *kṛt* suffix, the genitive shall be used for both the agent and the object. Example: *bhavataḥ śāyikā* ("your lying down"); *apām sraṣṭā* ("the creator of waters"). Why specify "agent and object"? [Example: *śastreṇa bhettā* ("the cutter with a weapon").

It might be argued as follows: here, the action is implied by the agent and the object; the verbal root alone expresses these. Of the root, there are two types of suffixes: *kṛt* and *tiṅ*. In the case of the employment of a *tiṅ* suffix, the prohibition [of the genitive] by the rule *na loka-* (Pāṇini 2.3.69) must apply. Consequently, by process of elimination, the genitive would occur only in connection with a *kṛt* suffix; so what is the purpose of explicitly mentioning *kṛt*? Do not say so, for it is necessary to exclude that which ends in a *taddhita* suffix, such as in the example *kṛtapūrvī kaṭam* ("one who has previously made a mat").

[Objection: But surely, in the analysis (*vigraha*) "the mat was made by him previously" (*kṛtaḥ kaṭaḥ pūrvamanenā*), since the suffix *kta* is prescribed when the object is expressed, the object is already denoted by that very [suffix]; therefore, the second case-ending (*dvitīyā*) should not occur. Likewise, the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*), which is its exception, should also not occur here, because of the governing rule of "when not already expressed" (*anabhihitādhikāra*). Furthermore, because the word *kṛta* is dependent on *kaṭa*, the compound would be difficult to obtain; and the same would apply to the *taddhita* suffix as well. If this is argued, it has been stated by Hari (Bhartṛhari): "In relation to a specific object, even though it has been consumed by words such as *kṛta* (past passive participles), another word 'made' (*kṛta*) functions independently of that specific [object]."
When the suffix -kta denotes the abstract state (bhāva) and the verb is thus intransitive,
then there occurs a connection between that [state] and the objects by means of an agent who possesses action.

"Just as an action that is formless and resides in [the stages of] 'gone' and so forth is connected with objects such as villages, so too is it connected in cases such as 'having previously done' (kṛtapūrvī). Thus [it is said].

The meaning of this is as follows: because words such as *kṛta* (made) are used in co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with words such as *kaṭa* (mat), they are connected to a specific object (*viśiṣṭakarman*). Even when [the specific object] has been extracted (*niṣkṛṣya*), that is, even when it has been experienced—referring to the state [expressed by] "a mat was made by him previously"—in that state, there is an absence of a compound formation (*vṛttiviraha*). A different word *kṛta*, which denotes the object in general (*karmasāmānyavacana*), is what functions and attains its application (*vṛtti*). The sense is that even in cases where the status of being an object is not intended to be expressed, such as in "it is not cooked here" (*neha pacyate*), a suffix is admitted to denote the object in general.

He states another opinion—that there is an affix in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) for roots whose object is not intended to be expressed—with the words "in the case of intransitivity. Now, one might object: even if the *kta* affix is applied in the sense of the abstract state or the general object, since there would be no requirement for a further relation, a compound could be formed by the rule *sup supā*. Then, by the rules *pūrvādiniḥ* (Pāṇini 5.2.86) and *sapūrvācca* (Pāṇini 5.2.87), the suffix *ini* could indeed be added in the sense of the agent. However, in the first alternative, the expression of the mat (*kaṭa*) by the *kta* affix would be unavoidable.

And as in the case of "kṣud upahantum" (to be able to destroy hunger), where the object of hunger (*kṣudhaḥ*) is expressed by a *kṛtya* suffix; let it not be so, because the meaning of the word *kṛta*, having become a single integrated unit with the meaning of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*), cannot be extracted and connected with the mat (*kaṭena*).

He states this very point with the words "therefore, [the case ending] is like that of an action" (*kriyāvat*). Now, one might object: "If there is no contact even through the action, how can there be an accusative case? Anticipating this doubt, he says "without a specific grasp" (*avigraha*). The meaning is: "devoid of a specific grasp" (*viśiṣya grahaḥ* = *grahaḥ*) means not being grasped as a primary factor (*aprādhānyena*), even though it is not explicitly apprehended. This is the underlying idea: a connection of the factors of action (*kāraka*) with an action is observed even when that action is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), as in the example "he made a mat" (*kaṭaṃ kṛtavān*). Furthermore, this word *kṛtapūrvī* is derived in the sense of "one by whom something was done previously" (*pūrvaṃ kṛtam anena*).

This results in the same meaning as the expression "he made it previously. In that case, the status of the mat (*kaṭa*) as the object (*karman*) is dependent upon the action of making (*karoti*). And since that [objecthood] is not expressed [by the suffix], it follows that, in the absence of the mention of *kṛt* [suffixes], the genitive case would indeed occur; thus the point is established.

It might be argued as follows: [In the verse] "odanaḥ pacyatetarām" (the rice is cooked exceedingly), and even in cases such as "gururdharitrī kriyatetarāṃ tvayā" (the earth was made heavy by you), the accusative case would apply to the rice and the earth because they are connected to the action through the very action [denoted by the suffix]. If it is claimed that the connection with the object occurs through the meaning of the *l*-suffix which has become a qualifier of the action, then let it be the same for the meaning of the *kta*-suffix as well; for there is no difference in the fact that, just as an action has a requirement (*ākāṅkṣā*) toward its factors (*kāraka*s), so too does a capacity have a requirement toward its possessor.

Granted that, in some way, there might be a function [of a word] by abandoning its primary meaning—as is frequently observed in cases such as *rājapuruṣa* (the king’s man), where a specific number is abandoned, or in *māsajāta* (born after a month), where the subordinate and principal status is abandoned—nevertheless, the mention of the *kṛt*-suffix is indeed redundant. This is because the prohibition is already established by the rule *na loka-* (Pāṇini 2.3.69). For the meaning of that rule is that [the genitive] does not occur in connection with an action expressed by a verbal root ending in a *niṣṭhā* suffix; this is because even in examples such as *grāmaṃ gatavān* ("he has gone to the village"), the case-factors (*kāraka*) are connected only with the action itself.

Nor should it be said that the mention of *kṛt* [suffixes] in the rule is intended to prevent the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) from being applied to the agent of the base meaning of the causative (*ṇic*)—as in "Yajñadatta causes Devadatta to cook"—on the grounds that the *ṇic* suffix is not a *kṛt*. For the prohibition is established simply by the phrase "not in connection with *la*" (*layoge na*). This means that the prohibition applies when there is a connection with an action conveyed by a verbal root (*laprakṛti*) or by a word ending in a *l*-suffix (*lāntapada*). And as for whether that action is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) or principal (*pradhānabhūta*), there is no restriction on this point.

However, the principle of the primary and the secondary (*gauṇamukhya-nyāya*) is not resorted to here, because [the rule] must conform to the intended meaning (*lakṣya*) and because of the commentary stating that "the *kāra* suffix is more extensive than the *svarita*. For this very reason, the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is obtained there. In examples such as *bhedikā devadattasya* ("Devadatta’s cutter") and *yajñadattasya kāṣṭhānām* ("Yajñadatta’s cutter of wood"), the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is also obtained from both agents for this same reason. Therefore, the mention of the *kṛt* suffix [in the rule] is redundant.

On this point, they say: the mention of *kṛt* [suffixes] is intended so that the rule applies as if it were a *kṛt* suffix, and not when there is the addition of a *taddhita* suffix—as in *vyākaraṇaṃ prājñaḥ*, where the suffix *aṇ* is added in its own sense (*svārthe*) according to Pāṇini 5.4.38 (*prajñādibhyaśca*). And for those who maintain this view, it follows that in an expression such as *pācakatamaḥ*, the genitive case is likewise prohibited. However, if one accepts forms such as *kartavyapūrvī* (as opposed to *kṛtapūrvī*), then once the compound has been formed with a word ending in *tavyat* and other such suffixes, the mention of *kṛt* serves to exclude such cases from the application of the rule.

Regarding the statement that the genitive suffix applies only to roots such as *ut* and others, one must seek out the usage of authoritative grammarians (*abhiyukta*). For instance, Bhaṭṭi says: *tad dharṣayairāmodamuttamam*. It is replied: this genitive is non-obligatory (*anityā*), because of the rule *tadarham* (Pāṇini 5.1.117). Furthermore, it has been stated in the *Akathita-sūtra* (Pāṇini 1.4.51) itself: when a *kṛt* suffix denoting the agent is applied to roots that take two objects, the genitive is fixed for the primary object (*pradhāna*), but for the secondary object (*guṇa*), it may occur in either way.

"When both [agent and object] are possible, [the sixth case ending] occurs for the object" (Pāṇini 2.3.66). Where there is the possibility of both [agent and object] in a formation with a *kṛt* suffix, the sixth case ending shall occur only for the object. Example: *āścaryo gavāṃ doho 'gopena* ("It is a marvel, the milking of cows by one who is not a cowherd"). It should be stated as a supplementary rule (*kārikā*) that this prohibition does not apply in the case of the use of the suffixes *-akā* and *-ā*. Example: *bhedikā bibhitsā vā rudrasya jagataḥ* ("The splitting or the desire to split the world by Rudra"). How then is it that there is no sublation by the suffix *-ktin*? This is explained in the commentary (*vṛtti*) on the sūtra *sthāgāpāpaco bhāve* (Pāṇini 3.3.95).

Thus, there is no sublation (*bādhā*) of *sīyuṭ* by *suṭ*; regarding this, the commentary on *Pāṇinisūtra* 3.4.107, *suṭtithoḥ*, states that Rakṣita says: "In the rule *apratyayāt* [3.3.102], the suffix *a* is understood here because of its primacy. However, in the word *bādhā*, the suffix *a* is applied according to *Pāṇinisūtra* 3.3.103, *gurośca halaḥ*. Alternatively, it should be understood that the third case ending is used because the sense of instrument (*karaṇatva*) is intended. Regarding the *vārttika* *śeṣe vibhāṣā*: some say this applies only to the domain of feminine suffixes; others say it is the diverse composition of the *sūtra* by Pāṇini or [the work] of Pāṇini.

Some maintain that the option (*vibhāṣā*) applies without distinction: "The instruction of words by the Teacher or of the Teacher" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 2.3.67); and "and [the genitive] after a *kta*-suffix denoting the present" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 2.3.67). When there is a connection with a *kta*-suffix having a present sense, the genitive case should be employed. This is an exception to the prohibition stated in "not with *loka*" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 2.3.69). For example: *rājñāṃ mato buddhaḥ pūjito vā* ("esteemed, known, or honored by kings"). Here, the *kta*-suffix is used in the sense of the present according to "and after [roots] meaning opinion, intellect, or honor" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 3.2.188). How then is the genitive used in connection with a *kta*-suffix denoting an abstract state (*bhāva*) in the neuter, as in *chātrasya hasitam* ("the laughing of the student")? It is established through the understanding that this is a residual case (*śeṣa*).
When there is an intention to express agency, only the third case ending is used, as in "chātreṇa hasitam" (the student laughed). (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.68)

*Adhikaraṇavācinaśca* (Pāṇini 2.3.68): In connection with a *kta*-suffix, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) shall be used when it denotes the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Example: *idameṣāṃ śayitam* ("this is where they slept"). Here, the sixth case is used for the agent (*kartṛ*). However, when a *kta* suffix is added to transitive verbs (*sakarmaka*), the sixth case is used for both the agent and the object, as there is no difference in their being unexpressed (*anabhihita*). Example: *idameṣāṃ bhuktam odanasya* ("this is what was eaten by them of the rice"). This restriction—"when both [agent and object] are applicable, [the sixth case is used] for the object"—applies specifically to the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*. In this context, regarding verbal roots meaning motion (*gatyartha*), this [restriction] does not apply.

In the sense of location (*adhikaraṇa*): *idameṣāṃ gatiḥ* ("this is the place they have gone to"). In the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*): *idam ete gatāḥ* ("these people have gone here"). In the sense of the object (*karman*): *idam ebhir gatam* ("this has been gone to by them"). In the neuter gender, expressing the abstract action (*bhāva*): *ihaibhir gatam* ("they have gone here"). When there is a desire to express the agent, it is *idameṣāṃ gatam*; and in that same context, when there is a desire to express the remaining relation (*śeṣa*), it is likewise [used]. (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.69)

Regarding the rule *nalokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛnām* (Pāṇini 2.3.69): the substitution of *ṇ* in the suffix *tṛn* has not been applied here because it would result in the destruction of the intended form. When these [suffixes] are used, the genitive case—which would otherwise be required by the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* (Pāṇini 2.3.65)—is prohibited. Examples of substitutes for *l* (the marker for the present stem) include: *odanaṃ pacan*, *pacamānaḥ*, *pecānaḥ*, and *pecivān*. How then are forms such as *babhrir vajram*, *papiḥ somam*, and *dadir gāḥ* to be explained? For *kikin* are neither *l*-markers nor substitutes for them.

This is not a fault; by the rule *kikinau liṭ ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.171), the functions (*kārya*) of the *liṭ* [perfect] tense are extended [to the suffixes *ki* and *kin*], but not the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of *liṭ*. For it is said: "When a specific [property] is extended, the general [category] is also extended. Examples: *kaṭaṃ cikīrṣuḥ* (desiring to make a mat). *kanyām alaṅkariṣṇuḥ* (desiring to adorn a maiden). Examples with the suffix *uka*: *vārāṇasīm āgāmukaḥ* (one who goes to Vārāṇasī). The prohibition [of the suffix *uka*] does not apply to the root *kam* in colloquial usage (*bhāṣā*). *purā sūryasya udetor ādheyaḥ* (it should be established before the rising of the sun). *purā krūrasya visṛpo virapśin* (O Virapśin, before the gliding of the cruel one). Examples with the past participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*): *odanaṃ bhuktavān* (he has eaten rice). *devadattena kṛtam* (done by Devadatta).

It is easy for you because of the sense of the *khal* suffix. The *soma* is easily drunk by you. [The rule] *tṛn* is a pratyāhāra (a contraction), beginning from the word *śatṛśānacau* up to the *nakāra* of *tṛn*. By this, there is also the inclusion of [suffixes] beginning with *śān*. Examples: *somaṃ pavamānaḥ* ("purifying the soma"). [This is formed by] *pūṅyajoḥ śānan* (Pāṇini 3.2.128). Example: *naṭam āghnānaḥ* ("striking the actor"). [This is formed by] *tācchīlyādiṣu cānaś* (Pāṇini 3.2.129). Example: *adhīyan pārāyaṇam* ("studying the Pārāyaṇa"). [This is formed by] *iṅdhāryoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.130), which prescribes the *śatṛ* suffix. Example of *tṛn*: *pātā sutaṃ indro astu somam* ("May Indra be the drinker of the pressed soma"). [In the case of the root] *dviṣ*, the *śatṛ* suffix is optionally used.

In the case of *mura* or *muraṃ* with the sense of "hating," there is a prohibition of the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhī) in all instances of the kāraka [relation]. However, the genitive of the residual relation (*śeṣe ṣaṣṭhī*) would certainly still apply. For example: *brāhmaṇasya kurvan* ("doing for a Brahmin"), *satyānuraktā narakasya jiṣṇavaḥ* ("those devoted to truth, victorious over Naraka"), and *chātrasya hasitam* ("the laughter of the student"). This also applies in cases such as *janikartuḥ* ("of the agent of birth") and so forth:

*ikṣvākūṇāṃ durāpe 'rthe tvadadhīnā hi siddhayaḥ* ("for even in matters difficult to attain for the Ikṣvākus, successes depend on you"), and *api vāgadhipasya durvacaṃ vacanaṃ tad vidadhīta vismayam* ("even the speech of the Lord of Speech might produce astonishment at that which is difficult to utter") (Kumārasambhava 2.2). In these cases as well, the genitive is used.

Alternatively, the construction is "the successes of the Ikṣvākus," and not "difficult for the Ikṣvākus to attain"; likewise, the construction is "the astonishment of the Lord of Speech," and not "difficult for the Lord of Speech to utter"—this is the general direction. Here, one should derive *ūkau* as *uḥ* and *ukaḥ*, and then analyze *laḥ* and *ūkau*. Because of the qualification by the letter *ū*, there is the rule of *tadantavidhi* (application of the rule to that which ends in the specified element). Due to the principle of *vyapadeśivadbhāva* (treating a single entity as if it possessed a designation), the prohibition applies even to the solitary [letter]. (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.1.62).

Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.70: *akenorbhaviṣyadādhamarṇyayoḥ*. When used with the word *aka* (a kṛt-affix denoting an agent) in the sense of the future, and when used with words expressing a debt (*ādhamarṇya*), the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) shall not occur. Examples: *edhānāhārako vrajati* ("He goes to fetch fuel"). *vrajaṅgāmī* ("One who goes to the cow-pen"). This has been explained in the context of the possibility of a second-case compound (*dvitīyā-samāsa*). Regarding the sense of debt (*ādhamarṇya*): *śataṃ dāyī* ("A debtor of a hundred [pieces]"). The term "future" (*bhaviṣyat*) is specifically emphasized here. Consequently, because the rule applies only to that which is prescribed under the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "the future," it does not apply in these cases: *varṣaśatasya pūrakaḥ* ("One who completes a hundred years"). *putrapautrāṇāṃ darśakaḥ* ("One who sees his sons and grandsons").

For this [suffix] is prescribed without distinction by Pāṇini’s sūtra 3.1.133, *ṇvultṛcau*, and not, like *tumuṇvulau* (Pāṇini 3.3.10), situated within the governing heading (*adhikāra*) of "that which is about to happen" (*bhaviṣyat*). In this context, the *Bhāṣya* has divided the rule to prevent a one-to-one correspondence (*yathāsaṃkhyam*): [one part applies to] "that which is about to happen," and [the other to] "in the sense of debt" (*ādhamarṇye*) according to Pāṇini 2.3.71.

*Vā kṛtyānāṃ kartari* (Pāṇini 2.3.71). The genitive case may optionally be used for the agent of *kṛtya* suffixes. Since the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti* (Pāṇini 2.3.65) would have made this obligatory, this is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*). Examples: *idam kartavyam kṛṣṇena* or *kṛṣṇasya*. Why specify "for the agent"? Consider: *geyo māṇavakaḥ sāmnām* ("the boy is to sing the Sāman hymns"). Because the rule *bhavyageya* (Pāṇini 3.4.68) prescribes the suffix for the agent, the object is not already expressed [by that suffix]. In this context as well, a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is made in the Bhāṣya: namely, *kṛtyānām*. The phrase "when both [agent and object] are applicable, [the sixth case is] not" (*ubhayaprāptau na*) follows from the previous rule.

"The cows are to be led to Vraja by Kṛṣṇa. In this example, the *kṛtya* suffix is used for the primary object, which is denoted by the word "cow" (*go*), as well as for the agent of the non-primary action. Since the agent is not expressed by the *kṛtya* suffix, the application of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would otherwise have been expected; however, it is prohibited [by this rule]. Consequently, the rule *kartari vā* applies: the genitive may optionally be used for the agent. Everything else [the prohibition of the genitive for the object and so forth] is withdrawn. (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.72)

*Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.72*: "With words having the sense of *tulya* (equal), except for *atula* and *upamā*, the third case ending is optionally used. When joined with words meaning "equal," the third case may optionally be used in the sense of the residual relation (*śeṣe*), or else the sixth case is used. For example: *tulyaḥ*, *sadṛśaḥ*, or *samaḥ* *kṛṣṇena* or *kṛṣṇasya*. Why [is it said] "except for *atula* and *upamā*"? Because there is no *tulā* (comparison/measure) or *upamā* (simile) of Kṛṣṇa. How then are the following usages to be explained: Kālidāsa’s “*tulāṃ yadā rohati dantavāsasā*,” and Māgha’s “*sphuṭopamaṃ bhūtisitena śambhunā*”? [These are explained by the fact that the word *tulya* is understood in those contexts.]

On this point, they say: *tolanam* (the act of weighing) is *tulā*. Mādhava maintains that [the form *tulā*] is correct by virtue of the irregularity (*nipātana*) "the elision of *ṇi* and the substitution of *aṅ*" in this very sūtra. *Upamitiḥ* (the act of comparison) is *upamā*. In that case, since the words *danta-vāsaḥ* and *śambhu* function as instruments (*karaṇa*) with respect to the meaning of the verbal root, the use of the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is entirely appropriate, as in examples such as "that by which something is compared. However, the present sūtra prescribes the third case specifically as an exception (*apavāda*) to the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) used for the remaining relations (*śeṣe*); it does not apply here—this is another matter. Alternatively, let the third case be applied according to Pāṇini 2.3.19: "The third case is used when joined with *saha* (together with), provided it denotes the principal [participant]."

"In the example: 'Of one who desires a comparison with the hair on its own head by means of those hairs growing from that very head,' it is said that the third case ending occurs even without the actual connection [to the word denoting the standard of comparison], as illustrated by the rule *vṛddho yūnā* (Pāṇini 1.2.65). Because of the inclusion of the word *artha* ('meaning') in the rule *tulyārthaiḥ*, the third case does not occur in connection with particles like *iva* which merely indicate the sense; for example: *gaur iva gavayaḥ* ('the gavaya is like a cow'), or *yathā gaus tathā gavayaḥ* ('as is a cow, so is a gavaya'). Since the particle *vā* is understood from the previous rule, the mention of *anyatarasyām* ('optionally') in this rule is for the purpose of carrying forward (*anukarṣaṇa*) the present option itself by means of the word *ca* ('and') in the subsequent rule. Otherwise, only the third case would have been carried forward, because of its immediate proximity."

(Pāṇini 2.3.73): "The dative [is used] also [after words expressing] *āyuṣya*, *madra*, *bhadra*, *kuśala*, *sukha*, *artha*, and *hita* when used in the sense of a blessing (*āśis*). The words ending with *sukha* form a *dvandva* compound. Then, by means of the word *atha*, a *bahuvrīhi* is formed. Thus, the word *artha* is connected individually with each member heard at the end of the *dvandva*. Since the words *madra* and *bhadra* are synonyms, one of them should not have been recited in the sūtra. However, some say that the word *artha* is also a separate cause [for the dative], and according to the commentary, the term *artha* is to be understood everywhere.

When these [words] are used in conjunction with a benediction (*āśis*) that is being expressed, the fourth case (*caturthī*) may optionally be employed; in the alternative, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used. For example: *āyuṣyaṃ cirañjīvitaṃ devadattāya* or *devadattasya bhūyāt* ("May there be long life for Devadatta"). Likewise: *madr*, *bhadra*, *kuśala*, *nirāmaya*, *sukha*, *śam*, *artha*, *prayojana*, *hita*, *pathya*—in such cases as "may there be," etc. It should be stated that the fourth case is used in connection with *hita*. Since this [rule] has its purpose fulfilled by the previous rule even when not a benediction, the option applies specifically in the case of a benediction. Why say "in a benediction"? (Objection: Because [the word] *āyuṣyaṃ* exists [as a quality] belonging to Devadatta.
Thus ends the third section (āhnika) of the third quarter (pāda) of the second book (adhyāya) in the illustrious Śabdakaustubha. And this quarter is completed.
The first lesson in the fourth chapter.

(Pāṇini 2.4.1) *dvigurekavacanam* ("A dvigu compound takes the singular ending"). It is called *vacanam* because it expresses (*vakti*); the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) by virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*). It is neuter in the general sense (*napuṃsakaṃ sāmānye*; Kāśikāvṛtti). A *samāhāra-dvigu* compound should express a single unified meaning. For it is established in the sūtra *taddhitārtha-* (Pāṇini 2.1.51) that *samāhāra* is indeed a formation denoting an abstract state (*bhāva-sādhana*). Thus, this [rule] is established by logical necessity (*nyāya*). Furthermore, it is commenced in order to ward off the misconception that it is a formation denoting an object (*karman-sādhana*), and for the sake of the application of the rule *sa napuṃsakam* (Pāṇini 2.4.17).
Furthermore, the author of the *Sūtras* is seen to exert effort even for the sake of removing potential misconceptions. For example:

(Pāṇini Sūtra 2.4.2) "And a *dvandva* compound [is singular] when referring to the limbs of living beings, musical instruments, or armies. A *dvandva* compound of limbs belonging to living beings shall have a single referent (*ekārtha*). The same applies to the limbs of musical instruments and the limbs of armies. Examples: *pāṇipādam* (hand and foot), *mārdaṅgikapāṇavikam* (the drummers and the pan-pipers), *rathikāśvāroham* (the charioteers and the horsemen). Here, "limb" (*aṅga*) refers to a physical part (*avayava*) in the case of living beings and armies; however, in the case of musical instruments, "limb" (*aṅga*) should be understood as that which assists (*upakāraka*). In words such as *mārdaṅgika*, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to Pāṇini Sūtra 4.4.55, *śilpam*, in the sense that "playing the *mṛdaṅga* drum is one's craft."

In examples such as *pāṇipādam*, since the rule *jātirapraṇinām* (Pāṇini 2.4.6) already establishes the formation, this specific statement is intended to prevent the mixing of genders (*vyatikara*). However, in cases such as *hastyaśvam* and *hastyaśvāya*, although they refer to parts of an army (*senāṅga*), the optional rule characterized by the term *paśu* takes precedence; thus, the optionality is established by the rule *vibhāṣā vṛkṣe* (Pāṇini 2.4.12), as settled in the *Bhāṣya* and *Kaiyaṭa*. Now, how is it that we have the expression *rathavājipattikariṇīsamākulam*? For there ought to be a neuter short vowel [by the rule *vibhāṣā vṛkṣe*].

It is said: one should understand that [the compound] *rathādisahitāḥ kariṇyaḥ* is a *madhyamapadalopī* (middle-term-elided) compound. Alternatively, the analysis (*vigraha*) is *rathaśca vājī ca*, and so forth; the singular number is used because it refers to a class (*jātāvekavacanam*). Since it will be stated later that "in the case of *phala*, *senā*, and so on, there is a plurality of constituent elements," the rule for singularization (*ekavadbhāva*) does not apply here. By this, [verses such as] Māgha’s *pātitairathanāgāśvaiḥ* and *itthaṃ rathāśvebhaniṣādināṃ praṇagaḥ* (Śiśupālavadha 12.1) are also explained; for in these cases too, there is either an elision of the middle term or an analysis using a word ending in the singular.

Alternatively, it is a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) of words that have already formed a *dvandva* compound. Thus, the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtras "tiṅastrīṇi trīṇi" (Pāṇini 1.4.101) and "luṭaḥ prathamasya" (Pāṇini 2.4.85) states: "Both are intended; there are many [instances of] *śakti* and *kiṭaka*. In the commentary on Māgha, the essential point is the alternative solution: that in the phrase "rathaturaṅgāśvebhe niṣīdanti," it is an *upapada-samāsa* with a word ending in the suffix *ṇini*.

Although the *dvandva* compound is prescribed for both *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction) and *samāhāra* (aggregation) by the rule "the *dvandva* is used in the sense of 'and' (*cārthe*)" (Pāṇini 2.2.29), and the singular number is already established because an aggregate (*samāhāra*) is a single entity, nevertheless, this section is for the purpose of restriction: that in the case of words denoting parts of living beings (*prāṇyaṅga*) and so forth, when used in the singular, it must be a *dvandva*—meaning specifically a *samāhāra-dvandva*. Nor should one take the opposite view, namely, that these [parts of living beings] form a *samāhāra* only [in the singular], because of the inclusion of the plural number in the rule "tiṣyapunarvasvoḥ" (Pāṇini 1.2.63). For that [plural marker] is employed to exclude the singular of the aggregate, as seen in the expression "this [cluster] of Tiṣya and Punarvasu."

(Pāṇini 2.4.3) *Anuvāde caraṇānām*: In a restatement (*anuvāda*), a *dvandva* compound of words denoting Vedic schools (*caraṇa*) shall be singular. The word *caraṇa* is primary when referring to specific Vedic branches (*śākhā*) such as the Kaṭha and Kālāpa; it is secondary (*gauṇa*) when referring to the persons who study those branches. Since both of these possess the designation of a genus (*jāti*) according to the rule "A gotra together with [words for] *caraṇas*" (Kātyāyana’s Vārttika), the status of being a genus is established for those denoting Vedic branches by the rule "Genus for non-living things" (Pāṇini 2.4.6). Therefore, in this context, even the secondary application—referring specifically to the persons—is what is intended. Example: *udagāt kaṭhakālāpam* ("The Kaṭhas and Kālāpas have risen").

The *Kaṭhaka* and *Kauthuma* [schools] became established. Here, when the *Kaṭhas* and *Kālāpas* had arisen and were well-established, two people made an agreement, saying, "We must go there," but having forgotten it, one remained behind. Regarding him, this is said: "Indeed, the *Kaṭhas* and *Kālāpas* have departed; why do you sit here? Therefore, this is a restatement (*anuvāda*). Those who study what was proclaimed by Kaṭha are the *Kaṭhas*. The suffix *ṇini* is applied because he was a pupil of Vaiśampāyana.

From *kaṭha* and *caraka*, [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied by Pāṇini 4.2.59, *tad adhīte tad veda*. Then, by Pāṇini 4.2.64, *proktālluk*, there is elision [of the suffix]. From the word *kalāpin*, [the suffix] *aṇ* is applied by Pāṇini 4.3.108, *kalāpino’ṇ*. By the Kātyāyana-vārttika beginning with *nāntasya ṭilope sabrahmacārī*, there is elision of the *ṭi* (the penultimate vowel). There is then elision of the suffix *aṇ* [indicating study]. By this, *kauthuma* is explained. However, when *udaya* and *pratiṣṭhā* are not being referred to, but rather are being made known as unknown, then the counter-example is: *udaguḥ kaṭhakālāpāḥ* ("The Kaṭhas and Kālāpas have risen").

It should be stated that [the suffix *kvasu*] occurs only after the roots *sthā* and *iṇ* when followed by *adyatanī*. Why "after *sthā* and *iṇ*" (*stheṇoḥ*)? [Consider: *anandiṣuḥ kaṭhakālāpāḥ* ("The Kaṭhas and Kālāpas did not rejoice"). Why "ending in *a* or *dyatani*" (*adyantāyām*)? [Consider: *udyanti kaṭhakālāpāḥ* ("The Kaṭhas and Kālāpas rise"). (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.2.111)

*Adhvaryukraturanapuṃsakam* (Pāṇini 2.4.4). The word *adhvaryu* indicates the Yajurveda. A *dvandva* compound consisting of non-neuter terms denoting sacrifices (*kratu*) that are either produced or prescribed therein shall be treated as singular. Examples: *arkāśvamedham*, *sāhnātirātram*. Why "sacrifices of the Adhvaryu"? [Counter-examples: *iṣuvajrau*, *udbhidvalabhidau*; for the injunctions for these are found in the same Veda. Why "non-neuter"? [Counter-examples: *rājasūyavājapeye*; for these two words are listed in the *ardharca* group [of neuter nouns], so when they are used in the neuter gender, this is the counter-example. (Pāṇini 2.4.5)

*Adhyayanato’viprakṛṣṭākhyānām* (Pāṇini 2.4.5): For those whose names are not remote—that is, proximate—due to the cause of study (*adhyayana*), a *dvandva* compound shall be treated as singular. For example: *padakakramakam*. One who studies the *padas* is called a *padaka*. According to *kramādibhyo vun* (Pāṇini 4.2.61), one who studies the *krama* is a *kramaka*. [The compound] *kramakavārttikam* [is formed as follows]: *vṛtti* refers to the *saṃhitā*; those who study that are *vārttikas*. Because of the inclusion of *uktha* and others in the list, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied. Since the *krama* must be studied after having studied the *padas*, the proximity is clear.

In the case of *kramaka-vārtika*, however, the proximity (*pratyāsatti*) to be understood is simply that the *krama* cannot be studied without having first studied the *saṃhitā*. Why say "from study" (*adhyayanataḥ*)? [Consider] "father and son" (*pitāputrau*). Why say "of those whose names are not separated by distance" (*aviprakṛṣṭākhyānām*)? [Consider] "the ritualist and the grammarian" (*yājñika-vaiyākaraṇau*). (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.4.6) *Jātir aprāṇinām* (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.4.6): A *dvandva* compound whose constituent members denote a genus (*jāti*), provided they do not refer to living beings, shall be singular. [Examples: *ārāśastri* ("the awl and the knife"), *ārāpratodaḥ* ("the awl and the goad"). Why say "genus" (*jāti*)? [Consider] *nandaka-pāñcajanyaiau* ("Nandaka and Pāñcajanya"); these two are proper nouns (*saṃjñāśabda*).

His sword is Nandaka, and his conch is proclaimed to be Pāñcajanya. What about non-living things? [The answer is: Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras. According to the maxim of "the negative particle (nañ) and the word 'iva'," there is a singular collective expression (*ekavadbhāva*) for substances and generic classes (*jāti*), but not for qualities or actions. For example: *rūpa-rasau* (color and taste); *gamana-ākuñcane* (going and contracting). This singular collective expression occurs only when the generic class (*jāti*) is predominant. However, when there is an intention to express specific individual substances (*dravya-viśeṣa*), one says *badarāmalakāni* (jujubes and myrobalans). But when the intention is to express the generic class (*jāti*), one says *badarāmalakam*. In this regard, the singular collective expression is optional; such is the natural implication of the Bhāṣya.

Accordingly, in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule *vibhāṣā vṛkṣamṛga* (Pāṇini 2.4.12), after introducing the *vārttika* beginning with *bahuprakṛtiḥ*, the examples *badarāmalakam* and *badarāmalakāni* are cited. Kaiyaṭa explains that according to the view of those who interpret the meaning as "when *badarāmalakāni* would otherwise be obtained," [the singular form] is indeed obligatory (*nityam eva*). For this very reason, the usage *oṣadhivanaspatīnām* found in the *bhāṣya* on the rule *tasya bhāvastvatalau* (Pāṇini 5.1.119) becomes consistent.

Kaiyaṭa, however, stating that there is no singular treatment (*ekavadbhāva*) because of the usage in the *Bhāṣya*, maintained that even when the genus (*jāti*) is intended to be expressed, the singular treatment does not occur. In this way, the passages from the *Bhāṣya* and Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the rule *laṭaḥ śatṛśānacau* (Pāṇini 3.2.124) are to be understood. If so, how is one to explain Bhāravi’s verse: *rañjitānu vividhāstaruśailāḥ* ("the various trees and mountains were colored")? Is it not the case here that specific individuals (*vyakti*) are intended to be expressed? True; it should be understood as "mountains together with trees."

*Viśiṣṭaliṅgo nadīdeśo'grāmāḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.7). The form *agrāmāḥ* is a Vedic plural used in place of the singular. A *dvandva* compound consisting of words denoting rivers or regions—provided they possess distinct genders (*viśiṣṭaliṅga*) and exclude villages (*agrāma*)—shall be treated as a singular. In this sūtra, all four terms should be understood as applying by extension to the whole compound (*dvandva*) through the properties of its parts. The expression *nadīdeśa* is an uncompounded designation. Example: *udhyaśca irāvatī ca* = *udhyerāvati*.

*Kuravaḥ* and *Kurukṣetram* form *kurukurukṣetram*. Why [is there] this difference in gender? [Consider] *gaṅgāyamune* and *madrakekayāḥ*. Why [is it specified] "river and country"? [Consider] *kukkuṭamayūryau* (a cock and a peahen). Why [is it specified] "not villages"? [Consider] *jāmbavam nagaram* (the city of Jāmbava) and *śālṛkinī grāmaḥ* (the village of Śālṛkinī), which together form *jāmbavaśālūkinyau*. Here, although the meaning of the first member (*pūrvapada*) is not a village, because the meaning of the second member (*uttarapada*) is a village, the prohibition is based on that. Thus it has been said: "The prohibition must be stated for villages on both sides."

The mention of "rivers" is because [they] are not a *deśa* (region). For a *janapada* (country) is indeed a *deśa*. For this very reason, mountains are not included; thus, Pāṇini’s sūtra 2.4.8 states: *kailāsaśca gandhamādanaṃ ca kailāsagandhamādane* ("Kailāsa and Gandhamādana form the compound *kailāsagandhamādane*") and *kṣudrajantavaḥ* ("small creatures").
In these cases, a *dvandva* compound shall be singular. For example: *yūkālikṣam* ("lice and nits"). Small creatures are those up to and including the mongoose (*ānakulāt*).

And for those whose enmity is eternal (Pāṇini 2.4.9): for those who have constant hostility, their *dvandva* compound shall be treated as singular. Examples include *govyāghram* (cow and tiger), *gajasiṃham* (elephant and lion), and so forth. Here, "enmity" (*virodha*) means hostility (*vaira*), and not such things as "incompatibility" (*sahānavasthāna*), because [if the latter were meant], there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as "shadow and sunlight" (*chāyātapau*). The word *śaśvat* indicates all three periods of time (*traikālya*). In the sense of "occurring therein," the suffix *vañ* is applied by Pāṇini 4.3.11 (*kālāṭ ṭhañ*). Although the suffix ends in *t*, the substitution of *ik* occurs by virtue of a specific grammatical exception (*nipātana*).

This is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the absence of *ṭilopa*—which would otherwise be obtained by the rule *avyayānāṃ bhamātre* (Kāśikāvṛtti)—is intended with reference to the general case, since it is not sublated by anything else. Therefore, some say that forms such as *kāndāvikā* are established thereby. In reality, however, *kandu* means a steamer; in that sense, the suffix *aṇ* is applied by the rule *saṃskṛtaṃ bhakṣāḥ* (Pāṇini 4.2.16), resulting in *kāndava*. Then, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied by the rule *tadasya paṇyam* (Pāṇini 4.4.51), resulting in *kāndāvikā*. Why is the word *śāśvatikaḥ* used [in the definition]? [Consider: Caitra and Maitra quarrel (*kalahāyete*).

By this, the usage of the poet Bhāravi—“*devāsurairamṛtamambunidhim mamantha*” (the gods and asuras churned the ocean for nectar)—is explained; for in that case, their [the gods'] activity is motivated by the nectar and so forth. Here, the meaning is that there is scope for the *dvandva* compound prescribed by the rule “*vibhāṣā vṛkṣamṛga*” (Pāṇini 2.4.12). The scope for *dvandva* compounds of animals (*paśu*) and birds (*śakuni*) is as follows: *mahājorabhram*, *mahājorabhrāḥ*; *haṃsacakravākam*, *haṃsacakravākāḥ*.

The scope of the rule *yeṣāṃ ca* (Pāṇini 2.4.1) is as follows: in the cases of *śramaṇabrāhmaṇam*, *mārjāramūṣakam*, *aśvamahiṣam*, and *kākolūkam*, where both [the rules *paśuśakunī ca* and *yeṣāṃ ca*] would apply, the option (*vibhāṣā*) provided by *paśuśakunī* takes precedence due to its later position; however, because it is restated by the word *ca* in *yeṣāṃ ca*, the compound becomes obligatory (*nityam*). (Pāṇini 2.4.10).

*Śūdrāṇāmaniravasitānām* (Pāṇini 2.4.10). For *śūdras* who are not excluded [from the community], a copulative compound (*dvandva*) shall be treated as singular. Examples: *takṣāyaskāram* (the carpenter and the blacksmith); *rajakatantuvāyam* (the washerman and the weaver). Here, the word *śūdra* refers to those other than the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*), and not specifically to the caste-nature of being a *śūdra*, because of the prohibition regarding those who are "not excluded" (*aniravasita*). The suffix *kta* is used here in the passive sense after the root *sī* preceded by the prefix *nirava*. *Niravasāna* means exclusion; and in this context, it is intended to mean exclusion from the [eating] vessel. Those by whom one has eaten, the vessel is not purified.

They are excluded from the vessels even by means of the purificatory rite prescribed by the authors of the Smṛtis, such as: "Bell-metal is purified by ash. What about those who have not been expelled? They are the Caṇḍālas and those who drink from the vessels of the dead. (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.4.11)

*Gavāśvaprabhṛtīni ca* (Pāṇini 2.4.11). These items, being *dvandva* compounds that have undergone singularization (*ekavadbhāva*), are correct. Examples: *gavāśvakam*, *gavāvikam*, *gavaiḍakam*, *ajāvikam*, *ajaiḍakam*. This rule is stated because the optional application of singularization for animal *dvandvas* would otherwise apply by default. Examples: *kubjavāmanam*, *kubjakairātam*, *putrapautram*, *śvacāṇḍālam*, *strīkumāram*, *dāsīmāṇavakam*, *uṣṭrakharam*, *śāṭīpracchadam*. Here, the recitation of words not denoting species of living beings is for the purpose of including multiple bases.

*Uṣṭraśaśam*, *mūtraśakṛt*, *mūtrapurīṣam*, *yakṛnmedaḥ*, *māṃsaśoṇitam*, *darbhapūtīkam*, *arjunapuruṣam*, *tṛṇolayam*, *dāsīdāsam*. Here, the rule *pumān striyā* (Pāṇini 1.2.67), which prescribes a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) when a masculine and a feminine noun are joined, does not apply. [Examples include: *kuṭīkuṭam*, *māṃsaśoṇitam*, and *bhāgavatībhāgavatam*. Regarding compounds beginning with *go* and *aśva*, there is the Vārttika: "In these cases, the Dvandva compound is formed according to the order in which the words are uttered."

The meaning is that in the *Gaṇapāṭha*, their specific forms are intended to be expressed, and the intent does not lie merely in the citation of the preceding and following words. Consequently, when the substitution of *avaṅ* is absent, it does not occur; as in: "Others than cows and horses are indeed non-animals; cows and horses are animals."

Pāṇini 2.4.12 states: *vibhāṣā vṛkṣamṛgatṛṇadhānyavyañjanapaśuśakunyaśvavaḍavapūrvāparādharottarāṇām*. The *dvandva* compound of the seven [categories] beginning with "trees" (*vṛkṣa*), as well as the three *dvandva*s beginning with "horse and mare" (*aśvavaḍava*), may optionally be singular. In the case of "trees" and the others, specific instances are included; for it is by means of the words "tree" and so forth that each individual *dvandva* is qualified. A single word "tree" is not itself a *dvandva*, nor is there the simultaneous employment of two [identical] words, because of the rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one).

The same applies to synonyms as well, because the formation of a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) is initiated even for dissimilar forms that possess the same meaning. Nor can one say "the tree and the *dhava* tree" (*vṛkṣaśca dhavaśca*), etc., because it has already been stated that the application of the *dvandva* compound is prohibited by rule between a general term and a particular term. Furthermore, one should not argue that this prohibition is non-obligatory because of the specific mention [in the rule] "among the Easterners and the Bharatas"; for even so, since usage such as "*vṛkṣadhavam*" is never observed, the prohibition itself remains operative in the present case. Therefore, it is established that only particulars are intended to be grasped here.

plakṣanyagrodham, plakṣanyagrodhāḥ; rurupṛṣatam, rurupṛṣatāḥ; kuśakāśam, kuśakāśāḥ; vrīhiyavam, vrīhiyavāḥ; dadhighṛtam, dadhighṛte; gomahiṣam, gomahiṣāḥ; tittirikapiñjalam, tittirikapiñjalāḥ; aśvabaḍavam, aśvavaḍavau; pūrvāparam, pūrvāpare; adharottaram, adharottare.

Regarding this, the *Vārttika* states: "The compound of *phala*, *senā*, *vanaspati*, *mṛga*, *śakuni*, *kṣudrajantu*, *dhānya*, and *tṛṇa* has many bases [but is singular]. The meaning is that for these, only a *dvandva* compound consisting of multiple bases is singular. This does not apply here in cases such as *badarāmalakau* (jujube and myrobalan), *rathikāśvārohau* (chariot-warriors and horsemen), or *plakṣanyagrodhau* (the *plakṣa* and *nyagrodha* trees). This *Vārttika* is supplementary to another rule and is not an independent prescriptive rule.

For if it were an injunction (*vidhi*), then if it were obligatory (*nitya*), it would—despite the multiplicity of constituents—apply obligatorily even to *vanaspati* and the like included in this sūtra, thereby overriding the optionality; whereas if they did not have multiple constituents, the optionality prescribed by the sūtra would apply. However, if it were optional (*vaikalpika*), then even for fruits and the like, it would override the obligatory singular collective formation (*ekavadbhāva*) obtained through other rules such as Pāṇini 2.4.6 (*nātiraprāṇinām*), and the optionality would instead apply when there is a multiplicity of constituents.

Nor should it be argued that the desired conclusion is already established by the observation of the *Bhāṣya* stating "badarāmalakaṃ, badarāmalakāni," for in that instance, "badarāmalakāni" is merely an occasional reading; furthermore, Kaiyaṭa has stated that even this reading is explained as follows: when "badarāmalakāni" is thus obtained, the obligatory singular collective form (*ekavadbhāva*) characterized by genus (*jāti*) applies. As for the alternative view mentioned by Kaiyaṭa—that an option is provided by this [sūtra] when the obligatory singular collective form would otherwise have applied—that is not the case here.

That [interpretation] is merely superficial, because it contradicts the subsequent Bhāṣya statement, "The *badara* and *āmalaka* fruits remain [as a dual]. For, if—as stated above—the present Vārttika were intended to prescribe an option (*vikalpa*) regarding compounds of many bases, then the obligatory singular treatment (*ekavadbhāva*) in other instances would be unavoidable; such is the direction of the argument.
(Pāṇini Sūtra 2.4.12)

Even in that case, if this were a residual rule (śeṣa) of that very [sūtra] because it is recited under "vibhāṣā vṛkṣa" (Pāṇini 2.4.12), then, although there would be no option regarding the non-multiplicity of the constituent bases in the case of *vanaspati* and so forth, the rule "jātiraprāṇinām" (Pāṇini 2.4.6) would apply as a permanent injunction (*nityavidhi*). Therefore, this is a residual rule for the entire section. Thus, when a *dvandva* compound of these—such as fruits and so on—becomes a singular unit either by this [present] rule or by another characteristic, it indeed possesses multiple constituent bases.

Therefore, in the case of "plakṣanyagrodhau," this option [of using the dual] does not apply as a compulsory rule under the rule *jātiraprāṇinām* (Pāṇini 2.4.6). The same applies to "vrīhiyavau," "kuśakāśau," and so forth.

However, regarding those [compounds] included in the present sūtra, the division of the scope is as follows: for those that do not denote living beings, since the rule *jātir aprāṇinām* (Pāṇini 2.4.6) applies obligatorily, an option is prescribed. And that [option] applies to them only with other members of their own class. Thus, when trees and so forth form a *dvandva* compound with others, there is either the obligatory application or the option according to the circumstances.
