For example, in the case of *vrīhikuśaplakṣam*, the rule *jātir aprāṇinām* (Pāṇini 2.4.6) applies obligatorily.

In the case of *plakṣaśabdasparśe* and *plakṣaśabdasparśāḥ*, however, the rule applies in both instances by virtue of Pāṇini 2.2.29: *cārthe dvandvaḥ*. Nor does the rule Pāṇini 2.4.6 (*jātiraprāṇinām*) apply here, because this is not a genus of substances (*adravyajātitvāt*). For it has been stated that the term *aprāṇinām* (of non-living beings) functions as a restrictive exclusion (*paryudāsa*). The mention of *paśu* (livestock), however, is for the purpose of setting aside the obligatory rule regarding the parts of an army (*senāṅga*), as exemplified by *hastyaśvādi*. Only the mention of *mṛgaśakuni* (wild animals and birds) remains to be addressed.

In this regard, the statement is expressed as follows: "A *dvandva* compound that is singular by virtue of the option (*vibhāṣā*) applies only to specific types of animals, and not to others. By this, it is established that for these [animals], when combined with others, there is only *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction). The same applies to the compounds *pūrvāparam* ("the former and the latter") and *adharottaram* ("the lower and the upper"). Although [the singularity] is already established because they are *paśu-dvandvas* (animal compounds), the specific mention of *aśvavaḍava* ("horse and mule") is for the purpose of a rule of direct prescription (*pratipadavidhi*).

In the case where there is a singular formation (*ekavadbhāva*), the rule *pūrvavadaśvavaḍavau* (Pāṇini 2.4.27) is superseded by *sa napuṃsakam* (Pāṇini 2.4.17). For the word *tat* refers to that which possesses the singular formation; thus, neuter gender is also established as being prescribed by the specific wording (*pratipadavihita*) for that which undergoes singular formation. However, the rule *pūrvavadaśvavaḍavau* applies in the alternative case where singular formation is absent: *aśvavaḍavau* (masculine dual), *aśvavaḍavān* (masculine plural).

(Pāṇini 2.4.13) *vipratiṣiddhaṃ cānadhikaraṇavāci* (Pāṇini 2.4.13). For words with contradictory meanings that do not denote substances (*adravyavācin*), a *dvandva* compound may optionally be singular. Here is the formulation of the rule: if a *dvandva* compound that is optionally singular is formed for words expressing contradictory meanings, then it must be only for those that do not denote substances. Consequently, for words denoting substances, there is only *itaretarayoga* (mutual connection). Example: *śītoṣṇe udake staḥ* ("cold and heat exist in the water"). Why "contradictory"? [Counter-example: *nandakapāñcajanyaṃ* ("the Nandaka and the Pāñcajanya [conch]").

In this case, even though the words denote substances (*dravya*), an optional compound in the sense of a collective (*samāhāra-dvandva*) certainly occurs. As for the counter-example "kāma-krodhau" (desire and anger) cited in the commentary, there too an optional singular form (*ekavadbhāva*) is unavoidable, just as in cases such as "śītoṣṇam" (cold and heat) or "sukhaduḥkham" (pleasure and pain). For it is established that the present sūtra is intended as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*).

Furthermore, if one were to assume that the intention [of the rule] is that the singular form occurs only for words denoting contradictory things when they do not denote substances (*adravyavācin*), this would contradict his own statement in the form of the question, "What is the purpose of [the condition] 'not denoting a substratum' (*anadhikaraṇavāci*)?"—given that in the example "cold and hot water" (*śītoṣṇe udake*), there would result the optional application of singular number (*ekavadbhāva*). It would also entail the violation of the natural sequence of the sūtra's wording. This is the general direction [of the argument]. (Pāṇini 2.4.14)

[The rule] *na dadhipayādīni* (Pāṇini 2.4.14) [applies]. These [pairs] shall not have a single form [by the elision of one member]. Examples: *dadhipayasī*, *madhusarpiṣī*, *sarpirmadhunī*. In these three cases, an option [to apply the rule for a single form] was obtained because they are seasonings (*vyañjana*). [However, this does not apply to: *brahmaprajāpatī*, *śivavaiśravaṇau*, *skandaviśākhau*. Nor should one suspect the application of the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) rule here based on the principle that it applies even to dissimilar forms (*virūpāṇām api*), as it is said:
"Skanda and Viśākha—these two sons were born."

Thus, because it has been determined that the *Mahābhārata* is not a mere enumeration (*paryāya*) [of names], the following pairs are established as *itaretara-yoga* (mutual conjunction) *dvandva* compounds by way of excluding them from being *samāhāra-dvandva* (collective) compounds: *parivrāj-kaushikau*, *pravargya-upasadau*, *shukla-kṛṣṇau*, *idhmā-barhiṣī* (the lengthening of the vowel occurs due to *nipātana*), *dīkṣā-tapasi*, *shraddhā-tapasi*, *medhā-tapasi*, *adhyayana-tapasi*, *ulūkhala-musale*, *ādya-avasāne*, *shraddhā-medhe*, *ṛk-sāme*, and *vāk-manase*. In this context, regarding *brahma-prajāpati* and so forth, the *itaretara-yoga* is established through the exclusion of the *samāhāra-dvandva*. This is due to their association with those [preceding examples].

The same applies to cases such as *dadhipayasī* (curd and milk). Therefore, one should not suspect that even though the optionality based on being consonants (*vyañjana*) has been prohibited there, the obligatory singular collective form (*ekavadbhāva*) characterized by genus (*jāti*) might still apply. Indeed, one should not suspect that the obligatory singular collective form characterized by genus might apply even when [the optionality] is prohibited. Furthermore, in the rule *ṣaṭsvasrādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.10), what was stated regarding the feminine is negated; it is negated in a general sense. And so he will say later: "But the fault lies in the dual number; therefore, 'both' is not [the case]."

Surely this would be so if there were a rule [vidhi] stating "of genus-names and names of living beings" (Pāṇini 2.4.6); however, that is a prohibition (niṣedha). And thus, because of that prohibition regarding both mutual conjunction (itaretarayoga) and collective aggregation (samāhāra) by that very sūtra under discussion, even the *dvandva* compound of items such as "curd and milk" (dadhipayas) would not be obtained.

To this it is replied: First, the two alternatives—that restrictive rules (*niyamavākya*) function either in the form of a positive injunction (*vidhi*) or in the form of a prohibition (*niṣedha*)—have been established in the *Pratyayalakṣaṇa* Sūtra and are supported by the *Bhāṣya* in rules such as *dyudbhyo luṅi* (Pāṇini 1.3.91). In that regard, since in rules such as *jātiraprāṇinām* (Pāṇini 2.4.6), one must resort to the alternative of functioning through a positive injunction (*vidhimukhatā*) in accordance with the requirements of the linguistic usage (*labhyānurodhena*), and since that [usage] is precluded by prohibitions such as *na dadhi* (Pāṇini 2.4.14), everything is well-established. (Pāṇini 2.4.15)

Regarding the rule *adhikaraṇaitāvattve ca* (Pāṇini 2.4.15): when the number of substances (*dravya*) is understood, the singular [form] would not apply. For example: *daśa dantoṣṭhāḥ* ("ten teeth and lips"). Now, it might be argued that it is established by logical principle (*nyāya*) that when the specific number of the items constituting the members of the compound is to be conveyed, only a *dvandva* with mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) is possible.

Otherwise, just as in the case of a *dvigu* compound such as "five or ten bundles of grass" (*pañcapūlyaḥ*, *daśapūlyaḥ*), the number ten would attach itself only to the aggregate (*samāhāra*) which is the primary element, and not to the individual members of the collection and so forth; what then would be the purpose of this prohibition? True, it is not by this rule that the *samāhāra-dvandva* is prohibited; rather, it is that very restriction—which dictates that for parts of living beings and the like, a *dvandva* must be an *samāhāra*—that is here prohibited. For if this prohibition did not exist, then in the case of "five [parts] here, namely face, belly, thigh, foot, and hand," the name *mādhukarī* (the honey-gathering bee-like alms-round) would now apply similarly to that.

In this way, there would be incorrectness (*asādhutva*) regarding such instances, because by the restrictive rule that [the *dvandva*] must be a collective compound (*samāhāra*) alone, the *dvandva* as a copulative compound (*itaretarayoga*) would be difficult to obtain. Consequently, the established meaning of the Sūtra is that there would be no restriction that when a number is understood, it must be expressed in the singular. Therefore, this [Sūtra] is intended as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) for the copulative *dvandva*. By this, in cases such as "ten teeth and lips" (*daśa dantoṣṭhāḥ*), since both the collective *dvandva* and the copulative *dvandva* would be difficult to obtain, the sentence itself should be employed.

This is refuted by the fact that both [possibilities] are prohibited: by the rule *adhikaraṇaitāvattve ca* and by the rule *prāṇyaṅgānāṃ samāhāra eva*. In cases such as "ten Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas," the *samāhāra-dvandva* must be prevented solely by the force of the reasoning previously stated.
(Pāṇini Sūtra 2.4.16)

The *vibhāṣā* (optionality) applies when proximity (*sāmīpya*) is the limiting factor for the quantity of the substratum (*adhikaraṇaitāvattva*). In such a case, there may be a restriction that the compound must be a collective (*samāhāra*) only; thus we have either *upadaśaṃ dantoṣṭham* ("the teeth and lips are near ten") or *upadaśā dantoṣṭhāḥ* ("the teeth and lips are nine or eleven"). The *avyayībhāva* compound, which is prescribed generally for any word ending in a case-suffix by the rule *avyayaṃ vibhakti* (Pāṇini 2.1.6), also occurs with numerals. However, the *bahuvrīhi* is specifically prescribed for this purpose by the rule *saṅkhyayāvyayāsannā* (Pāṇini 2.2.25).

In that regard, when the option for a single unified meaning (*ekavadbhāva*) is adopted, the *avyayībhāva* compound is subsequently applied. However, the state of having a single meaning (*ekārthatva*) is itself more intrinsic (*antaraṅga*) than the state of having a unified meaning; and within that unity of meaning, the *avyayībhāva* is predominant because it primarily expresses proximity (*sāmīpya*). Even though the *avyayībhāva* is devoid of number (*niḥsaṅkhya*), its unity of meaning should nevertheless be understood as consisting in the absence of differentiation. As for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), it arises from the intention to express non-difference between the proximity and that which possesses it. Furthermore, the limitation of the substratum (*adhikaraṇaitāvattva*) results from the intention to express non-difference between the aggregate (*samāhāra*) and that which constitutes the aggregate (*samāhārin*).

In the alternative view, however, when there is a plurality of referents (*bahu-artha*), only a *bahuvrīhi* compound is employed as the subsequent member (*anuprayoga*). Its status as having a plurality of referents arises because the proximate element (*samīpin*) is predominant. If, on the other hand, only an *avyayībhāva* were employed in both cases, then because it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), there would be an absence of plurality, and thus the plural number would not occur. Or, even if that [plural number] were present, once the *na-lopa* (elision of *na*) had been applied, the form would not be *upadaśāḥ*. But if a *bahuvrīhi* alone is employed as the subsequent member, then the genitive case would occur—as in *upadaśasya pāṇipādasya*—whereas one intends for it to be *upadaśaṃ pāṇipādasya*. Therefore, the previously stated [view] alone is elegant. (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.4.17)

"An aggregate (samāhāra) is neuter" (Pāṇini 2.4.17). A *dvigu* compound and a *dvandva* compound denoting an aggregate shall be neuter. This is an exception to the rule that the gender of a compound follows the gender of its final member (*paravalliṅga*). Examples: *pañcagavam* ("a collection of five cows"), *dantoṣṭham* ("teeth and lips"). Since the term "aggregate" is already understood from the context of this section, the explicit mention of "this" (*sa*) is for the purpose of including even those *dvandva* compounds denoting aggregates that are not explicitly mentioned within this specific section. Thus, it is stated in the rule "for *yu* and *vu*, [substitute] *an* and *ak*" (Pāṇini 7.1.1): if *yu* and *vu* were taken as a *dvandva* compound denoting an aggregate, they would become neuter by virtue of the rule "an aggregate is neuter" (Pāṇini 2.4.17).

For this very reason, it is stated: "Technical terms and paribhāṣās [apply] at the time of their operation. (Kātyāyana’s Vārttika). A *dvigu* compound whose final member ends in *a* is desired in the feminine. Under the governing rule *ataḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.91), the prescription of the suffix *ṅīp* by the rule *dvigoḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.21) is the indicator (*liṅga*) for this case. Example: *pañcamūlī*. [Kātyāyana’s Vārttika: "A [dvigu] ending in *vā* [is optionally feminine]. Example: *pañcakhaṭvī*, *pañcakhaṭvī*, or *pañcakhaṭvam*. In the alternative where femininity applies, there is the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upasarjana-hrasvatva*). [Kātyāyana’s Vārttika: "In a *dvigu* in the feminine, there is the elision of the *n* of a stem ending in *an*, and the suffix is optional. Examples: *pañcatakṣam*, *pañcatakṣī*.

Because of the prohibition of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* rule by the metarule "and when it is the latter member of a compound, [the rule] regarding what is not the beginning of a word applies" (*kāovāo*), there is an absence of *pada*-status; thus, the mention of the elision of *n* is made. This is a prohibition for those ending in *pātra* and so forth: *pañcapātram*, *tribhuvanam*, *caturyugam*, *dvisamāsam*. The group beginning with *pātra* is an *ākṛtigaṇa*. (Pāṇini 2.4.18)

*Avyayībhāvaś ca* (Pāṇini 2.4.18). This [compound] shall be neuter. Examples: *adhistri*, *unmattagaṅgam*. Since it was previously stated that an *avyayībhāva* whose prior member is predominant is without gender (*aliṅga*), whereas one whose other member (the subsequent member) is predominant would take the gender of its qualifier (*viśeṣyaliṅgatva*), this rule is now stated. The particle *ca* (and) is for the purpose of including what has not been mentioned. Its result is seen in the *Kārikāvākya*: "After *puṇya* and *sudina*, [the word] *ahan* [becomes neuter]. Thus: *puṇyāham*, *sudināham*. In the case of a *karmadhāraya*, [the suffix] *ṭac* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.4.91: "After *rājan*, *ahan*, and *sakhi* [the suffix *ṭac* is added]."

This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule *rātrānhāhāḥ puṃsi* (Pāṇini 2.4.29). The word *sudina* denotes that which is praiseworthy (*praśasta*). Accordingly, it is employed [in the following verse]: "On auspicious days (*sidināsu*), this work of the assembly should be recited especially by one who is learned, and by oneself as well."

Therefore, one should not suspect a contradiction in the simultaneous use of the words *dina* and *ahaḥ* here. Regarding the rule *pathaḥ saṅkhyāvyayādeḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.74), which prescribes the suffix *aC*, we have *tripatham* (the path of three). *Vipatha* (a bad path) is a *prādi*-compound. How then is the Amarakośa consistent with its statement: "Also *atipanthaḥ* and *supanthaḥ*" (Amara 2.1.16)? It is explained thus: the word *pathaḥ* [in the rule] refers to the form ending in the samāsānta suffix; the meaning is that the word *patha*, when it ends in the samāsānta suffix and follows a numeral or an indeclinable (*avyaya*), is neuter.

Regarding the reading *pathaḥ klībatā*, it should be understood that because the word *patha* (in compounds such as *saṅkhyādi-patha*) invariably takes the suffix *a* [as a samāsānta], by association with it, even indeclinables (*avyaya*) and others of that kind are understood to be taken only when they likewise possess that suffix. Thus, the *Klībaliṅgakārikā* states: "The word *patha* [takes the neuter gender] when following a numeral or an indeclinable. However, there is no such suffix here [in the case of *satpatha*], due to the prohibition in Pāṇini’s sūtra 5.4.69: *na pūjanāt*. How then is the usage "satpathaścārcite'dhvani" (and *satpatha* means a respected road) to be explained? It is because of the specific enumeration [of words] with *su* and *ati* alone [as taking the suffix]. Now, how is this—?

Regarding this entry in the *Amara-kośa* (Aokoo2-1-16), Kṣīrasvāmin, Durghaṭavṛtti, and others state that the reading should be *vipatham* and *kāpatham*, in accordance with the *Liṅgakārikā* and other authorities. However, if this were the case, then the neuter gender found even in the *Rabhasa-kośa*—in its verse "the two, *vipatha* and *kāpatha*, are in the masculine"—would have to be regarded as a mere scribal error (*prāmādika*). In reality, however, from the root *pat* (to go) with the suffix *ac* (pacādyac), one who traverses or pervades is called *patha*; thus, this word ends in the vowel *a*. Accordingly, the *Trikāṇḍaśeṣa* states: "The words *vāṭa*, *patha*, and *mārga* are synonyms for road."

Therefore, there is no masculine gender in the compound. Nor should it be argued that even if *vipatha* were thus established, *kāpatha* would not exist because the substitution of *kā-* would be difficult to obtain; for that [substitution] is possible by the rule *īṣadarthe ca* (Pāṇini 6.3.105), since [in this case] the sense of censure results from the meaning. As for what Mādhava stated—that if a form ending in *a* were accepted, the sūtra *patho vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 5.4.72) would become redundant—[that objection is refuted].

In this regard, the following is the solution: By the force of the specific mention of the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) in the rule *apathaṃ napuṃsakam* (Pāṇini 2.4.30), the application of the rule *nañastatpuruṣāt* (Pāṇini 5.4.71) is necessarily set aside. Nor is that [mention of *apatham*] a reference to a stem ending in *a*, for if it were, then by the same logic in the rule *pathaḥ saṅkhyāvyayādeḥ* (Kātyāyana-vārttika), forms such as *apathaḥ*, *vipathaḥ*, and *kāpathaḥ* would fail to be established.

Furthermore, after the sūtra *rātrānhāhāḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.29), a vārttika is recited in the sūtra *apathaṃ napuṃsakam* (Pāṇini 2.4.30). Thus, in accordance with the context, it is logical that the reference is made precisely to the form where the samāsānta suffix has been applied, as this is established by tradition. For this reason, Kaiyaṭa, suspecting that the purpose of the sūtra *apathaṃ napuṃsakam* is already covered by the vārttika, states that there is no fault because the sūtra is an ancient [independent] rule (*prācyatvāt*).

This being the case, it should be noted that the rule *patho vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 5.4.72) is intended to establish the form *apanthāḥ*, and thus there is no contradiction between the earlier and later statements of Amara.

Let us return to the subject at hand—this prescription of the neuter gender is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule of taking the gender of the final member (*paravalliṅgatā*). Consequently, it does not apply in the case of the *bahuvrīhi* compound *vipathā nagarī* ("the city beyond the path"), nor even in *atipathā* ("having transcended the path"). For in these cases, the rule "In *dvigu*, *prāpta*, *āpanna*, *alaṃpūrva*, and compounds with a *gati* as the first member, [the neuter gender] does not [apply]" (Kāśikāvṛtti) prohibits the taking of the gender of the final member. If this is so, how is Kaiyaṭa’s statement—that upon taking *utpatham* as the illustrative example, it is a *tatpuruṣa* by the rule "A *ku* or a *gati* [is compounded with another word]" (Pāṇini 2.2.18)—not contradicted?

This is not so; for in that case, the analysis (*vigraha*) is not "the path has risen" (*patha udgataḥ*) and so forth, but rather "an excellent path" (*utkṛṣṭaḥ panthā*). And thus, the rule for the gender of the final member (*paravalliṅga*) would indeed apply. Therefore, it is established that this prescription of gender applies only when the meaning of the final member is predominant. This is clear in the work of Mādhava. As for the example *supatham* cited in the *Vṛtti*, Mādhava maintains that there the word *su* means "extensiveness" (*vaipulya*) and not "praise," and thus the compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) is applied.

Since an action (*kriyā*) is of a non-substantial nature (*asattvarūpa*), it follows that its qualifiers would likewise lack gender. Regarding this, they say that although this statement was not included in the *Vārttika*, it was nevertheless formulated by the author of the *Vṛtti*. Examples are: *mṛdu pacati* (he cooks softly) and *prathamaṃ pacati* (he cooks first). Alternatively, this is established by the rule: "The neuter is used for the general" (*sāmānye napuṃsakam*). For this very reason, this [rule] does not apply to words with fixed genders (*niyataliṅga*). Example: *ādiṃ pacati* (he cooks the beginning). The meaning is: he performs that softening (*viklitti*) which constitutes the beginning.

The accusative case ending (*dvitīyā*) is used because [the word *bhāvanā*] functions as the object (*karman*) with respect to the "appropriation of the elements" (*dhātūpāttabhāvanā*), or because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that [object]. For this very reason, the author of the *Mahābhāṣya* states in the rule *sakṛllvau* that "the *yaṇ* [substitution] occurs after a [word ending in] a kāraka. Nor should one fear that all kārakas would consequently become neuter because they are adverbs (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), for kārakas are essentially the meanings expressed by case endings (*vibhakti*). Although the substratum of power (*śaktyādhāra*) is indeed a substance (*dravya*) and the meaning of a nominal stem (*nāmārtha*), [this does not preclude their status as kārakas].

Nevertheless, it is not a qualifier of the action itself, but rather a qualifier of the *kāraka* (participant) that has become a qualifier of the action; this is how it should be understood. For this very reason, the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that the meaning of a noun does not connect with the meaning of a verbal root through a relation of difference (*bheda*).

Even in expressions such as *stokaṃ pacyate* ("a little is being cooked"), there is no denotation of the rice (*taṇḍula*) and so forth as something pervaded by the meaning of the verbal root; rather, it is not even included within the scope of the root. This is because, by the force of the qualifier in the rule *bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.69), the term "object" (*karman*) is understood to refer to an external object, and since the same conclusion follows for the rule *laḥ karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 3.4.69). Therefore, that which is included within the scope of the root is qualified only by a word ending in the accusative case, and not by a word ending in the nominative case conditioned by its having been already denoted (*abhihitatva*).

Nor is there a genitive case characterized by connection with a *kṛt*-suffix in the expression "the cooker of a small amount of rice" (*stokam odanasya paktā*); however, where a specific meaning of the verbal root is construed as an instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to the productive operation (*bhāvanā*), there the qualifiers must necessarily end in the instrumental case, as in "one should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma. This is clear from the commentary on the rule *karaṇe yajaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.85) in both the *Vṛtti* and the *Padamañjarī*.

Nor should it be argued that, in this case, the injunction "one should sacrifice properly with the Jyotiṣṭoma" would be untenable; for that is indeed tenable when [the adverb] functions as a qualifier of the productive operation (bhāvanā). In that context, the word must end in the nominative case. However, since the action itself may be treated as an artificial object (*karma*) because it is pervaded by acts such as seeing or praying, the accusative case is used even when it qualifies that [action], as in the rule stating that qualifiers of an action take the neuter gender. Furthermore, the singular number is also the general rule (*utsarga*).

In examples such as *hataśāyikāḥ śayyante*, even though the plural number occurs, this is because it will be explained under the rule *sārvadhātuke yak* (Pāṇini 3.1.67). This is the general direction [of the argument]. As for the use of the neuter gender in expressions like *prātaḥkamanīyam* when qualifying an indeclinable (*avyaya*), although the neuter gender is the same, nevertheless only the nominative singular is used and not the accusative singular, because there is no sense of being an object (*karmatā*). However, in the case of *prātarādi*, the gender is indeed fixed; this is the general direction.

Although these Vārttikas are recited in the Bhāṣya under the rule "apathaṃ napuṃsakam" (Pāṇini 2.4.30), they have nevertheless been explained here in accordance with the Vṛtti, with the intention that they are intended to explain the meaning indicated by the particle *ca* in the rule "avyayībhāvaśca" (Pāṇini 4.3.59). (Pāṇini 2.4.19)

"A *tatpuruṣa* [compound] that is neither *nañ* nor *karmadhāraya*" (Pāṇini 2.4.19). This is an introductory heading (*adhikāra*). The word *karmadhāraya* here refers primarily to the state of being a *karmadhāraya*. It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound containing a *dvandva* within it, with the negative particle *nañ*: the meaning is that a *tatpuruṣa* is one in which both the negative particle (*nañ*) and the state of being a *karmadhāraya* (*karmadhārayatva*) do not exist. He will state later: "Optionally, [compounds ending in] *senā*, *surā*, etc. (Pāṇini 2.4.25). Why say "*tatpuruṣa*"? [Consider: *dṛḍhaseno rājā* ("the king Dṛḍhasena"). Why say "devoid of *nañ*"? [Consider: *asenā* ("without an army"). Why say "devoid of the state of being a *karmadhāraya*"? [Consider: *paramasenā* ("the supreme army").

We shall explain later in the *Madhyama-sūtras* itself that this topic is not very useful there. (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.4.20): "In the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*), [the word] *kanthā* [is neuter] among the *Uśīnara*s. A *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in *kanthā* is neuter if it is the name of a *kanthā* (woolen cloth) produced in the country of the *Uśīnara*s. For example: the descendants of Suśama are the *Sauśamayas*; their *kanthā* is *sauśamikantham*. Why "in the sense of a name"? [Consider: *vīraṇakanthā* (a mat made of *vīraṇa* grass). Why "among the *Uśīnara*s"? [Consider: *dākṣikanthā* (the *kanthā* of Dakṣi). Here, a beginningless (*anādi*) name is understood.

And that [compound] among the Uśīnaras is a *tatpuruṣa* distinct from that [previous type], consisting of a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), and there is no *karmadhāraya* here; this is the result of the limited scope [of the rule].
(Pāṇini Sūtra 2.4.21)

*Upajñopakramantatadādyācikhyāsāyām* (Pāṇini 2.4.21). That which is known (*upajñāyate*) is an *upajñā*. The suffix *aṅ* is applied in the sense of the object by the rule *ātaścopasarge* (Pāṇini 3.1.136). That which is undertaken (*upakramyate*) is an *upakrama*; the suffix *ghañ* is applied in the sense of the object. By the rule *nodāttapadeśasya* (Pāṇini 7.3.34), the prohibition of *vṛddhi* applies. A *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in *upajñā* or *upakrama* shall be neuter when one intends to express the beginning—that is, the priority—of those two, namely the *upajñā* or the *upakrama*.

"A work whose discovery is by Pāṇini" is *pāṇinyupajñaṃ granthaḥ*; "kindness whose beginning is with you" is *tvadupakramaṃ saujanyam*. Here, it is made known that in the derivation of words (*śabdavyutpatti*), the speaker’s intention alone (*vivakṣā*) is the regulating factor, and not the actual state of things (*vastusthiti*). Therefore, when there is merely an intention to express a relationship of action [rather than a relationship of origin], one does not say, for example, *devadattopajño rathaḥ* ("a chariot whose discovery is by Devadatta"). In this case, without a genitive tatpuruṣa compound, the result of the governing rule (*adhikāraphala*) would not be obtainable because the status of being "that which begins with him" (*tadāditva*) would not be understood. (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.4.21–22).

*Chāyā* [is neuter] when there is multiplicity (Pāṇini 2.4.22). A *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in *chāyā* shall be neuter if it denotes a multitude of shadows. This implies that the word *chāyā* follows a preceding member which presents those obscuring substances which, by coming together, produce a shadow that serves as a means of subsistence for many. For this very reason, the governing rule (*adhikāra*) does not apply here [to the subsequent rules]. *Ikṣūṇāṃ chāyā* = *ikṣucchāyam*. This is an exception to the optional rule beginning with *vibhāṣā senā* (Pāṇini 2.4.25).

How then is the expression *ikṣucchāyāniṣādinyaḥ* (RV 10.74.20) to be explained? It is said: the elision of the prefix *ā-* must be understood here, meaning "seated all around" (*āsamantān niṣādinyaḥ*). According to Pāṇini 2.4.23, *sabhā rājāmanuṣyapūrvā*: a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in *sabhā*, when preceded by a word for "king" (*rājan*) or a word that is not a human being (*amanuṣya*), shall be neuter. For example: *inasabham* ("the assembly of the Lord"), *īśvarasabham* ("the assembly of the Sovereign"). This is intended only for synonyms [of "king"]. Thus, there is a split-compound (*cheda*) as *a-rājā*. By the maxim of "negation joined with 'iva' or a similar term," the word *arājā* is taken to mean one who resembles a king, that is, a synonym for "king. Therefore, it does not apply here in cases such as *rājasabhā* ("the king's assembly") or *candraguptasabhā* ("Candragupta’s assembly").

How is it that in the *Kīcakavadha* we find the phrase “*nṛpatisāmagamanna vepamānā*” (*Māgha-bhāṣya*)? Rakṣita explains that this is because *nṛpati* denotes a specific type of king, similar to *gajapati*. Alternatively, having first formed a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning “a hall (*sabhā*) whose lord (*pati*) is a man (*nṛ*),” a subsequent *karmadhāraya* is applied. Because the rule *anañ-karmadhārayaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.19) continues to apply, there is no neuter gender. The word *amanuṣya*, by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), refers to Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and the like; thus, *rakṣaḥ-sabham* [is valid]. However, because the conventional meaning is absent here, *kāṣṭha-sabhā* [is not so used]. (Pāṇini 2.4.24).

And [the word] *aśālā* (Pāṇini 2.4.24). The word *sabhā* denotes both a "hall" (*śālā*) and an "assembly" (*saṅghāta*). In that regard, when preceded by *rājan* or a non-human [term], the neuter gender of the preceding member was stated by the previous rule; however, for that which denotes an assembly, this [rule] prescribes [the neuter gender]. For example: *strīsabham*, meaning "an assembly of women" or "a group of women. Why say "not a hall"? Consider *anāthasabhā*, meaning "a hut for the destitute. (Pāṇini 2.4.25)

Pāṇini Sūtra 2.4.25: *vibhāṣā senā-surā-cchāyā-śālā-niśānām*. For a *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in these [words], there may optionally be neuter gender: *brāhmaṇasenam*, *brāhmaṇasenā*; *yavasuram*, *yavasurā*; *kuḍyacchāyam*, *kuḍyacchāyā*; *gośālam*, *gośālā*; *śvaniśam*, *śvaniśā*. They say that *śvaniśā* refers to the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa-caturdaśī*), for it is well known that dogs dwell (*upavasanti*) on that day. Regarding this, the Śābara-bhāṣya on the section concerning animals states: "We see that dogs dwell on the fourteenth day. (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.4.26).

In a *dvandva* and a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the gender of the final member alone shall prevail. For example: *kukkuṭamayūryāvimau* (this pair consists of a cock and a peahen), *mayūrīkukkuṭāvimau* (this pair consists of a peahen and a cock); and *ardhapippalī* (half of a long pepper).

This might be the case: if by this [rule] the fact that the gender of a compound follows the gender of its final member (*paravalliṅgatva*) were being extended [to other compounds], then by the rule *pūrvavadaśvavaḍavau* (Pāṇini 2.4.27) as well, for the sake of logical consistency (*nyāyasāmyāt*), it would have to be extended to the compound itself. Consequently, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* would be heard, because even though the meaning of the compound is masculine, the femininity of the meaning of the final member (*uttarapadārtha*) has not departed. As for the claim that there is a shortening [of the vowel] by the rule *gaustriyoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.2.48), [that is incorrect].

That is not so; for in the rule *cārthe dvandvaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.2.29), although all members are indicated in the nominative case, they lack the designation of *upasarjana* because of the governing rule *anekam* [which applies to multiple words], and because that designation is etymological (*anvartha*). Precisely for this reason, it is stated that there is no shortening [of the vowel] in the compound *rājakumārī* (king’s daughter). And for this very reason, there is no shortening in *kukkuṭamayūryau* (cock and peahen). Now, one might object: let the etymological nature of the designation be disregarded; thus, the form *aśvavaḍavau* would be established.

In the case of *rājakumārī kukkuṭamayūryau* ("the princess and the two—cock and peahen"), however, once the shortening (*hrasva*) has been applied, [the feminine suffix] is restored again from the feminine affix (*strīpratyaya*). Thus, the form is established. As it has been said: "The gender of the subsequent [member applies] to both the word and its meaning. For indeed, by the term *liṅga*, both the suffix denoting gender and the meaning are understood, because of the adoption of the principle of *tantra* (simultaneous application). And thus, the gender of the compound as a whole—whether it be a *dvandva* or a *tatpuruṣa*—shall be like that of the subsequent member; likewise, the suffix denoting that [gender] shall be like that of the subsequent member. This is the meaning of the sūtra.

And thus, in cases such as "substance and quality" (*dravyaguṇau*) or "quality and action" (*guṇakarmaṇī*), where a suffix denoting gender cannot occur, only the meaning is extended by analogy (*atideśa*). But when both are possible, both are [extended], as in "cock and peahen" (*kukkuṭamayūryau*). Consequently, even though the original (*aupadeśika*) form has a short vowel, there will be the hearing of the [long] vowel resulting from the analogical extension. Nor should a short vowel be suspected again, because [the compound] is not a subordinate member (*anupasarjana*) and because anything other than that is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadikatva*).

Nor should it be argued that even in cases such as *dattāgārgyāyaṇyau* and *dattākārīṣagandhye*, once the shortening has been applied, the suffixes *phak* and *yaṅ* would arise again from the compound; for this is not the case, since by the rule *bhasyāṭaḍhe taddhite* (Kāśikā Vārttika), the previously produced *y* can be elided, which is the desired result. This is incorrect, because in the case of *dattā ca yuvatiśca dattāyuvatī*, there would result the undesirable hearing of two *ti*-suffixes (*tip*), since *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine substitution) is impossible there due to the presence of the *abha* designation.

Therefore, it is established that there is no status as a subordinate member (*upasarjanatva*) in a *dvandva* compound precisely because [the term] is etymologically significant (*anvarthatva*). Consequently, in the case of "aśvavaḍavau," another means must be stated for the removal of the feminine suffix.

To this it is replied: In the rule *vibhāṣā vṛkṣamṛga* (Pāṇini 2.4.12), the elision of the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is prescribed as a nipātana (irregularity) in the case of *aśvavaḍavā*. As it has been said: "If it is argued that the gender [of the compound] would be other than that of its constituents, the statement regarding the elision of *ṭāp* in *aśvavaḍavā* is established by way of nipātana. Furthermore, there is the metarule: "A prohibition must be stated for *dvigu*, *prāpta*, *āpanna*, *alaṃpūrva*, and *gati* compounds. For example: *pañcakapālaḥ puroḍāśaḥ* ("a sacrificial cake prepared in five potsherds"), *prāptajīvikaḥ* ("one who has obtained a livelihood"), and *āpannajīvikaḥ* ("one who has entered upon a livelihood").

*alaṅkumāriḥ* (one who has no interest in girls), *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* (one who has departed from Kauśāmbī). However, this [rule] is rejected in the Bhāṣya. For it is said: the mention of *tatpuruṣa* need not be made; let it simply be that "the gender of a *dvandva* is like that of its final member. How then do we account for *pūrvakāyaḥ* (the front part of the body) and *arddhapiplī* (half a long pepper)? Even the *ekadeśisamāsa* (partitive compound) need not be commenced. This is simply a *karmadhāraya*: "that which is both prior and a body," and "that which is both half and a long pepper. Consequently, by virtue of the predominance of the meaning of the final member, the gender of the compound follows that of the final member.

Nor should it be said that the *ekadeśi-samāsa* (part-whole compound) must necessarily be formulated for the purpose of precluding the *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa* (genitive compound); for this is not desired by the author of the Sūtras, and because of non-expression (*anabhidhāna*). To explain: in the rule *dvitīyatṛtīya-* (Pāṇini 2.2.3), the inclusion of the term *anyatarasyām* indicates that even the author of the Sūtras does not desire a *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa* there; furthermore, it has already been stated that the author of the Bhāṣya also does not desire a *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa* with the word *ardha*. As for the case of *pūrvāpara*, however, a *ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa* will not occur due to non-expression.

Moreover, this rejection [of the suffix] is weak, because it has been stated in the Bhāṣya itself regarding the rule for the suffix *san* that "resorting to non-expression is the resort of those who have no other way" (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.7).

*Pūrvavad-aśva-vadavau* (Pāṇini 2.4.27). The dual number is not mandatory (*atantram*). This is an extension of the meaning (*arthātideśa*), serving as an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule regarding the gender of the subsequent member (*paravalliṅgatā*). Examples include *aśvavaḍavau*, *aśvavaḍavān*, and *aśvavaḍavair javanaiḥ*. However, in the case of a collective compound (*samāhāradvandva*) under the rule *vibhāṣā vṛkṣa-* (Pāṇini 2.4.12), the form *sa napuṃsakam* (Pāṇini 2.4.17) applies exclusively. This is because the specific mention of *aśvavaḍavau* is intended for the purpose of referring back [to this specific pair] by means of the pronoun *tat*; otherwise, since the result would have been established by the mention of *paśu* alone, its inclusion would be redundant, as has been stated. (Pāṇini 2.4.28)

In the Vedic language (*chandas*), the terms *hemanta* and *śiśira* [form a dvandva compound] as well as *ahar* and *rātra*. The term "as before" (*pūrvavat*) is understood here. Thus, *hemanta* and *śiśira* form the compound *hemantaśiśirau*. Here, this should be noted: the word *śiśira* is used in both the masculine and neuter genders. Accordingly, in the rule *cakravajrāndhakāra-* (Pāṇini 2.4.30), the venerable Pāṇini states: "darkness and *śiśira* are neuter. Amara also says: "Hemanta and *śiśira* are not feminine" (Amara-kośa 1.4.19).

And thus, in this very sūtra, [the form] *ahorātrāḥ* attains the masculine gender by the rule *rātrānhāhāḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.29). Its dual ending is internal; it prescribes the dual for *ahorātra*. Nor should it be said that this is established through *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) from a collective *dvandva* compound, because even in that case, the masculine gender will be stated in a subsequent sūtra. It will be stated that there is a reversal of gender in the Vedic language (*chandas*), and this is its detailed elaboration. But in common usage (*loka*), however, [the forms] *hemantaśiśirau* [are used] when referring to suffering, and *ahorātrau* when referring to merit. (Pāṇini 2.4.29)

*rātrānhāhāḥ puṃsi* (Pāṇini 2.4.29): compounds ending in these [words]—namely *rātri*, *ahan*, and *ahar*—are masculine only. The first part of the night is *pūrvarātraḥ*. This is a *ekadeśisamāsa* (compound denoting a part of a whole). The suffix *ac* is added as a compound-ending by the rule *ahaḥ sarvaikadeśa-* (Pāṇini 5.4.87). Thus, *pūrvāhṇaḥ*. By the rule *rājāhaḥsakhibhyaṣṭac* (Pāṇini 5.4.91), the suffix *ṭac* is applied. By the rule *anho'nh etebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.88), the substitute *anhan* is used for *ahan*. By the rule *anho'dantāt* (Pāṇini 8.4.7), the substitution of *ṇ* occurs. Thus, *dvyahaḥ*.

In the rule *na saṃkhyādeḥ samāhāre* (Pāṇini 5.4.89), there is an absence of the substitution of *an*. By the rule *anhaṣṭakhoreva* (Pāṇini 6.4.185), there is the elision (*ṭilopa*) of the final vowel. This rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule regarding the gender of the subsequent member (*paravalliṅga*). However, in the commentary (*vṛtti*), it is stated that "these are masculine. In that context, the meaning should be understood as "those ending in these [words]. As for the argument that once the words beginning with *rātra* have been made masculine by this rule, the gender of the compound ending in them is established simply by the rule *paravalliṅgam* (Pāṇini 2.4.26)—that is not correct, because in the case of a collective compound (*samāhāra*), the neuter gender would otherwise result.

For the exception to its being neuter is the rule *sa napuṃsakam* (Pāṇini 2.4.17). Nor can it be argued that its neuter gender is merely a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), because that would contradict the examples given by the author of the Vṛtti, namely *dvirātraḥ* and *trirātraḥ*. For that [usage] has been explained by everyone as a *dvigu* compound in the sense of a collective (*samāhāra*). Even Amarasimha employed it thus: *tena tu triṃśadahorātraḥ* (Amarakośa 1.4.12).

Thus it is said: "By a month [of thirty days], there shall be a day-and-night" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.22). Therefore, this rule for the masculine gender applies specifically to that which ends in such a compound. Although, by virtue of proximity, this is an exception only to the rule regarding the gender of the subsequent member (*paravalliṅgatā*), nevertheless, because it is a later rule, it subverts the neuter gender.

In this regard, the following should be considered: while the masculine gender may apply to the term *ahorātraḥ* according to the method stated above, the masculine gender asserted by the author of the Vṛtti, Haradatta, and others for *dvirātra* and similar compounds is inconsistent; for in those cases, there is no rule prescribing a specific neuter gender. Thus states the sūtra of the Liṅgānuśāsana: "The words *āpatha*, *puṇya*, and so forth, are neuter" (Liṅgasūtra 132), and "A word for night preceded by a numeral [is neuter]" (Liṅgasūtra 132).

Amarasiṃha also says: "The word *rātra* [forming a compound] preceded by a numeral" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.2.25), and "The word *gaṇarātra* [is used for] many nights" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.6). Regarding [the words] *anuvāka* and so forth, it should be stated that they are masculine (*puṃsi vaktavyam*). Examples: *anuvākaḥ*, *śaṃyuvākaḥ*, *sūktavākaḥ*. These are technical names for specific types of sentences. Since these would otherwise be neuter as they end in the suffix *ghañ* used in the sense of the object (*karman*), this rule is stated [to establish their masculinity]. (Pāṇini 2.4.30)

*Apatham* is neuter (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 2.4.30). This word shall be neuter when it occurs in a *tatpuruṣa* compound; however, in other compounds, we have *apatho deśaḥ* (a pathless region) and *apathā nagarī* (a city without a path). Because the form is specified here as ending in the *samāsānta* suffix [with the elision of the final syllable], it does not apply here in the case of *apanthāḥ*. *Ardharcāḥ* are both masculine and neuter (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 2.4.31). Words beginning with *ardharca* may be used in the masculine or the neuter. These are collected in the *Gaṇaratna*; for example: [The list follows: ardharca, māṇavaka, chātraka, vṛndāraka, yūthaka, dhāraka, kuṇḍala, kaṭaka, śaṅkha, śikhara, gṛha, sāra, nicaya, viṭapa, pustaka, kuṭīra, maṇḍapa, droṇa, karṇa, pātra, kamaṇḍalu, khalīna, kapāṭa, kaparda, khaṇḍa, dara, dāḍima, nidāgha, niryāsa, pravāla, bhūta, bhavana, bhāga, bhāgya, bhājana, bhasman, maṅgala, mukuṭa, muṇḍa, yauvana, rajata, ratha, taṭa, viṭapa, viśāla, śukra, śukla, śubhra, śṛṅga, śvabhra, saktu, sārathi, stamba, sthapati, snāna, hṛda, hṛdaya. (Note: The specific items in the *gaṇa* are listed above.)

The words *ardharca*, *dhvaja*, *kuñja*, *śīdhu*, *madhava*, *varcas*, *kūrca*, *āḍhaka*, *paṅka*, *anīka*, *pināka*, *niṣka*, *kapaṭa*, *aṣṭaṅka*, *kirīṭa*, *kuṭa*, *kūṭa*, *kaṅkaṭa*, *karvaṭa*, *aṇḍa*, *śakaṭa*, *valmīka*, *sānu*, *unaṭa*, *khaṇḍa*, *udyoga*, *viḍaṅga*, *śṛṅga*, *saraka*, *puṅkha*, *vraja*, and *modaka* [are masculine]. The word *madhu* is of two genders (*dviliṅga*) when it means nectar (*makaranda*), wine (*madya*), and honey (*mākṣika*). It denotes nectar, wine, and also honey.
"By virtue of its inclusion in the *ardharca* group [of stems], the word *madhu* is used in both the masculine and neuter genders."

Thus says Śāśvata. However, Amara states: "Mārdvīka and madhu [are neuter], but not in the two genders. But *caitra* and *daitra* are masculine only. *Varcaska* means feces; *kūrca* means a long beard; *āḍhaka* is a specific measure of capacity; *paṅka* means mud or sin; *anīka* means an army; *pināka* refers to the bow or trident of Rudra; *niṣka* is an ornament; *kapaṭa* is a pretext; *ṭaṅka* is a stone-cutter's chisel; *kirīṭa* is a crown; *kuṭa* is a jar; *kūṭa* means a heap or deceit; *kaṅkaṭa* is armor.

*Karvaṭa*: a village surrounded by rivers and the like; *kheṭaka*: a village; *aṇḍa*: the laying of eggs by birds and other creatures; *naṭa*: a specific type of dancer; *khaṇḍa*: a product of sugarcane and a fragment; *udyoga*: exertion or enthusiasm; *viḍaṅga*: a medicinal herb; *saraka*: liquor; the rest are well known. *Śoka*: a paste for the head and a heap of awns; *śulka*: toll or tax; *nidāgha*: summer heat; *nakha*: nail; *bāṇa*: arrow; *droṇa*: a measure; *suvarṇa*: gold; *bhūṣaṇa*: ornament; *raṇa*: battle; *kārṣāpaṇa*: a coin; *toraṇa*: an arched gateway; *kāṇḍa*: section, arrow, or stalk; *tāṇḍava*: a type of dance; *daṇḍa*: staff or punishment; *maṇḍa*: scum or essence; *piṭaka*: a small box or boil; *sakta*: flour; *taṭāka*: a pond; *vraṇa*: a wound; *peṭa*: a basket; *mañcaka*: a bedstead; *vārabāṇa*: armor; *caraṇa*: foot; *vastra*: cloth; *ambara*: garment; *airāvata*: the elephant of Indra.

*Kalka* means medicinal extract, deceit, or sin; *śūka* means the awn of grain or a needle; *śulka* means a toll-house or a source of revenue such as a ferry; *droṇa* refers to a specific measure of capacity or a species of bird; *bhūṣaṇa* means an ornament; *kāṇḍa* denotes an arrow, a stalk, a section, the rainy season, or something contemptible; *maṇḍa* is the liquid portion of curd and similar substances; *piṭaka* is a specific vessel made of bamboo; *peṭa* means a collection or multitude; *airāvata* is Indra’s elephant;
and *caraka*, *maṭha*, *viṭhaṅka*, *kṣveḍita*, *abhūtavṛtta*, *prayuta*, *ghṛta*, *vasanta*, *hastabusta*, and *aparāṅmukha* [are other examples].

*Palitaphalaka-kaṇṭā*: A specific treatise (*caraka-grantha*) concerning the hundred thousand nests of grass belonging to various types of karma. *Maṭha*: The dwelling place of ascetics. *Viṭaṅka*: A pigeon-cot (the cornice of a roof). *Kṣveḍita*: A particular kind of pleasant sound. *Bhūta*: This word has two genders when referring to a *piśāca*; however, as a verb (*kriyāśabda*), it takes the gender of the noun it qualifies (*viśeṣyaliṅga*). *Vṛtta*: Conduct or character. He employs ten lakhs [of coins]. *Ghṛta*: Clarified butter (*ājya*). *Hasta*: The hand. *Busta*: A meat-filled roll (*māṃsa-śaṣkulī*). *Palita*: One with grey hair. *Phalaka*: A shield. *Kaṇṭa*: Sin. "One of such a name" and "one of such an action"—the meaning is "one who performs this task."
"Karma is considered to be masculine or neuter when it denotes the object or the action.

Thus says Rudra. "Youvana" is the second stage of life. "Udyāna" means a garden; "yāna" means a vehicle. "Tīrtha," "protha," "nalina," "pulina," "steya," "yodha," "auṣadha," "sthāna," "śūrpa," "nidhana," "śayana," "dvīpa," "puccha," and "āyudha" are [neuter].
A herd, excrement, a corpse, a heap of filth, excellent colors, seats, umbrellas, space, protective amulets, dice-patterns, forests, and rains.

*Protha* means the nose of a horse; *steya* means theft; *yodha* means a warrior; *auṣadha* means medicine; *sthāna* means a support or place; *śūrpa* means a winnowing basket; *nidhana* means death; *śayana* means a bed; *yūtha* means a herd of animals; *gūtha* means excrement; *kuṇapa* means a corpse; *kutapa* means a specific type of woolen blanket; *varṇa* means a syllable; *pratisara* means a bracelet; *mukha* means the face. *Aṣṭāpada* refers to gold, meaning that which has its foundation (*pada*) in eight metals (*loha*). The lengthening of the vowel is according to the rule *aṣṭanaḥ saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 6.3.125). *Araṇya* means a forest; *varṣa* means a year.

The *kamaṇḍalu* (water-pot), the *maṇḍapa* (pavilion), the *kuṭṭima* (paved floor), the *mābuda* (a type of water-lily), the *avataṃsa* (ear-ornament), the *pārā* (a type of bird), the *śatamāna* (a weight of gold), and *candana* (sandalwood);
likewise, the *samāna* (equal), the *pūṣā* (the sun), the *dṛḍha* (firm), the *mūṣika* (mouse), the *odana* (boiled rice), the *dina* (day), and the *vitāna* (canopy) when it is red (*lohita*).
*Arbuda* means ten *koṭis*. However, as a mountain, it is masculine. Thus says the *Medinī*: [The text continues with the relevant verses from the Medinīkośa regarding these terms.]

*Arbuda* refers to a mass of flesh (*māṃsapuruṣa*) or ten crores; it does not refer to a woman. It also denotes a specific mountain. *Avataṃsa* means an ornament for the head, including one with a peak (*seśara*). *Pāra* means the further shore (*paratīra*). *Śatamāna* is a weight of silver (*rūpyapala*). *Samāna* means similar (*sadṛśa*). *Pūṣa* is the exudation from a seal-ring (*mudrā*) and so forth. *Mūṣika* is a rat (*ākhu*). *Odana* is boiled rice (*kūra*). *Dina* is a day (*divasa*). *Lohita* is blood (*śoṇita*). When denoting a quality, however, it follows the gender of the word it qualifies (*vācyaliṅga*). *Aṃsa*, *kṣīra*, *kaṣāya*, *bimba*, *viṭapa*, *netra*, *avyaya*, *śekhara*, *kedāra*, *āśrama*, *śalya*, *śūla*, *valaya*, *bāla*, *tamāla*, and *mala*.

The groves, the embers, the pleasure-parks, the darts, the juices, the vessel, the purifier, the city, the middle, the base, the lotus-fiber, the circle, the fire, the stalk, the sprout, and the blue lotus.

*aṃsaḥ* means the shoulder (*skandha*). *Kṣīra* means milk (*dugdha*). *Kaṣāya* is an astringent taste (*tuvara-rasa*). *Bimba* means a circle (*maṇḍala*). *Viṭapa* means a trunk and a branch (*stambha* and *śākhā*). *Netra* means the eye (*nayana*). The word *avyaya* (indeclinable) follows with "atha" and so forth. *Śekhara* means a crest-jewel (*āpīḍa*). *Kedāra* means a field (*kṣetra*). *Āśrama* means a hermitage, the dwelling place of a sage (*muni-sthāna*). *Śūla* means a weapon and a specific type of disease. *Valaya* means a bracelet, an ornament for the hand. *Bāla* means a child (*śiśu*) and hair (*keśa*). *Tamāla* is a specific type of tree. *Mala* means sin (*pāpa*) and excrement (*viṭ*). *Gulma* means a thick stalk or clump (*prakāṇḍa*). *Aṅgāra* means burnt wood (charcoal).

*Vihāra* means a place of play. *Rasa* refers to sweet and other tastes. *Pātra* means a vessel; according to Amara’s definition, "In three senses, *pātra*, *puṭī*, and *vāṭī*," the term here excludes non-application (i.e., it applies to the specific meaning of a vessel), but its intended sense does not exclude other applications either. Similarly, *pavitra* means purifying (*pāvana*), and *puraḥ* and *purī* are likewise used. *Budhna* is the lower part. *Nala* is a hollow grass. *Nāla* is the stalk of lotuses and the like; this word is also feminine, as Śrīharṣa says: "We worship the *nālā*s, which are like the tips of lotus-stalks. *Pravāla* means a sprout and coral.
Jṛmbha, Vajra, Kabandha, Karṣaka, Kukuda, Cakra, Andhakāra, Aṅkuśa, Vaktra, Saṅgama, Deha, Dāḍima, Hima, Patra, Bala, Valkala,
Kārpāsa, Āmiṣa, Kāśa, Kośa, Kusuma, Pragrīva, Māseka, Sā, Niryāsa, Kalaśa, Ambarīṣa, Kalala, Māṣa, Karīṣa, and Kuśa.

*Jṛmbha* and *jṛmbhaṇa* mean yawning. *Vajra* refers to a thunderbolt, a diamond, or a thunderbolt-shaped weapon. *Kabandha* means a headless trunk. *Karṣa* is one-fourth of a *pala*. *Kakuda* denotes the preeminent, the shoulder of a bull, and the insignia of royalty. *Cakra* is a wheel or a part of a chariot. *Aṅkuśa* is a goad. *Vaktra* means the mouth. *Saṅgama* is the confluence of rivers and the like. *Deha* is the body. *Dāḍima* is a specific type of fruit (the pomegranate). *Hima* is frost or snow. *Patra* means a leaf or a vehicle. *Bala* means strength or an army. *Kusuma* is a flower. *Pragrīva* is a window.

A *māsa* consists of thirty days and nights. *Ikkasa* and *cikkasa* refer to the flour of wheat and other grains; however, Amara read *cikkasa* in the *ardharca* section and elsewhere. *Niryāsa* is the exudation or resin of trees and the like. *Kalaśa* means a jar. *Ambarīṣa* refers to a frying pan. *Kalala* is a specific stage of transformation of semen and blood. *Māṣa* denotes both a specific measure of weight and a specific type of grain. *Karīṣa* is dried cow dung. As for the distinction regarding the scope of the word *kuśa*, it will be explained during the commentary on the grammatical rule (*liṅgānuśāsana-sūtra*) beginning with "daṇḍamaḍa."
The roots of the pestles are like buds; the bodies of the side-vessels are like ears of grain; the stalks are like lotuses and ploughs;
there are fragments and earrings; the shackles are like husks and straw; the pillars have the nature of auspiciousness; the large cups are like poison; and the skull is worshipped with oil.

*Mūla* means root; *śiphā* means the same. *Pātrī* refers to a sacrificial implement. *Kamala* means a lotus. *Hala* means a plough. *Caṣāla* is a specific type of sacrificial vessel. *Khaṇḍala* means a fragment or piece. *Phala* means purpose or result. *Śāla* is a specific species of tree. *Śīla* means conduct or character. *Viṣa* refers to poisons such as the *vatsanāga* and others. *Caṣaka* is a drinking vessel for honey-wine (*madhu*). *Pūla* is a bundle of tied grass.
The battle was the sacrificial bath; the fast was the Rājasūya; the cups were the days; the Kaṃsa vessel was the Vājapeya sacrifice; and the gold was the sacrificial fee.
The bellies, the chests, the bodies, the cries, the forests, the kingdoms, the drums, the house-doors, and the cocks are the dwellings of the flesh-eaters.

*vāraḥ* means turn or sequence. *Kaṃsaḥ* (masculine) refers to a drinking vessel; this is the meaning according to Amarakośa 2.9.33. *Daraḥ* denotes fear, disease, and the small. *Śarīraḥ* means the body. *Ārāvaḥ* means sound. The word *gṛha* is used in the neuter as a general term for a house; however, in the masculine, it occurs only in the plural. Amarasimha states in 2.2.18: "The words *kavāṭa* and *arara* are synonyms. We shall explain in the rule Pāṇini 3.2.98 (*śaktau hastikapāṭayoḥ*) that the word *kapāṭa* is also correct in this very sense. *Ārdraḥ* refers to ginger (*śṛṅgavera*). *Dhāma* means both a house and splendor.
Padma, āṣāḍhaka, kapittha, ṣaṣṭika, kula, ambhoja, vāja, amṛtā, sthūla, dyūta, khalīna, loha, kavaca, aśoka, kṣaya, anekapa, śaṅkha, taṇḍaka,
dharma, carman, rajata, sneha, asi, haṃsa, apara, sāra, saindhava, madhya, adhvara, dhanus, māna, stana, and sthāṇu.

*Padma* is masculine when meaning a treasure, but it has two genders (masculine and neuter) when meaning a lotus. *Āṣāḍha* refers to the staff of a religious student (*vratidaṇḍa*) and the month [of that name]. *Kapittha* is a specific type of tree; however, it is also read as *kavīya*, which means the rope for binding the mouth of a horse. And it was said by Bopālita: "The word *karīkhalīna* or *kavīya* is feminine or masculine, meaning 'the equipment for the horse's mouth'. *Ṣaṣṭika* is a variety of rice. *Kula* means lineage and house. *Ambhoja* is a lotus. *Vāja* means a feather. *Amṛta* means water. *Aśoka* is a tree.

*Kṣaya* means a house. *Anekapa* means an elephant. *Śaṅkha* is masculine when meaning a treasure-trove, but is of two genders when meaning a conch-shell. *Taṇḍaka* is a specific type of text for the Sāmavedic chanters (*chandoga*). *Carman* means a skin; *ajina* means a deerskin. *Rajata* means silver. *Sneha* means affection. *Asi* means a sword. *Apara* means another. *Sāra* means strength. *Saindhava* means salt. *Māna* means pride. *Sthāṇu* means a stake or post.
The Mahimanetra, Kapañcaka, Daṇḍaka, Krakaca, Śambala, Kuṇḍa, and Kandara hells.
The deities of the vital points of Kaṭakamālava, with their peaks as filaments and their wood as fistulae.

*Mahiman* means greatness; *netraka* means a chain or thorn; *pañcaka* means width; *daṇḍaka* is a specific type of meter; *krakaca* is a tool for splitting wood and the like; *śambala* means provisions for a journey; *kuṇḍapa* is a specific sacrifice; *kandarā* (cave) is used in the feminine as well; *mālava* is a specific region; *marmara* is the rustling sound of dry leaves; *daivata* means a deity; *dāru* means wood.

The lamp, the effort, Brahmā, and the covering; the site, the vow, the half-offering, and the designation; the field, the moment, wealth, the seed, the palace; the dust, the surface, the hair-cloth, and the sky.
*Dīpa* means a particular kind of light; *bhāva* means intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); *vāstu* means a house; *arma* means a cataract of the eye; *dhana* means wealth; and *paṭa* means a garment.
The huts were their bows, the sins of men were their arrows, the hollows of the world were their bowstrings, and the earth was their target;
with the roots of celestial sandalwood as their arrows, they made the cities the targets for their flight through the sky.

*Uṭaja* means a leaf-hut (*parṇaśālā*). *Cāpa* means a bow (*dhanuḥ*). *Pātaka* means sin (*pāpam*). *Gāṇḍiva* is the bow of Arjuna. It also has a long middle vowel. This is clear from the commentary (*vṛtti*) and other sources on the rule *gāṇḍyajagātsañjñāyām* (Pāṇini 5.2.110).
Camphor, silk garments, sixty-year-old *uśīra* root, *gāṇḍī* reeds, resin, bellows of matching color,
oil-cakes, books, fingernails, arrows, pieces of sugar-cane, *vainītaka* cloth, leopard claws, and counterfeit gold.

*Karpūra* is *ghanasāra*. *Kūrpāsaka* is a bodice (*kañcuka*). *Ṣaṣṭi* is a word denoting a number. *Uśīra* is *nalada*. *Niṣṭheva* is spitting (*niṣṭhīvana*). *Bhastrā* is a leather pouch (*carma-kośa*), and [the form] *bhastrā* [also exists]. *Pusta* is a book (*pustaka*). *Nakhara* is a nail (*nakha*). *Iṣu* is an arrow (*bāṇa*); this [word] is also feminine. As Amara states: "The words *patrī*, *ropa*, and *iṣu* are used in both genders" (Amarakośa 2.8.87). And so Śrī Harṣa, having begun with "If flowers are the arrows of Smara," employed [the word] in the verse: "That these [arrows] struck my heart... (Naiṣadhacarita 1.45).

*Khaṇḍa* is a collection of lotuses and the like; *vainītika* refers to that which belongs to those who are disciplined (*vinīta*); it is a vehicle carried by men. *Dvīpī* is a tiger; *ārakūṭa* is brass. But Amara says: "The remainder [of the list] consists of both masculine and neuter genders: *ardharca*, *piṇyāka*, *kaṇṭaka*, *modaka*, *taṇḍaka*, *ṭaṅka*, *śāṭaka*, *karpaṭa*, and *arbuda*."
Pātaka, udyoga, caraka, tamāla, āmalaka, naḍa;
kuṣṭha, śatamāna, arma, śambala, avyaya, tāṇḍava;
kavīya, kanda, kārpāsa, pārāvāra, and yugandhara.
In the Vedic tradition, the gender of words such as *yūpa*, *pragrīva*, *pattrī*, *veṣa*, *pūṣan*, and *camasa* is fixed;
likewise, for words beginning with *ardharca* and those starting with *ghṛta*, their masculine gender and so forth are established as certain.
If that [reason] exists even in the world outside the subject, then let it be [considered] as *śeṣavat* (the remainder). Thus [it is said].

*Arma* means an eye disease. Its commentators state that the suffix *man* is an *auṇādika* (irregular) suffix, according to the rule "arti-stu-su-hu-sṛ" (*Uṇādisūtra* 1.145). *Śambala* begins with either the palatal *ś* or the dental *s*; these same commentators [hold this view]. Here, although words ending in *cikkasa* are listed in the *ardharcādi* group, and words such as *kūṭa*, which are not feminine, have been mentioned previously in their respective places, it is stated that for other words not included here, the masculine gender and so forth are well-known exceptions.

Therefore, it is understood that in common usage, words such as *ghṛta* (clarified butter), *kṣīra* (milk), *dāru* (wood), *loman* (hair), *āsana* (seat), *mukha* (mouth), and *śarīra* (body) possess fixed genders. Nevertheless, because they are absent from the works of the Three Sages (*Munitraya*), their status as Vedic is baseless. For this very reason, they say that [the author] stated "even in common usage" (*loke 'pi*) and so forth out of dissatisfaction. This is correct, because the sūtras governing gender (*liṅgānuśāsana*) concerning subjects such as *ghṛta* operate as being common to both the world and the Veda. Likewise, all other words that are determined to be masculine or neuter by means of lexicons (*kośa*) and other sources should be understood as included among the *ardharcādi* group.

Now, by way of a digression, the sūtras of Pāṇini’s *Liṅgānuśāsana* (Instruction on Gender) are being explained, as they have been employed in the application of the extension rule (*atideśa*) "the gender of the other [word] follows" (*paravalliṅgam*).
Gender. Feminine. These are mentioned in the *adhikāra-sūtra* (governing rule).

Those ending in the vowel *ṛ*—namely *mātṛ*, *pitṛ*, *svasṛ*, *yātṛ*, and *nanāndṛ*—are exclusively feminine. These five alone are feminine because, while the prohibition of the suffix *ṅīp* applies specifically to the seven beginning with *svasṛ*, forms such as *kartrī* end in *ī* due to the suffix *ṅīp*. As for *tisṛ* and *catasṛ*, although they are prescribed as substitutes in the feminine, the bases *tri* and *catur* do not end in *ṛ*.

A verbal root (*dhātu*) ending in the suffix *an* or *ū* is feminine: e.g., *avaniḥ* (the earth) and *camūḥ* (an army). Why is the mention of the "suffix" (*pratyaya*) necessary? [To exclude] *dyūḥ* (heaven), which is derived from the root *div* with the suffix *kvip*. It follows the gender of its substantive (*viśeṣyaliṅga*).
*aśani*, *bharaṇi*, and *araṇi* are masculine; for example, *iyam aśaniḥ* or *ayam aśaniḥ*. Roots ending in the suffixes *-min* and *-ni* are feminine; for example, *bhūmiḥ* and *glāniḥ*.
*Vanhi*, *vṛṣṇi*, and *agni* are masculine; this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding rule.
The words *śroṇi*, *yoni*, and *ūrmi* are feminine when referring to a male. This [word] *śroṇi* may be either feminine (*iyam*) or masculine (*ayam*).
It ends in the suffix *ktin*. This is clear. Regarding *kṛti* and so forth: it also ends in the vowel *ī*. A word ending in the suffix *ī* is feminine, as in *lakṣmīḥ*.

And [words] ending in *ūṅ* and *āp*. *kurūḥ* (the Kuru women). *vidyā* (knowledge). A monosyllabic word ending in *y*. *śrīḥ* (prosperity), *bhūḥ* (earth). Why "monosyllabic"? As in *pṛthuśrīḥ* (one of great prosperity). From twenty up to ninety. *iyam viṃśatiḥ* (this is twenty), *triṃśat* (thirty), *catvāriṃśat* (forty), *pañcāśat* (fifty), *ṣaṣṭiḥ* (sixty), *saptatiḥ* (seventy), *aśītiḥ* (eighty), *navatiḥ* (ninety).
*Dundubhi* [is feminine] when referring to dice. This *dundubhi*. What about when it refers to dice? "This *dundubhi*" means a particular kind of musical instrument or a demon (*asura*).

*Nābhi* [is feminine] when not referring to a Kṣatriya. This *nābhi*. Both [words] are masculine elsewhere. *Dundubhi* and *nābhi* are masculine when outside the aforementioned domains. *Nābhi* as a Kṣatriya. How then—

"Bearing the beauty of navels accompanied by waistbands, with [thighs] as tender as the petals of a blooming lotus" (Kumārasambhava 8.25)—thus says Bhāravi. It is said in reply: in cases such as *dṛḍhabhaktiḥ*, the word *komalaiḥ* should be understood as a neuter used in a general sense. However, in reality, according to the Mahābhāṣya—"Gender is not to be prescribed, for gender depends on common usage"—masculinity is also correct here. For this very reason—
The word *pumān* refers to a chief among men, a king, a wheel, or a Kṣatriya;
it denotes a living being when used in the dual number, and in the feminine (*pumān*), it signifies musk.
Thus says the Medinīkośa. Rabhasa also says: "The word nābhi denotes a chief king or a kṣatriya in the masculine; it refers to a vital organ (of the body) in both genders;
it means the nave of a wheel or a preeminent person in the feminine; and it signifies musk."
In this same manner, it should be understood in other instances as well.

The suffix *tal* [forms feminine nouns]. This occurs in the feminine gender: the state of being white is *śuklatā*; the duty of a Brahmin is *brāhmaṇatā*; a collection of villages is *grāmatā*; and a deity itself is *devatā*. [The following are] names for earth, lightning, river, creeper, and woman: *bhūmi* is *bhūḥ*; *vidyut* is *saudāmanī*; *sarit* is *nimnagā*; *latā* is *vallī*; and *vanitā* is *yoṣit*.
The word *yādas* is neuter; the term *yādaḥ*, although denoting a river, is also neuter.
*bhās*, *sruk*, *srak*, *diś*, *uṣṇih*, and *upānah*—these are feminine. For example: "this is *bhā*" (*iyaṃ bhā*), and so forth.

*Sthūṇā* and *ūrṇā* are also neuter. These two exist as both feminine and neuter: *sthūṇam* / *sthūṇā*; *ūrṇam* / *ūrṇā*. Among these, *sthūṇā* is a wooden pillar with two notches; *ūrṇā*, however, is the wool of sheep and the like. [The rule] "after *gṛha* and *śaśa*, [the word is] neuter" is for the purpose of restriction. When preceded by *gṛha* and *śaśa*, *sthūṇā* and *ūrṇā* are neuter respectively: *gṛhasthūṇam*; *śaśorṇam*. Amara states: "The compound *śaśorṇa* refers to the wool of a hare. (*Amarakośa* 2.9.108).
*prāvṛṭ*, *vipruṭ*, *ruṭ*, *tṛṭ*, *viṭ*, and *tviṣ*—these [words] are feminine.
*darvī*, *vid*, *vedī*, *khaṇī*, *śāṇī*, *aśri*, *veśī*, *kṛṣī*, *auṣadhī*, *kaṭī*, and *aṅgulī*—these are feminine; optionally, they take the suffix *ṅīṣ*. Thus: *darvī* or *darvi*, and so forth.

*tithi*, *nāḍī*, *ruci*, *vīci*, *nālī*, *dhūli*, *kiki*, *elā*, *chavi*, *rātri*, and others are likewise [feminine]. For example: "this is a *tithi*" (*iyaṃ tithiḥ*), and so on. However, Amara says: "*tithayaḥ* [are] in both genders" (*tithayo dvayoḥ*). Accordingly, Bhāravi writes: "Of him, there were many *tithis* upon the earth" (*tasya bhuvi bahutithāstithayaḥ*). For if it were feminine, it would have been *bahutithyaḥ*. And Śrīharṣa writes: "All the *paurṇimā-tithis* at night."

*Śaṣkulī*, *rājikā*, *kuṭī*, *aśani*, *varti*, *bhrakuṭi*, *truṭi*, and *valipaṅkti*—these also may be feminine. This is *śaṣkulī*. *Pratipad*, *āpad*, *vipad*, *saṃpad*, *śarat*, *saṃsat*, *pariṣad*, *uṣas*, *saṃvit*, *kṣut*, *punaḥ*, *mud*, and *samidh*—this is *pratipad*, and so forth. *Uṣas* means "shining"; it is the deity presiding over the dawn. *Āśis*, *dhūḥ*, *pūḥ*, *gīḥ*, and *dvāras*—this is *āśis*, and so forth.

The words *apsu-mat*, *samanaska*, and *sikatā* denote the plural number of years (*varṣa*). The five words beginning with *abadī* (referring to flowers) are feminine and denote plurality. For example: *imā āpaḥ* ("these waters"); "sumanas" [as a flower] is feminine according to Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.4.27; and "sumanā" [as a jasmine] is feminine according to Aṣṭādhyāyī 2.4.72. However, when denoting a deity, it is masculine only, as in "suparvāṇaḥ sumanasaḥ" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.1.7). Plurality is the general rule, though it is not absolute, as evidenced by the usage in the Bhāṣya on the *arthavat-sūtra*: "Even a single grain of sand (*sikatā*) is incapable of yielding oil."

This is because of the statement "she gives birth every year" (*samāṃ samāṃ vijāyate*) and the commentary (*bhāṣya*) which reads *samāyāṃ samāyām*. Furthermore, Haradatta likewise explains the phrase "the two *sumanas* flowers were not smelled" (*aghrāsātāṃ sumanasau*) in his commentary on the rule *vibhāṣā ghrādheṭ* (Pāṇini 2.4.78).
*srak*, *tvak*, *jyok*, *vāk*, *yavāgūḥ*, *nauḥ*, *sphik*. This is *srak*; *tvak*; *jyok*; *vāk*; *yavāgūḥ*; *nauḥ*; *sphik*.
To be connected with the limit of the moment. This is the moment. The limit. To be connected.
And the *culliveṇikhāryas* [are also included]. This is clear.
And [the examples include] stars, the moon, moonlight, and so forth.
The word *śalākā* is always feminine. The inclusion of the term "always" (*nitya*) indicates that there are occasional exceptions for other words.
Thus ends the section on women.
A man; this is the qualification.

[These] end in the suffix *ghañ*: *pākaḥ* (cooking), *tyāgaḥ* (renunciation), *karaḥ* (hand), *garaḥ* (poison). This [suffix] occurs only in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*), because when the abstract action is qualified by neuter gender, it is restricted by *ktalyuḍ*; but when qualified by feminine gender, it is excluded by *ktin* and other suffixes, leaving this as the remainder. However, when denoting an object (*karman*) and so forth, even words ending in *ghañ* follow the gender of the substantive they qualify. Thus says the Bhāṣya: "The connection will continue to apply. And those ending in *ghañ*: *vistaraḥ* (expansion), *gocaraḥ* (range), *cayaḥ* (accumulation), *jayaḥ* (victory), and so on. The words *bhaya*, *liṅga*, *bhaga*, and *pada* are neuter. These are neuter: *bhayam* (fear), *liṅgam* (mark/sign), *bhagam* (fortune/vagina), *padam* (foot/step).
A word ending in the suffix *naṅ* is masculine: *yajñaḥ*, *yatnaḥ*.

The suffix *yāc* (in the feminine) is an exception to the preceding rule. A word ending in the *kip* suffix is *ghu* and shall be masculine: *ādhiḥ*, *nidhiḥ*, *udadhiḥ*. Why "ending in *kip*"? [Consider] *dānam*. Why "*ghu*"? [Consider] *jajñir bījam*.
*iṣudhiḥ* is both feminine and masculine. The word *iṣudhi* is used in the feminine and the masculine genders; it is an exception to the preceding rule.

The following words are used in the masculine: *deva*, *asura*, *ātman*, *svarga*, *giri*, *samudra*, *nakha*, *keśa*, *danta*, *stana*, *bhuja*, *kaṇṭha*, *khaḍga*, *śara*, and *paṅka*. *Devāḥ* (gods) means *surāḥ*; *asurāḥ* means *daityāḥ*. *Ātmā* means the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*). *Svargaḥ* means the celestial realm (*nāka*). *Giriḥ* means a mountain (*parvata*). *Samudraḥ* means the ocean (*abdhi*). *Nakhaḥ* means a fingernail (*kararuha*). *Keśaḥ* means hair on the head (*śiroruha*). *Dantaḥ* means a tooth (*daśana*). *Stanaḥ* means a breast (*kuca*). *Bhujaḥ* means an arm (*doḥ*). *Kaṇṭhaḥ* means the throat (*gala*). *Khaḍgaḥ* means a sword (*karavāla*). *Śaraḥ* means an arrow (*mārgaṇa*). *Paṅkaḥ* means mud (*kardama*), and so forth.

*Triviṣṭapa* and *tribhuvana* are neuter. This is clear. *Triviṣṭapa* means the third world (*tṛtīyaṃ viṣṭapaṃ*). Since it would have been expected to be masculine by virtue of being a name for heaven (*svarga*), this rule is commenced [to specify its gender].
*Dyauḥ* is feminine. Both *dyo* and *div* are included here by way of a common grammatical framework (*tantra*).
*Iṣu* and *bāhu* are feminine, and by the word "and" (*ca*), they are also masculine.

The words *bāṇa* (arrow) and *kāṇḍa* (shaft) are neuter; by the word *ca* (and), they are also masculine. The group of four sūtras beginning with *triviṣṭapa* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule for *devāsura*. Words ending in *n* are masculine: *rājā* (king), *takṣā* (carpenter). Nor is there over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to words such as *carma* (skin) or *varma* (armor), because this will be stated in the section on neuters under the rule *mandvyacko 'kartari* (Liṅgānuśāsana Sūtra 145). Names for sacrifice, man, cheek, ankle, and cloud: *kratu* is sacrifice (*adhvara*); *puruṣa* is man (*nara*); *kapola* is cheek (*gaṇḍa*); *gulpha* is ankle (*prapada*); *megha* is cloud (*nīrada*).
*Abhra* is neuter; this is an exception to the preceding rule.

Words ending in *u* [are as follows]: this [suffix] occurs in the masculine, as in *prabhuḥ* (lord) and *ikṣuḥ* (sugarcane). [The word] *hanuḥ* is feminine when it means a type of harlot (*haṭṭavilāsinī*), the commencement of a dance, or a disease.

The *Medinī* states: "In the sense of a part of the cheek, [the word *kapolā* is feminine]. The *Amara* states: "The word *kareṇu* is feminine when referring to a female elephant (*ibhī*), and masculine when referring to a male elephant (*ibha*). However, the scope of the present sūtra consists of cases not covered by such specific rules. And it has been said:
"The rule for the remaining genders is pervasive, provided it is not sublated by specific rules.
This applies elsewhere as well.

The words *dhenu*, *rajju*, *kuhū*, *sarayu*, *tanu*, *reṇu*, and *priyaṅgu* are feminine; however, in a compound, *rajju* may also be masculine, as in *karkaṭarajjvā* (with a crab-rope) and *karkaṭarajjunā* (by a crab-rope).

The words *śmaśru*, *jānu*, *vasu*, *svādu*, *aśru*, *jatu*, *trapu*, and *tālū* are neuter. *Vasu* denotes wealth (*artha*). Why "denoting wealth"? [As in: *vasuḥ* [meaning] a ray, fire, or the Lord of Wealth (Kubera). [In the *Kaumudī*, the reading is expanded to: *madgu*, *madhu*, and *sīdhu*—these are also neuter. Furthermore, *sīdhu*, *sānukam*, and *kamaṇḍalu* are neuter; and because of the word "also" (*ca*), they are masculine as well. This *madgu* [is masculine]; this *madgu* [is neuter]. Words ending in *r* [are as follows]: *meruḥ*, *setuḥ*.

The words *dāru*, *kaseru*, *jatu*, *vastu*, and *mastu* are neuter. The rule regarding the suffix *rut* (which would otherwise cause the masculine gender) is hereby set aside. For example: *idaṃ dāru* (this wood). The word *saktu* is both neuter and—by virtue of the particle *ca* ("and")—masculine. Thus: *saktaḥ* (masculine) and *saktaḥ* (neuter).

Up to the word *raśmi*, the suffix *akāra* (the letter *a*) is the final phoneme [of the nouns under discussion]. As he will state later: "*raśmi* is the name for a ray of light or a day" (*liṅgasūtra* 100), the phrase "up to this point, the final phoneme is *akāra*" is understood as the governing rule (*adhikāra*).
A word having *ka* as its penultimate letter and ending in *a* is masculine: *stabakaḥ*, *kalkaḥ*.
The words *cibuka*, *śālūka*, *prātipadika*, *aṃśuka*, and *ulmuka* are neuter; this is an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding rule.

The words *kaṇṭaka*, *anīka*, *saraka*, *modaka*, *caṣaka*, *mastaka*, *pustaka*, *taḍāka*, *niṣka*, *śuṣkavarcaska*, *pināka*, *bhāṇḍaka*, *piṇḍaka*, *śaṇḍaka*, *piṭaka*, *tālaka*, *phalaka*, and *pulāka* are neuter; however, they may also be masculine after the suffix *ac*. For example: "this is a *kaṇṭaka*" (*ayaṃ kaṇṭakaḥ*) or "this is a *kaṇṭaka*" (*idaṃ kaṇṭakam*), and so forth. **Words ending in *ṭ* (ṭopadha):** A word ending in *ṭ* and terminating in *a* is masculine. Examples: *ghaṭaḥ* (pot), *paṭaḥ* (cloth). However, *kirīṭa*, *mukuṭa*, *lalāṭa*, *vaṭa*, *vīṭa* (as in the *Kaumudī*), *śṛṅgāṭaka*, *rāṭa*, and *loṣṭa* are neuter. Examples: *kirīṭam*, etc.

The words *kuṭa*, *kuṭaka*, *paṭaka*, *vāṭaka*, *karpaṭa*, *naṭa*, *nikaṭa*, *kīṭa*, and *kaṭa* are neuter; however, with the suffix *ca*, they are masculine—as in *kuṭaḥ* or *kuṭam*, and so forth. A word ending in *ṇa* (ṇopadha) and ending in *a* is masculine: *guṇaḥ*, *gaṇaḥ*, *pāṣaṇaḥ*.
The words *ṛṇa*, *lavaṇa*, *parṇa*, *toraṇa*, *raṇa*, and *uṣṇa* are neuter. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the preceding rule.
The words *kārṣāpaṇa*, *svarṇa*, *suvarṇa*, *vraṇa*, *caraṇa*, *vṛṣaṇa*, *viṣāṇa*, *cūrṇa*, and *tṛṇa* are neuter.
And [the suffix] *at* is used in the masculine.
A word ending in the suffix *thak* [is udātta on its final syllable]: *rathaḥ*, *prasthaḥ*.
Regarding the word *kāṣṭha*: according to the *Kaumudī*, "the forms *kth*, *oktha*, and *uktha* are neuter. For example: "this wood" (*idaṃ kāṣṭham*), and so forth.

However, when meaning "direction," *kāṣṭhā* is feminine: "these directions" (*imāḥ kāṣṭhāḥ*). Furthermore, the words *tīrtha*, *protha*, *yūtha*, and *gātha* are neuter; because of the word "and" (*ca*) [in the rule], they are also masculine: "this sacred ford" (*ayaṃ tīrthaḥ*) or "this sacred ford" (*idaṃ tīrtham*).

[The following words ending in] *a* [are] not neuter: those ending in *ina*. [Examples: *phenaḥ* (foam). The following words ending in *a* are neuter: *jaghana*, *ajina*, *tuhiṇa*, *kānana*, *vana*, *vṛjina*, *vipina*, *vetana*, *śāsana*, *sopāna*, *amithuna*, *śmaśāna*, *ratna*, *nimna*, and *cinha*. *yātrā*, *mātrā*, *bhastrā*, *daṃṣṭrā*, and *varatrā* are exclusively feminine.

*Bhr̥tra*, *amitra*, *chātra*, *putra*, *mantra*, *vṛtra*, *meḍhra*, and *oṣṭha* are [names] used in the masculine. This one is *bhr̥tra*. *Amitra* means "not a friend. As Māgha says: "His friends became his enemies" (*tasya mitrāṇyamitrāste*, Śiśupālavadha 2.101). And it is said: "The two words *amitrau* may mean both enemies and friends. As for what Haradatta stated regarding the rule *dviṣo'mitre* (Pāṇini 3.2.131)—namely, that the suffix *itrac* is applied by the Uṇādi rule *amerdviṣati cit* (Uṇādisūtra 626), resulting in *amitra* from the root *am*—the fact that the word has the acute accent on the middle syllable (*madhyodātta*) in examples such as "he would distress a friend" (*mitrasya vyathayet*) must be considered problematic.

The same applies to negative compounds (*nañ-samāsa*). To suggest that there would also be the adoption of the gender of the final member (*paravalliṅgatā*) is another flaw [in their argument], which stems from a failure to properly examine the sutra under discussion. Furthermore, the raising of the objection regarding accentuation (*svaradoṣa*) is based on a failure to recall the sixth-century rule: *naño jaramaramitramṛtāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.2.116). This is the general direction [of the critique]. [The words] *patra*, *pātra*, *pavitra*, *sūtra*, and *chatra* are used in the masculine as well.

The terms for army, heroism, battle, city, and war are as follows: *bala*, *vīrya*, *āhava*, and *saṅgrāma* are masculine. Regarding *padma*, *kamala*, and *utpala*: these words, though denoting flowers, may be of both genders. Amara also states: "Or *padma* and *nalina* are masculine" (Amarakośa 1.10.40). Thus, the commentary on the *ardharca*-group rule—which states that *padma* meaning "aquatic plant" is exclusively neuter—is to be understood as representing an alternative opinion (*matāntara*). *Āhava* and *saṅgrāma* are masculine.
The word *āji* is used only in the feminine gender.
