For example: *abhṛśo bhṛśo bhavati* ("one who was not intense becomes intense") results in *bhṛśāyate*. The word *ca* ("and") here indicates a cumulative conjunction (*anvācaya*) and not a restrictive conjunction (*sanniyoga*), because otherwise the listing of vowel-ending (*ajanta*) words in the *bhṛśādi* group would become redundant.

If *acveḥ* were an absolute negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), then there would clearly be an "unintelligible compound" (*asamarthasamāsa*) and a "splitting of the sentence" (*vākyabheda*). Furthermore, since the suffix *cvi* is prescribed in connection with the verb *bhavati*, the meaning [of the base] is already expressed by the employed *bhavati* itself; thus, the suffix *kyaṅ* would not even be applicable, rendering the prohibition useless. Therefore, it is appropriate to take it as an exclusionary negation (*paryudāsa*). Accordingly, by the maxim of "the negative particle joined with *iva*," similarity is obtained, and it is stated that [the suffix applies] to those bases where there is the transformation of something into what it was not before (*abhūtatadbhāva*). Consequently, it does not apply here: *na kva divā bhṛśā bhavanti*.

The meaning is: where in the daytime do those stars and other luminaries that are very bright at night exist? Here, the forms *sumanas*, *unmanas*, *durmanas*, and *abhimanas* are recited [in the list]. Regarding this, a doubt arises: since the entire complex becomes a verbal root (*dhātu*) when the suffix *kyan* follows a compound, there would be a fault in the application of the augment *aṭ*, the suffix *lyap*, and reduplication. To illustrate: while forms such as *svamanāyata* and *udamānayata* are desired, forms such as *asumanāyata* and *aunmanāyata* would result. Similarly, in cases such as *sumanāyitvā*, the suffix *lyap* would be incorrect.

However, if words such as *su* were to enter into the body of a *ktvā*-affixed form, then because there would be no other word distinct from it, a compound (*samāsa*) would not exist; and in the absence of a compound, the suffix *lyap* would not occur, resulting in forms such as *sumanāyitvā*. Similarly, when a desiderative (*san*) follows a form ending in *kyaṅ*, and the first monosyllable (*ekāc*) of that desiderative undergoes reduplication, forms such as *susumanāyiṣate* would result; yet *sumimanāyiṣate* and so forth are what is desired.

Regarding this, they say: The root *saṃgrāma* is listed among the curādīḥ (cur-ādi group) with the meaning "to fight. It should not have been listed there. Since the suffix *ṇic* is already established for the word *saṃgrāma*—which denotes "fighting"—by the rule *tat karoti* (Gaṇasūtra), its inclusion [in the cur-ādi list] must serve either as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*) or as an explanatory indication (*jñāpanārtha*). As a restrictive rule, it means: "If a suffix that causes the designation *dhātu* (verbal root) occurs after a form accompanied by a prefix (*sopasarga*), it occurs only after the root *saṃgrāmi*, and not after any other. Alternatively, as an explanatory indication, it shows that when a suffix causing the designation *dhātu* is intended to be applied to a composite form (*saṃghāta*) consisting of a prefix and a root, the prefixes are treated as separate from the root.

"But [the suffix] *pratyaya* is [derived] from the *pariśiṣṭa* (supplement) itself. For the root *saṃgrāma*, being listed in the *curādi* group, is read with its prefix (*sopasarga*) as a single composite unit; it is not a separate word whose parts resemble a prefix, such as the root *āplṛ* in the sense of "pervasion. Consequently, the optional substitution of the *parasavarṇa* (the following sound) occurs by the rule *vā padāntasya* (Pāṇini 8.4.59). The purpose of reading it as a composite unit is seen in forms such as *asaṃgrāmayata śūraḥ*, *saṃgrāmayitvā*, and *sisaṃgrāmayiṣate*.
Therefore, according to the aforementioned method, the result is either a restrictive rule (*niyama*) or an explanatory indication (*jñāpana*).

Regarding this, Haradatta says: "This root *saṃgrāmayati* is intended to be *anudātta-it* (having an indicatory vowel *it* that is unaccented). Consequently, its recitation [in the Dhātupāṭha] would be for the purpose of attaching an indicatory letter (*anubandha*) so as to effect the *ātmanepada* endings, just as in the case of roots like *galbh*. Therefore, how could it serve as a restrictive rule or an indicator (*jñāpaka*)? Furthermore, if the recitation were merely for the purpose of attaching an indicatory letter, one should have simply read 'grāma yuddhe'; the prefix *sam-* would then be understood as a mere dyotaka (indicator) by virtue of its observation in actual usage, just as the prefix *adhi-* is understood in the case of the roots *iṅ* and *ik*."

Therefore, it must be stated that the specific reading mentioned previously indeed possesses the aforementioned result; for if this were not the case, then just as the augment *āṬ* does not occur before the roots *iṅ* and *ika*, it would likewise not occur before this [root] either.

Regarding this, Mādhava maintains that the fact that this [root *man*] is marked as *anudātta* is un-Pāṇinian; thus, since the reading serves this specific purpose, there is no violation of the *jñāpaka*. However, this contradicts Kaiyaṭa’s statement that "the root *saṃgrāmayati* should be understood as *anudātta*. Furthermore, Haradatta has established the following as his final conclusion (*siddhānta*): there is no compound of the word *manas* with [words beginning with] *su* and so on; rather, these are uncompounded and serve as qualifiers of the meaning of the suffixes, while the word *manas*—in the context of a derivative formation (*vṛtti*)—refers to one who possesses it (i.e., the quality of having a mind). Thus, the meaning of "one becomes well-minded" (*manaḥsvī suṣṭhu bhavati*) and so forth is derived.

That too is refuted by the fact that it contradicts what will be stated by the author of the Bhāṣya and others regarding the rule *prabhau parivṛḍhaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.21): when one says "he makes [someone] powerful" (*parivṛḍham ācaṣṭe*), the suffix *ṇic* is applied, and once the suffix *ktvā* has been added, the form *parivraḍhayya* occurs with the suffix *lyap*. For in that case, as here, it is not possible for [the word] to function as a qualifier of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*). If it is asked, "How then is the desired meaning established in this instance? [the answer follows].

To this it is replied: the base *saṅgrāma* is listed in the *curādi* group because it is derived under the heading of the suffix *man* by the rule *graserā ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.148), which states that the suffix *man* is added to *gras* with the replacement of the root vowel by *ā*. It is not, however, a verbal root (*dhātu*). Since the addition of the causative suffix *ṇic* is already established for it by the previously introduced *gaṇa*-sūtra *tat karoti* (Gana-sūtra), the attachment of the indicatory letter (*anubandha*) is merely for the sake of a specific result, just as in the case of roots such as *galbh*.

This being the case, even when it is said, "this word *grāma* [is used] in the sense of 'battle'," since the word *grāma* itself does not apply to battle, the word *saṅgrāma* is indeed obtained by implication (*sāmarthyāt*). And in that context, it is also easily established that the specific form *saṅgrāmi* possesses the status of a verbal root (*dhātu*), because the technical designation (*sañjñā*) prescribed by the rule *sanādyantāḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.32) rests upon the entire aggregate of both the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*).

By this, the counter-argument regarding *iṅ* and *ika* is refuted; for in that case, there is a disparity, since the designation of verbal root (*dhātusañjñā*) depends upon the specific wording and does not touch upon the qualified form. And thus, the specific reading "saṅgrāma" indicates that "a preceding member which has the same form as a prefix is separated when a suffix that triggers the designation of a verbal root is intended to be applied."

And since that [compound] is synonymous with its subsequent member—which serves as the base for the suffixes that trigger the designation *dhātu*—it possesses semantic capacity (*samartha*) even with the specific meaning constituted by that [subsequent member], namely the form ending in *-ktvā*. Consequently, by the rule "kṛnmejantaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.1.39) and because the term *prādi* is included in the rule "kugatiprādayaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.2.18), it forms a compound; thus, forms such as *parivraḍhayya* are established. This same process applies to cases such as *avajigalbhiṣate*, *avāgalbhata*, and *avagalbhya*.

Nor does this contradict the sixth Vārttika, *uṣyomāṅkṣvāṭaḥ*, nor its commentary regarding the form *auḍhīyat*; for we accept that an indicatory mark (*jñāpaka*) applies only to cases of the same class as itself—namely, where the preceding member is actually heard [as such], and not where it has been replaced by a substitute. In this regard, the works of the Bhāṣya, the Vārttikas, the Dhātuvṛtti, and others are supportive; let those who value excellence reflect upon this. Consequently, certain usages such as *pramāṇayitvā* and *vicārayitvā* are merely due to negligence.

For this very reason, Sudhākara and others, who cite *śrāpayati* and *jyāpayati*, as well as Śākaṭāyana and others, who cite *śrapayati* and *jyapayati*, are refuted by those who maintain that the root is *praśasya*. This is because, by separating the prefix *pra* and deriving the causative suffix (*ṇic*) from the word *śasya* alone, the forms *śra* and *jya* would not be applicable. For this same reason, Mādhava and others have accepted only *praśasyayati*.

By this, the authors of the *Dhātucandrodaya* and others, who cite examples such as *apaprāvat* (he spoke of the rainy season) and *avivīrat* (he spoke of a plant), are refuted. The meaning made known by the inclusion of the root *saṅgrāmayati* must somehow be justified by relying on the knowledge that the rule is non-universal (*anitya*), based on the force of the sixth-century Bhāṣya-vārtika: *usyomāṅkṣvāṭaḥ*. This is the direction of the argument.

The words beginning with *bhṛśa*, however, are illustrated in Mādhavīya in accordance with their recitation in the *gaṇa* lists of the *Śloka*. For example: *bhṛśāyate*, *capalāyate*, *mandāyate*, *paṇḍitāyate*, *rehāyate*. Regarding the word *reha*, the *Gaṇavṛtti* states that it occurs in the sense of "in secret," "cruelty," and "the cessation of the desire for alms. *Tṛpāyate*; *tṛpa* means both the moon and the ocean. *Vehāyate*; *vehad* means a female that destroys the fetus. *Adharāyate*; the *Gaṇavṛtti* states: "Adhara means a fool and also a lotus (*puṣkara*)."

*ojāyate*, *varcāyate*; in the context of grammatical derivation (*vṛtti*), the words *ojas* and *varcas* refer to that which possesses those qualities. *rephāyate*; according to the *Gaṇavṛtti*, *rephaḥ* means "full of anger. *durmanāyate*, *sumanāyate*, *unmanāyate*, *utsukāyate*. *śaśvāyate*, *bṛhāyate*; these two [roots] end in *-ta*. Regarding the rule *subāmantrite* (Pāṇini 2.1.2), it should be added as an extension (*upasaṃkhyeya*) that a prefix (*upasarga*) attached to *manas* behaves like a subsequent member of a compound.

By this, it is understood from an examination of the Bhāṣya on the present sūtra that in forms such as *sumanāyate*, the *nighāta* (anudātta accentuation) prescribed by Pāṇini 8.1.28 (*tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*) does not occur; whereas in forms such as *devadattaḥ sumanāyate*, the *nighāta* does occur for the verb along with its prefix. These verses [cited] belong to the Gaṇapāṭha under the *bhṛśādi* group. However, in the Gaṇavṛtti, the word *bṛhat* is not recited, while the word *bhadra* is indeed recited.

And the word *kandhara* [is derived as follows]: the *kandharā* is a ligament (*snāyu*) that has the appearance of a thick cord, is unjoined, and is situated within the skin; one who possesses that is *kandhara*. The suffix *ac* is applied in the sense of possession according to Pāṇini 5.2.127 (*arśaādibhyo'c*), and [the compound formation] according to Pāṇini 3.1.13.

Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.13 states: *lohitādibhyaḥ ḍājbhyaḥ kyaṣ*. The suffix *kyaṣ* occurs after the words beginning with *lohita* and after those ending in *ḍāc*, in the sense of "becoming" (*bhavati*). By the rule *vā kyaṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.90), [the Ātmanepada endings are optionally used]: *lohitāyati* or *lohitāyate*. Here, by the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the word *abhūta* from the preceding rule, the scope is restricted to cases of "becoming what one was not before" (*abhūtatadbhāva*). This [condition] is not a qualifier for the suffix *ḍāc*, because such a case is impossible [for a word already ending in *ḍāc*]. The analysis (*vigraha*) is: "that which was not red becomes red. Similarly: *paṭapaṭāyati*, *paṭapaṭāyate*.

Even without connection to the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, or *as*, the suffix *ḍāc* occurs here after a word ending in *ḍāc* precisely because of the force of its specific rule (*vidhānasāmarthya*). This is because the root *bhū*, whose meaning has already been expressed by *kyaṣ* prescribed in the sense of "becoming" (*bhavatyartha*), cannot be employed here [alongside it]. Regarding this, there is a Vārttika:

"The statement that *kyaṣ* is prescribed after [the roots] *lohita* and *ḍāj*, while the others [are included] among the *bhṛśādi* group, is intended as a refutation of the word *ādi* (‘and so forth’). The meaning is that these six—*nīla*, *harita*, *manda*, *phena*, *dāsa*, and *manda*—which are listed after the word *lohita*, should be understood as belonging to the *bhṛśādi* group. Furthermore, both the *k* and *ṣ* of *kyaṣ* are also refuted; for instance, the *k* is clearly not for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, because a prohibition is impossible for that which has not even arisen."

Nor is it for the sake of general inclusion by the rule *naḥ kye* (Pāṇini 1.4.15), because [the long vowel] is prescribed only after a suffix ending in *n*. Nor is it for the sake of the rules *āpatyasya ca taddhite 'ni* and *kyacvyośca* (Pāṇini 6.4.151, 152), since it would be more appropriate simply to say *yāc chandasi*. And this is logical, as we see [the form] even from a root ending in *ya*, such as *kaṇḍvādi-yaganta* in the example *śakunam bhuraṇyum*. Nor is it for the sake of applying the lengthening rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.25) in the case of *lohitāyate*, because the term *kṅiti* does not recur there.

If it is argued that the recurrence [of the word *hal*] is necessary for the sake of forms such as *uruyā* and *dhṛṣṇuyā*, we say no; for here, in place of the third case-ending, the substitution *yā* occurs by the rule *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39). And this is Vedic (*chāndasa*). In that context, even the short vowel will be Vedic, just as in the example *upagāyantu sāpatnayo garbhiṇayaḥ*. Nor is it intended for the purpose of including the general term in the rule *kyasya vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 6.4.50), because the word *hal* continues to recur from the previous rule.

This [suffix *ya*] does not occur after a word ending in a consonant (*halanta*), nor is it for the purpose of qualifying [the rule] "optionally after a *kyaṣ*-ending root" (Pāṇini 1.3.90), because the sūtra would have been formulated simply as "vā syāt. Nor does this lead to an over-extension in cases such as *pāśyā* from the rule "the suffix *ya* after *pāśa* and others" (Pāṇini 4.2.49); for that section is intended as a restriction (*niyama*) regarding those verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) prescribed by general rules. Furthermore, there are no verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*) ending in the *ya* of the *pāśa* group. If it is argued that they do exist after roots ending in the *kvip* affix used in the sense of "behaving like" (*ācāra-kvip*), we say no; because of the intervention of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*, and because even in a rule concerning what precedes, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) retains its status as the original element (*sthānivadbhāva*).

Nor should one fear an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) [of the suffix] from words such as *daṇḍya* and *vadhya*, which end in the *kvip* suffix used in the sense of habitual action (*ācāra*), because it will be stated in the fifth [chapter] that in those cases the suffix is *yat*—due to the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of *yat* from the preceding rule "daṇḍādibhyaḥ" (Pāṇini 5.1.65)—and not the suffix *yap*. For this very reason, the letter *ṣ* [in the rule] is also redundant. Its purpose might be thought to be the prevention of the inclusion of general terms in rules such as "vā kyaṣaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.170) and "kyasya vibhāṣā" (Pāṇini 6.4.50); however, all of that has already been refuted.

Therefore, having omitted the word *ādi* and the letter *ṣ*, the rule "yaḥ after *lohita* and words ending in *ḍāp*" was established in the Bhāṣya. However, if there exists an expression for a verbal noun (*ācārakviP*) such as "one who behaves like a member of an assembly" (*sabhya*)—as in the case of *sabhāyāḥ yaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.4.105)—then the rule should have been formulated as "vā yaṣaḥ. Or rather, let there be only the letter *ṣ*; the remainder would indeed be redundant. The author of the Vṛtti, however, considers the meaning of the Vārttika to be something else.

For instance, it is not that the inclusion of "beginning with" (ādi) is rejected by this [rule]; rather, it is said that those six [words] which have been recited—namely *nīla* and so forth—are extracted from there and inserted among *bhṛśa* and the others. However, for those not recited, only *kyaṣ* is used. And these [unrecited words] are obtained because [the group] is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open-ended class). As for the evidence (*jñāpaka*) for its being an *ākṛtigaṇa*, it is the letter *k* in *kyaṣ* in the rule *naḥ kye* (Pāṇini 1.4.15), which serves to include the general category [of words ending in *n*], and the letter *ṣ* to prevent the elision of that [nasal]. For indeed, among the [words] actually recited, such as *lohita* and so on, there is none that ends in *n*. And the author of the *Gaṇavṛtti* has collected those [words] established by the *ākṛtigaṇa* nature.
Redness, blackness, and suffering; joy, pride, and pleasure;
fainting, sleep, and compassion; smoke, the heart, and the skin—these are the qualities of the Karumānti.

The forms *nidrākaroti*, *ādayaḥ*, and so forth, occur in the sense of "functioning" (*vṛtti*) with respect to that [sleep]. For example: *nidrāyati*, *nidrāyate*, and so on. All of this, however, should be disregarded because it contradicts the Bhāṣya. Furthermore, it is clearly understood that even for the author of the Vārttika, who states "*lohitādibhyaḥ*," the intention was to dispense with the word "ādi. Otherwise, he would have simply said "*lohitāt*."

For this very reason, we stated in our discussion on the *kyaṅ* suffix that although the entry in the *Kalpataru*—"in the case of *vidvasyamāna*, [the suffix] *kyaṣ* applies after roots such as *lohita* ending in *ḍāc*"—is possible according to the method of the *Vṛttikāra*, it is merely a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*) because it contradicts the *Bhāṣya*.

It might be argued: "Let there be the rule *kyaṣ ca*; because of the word *ca*, let there also be *kyaṅ*. In that case, the *parasmaipada* would apply in the *kyaṣ* alternative, while the *ātmanepada* would apply in the *kyaṅ* alternative; thus, the rule *vā kvaṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.90) need not exist. This is not so. According to the maxim *prātipadikagrahaṇe liṅgaviśiṣṭasyāpi grahaṇam* (Paribhāṣā 73), when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is mentioned, it includes the form qualified by gender as well. Thus, from the word *lohinī* with the suffix *kyaṣ*, the two forms *lohinīyati* and *lohinīyate* are desired. However, if *kyaṅ* were applied, the rule *kyaṅmāninośca* (Pāṇini 6.3.36) would cause the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*), resulting in *lohitāyate*. Since there is a difference in the resulting forms, the rule *vā kvaṣaḥ* is necessary. (Pāṇini 3.1.14)

*Kaṣṭāya kramaṇe* (Pāṇini 3.2.14). In the word *kaṣṭe*, [it means] *kṛcchra* (difficulty/suffering). According to the rule *kṛcchragahanayoḥ kaṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.22), there is an absence of the augment *iṭ* when *kaṣ* is used in the sense of *kṛcchra*. By that [word], a sinful action (*pāpa-karman*) characterized by that [difficulty] is indicated. *Kramaṇa* means exertion (*utsāha*); for in the sūtra *vṛttisargatāyaneṣu* (Pāṇini 1.3.38), it is stated that "exertion (*sarga*) is effort (*utsāha*). Therefore, this is the meaning: the suffix *kyaṅ* occurs after the word *kaṣṭa* ending in the dative case when the sense of exertion is intended. *Kaṣṭāya kramate* becomes *kaṣṭāyate*. The meaning is: he exerts himself to perform a sinful action.

It should be stated that [the suffix *kyaṅ*] is applied after the words *satra*, *kakṣa*, *kaṣṭa*, *kṛcchra*, and *gahana* when there is a desire to act like a *kaṇva*. *Kaṇva* means "evil. In the context of verbal derivation (*vṛtti*), these words are synonyms for evil. After these words ending in the accusative case, *kyaṅ* is applied when there is a desire to act. The analysis (*vigraha*) is not expressed by its own constituent parts (*asvapadena*): "he desires to act like evil" (*pāpaṃ cikīrṣati*). Thus: *satrāyate*, *kakṣāyate*, *kaṣṭāyate*, *kṛcchrāyate*, *gahanāyate*.

[The suffix] *kyaṅ* is applied after the word *karman*, when combined with *romantha* and *tapas*, in the sense of *varti* (swallowing/turning back) and *cara* (wandering), respectively. (Pāṇini 3.1.15). The word *karmaṇaḥ* is in the ablative case, because it is in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with *romanthatapobhyām*. It is in the singular number because it is connected to each [of the two words] individually. Regarding *varti*: although the suffix *yuc* would normally apply to the causative form of the root *vṛt* by Pāṇini 3.3.107 (*ṇyāsaśrantho yuc*), the suffix *ktin* is used here instead due to this very rule being a specific irregularity (*nipātana*). Regarding *carateḥ*: the suffix *kvip* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) because the root belongs to the *sampadādi* group. Thus, after the two objects *romantha* and *tapas*, the suffix *kyaṅ* occurs in the respective senses of *varti* and *cara*. One who turns the cud over is called *romanthāyate*.

It should be stated that this refers to "the movement of the jaw" (*kāovāo*). Here, by the movement of the jaw, one understands the chewing of what has been bitten, drawing it back into the region of the mouth. Regarding the example *neha kīṭo romanthaṃ vartayati* ("here the insect does not ruminate"), Haradatta, the author of the *Nyāsa*, explains that it means "the insect makes round [into a ball] the substance that has emerged from the region of the anus. Kaiyaṭa, however, explained it as meaning "the insect eats [the substance] that has emerged from the region of the anus. In *tapasyati*, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) ending would have been required here; therefore—

It should be stated that *tapas* takes the *parasmaipada* [ending] as well (*kāovāo*). And thus, it would have been more appropriate to include the word *tapaḥ* in the very sūtra beginning with "namovariva" (Pāṇini 3.1.19). However, it was not done in that way.

(Pāṇini 3.1.16) "After *bāṣpa* and *ūṣman*, when there is the act of emitting, [the suffix] *kyaṅ* [is added]. The term *kyaṅ* is understood to carry over [from the previous rule]. He emits vapor: *bāṣpāyate*. He emits heat: *ūṣmāyate*.

(Pāṇini 3.1.17) *śabda-vaira-kalaha-abhra-kaṇva-meghebhyaḥ karaṇe* || The suffix *kyaṅ* occurs after these [words] used as objects in the sense of "doing" (*karoti*). From *śabda*: he makes sound → *śabdāyate*. Likewise: *vairāyate*, *kalahāyate*, *abhrāyate*, *kaṇvāyate*, *meghāyate*. Since the suffix *ṇic* would have applied by the rule *tatkaroti* (Gaṇasūtra), this [rule] is commenced. In some cases, *ṇic* is also desired—namely, *śabdayati*. For that purpose, the author of the Nyāsa states that the letter *ca* is carried over here from the rule *bhṛśādibhyo bhuvi* (Pāṇini 3.1.12) by means of the "frog-leap" (*maṇḍūkapluti*) method. Regarding this, there is a Vārttika:
And from *sudina* and *durdina*, [the suffix] *kāya* is optionally applied (*kāovāo*). [Examples: *sudināyate*; *durdināyate*.
Also, from *nīhāra*, [the suffix] *kāya* is optionally applied (*kāovāo*). [Example: *nīhārāyate*.

The inclusion of *aṭṭā*, *śīkā*, *koṭā*, *poṭā*, *soṭā*, *pruṣṭā*, and *pluṣṭā* must be made [in the list]. *Poṭā* refers to a woman possessing the characteristics of both male and female; others besides this are verbal roots, according to Mādhava in his *Subdhātuvṛtti*. *Aṭa* (meaning "to go," *bhvādigaṇa*, *parasmaipada*, 296): from *aṭati*, the suffix *ac* is applied and then *ṭāp*; that which performs this is *aṭāyate*. *Aṭṭa* (meaning "to transgress" and "to injure," *curādigaṇa*, 28): by the rule *gurośca halaḥ* (*Pāṇini* 3.3.103), the suffix *a* is added—thus *aṭṭā*; that which performs this is *aṭṭāyate*. *Śīkṛ* (meaning "to sprinkle," *bhvādigaṇa*, *ātmanepada*, 75): beginning with the palatal sound (*tālavyādi*).

Dhanapāla and Kāśyapa, however, hold that it begins with *d* (i.e., *duṭ*). Regarding the *a*-suffix after a heavy syllable (*gurośca halaḥ*), Mādhava explains the verbal root in question as follows: one who performs the act of *śīkā* (a woman of ill repute) is said to "act like a *śīkā*" (*śīkāyate*). The root *kuṭ* meaning "crookedness" (*kauṭilye*) belongs to the *tudādi* class; with the causative suffix *ṇic*, it becomes *koṭayati* or *koṭayate*, and one who performs that act is *koṭā*, who then "acts like a *koṭā*" (*koṭāyate*). The term *poṭā* has already been mentioned; one who acts like her is *poṭāyate*. If the reading is *soṭā*, the meaning of the verbal root must be sought elsewhere.

In the reading *moṭā*, however, *muṭ* belongs to the curādi group in the sense of "crushing" (*sañcūrṇana*), and to the bhvādi group in the sense of "showing" (*pradarśana*). In the tudādi group (tuopao94), it occurs in the senses of "showing" and "thrusting. Thus, from *moṭayati*, we derive *moṭā*; and from *moṭāyate*. From *pruṣ* and *pluṣ* in the sense of "burning" (*dāha*) [bhyāopao55,56], the suffix *kta* is applied in the passive sense (*karmaṇi ktaḥ*), resulting in *pruṣṭā* and *pluṣṭā*. One who causes these to be done is expressed as *pruṣṭāyate* and *pluṣṭāyate*.

Ujjvaladatta, however, in his commentary on the sūtra *aśūprūṣilaṭikaṇikhaṭiviśibhyaḥ kvan* (Uṇādi-sūtra 157), cites Ratnamati’s statement: "*pruṣvaḥ syād ṛtusūryayoḥ*" ("*pruṣva* may mean the season or the sun") and "*pruṣvā jalakaṇikā*" ("*pruṣvā* means a drop of water"). Citing the root *pluṣ* in the sense of "moistening" (*snehanādi*) as his example for the form "*pruṣvāyate*," he has introduced the reading "*pruṣvā*" here in the Vārttika (Pāṇini-sūtra 3.1.18).

*Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.18*: *sukhādibhyaḥ kartṛvedanāyām*. The word *kartṛ* (agent) is a separate word with its genitive case ending elided (*lupta-ṣaṣṭhīka*). *Vedanā* means knowledge (*jñāna*). [The term is derived] from the root *vid* (meaning "to perceive," "to declare," or "to dwell") belonging to the *curādi* class; from this, after adding the causative suffix *ṇic*, the suffix *yuc* is applied in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*) by *Pāṇini Sūtra 3.3.107* (*ṇyāsaśrantho yuc*). Alternatively, it is formed by the supplementary rule (*aupasaṅkhyānika*) *ghaṭṭivandividibhyaśca*. And the status of being the agent (*kartṛtva*) is relative to the action of perceiving mentioned in the scripture.

This is the meaning: the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied after words such as *sukha* (happiness), which are objects related to the agent of the action of feeling (*vedana*) by way of being inherent in that agent, when the sense is "feeling. For example: *sukhaṃ vedayate* → *sukhāyate* ("he feels happiness"). Why is the mention of the "agent" (*kartṛ*) necessary? [Consider: *sukhaṃ vedayate prasādhako rājñaḥ* ("the attendant feels happiness for the king"). This root *vid* belongs to the *ākusmīya* group. Thus, the reading of the *parasmaipada* form *vedayati* found in some texts is an error. Regarding this, the author of the *Ślokagaṇa* says:

*sukha-duḥkha-gahana-kṛcchra-stṛpra-alīka-pratīpa-karuṇāś-ca | kṛpaṇaḥ soḍhaḥ—iti ime sukhādayo daśa gaṇe paṭhitāḥ ||* "These ten, beginning with *sukha*, are recited in the list: *sukha*, *duḥkha*, *gahana*, *kṛcchra*, *stṛpra*, *alīka*, *pratīpa*, *karuṇa*, *kṛpaṇa*, and *soḍha*."
*Soḍham* means endurance or overcoming. In the *Gamaratnamahodadhi*, however, the word *āsram* is also listed here [as a synonym].
(Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.19)

Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.19: *namovarivaścitraṅaḥ kyac*. The term "instrument" (*karaṇa*) from the preceding rule does not carry over here; rather, by the inherent nature of its expressive power, it refers here specifically to a particular action. Therefore, the suffix *kyac* is applied after *namas-* in the sense of worship, after *varivas-* in the sense of service, and after *citraṅ-* in the sense of wonder. *namasyati devān*: the meaning is that he worships the gods with prostration. *varivasyati gurūn*: the meaning is that he serves his teachers. *citrīyate*: the meaning is that he is amazed; [this is used] at the end of the form *viśmāyayate*.

And likewise, regarding the illusory deer (*māyāmṛga*), Bhaṭṭi says: "Then, being struck with wonder (*citrīyamāṇaḥ*). Here, because the marker *ṅ* is applied to the root *citri*, it must be stated that a grammatical feature (*liṅga*) applied to a constituent part serves as a qualifier for the whole. This being the case, the *ātmanepada* ending occurs after the form ending in *kyac*. Nor should it be argued: "In this way, let the word *citra* also be included in the rule *śabdavairakalahābhrātikārṣṇyaprātipadakebhyaḥ kyaṣ* (Pāṇini 3.1.17), so that the *taṅ* (the *ātmanepada* endings) will occur by means of *kyaṣ* itself. For if that were the case, the substitution of *ī* [for the vowel] by the rule *kyaci ca* (Pāṇini 7.4.33) would not take place.
Therefore, the suffix *kyac* alone should be applied, and the *ṅ* marker [to its root]. (Pāṇini 3.1.20)

[The suffix *ṇiṅ* is applied after the words] *puccha*, *bhāṇḍa*, and *cīvara*. Since the term *karaṇa* (instrument) is understood [from the previous rule], [the suffix is applied] to denote specific actions: lifting up (*udāsana*), throwing away (*vyasana*), and tossing around (*paryasana*) in the case of *puccha*; and gathering together (*samācayana*) in the case of *bhāṇḍa*. *Lifting up* (*udāsana*) means raising up. *Throwing away* (*vyasana*) means various or contrary ways of raising up. *Tossing around* (*paryasana*) means throwing all around. Examples: *utpucchayate* (he lifts up his tail), *vipucchayate* (he throws his tail away), *paripucchayate* (he tosses his tail around). From *bhāṇḍa*, [the suffix is applied] in the sense of gathering together (*samācayana*). Gathering together means making into a heap. Example: *sambhāṇḍayate* (he gathers the goods together); the meaning is that he collects the goods (*bhāṇḍāni*) into a heap.

[The suffix] *kā* [is applied after the root *ci*] in the sense of acquiring or wearing a robe (*cīvara*). A monk "acquires a robe" (*saṃcīvarayate*) means he either acquires robes or wears them. The letter *ṇ* in the causative marker *ṇiṅ* is for the purpose of including the general [root *ci*], and not for the purpose of *vṛddhi* strengthening, because that is impossible. The letter *ṅ* is for the purpose of preventing [the application of other rules] and for the purpose of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). For this very reason, roots such as *puccha* are not included in the subsequent rule.

Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.21: *muṇḍamiśraślakṣṇalavaṇavratavastrahala-kalakṛtatūstebhyo ṇic*. The suffix *ṇic* is applied after these ten [words] in the sense of the root *kṛ* ("to do/make"). *Muṇḍam karoti* becomes *muṇḍayati* (he shaves). *Miśrayati* (he mixes). *Ślakṣṇayati* (he smoothes). *Lavaṇayati* (he seasons with salt). Regarding *vrata*: according to Kātyāyana’s Vārttika, it is used in the sense of "eating" and "abstaining from eating. *Payo vratayati* (he observes a milk-vow) or *śūdrānnam vratayati* (he abstains from the food of a Śūdra).

[The suffix] *kya* occurs after the word *vastra* in the sense of "covering. [Thus one forms] *saṃvastrayati*. Here, the meanings of the word *vrata* are "eating" and "abstinence from it," whereas the meaning of the word *vastra* is "covering. The suffix, however, has the sense of the root *kṛ* ("to do"). And the word *vrata* is indeed heard in the sense of eating: "Whatever milk is his *vrata*, that increases his very self"; "Manu was one who had three *vratas*; the Asuras were two-*vrata*; the gods were one-*vrata*. And in the *Paspaśā*: "And by this [method], even dog-meat and such things can be made into a *vrata* (consumed as a religious observance)."

This very word *vrata* functions, by means of indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on its opposite, to denote the cessation [of an action], just as in the case of *darśa* and other such terms. Mādhava states that in the expression "he clothes himself in a cloak" (*saṃvastrayati prāvāram*), the meaning is "he covers himself with a cloak. From the three roots beginning with *hali*, the suffix is applied when there is the sense of grasping: from *hali*, *haliṃ gṛhṇāti* becomes *halayati*; from *kali*, *kaliṃ gṛhṇāti* becomes *kalayati*; from *kṛta*, *kṛtaṃ gṛhṇāti* becomes *kṛtayati*. From *tūsta*, in the sense of pulling out, one forms *vitūstayati* (as in *tūstāni vihanti*). Śrībhadra says, "tūsta is hair," while the *Nyāsa* explains it as "hair that has become matted. The *Vaijayantī* lexicon identifies it as "sin."

It might be argued: "All this is already established by the rule *pratipadikāddhātvarthe* (Gaṇasūtra). Nor is there a restriction regarding the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) in that context by means of the rule *tat karoti* (Gaṇasūtra), since forms such as *atyararājat* ('he surpassed the king') are also desired. If one asks, "Then what is the purpose of the rule concerning *muṇḍa* and so forth?"—to this they reply: This [rule] is for the sake of deriving the causative suffix (*ṇic*) even from words that require a complement, as in *muṇḍayati māṇavakam* ('he shaves the boy'), *miśrayaty annam* ('he mixes the food'), *ślakṣṇayati vastram* ('he polishes the cloth'), and *lavaṇayati vyañjanam* ('he seasons the condiment'). Furthermore, it is for the sake of the irregular substitution of *at* for the vowels of *halika* and *krīḍa*. Thus says the Vārttika:

The designation of *halika* and *kalika* as ending in the vowel *a* is for the purpose of prohibiting their treatment as *san*-like (*sanvadbhāva*). For instance, when *halika* or *kalika* is in the state [of derivation], the rule *aco ñṇiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.115) would require Vṛddhi, and by the rule *ṇāviṣṭhavad* [the suffix *ṇa*] being treated like *iṣṭhan*, the *ṭi*-elision would also apply. In that case, the elision is non-permanent (*anitya*) because it is superseded by the attainment of another form; however, the Vṛddhi is permanent because it does not apply once the *ṭi*-elision has taken effect.

Since both [rules] are non-eternal (*anitya*), when *vṛddhi* has been applied, the elision (*lopa*) would occur before the substitution of *aikāra* with *āy*, because of the priority (*paratva*) [of the rule for elision] and because a rule concerning phonemes (*vārṇa*) is stronger than one concerning a stem (*āṅga*). Consequently, this [stem] would not be one that loses its *nakāra* (*anaglopin*), and thus the treatment as having a *saN*-augment (*sanvadbhāva*) according to Pāṇini 7.4.93 would apply. Furthermore, it should not be argued that there is no fault because of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) by Pāṇini 7.4.94, since that is separated [from the *laghu*] by that [substitution]. For [the rule states]: "When a *ṇi* followed by *caṅ* is present, the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) of that which is the *aṅga* [ending in *ṇi*] is followed by a *laghu*; for that, there is the treatment as *saN* and the lengthening of the *laghu*."

In the commentary presented by Kaiyaṭa as the view of "some" (ekīyamata), which was favored by Haradatta and others, the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (the treatment of a substitute as the original) is irrelevant. Even according to the views of the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa—namely, that the rule applies to the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) occurring after a light vowel (*laghu*) in a *ṇi*-affix followed by *caṅ*—since the reduplication occurs only after the elision of the *ṭi* (the penultimate vowel) has taken place, it is not something seen as preceding the designated vowel (*ādiṣṭādacaḥ pūrva*). Therefore, when an operation is to be performed regarding what is seen as preceding the designated vowel, the prescribed status of being a *sthānivat* does not apply; this is the meaning. [The phrase] "as something seen as preceding the designated vowel" [is used].

Because the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) would not apply here. However, if *at* is prescribed as an *anipātana* (an irregular, non-technical term), then even though *vṛddhi* occurs by virtue of its higher priority, only the *ag* portion is elided; thus, neither the *sanvadbhāva* nor the lengthening takes place. Consequently, from roots such as *bal* and *paṭ*, when followed by *ṇic*, one obtains *abībalat* and *apīpaṭat*, and not *ababalat* and *apapaṭat*.

It might be argued that this contradicts the Bhāṣya on Pāṇini 7.4.1 (*ṇau caṅi*), for there it is established that elision (*lopa*) is stronger than *vṛddhi*. And this is logical, because even when another form of the word is obtained, permanence (*nityatva*) is sometimes accepted based merely on the fact that an operation applies whether [the other rule] has been performed or not. As it says: "Because the *vuK* augment after *bhū* is permanent," and so forth. Furthermore, the evidence here is the inclusion of the term *ag* as a *pratyāhāra* (abbreviation) in the rule Pāṇini 7.4.2 (*nāglopiśāsvṛditām*).

For instance, when there is a *vṛddhi* [substitution] after words ending in an *a*-vowel or having an *a*-vowel as their penultimate letter, as well as after words ending in an *ṛ*-vowel, it is only the *a*-vowel that is elided. In that case, one should simply state: "not for those [words] whose [penultimate vowel] does not undergo elision (*alopinām na*). However, in the case of words ending in an *i*-vowel or an *u*-vowel, once the *vṛddhi* has been applied, it is the *au*-vowel that is elided, and not the *a*-vowel.

It should not be argued that in examples such as *asasvāmat* (from *svāmin*), *ajugomat* (from *gomin*), *apaprādat* (from *prāduḥ*), *ayayādat* (from *yādṛśa*), and *atatādat* (from *tādṛśa*)—where the elision of the initial vowel occurs because the rule for *vṛddhi* does not apply—the mention of the suffix *aṅ* [in Pāṇini 6.4.72] is intended to prevent the shortening of the vowel; for due to the lack of conventional usage (*anabhidhāna*), the causative suffix (*ṇic*) does not arise at all in those cases. This is understood from the fact that the author of the Bhāṣya supports [the view of] its being an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

Nor should it be argued that even in this case, in the example *asasraijat* (he caused [him] to unstring), the mention of *aglopa-* (loss of a vowel) in Pāṇini 6.4.123 would be for the purpose of preventing the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) when the suffixes *vin* and *matup* are elided—since there is indeed an indication to that effect in the Bhāṣya on Aṣṭādhyāyī 6.4.143 (*ṭeḥ*), where *srajayati* is cited as an example. For even so, the absence of vṛddhi in *srajayati* is accepted as the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), because the author of the Bhāṣya on 6.4.143 cites *srajayati* as the illustration, or else by the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) *āṅgavṛtte punarvṛttāvavidhiḥ* ("when an operation has already taken place within a stem, a subsequent operation does not apply again").

Since there would be no occurrence of *vṛddhi*, the short-vowel substitute (*hrasva*) for the penultimate (*upadhā*) would not exist at all; therefore, the inclusion of the pratyāhāra [in the rule] indicates that the *ṭilopa* occurs prior to the *vṛddhi*. If it is asked: "How then can it be said here that the *ṭilopa* occurs after the *vṛddhi* has taken place?"

Regarding this, Mādhava has set forth three views in his *Subdhātuvṛtti*: one view holds that "vṛddhi [occurs] because it is subsequent" is the primary position (*mukhya-pakṣa*), whereas "elision (*lopa*) is stronger than vṛddhi" is merely a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*); another view is the opposite of that; and yet another view, based on the authority of two *bhāṣya* passages, maintains that since elision of the *ṭi* suffix may occur optionally either before or after the vṛddhi, both forms *apapaṭat* and *apīpaṭat* are correct. Thus, he has recorded all three opinions.

The distinction here is that the first view belongs to Haradatta, the second to Kaiyaṭa, and the third to others. An investigation into their relative strength will be conducted later. Furthermore, this distinction pertains to a domain different from that of the suffix *ṇi*. However, in the case of *ṇi* followed by *ṇic*, the elision of *ṇi* occurs first—either by the rule of "exception" (*vipratiṣedha*) according to the maxim "the elision of *ṇi* and *ṇal* [take precedence]," or because it is an exception (*apavāda*) according to the method of extraction (*niṣkarṣa*). Regarding the shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hrasvatva*), the treatment as *sannat* (like the desiderative), and the lengthening, we shall explain in the seventh [chapter] that the form is indeed *avīvadat*, either due to the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) "ṇerṇici" or because of the designation of the class-form (*ṇyākṛti-nirdeśa*).

Let us return to the subject at hand. In the sūtra beginning with *muṇḍa*, the inclusion of certain items is for the sake of elaboration (*prapañca*). All the items starting with *muṇḍa* ought to have been read in that very sūtra, namely *satyāpapāśa-* (Pāṇini 3.1.25). For in this way, a single unified statement (*ekavākyatā*) would be obtained, and there would be the economy of not having to include the causative marker *ṇic* twice. However, it was not done in that manner. (Pāṇini 3.1.22)

Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.22: *dhātor ekāco halādeḥ kriyāsamabhihāre yaṅ*. From a root (*dhātu*) that consists of a single vowel (*ekāc*), begins with a consonant (*halādi*), and denotes an action that is being repeated (*samabhihriyamāṇakriyāvṛtti*), the suffix *yaṅ* shall be applied in its own sense (*svārthe*). Here, "repetition" (*samabhihāra*) means either frequency (*paunaḥpunya*) or intensity (*bhṛsārtha*). Although the primary meaning of the word *samabhihāra* is the heaping together (*rāśīkaraṇa*) of scattered things into one place, this is only possible for things such as grain and the like; it cannot apply to the action denoted by a verbal root, because action is formless (*amūrtatva*).

Therefore, a secondary (gauṇa) meaning is understood. And that [meaning] is not the denoted object (vācya) of the suffix, because it would result in the suffix becoming the qualificand (viśeṣya) with respect to the meaning of the stem; rather, it is the indicated (dyotya) meaning. For this very reason, the established path is that suffixes such as *ṭāp* and *tarap* are merely those which express their own inherent meaning (*svārthika*). However, when the general rule of the primacy of the stem-meaning is abandoned—even in the case of *ṭāp* and other suffixes, just as in the case of finite verbs—then the position that *ṭāp* and others are denoters (*vācaka*) is indeed possible.

And this [application] has been accepted even in the Bhāṣya regarding the rules for the *yaṅ* suffix and so forth, as is clear from various places therein. One cooks excessively or repeatedly: *pāpacyate*. The lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule "the long vowel [is substituted] for a non-*kit* [root]" (Pāṇini 7.4.83). It shines intensely: *dedīpyate*. The *guṇa* [substitution] occurs by the rule "there is *guṇa* in the case of *yaṅ* and its elision" (Pāṇini 7.4.82).

If it is asked: "Why is there not a doubling of the word here by the rule *nityavīpsayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.4), or by the Vārttika *kriyāsamabhihāre ca*?"—the answer is that the frequent repetition (*kriyāsamabhihāra*) is already indicated by the suffix *yaṅ* itself. Nor should it be argued that, on these grounds, doubling would likewise not occur in cases such as *lunīhi lunīhi*; for in that case, the particle *hi*, which is identical in form to the imperative (*loṭ*), requires doubling as an auxiliary to indicate the frequent repetition, otherwise ambiguity would arise. However, *yaṅ* does not function in this way; thus, there is a difference between the two cases.

What is the purpose of [specifying] "from a verbal root"? It is so that [the suffixes] may have the status of being *ārdhadhātuka*. By means of this, forms such as "bruvo vaciḥ" (P. 2.4.53) are established. What is the purpose of [specifying] "monosyllabic" (*ekāca*)? [Consider: *punaḥpunar jāgarti* ("he wakes up again and again"). What is the purpose of [specifying] "beginning with a consonant" (*halādeḥ*)? [Consider: *bhṛśam īkṣate* ("he looks intensely"). The *ṅit*-status of the *yaṅ* suffix is for the sake of preventing *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, and *niṣṭhā*-substitution, as in *bobhūyate* and *marīmṛjyate*.

Nor should it be argued that, because the [suffix] has already fulfilled its purpose with respect to the individual constituent (*avayava*), it would not qualify the whole (*samudāya*) and thus the *ātmanepada* ending would not occur after a root with the *yaṅ* affix; for this has been explained in detail in the very sūtra "anudāttaṅita ātmanepadam" (Pāṇini 1.3.12), which states that the [ending] occurs after a root ending in a *ṅit* suffix. Regarding the examples "he shines intensely" (*bhṛśaṃ śobhate*) and "it pleases intensely" (*bhṛśaṃ rocate*), the *Bhāṣya* states that the *yaṅ* affix does not apply here due to a lack of conventional usage (*anabhidhāna*).

If it is asked: "How then do the authors of the *Dhātuvṛtti*, while explaining the roots *ruca* (to shine) [DhP 1.746] and *śubha* (to beautify) [DhP 10.41], cite *rorucyate* and *śośubhyate* as examples? They reply: "Because the *Mahābhāṣya* mentions the sense of 'intensity' (*bhṛśārtha*), it occurs precisely when there is repetition (*paunaḥpunya*). Furthermore, according to the *Dhātucandrodaya*, since *śobhate* is cited as an example for the *śap*-affix, the *yaṅ* suffix certainly occurs for the root belonging to the *tudādi* class. [This is supported by the rule: "The inclusion of *sūci*, *sūtri*, *mūtri*, *aṭi*, *arti*, *aśu*, and *ṛṇu* [in the list of roots taking *yaṅ*]."

The roots *sūc* (meaning "to hint," Dhatupatha 3.41), *sūtr* (meaning "to loosen," 3.76), and *mūtr* (meaning "to urinate," 3.161)—as well as both forms of *aś*, namely *aś* (meaning "to eat," Kryādi 51) and *aś* (meaning "to pervade," Svādi 18)—are all included here. Among these, the first three [roots] do not qualify for the present rule because they consist of more than one consonant (*anekāl*). The others do not qualify because they do not begin with a consonant (*ahalādi*). As for *ūrṇu*, it does not qualify because it consists of more than one consonant and does not begin with a consonant; therefore, this rule is stated for its sake. However, in this case, the desired result for *ūrṇu* is already established by the application of the *ṇuvat*-substitution that will be mentioned later. Examples: *sosūcyate*, *sosūtryate*.

The roots *sūci* and *sūtri* end in vowels. After adding the causative suffix *ṇic* (belonging to the *cur*-class), there is elision of the vowel *a*. Then follows the intensive suffix *yaṅ*, elision of *ṇi*, reduplication, and by Pāṇini 7.4.60 (*halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*), all but the first consonant of the reduplicated syllable are dropped. Guṇa is applied to the reduplicated syllable. However, the substitution of *ṣ* for the following letter does not occur because it is not an original substitute (*anādeśatvāt*). Nor are these two roots *ṣopadeśas* (roots taught with an initial *ṣ*), because they end in a vowel and thus consist of more than one syllable. For the definition of a *ṣopadeśa*—which excludes roots such as *seksṛ* and others—implies that similarity to those [monosyllabic roots] requires them to consist of a single syllable; this is the established conclusion. Furthermore, the examples given in the Bhāṣya, namely *sosūcyate* and *sosūtryate*, serve as proof for this point.

This is precisely the intention of Mādhava as well, who states that in the definition of *ṣopadeśa* (roots with an initial sibilant), the property of having a single vowel (*ekāctva*) must be included as a qualification. This is formulated [in the following examples]: *aṭāṭyate*. Since it will be stated later that the genitive case in Pāṇini’s rule 6.1.2, *ajāder dvitīyasya*, [refers to the second syllable], [the reduplication applies there]. [In the case of] *arāryate*, there is *guṇa* substitution by Pāṇini’s rules 7.4.28 (*guṇo 'rtisaṃyogādyoḥ*) and 7.4.30 (*yaṅi ca*), and the doubling of the *rya* sound.

Nor does the prohibition of doubling for the letter *r* apply here by the rule "nandrāḥ saṃyogādayaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.3), because the author of the Vṛtti on the sixth [chapter] states: "This prohibition does not apply when [the *r*] is followed by a *y*. Nor is this without authority, for the very Bhāṣya on the present sūtra—"arārthataḥ"—serves as proof in that regard. *aśāśyate*. *ūrṇonūyate*. The root *muc* is used in the sense of covering (*ācchādane*). This [root] has *n* as its penultimate letter (*nopadha*). Its *ṇ*-substitution occurs according to the eighth [chapter]. Because that [substitution] is considered "not established" (*asiddha*), the word *nu* undergoes doubling.

The rule *pūrvatrāsiddham* (Pāṇini 8.2.1), which states that what precedes is as if non-existent, is not universally valid regarding reduplication (*advirvacane*), because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule *ubhau sābhyāsasya* (Pāṇini 8.4.29). It might be argued as follows: In the case of *lunīhi-lunīhi evāyaṃ lunāti*, the imperative (*loṭ*) would be superseded by the intensive suffix (*yaṅ*). For the *yaṅ* is internal (*antaraṅga*), since it depends only on the repetition of the action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*), whereas the imperative is external (*bahiraṅga*), because it is prescribed for the agent, object, or state when there is a connection between verbal roots based on a distinction in the action. If so, where does the imperative find its scope? It finds it in cases with more than one vowel (*anekāc*) and those beginning with a vowel other than *a* (*ajādau*). For example: *jāgṛhi-jāgṛhi evāyaṃ jāgarti* ("He keeps waking up") and *īkṣasva-īkṣasva evāyam īkṣate* ("He keeps looking").

Regarding this, they say: the word *vā* ("or") is understood [from the previous rule]. When *yaṅ* does not apply, then the *loṭ* suffix will apply. (Pāṇini 3.1.23) *nityaṃ kauṭilye gatau*: when a verbal root denotes motion (*gati*), *yaṅ* shall necessarily (*nityam*) occur only when crookedness (*kauṭilya*) is to be expressed, and not for the intensification of action (*kriyā-samabhihāra*). From the roots *kramu* (to step, DhP 4.74) and *drama* (to move, DhP 4.67), we have *caṅkramyate* and *dandramyate*. Because of the inclusion of the word *nityam* for the sake of restriction, it does not occur here: *bhṛśaṃ krāmati* ("he strides intensely").

Now, one might object: just as by the rule "vaḍavāyā vṛṣe vācye," the suffix *ap* which would have applied to the offspring is set aside and another is prescribed; or just as by the rule "ñītaḥ ktaḥ," the suffix *kta* which would have applied to the past tense is set aside and another is prescribed for the present tense—so too here, since *yaṅ* is prescribed after any verbal root (*dhātu*) for the intensification of action (*kriyā-samabhihāra*), while it is prescribed after roots meaning motion (*gati-vacana*) for crookedness (*kauṭilya*), the sublation [of the former by the latter] is established by the very logic of the "curd and Kauṇḍinya" maxim (*takra-kauṇḍinya-nyāya*). True; for this very reason, the mention of the word "nitya" (constant/always) in the Bhāṣya and Vārttika has been rejected.
(Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.24)

Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.24: *lupasada-carajapajabhada-ha-daśa-gṛbhyaḥ bhāvagarhāyām*. The suffix *yaṅ* shall be applied after these [roots] when the reproach (*garhā*) regarding the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is to be expressed. *lup* (DhP 10.151): "to cut. *sad* (DhP 4.879): "to perish," etc. Regarding the root *sad*: Haradatta states that the causative form *sādayati* derived from the curādi class root *āṅ-sad* (DhP 10.299), which means "to go" (*padyarthe*), is not included here because of the continued application of the rule *ekācaḥ* ("after a one-vowel root"). However, this is questionable; for when the base form (*prakṛti*) is mentioned, there is no possibility of including anything additional, such as a causative suffix (*ṇic*).

Otherwise, since even forms such as *lup* or those ending in the causative suffix *ṇic* would have to be excluded, there would be no reason for mentioning only *sad*. [The roots are: *cara* (to move, *bhvādigaṇa*, 560); *japa* (inarticulate speech, *bhvādigaṇa*, 396); *jabhī* (to yawn, *bhvādigaṇa*, 388); *daha* (to burn to ashes, *bhvādigaṇa*, 1016). Precisely because of this, by the rule of irregularity (*nipātana*), there is the elision of *na* when the *yaṅ* suffix is dropped: *dandaśīti*. *gṝ* (to swallow, *tudādigaṇa*, 130); *gṝ* (sound, *kryādigaṇa*, 26).

In this regard, some maintain that because of its association with roots whose vowel is not subject to modification (*adanta-vikaraṇa*), only the root *tud* and others are intended; others hold that both [roots ending in *u* and those ending in *ū*] are included. *Lolupyate* means "he repeatedly cuts in a contemptible manner. *Sāsadyate*. *Cañcūryate*. Here, by the rule *caraphalośca* (Pāṇini 7.4.87), the augment *nuK* is inserted; then by *utparasyātaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.88) and *hali ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.2), there is lengthening of the vowel. *Jañjapyate*. *Jañjabhyate*. *Dandahyate*. *Dandaśyate*.

The suffix *nu* is applied to the four roots beginning with *jap* (as prescribed by Pāṇini 7.4.86: *japajabhadahadaśabhañjapaśāñca*) for their repetition (*abhyāsa*). Thus, from *nijegilyate*: by [the rule] *ṛta iddhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.100), the substitution of *i* for *ṛ*; then the doubling (*dvirvacana*) of the root; then the *guṇa* strengthening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*); and when the form *jegirya* is established, the substitution of *l* for *r* occurs by *gro yaṅi* (Pāṇini 8.3.20). Nor does the lengthening (*dīrgha*) prescribed by *hali ca* (Pāṇini 6.4.2) apply here on account of its higher status in the order of rules, because that rule is considered asiddha (not yet effective) relative to the present operation. Once the substitution of *l* has been made, the lengthening does not occur because the conditions for it have been subverted.

What does "he cultivates" (bhāveti) mean? It is so that [the rule] may not apply in cases of censuring the means (*sādhana*): "The low-born man (*vṛṣala*) mutters the mantra. Here, because there is no lapse in accent, phoneme, and so forth, there is no censure [of the action itself]. However, the means designated as the agent (*kartṛ*) is censured, because a Śūdra lacks qualification for the Veda. The inclusion of the word "always" (*nitya*) continues here for the sake of restriction; its explanation is as before.

Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.25: *satyāpa-pāśa-rūpa-vīṇā-tūla-śloka-senā-loma-tvac-varma-varṇa-cūrṇa-curādibhyo ṇic*. The suffix *ṇic* shall be applied after these [words]. Since the formation would already be established by the rule "after nominal stems beginning with *satya* and ending with *cūrṇa*, in the sense of verbal action" (*dhātvarthe*), this specific statement is for the purpose of adding the augment *apuk* to *satya*; for the others, it serves as an elaboration (*prapañca*); and in cases such as *mālinyā upaślokayati* ("he praises the courtesan"), it is for the purpose of allowing the suffix to arise even after a word that requires a complement (*sāpekṣa*).

Although the term "in the sense of the root-meaning" (dhātvarthe) is stated without qualification, the specific meaning obtained through the inherent nature [of the suffix] is pointed out by the author of the Vṛtti and others. For example: *satyāpayati* means "he declares the truth"; for the Bhāṣya says, "he makes it true."

The augment *āpuk* should be stated after the roots *arth*, *vid*, and *sat*. Due to the force of the statement regarding *āpuk*, there is no elision (*tilopa*) [of the penultimate vowel]; thus, it causes one to understand *arthāpayati*. Some say that since the result would have been established by *puk* alone, the explicit mention of the vowel *ā* is for the purpose of prescribing it from another rule, and by this, forms such as *likhāpayati* are established. That is not correct, because it contradicts the Bhāṣya which states, "the augment *puk* alone will be applied. Therefore, they say that *likhāpayati* is simply an incorrect usage.

Regarding the usage in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*, "he causes the feet to be washed," Haradatta and others maintain that this is to be justified by the principle that "the seers act according to the Vedic meters. He releases the noose: *vipāśayati*. He looks at the form: *rūpayati*. He sings along with the lute: *upavīṇayati*. He scrapes with cotton: *anutūlayati* the tip of a blade of grass; Haradatta says the meaning is "he scratches" (*anukuṣṇāti*) or "he rubs against" (*anughaṭṭayati*). He praises with verses: *upaślokayati*.

In *abhiṣeṇayati* ("he marches with an army"), the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by Pāṇini 8.3.65 (*upasargāt sunoti*). In *abhyaṣeṇayat*, the substitution of *ṣ* occurs by Pāṇini 8.2.63 (*prāk sitādaḍvyavāye 'pi*). From the root *tvac* in the sense of "covering" (*saṃvaraṇe*), the suffix *gha* is applied by Pāṇini 3.3.118 (*puṃsi sañjñāyām*). In *tvacayati* ("he covers"), there is no vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) of the penultimate vowel because the elision of the *ṭi* (the *a* of *tvaca*) is treated as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*).

From the very root mentioned above, which ends in a consonant, the suffix *ṇic* is applied by the rule *tat karoti* (Gaṇasūtra), as in *tvacayati*; here, the *vṛddhi* strengthening of the penultimate vowel indeed occurs. By the rule *prakṛtyaikāc* (Pāṇini 6.4.163), there is no elision (*ṭilopa*) of the suffix. Therefore, it should be understood that in the sūtra, the letter *a* in *tvacaḥ* is intended to be significant (*vivakṣita*), and not merely for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*), as is the case with *satyāpeta*. He arms himself with armor: *saṃvarmayati*. He assumes a color: *saṃvarṇayati*. He scatters with powders: *avacūrṇayati*. From roots such as *cura*, the suffix *ṇic* is added in the sense of the root itself (*svārthe*): *corayati*, *cintayati*. (Pāṇini 3.1.26)

*Hetumati ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.26). *Hetu* is the instigator (*prayojaka*) of the agent; that which possesses the activity of such an instigator—namely, an impulsion (*pravartanā*)—is called *hetumat*. When this [impulsion] is to be expressed, the suffix *ṇic* is added to the verbal root. For example: *pācayati devadatto yajñadattena* ("Devadatta causes Yajñadatta to cook"). The meaning is: the impulsion residing in Devadatta has as its object the activity conducive to the softening [of the rice] located in Yajñadatta. Impulsion is of many kinds: command (*preṣaṇa*), entreaty (*adhyeṣaṇa*), and acting in a manner conducive to that [action]. Command is the impelling of an inferior person, such as a servant; it means an order.

*Adhyeṣaṇā* (solicitation) is the urging of one worthy of worship, such as a teacher; it means a request. Its corresponding performance is also manifold, consisting of *anumati* (consent), *upadeśa* (instruction), and *anugraha* (favor). Among these, one without whose consent an action cannot be accomplished is a prompter (*prayojaka*) by mere consent, such as a king and the like. A physician and others, however, are prompters merely through instruction, such as saying, "The fever patient should drink a decoction."

Furthermore, he who stops someone fleeing while being pursued by another with the intent to kill is indeed an instigator (*prayojaka*), because he acts as a facilitator for the killer. Thus, in this context, these specific distinctions are to be understood from the meaning, the context, and other factors. However, the general sense of "incitement" (*pravartanā-sāmānya*) that pervades all cases is the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*). And since that [general sense] is the primary denotation (*śakya*) of the *ṇic*, this is the principal view. The alternative view—that it is merely indicated (*dyotya*)—is also established in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*).

Although, because the word *hetu* (cause) is inherently relational, when one says "possessing a cause" (*hetumān*), that very thing toward which there is causality is understood—just as when one says "having a father" (*pitṛmān*), the son is understood—and such a "cause" is designated as *hetu* within the section on *kārakas*, namely the agent (*kartṛ*) and the action (*kriyā*), making it logical for either the agent or the cooking to possess causality; nevertheless, because of the governing rule *karaṇe* ("in the sense of instrument"), the agent is not taken here, nor is the cooking, since that is already expressed by the verbal root itself. Rather, it is that which [is related] in relation to the cooking and the cooker...

The established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that in common worldly usage, the very operation (*vyāpāra*) of a cause, which is by its own nature well-known as the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), is expressed by the word "cause" (*hetu*); and thus, the rule *hetutaḥ* alone would have been appropriate. The meaning would then have been: "the causative suffix (*ṇic*) occurs when the cause functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*). However, it was not formulated in that way.

In this context, although it has been described in the Bhāṣya and other works that the suffix *ṇic* is merely indicative (*dyotaka*)—on the grounds that both the result and the operation are denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*), and because the property of being an operation conducive to softening (*viklitti-anukūla-vyāpāra*) is easily found even in the case of commanding (*preṣaṇa*) and so forth, such that even that [commanding] could be considered the meaning of the root *pac*—nevertheless, this is merely a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*). For instance, it is specifically the particular operation beginning with placing [the pot] on the fire (*adhiśrayaṇa*) that constitutes the meaning of the root *pac*.

However, [the agent] prior to that [state] is not [denoted], because the term "pacati" (he cooks) is not employed during the stage of buying [grain] and so forth; otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, occasional usage can be accounted for as being figurative (*bhākta*), and because the difference in meaning between *pacati* and *pācayati* is established by experience. Moreover, one must accept the established rule that "that which is the agent (*kartṛ*) in the root-sense (*aṇau*) becomes the object (*karman*) in the causative sense (*ṇau*)," and so on. In cases such as *praṇāyayati* and *abhiṣāvayati*, when a prefix (*upasarga*) indicates a specific quality residing in the meaning of the verbal base (*prakṛtyartha*), the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* and *ṣ* for *s* occurs due to the presence of the causative suffix (*ṇic*).

But it is not so in the case of a relationship, as is clear from the eighth [chapter]. Therefore, one should not be overly insistent on this position. It might be argued: "If the mere instigation (*pravartanā*) is the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), then there would be the undesirable consequence of *ṇic* being a synonym for the imperative (*loṭ*) and other such suffixes. Consequently, when one ought to say 'May you ask me,' the causative suffix would also be employed. To this we reply: The instigator of an agent is indeed the "efficient cause" (*hetu*); however, the object of the command has not yet been determined as an agent. Thus, the distinction is that the meaning of *ṇic* is an instigation conditioned by the activity of the one to be prompted, whereas the meaning of the imperative is the instigation alone. And it has been said:
"But when there is an injunction regarding the mere substance, the *loṭ* suffix is prescribed for [roots such as] *pṛccha* (to ask) and so on;
however, when there is the employment of that which possesses an action, that is the domain of the *ṇic* suffix.

Furthermore, the meaning of the *loṭ* suffix is instigation (*prayukti*), which is a property of the instigator (*prayoktṛ*). But the meaning of the *ṇic* suffix has an unspecified agent. For in "Cook! (*paceti*), the instigation is understood as belonging to the speaker alone; but in "He causes to cook" (*pācayati*), it belongs to someone other than the speaker.

The addition *tatkaroti* (he does that) is prescribed by the Sūtra (*kāovāo*) in the sense of "doing that" and so forth. This meaning, though already established by the recitation of the *gaṇa*, is also demonstrated by this supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*). Here, in the expression *karoti*, only the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*) is intended, not the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*). Consequently, from the causative form (*ṇyantāt*), the *la*-suffixes are established for the meanings of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*), as well as for the past and future tenses, and for the dual and plural numbers. Mādhava maintains that this *ṇic* suffix is applied directly to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself, and not to a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*).

And this is appropriate, because the governing rule *supaḥ* has been interrupted here. Furthermore, among the *curādi* roots, it is recited thus: “From a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), when the meaning of a verbal root is to be expressed, [the suffix] *ṇic* is added diversely (*bahulam*), and the operations of the suffix *iṣṭhan* also apply”; “he does that,” “he describes that”; “he surpasses by means of that”; and “from the agent or the instrument, when the meaning of a verbal root is to be expressed. The meaning of this is: *ṇic* shall be added to a nominal stem when a specific meaning of a verbal root is to be expressed, and diversely the grammatical operations of the suffix *iṣṭhan* shall apply to it.

It transcends the bank; it causes [the boat] to go up the bank. This is an elaboration (*prapañca*) of the rule *tat karoti* and so forth. And thus, because the rule begins with the term *prātipadikāt* (from a nominal stem), this is not an injunction based on a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*). Likewise, the present Vārttika has the same meaning and functions in the same way. However, the rule *tenātikrāmati* (Kāśikāvṛtti) is merely an elaboration of the rule *kartṛkaraṇād*.

The inclusion of the term "agent" (*kartṛ*) is specifically as a qualifier for the "instrument" (*karaṇa*), intended to dispel the doubt that only those things well-known in the world as instruments—such as the eyes and so forth—are to be understood here. Otherwise, [the suffix] would apply only in cases such as *cakṣuṣā paśyati* ("he sees with the eye") or *cakṣayati* ("he causes to see"), but not in cases such as *karibhir avabadhnāti* ("he binds with elephants") or *avakarayati* ("he causes to bind"). Thus, the words *tena* ("by that") and *tat* ("that") are indicative of both the object (*karman*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*); the meaning is: from a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that conveys either an instrument or an object.

If, however, the suffix were produced after a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), then in forms such as *atihastayati* (derived from *hastinā atikrāmati* with the causative suffix *ṇiC*), once the case-suffix has been elided and the *ṭi*-portion has been elided, the status of being a *pada* would still apply due to the intermediate case-suffix, and thus *jaś*-ness (the substitution of a voiced stop) would occur. Nor can the elision of the *ṭi* be considered *sthānivat*, because it is a substitute for both a vowel (*ac*) and a consonant (*hal*). Haradatta, however, maintains that the causative suffix *ṇiC* follows a word ending in a case-suffix. As he says: "The word 'tat' is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of a word ending in the second case. On this view, there is no risk of the application of *pada*-operations, because the designation *bha*—extended by the rule *iṣṭhavad*—supersedes the status of being a *pada*.

For this very reason, in examples such as *paṭiṣṭha*, when the suffix *iṣṭhan* follows a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), operations pertaining to a "word" (*pada*), such as the substitution of *jaś* (the voiced unaspirated stops), do not take place. Furthermore, even in the opinion of Mādhava, this is the only way to explain cases such as *srajayati* ("he causes [him] to wear a garland"), which derives from *sragviṇam ācaṣṭe*. This is because, when the suffixes *vin* and *matup* are elided after a word ending in a case-suffix, the base remains a word ending in a case-suffix; thus, by the rule of "assuming the presence of a suffix" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), the application of word-level operations would clearly follow. Therefore, it is established here that according to different opinions, the causative suffix *ṇic* is added either after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) or after a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*).

Even under the first view, since there is a grasping of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) in some way or another, and because of the principle that a term including gender (*liṅga-viśiṣṭa-grahaṇa*) includes its gendered forms, the operation occurs even from a base ending in *ṅī* or *āp*. For this very reason, in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *ṇāviṣṭhavan*, regarding the extension (*atideśa*) expressed as *iṣṭhavat*, the state of being masculine (*puṃvadbhāva*) is also mentioned as a purpose, along with the statement: "for the sake of the masculine state, the elision of *ṭi*, the elision of *yaṇ* etc., and the elision of *vin* and *mat*. And it is clear in the *Akara* (the *Mahābhāṣya*) on the sixth [chapter] that this is merely illustrative (*diṅmātra*) and not an exhaustive enumeration (*parigaṇana*). We shall, however, elaborate upon the examples: *enīm ācaṣṭe* results in *etayati*.

One says *haritayati* when expressing "one who is like a *hariṇī* (a female deer). Nor should it be asked here, "How can there be an extended application (*atideśa*) of the rule for masculine forms (*puṃvadbhāva*), since no specific rule for it has been prescribed in the context of the suffix *iṣṭhan*? For when there is an extended application of a specific case, the general rule is also necessarily extended. Indeed, when it is said, "One should behave here as one does toward Vasiṣṭha," the status of being a Brāhmaṇa—which is based on the general category—is also extended. Likewise, here too, the masculine form is applied because the suffix is a *taddhita* that causes the technical designation *bha*; thus, there is no fault.

One might object: "In forms such as *nanv-etad-ī*, once the feminine suffix *ṅīp* has been elided by the elision of the *ṭi*-portion (*ṭilopa*), the nasal *n* should also be elided, since it is prescribed in grammatical conjunction (*sanniyogaśiṣṭa*) with that suffix. Thus, since the purpose is already served by the elision of the *ṭi*-portion alone, for what reason was *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like substitution) also cited separately in the Bhāṣya as having its own distinct purpose?"

Regarding this, Kaiyaṭa states: "This [rule] is intended to indicate the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of the *sanniyogaśiṣṭa* paribhāṣā (Pā. Bhāṣya 88). Therefore, he says that in the forms *aineyaḥ* and *śyaineyaḥ*, even though the elision (*lopa*) of the *y* by the rule *yasya* (Pā. Sū. 6.4.49) has taken place, the *n* is not removed. Haradatta, however, mentions another result as being the opinion of others: one says *aiḍabiḍayati* when expressing the act of describing *iḍabiḍa*; likewise, *dāradayati* for *darada*. The word *iḍabiḍa* denotes both a country (*janapada*) and a Kṣatriya caste.

Therefore, from the word *darat*—which is a term for a region (*janapadaśabda*) derived from a *kṣatriya* name—the suffix *añ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.168, and further by the rule 4.1.174 (*dvyañmagadha*). Since the application of *añ* and the other suffixes is prescribed up to the end of the fourth chapter, there is elision (*luk*) by 4.1.177 (*ataśca*). The meaning of the sūtra is that the *tadrāja* suffix in the form of the vowel *a* is elided in the feminine. Consequently, *iḍabiṭ* and *darat* are feminine; whereas *aiḍaviḍa* and *dārada* are masculine.

And by the statement "like the masculine," when the feminine word is extended [by *atideśa*] to the masculine word, the desired result is established. Nor should it be suspected that, because it is a genus (*jāti*) by virtue of being a clan-name (*gotra*), the prohibition of the masculine-like form (*puṃvadbhāva*) by Pāṇini 6.3.41, "and of a genus," would apply; for it will be stated later that this prohibition does not apply to what is prescribed by a supplementary rule (*aupasaṃkhyānika*). Nor should it be argued that, even so, since the rule "after a quality-word beginning with *aj* etc., only when followed by *iṣṭhan*" (Pāṇini 5.3.58) precludes the possibility of these two suffixes (*iṣṭhan* and *īyasun*) occurring after such words, how can there be an extension (*atideśa*) of the form "like that" (*tadvat*)? For the extension is not only of what has been actually seen in the case of *iṣṭhan*, but rather of what is possible. Otherwise, in forms such as *atirājayati*, the elision of the *ṭi* suffix would not occur.
If it is asked, "In this view, how are forms such as *aiṇeyaḥ* and *śyaineyaḥ* established?

Mādhava replies: By citing examples such as *aiḍabiḍayati*—which cannot be explained otherwise—and then citing *etayati* and *śyetayati*, the author of the Bhāṣya indicates that the *paribhāṣā* "taught as taught in conjunction" (*sanniyogaśiṣṭa*) is not universally obligatory (*anitya*).

In reality, although the rule for *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine treatment) finds its scope of application in forms like *ekākṣu* and the absence of *ṭilopa* in words that do not denote a masculine (*abhāṣitapuṃska*), in cases such as *etayatī*, it is precisely *puṃvadbhāva* that must be understood [to apply] due to its being *antaraṅga* (more internal). This is because, as stated in the rule "and it is established prior to the formation of the suffix" (*siddhaśca pratyayavidhau*), it operates even before the suffix arises. For this very reason, the formation of the word without the nasal *n* is established.

Nor should it be argued that even when the *ṭi*-lopa occurs here, the removal of the letter *n* is easily obtained by the principle of "being taught in conjunction" (*sanniyogaśiṣṭa*); for if the removal of the letter *n* were to be effected by that principle, the status of being a "substitute" (*sthānivadbhāva*)—by the rule "when a subsequent [element] is substituted for an *ac*" (Pāṇini 1.1.57)—would be unavoidable.

For this very reason, in cases such as *pañcendraḥ* (meaning "that which has five Indrāṇīs as its deities"), where the hearing of the augment *an* would otherwise result by virtue of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*), the mention of *luk* in the Vārttika "kvilugupadhā... is clearly stated in the Bhāṣya, the Vārttikas, and other works, for the purpose of prohibiting that status of being a substitute. For this same reason, the form *abhyāsekārasahitamaitad* is established. However, if there were a *ṭi*-lopa, then—whether at the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyā*) or in the final form (*pariniṣṭhita*)—there would be no application of the status of being a substitute because the condition of being followed by an *a*-vowel would be absent; consequently, the aforementioned form would not be established.

It should be noted that there is no application of the *sthānivadbhāva* rule even for the elision (*allop*), because although that elision is caused by the suffix *ṅī*, it is not caused by the suffix *ṇic*.

He describes *pṛthu* [as such]; he causes it to expand (*prathayati*). In the case where the elision of the suffixal *ṭi* occurs prior to the *vṛddhi* [substitution], because the root is *aglopi* (having its initial vowel elided), the rule *sanvallaghuni* (Pāṇini 7.4.93) does not apply, and thus we have *apaprathat*. Alternatively, because the *vṛddhi* substitution takes precedence, and because the root is no longer *aglopi* due to the elision of the *ṭi* occurring before the *āvādeśa*, we have *apiprathat*. Both of these options are explained in detail under the rule *muṇḍamiśra* (Pāṇini 3.1.21). Similarly, one who describes *mṛdu* [as such] is *mradayati*. The forms are *amamradat* and *amimradat*. Likewise: *bhraśayati*, *kraśayati*, *draḍhayati*.

And because these [roots] are invariably *aglopi* (losing their penultimate vowel) before the suffix *caṅ*, they all take the single form: *ababhraśat*, *acakraśat*, *adadraḍhat*. *parivraḍhiyati*. Here, because the prefix (*upasarga*) is separated [from the root], we have *paryavraḍhayata* and *paryavavraḍhat*. One should remember these six—*pṛthu*, *mṛdu*, *bhṛśa*, *kṛśa*, *dṛḍha*, and *vṛḍha* preceded by *pari*—in the rule for the substitution of *ra*.

One says "he speaks poetically" (*kavayati*) or "he makes proficient" (*paṭayati*). The forms are *acakavat* and *acīkavat*; *apapaṭhat* and *apapiṭhat*. From "he described a young girl" (*kumārīmākhyāt*), we derive *acukumārat*. Here there is only one form; for according to the interpretation of Kaiyaṭa and others regarding the meaning of the two rules—"as in the case of *saN*" (*sanvallaghuni*, Pāṇini 7.4.93) and "lengthening of the short vowel" (*dīrgho laghoḥ*, Pāṇini 7.4.94)—it refers to the reduplication (*abhyāsa*) when a *ṇiC* followed by *Caṅ* follows, provided that the short vowel immediately preceding it is the one in question. Since, in this instance, there is no short vowel following the reduplication, [the rule does not apply].

And because that [root] is followed by *caṅ* and then by *ṇi*, there is no occasion for the application of the rule regarding vowel lengthening (*dīrghatva*). Even according to the view of Haradatta and others—that "when a root ending in *ṇi* is followed by *caṅ*, the reduplicated syllable of the stem which is followed by a light vowel" applies—there is no elision of a vowel (*aglopin*) in the case of the word *kumārī*, even though the *vṛddhi* substitution has occurred due to its treatment as masculine (*puṃvadbhāva*). Thus, one says *ananadat* and so forth, having caused the river to speak.
