Now, one might object: according to Kaiyaṭa’s view, by the maxim *yenāvyavadhānaṃ tena vyavahite 'pi*, let the treatment as *san*-like (*sanvadbhāva*) indeed apply in cases such as *ajīharat* where there is an intervention by a single consonant; but how could it apply in cases like *acikṣaṇat*? The answer is that this is because the rule *atsmṛdṛtvarapra* (Pāṇini 7.4.95), which prescribes the substitution of *at* for the root vowel in forms such as *asasmarat* to prevent the application of *it*, indicates that the operation takes place even when there is an intervention by a *saṃyoga* (conjunct consonant). Thus, *aujaḍhat* (he described [the act of] carrying) from *ūḍham ākhyat*, and *aujiḍhat* (he described [the act of] carrying) from *ūḍhim ākhyat*. Similarly, *karayati* (he causes to do) from *kartāram ācaṣṭe*, and *bharayati* (he causes to support) from *bhartāram*.

He causes the milker to milk: *dogdhāraṃ dohayati*. Some say that by the rule *tuśchandasi* (Pāṇini 5.3.59), the elision of the suffix *-tṛ* is also extended to the causative (*ṇic*). Others, however, argue: "Let it be granted that this [elision] taught for the Vedic language is extended to the causative only within the Vedic language. But how would it apply in the common language (*bhāṣā*)? Therefore, in the common language, forms such as *karttayati* (he causes to make) are derived only through the elision of the *ṭi*. He describes you or me: *tvāpayati*, *māpayati*.

In this context, by the rule *pratyayottarapadayośca* (Pāṇini 7.2.98), for the forms *yuṣmad* and *asmad*—which denote a single referent—the substitutes *tvam* and *au* replace the portions ending in *map*. Regarding the form *tvādayati*, one opinion holds that because the substitution of the single substitute (*pararūpa*) by the rule *ato guṇe* (Pāṇini 6.1.97) is preceded by the elision of the final vowel (*ṭilopa*), which is obligatory, the subsequent *vṛddhi* and *puk* augmentations apply. However, in reality, since an internal operation (*antaraṅga*) is stronger than even a subsequent one, the *pararūpa* substitution takes effect first; consequently, by the rule *prakṛtyaikāc* (Pāṇini 6.4.163), there is no elision of the suffix, and after the *upadhā-vṛddhi*, the forms are indeed *tvādayati* and *madāyati*. This is the view of many scholars.

The statement that *prakṛtyaikāc* (Pāṇini 6.4.163) is refuted by the Bhāṣya is intended merely to show that it is otherwise established (*anyathāsiddhi*) in certain specific instances. For example, among those cited by the author of the Vṛtti, forms such as *preṣṭha* and others are established by the rule *ābhaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.162); even if that [rule] were omitted, they would be established by the force of the vocalization of the vowel *a*, just as in *jyeṣṭha*. Furthermore, in the case of the suffixes *iṣṭhan*, *īyasun*, and *īyas*, the Bhāṣyakāra does not intend [the application of 6.4.163] even for what remains when a multi-syllabic stem is present, because the elision of the *ṭi* (the final syllable) occurs when there is the elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *vin* and *matup*.
Because that which constitutes an exception to *luk* operates within that same alternative (*pakṣa*),
this [objection] applies equally to the elision of *tṛ*, since it too operates [only] when *kaniṣṭha* and so forth are present.

We shall explain that the works of Kaiyaṭa, Mādhava, and others are favorable to this view. Others, however, maintain that by the paribhāṣā *aṅgavṛtte* (Pāṇini Bhāṣya 94), one should not apply the vṛddhi [substitution] and thus derive forms such as *tvadayati* and *madayati*. In the case of *yuṣmayati* and *asmayati*, derived from *yuvām* or *āvām* with the suffix *ācaṣṭe* [denoting the causative sense of "to speak"], although in the rule *yuvāvau dvivacane* (Pāṇini 7.2.92) the term *dvivacane* is taken to mean "in the sense of the dual," nevertheless, the substitutes *yuvā-* and *āvā-* do not occur here because they are not followed by a case-ending (*vibhakti*). For Mādhava and others hold that the *ṇic* suffix is added directly to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself.

Even according to Haradatta’s view—that [the suffix] follows a word ending in a case-suffix—the case-ending is elided by the maxim "even internal [rules] are set aside" (*antaraṅgān api*). Thus, from *tvām* or *tvām atikrāntaḥ*, we derive *atitvām*; and from *tvām atikrāntān*, we derive *atitvān*. In the forms *atitvayati* and *atimayati* (meaning "he speaks of one who has surpassed you" or "me"), the substitutes *tvam* and *mām* are applied to *yuṣmad* and *asmad* because they denote a single entity, according to Pāṇini 7.2.98: *pratyayottarapadayoś ca*. Mādhava holds that the single-substitute (*pūrvarūpa*) occurs first because it is an internal rule (*antaraṅga*), and subsequently, the *ṭi*-portion is elided.

That is questionable, because by separating the prefix [from the base], there would be *prakṛtibhāva* (the preservation of the original form) according to Pāṇini’s sūtra 6.4.163, *prakṛtyaikāc*. Therefore, one should understand it as *atitvādayati* and *atimādayati*. Even here, according to the view that the elision of *ṭi* (*ṭilopa*) occurs before the substitution of the single substitute for the preceding and following sounds (*pararūpa*)—because it is obligatory—the forms are *atitvāpayati* and *atimāpayati*. One who describes someone as having surpassed you both (*yuvām*), us two (*āvām*), or you all (*yuṣmān*), or us all (*asmān*), is said to *atiyuṣmayati* or *atyasmayati*.

Now, a certain distinction regarding the formation of stems with the suffix *kvip* after a causative (*ṇic*) root is stated. In that regard, when the object to be designated (*ākhyeya*) is singular—as in "he designates you" (*tvām*) or "me" (*mām*)—the nominal stems are threefold according to the previously mentioned difference of opinion: *tvāp*, *māp*; *tvād*, *mād*; and *tvad*, *mad*. When the object to be designated is plural—as in "he designates you two" (*yuvām*), "us two" (*āvām*), or "you all" (*yuṣmān*), "us all" (*asmān*)—there is an absence of the forms *tva* and *mama*. Consequently, after the causative suffix *ṇic*, the *ṭilopa* (elision of the penultimate vowel) occurs; then, upon the application of *kvip*, the *ṇilopa* (elision of the causative marker); and finally, the elision of the single-consonant suffix *k* (*apṛktalopa*). Thus, the nominal stems become *yuṣma* and *asma*, ending in *-m*. From these, the case endings (*svādayaḥ*) are subsequently applied.

In that regard, from the eight nominal stems (*prātipadika*) as well, the substitutions for the case endings (*vibhakti*) are prescribed by seven rules according to their respective cases: *ṅeprathamayoram* (Pāṇini 7.1.28), *śaso na* (7.1.29), *bhyaso'bhyam* (7.1.30), *pañcamyā at* (7.1.31), *ekavacanasya ca* (7.1.32), *yuṣmadasmadbhyāṃ ṅaso'ś* (7.1.27), and *sāma ākam* (7.1.33).

Thus, the substitution of *ā* prescribed by the three rules—"yuṣmadasmadoranādeśe" (Pāṇini 7.2.86), "dvitīyāyāñca" (7.2.87), and "prathamāyāśca dvivacane bhāṣāyām" (7.2.88)—as well as the substitution of *ya* prescribed by "yo'ci" (7.2.98), indeed take place. Furthermore, the elision of the final syllable (*śeṣe lopaḥ*) occurs when it is explained as the elision of the final [vowel] before any case-ending other than those that serve as the cause for the *ā* and *ya* substitutions.

If one adopts the interpretation that the word *śeṣa* refers to the remainder [of the suffixes] following a stem ending in *m*, resulting in the elision of the *ṭi*-portion (*ṭilopa*), then this does not occur at all when there is more than one thing to be designated (*ākhyeya*). For in that case, what would have been removed by the elision of the *m* (via the rule *śeṣe lopena*) is already removed by the elision of the *ṭi* itself through the application of the rule *ṇāviṣṭhavad iti vaktavyam*. However, when there is only one thing to be designated, it certainly does occur, because the elision of the *ṭi* has not yet taken place. According to the view that "having accepted the elision of the *ṭi*, the status of ending in *p* is achieved through the augment *puK*," this [substitution] does not occur at all; for since the substitution of *yaT* is prescribed for vowels (*aj-ādi*), the substitution of *āT* results only in the case of consonants (*hal-ādi*).

The substitutions prescribed by the four sūtras—"tvāhau sau" (Pāṇini 7.2.94), "yuyavayau jasi" (Pāṇini 7.2.93), "tubhyamahyau ṅayi" (Pāṇini 7.2.95), and "tavamamau ṅasi" (Pāṇini 7.2.96)—do not occur at all when there is identity of the person addressed (*ākhyeya*), because the element ending in *m* (*maparyanta*) is absent. However, they are optional when there is duality or plurality of the person addressed.

For instance, regarding the rule *maparyantasya* (Pāṇini 7.2.19): since the form *māntasya* alone would have sufficed, one opinion holds that by the force of including the word *pari*, the substitutes do not apply while *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are in the state of being *mānta*. Another opinion holds that in the absence of the inclusion of *pari*, the substitutes would apply only to what ends in *m*; however, when *pari* is present, they apply both to what ends in *m* and to what exceeds it. Both of these views will be explained under that very same sūtra. And because of this difference of opinion, an option (*vikalpa*) results here.

In that regard, when there are two things to be expressed (ākhyeya), although *tvā*, *āha*, and so forth would apply by virtue of their higher status (*paratva*) over *sṛj*, *ṅe*, and *ṅasi*, in other numbers such as *au* and *am*, the forms *yuvau* and *āvau* certainly exist according to one view because they follow the case endings; however, according to another view, neither *tvā* and so forth nor *yuvau* apply—this is the distinction.

Now, regarding the forms: when the object denoted (*ākhyeya*) is the same, *tvām* and *mām* are used. However, according to those who maintain that there is no *vṛddhi* [in the case of *tvad* and *mad*], when the suffix is elided by the rule for the "remainder" (*śeṣe lopaḥ*), the forms are *tvam* and *mam*. Even in the view where the elision of the suffix (*ṭilopaḥ*) occurs in the "remainder," and that [elision] does not apply to the verbal base *ācakṣāṇa*, it has been stated that *tvām* and *mām* indeed exist when the object denoted is the same. But in the case of forms ending in *-p* (i.e., *tvat* and *mat*), the forms *tvāpam* and *māpam* occur optionally. Thus, by way of summary, there are three forms. In the dual of *auṅ*, there is only one form: *tvām* and *mām*. By the rule "and in the dual of the nominative" (*prathamāyāśca dvivacane*), the suffix *āv* is applied.

In the *jas* [case-ending], there are three forms: *sā*, *iva*, and *trīṇi*; in the remaining cases, due to the optional elision (*lopasya*) of the final *p* and *t* sounds. In the *am* and *auṭ* endings: *tvām*, *mām*; *tvān*, *mān*. By the rule *dvitīyāyāñca* (Pāṇini 7.2.77), there is the substitution of *ā* [for the final vowel]. In the *āṅ* ending: *tvāyā*, *māyā*; but when there is no *vṛddhi*, it is *tvayā*, *mayā*. *Tvābhyām*, *mābhyām*; *tvābhiḥ*, *mābhiḥ*. In the *ṅi* ending, *am* is substituted; by the rule *śeṣe lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.90), there is elision of the final portion. When the *vṛddhi* alternative applies, by the rule *āto dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.140), there is elision of the *ā*: *tvam*, *mam*. In the other alternative, *tvāpam*, *māpam*. *Tvābhyām*, *mābhyām*.

*tvābhyam*, *mābhyam*. In the case of the suffix *bhyam*, there is elision (*lopa*) of the remainder [of the stem]. However, in the alternative view where *abhyam* is the substitute, when the remainder is elided and the *ā*-elision (*āllopa*) occurs, the forms are *tvabhyam* and *mabhyam*. This is likewise in the case of the non-vṛddhi alternative. In the alternative where *āp* is present, the forms are *tvāpabhyam* and *māpabhyam*. In that context, regarding the suffix *bhyam*, by the paribhāṣā "aṅgavṛtta" (Pābhā 94), the substitution of *e* (by Pāṇini 7.3.103, "in the plural, before *jhal*, *e*") does not take place. Thus, the forms are *tvat*, *mat*. When the remainder is elided, in the vṛddhi alternative, there is *ā*-elision: *tvāpat*, *māpat*. [The forms] *tvābhyām*, *mābhyām*; *tvat*, *mat*; *tvāpat*, *māpat*.

*tva*, *mā*; *tvāpa*, *māpa*; *tvāyoḥ*, *māyoḥ*; but when not subject to vowel strengthening (*avṛddhi*), *tvayoḥ*, *mayoḥ*; *tvākam*, *mākam*; *tvāpākam*, *māpākam*; *tvāyi*, *māyi*; *tvāyoḥ*, *māyoḥ*; but when not subject to vowel strengthening, *tvayi*, *mayi*; *tvayoḥ*, *mayoḥ*; *tvāsu*, *māsu*.

And thus, when the person denoted is the same (*ākhyeyaikye*), determine with one mind that there are three forms for the nominative (*su*) and accusative (*jas*), two for the dative (*caturthī*) and the locative plural (*bhyas*), and two forms for the genitive-locative dual (*ṭau*) and the locative singular (*ṅi*), as well as for the dative plural (*bhyas*).

However, this should be noted: since the rule *kṛtaḥ kartary asaṃjñāyām* states that [the suffix] is dependent on the gender of the substantive (*viśeṣyanighna*), when [the word] *ācakṣāṇa* is neuter, the case endings *su* and *au* are not *sarvanāmasthāna*. Consequently, by the rule *āto dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.140), the long *ā* is elided, resulting in the forms *tvam* and *mam* alone. For those who maintain that there is no vowel lengthening (*avṛddhi*), in the vocative, the *hal* [consonant] is elided by the rule *eṅhrasvāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.69), resulting in *he tvā* and *he ma*.

Regarding the feminine gender (*strītva*), the suffix *ṭāp* would have been applicable; however, this is to be resolved by the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā* (Pāṇini 1.1.67). As for the two alternative solutions proposed for the case of the simple [word]—namely, "due to the absence of gender" (*aliṅgatvāt*) or "due to the elision of the *aT*" (*aṭ-ṭilopāt*)—those do not apply here. This is the general direction [of the argument].

Now, when there are two objects to be expressed, the forms are as follows: in the nominative singular (*sau*), *tvam* and *aham*; in the absence of the substitution of the base (*prakṛti*), *yuṣam* and *asam*; and when the elision (*lopa*) of the suffix is also absent, *yuṣmam* and *asmam*. Thus, there are three forms each. In the dual: *yuvām* and *āvām*; *yuṣām* and *asām*. In the plural with the suffix *jasi*: *yūyam* and *vayam*; *yuṣam* and *asam*; *yuṣmam* and *asmam*. In the dual of the instrumental (*am-auṭoḥ*): *yuvābhyām* and *āvābhyām*; *yuṣābhyām* and *asābhyām*. In the plural of the instrumental (*yuvābhiḥ*, etc.): *yuvābhiḥ* and *āvābhiḥ*; *yuṣābhiḥ* and *asābhiḥ*. In the singular of the instrumental (*yuvayā*, etc.): *yuvayā* and *āvayā*; *yuṣyā* and *asyā*. In the singular of the genitive (*yuṣmad-asmadbhyām ṅasaḥ*): *tava* and *mama*; *yuṣa* and *asa*; *yuṣma* and *asma*. In the dual of the genitive (*yuṣmad-asmadbhyāṃ ṅasoḥ*): *yuvayoḥ* and *āvayoḥ*; *yuṣyoḥ* and *asyoḥ*. In the plural of the genitive (*yuṣmad-asmadbhyāṃ ṅasām*): *yuṣmākam* and *asmākam*; *yuṣām* and *asām*; *yuṣmān* and *asmān*. In the singular of the locative (*yuṣmad-asmadbhyāṃ ṅi*): *tvayi* and *mayi*; *yuṣi* and *asi*; *yuṣmi* and *asmi*. In the dual of the locative (*yuṣmad-asmadbhyāṃ ṅyoḥ*): *yuvayoḥ* and *āvayoḥ*; *yuṣyoḥ* and *asyoḥ*. In the plural of the locative (*yuṣmad-asmadbhyāṃ ṅiṣu*): *yuṣmāsu* and *asmāsu*; *yuṣāsu* and *asāsu*; *yuṣmasu* and *asmatsu*. Thus, the complete paradigm is established. As for the vocative (*sambuddhau*), it is the same as the nominative (*prathamāvat*). However, in the case of the singular, the form *he* is optionally substituted for the vocative suffix (*sambuddhyāḥ sau vā heḥ*). Therefore, the forms are: *he tvam*, *he aham*, *he yuṣam*, *he asam*, *he yuṣmam*, *he asmam*. In the dual and plural, they are the same as the nominative. Thus, the declension of *yuṣmad* and *asmad* is completed. One should understand that the forms of *bhavat* are similar to those of *yuṣmad*. The forms of *kim* are as follows: *kaḥ*, *kau*, *ke*; *kam*, *kau*, *kān*; *kena*, *kābhyām*, *kaiḥ*; *kasmai*, *kābhyām*, *kebhyaḥ*; *kasmāt*, *kābhyām*, *kebhyaḥ*; *kasya*, *kayoḥ*, *keṣām*; *kasmin*, *kayoḥ*, *keṣu*. The forms of *idam* are as follows: *ayam*, *imau*, *ime*; *imam*, *imau*, *imān*; *anena*, *ābhyām*, *ebhiḥ*; *asmai*, *ābhyām*, *ebhyaḥ*; *asmāt*, *ābhyām*, *ebhyaḥ*; *asya*, *anayoḥ*, *eṣām*; *asmin*, *anayoḥ*, *eṣu*. The forms of *adas* are as follows: *asau*, *amū*, *amī*; *amum*, *amū*, *amūn*; *amunā*, *ābhyām*, *amībhiḥ*; *amuṣmai*, *ābhyām*, *amībhyaḥ*; *amuṣmāt*, *ābhyām*, *amībhyaḥ*; *amuṣya*, *anayoḥ*, *amīṣām*; *amuṣmin*, *anayoḥ*, *amīṣu*. In all these cases, when operations such as substitution of the root (prakṛti), replacement (ādeśa), yaṅ, ātva, and elision (lopa) are to be performed, the elision of the causative suffix (ṇilopa) is not treated as "as if it were present" (na sthānivat), because it has been elided by the rule *kvo lopaḥ*; this is the general direction.

One says *śāvayati* when expressing a dog (*śvan*). When the form *śvan-i* is established, two elisions of the *ṭi*-portion (*ṭilopa*) are applicable by the extension (*atideśa*) rule "as in the case of *iṣṭhan*" (*iṣṭhavad-bhāva*): one by Pāṇini 6.4.143 (*ṭeḥ*), and the other by 6.4.144 (*na-staddhite*). Among these, the rule 6.4.163 (*prakṛtyaikāc*)—which prescribes the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) for monosyllabic bases—applies specifically to the elision governed by 6.4.143 (*ṭeḥ*) according to the maxim of "that which was not previously applicable" (*yenāprāptinyāya*). Consequently, even though that [specific] elision has been set aside, the elision governed by 6.4.144 (*na-staddhite*) still takes place.

Then, by the extension of the designation *bha*—as prescribed by the rule *iṣṭhavad*—there occurs the *samprasāraṇa* of the letter *va*, followed by *vṛddhi* and the substitution of *āv*. Nor should it be argued that because the rule *orguṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.146) was observed to apply to the preceding element in forms such as *daviṣṭhaḥ* (with the suffix *iṣṭhan*), it should likewise be extended here; for when that [substitution] is to be performed, both the *samprasāraṇa* and the elision of *ṭi* are considered *asiddha* (non-existent) by the rule *asiddhavad atra* (Pāṇini 6.4.22).

Others, however, maintain that in cases such as *brahmiṣṭhaḥ*, because the rule "ṭeḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.155) applies later than the elision of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* caused by the presence of the letter *n*, it is precisely "ṭeḥ" that operates. That [elision] is here precluded by the status of the base (*prakṛtibhāva*). Furthermore, since the rule "nastaddhite" (Pāṇini 6.4.144) is never observed to apply after the superlative suffix *iṣṭhan*, it is not extended here; thus, they say the form is *śunayati* due to the prior occurrence of semi-vowel vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) and the subsequent substitution of the penultimate vowel.

Nor should it be argued that because the two instances of *ṭilopa* are *ābhīya*, they are mutually *asiddha*, and thus how can there be a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*)? For it will be stated later that in the case of a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*), the status of being *ābhīya* does not apply to what is mutually *asiddha*. Regarding the form *vidvayati* (from *vidvas* with the causative suffix *ṇiC* and subsequent *ṭilopa*), the followers of Durga hold that this occurs when one expresses "he causes a learned man (*vidvas*) to speak. Regarding this, Ātreya maintains that the absence of *saṃprasāraṇa* is problematic and requires further consideration.

The restoration [of the vowel] should be understood according to the *paribhāṣā* rule *aṅgavṛtte punarvṛttāvavidhiḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.56). Regarding the form *vidāvayati*, some say that after the *saṃprasāraṇa*, the *vṛddhi* substitution, and the replacement with *āv*, this is the result; others, however, say *vidayati*. For instance, because it is obligatory (*nitya*), the *saṃprasāraṇa* occurs before the elision of the suffixal *ṭi*; then, due to its being an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), the *pūrvarūpa* sandhi follows, and subsequently the elision of the *ṭi*. Nor is the elision of the *ṭi* itself obligatory, as it is non-obligatory (*anitya*) because it applies to a different word-form (*śabdāntara*).

If it is argued that the attainment of a different word does not occur merely through *samprasāraṇa*, but rather through the formation of the *pūrvarūpa* [single-substitute], according to the principle: "That whose cause is destroyed by another rule is considered non-eternal" (Paribhāṣā 48), we say no; for Haradatta and others have stated that the rule "yasya ca... is not universally applicable (*asārvatrika*). Thus, from *udañc*, one says *udīcayati*. Here, because the prefix is separated, the suffix *ṇic* is applied after the word *ac* from which the *n* has been elided.

By the rule *prakṛtyaikāc* (Pāṇini 6.4.163), there is no elision of the suffix *ṭi*. Since the designation *bha* applies by the extended application (*atideśa*) of the rule *iṣṭhavad* [from Pāṇini 6.4.155], the elision of the vowel *a* would have occurred by the rule *acaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.138); however, this is precluded by the rule *uda īt* (Pāṇini 6.4.139), which prescribes the substitution of *ī* for the final *u*. In the case of the *caṅ* [aorist marker], the form is *udaicicat*. Here, because the elision of the *ṇi* suffix is treated as if it were not present (*sthānivadbhāva*) by the rule *dvirvacane'ci* (Pāṇini 1.1.59), the word *ci* undergoes reduplication according to the rule *ajāderdvitīyasya* (Pāṇini 6.1.2). Then, the augment *āṭ* is added to the stem, resulting in the *vṛddhi* strengthening.

In *lyap*, because there is an absence of the condition of being preceded by a light vowel (*laghupūrvatva*), the substitution of *ay* does not occur; thus, after the elision of the *ṇi* suffix, one says *pratīcayati* (he causes to face west). Here, the elision of *at* occurs by Pāṇini 6.4.138 (*acaḥ*), and the lengthening of the preceding syllable occurs by Pāṇini 6.3.138 (*cau*). In the case of the *caṅ* (reduplication), when *aṭ* is inserted before the syllable *ci*, and the *yaṇ* substitution takes place, one says *pratyacicat*. In the alternative view where there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) according to Pāṇini 6.1.127 (*iko'savarṇe*), one says *pratyacicat*. With *lyap*, it is *pratīcya*. One who describes *samyañcam* (one who is well-directed) says *samīcayati*.

From the root *añc* with the prefix *caṅ*: *samyacicat*, *sami acicat*. The gerund is *samīcya*. [The word] *tiryak* is derived from *tiras-añcati*; by the rule *titasitaryalope* (Pāṇini 6.3.94), there is the substitution of *tiri* for *tiras*. One causes someone to go crosswise by saying *tam ācaṣṭe*, which results in *tirāyayati*. Through the application of the *iṣṭhavan-bhāva* (the treatment as if it were the superlative suffix *iṣṭha*), there is the elision of the *ṭi* (the *ac*) of the root *añc*, and then the *vṛddhi* and *āy* substitutions. Nor should it be asked: "If there is the elision of *añc* here, how can there be the substitution of *tiri* for *tiras*? For the condition *alope* (in the absence of elision) in the rule *acaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.138) serves to prevent the substitution of *tiri* when an elision occurs, because that [elision] is immediately contiguous.

In this case, although the elision (*lopa*) of *tireḥ* would be applicable whether the *vṛddhi* and *āy* have been applied or not, it does not take place by virtue of the *paribhāṣā* "aṅgavṛtte punarvṛttāvavidhiḥ" (Pāṇinian tradition 94). Alternatively, according to the logic of the *ciṇoluṅnyāya*, since the first-applied *ṭi*-elision is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) by the rule "asiddhavadatra" (Pāṇini 6.4.22), a further *ṭi*-elision does not occur. For this very reason, because *tireḥ* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) by virtue of being a *sthānin*, the *ṭi*-elision that would otherwise apply by the rule "avyayānāṃ bhamātre" (Kātyāyana-vārttika) also does not take place.

Thus, by the rule *yasya* (Pāṇini 6.4.148), elision (*lopa*) also does not occur, because it is superseded by the subsequent *vṛddhi* [substitution]. In the case of *caṅ*, because the root begins with a vowel (*aglopi*), there is no shortening of the penultimate vowel (*upadhā-hasva*); hence, *atitirāyat*. [The word] *sadhraṅ* is formed from *saha añcati* ("he goes together"), according to the rule *sa hasya sadhriḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.95). One who causes *sadhryañc* to speak is expressed as *sadhrāyayati*. [In the *caṅ* form,] *asasadhrāyat*; as before, there is again no elision of the *ṭi* suffix.

It might be argued: if the basis for the non-application of the *ṭilopa* (elision of the suffix *ṭi*) when the vowel *i* of *tri* and *stri* undergoes the substitution of *ik* is the principle that [an operation] is treated as *asiddha* (non-existent) according to the rule regarding *ciṇ* and *luṅ*, then the form *kumārayati*—derived from *kumārīm ācaṣṭe*—"he describes a young girl"—would not be established. For in that case too, since the masculine treatment (*puṃvattva*) applies by virtue of the *iṣṭhavadbhāva* (the treatment as if it were the superlative suffix *iṣṭhan*), that very [masculine treatment] would result in the *asiddha* status of the elision of the vowel *ā* of *kumārī*. If this is said, it is not so. This is because it is accepted that "the locus of operations being extended [by analogy] is precisely the locus of their original production," and because the masculine treatment is governed by the rule *bhasyāḍhe taddhite* (Pāṇini 6.4.149).

This occurs even before the application of the *ābhīya* rules. For this very reason, the author of the Bhāṣya has cited: *lohinīm ācaṣṭe lohitayati* ("he describes her as red"). *Viṣvadryañcam ācaṣṭe viṣvadrāyayati*; *devadryañcam ācaṣṭe devadrāyayati*. By the word *ca* in the rule *viṣvag-devayoś-ca* (Pāṇini 6.3.92), when the substitute *dryañc* is applied to a pronoun, one says *sarvadrāyayati*. When the substitute *dryañc* is applied to *adas*, one says *amumuyāyati*, *adamuyāyati*, or *adadrāyayati*. In the *caṅ* formation, because it begins with a vowel (*ajādittvāt*), there is reduplication of the second syllable.

Because it is an *aglopi* (a stem that loses its final vowel), there is no shortening of the penultimate vowel (*nopadhāhrasvaḥ*). Thus: *āmumumuāyat*, *ādadamuāyat*, *ādadadrāyat*. In the first case, because of the rule "that which is not established is as if non-existent prior to reduplication" (*pūrvatrāsiddhīyamadvirvacane*), the substitution of *m* (*mutva*) is treated as non-existent, and thus there is no shortening. He causes *im* to be expressed: *āyayati*. Because of the rule "a monosyllabic root remains in its original form" (*prakṛtyaikāc*), there is no elision of the suffixal *ṭi*, and after the application of *vṛddhi*, the substitution of *āy* occurs. In the *caṅ* (the causative aorist), when the penultimate vowel is shortened and the second syllable is reduplicated, one says: *mā bhavān ayiyat*.

Furthermore, one should not suspect that the status of *sthānivadbhāva* (being like the original) applies to the *vṛddhi* substitution and so forth on the grounds that "when a reduplication is to be performed, what has been effected by a *ṇi*-affix is treated as the original"; for that [rule] applies where the reduplication is obtained of the form of the original (*sthānin*), whereas here, according to Mādhava, the reduplication belongs to the *ṇi*-affix itself.

In reality, however, in order to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of *acikīrtat*, we have already stated in the very rule *dvirvacane'ci* (Pāṇini 1.1.59) that—relying on the fact that the *jñāpaka* "oḥ puyaṇji" (Pāṇini 7.4.80) applies only to its own class of similar cases—the operation of *sthānivadbhāva* occurs only when the subsequent portion (*uttarakhaṇḍa*) does not contain the letter *v*. This is also clearly evident in the commentary on the rule *urat* (Pāṇini 7.4.66) in works such as the *Rakṣita* and the *Padamañjarī*.

There is no insistence that the absence of an *a*-vowel in the posterior member (*uttarakhaṇḍa*) must necessarily result from actual application [of a rule], but rather that it may also occur during the stage of grammatical derivation (*prakriyāvasthā*). Therefore, in the case of *aujiḍhat* and *apīpyat*, even though the *a*-vowel is removed from the posterior member by the elision of the suffix (*ṭilopa*) following reduplication, and by the rule *lopaḥ pivateḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.49), there is no defect. [Example: From the root *bhū*, one says *bhāvayati* ("he causes to be"). In the *caṅ* (the reduplicated aorist marker), we have *abībhavat*. Because of the status of being a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) for what was formed in the causative (*ṇau*), the word *bhū* undergoes reduplication.

Again, in the subsequent portion, there is lengthening and shortening; then, by virtue of the *sanvadbhāva* [treatment as if followed by *saN*], there is *itva* (the substitution of *i*) according to Pāṇini 7.4.80 (*oḥ puyaṇjyapare*); and finally, there is lengthening according to Pāṇini 7.4.94 (*dīrgho laghoḥ*).

Now, one might object: "In this case, when *bhū* is doubled, the operations of *vṛddhi*, lengthening, and shortening have taken effect in the second part [of the reduplication]. Consequently, since the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*) precedes a vowel that has not been subject to the rules of the present context (*anādiṣṭādacaḥ pūrvatvāt*), when the substitution of *i* for *u* (by *puyaṇjīti*) is to be applied on the basis of its being treated like the desiderative stem (*sanvadbhāva*), how can there be an *i*-substitution? For, by the rule *ṇau caṅi* (Pāṇini 7.4.1), the short vowel [of the reduplication] becomes subject to the status of a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original long vowel) by *acaḥ parasmin* (Pāṇini 1.1.57); thus, because a non-light vowel (*alaghu*) follows, how could the *i*-substitution occur? To this it is replied: [The answer lies in the fact that] both the *i*-substitution prescribed by *oḥ puyaṇji* (Pāṇini 7.4.80) and the extension of the *sanvadbhāva* treatment...

Because of the force of the initial application [of the rule], the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) does not apply here. In *abubhravat* (he described the eyebrows), that *yaṇ* which follows an *avarga* letter is not followed by the reduplicated syllable; and that which is followed by the reduplicated syllable is not followed by an *avarga* letter. Thus, there is no substitution of *it*. In *aśiśrayat* (he caused to lean), the word *śri* undergoes reduplication because of the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivattva*) for what was formed in the causative suffix (*ṇau*). He described the sound *he*: *ajīhayat*. He described a cow: *ajūgavat*. He described wealth: *arīrayat*. He described a boat: *anūnavat*. He described his own horse: *svāśaśvat*. And from *svar*, [we have] *svaryati*.

According to the rule *avyayānāṃ bhamātre* (Kātantra-vṛtti), there is the elision of the *ṭi* suffix. However, regarding the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*) by the rule *prakṛtyaikāc* (Pāṇini 6.4.163), it is stated that—by the principle of *yenāprāpte* (Pāṇini-bhāṣya 59) and due to immediate proximity (*ānantarya*)—this applies only to the elision of *ṭi* prescribed by *ṭeḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.155) and not to any other. Since the elision of *ṭi* has already occurred when the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied, it is considered a *sthānivadbhāva*; thus, some maintain that the word *svar* undergoes reduplication as *asasvad*.

The status of being a *sthānin* (original element) applies only to a substitute (*ādeśa*) for a vowel (*ac*). However, since this [substitute] is for a consonant (*jhal*), there is an absence of *sthānivadbhāva*; thus, according to others, when the word *su* undergoes reduplication, the form is *asisvat*. He causes many to speak: *bhāvayati*. Here, because the suffix *iṣṭhan* is prescribed by Pāṇini 6.4.159, *iṣṭhasya yiṭ ca*, the substitution of *bhū* for *bahu* occurs. The augment *yiṭ*, however, does not apply; for, by observing the locative case in the word *ṇau* within the rule, the suffix *vati* is applied to the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) *iṣṭhavat* as if it were also in the locative case. Thus, the meaning is "as if in the state of *iṣṭha*."

According to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that when the suffix *iṣṭhan* follows, only the grammatical operation applicable to the preceding element is extended, and not the operation of *iṣṭhan* itself—and furthermore, because the statement "of the nominal stem" (*prātipadikasya*) is intended to prevent the extension of operations belonging to the suffix—Kaiyaṭa, in his commentary on the rule *ṭeḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.155), cites *bhāvayati* as an example. He notes that since the substitution of *bhū-* for *bhu-* is taught in conjunction with the insertion of *yiṭ*, this substitution would also be absent in the absence of *yiṭ*; thus, he presents *bāhayati* as the opinion of certain authorities (*ekīyamata*).

However, considering that [the term] *bhāvayati* possesses greater authority precisely because it is supported by logical reasoning (*sopapattikatva*), he stated "he causes to exist" (*bhāvayati*) as his own position, while stating "he brings into being" (*bhāvayati*) according to the opinion of others. For this very reason, it was stated that even in the case of human effort (*puruṣakāra*), one should consider that it "brings into being."

In reality, however, Kaiyaṭa’s position alone is superior. Thus, the rule *iṣṭhavad* is an extension (*atideśa*) of grammatical operations, because the operation itself is primary. Consequently, the very mention of *iṣṭhavad* serves as the prescriber here for those [operations] observed in the base form; it is that which prescribes the substitution of *bhū*. And thus, the absence of a mandatory co-occurrence (*sanniyoga*) is quite clear. In the systems of Candra, Kumāra, and Śākaṭāyana, however, having prescribed the augment *yuk* only after *bahu* in the suffix *iṣṭhan*, they accept the form *bhūyayati*. [Similarly,] from *sthūla* one forms *sthavayati*, meaning "he describes as large."

It causes to go far (*dūrīkaroti*), it separates the young man (*yuvānaṃ yavayati*), it shortens (*hrasvayati*), it throws (*kṣepayati*), it grinds (*kṣodayati*). In these first examples, the *guṇa* [substitution] would have been subject to the rule *aco ñṇiti* (Pāṇini 7.2.115), which prescribes *vṛddhi*; however, it does not occur either by the principle *aṅgavṛtte punarvṛttāvavidhiḥ* (Paribhāṣā 94) or by the inclusion of the term *bahulam* in the rule *prātipadikāddhātvarthe bahulam* (Gaṇasūtra).

Even from the word *yuvati*, when the suffix *iṣṭhan* is applied, by the rule "the [form] qualified by gender" (*liṅgaviśiṣṭa*) [Pāṇini 6.3.35], and because the elision of the subsequent *yaṇ*-class sounds and so forth occurs by the rule "sthūla-dūra... (Pāṇini 6.4.156), and since that [operation] is extended to the denominative (*ṇic*) as well, the form is simply *yavayati*. Alternatively, once the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) has been applied, that same form results from the elision of the subsequent *yaṇ*-class sounds and so forth.
While the sun, by its rays mingled with droplets of spray, drives away [the heat] through its descent...

Sudhākara and others maintain that this usage by Kālidāsa is questionable; however, in reality, it can be resolved as meaning "he makes him go far" (*dūram ayate*) or "he makes him distant" (*dūrāt taṃ karoti*). [Similarly,] from *sragvin* (one who wears a garland), one derives *srajayati* (he causes someone to wear a garland). Here, due to the extended application (*atideśa*), there is the elision of the suffix *vin*. The elision of the *ṭi* portion does not occur by the rule *prakṛtyaikāc* (Pāṇini 6.4.163). Furthermore, it is established in the Bhāṣya that the vowel-vṛddhi prescribed by *ata upadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.116) does not take place here, on the basis of the principle *aṅgavṛtte punarvṛttāvavidhiḥ* (the rule of non-application when an operation has already occurred within the base).

One says "possessing cows" (*gomantam*) as *gāvayati*; when the suffix *matup* is elided, there is a *vṛddhi* [substitution] by Pāṇini 7.2.115 (*aco ñṇiti*). In the case of the *caṅ* [aorist], because the root has lost its final vowel (*aglopi*), the rules for *asanvat* behavior, lengthening, and so forth do not apply: *asasrajat*, *ajugavat*, etc. One says "young" or "small" as *kanayati*, according to Pāṇini 5.3.64 (*yuvālpayoḥ kananyatarasyām*). In the alternative, one says *yavayati*. The same applies when analyzing the compound as "a young woman" or "a small thing. One says "near" as *nedayati*. One says "certainly" as *sādhayati*.

Regarding the rule *antikabāḍhayornedasādhau* (Pāṇini 5.3.63): one expresses that which is excellent by saying *praśasyayati*. Here, the suffixes *śra* and *jya*—prescribed by the rules *praśasyasya śraḥ* and *jya ca* (Pāṇini 5.3.60–61)—do not occur; Mādhava maintains this because the prefix (*pra*) is treated as separate [from the base]. As for what was cited by Sudhākara as *śrāpayati*, and what was cited by Śākaṭāyana as *śrayati* and *jyayati*, all of that is to be disregarded due to its contradiction with the Bhāṣya. One expresses that which is old by saying *vṛddham ācaṣṭe* = *vṛddhayati*; [one expresses it] by saying *jyāpayati*.

And this substitution of *jva* is optional with the substitution of *varṣa*. According to Pāṇini’s sūtra 6.4.157, *priya-sthira-* etc., the prefix *prādi* [is applied]: one who expresses *priya* (dear) is called *prāpayati*; *sthira* becomes *sthāpayati*; *sphira* becomes *sphāpayati*; *uru* becomes *varayati*—thus Mādhava says regarding the verbal root *sub*. However, regarding the verbal root *ūrṇu*, he himself cited an example of *vṛddhi*: *bahulaṃ bahayati*, *guruṃ garayati*, *vṛddhaṃ varṣayati*. *Tṛpra* means suffering; one who expresses that is *traṣayati*. *Dīrgha* becomes *drāghayati*. *Vṛndāraka* becomes *vṛndayati*.
Thus ends the detailed exposition of examples for the treatment as if it were the superlative suffix (*iṣṭhan*).

Let us return to the subject at hand: one who composes a *sūtra* is called a *sūtrakāra*. Here, in the sentence "he composes the *sūtra* of grammar" (*vyākaraṇasya sūtraṃ karoti*), the word *sūtra* denotes the *sūtra* as a substance (*dravya*). Furthermore, the meaning of the word "grammar" (*vyākaraṇa*) is the aggregate of both the characterized (*lakṣya*) and the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Because of the relationship of part and whole (*aṃśāṃśibhāva*) between these two, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is employed.

Regarding the verse, there are two positions: [first] that the word *sūtra* is redundant, or [second] that it refers to the sense of "to make. In either case, since the *sūtra* is but a part of the meaning of the word (*padārthaikadeśa*), the grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) is not connected with it; rather, it is connected only with the sense of "making. Thus, in the expression "*vyākaraṇaṃ sūtrayati*" (he formulates the grammar), the accusative case alone occurs. Furthermore, even there, when a general relationship is intended, the genitive case certainly occurs, as in "*mātuḥ smarati*" (he remembers his mother); such is the direction of the argument.

"From *ākhyāna*, [the suffix] *ṇic* is added in the sense 'he expresses that'; there is elision of the *kṛt*-suffix, restoration of the original form, and the case-role is as in the original. (Kāśikāvṛtti). *Ākhyāna* means "that which is narrated"; the suffix *lyuṭ* is used for the object due to the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*). According to the ancients, by the word *ākhyāna*, the word expressing that [action] is understood, because it is impossible for the meaning itself to be a *kṛdanta* [derivative].

In reality, however, the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*). One who narrates the "slaying of Kaṃsa" (*kaṃsavadha*) is said to "cause Kaṃsa to be slain" (*kaṃsaṃ ghātayati*). Here, because the mention of a *kṛt*-suffix includes that which is preceded by a prefix (*gati*) or a kāraka, the word *kaṃsavadha* is a *kṛdanta* (a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix) signifying narration. From that nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in the second case, the causative suffix *ṇic* is added. There is elision (*luk*) of the *ap* portion of the *kṛt* suffix. That which is the base (*prakṛti*) of that very [suffix], namely *han*, remains in its own form, having abandoned its modification.

Although it is already established that when *luk* (elision) has occurred, the substitution *vadh*—which is taught as being in obligatory association (*sanniyogaśiṣṭa*) with it—is necessarily withdrawn, since by the rule *hanaśca vadhaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.76), the suffix *ap* and the substitute *vadh* are taught in obligatory association; nevertheless, Kaiyaṭa, Haradatta, Mādhava, and others maintain that the statement regarding the restoration of the original form (*prakṛtipratyāpatti*) is intended to prevent the occurrence of *kutva* (the change of *y* to *k*) in the example *sītāyogam ācaṣṭe sītayā yojayati*, because in this case, *kutva* is not taught in obligatory association with anything else.

In reality, however, since that [result] is established by the very principle of *nimittāpāya* (Pao-bhāo 57), this [sūtra] is intended to indicate its non-eternality (*anityatva*). The conclusion is as follows: even for those who claim, "This is neither a statement [of a rule] nor a principle," they nevertheless invoke the *akṛtavyūha* paribhāṣā (Pao-bhāo 57) as a substitute for that [principle]; thus, it is precisely the non-eternality of that [paribhāṣā] which is indicated by this [sūtra]. This has been explained by us in detail under the sūtra *acaḥ parasmin* (Pāṇini 1.1.57).

And thus, when the form *kaṃsahan* is established, the designation of a base (*aṅga*) and the designation of a verbal root (*dhātu*) would apply only to that which is qualified by *kaṃsa*; consequently, there would be the fault of [the augment] *aṭ* and [the reduplication] of the root. Therefore, it is stated: "The grammatical relation (*kāraka*) is like that of the original base."

The meaning of this is as follows: "prakṛti" refers to the base form of the causative suffix (*ṇic*). The suffix *vati* is applied after a word ending in the genitive case. Whatever *kāraka* (grammatical participant), such as Kaṃsa, belongs to a *kṛt*-derived verbal root like *han*, that very form remains when it is not included within the verbal root of the causative (*hetumaṇṇic*), provided it ends in the accusative case. For this very reason, the hearing of the letter *n* in the expression "he causes the king to come" (*rājānam āgamayati*)—derived from "he describes the coming of the king" (*rājāgamanam ācaṣṭe*)—is also logically justified.

By this extended application (*atideśa*), since it is established that the *kāraka* (the agent) is not included within the verbal root (*dhātu*), the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied only after [roots] distinct from those, such as *vad*. By this, forms such as *kaṃsam ajīghatat*—where the augment *aṭ* and reduplication occur—are established according to one's desire. [Objection: Even so, would the substitution of *k* for *h* by "ho hanteḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.54) and the substitution of *t* for *han* by "hanasto 'ciṇṇaloḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.32) not fail to apply? [If you argue: "Because when a verbal root is mentioned by its own form, the operation is understood to apply to a suffix belonging to that [root]" (Paribhāṣā 90)?

Regarding this, Haradatta, Mādhava, and others state: "In the rule *prakṛtivat ca*, the word *ca* (and) is to be construed out of its order; it should be understood immediately after the word *kārakam*. Furthermore, the word *kāryam* (the grammatical operation) is to be supplied by ellipsis. The meaning is: whatever *kāraka* (participant in an action) is found in the case of a *ṇic* affix caused by a motive (*hetumaṇṇic*), the same applies here; and whatever operation occurs there—such as the augment *aṭ*, reduplication, *tatva*, *kutva*, and so forth—that too occurs here in the same way. And in this context, both the augment *aṭ* and reduplication are established by two separate rules of extension."

The distinction is that unmixed examples include [verbs] beginning with the second [conjugation class] and those involving *kutva* (the change of *k* to *g*) and so forth. Here, there is no insistence on the causative (*ṇic*) suffix being used only in the specific narratives of the *Kaṃsavadha*, *Subhadrāharaṇa*, and others; rather, it applies to the mere act of narration. Therefore, one says *rājānam āgamayati* ("he causes the king to come") when expressing *rājāgamanam* ("the coming of the king"). Although in this case the king was the agent (*kartṛ*) in the base form (*prakṛti*) [of the root], nevertheless, in the causative (*hetumaṇṇic*) of the root *gam*, he becomes the object (*karman*) by the rule *gatibuddhipratyavasānārthaśabdakarmākarmakāṇām aṇikartā sa ṇau* (Pāṇini 1.4.52); and the same applies here as well.

Although the base portion (*prakṛtibhāga*) of the word *rājānam* is a *pada* by virtue of the intermediate sixth case (*antarvartinī ṣaṣṭhī*), nevertheless, the nasal *ṇ* is indeed heard [in the form *rājñā*] due to the force of the transfer of form (*rūpātideśa*). In the example “he causes Devadatta to cook” (*devadattapākam ācaṣṭe* → *devadattena pācayati*), the third case ending alone occurs; this is because, by the rule “*gati-buddhi-*” (Pāṇini 1.4.52), the status of being an object (*karmatva*) is removed, and the status of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) alone remains. This is the general direction of the argument.

And regarding an activity whose purpose is to be seen (*dṛśyarthā pravṛttiḥ*): "the sporting of deer" is *mṛgaramaṇam*; this is a compound with the sixth case in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ-ṣaṣṭhī*). One expresses that [activity] as "he causes the deer to sport" (*mṛgān ramayati*). This rule is stated for the purpose of ensuring that the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied only when the verb form expresses an activity whose purpose is to be seen by the agent who is being informed, and not otherwise. That is to say, this verbal operation (*vṛtti*) in the form of a verb is [restricted] if it has the sense of being seen.

Therefore, in the case where one who is himself experiencing the deer's sporting describes it to another in order to show it, the usage is *mṛgān ramayati* ("he causes the deer to sport"). However, when one who has seen the deer's sporting in the forest comes to a village and describes it to another, saying, "The deer sport there in this way," then in that instance of communication to be understood, the expression is simply the sentence *mṛgaramaṇam ācaṣṭe* ("he describes the deer's sporting").

On this point, Kaiyaṭa and others state that the restriction "only when [the causative] has the sense of 'seeing'" applies specifically to cases such as the roaming of deer, and is not universal; therefore, they maintain that the causative suffix (ṇic) must indeed occur even in cases like the arrival of a king, despite the absence of the activity of seeing.

"Furthermore, there is elision [of the suffix *aṅ*] when expressing a limit (*maryādā*) involving the complete connection of time (*kālātyantasaṃyoga*). Here, the phrase "following a narrative" (*ākhyānāt*) does not apply. The remainder is as before. The meaning is that when the complete connection of time with the action of narrating—which is present in proximity—is to be conveyed, there is the causative suffix *ṇic*, and there is elision of the suffix *aṅ* which expresses a limit. An example is *vivasanam* or *vivāsaḥ*, meaning "passing by" or "transgressing"; [this is formed with] the suffix *ghañ*. Then, "the passing by of the night" (*rātrervivāsaḥ*) is a compound with a genitive case in the sense of the agent (*kartṛṣaṣṭhyā*).

Then, by the rule *āṅ maryādābhividhyoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.13), there is an *avyayībhāva* compound with *āṅ*. *Ārātrivivāsam ācaṣṭe* means "he tells [the story] until the end of the night. The meaning is that he tells stories for as long as the night has not passed.

In the case of *vasikriyā* (the act of subduing), which functions as the agent (*kartṛ*), the night (*rātri*) becomes the object (*karman*) when the causative suffix (*ṇi*) is applied; this is because the root *vas* is intransitive (*akarmaka*). Similarly here, the night also becomes the object when the causative suffix is applied. Since the word *rātrim* has its sixth case ending elided (*lupta-ṣaṣṭhyanta*), the preceding member (*prakṛti-bhāga*) is a *pada*. Consequently, the optional *prakṛti-bhāva* (non-application of sandhi rules) prescribed by Pāṇini 6.1.127 (*iko’savarṇe*) would apply, but it is precluded here by the extension (*atideśa*) of the form from the preceding rule. In this context, although the meaning of the causative base (*ṇic-prakṛti*) is not explicitly stated, it is understood through implication.

However, the word expressing that [meaning], such as "bhārakakathām" and so forth, should not be employed here. For when that is used in co-utterance, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) itself does not arise, due to non-usage (*anabhidhāna*). And the proof for this is precisely the rejection (*pratyākhyāna*) by the author of the Bhāṣya which will be mentioned later. Indeed, a rejection based on a difference in result will become clear at the very occasion of the rejection itself. Likewise, regarding the previously mentioned explanation of "prakṛtivacca kārakam" as involving an inversion of the order of words through ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*), the rejection by the author of the Bhāṣya serves as the authority; such is the direction of the argument.

[The rule] *citrikaraṇe prāp-* [is applied]. Excluding the word "ākhyānāt" (from narration), the remainder is connected [to the previous rule]. When a sense of performing a marvelous feat (*āścaryakaraṇa*) is implied following a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix, the affix *ṇic* shall be added to the root in the sense of "attaining" (*prāptau*), with the elision of the *kṛt* suffix and so forth as before. For example: *ujjayinyāḥ prasthito māhiṣmatyāṃ sūryodgamanaṃ prāpnoti sūryam udgamayati* ("Setting out from Ujjayinī, he attains sunrise at Māhiṣmatī; he causes the sun to rise [at Māhiṣmatī]"). Here, since Māhiṣmatī is a distant place from Ujjayinī, the fact that he traverses such a distance before sunrise constitutes a marvelous feat.

By the rule *prakṛtivacca kārakam*, the sun (*sūrya*) retains its status as a separate [agent]. Since it is stated that [the causative suffix] applies only to the root *saṃgrāmayati* when accompanied by a prefix, the word *ut* is separated [from the root]. Because the sun is the object (*karman*) in the causative form with the causal suffix (*hetumaṇṇic*), it is also the object here; thus, one says "he caused the sun to rise" (*sūryam udagamayat*), and so forth.

[The suffix] *ṇica* [is applied] after a word expressing conjunction with a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra-yoga*) in the sense of "he knows. The remainder is as before. The meaning is that the conjunction with the *puṣya* [constellation] has the agent as its object; that is, the conjunction. For the *puṣya* joins—that is, connects—with the moon. Here, because the object is also understood, the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) for the agent does not occur due to the restriction [stated in] Pāṇini 2.3.66 (*ubhayaprāptau*), and thus the third case (*tṛtīyā*) is used, just as in the rule Pāṇini 1.4.28 (*antarddhau yenādarśanamicchati*).

"He knows the conjunction with Puṣya" (*puṣyayogaṃ jānāti*) means "he joins [the moon] with Puṣya" (*puṣyeṇa yojayati*). Since the agent of the root *yuj* (Puṣya) is not included among the agents of the motion and so forth [of the causative], it does not become an object (*karman*) when the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied due to the causal sense; rather, it retains its status as an agent (*kartṛ*). Here too, it is the same, and therefore the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) alone is used. Furthermore, this collection of Vārttikas beginning with "from a narrative, the Kṛt-suffix" (*ākhyānātkṛtaḥ*) has been rejected by both the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika itself, because the various examples (*lakṣyajāta*) belonging to them can be easily established through metaphorical attribution (*āropa*). For instance, the expression "he causes Kaṃsa to be killed" (*kaṃsaṃ ghātayati*) is simply such an attribution.

For those who are the explanatory teachers of actors imitating Kaṃsa and others, they cause the actor imitating Kaṃsa—who is perceived by the audience with the cognition that he is Kaṃsa—to be slain, as it were, by Vāsudeva appearing in that very same form. Those who explain a painting in such a sequence as "This is Mathurā, this is the palace, here has the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva entered," and so forth—they too act in exactly the same way.

Even those known as *granthikas* (reciters of texts) who, while reciting a book, narrate the "Slaying of Kaṃsa," they too—as if bringing about those various actions—produce a certainty regarding the objects denoted by each respective word. Thus, the metaphorical attribution (*āropa*) is clear. Furthermore, in established usages such as "Go! Kaṃsa is being slain," "Go! He will be slain," or "What is the use of going? Kaṃsa has already been killed here," this same principle applies even to you. For in these cases, the rule for the causative suffix (*ṇic*) does not provide any assistance, since the causative suffix is absent in the examples cited. And it has been said:

"And one regards Kaṃsa and others—who have had their forms superimposed by words and who have entered the domain of the intellect—as if they were directly perceived (pratyakṣa), [and as] the means [of an action].

This should be understood similarly in cases such as "he causes the king to come" (*rājānam āgamayati*). For in cases like "he brings the king" (*rājānam ānayati*), since there is no *ṇic* suffix, this is indeed the only way to explain it. Even in "he makes the night pass" (*rātrim vivāsayati*), the superimposition is that "the night has been made to go by him" through the telling of various stories. And in cases such as "he led the night away" (*niśām nināya*), this is likewise the only way for you to explain it as well.

In the expression "he causes the sun to rise," there too is a superimposition of the relationship between the prompted and the prompter; however, the basis for this is simply the accomplishment of Devadatta's intended purpose, namely, "May I obtain the rising of the sun at Māhiṣmatī. For whoever is impelled by another accomplishes that person's intended object. In that regard, even though disciples and others act for the sake of their own welfare, they certainly aim toward the intended purpose of the teacher as well.

However, there is a disparity in that the sun does not act with the intended destination of Devadatta in mind. Nevertheless, there is no harm in the metaphorical attribution (āropa) as long as the desired purpose is accomplished. Similarly, in the case of "yojayati puṣyeṇa" ("he joins [the moon] with Puṣya"), because the conjunction with Puṣya is revealed to everyone through the study of the science of astronomy (jyotiḥ-śāstra), the metaphorical attribution "as if he were joining" is applied.
Thus ends the second Āhnika of the first Pāda of the third Adhyāya in the Śabdakaustubha.
The third section (āhnika) of the first quarter (pāda) of the third chapter (adhyāya).

(Pāṇini 3.1.27) *kaṇḍvādibhyo yak*: The suffix *yak* occurs after the roots beginning with *kaṇḍū* in their own sense (*svārtha*). From the root *kaṇḍūñ* (P. 6.4.24), we derive *kaṇḍūyati* or *kaṇḍūyate*. It should not be said that *kaṇḍū* and the others are merely nominal stems (*prātipadika*), because their status as verbal roots (*dhātu*) is established by the fact that the suffix *yak* is marked with *k* (indicating *kittva*), which serves to prohibit *guṇa* substitution. Nor should it be argued that the recurrence of the term "root" (*dhātoḥ*) [from the previous rule] would then be redundant; for that term is necessary to exclude the nominal stems.

Nor should it be said that these are merely verbal roots (dhātu), because for some among the *kaṇḍvādi* group, their status as nominal stems (*prātipadika*) is established by their being listed with a long vowel. For if they were indeed only verbal roots, then the mention of the suffix *ya* [in Pāṇini 3.1.27] would have to be set aside and it must be accepted that *ya* is obligatory; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of forms such as *kaṇḍavati* in the *śab* class and so forth.

This being the case, since the form *kaṇḍūyati* and others would be established even from a short-final root by applying the *yaka* suffix and the lengthening rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ dīrghaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.25)—just as in the case of *mantūyati* and so on—what is the purpose of reading the long vowel? Therefore, it is established that the *kaṇḍvādi* roots are of two kinds: both verbal roots (*dhātu*) and nominal stems (*prātipadika*), as indicated by the two indicators, namely the *kit* designation and the lengthening. And it has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "Because it occurs in the section on verbal roots, and because the suffix *ka* is attached to it, and because he [the author] has prescribed this lengthening, I consider the verbal root to be optionally specified."

In this context, because the governing topic is *dhātu* (verbal roots), the suffix is added to the roots themselves; and it is the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that this suffix is obligatory (*nitya*).

It might be argued: "Let these [forms] simply be nominal stems (*prātipadika*); let the long vowel in their recitation and the *kittva* of the suffix be abandoned. This cannot be said, for if that were the case, the lengthening prescribed by Pāṇini’s rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ...* (Pāṇ. 7.4.25) would not apply here, as that rule is conditioned by the presence of a suffix marked with *ṅ*. Nor can it be argued that this leads to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in forms such as *uruyā* and *dhṛṣṇuyā*, since those are Vedic (*chāndasa*).

Nor should it be argued that if *yaK* were obligatory, the form *kaṇḍūḥ* would not be established; for from the word *kaṇḍūya*, by adding the suffix *kvip* in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*) under the *saṃpadādi* group, there is elision of the *a* by Pāṇini 6.4.48 (*al-lopaḥ*), and subsequently the elision of *y* by Pāṇini 6.1.66 (*lopo vy-oḥ*), whereby the form is successfully derived. Nor should one suspect that the elision of *a* (the *al-lopa*) would be subject to the rule of *sthānivadbhāva* regarding the elision of *y*, because this is prohibited by Pāṇini 1.1.58 (*na padānta...*).

Nor should it be argued that *uvaṅ* substitution would occur due to the *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being as if occupying the original position) of the elision of the *al*; for if *sthānivadbhāva* were present, the root would still end in an *akāra*, and thus *uvaṅ* would not apply in the first part [of the derivation]. If it is then asked, "In that case, let there be *yaṇ* substitution"? Let it be so; we shall apply *ūṭh* to that [resulting form]. Nor should it be argued that when *ūṭh* is to be applied, the elision of *al* prevents the presence of a *kvip* suffix by virtue of *sthānivadbhāva*; for the letter *v* is indeed prior to the *ac* (vowel) that serves as the point of reference (*ādiṣṭa*). But surely, the quality of being prior to the *ac* that serves as the point of reference exists precisely through the medium of the *sthānin* (the original element)?

Nor is Mādhava’s statement—that there is no extension (atideśa) because this [quality] is not prescribed by the grammatical treatise (asāstrīya)—correct; for since the extension "ataḥ parasmim" (Pāṇini 1.1.57), which must be applied on the basis of its being prior to an unspecified vowel (anādiṣṭādacaḥ pūrvatvam), is itself scripturally sanctioned (śāstrīya), an extension of an extension (atideśātideśa) via the rule "sthānivat" (Pāṇini 1.1.56) is unavoidable.

If it is argued that otherwise the mention of *savarṇa* in the rule *na padānta* (Pāṇini 1.1.58) would result in being purposeless, we say no; for it has already been established that the status of being "prior to a vowel" (*pūrvatva*) by way of the substitute (*sthānin*) is not universal. For this very reason, once *ūṭ* has been applied, *uvaṅ* does not apply again. Alternatively, due to the prohibition "that which is elided before *kvip* is not treated as a substitute" (*kā-vā*), let there simply be no *yaṇ*-substitution at all.

[Objection: But even so, in forms such as *kaṇḍvau*, since the condition of being preceded by a conjunct (*saṃyoga-pūrvakatva*) applies, the rule *oḥ supi* (Pāṇini 6.4.83) would not apply, and consequently *uvaṅ* would occur—do you mean this? [Reply: Let it be; we shall effect *ūṭh* by means of the *pratyaya-lakṣaṇa* (the technical application of a suffix) for the *kvip* suffix. Therefore, these are indeed nominal stems (*prātipadika*), and the lengthening and the *kit*-designation are useless—is this your point? [Reply: Not so. Because *uvaṅ* is *asiddha* (non-existent) due to its being *bahiraṅga* (extrinsic), whereas *ūṭh* is weaker [and thus superseded].

Furthermore, according to the aforementioned reasoning, forms such as *mantūḥ* would arise just like *kaṇḍūḥ*, and forms such as *mantuḥ* would not be established. Now, if the option (*vā*) from Pāṇini’s sūtra 3.1.7 (*dhātoḥ karmaṇaḥ*) were to be carried over [here], then although *mantuḥ* and so forth—with the short vowel—would be established, nevertheless, by means of the elision of *al* and the elision of *ya* (as in *kaṇḍūḥ*), the form *mantūḥ* would also result. Likewise, on the view that the suffix *kyap* does not arise, the form *kaṇḍuḥ* would also result just like *mantuḥ*.

Furthermore, if the suffix *ya* were applied to *sukha* and other such words, because that [suffix] would not be an *ārddhadhātuka*, the elision of the final *a* (by Pāṇini 6.4.48) would not occur; consequently, by the rule "akṛtsārva" (Pāṇini 7.4.25), the vowel would be lengthened, resulting in forms such as *sukhāvati*. However, forms such as *sukhyati* are what is intended. If, on the other hand, the word were taught as ending in a consonant (*halanta*), then forms ending in *a*, such as *sukham* and *duḥkham*, would not be established. Therefore, the [explanation] exactly as it stands is the most elegant.

But even so, although forms such as *kaṇḍvau* and *mantuḥ* are established by means of nominal stems (*prātipadika*), nevertheless, undesirable forms would certainly arise from [roots] ending in *yaK* when followed by *kviP*. For example: from *kaṇḍūyati*, one would get *kaṇḍuvau* and *kaṇḍuvaḥ*; from *mantūyati*, one would get *mantūḥ*; and from the class beginning with *sukha*, one would get *suk* and so forth, ending in a consonant (*hal*). This is not a fault, because *kviP* simply does not arise after roots ending in *yaK*. For it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "The suffix *kviP* will not be seen after these."

How then is the suffix *ap* applied to the root *kaṇḍūyati* [to form] *kaṇḍūḥ*, as stated in the rule *na padānta* (Pāṇini 1.1.58)? Understand that this occurs even when the suffix *kvip* follows a form ending in *kyac*. In that case, the form *kaṇḍuvau* is indeed desired with the substitution of *uvaṅ*. Similarly, it should be understood that the same applies when *kvip* follows a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *ācārakvip* or *ky-aṅ*.

It might be argued: "Let the *kaṇḍvādi* items be simply nominal stems (*prātipadika*); let them remain long as they are in the original list, let the letter *k* be discarded, and let the mention of the suffix *vā* be carried over [from Pāṇini 3.1.20]. Furthermore, our position is the same regarding the non-occurrence of *kvip* after a stem ending in *ya*. So what is the point of treating the *kaṇḍvādi* items as verbal roots (*dhātu*)? [Response: No, because according to the reasoning already stated, forms such as *sukhyati* would not be established. If a suffix were added to a nominal stem, that suffix would not be considered *ārdhadhātuka*, and consequently, the form would have to be *sukhāyati*; this is indeed a manifest flaw.

As for what is stated in the *Kaumudī*—"The suffix *yak* occurs in the sense of the root *kṛ* (to do); since both roots and nominal stems [can serve as bases], the *kaṇḍvādi* group is of two kinds; thus, 'he scratches' (*kaṇḍūyate*) [is derived from] *kaṇḍū*. Because it is a nominal root (*nāmadhātu*), the suffix *ya* is desired; and since reduplication would otherwise apply, it is stated that for the *kaṇḍvādi* group, the third syllable is reduplicated"—all of this contradicts the original source (*ākara*) and is beset by numerous defects. For instance, by the explanation "in the sense of *kṛ*," the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the term "instrument" (*karaṇe*) is obtained. But that is redundant, because [the required meaning] is obtained even without the recurrence of the mere sense of the root.

Furthermore, because there is no connection (*anvaya*) with anything additional [beyond the verbal root], the demonstration of the analytical derivation (*vigraha*) as "he performs scratching" (*kaṇḍūṃ karoti*) is also incorrect. Moreover, the claim that this is due to its being a nominalized root (*nāmadhātu*) is all the more untenable, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that the suffix *yaK* occurs only after verbal roots (*dhātu*) within the governing context of "roots. If, on the other hand, you admit that *yaK* occurs after a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself, then in the present tense (*laṭ*) and so forth, forms such as *kaṇḍavati* would result.

Now, if you intend that the *kaṇḍvādi* items are indeed nominal stems (*prātipadika*), then forms such as *sukhyati* would not be established; furthermore, there would be a contradiction with your own statement that "the *kaṇḍvādi* items are of two kinds. As for the contradiction with the original source (*ākara*), it is quite evident, so let us leave it at that for now.

However, some esteemed scholars somehow justify this entire section on grammatical derivation (*prakriyāpraghaṭṭaka*), even though it is marred by numerous defects. For instance, they argue that *kaṇḍvādi* is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and that this text belongs to the alternative view where the suffix *yak* is optional after such stems; hence it is stated that [the suffix] occurs "in the sense of the root *kṛ*" (*kṛñarthe*). Furthermore, they provide the analysis as "he performs scratching" (*kaṇḍūṃ karoti*). Indeed, this analysis would not be possible if *yak* were obligatory either after verbal roots or after nominal stems. Thus, the statement that [these words] are denominative verbs (*nāmadhātu*) and so forth is also entirely correct.

If it is asked, "How then is this twofold nature stated?"—the intention is that when they end in *ya*, they are verbal roots (*dhātu*), whereas in their isolated state they are nominal stems (*prātipadika*). Alternatively, the term "verbal root" is used figuratively for those elements that constitute parts of a root ending in *ya*. The twofold nature arises from the distinction between states based on the presence or absence of suffixes. Nor should it be argued that in forms such as *sukhyati*, the rule "elision of *at*" (Pāṇini 6.4.64) would not apply; for since *yak* is marked with the *k*-sign, it necessarily possesses the status of an *ardhadhātuka* suffix, and this is established both by necessity and by parsimony.

For this very reason, it was stated simply as "of two kinds" and not that "yaṅ occurs after roots [only]"; although this contradicts the Bhāṣya and other authorities, let it be accepted somehow, since there is no disagreement regarding the actual linguistic usage (*lakṣya*).

Now, the examples: 1. *kaṇḍūñ* (root *kaṇḍū*) in the sense of rubbing the limbs. A suffix (*liṅga*) applied to a part [of a word] qualifies the whole. This applies hereafter as well. *kaṇḍūyati*, *kaṇḍūyate*. 2. *mantu* in the sense of offense; some say in the sense of anger. *mantūyati*. Candragomin, however, having read it with the marker *ñ* (*ñit*), also says *mantūyate*. 3. *valgu* in the sense of praise and excellence. *valgūyati*. "Simultaneously with that beautiful [glance] which opened... 4. *asu* in the sense of affliction. *asūyati*. *asūyuḥ*. Mādhava states that the suffix *u* is added by the rule *mṛgayvādayaśca* (Uṇādi-sūtra 39). By this—

"The virtuous, being free from envy, indeed accept the words of those who love them. Thus is the usage of Bhaṭṭi explained. However, some read the roots as *as* and *asūñ*; they say that from the first, which ends in *s*, comes *asyati*, and from the second, which ends in a long vowel, come *asūyati* and *asūyate*. 6. *leṭ* and 7. *loṭ* mean "shaking," "being in front," and "sleeping. One says *leṭyati* and *loṭyati*. The forms are *laṭitā* and *loṭitā*, with the elision of *a* and the elision of *y*. Some say that *leṭ* and *loṭ* have the meaning of "shining"; Mādhava says "being in front" means "the state of being in front."

In this regard, some, relying on the word *pūrva* as an indication of the verbal root (*prakṛti*), cite *pūrvyati* as an example. Accordingly, Bhaṭṭamalla has stated among the group of mental functions (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*): "One lies down (*śete*), slumbers (*drāyati*), sleeps (*nidrāti*), rests (*sasti*), sleeps (*svapiti*), *pūrvyati*, slumbers (*nidrāyate*), reclines (*saṃviśati*), is absorbed in sleep (*nidrāyāṃ saṃsti*), and is languid (*mandate*)."

The meaning of this has been stated in the *Dhātucandrodaya*: "The ten roots beginning with *śī* are declared to mean 'sleeping. *Pas* is [the root] for dreaming; it belongs to the *adādi* (second) class. Some have recited it as 'ṣasi śayane' (to lie down)," according to Kṣīrasvāmī in that very same work. Furthermore, it begins with the statement that *pūrvyati* ends in the *ya*-affix of the *kaṇḍvādi* class. Likewise, Deva has also said:
"As for the form *pūrvyati*, since it is seen among the *kaṇḍvādi* roots, it is used in the sense of dreaming."

Furthermore, this [interpretation] has been refuted by the *Puruṣakāra* itself on the grounds that it is incorrect because the word is not listed earlier in the *gaṇa-pāṭha*, which lacks explicit definitions of meaning in the *Amoghā* commentary on Sākaṭāyana’s *Dhātuvṛtti*. This is indeed correct, for Javāditya also reads it simply as "leṭ" and "loṭ," and Haradatta explains it in his *Ghautya* as "in the state of being prior" (*pūrvabhāve*) and "in dreaming" (*svapne*). By this, in the *buddhi-varga*, when something is brought within the range of the mind (*manasāgocarīkāre*), one says "he intends" (*manasyati*) in the sense of "being in the mind."

Thus, even the statement of Bhaṭṭamalla is refuted, as the same logic applies. For Jayāditya specified only "asu," whereas Haradatta, having begun with "Now follows the explanation of the meanings of the *kaṇḍvādi* roots" and while commenting on the *kaṇḍvādi* list, took up the term "asu" as a lemma (*pratīka*) and explained it as "in the sense of mental affliction."

For this very reason, even for those who read "asu manasa utāpa," the word "manasa" is a genitive singular functioning as an adjective qualifying the affliction (*upatāpa*), and not a citation of the verbal root; this is because such an interpretation would contradict the *Vṛtti*, the *Padamañjarī*, and other works. Furthermore, there is indeed dissatisfaction with the explanation of the author of the *Dhātucandrodaya*, who, despite explaining at great length that "manasyati" is formed from the *kaṇḍvādī* class with the suffix *yak*, finds it unsatisfactory.

For this same reason, having adopted the reading "manasyate" and having stated that the suffix *kyaṅ* occurs after the word "manas" when it functions as a derivative form (*vṛtti*), he concluded, "This is most excellent."

8. *lelā* in the sense of shining: the Śruti says, "He meditates, as it were; He flickers, as it were. 9. *iras*, 10. *iraj*, 11. *irañ* in the sense of envy: *irasyati*, *irajyati*, *īryati*, *īryate*. There is lengthening [of the vowel] by Pāṇini’s sūtra 6.4.123 (*hali ca*). These three roots also have other meanings according to their respective contexts. For instance, in the mantra "O Agni, ruling (*irajyan*), spread forth with living beings," Bhaṭṭabhāskara and others maintain that this [root] has the meaning of shining.

In the mantra "irajyantāvasavyasya bhūreḥ," the root *iraj* is used in the sense of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). Although the root *iryati* is stated to mean both "to move" and "to stand on a path"—as Amara says: "Caryā, however, is īryā; it is standing on a path" (Amarakośa 2.7.38)—the *Gaṇaratnamahodadhi* states: "The root *iyas* is used in the sense of sovereignty. Thus: *iyasyati*. 13. *uṣas* in the sense of dawn: *uṣasyati rātriḥ* ("the night dawns"). 14. *ved* in the sense of cheating and sleep: *vedyati*. 15. *medhā* in the sense of quick apprehension: *medhāyati*. 16. *kuṣubha* in the sense of throwing: *kuṣubhyati*.

17. *magadha* in the sense of surrounding; others say in the sense of being a low servant. *magadhyati*. 18. *tanta* and 19. *paṃpa* in the sense of suffering. *tantasyati*. *paṃpasyati*. 20. *sukha* and 21. *duḥkha* in the sense of performing that [action]. By the word "that," the meanings of pleasure and pain are intended. The meaning is: in an action consisting of pleasure or pain. *sukhyati*. *duḥkhyati*. The meaning is: one experiences pleasure or pain. 22. *sapara* in the sense of worship. This [root] ends in *a*; [it is found] in the *Mahodadhi*. *saparyati*. 23. *arara* in the sense of the work of a spoke (*ārā*).

*Ārā* means a goad; it is *araryati*. 24. *Bhiṣaja* in the sense of medical treatment; it is *bhiṣajyati*. 25. *Bhiṣṇaja* in the sense of service; it is *bhiṣṇajyati*. [As in: "O Maghavan, Sarasvatī serves you" (*sarasvatī tvā maghavann abhiṣṇak*). Here there is a Vedic elision (*chāndaso luk*). 26. *Iṣudha* in the sense of holding arrows; it is *iṣudhyati*. 27. *Racaṇa*, 28. *Varaṇa* in the sense of going; it is *caraṇyati*, *varaṇyati*. 29. *Curaṇa* in the sense of stealing; it is *curaṇyati*. 30. *Turaṇa* in the sense of speed; it is *turaṇyati*. 31. *Bhuraṇa* in the sense of supporting and nourishing; others say it means "supporting and moving."

*bhuraṇyati* (32). *gadgadi* means faltering speech; [from this root] *gadgadyati*. (33) *elā*, (34) *kelā*, (35) *khelā*—these mean sporting; [from these roots] *elāyati*, *kelāyati*, *khelāyati*. (36) *elā* also means standing still. (37) Others say it is *ilā*; [from this] *ilāyati*. (38) *lekhā* means faltering as well; [from this] *lekhāyati*. Others hold that this [root] ends in *a*; in that case, there is the elision of *at* (Pāṇini 6.4.48), and thus *lekhyati*. (39) *liṭa* means smallness or contempt; [from this] *liṭyati*. (40) *lāṭa* means living; [from this] *lāṭyati*. (41) *hṛṇīṅ* means anger and shame.

"How does the childless earth feel ashamed?"—thus says Śrīharṣa. (42) *mahīṅ* is used in the sense of worship (*pūjā*). Here, "worship" refers to the state of being the agent of the act of being worshipped; therefore, this root is intransitive (*akarmaka*). *Mahīyate* means "he attains worship. As stated in the Bhāṣya: "And his mother and father are honored (*mahīyete*) in the heavenly world. (43) *rekhā* is used in the senses of praise (*ślāghā*) and attainment (*āsādana*). *Āsādana* means reaching or causing to reach. *Rekhāyati* means "he experiences praise" or "he causes [another] to experience praise. (44) *dravas* is used in the senses of distress (*paritāpa*) and service (*paricaraṇa*).

45. *tiras* in the sense of disappearance: *tirasyati*. 46. *dravas* in the senses of heating and attending upon: *dravasyati*. 47. *uras* in the sense of strength: *urasyati*, meaning "he becomes strong. 48. *taraṇa* in the sense of going: *taramyati*. 49. *payas* in the sense of spreading: *payasyati*. 50. *sambhūyas* in the sense of becoming abundant: *sambhūyasyati*. 51. *ambara* and 52. *saṃvara* in the sense of covering: *ambaryati*, *saṃvaryati*.

In the *Gaṇaratnamahodadhi*, because these belong to the class of *ākṛtigaṇas* (classes defined by their form), it is stated that from roots such as *raidhaval* one forms *rāyati* and *dhavalyati* by adding the suffix *yak*. It will be stated later that for roots belonging to the *kaṇḍvādi* class, there is reduplication of the third syllable (*tṛtīyasya dve*). Consequently, with the suffix *san*, one forms *kaṇḍūyiyiṣati*, and so forth. (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.28)

*Pagu-pū-dhūpa-vichi-paṇi-panibhya āyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.28). The suffix *āya* is added to these roots in their own sense (*svārthe*). *gup* (to protect, *bhvādi*, 395): *gopāyati*. *dhūp* (to heat, *bhvādi*, 396): *dhūpāyati*. *vicch* (to go, *tudādi*, 143): *vicchāyati*. Because of the force of its inclusion in the *tudādi* class, the suffix *śa* is not applied after the form ending in *āya*; rather, [the suffix] *śap* is applied. Thus, one says both *vicchāyanati* and *vicchāyati*. According to *ācchī* (Pāṇini 7.1.80), there is an optional application of the augment *num*.

Others, however, on the strength of its inclusion in the *tudādi* list, say that the *āya* suffix is optional even for this root when followed by a *sārvadhātuka* suffix. Regarding the roots *paṇa* (DhP 4.40) and *pana* (DhP 4.41), meaning "to bargain" and "to praise": although one might expect them to be read together as *paṇapana*, the fact that they are read separately as *pana ca* indicates that this [root *pana*] applies only to the sense of "praising. By association with it, the *āya* suffix is also applied to *paṇ* only in the sense of "praising. Since the *anubandha* (the marker *ṇ*) serves its purpose only in the case of the simple root, the *ātmanepada* ending does not occur after the form ending in the *āya* suffix. Thus, *paṇāyati* and *panāyati* mean "he praises. However, regarding "bargaining," Jayāditya and others cite the example: *śatasya paṇate* ("he bargains for a hundred").

Others, however, maintain that the suffix *āya* is also desired for the sake of expressing worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). Thus says Bhaṭṭi: "And he did not find [merchandise] for sale among the merchants" (*na copalebhe vaṇijāṃ paṇāyām*). Even in this view, in forms such as *paṇiṣyate* and *paṇāyiṣyati*, the *anubandha* (the marker *ṅ*) serves its purpose only when the root is used alone. For this very reason, even from the root *pan*, when the suffix *āya* is added, only the *parasmaipada* (active voice) occurs. (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.3.29).

*ṛterīyaṅ* (Pāṇini 3.1.29): *ṛti* is a root found in the Sūtras; from it, the suffix *īyaṅ* occurs. Thus, *ṛtīyate*. Although the *ṅ*-marking of *īyaṅ* serves its purpose by prohibiting *guṇa*, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) still applies because the verbal base ends in a *ṅ*-marked suffix, just as in the case of bases ending in *yaṅ*. We have already explained how this is so under the rule *anudāttaṅitaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.12).
