Since [the form] *śaṅ* is already established by the rule *ṛteśchaṅ*, the explicit mention of *īyaṅ* is for the purpose of indicating that suffixes such as *āyan* and others do not apply to verbal roots (*dhātu*) or primary suffixes (*pratyaya*). Consequently, forms such as *śaṅkhaḥ*—derived from the root *śam-* with the suffix *kha*—are established; so say the authors of the *Vṛtti* and others. Haradatta, however, offers a counter-argument (*pratibandī*), stating that since the rule "when two things are compared or when there is a distributive sense, the suffixes *tarap* and *chasun*" could have been stated simply as "when there is a comparison," the explicit mention of *īyasun* would indicate that even in the case of suffixes applied to verbal roots, suffixes like *āyan* and others are absent.

In this context, the mention of the suffix *īyasun* is solely for the sake of brevity in grammatical derivation (*prakriyālāghava*) and not for the purpose of providing a technical indication (*jñāpana*), because [if it were for the latter], the suffixes *āyan* and others would be rendered without scope. Nor is there a lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanāviraha*), as the very Vedic-style (sūtra-like) references such as "ṇyakṣatriya" (Pāṇini 2.4.58) serve as that determining factor; this is the resolution to be understood. Furthermore, the commentary states that the root *ṛti*, which is Vedic (*sautra*), occurs in the sense of "compassion" (*ghṛṇā*).

Although the word *ghṛṇā* has multiple meanings—according to the rule "ghṛṇā means both loathing (*jugupsā*) and compassion (*kṛpā*)"—nevertheless, in this context it signifies only loathing, because Haradatta and others maintain that the word *ṛtīyā* is listed in the lexicons as a synonym for *bībhatsā* (disgust). Bhaṭṭamalla, however, in his *Ākhyātacandrikā*, within the third section on polysemous words, favored its having multiple meanings by reading: "ṛtīyate [is used] in the senses of 'fie! (*dhik*) and loathing (*ghṛṇā*)."

Thus speaking, even Amara is in agreement here. For if he intended the meaning to be merely "disgust," he would have clearly recited [the rule] as "haṇīyā ca jugupsane. However, by employing the word *ghṛṇā* in its various senses, Kṛṣṇaprabodha in his commentary on the *Padacandrikā*, the *Dhātucandrodaya*, maintains that the root *ṛ* also possesses that same range of meanings. But when there is a desire to express an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, in the alternative where *īyaṅ* does not occur, the *parasmaipada* alone is used because it is the "remainder" (*śeṣa*). [Conjugations: *ānarta*; *artiṣyati*; *ārtīt*; *ārtiṣyat*. As for the author of the *Prasāda*, who provides examples of the *ātmanepada* here, he is certainly mistaken.

(Pāṇini 3.1.30) *Kameṇiṅ* (Pāṇini 3.1.30). [The suffix] *ṇiṅ* is applied in the sense of the root's own meaning (*svārthe*). Thus, *kāmayate*. Now, one might object: here, by the rule *ata upadhāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.116), a *vṛddhi* [strengthening] would be required, but its prohibition applies by the rule *ṅkiti ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.5). Nor can it be argued that the *vṛddhi* occurs due to the force of the *ṇit* designation [of the suffix], since that designation has already served its purpose through the specific rule *ṇeraniṭi* (Pāṇini 6.4.51). Furthermore, it should not be said that the letter *ṅ* has already served its purpose by indicating the *ātmanepada* [middle voice] ending; for even so, the strength of the prohibition remains intact.

Nor should it be argued that the statement "na kamyamicamām" (Pāṇini’s Gaṇasūtra) is intended to prohibit the designation *mit* for the purpose of preventing *vṛddhi*, and that this rule, being otherwise redundant in the absence of *vṛddhi*, serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for *vṛddhi* in this context; for the prohibition of the *mit* designation remains meaningful as a means of precluding the optional lengthening (*dīrgha*) prescribed by the rule "ciṇṇamulordīrgho’nyatarasyām" (Pāṇini 6.4.93), which would otherwise apply when the affixes *ciṇ* and *ṇamul* follow a root ending in *ṇi*.

Nor should it be argued that one might abandon the mention of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) there and instead allow the original short vowel (*hrasva*) to be optional, so that even the prohibition of the *mit* designation for the root *kam* would not be necessary; for if the suffix *ṇic* were applied to the form ending in *yaṅ* (i.e., *kāmy*), and then another *ṇic* were added, followed by *ciṇ* or *ṇamul*, the two resulting forms—*aśami* / *aśāmi*; *śamaṃ śamam* / *śāmama śāmam*; *aśaṃśami* / *aśaṃśāmi*; *śaṃśamaṃ śaṃśamam* / *śaṃśāmaṃ śaṃśāmam*—could not be accounted for without the mention of the long vowel.

For with respect to a long-vowel rule (*dīrghavidhi*), there is no *sthānivadbhāva* (the status of being as if the substitute were the original) for the elision of *ṇi* and *ṇya*, due to the prohibition in Pāṇini 1.1.58 (*na padānta*). However, with respect to a short-vowel rule (*hrasvavidhi*), since *sthānivadbhāva* does apply, if the *ṇic* following *ciṇ* or *ṇamul* were separated from the root by *ṇi* and *ṇya*, the optional shortening would not take effect. This is according to the literal wording of the sūtra. But according to the alternative view—that once it is stated that "what is established by what is *asiddha* in the preceding" (*pūrvatrāsiddhīyam*), there is no need to include the mention of *savarṇa*, *anusvāra*, and so forth—the desired result is established because the general form (*ākṛti*) of *ṇi* remains identical even when a *ṇic* is added to a stem already ending in *ṇic*.

Regarding the form *śaṃśāmam śaṃśāmam*, we have already explained under the rule *na padānta* (Pāṇini 1.1.58) that it is derived from the root with the *yaṅ*-luṅ suffix followed by the *ṇamul* suffix. Even in this alternative analysis (*niṣkṛṣṭapakṣa*), the mention of the long vowel (*dīrghagrahaṇa*) in the rule *ciṇṇamuloḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.93) must indeed be maintained. For instance, take the root *heḍṛ* ("to disregard"), which belongs to the *ghaṭādi* group. By the rule *mitāṃ hrasvaḥ*, the penultimate vowel becomes short, resulting in *hiḍayati*. Here, if the short vowel were optionally applied when the *ciṇ* or *ṇamul* suffixes are added, the forms would be *ahiḍi* or *aheḍi*.

In the case of the long vowel, however, the forms *ahiḍi* and *ahīḍi* occur. Thus, since the optionality of lengthening for the root *kam* would also apply in the *ciṇ* and *namul* suffixes, the prohibition of the *mit*-designation—which serves its purpose by excluding that [lengthening]—is not capable of indicating [the occurrence of] *vṛddhi*. Furthermore, regarding the rule "āyādaya ārdhadhātuke vā" (Pāṇini 3.1.31), when the *ṇiṅ* is absent and the *ṇic* is applied, *vṛddhi* occurs; yet, the prohibition of the *mit*-designation is intended to prevent the shortening prescribed by "mitāṃ hrasvaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.92). Therefore, in no way does this [prohibition] indicate *vṛddhi*.

If it is argued that, therefore, some means must be stated to prevent the prohibition [of *guṇa*] by the rule *ṅkiti ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.5), this is true; however, that very means has already been stated: [the application of the suffix *ka* occurs] from the section on *taddhita* and *kāmya* beginning with *ik* (Pāṇini 3.1.31).

*Āyādaya ārdhadhātuke vā* (Pāṇini 3.1.31). When there is the intention to express an *ārddhadhātuka* affix, the suffixes beginning with *āya* may optionally occur. For example: *jugopa*, *gopāyāñcakāra*; *ānarta*, *ṛtīyāñcakre*; *kāmayāñcakre*, *cakame*. Here, if the term *ārddhadhātuke* were a locative of posteriority (*parasaptamī*), the meaning would be that once the suffixes beginning with *āya* have commenced, they are optionally withdrawn when an *ārddhadhātuka* follows. In that case, there would be many faults.

For instance: when the feminine gender is intended for a word ending in the suffix *āya*, if the suffix *a* were applied according to Pāṇini 3.3.102 (*apratyayāt*), then in the case where the suffix *āya* is dropped, the undesired form *gopā* would result, and the desired form *guptiḥ* would not be established. Similarly, from the word *ṛtīya*, when the *liṭ* suffix is applied, because it ends in a suffix, the *īya* suffix would be dropped; consequently, one would obtain *ṛtāñcakāra* instead of *ānarta*. Likewise, in forms such as *artitāsi*, *artiṣyati*, *ṛtyāt*, and *ārtīt*, the parasmaipada (active voice) endings would not occur.

Likewise, since the substitution of *īyaṅ* for the root *tās* (the desiderative suffix) would serve as a cause for the application of the rule *na dhātulopa ārdhadhātuke* (Pāṇini 1.1.4)—which prohibits [guṇa and vṛddhi] when an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix follows—the *guṇa* conditioned by that [substitution] would not occur. Now, if it were argued: "By this [rule], the non-application is not made optional; rather, only its application is prescribed," even then, does this [new rule] form a single syntactic unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the rules prescribing *āy* and so forth, or is it a separate syntactic unit (*bhinnavākyatā*)? In the first case, the meaning would be: "When an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix follows, *āy* is optionally substituted [for the final vowel of the root]. The same would apply to the subsequent cases as well. Consequently, *āy* and the other substitutions would occur only optionally before an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix, but they would never occur before a *sārvadhātuka* suffix.

Now, it might be argued: since the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*) is evident—given that one could have simply stated *ārdhadhātuke vā* within the rule for *gup* and others, rather than having to formulate *āyādaya*—the fact that the author has instead tolerated this complexity and composed a separate rule, *āyādaya ārdhadhātuke vā*, indicates through its power that there is a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) based on a distinction of function. Consequently, the meaning is as follows: the general rule (*utsarga*) is that *āy* and the other suffixes are obligatory after roots such as *gup*; however, when an *ārdhadhātuka* affix follows, they are optional.

And thus, like a suffix with an indicatory letter (*vikaraṇa*), the *āya* and other affixes would apply when a suffix follows. Consequently, from the root *gup* with the suffix *ktin*, if the *āya* alternative were applied, after the elision of *a* and the elision of *ya*, the undesirable form *gopātiḥ* would result, and the desired form *gopāyā* would not be established. Therefore, the interpretation of the locative case [in Pāṇini 3.1.32] as "when a suffix follows" is indeed faulty here. **Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.32:** *sanādyantā dhātavaḥ* ("Those ending in *san* and so on are verbal roots"). Verbal roots ending in *san* and the rest, up to those ending in *ṇiṅ*, as well as the final members (*anta*) of such groups—namely, those composite forms whose last constituent is one of these suffixes—should receive the designation of "verbal root. Examples: *jugupsate* ("he feels aversion"), *kāmayate* ("he desires").

Regarding the rule *suptiṅantaṃ* (Pāṇini 1.4.14), the inclusion of the term *anta-* ("ending in") is for the purpose of reviving the principle that "when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned in a rule prescribing a technical name (*saṃjñā*), the paribhāṣā 'the mention of a suffix [includes only the suffix itself]' does not apply. It is not an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*), because that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) and would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that a whole aggregate such as "Devadatta" in the phrase "Devadatta wishes to act" (*devadattaś cikīrṣati*) would be designated as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). In the case of a revival (*pratiprasava*), however, there is both brevity (*lāghava*) and the absence of the aforementioned defect; this is quite clear.

The rule *sanādyantāśca* was not formulated immediately after *bhūvādayaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.1), because the exact extent of the suffixes beginning with *san* is not known. If one asks why the rule was not instead formulated as *saṅantāśca*, relying on the *ṅ* of *ṇiṅ* to form a pratyāhāra, [the answer is] that this would lead to ambiguity, since the letter *ṅ* also occurs in *caṅ* and other such suffixes. It would have been more appropriate to formulate the rule as *bhūvādayaśca* immediately after *sanādyantāḥ*; however, it was not done in that way.

This sūtra has been rejected in the Bhāṣya. For instance, in the case of a compound where the original meaning is abandoned (jahatsvārthā vṛtti), it is the complexes such as *cikīrṣa* and *jihīrṣa* that possess meaning, while their constituent parts are meaningless; furthermore, in the rule "all [elements] are substitutes for all words," the relationship between the substituendum (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) is restricted to those elements that possess meaning. It has been stated that in rules such as "eruḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.91), the form *testuḥ* is what results.

In this way, here too, when there is the occasion for the root *iṣ* [meaning "to desire"] as qualified by the act of making (*karaṇa*), the word *cikīrṣa-* [arises]; similarly, when there is the occasion for the root *iṣ* functioning with the meaning of taking (*haraṇa*) as qualified [by the object], the word *jihīrṣa-* [arises]; when there is the occasion for the root *gup*, the word *gopāya-* [arises]; and when there is the occasion for the root *iṣ* functioning with a desire qualified by a son, the word *putrīya-* [arises]. In such cases, the status of being a verbal root (*dhātutva*) is established through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute behaves like the original), just as in the case of *jagdhi-* and others, or as the property of being a suffix (*tiṅtva*) exists in *pacatu*.

It might be argued: "In the *sthānivadbhāva* rule, forms such as *cikīrṣā* cannot be included by the word *ādeśa*, because the term *ādeśa* is conventionally restricted to those substitutes that replace an original element (*sthānin*) specified by a genitive case ending. This is not so. Since the status of being a substitute is already obtained by the very mention of *sthānivat*, the inclusion of forms like *cikīrṣā* is easily achieved by taking the etymological meaning—"that which is directed toward" (*ādiśyate*)—based on the force of the explicit mention of the term [in the rule], just as in the case of *testuḥ* and others which are inferred. Thus, they are readily grasped.

Nor should it be said that the substitution [of *putrīya-*] and so forth applies only to a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) and not to the root *iṣ* itself; for, since the status of being a verbal root (*dhātutva*) is established as necessary by such indicative marks as "even a slight distinction" (Pāṇini 1.3.90), it is determined—so as to account for that—that the substituends are precisely those which convey the action, such as "desire" (*icchā*), "conduct" (*ācāra*), and "becoming" (*bhū*). This is the general direction. (Pāṇini 3.1.33)

*syatāsī lṛluṭoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.33). The term *lṛ* is a general designation for both *lṛṅ* and *lṛṭ*. When *lṛ* (referring to *lṛṅ*) or *luṭ* follows a verbal root (*dhātu*), the suffixes *syat* and *tāsī* are applied respectively. Examples: *akariṣyat* (he would have done), *kariṣyati* (he will do), and *śvaḥ kartā* (he is to do tomorrow). Jayāditya maintains that the vowel *i* in *tāsī* is marked with the technical designation *it*.

To illustrate: in the case of *mantāhantā*, when we have *man tās ā* and *han tās ā*, after the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant), the stem (*aṅga*) ending in *-tā* becomes subject to the *ḍāp* suffix. Consequently, the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*), which is the letter *a*, would be subject to elision by the rule *aniditām* (Pāṇini 6.4.24). To prevent this, one must maintain that the root *tās* is marked with an indicatory *it*. Nor should it be argued that because the elision of the *ṭi* is considered "as if not having taken effect" (*asiddha*) due to its being an *ābhīya* operation, the letter *n* is not the penultimate vowel; for the rule *ābhāt* (Pāṇini 6.4.22) has been rejected in the *Mahābhāṣya*.

Even according to the view of the Sūtra, the *asiddha* status [of the augment *āṬ*] is non-eternal (*anitya*). In this regard, the inclusion of the long vowel marker *ta* (i.e., *tapara*) in the rule "the elision of *a* in the case of *śn* and *as*" (Pāṇini 6.4.111) is the indicative mark (*liṅga*). For that [marker] is intended so that [the elision] does not occur in forms such as *āstām* and *āsan*. Since the elision would not even arise there due to the *asiddha* status of *āṬ*, the *tapara* marker, being otherwise redundant, indicates the non-eternality of the *asiddha* status.

Therefore, in the forms *debdhatuḥ* and *debdhuḥ*, because the *liṭ* [affix] is marked with *kittva* after the roots *śranthi*, *granthi*, *dambhi*, and *svañji*, there is elision of the *na* [augment]; and since that [elision] is not considered *asiddha*, the substitution of *etva* and the elision of the reduplication (*abhyāsalopa*) take place. Likewise here as well, in the absence of the *asiddha* status of the *ṭilopa*, the elision of *na* which would otherwise have occurred is prevented by the fact that [the suffix] is marked with *it*.

Nor should it be argued that, since the mention of the term *dhātu* (root) in the rule for the insertion of *num* serves its purpose by excluding the *tās-* affixes, the intended meaning—that *num* occurs only during the stage of the root's formal instruction (*upadeśa*)—would not be established; for one must rely on the very statement: "In the rule for *num*, the mention of 'as if in the state of formal instruction' (*upadeśivad-vacanam*) is for the sake of establishing the suffix," or else on the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) found in the citation of the root with *num* and *k* in the rule "dhinvikṛṇvyoḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.80).

Vāmana, however, with the intention that "the letter *i* in *tāsi* is for the sake of pronunciation," considers that the mention of "root" (*dhātu*) in the rule *idito num dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.58) is for the purpose that the augment *num* should occur only during the stage when the word is still designated as a root (*dhātupadeśāvasthā*). According to his view, it should be understood that in forms such as *mantā* and *hantā*, the elision of *na* (*nalopa*) does not take place because the elision of *ṭi* (*ṭilopa*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*).

This is now considered: do the *vikaraṇas* such as *sya*, which are prescribed by taking the letter *l* as their cause, occur while the verbal root is still in the state of *l* (*la-avasthā*), or rather after the substitutes for *l* (*lādeśa*) have been applied? In the first view, once the state of *l* has reached the suffix *tās* and its acute accent on the beginning of the affix (*pratyayādyudātta*) has been applied, the substitutes for *l* would occur; consequently, their accent would be "later-prescribed" (*satiśiṣṭa*). And thus, the rule prescribing the unaccented nature (*anudātta*) of the *lasārvadhātuka* following *tās* would be merely a rule for what was not otherwise obtained (*aprāptavidhi*).

And this being the case, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the *Ṣaṣṭha-adhyāya*—namely, that "even a suffix accent (*vikaraṇasvara*) that remains by virtue of being subsequently prescribed does not subvert the accent of the *lasārvadhātuka*"—would be violated. Consequently, in the example "yā dampatī samanasā sunute," since the suffix accent would be stronger as the one remaining by subsequent prescription, the finite verb (*tiṅanta*) would have its middle syllable acute (*madhyodātta*). However, an acute on the final syllable (*antodātta*) is desired. A similar clear defect would arise in examples such as "prīṇītāśvān" and "hinvanti sūram."

In the second view, however, since the accent of *tās* (the affix *tāsi*) is *satiśiṣṭa* (remaining after others have been applied), the fact that the *lasārvadhātuka* affixes are unaccented is already established by the rule of *śeṣanighāta*; thus, the explicit mention of *tāsi* in the rule serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). Nevertheless, forms such as *gamiṣyati* and *paṭhiṣyati* would not be established. For instance, *sārvadhātuke yak* (Pāṇini 3.1.67) is a general rule (*utsarga*), while *śa* and the like, as well as *syat* and the like, are its exceptions (*apavāda*). Among these, the scope of *śa* and the like is exemplified by *gacchati* and *paṭhati*, whereas the scope of *syat* and the like is exemplified by *gaṃsyate* and *paṭhiṣyate*.
In the cases of "gamiṣyati" and "paṭhiṣyati," where both [suffixes] would apply, the suffix *śap* prevails due to its higher position in the order of rules.

Now, it might be argued that there is no relationship of general rule (*utsarga*) and exception (*apavāda*) between *yaK* and *śaP* and so forth, because they have distinct domains of application. For in the rule prescribing *yaK*, the mention of "bhāva" (intransitive action) and "karman" (object) is understood as a carry-over (*anuvartate*). And that must necessarily be carried over so that *yaK* does not occur after roots such as *pac* or *paṭh* when *śaP* follows—as in *pacati* or *paṭhati*. Even so, forms such as *gamiṣyati* and *paṭhiṣyati* might indeed be established, since *yaK* and *śaP*, as general rules, can be superseded by *syati* and other suffixes which act as exceptions. However, forms such as *deviṣyati* and *seviṣyati* would simply not be established at all.

For instance, regarding the affixes (vikaraṇas), there is the general rule for *yak* and *śap*, while *śyan* and so forth, as well as *syādi* and so forth, are their exceptions. The scope of *śyan* and the others is seen in forms such as *dīvyati* and *sīvyati*; whereas the scope of *syādi* and the others is seen in *pakṣyate*. However, in cases where both would apply, such as *deviṣyati* and *seviṣyati*, the *śyan* and other affixes would occur by virtue of their higher priority (*paratva*).

This has been explained in various ways in the Bhāṣya. For instance, the substitutes for *śap*, such as *śyan* and so forth, will be prescribed; this is because the ablative case in the rule "divādibhyaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.69), which is carried over [from the previous sūtra], is interpreted as a genitive case referring to the agent (*kartṛ*), following the principle that a nominative case (*śap*) is understood. And thus, in the domain of *syat* and other [suffixes], there is no *śap* at all after roots beginning with *div*, because it is superseded by the exceptions (*apavāda*) consisting of *syat* and the others. Consequently, its substitutes, such as *sya* and so forth, are certainly ruled out from the start.

Alternatively, in rules such as *divādibhyaḥ śyan* (Pāṇini 3.1.69), the suffixes beginning with *sy-* will be understood by way of *anuvṛtti*. That is to say: after roots of the *div*-class, *śyan* occurs; however, for the *lṛt* and *luṭ* [suffixes], *syatāsī* occur. [The rule] "after *div*-class roots" applies in the same way hereafter. If this is so, why should the suffixes beginning with *sy-*—which would apply precisely at the stage of the *la* [marker]—wait for the arising of the *sārvadhātuka* designation?

Consequently, the objection—asking how the statement that the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes are *anudātta* (unaccented) in the rule for *tās-* can serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the aforementioned meaning—is refuted; for in rules such as "sārvadhātuke yak" (Pāṇini 3.1.67), the occurrence of a *sārvadhātuka* suffix must be awaited precisely by virtue of its recurrence (*anuvṛtti*). Alternatively, let the *śyan* and other affixes not be substitutes for *śap*, and let them not recur in subsequent rules; however, in forms such as *deviṣyati*, the *lādeśas* (affixes beginning with *la*) would indeed apply first, overriding the *syādi* affixes due to their higher status (*paratva*).

It should not be argued that these [substitutions] are not permanent because, up until the end of the third chapter, the domain is that of verbal roots (*dhātu*), and thus, due to the intervention of *sy*-suffixes, the *l* suffix following a root would not exist, resulting in the non-application of the substitutes. This is because the substitutes for *l* are indeed permanent, by relying on the qualification of the rule "of *l* prescribed after a root" (*dhātorvihitasya lasya*) as referring specifically to what has been prescribed. And so, once the *l*-substitutes have been applied, both sets—those beginning with *sy-* and those beginning with *śyan*—would be applicable.

In that case, by virtue of being *antaraṅga* (internal), only the *sy*-suffixes will occur, and not the *śyan*-suffixes; for the latter are *bahiraṅga* (external) as they depend upon the status of being a *sārvadhātuka* suffix and the specific meaning of the agent (*kartṛ*).

(Pāṇini 3.1.34) *sibbahulaṃ leṭi* (Pāṇini 3.1.34). The suffix *sip* is optionally applied to a verbal root when *leṭ* follows. [Example: *joṣiṣat*. [Root: *juṣī* in the sense of "pleasure" and "service" (Dhātupāṭha 8). It is *anudātta*-accented. The Parasmaipada ending occurs by irregular substitution (*vyatyaya*). [The suffix] *sip* [is added], followed by *iṭ*. By *leṭo'ḍāṭau* (Pāṇini 3.4.94), *aṭ* is added in place of *tip*. By *itaśca lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.97), the *ikāra* is elided. Because of the mention of "optionally" (*bahulagrahaṇa*), it does not occur here: *patāti didyut*.

In Vedic (chandas), the *ṇit* designation should be stated as being frequent (*bahu-lam*). [Examples are: *pra ṇa āyūṃṣi tāriṣat* and *ayāṃivāṃ savitā sāviṣat*; because of the *ṇit* designation, there is vṛddhi [of the root vowel]. In *devasya heḍo 'vayāsisīṣṭhāḥ*, here [the suffix] *liṅ* follows the root *yā* preceded by *ava*. Due to the statement "frequently" (*bahu-lavacanāt*), there is *sip*, *thās*, *sīyuṭ*, and *suṭ*, along with *iṭ*. The prohibition [of *iṭ*] by Pāṇini 7.2.10, "after a monosyllabic root that is anudātta in its original form (*upadeśe*)," does not apply here, because of the intervention of *sip*. The absence of *ṣatva* for the *s* of *sīyuṭ* is a Vedic peculiarity (*chāndasaḥ*).

The *nighāta* (elision of accent) applies by the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ* (Pāṇini 8.1.28). However, when used in conjunction with the word *yat*, the form *yāsisīṣṭhāḥ* is intended to have its first syllable accented (*ādyudātta*). Although the word would otherwise result in being *antodātta* (accented on the final syllable) because the suffix *thās* is inherently acute according to the accent of the affix (*pratyayasvara*), nevertheless, as stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "Even by breaking the rule, one should perform the *sapi*-operation after discarding *sip*," once *sap* is applied, [the suffix] is followed by what is taught with *a* (*adupadeśa*), and by virtue of being a *sārvadhātuka* due to the rule *chandasyubhayathā* (Pāṇini 3.4.117).

The desired result is achieved through the fact that the *sārvadhātuka* affixes are *anudātta* (unaccented). If the *sap* [the suffix *śap*] were not *pit*, then by the rule regarding the "cessation of the acute accent" (*udāttanivṛttisvara*), the *iṭ* augment would become acute. Therefore, it is established here that the *sap* is marked as *pit* for the sake of the final accent. However, according to the literal wording of the sūtra, the *pit* designation is indeed redundant. Accordingly, the Vārttika states: "The purpose of making it *kit* is useless because it lacks a vowel (*anackatvāt*). If it is argued that it is for the sake of making the *iṭ* unaccented, [we reply] that this is already established by the rule that augments are *anudātta*. (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.35).

"Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.35: *kāspratyayādāmamantre liṭi* (after the root *kāsa-* and after [roots] ending in affixes, the augment *ām* is added before the *liṭ* [perfect tense] suffix, but not in a mantra). The root *kāsṛ* (meaning 'to sound contemptuously') belongs to the *bhvādi* class (624). Examples: *kāsāñcakre*, *lolūpāñcakre*. Why say "not in a mantra"? Consider: *kṛṣṇo nonāva* ("Kṛṣṇa bellowed repeatedly"). Why was it not stated as "*acchandasī*" (except in Vedic verse)? Because it is desired even in the Brāhmaṇas, as seen in examples such as: *putramāmantrayāmāsa* ("He addressed his son") and *atha ha śunaḥ śeṣa īkṣāñcakre* ("Then Śunaḥśepa looked about") from the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (7.3)."

It should be stated that "having more than one vowel" (*anekāc*) [is the condition] for the purpose of forms such as *culumpāñcakāra* (Kāśikāvṛtti). *Culumpāñcakāra*: this is correct by the force of the statement of the author of the *Tīrthārttika* on *culumpati*. Here, in order to avoid under-extension (*avyāpti*) and over-extension (*ativyāpti*), it has already been explained previously that the mention of the suffix (*pratyaya*) should be removed and, in its place, the mention of "having more than one vowel" (*anekāc*) should be made. Examples: *cakāsāñcakāra*, *daridrāñcakāra*.

Regarding the rule *āta au ṇalaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.1.34), although the vowel *o* should have been prescribed [for the substitution of the suffix *ṇal*], the prescription of *au* is for the purpose of ensuring that *au* is heard even when the vowel *ā* is elided by the rule *daridrāterārdhadhātuke lopaḥ* (Kāśikāvṛtti). Therefore, they say that the form *dādaridrau* also occurs.

The [augment] *ām* does not apply to the root *ūrṇu*, because of the extended application (*atideśa*) of its treatment as being like *nu*. Nor should it be argued that even so, by the subsequent rule "ijādiḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.36), *ām* would necessarily occur regardless of whether the root has more than one vowel; for that rule also does not apply here due to the force of its placement among the results of the treatment as *nu*—as indicated by the statement "and for the purpose of prohibiting *ām*" (*āmaśca pratiṣedhārtham*)—and because the author of the Bhāṣya, adopting the recitation of the sūtras in *saṃhitā* form, states "anṛcchodayāyāsaḥ," thereby prohibiting *ām* after a root ending in *u* through the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the *u* in "anṛcchu-u."

If it is argued that, in this way, after the word *u* with the *kvip* suffix for habitual action, the augment *ām* prescribed by the rule *ijādeḥ* would apply—and that the example previously cited, which is accepted by Mādhava and others, would thus contradict this Bhāṣya—[the answer is: no, because that [example] is possible under the first alternative. Under the second alternative, however, let there be no *ām*, since we accept that a form may remain unapplied according to the specific characteristics of the grammatical system.

Alternatively, by means of a *praśliṣṭanirdeśa* (a compound-like reading) of "uśca uśca," there is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) specifically of that which ends in /u/ and possesses a heavy vowel (*gurumataḥ*). And this [exclusion] is a supplement (*śeṣa*) only to the rule "ijādeḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.36). Consequently, for words such as *valgū* and *phalgū*, which end in *kvip*, the suffix *ām* indeed occurs due to their having more than one syllable (*anekāctva*); thus everything is well-established. Regarding this, the *Kāśikā* states: "Because it ends in /a/, the *ām* of *vid* is not an *it*; likewise, because of the prescription of *ām* for *āsa* and *kāsa*, there is the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*), as in the case of *katanta*."

The meaning of this is as follows: *amittva* (non-shortness) is the absence of being short (*mit*). The letter *m* of *ām* does not receive the technical designation *it* by the rule *halantyam* (Pāṇini 1.3.3). Why? Because it is *at*, that is, because it is situated near the end (*anta*) of the word; in other words, because it possesses the vowel *a* near [the end] at the time of its prescription in the sūtra.

In this context, he states as a corollary: "The absence of *guṇa* [vowel strengthening] for *vid* is likewise [due to its being treated as] ending in *a*. The meaning is that it is precisely because it ends in *a*. For in the rule *uṣavidajāgṛbhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.38), the fact that *vid* ends in *a* is established by way of its association with the suffix *ām*. Therein, because of the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) regarding the elision (*alopa*), *guṇa* does not occur. However, if the vowel *a* were intended in the very root-list (*dhātupāṭha*) entry for *vida jñāne*, then forms such as *vetti* would not be established, due to the undesirable consequence of hearing the vowel *a* [in those forms].

Now, even while accepting that the suffix *ām* ends in *m*, he states the evidence for its not having the designation *mit*: "And because of the prescription of *ām* for the roots *ās* and *kās*. The phrase "the non-*mit*-status of *ām*" is to be supplied. By the two rules "and for *day*, *āya*, and *ās*" (Pāṇini 3.1.37) and "after the root *kās* and a suffix" (Pāṇini 3.1.35), the prescription of *ām* for *ās* and *kās* implies that *ām* does not have the designation *mit*. For if it were *mit*, the *ām* added to *ās* and *kās* would follow the final vowel *ā*; and in that case, by the rule for homogeneous long vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*), it would be redundant. This is the intended meaning.

Indeed, if it were the view that [the suffix] ends in *a*, one would have to state the rule as *āmāmantra* (Pāṇini 2.3.49); therefore, he says: "there is a single substitute for the subsequent form" (*pararūpam*). The sense is that, just as in the rule "in all cases, after words beginning with *lohita* and ending with *kanta*" (Pāṇini 4.1.18), there is a single substitute by virtue of a specific grammatical derivation (*nipātana*), or because the word belongs to the *śakandhv-ādi* group, so too is it here.
(Pāṇini 3.1.36)

Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.36: *ijādeśca gurumato 'nṛcchaḥ*. The suffix *ām* is applied after a root beginning with *i*, provided it is heavy (*gurumat*) and different from the root *ṛcch*, when the suffix *liṭ* follows—but not in a mantra. Examples: *īhāñcakre*, *ūhāñcakre*. Why does the sūtra say "beginning with *i*" (*ijādeḥ*)? Consider *tatakṣa* (from *takṣ*). Why does it say "heavy" (*gurumataḥ*)? Consider *iyeṣitha* (from *iṣ*). If one objects: "But even here, once the *guṇa* substitution has taken place, the root is indeed heavy," we reply: True. However, because the condition of being heavy depends on its immediate proximity to the *liṭ* suffix, the *ām* suffix is not applied here by the technical rule known as *sannipātalakṣaṇo vidhiranimittaṃ tadvighātasya* ("a grammatical operation conditioned by a specific combination of elements does not become the cause for the destruction of that very combination"). Thus, the heaviness [of the root] is lost once the *guṇa* occurs.

Alternatively, the term *liṭi* (in the periphrastic perfect) is a qualifier of what is prescribed [by the rule]. It means: "when that *liṭ* which is prescribed after a root beginning with *ij* and having a heavy vowel (*gurumat*) [is present]. Consequently, the substitution will not occur because of the heaviness [of the stem] caused by the presence of the *liṭ* suffix. Why say *anṛcchaḥ* ("except for *ṛcch*")? Consider *ānarccha*, *ānarcchatuḥ*, *ānarcchuḥ*. The expression *anṛccha* could have been omitted; for by the very indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the prescription of *guṇa* substitution in the *liṭ* by the rule *ṛcchatyṝtām* (Pāṇini 7.4.11), the application of *ām* is precluded.

Nor should it be said that in this context, by the term *ṛcchati*, there is a reference to the root *ṛ* itself by means of the *śitap* (the suffix *tiP* with the marker *ś*); for the root *ṛ* is included [in the rule] by its own form through the long vowel *ṝ* according to Pāṇini 6.1.101 (*ṛcchatyṝtām*). And the plural number [in the sūtra] is the proof for this inclusion. Regarding this, the Ślokavārttika states: "The substitution of *ṇu* for *ūrṇu* must be stated; the established usage of the intensive (*yaṅ*) is the purpose. Furthermore, it is for the sake of prohibiting the augment *ām*, because here [in the sūtra] the term 'monosyllabic' (*ekāc*) is employed."

In this context, there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the state of being a verbal root (*bhāva*) to the intensive suffix *yaṅ*. However, there is no extension of the absence of *ām* or *iṭ*, because those two do not exist [in the base form]. *Iḍ-upagraha* refers to the prohibition of *iṭ*. The word "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) is in the ablative case according to Pāṇini 2.3.25. Furthermore, the result here functions as the cause, just as in the expression "he dwells for the sake of study" (*adhyayanena vasati*). While the term "single-vowel root" (*ekāca*) is understood from the previous rule, the prohibition of *iṭ* applies by Pāṇini 7.2.11 (*śryukaḥ kiti*). For that reason as well, the application of the *ṇu*-suffix-like behavior (*ṇuvadbhāva*) must be stated; such is the meaning. Examples: *proṇonūyate*, *proṇunāva*, *proṇutaḥ*, *proṇutavān*. (Pāṇini 3.1.37)

Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.37: *dayāyāsaśca*. After these roots, the suffix *ām* occurs before the *liṭ* (perfect tense). The roots are: *daya* (in the sense of giving, going, and protecting; *bhvādi*, *ātmanepada*, no. 482), *aya* (in the sense of going; *bhvādi*, *ātmanepada*, no. 475), and *ās* (in the sense of sitting; *adādi*, *parasmaipada*, no. 11). All three are *anudātta*-accented. Examples: *dayāñcakre*, *palāyāñcakre* (where the substitution of *l* for *y* occurs by Pāṇini Sūtra 8.2.19: *upasargasyāyatau*). *āsāñcakre*. Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.38.

*Uṣavidajāgṛbhyo 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 3.1.38). After these roots, *ām* may optionally be used before the *liṭ* suffix. *Uṣ* (in the sense of burning, *bhvādi* 698); *vid* (in the sense of knowing, *adādi* 54). The inclusion here is not of the two *ātmanepada* roots meaning "to exist" and "to deliberate," nor of the *ubhayapada* root meaning "to obtain," because of the association with the two *parasmaipada* roots *uṣ* and *jāgṛ*. Examples: *oṣāñcakāra*, *uvoṣa*; *vidāñcakāra*, *viveda*—here, due to the irregularity (*nipātana*) of having a final *a* when *ām* follows, there is no *guṇa* substitution; *jāgarāñcakāra*, *jajāgāra*. (Pāṇini 3.1.39)

*Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.39*: *bhī-hī-bhṛ-huvāṃ śluvac ca*. After these roots (*bhī*, *hī*, *bhṛ*, *hu*), when the *liṭ* suffix follows, there is optionally the *ām* affix; and for these [roots], the grammatical operation is as if there were *ślu*. What, then, is that [operation]? It is reduplication and the substitution of *i* for the root vowel. Thus: *bibhayāñcakāra*, *bibhāya*; *jirhayāñcakāra*, *jihrāya*; *vibharāñcakāra*, *babhāra*; *juhavāñcakāra*, *juhāva*. Here, reduplication occurs for all of them, but the substitution of *i* occurs only for *bhṛ*, because it is prescribed by the rule *bhṛñām it* (Pāṇini 7.4.76) specifically when *ślu* follows. (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.40)

Pāṇini 3.1.40 states: *kṛñ cānuprayujyate liṭi* ("And *kṛñ* is employed after [the verb] in the *liṭ* [perfect]"). After the suffix *ām*, the root *kṛñ* is employed when the *liṭ* follows. The term *kṛñ* here is a pratyāhāra (abbreviated designation) formed by the letter *ñ* from the rule *kṛño dvitīya-* (5.4.58), which itself refers back to the rule *kṛbhvasti-* (5.4.50). By this, the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* are to be understood.

And the proof for this is the inclusion of the term *kṛ* in the rule *āmpratyayavatkṛño 'nuprayogasya* (Pāṇini 3.1.40). Due to the force of the term *anuprayoga*, there is no substitution of *bhū* for *as*. Otherwise, he would have simply said, "*kṛ* is employed after [the root]". Examples are: *yācayāṃcakāra*, *yācayāmbabhūva*, and *yācayāmāsa*. Here, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings occur for the *as* that is employed as an auxiliary (*anuprayukta*) when the sense is that of a state (*bhāva*) or an object (*karman*). Regarding that, they disagree concerning the forms when *eś* and *iṭ* are applied.

For instance: in both cases, when the substitution of *ha* is applied by Pāṇini’s rule 7.4.52 (*ha eti*), some say the form is *īkṣāmāhe*. Others say that because of its association with *tasi*, the substitution of *ha* occurs only before the augment *iṭ*. Still others maintain that due to that very association, the substitution of *ha* occurs only before a sārvadhātuka suffix; thus, they claim the form in both instances is *īkṣāmāse*. One might object: this form ending in *ām* has an unmanifested meaning, for neither a specific grammatical relation (*kāraka*) nor a specific number is understood from it. Since the required specific meaning can be obtained through logical application (*nyāya*) itself, what is the purpose of this rule?

To this it is replied: When there is a desire to express the mere action (*kriyā*) alone, while the grammatical factor (*kāraka*) and its number (*saṅkhyā*) are not intended to be expressed, such usages as *pākapreraṇā jātā* ("the instigation of cooking has arisen") are indeed accepted by all. In that context, since the mere form *pācayāmi* would naturally result [as the sole expression], this [rule] is intended to prevent that. Furthermore, just as in the case of the roots *asti* and *bhavati*, the use of *vidyati* would also naturally result; this [rule] is intended to prevent that as well.

Furthermore, this sūtra is intended for the purpose of employing a verb in its primitive sense (*prākṛtārtha*) as a general term (*sāmānyavācaka*) following a verbal root from which the causal suffix (*ṇic*) has been removed (*nivṛttapreṣaṇāt*). Moreover, it ensures that the usage occurs only after [the causative action] and not before; thus, forms such as *cakre* and *īkṣām* do not occur. Furthermore, immediate succession is the primary sense of "after"; thus, this rule also serves to exclude cases where there is an intervention. Consequently, forms such as *īkṣāṃ rājā cakre* do not occur.

How then is it that the *Bahvṛcabrāhmaṇa* states: "The king indeed made them intoxicated" (*tān ha rājā madayāmeva cakāra*)? Understand that this is due to Vedic usage (*chāndasatvāt*). How then do we find in the *Bhaṭṭikāvya*: "They made the paths of the city muddy" (*ukṣāmpracakrurnagarasya mārgān*) and "He caused fear" (*bibhayāmpracakārāsau*)? And how in the *Raghukāvya*: "He first caused him to fall, and he fell afterwards" (*taṃ pātayāṃ prathamamāsa papāta paścāt*) and "He who caused Nahuṣa to fall" (*prabhraṃśayāṃ yo nahuṣañcakāra*)? They say that these are merely errors, because they contradict the *Vārttika* rule which states: "[The suffix *ām* is used] for the purpose of preventing the inversion [of sequence] and for the purpose of preventing the intervention [of other words]."

In this context, because the root *kṛ* (and by extension *bhū* and *as*) denote both general and specific meanings, it should be understood that there is a relation of non-difference (*abhedānvaya*) between their respective referents. For this very reason, although *sampad* is included within the pratyāhāra [formed by *san* and *kṛt*], its subsequent employment (*anuprayoga*) does not occur, because its meaning would not be connected [with the primary verb]. As for the argument that, due to the governing rule of "root" (*dhātu*) from Pāṇini’s sūtra 3.1.32 (*sanādyantā dhātavaḥ*), there can be no subsequent employment of the entire complex consisting of a root and a prefix—this is incorrect; for even so, the root *pad* itself, which is the element here, must be excluded precisely by the method already stated.

And thus, because the general [meaning] culminates in a particular when a particular is present, the expression of particulars such as the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) inherent in that [general meaning] results in nothing other than the expression of particulars inherent in the *āma*-ending. For this very reason, since the two verbs *bhū* and *as* used in subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) become transitive by virtue of the *āma*-ending, the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) is formed with them in the sense of the object (*karman*). Accordingly, Māgha says: "He bore his umbrella" (*tasyātapatraṃ bibharāṃbabhūve*). And Śrīharṣa says: "Even at the height of summer, the nights did not bear the weight of darkness. (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.41)

*vidāṅkurvantu ity anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 3.1.41). When *loṭ* follows the root *vid*, the following is optionally prescribed as a nipātana: the absence of guṇa, the elision (*luk*) of the *loṭ* suffix, and the subsequent employment (*anuprayoga*) of the root *kṛñ*. The word *iti* serves to indicate all the various forms of the *loṭ* suffixes. The use of the third person plural in the rule is merely for the sake of common usage. [Examples: *vidāṅkarotu*, *vidāṅkurutām*, *vidāṅkurvantu*. (Pāṇini 3.1.42)

"abhyutsādayām, prajanayām, cikayām, ramayāmakaḥ, pāvayām, kriyāt, vidāma, akran"—these are irregularly formed (nipātita) in the Veda (chandas). The suffix *ām* is applied in the *luṅ* (aorist) after the causatives (*ṇyanta*) of the roots *sad*, *jan*, and *ram*. After the simple root *ci* as well, *ām* is applied in the *luṅ*, followed by reduplication and the change of *c* to *k* (*kutva*). The auxiliary verb *akṛ* is employed with each of these four forms. Furthermore, after the causative of *pav* or *pū*, the suffix *ām* is applied in the *āśīr-liṅ* (precative), and the auxiliary verb *kriyāt* is employed.

In the *luṅ* tense, there is an absence of *guṇa*, and the suffix *an* is employed after the root *kṛ*. In the form *akaḥ*, this is the *tip* ending of *kṛñ* in the *luṅ* tense. By the rule *mantre ghasa* (Pāṇini 2.4.81), there is elision (*luk*) of the *cli* suffix, and by *halṅyādi* (Pāṇini 6.1.68), there is elision of the *tip* ending. The form *akran* is the plural of that same [root] in that very tense. *Abhyutsādayāmakaḥ* and *abhyudasīṣadat* occur in the alternative [form] and in the common language (*bhāṣā*). *Prajanayāmakaḥ*, *prājījanat*; *cikayāmakaḥ*, *acaaiṣīt*; *rāmayāmakaḥ*, *arīramat*; *pāvayāṃkriyāt*, *pāvyāt*; *vidāmakran*, *avediṣuḥ*.
Thus ends the third Āhnika of the first Pāda of the third Adhyāya in the illustrious Śabdakaustubha.
The Fourth Daily Lesson of the First Quarter of the Third Chapter.

(Pāṇini 3.1.43): *cli luṅi*. The suffix *cli* shall be applied to a verbal root (*dhātu*) when the suffix *luṅ* follows. The letter *i* in *cli* is for the purpose of general reference (*sāmānyagrahaṇa*). The letter *c* is for the sake of the accent (*svarārtha*), as will become clear in the subsequent rule. Its substitutes, such as *sij* and others, will be stated hereafter. Now, one might ask: "If this is so, what is the purpose of the suffix *cli*? Let the suffix *sij* itself be the general rule (*utsarga*), and let *ksa* and the others be its exceptions (*apavāda*)."

And it is not the case that, in the rule *mantra ghasa* (Pāṇini 2.4.81), since the single term *liṭ* could suffice for all verbal roots (*dhātu*), the term *cli* should have been employed for the sake of brevity. For otherwise, the mention of *aṅ* would be for the sake of the roots *ghas*, *naś*, and *gam*; the mention of *caṅ* would be for the sake of those ending in long *ā*, because *dheṭ* is included among them, as there is *caṅ* for it by the rule *vibhāṣā dheṭśvyoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.49); and the mention of *sic* would be for the sake of other verbal roots.

If, however, the elision (*luk*) of the *ciṇ* suffix prescribed by Pāṇini 3.1.61 (*dīpajana...*) is observed in Vedic usage for the root *jan*, then one must argue that three or four mentions of the term would have to be made [in the rule]; for even in the case of accepting *cli*, the mention of three—namely *cli*, *cli*, and *li*—is equal when the rules "cli luṅi," "cleḥ sic," and "mantre ghasa" (Pāṇini 3.1.43, 44; 2.4.81) are taken together.

Nor should it be argued that even if there is parity according to the aforementioned method, there is another parsimony (*lāghava*) in the *cli* view, because in the rule *gāti-sthā-* (Pāṇini 2.4.77), one could remove the word *sic* and substitute *liḥ* in its place, and then carry that very term forward into the rules for *mantre ghasa-* etc. To say this is to imply either that the elision of *li* (*ler-luk*) is an exception (*apavāda*) to *sic* and other substitutes even before those substitutes have been applied, or else that the status of being a *sthānin* does not apply once the substitutes have been applied.

Not the first [alternative], because in forms such as *aguḥ* and *asthuḥ*, since there is an absence of what follows the suffix *sic*, the rule *sijabhyasta* (Pāṇini 3.4.109) would fail to apply, resulting in the non-occurrence of *jus*. Nor can *jus* be applied by the rule *ātaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.110), because the term *sic* is also understood to carry over (*anuvṛtti*) into that rule.

Now, it might be argued: "In the sūtra *ātaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.110), the mention of *sic* does not carry over; thus, in forms such as *aguḥ*, that [mention] serves for the purpose of a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*) and not for the purpose of a restrictive rule (*niyama*), because there is nothing to be excluded. Nor can *abhūvan* be the thing to be excluded, since in that case there is no possibility of the application of *jus* at all. Furthermore, there is no possibility of the application of *sijabhyasta* (Pāṇini 3.4.109), because the position has now been adopted that the elision (*luk*) occurs precisely in the state of the suffix *la*."

Nor should it be argued that, by the same logic, in the case of *avān* as well, the *jus* substitution would necessarily apply by the rule *ātaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.110); for this objection is refuted by the restrictive rule *laṅaḥ śākaṭāyanasyaiva* (Pāṇini 3.4.111), which allows for the optionality of the substitution. Even so, in forms such as *mā hi gātām* and *mā hi syātām*, the accent prescribed by the rule *ādiḥ sivo 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 6.1.178) would not be established. Therefore, it remains settled that the first position—that the elision occurs in the state of the *l* suffix—is indeed defective.

Not the second [alternative], for if that were the case, then by the rule *vibhāṣā ghrādheṭ* (Pāṇini 2.4.78), there would be elision (*luk*) only of the substitutes for *cli*; consequently, this elision would also apply to the *liṅ* substitute of *dheṭ*. In that situation, when the *caṅ* is optionally applied by the rule *vibhāṣā dheṭśvyoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.49), and the *sic* is applied in the alternative case, its elision (*luk*) or non-elision (*aluk*) results in the desired forms: *adhāt*, *adhātām*, *adhuḥ*; and *adhāsīt*, *adhāsiṣṭām*, *adhāsiṣuḥ*.

In the case of *caṅ* as well, when the *luk*-elision does not apply, the forms *adadhat*, *adadhatām*, and *adadhan* are established. However, in the view that the rule *na lumatā* (Pāṇini 1.1.63) serves as an indicator (*nirddeśa*) for the governing heading (*aṅgādhikāra*), reduplication would occur by virtue of the *pratyayalakṣaṇa* principle; thus, a fourth form, *adadhāt*, would also result in the *luk*-elision alternative.

The rule *na lumatā* (Pāṇini 1.1.63) is not a reference to the governing heading (*adhikāra*) on "stem" (*aṅga*); rather, whether [the element] is a stem or not a stem, when a suffix is elided by *lumat*, everything that would otherwise apply to the preceding element is prohibited. According to this primary view, since the doubling (*dvitva*) does not take effect when the *caṅ* is elided, the form is exactly the same as when the *sic* suffix is elided; thus, although there is no fault in forms such as *adhāt*, nevertheless, in the plural, the undesirable fourth form *adhān* would indeed occur. However, the three desired forms—*adhuḥ*, *adhāsiṣuḥ*, and *adhān*—are intended.

Regarding the form *adadhan*: one should not argue that the suffix *jus* will apply by Pāṇini 3.4.110 (*ātaḥ*) even when there is elision (*luk*) of the *caṅ* suffix, because in that rule the word *sicaḥ* (after the root *sic*) is understood as a governing term (*anuvṛtti*). Otherwise, since its status as a restrictive rule (*niyamārthatā*) would be untenable, *jus* would undesirably apply to *abhūvan* by the principle of "as if the suffix were present" (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), according to Pāṇini 3.4.109 (*sijabhyastavidibhyaśca*). [Objection: But I shall state [in a subsequent rule]: "And [the suffix *jus* applies] after *cli*, after reduplicated forms (*abhyasta*), and after *vidi*. In this way, even when there is elision of *caṅ*, *jus* will apply because it follows immediately after *cli*.

If you argue: "Even in the rule *ātaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.110), by the very continuation of the mention of *liṅ*, the restriction will ensure that *jus* does not occur in forms such as *abhūvan*. Furthermore, in cases like *mā hi gātām*, the accentuation governed by *ādiḥ sicaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.187) is also established. Thus, the view that *luk* occurs after the substitutes have been applied is entirely unassailable," [we reply]: No. For if you were to state the rule as *cli-abhyasta*, then a fault would arise regarding *ksa*, *āṅ*, and *caṅ*; for in *adhukṣan*, *avocan*, and *adadhan*, *jus* would undesirably apply even there.

Therefore, one should simply state *sij-abhyasta* [in Pāṇini 6.1.5]. And in the rule *ātaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.110), the mention of *sic* must be carried over [from the previous rule]. If this were the case, then in the absence of *caṅ* (*caṅ-luki*) in the plural, the form *adhān* would result; thus, the defect remains exactly as it was. Consequently, in the rule *gāti-sthā* (Pāṇini 2.4.77), one should simply state *sicaḥ*. Therefore, even in the alternative view that accepts *cli*, the inclusion of all three—*cli*, *cleraḥ*, and *leraḥ*—is equal. On the contrary, by not employing *cli*, there is great economy of effort (*mahallāghavam*).

If it is argued: "In the rule *mantre ghasa* (Pāṇini 2.4.81), etc., only the term *aṅ* should have been mentioned; however, *sic* is to be understood by being carried over (*anuvartita*) from the rule *gātisthā* (Pāṇini 2.4.77). For the roots *dheṭ* and *jan*, both *caṅ* and *ciṇ* are optional; thus, those examples cited for the elision (*luk*) are already established by the elision of *sic* itself. Nor should it be said that in this way the accent prescribed by *ādiḥ sico 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 6.1.187) would apply, because even if *caṅ* and *ciṇ* were included [in the rule], that optional accent would still be unavoidable. Therefore, the rule *cli luṅi* (Pāṇini 3.1.43) is indeed redundant. [This is the objection.]

Regarding this, they say: if *cli* were non-existent, then in the rule *mantra ghasa* (Pāṇini 2.4.81), for those [roots] from which there is the elision (*luk*) of *sic*, the accentuation prescribed by *ādiḥ sicaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.187) would apply. But when this [substitution of *cli*] exists, because of the elision of *cli* while it is still in the state of *la*—as indicated by the term *leḥ*—there is no *sic*, and thus the accentuation occurs according to the respective rules. Furthermore, if *sic* were elided after roots ending in long *ā*, the substitution of *jus* would result; however, if *cli* is elided, the substitution of *anti* alone occurs.

Furthermore, in the rule *śala igupadhāt* (Pāṇini 3.1.45), the term *cli* must be understood even for the purpose of qualifying *aniṭaḥ*. For if *cli* were absent, the phrase *aniṭaḥ* would qualify the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself; consequently, forms such as *aghukṣat* would not be established. If it is argued that because [the root] is marked with the *udic* indicator, there is an optional *iṭ*, and thus by its occasional absence it is indeed *aniṭ*, then the suffix *ksa* would apply invariably. In that case, forms such as *aguhīt* would not be established.

If, however, "aniṭaḥ" (of that which lacks an *iṭ* augment) is taken as a qualifier of the *cli* suffix, then it is established as desired: when the *cli* is *aniṭ*, there is *ksa*, and when it is *seṭ*, there is *sic*. Therefore, it is settled that the result of the *cli* suffix is the irregular accent (*yatāyatha-svara*) and the final *t* in forms such as *aguhīt*.

In the Bhāṣya, however, the suffix *cli* has been rejected. As for what was said—that by the rule *ādiḥ sicaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.187), the accent would be on the beginning—that is not so; because that [rule] is optional, the desired accent is established without obstruction. Furthermore, since all such options are restricted (*vyavasthita*) in Vedic usage, an undesirable result cannot be imposed. As for the claim that *jus* would occur after roots ending in long *ā*, that too is incorrect, because there is no such example in the Mantras. And on this point, the very rejection by the author of the Bhāṣya is the authoritative proof.

As for the objection that [the form] *aguha* would not be established, that too is incorrect; for roots such as *guh* differ based on the presence or absence of the augment *iṭ* when it is optionally applied. In this regard, Kaiyaṭa has described the intention of the venerable Bhāṣyakāra [Patañjali] as follows: "The suffix *sic* is applied after those [roots] which take *iṭ*, whereas *ksa* is applied after those which do not.
(Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.44)

*cleḥ sic* (Pāṇini 3.1.44). The substitute *sic* shall take the place of *cli*. Regarding the vowel *i*, there are two views: that it is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*), or that it bears the technical designation *it*; both have been explained under the rule *hanaḥ sic* (Pāṇini 1.2.14). The letter *c* is for the sake of accentuation (*svarārtha*). In *mā hi lāvīt*, the fact that the augment *iṭ* is unaccented (*anudātta*)—which would otherwise apply by the rule "augments are unaccented"—is overridden because both the original element (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) are marked with two *ci*t markers. As for the rule concerning the accent of the suffix *kāṃcat*, there are two exceptions: the unaccented nature of augments and the accent produced by a *ci*t marker.

In that regard, the first [point] was made known during the rule for *yāsuṭ* as being within its own scope; however, the *cit*-accent belongs to the sixth [chapter]. There, in the case of a conflict between an exception (*apavāda*) and a prohibition (*vipratiṣedha*), the *cit*-accent alone prevails because it is subsequent; so why [attribute] the *cit* status to *sic*? That is not correct, for the unaccented nature of an augment (*āgama-anudāttatva*) is indeed desired even in the case of primary augments (*prakṛty-āgama*) such as *ānu* and others.

Furthermore, since the acute accent on the *cit* [suffix] applies to words such as *kuṇḍina*, how could these two [the *sicaḥ* and *niṣṭhāyāḥ* rules] be exceptions (*apavāda*) to the accent of the suffix? Moreover, in this case, even the posteriority of the *cit*-accent does not exist, because the rule "as if it were the original" (*sthānivat*) is an extension of the operation (*kāryātideśa*). Therefore, since there is no distinction due to the unaccented nature of the augment (*āgama*), every accent would be sublated; thus, the *cit*-designation for *sic* is intended to prevent that sublation.

Nor can that [substitution] be precluded by the very capacity of the *liṅ* suffix itself, because in the rule *mantre vasaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.81), the mention of *liḥ* as a general term makes that [capacity] purposeful. Otherwise, since this [suffix] is without an indicatory letter (*anubandha*), only it would be grasped, and not *liṭ*. Consequently, in the rule *āmaḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.81), since a *liḥ* without an indicatory letter is impossible, the term *liḥ* would not be carried over [as an anuvṛtti].

Furthermore, because it is subsequent and internal (antaraṅga), when the suffixes *tiP* and so forth are subsequently elided, the form *kārayām* would—by virtue of the rule on the characteristics of suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*)—be considered a finite verb (*tiṅanta*). Consequently, in the example *devadattaḥ kārayāñcakāra*, the suffix *ām* would be unaccented (*nighāta*), while what follows it would remain accented. Therefore, in the rule *āmaḥ*, the term *leḥ* must indeed be carried over (as an *anuvṛtti*). For that purpose, a general reference to the suffix *liṭ* must be stated in the preceding rule; otherwise, the letter *c* in *cleḥ* would be rendered purposeless, as its function is to prevent the obstruction of that general reference. However, in the view where *cli* is rejected, the unaccented nature of the augment is set aside by the fact that *sic* itself possesses the property of being marked with *C*.

It should be stated that *sij* [is applied] after the roots *spṛś*, *mṛś*, *kṛṣ*, *tṛp*, and *dṛp* (from the *Kātantra-vyākaraṇa*). After *spṛś* "to touch" (*tudādigaṇa* 142), *mṛś* "to touch/grasp" (*tudādigaṇa* 145), and *kṛṣ* "to scratch/draw" (*bhvādigaṇa* 1015)—for which the suffix *ksa* would otherwise be prescribed—[the suffix *sij* is applied]. After *tṛp* "to satisfy/delight" and *dṛp* "to rejoice/release"—for which *aṅ* is prescribed because they belong to the *puṣādi* group—the suffix *sij* is also permitted as an alternative. Examples: *asprākṣīt*, *aspārkṣīt*, *aspṛkṣat*; *amrākṣīt*, *amārkṣīt*, *amṛkṣat*; *akrākṣīt*, *akārkṣīt*, *akṛkṣat*.

*atṛpsīt*, *atārpsīt*, *atṛpat*; *adrāpsīt*, *adārpsīt*, *adṛpat*. In the *Prakriyākaumudī*, however, having inserted *sṛp* and *ṇap* into the present *vārttika*, two further forms, *asrāpsīt* and *asārpsīt*, are also cited. That, however, should be disregarded because it is not sanctioned by authoritative tradition (*aprāmāṇikatvāt*). (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.45)

Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.45: *śala igupadhādaniṭaḥ ksaḥ*. The suffix *ksa* is substituted for the *cli* (the augment of the aorist) following a verbal root that ends in *śal*, has a penultimate *iK* vowel (*i*, *u*, or *ṛ*), and is *aniṭ* (lacking the *iṭ* augment). Examples: from *duh* (to milk), *adhukṣat*; from *lih* (to lick), *alikṣat*. Why "ending in *śal*"? Consider *abhaitsīt* (he split); here the root ends in *t*, not *śal*. Why "having a penultimate *iK* vowel"? Consider *abhaitsīt*; here the penultimate vowel is *ai*, which is not an *iK*. Why "having a penultimate *iK* vowel"? Consider *adhākṣīt* (he burnt); here the penultimate vowel is *ā*, which is not an *iK*. Why "being *aniṭ*"? Consider *akoṣīt* (he was angry); this root takes the *iṭ* augment. Regarding the alternative view that rejects the existence of the *cli* suffix, it has already been stated that the term "*aniṭaḥ*" serves as a qualifier for the verbal root itself.

Although the *guṇa* substitution would indeed apply to the root even before the suffix *kso* is added, it nevertheless does not take place due to the force of the qualification *ig-upadhāt* (Pāṇini 1.2.26). Nor should it be argued that even after the *guṇa* has occurred, the suffix *kso* may still apply by resorting to the notion of what was previously so (*bhūtapūrvagatyā*) or by relying on a qualification based on the form as it was prescribed; for this would result in the rule prescribing the *kit* marker being rendered useless. Furthermore, it cannot be claimed that the *kit* marker is intended as a qualification for the rule *ksasyāci* (Pāṇini 7.3.72), since that rule is already established by the reading *sasyāci* alone.

Nor should it be argued that, in this way, there would be the undesirable consequence of the forms *vatsase* and *vatsā* from the roots *vṛt*, *vad*, *ihan*, *kam*, and *kaṣ* [by applying the suffix *sa*]; for even in the rule *lugvā duha-* (Pāṇini 7.3.73), the word *sasya* is understood as being carried over from the previous rule *sasyāci*. Thus, it is easy to maintain that among the roots beginning with *duh*, only those for which [the elision] is possible are included in the preceding rule as well. Therefore, it is established that by the force of the inclusion of the *kit* marker, there is no *guṇa* substitution. (Pāṇini 3.1.46) *śliṣa āliṅgane* (Pāṇini 3.1.46). Here, the rule is divided:

Regarding *āliṅgane* (in the sense of embracing): this substitution of *ks* for the following *cli* of the root *śliṣ*, which is *aniṭ*, occurs only in the sense of embracing (*āliṅgana*), and not in other senses. Thus, while *aṅ* has scope in other senses, it is superseded by *ks* in the case of embracing. For example: *aślikṣat kanyāṃ devadattaḥ* (Devadatta embraced the girl). For here, the root *śliṣ* functions in the sense of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), and not in the sense of embracing (*āliṅgana*), which is synonymous with *upagūhana* or *pariṣvaṅga*. [Objection: But in this case, the suffix *ks* would be unavoidable by the rule *śala igupadhāt* (Pāṇini 3.1.45).

If it is argued: "By the restriction 'only in the sense of embracing' (*āliṅgane eva*), according to the maxim *anantarasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.54), that application of *śliṣ* which would otherwise result is restricted for the purpose of excluding *aṅ*, but nothing prior to that [application] is also restricted"? No, because by the power of the *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule), all applications of *ksa* are restricted. Furthermore, since *aṅ* does not apply in the middle-voice (*ātmanepada*), only *sij* remains as the final outcome. But even so, why is this a restriction on the *ādeśa* (substitute)—that is, "only in the sense of embracing"—and why could it not rather be a restriction on the meaning, namely, "in the sense of embracing, only *ksa* [is applied]"? Consequently, in the sense of embracing, let there simply be no *aṅ*.

If it is argued that in the *ātmanepada*, even in the sense of "not embracing," the suffix *kso* would still be unavoidable by the preceding rule, [the reply is]: True; although both types of restriction (*niyama*) are possible here, only the restriction on the affix (*pratyayaniyama*) is adopted—either because it conforms to the attested usage (*lakṣya*), or because it is primary due to being indicated by the case-ending of the thing to be prescribed (*vidheya*), or because of the explanation given by the author of the Bhāṣya—and thus there is no fault. Regarding the connection with the word *śliṣ*, why is it specified as "not taking the augment *iṭ*" (*aniṭaḥ*)? It is so that only the root *śliṣ* mentioned in "śliṣa āliṅgane" (DhP 1.3.20) may be understood.

Let there be no inclusion of the root *śliṣ* (meaning 'to burn', *bhvādigaṇa*, parasmaipada, 703) which takes the augment *iṭ*. Since that [root] is excluded precisely because it possesses an *anubandha*, the term "not taking *iṭ*" (*aniṭaḥ*) is not strictly necessary; this is the direction [of the argument].

Furthermore, the suffix *ksa*, established by the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) for the root *śliṣ*, according to the maxim of "an exception [applies] before [the general rule]" (*purastādapavāda*), subverts only the *aṅ* suffix, but not the *ciṇ*; thus, in the case of "the girl was embraced by Devadatta" (*samāśleṣi kanyā devadattena*), the form with *ciṇ* alone occurs. (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.47).

*na dṛśaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.47). The suffix *ksa* shall not occur after the root *dṛś*. [Examples: *adarśat*, *adrākṣīt*. In the alternative where *aṅ* applies by the rule *irito vā* (Pāṇini 3.1.47), there is *guṇa* substitution by the rule *ṛdṛśo’ṅi* (Pāṇini 7.4.16). In the alternative where *sic* applies, there is *am* substitution by the rule *sṛjidṛśorjhali* (Pāṇini 6.1.58). (Pāṇini 3.1.48)

*ṇi-śrudru-srubhyaḥ kartari caṅ* (Pāṇini 3.1.48). After these roots, *caṅ* shall be substituted for *cli* when *luṅ* follows that expresses the agent (*kartṛ*). The term *ṇi* is a general designation for both *ṇiṅ* and *ṇic*. Examples: *acīkamata*, *acīkarat*, *aśiśriyat*, *adudruvat*, *asusruvat*. Why "when expressing the agent"? Consider: *akārayiṣātāṃ ghaṭau devadattena* ("the two pots were caused to be made by Devadatta"). The *ṅ* in *caṅ* is for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa*; the *c* is for the purpose of specifying [the substitute] as *caṅ*.

If *aṅ* were prescribed [by the rule *aṅ*], there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) because *aṅ* occurs after roots such as *as* and *vac* (Pāṇini 3.1.52), and *ic* occurs after roots such as *ṣid* and *bhid* (Pāṇini 3.3.104). However, if *ṅ* were applied specifically in rules such as *ṇiśri* (Pāṇini 3.1.48), then it would be possible to omit the status of being a *cit*. The supplementary rule (*kārikā*) states: "An addition for the root *kam*. This is intended for cases where *āniṅ* does not exist, according to the rule "āyādaya ārddhadhātuke vā" (Pāṇini 3.1.31). For example: *acakamata*. Regarding this, the Bhāṣya says:
"They go to the celestial realm (*nāka*), which is desired happiness, by means of well-yoked mares as chariots."
Then those who travel on foot, speaking what they have reflected upon, proceed.

The meaning of this is as follows: Although the two words *acakamata* and *acīkamata* are equally correct (*sādhutva*), because the form *acakamata* requires recourse to specific grammatical rules (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*), there is a greater effort (*kleśādhikya*) in its employment, and thus a greater reward (*phalādhikya*). Therefore, when asked what the form of the root *kam* is in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense, those who say "it is *acakamata*" go to heaven in well-yoked chariots. But those by whom "it is *acīkamata*" was said go as "foot-scratchers" (*patkāṣiṇaḥ*), rubbing their feet [on the ground].
In the expression "foot-scratchers," the word *pāda* is replaced by *pad* according to Pāṇini Sūtra 6.3.54: *himakāṣihatiṣu ca*.

Others, however, explain it thus: those who have said "he desired to act" (*akamiṣṭa*) are themselves referred to by the word *akamiṣṭa* through figurative usage. These people, even though they travel on well-yoked mares and chariots, do not obtain happiness because of their utterance of a corrupt word (*apaśabda*). But those who speak the form *acīkamata*, even if they are foot-scratching mendicants (*patkāṣin*), proceed with happiness. (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.49)

Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.49: *vibhāṣā dheṭśvyoḥ*. After these two roots (*dheṭ* and *śvi*), the substitute *caṅ* may optionally be applied to the suffix *cli*. Thus, we have *adadhat*. In the alternative case where *sic* is used, there is optionally elision (*luk*) by Pāṇini Sūtra 2.4.78: *vibhāṣā ghrādheṭ*. Hence, *adhāt* or *adhāsīt*. For *śvi*, in the alternative case, *aṅ* is applied by Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.78: *jṝstambhu*. By Pāṇini Sūtra 7.4.78: *śvayateraḥ*, the vowel *a* is substituted for the root-final. Since the rule for Vṛddhi is prohibited before *sic*, Guṇa is applied, resulting in *aśvayīt*. The phrase "in the active voice" (*kartari*) applies here as well: *adhiṣātāṃ gāvau vatsena*. This is the dual form in the passive sense (*karmaṇi*). By Pāṇini Sūtra 1.2.27: *sthāghvoricca*, the suffix is marked with *k* and the vowel *i* is substituted [for the final of *dhā*]. Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.50: *na māṅyoge*. [This sūtra prohibits the augment *āṬ* after the prohibitive particle *māṅ*.]

*Gupeśchandasī* (Pāṇini 3.1.50): After the root *gup*, the suffix *caṅ* may optionally replace *cli* in the Vedic language (*chandas*). This rule applies only in cases where the *āya*-pratyaya is absent, because the root is cited in its bare form in the sūtra. *imān no mitrāvaruṇau gṛhānajūgupataṃ yuvam* ("O Mitra and Varuṇa, you two have protected these houses of ours"). [Root: *gup* in the sense of "protection" (*bhvādi-gaṇa*, no. 395); [Tense: *luṅ*; [Person: second person dual, *thas* replaced by *tam*. Regarding the lengthening of the reduplicated syllable, Haradatta states that this is governed by Pāṇini 6.1.7, *tujādīnāṃ dīrgho'bhyāsasya* ("there is lengthening of the reduplicated syllable for roots beginning with *tu* etc."). However, in the *Kalpasūtras*, the short vowel is generally read.

In the alternative view (*pakṣe*), [the forms are] *agauptam* and *agopiṣṭam*. In the absence of *iṭ* due to the marker *ū*, there is *vṛddhi* by Pāṇini 1.1.2 (for the root *gup*). The elision of *sic* occurs by Pāṇini 8.2.26. In the view where *iṭ* is present, there is a prohibition of *vṛddhi* by Pāṇini 7.2.4, and thus *guṇa* applies. In the view involving the *āya* suffix, the form is *agopāyiṣṭam*. Thus, there are four forms in the Vedic language (*chandasi*). In the spoken language (*bhāṣā*), however, there are three forms, excluding the one ending in *caṅ* (the reduplicated aorist). (Pāṇini 3.1.51)

Regarding *nonayati*, *dhvayati*, *elayati*, and *ardayati* (Pāṇini 3.1.51): after these causative forms (*ṇyantebhyaḥ*), the *caṅ* substitute for the *cli* suffix shall not occur in the Vedic language (*chandasi*). Example: *mā tvāyato jarituḥ kāmam ūnayīḥ*. "O [Agni], do not diminish the desire of the singer who seeks you. The meaning is: "Do not make the desire—the longing—of me, the singer or praiser who seeks you (*tvāyataḥ*), deficient (*ūnam*). In the common language (*bhāṣāyām*), it is *mā ūnayaḥ*. The root *ūna* is used in the sense of "diminution" (*parihāṇe*) [Dhātupāṭha 356].

In the *cur* class, the root is considered to end in a long vowel (*adanta*) due to the suffix *ṇic*. When the *caṅ* suffix follows, because the elision (*al-lopa*) of the *ṇi*-caused *kṛt* suffix is treated as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*), the rule "the second syllable beginning with a vowel" (Pāṇini 6.1.2) causes the reduplication of the syllable *naś*. Due to the fact that the root has lost its penultimate vowel (*aglopitva*), the rules regarding the *sanvadbhāva*, the lengthening of the penultimate vowel, and the shortening of the penultimate vowel do not apply. In this regard, the reading *auninat* is generally found in both the *Vṛtti* and the *Padamañjarī*; however, the *ikāra* in the reduplicated syllable there is an error. This point was clarified by us under the rule "when a vowel follows the reduplication" (Pāṇini 1.1.59).

"May Agni, smelling of smoke, not make you *dhvan* (resound). The root *dhvan* meaning 'to sound' belongs to the *curādi* class; it is both *adanta* (ending in *a*) and *nānta* (ending in *n*). In the *bhāṣā* (vernacular/classical usage), however, because it loses its final vowel (*aglopi*), it does not take the *sanvadbhāva* treatment. Thus: *adadhvanat*. But for the *ghaṭādi* group, because it does not lose its final vowel (*anaglopi*), it is *adidhvanat*. In the *bhāṣā*, *ailayīt* and *aililat*. The root *ila* meaning 'impulsion' belongs to the *curādi* class. In the *bhāṣā*, *ārdayīt* and *ārdidat*. The root *arda* meaning 'going' and 'begging' belongs to the *bhvādi* class, while *arda* meaning 'injury' belongs to the *curādi* class as a causative (*hetumaṇṇic*) form.

In this sūtra, the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *chandasi* (in Vedic) is the view accepted by the great treatises such as the *Vṛtti*. Thus says Bhaṭṭi: "Janaka made him grasp that bow with which Pinākin tormented the city of the Daityas.

However, in the *Prakriyākaumudī*, it is stated that both [the terms *chandasi* and *vibhāṣā*] apply even in common usage (*loke*). Its intention is that *chandasi* does not recur, while *vibhāṣā* does. But this is incorrect, because it would render the negative particle (*nañ*) in the sūtra redundant and would contradict all the great treatises; let us leave it at that.

(Pāṇini 3.1.52): *asu*, *vac*, and *khyā* take the suffix *aṅ*. *Asu* means "to throw" (*diopao3*); *vac* means "to speak" (*aopao52*); *brūño* (*aouo34*) is replaced by *vaci*; and *khyā* means "to tell" (*aopao50*), being the substitute for *cakṣiṅ* (*aoāo7*), according to the ancients. In reality, however, *khyāti* applies only to the domain of *sārvadhātuka* affixes; here, however, only the substitute [form] is intended. After these roots, *aṅ* shall be the suffix when *luṅ* follows in the sense of the agent.

Since the substitution of *aṅ* for the root *as* (to throw) is already established by its inclusion in the *puṣādi* group, its mention here again is for the sake of the *ātmanepada* endings. Thus: *paryāsthata*, *paryāsthetām*, *paryāsthanta*. The *ātmanepada* occurs optionally after prepositions due to the rule: "The option [for *ātmanepada*] is stated for the roots *as* and *ūh* following a prefix" (*kāśikāvṛtti*). [The suffix] *aṅ* is applied. For the root *as*, there is the augment *thuk*. However, in the case of the reflexive-passive (*karmakartṛ*) voice, *ciṇ* applies because it is subsequent; otherwise, *aṅ* applies. Thus: *paryāsi*, *paryāsthetām*, *paryāsthanta*. [From the root *vac* (to speak): *avocat*, *avocatām*, *avocan*. [The substitution of] *um* [for the final vowel of *vac*] occurs before the suffix *aṅ* according to Pāṇini 7.4.20.

*akhyat*, *akhyatām*, *akhyan*. Why [is it specified] "in the active voice" (*kartari*) in Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.64, *āto lopaḥ*? So that it does not apply in the passive (*karmaṇi*), but rather only so that the suffixes *ciṇ* and *sic* may occur: *nirāsi*, *nirāsiṣātām* (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.53).

*lipi-sici-vhaśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.53). After these roots, *aṅ* shall be the substitute for *cli*. *lipa* (to smear) [Dhātupāṭha 1.53]: *alipat*. *ṣica* (to sprinkle) [Dhātupāṭha 1.54]: *asicat*. *vheñ* (in the sense of rivalry and sound) [Bhvādigaṇa 1.33]: *avhat*. However, it was not stated as "*asyati-vakti-khyāti-lipi-sici-vha*" because, had it been a single sūtra, there would have been an option (*vikalpa*) even for *asyati* and the others due to their recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) in the subsequent rule. (Pāṇini 3.1.54)

*Ātmanepadeṣv anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 3.1.54). Since the previous rule would have made [the substitution] compulsory, this one makes it optional. *alipata*, *alipta*; *asicata*, *asikta*. When there is no *aṅ* augment, [the substitute] *sic* is used. By *jhalo jhali* (Pāṇini 8.2.26), there is elision of the *s*. Because of the *kit* designation by *liṅsicāv ātmanepadeṣu* (Pāṇini 1.2.11), there is an absence of *guṇa*. *avhata*, *avhāsta*. (Pāṇini 3.1.55)

Pāṇini 3.1.55: *puṣādidyutādyḷditaḥ parasmaipadeṣu*. For roots beginning with *puṣ*, those beginning with *dyut*, and those marked with the indicatory letter *ḷ* (ḷdit), the substitute *aṅ* is applied in place of the suffix *cli* when followed by Parasmaipada endings. The group of roots beginning with *puṣ* (*puṣādi*) consists of *puṣa* (to nourish) and *śuṣa* (to dry)—as seen in Dhatupatha 76 and 77—extending until the end of the first section of the Dhatupatha. As for the occurrence of the term *vṛt* (meaning "ends here") after *ṣṇiha* (to love) in the middle of this list (Dhatupatha 94), that is intended to mark the end of the *radhādi* group.

In this regard, the authority is the statement of the Vārttikakāra regarding the sūtra *asyativakti* (Pāṇini 3.1.52): "The inclusion of the root *as* [in that rule] is for the sake of the ātmanepada, because [the *puṣ* under discussion here] belongs to the *puṣādi* group. Examples are: *apuṣat*, *aśuṣat*. However, the root *puṣ* belonging to the *bhūvādi* class—such as *puṣa* in the sense of nourishing (*puṣṭau*), and *śriṣu*, *śliṣu*, *pruṣu*, *pluṣu* in the sense of burning (*dāhe*) [Bhūvādi 71–75]—is not included here. This is known from the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) consisting in the separate listing of the *dyutādi* roots; for those very roots are recited there [in the *dyutādi* list] immediately after *puṣ*.

Even the root *puṣ* (meaning "to nourish") and *muṣ* (meaning "to steal"), which are listed among the *kryādi* roots (DhP 5.7–8), are not included here. For in that [list], there are only four roots; and if those were intended to be included, they would have been made with the marker *ḷ*.
