As for what Haradatta stated—that [the desired forms] are established by the fact that [the roots] have a circumflex accent (*svarita*) and so forth—that is incorrect, because those [four roots] lack an indicatory letter (*anubandha*), and thus, even though *grah* has a circumflex accent, the meaning of the word "etc. (*ādi*) cannot be obtained. If, however, the word "etc. refers to the suffix *aṅ*, then the meaning of the word "also" (*api*) cannot be obtained. This is the general direction of the argument.

If it is asked, "Why then, in the Siddhānta [the Pāṇinian system] as well, are the roots beginning with *puṣ* and those beginning with *dyut* not listed as having the marker *lṛt*?"—the answer is: No, because listing the letter *lṛ* for each one would result in the fault of excessive complexity (*viparīta-gaurava*). Nor can the letter *lṛ* be indicated by another marker (*anubandha*), for that would lead to the impossibility of accomplishing their respective grammatical operations (*kārya*), since among them there exist roots marked with *ā*, *ī*, *u*, and *ū*. For example, among the *puṣ*-class roots, we have *ñiṣvidā* (in the sense of "oozing from the body") and *madī* (in the sense of "joy").

The roots *śam* (in the sense of pacification) and *ṣidhū* (in the sense of accomplishment) are recited [in the *dhātupāṭha*]. Furthermore, among the *dyutādi* group, *śvitā* (in the sense of color), *ñimidā* (in the sense of moistening), *ñiṣvidām* (in the sense of moistening and releasing), *sraṃsu* and *dhvaṃsu* (in the sense of falling down), *syandū* (in the sense of flowing), and *kṛpū* (in the sense of capability) are recited. [Examples: *adyutat*, *aśvitat*. By the rule *dyudbhyo luṅi* (Pāṇini 1.3.91), the *parasmaipada* (active voice) is optionally applied.

The root *gam* (from the *bhvādi* class) takes the form *agamat*. Why specify "in the parasmaipada endings"? [Consider: *adyotiṣṭa*. In this case, it would have been more appropriate to list "puṣa, dyuta, etc. with only a single term *ādi*, just as in the rule *nandigrahipacādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.134). However, it was not done in that way; such is the fact. (Pāṇini 3.1.56)

Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.56: *sartiśāstyartibhyaśca*. After these roots, *aṅ* shall be substituted for *cli*. Only the root *śās* (meaning "to instruct," Dhātu-pāṭha 65) is intended here, because it occurs in conjunction with *sṛ* and *ṛ*, both of which are parasmaipada roots. The ātmanepada root *āṅ-śās* (meaning "to desire," Dhātu-pāṭha 12) is not included here. Furthermore, regarding *ṛ* and *sṛ*, only the roots belonging to the *juhotyādi* class (Dhātu-pāṭha 16 and 17, meaning "to go") are intended here, due to their association with *śās*, which lacks the *śap* suffix. Therefore, for the roots belonging to the *bhvādi* class, only *sic* is applied.

By means of the word *ca*, the term “*parasmaipadeṣu*” (in the case of parasmaipada endings) is drawn forward [from the previous rule]. However, that [term] is for the sake of what follows and does not connect here, because of the force of the composition being made as a separate rule (*pṛthagyoga*). For otherwise, he would have simply recited: “*puṣādidyutādyḷditsartiśāstyartibhyaḥ*”. In this way, both the separate mention of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) and the particle *ca* would not need to be made. Alternatively, by means of the “frog-leap” (*maṇḍūkapluti*), the mention of *parasmaipada* will be connected only with the subsequent [rule].

Alternatively, it should be explained as: "The root *śās*, which is seen [to take] the *parasmaipada* when attracted here [by the preceding rule]. The commentary of Kaiyaṭa on the sūtra "śāsa idaṅhaloḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.34) should also be understood in this way. *sartum*—he ran. By the rule "ṛdṛśo’ṅi" (Pāṇini 7.4.16), there is guṇa substitution. *aśiṣat*—he commanded. By the rules "śāsa idaṅhaloḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.34) and "śāsivasighasīnāṃ ca" (Pāṇini 8.3.60), there is the substitution of *ṣ*. *ārat*—they moved. "samanyavo yatsamaranta senāḥ"—when the armies, filled with fury, came together.

Regarding the rule *samo gamyṛcchibhyām* (Pāṇini 1.3.29), the Ātmanepada ending is applied by the Vārttika *arttiśrudṛśibhyaśca*. The absence of the augment *aṭ* is due to the rule *bahulaṃ chandasyamāṅyoge’pi* (Pāṇini 6.4.75). Bhaṭṭi says: "My desired intentions were fulfilled when you arrived. As for the example with the *sic* suffix provided in the Bhāṣya under *samo gamyṛcchi* (1.3.29), we have already stated that this refers to the root belonging to the *bhūvādigaṇa*.

(Pāṇini 3.1.57) *irito vā*: After a verbal root ending in the vowel *i* (or *ī*), the suffix *aṅ* may optionally replace *cli* in the *parasmaipada* endings. Examples: *abhidat*, *abhaitsīt*. Why "in the *parasmaipada* endings"? [Consider: *abhitta*; here, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings are used because the root is marked with a svarita accent. (Pāṇini 3.1.58)

Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.58: *jṝ-stambhu-mrucu-mluca-grucu-glucu-gluñcu-śvibhyaś-ca*. After these roots, the suffix *aṅ* is optionally substituted for *cli*. *Jṝ*: *ajarat*, *ajārīt*. *Stambhu*: A root belonging to the *sautra* (artificial) class. *astabhat*, *astambhīt*. *Mṛcu* and *mrucu*: Meaning "to go" (*bhvādigaṇa*, roots 195, 196). *amrucat*, *amrocīt*. *amlucat*, *amlocīt*. *Grucu* and *glucu*: Meaning "theft" (*bhvādigaṇa*, roots 197, 198). *agrucat*, *agrocīt*. *Gluñcu*: Meaning "to go" (*bhvādigaṇa*, roots 201, 202). *aglucat*, *agluñcīt*. *Śvi*: *aśvat*, *aśvayīt*.

He caused to move (*aśiśviyat*). This has been explained under *Pāṇini Sūtra* 3.1.41: "There is an option regarding the roots *dhēṭ* and *śvi*. Although three forms are established even by employing only one of the two roots *gluc* and *gluñc*, nevertheless, when both *gluñc* and *gluc* are included, there are two forms: *aglucat* and *aglucīt*. From *gluc* with the suffix *sic*, we have *aglocīt*. Likewise, when *gluc* is employed, its forms are *aglucat* and *aglocīt*; whereas from *gluñc*, we have *agluñcīt*. Nevertheless, both were included by the author of the *Sūtras* because of a difference in meaning.

The author of the Bhāṣya, however, has stated that because verbal roots possess multiple meanings (*anekārthatva*), the desired result is established [by the rule itself], and thus one or the other [of the two rules] need not be formulated. By this, the opinion of certain scholars proposed by Jayāditya—that due to the force of employing both rules, the nasalization of *gluñc* does not occur—is refuted, as it contradicts the Bhāṣya. (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.59)

*kṛ-mṛ-dṛ-ri-hibhyaś-chandasi* (Pāṇini 3.1.59). After these roots, *aṅ* may optionally be substituted for *cli* in the Vedic language. Examples: *akarat*, *amarat*. Here, the Parasmaipada ending is used by way of transposition (*vyatyaya*). *adarat*: "When he climbed from ridge to ridge. However, it should be noted that the statement made in the Ṛgbhāṣya while explaining this verse—namely, that because the rule is conditioned by a technical designation (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*), the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel does not occur—is merely a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*). In the worldly language (*loka*), however: *akārṣīt*, *amṛta*, *adārīt*, *aruksat*. (Pāṇini 3.1.60)

*Ciṇ* [is substituted] for *cli* after [a verbal root ending in a vowel] before the suffix *ta*. (Pāṇini 3.1.60) The root *pad* (meaning "to go")—from this, *ciṇ* shall be substituted for *cli* when the suffix *ta* follows. Here, only the singular number of the *ātmanepada* is intended to be included, and not that which is prescribed by the rule *tasthasthamipām* (Pāṇini 3.4.101), because such a suffix is impossible here since the root is *ātmanepadi*. The word *vā* ("optionally") is no longer in force, because the term *anyatarasyām* ("either of the two") is employed in the subsequent rule. Examples: *udapādi sasyam* (the crop arose); *samapādi bhaikṣam* (alms were obtained). Why is it said "before *ta*"? Consider: *udapatsātām* (they two arose); *udapatsata* (they all arose). (Pāṇini 3.1.61)

Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.61: *dīpajana-budha-pūritāyipyāyibhyo 'nyatarasyām*. After these roots, the suffix *ciṇ* may optionally occur in place of *cli* when followed by the personal endings of the aorist (*te*). Examples: *adīpi*, *adīpiṣṭa*; *ajani*, *ajaniṣṭa*; *abodhi*, *abuddha*; *apūri*, *apūriṣṭa*; *atāyi*, *atāyiṣṭa*; *apyāyi*, *apyāyiṣṭa*. In this context, the roots *janī* (in the sense of "manifestation") and *budha* (in the sense of "understanding") from the *divādi* class are understood.

As for the *jan* in the sense of "producing" (belonging to the *bhvādi* class), the *budh* in the sense of "awakening" (belonging to the *divādi* class, *budha* 883), and the *budhi* in the sense of "understanding" (belonging to the *bhvādi* class, *budhi* 100)—these are not included here, because [the rule] intends to include only those two forms of *jan* and *budh* that are invariably middle-voiced (*ātmanepada*) and belong to the *divādi* class, due to their association with *dīp* and *pūr*. As for what Mādhava stated—that due to the association with intransitives (*akarmaka*), only the intransitive forms are intended—[that is incorrect].

That is to be considered; for there would be a contradiction with such usages as "Nārada awakened him in due course" (*kramādamuṃ nārada ityabodhi saḥ*) and "he awakened her whose eyes were tormented by the pain of waking" (*abodhitajjāgaraduḥkhākṣiṇīm*). Furthermore, this option (*vikalpa*) applies only when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed. However, in the case of the abstract action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*), the suffix *ciṇ* necessarily occurs because it is subsequent [in the order of rules], or because the term "agent" (*kartari*) is understood to carry over [from the previous rule] here. (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.62)

*acaḥ karmakartari* (Pāṇini 3.1.62). After a verbal root ending in a vowel (*ac*), the suffix *ciṇ* optionally occurs when the suffix *ta* follows, provided the action is expressed as being performed by the object itself (*karmakartṛ*). This is an optional rule (*vibhāṣā*) that applies where [the suffix] would otherwise be mandatory. Examples: *akṛta* *mā kaṭaḥ svayameva* ("The mat made itself"). *alāvi* / *alaviṣṭa* *kedāraḥ svayameva* ("The field harvested itself"). Why "after a vowel" (*acaḥ*)? Consider: *abhedi* *kāṣṭhaṃ svayameva* ("The wood split itself"). Here, the root ends in a consonant, so *ciṇ* does not apply. Why "when the action is performed by the object itself" (*karmakartari*)? Consider: *akāri* *kaṭo devadattena* ("The mat was made by Devadatta"). Here, the agent is Devadatta, not the object itself. (Pāṇini 3.1.63)

*Duhaśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.63): After the root *duh*, the suffix *ciṇ* may optionally occur when the *cli* suffix follows and the *ta*-suffix (the third person singular ending) is present in the sense of the object acting as the agent (*karmakartṛ*). Examples: *adodhi* or *adugdha* *gauḥ* svayameva* ("the cow milked itself"). When *ciṇ* occurs in the sense of the impersonal passive (*bhāve*), there is optionally the elision (*luk*) of the *kṣa*-suffix by the rule *lugvā duha* (Pāṇini 7.3.73). In the alternative case, the form is *adhukṣata*. Why specify "in the sense of the object acting as the agent"? So that *ciṇ* alone may occur in the case of a pure object (*śuddhakarmaṇi*), as in: *adodhi gauḥ gopālena* ("the cow was milked by the cowherd"). This is an optional rule where [otherwise] there would have been no application, because of the prohibition of *ciṇ* by the rule *na duhasnunamāṃ yakciṇau* (Pāṇini 3.1.89).
In that context, the mention of *duhi* is for the purpose of excluding [the application of] *yak*; however, the mention of *ciṇ* is for the sake of including *snuki*.

(Pāṇini 3.1.64) *na rudhaḥ*: The affix *ciṇ* is not applied after the root *rudh* when it occurs with the *karmakartṛ* (the agent who is simultaneously the object). Example: *aruddha gauḥ svayam eva* ("The cow blocked itself"). However, in the case of the pure passive (*śuddhe karmaṇi*), it is: *arodhi gaur gopālena* ("The cow was blocked by the cowherd"). Only the root *rudhir* in the sense of "obstructing" (*āvaraṇe*) is understood here, and not the root *ano rudha* in the sense of "desiring" (*kāme*), because in the latter case, the state resides in the agent (*kartṛsthabhāvakatvena*), and thus there can be no *karmakartṛ*.
(Pāṇini 3.1.65)

Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.65: *tapo'nutāpe ca* (The affix *ciṇ* shall not replace *cli* in the case of the *karmakartṛ* [the agent who is also the object], and also when there is repentance). The term *anutāpa* means subsequent regret (*paścāttāpa*). Its inclusion is for the purpose of excluding the *akarmaka* (intransitive) sense. For in that case, the prohibition applies even to the *bhāva* (impersonal action) and *karman* (object) voices. This is so even in instances where the status of being like the object (*karmavadbhāva*) is extended by the rule *karmavat karmaṇā* (Pāṇini 3.1.87), as in: *atapta tapas tāpasaḥ*, meaning "the ascetic performed penance. (That is, he acquired penance.)

In this context, the application [of the rule] arises from the extended application (*atideśa*) of *karmavattva* (the status of being like an object) by the rule *tapastapaḥkarmakasyaiva* (Pāṇini 3.1.88). Regarding *anutāpa* (remorse): *anvatapta pāpena*. The meaning is that he was subsequently struck down by that sinful action which was previously committed. The *lakāra* (verbal suffix) occurs in the sense of the pure action (*karman*). The third case (*tṛtīyā*) in *pāpena* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). Alternatively, when the action is not intended to be expressed, or when *tapas* means "sorrow," the *lakāra* occurs in the sense of the state (*bhāva*). In this case, the third case is used in the sense of the cause (*hetu*).

But when the agent-as-object (*karmakartṛ*) of the root *tap*—which signifies the act of heating and whose action resides in the object—is intended to be expressed, then the ātmanepada suffix is applied by the extended rule *akarmavat karmaṇā* (Pāṇini 3.1.87). Even in that case, the instrumental case is used for the causal agent (*hetu*) according to Pāṇini 3.1.66.

*Ciṇ* [is substituted] for *cleḥ* (the affixes of the aorist) when expressing the sense of the impersonal (*bhāva*) or the passive (*karman*), provided that the suffix *ta* follows. *abhāvi bhavatā* ("it was become by you"). *akāri kaṭas tvayā* ("the mat was made by you"). The mention of *ciṇ* is for the sake of clarity, because the mention of *ciṇ* continues from the rule *ciṇ te padaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.60), just as the mention of *te* does. As for the mention of *anyatarasyām* in the rule *dīpajanabudhipūritāyiśvyaidhijvalaśucalaṣapatapadāmacaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.61), it has ceased its application precisely at the rule *na rudhaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.64).

Otherwise, the negative particle (*nañ*) would result in being redundant. Nor should it be argued that the prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) alone continues to apply here, because a prohibition must be preceded by a prior application (*prāpti*), and there is no application of *ciṇ* for either the action itself (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*) by any [rule].

Furthermore, one should not argue that the *bhāṣya* on the present sūtra establishes a specific purpose for the repetition of the term *ciṇ*, namely that the suffix *ksa*—which is prescribed by the distinct rule "śliṣaḥ"—might otherwise subvert this *ciṇ* just as it subverts the *aṅ* of the *puṣādi* class; therefore, the repetition of *ciṇ* is intended so that *ciṇ* alone occurs here and *ksa* does not. This is because that [purpose] is also merely optional. For that statement was made with reference to the whole (*samudāya*).

However, when reference is made to the individual part (*avayava*), it has already been stated that, according to the maxim of the prior exception (*purastādapavāda*), the *ksa* of the root *śliṣ* subverts only the *aṅ* and not the *ciṇ*. (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.67)

*Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.67*: *sārvadhātuke yak*. When a *sārvadhātuka* suffix follows, the affix *yak* is added to a verbal root (*dhātu*) provided it expresses the sense of the action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*). Examples: *āsyate* (he sits), *śayyate tvayā* (you lie down). In the case of *śīṅ*, the substitution of *ay* occurs by *Pāṇini Sūtra 7.4.22*: *ayaṅ yi ṅkiti*. Example: *kriyate kaṭaḥ* (the mat is being made).

The scope for the rule "the *yaK* affix occurs here when there is an object" (*iha karmaṇi yaK bhavati*) is, for example, in the case of a pure object: *pacyate odanaḥ* ("the rice is cooked"). The scope for the *śap* affix [indicating the agent] is, for example, in the case of a pure agent: *pacati*. When both [affixes] would apply simultaneously in the case of a reflexive object-agent (*karmakartṛ*), one must provide an additional rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for the prescription of *yaK* in the case of the reflexive object-agent. [Objection: It need not be stated. It is established by the extension of the operation (*kāryātideśa*). For it is precisely by the rule *karmavat kartari* ("the agent is like the object") that *yaK*, the middle voice endings (*ātmanepada*), and so forth, are prescribed; thus, *yaK* alone is the subsequent [operation].

Even under the view that this is an extension (*atideśa*) from the *Śāstra*, the *ya*-affix alone will occur in the case of the object-agent (*karmakartṛ*), due to the *jñāpaka* rule: "The *yak* and *ciṇ* affixes do not occur after the roots *duh*, *snu*, and *nam*" (Pāṇini 3.1.89). Here, this should be noted: the meanings of the *l*-suffixes are the state (*bhāva*), the object (*karman*), and the agent (*kartṛ*). This follows from the rule: "The *l*-suffixes [occur] in the sense of the object and in the sense of the state for intransitive roots" (Pāṇini 3.4.69). For in that rule, the word "agent" (*kartari*) is drawn over by the particle *ca*; and it was established in the preceding rule that this [word "agent"] serves to provide the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*).

Furthermore, in the subsequent rule *tayoḥ eva kṛtya-* (Pāṇini 3.4.70), it is likewise; thus, by virtue of this "sandance" (the inclusion between two similar rules) and the context of the majority of readings (*prāyapāṭha*), it is appropriate that even in the intervening cases, the meaning is simply the presentation of the objects of expression. The agent is the substratum of the action denoted by the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), which is the primary element, and the object is the substratum of the result (*phala*). Since both the result and the operation (*vyāpāra*) are already conveyed by the verbal root itself, the meaning of the *l*-suffixes (*lakāra*) is merely the substratum, because the meaning of a word must be that which cannot be obtained from any other source.

Consequently, that same meaning belongs to the *tiṅ* suffixes as well, because they are substitutes (*ādeśa*) for the *la*-suffixes, and a substitute is capable of expressing only the meaning of its original base (*sthānin*). They manifest the status of being *vikaraṇas*, whereas *yak* and *ciṇ* express the result [of the action]. If it is argued: "Let the opposite be the case; according to the natural sense of the grammatical rule *'kartari śap'* (Pāṇini 3.1.68) and others, let *śap* and so forth be the denoters (*vācaka*), while the *lakāra*s are merely indicators (*dyotaka*)," we say no. For even in the absence of *śap* and the rest in the *liṅ* (optative), *liṭ* (perfect), and in the *adādi* and *juhotyādi* classes of verbs, those meanings are still cognized. Although—sometimes, even in the absence of *tiṅ* suffixes, all three [agent, object, and instrument] are cognized.
One who acts without tranquility goes [to suffering] merely by the proximity of the *ciṇ* and *śap* suffixes.
In expressions such as *adoga-bibharti*, the cognition of an agent occurs even when there is only a verbal root (*dhātu*);
likewise, in expressions such as *āsate*, the cognition of an agent occurs even in the absence of a verbal root.

Nevertheless, in that regard, according to the opponent's view, it is the [suffix] that has been elided which conveys the meaning through recollection; however, for us, since we accept the stated principle that "that which remains denotes the meaning of what is being elided," everything is well-established. In this context, the *tiṅ* suffix, while expressing the agent and the object, also conveys the number residing in them; thus, when there is duality or plurality of the agent or the object, the dual and plural endings respectively occur.

In the case of a *bhāva* (action), however, the suffix *laṭ* denotes or indicates the action itself, which constitutes the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) and has reached a state of non-substantiality (*asattvāvasthāpanna*). In that case, there is only the third person singular; neither the second nor the first persons occur, because there is an absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the words *yuṣmad* ("you") and *asmad* ("I"). Nor do the dual or plural numbers occur, because duality and plurality are not perceived. As for the singular number, it follows from the *Bhāṣya*: "The singular shall be established as the general rule (*utsarga*)."

In this regard, even the use of the plural number is a general rule (*utsarga*), for that is accepted in the *Bhāṣya* in such examples as "the camel-sittings are being sat" (*uṣṭrāsikā āsyante*) and "the dead-lying-downs are being laid" (*hataśāyikāḥ śayyante*). For indeed, the sittings of camels are distinct from one another by their very nature; and the dead lie down in various ways—face up, face down, with limbs scattered, hair disheveled, garments fallen, and so forth. Due to this similarity, even for the action (*bhāva*) denoted by the verb, a plural number occurs precisely because a distinction is perceived within its own nature.

Even without the employment of the word *iva*, the sense of "as if" is understood, according to the maxim that "a word denoting one thing is applied to another. Thus, the meaning here is: "Just as there are various kinds of couches for those who have been slain, so too are they made by Devadatta and others. And in this way, the forms *āsikāḥ* and *śāyikāḥ* are in the accusative plural; they function as adverbs of action (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) and thus possess the status of an object (*karman*).

Nor should it be argued that, in this case, there would be neither the neuter gender nor the singular number; for, since the rule *striyāṃ ktin* (Pāṇini 3.3.94) governs the context, the feminine gender is determined, which precludes the application of the maxim *sāmānye napuṃsakam* (the neuter is used for the general), and because the singular number is determined by the plurality [of the objects denoted], the singular does not apply—this is the direction of the argument.

However, some, considering that this *lakāra* suffix denotes the object (*karman*), maintain that the words *āsikā* and *śāyikā* are in the nominative case. For instance, since *āsikā* and *śāyikā* denote states (*bhāva*), they function as objects according to the rule "time, state, and distance to be traversed" (*kāla-bhāvādhvagantavya*); thus, the *l*-suffix occurs in the sense of the object, as in the example "one sleeps for the duration of milking a cow" (*godohaḥ supyate*). Furthermore, in the cases of *uṣṭrāsikā* ("the camel-sitting") and *hataśāyikā* ("the dead-man-laying"), the sitting and lying—which are presented by the verbal roots of the respective denominatives—function as qualifiers with respect to the act of sitting and lying, just as the milking of cows functions with respect to sleeping.

Furthermore, the delimiting nature (*paricchedakatva*) of the *āsikā* and *śāyikā* is mediated through similarity (*sādṛśya*), whereas that of the *godoha* is through a temporal adjunct (*kālopādhi*); this is another matter. Kaiyaṭa and others maintain that this [delimiting function] certainly occurs even when there is a different intention to express (*vivakṣāntara*).

However, it has been stated by the author of the Bhāṣya that plurality (*bahutva*) is accepted even when the suffix *la* is prescribed in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*). Nor should it be argued that this would undermine the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that the *bhāva* expressed by a verb (*ākhyāta*) exists in a non-substantial state (*asattvāvasthāpanna*); for here, "non-substantial state" is intended to mean the absence of connection with gender (*liṅga*) and the absence of connection with case-roles (*kāraka*) such as the instrument (*karaṇa*).

For this very reason, there is no inconsistency even when the action, which constitutes the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) in cases such as *pacati bhavati* ("he is cooking," i.e., "he is becoming a cooker"), *pacyate bhavati* ("it is being cooked, i.e., it is becoming something cooked"), or *paśya mṛgo dhāvati* ("look, the deer is running"), is connected to another action by way of being its agent (*kartṛ*) or its object (*karman*). Nor does this entail an identity with the meaning of *ghañ*-affixes and the like; for the *bhāva* (action/state) expressed by *ghañ* and similar suffixes possesses gender and is connected to all the case-factors (*kārakas*) as appropriate—thus the difference between the two is evident. In this matter of difference, the regulating factor is simply the nature of the word’s expressive power (*śabdaśakti*), which is to be inferred on the strength of experience.

This has been stated: "An action expressed by a *kṛt* suffix appears like a substance (*dravya*). Even in the case of *tumun* and other such suffixes, there is no denotation of a substantial entity (*sattvārtha*). This will become clear from the *Vārttika*: "The *avyaya-kṛt* suffixes [denote] the abstract action (*bhāva*). Even in the case of non-*avyaya* *kṛt* suffixes, as in "you must lie down" (*śayitavyaṃ bhavadbhiḥ*), the number one alone is construed with the meaning, and not duality and so forth; this should be distinguished according to experience and according to the grammatical rule (*yathākāraṇam*). (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.68)

Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.68: *kartari śap*. When a *sārvadhātuka* suffix denoting the agent (*kartṛ*) follows, the affix *śap* is added to the verbal root (*dhātu*). The letter *p* is for the sake of accent (*svarārtha*) and to prevent the application of the *ṅit*-designation. The letter *ś* serves to denote a *sārvadhātuka* suffix and to serve as a qualifier in rules such as Pāṇini Sūtra 7.1.81 (*śapśyanor...*). Examples: *pacati*, *paṭhati*. The mention of the term "agent" (*kartṛgrahaṇam*) will be utilized in the rule Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.87 (*karmavat karmaṇā*).

In this case, however, there is no harm even though the general rule "the *śap* affix occurs after a verbal root in the *sārvadhātuka* [domain]" applies; for since the *yaṅ* affix and others are exceptions (*apavāda*) in the case of the passive and middle voices (*bhāvakarman*), the *śap* affix is restricted solely to the active voice (*kartṛ*). Nor should it be argued that the mention of "passive and middle" (*bhāvakarma*) does not carry over into the rule for *yaṅ*, because if it did not, *yaṅ* would undesirably apply to forms like *pacati* by taking the *śap* affix itself as its cause. (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.69) *Śyan* occurs after roots beginning with *div*. (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.69) This is an exception to *śap*. Examples: *dīvyati*, *sīvyati*. The root *mṛg* in the sense of "searching" (*anveṣaṇe*) is listed among the *cur*-class (*curādi*) roots ending in *a* as being *ātmanepada*. Regarding that—

"This Supreme Person seeks the further shore of the milk-ocean," and so forth. Because it is also listed among the *divādi* roots, "mṛgyati" is correct. Haradatta and others maintain that the word *mṛga* should be regarded as belonging to the *kaṇḍvādi* group [of roots].
(Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.70).

Or [the suffix] *śyan* is optionally applied after the roots *bhrāś*, *bhlāś*, *bhram*, *kram*, *klam*, *tras*, *truṭ*, and *laṣ* (Pāṇini 3.1.70). *ṭubhrāśṛ* and *ṭubhlāśṛ* mean "to shine" (*dīptau*; Dhātupāṭha 849, 850). *bhramu* means "unsteadiness" (*anavasthāne*; Dhātupāṭha 99) and "movement" (*calane*; Dhātupāṭha 865); both are included here. *kramu* means "stepping" (*pādavikṣepe*; Dhātupāṭha 474). *klamu* means "weariness" (*glānau*; Dhātupāṭha 1010). *trasī* means "agitation" (*udvege*; Dhātupāṭha 11). *truṭī* means "cutting" (*chedane*; Dhātupāṭha 95). *laṣa* means "desire" (*kāntau*; Dhātupāṭha 913).

The roots *bhrāś*, *bhlāś*, and *bhram* belong to the *divādi* class in the sense of "not remaining steady" (*anavasthāna*), while *truṭ* belongs to the *tudādi* class; the others belong to the *bhūvādi* class. Therefore, this option applies to both groups. Thus: *bhrāśyate*, *bhrāśate*; *bhlāśyate*, *bhlāśate*; *bhrāmyati*, *bhramati*. For the *divādi* root *bhram*, there is lengthening in the *śyan* affix by Pāṇini 7.3.74, "There is lengthening for the eight roots beginning with *śam* before *śyan*. However, for the *bhūvādi* root, this does not occur, as it is not among those beginning with *śam*. [Likewise: *krāmyati*, *krāmati*.

The lengthening [of the vowel] occurs by the rule *kramaḥ parasmaipadeṣu* (Pāṇini 7.3.76). And because of the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *śiti*, this [lengthening] applies both to the *śap* and the *śyan* suffixes. However, in the *Kaumudī*, after explaining that "there is lengthening of *kram* in the presence of *śap*," a short vowel is cited as the example for *śyan*; that is indeed incorrect. [Examples are: *klāmyati*, *klāmati*. The lengthening occurs by the rule *ṣṭhivuklamucamāṃ śiti* (Pāṇini 7.3.75). The inclusion of *klam* in the list of roots beginning with *div* is for the sake of the grammatical operations (*kārya*) pertaining to the *puṣādi* group.

In the *Kaumudī*, however, it is stated that for the root belonging to the *bhūvādigaṇa*, "klamati" [is used]; that is indeed un-Pāṇinian. [The forms] *trasyati* and *trasati* [are derived from the root *tras*]. Haradatta maintains that the purpose of including *tras* in the *divādigaṇa* is to be considered. [The forms] *truṭyati* and *truṭati*; *laṣyati* and *laṣati*. (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.71) *yaso'nupasargāt*: After the root *yas* when not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*), the affix *śyan* may optionally occur. Thus, *yasyati* or *yasati*. Why "not preceded by a prefix"? [Consider] *āyasyati* and *prayasyati*. Here, *śyan* occurs invariably, because the root *yasu* meaning "exertion" (*prayatna*) belongs to the *divādigaṇa*.

(Pāṇini 3.1.72) *saṃyasaśca*: After the root *yas* preceded by the prefix *sam*, the affix *śyan* is optionally applied. Thus, one forms *saṃyasyati* or *saṃyasati*. Here, it would have been more appropriate to state simply "after *yas* and *saṃyas*," for the desired result is achieved through the restrictive rule that if there is a prefix, the affix applies only after *saṃyas* and not after *prayas* and so forth. (Pāṇini 3.1.73)

*svādibhyaḥ śnuḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.73). This is clear. From the root *su* (to press), one forms *sunoti*. Because the root *ṣiñ* (in the sense of binding) is listed both in the *svādi* and *kryādi* groups, both forms *sinoti* and *sināti* occur. *śruvaḥ śṛ ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.74). The suffix *śnu* is applied after the root *śru*, and by virtue of its application, the root undergoes the substitution *śṛ*. Thus, one forms *śṛṇutaḥ* and *śṛṇvanti*.

(Pāṇini 3.1.75) *akṣo 'nyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 3.1.75). The root *akṣū* in the sense of "pervading" (*vyāpti*) belongs to the Bhvādi class. From this root, the suffix *śnu* may optionally occur. Thus: *akṣṇoti*, *akṣati*. (Pāṇini 3.1.76)

The suffix *śnu* may optionally be applied after the root *takṣ* when it means "to make thin" (*tanūkaraṇe*). Thus, one says *kāṣṭhaṃ takṣṇoti* or *takṣati*. Why "when meaning to make thin"? Consider *santakṣati*, which means "he reviles with words. After the roots beginning with *tud* (the *tudādi* class), the suffix *śa* is applied. Thus, from *tud* we have *tudati*, and from *nud* we have *nudati*. When the forms *tud-ti* and *nud-ti* are established, the suffix *śa*—being obligatory (*nitya*)—prevents the application of *guṇa* (vowel strengthening), which would otherwise apply by virtue of its higher status (*paratva*) in the order of rules.

(Pāṇini 3.1.78): *rudhādibhyaḥ śnam* (Pāṇini 3.1.78). After these [roots], the suffix *śnam* shall occur. Because it is marked with the indicatory letter *m*, it follows after the final vowel. By the maxim of the curd and the Kauṇḍinya, this [suffix] sets aside the *śap* [augment]. The letter *ś* is for the purpose of specification, as in the rule *śnānnalopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.23). If it were stated simply as *nānnalopaḥ*, then [the elision of *n*] would also occur in forms such as *yajñānām* and *yatnānām*.

Nor should it be argued that once the lengthening [of the vowel] has been applied by the rule *nāmi* (Pāṇini 6.4.3), the designation *nāt* will not occur because that designation no longer exists; for since a form modified in one part is not different from the original, the designation *nāt* remains possible even when the vowel is long. Furthermore, due to its higher status in the order of rules (*paratva*), the elision (*lopa*) must take effect.

Nor should it be argued that, because [the suffix] is further than that, the long vowel should apply by the rule *supi ca* (Pāṇini 7.3.102); for by the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā* (Pāṇini Bhāṣya 87), that [rule] does not apply here. Nor should it be argued that, in this case, the long vowel by the rule *nāmi* (Pāṇini 6.4.3) would likewise not occur in forms such as *rāmāṇām*; for since the very commencement [of the rule *nāmi*] possesses its own force (*ārambha-sāmarthya*), the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā* does not apply when the long vowel is to be effected by the rule *nāmi*.

The lengthening [of the vowel] by Pāṇini-sūtra 6.1.102 (*supi ca*) has its utility in forms such as *rāmābhyām* and the like; therefore, it is not intended to subvert the *sannipātaparibhāṣā*. As for what Haradatta stated—that because of the citation *kaṣṭāya*, the lengthening will occur by virtue of a general indicator (*jñāpaka*), and even so, since this would be subject to the status of a *sthānivadbhāva* in a rule concerning what precedes, this would still be the word *naś* itself, and thus the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) would necessarily occur—[that is incorrect].

That is questionable: while it may be granted that a *paribhāṣā* does not apply in certain instances due to its dependence on a general indicator (*jñāpaka*) in accordance with the observed forms (*lakṣya*), why should its general application be abandoned here? If you argue that it is precisely for the sake of establishing forms such as *yatnānām*, we reply: since it was just stated that the form is not established even when the long vowel is present, and because you yourself will later state that the form remains unestablished.

Furthermore, the rule "pūrvasmādvidhau" (P. 1.1.56) is far too broad; for its established meaning is "from that which has been relied upon as the cause immediately preceding. Now, in this case, the mere consonant *n* which precedes the undesignated vowel (*anādiṣṭādacaḥ*) is not relied upon as the cause. And as for the cause—the cluster consisting of the *n* and the vowel *ā*—that does not precede the undesignated vowel. Therefore, this argument is trivial. Consequently, by the method previously stated, there is the application [of the rule] because that which undergoes partial modification is non-different from the original. The letter *ś* is for the purpose of specification, namely, that it applies only before a long vowel.

Even so, there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) in cases such as *viśnānām* or *praśnānām*, because [the suffixes] are devoid of meaning (*anarthakatvāt*). Nor should it be argued that the same applies to the *vikaraṇa* [suffixes] as well; for according to the view of some (ekadeśimatam), those [suffixes] possess denotative power (*vācakatva*), and even according to the primary view (mukhyamatam), they possess meaning through the sense they indicate (*dyotyena arthena arthavattvāt*). For this very reason, although the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) of a suffix is based on its meaning, when *śnam* is applied, the designation *it* for the letter *ś* is established by Pāṇini’s rule *laśakvataddhite* (Pāṇ. 1.3.8).

Furthermore, by the paribhāṣā *lakṣaṇapratipadokta* (Pā. 1.1.68), there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *viśnānām*. Therefore, it is established that the letter *ś* in *śnam* is for the purpose of specification (*viśeṣaṇa*) in the rule *śnānnalopaḥ* (Pā. 6.4.23). Nor should it be argued that its purpose is to prevent the designation of *ardhadhātuka*; for if that designation were present, then in *anakti*, *bhanakti*, the elision (*lopa*) of the *a* [of the suffix] would occur; in *ruṇaddhi* and *bhinatti*, *guṇa* substitution would occur; and in *hinasti* and *tṛṇoḍhi*, the augment *iṭ* would occur.

If it is argued that the rule *neḍ vaśi* (Pāṇini 7.2.8) does not apply here because [the element *śnam*] is not a *kṛt* suffix, we say no; for even though it is an *ārdhadhātuka* affix, there is no harm [in its application]. And if it is further argued that this would result in a triad—namely, elision (*lopa*), *guṇa*, and *iṭ*—as previously stated, we say no; because all three are indeed augments (*āgama*), and the portion preceding *śnam* does not constitute a complete stem (*aṅga*).

To explain: the meaning of the rule *yasmāt pratyayavidhiḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.13) is this: when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is being prescribed, that which is designated by the ablative case—such as "from a root" (*dhātoḥ*) or "from a nominal stem" (*prātipadikāt*)—is the *aṅga* (base) with respect to what follows it. However, in the present case, that which is designated by the ablative—"from roots beginning with *rudh*" (*rudhādibhyo dhātubhyaḥ*)—the suffix does not follow it; and that part preceding which the suffix follows is not designated by the ablative when the suffix is being prescribed. This is the general principle. [Examples: *ruṇaddhi*, *bhinatti*. (Pāṇini 3.1.79)

*Uḥ* after *tan*-class roots and *kṛñ* (Pāṇini 3.1.79). The suffix *u* shall be applied after the roots beginning with *tan* and after *kṛñ*. [Examples: *tanoti*, *karoti*. The mention of *kṛñ* has been rejected in the Bhāṣya, since [the form] is established by its very inclusion in the *tan*-class. [Objection: Let it be for the sake of a restrictive rule (*niyama*) regarding the operations specific to the *tan*-class.

If it is argued that because of the rule *tanādibhyastathāsoḥ* (Pāṇini 2.4.79), which provides for the optional elision (*luk*) of the *sic* suffix, the two forms *akṛta* and *akṛthāḥ* would not occur [since the *sic* would always be elided], this is not so. Even though there is an option regarding the elision, when that elision does not take place, the desired form is established by the elision prescribed by *hrasvādaṅgāt* (Pāṇini 6.1.68). Furthermore, an optional rule does not sublate a mandatory one, because the mandatory rule is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) with respect to the optional one.

Nor can it be argued that, by the principle that "an exception [apavāda] prevails over a general rule [utsarga] due to the authority of the specific statement," the reading of *kṛ* in the *tan*-class (the *tanādi-gaṇa*)—which would otherwise be established as *asiddha*—is set aside by this rule, resulting in an optionality that overrides the obligatory application; for the purpose of the reading of *kṛ* in the *tanādi-gaṇa* is already fulfilled by its inclusion in the rules for the derivation of verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇa-vidhi*). Furthermore, the optionality is already fulfilled in cases such as *atathāḥ*. On the contrary, if the mention of *kṛ* were actually made, then because the reading of *kṛ* among the *tanādi*s would serve another purpose, the optionality would override the obligatory rule according to the maxim *yenāprāpte* (Pāṇini 1.4.2).

The inclusion of the term *kṛñ*, however, would serve the purpose of ensuring that its recitation among the *tan*-class roots (*tanādayaḥ*) is not rendered superfluous by the rule for the introduction of verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇa*). Therefore, it is more appropriate to simply omit the mention of *kṛñ*.

(Pāṇini 3.1.80) *dhinvikṛṇvyora ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.80). For the roots *dhivi* (meaning "to delight," *bhvādi*, *parasmaipada*, no. 594) and *kṛvi* (meaning "to injure" or "to do," *bhvādi*, *parasmaipada*, no. 599), there shall be the substitution of the vowel *a* for the final [consonant], and the suffix *u* shall also be applied. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *śap*. By the rule *ato lopaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.48), the [final] *a* is elided; because of its status as a *sthānivat* (as if it were the original element), the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadha-guṇa*) does not take place. Thus: *dhinoti*, *kṛṇoti*. The mention of these two roots with the *num* augment attached is for the purpose of indicating that the application of the *num* augment occurs only during the stage of the original instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*).

Therefore, in the rule for the insertion of *num*, the statement "the mention of 'as if it were taught' (*upadeśivad-vacanam*) is for the sake of establishing the status of the suffix" need not be made. Furthermore, on the view that the vowel *i* in *sic* and *tās* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇārtha*), even the mention of *dātuḥ* in the rule for *num* need not be made, because what that [mention] was intended to indicate is already indicated by this very [rule].
(Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.81)

*krī-ādibhyaḥ śnā* (Pāṇini 3.1.81). This is clear. [Examples: *krīṇāti*, *prīṇāti*. *stambhu-stumbhu-skambhu-skumbhu-skuñ-bhyaḥ śnuś-ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.82). The first four are from the Sūtra collection (*sautra*). *skuñ* means "to flow" (*āpravaṇe*) [Dhātupāṭha 6]. From these, there shall be the suffix *śnā* as well as *śnu*. [Examples: *stabhnāti*, *stabhnoti*; [in the second person singular imperative: *stabhāna*, *stabhnuhi*. *stubhnāti*, *stubhnoti*. *skabhnāti*, *skabhnoti*. *skubhnāti*, *skubhnoti*. *skunāti*, *skunīte*.

By virtue of the capacity for the *udit* marker, even those verbal roots (*dhātu*) mentioned in the Sūtras possess all meanings; however, this [marker] does not have as its sole domain the *vikaraṇa* suffixes.

(Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.82): *halaḥ śnaḥ śānajjhau*. After a consonant, the suffix *śnā* is replaced by *śānac* when followed by the imperative (*loṭ*) ending *hi*. Examples: *puṣāṇa*, *muṣāṇa*. [This is] the imperative (*loṭ*), second person singular (*sip*), which is replaced by *hi*.

(Pāṇini 3.1.81): *kr̥ñādibhyaḥ śnā*. For that [suffix], there is *śānac* [in the present participle]; because it possesses the *cittva* property, it is udātta-accented on the final syllable. Due to the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of the *sannipāta-paribhāṣā*, there is elision (*luk*) of the augment *hi*. Why [is the condition] *halaḥ* [stated]? [Consider: *kr̥mīhi*. Why [is the condition] *hau* [stated]? [Consider: *puṣṇāti*. The mention of the original element (*sthānin*) as *śnaḥ* is for the sake of obtaining its status as a substitute (*ādeśatva*). Otherwise, this would indeed be a different suffix altogether. If it is asked, "Let it be so; what is the fault?", we say no, because in cases such as *pacati* and *paṭhati*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of *śānac* replacing *śap*.

Nor should it be argued that the rule *kryādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.81) is understood [in the present context], for that would result in the non-establishment of the four forms *stabhāna*, *stubhāna*, etc. Furthermore, it is not possible to carry forward the roots beginning with *stambh* [from 3.1.82], because the suffix *śānac*—being specifically prescribed—would subvert both *śna* and *śnu*, leading to the undesirable consequence of the non-establishment of forms such as *stabhnuhi*. Nor can it be argued that *śnu* is also carried forward [from 3.1.74], for that would entail the undesired application of *śnu* even to the *kryādi* group.

Furthermore, there is no evidence for the rule that *śnu* occurs only after roots such as *stambh*, while *śānac* occurs after those [roots] as well as after those beginning with *krī*; therefore, let it remain exactly as in the original arrangement (*yathānyāsam*). Haradatta maintains that the purpose of adding the marker *ś* to *śānac* must be considered, since the desired result is already established through the principle of *sthānivadbhāva*.

Regarding this, there is the following reflection: this [statement] is intended to indicate that the prohibition "in some cases, even when an operation dependent on [the affix] follows" applies even in the case of the prescription of *an*. Consequently, according to the view of the Vārttika, *ī* does not occur in *brūtāt*; however, according to the view of the Bhāṣya, the *ṅit*-character is not necessarily present in *bhaviṣīṣṭa*. This has been clarified by us under the rule *ṅiti ca* (Pāṇini 1.1.5). (Pāṇini 3.1.84)

In the Veda, the suffix *śānac* is also used [after roots ending in long vowels]. Because of the word "also" (*api*), it is used after the suffixes *śatṛ* and *kvasu*. *gṛbhāya jivhayā madhu* ("Seize the honey with your tongue"). *badhāna devasavitaḥ* ("Bind, O divine Savitṛ"). By the rule *hṛgrahorbhaśchandasi* (Kātyāyana-vārttika), the *h* of the root *gṛh* becomes *b*. By the rule *aniditām* (Pāṇini 6.4.24), there is elision of the *n* of the root *bandh*. *yoskabhāyaduttaram* ("He who propped up the higher [heaven]"); the meaning is *askabhnāt* ("he propped up"). (Pāṇini 3.1.85)

*Vyatyayo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.1.85). The *vikaraṇas* have been introduced; in the Vedic language (*chandas*), there may be a frequent transposition (*vyatyaya*) of them. Transposition means "going beyond" (*vyatigamana*). From the root *iṇ* preceded by *vyati*, the suffix *ac* is applied in the sense of a state (*bhāve*) according to Pāṇini 3.3.56. Sometimes it means "mutually entering each other's domain. For example: *kaṇḍāni bhedati*. Where *bhinatti* would be expected [in Classical Sanskrit]. Also: *na hy asyā aparañcana jarasā mriyate patiḥ*. Where *mriyate* would be expected. And: *jīvaccāmaravāsādho vyādham ājīvam āmaraḥ*.

This may also be resolved by observing the Vedic usage found in the Purāṇas and other texts. In the phrase *indro vastena neṣatu*: the verb *nī* (to lead) is in the imperative (*loṭ*), second person plural (*tip*). There are two affixes (*vikaraṇa*): *śap* and *sip*. In *indreṇa yujā taruṣema vṛtram*: the meaning is "may we overcome" (*tarema*). The verb *tṛ* (to cross/overcome) is in the optative (*liṅ*) used for injunctions and so forth, second person plural (*mas*). There are three affixes: *uḥ*, *sip*, and *śap*. The root undergoes *guṇa* strengthening. When the form *taruṣ mas* is established, the *s* is elided according to Pāṇini 3.4.11 (*nityaṃ ṅitaḥ*). Then the augment *yāsuṭ* is applied. By Pāṇini 7.2.80 (*ato yeyaḥ*), *ya* replaces *i*; subsequently, there is the elision of *y*.

"Guṇa is substituted for [the vowels] *a* and *ā*" (Pāṇini 6.1.87). The inclusion of the term *bahulam* ("diversely") is intended to indicate that all grammatical rules may have exceptions. Thus says the Bhāṣya:

"The author of the Śāstra intends the transposition of case endings (*suptiṅ*), voice (*upagraha*), gender (*liṅga*), person (*nara*), tense (*kāla*), the letter *h*, accent (*svara*), the agent (*kartṛ*), and the suffix *yaṅ*; and this [transposition] is also established by means of *bāhulaka*."

There is an interchange of case endings (*supām vyatyayaḥ*): [the word] *yuktāmātā* occurs in place of *dakṣiṇāyāḥ*, where one would expect *dakṣiṇasyām*. And there is an interchange of verbal suffixes (*tiṅām*): [the word] *takṣati* occurs in place of *takṣanti*, as in *ye aśvayūpāya takṣati*. The term *upagraha* (verbal mood/voice) denotes that which is indicated by the substitutes for *l* (the verbal suffixes), which takes the form of a specific means of accomplishing the action (*kriyāsādhanaviśeṣarūpa*), such as whether its purpose is for oneself or for another. As it has been said:
"That distinction of meaning which is sometimes perceived from the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), and which is also [perceived] from other substitutes for *l*, they consider that to be *upagraha*."

In the expressions *ātmanepadāt* and *lādeśāt*, the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used in the sense of cause. However, here the word *upagraha* (verbal suffix) is used figuratively (*lakṣaṇayā*) to refer to the *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada* endings which serve as the means for that cognition. *brahmacāriṇamicchate*: where *icchati* was expected. *pratīpamanya ūrmiryudhyati*: where *yudhyate* was expected. *madhostṛptā ivāsate*: where *madhunaḥ* was expected. Although in the common language (*bhāṣā*) the word *madhu* has both genders because it belongs to the *ardharcādi* group, nevertheless, its application is restricted to specific meanings. Thus—it denotes the nectar of flowers (*makaranda*), wine (*madya*), or honey (*mākṣika*).
Due to its inclusion in the *ardharcādi* group, the word *madhu* is used in both the masculine and neuter genders.

Thus, according to the *Śāśvatika* [lexicon], it is feminine; however, in the sense of "immortal" (*amṛta*), it is exclusively neuter. For this very reason, an example of its irregular usage has been provided. Māgha, however, says: "A bee, having become indifferent to the splendor of the blossoms of creepers—splendors overflowing with delicious nectar—surely approaches their lip-honey out of a longing for the name 'drinker of nectar' (*amṛtapāna*)."

In this context, one who employs the masculine form of the word *madhu* as a synonym for *amṛta* (nectar) should be questioned, according to the *Śāśvata* lexicon. *Naraḥ* means *puruṣaḥ* (man). *Adhāsavīraiḥ daśabhir viyūyāḥ*—where *viyūyāt* is expected [as the correct form]. The root *yu* (to mix), preceded by the prefix *vi*, is used in the benedictive (*liṅ*) mood. *Kāla* is a suffix denoting time; [the phrase] means "on the morrow" (*śvas*) by one who is about to establish the sacred fires (*agnīn ādhāsyamānena*). The *lṛṭ* suffix is used in place of the *luṭ* suffix. *Hal-triṣṭubhaujaḥ śuphitam ugravīram*.

Regarding the substitution of *pha* for *bha* in the sense of "beauty" (*śobhā*) in the *Āśvalāyana-sūtra*, Haradatta maintains that in the *Taittirīya* [Saṃhitā], only the letter *bha* is recited. However, in reality, even in the *Āśvalāyana-sūtra*, only the letter *bha* is recited. The example of the transposition of consonants (*hal-vyatyaya*), namely "it is obtained as *suhitam*," is clear according to the *Bhāṣya*. [Example: "Let the pregnant wives sing praises to me. (*ac-upagāyantu māṃ patnayo garbhiṇyaḥ*)

The substitution of a short vowel for a long one and the transposition of vowels will be explained under the rule *parādiś chandasi bahulam* (Pāṇini 6.2.199). Haradatta maintains that the word *kartṛ* (agent) is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all grammatical factors (*kāraka*), and thus it refers to the transposition of case-endings (*vibhakti*) that express them. However, if this were the case, the purpose would already be served by the words *sup* and *tiṅ* alone; therefore, one should cite as examples the transposition of primary suffixes (*kṛt*), secondary suffixes (*taddhita*), and so forth, which also express grammatical factors.

And likewise, in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the sūtra *karmaṇyaṇ* (Pāṇini 3.2.1), it is stated that there is a transposition (*vyatyaya*) of suffixes in the Vedic language (*chandasi*). We shall clarify that point in that very place. The term *yaṅ* is a pratyāhāra (abbreviated designation), beginning with the letter *ya* of *yak* and ending with the *ṅ* of *liṅyāśiṣyaṅ* (Pāṇini 3.1.86). A transposition of these has already been illustrated. Thus, the author of the treatise, Pāṇini, intends a transposition of *sup*, *tiṅ*, and so forth. And this is established by means of *bāhulaka*. [The word] *bahula* means that which takes or receives many meanings; its state is *bāhulaka*. The suffix *vuñ* is applied here because it belongs to the *manojñādi* group.

(Pāṇini 3.1.86) *liṅyāśiṣyaṅ* (Pāṇini 3.1.86). In the Vedic language (*chandas*), the suffix *aṅ* shall be applied to a verbal root when the optative (*liṅ*) in the sense of benediction (*āśis*) follows. This *aṅ* is observed primarily after the roots *sthā*, *gā*, *gam*, *vac*, *vid*, *viś*, *kṛ*, *ruhi*, and *hi*. For example: *upastheyaṃ vṛṣabhaṃ tūryāṇām* ("May he be approached, the bull of the swift ones"). In this case, the optative (*liṅ*) with the prefix *upa-* is used in the sense of benediction. The suffix *am* replaces *mip* (the first person singular ending), and because of the rule *chandasyubhayathā* (Pāṇini 6.4.86), there is also the designation of *sārvadhātuka*. Consequently, by the rule *liṅaḥ salopo 'nantyasya* (Pāṇini 7.2.71), there is the elision of the *s* [of the augment *yāsuṭ*].

In the case of the suffix *aṅ*, [the rules] "āto lopaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.64) and "ato yeyaḥ" (Kātyāyana-vārttika 7.2.80) apply. One should approach the truth (*satyam upageyam*); we would go to the house of the one who knows (*gamaema jānato gṛhān*). We would speak the mantra to Agni (*mantraṃ vocemāgnaye*). [By the rule] "vaca um" (Pāṇini 7.4.20), one would know this [truth] which has entered the mind (*videyamenāṃ manasi praviṣṭām*). I shall perform the vow; may I be able to do so (*vrataṃ cariṣyāmi tacchakeyam*). May we ascend the flowing river for our well-being (*asravantīm āruheamāsvastaye*). The suffix *ag* should be stated after the root *dṛś* (Kātyāyana-vārttika). [Thus one says: "May I see my father and mother" (*pitaraṃ ca dṛśeyaṃ mātaraṃ ca*). However, if the suffix *aṅ* were present, there would be *guṇa* substitution by the rule "ṛdṛśo'ṅi" (Pāṇini 7.4.16). Now, how is it that one says "we would resort to the great refuge" (*upastheyāṃ śaraṇaṃ bṛhanta*)? For in that case, *sthemā* would be expected [by the rule "sthāgāpāpaco bhāve" (Pāṇini 3.3.95)].

Regarding this, the commentary (*bhāṣya*) states: "Because [the suffix] *liṅ* is *sārvadhātuka*, there is the elision of *s*; because it is *ārdhadhātuka*, there is the substitution of *e*. The intended meaning is that this is according to the rule *er liṅi* (Pāṇini 6.4.67). Furthermore, the augment *aṅ* need not be applied here, due to the principle of diversity (*bāhulaka*). Thus ends the fourth section (*āhnika*) of the first quarter of the third chapter in the venerable *Śabdakaustubha*.
The Fifth Daily Lesson of the First Quarter of the Third Chapter.

(Pāṇini 3.1.87): *karmavat karmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ*. By the word *karman*, one's own action (*svaniṣṭhā kriyā*) is indicated. An agent expressed by a verbal suffix (*lakāra*) who possesses an action equal to that residing in the object (*karmastha*) shall be treated like the object (*karmavat*). The mention of two *lakāras* [in the sūtra] is due to the rule *vyatyayo bahulam liṅyāśiṣyaṅ* (Pāṇini 3.1.85, 86), or else the *lakāra* is mentioned as having been elided. The elision occurs either by *saṃyogāntasya* (Pāṇini 8.2.23) or by *halo yamām* (Pāṇini 8.4.64).

And that term *lakāra*, which is carried over here, should be transformed into the genitive case, or its genitive ending should be elided; and the meaning of the genitive is "the state of being denoted" (*vācyatva*). From the rule *kartari śap* (Pāṇini 3.1.68), the term *kartṛ* (agent) is carried over and transformed into the nominative case. By this, the intended meaning is obtained. The purposes [of this rule] are the application of the *ya*-affix, the *ātmanepada* endings, the *ciṇ* affix, and the *ciṇvad-bhāva* treatment. For example: *bhidyate kāṣṭhaṃ svayameva* (The wood splits by itself); *abhedi kāṣṭhaṃ svayameva* (The wood split by itself); *kāriṣyate kaṭaḥ svayameva* (The mat will be made by itself).

These three examples illustrate the middle voice (*ātmanepada*); the distinction is that they correspond respectively to the suffixes *yak*, *ciṇ*, and the state of *ciṇvad-bhāva*. When the instigation [to act] has ceased, the object remains within a portion of its own action; as its status as an object ceases, it persists in its status as an agent.

In this state, because the roots are intransitive (*akarmaka*), the *l*-suffixes occur in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) and the action itself (*bhāva*). Among these, when they occur in the sense of the agent, although the forms would normally be those of the simple active voice (*śuddha-kartari*), there is an extended application (*atideśa) based on the following principle: "The agent of the roots *bhid* (to split) and *kṛ* (to do), which expresses the *l*-suffixes, possesses an action equal to that [action] which belonged to the wood when it was the object in the previous state—namely, the action consisting of being split for *bhid*, and the action consisting of arising in the mat for *kṛ* as its object. Consequently, the four suffixes beginning with *yaṅ* (*yaṅ*, *yaṅluk*, *san*, and *kyac*) are applied.

Just as there is intransitivity for a verb when the causal suffix (*ṇic*) has been removed, and just as an action may in some cases reside in the object (*karman*) and in others not, so it has been explained in the rule *ṇeraṇau* (Pāṇini 1.3.67). Why does the rule specify "by the object" (*karmaṇā*)? So that [the designation of agent] does not apply to those actions equal to the action of the instrument (*karaṇa*) or the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). For example: *sādhvasiś chinatti* ("the sword cuts well") and *sādhu sthālī pacati* ("the pot cooks well").

If it is argued that here, in the state of being an instrument (*karaṇa*) or a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), the operation of the sword or the pot, although existing in reality, is not denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*), what follows from this? For in this sūtra, the verbal root’s denotation of the action (*kriyā*) which serves as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) for the similarity is not explicitly assumed by the words [of the sūtra], such that the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would not occur even without the mention of "object" (*karman*). Furthermore, actions residing in the agent (*kartṛstha-kriyā*) are also to be excluded by this very rule, such as: "the village goes by itself," "the elephant mounts by itself," "the meaning of the scripture attains [him]," "he remembers," and "he has faith," and so forth.

If it is objected: "In that case, since effort (*yatna*), which is the meaning of the root *kṛ*, resides in the agent just like knowledge (*jñāna*) or desire (*icchā*), how can 'the mat will be made by itself' (*kāriṣyate kaṭaḥ svayam eva*) be cited as an example? [Response: No, because it has already been explained that the root *kṛ* has the sense of "producing" (*utpādana*). What is expressed by the *lakāra* (verbal suffix)? [The answer is: It is so that the *lakāra* does not arise in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*), as in "the granary splits by itself" (*bhidyate kusūlena*). If this extension (*atideśa*) were applied here, the accusative case would result for the *kusūla*.

Furthermore, in the absence of the qualification "being denoted by the *lakāra* suffixes," the *kṛtya* and *khalartha* suffixes would apply to this [intransitive] agent, as in: *bhettavyaḥ kusūlaḥ svayam eva* ("the granary is to be split by itself") and *īṣadbhedaḥ kusūlaḥ svayam eva* ("the granary is slightly split by itself"). However, it is desired that they apply only to the action (*bhāva*), as in: *bhettavyaṃ kusūlena* or *kusūlasya*. The genitive case may optionally be used according to Pāṇini 2.3.71, *kṛtyānāṃ kartari vā*, as in: *īṣadbhedaṃ kusūlena*.

As for what was stated here in the Vārttika—"there is a prohibition regarding the *kṛtya*, *kta*, and *khal* suffixes"—the mention of the *kta* suffix there is not intended to be significant; rather, it was included here because of its common recitation alongside them elsewhere. For indeed, since these roots are intransitive (*akarmaka*), the *kta* suffix occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) by the rule "gatyarthākarmaka... (Pāṇini 3.4.72). Accordingly, in the case of the rule "of the root *si* [when] having 'swallowing' as its object and the agent as its subject" (Kāśikāvṛtti), the *niṣṭhā* nasalization will be illustrated with the example "the morsel has been swallowed by itself" (*sino grāsaḥ svayameva*), where the *kta* suffix denotes the agent.

Others, however, say that the mention of the *kta* suffix is indeed intended, because the example “*gavā dugdhaṃ payaḥ*” (milk [was] milked by the cow) is possible. For here, since the cow is both object and agent (*karmakartṛ*), when the extension of the rule for objects (*karmavad-atideśa*) applies, the *kta* suffix would occur. This is not so in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), where the rule *Pāṇini-sūtra 3.4.72*, *gatyarthākarmaka...*, does not apply, because [the verb] is transitive due to having an object in the form of the milk.

Nor should it be argued that, precisely because it is transitive (*sakarmaka*), the extended application (*atideśa*) of the rule *karmavat* will not occur; for there is a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) stating, "The roots *duh* and *pac* [are treated as *karmavat*] in many instances when they are transitive. Nor can it be claimed that the operation occurs solely by virtue of the mention of the word "many" (*bahula*), since that term has been rejected in the *Bhāṣya*. This is the general direction of the argument.

However, the mention of *vat* (the suffix *-vat*) can be omitted. For instance, let there simply be the designation of "object" (*karman*) for the agent denoted by the *l*-suffixes. Nor can it be argued that the designation of "agent" is sublated by the designation of "object," because—unlike in the governing rule concerning the application of a single designation (*ekasaṃjñādhikāra*)—designations may coexist elsewhere. Furthermore, one should not say that in such a case the *lo* suffix would not occur due to the absence of transitivity (*sakarmakatva*), because [the desired result] is established through the sequence of operations. Indeed, the designation of "object" awaits the production of the *l*-suffixes, since that [designation] is prescribed specifically for the agent denoted by those *l*-suffixes.

Therefore, since the status of being intransitive (*akarmakatva*) persists from the outset, the rule for the suffix *la* in the sense of the action (*bhāva*) and the agent (*kartṛ*)—namely, *bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.69)—remains unimpeded. But even so, one might object that the *yaK* (passive) and *ātmanepada* endings would not occur; for the *yaK* and *śap*, which have scope in the case of pure objects and agents respectively, would apply by virtue of their higher priority (*paratva*), resulting in the application of *śap*. This is because there would be a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) between the *ātmanepada* prescribed by *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.13) and the *parasmaipada* prescribed by *śeṣātkartari* (Pāṇini 1.3.78).

If it is argued that [the suffix *śap*] should not apply because it is subsequent [to other rules] and because the *parasmaipada* endings would otherwise be required, we say no. This is because the general rule (*utsarga*) "śap after a verbal root before a *sārvadhātuka* ending" can still operate by excluding those domains already occupied by the exception (*apavāda*), namely the *yak* prescribed for the states of being (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*). Consequently, the mention of the agent (*kartṛ*) in the sūtra "śap after [a root] denoting an agent" is superfluous. Its purpose is this: "So that *śap* and the others may occur when the agent is indeed the agent, but they should not occur in the case of a 'reflexive agent' (*karmakartṛ*)."

Now, one might object: "In this view of Haradatta, since the suffix *yaK* is prohibited by the rule *na duha* (Pāṇini 3.1.89), the *śap* [suffix] would not occur. Consequently, there would result the occurrence of forms without verbal suffixes (*nirvikaraṇa*), just as in the case of the optative (*liṅ*) and the perfect (*liṭ*). If this is raised, [the response is: In that case, the rule *kartari* is split; and in the rule *bhāvakarmaṇoḥ*, it is also split into *bhāve* and *karmaṇi*. Then, carrying forward the term *karmaṇi* from the subsequent rule, *yaK* occurs when the agent (*kartṛ*) is in the objective state (*karman*), serving as an exception (*apavāda*) to *śap*. In rules such as *na duha*, because there is no such exception, the general rule (*utsarga*) remains in force once again.

And this explanation is established in the Bhāṣya itself regarding the rule for *yaṅ*. Thus, first of all, *yaṅ* is established; this is also because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule *na duhasnunamām* (Pāṇini 3.1.89). Likewise, by carrying forward the word "agent" (*kartari*) from the rule *kartari karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 1.3.14), the explanation is that "the Parasmaipada occurs when the agent is indeed the agent, but not when the agent is also the object (*karmakartṛ*)," and thus the Ātmanepada is applied. Therefore, it is established that even if the mention of the suffix *vat* is omitted, everything desired is accomplished.

However, when the suffix *vat* is employed, it is quite clear that this is an extension (*atideśa*). And that [extension] is sixfold, based on the distinctions of form, cause, identity, designation, treatise, and operation; this was explained in the rule *sthānivat* (Pāṇini 1.1.56). But here, the first three are impossible. Furthermore, an extension by way of designation does not differ from the position of a technical name (*saṃjñā*); in that case, the use of the suffix *vat* would be redundant. Therefore, only two remain.

Even in that case, regarding the extension (*atideśa*) of the rule, one would have to resort to the previously mentioned effort for the sake of establishing the *yaṅ* and the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), which results in complexity. Moreover, since this is the primary purpose for which the other extensions exist, this must be an extension of the operation (*kāryātideśa*) itself. Nor should it be argued that under this view the accusative (*dvitīyā*) would also be extended, such that in the expression *bhidyate kusūlena*, when the suffix denotes the state (*bhāva*), the accusative would occur in the sense of the agent; for it has been stated that "the extension of the object-like status applies only to the agent expressed by the suffix."

Even so, there is no occurrence of the aforementioned fault in the case of "the granary is split" (*bhidyate kusūlaḥ*), because the accusative case does not apply since [the object] has already been expressed. If it is objected that there is no governing rule for what is "not expressed" (*anabhihitādhikāra*) here, that is true; nevertheless, by the force of the suffix *-vat* (in *karmavat*), just as a suffix occurs when the object is unexpressed, it would likewise be obtained when the agent is unexpressed. Therefore, it has already been stated that there is indeed expression [of the agent].

[Objection: But surely, when the causal operation (*preṣaṇa*) has ceased, verbs such as *lunāti* (he cuts) and *bhinatti* (he splits) become intransitive, just like [the verb] *dvidhā bhavati* (it becomes two). Therefore, how can there be "an action equal to that of the agent" (*tulyakriyatvam*) with respect to the object (*karman*) in those cases? [Reply: No, for we do not mean that the equality of action is with respect to whatever is the object in this particular usage; rather, it is with respect to whatever was the object in another usage. [Objection: If that were so, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as "Devadatta cooks rice" (*pacaty odanaṃ devadattaḥ*) and "The rice ripens by itself" (*rādhyaty odanaḥ svayameva*). [Reply: Regarding this, the Vārttika states:

"If it is seen as the object [of the action] in the same verbal root (dhātu) or in the same base (kāya)," so it is said. This is established by logic (*nyāyasiddha*); for the term "verbal root" (*dhātu*) is understood to carry over (*anuvartate*), and since the agent and the object cannot exist apart from the verbal root, that which is established by implication (*sāmarthya*) alone is stated again for the purpose of expressing singularity (*ekatva-vivakṣā*). Thus, it means: when there is an action in a certain verbal root, the agent of that very root is one who possesses an action equal to that of the object. Therefore, this does not apply when there is a difference in the verbal roots.

It might be argued as follows: even for a single entity, agency and objecthood are observed through a difference in form, as in "you know yourself by yourself. And likewise, in cases such as "the rice is being cooked" (*odanaḥ pacyate*), let the *L*-suffix (the passive marker) apply directly to the primary object itself; what then is the need for resorting to the theory of "withdrawn instigation" (*nivṛttapreṣaṇatva*) or for the extended application (*atideśa*) "like the object" (*karmavat*)? Nor should it be said that if this were the case, the *L*-suffix would not occur in the abstract sense (*bhāve*) in "it is split by a spike" (*bhidyate kusūlena*), for we accept that very consequence. Indeed, let that [abstract sense] also occur only when there is an object. (Pāṇini 3.1.89)

On this point, they say: if it were so, then by the rule "na duhasnunamām" (Pāṇini 3.1.89) and others, the distinction of scope regarding the prohibition of *yak* and *ciṇ* would not be obtained. Furthermore, in cases such as "the staff bends" (*namati daṇḍaḥ*) or "the mat causes itself to be made" (*kārayate acīkarata vā kaṭaḥ*), even though *yak* and *ciṇ* are prohibited, the suffixes *śap* and *caṅ* would not occur, because [the object] lacks the status of an agent (*akartṛtvāt*). Moreover, the usage "the rice cooks" (*pacaty odanaḥ*) would also result as an undesirable consequence. Therefore, one must indeed begin the rule of extended application (*atideśasūtra*) by resorting to the state where the instigation has ceased (*nivṛttapreṣaṇatā*).

It should be stated [as a Vārttika]: "When the agent has an action equal to that of the instrument (*karaṇa*), it frequently behaves like the object (*karman*). (Kāśikāvṛtti). He surrounds the tree with thorns (*parivārayati vṛkṣaṃ kaṇṭakaiḥ*). The thorns surround the tree (*parivārayante vṛkṣaṃ kaṇṭakāḥ*). Here, the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is established. Nor is its establishment possible by the rule *ṇicaśca* (Pāṇini 1.3.74), because that rule applies only when the fruit of the action goes to the agent (*kartṛgāmi*). In this case, however, the middle voice is desired even in the absence of such a fruit. Due to the inclusion of the term "frequently" (*bahulam*), it does not apply here: "The sword cuts well" (*sādhu asis chinatti*).

A prohibition must be stated for transitive verbs (*sakarmaka*). Examples: *anyonyam āśliṣyataḥ* (they embrace each other); *anyonyam spṛśataḥ* (they touch each other). And this is established by logic (*nyāyasiddha*). For when it is said, "that agent whose action is equal to an action residing in the object," what is understood from the proximity [of the words] is this: that the very action through which one becomes an agent is the same action that serves as the basis for the status of being an object. But this is not the case here, because even for one who does not embrace himself, the status of being an object is possible when he is embraced by another.

This is because, although the two operations conducive to the result called "conjunction" (saṃyoga) which inheres in another [substance]—both consisting of motion and expressed by a single verbal root—are distinct only in their essential natures. By this, the expression "the splitting granary splits the vessels" is also explained. For even though the process of splitting occurs in the granary by chance, it is not the cause of the status of being the object (*karman*) residing in the vessels; for even while the granary itself does not split, it indeed splits the vessels as they fall upon it.

[Objection: Even so, in the case of roots such as *pac* and *rudh*, which are inherently transitive (*dvikarmaka*), even when one of their two objects is treated as the agent (*kartṛ*), they remain transitive in their other state; thus, the status of being "like the object" (*karmavadbhāva*) would still apply. To prevent this, a specific prohibition for transitive roots must indeed be formulated. [Response: This is established through a formal division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). For instance: first, *tapeḥ*. This means that the prohibition applies only to the root *tap* when it is transitive, and not to any other root. Then, *tapaḥ karmakasyaiva*. Here, the word *tapeḥ* is understood to carry over from the previous rule. Alternatively, a division of the rule will be made in the Vārttika itself: [The Vārttika states: "In the case of *tap*, [the prohibition applies] only when it is transitive. Then: "And [the prohibition applies] only to that which has *tap* as its object. Here, *tapeḥ* is understood to carry over. Or else: "In the case of *tap*, [the prohibition applies] only when it is transitive. Then: "And [the prohibition applies] only to that which has *tap* as its object. Here, *tapeḥ* is understood to carry over. Thus, the desired result is achieved.

*Duhipacyorbahulaṃ sakarmakayoḥ*. Here, the statement "of *duh* and *pac*, when they have an object" (*duhipacyoḥ sakarmayoḥ*) constitutes one sentence for the purpose of restriction: "only of *duh* and *pac*, and not of others. Thus: *dugdhē gōḥ payaḥ* ("the cow yields milk") and *tasmād udumbaraḥ salōhitaṃ phalaṃ pacyatē* ("therefore the udumbara tree bears red fruit"). In these cases, the cow and the udumbara tree are both objects and agents (*karmakartṛ*). It should be noted that the Vārttika on the sūtra *akathitaṃ ca* (Pāṇini 1.4.51) provides support for this.

The second statement, "bahulam" (variously), is intended to prevent over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *odanaṃ pacati* ("he cooks the rice"). However, that [statement] has been rejected in the Bhāṣya. For the rule *duhipacyoḥ* refers to the object-agent (*karmakartṛ*). Is it a prescriptive or restrictive rule only for those cases where the action is identical to that which resides in the object? In either case, there is no possibility of over-extension in examples such as *odanaṃ pacati*. Nor is the mention of "variously" (*bahulam*) for the sake of the active voice (*parasmaipada*) in the case of the object-agent alone, because that is not desired; such is the direction of the argument.

Regarding the roots *sṛj* and *yuj*, the suffix *śyan* [is introduced] optionally (in the *kārita* sense). It should be stated that for these two transitive roots, the agent frequently behaves like the object (*karmavat*). And *śyan* is an exception to *yaṅ*.

It should be stated that [the suffixes] *ya* and *ciṇ* are applied to the agent itself when the agent is one endowed with faith (*śraddhopapanne kartari*). Thus, the student (*brahmacārī*) is made to create (*sṛjyate*) or is joined to yoga (*yujyate*). When the *śyan* affix is present, the root (*prakṛti*) retains its initial udātta accent. However, if the *yak* affix were used, then because the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes are anudātta, the udātta accent would belong to the *yak* itself. In the *Kaumudī*, however, it is stated: "Some [grammarians] hold that *yak* and *ciṇ* are applied to the agent after the root *sṛj* when the agent is endowed with faith. In that context, the mention of *yag* is incorrect, and there is a deficiency due to the failure to mention the middle voice (*ātmanepada*); such is the direction of the argument.

Regarding the roots signifying adornment (*bhūṣā*), those beginning with *kṛ* (the *kirādi* group), and those ending in the desiderative suffix (*san*), it must be stated that the *yak* and *ciṇ* affixes do not occur, except in the case of the ātmanepada. The meaning is that for these roots denoting adornment, for the *kirādi* group, and for those ending in *san*, the passive (*yak*) and periphrastic passive (*ciṇ*) are excluded. Examples: *alaṃkurute kanyā svayameva* (The maiden adorns herself); *alamakṛta* (She adorned herself). Since the result of the action—namely, beauty—is observed to reside in the object, adornment is considered to reside in the object (*karmasthā bhūṣā*).

However, since the prohibition of *yak* and *ciṇ* for roots meaning "adornment" (*bhūṣā*) ending in *ṇic* is already established by the rule to be stated later, these do not serve as primary examples here: *bhūṣayate kanyā svayam eva* (the girl adorns herself). *abubhūṣata kanyā svayam eva* (the girl did not adorn herself). *avakirate hastī svayam eva* (the elephant scatters [dust] himself). *avākīrṣṭa hastinaṃ kaścit* (someone scattered [dust] upon the elephant). [The elephant] scatters with dust and the like; in that case, because of ease, the elephant is intended to be expressed as the agent. *girate* (he swallows). *agīrṣṭa* (he was swallowed). The *kirādi* group is a sub-group within the *tudādi* class.

The root *san* (to wish) is inherently *kartṛsthakriya* (having an action residing in the agent); thus, [in the desiderative] one says *kaṇṭaḥ svayam eva cikīrṣate* ("the throat itself desires to act"). [In the past tense] one says *acikīrṣiṣṭa*. Here, although the desire (*icchā*) resides in the agent, it is considered *karmasthakriya* (having an action residing in the object) with respect to the action of "acting" (*karoti*).
(Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.88).

*Tapas-tapaḥ-karma-kasyaiva* (Pāṇini 3.1.88). The root *tap* (meaning "to heat," from the *bhvādi* class, No. 1010): its agent shall be treated like the object (*karmavat*), but only when *tapas* is the object, not when it has any other object. The *Vṛtti* states that this is for the purpose of a specific rule due to the difference in action. For instance, ascetic practices such as fasting (*upavāsa*) and so forth "heat" (*tapanti*) the ascetic; the meaning is that they cause him suffering. Thus, when the ascetic is the object, the meaning of the root *tap* is "causing suffering"; but when he is the agent, the meaning is "earning" or "acquiring."

The ascetic (*tāpasa*) performs austerity (*tapas*); that is to say, he acquires [merit through] austerity. Now, one might object: even so, the action characterized by the heating of the body is identical in both states, for there is no activity of the ascetic called "acquisition" other than the heating of the body. If this is so, why did the author of the *Vṛtti* not accept the view that it serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārthatva*), which is the position supported by the *Bhāṣya*?

On this point, they say: although bodily heat exists in reality, it does not appear as such from the word; rather, it appears only as "exertion" (*arjana*). Otherwise, it would be impossible for *tapas* (heat/exertion) to function as the object (*karman*) of the action. Thus, because there is an absence of identical action (*tulyakriyatva*), the suffix indeed has the sense of an injunction (*vidhi*).
