In the *luṅ* [aorist] form: *atapta tapas tāpasaḥ* ("the ascetic performed penance"). Because of the prohibition of *ciṇ* by the rule "tapo 'nutāpe ca" (Pāṇini 3.1.65), the suffix *sic* is used. Its elision occurs by the rule "jhalo jhali" (Pāṇini 8.2.26).

What is the purpose of [specifying] "of that which has the action of heating" (*tapaḥkarmaka*)? [Consider: "The goldsmith heats the gold. But the particle *eva* is indeed redundant. If it is argued that the connection of that which is heard [in the sūtra] must be stated, that is true; however, by splitting the sentence, the connection has already been demonstrated in some way.
(Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.89)

*Na duhasnunamāṃ yak-ciṇau* (Pāṇini 3.1.89). For these [roots], *yak* and *ciṇ* do not occur. This is a prohibition of those [suffixes] which would otherwise be applicable by the extended application (*atideśa*) of the rule that a root behaves like its object (*karmavat*). This is according to the principle of "the non-prohibition of what is immediately preceding" (*anantarasya*). Therefore, they do indeed occur in the case of a pure object (*śuddhe karmaṇi*) and in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*). By this rule, *yak* is prohibited for the root *duh*; however, *ciṇ* had already been made optional by the rule *duhaśca* (3.1.63). Thus: *dug-dhe gauḥ svayam eva* ("The cow milks itself"); *adugdha*, *adohi gauḥ svayam eva* ("The cow was milked by itself").

The suffix *śap* is prohibited; it is elided because [the root] belongs to the *adādi* class. By Pāṇini 8.2.32 (*dāderghaḥ*), *gh* is substituted for *dh*. By Pāṇini 8.2.40 (*jhaṣastathordho'dhaḥ*), *dh* is substituted for *th*, and then *jaś*-tva (substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop) applies. Regarding the rule "for *duh* and others when the object is not the primary one" (*apradhāne duhādīnām*), there is a desire to express the agency (*kartṛtva*) of that object upon which the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) is placed; however, the primary object remains simply an object. [Example: "The earth, milked by his virtues, yields treasures for him who is like a treasure-house. (*svayaṃ pradugdhe'sya guṇairupasnutā vasūpamānasya vasūni medinī*)

As in the example *itivat*. In the case of the substitution of *ciṇ* for *ārdhadhātuka*, there is *ksa*; however, because of the rule "there is elision (*luk*) when *u* follows," [the *ksa*] is elided. Thus: *prasnute*. In the past tense, *prāsnoṣṭa*; since *ciṇ* is prohibited, *sic* is applied. "The staff bends by itself" (*namate daṇḍaḥ svayameva*). It was bent: *anaṃsta*. Here, the root *nam* has the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) included within it. In that regard, just as in the cases "Devadatta causes the staff to bend" (*namayati daṇḍaṃ devadattaḥ*) and "the staff bends by itself" (*namayate daṇḍaḥ svayameva*), where the action resides in the object (*karmasthakriyatva*) of the causative form, so too should it be understood here.

Regarding the prohibition [of the *ātmanepada*] for roots ending in *yak* and *ci*, there is a supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) concerning causative roots in *ṇic*, as well as the roots *śri* and *brū*: "The mat causes itself to be made" (*kārayate kaṭaḥ svayameva*). "He had it made" (*acīkarata*). "The staff raises itself" (*ucchrayate daṇḍaḥ svayameva*). Because it begins with the vowel *u*, it is included among those roots whose action resides in the object (*karmastha*). The followers of Bhāradvāja recite:

There is an addition [to the rule] regarding the roots *niśranthi*, *granthi*, and *brū* when they are used in the Ātmanepada and are intransitive. In this context, the term *ṇi* is a general designation for both *ṇiṅ* and *ṇic*. An example of *ṇic* has already been cited. An example of *ṇiṅ*: *puccham udasyati* (he raises his tail) becomes *utpucchayate gauḥ* (the cow raises her tail). When the sense of causation (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) is inherent in it—*utpucchayate gām* (he causes the cow to raise her tail)—and then, due to an excess of ease, there is a desire to express the cow itself as the agent—*utpucchayate gauḥ svayameva* (the cow raises her tail by herself). *Udapupucchata* (she raised her tail repeatedly). Here, since the suffixes *yak* and *ciṇ* are prohibited after a root with *ṇic*, the suffixes *śap* and *caṅ* occur.

In the *Kaumudī*, however, it is stated that there is no *caṅ* affix when the agent is also the object (*karmakartṛ*). The example given, *akārayiṣṭa*, is indeed incorrect. [The roots] *śrantha* and *grantha* mean "to string together" (*sandarbhe*); they belong to the *curādi* class, specifically the *ādhṛṣīya* subgroup. They are included here in the sense of their forms when the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is absent. Devadatta strings a book (*granthaṃ granthati*); he strings a girdle (*mekhalāṃ śranthati*). When the act of stringing occurs spontaneously, one says *granthaḥ svayameva*. The forms are *agranthiṣṭa* and *aśranthiṣṭa*. These two roots are also listed in the *kryādi* class; they are likewise included here.

It unravels; it knots itself. Those verbal roots which are specified as being intransitive (*akarmaka*) for the purpose of prescribing the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) serve as examples here when they have an internalized causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) and the sense of instigation has subsequently ceased (*nivṛttapreṣaṇa*). For example: "After the root *vi* when it has sound as its object" and "also when it is intransitive" (Pāṇini 1.3.34, 35). *Saindhavā vikurvate*: the horses prance; the meaning is that they gallop. *Tān vikaroti*: he causes them to prance; the meaning is that he makes them gallop. Again, due to ease of performance, when the horses themselves become the agents: *Saindhavā vikurvate svayameva*: the horses prance by themselves. *Vyakṛṣata*.

As for what is recited in the *Vṛtti*—"he strikes the boy; the boy strikes himself"—that is incorrect, because the form "he strikes the boy" (*āhanti māṇavakam*) is transitive and lacks the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), according to Haradatta. Others, however, say: the rule "middle voice for roots that are intransitive" (*ātmanepada-akarmaka*) is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the verbal root itself. And since this root *han*—in the rule *āṅo yamahanaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.28)—is intransitive when the object is not intended to be expressed, it is then the cause for the middle voice. Therefore, even though it is transitive here, the example is not contradictory. (Pāṇini 3.1.90)

Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.90: *kuṣirajoḥ prācāṃ śyan parasmaipadaṃ ca*. The roots *kuṣ* (to extract) [DhP 4.6] and *rañj* (to color) [DhP 10.24], according to the Eastern grammarians, take the suffix *śyan* and the *parasmaipada* endings when used in the sense of the object acting as its own agent (*karmakartṛ*). This is an exception to the rule for *ātmanepada* endings. Examples: *kuṣyati pādaḥ svayam eva* (the foot extracts itself); *rajyati vastraṃ svayam eva* (the cloth colors itself). The mention of "according to the Easterners" (*prācām*) indicates that this is optional. Thus, one may also say: *kuṣyate* or *rajyate*.

Following the rule *na duha* (Pāṇini 3.1.89), the suffix *yak* is understood as being prohibited (*neti*), and in that very context, the suffix *śyan* is prescribed. Furthermore, the *parasmaipada* (active voice) is taught in connection with that [suffix]. Consequently, in the scope of the benedictive (*āśīrliṅ*), the perfect (*liṭ*), and the *syādi* (future, conditional, etc. suffixes, neither *śyan* nor the *parasmaipada* occurs. For example: *koṣiṣīṣṭa pādaḥ svayameva* (the foot may be rubbed by itself); *raṅkṣīṣṭa vastraṃ svayameva* (the garment may be dyed by itself); *cukuṣe* (it was rubbed); *rarañje* (it was dyed); *koṣiṣyate* (it will be rubbed); *raṅkṣyate* (it will be dyed); *akoṣi* (it was rubbed); *arañji* (it was dyed), and so forth.

There is a distinction regarding the accent and the augment *num* between the suffixes *śyan* and *yak*: *kuṣyantī jaṅghā* ("the thigh that scratches"). With *śyan*, by Pāṇini 7.1.81 (*śapśyanornityam*), the augment *num* is applied, and because it is marked with *n* (a *nit*), the word is acutely accented on its first syllable. However, with *yak*, by Pāṇini 7.1.80 (*ācchīnadyoḥ*), the application of *num* is optional; furthermore, since the *lasārvadhātuka* suffixes are unaccented, the acute accent would fall on *yak* itself. (Pāṇini 3.1.91).

*dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.91). This is an *adhikāra* (governing rule) extending up to the end of the third book (*adhyāya*). Although the term *dhātu* (root) continues to apply from the sūtra *dhātor ekāco halādeḥ* (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.22), the term *dhātu* is repeated here so that the designation *ārddhadhātuka* may be understood as dependent upon the operation of the word itself. Otherwise, in forms such as *lūbhyām* and *pūbhyām*, the augment *iṭ* would apply to the suffix *bhyām* and the *guṇa* substitution would apply to the base (*prakṛti*). However, because the rule is formulated specifically with *dhātoḥ*, these do not occur.

Furthermore, this [rule] is also for the purpose that the designation *kṛt* and the designation *upapada* should apply specifically within this section concerning verbal roots (*dhātu*). Otherwise, they would apply even to preceding rules; consequently, in the case of *kariṣyati*, since the suffix *syat* would receive the designation *kṛt*, the word ending in a *kṛt* suffix would be a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and the nominative singular suffix *su* would arise—because the singular number is the default—and because of the inclusion of the term "number" (*vacana*) in the rule *prātipadikārtha-* (Pāṇini 2.3.46).

Likewise, [if the rule were not as stated], the meaning of Pāṇini’s sūtra 3.1.43, *cli luṅi*, would be that *cli* occurs when a form ending in *luṅ* is the governing word (*upapada*). Furthermore, because of the application of the rule regarding optional forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*) in the preceding context, there would be a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of *sic* with *ksa* and other suffixes. Therefore, it is established that the word *dhātoḥ* ("after a root") must be included. And this [word] can be dispensed with. Thus, it remains established that the word *dhātoḥ* must be included. And this can be refuted. Thus, it remains established that the word *dhātoḥ* must be included. And this can be refuted.

For instance, the mention of the word *dhātu* in the rule *śami dhātoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.14) will itself be carried forward as a second [governing] term for the technical designations *sārvadhātuka* and *ārdhadhātuka*. Furthermore, the technical designations *kṛt* and *upapada*, as well as the rule regarding dissimilar forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*), will be explained by means of this very governing context (*adhikāra*), just like the rules *pratyayaḥ* and *paraśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.1–2). Consequently, there is no possibility of that [designation] applying to what precedes. (Pāṇini 3.1.92)

*Upapada* [is defined as] that which stands in the locative case (Pāṇini 3.1.92). A word such as *kumbha*, which stands as the object (*karman*) and so forth to be expressed in a word ending in the locative case, is termed *upapada*. And only when that exists, the suffix to be mentioned hereafter shall occur, by virtue of the force of this technical designation (*mahāsaṃjñā*). Here, "word" (*pada*) is the term being defined. Therefore, the paribhāṣā concerning semantic competency (*samartha*) is operative. The locations where this technical term is applied are "an *upapada* [forms a compound] with a non-finite verb" (Pāṇini 2.2.19), etc. (Pāṇini 3.1.93).

*kṛdatiṅ* (Pāṇini 3.1.93): Within this governing context of verbal roots (*dhātu*), an affix other than *tiṅ* shall bear the technical designation *kṛt*. Examples: *kartavyam*, *karaṇīyam*. Why say "other than *tiṅ*" (*atiṅ*)? [Consider: *cīyāt*. The locations where this designation applies include rules such as *kṛttaddhitasamāsāśca* (Pāṇini 1.2.46) and others. The term "other than *tiṅ*" (*atiṅ*) could be omitted. How would one account for *cīyāt*? It is established by means of an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

In the rule *akṛtsārvadhātukayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.25), since the term *akṛt* alone would have sufficed, the inclusion of the term *sārvadhātuka* indicates that "the designation *kṛt* does not apply to *tiṅ* suffixes. Nor should it be argued that the inclusion of *sārvadhātuka* is for the purpose of excluding the *śyan* affix; for among the roots beginning with *div*, there is no short-vowel-ending root that ought to take a long vowel, and thus there is nothing to be excluded. However, in the *Bhāṣya*, the acceptance of the *tiṅ* suffixes having the *kṛt* designation is indeed maintained.

Nor should it be argued that, because a word ending in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) would thus be a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), case endings such as the nominative (*svādi*) would arise; for [the meanings of] number, such as singularity, have already been expressed by the verbal suffix itself. Nor does the inclusion of the term "number" (*vacana*) in the rule lead to that consequence even when [the meaning] has been expressed, since that term serves its purpose in examples such as *ekaḥ* ("one"). This is because the rules *atiśāyane tamabiṣṭhanau* (Pāṇini 5.3.55) and *tiṅaśca* (Pāṇini 5.3.56) indicate that words ending in verbal suffixes are not considered to end in nominal suffixes (*asubanta*).

Even so, there is no risk of the *tuk* augment applying in cases such as *pacati* and *paṭhati* by virtue of the rule *hrasvasya piti kṛti* (Pāṇini 6.1.71), because in the rule prescribing *tuk*, the term *dhātu* (root) is understood to carry over from the preceding rule *dhātvādeḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.64). If it is argued that even so, the *tuk* would still apply in forms such as *cikīrṣati* and *jihīrṣati*, we say no; for these are intervened by the *śap* suffix. If it is argued that once the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) has been applied, there is no intervention, we say no; because of the status of a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) in respect to a preceding operation.

Nor does the status as being like the original (sthānivadbhāva) set aside the status as being like the end (antavadbhāva) on account of its being subsequent, because that [rule regarding antavadbhāva] will be rejected. Nor should it be argued that even so, if the prohibition "not after a verbal suffix" (atiṅ) were rejected, then in the case of *paceran*, there would be elision of the *n* due to its being at the end of a nominal stem (prātipadikānta); for by the very force of the pronunciation of the letter *n* in the rule "ran replaces jha" (Pāṇini 3.4.105), the elision does not take place.

If it is argued that in this case, in the form *cīyāt*, the long vowel would not occur because it is a *kṛt*-suffix ending in *y*, there is no such fault. The prohibition concerning *sārvadhātuka* suffixes indicates that "the prohibition [of lengthening] applies to non-*kṛt* suffixes does not operate in the case of *tiṅ*s.

Nor should it be said that even so, in a *tiṅ*-compound, the accent of the following *kṛt*-suffix (*kṛduttarapada-svara*) would apply; for we accept this as the desired result (*iṣṭāpatti*), since the reading is undisputed in instances such as *yo jāta eva paryabhūṣāt*, and furthermore, because the mention of *kṛt* in the rule *gatikārakopapadātkṛt* (Pāṇini 6.2.139) will be rejected (*pratyākhyāsyamāna*). This is the direction of the argument.
Thus ends the fifth section of the first quarter of the third chapter in the illustrious Śabdakaustubha.
The sixth section (āhnika) of the first quarter (pāda) of the third chapter (adhyāya).

(Pāṇini 3.1.94) *vā'sarūpo'striyām* (Pāṇini 3.1.94). This is a *paribhāṣā* (metarule). Within this governing context of verbal roots (*dhātu-adhikāra*), except where there is a governing context for feminine suffixes (*stry-adhikāra*), the word *vā* ("optionally") applies wherever a dissimilar (*asarūpa*) apavāda suffix is prescribed. Thus, just as in the case of "the optionality [of the apavāda] for *dadāti* and *dadhati*" (Pāṇini 3.1.139), since the apavāda is understood from the scripture as being optional, the corresponding *utsarga* (general rule) likewise operates in its alternative form. For instance, although *ka* is an apavāda for roots ending in *i*, *u*, or *ṛ* as penultimates (*ig-upadha*), for *jñā*, *prī*, and *kṛ*, the suffixes *ṇvul* and *tṛc* also occur in those same domains.

[Vikṣepakaḥ] means one who causes distraction, a distractor, or a distraction itself. And it is not the case that, in the domain of [the suffix] *ka* prescribed by "āto 'nupasarge kaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.3), the rule "karmaṇy-aṇ" (Pāṇini 3.2.1) would also optionally apply. If you argue that this [suffix *ka*] is of the same form [as *aṇ*], what of it? For it is well known that in the rules concerning *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, the word *ikaḥ* (from Pāṇini 1.1.3) is understood as being present in the rule for *ka* as well—otherwise, even suffixes such as *ṇvul* would be difficult to obtain.

If it is asked: "When *satyām* is present, why would the application of the rule for the same form (*sarūpa*) not also occur optionally?"—True. By virtue of the mention of "dissimilar" (*asarūpa*), this optionality applies only with respect to that [form] toward which there is dissimilarity; however, with respect to any other, it is simply a sublater (*bādhaka*). Thus, there is no fault. Consequently, the resulting meaning is: "A dissimilar apavāda suffix shall be a sublater of the general rule (*utsarga*). Why does it say "not in the feminine" (*astriyām*)? [Consider] *cikīrṣā*; here, *ktin* does not occur. The mention of "feminine" (*strī*) is intended as a svarita accent.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that since the scope of a governing rule (*adhikāra*) is understood through the *svarita* accent, there is no optionality within the governing rule "striyāṃ ktin" (Pāṇini 3.3.94). If, however, it were stated that [the prohibition] applies when the feminine gender is to be expressed (*abhidheya*), then the suffixes *ṇvul* and *tṛc* would not occur in the case of the word *vikṣepikā* / *vikṣeptrī*. Furthermore, if it were argued that the prohibition applies only to those [suffixes] prescribed after the word "striyām" has been explicitly uttered, then the suffix *ktin* would not occur in the case of *vyāvakrośī* / *vyāvakruṣṭiḥ* in the domain of the reciprocal action suffix *ṇac*, because both [suffixes, *ṇvul* and *ktin*], are prescribed after the word "striyām" has been uttered.

Regarding this, some say that since both the general rule (*utsarga*) and the exception (*apavāda*) are situated within the domain of feminine suffixes (*stryadhikāra*), this [suffix *ghañ*] is a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*). Others, however, maintain that it applies even to the exception alone. In the former view, in the case of *āsana* and *āsya*, there is co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) with the suffix *ṇyat* (Pāṇini 3.1.124), which is an exception to the suffix *yuc* prescribed under the domain of feminine suffixes; however, there is no co-occurrence with *ktin* and other such suffixes for *ghañ*, because they do not express the same meaning. In the second position, however, the non-co-occurrence of *ghañ* with *ktin* and others is established.

Regarding the term *āsya* here, the distinction is that the suffix *ṇyat* is applied according to Pāṇini’s rule 3.3.113, *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*. Now, does similarity (*sārūpya*) pertain to the actual usage (*prayoga*) or to the grammatical instruction (*upadeśa*)? It cannot be the first, because in cases involving *kvip* and other such suffixes—as in *grāmaṇīḥ* and *grāmarṇyaḥ*—suffixes like *aṇ* would fail to apply. For *kvip* and the others possess no form in actual usage, since their elision is prescribed.

If it is argued that the latter [alternative] is not tenable because it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as *kaṇ*, which differ from the *anubandha* [of the root], we say: no. This is because there is no fault in the second position since *anubandhas* are non-conclusive (*anaikāntika*). Even if they were conclusive (*aikāntika*), this is known from the evidence of the rules: "Non-similarity [of roots] is not caused by *anubandhas*" (Pāṇini Bhāṣya 8) and "There is an option for the roots *dā* and *dhā*" (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.139).

Otherwise, because of the dissimilarity (*asārūpya*) caused by the suffixes themselves, the forms *dāyaḥ* and *dhāyaḥ* would apply even in the domain of *śa* (the *śit* affix) for *dadaḥ* and *dadhaḥ*, as they would also apply to the affix *ṇa*; so what is the purpose of including the mention of *vibhāṣā*? This *vāsarūpa* paribhāṣā is non-eternal (*anitya*), as indicated by the inclusion of both *kṛtya* and *tṛc* in Pāṇini Sūtra 3.3.169, *arhe kṛtyatṛcaśca*. Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that "in the case of *kta*, *lyuṭ*, *tumun*, and affixes having the sense of *khal*, the rule of *vāsarūpa* does not apply" (Paribhāṣenduśekhara 77). Thus: *hasitaṃ hasanaṃ chātrasya* ("the laughing, the act of laughing, of the student").

In this context, *ghañ* does not apply where *ktalyuṭ* would otherwise occur. Regarding *tumun*: *icchati bhoktum* ("he desires to eat"). Here, the *loṭ* [imperative] does not occur by the rule "in the sense of desire, the *liṅ* and *loṭ* [are used]" (Pāṇini 3.3.157). However, the *liṅ* certainly does occur, because of the statement "and the *liṅ*" (Pāṇini 3.3.159). Thus, by this very restriction (*niyama*), the occurrence of *loṭ* here is easily avoided. Therefore, the mention of *tumun* here is merely for the sake of appearance. Regarding the sense of *khal*: *āto yuc*—*īṣatpānaḥ* ("easy to drink"); here, *khal* does not occur.

One might argue: "Surely, since the rule *stryadhikārāt* (Pāṇini 3.3.94) begins, one should simply accept that the principle of *vāsarūpa* (Pāṇini 3.1.94) no longer applies. This is not so; for otherwise, forms such as *āsitvā bhuṅkte* ("having sat, he eats") and *āsyate bhoktum* ("he is seated in order to eat") would result in being unestablished. For here, because sitting is for the sake of eating, its status as a prior action (*pūrvakālatā*) is understood. Moreover, the suffix *ktvā* is taught under the heading of the sense of *tumun* (infinitive), and thus it denotes the abstract state (*bhāva*). The *l*-suffixes (tense/aspect markers) also denote the same [abstract state]. Consequently, because they share the same domain (*samānaviṣayatva*), there would be a relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*).

Regarding the statement in the *Kaumudī* commentary that "because there is no absence of the rule for dissimilar suffixes (*vāsarūpavidhi*) after the sūtra *striyāṃ ktin* (Pāṇini 3.3.94) [which precedes] the sūtra *praiṣātisarga* (Pāṇini 3.3.163)," this is contrary to the original source (*ākara*). This is the direction of the argument.
(Pāṇini 3.1.95)

*kṛtyāḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.95). This is an *adhikāra* (governing heading). The specific limit [of its application] is established through an indicator (*jñāpaka*). In the rule *arhe kṛtyatṛcaśca* (Pāṇini 3.3.169), although one could have simply said *kṛtyāḥ*, the inclusion of *tṛc* is an indicator that the designation *kṛtya* is applied prior to the rule *ṇvultṛcau*. The points where this designation is applied are such as *kṛtyānāṃ kartari vā* (Pāṇini 2.3.71) and others. The plural number is used for the purpose of including those not explicitly mentioned.

By this, it is indicated by the very sūtra "kelimara upasaṃkhyānam" (Kāśikāvṛtti) and so forth. In this sūtra, the author of the Vṛtti added the phrase "prāṅ ṇvulaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.96). Regarding "tavyat-tavya-anīyar" (Pāṇini 3.1.96): these suffixes shall apply only to verbal roots (*dhātu*). The letter *t* and the letter *r* are for the sake of accentuation (*svarārtha*). [Examples: *kartavyam*, *karaṇīyam*.

The suffix *ṇyat* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) [to form] *vāstavya*. This refers to the root *vas* in the sense of "dwelling" (*nivāse*, *bhvādi*, *parasmaipada*, 1030), and not to the root *vas* in the sense of "covering" (*ācchādane*, *adādi*, 13) which takes the *lu*-class suffix. Because of the rule stating "only to those two [roots]," the suffix would not have been applicable in the sense of the agent; hence this specific statement. Thus, one who dwells is a *vāstavya*. Alternatively, it is a word ending in a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). One who exists in a dwelling (*vāstu*) is a *vāstavya*; the suffix *yat* is applied because it belongs to the *dig-ādi* group. There is no difference in accent between [the forms] *vāstavya* and *avāstavya*.

For when the suffix *tavyat* is used, the final syllable is udātta according to Pāṇini 6.2.160: *kṛtyokeṣṇuccārvādayaśca*; however, when the suffix *yat* is used, it is by means of Pāṇini 6.2.156: *yayatoścātadarthe*.

*kelimaḥ* is an addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) [to the rules]. It has been stated that this is indicated by the plural form *kṛtyāḥ*. The letter *ka* is for the purpose of prohibiting *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*; the letter *ra* is for the sake of the accent. *Pacelimā māṣāḥ* means "the beans are to be cooked" (*paktavyāḥ*). *Bhidelimāḥ saralāḥ* means "the pine trees are to be split" (*bhettavyāḥ*). Regarding the pure passive (*śuddhe karmaṇi*), the suffix is established in the Bhāṣya. However, the author of the Vṛtti says, "This is desired even in the sense of the agent as object" (*karmakartari*), which contradicts the Bhāṣya. (Pāṇini 3.1.97)

*aco yat* (Pāṇini 3.1.97). The suffix *yat* shall occur after a verbal root ending in a vowel. Examples: *ceyam*, *jeyam*. Now, one might object: "Why not simply specify *yat* in the preceding rule itself and omit the mention of 'vowels' (*aj*)? Since the author will state later that *ṇyat* occurs after roots ending in consonants (*hal*), by process of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), *yat* will apply only to those ending in vowels. [Response: This is for the purpose of ensuring that the suffix applies even to those that were previously vowel-ending [but are now consonant-ending]. Examples: *ditsyam*, *dhitsyam*.

For here, when the roots *dāñ* and *dhāñ* take the desiderative suffix (*san*), resulting in the forms *ditsa-* and *dhitsa-*, one might argue that since the condition for the suffix *ṇyat* is met by relying on the locative case *ārddhadhātuke* (Pāṇini 3.4.114)—which refers to the context of the affix—the elision of the *a* of *san* would result in a form ending in a consonant (*halanta*), and thus *ṇyat* should apply. However, because of the explicit mention of the vowel *a* (*aj-grahaṇa*) in the rule, the suffix applies by relying on the fact that the root previously ended in a vowel (*ajantatva*). Consequently, the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*) is applied by the rule *yato 'nāva-* (Pāṇini 6.1.213). If *ṇyat* were applied instead, the circumflex accent (*svarita*) of the suffix marker *ti* would have occurred. In cases such as *cikīrṣyam*, however, there is no difference between *ṇyat* and *yat*.

Because of the continued application of the term *dvyañ* (containing two vowels) in the rule *yato'nāvaḥ*, if the locative case in *ārddhadhātuke* were taken as a *parasaptamī* (indicating sequence), then the mention of *añ* here would indeed be unnecessary. [However, this is not the case, as follows: An addition (*upasaṃkhyāna*) must be made for the roots *taki*, *śasi*, *cati*, *yati*, and *janī*.

*taki* (in the sense of laughing; *bhvādi*, *parasmaipada*, 117). *śasu* (in the sense of harming; *bhvādi*, *parasmaipada*, 728). *cati* (in the sense of begging; *bhvādi*, *ubhayapada*, 890). *yati* (in the sense of effort; *bhvādi*, *ātmanepada*, 30). *janī* (in the sense of coming into being; *divādi*, *ātmanepada*, 43). [The resulting forms are: *takyam*, *śasyam*, *catyam*, *yatyam*, *janyam*.

In this context, the rule *jana-* (Pāṇini 6.1.213), which serves the purpose of [preserving] the accent, is not required because there is no difference in form even when the suffix *ṇyat* is applied, due to the prohibition of *vṛddhi* by the rule *janivadhyośca* (Pāṇini 7.3.35). Haradatta states that some also read *śaṃs-* here; by that, the initial acute accent (*ādyudātta*) is established in the forms *narāśaṃsyam* and *rādhyam*. However, it should be understood that in the alternative where it is not so read, the form is established by adding *yat* to the causative (*ṇyanta*) stem. They say this, but all of this is to be disregarded, as it is rooted in a forgetfulness of the sūtra *īḍavanda-* (Pāṇini 6.1.214) and others.

Or [the suffix] *yat* is applied after the root *han*, and by its connection with that suffix, the substitution of *vadha* must be stated; this is the meaning. Thus we have *vadhyaḥ* and *ghātyaḥ*. In the absence of *yat*, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied, and by the rule "hanasto 'ciṇṇaloḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.32), there is the substitution of *t* for the *n*. Then, by the rule "ho hanteḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.54), there is the substitution of *k* (i.e., *gh*).

Although the form *vadhyaḥ*—derived from the rule *vadham arhatīti vadhyaḥ*—can also be established by the secondary suffix *yat* under the governing rule *yati* (Pāṇini 4.4.91) and the specific rule *daṇḍādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.66), nevertheless, in cases such as *asivadhyaḥ* ("slayable with a sword") and *musalavadhyaḥ* ("slayable with a mace"), a compound would not be established. However, when [the suffix] *kṛt* is used, it is established by the rule *kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā* (Pāṇini 2.1.32).

Nor should it be argued that, once the analysis *na asivadharm arhati* has been performed, the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) may be applied directly from the compound itself; for the word *vadha* is listed alone among the items beginning with *daṇḍa*, and because the rule of extension to [words] ending in that [suffix] is prohibited, and because there would be a difference in accent. For if the suffix *yat* were added to the word *asivadha*, the circumflex (*svarita*) accent would result according to Pāṇini 6.1.185 (*tit svaritam*). However, when there is a compound with a *kṛt*-derived word, by the rule of the original accent of the final member of a *kṛt*-derivative (*kṛduttarapada-prakṛtisvara*), the word *vadhya* is accented on its first syllable.

For this very reason, one should not claim that there is a compound with the word *vadhya* ending in a *taddhita* suffix according to Pāṇini 2.1.4 (*sup supā*), because that would result in the word being oxytone (*antodātta*). Furthermore, in the word *vadhya*, which ends in a *kṛt* or *taddhita* suffix, the specific distinction created by the presence of the suffix *ka* exists. By this, the Bhāṣya—which aims to reject the Vārttika *girau ḍaś chandasi*—is also refuted. Consequently, rules such as Pāṇini 4.3.38 (*kṛtalabdhakrītakuśalāḥ*) find their proper application; such is the direction of the argument.

By a careful examination of the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on this point and other sources, it is understood that there is no distinction between the uncompounded form *vadhyam* and [the compound]. Thus, the rule is simply *daṇḍādibhyaḥ*, with *yat* being supplied from the context. Mādhava, in his commentary on the root *han*, clarified that the reading *daṇḍādibhyo yat* without the anubandha is erroneous.

Upon a careful examination of Haradatta’s work, however, it appears that the intended meaning of the Bhāṣya is that this rule—which is read even in the section on the *vidhi* (prescriptive rules) in the Bhāṣya and other texts—should instead be placed immediately before the rule "mṛjervibhāṣā" (Pāṇini 3.1.113) regarding the formation of the *kyap* suffix; for this results in greater brevity by avoiding the formulation of an optional alternative (*vikalpa*). Even under that view, the word *vadhya* is udātta on its first syllable due to the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*), whereas the *kyap* suffix is anudātta because it is marked with the *pi*-diacritic.

Furthermore, in the case of a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), the desired result is achieved through the application of Pāṇini Sūtra 6.2.160, *yayatoścātadarthe kṛtyoktaṣṇuccārvādayaśca*; moreover, it is precisely when uncompounded that the absence of distinction is to be conveyed (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.98).

Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.98: *adupadhāt* || The suffix *yat* shall be applied after a verbal root ending in a labial (*pa-varga*) consonant and having *a* as its penultimate vowel (*upadhā*). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *ṇyat*. Examples: *śapyam*, *labhyam*. Why [is it said] "after a labial"? Consider *vākyam*; here, by Pāṇini Sūtra 7.3.52 (*cajoḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ*), there is the substitution of *ku* (i.e., *k* for *c* and *j*). Why "having *a* as its penultimate vowel"? Consider *kopyam*. Why is the *t* in *tapara* (the *a* with the *t*) used? Consider *āpyam*. From the roots *kup* (DhP 1.27) meaning "to be angry" and *āplṛ* (Svādi 14) meaning "to pervade," when the suffix *ṇyat* is applied, the accent falls on the suffix-initial (*titsvara*). However, if the suffix *yat* were applied instead, the accent would be governed by Pāṇini Sūtra 6.1.213 (*yato 'nāvaḥ*). Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.99: *śakisahośca* || This is clear. Examples: *śakyam*, *sahyam*.

(Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.100): *gadamadacarayamaś cānupasarge*. The locative case is used here by transposition in the sense of the ablative. The suffix *yat* shall be applied after these roots when no prefix (*upasarga*) precedes them: *gadyam*, *madyam*, *caryam*, *yamyam*. Why "without a prefix"? As in: "This is not to be spoken (*nigādyam*) concerning the Nishadhan. [Examples with prefixes: *pramādyam*, *pracāryam*. Since the application of *yat* after the root *yami-* is already established by the preceding rule, this statement is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtham*), so that it may apply only when there is no prefix and not when there is one. Thus, [the forms] *prayamyam* and *saṃyamyam* are excluded.

How then are [the following] to be understood: “*tena na tatra bhaved viniyamyam*,” “*aniyamyasya nāyuktiḥ*,” and “*tvayā niyamyā nanu divyacakṣuṣā*”? This is simply a faulty reading (*pramādapāṭha*). Haradatta maintains that one must read *viniyāmyam* and so forth with a long vowel. Others hold that *niyamya* means “one who is skillful (*sādhu*) in restraint (*niyama*),” according to Pāṇini 4.4.98 (*tatra sādhuḥ*). Still others say that the word *kevalāt* is used, forming a compound with the word *ni-* [to produce *niyamya*].

*Ācārya-rāṅi cāgurau* (Kātyāyana-vārttika). This Vārttika is for the purpose of including the sense of a preposition (*upasarga*). *Ācārya-deśaḥ*: meaning "one who is to be approached" (*gantavya*). Why "not when it means a teacher" (*agurau*)? [Because] *ācāryo guruḥ* ("the teacher is the guru"). (Pāṇini-sūtra 3.1.101)

*Avadya*, *paṇya*, and *varya* are irregularly formed (*nipātana*) in the senses of "blameworthy," "to be sold," and "prohibition" respectively (Pāṇini 3.1.101). These three terms—*avadya* and the others—are established as irregular forms corresponding respectively to the meanings "blameworthy" (*garhya*) and so forth. In that context, when the prefix *nañ* is used with the root *vad*, both the suffixes *yat* and *kyap* would apply by virtue of the rule "after *vad*, when a *sup*-ending word follows, *kyap* and [the general *yat*] are applied" (Pāṇini 3.1.106). This irregular formation (*nipātana*) serves a dual purpose: to ensure that *yat* alone is used, and to restrict its application specifically to the sense of "blame. Thus, *avadya* means "sin" (*pāpa*), because it is not fit to be spoken. Why "blameworthy"? Consider the example: "The names of one's teachers are not to be uttered" (*anudyaṃ gurunām*). For while those names are indeed not blameworthy, they are simply not fit to be uttered.
One who desires his own welfare should not utter his own name, nor the name of his teacher, nor the name of one who is extremely wretched, nor the names of his eldest child or his wife.

This is according to the traditional rule (*smṛti*). Here, by the rule *vadaḥ supi* (Pāṇini 3.1.106), only the suffix *kyap* occurs. Because it belongs to the *yajādi* class, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*). By the rules *nalopo nañaḥ* and *tasmānnuḍaci* (Pāṇini 6.3.73, 74), the elision of the *n* of the negative particle is applied, and the augment *nuṭ* is added after that. Regarding the word *paṇya*, although the suffix *ṇyat* would have been expected from the root *paṇ* in the sense of "dealing," this specific form is prescribed [by the rule *paṇa vyavahāre*]. Thus, *paṇyaḥ kambalaḥ* ("a woolen blanket for sale") and *paṇyā gauḥ* ("a cow for sale"). However, *pāṇyam* has a different meaning; it means "worthy of praise.

Even though the word *paṇitavya* is common to both meanings, because the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) serves to establish a conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), and because the word *paṇya* is conventionally restricted to things intended for trade, the restriction of meaning is obtained. And it has been said:

"Roots, suffixes, tenses, and moods are for the purpose of attaining [specific forms], while the restriction [of suffixes] and the irregular formations (nipātana) are for the purpose of establishing conventional usage. Regarding the root *vṛṅ* in the sense of "choosing" (*saṃbhaktau*, DhP 3.1.37): from this root, the suffix *yat* is applied to form *varya*. The phrase "a maiden to be chosen by no less than a hundred thousand" indicates that the words *śata* and *sahasra* here denote indefinite numbers; the meaning is that there is no fixed limit on the number of suitors who may choose the maiden. This is an irregular formation (*nipātana*) specifically from the root *vṛṅ*, because it is only in that context that the possibility of non-restriction (*anirodha*) arises. Therefore, from the root *vṛñ* in the sense of "choosing" (*varaṇe*, DhP 10.286), only the suffix *kyap* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.109 (*eti-stu-śā-s-* etc.), resulting in the form *vṛtyā*.

In this sūtra, *avadya* and the following terms are separate words lacking case-endings (*avibhaktika*), and not a dual-ended (*jasant*) *dvandva* compound. Consequently, *varya* is prescribed as a feminine form only. However, in the masculine, the suffix *ṇyat* applies according to Pāṇini 3.1.124 (*ṛhaloḥ*), resulting in *vāryāḥ* for the officiating priests (*ṛtvijaḥ*); such is the opinion of the author of the Vṛtti. Nor should one suspect the application of the suffix *kyap* here by Pāṇini 3.1.109 (*etistu*), because it will be stated later that in that rule only the root *vṛñ* (to choose) is intended, and not *vṛṅ* (to choose). Bhaṭṭi, however, considering the reference to be a *dvandva* with a *jas* ending, employed the masculine form *yata*.
"Sugrīva is my friend, he who possesses beautiful prowess"—thus [it is said].
The same applies to *puruṣottama* and others. (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.102)

*Vahyam* is an irregularly formed term (*nipātana*) when it denotes an instrument (*karaṇa*). *Vahyam* means "that by which one carries"; thus, a cart (*śakaṭa*) is called *vahyam*. Why "when it is an instrument"? [In other cases] it is *vāhyam*, meaning something else that is the object of carrying (*vahanakarma*).
(Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.102–103)

*aryaḥ svāmivaiśyayoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.103). From the root *ṛ* "to go" (*bhvādigaṇa*, parasmaipada, 961), although the suffix *ṇyat* would normally apply, the suffix *yat* is here prescribed as a nipātana (irregular formation). Thus, *aryaḥ* means either a master (*svāmin*) or a Vaiśya. Why specify "of a master or a Vaiśya"? [Because] an *ārya* who is a Brāhmaṇa means one who is "to be attained" (*prāptavya*). Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "In the sense of 'master,' there is also udātta accent on the final syllable. However, when it refers to a Vaiśya, by the rule *yato'nāvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.213), it is simply udātta on the first syllable.

Now, if it is asked: "What is the case when the word *vaiśya* denotes both [a Vaiśya and] a master (*svāmin*)?"—if the intention is to express its status as a Vaiśya, it is udātta on the first syllable; if the intention is to express its status as a master, it is udātta on the final syllable. For this very reason, the term *ākhyā* ("designation") was included in the *phiṭ-sūtra*: "The word *arya*, when it is a designation for a master. Thus, the resulting meaning is that in such a context, one must certainly not intend to express both meanings simultaneously. (Pāṇini Sūtra 6.2.104)

The word *upasaryā* is derived from the root *sṛ* preceded by *upa*, belonging to both the *bhūvādika* and *juhotyādika* classes, with the suffix *yat* applied when the cow has reached the proper time for conception during her first pregnancy. It means a cow fit to be approached by a bull for the purpose of impregnation. Why is it specified "at the proper time for conception"? Consider: *śaradi madhurā upasāryā*, meaning "the city of Madhurā is to be visited in autumn"; here the suffix is *ṇyat* used in the sense of the object (*karman*).

Regarding the word *kālya* here: while the phrase *tadasya prāptam* ("that has been reached by him") is in effect, the suffix *yat* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.1.107 (*kālād yat*). *Prajana* means "procreation"; the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). By Pāṇini 7.3.35 (*janivadhyośca*), the prohibition of *vṛddhi* applies. (Pāṇini 3.1.105).

*Ajaryaṃ saṅgatam* (Pāṇini 3.1.105). The suffix *yaṅ* is prescribed after the root *jṛ* preceded by the negative particle *nañ* when used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), provided that *saṅgatam* is the object to be qualified. The word *saṅgatam* is derived from the neuter abstract noun (*bhāva*) using the suffix *kta*. Thus, *ajaryam* means "the association of the virtuous which does not decay. Here, one should not take the meaning to be that the entire compound *ajaryam* has *saṅgatam* as its expressed referent (*vācya*), because such a simultaneous usage would be untenable in the examples. Nor can this simultaneous usage be explained as being merely for the sake of commentary, like the expression "a jar is a *kalaśa*," because of the usage found in Bhāravi’s poem: *tena saṅgatam āryeṇa rāmājaryaṃ kuru drutam* ("Therefore, quickly form an undecaying association with that noble Rāma").

"By means of deer, he bound himself again to the bondage of the body with that which is taught by old age as being 'not to be worn out' (ajarīyam). This usage by Kālidāsa must be explained by supplying the word "saṅgatam" (association). What is the association? It is the "ajaritā kambalaḥ" (the non-wearing woolen blanket). Since it is stated that [the suffix] occurs in the sense of the agent, the suffix *ṇyat* occurs even when the state (*bhāva*) has the "association" as its agent: "ajāryaṃ saṅgatena" (Pāṇini 3.1.106).

Regarding the rule *vadaḥ supi kyap ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.106): the author of the Vṛtti states that the term *anupasarge* ("when there is no prefix") is understood [from the previous rule] to apply here as well. Thus, when the root *vad* is followed by a nominal stem (*sup*) as an upapada and is not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*), the suffix *kyap* shall be applied, and optionally *yat*. Examples are *brahmodyam* and *brahmavadyam*. Here, *kyap* is used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*); as before, there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*). *Brahman* means the Veda; the meaning is "the speaking of that."

If it is objected: "Is it not the case that a *kṛt* suffix in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*) is difficult to obtain after a transitive verb, since it will be stated later [in Pāṇini’s sūtras] that 'the *kṛt* suffixes in the sense of an abstract action occur after intransitive verbs' (Pā. 3.4.69) and 'the *kṛtya*, *kta*, and *khal*-affixes occur only after those two [verbs]' (Pā. 3.4.70)? True; however, there is no such fault here because the term 'abstract action' (*bhāva*) from the subsequent sūtra is drawn back [into this one]."

Although the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *anupasarga* (not being preceded by a prefix) in this sūtra is established in the Vṛtti, the Bhāṣya, and other works, it is nevertheless not strictly necessary. This is because the inclusion of the term *upasarga* in the sūtra *satsūdviṣa-* (Pāṇini 3.2.61) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that "in other instances where *sub* is mentioned, *upasarga* is not included," as will be stated later; thus, the point is already understood. Furthermore, the result—that there is no [application] when a prefix is present—is beyond dispute. Therefore, in this context, we have *ṇyadeva-pravādyam*, *anuvādyam*, and *apavādyam*.

As for the term "anūdyam" used in the *Bhaṭṭavārttika* within the section on Grammar (*Vyākaraṇādhikaraṇa*), it is clearly explained in the *Nyāyasudhā* that this can be somehow resolved by applying the suffix *kyap* with the word "anu" as an attendant (*upapada*) in the sense of certainty, followed by a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*). Regarding the rule *bhuvo bhāve* (Pāṇini 3.1.107): the suffix *kyap* occurs after the root *bhū* when an *upasarga*-less nominal stem (*sup*) is the attendant (*upapada*), in the sense of state (*bhāva*). As for why [the word *anupasarge*] does not carry over [from the previous rule], it is because it was not drawn forward (*anukṛṣṭa*) in the preceding sūtra. Examples: *brahmaṇo bhāvaḥ* = *brahmabhūyam*. Only when there is a nominal stem (*sup*)—as in *bhavyam*. Only when there is no *upasarga*—as in *prabhavyam*.

If it is argued: "But surely, when not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*), the root *bhū* is intransitive; therefore, it will apply only to the abstract state (*bhāva*). So what is the purpose of explicitly mentioning 'the abstract state' (*bhāva*)? Do not say so. For [if it were not mentioned], there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of its application to the object (*karman*) when the sense is 'to obtain'; and even from the root meaning 'to exist,' there would be the undesirable consequence of its application to time and other such objects of action (*kāla-karman*). Furthermore, it is for the sake of the subsequent rules. (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.108)

*hanasta ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.108). After the root *han*, when it is followed by a nominal ending (*subanta*) that is not a prefix (*anupasarga*), the suffix *kyap* occurs in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*), and the letter *t* is substituted for the final [n]. Thus, *brahmahatyā*. By its very nature, a word ending in the suffix *kyap* prescribed by this rule is feminine in gender in common usage. However, in the Vedic language (*chandas*), even neuter gender is accepted, as in: *sanādeva dasyuhatyāya jajñiṣe*.

In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), the suffix *kyap* should be stated as an option for feminine nouns. [Example: "He who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice overcomes even the murder of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyām tarati*). Why [is the condition] "after a root ending in *su*" (*supi*) mentioned? [Counter-example: "The striking (*ghātaḥ*) proceeds. However, the suffix *ṇyat* does not apply here, because its prescription is for the abstract state (*bhāve*) after a transitive root. Even when the root is intransitive due to the non-intentionality of the object (*karmāvivakṣāyām akarmakatve’pi*), [the suffix *ṇyat*] still does not apply, because it is not so taught. [The rule applies] only when there is no prefix (*anupasarge*). [Counter-example with prefix: "The striking (*praghātaḥ*) proceeds. (Pāṇini 3.1.109)

The suffix *kyap* is applied after the roots *i*, *etu*, *śās*, *vṛ*, *dṛ*, and *juṣ* (Pāṇini 3.1.109). The phrase "after a verbal root ending in a vowel, when no prefix is present, and denoting an action (*bhāva*)" is no longer in force here. The suffix *kyap* shall apply after these [roots]. In the word "eti," only the root *iṇ* is intended to be included, not the roots *iṅ* (to study) and *ik* (to go), because those two are used only with the prefix *adhi*, and thus the mention of "eti" would otherwise be untenable. Accordingly, the form *etya* was employed in the *Mahābhāṣya*: "Thus is grammar [studied] even today for the protection of the Vedas. Some, however, citing the statement "it should be stated that *ik* is treated like *iṇ*" (*kārikā-vārttika*), cite *adhītyam* as an example. Thus: *ityaḥ*.

How, then, is the word *upeya* derived? It is formed from the root *iṅ* (meaning "to go," *dioāo* 37), belonging to the *divādi* class, with the suffix *yat*. Thus, it means "one who is to be praised" (*stutyaḥ*). Regarding the word *śiṣyaḥ*: by the rule *śāsa idaṅhaloḥ* (*pāosūo* 6.4.34), the vowel *i* is substituted [for the final *ā*], and by the rule *śāsivasi* (*pāosūo* 8.3.60), the letter *ṣ* is substituted [for the *s*]. The root *āṅaḥ śāsu* in the sense of "desire" (*icchāyām*, *aoāo* 12) is also included here because there is no distinction made. Consequently, the form *āśāsyam* has its middle syllable accented (*madhyodātta*) according to the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*). However, if the suffix *ṇyat* were used, the suffix would be circumflex-accented on the final syllable (*antasvaritatva*) according to the rule *gatikārakopapadātkṛt*.

However, some maintain that only the root *śās* (in the sense of "instruction," *anuśiṣṭau*, Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.55) is intended here. The inclusion of *vṛ* refers to *vṛñ* (the causative/secondary root), and not to *vṛṅ* (the primary root meaning "to choose"), because of the evidence provided by the fact that both roots are included due to their association with the preceding and following ones. This is indicated by the rule "īḍavandavṛśaṃsaduhāṃ ṇyataḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.21), which prescribes the acute accent on the initial syllable of the word *vārya*. For in that rule, due to the association with *īḍ* and *vand*, which have vowel-initial verbal suffixes (*akāra-vat-pratyaya*), it is the *ātmanepada*-forming root *vṛṅ* that is understood. Thus: *vṛtyaḥ*, *dṛtyaḥ*, *juṣyaḥ*.

The re-mention of *kyap* while [the rule for] *kyap* is already in force is for the purpose of overriding an overriding rule (*bādhakabādhanārtham*). Consequently, by overriding the suffix *ṇyat* prescribed by the rule "orāvaśyake" (Pāṇini 3.1.125), only *kyap* occurs. To illustrate: in this sūtra, the application of the mention of *stauti* finds its scope in cases where necessity is not intended, such as *stutya*; the scope of "orāvaśyake" is found in *avaśyalāvyam*. In the case of *avaśyastutyaḥ*, where both would apply, *ṇyat* would occur by virtue of being the subsequent rule; however, due to the re-mention of *kyap*, only *kyap* occurs.

It should be stated that [the suffix *yat*] is optionally applied after the roots *śaṃs*, *duh*, and *guh* (as per the Kāśikāvṛtti): *śasyam* or *śaṃsyam*; *duhyam* or *dohyam*; *guhyam* or *gohyam*. This point is established in the Vṛtti itself. However, it does not appear in the Bhāṣya; therein, the form for *śaṃs* is established by the authority of two rules: "The substitute *śra* replaces *praśasya*" (Pāṇini 5.3.60) and "The augment *iṭ* is added to the roots *iḍ*, *vand*, *vṛ*, *śaṃs*, and *duh* when followed by the suffix *ṇyat*" (Pāṇini 6.1.214). As for the other two roots (*duh* and *guh*), their source must be sought elsewhere.

There is an addition [to the rule] regarding the formation of a name from the root *añj* preceded by the prefix *ā*. The root *añj* (meaning "to manifest," "to smear," etc. takes the suffix *kyap* in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) due to its frequent occurrence (*bāhulaka*). By the rule *aniditāṃ hala upadhāyāḥ kṅiti* (Pāṇini 6.4.24), there is elision of the nasal (*n*), resulting in *ājyam*. If one asks: "Why is it not stated that the elision of the nasal occurs specifically before the suffix *ṇyat*?"—the answer is no, because that would result in the substitution of *kutva* (the change of *j* to *g*) and the application of the accent of a *tit* suffix. Therefore, this word ends in *kyap* alone. If one objects: "In that case, the rule for *avagraha* (word-separation in the Pada-pāṭha) would apply, which is not desired, since the makers of the Pada-text do not separate it—as seen in such passages as *'ājyaṃ kimāsītparidhiḥ ka āsīt'*"—[the response is: No, for there is no such fault. The *avagraha* does not occur here because the word is treated as a single unit in the context of the ritual or the specific derivation intended. Thus, the form *ājyam* is established.

Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "The authors of the *pada-pāṭha* are not to be followed by the author of the grammatical rules (*lakṣaṇa*); rather, the author of the grammatical rules is to be followed by the authors of the *pada-pāṭha*. The intention here is as follows: the *saṃhitā* alone is eternal, whereas the separation of words (*padaviccheda*) is a human convention. For this very reason, because there is no certainty regarding the meaning [of such divisions], they do not perform *avagraha* (separation). For example, in the word *haridrava*.

In this regard, there arises a doubt as to whether the word *hari* ends in the vowel *i*, or whether the word *harit* ends in the consonant *t*. Furthermore, having introduced the mantra "vanena vāyaḥ" with the statement, "Śākalya read it as 've'ti and 'caya' iti," Yāska refutes this by pointing out that if it were so, the word *adhāyi* would have resulted in an udātta accent due to the application of the augment *aṭ*; subsequently, establishing the conclusion that "vāya" means "the offspring of Vi" (*verapatyam*) as a single compound, Yāska makes it perfectly clear that the division of words (*padavibhāga*) is a human construct.

Furthermore, regarding the statement, "Moreover, the *avagraha* occurs when there is a word-boundary (*padatva*), but not when there is none; thus both [rules] are merely conventional assertions to be followed out of deference to traditional usage," this is because there is no *avagraha* in such cases as "īyivāṃsam atis tridhaḥ" and "devayanto yathāmatim. Conversely, there is an *avagraha* in cases such as "īyivāṃsam atis tridhaḥ" and "devayanto yathāmatim. This is the general direction. However, in the *Prakriyākaumudī*, it is stated that for the root *aj* in the sense of "going" and "throwing" (*bhvādi-gaṇa*, 230), the form is *ājyam*; but that contradicts the *Mahābhāṣya* and is inconsistent with the meaning, and thus should be disregarded by authoritative scholars.
(Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.110)

Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.110: *ṛdupadhāccāklṛpicṛteḥ*. The suffix *kyap* shall be applied after a verbal root that has *ṛ* as its penultimate vowel (*upadhā*), with the exception of the roots *kṛp* and *cṛt*. *Vṛt*: *vṛtyam*. *Vṛdh*: *vṛdhyam*. Why is it said "with the exception of *kṛp* and *cṛt*"? [Consider: *kṛp* (in the sense of capability, *bhvādigaṇa*, no. 763): *kalpyam*. Because the substitution of *l* for *r* in *kṛp* is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) [at the time of applying this rule], and because *ṛ* and *ḷ* are prescribed to have the same phonetic class (*savarṇa*) designation, the root still possesses an *ṛ* in its penultimate position. *cṛt* (in the senses of harming and tying, *tudādigaṇa*, no. 44): *cartyam*.

What is the purpose of the long vowel marker (tapara)? In the case of the root *kṝ* (meaning "to scatter," *cuādigaṇa* 120), when the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is absent, only *ṇyat* occurs: *kīrtyam*. This very use of the long vowel marker is the evidence for the rule that "the *curādi* roots are not necessarily [restricted to] having the causative suffix. However, when the causative suffix is present, whether the suffix is elided or not, it is exactly like the word *ditsyam*. Consequently, by the rule *yato 'nāvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.213), the initial syllable is udātta-accented. (Pāṇini 3.1.111).

*ī ca khanaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.111). The suffix *kvip* shall be applied after the root *khan*, and the vowel *ī* shall be substituted for the final letter [of the root]. The mention of the long vowel (*ī*) is for the purpose of including the short vowel (*i*) by means of *praśleṣa* (conjunction). Therein, the second *i* is for the purpose of precluding the substitution of *ā* by the rule *ye vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 6.4.43). Otherwise, the scope of *ye vibhāṣā* would be *khāyate* and *khanyate*; whereas the scope of the [substitution of] *i* would be that alternative in which the substitution of *ā* does not occur. When both [substitutions] would apply in the case of the *ā*-substitution, the substitution of *ā* would take effect because it is subsequent and internal (*antaraṅga*).

In the rule *ye vibhāṣā*, the locative case is one of domain (*viṣaya-saptamī*). Thus, when the suffix beginning with *y* is present in the mind, the substitution of *ā* (ātvam) is internal (*antaraṅga*). This substitution of *i* (ittvam), however, is external (*bahiraṅga*) because it is prescribed together with the suffix *kyap*. Therefore, having adopted the position that in *ye vibhāṣā* the locative denotes the domain, the author of the Sūtra performed the vocalization of the long vowel (*dīrghoccāraṇam*). But the author of the Bhāṣya rejected this by adopting the locative of contiguity (*parasaptamī*). For in the view of the locative of contiguity, the substitution of *i* is internal, since it is prescribed without depending on a subsequent cause.

For that [substitution] is prescribed by the rule of *kyaṅ-sanniyoga*; and thus, it alone is the sublater of the short vowel (*atva*). If it is argued: "Even if the substitution of a short vowel occurs, and subsequently the *guṇa* substitution of *ā* takes place with the preceding vowel, the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) would still be considered 'unestablished' (*asiddha*) by the rule *ṣatvatukorasiddhaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.86). Consequently, by the rule *hrasvasya piti kṛti tuk* (Pāṇini 6.1.71), the *tuk* augment would apply; therefore, the long vowel (*dīrgha*) itself must be prescribed"—we say no. This is because it will be stated later that the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) between the end of a word and the beginning of a word is unestablished (*asiddha*) for the application of the *tuk* augment, but not any other [single-substitute].

Otherwise, in the case of *vṛkṣe chatram*, because the *ād-guṇa* [substitution] would be treated as non-established (*asiddha*) with respect to the locative suffix *ṅi*, the rule *che ca* (Pāṇini 6.1.73) would cause the obligatory insertion of *tuk* based on the short vowel; however, what is desired is that the rule *dīrghāt padāntādvā* (Pāṇini 6.1.75–76) applies—this is the direction. The rule *bhṛño’saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 3.1.112) states: after the root *bhṛ*, the suffix *kyap* shall occur when it does not denote a technical name (*saṃjñā*). Thus, *bhṛtyāḥ karmakarāḥ* ("servants who are to be supported"), meaning they are those who ought to be maintained. Consequently, this is a word denoting an action (*kriyāśabda*), and not a proper name.

The suffix *kyap* is generally used in the sense of the feminine (*samā*); however, this Vārttika provides for its optional use even when it is already established by rule as being obligatory in non-technical senses (*asaṃjñā*). Examples: *sambhūtiḥ*, *sambhāryā*. Why "in a non-technical sense"? Consider *bhāryaḥ*, which refers to a Kṣatriya.
Since the word *bhārya* is observed in the masculine in the sense of a name (*saṃjñā*), the form *bhāryā* would not be established [by Pāṇini 3.1.104] in that context.
But since there is a governing rule for the abstract state (*bhāva*) in the feminine, *bhāryā* is thus established.
Alternatively, it is recorded in the grammatical tradition that the suffix *kṛtya* is frequently used in the sense of a nominalization (*saṃjñā*);
thus, she is just like a wife (*patyam*), just like a bride (*janyam*), and just like a wall (*bhitti*).

The meaning of this is as follows: for you, the author of the Sūtras, the word *bhāryā* would not be established; for, setting aside [the suffix] *ṇyat*, there would be the contingency of *kyap* by virtue of the rule "In the sense of a name, after the roots *samaja*, *niṣad*, etc. (Pāṇini 3.3.99). Now, one might argue: "Since the prohibition of *kyap* in the sense of a name is established by force of the prohibition in the current sūtra 'After the root *nṛñ*, not in the sense of a name' (Pāṇini 3.1.112), the *kyap* that would otherwise apply to the root *bhṛñ* by another rule such as 'In the sense of a name' (Pāṇini 3.3.99) will not occur when it refers to a name."

Nor is the term "in the sense of a name" (*saṃjñāyām*) redundant there, because it has its purpose fulfilled in other verbal roots; having raised this objection, he says "in the sense of a name," etc. The word "of the prohibition" (*pratiṣedhasya*) is to be supplied as the remainder. This is because the prohibition of the [suffix] *it* in the rule "not when not a name" (*asaṃjñāyām*) has already served its purpose in the masculine form "a Kṣatriya named Bhāryā," since it is seen there that the purpose is fulfilled. Thus, the point is that there is no further capacity [for the suffix]. Therefore, the objection that the word *bhāryā* cannot be established remains valid.

He states the answer: "There is the governing rule of *bhāva* (abstract state) with respect to the feminine. But surely, in the sūtra *saṃjñāyāṃ samaja-* (Pāṇini 3.3.99), the author of the Vṛtti will say that the term *bhāve* is not intended as a restrictive accent (*svarita*), and thus the previous governing rule [of *karaṇe*] alone applies. And this is logical, given such examples as *samajanti tasyām iti saṃjvā* ("they assemble therein, thus it is a 'gathering place'") and *niṣīdanti tasyām iti niṣadyā* ("they sit therein, thus it is a 'seating place'"). So how can it be said that "there is the governing rule of *bhāva* with respect to the feminine"? True.

In the section on feminine nouns (*strī-prakaraṇa*), when the suffix *kyap* is prescribed by rules such as "in the sense of a name (*saṃjñāyām*) after the root *sam-aj*" and so forth, there exists an operation (*vyāpāra*) characterized by the assumption of the state (*bhāva*) as the denoted meaning. Due to the inherent nature of the word’s expressive power (*śabda-śakti-svābhāvya*), the suffix *kyap* applies only to the state (*bhāva*) and not to the object (*karman*).

Out of dissatisfaction with this [explanation], he says "Alternatively" (*athavā*). That by which one does not fall is *apatya* (offspring). Although the suffix *yat* is prescribed after bases ending in vowels (*ajanta*) in the sense of abstract state (*bhāva*) or action (*karman*), here it occurs after a base ending in a consonant (*halanta*) in the sense of instrument (*karaṇa*). In the word *janya*, *yat* likewise follows a consonantal base; in *bhitti*, the suffix *ktin* occurs in place of *aṅ*—as prescribed by Pāṇini’s rule *ṣidbhidādibhyo’ṅ* (Pāṇ. 3.3.104)—which would otherwise have applied. Just as all this occurs by virtue of the principle of diversity (*bāhulaka*), so too in the case of the word *bhāryā*, the suffix *ṇyat* occurs in place of *kyap*. This is the meaning.

Alternatively, this may be resolved as follows: in the rule for the suffix *kyap*, only the root *bhṛ* from the *bhvādi* class (*bhṛñ bharaṇe*, Dhp. 1.923) is taken, and not the root *ḍubhṛñ* from the *juhotyādi* class (*ḍubhṛñ bharaṇe*, Dhp. 3.5), because the former has two indicatory letters (*anubandha*). Thus, the word *bhāryā* is derived without any obstacle either from *vibhṛ*—as in the form *bhṛñ bharaṇe* with a long vowel (*dīrghānta*) belonging to the *kryādi* class—or from the *kryādi* root itself, by means of the suffix *aṇ*. (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.113).

*mṛjer vibhāṣā* (Pāṇini 3.1.113). Since the suffix *kyap* would apply obligatorily because the root has *ṛt* as its penultimate letter (*ṛdupadha*), this sūtra is for the purpose of providing an option. Thus we have *parimṛjyaḥ* and *parimārgyaḥ*. In the alternative case where the suffix *ṇyat* is applied, there is vocalic strengthening (*vṛddhi*) by *mṛjer vṛddhiḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.114), and the substitution of *k* (known as *kutva*) by *cajoḥ kughiṇṇyatoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.52).
The words *rājasūya*, *sūrya*, *mṛṣodya*, *rucya*, *kupva*, *kṛṣṭapacya*, and *āvavya* [are formed with the suffix *kyap*]. (Pāṇini 3.1.114)

These seven words ending in *kyap* are derived as irregular forms (*nipātana*). In the sense that a consecrated Kṣatriya is a *rājā* (king), and that [Soma] is to be pressed—that is, produced—by means of the pressing-rite, the suffix *kyap* is applied in the objective sense (*karman*). The lengthening of the vowel is also an irregularity for the sake of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). Alternatively, Soma in its form as a creeper is the *rājā*, as seen in such passages as "they purchase the king. In the sense that he is pressed—that is, crushed—here, the suffix *kyap* is applied in the locative sense (*adhikaraṇa*). The irregular derivation is for the sake of conventional usage.

Therefore, there is no over-extension [of the term] in the case of the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) and so forth under the first view, nor in the case of the *jyotiṣṭoma* and so forth under the second view. Furthermore, the word *rājasūya* is both masculine and neuter because it belongs to the *ardharcādi* group. *Sūrya* means "he who moves through the path of the sky. From the root *sṛ* ("to go," *bhvādigaṇa*, *parasmaipada*, 960), the suffix *kyap* is applied in the sense of the agent; by irregular derivation (*nipātana*), the vowel *u* is substituted, followed by the substitution of *ra* for the semivowel, and lengthening according to Pāṇini 8.2.77 (*hali ca*). Alternatively, it is derived from *ṣū* ("to impel," *tudādigaṇa*, 128).

In the sense of "impelling the world toward a good action" (*suvati-karmaṇi lokaṃ prerayati*), when the suffix *kyap* is applied to the root *su*, the augment *ruṭ* is also prescribed as a *nipātana*. After the root *vad* with the prefix *mṛṣā*, the suffix *kyap* is used in the passive sense (*karmaṇi*). Since the suffix *yat* would otherwise be applicable, *kyap* is prescribed here as mandatory. This word is *viśeṣyanighna* (its gender depends on the noun it qualifies). As Māgha says in the *Śiśupālavadha* (4.10): "The qualities of loftiness and beauty found in poets whose speech is unrestrained do not become false [when described]. The word *rucya* means "that which shines"; the suffix *kvap* is applied in the active sense (*kartari*).

The substitution of *ku* for the initial [guttural] of *gup* and others occurs when forming a technical name (*saṃjñā*). Thus, *kupya*. This is a term for wealth other than gold and silver. *Kṛṣṭapacyāḥ* refers to those that ripen by themselves in a ploughed field; this is an irregular formation (*nipātana*) used with the agent as the subject (*karmakartṛ*). Here, the acute accent on the final syllable is also irregularly applied. But when the object (*karman*) is intended, it becomes simply *kṛṣṭapākyaḥ*. *Avyathyaḥ* means "that which does not waver"; here the suffix *kyap* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*). On this point, there are Vārttikas: "In the case of *sū*, *ruc*, and *vyath*, the suffix *kyap* is used in the sense of the agent."
And after the roots *sū* and *sarti*, there is the substitution of *u* for the *ṛ* of the root *sṛ* (according to the Kātantra-vyākaraṇa).
Alternatively, [the suffix] *ruṭ* is added to the root *sū* [to form *sūru*] (*kāśikāvṛtti*). [The word] *kupya* [is formed with the suffix *kyap*] when it is a proper name (*kāśikāvṛtti*).

"The roots *bhid* and *ujjh* [take the suffix *kyap*] when referring to a river" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 3.1.115). The suffix *kyap* is applied to the roots *bhid* and *ujjh* in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*), and there is the substitution of *dh* for the final letter of *ujjh*. That which breaks the bank is *bhidya*; that which abandons the water is *uddhya*. Why "when referring to a river"? [Counter-examples: *bhettā* (one who breaks), *ujjhitā* (one who abandons). (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 3.1.116)

*Puṣya-sidhyau nakṣatre* (Pāṇini 3.1.116). The suffix *kyap* is prescribed after the roots *puṣ* and *sidh* when used in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), provided that a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) is to be expressed. [The word] *puṣya* is so called because "in this [mansion], undertakings flourish" (*puṣyanti asmin ārabdhā arthāḥ*). [The word] *sidhya* is so called because "in this [mansion], things succeed" (*sidhyanti asmin*). Why specify "when a lunar mansion is to be expressed"? [To exclude cases such as] nourishing (*poṣaṇam*) or succeeding (*sedhanam*). The words *puṣya* and *sidhya* are synonyms; however, they appear as a *dvandva* compound in the rule because the rule intends to refer to their specific forms. Amara states: "In the [mansion] *puṣya*, [the names] *sidhya* and *tiṣya* are used."

In this context, from the root *tuṣ* in the sense of "to be satisfied" (*tuṣṭau*), the suffix *ṇvuc* is applied in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*) by virtue of the rule of multiplicity (*bāhulakāt*). By the nipātana rule "sūryatiṣya... (*Pāṇini 6.4.149*), the vowel *u* is replaced by *i*, resulting in *tiṣyaḥ*. In his commentary on Amarakośa 3.3.155, Kṣīrasvāmī states that [the word] is derived from the root *tviṣ* in the sense of "to shine" (*dīptau*) (*bhvādi-gaṇa*, no. 1026), ending in the Uṇādi suffix *yak* according to the rule "adhnyādayaśca" (*Uṇādisūtra* 561). The elision of the *v* is due to nipātana (*Pāṇini 3.1.117*).

The suffix *kyap* is irregularly applied (*nipātyate*) after the roots *pūṅ*, *nīñ*, and *ji* when the objects *muñja*, *kalka*, and *halisūpa* are to be expressed, respectively. The root *pūṅ* (meaning "to purify," from the *bhvādigaṇa*) is preceded by the prefix *vi*. *Vipūya* refers to the *muñja* grass. The meaning is: "it must be purified for the purpose of making ropes and the like. *Muñja* is a specific type of grass. *Vinīya* refers to a medicinal paste (*kalka*). This word *kalka* exists [in the sense] of a specific ground medicinal substance. For example:
"A paste consisting of one part each of *pathyā*, ginger, and rock salt should be drunk daily for the destruction of all diseases."

And regarding the word *pāpa* (sinful/evil): beginning with the statement, "Austerity is not a stain, study is not a stain," some [commentators] say that the suffix *-ya* here denotes something belonging to *tamas* (the quality of darkness). Haradatta, however, says it is used without such distinction. Thus Māgha employed it: "with devotion expanding through unrestrained agitation" (*avinīya-sambhrama-vikāsibhaktibhiḥ*). The root *ji* (to conquer) belongs to the *bhvādigaṇa* (Pāṇini 1.3.1). The word *jitya* means a plough (*halī*). Its meaning is "that which is to be drawn by force. A great force is called a *halī*. It refers to a thick wooden beam used for leveling the furrowed ground. The forms *vipavyam*, *vineyam*, and *jeyam* follow accordingly. In all these cases, the suffix *yat* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.97 and 3.1.118.

After the roots *prati* and *api*, the suffix *kyap* is applied to the root *grah*. That which is not to be accepted by one who is intoxicated is "not-to-be-accepted" (*apratigṛhya*). Therefore, it is "not-to-be-grasped" (*anāpigṛhya*).
(Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.119)

It should be stated that this applies to the Vedic language (*chandas*) (as per *Kāśikāvṛtti*). In common worldly usage (*loka*), however, we have *pratigrāhyam* and *apigrāhyam*. The suffix *kyap* is applied after the root *grah* [with the prefix *pra-*]. [The example is] *pragṛhyaṃ padam*. The commentary (*vṛtti*) states that the technical designation *pragṛhya* is prescribed for that [word]. Although the designation *pragṛhya* applies to dual endings and so forth which are parts of a word (*padāvayava*) and not to the word as a whole (*pada*), nevertheless, one should understand that the property of a part is metaphorically attributed to the whole. Alternatively, this word *pada* is taught here in its etymological sense (*yaugika*), meaning "that by which a meaning is understood" (*gamyate 'nenārthaḥ*).

In this context, the meaning of *asannikarṣa* (non-proximity) refers to houses; for in examples such as *agnī atra*, due to the absence of *yaṇ*-substitution resulting from the *prakṛtibhāva* rule, the vowels are not in close proximity to one another because they are separated by even a small amount of time. Thus, the *Bahvṛca-prātiśākhya* states: "The opening (*vivṛtti*) occurs between vowels, and that [opening] is called *svarabhakti*. Furthermore, the duration of *svarabhakti* is stated in that same work to be either half a *mātrā*, a quarter *mātrā*, or, in longer cases, one and a half *mātrās*.

Thus, the resulting meaning is that the interval between two consonants, known as *vivṛtti*—a period devoid of phonemes—is sometimes half a *mātrā* and sometimes a quarter *mātrā*. This rule is to be understood from the *Śikṣās*. Regarding the term *avagṛhya*, the commentary (*vṛtti*) states: "A word for which an *avagraha* is made. *Avagraha* means separation. Here too, the meaning of the root *grah* is as before; furthermore, according to the *Prātiśākhya*, "the *mātrā* is a short vowel, and it is the interval between *avagrahas*."

Regarding this, Haradatta maintains that at the time of *pada*-formation, only the first member of a compound is to be treated as *avagṛhya*. However, this is merely an illustration, since forms such as *haribhiḥ* are also to be included. Therefore, the established rule is that whatever portion of a word falls under the designation *mahāpada* and is recited separately at the time of *pada*-formation, all of that is *avagṛhya*. One whose nature is to act according to his own will is *svairī*, meaning independent. One who is not *svairī* is *asvairī*, meaning dependent. These are called *gṛhyakāḥ*; the sense is "those who have been taken hold of" (*gṛhītakāḥ*). The suffix *kan* is applied in both cases to express compassion. By this, parrots and other birds rendered dependent through confinement in cages and the like are meant.

"Those attached to their homes are birds and beasts; they are clever and they are domestic," says Amarasimha. In the sense of "external"—as in *grāmagr̥hyā* or *nagaragr̥hyā senā*—the meaning is "an army situated outside the village or city. Due to the feminine gender indication, [the suffix] does not apply to the masculine or neuter genders. In the alternative sense of "belonging to a side" (*pakṣe bhavaḥ*), one has *pakṣyaḥ*; the suffix *yat* is applied because it belongs to the *digādi* group. Examples include *vāsudevagr̥hyaḥ* and *āryagr̥hyaḥ*, which mean "one who has taken refuge in that side" (i.e., *tatpakṣāśrita*). (Pāṇini Sūtra 4.3.120).

The rule *vibhāṣā kṛvṛṣoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.120) states that the suffix *kvap* shall be applied after the roots *kṛ* and *vṛṣ*; alternatively, the suffix *ṇyat* may be used. Thus we have *kṛtyam* and *kāryam*. The root *vṛṣu* (meaning "to sprinkle," from the *bhvādigaṇa*) yields *vṛṣyam* and *varṣyam*. The rule *yugyañ ca patre* (Pāṇini 3.1.121) prescribes that *yugya* is formed with the suffix *kyap* after the root *yuj* when it means "a vehicle" (*patra*). A vehicle is that by which one travels (*patanti anena*). The suffix *ṣṭran* is applied in the sense of an instrument according to the rule *dāmnīśasa-* (Pāṇini 3.2.182). In this specific sense, the suffix *kyap* is applied to *yuj* in the sense of the object (*karman*), and the substitution of *g* for *j* (*kutva*) is also prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*). Thus, *yugya* refers to a "draft ox. Why "in the sense of a vehicle"? Consider *yogyam*, which is something else; here, the suffix *ṇyat* is used, and the substitution of *g* for *j* occurs by the rule *cajoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.52).

Regarding this, Haradatta states: This is established by the suffix *yat* [taught] prior to the *hitīya* section, namely by the rule *tadvahati rathayugaprāsaṅgam* (Pāṇini 4.4.76). There is also no difference in accent: when the suffix *kyap* is applied, there is the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*); when *yat* is applied, there is the initial acute (*ādyudāttatva*) according to the rule *yato ’nāvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.213). Even in the case of *ayugyam*, there is no difference in accent, because in both instances—by the rules *yayatoścātadarthe* (Pāṇini 6.2.156) and *kṛtyokeṣṇuccārvādayaśca* (Pāṇini 6.2.160)—the final acute (*antodāttatva*) is prescribed.
Therefore, this sūtra could have been omitted.

In this regard, the following must be stated: Even though forms such as *yugyo gauḥ* ("an ox for a yoke") are established [by this rule], the example *yugyo hastī* ("an elephant for a yoke") cited in the commentary (*vṛtti*) is not established by a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), for an elephant does not carry a yoke. It is, however, established by a primary derivative suffix (*kṛt*), since it is "yoked" (*yujyate*) for connection with a rug or similar object. Furthermore, if this sūtra did not exist, the form *yogyo gauḥ* would also result from the suffix *ṇyat*. Moreover, there is indeed an optional difference in accent, because in examples such as *kratur bhavaty ukthyaḥ*, the acute accent on the suffixal vowel (*tisvara*) is observed.

In the view propounded by the author of the Vedabhāṣya—that the rule *yato 'nāvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.213) applies only to those words ending in two syllables (*dvyacka*) that have a monosyllabic base (*ekācprakṛtika*)—the difference in accentuation (*svarabheda*) would be unavoidable; such is the direction of the argument. (Pāṇini 3.1.122)

*Amāvasyad anyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 3.1.122). The word *amā* occurs in the sense of "together with," as seen in examples such as *amātyaḥ* ("minister"). When this word is used as an upapada, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied to the root *vas* in the sense of location (*adhikaraṇa*). When the resulting *vṛddhi* [strengthening] has taken place, a short vowel is optionally substituted by nipātana (irregular prescription). Through this very nipātana, the conventional meaning of a specific time is obtained. Because the moon and the sun dwell together (*amā saha*) in close proximity on this day, it is called *amāvasyā* or *amāvāsyā*.

Because that which is modified in one part is not considered different [from the original], the taddhita suffix prescribed after citing the form with a long middle vowel in *amāvāsyāyā vā* (Pāṇini 4.3.30) is established even from the form with a short middle vowel. However, if one were to rely on the view that this is an optional archaic substitution (*nipātana*) for the form ending in the suffix *yat*, then, in the absence of *yat*, the suffix *ṇya* itself would be difficult to obtain in the locative sense as *amāvāsyā*.

Even if it were obtained through the rule *bāhukālāt* (Pāṇini 4.3.61), nevertheless, in the rule *amāvāsyāyā vā*, the mention of the form ending in *ṇya* would not include the form ending in *yat*. Furthermore, in the case of the suffix *ṇya*, there would be no compound with an upapada.

If it is argued that [the form] will occur because [the compound] belongs to the *mayūravyaṃsaka* group (Pāṇini 2.1.72), even so, by the rule "after a root, a kāraka, or an upapada" (Pāṇini 6.2.139), the accent would not be as required; rather, it would be oxytone (*antodātta*). However, what is desired is precisely the accent of the *tit* suffix (Pāṇini 6.1.185), as seen in examples such as *amāvāsyā*, *subhagā*, and *susevā*, as well as in *yadāgneyo 'ṣṭākapālo 'māvāsyāyām*, where both the svarita accent on the word *sva-* and the general rule for the remaining cases (*śeṣanighāta*) are recited.
