Therefore, one must accept the explanation exactly as it is stated: "When there is vṛddhi, the short vowel is optionally substituted for the suffix *-ṇya*. And thus says the Bhāṣya:
I cause the two vowels *a* and *m* to fall together as a single entity (*nipātayāmi*) to prevent their increase;
likewise, their occurrence as one and my own accent are thereby established.

In this context, the dual-number designation is based on a distinction between individual instances; "of one" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. Regarding "the two ending in -ṇya"—that is, those ending in the suffix -ṇya—I prescribe the short vowel for one of them, namely the absence of vṛddhi, when preceded by *am* or *ā* in the case of the root *vas*. This statement is made by the author of the Sūtra as if they had attained identity [with the tradition]. That being so, the fact that there is a single secondary derivative (*taddhita*) application for those two words is established, because that which undergoes a partial modification is not different [from the original]. For me, who prescribes it thus, the accent is also established. And that has already been explained.

Nor should it be argued that even in the established system (*siddhānta*), the original accent of the subsequent member (*uttarapadaprakṛtisvara*) is difficult to obtain because, in the absence of the locative case in the rule, the designation *upapada* does not apply, and thus there is no status of being "subsequent to an *upapada*"—for the intention is that the locative case is indicated by its elision (*luk*) in the form "amā" (Pāṇini 2.4.82). (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.123)

In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), the following seventeen words—*niṣṭarkya*, *devahūya*, *praṇīya*, *unnīya*, *ucchiṣya*, *marya*, *starya*, *adhvaryu*, *khanya*, *khānya*, *devayajyā*, *pṛcchya*, *pratiṣīvya*, *brahmavādya*, *bhāvya*, *stāvya*, *upacāyya*, and *pṛḍā*—are irregularly formed (*nipātyante*). Regarding *niṣṭarkya*: from the root *kṛtī* (meaning "cutting," Dhp. 1.769), although the suffix *kyap* would normally apply after the prefix *nis*, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied instead; there is a transposition of the first and last letters [of the root], and the substitution of *ṣ* for the *s* of *nis* is also irregularly prescribed. Thus: *niṣṭarkyaṃ cinvīta paśukāmaḥ* ("One desiring cattle should pile the *niṣṭarkya* altar").

When the word *deva* is the preceding term (*upapada*), the suffix *kyap* is added to the roots *hve* (to call) or *hu* (to offer); there is lengthening of the vowel and the absence of the *tuk* augment. Thus: *uddevahūye* ("in the calling of the gods"). Here, the suffix *kyap* is added to the root *nī* preceded by *pra* and *ud*: *praṇīyaḥ* ("to be led forward") and *unnīyaḥ* ("to be lifted up"). From the root *śiṣ* preceded by *ud*, the suffix *kyap* is added: *ucchiṣyam* ("that which remains"). From the roots *mṛ* (to die, Dhatupatha 1.23), *stan* (to cover, Dhatupatha 1.6), and *dhvṛ* (to be crooked, Dhatupatha 1.164), the suffix *yat* is added: *maryaḥ* ("man"), *staryā* ("female animal"), and *dhvaryaḥ*. The form *staryā* is a specific irregular derivation (*nipātana*) occurring only in the feminine. The form *dhvaryaḥ* is likewise derived from *dhvṛ*.

From the root *khan* (to dig), [the forms] *khanya* and *khānya* [are derived]. When the word *deva* is an upapada, the suffix *ya* is applied to the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), as in: *śundhadhvaṃ daivyāya karmaṇe devayajyāyai*. Since the suffix accent would result in an oxytone (*antodātta*), the rule for the original accent of the final member of a *kṛt*-derivative compound applies. This specific formation is restricted to the feminine gender. From the root *prach* (to ask) preceded by *ā*, the suffix *kyap* is applied: *āpṛcchyam dharuṇaṃ vājyarṣati*. From the root *sīv* (to sew) preceded by *prati*, the suffix *kyap* is applied along with the change of *s* to *ṣ*: *pratiṣīvyaḥ*.

When *brahman* is the upapada, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied [to the root *vad*]. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the two suffixes *kva* and *kyap* which would otherwise be applicable by Pāṇini 3.1.106: *vadaḥ supi kyap ca*. Thus, we have *brahmavādyam*. Now, how is it that we find "they speak the *brahmodyam*" (Ṛgveda-Śrautasūtra 2.4)? For if the suffix *ṇyat*, which is specifically prescribed for the Vedic language (*chandas*), were to supersede the suffix *kyap*—which finds its application in the common language (*loka*) by the rule "vadaḥ supi"—then there would be the undesirable consequence of such a sublation. Nor can one argue that this is permissible because of the rule *vāsarūpa* (Pāṇini 3.1.94). True; however, one should understand that here there is a reversal of the *kṛt* suffixes.

For it has been stated: "And [the suffix *ṇyat* is applied] after roots ending in *kāla*, *hal*, or a vowel, and after those having a *kartṛ* (*yaṅ*). In that context, we have already explained that the mention of *kartṛ* refers to *kṛt* suffixes. From the roots *bhū* and *stu*, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied, resulting in *bhāvyaḥ* and *stāvyaḥ*. After the root *ci* preceded by the prefix *upa*, the suffix *ṇyat* is applied and the substitution of *ā* for the penultimate vowel is prescribed when *pṛḍa* is the subsequent member of the compound. The root *mṛḍ* means "to be gracious," and *pṛḍ* means "to cook" (Dhātupāṭha 4.47, 48). From this [root *pṛḍ*], the suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule for roots with an *ig* vowel as the penultimate letter, resulting in *upacāyyapṛḍa*. It should be stated that [this applies only when the word] *hiraṇya* follows. Otherwise, it is simply *upaceyapṛḍa*. Regarding this, there is a Vārttika:
One should know that in *niṣṭarkya*, there is a transposition; the change of *ni* to *ṣ* occurs by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*).
In *upacāyya*, the suffix *ṇyat* and the substitution of *ā* for *i* are both irregularly prescribed.

The suffix *ṇyat* occurs after one root, and the suffix *kyap* occurs after four; likewise, the suffix *yat* occurs after four roots. The suffix *ṇyat* occurs after one root, the word *yaś* occurs after two, the suffix *kyap* occurs after two, and the rule for *ṇyat* applies to four.

"ṇyatvayam" means the extreme reversal of the beginning and the end. Regarding "from four," the suffix *kyap* is applied to the four roots beginning with *devahūya*; there is a distinction in the root *nī* due to the difference in prefixes. "Two *kyaps*" means that two [suffixes] are applied to two roots. "The prescription of *ṇyat* occurs four times" is a form ending in the suffix *suc*; the meaning is that the suffix *ṇyat* is prescribed on four occasions.

(Pāṇini 3.1.124): *ṛhalorṇyat*. The suffix *ṇyat* occurs after a verbal root ending in the vowel *ṛ* or in a consonant (*hal*). Examples: *kāryam*, *hāryam*, *vācyam*, *pācyam*. In the rule, the genitive case is used in the sense of the ablative (*pañcamyarthe ṣaṣṭhī*). Furthermore, the term *ṛ* here refers to the phoneme *ṛ* and not to the root *ṛ* (to go), because it is mentioned alongside *hal* (consonants), and because of the technical indication in the rule *paraṅkāryam* (Pāṇini 1.4.2). This is also supported by the evidence of the rule *īḍavandavṛśaṃsaduhāṃṇyataḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.214). Regarding this, there are the following Vārttikas:

The rule for *ṇyat* after the root *sṛj* when preceded by *pāṇi* (Kāśikāvṛtti). This is an exception to the application of *kyap*, which would otherwise apply because the root has a short *ṛ* as its penultimate vowel (*ṛdupadha*). A rope released with the hands is called *pāṇisargyā*. It should be stated that [the suffix applies] also after [the root *sṛj*] preceded by *sam-ava*: *samavasargyā*.

It should be stated [in the *Kāśikāvṛtti*]: "And after the roots *lap* and *dabh*. Thus, *apalāpyam* and *avadābhyam*. These are exceptions (*apavāda*) to the rule "poradupadhāt" (Pāṇini 3.1.98), which would otherwise have applied. Although the root *dabh* is not listed among the verbal roots (*dhātu*), it is valid—like *culump* and others—because of the statement in the *Vārttika* and because of the inclusion of the term "variously" (*bahulam*) in the rule "bahulam etan nidarśanam" (Dhātupāṭha, Curādigaṇa). Accordingly, it is employed in such usages as: "Neither do they perish, nor does the thief deceive them," and "Viṣṇu is the protector, the undeceivable."

Jayāditya, however, having read the first two *vārttikas* under the rule *eti-stu-śāsvṛ-* (Pāṇini 3.1.109), inserts *lap* between the two roots mentioned in the third *vārttika*, and having placed it above *rap* in the rule *āsuyuvapi-* (Pāṇini 3.1.126), he includes *dabh* by means of the particle *ca* used for the purpose of collecting what has not been explicitly stated. In this regard, it should be noted that the resulting dissimilarity (*vairūpya*) is entirely without foundation. (Pāṇini 3.1.125)

Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.125: *orāvaśyake* || The suffix *ṇyat* is applied after a verbal root ending in *u* when the sense of necessity (*āvaśyaka*) is to be expressed. Necessity (*avaśyam bhāvaḥ*) is called *āvaśyakam*. [The suffix] *vuñ* is added because it belongs to the *manojñādi* group. [In this group,] there is elision of the *ṭi* portion [of an indeclinable] before any nominal suffix beginning with a consonant (*bha*). Examples: *lāvyam*, *pāvyam*. Although the meaning has already been expressed [by the suffix], usage of the word itself is sometimes seen due to disregard for brevity (*lāghava*). Example: *avaśyalāvyam*. Here, even though a compound formed with an *upapada* is impossible, the compound is justified because the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group is an *ākṛtigaṇa*. It should be understood that the preservation of the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the second member also occurs there by virtue of a specific grammatical exception (*nipātana*). Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.126.

Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.126: *āsuyuvapirapitrapicamaśca*. The suffix *ṇyat* shall be applied after the root *su* preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, as well as after the roots *yu*, *vap*, *rap*, *trap*, and *cam*. This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the suffix *yat* which would otherwise be applicable according to Pāṇini Sūtras 3.1.97 and 98 (*aco yat* and *poradupadhāt*). It has been stated here that the root *lap* was inserted above *rap* by the author of the Vṛtti. *Suñ* (meaning "to press") [Dhātupāṭha 1.450]: *āsāvyam*. *yu* (meaning "to mix") [Dhātupāṭha 2.3]: *yāvyam*. However, the root *yuñ* (meaning "to bind") [Dhātupāṭha 7.7] is not included here because it possesses an *anubandha* (the letter *ñ*). *vap*: *vāpyam*. *rap*: *rāpyam*. *trap*: *apatrāpyam*. *cam*: *ācāmyam*. (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.127)

*Ānāyyaḥ* [is used] in the sense of *anitya* (Pāṇini 3.1.127). From the root *nī* preceded by the prefix *āṅ*, the suffix *ṇyat* and the substitution of *ā* for the root vowel are irregularly prescribed (*nipātyete*). This irregular prescription is also for the sake of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). It does not apply to [the word] *ānāyya* as listed in the *ghaṭādi* group; rather, it applies specifically to a particular *dakṣiṇāgni* (southern sacrificial fire). For instance, the source (*yoni*) of the *dakṣiṇāgni* is optionally considered to be from the house of a wealthy Vaiśya, from the *bhrāṣṭra* (roasting fire), or from the *gārhapatya* (householder's fire). In that case, when it is brought from the *gārhapatya* together with the *āhavanīya* (offering fire) such that they share a single source, it is precisely there that this irregular prescription applies. And its *anityatva* (non-permanence) follows from the fact that it is not continuously kindled. On this point, the Bhāṣya states:
If it is argued that the fire brought from elsewhere is non-eternal, then [the rite] would be performed in the Dakṣiṇāgni;
however, one should know that it occurs in a single source (ekayoni), for otherwise it would be merely an Āhavanīya fire.

Immediately after the word *cet*, the phrase "the over-extension [of the rule] to jars and the like" (*ghaṭādiṣvatiprasaṅga*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Regarding the form *bhavet*, the optative suffix (*liṅga*) is used in the sense of possibility; the meaning is that by means of this grammatical irregularity (*nipātana*), the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) is made possible. In the phrase "in a single source" (*ekayonau*), the words "together with the Āhavanīya fire" (*āhavanīyena saha*) are to be understood as the ellipsis. Regarding the term *āneya*, the meaning is that the suffix *yat*—prescribed by Pāṇini’s sūtra 3.1.97 (*aco yat*)—is applied to the non-eternal jar and so forth, as well as to the Dakṣiṇāgni fire which has a different source (*bhinnayoni*). (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.128).

*praṇāyyaḥ* means "one who is not honored" (*asammataḥ*). *Sammānanam* (honoring) is *sammatiḥ*. Here, the intended meaning is the activity of the object (*karma-vyāpāra*) consisting in approaching a state that is an object of affection. Likewise, devotion toward an object of enjoyment is also *sammatiḥ*. Both meanings are intended here by virtue of the *tantra* principle (the simultaneous application of multiple senses). Therefore, the substitution of *vyad* for the root *ṇī* (to lead) is prescribed after the prefix *pra-* when used with reference to one unworthy of honor or one who is disinterested. Thus, *praṇāyyaś coraḥ* ("an unworthy thief"). [As stated: "A father should teach the Veda to his eldest son, to a worthy pupil (*praṇāyya*), and to no one else whatsoever. (Pāṇini 3.1.129)

The forms *pāyya*, *sānnāyya*, *nikāyya*, and *dhāyyā* are irregularly derived (nipātana) in the senses of a measure (*māna*), an oblation (*havir*), a dwelling (*nivāsa*), and a *sāmidhenī* verse, respectively. Four [terms] are thus substituted for four [roots], corresponding to their order: 1. *Pāyya* means a measure (*māna*). It is that by which something is measured (*mīyate 'nena mānam*). From the root *māṅ* (to measure), the suffix *ṇyat* is applied in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*). By the rule *āto yuk ciṇ-kṛtoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.33), the augment *yuk* is inserted. Furthermore, the substitution of *p* for the initial *m* of the root occurs due to this irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Any other thing that is measured is simply called *meyam*. 2. *Sānnāyya* refers to a specific type of oblation (*havir-viśeṣa*). It is so called because it is properly led (*samyaṅ nīyate*) toward the fire for the purpose of offering (*homārtham*). 3. *Nikāyya* means a dwelling (*nivāsa*). 4. *Dhāyyā* refers to a *sāmidhenī* verse. These are the four forms established through these specific grammatical substitutions.

The root *nī* preceded by the prefix *sam* takes the suffix *ṇyat*, undergoes the substitution of *ā* for *ai*, and the lengthening of the vowel following the prefix is irregularly prescribed (*nipātana*). This is the name for the curd and milk that are ordained [in the ritual] as "curd for Indra" (*aindraṃ dadhi*) on the new moon day and "milk for Indra" (*aindraṃ payaḥ*) on the new moon day.

Māgha, however, taking the literal sense, employed it for sacrificial oblations (*havis*) in general: "Every night, having recited the *sāmidhenī* verses according to the rules with resonant sounds, those who maintain the sacred fires—whose light is unextinguished—[enter the hall]."

"The fire, having consumed the oblation offered by the foremost among those who have become travelers on the path that destroys the flood of heavy sins committed, now devours the sacrificial food of the virtuous. (Mālatīmādhava 11.41)

One should not argue that this [verse] might also refer specifically to curds and milk; for since it is recited after first describing the rising and setting of the moon and then introducing the rising of the sun, it pertains to the first day of the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapratipad), at which time the combination of curds and milk is impossible. Furthermore, it should be understood that a word denoting a specific type of oblation (havis) may function as a metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) for the oblation in general or for another specific variety. "Nikāyya" means a dwelling place. It is derived from the root *ci* with the prefix *ni*, in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*), with the suffix *ṇyat*; the substitution of *ā* for the initial vowel (*āy-ādeśaḥ*) and the change of the initial *c* to *k* (*katvam*) are both irregularly prescribed (*nipātyate*).

The etymological analysis (*vigraha*) is: "that in which grain and other things are accumulated. The other [meaning] is that which is to be accumulated. The word *nikāya* also exists in this very sense; it will be derived under Pāṇini 3.3.41: "In the senses of dwelling, piling up, body, and funeral pyre, there is the substitution of *ka* for the initial [of the root]. The suffix *ṇyat* is applied to the root *dhā* in the sense of *sāmidhenī*. That which is for the placing of fuel-sticks (*samidh*) is a *sāmidhenī*. According to the Kāśikāvṛtti: "The suffix *ṣeṇyaṇ* is used in the sense of placing fuel-sticks. The verses beginning with "pravovājāḥ" are the *sāmidhenīs*.

And here, not every *sāmidhenī* verse is called a *dhāyyā*; rather, it is specifically the verse beginning with "apṛthupājā amartyaḥ," which is inserted among the *samidhyamānavatī* and *samiddhavatī* verses in the modified rituals (*vikṛtis*). In the Sūtra, the mention of *sāmidhenī* is intended as an illustration for the context of ritual application. Accordingly, the term is seen even in what is not a *sāmidhenī*, such as in the statement: "He recites the *dhāyyās*: 'Agni is the leader' and 'O Soma, you with your rites'"; this is the injunction for the *marutvatīya* hymn in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.

In this regard, Haradatta’s statement—that the suffix *ṇyat* is applied in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*) because "by means of this [verse] the firewood is placed"—applies to instances such as "pṛthupājāḥ. However, Mādhava’s statement—that the suffix *ṇyat* is applied in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*) because "it is placed (*dhīyate*)," thus forming *dhāyyā*—is common to cases such as "agnirnetā. The distinction is that all these particulars are obtained through the fact that the irregular derivation (*nipātana*) serves to establish conventional usage (*rūḍhi*).
(Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.130)

*kratau kuṇḍapāyyasañcāyyau* (Pāṇini 3.1.130). These two are irregularly formed (*nipātita*) when a sacrifice (*kratu*) is to be expressed. In that context, when the word *kuṇḍa* ending in the third case is an attendant word (*upapada*), the suffix *yat* is irregularly applied to the root *pā* (to drink) in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), and the augment *yuk* is added. Thus, because the Soma is drunk in this [sacrifice] by means of a *kuṇḍa*, it is called the *kuṇḍapāyya* sacrifice.

If it is argued: "In this case, let only the suffix *ṇyat* be prescribed by way of a special rule (*nipātana*), because it is the subject under discussion; thus, *yuk* need not be prescribed, as it would already be established by the rule *āto yuk* (Pāṇini 7.3.33). This also provides economy of expression (*lāghava*),"—it is not so. For then the acute accent (*titsvara*) would undesirably apply. However, the initial acute accent (*ādyudāttatva*) is desired, as established by the rule *yato ’nāvaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.213), since that very accent is finalized by the rule regarding the original accent of the second member of a compound (*kṛduttarapadaprakṛtisvara*). And thus it is employed in usage: "That which is your *śṛṅgavṛṣa*, the *praṇapāt*, the *kuṇḍapāyya*."

The suffix *ṇyat* is prescribed after the root *ci* preceded by the prefix *sam*, and the substitution of *āy* is also applied by way of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). That which is gathered together is called a *sañcāyya* sacrifice. Why is it specified "in the case of a sacrifice" (*kratāv*)? [To show that] *kuṇḍapānam* [is] *sañceyaḥ*.
(Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.131)

*agnau paricāyyopacāyyasamūhyāḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.131). These are irregularly formed (*nipātyante*) when "fire" (*agni*) is the object denoted. Here, "fire" does not mean the burning flame itself, but rather a specific place constructed by piling bricks for the purpose of maintaining that fire; it is because the term is conventionally established (*nirūḍha*) in that sense alone. From the root *ci* ("to pile") preceded by *pari* and *upa*, the suffix *ṇyat* and the substitution of *ā* for *i* are irregularly prescribed: *paricāyyaḥ* and *upacāyyaḥ*. From the root *ūh* ("to carry") preceded by *sam*, the vocalization (*saṃprasāraṇa*) and lengthening are irregularly prescribed: *samūhyaṃ cinvīta paśukāmaḥ* ("one desiring cattle should pile the *samūhya*").

What is the purpose of the restriction "in the sense of *agni*"? [Consider the examples: *pariceyam*, *upaceyam*, *saṃvāhyam*. Here, from the root *ūh* (DhP 6.49, *ūhavitarke*) preceded by *sam*, which—due to its polysemy—is used in the sense of *vah* (to carry), the form *samūhyam* is established by adding the suffix *ṇyat* because the root ends in a consonant (*hal*). And this is appropriate, because in the Brāhmaṇa the word *samūhya* is etymologically explained with the root *ūh* in the sense of *vah*: "One desiring cattle should pile the *samūhya* altar. Man is indeed cattle; thus he piles it for him with cattle. And so it has been stated by the author of the Vārttika:

The word "samūhya" is a redundant expression because [the formation] is already established by the general rule. If it is argued that it is for the sake of the specific meaning [of *ūha*], it is already established because the root *vah* has that same meaning. Furthermore, it is established in the Brāhmaṇa by the analysis of the compound as *ūhi-vigraha*.
(Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.132)

In the rule *cityāgnicitye ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.132), the suffix *kyap* is irregularly prescribed (*nipātyate*) for the word *citya* when used in the sense of the object (*karman*). This is an exception (*apavāda*) to [the general rule] *yataḥ*. By the accent of the verbal root, the word is udātta on its first syllable. That which is piled up (*cīyate*) is the *citya* fire-altar (*agni*). The piling of the fire-altar is *agnicityā*. Here, the suffix *yak* is irregularly prescribed along with the augment *tuk*, but not *kyap*. Consequently, the word has an udātta accent on its final syllable. In this sūtra, the term "in the case of fire" (*agnau*) is understood from the previous rule; however, that qualifies only the word *citya* and not the word *agnicityā*, because the latter is prescribed as a formation in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*). Therefore, in cases other than those involving fire, the form is simply *ceya*.
The ritual duties are completed.

(Pāṇini 3.1.133) *ṇvultṛcau*: The suffixes *ṇvul* and *tṛc* occur after a verbal root (*dhātu*). From this point until the end of the chapter, by the general rule stated as "kṛt [suffixes] in the sense of the agent" (Pāṇini 3.4.67), these affixes denote the agent. Examples: *pācakaḥ* (one who cooks), *paktā* (one who cooks). In the case of *tṛc*, the letter *c* is for the purpose of preventing the loss of the general designation [of the suffix]. This is seen in rules such as "tuśchandasi" (Pāṇini 5.3.59) and "turiṣṭhemeyaḥsu" (Pāṇini 6.4.154). Consequently, even in the rule "aptṛn" (Pāṇini 6.4.11), it would be more appropriate to mention the form simply as "aptṛsvasṛ," rather than separately mentioning "tṛn" and "tṛc."

(Pāṇini 3.1.134): *nandigrahipacādibhyo lyuṇinyacaḥ*. After roots beginning with *nandi*, [the suffix] *lyu* is applied; after those beginning with *grahi*, *ṇini*; and after those beginning with *pac*, *ac*. Furthermore, the groups *nandi*, *grahi*, *paci*, and so forth, are not included as they are listed in the Dhātupāṭha. Rather, those which constitute the radical portions (*prakṛtibhāga*) within nominal groups (*prātipadikagaṇa*) such as *nandana*, *ramaṇa*, and the like, are here extracted mentally and taken up. If it is asked: "In that case, what is the purpose of this rule, since the correctness of words such as *nandana* and others is established simply by their being listed in the Gaṇapāṭha?"

Regarding this, Haradatta says: "If this [Gaṇapāṭha] did not exist, it would not be required because it would be of no use anywhere within the Aṣṭādhyāyī. His intention is as follows: Grammar is a science whose purpose is the restriction of word-forms (svarūpa-niyama), asserting that "only these [forms] are correct. And according to the maxim, "All of that is indeed contained within the Sūtras," the science consists of the Sūtras themselves. Consequently, whatever is not made the subject of the Sūtras by any means would—like the word *gāvī* and others—be liable to the consequence of being incorrect (*asādhutva*) by implication.

The suffix *lyu* (i.e., *an*) is applied after the causative forms of the roots *nandi*, *vāśi*, *mādi*, *dūṣi*, *sādhi*, *vardhi*, *śobhi*, and *rocibhi*, when used as proper names (*saṃjñāyām*). *ṭunadi* (in the sense of prosperity; *bhvādi*, *parasmaipada*, 67): that which causes joy is *nandanaḥ*. *vāśṛ* (in the sense of sound; *divādi*, *ātmanepada*, 77): *vāśanaḥ*. *madī* (in the sense of exhilaration; *divādi*, *ātmanepada*, 1–2): *madanaḥ*. *duṣa* (in the sense of corruption; *divādi*, *ātmanepada*, 79): by the rule *doṣo ṇau* (*Pāṇini* 6.4.90), the vowel *u* is substituted [for *u*], resulting in *dūṣaṇaḥ*. *rādha* and *sādha* (in the sense of accomplishment; *svādi*, *parasmaipada*, 16, 17): a Brahmin who accomplishes the sacrifice is *yajñasya sādhanaḥ*. Since the suffix *lyu* denotes the agent (*kartari*), it takes the masculine gender.

How then [should one explain] the expression “a cow is the means of the oblation for the Hotṛ priest”? [The suffix] *lyuṭ* (ana) is used here in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*), and it will be neuter because it expresses a general quality. [From the root] *vṛdh* (DhP 1.760), meaning "to increase": *vardhanaḥ*. [From the roots] *śubh* and *śumbh* (DhP 6.41, 42), meaning "to beautify": *śobhanaḥ*. [From the root] *ruc* (DhP 1.746), meaning "to shine": *rocanaḥ*.

The suffix *ana* is applied after roots ending in *sah*, *dam*, and *tap* when forming names (Pāṇini 3.2.157). *sah* in the sense of endurance (*marṣaṇa*): *sahanaḥ*. *tap* in the sense of heating or tormenting (*santāpa*): *tapanaḥ*. *dam* in the sense of subduing (*upaśama*): *damanaḥ*. *jap* and *jalp* in the sense of distinct speech (*vyaktā vāk*): *jalpanaḥ*. *ram* in the sense of sporting (*krīḍā*): *ramaṇaḥ*. *dṛp* in the sense of exhilaration and release (*harṣa-vimocana*): *darpaṇaḥ*. *krad* in the sense of calling out and weeping (*āhvāna-rodana*): *saṅkrandanaḥ*.

From the root *kṛṣ* in the sense of "plowing" (*bhvādigaṇa*, parasmaipada, 1015), we have *saṅkarṣaṇa*. From *hṛṣ* in the sense of "delighting" (*bhvādigaṇa*, parasmaipada, 710), we have *harṣaṇa*. From *ard* in the sense of "injuring" (*bhvādigaṇa*, parasmaipada, 55), [the term] *janārdana* is derived from the fact that he "afflicts people" (*janam ardayati*). Although the suffix *aṇ* would have been expected here according to the rule for the object (*karman*), it is understood that the same applies in subsequent cases when an object is used as an upapada. From *yu* in the sense of "mixing" (*adādigaṇa*, parasmaipada, 23), we have *yavana*. From *ṣūd* in the sense of "flowing" or "destroying" (*bhvādigaṇa*, ātmanepada, 25), [the term] *madhusūdana* is derived from the fact that he "destroys the demon named Madhu. From *ñibhī* in the sense of "fear" (*juhotyādigaṇa*, parasmaipada, 2).

From the root *bhī* preceded by *vi*, with the suffix *ṇic*, the augment *ṣuk* is applied according to Pāṇini 7.3.40 (*bhiyo hetubhaye ṣuk*), resulting in *vibhīṣaṇaḥ*. From *lūñ* (meaning "to cut," Dhatupatha 11), the change to *ṇatva* occurs by irregular derivation (*nipātana*), resulting in *lavaṇaḥ*. From *ṇaś* (meaning "disappearance," Dhatupatha 88) and *damu* (meaning "to subdue," Dhatupatha 97), these take the suffix *ṇyat*. One who destroys wealth is *vittanāśanaḥ*; one who subdues a family is *kuladamanaḥ*, as is *śatrudamanaḥ*. Thus ends the group beginning with *nandi*.

*Graha* (in the sense of seizing): *grāhī*. *Ṣaha* (in the sense of enduring): *sahī*. *Dasu* (in the sense of wasting away): *uddāsī*. *Bhasa* (in the sense of threatening and shining): *udbhāsī*. From the root *sthā*, by [Pāṇini 7.3.33] *āto yuk ciṇ-kṛtoḥ*, [we derive] *sthāyī*. *Matri* (in the sense of secret counsel; belonging to the curādi class): *mantrī*. *Arda* (in the sense of harming): *samardī*.

[The suffix *ini* is applied after the roots] *rakṣ*, *śru*, *vap*, and *śo* when preceded by *ni*. *rakṣ* in the sense of protection (*bhvādigaṇa*, parasmaipada, 659): *nirakṣī*. *śru* in the sense of hearing (*bhvādigaṇa*, parasmaipada, 967): *niśrāvī*. *ḍuvap* in the sense of sowing seeds (*bhvādigaṇa*, ubhayapada, 1028): *nivāpī*. *śo* in the sense of making thin (*divādigaṇa*, parasmaipada, 39): *niśāyī*. These four are preceded by *ni*.

[The suffix *ini* is applied] after the roots √yāc, √hṛ, √vyāhṛ, √vraj, √vad, and √vas, provided they are not preceded by the prefix *a*. (Pāṇini 3.2.156) √yāc (yācati) in the sense of begging (Bhvādi 888). √hṛ (harati) in the sense of taking away (Bhvādi 924). √vraj (vrajati) in the sense of going (Bhvādi 254). √vad (vadati) in the sense of distinct speech (Bhvādi 1034). √vas (vasati) in the sense of dwelling (Bhvādi 1034). Examples: ayācī (one who does not beg) avyāhārī (one who does not speak) asaṃvyāhārī (one who does not converse) avrājī (one who does not wander) avādī (one who does not speak) avāsī (one who does not dwell)

[Gaṇasūtra 6.1.193]: For verbal roots ending in *a* that have inanimate agents, the suffix *ṇin* is applied [to form a future passive participle], provided they have meanings for which [the suffix *ṇyat*] is prohibited. Examples: *akārī* (one who has done), *ahārī* (one who has taken). In *viśayī* from the root *śīṅ* (to sleep), there is no *vṛddhi* due to irregularity (*nipātana*). In *viṣayī* from the root *ṣiñ* (to bind), there is no *vṛddhi* as before. Regarding this, Vardhamāna states in his commentary on the *Gaṇaratnamahodadhi* that the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* also occurs here by irregularity. The *Vṛtti* states: "In the sense of 'country,' *viśayī* and *viṣayī*. The suffix *ṇin* is applied after [the root *bhu*] with the sense of "overpowering" (*abhibhāvī*) when referring to the past (*bhūte*).

*Abhibhūta-vān* means one who has overcome; *abhibhāvī* means one who overcomes. *Rādha* in the sense of accomplishment (*saṃsiddhi*) [forms] *rādhitā*; *rudhir* in the sense of covering (*āvaraṇa*) [forms] *avarodhī* and *uparodhī*. *Paribhāvī*: here the absence of *vṛddhi* is prescribed as an irregularity (*nipātana*). Thus ends the *grahādi* group. *Ḍupacaṣ* in the sense of cooking (*pāka*) [is from] *bhvādi*, class 1021; *vaca* in the sense of speaking (*paribhāṣaṇa*) [is from] *adādi*, class 53, and so forth.

This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). Accordingly, in the rule *śivaśamariṣṭasya kare* (Pāṇini 4.4.143), the suffix *ac* is applied to the root *kṛ*; and in the rule *karmaṇi ghaṭo'ṭhac* (Pāṇini 5.2.35), it is applied to the root *ghaṭ*. Likewise, by the rule *yaṅo'ci ca* (Pāṇini 2.4.74), the elision (*luk*) of *yaṅ* is prescribed when this suffix *ac* follows. Furthermore, it is stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "The suffix *ac* should be mentioned after all verbal roots."

If one asks, "For what purpose, then, is the sequential enumeration of *pac* and the others? [The answer is: It is for the purpose of attaching *anubandhas* (indicatory letters) in cases such as *nadaṭ*, and for the purpose of setting aside [the application of] suffixes that have a word denoting an object (*karma-upapada*) or those whose penultimate vowel is *i* (*igupadha*). For other [roots], however, it is for the sake of elaboration (*prapañca*). To illustrate: *nadaṭ*, *bhaṣaṭ*, *plavaṭ*, *caraṭ*, *garaṭ*, *taraṭ*, *coraṭ*, *devaṭ*, *sūdaṭ*—these end in *ṭ*. In the root *nad* (meaning "inarticulate sound," *bhvādigaṇa*, *parasmaipada*, 54), the *ṭ* is for the purpose of [forming] the feminine suffix *ṅīp*; thus, *nadaḥ* and *nadī*. In the root *bhaṣ* (meaning "to scold," *bhvādigaṇa*, *parasmaipada*, 696), [the suffix *aṭ* is applied] to form *bhaṣī*.

*Plu* (in the sense of moving, *bhvādigaṇa*, 983) forms *plavī*; *car* (in the sense of moving, *bhvādigaṇa*, 560) forms *carī*; *gṝ* (in the sense of swallowing, *tudādigaṇa*, 130) forms *garī*; *tṝ* (in the senses of floating and crossing over, *bhvādigaṇa*, 994) forms *tarī*; *cur* (in the sense of stealing, *curādigaṇa*, 1) forms *corī*; *div* (in the sense of playing and so forth, *divādigaṇa*, 7) forms *devī*; *sūd* has already been explained [as meaning "to kill"]; it forms *sūdī*; *miṣ* (in the sense of rivalry, *tudādigaṇa*, 72) forms *meṣaḥ*; *kup* (in the sense of anger, *divādigaṇa*, 127) forms *kopaḥ*; *sūplṛ* (in the sense of moving, *bhvādigaṇa*, 1008) forms *sarpaḥ*. Here, in the case of *div* and the others, the suffix *ka* would have applied because they end in an *ik* vowel as their penultimate (*igupadha*).

One who supports a paramour is called *jārabharā*; one who cooks a dog is called *śvapacā*. In these two cases, the suffix *aṇ* would have been required by rule [Pāṇini 3.2.1]. However, because the word *śvapāka* is listed among the *nyaṅkvādi* group, Kaiyaṭa and others maintain that the suffix *aṇ* is optionally applied even when it is not denoting the object (i.e., under Pāṇini 3.2.1). The distinction is that the inclusion of roots such as *jṝṣ* and *mṛṅ* in that list is merely for the sake of elaboration (*prapañcārtha*).
(Pāṇini 3.1.135)

Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.135: *igupadhajñāprīkiraḥ kaḥ*. The suffix *ka* is applied after verbal roots that have a vowel (*i*, *u*, or *ṛ*) as their penultimate letter (*upadha*), as well as after the roots *jñā*, *prī*, and *kṝ*. Examples: *vikṣipaḥ* (one who scatters); *vilikhaḥ* (one who scratches); *vibudhaḥ* (one who awakens); *kṛśaḥ* (one who is emaciated). Regarding *jña*: from the root *jñā* (to know), the suffix *ka* is added. By Pāṇini Sūtra 6.4.44 (*āto lopa iṭi ca*), the long *ā* is elided, resulting in *jñaḥ* (one who knows). Regarding *priya*: from the root *prī* (to satisfy/delight, kryādigaṇa, class 9), the substitution of *iyaṅ* occurs. From *prīṇāti* (he delights), *priyaḥ* is formed. Regarding *kira*: from the root *kṝ* (to scatter, tudādigaṇa, class 6), by Pāṇini Sūtra 7.1.100 (*ṛta iddhātoḥ*), the *ṛ* is replaced by *i*. From *kirati* (he scatters), *kiraḥ* is formed.

In the *sūtra*, however, regarding the *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction) *dvandva* compound, one should understand that there is a substitution of the singular ablative case ending (*pañcamī-ekavacana*) for the word *ṛ*. Since the word *ṛ* is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of a verbal root, by the extended application (*atideśa*) rule "an imitation is like its original" (*prakṛtivadanukaraṇam*), the substitution of *i* for *ṛ* occurs. In a *samāhāra* (collective) *dvandva*, however, because of the neuter gender, the vowel would be shortened, and thus the substitution of *i* would not take place. (Pāṇini 3.1.136) *ātaścopasarge*: When a prefix (*upapada*) beginning with a vowel follows a verbal root ending in long *ā*, the suffix *ka* is applied. This is an exception to the suffix *ṇa* which would otherwise be obtained by the rule *śyādvyādhā* (Pāṇini 3.1.141). Examples: *prasthaḥ*, *suglaḥ*, *sumlaḥ*.

(Pāṇini 3.1.137): *pāghrādhmādheḍdṛśaḥ śaḥ*. After these five roots, the suffix *śa* occurs. Thus: *pibati* → *pibaḥ*; *jighraḥ*; *dhamaḥ*; *dhayaḥ*. In the feminine, however, the suffix *ṭāp* is applied, resulting in *dhayā*. Although the root *dheṭ* has the marker *ṭi*, which would require the suffix *ṅīp* here just as in the case of *stanandhayī*, nevertheless, some maintain that the word "in the presence of a prefix" (*upasarge*) is understood in this rule, so that *ṅīp* applies only after a stem ending in the suffix *khaś* and not after one ending in the suffix *śa*; however, this view is not accepted by many.

And thus Śrī Harṣa employed [the word]: *phalāni dhūmasya dhayānadhomukhān* ("drinking the fruits of smoke with faces turned downwards"). It is also heard [in scripture]: *yadā paśyaḥ paśyate rukmavarṇam* ("when the seer sees the golden-colored one"). Here, there is the inclusion of the root *dhā* (to drink), and not of *pā* in the sense of "protection" (*pā rakṣaṇe*, DhP 4.60), because that belongs to the *lug*-class (which lacks a suffix). There is a prohibition regarding *ghrā* when used as a name (*ghraḥ sañjñāyāṃ pratiṣedhaḥ*). And in this regard, the Vārttika rule *vyāghrādibhiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.56) is the indicative mark. [Examples: *vyāghraḥ*. [The suffix] *ka* is applied by the rule *ātaścopasarge* (Pāṇini 3.1.136). (Pāṇini 3.1.138).

*Anupasargāllimpavindadhāripārivedyudejicetisātisāhibhyaśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.138). After the roots *limp*, *vind*, and the others listed, provided they are not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*), the suffix *śa* shall be applied. Thus, one who smears is *limpaḥ*; one who finds is *vindaḥ*. In the rule, the forms *limpa* and *vinda* are cited with the nasal augment (*num*) already present, as it will occur in the subsequent formation; therefore, other conjugational suffixes (*vikaraṇa*) are not included. Furthermore, only the root meaning "to obtain" (*lābha*) is intended here [for *vind*].

The roots *dhṛñ* in the sense of "holding" (*bhvādigaṇa*, 925) and *dhṛṅ* in the sense of "remaining" (*tudādigaṇa*, 132) are both included here; thus, [the form] is *dhārayaḥ*. Now, how is it that Śrīharṣa says, "na mahyamatrottaradārayasya te"? For, by virtue of its higher status, the suffix *aṇ* ought to apply in the sense of the object, as in the case of *sūtradhāra* and similar words. And so says the Vārttika: "A word with an object as its upapada [takes the suffix *aṇ*] by way of an exception (*vipratiṣedha*) over [a word ending in] the vowel *a* when there is no upapada" (*kāśikāvṛtti*).

True; since the suffix *aṇ* would not apply when there is a desire to express that [the action] is subordinate (*śeṣatva*) to the object, once the suffix *śa* has been applied, the compound will be formed with that which ends in the sixth case denoting subordination (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*). By this, forms such as *gaṅgādhara*, *bhūdharā*, and *jaladhara* are explained. The root *pāra* (in the sense of "completion of an action") belongs to the *curādi* group: that which causes one to reach the end is *pārayaḥ*. The root *vid* (in the senses of "consciousness," "narration," etc. belongs to the *curādi* group, or it may be any root meaning "knowledge" and so forth with the causative suffix *ṇic*: that which makes known is *vedayaḥ*. The root *ejṛ* (in the sense of "trembling") belongs to the *bhvādi* group with the causative suffix *ṇic*: that which causes agitation is *udejayaḥ*.

The root *cit* (in the sense of "perception") belongs to the *curādi* class. Thus, one who causes to perceive is a *cetayaḥ*. Bopadeva maintains that the root *sati* (in the sense of "happiness") ends in the causative suffix (*ṇic*) of the *curādi* class. Haradatta maintains that *sāti* is a Vedic root ending in the causative suffix (*hetumaṇṇic*). [Thus we have] *sātayaḥ*. By the rule of alternative forms (*vāsarūpa-nyāya*), when the suffix *kvip* is applied, it becomes *sāt*. Alternatively, by treating it as belonging to the *sampadādi* group, the suffix *kvip* may be used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*). In this way, on the strength of scriptural passages such as "He indeed causes bliss" (*eṣa evānandayati*), Brahman is the "one who causes bliss" (*ānandayitṛ-vijñāna*); and on the strength of passages such as "Brahman is bliss" (*ānandaṃ brahma*), Brahman is "of the nature of bliss" (*ānanda-rūpa*). This is the meaning of the word *sat*. Those in whom this exists are *sāttvantaḥ*, namely, the devotees (*bhaktāḥ*).

By this, [the derivation of] "sātvatāṃ pataye namaḥ" and so forth is explained. Those who claim that *sāt* is simply *sat* (being) and assert its status as an archaic Vedic form (*ārṣatva*) are thus refuted. [The root] *ṣad* (to endure) [DhP 1.877] is either from the *bhvādi* class or a causative (*ṇic*) derivative; those who possess it are *sāhayaḥ*. In the examples, after the roots *lip* and *vind*, the suffix *śa* is applied by Pāṇini 3.1.77 ("*tudādibhyaḥ śaḥ*"), and the augment *num* is added by 7.1.59 ("*śe mucādinām*"). In the case of *dārayati* and others, there is the substitution of *guṇa* and *ay* [for *i*]. Why [is it specified] "after a prefixless [root]"? [Consider] *pralipaḥ*. It should be stated: "After *lip* when preceded by *ni*" (Vārttika). The gods named *nilimpāḥ* [are derived thus].

It should be stated that [the suffix *ghañ*] is applied after the root *vid* when preceded by words such as *go-* (*gavādiṣu*) in the sense of a proper name (*saṃjñāyām*). Examples: *govindaḥ*, *aravindaḥ*. The spokes (*araḥ*) are the wooden pieces situated between the hub (*nābhi*) and the rim (*nemi*) of a wheel; the petals, being shaped like those spokes, receive the designation of that word (*tacchabdabhāñji*) due to their similarity. This rule is intended to set aside the application of the suffix *aṇ* in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*) [as prescribed by Pāṇini 3.2.1].
(Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.139)

Regarding the roots *dadāti* and *dadhati*, there is an option (Pāṇini 3.1.139). The suffix *śa* may be applied; alternatively, by Pāṇini 3.1.141 (*śyādvyadhā*), the suffix *ṇa* is applied. Thus: *dadaḥ*, *dadhaḥ*, *dāyaḥ*, *dhāyaḥ*. This applies only when there is no prefix (*anupasargāt*). For example: *pradaḥ*, *pradhaḥ*. The roots *dada* (meaning "to give," *bhvādi* 17) and *dadha* (meaning "to hold," *bhvādi* 8) form *dadaḥ* and *dadhaḥ* when followed by an *ac* vowel in the ārdhadhātuka suffix *a*. When followed by the suffix *ṇa*, they form *dāyaḥ* and *dhāyaḥ*. True, this rule is for the sake of accentuation (*svarārtham*): [e.g.,] *adadaḥ*, *adadhaḥ*.

In this case, the initial syllable is to be udātta by virtue of the accent of the negative particle *nañ*; however, if it were to end in a vowel (*ajanta*), it would instead be antodātta according to Pāṇini 6.2.157 (*ackāvaśaktau*). Thus, there is a great difference. (Pāṇini 3.1.140)

"From the roots beginning with *jvaliti* and ending with *kas*, the suffix *ṇa* [is optionally applied]" (Pāṇini 3.1.140). The word *iti* has the sense of "beginning with. Thus, from the roots starting with *jvala* (in the sense of "shining," bhvādi class, no. 856) and ending with *kasa* (in the sense of "going," bhvādi class, no. 885), the suffix *ṇa* may optionally occur. Examples: *jvalaḥ*, *jvālaḥ*; *calaḥ*, *cālaḥ*. The rule applies only when there is no prefix (*anupasargāt*); hence, *prajvalaḥ* (with the prefix *pra*). For those who read *vṛt* after having studied *kasi*, the inclusion of the term *kasant* (ending with *kas*) is of doubtful utility.

Although the root *jval* (to blaze) is listed twice—in the *jvalādi* group and subsequently in the *ghaṭādi* group—it is only the second occurrence that is intended here. This is because the inclusion in the *ghaṭādi* group serves its purpose in establishing the technical designation *mit*, whereas the other listing has no other function. Furthermore, within the *jvalādi* group, the root *bhram* is listed as "bhramu calane" (DhP 1.491). From this, the form *bhramaḥ* is derived with the suffix *ṇa*, due to the prohibition of *vṛddhi* by Pāṇini’s rule "nodāttopadeśasya" (7.3.34).

However, the inclusion of *bhram* in the *jvalādi* group is for the sake of accentuation; it ensures that in the word *abhramaḥ*, the accent does not fall on the first syllable according to the rule "ackāvaśaktau" (6.2.157).

The term *tan* is included in the *uṇādi* suffixes (*kāovāo*). [The word] *avatānaḥ* is derived from the root *tan* with the prefix *ava*. In this *vārttika*, neither the rule "with the suffix *ap*" nor the rule "when there is no prefix" (*anupasargāt*) is connected [to the root].
(Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.141).

*Śyai*, *vyadha*, *asru*, *saṃsru*, *tiṇ*, *ava-sā*, *ava-hṛ*, *lih*, *śliṣ*, *śvas* (Pāṇini 3.1.141). The phrase "without a prefix" (*anupasargāt*) has ceased to apply here, because it is mentioned again in the subsequent rule. Consequently, the mention of "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) connected with that also ceases to apply. The suffix *ṇa* shall be applied after the roots beginning with *śyaiṅ*. Although the root *śyaiṅ* (meaning "to go," *bhvādi* class, no. 988) would have been established by its very ending in long *ā*, it is specifically mentioned here to block the application of the suffix *ka* when a prefix is present. Thus: *avasyāyaḥ*, *pratiśyāyaḥ*. [In these forms,] the augment *yuk* is applied according to Pāṇini 7.3.33 (*āto yuk ciṇ-kṛtoḥ*).

By this, the inclusion of the root *vas* (to dwell) is explained: *vāsaḥ*, *dhāyaḥ*. In this sūtra, there is a *praśleṣa* (conjunction) of "śyā-āt," but it does not refer to the substitution of *yaṇ* for *śī*, nor to the root *at*, nor to roots ending in *ac* such as *yat* and others, nor to those ending in *a*. In this matter, the commentary alone is the refuge. From *vyadh* (to strike, Dhp. 7.5): *vyādhaḥ*. From *sru* (to flow, Bhu. 1.960), preceded by *āṅ* and *sam*: *āsrāvaḥ*, *saṃsrāvaḥ*. From *iṇ* (to go, Pā. 2.35), preceded by *ati*: *atyāyaḥ*.

The root *ant* [is used] in the sense of "concluding act" (*antakarmaṇi*) [Pāṇini 3.3.41]. The root *hṛ* [is used] in the sense of "taking away" (*haraṇe*) [Pāṇini 3.3.40]; preceded by *ava*, it forms *avahāraḥ*. The root *lih* [is used] in the sense of "tasting" (*āsvādane*) [Pāṇini 3.3.62], forming *lehaḥ*. The root *śliṣ* [is used] in the sense of "embracing" (*āliṅgane*) [Pāṇini 3.3.74], forming *śleṣaḥ*. The root *śvas* [is used] in the sense of "breathing" (*prāṇane*) [Pāṇini 3.3.62], forming *śvāsaḥ*. [This is governed by] Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.142.

Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.142: *du-nor-an-upasarge*. After the roots *du* and *nī*, when no prefix (*upasarga*) precedes them, the suffix *ṇa* is applied. From *du* (meaning "to burn"), we derive *dāvaḥ* ("forest fire"). Here, because of its association with *nī*, the root *du* with the indicatory letter (*anubandha*) *ṇ* is understood; however, from the root *du* without the indicatory letter (*niranubandhaka*), the suffix *ac* (by Pāṇini 3.1.134) is applied, resulting in *davaḥ*. Alternatively, it may be derived as an instrument (*karaṇa-sādhana*) ending in *ap* (by Pāṇini 3.3.57), yielding *davaḥ*. Amara states: "The words *dava* and *dāva* refer to forest fires. From *nī* (meaning "to lead"), we derive *nāyaḥ*. Why "when no prefix precedes"? Consider *pradavaḥ* and *praṇayaḥ*. (Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.143).

The term *grāha* is optionally [treated as such] by the rule *vibhāṣā grahaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.143). The suffix *ṇa* shall apply; alternatively, the suffix *ac*. This is a *vyavasthitavibhāṣā* (restricted option). Therefore: *jalacara-grāhaḥ* (an aquatic creature), *jyotiṣi-grahaḥ* (a planet). It should be stated that this also applies to the root *bhū*: (*kārikā-vārttika*). *Bhavaḥ* means a god and the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). *Bhāvāḥ* means categories of things (*padārthāḥ*). This statement does not exist in the *Mahābhāṣya*. However, "the things" (*bhāvāḥ*) should be understood as derived from the root *bhū* belonging to the *curādi* class with the causative suffix *ṇic*, followed by the suffix *ac* in the sense of attainment (*prāpti*). (Pāṇini 3.1.144)

*Gahe kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.144). After the root *grah*, the suffix *ka* occurs when "house" (*geha*) is the agent. That which seizes grain and so forth is a "house" (*gṛha*). Because they reside therein, "wives" (*dārāḥ*) are called "houses. The word *gṛha* belongs to the *ardharca* group [of neuter nouns]. In that context, it is masculine and ends only in the plural; however, as a neuter, it expresses the thing itself [the dwelling]. Both types [masculine and neuter] primarily denote a dwelling, while in the sense of "wife," they are used figuratively. And thus it is said: "They do not call a house a 'house'; the wife is called the 'house'."

Thus, people employ the term in its primary sense when referring to a house. However, the Vṛttikāra, by resorting to either *tantra* (repetition) or *āvṛtti* (iteration), indicates two meanings for the word *geha* in the sūtra; since the suffix is prescribed there, he maintains that the word *gṛha* is used in its primary sense even when it refers to wives. Furthermore, Nyāsakāra and Haradatta hold that the word *geha* is an adjective qualifying the agent who is the meaning of the suffix, and not a governing word (*upapada*), because of the specific mention in the rule: "in connection with the master of the house" (Pāṇini 4.4.90).

Regarding the statement *gṛha-grahaṇe* (cuoāo 367): since the word *gṛha* can be established through the addition of the suffix *ṇic* to the root *grah* (belonging to the *cur*-class) followed by the suffix *ac* (as per Pāṇini 3.1.134), or by the suffix *kap* (as per Pāṇini 3.1.135) with the understanding that the *bhū*-class roots serve as an illustration for all roots ending in *i*, this indicator (*jñāpaka*) is weak, as the specific mention [of *gṛha*] could be accounted for otherwise. However, it should be noted that its status as a qualifier of the agent is established solely through traditional interpretation (*vyākhyāna*).
In reality, since the word *gṛha* is established in the manner already stated, the rule *gehe kaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.145) could have been omitted; such is the direction of the argument.

Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.145: *śilpini ṣvun*. The suffix *ṣvun* occurs after a verbal root when the agent is a craftsman (*śilpin*). Skill in action is *śilpa*; one who possesses that is a *śilpin*. Because of its association with the preceding [sūtras], the term "*śilpini*" also qualifies the meaning of the suffix itself. Regarding this, the Bhāṣya provides a restrictive enumeration: "after the roots *nṛt*, *khan*, and *rañj*. Examples: *nartakaḥ* (male dancer), *nartakī* (female dancer); *khanakaḥ* (digger), *khanakī* (female digger).

The statement that *jan*, *jṝ*, *ṣṇas*, and *rañj* take the suffix *am* (Pāṇini 3.2.176, with the Gaṇasūtra *janījṝṣṇasurañjo'mantāśca*) indicates—according to Nyāsakāra, Haradatta, and others—that the nasal is sometimes elided even when *aṅ* follows *sañj*. Thus, the Vārttikas "after *rañj* with *ṇi*, [the suffix *ap* is added] in the sense of 'deer-pleasing'" (*rañjerṇau mṛgaramaṇe*) and "an addition for *rajaka*, *rajan*, and *rajas*" (*rajakarajanarajassūpasaṅkhyānam*) are merely restatements of meanings established by this indication. [Examples: *rajakaḥ* (a washerman), *rajakī* (a washerwoman)—the latter having the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* because of the marker *ṣit*.

According to the Bhāṣya, however, the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not apply. For instance, in the sixth [chapter], the author of the Bhāṣya stated—"these are *auṇādika* derivatives from the root *kit*"—in order to reject the Vārttika which proposes the addition of "rajaka-rajanarajaḥsu" [to the rule].

Regarding this, Kaiyaṭa states: *rājakaḥ* is formed with the suffix *kvun* by Pāṇini 3.1.146 (*kvun śilpisaṃjñayoḥ*). *Rajanam* is formed with the suffix *kyun* by Pāṇini 3.2.157 (*rañjeḥ kyun*). *Rajaḥ* is formed with the suffix *asun*, which is marked with the *k*-sign, by Pāṇini 3.3.118 (*bhūrañjibhyāṃ kit*). However, in the case of *rajakī*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied because of her connection to a male (*puṃyoga*). The intention of the author of the Bhāṣya is that if there is no such connection to a male, the suffix *ṅīṣ* should not occur. Thus, according to the view of the Bhāṣya, the suffix *ṣvun* is prescribed only after the roots *nṛt* and *khan*, and not after *rañj*. (Pāṇini 3.1.146)

Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.146: *gāthaka*. The suffix *thakan* is applied after the root *gai* when the agent is an artisan (*śilpin*). Thus, *gāthakaḥ* (a singer by profession). Although there is no distinction among the various roots beginning with *gā*, it is the root *gai śabde* (DhP 1.942) that is understood here, and not *gāṅ gatau* (DhP 1.975). For the suffix *thakan* is capable of denoting an artisan only in the sense of "singing. Pāṇini Sūtra 3.1.147: *ṇyuṭ ca*. The suffix *ṇyuṭ* is also applied after the root *gai* when the agent is an artisan. Thus, *gāyanaḥ* (masc. and *gāyanī* (fem.). The separation of this rule (*yogavibhāga*) is for the purpose of its continued application (*anuvṛtti*) in the subsequent rules.

(Pāṇini 3.1.148) *haśca vrīhikālayoḥ*: The suffix *ṇyuṭ* is applied after the roots *jahāti* and *jihīte* when denoting a type of rice (*vrīhi*) or a period of time (*kāla*) as the agent. In the sense "it leaves behind water," *hāyana* refers to a type of rice; [the etymology is] "because it increases (*vardhana*) the water. Alternatively, the analysis is "it abandons (*jihīte*) the water"; the meaning is that it generally requires water. They say that specific varieties of rice produced in arid regions (*jāṅgala-deśa*) are called *hāyana*.

The word *hāyana* means a year (*varṣa*), because it abandons (*jahāti*) all states during the state of dissolution (*pralayāvasthā*), or because it goes (*jihīte*)—that is, it pervades—as a delimiting factor. Here too, the rule regarding the restriction to the words *vrīhi* and *kāla* does not apply, as indicated by the evidence of the rule "tricaturbhyāṃ hāyanasya" (Pāṇini 5.1.29).

*Prusṛlvaḥ samabhihāre vun* (Pāṇini 3.1.149). The suffix *vun* shall be applied after these [roots] when denoting an agent who performs an action well (*sādhukārī*). By the mention of *samabhihāra* ("repetition" or "frequency"), proficiency (*sādhukāritva*) is indicated, because of the constant association [of the two]. For the general rule (*utsarga*) is that whoever repeatedly performs a particular action attains skill (*kauśala*) therein. Consequently, the suffix occurs even for one who performs an action well only once; however, it does not occur for one who performs it poorly even many times. Examples: *pravakaḥ*, *sarakaḥ*, *lavakaḥ*. In the sūtra, *prusṛlvaḥ* is the nominative plural (*jas*) used in place of the ablative. (Pāṇini 3.1.150)

And [the suffix] *vuñ* is added after a verbal root when it denotes a blessing (*āśis*) (Pāṇini 3.1.150). When a root expresses an object that is the focus of a prayer for something not yet attained, the suffix *vuñ* occurs in the sense of the agent. Examples: *jīvatāt* → *jīvakaḥ* ("one who may live"); *nandatāt* → *nandakaḥ* ("one who may rejoice"). Here, "blessing" is a property of the speaker. This utterance by a father or the like refers to the son or another person who is the agent of living or rejoicing—states which have become objects of the desire residing in the father or the like. Thus ends the sixth section of the first quarter of the third chapter in the venerable *Śabdakaustubha*. And the quarter is completed.
